To the Duke of Béjar

Marquis of Gibraleón, Count of Benalcázar and Bañares, Viscount of La Puebla de Alcocer, Lord of the towns of Capilla, Curiel and Burguillos

Trusting in the generous welcome and the honour that Your Excellency shows to books of every kind, as a prince so inclined to favour the fine arts — and above all those which, being noble, do not stoop to serve the common crowd or to make money out of it — I have determined to bring The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha into the light under the shelter of Your Excellency's most illustrious name. And with the respect I owe to greatness of that order, I beg you to receive him kindly into your protection, so that in your shadow he may dare to appear safely before the judgement of certain persons who, keeping strictly within the bounds of their own ignorance, are in the habit of condemning other men's work with more severity than justice. For he goes out stripped of that precious ornament of elegance and learning which usually clothes works composed in the houses of men who know things; and I trust that when Your Excellency's good sense considers how well I meant it, you will not despise the smallness of so humble a service.

Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra

Prologue

Idle reader: you can take my word for it, without my having to swear to it, that I wish this book, being the child of my brain, were the handsomest, the liveliest and the cleverest that anyone could imagine. But I have not been able to break the law of nature, by which every thing brings forth its own likeness. And so what could my barren and ill-cultivated wit bring forth but the history of a son who is dry and shrivelled and wilful and full of odd notions that never occurred to anybody else — a son, in short, conceived in a prison, where every discomfort has its lodging and every mournful noise makes its home? Peace and quiet, a pleasant place, cheerful fields, clear skies, the murmur of streams, a mind at rest — these do a great deal to make even the most barren muses fertile, and to bring into the world offspring that fill it with wonder and delight. It happens sometimes that a man has an ugly son with no charm at all, and the love he bears him ties a blindfold over his eyes so that he cannot see his faults; on the contrary, he takes them for talents and beauties, and repeats them to his friends as wit and elegance.

But I — who only seem to be Don Quixote's father, and am really his stepfather — have no wish to swim with the current of custom, or to beg you, dearest reader, very nearly in tears, as others do, to forgive or overlook the faults you may see in this son of mine. You are neither his relation nor his friend; you have your own soul in your own body and as free a will as the best of them; you are in your own house, where you are lord of everything, as the king is of his taxes; and you know the saying — under my own cloak, I can kill the king. All of which lets you off every kind of deference and obligation, so that you may say whatever you like about this history without fear of being run in for the bad you say of it or rewarded for the good.

I should have liked to give it to you plain and naked, without the ornament of a prologue, or the endless catalogue of the customary sonnets, epigrams and tributes that are usually stuck at the front of books. Because I can tell you that, although the book cost me some labour, nothing cost me more than making this preface you are now reading. Many a time I took up the pen to write it, and many a time I put it down again, because I did not know what to say. And once, when I was sitting stuck — the paper in front of me, the pen behind my ear, my elbow on the desk and my cheek on my hand, wondering what on earth to write — a friend of mine came in unexpectedly, a witty man and a shrewd one, who saw me sunk so deep in thought and asked me what was the matter. I made no secret of it. I told him I was thinking about the prologue I had to write for the history of Don Quixote, and that it had got me into such a state that I no longer wanted to write it, still less to bring the deeds of so noble a knight out into the light at all.

"Because how do you expect me not to be worried," I said, "about what that ancient lawgiver they call the public will say when it sees that, after all these years asleep in the silence of oblivion, I come out now, with all my years on my back, carrying a legend as dry as a rush mat, barren of invention, poor in style, thin in ideas and destitute of every kind of learning and doctrine — with no notes in the margins and no annotations at the end, the way I see other books have, however made-up and worldly they may be, so crammed with sayings from Aristotle and Plato and the whole herd of philosophers that they fill the reader with admiration and get their authors a reputation as well-read, learned, eloquent men? And then when they quote Holy Scripture! People will say they are so many St Thomases and Doctors of the Church, keeping up a decorum so ingenious that in one line they paint a distracted lover and in the next preach a nice little Christian sermon, which is a joy and a treat to hear or to read. My book will have none of this. I have nothing to note in the margin and nothing to annotate at the end, and I have no idea which authors I have followed, so as to put them at the front as everybody else does, in alphabetical order, beginning with Aristotle and ending with Xenophon and Zoilus or Zeuxis — even though one of them was a slanderer and the other a painter. My book will also have to do without sonnets at the front, or at least without sonnets by dukes, marquises, counts, bishops, great ladies or celebrated poets — though if I asked two or three tradesman friends of mine, I know they would give me some, and such that the ones by our most famous names in Spain could not touch them.

"In short, my dear sir and friend," I went on, "I have decided that Señor Don Quixote shall stay buried in his archives in La Mancha until heaven provides someone to furnish him with all the things he lacks. I find myself incapable of supplying them, out of my own inadequacy and want of learning, and because I am naturally idle and too lazy to go hunting for authors to say what I can perfectly well say without them. This is the cause of the suspense and abstraction you found me in — reason enough, I should think, given what you have just heard."

My friend, hearing this, struck himself on the forehead, let off a great volley of laughter, and said:

"Good God, brother, you have just cured me of an error I have been living in the whole time I have known you, all of which I have taken you for a sensible and prudent man in everything you did. But now I see you are as far from it as heaven is from earth. How is it possible that things of so little consequence, and so easily put right, have the power to stop and stupefy a mind as ripe as yours, and one so used to breaking through and trampling over much greater difficulties than these? On my faith, this does not come from any lack of ability, but from a surplus of laziness and a famine of common sense. Would you like to see whether what I say is true? Then pay attention, and you shall watch me demolish every one of your difficulties in the time it takes to open and shut your eyes, and put right all the defects that you say hold you up and make you afraid to bring out into the light of the world the history of your famous Don Quixote, the light and mirror of all knight-errantry."

"Tell me, then," I answered, "how do you propose to fill up the emptiness of my fear and bring the chaos of my confusion into daylight?"

To which he replied:

"The first thing that troubles you — the sonnets, epigrams and tributes you lack for the opening, and the fact that they ought to be by weighty people with titles — can be cured by your taking a little trouble and writing them yourself. Then you can christen them and put whatever name you please to them, fathering them on Prester John of the Indies or the Emperor of Trebizond, both of whom, I have it on good authority, were famous poets. And if they were not, and there should be some pedants and university men who snap at you behind your back and mutter about the truth of it, don't give twopence for them; because even if they prove the lie on you, they can't cut off the hand you wrote it with.

"As for citing in the margins the books and authors you took the sayings and maxims in your history from, all you have to do is work in, wherever it fits, some maxims or bits of Latin that you happen to know by heart — or that at least cost you very little trouble to look up. For example, when you are dealing with liberty and captivity, put:

Non bene pro toto libertas venditur auro.

[Liberty is not well sold for all the gold in the world.]

And then in the margin cite Horace, or whoever said it. If you are dealing with the power of death, come straight in with:

	Pallida mors aequo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas,
	Regumque turres.

[Pale death knocks with the same foot at the cottages of the poor and the towers of kings.]

If it is the friendship and love that God commands us to feel towards our enemy, get yourself into Holy Scripture at once, which you can do with the smallest amount of curiosity, and quote the words of God himself, at least: Ego autem dico vobis: diligite inimicos vestros. [But I say unto you: love your enemies.] If it is evil thoughts, come in with the Gospel: De corde exeunt cogitationes malae. [Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts.] If it is the unreliability of friends, there is Cato ready with his couplet:

	Donec eris felix, multos numerabis amicos,
	tempora si fuerint nubila, solus eris.

[While you are prosperous you will count many friends; if the weather turns cloudy, you will be alone.]

And with these scraps of Latin and others like them they will at least take you for a scholar, and being one is no small honour and profit these days.

"As for putting annotations at the end of the book, you can safely manage it like this. If you name some giant in your book, make him the giant Goliath, and with that alone, which will cost you next to nothing, you have a fine long note, since you can put: The giant Golias, or Goliath, was a Philistine whom the shepherd David killed with a great stone in the valley of Terebinth, as is told in the Book of Kings, in whatever chapter you find it written. After that, to show yourself a man learned in humane letters and a cosmographer, arrange for the river Tagus to be mentioned somewhere in your history, and you will find yourself with another famous note, thus: The river Tagus was so called after a king of the Spains; it rises in such and such a place and dies in the ocean, kissing the walls of the famous city of Lisbon; and it is thought to have golden sands, etc. If you are dealing with thieves, I will give you the story of Cacus, which I know by heart. If with loose women, there is the Bishop of Mondoñedo, who will lend you Lamia, Laida and Flora, and a note on them will do your credit no harm. If with cruel women, Ovid will hand over Medea. If with enchantresses and witches, Homer has Calypso and Virgil has Circe. If with valiant captains, Julius Caesar will lend you himself in his own Commentaries, and Plutarch will give you a thousand Alexanders. If you are dealing with love, with two ounces of Italian you will run straight into Leone Ebreo, who will fill your measure to the brim. And if you would rather not go abroad for it, you have Fonseca's On the Love of God at home, in which everything is summed up that you, or the most ingenious man alive, could want on the subject. In short, all you have to do is see that these names get mentioned, or these stories touched on, in your own; and leave the business of the notes and marginal citations to me, for I promise you I will fill your margins and use up four sheets of paper at the end of the book.

"Now let us come to the list of authors that other books have and yours lacks. The cure for that is very easy, because you have nothing to do but look for a book that cites them all, from A to Z, as you say. Then you put that same alphabet into your own book; and although the lie is perfectly obvious, since you had so little need to make use of them, it doesn't matter in the least. Perhaps there will even be somebody simple enough to believe that you have drawn on all of them in that plain, straightforward history of yours; and if it serves no other purpose, at least that long catalogue of authors will do to give the book a sudden air of authority. Besides, nobody is going to set about checking whether you followed them or not, since there is nothing in it for him.

"What is more — now that I come to think of it properly — this book of yours has no need whatever of any of the things you say it lacks, since the whole of it is an attack on books of chivalry, which Aristotle never thought about, and St Basil said nothing about, and Cicero never came across. Its fabulous absurdities have nothing to do with exactness of truth or with the observations of astrology; geometrical measurements are of no importance to it, nor is the refutation of arguments used in rhetoric; and it has no reason to preach at anybody, mixing the human with the divine, which is a kind of mixture no Christian understanding should ever be dressed in. It has only to make use of imitation in what it writes; and the more perfect that imitation is, the better the writing will be. And since this piece of writing of yours aims at nothing more than destroying the authority and standing that books of chivalry have in the world and among the common people, there is no reason for you to go begging maxims from philosophers, counsels from Holy Scripture, fables from poets, speeches from rhetoricians or miracles from saints. Just see to it that your sentences come out plainly, in meaningful, decent, well-placed words, and that your prose runs full and cheerful; paint what you mean as far as you can and as well as you possibly can, and make your ideas understood without tangling them up and darkening them. See to it, too, that reading your history makes the melancholy man laugh, and the cheerful man laugh harder; that the simple man is not bored, the clever man admires the invention, the serious man does not despise it and the prudent man cannot help praising it. In a word, keep your eye fixed on pulling down that ill-founded machine of chivalric books, hated by so many and praised by a great many more. If you managed that, you would not have managed a small thing."

I listened in complete silence to what my friend said, and his arguments stamped themselves on me so firmly that I approved them without any argument at all and decided to make my prologue out of them. In it, gentle reader, you will see the good sense of my friend, my own good fortune in finding such an adviser at a moment of such need, and your own relief at finding the history of the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha so honest and so free of complications — a man of whom the whole population of the district of the plain of Montiel holds the opinion that he was the chastest lover and the bravest knight seen in those parts for many years. I do not want to make too much of the service I am doing you in introducing you to so noble and honourable a knight; but I do want you to thank me for making you acquainted with the famous Sancho Panza, his squire, in whom, to my mind, I have concentrated for you every squirely grace that lies scattered through the whole pack of worthless books of chivalry.

And with that, God give you health, and may he not forget me. Vale.

Verses for the Book of Don Quixote of La Mancha

[Modern note: what follows is a set of commendatory poems supposedly written by Amadís of Gaul, Orlando, the Lady Oriana and other characters out of the very romances the book is attacking — a parody of the puffs that real books of the day carried at the front. Two of them are in what the Spanish calls versos de cabo roto, "broken-tail verse": the last syllable of every line is lopped off. It makes the rhyme and mocks affected poets at the same time, and the English does the same thing, so read the half-words aloud and let your ear finish them.]

Amadís of Gaul, to Don Quixote of La Mancha

Sonnet

	You who copied out the weeping life
	that I led, absent and disdained, up there
	on the great bare crag of the Poor Rock,
	turned from cheerfulness to penitence;
	you whose eyes gave you your only drink,
	abundant liquor, though it tasted salt,
	and who, with silver, tin and copper taken
	from you, were fed by earth on earth itself:
	live certain of this, that eternally —
	as long, at least, as in the fourth sphere
	the golden Apollo spurs his horses on —
	you will keep a clear name for courage;
	your country will stand first among them all;
	and your wise author, unique in the world, alone.

Don Belianís of Greece, to Don Quixote of La Mancha

Sonnet

	I broke, I hacked, I dented, said and did
	more than any knight errant in the world;
	I was skilful, I was brave, I was arrogant;
	I avenged a thousand wrongs, undid a hundred thousand.
	I gave Fame such deeds as make a man eternal;
	I was a courteous and an attentive lover;
	every giant was a dwarf to me,
	and I gave satisfaction in every duel.
	I had Fortune prostrate at my feet,
	and my good sense dragged bald Occasion
	about by the forelock as it pleased.
	But although my luck was always seen
	perched above the very horn of the moon,
	I envy your exploits, great Quixote!

The Lady Oriana, to Dulcinea of El Toboso

Sonnet

	Oh, that I had, lovely Dulcinea,
	for greater comfort and for greater peace,
	set Miraflores down in El Toboso,
	and traded my London for your village!
	Oh, that I could have dressed both soul and body
	in your desires and in your livery,
	and watched some unequal battle fought
	by the famous knight you made so fortunate!
	Oh, that I had got away as chastely
	from the lord Amadís as you did
	from the well-behaved gentleman Don Quixote!
	Then I should have been envied and not envious,
	and the time that was sad would have been merry,
	and I should have had the pleasures without the bill.

Gandalín, Squire to Amadís of Gaul, to Sancho Panza, Squire to Don Quixote

Sonnet

	Hail, famous man, to whom Fortune,
	when she put you into the squiring trade,
	arranged things so gently and so sensibly
	that you got through it without a single mishap.
	The spade and the sickle no longer quarrel
	with knight-errantry; plain squiring is
	the fashion now, and by it I accuse
	the proud man who tries to trample on the moon.
	I envy you your donkey and your name,
	and I envy your saddlebags just as much,
	which showed what a shrewd provider you were.
	Hail again, Sancho! So good a man
	that to you alone our Spanish Ovid
	makes his bow — and a smack on the back of the neck with it.

Orlando Furioso, to Don Quixote of La Mancha

Sonnet

	If you are not a peer, you have had none:
	you could have been a peer among a thousand peers;
	nor can there be one where you are to be found,
	unconquered conqueror, never yet conquered.
	Orlando I am, Quixote, who, lost

The Knight of Phoebus, to Don Quixote of La Mancha

Sonnet

	My sword was never the equal of yours,
	Spanish Phoebus, courtier full of curiosity;
	nor was my hand, that was a lightning-bolt
	where day is born and where day dies, the equal of your glory.
	I despised empires; the monarchy
	the red East offered me I left behind,
	all for the sake of seeing the sovereign face
	of Claridiana, my beautiful dawn.
	I loved her as a rare and single miracle;
	and, banished in her disgrace, hell itself
	feared this arm of mine, which tamed its fury.
	But you, illustrious Gothic Quixote,
	are eternal in the world for Dulcinea's sake,
	and she, for yours, is famous, chaste and wise.

From Solisdán, to Don Quixote of La Mancha

Sonnet

	Albeit, Sir Quixote, that such foolishness
	hath tumbled all thy brainpan out of joint,
	yet shall no man reproach thee ever
	as one of vile and filthy deeds.
	Thy feats shall be the judges of it,
	sith thou hast gone about undoing wrongs,
	being a thousand times well cudgelled
	by rogues and knaves and low-born varlets.
	And if thy fair Dulcinea should
	commit some discourtesy against thee,
	and show no kindly face towards thy griefs,
	in such mischance let this be thy comfort:
	that Sancho Panza was a poor go-between,
	he a fool, she hard, and thou no lover at all.

Dialogue between Babieca and Rocinante

Sonnet

	B. How is it, Rocinante, you're so thin?
	R. Because one never eats, and always works.
	B. But what about the barley and the straw?
	R. My master doesn't leave me a mouthful.
	B. Go on with you, sir, you're very badly bred,
	using that ass's tongue of yours on your master.
	R. He's an ass from the cradle to the grave.
	Do you want to see it? Look at him in love.
	B. Is it stupid to love? R. It isn't very clever.
	B. You're getting metaphysical. R. It's because I don't eat.
	B. Then complain of the squire. R. That's not enough.
	How am I to complain of what ails me,
	if the master and the squire, or the steward,
	are every bit as much hacks as Rocinante?

Part One (1605)

Chapter 1: Which Treats of the Character and Daily Habits of the Famous Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha

In a village of La Mancha, whose name I have no wish to remember, there lived not long ago one of those gentlemen who keep a lance in the rack, an ancient leather shield, a bony old nag and a greyhound for coursing. A stew with rather more beef than mutton in it, cold meat salad most evenings, "griefs and groans" — bacon and eggs — on Saturdays, lentils on Fridays and the odd pigeon by way of a treat on Sundays: this ate up three quarters of his income. The rest of it went on a coat of fine black cloth, velvet breeches for holidays with the slippers to match, and on weekdays he did himself proud in the best homespun he could get. He kept in the house a housekeeper the wrong side of forty, a niece not yet twenty, and a lad for the field and the market who could saddle the nag and handle the pruning-hook. Our gentleman was getting on for fifty. He was strongly built but lean, thin in the face, a great early riser and a keen huntsman. They say his surname was Quixada, or Quesada — the authorities who write about this differ on the point — though the likeliest guess is that it was Quexana. But that hardly matters to our story; it is enough that the telling of it does not stray a hair's breadth from the truth.

You must know, then, that in his idle hours — which were most of the year — this gentleman gave himself up to reading books of chivalry, with such passion and such pleasure that he all but forgot his hunting and even the running of his property. His curiosity and his folly went so far that he sold acres of good arable land in order to buy books of chivalry to read, and carried home every one of them he could get hold of. Of all of them, none pleased him so well as those written by the famous Feliciano de Silva, because the clarity of his prose and those tangled arguments of his struck him as pearls beyond price — above all when he came to the wooings and the challenges, where he would often find written: The reason of the unreason with which my reason is afflicted so weakens my reason that with reason I complain of your beauty. Or again: The high heavens that with their stars divinely fortify you in your divinity make you deserving of the deserts that your greatness deserves.

Over sentences like these the poor gentleman lost his wits. He would lie awake trying to understand them and dig the sense out of them, which Aristotle himself could not have done if he had come back to life for that single purpose. He was not altogether happy about the wounds Don Belianís gave and took, since he reckoned that however great the surgeons who had treated him, his face and his whole body must be covered in scars and seams. Still, he praised the author for ending his book with the promise of that never-ending adventure, and many a time he felt the itch to take up a pen and finish it off exactly as promised there. He would have done it too, and made a success of it, if greater and more constant preoccupations had not got in his way.

He often argued with the curate of his village — a learned man, a graduate of Sigüenza — about which had been the better knight, Palmerín of England or Amadís of Gaul. But Master Nicholas, the barber of that same town, said that neither of them came near the Knight of Phoebus, and that if anyone could be compared to him it was Don Galaor, brother of Amadís of Gaul, because he had a temper suited to anything; he was not a squeamish knight, nor such a weeper as his brother, and in the matter of courage he was not a step behind him.

In short, he buried himself so deep in his reading that his nights went by from dusk to dawn and his days from dawn to dusk; and so, from too little sleep and too much reading, his brain dried up on him and he went out of his mind. His imagination filled with everything he had read in the books — enchantments and quarrels, battles and challenges, wounds, wooings, love affairs, tempests and impossible nonsense; and it planted itself so firmly in his head that the whole machinery of those dreamed-up, drummed-up inventions was true, that for him there was no more certain history in the world.

He used to say that the Cid Ruy Díaz had been a very good knight, but that he was nothing beside the Knight of the Burning Sword, who with a single backhand had split two huge and monstrous giants down the middle. He thought better of Bernardo del Carpio, because at Roncesvalles he had killed the enchanted Roland by using the trick of Hercules, who throttled Antaeus, the son of Earth, in his arms. He spoke very well of the giant Morgante, because although he came of that giant brood, who are all overbearing and ill-mannered, he alone was civil and well brought up. But above all of them he approved of Reinaldos of Montalbán, and most of all when he saw him ride out of his castle and rob everyone he met, and when overseas he stole that idol of Mahomet which was solid gold, according to his history. As for the traitor Ganelon, he would have given his housekeeper for the chance of a good kicking at him — and thrown in his niece as well.

In the end, his wits now completely gone, he fell into the strangest notion that any madman in the world ever fell into: it seemed to him right and necessary, both for the increase of his own honour and for the service of his country, that he should turn knight errant and go off through the world with his armour and his horse to look for adventures, and to practise everything he had read that knights errant practised — righting every kind of wrong, and putting himself in the way of dangers and difficulties from which, once he had come through them, he would win eternal name and fame. The poor man already saw himself crowned by the strength of his own arm as at the very least Emperor of Trebizond; and so, in the grip of these delightful thoughts and carried away by the extraordinary pleasure he took in them, he set about putting his wishes into practice.

The first thing he did was to clean up a suit of armour that had belonged to his great-grandfathers and had lain rusting and mildewed in a corner, forgotten, for centuries. He cleaned and repaired it as best he could, but then he saw that it had one great defect: it had no closed helmet, only a plain headpiece. Here his ingenuity came to the rescue. He made a kind of half-helmet out of cardboard which, fitted to the headpiece, gave the appearance of a whole one. It is true that in order to test whether it was strong and could stand up to a sword-cut, he drew his sword and gave it two blows; and with the first he undid in an instant what he had taken a week to make. It did not please him at all, the ease with which he had knocked it to pieces, and to guard against that danger he made it over again, putting bars of iron inside it, in such a way that he was satisfied with its strength; and without caring to test it a second time, he pronounced it and held it to be a helmet of the very finest make.

Next he went to look at his nag; and although the beast had more cracked quarters in its hooves than there are quarter-pieces in a coin, and more blemishes than Gonella's horse, which tantum pellis et ossa fuit — was nothing but skin and bone — it seemed to him that neither Alexander's Bucephalus nor the Cid's Babieca was a match for it. Four days went by while he thought what name to give it; because, as he said to himself, it was not right that the horse of so famous a knight, and so good a beast in itself, should go without a name of its own. He tried to fit it with one that would declare what it had been before it belonged to a knight errant, and what it was now; for it stood to reason that when its master changed his condition it should change its name too, and take one that was famous and resounding, as suited the new order and the new profession it had now entered. And so, after a great many names that he made up and rubbed out and struck off, added to, pulled apart and put together again in his memory and his imagination, he ended by calling it Rocinante — a name which struck him as lofty, resounding, and expressive both of what the animal had been when it was a common hack, and of what it was now: the first and foremost hack in the world.

Having found a name for his horse, and one so much to his liking, he wanted to find one for himself, and he spent another eight days on that thought, and at the end of it decided to call himself Don Quixote. Which is why — as has been said — the authors of this most truthful history concluded that his name must certainly have been Quixada, and not Quesada, as others have tried to make out. But remembering that the valiant Amadís had not been content to call himself Amadís and nothing more, but had added the name of his kingdom and country in order to make it famous, and called himself Amadís of Gaul, he too, like a good knight, resolved to add the name of his own country to his own and call himself Don Quixote of La Mancha — by which, to his mind, he declared his lineage and his birthplace to the life, and honoured his country by taking his surname from it.

So, with his armour cleaned, his headpiece turned into a helmet, a name found for his nag and his own name settled, he decided that the only thing still wanting was a lady to fall in love with; for a knight errant without a love is a tree without leaves or fruit, a body without a soul. He said to himself:

"If, for my sins, or by my good luck, I should run into some giant hereabouts, as commonly happens to knights errant, and knock him down at the first charge, or split him through the middle, or in short defeat him and force him to surrender — will it not be as well to have someone to send him to as a present, so that he may go in and fall on his knees before my sweet lady and say, in a humble, submissive voice: 'Madam, I am the giant Caraculiambro, lord of the isle of Malindrania, who was defeated in single combat by the never-sufficiently-to-be-praised knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, who commanded me to present myself before your grace, that your highness might dispose of me as she pleases'?"

Oh, how our good gentleman enjoyed himself when he had made that speech — and still more when he had found someone to call his lady! It happened, so it is believed, that in a village near his own there was a good-looking farm girl he had been in love with for a time, though as far as anyone knows she never learned of it or gave it a thought. Her name was Aldonza Lorenzo, and it seemed to him a good idea to give her the title of mistress of his thoughts. Looking for a name for her that should not clash too much with her own, and that should lean and point towards a princess and a great lady, he ended by calling her Dulcinea of El Toboso, because she came from El Toboso — a name which struck him as musical and out of the ordinary and full of meaning, like all the others he had settled on for himself and for everything belonging to him.

Chapter 2: Which Treats of the First Sally the Ingenious Don Quixote Made from His Own Country

These preparations made, he would wait no longer to put his plan into effect, urged on by the thought of how much the world was losing by his delay — such was the number of wrongs he meant to right, injuries to redress, injustices to mend, abuses to reform and debts to settle. And so, without telling a soul what he intended, and without anybody seeing him, one morning before daybreak — it was one of the hot days of July — he put on the whole of his armour, mounted Rocinante, fitted on his badly made helmet, slipped his shield onto his arm, took up his lance, and by the back gate of a yard rode out into the open country, hugely pleased and delighted to see how easily he had made a beginning on his heart's desire.

But no sooner was he in the open than a terrible thought struck him, one that very nearly made him abandon the whole enterprise before it started: it came into his head that he had not been dubbed a knight, and that by the laws of chivalry he neither could nor should take up arms against any knight; and that even if he had been dubbed, as a new knight he was bound to wear plain white armour with no device on his shield until he had earned one by his own efforts. These thoughts made him waver in his purpose; but his madness being stronger than any argument, he resolved to have himself dubbed a knight by the first man he met, in imitation of a great many others who had done the same, as he had read in the books that had brought him to this pass. As for the white armour, he meant to scour his own, when he got the chance, until it was whiter than ermine. With that he settled his mind and rode on, taking whatever road his horse chose, in the belief that this was where the whole force of adventure lay.

As he rode along, our brand-new adventurer talked to himself, saying:

"Who can doubt that in ages to come, when the true history of my famous deeds is brought to light, the sage who writes them down will begin his account of this my first sally, so early in the morning, in this manner? — 'Scarcely had ruddy Apollo spread over the face of the wide and spacious earth the golden threads of his beautiful hair, and scarcely had the little painted birds with their forked tongues greeted in sweet and honeyed harmony the coming of the rosy dawn, who, leaving the soft bed of her jealous husband, was showing herself to mortals through the doors and balconies of the Manchegan horizon, when the famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, leaving the idle feathers of his bed, mounted his famous horse Rocinante and began to ride across the ancient and well-known plain of Montiel.'"

And it was the truth that he was riding across it. He went on:

"Happy the age and happy the century in which my famous exploits shall come to light — exploits worthy to be carved in bronze, cut in marble and painted on panels as a memorial for the future! And you, wise enchanter, whoever you may be, whose business it will be to chronicle this extraordinary history, I beg you not to forget my good Rocinante, my eternal companion on all my roads and journeys!"

Then he would begin again, as though he really were in love:

"O Princess Dulcinea, mistress of this captive heart! Great wrong have ye done me in dismissing me and reproaching me with the harsh command that I appear no more before your beauty. May it please you, lady, to be mindful of this heart of yours in bondage, that suffers so many sorrows for love of you."

He went on stringing together other absurdities of the same kind, all in the manner his books had taught him, imitating their language as closely as he could; and all the while he rode so slowly, and the sun climbed so fast and beat down so hot, that it would have been enough to melt his brains if he had had any.

He rode almost the whole of that day without anything happening worth telling, which drove him to despair, because he wanted to run into somebody at once, immediately, on whom he could test the strength of his mighty arm. There are authors who say his first adventure was the one at Puerto Lápice; others say it was the windmills. But what I have been able to establish in the matter, and what I have found written in the Annals of La Mancha, is that he rode all that day, and that at nightfall his nag and he were worn out and dying of hunger; and that, looking about him in every direction to see whether he could make out some castle or some shepherds' hut where he might take shelter and do something about his great hunger and want, he saw an inn not far from the road he was on — which was as though he had seen a star guiding him, not to the porch, but to the very palace of his redemption. He pushed on, and reached it just as night was falling.

There happened to be standing at the door two young women of the sort they call women of the town, who were on their way to Seville with some carriers who had chanced to break their journey at that inn for the night. And since to our adventurer everything he thought or saw or imagined seemed to be made and to happen after the fashion of what he had read, the moment he saw the inn it presented itself to him as a castle with its four towers and its spires of shining silver, complete with drawbridge and deep moat and all the trimmings that such castles are painted with. He came up towards the inn — which to him was a castle — and a little way off he reined Rocinante in, waiting for some dwarf to show himself between the battlements and blow a trumpet to signal that a knight was arriving at the castle. But seeing that they were slow about it, and that Rocinante was in a hurry to get to the stable, he went up to the door of the inn and saw the two loose women standing there, who seemed to him two beautiful maidens or two graceful ladies taking their ease in front of the castle gate.

Just then it happened that a swineherd who was rounding up a drove of pigs from some stubble-fields — pigs, begging your pardon, but that is what they are called — blew his horn, at which signal they gather; and instantly Don Quixote had what he wanted, which was a dwarf giving notice of his arrival. So with extraordinary satisfaction he came up to the inn and to the ladies, who, seeing a man of that sort coming, armed and carrying lance and shield, were frightened and were going indoors. But Don Quixote, gathering from their flight that they were afraid, raised his pasteboard visor, uncovered his dry and dusty face, and said to them with a courteous air and in a calm voice:

"Flee not, your graces, nor fear any discourtesy; for the order of chivalry which I profess neither touches nor concerns the doing of any to anyone, and least of all to maidens as highborn as your presences declare you to be."

The girls stared at him, hunting with their eyes for the face that the wretched visor hid; but when they heard themselves called maidens, a thing so far outside their line of business, they could not keep from laughing, and they laughed so hard that Don Quixote took offence and said:

"Modesty becomes the fair, and moreover it is great foolishness to laugh at a slight cause; but I say this not to vex you or to make you show ill temper, for mine is nothing but to serve you."

The language, which the ladies did not understand, and the sorry figure our knight cut, only increased their laughter and his annoyance; and it would have gone a good deal further if at that moment the innkeeper had not come out — a man who, being very fat, was very peaceable. Seeing that misshapen figure armed with such ill-matched equipment as the bridle, lance, shield and corselet, he came within an inch of joining the maidens in their expressions of delight. But in the end, in some awe of that whole apparatus of hardware, he decided to speak civilly, and said:

"If your worship, sir knight, is looking for lodging, then apart from a bed — for there is not one in this inn — everything else will be found here in great abundance."

Don Quixote, seeing the humility of the governor of the fortress (for that is what the innkeeper and the inn seemed to him), replied:

	"For me, sir castellan, anything will serve, for
	my trappings are my arms,
	my resting is to fight,

and so on."

The landlord thought he had been called a Castilian because he had been taken for one of the honest men of Castile, though in fact he was an Andalusian from the beach at Sanlúcar, no less a thief than Cacus and no less a rogue than a student page. So he answered:

"In that case, your worship's bed must be the naked rock and your sleep a perpetual watch; and if that is so, you may safely dismount, in the certainty of finding in this hovel occasion, and occasions, for not sleeping at all for a whole year, let alone for one night."

And saying this he went to hold the stirrup for Don Quixote, who dismounted with great difficulty and effort, like a man who had not broken his fast all that day.

He then told his host to take particular care of his horse, because it was the finest piece of horseflesh that ever ate bread in this world. The innkeeper looked it over and did not think it half as good as Don Quixote said; but he settled it in the stable and came back to see what his guest wanted. The maidens, who had by now made it up with him, were taking his armour off; and although they had got the breastplate and backpiece off him, they never could work out how to unfasten the gorget or get off the makeshift helmet, which he wore tied on with green ribbons. The knots could not be undone and the ribbons would have had to be cut, and to this he would not agree on any terms; so he spent the whole of that night with his helmet on, and made the drollest and strangest figure imaginable. And while they were disarming him — since he supposed that these battered and much-travelled creatures were great ladies of that castle — he said to them very gracefully:

	"Never was a knight so well
	waited on by ladies
	as Don Quixote was
	when he came from his village:
	damsels tended him;
	princesses, his hack —

or Rocinante, for that, my ladies, is my horse's name, and Don Quixote of La Mancha is mine. And although I had no wish to reveal myself until the deeds done in your service and for your good should have revealed me, the necessity of fitting this old ballad of Lancelot to the present occasion has caused you to learn my name before its proper season. But the time will come when your ladyships shall command and I obey, and the strength of my arm shall show how much I desire to serve you."

The girls, who were not used to hearing rhetoric of that kind, said not a word; they only asked whether he would like anything to eat.

"I would eat anything at all," answered Don Quixote, "because, as I understand it, it would do me a great deal of good."

It happened, as luck would have it, to be a Friday, and there was nothing in the whole inn but a few helpings of a fish that in Castile they call pollack, in Andalusia salt cod, in some places dried cod and in others little trout. They asked him whether his worship would perhaps eat some little trout, since there was no other fish to give him.

"So long as there are plenty of little trout," answered Don Quixote, "they can do duty for one trout; because it is all one to me whether I am given eight reals in small change or in a single piece of eight. What is more, these little trout may well be like veal, which is better than beef, or kid, which is better than goat. But whatever it is, let it come at once, for the labour and the weight of arms cannot be borne without the government of the guts."

They set his table for him at the inn door, for the cool of it, and the landlord brought him a portion of the badly soaked and worse cooked salt cod, and a loaf as black and grimy as his armour. But it was a thing to make you shout with laughter to watch him eat; because, with his helmet on and the visor up, he could get nothing into his mouth with his own hands unless somebody put it there for him, so one of the ladies had to do him this service. As for giving him a drink, that was impossible, and would have stayed impossible if the innkeeper had not bored out a reed and put one end in his mouth and poured the wine in at the other; and all this he took patiently rather than break the ribbons of his helmet.

While this was going on, a pig-gelder happened to arrive at the inn, and as he came up he blew his cane whistle four or five times — which finally settled it for Don Quixote that he was in some famous castle, and that they were serving him with music, and that the pollack was trout, the bread white, the whores ladies and the innkeeper the castellan of the castle; and so he counted his decision and his setting out well repaid. But what worried him most was that he had not yet been dubbed a knight, since it seemed to him that he could not lawfully enter on any adventure without first receiving the order of chivalry.

Chapter 3: Which Tells the Comical Way Don Quixote Had Himself Dubbed a Knight

And so, tormented by this thought, he cut short his scanty inn supper; and when it was over he called the innkeeper, shut himself up with him in the stable, fell on his knees before him and said:

"Never will I rise from where I am, valiant knight, until your courtesy grants me a boon that I wish to ask of you, one that will redound to your praise and to the good of the human race."

The innkeeper, seeing his guest at his feet and hearing this sort of language, stood staring at him in confusion, not knowing what to do or say, and kept insisting that he get up; but Don Quixote would not, until he had to tell him that he granted the boon he was asking.

"I expected no less of your great magnificence, my lord," answered Don Quixote. "And so I tell you that the boon I have asked of you, and that your generosity has granted me, is that tomorrow morning you shall dub me a knight; and that tonight I shall keep watch over my arms in the chapel of this castle of yours; and tomorrow, as I have said, what I so much desire shall be accomplished, so that I may go, as is proper, through all four quarters of the world in search of adventures on behalf of the needy — which is the business of chivalry and of knights errant such as I am, whose desire is bent upon deeds of that kind."

The innkeeper, who, as has been said, was something of a sly rogue and already had some suspicions of his guest's want of wits, was quite convinced of it when he heard this speech; and, in order to have something to laugh at that night, he decided to humour him. So he told him he was entirely right in what he wanted and asked for, and that such a resolution was proper and natural in knights as distinguished as he appeared to be and as his gallant bearing showed him; and that he himself, in the years of his youth, had followed that honourable profession, going about the world in various parts in search of adventures — not omitting the Percheles of Málaga, the Isles of Riarán, the Compass of Seville, the Little Market of Segovia, the Olive Grove of Valencia, the Rondilla of Granada, the beach at Sanlúcar, the Colt of Córdoba, the Taverns of Toledo and various other places, where he had exercised the nimbleness of his feet and the deftness of his hands, doing a great many wrongs, courting a great many widows, undoing a few maidens and swindling a few minors; and, in short, making himself known in nearly every court and tribunal in the whole of Spain. And that at last he had retired to this castle of his, where he lived on his own property and other people's, taking in all knights errant of whatever rank and condition, purely out of the great affection he had for them and so that they should share their goods with him in payment of his good will.

He told him also that in this castle of his there was no chapel where he might keep watch over his arms, because it had been pulled down to be built again; but that in case of necessity he knew that the watch could be kept anywhere, and that tonight he might keep it in a courtyard of the castle; and that in the morning, God willing, the proper ceremonies would be performed, so that he should be dubbed a knight, and so much a knight that there could be no more of one in the world.

He asked whether he had any money with him. Don Quixote answered that he had not a farthing, because he had never read in the histories of knights errant that any of them had carried any. To this the innkeeper said that he was mistaken; that although it was not written down in the histories — because it had seemed to their authors that there was no need to write down a thing so obvious and so necessary to carry as money and clean shirts — that was no reason to believe they had not carried them. He might take it as certain and established that all the knights errant that so many books are stuffed and crammed with carried well-lined purses against whatever might befall them; and that they likewise carried shirts and a little box full of ointments to treat the wounds they took, because it was not every time that in the fields and deserts where they fought and came off wounded there was somebody to treat them — unless indeed they had some wise enchanter for a friend, who would come to their aid at once, carrying through the air on a cloud some damsel or dwarf with a flask of water of such virtue that on tasting a single drop of it they were instantly healed of their cuts and wounds as though they had never had anything the matter with them. But in the absence of that, knights in past ages had thought it right that their squires should be provided with money and other necessaries, such as lint and ointments for dressing wounds; and when it happened that such knights had no squires, which was seldom and rarely, they carried everything themselves in a pair of very slim saddlebags that hardly showed at all, slung behind the saddle as though it were something of greater importance — because, except on some such occasion, this business of carrying saddlebags was not much approved of among knights errant. And for this reason he advised him — since he might still command him as his godson, which he was so soon to become — not to travel from now on without money and without the provisions mentioned, and he would find how well off he was with them when he least expected it.

Don Quixote promised to do what he was advised with the greatest exactness; and so orders were given for him to keep watch over his arms in a large yard at one side of the inn. Gathering them all up, Don Quixote laid them on a trough that stood beside a well, and, slipping his shield onto his arm, took up his lance and began to pace up and down in front of the trough with a noble bearing; and as he began his pacing, night began to fall.

The innkeeper told everybody in the inn about his guest's madness, the watch over the arms and the dubbing he was expecting. They marvelled at so strange a kind of madness and went to watch him from a distance, and saw that with a calm air he sometimes paced up and down, and sometimes, leaning on his lance, fixed his eyes on the armour and did not take them off it for a long while. Night had closed in completely, but the moon was so bright that it could compete with the body that lent it its light, so that everything the new knight did was plainly seen by everybody.

Just then it occurred to one of the carriers in the inn to go and water his string of mules, and for that it was necessary to move Don Quixote's armour off the trough. Seeing him come, Don Quixote said to him in a loud voice:

"O thou, whoever thou art, presumptuous knight, that comest to lay hands on the arms of the most valiant errant that ever girded sword! Look to what thou doest, and touch them not, unless thou wouldst leave thy life in payment for thy presumption."

The carrier took no notice of these words — and it would have been better for him if he had, since he would have been taking care of his health. On the contrary, he took hold of the straps and flung the armour a good way from him. Seeing which, Don Quixote raised his eyes to heaven and, fixing his thoughts — so it appeared — on his lady Dulcinea, said:

"Help me, my lady, in this first insult offered to this breast of yours that is your vassal; let not your favour and protection fail me in this first trial."

And saying this and more to the same effect, he let go his shield, raised his lance in both hands and brought it down on the carrier's head with such a blow that he knocked him to the ground so badly hurt that if he had followed it with a second there would have been no need of a surgeon to treat him. That done, he gathered up his armour and went back to pacing with the same composure as before.

A little later, without anyone knowing what had happened — for the carrier was still stunned — a second one came up with the same intention of watering his mules; and as he went to move the armour and clear the trough, without a word and without asking anyone's help, Don Quixote let go his shield again, raised his lance again, and without breaking it to pieces made more than three of the second carrier's head, for he split it in four. At the noise all the people in the inn came running, the innkeeper among them. Seeing this, Don Quixote got his shield on his arm, laid his hand on his sword and said:

"O lady of beauty, strength and vigour of this feeble heart of mine! Now is the time to turn the eyes of your greatness upon this captive knight of yours, who awaits so great an adventure."

With this he recovered, as it seemed to him, such courage that if all the carriers in the world had attacked him he would not have taken a step back. The comrades of the wounded men, seeing the state they were in, began at a distance to rain stones down on Don Quixote, who sheltered himself as best he could behind his shield and dared not leave the trough for fear of abandoning his armour. The innkeeper shouted to them to leave him alone, because he had already told them the man was mad, and being mad he would get off even if he killed the lot of them. Don Quixote was shouting too, and louder, calling them treacherous cowards, and saying that the lord of the castle was a base-born scoundrel of a knight to allow knights errant to be treated in such a way, and that if he had received the order of chivalry he would have made him understand his treachery:

"But as for you, foul and low rabble, I take no account of you at all. Throw, come on, come here and do me what harm you can, and you shall see what payment you get for your folly and your insolence."

He said this with such spirit and such fearlessness that he put a terrible fright into his attackers; and for that reason, and because of the innkeeper's arguments, they stopped throwing, and he let the wounded be carried off and went back to his watch with the same quiet composure as before.

The innkeeper did not much care for his guest's jokes, and decided to cut it short and give him the confounded order of chivalry at once, before any further misfortune occurred. So, going up to him, he apologised for the insolence that low sort of people had shown him without his knowing anything about it, though they had been well punished for their presumption. He told him, as he had told him already, that there was no chapel in the castle, and that for what remained to be done none was needed; that the whole point of being dubbed a knight lay in the blow on the neck and the stroke on the shoulder, according to what he knew of the ceremonial of the order, and that this could be done in the middle of a field; and that he had already fulfilled the requirement about watching over the arms, since two hours' watch was enough, and he had stood more than four.

Don Quixote believed the whole of it, and said that he was there ready to obey him, and to finish it off as quickly as he could; because if he were attacked again once he was dubbed a knight, he did not intend to leave a soul alive in the castle, except those his host might tell him to spare, whom he would spare out of respect for him.

Warned and thoroughly alarmed by this, the castellan promptly brought out a ledger in which he entered the straw and barley he issued to the carriers, and with a candle-end that a boy fetched him, and with the two damsels already mentioned, he came to where Don Quixote was and told him to kneel. Then, reading out of his account-book as though he were saying some devout prayer, in the middle of the reading he raised his hand and gave him a good blow on the neck, and after it, with the man's own sword, a handsome stroke across the shoulder, muttering all the while under his breath as though he were praying. That done, he ordered one of the ladies to gird on his sword, which she did with great composure and discretion — and no little was needed to keep from bursting with laughter at every point of the ceremony; but the feats they had already seen from the new knight kept their laughter within bounds. As she girded on the sword, the good lady said:

"God make your worship a very fortunate knight and give you good luck in your fights."

Don Quixote asked her what she was called, so that he might know from then on to whom he was indebted for the favour received; because he meant to give her some share of the honour he would win by the strength of his arm. She answered very humbly that she was called La Tolosa, and that she was the daughter of a cobbler from Toledo who lived by the little stalls of Sancho Bienaya, and that wherever she might be she would serve him and hold him for her lord. Don Quixote begged her, for love of him, to do him the favour of taking a title from then on and calling herself Doña Tolosa. She promised she would; and the other buckled on his spur, and with her he had almost the same conversation as with the lady of the sword. He asked her name, and she said she was called La Molinera, and that she was the daughter of an honest miller of Antequera; and Don Quixote begged her too to take a title and call herself Doña Molinera, offering her fresh services and favours.

These ceremonies, never before seen in this world, having been rushed through at the gallop, Don Quixote could not wait to be in the saddle and out looking for adventures. Saddling Rocinante at once, he mounted, embraced his host, and thanked him for the favour of dubbing him a knight in such extraordinary terms that there is no possibility of setting them down. The innkeeper, to see him out of the inn, answered him with no less rhetoric, though in rather fewer words, and without asking him for the price of his lodging let him go, and good riddance.

Chapter 4: Of What Happened to Our Knight When He Left the Inn

It must have been daybreak when Don Quixote rode out of the inn, so pleased with himself, so gallant, so overjoyed at finding himself dubbed a knight that the delight of it burst the girths of his horse. But remembering his host's advice about the very necessary provisions he ought to carry with him, and particularly the money and the shirts, he decided to go home and fit himself out with everything, and with a squire as well, reckoning on taking on a labourer who was a neighbour of his, a poor man with children, but very well suited to the squirely office of chivalry. With this in mind he turned Rocinante towards his village, and the horse, all but recognising his old haunts, set off so willingly that he seemed not to be putting his feet on the ground at all.

He had not gone far when it seemed to him that from a thicket on his right hand came faint cries, like somebody in distress; and he had hardly heard them before he said:

"I give thanks to heaven for the favour it does me, in putting occasions so promptly before me in which I can do what I owe to my profession and gather the fruit of my good intentions. These cries are certainly from some man or woman in need, who requires my favour and assistance."

And turning the reins, he headed Rocinante towards where the cries seemed to be coming from. A few steps into the wood he saw a mare tied to an oak, and tied to another a boy stripped to the waist, about fifteen years old, who was the one crying out — and not without cause, for a strapping farmer was laying into him with a belt, and every stroke came with a reproof and a piece of advice. He was saying:

"Hold your tongue and keep your eyes open."

And the boy was answering:

"I won't do it again, sir; by Christ's Passion, I won't do it again; I promise to look after the flock more carefully from now on."

Seeing what was going on, Don Quixote said in an angry voice:

"Discourteous knight, it ill becomes you to set upon one who cannot defend himself. Get on your horse and take your lance" — for there was a lance too, leaning against the oak the mare was tethered to — "and I will make you understand that what you are doing is the work of cowards."

The farmer, seeing that figure covered in armour standing over him and brandishing a lance in his face, gave himself up for dead, and answered civilly:

"Sir knight, this boy I am punishing is a servant of mine, employed to look after a flock of sheep I have hereabouts, and he is so careless that I lose one every day. And when I punish him for his carelessness — or his roguery — he says I do it out of meanness, so as not to pay him the wages I owe him; and before God and on my soul he lies."

"'Lies', in my presence, you vile peasant?" said Don Quixote. "By the sun that shines on us, I have half a mind to run you through with this lance. Pay him at once, without another word; if not, by the God who rules us I will finish and annihilate you on this spot. Untie him this minute."

The farmer hung his head and, without a word in reply, untied his servant. Don Quixote asked the boy how much his master owed him. He said nine months at seven reals a month. Don Quixote did the sum and found it came to sixty-three reals, and told the farmer to pay it out on the spot unless he wanted to die for it. The frightened peasant answered that, in the pass he was in and by the oath he had sworn — and he had not sworn anything yet — it was not so much, because there had to be deducted and taken into account three pairs of shoes he had given him and a real for two bleedings when he had been ill.

"That is all very well," replied Don Quixote, "but let the shoes and the bleedings stand against the lashes you have given him without any fault of his; for if he wore out the leather of the shoes you paid for, you have worn out the leather of his body; and if the barber let his blood when he was ill, you have let it when he was well. So on that score he owes you nothing."

"The trouble is, sir knight, that I have no money here. Let Andrés come home with me and I will pay him real by real."

"Me go with him?" said the boy. "Not on your life! No, sir, not for a moment; because the minute he gets me alone he'll flay me like a St Bartholomew."

"He will do nothing of the kind," replied Don Quixote. "It is enough that I command him, and he will respect me; and provided he swears it to me by the order of chivalry he has received, I will let him go free and guarantee the payment."

"Just listen to what your worship is saying, sir," said the boy, "for this master of mine is no knight and has never received any order of chivalry at all; he is Juan Haldudo the rich man, from over at Quintanar."

"That matters little," answered Don Quixote, "for there may well be knights among the Haldudos; besides which, every man is the son of his own deeds."

"That's true enough," said Andrés, "but this master of mine — what deeds is he the son of, when he denies me my wages and my sweat and labour?"

"I do not deny them, brother Andrés," answered the farmer; "and do me the kindness of coming with me, and I swear by all the orders of chivalry there are in the world to pay you, as I have said, real by real, and perfumed into the bargain."

"I let you off the perfume," said Don Quixote. "Give them to him in reals and I shall be satisfied. And mind you keep your oath; if not, by that same oath I swear to come back and look for you and punish you, and I shall find you even if you hide better than a lizard. And if you want to know who lays this on you, so as to feel more truly bound to carry it out, know that I am the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, the undoer of wrongs and injustices. And so God be with you, and do not let what you have promised and sworn slip out of your mind, on pain of the penalty pronounced."

And so saying he spurred Rocinante and was soon well away from them. The farmer followed him with his eyes, and when he saw that he had passed out of the wood and was no longer in sight he turned to his servant Andrés and said:

"Come here, my son, I want to pay you what I owe you, as that undoer of wrongs commanded me."

"I'll swear you do," said Andrés. "And how right your worship will be to carry out the orders of that good knight — may he live a thousand years! Seeing how valiant he is and what a good judge, by St Roch, if you don't pay me he'll come back and do exactly what he said."

"I'll swear to that too," said the farmer; "but out of the great affection I bear you, I want to increase the debt so as to increase the payment."

And taking him by the arm he tied him to the oak again, where he gave him so many lashes that he left him for dead.

"Now call, Señor Andrés," said the farmer, "for the undoer of wrongs, and you'll see how he doesn't undo this one. Though I don't think it's finished being done yet, because I have a mind to flay you alive, as you were afraid of."

But in the end he untied him and gave him leave to go and look for his judge, so that he might execute the sentence pronounced. Andrés went off rather glum, swearing to go and find the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha and tell him point by point what had happened, and that he would have to pay for it sevenfold. For all that, he went off crying and his master stayed behind laughing.

And that was how the valiant Don Quixote undid the wrong; and he, delighted with what had happened and thinking he had made a most fortunate and lofty beginning to his knighthood, rode on towards his village in great satisfaction with himself, saying under his breath:

"Well may you call yourself the most fortunate of all the women alive on earth today, O beauty above all beauties, Dulcinea of El Toboso — since it has fallen to your lot to have subject and surrendered to your every wish and pleasure so valiant and so renowned a knight as Don Quixote of La Mancha is and shall be; who, as all the world knows, received the order of chivalry yesterday and today has undone the greatest wrong and injury that injustice ever framed or cruelty ever committed. Today he struck the whip from the hand of that pitiless enemy who was flogging that delicate child for no reason at all."

At this point he came to a place where the road divided into four, and at once there came into his mind those crossroads where knights errant used to stop and consider which of the roads to take; and to imitate them he sat still a while, and after thinking it over very thoroughly he dropped the rein and left his own choice to the horse's, and the horse followed his original intention, which was to make for his own stable.

After going about two miles, Don Quixote made out a great crowd of people, who, as it turned out afterwards, were some merchants of Toledo on their way to buy silk in Murcia. There were six of them, riding under sunshades, with four servants on horseback and three muleteers on foot. Don Quixote had hardly caught sight of them before he imagined this must be some fresh adventure; and, so as to copy in every way he could the passages he had read in his books, it seemed to him that here was one made to measure that he had been meaning to attempt. So with a noble bearing and great resolution he settled himself firmly in the stirrups, gripped his lance, brought his shield up to his chest, and, planting himself in the middle of the road, waited for those knights errant to come up — for that is what he took them for and judged them to be. And when they had got near enough to see and hear him, Don Quixote raised his voice and said, with an arrogant gesture:

"Let all the world stand still, unless all the world confesses that there is not in all the world a maiden more beautiful than the Empress of La Mancha, the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso."

The merchants stopped at the sound of this speech, and to look at the strange figure of the man who made it; and from the figure and the speech they saw at once that its owner was mad. But they wanted to see at their leisure where this confession they were being asked for would end, and one of them, who was something of a joker and very shrewd indeed, said to him:

"Sir knight, we do not know who this good lady you speak of may be. Show her to us; and if she is as beautiful as you make out, we will willingly and without any compulsion confess the truth that you require of us."

"If I showed her to you," replied Don Quixote, "what merit would there be in your confessing so obvious a truth? The whole point is that without seeing her you must believe it, confess it, affirm it, swear it and defend it; and if not, you are at war with me, you monstrous and arrogant people. Whether you come at me one by one, as the order of chivalry requires, or all together, as is the custom and the bad practice of your breed, here I stand and wait for you, trusting in the right that is on my side."

"Sir knight," said the merchant, "I beg your worship, in the name of all these princes here present, that — so as not to burden our consciences by confessing a thing we have never seen or heard of, and one so much to the prejudice of the empresses and queens of the Alcarria and Extremadura — your worship will be so good as to show us some portrait of this lady, even if it is no bigger than a grain of wheat; for you can tell the whole skein by a single thread, and we shall be satisfied and easy in our minds, and your worship will be content and paid off. In fact I think we are so far on your side already that even if her portrait shows us she is blind in one eye and that the other runs vermilion and brimstone, we would still, to oblige your worship, say everything you like in her favour."

"It runs nothing of the kind, you infamous rabble," answered Don Quixote, blazing with rage. "It runs nothing of the kind, I tell you, but amber and civet packed in cotton wool; and she is neither one-eyed nor hunchbacked, but straighter than a spindle out of the Guadarrama. But you shall pay for the enormous blasphemy you have uttered against beauty as great as my lady's."

And saying this he charged with his lance levelled at the man who had spoken, with such fury and rage that if good luck had not arranged for Rocinante to stumble and fall halfway there, it would have gone badly for the bold merchant. Rocinante went down, and his master rolled a good distance across the field; and, trying to get up, he never could — such an encumbrance were the lance, shield, spurs and helmet, together with the weight of that ancient armour. And while he was struggling to get up and failing, he kept saying:

"Fly not, cowardly people! Stay, base creatures! It is not by my own fault that I lie here, but by my horse's."

One of the muleteers, who cannot have been very well disposed, hearing the poor fallen man come out with all this arrogance, could not put up with it without answering him across the ribs. Going up to him, he took the lance, and after breaking it in pieces he began with one of them to give our Don Quixote such a beating that, in spite of all his armour, he ground him like grain. His masters shouted at him not to lay it on so hard and to leave the man alone, but the lad's blood was up and he would not leave the game until he had staked the whole rest of his rage; and fetching the other pieces of the lance he finished breaking them up on the wretched fallen man, who through that whole tempest of blows never shut his mouth, but went on threatening heaven and earth and the brigands, which was what they seemed to him.

The lad wore himself out, and the merchants went on their way with something to talk about for the rest of it — the poor cudgelled knight. And he, when he saw himself alone, tried once more whether he could get up; but if he could not do it when he was sound and well, how was he to do it now, pounded and half destroyed? And still he counted himself fortunate, since it seemed to him this was a misfortune proper to knights errant, and he put the whole of it down to his horse's fault; and it was not possible to get up, so bruised was he in every part of his body.

Chapter 5: In Which the Story of Our Knight's Misfortune Is Continued

Finding, then, that he really could not stir, he decided to fall back on his usual remedy, which was to think of some passage out of his books; and his madness brought to his mind the one about Valdovinos and the Marquis of Mantua, when Carloto left him wounded in the mountains — a story known to children, not unfamiliar to young men, celebrated and even believed by old ones, and for all that no truer than the miracles of Mahomet. This struck him as made to measure for the situation he was in; and so, with every appearance of great suffering, he began to roll about on the ground and to say in a failing voice the very words they say the wounded knight of the wood said:

	Where art thou, lady mine,
	that thou grievest not at my pain?
	Either thou knowest it not, lady,
	or thou art false and disloyal.

And in this manner he went on with the ballad as far as those lines that say:

	O noble Marquis of Mantua,
	mine uncle and lord by blood!

And as luck would have it, when he got to this line a labourer from his own village and a neighbour of his happened to be passing, on his way back from taking a load of wheat to the mill. Seeing a man lying there, he came up and asked him who he was and what was wrong with him that he was complaining so mournfully. Don Quixote had no doubt at all that this was the Marquis of Mantua, his uncle; and so he answered nothing but went on with his ballad, in which he gave an account of his misfortune and of the love affair between the Emperor's son and his own wife — all exactly as the ballad sings it.

The labourer stood amazed, listening to this nonsense; and taking off the visor, which was already in pieces from the beating, he wiped his face, which was covered in dust; and he had hardly wiped it before he recognised him and said:

"Señor Quixana" — for that must have been his name when he was in his right mind and had not yet gone from a quiet gentleman to a knight errant — "who has put your worship in this state?"

But he only went on with his ballad in answer to everything he was asked. Seeing this, the good man got off his breastplate and backpiece as best he could, to see whether he had any wound; but he saw no blood and no mark of any kind. He tried to get him up off the ground, and with no little trouble hoisted him onto his own donkey, which seemed to him the steadier mount. He gathered up the armour, down to the splinters of the lance, and tied it all on Rocinante; and taking the horse by the rein and the ass by the halter, he set off towards his village, deep in thought at the nonsense Don Quixote was talking. And Don Quixote was no less deep in it, for being so pounded and broken that he could hardly keep his seat on the little donkey, and letting out sighs from time to time that carried up to heaven — so that once again he obliged the labourer to ask him to say what was wrong with him. And it seems as though the devil himself was bringing into his memory the tales that fitted his circumstances, because at that moment, forgetting all about Valdovinos, he remembered the Moor Abindarráez, and how the governor of Antequera, Rodrigo de Narváez, took him prisoner and carried him captive to his stronghold. So that when the labourer asked him again how he was and what he felt, he answered with the same words and speeches that the captive Abencerraje made to Rodrigo de Narváez, exactly as he had read the story in Jorge de Montemayor's Diana, where it is written down — making such apt use of it that the labourer was consigning himself to the devil at having to listen to such a machine of foolishness. By which he understood that his neighbour was mad, and he hurried on to reach the village so as to escape the tedium Don Quixote's long harangue was causing him. At the end of it Don Quixote said:

"Let your worship know, Señor Don Rodrigo de Narváez, that this beautiful Jarifa I have mentioned is now the lovely Dulcinea of El Toboso, for whom I have done, do and shall do the most famous deeds of chivalry that have been, are being or ever will be seen in this world."

To which the labourer answered:

"Look here, sir, sinner that I am — I am not Don Rodrigo de Narváez, nor the Marquis of Mantua, but Pedro Alonso, your neighbour; and your worship is not Valdovinos nor Abindarráez, but the honourable gentleman Señor Quixana."

"I know who I am," answered Don Quixote, "and I know that I can be not only the men I have named, but all the Twelve Peers of France as well, and all the Nine Worthies too; for my exploits will outdo everything they all did together and every one of them did singly."

With this talk and more like it they reached the village about nightfall; but the labourer waited until it was a little darker, so that the battered gentleman should not be seen making such a poor horseman. When it seemed to him the right time, he went into the town and up to Don Quixote's house, which he found in an uproar. The curate and the barber of the village were there, both of them great friends of Don Quixote, and the housekeeper was shouting at them:

"What does your worship think, Señor Licentiate Pero Pérez" — for that was the curate's name — "of my master's misfortune? Three days now and no sign of him, nor of the nag, nor of the shield, nor the lance, nor the armour. Miserable woman that I am! I am convinced — and it is as true as that I was born to die — that those cursed books of chivalry he has, and reads so constantly, have turned his brain. Now I remember hearing him say many a time, talking to himself, that he wanted to turn knight errant and go off through the world looking for adventures. Let those books be commended to Satan and Barabbas, for having ruined the finest understanding in the whole of La Mancha."

The niece said the same, and more besides:

"You should know, Master Nicholas" — that was the barber's name — "that many a time it happened that my uncle would be reading these heartless books of misfortunes for two days and nights together, at the end of which he would throw the book out of his hands, lay hold of his sword and go slashing at the walls; and when he was thoroughly worn out he would say he had killed four giants as big as four towers, and the sweat that ran off him from tiredness he said was blood from the wounds he had taken in the battle. Then he would drink off a great jug of cold water and be well and calm again, saying that the water was a most precious potion brought him by the sage Esquife, a great enchanter and a friend of his.
