But I am to blame for the whole thing, for not telling your worships about my uncle's ravings so that you could have done something about it before it came to this, and burnt all these excommunicated books — for he has plenty of them, and they thoroughly deserve to be burned, as if they belonged to heretics."

"That is what I say too," said the curate, "and upon my word tomorrow shall not pass without a public trial being held on them and their being condemned to the fire, so that they may not give anyone else who reads them the chance of doing what my good friend must have done."

The labourer and Don Quixote were listening to all this, and it finally made the labourer understand what was the matter with his neighbour; so he began to call out:

"Open, your worships, to Sir Valdovinos and to my lord the Marquis of Mantua, who comes sorely wounded, and to the Moorish lord Abindarráez, brought captive by the valiant Rodrigo de Narváez, governor of Antequera."

At these shouts they all came out, and as the men recognised their friend and the women their master and uncle, who had still not got down from the donkey because he could not, they ran to embrace him. He said:

"Hold, all of you. I come sorely wounded through my horse's fault. Carry me to my bed and send, if it be possible, for the wise Urganda, to treat and examine my wounds."

"Just look at that, confound it!" said the housekeeper at this. "Didn't my heart tell me exactly which foot my master was limping on! Come up, your worship, and welcome; for without that Hurgada of yours coming we shall know how to cure you here. Cursed, I say again, and a hundred times over, be these books of chivalry, that have brought your worship to this!"

They carried him to bed at once, and searching him for wounds could find none; and he said it was all bruising, from having taken a great fall with Rocinante his horse while fighting ten giants, the most outrageous and audacious that were to be found in a great part of the earth.

"Aha!" said the curate. "So there are giants in the dance, are there? By the holy cross, I will burn them tomorrow before nightfall."

They asked Don Quixote a thousand questions, and to none of them would he answer anything except that they should give him something to eat and let him sleep, which was what mattered most to him. This was done, and the curate questioned the labourer at great length about how he had found Don Quixote. He told him the whole of it, with the nonsense he had talked when he found him and while he was bringing him home; which only made the licentiate keener to do what he did the next day, which was to call on his friend Master Nicholas the barber and go with him to Don Quixote's house.

Chapter 6: Of the Great and Comical Inquisition the Curate and the Barber Held in the Library of Our Ingenious Gentleman

He was still asleep. The curate asked the niece for the keys of the room where the books were — the authors of the mischief — and she gave them to him very willingly. They all went in, the housekeeper with them, and found more than a hundred large volumes, very handsomely bound, and a good many small ones. The moment the housekeeper saw them she hurried out of the room again and came back with a bowl of holy water and a sprinkler, and said:

"Take this, your worship, Señor Licentiate, and sprinkle the room, in case there should be here one of those enchanters the books are full of, and he should put a spell on us in return for the one we mean to put on them by driving them out of the world."

The licentiate laughed at the housekeeper's simplicity, and told the barber to hand him the books one at a time so that he could see what they were about, since there might be some that did not deserve punishment by fire.

"No," said the niece, "there is no reason to spare a single one, because they have all done the damage. It would be better to throw them out of the window into the yard, make a pile of them and set fire to it; or else take them out to the stable-yard, and there make the bonfire, and then the smoke will not be a nuisance."

The housekeeper said the same: such was the eagerness the two of them had for the death of those innocents. But the curate would not agree to it without at least reading the titles. And the first that Master Nicholas put into his hands was The Four Books of Amadís of Gaul, and the curate said:

"There seems to be something providential in this; because I have heard it said that this was the first book of chivalry printed in Spain, and that all the rest have taken their beginning and origin from it. And so it seems to me that, as the founder of so bad a sect, we ought to condemn it to the fire without any excuse."

"No, sir," said the barber, "for I have also heard it said that it is the best of all the books that have been written in that line; and so, as being unique in its art, it ought to be pardoned."

"That is true," said the curate, "and for that reason its life is spared for now. Let us see that other one next to it."

"It is," said the barber, "The Exploits of Esplandián, the lawful son of Amadís of Gaul."

"Then in truth," said the curate, "the goodness of the father shall not save the son. Here, mistress housekeeper: open that window and throw him into the yard, and let him make a beginning to the pile for the bonfire we are going to have."

The housekeeper did it with great satisfaction, and the good Esplandián went flying into the yard to wait with all patience for the fire that threatened him.

"On we go," said the curate.

"This next one," said the barber, "is Amadís of Greece; and I believe all the ones on this side are of the same family as Amadís."

"Then let them all go into the yard," said the curate; "for rather than not burn Queen Pintiquiniestra, and the shepherd Darinel and his eclogues, and the devilish tangled speeches of the man who wrote them, I would burn my own father along with them, if he came about in the shape of a knight errant."

"I am of that opinion," said the barber.

"And so am I," added the niece.

"Well then," said the housekeeper, "hand them over, and out into the yard with them."

They gave her the books, which were many, and she saved herself the stairs by pitching them down out of the window.

"Who is that tub of a thing?" said the curate.

"That," answered the barber, "is Don Olivante de Laura."

"The author of that book," said the curate, "was the same man who wrote The Garden of Flowers; and to tell the truth I cannot make up my mind which of the two books is the more truthful — or, to put it better, the less lying. All I can say is that this one goes into the yard for being absurd and arrogant."

"This next is Florismarte of Hyrcania," said the barber.

"So Sir Florismarte is here, is he?" replied the curate. "Then upon my faith he shall come to a quick end in the yard, in spite of his strange birth and his celebrated adventures; the hardness and dryness of his style allow of nothing else. Into the yard with him and with that other one, mistress housekeeper."

"With pleasure, sir," she would answer; and she carried out her orders with great cheerfulness.

"This is The Knight Platir," said the barber.

"That is an old book," said the curate, "and I find nothing in it that deserves pardon. Let it join the others without argument."

And so it was done. They opened another book and saw that it was called The Knight of the Cross.

"For the sake of so holy a name as this book bears, its ignorance might be forgiven; but then there is the saying: behind the cross stands the devil. Into the fire with it."

Taking up another book, the barber said:

"This is The Mirror of Chivalry."

"I know his worship already," said the curate. "In there go Sir Reinaldos of Montalbán with his friends and companions, greater thieves than Cacus, and the Twelve Peers, with that truthful historian Turpin. And to tell the truth I am inclined to sentence them to no more than perpetual banishment, if only because they have a share in the invention of the famous Matteo Boiardo, out of which the Christian poet Ludovico Ariosto also wove his cloth. And if I find Ariosto here, and speaking any language but his own, I shall show him no respect whatever; but if he speaks in his own tongue, I shall put him on my head."

"Well, I have him in Italian," said the barber, "but I don't understand him."

"Nor would it be a good thing if you did," answered the curate; "and here we would gladly excuse that captain for not having brought him to Spain and made a Castilian of him, for he stripped him of a great deal of his native worth. And the same will be done by everyone who tries to turn books of verse into another language: however much care they take and however much skill they show, they will never reach the pitch those books had at their first birth. In short, I say that this book, and all that are found dealing with these matters of France, should be thrown and deposited in a dry well until we can decide with more deliberation what is to be done with them — always excepting a certain Bernardo del Carpio that is going about, and another called Roncesvalles; for these, the moment they come into my hands, shall pass into the housekeeper's and out of hers into the fire, without any reprieve."

The barber confirmed the whole of it and thought it well and very rightly said, believing the curate to be so good a Christian and so great a friend of the truth that he would not say otherwise for anything in the world. And opening another book, he saw it was Palmerin of the Olive, and next to it another called Palmerin of England; seeing which, the licentiate said:

"Let that olive be split into kindling at once and burned until not even its ashes are left; and let that palm of England be kept and preserved as something unique, and let a case be made for it like the one Alexander found among the spoils of Darius, which he set aside for keeping the works of the poet Homer in. This book, my friend, has authority on two counts: first because it is very good in itself, and secondly because it is said that a wise king of Portugal wrote it. All the adventures at the castle of Miraguarda are excellent and very skilfully done; the speeches are courtly and clear, and observe and respect the character of the speaker with great propriety and understanding. So I say, saving your better judgement, Master Nicholas, that this one and Amadís of Gaul go free of the fire, and all the rest perish without any further sifting and searching."

"No, my friend," replied the barber. "This one I have here is the celebrated Don Belianís."

"Then that one," replied the curate, "along with its second, third and fourth parts, needs a little rhubarb to purge its excess of bile; and everything about the Castle of Fame will have to come out, and other impertinences of more consequence. For that they are given the longest term the law allows, and according as they mend, so shall they be treated with mercy or with justice. In the meantime keep them at your house, friend, but do not let anybody read them."

"With pleasure," answered the barber.

And without wishing to tire himself out reading any more books of chivalry, he told the housekeeper to take all the big ones and pitch them into the yard. This was not said to a fool or a deaf woman, but to one who was keener on burning them than on weaving a length of cloth, however large and fine. Grabbing nearly eight at once, she flung them out of the window; and taking so many together, one fell at the barber's feet, and he had a fancy to see whose it was, and saw it said: The History of the Famous Knight Tirant lo Blanc.

"Bless me!" said the curate, with a great shout. "So Tirant lo Blanc is here! Give him to me, friend; I reckon I have found in him a treasure of enjoyment and a mine of amusement. Here is Don Quirieleison of Montalbán, that valiant knight, and his brother Tomás of Montalbán, and the knight Fonseca, and the battle the brave Tirant fought with the mastiff, and the witticisms of the damsel Pleasure-of-my-life, and the loves and the wiles of the widow Repose, and the lady Empress in love with Hippolyte her squire. I tell you truly, friend, that for its style this is the best book in the world: here the knights eat, and sleep, and die in their beds, and make their wills before they die, with all sorts of things that every other book of the kind goes without. For all that, I tell you that the man who wrote it deserved, for not having done so many foolish things on purpose, to be sent to the galleys for the rest of his days. Take it home and read it, and you will see that everything I have told you about it is true."

"I shall," answered the barber. "But what are we to do with these small books that are left?"

"These," said the curate, "cannot be books of chivalry, but of poetry."

And opening one, he saw it was the Diana of Jorge de Montemayor, and said, thinking all the rest were of the same kind:

"These do not deserve to be burned like the others, because they do not do, and will not do, the harm the books of chivalry have done. They are books of the understanding, and nobody is the worse for them."

"Oh, sir!" said the niece. "Your worship may perfectly well order these to be burned like the rest; because it would be no great wonder if, my uncle having been cured of his chivalry sickness, he should read these and take it into his head to turn shepherd and go wandering about the woods and meadows singing and playing — and, what would be worse, turn poet, which they say is an incurable and catching disease."

"The young lady speaks the truth," said the curate, "and it will be as well to take this stumbling-block and occasion of sin out of our friend's way. And since we are beginning with Montemayor's Diana, I am of the opinion that it should not be burned, but that everything about the wise Felicia and the enchanted water should be cut out of it, and nearly all the longer verses; and let it keep, and welcome, its prose and the honour of being first in that line of books."

"This next," said the barber, "is the Diana called the second, by the man from Salamanca; and this is another with the same name, whose author is Gil Polo."

"Then let the one from Salamanca," answered the curate, "go and swell the number of the condemned in the yard; and let Gil Polo's be kept as if it were by Apollo himself. And get on, friend, and let us hurry, for it is growing late."

"This book," said the barber, opening another, "is The Ten Books of the Fortune of Love, composed by Antonio de Lofraso, a Sardinian poet."

"By the holy orders I received," said the curate, "since Apollo was Apollo and the muses muses and poets poets, so amusing and so preposterous a book as this has never been written; and in its own way it is the best and the most singular of all that have come out in that line into the light of the world; and the man who has not read it may reckon he has never read anything enjoyable in his life. Give it to me, friend, for I value having found it more than if somebody had given me a cassock of Florentine cloth."

He put it aside with the greatest satisfaction, and the barber went on:

"These next are The Shepherd of Iberia, The Nymphs of Henares and Disenchantments of Jealousy."

"Then there is nothing to be done," said the curate, "but hand them over to the secular arm of the housekeeper; and let nobody ask me why, or we should never be finished."

"This next is The Shepherd of Fílida."

"That is no shepherd," said the curate, "but a very polished courtier. Let it be kept like a precious jewel."

"This big one here," said the barber, "is called Treasury of Various Poems."

"If there were not so many of them," said the curate, "they would be more esteemed. This book needs weeding and cleaning of certain low things it has among its fine ones. Let it be kept, because its author is a friend of mine, and out of respect for other more heroic and lofty works he has written."

"This one," the barber went on, "is the Songbook of López Maldonado."

"The author of that book," replied the curate, "is also a great friend of mine, and his verses in his own mouth astonish anyone who hears them; and such is the sweetness of the voice he sings them in that it enchants you. He is a little long in the eclogues, but there was never too much of a good thing. Let it be kept with the chosen ones. But what book is that beside it?"

"The Galatea, by Miguel de Cervantes," said the barber.

"That Cervantes has been a great friend of mine for many years, and I know he is better versed in misfortunes than in verses. His book has something of good invention about it; it proposes something and concludes nothing. We must wait for the second part he promises; perhaps with amendment it will win the whole of the mercy that is now refused it. In the meantime, until we see, keep him shut up at your house, friend."

"With pleasure," answered the barber. "And here come three all together: The Araucana, by Don Alonso de Ercilla; The Austríada, by Juan Rufo, magistrate of Córdoba; and The Monserrat, by Cristóbal de Virués, a Valencian poet."

"All three of those books," said the curate, "are the best that have been written in heroic verse in the Castilian tongue, and can compete with the most famous of Italy. Let them be kept as the richest treasures of poetry that Spain possesses."

The curate grew tired of looking at any more books, and so, without further examination, he wanted all the rest burned wholesale. But the barber had already opened one that was called The Tears of Angelica.

"I should have wept them myself," said the curate on hearing the name, "if I had ordered such a book to be burned; because its author was one of the famous poets of the world, not only of Spain, and he was outstandingly happy in his translation of some of Ovid's fables."

Chapter 7: Of the Second Sally of Our Good Knight Don Quixote of La Mancha

At this point Don Quixote began to shout:

"Here, here, valiant knights! Here is where you must show the strength of your mighty arms, for the courtiers are getting the best of the tournament!"

Running to see what all this noise and commotion was about, they got no further with the inquisition into the books that were left; and so it is believed that The Carolea and The Lion of Spain went into the fire unseen and unheard, along with The Deeds of the Emperor, written by Don Luis de Ávila, which must undoubtedly have been among those still to come; and perhaps, if the curate had seen them, they would not have suffered so severe a sentence.

When they reached Don Quixote he was already out of bed and still shouting and raving, laying about him on all sides with cuts and backstrokes, as wide awake as if he had never slept at all. They got hold of him and forced him back into bed; and after he had quietened down a little he turned to the curate and said:

"Certainly, my lord Archbishop Turpin, it is a great disgrace to those of us who call ourselves the Twelve Peers to let the courtier knights carry off the victory in this tournament so tamely, when we adventurers have won the prize on the three preceding days."

"Be quiet, my friend," said the curate. "God will be pleased to let the luck change, and what is lost today may be won tomorrow. Look to your health for the present, for it seems to me your worship must be excessively tired, if you are not sorely wounded."

"Wounded, no," said Don Quixote, "but pounded and broken, there is no doubt of that; because that bastard Don Roland has beaten me to a pulp with the trunk of an oak, and all out of envy, because he sees that I alone stand against his exploits. But my name is not Reinaldos of Montalbán if, when I get out of this bed, I do not make him pay for it, for all his enchantments. And for now, let them bring me something to eat, for I know that is what I need most, and leave the revenging to me."

They did so: they gave him something to eat and he fell asleep again, and they were left astonished at his madness.

That night the housekeeper burned and consumed every book there was in the yard and in the whole house; and some must have gone up in the flames that deserved to be kept in perpetual archives. But their luck, and the laziness of the inquisitor, did not allow it; and so the proverb was fulfilled in them, that sometimes the just pay for sinners.

One of the remedies the curate and the barber hit on for their friend's complaint was to have the room where the books had been walled and plastered up, so that when he got up he should not find it — perhaps if the cause were removed the effect would cease — and to say that an enchanter had carried them off, room and all. This was done with great speed. Two days later Don Quixote got up, and the first thing he did was go and look at his books; and, not finding the room where he had left it, he went about from one place to another looking for it. He would come to where the door used to be and feel for it with his hands, and turn his eyes this way and that over everything without saying a word; but after a good long while he asked his housekeeper which way the room with his books was. The housekeeper, who had been thoroughly briefed on what she was to answer, said:

"What room, or what nothing, is your worship looking for? There is no room and no books in this house any more, because the devil himself carried the whole lot away."

"It was not the devil," put in the niece, "but an enchanter who came on a cloud one night, the day after your worship left here; and getting down off a serpent he was riding, he went into the room, and I don't know what he did in there, but after a little while he flew out through the roof and left the house full of smoke. And when we thought to look at what he had done, we could see neither book nor room. Only my mistress and I remember very well that as the wicked old man was leaving he called out in a loud voice that, because of a secret enmity he bore the owner of those books and that room, he had done damage in this house that would be seen afterwards. He said too that he was called the sage Muñatón."

"He would have said Frestón," said Don Quixote.

"I don't know," answered the housekeeper, "whether he was called Frestón or Fritón; all I know is that his name ended in -tón."

"So it does," said Don Quixote. "He is a wise enchanter, a great enemy of mine, who has a grudge against me, because he knows by his arts and his learning that in the course of time I am to fight in single combat with a knight he favours, and that I am to defeat him without his being able to prevent it; and for that reason he does me every ill turn he can. And I tell him that he will have a hard time contradicting or avoiding what heaven has ordained."

"Who doubts it?" said the niece. "But who is asking your worship to get mixed up in these quarrels, uncle? Wouldn't it be better to stay peacefully at home and not go wandering about the world looking for bread better than wheaten, without stopping to think that many go for wool and come back shorn?"

"Oh, niece of mine," answered Don Quixote, "how badly you have reckoned it up! Before anybody shears me I shall have plucked out and pulled off the beard of every man who so much as thinks of touching the tip of a single hair of mine."

Neither of them cared to answer him back any further, because they saw that his temper was rising.

The fact of the matter is that he stayed at home for a fortnight very quietly, giving no sign of wanting to repeat his first ravings; during which days he had the most delightful conversations with his two friends the curate and the barber, in which he maintained that what the world stood in most need of was knights errant, and that in him knight-errantry should be brought back to life. The curate sometimes contradicted him and sometimes agreed, because without keeping up that device there was no getting on with him at all.

During this time Don Quixote worked on a labourer who was a neighbour of his, an honest man — if that title can be given to a man who is poor — but with very little salt in his headpiece. In short, he said so much to him, and persuaded and promised him so much, that the poor peasant made up his mind to go off with him and serve him as squire. Among other things Don Quixote told him that he should be ready to come willingly, because some adventure might befall in which, in the twinkling of an eye, he might win an isle and leave him governor of it. On the strength of these promises and others like them, Sancho Panza — for that was the labourer's name — left his wife and children and took service as his neighbour's squire.

Don Quixote then set about getting money; and by selling one thing and pawning another, and coming off badly on all of them, he raised a reasonable sum. He also fitted himself out with a round shield, which he borrowed from a friend, and, patching up his broken helmet as best he could, he warned his squire Sancho of the day and hour he meant to set out, so that he could provide himself with whatever he thought he most needed. Above all he charged him to bring saddlebags. Sancho said he would, and that he was thinking of bringing an ass he had, a very good one, because he was not used to going far on foot. Over the ass Don Quixote hesitated a little, casting about in his memory to see whether any knight errant had ever had a squire mounted asswise; but none came to mind. All the same, he decided that he should bring it, meaning to fit him out with a more honourable mount as soon as there was occasion, by taking the horse off the first discourteous knight he met. He provided himself with shirts and everything else he could, following the advice the innkeeper had given him. And all this being done and settled, without Panza taking leave of his children and wife, or Don Quixote of his housekeeper and niece, they left the village one night without a soul seeing them; and they rode so far that by daybreak they reckoned themselves safe from being found even if they were searched for.

Sancho Panza rode along on his donkey like a patriarch, with his saddlebags and his wineskin, and with a great longing to see himself governor of the isle his master had promised him. Don Quixote happened to take the same route and road he had taken on his first journey, across the plain of Montiel, which he crossed with less discomfort than the time before, because it was early morning and the sun's rays struck them slantwise and did not tire them. Then Sancho Panza said to his master:

"Mind your worship doesn't forget, sir knight errant, what you promised me about the isle; for I shall know how to govern it, however big it may be."

To which Don Quixote answered:

"You must know, Sancho Panza my friend, that it was a very common practice among the knights errant of old to make their squires governors of the isles or kingdoms they won; and I am determined that so gracious a custom shall not fail through me. On the contrary, I mean to improve on it: because they sometimes, and perhaps most times, waited until their squires were old; and then, when the men had had their fill of service and endured bad days and worse nights, they gave them some title of count, or at most marquis, of some valley or province of no great size. But if you live and I live, it may very well be that before six days are out I shall win a kingdom with others attached to it, exactly suited for crowning you king of one of them. And do not think it much, for things and events come to such knights in ways so unheard-of and unimagined that I might easily give you even more than I promise."

"In that case," answered Sancho Panza, "if I were to be a king by one of these miracles your worship talks about, then at the very least Juana Gutiérrez, my old woman, would come to be a queen and my children princes."

"Well, who doubts it?" answered Don Quixote.

"I doubt it," replied Sancho Panza; "because I reckon that if God rained kingdoms down on the earth, not one of them would sit well on the head of Mari Gutiérrez. I tell you, sir, she isn't worth twopence as a queen. Countess would suit her better, and even that with God's help."

"Leave it to God, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "and He will give what suits you best. But do not lower your spirits so far as to be content with anything less than being a governor."

"I won't, sir," answered Sancho, "especially having so distinguished a master as your worship, who will know how to give me whatever is good for me and whatever I can carry."

Chapter 8: Of the Good Fortune the Valiant Don Quixote Had in the Dreadful and Never-Before-Imagined Adventure of the Windmills, with Other Events Worthy of Happy Remembrance

At this point they caught sight of thirty or forty windmills that stand on that plain; and as soon as Don Quixote saw them he said to his squire:

"Fortune is guiding our affairs better than we could have wished. Look over there, Sancho Panza my friend, where thirty or more monstrous giants are showing themselves, with whom I mean to do battle and take all their lives; and with their spoils we shall begin to grow rich. For this is a righteous war, and it is a great service to God to sweep so evil a breed off the face of the earth."

"What giants?" said Sancho Panza.

"Those you see over there," answered his master, "with the long arms; some of them have arms very nearly two leagues long."

"Look, your worship," answered Sancho, "those things over there aren't giants, they're windmills, and what look like arms on them are the sails, which the wind turns and makes the millstone go round."

"It is quite clear," answered Don Quixote, "that you are not versed in this business of adventures. They are giants; and if you are frightened, get out of the way and set yourself to praying while I go into fierce and unequal battle with them."

And saying this he put spurs to his horse Rocinante, paying no attention to the shouts his squire Sancho was giving him, warning him that beyond any doubt they were windmills and not giants that he was going to attack. But he was so set on their being giants that he neither heard his squire Sancho's shouts nor made out what they were, though he was already quite close; on the contrary, he went on calling at the top of his voice:

"Fly not, cowards and vile creatures, for it is one knight alone who attacks you!"

Just then a little wind got up and the great sails began to move, seeing which Don Quixote said:

"Though you wave more arms than the giant Briareus, you shall answer to me for it."

And saying this, and commending himself with all his heart to his lady Dulcinea, begging her to help him in this pass, well covered by his shield and with his lance in the rest, he charged at Rocinante's full gallop and rammed the first mill in front of him. He drove his lance into the sail, and the wind turned it with such fury that it smashed the lance to pieces, carrying horse and knight along with it, and Don Quixote went rolling across the field very badly knocked about. Sancho Panza came to the rescue at his donkey's full run, and when he got there he found his master could not stir, such a fall had Rocinante given him.

"God help us!" said Sancho. "Didn't I tell your worship to look carefully at what you were doing — that they were only windmills, and nobody could take them for anything else unless he had windmills of the same sort in his own head?"

"Be quiet, Sancho my friend," answered Don Quixote. "Matters of war, more than any others, are subject to continual change. What is more, I believe — and it is the truth — that the sage Frestón who stole my room and my books has turned these giants into windmills, to rob me of the glory of defeating them: such is the enmity he bears me. But in the end, in the very end, his wicked arts will avail him little against the goodness of my sword."

"God grant it, as He can," answered Sancho Panza.

And helping him to his feet, he got him back up onto Rocinante, whose shoulder was half out of joint. Talking over the adventure just past, they took the road for Puerto Lápice, because Don Quixote said it was impossible not to find many and various adventures there, it being a much-travelled place. But he rode along very downcast at having lost his lance; and saying so to his squire, he added:

"I remember reading that a Spanish knight called Diego Pérez de Vargas, having broken his sword in a battle, tore a heavy branch or bough from an oak, and with it did such things that day, and pounded so many Moors, that he was given the surname Machuca — the Pounder — and he and his descendants from that day on were called Vargas y Machuca. I tell you this because from the first oak or elm that offers itself I mean to tear off a bough as good and as heavy as that one; and I intend to do such deeds with it that you will count yourself fortunate to have deserved to come and see them, and to be a witness of things that will hardly be believed."

"In God's hands," said Sancho. "I believe every word your worship says. But straighten up a bit, because you seem to be riding all on one side — it must be the bruising from the fall."

"That is the truth," answered Don Quixote; "and if I do not complain of the pain, it is because knights errant are not allowed to complain of any wound, even if their guts are coming out through it."

"If that's so, I have nothing to say," answered Sancho. "But God knows I'd be glad enough if your worship did complain when something hurt. For myself, I can tell you I shall complain of the very smallest pain I get — unless that rule about not complaining applies to the squires of knights errant as well."

Don Quixote could not help laughing at his squire's simplicity, and told him he might very well complain, how and when he liked, whether he felt like it or not; for so far he had read nothing to the contrary in the order of chivalry. Sancho pointed out that it was dinner time. His master answered that for the present he had no need of it, and that Sancho might eat whenever he pleased. With this permission Sancho settled himself as comfortably as he could on his donkey, and taking out of the saddlebags what he had put into them, he rode along behind his master eating very deliberately, and from time to time tilting up the wineskin with such relish that the most pampered tavern-keeper in Málaga might have envied him. And while he went along in this fashion, taking pull after pull, he had no memory of any promise his master had made him, and thought it no hardship at all, but a great rest, to go about looking for adventures, however dangerous they might be.

In the end they spent that night among some trees, and from one of them Don Quixote tore off a dry branch that could very nearly serve him as a lance, and fitted to it the iron head he took off the one that had broken. All that night Don Quixote did not sleep, thinking about his lady Dulcinea, so as to conform to what he had read in his books, where knights would go many nights without sleeping in the forests and the wilderness, occupied with the memory of their ladies. Sancho Panza did not spend it in that way; having his stomach full, and not with chicory water, he carried the whole night off in a single sleep, and neither the sun's rays striking him in the face nor the singing of the birds, who greeted the coming of the new day in great numbers and very merrily, would have been enough to wake him if his master had not called him. As he got up he gave the wineskin a squeeze and found it rather thinner than the night before, and his heart sank, for it seemed to him they were not on a road that would soon make good the shortage. Don Quixote would not breakfast, because, as has been said, he had taken to living on delicious memories. They went back to the road they had started on for Puerto Lápice, and about three in the afternoon they came in sight of it.

"Here," said Don Quixote when he saw it, "we can dip our hands up to the elbows, brother Sancho Panza, in what they call adventures. But note that however great the dangers you may see me in, you are not to lay hand on your sword to defend me, unless you see that those attacking me are riff-raff and low people, in which case you may certainly help me. But if they are knights, it is in no way lawful or permitted you by the laws of chivalry to help me, until you are dubbed a knight yourself."

"Certainly, sir," answered Sancho, "your worship shall be very well obeyed in this; and all the more since I am naturally peaceable and no friend to getting into brawls and quarrels. Though it's true enough that where defending my own person is concerned I shan't take much account of those laws, since both divine and human law allow every man to defend himself against anyone who tries to wrong him."

"I say no less," answered Don Quixote; "but in this matter of helping me against knights you must keep your natural impulses in check."

"I say I'll do it," answered Sancho, "and I'll keep that commandment as well as I keep Sunday."

While they were talking, two friars of the order of St Benedict appeared on the road, mounted on two dromedaries — for the two mules they were riding were no smaller than that. They were wearing travelling goggles and carrying sunshades. Behind them came a coach, with four or five horsemen escorting it and two muleteers on foot. In the coach, as it turned out afterwards, was a Basque lady on her way to Seville, where her husband was, on his way out to the Indies with a very honourable appointment. The friars were not travelling with her, though they were on the same road; but Don Quixote had hardly caught sight of them before he said to his squire:

"Either I am much mistaken, or this is going to be the most famous adventure ever seen; because those black shapes over there must be, and beyond any doubt are, enchanters carrying off some princess they have stolen in that coach, and it is my business to undo this wrong with all my might."

"This is going to be worse than the windmills," said Sancho. "Look, sir, those are friars of St Benedict, and the coach must belong to some travellers. Look, I tell you to look very carefully at what you are doing, in case it's the devil deceiving you."

"I have told you already, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "that you know very little about the business of adventures. What I say is true, and you shall see it now."

And saying this he rode forward and placed himself in the middle of the road the friars were coming along; and when they had got close enough for him to think they could hear what he said, he called out in a loud voice:

"Devilish and monstrous crew, release this instant the noble princesses you are carrying off by force in that coach; or else make ready to receive a swift death, as the just punishment of your evil deeds."

The friars reined in and stood amazed, both at Don Quixote's figure and at his words, to which they answered:

"Sir knight, we are neither devilish nor monstrous, but two religious of St Benedict going along our road; and we do not know whether or not there are any princesses being carried off by force in that coach."

"Soft words are wasted on me, for I know you already, you perfidious rabble," said Don Quixote.

And without waiting for any further answer he spurred Rocinante and, with his lance levelled, charged the first friar with such fury and determination that if the friar had not let himself drop off the mule he would have brought him to the ground against his will, and badly wounded too, if he had not fallen dead. The second religious, seeing how his companion was being treated, dug his heels into the castle of his good mule and began to gallop across that plain, lighter than the wind itself.

Sancho Panza, seeing the friar on the ground, got nimbly down off his donkey, went at him and began to strip off his habit. Then two of the friars' servants came up and asked him why he was undressing him. Sancho answered that it belonged to him by right, as the spoils of the battle his master Don Quixote had won. The servants, who were not up to jokes and knew nothing about spoils or battles, seeing that Don Quixote had ridden off some way and was talking to the people in the coach, set on Sancho and knocked him down; and without leaving a hair in his beard they kicked him to a pulp and left him stretched on the ground without breath or sense. And without stopping a moment the friar got back on his mule, thoroughly frightened and cowed and with no colour in his face; and as soon as he was in the saddle he spurred after his companion, who was waiting for him a good way off to see how this alarm would turn out; and without waiting for the end of the whole business they went on their way, crossing themselves more often than if they had had the devil at their backs.

Don Quixote, as has been said, was talking to the lady in the coach, saying:

"Your beauty, my lady, may now dispose of your person as best pleases you, for the arrogance of your abductors lies in the dust, brought down by this strong arm of mine. And so that you may not be in pain to know the name of your deliverer, know that I am called Don Quixote of La Mancha, knight errant and adventurer, and captive of the peerless and beautiful Doña Dulcinea of El Toboso. And in payment of the benefit you have received from me, I want nothing but that you return to El Toboso and present yourself on my behalf before that lady, and tell her what I have done for your liberty."

Everything Don Quixote was saying was overheard by one of the squires escorting the coach, a Basque; who, seeing that he would not let the coach go forward but insisted that it must turn straight back to El Toboso, went up to Don Quixote and, taking hold of his lance, said to him in bad Castilian and worse Basque:

"Go, knight, and badly go thou; by the God that made me, if not leave coach, so kill thee as art here Biscayan."

Don Quixote understood him perfectly well, and answered with great composure:

"If thou wert a knight, which thou art not, I would already have punished thy folly and thy presumption, thou wretched creature."

To which the Basque replied:

"I no gentleman? I swear to God thou liest as Christian. If lance throwest and sword drawest, the water how soon shalt see thou carriest the cat! Biscayan on land, gentleman on sea, gentleman by the devil; and thou liest, and look to it if other thing sayest."

"Now shalt thou see, said Agrajes!" answered Don Quixote.

And throwing his lance on the ground, he drew his sword, got his shield on his arm and went at the Basque, determined to take his life. The Basque, seeing him come like that, would have liked to get down off the mule — which, being one of the bad hired sort, was not to be trusted — but could do nothing except draw his sword. It was lucky for him that he was next to the coach, from which he was able to snatch a cushion that served him as a shield; and then they went at each other as though they were two mortal enemies. The rest of the party wanted to make peace between them, but could not, because the Basque kept saying in his tangled speech that if they would not let him finish his battle he would kill his own mistress and everybody else who got in his way. The lady in the coach, astonished and terrified at what she was seeing, told the coachman to draw off a little way, and from a distance watched the fierce contest; in the course of which the Basque dealt Don Quixote a great slash on the shoulder, over the top of his shield, which, if it had landed undefended, would have opened him down to the waist.

Don Quixote, feeling the weight of that outrageous blow, gave a great shout, saying:

"O lady of my soul, Dulcinea, flower of beauty, come to the help of this knight of yours, who to satisfy your great goodness finds himself in this hard pass!"

The saying of this, and the gripping of the sword, and the covering himself well with his shield, and the charging at the Basque, were all one movement, for he had made up his mind to stake everything on the hazard of a single stroke.

The Basque, seeing him come at him like that, understood his courage well enough from his boldness, and resolved to do the same as Don Quixote; and so he waited for him well covered by his cushion, without being able to turn the mule one way or the other, for by now, out of sheer weariness and being unused to such childishness, it could not take a step.

So on came Don Quixote, as has been said, against the wary Basque, with his sword raised and his mind made up to split him down the middle; and the Basque was waiting for him with his sword up too and padded with his cushion; and all the bystanders were terrified and hanging on what would come of those enormous blows they were threatening each other with. And the lady in the coach and the rest of her maids were making a thousand vows and offerings to all the images and houses of devotion in Spain, that God might deliver their squire and themselves from the great danger they were in.

But here is the trouble with all this: that at this exact point the author of this history leaves the battle hanging, pleading that he found nothing more written about these exploits of Don Quixote than what he has already set down. It is true that the second author of this work refused to believe that so remarkable a history could have been abandoned to the laws of oblivion, or that the wits of La Mancha could have been so incurious as not to have among their archives or in their desks some papers dealing with this famous knight. And so, with that idea, he did not despair of finding the end of this delightful history, which, heaven being favourable to him, he did find in the manner that shall be told in the second part.

Chapter 9: In Which Is Concluded and Ended the Stupendous Battle Between the Gallant Basque and the Valiant Manchegan

Part Two of the Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha

We left, in the first part of this history, the valiant Basque and the famous Don Quixote with their swords raised and bare, on the point of dealing two such furious downstrokes that, if they had landed squarely, they would at the very least have split and cleft the pair of them from top to bottom and opened them up like a pomegranate; and at that most uncertain moment the delicious history stopped and was cut off short, without its author giving us any notion where what was missing might be found.

This caused me great distress, because the pleasure of having read so little turned into annoyance at the thought of how poor a road there was to finding the great deal that, to my mind, was missing from so appetising a tale. It seemed to me impossible and against all good custom that so good a knight should have lacked some sage to take on the writing of his unheard-of exploits — a thing that never failed any of the knights errant,

	of those that people say
	go out upon their adventures,

because every one of them had one or two sages ready made, who not only wrote down their deeds but painted their smallest thoughts and trifles, however hidden. And so good a knight could not have been so unfortunate as to lack what Platir and others like him had in abundance. So I could not bring myself to believe that so gallant a history had been left maimed and crippled, and I laid the blame on the malice of time, the devourer and consumer of all things, which had either hidden it away or consumed it.

On the other hand, it seemed to me that since among his books there had been found such modern ones as Disenchantments of Jealousy and The Nymphs and Shepherds of Henares, his history must be modern too; and that even if it was not written down, it would be in the memory of the people of his village and of the villages round about. This notion left me confused and eager to know, really and truly, the whole life and miracles of our famous Spaniard Don Quixote of La Mancha, the light and mirror of Manchegan chivalry, and the first in our age and in these calamitous times to take up the labour and exercise of errant arms, and the righting of wrongs, the succouring of widows and the protection of those maidens who used to go about with their whips and their palfreys and the whole of their virginity on their backs, from hill to hill and from valley to valley; for unless some scoundrel, or some peasant with an axe and a steel cap, or some monstrous giant, forced them, there were maidens in past ages who at the end of eighty years, in the whole of which they had never once slept under a roof, went to their graves as intact as the mothers who bore them.

I say, then, that for these and many other reasons our gallant Quixote deserves continual and memorable praise; and some is not to be denied me either, for the labour and diligence I put into looking for the end of this agreeable history — although I know very well that if heaven, chance and fortune had not helped me, the world would have gone short of the pastime and the pleasure that anyone reading it attentively may have from it for very nearly two hours. Now, the finding of it happened in this way.

I was one day in the Alcaná of Toledo when a boy came up to sell some old notebooks and papers to a silk merchant; and since I am fond of reading, even torn papers in the street, moved by this natural inclination of mine I took up one of the notebooks the boy was selling, and saw that it was in characters I recognised as Arabic. And although I recognised them I could not read them, so I looked about to see whether there was any Spanish-speaking Moor about who could read them for me; and it was not very hard to find an interpreter of that kind — indeed, if I had been looking for one of a better and older language, I should have found him. In the end luck provided me with one; and telling him what I wanted and putting the book into his hands, he opened it in the middle, read a little of it, and began to laugh.

I asked him what he was laughing at, and he answered that it was at something written in the margin of that book by way of a note. I asked him to tell me what it was; and he, still laughing, said:

"Written here in the margin, as I said, is this: 'This Dulcinea of El Toboso, so often mentioned in this history, is said to have had the best hand for salting pork of any woman in the whole of La Mancha.'"

When I heard "Dulcinea of El Toboso" I was thunderstruck and left hanging, because it came to me at once that these notebooks contained the history of Don Quixote. With that idea I pressed him to read the beginning; and doing so, turning the Arabic straight into Castilian, he said it read: History of Don Quixote of La Mancha, written by Cide Hamete Benengeli, an Arab historian. It took a great deal of discretion to hide the delight I felt when the title of the book reached my ears; and snatching them from under the silk merchant's nose, I bought all the papers and notebooks from the boy for half a real — though if he had had any sense and had known how much I wanted them, he might safely have promised himself and carried off more than six reals from the sale.

I then went off with the Moor into the cloister of the cathedral, and begged him to turn all the notebooks that dealt with Don Quixote into Castilian, taking nothing away and adding nothing, offering him whatever payment he liked. He was satisfied with two arrobas of raisins and two bushels of wheat, and promised to translate them well and faithfully and very quickly. But I, to make the business easier and not to let go of so fine a find, took him home with me, where in a little over a month and a half he translated the whole of it, exactly as it is set down here.

In the first notebook there was a very lifelike picture of Don Quixote's battle with the Basque, both of them in the very posture the history describes, with their swords raised, the one covered by his shield and the other by his cushion, and the Basque's mule so true to life that you could tell it was a hired one a bowshot off. At the Basque's feet was written a label saying Don Sancho de Azpeitia, which must undoubtedly have been his name; and at Rocinante's feet was another that said Don Quixote. Rocinante was marvellously painted, so long and lanky, so wasted and thin, with such a backbone and so confirmed a consumptive, that he showed quite plainly with what care and propriety the name Rocinante had been given him. Next to him was Sancho Panza, holding his donkey by the halter, at whose feet was another label saying Sancho Shanks; and it must have been because, as the picture showed, he had a big belly, a short body and long shanks, and for that he must have been given the names Panza and Zancas — Paunch and Shanks — by which the history sometimes calls him. There were some other small details worth noticing, but they are all of little importance and do not bear on the true relation of the history; and no relation is a bad one so long as it is true.

If any objection can be raised against the truth of this one, it can only be that its author was an Arab, since it is very much in the nature of that nation to be liars; though as they are such enemies of ours, one may sooner suppose that he fell short in it than went too far. And so it seems to me; because where he could and should have let his pen run out in praise of so good a knight, he seems deliberately to pass over it in silence — a thing badly done and worse thought of, since historians ought to be exact, truthful and in no way partial, and neither interest nor fear, rancour nor affection should make them swerve from the road of truth, whose mother is history, rival of time, storehouse of deeds, witness of the past, example and counsel to the present, warning to what is to come. In this one I know there will be found everything anyone could wish for in the most agreeable history; and if anything good is missing from it, it is my belief that the fault lay with that dog of an author rather than with the subject. In short, its second part, following the translation, began in this way:

With the cutting swords of the two valiant and angry combatants raised on high, it looked as though they were threatening heaven and earth and the abyss, such was the boldness and bearing they had. And the first to bring down his blow was the choleric Basque, who struck with such force and such fury that, if his sword had not turned in mid-course, that single stroke would have been enough to put an end to the fierce contest and to all our knight's adventures. But his good fortune, which was keeping him for greater things, twisted his opponent's sword, so that although it caught him on the left shoulder it did him no other damage than to strip that whole side of its armour, carrying away with it a good part of the helmet along with half an ear; all of which came down with a dreadful crash, leaving him in a very bad way.

God help me — who is there that could properly tell now the rage that entered our Manchegan's heart when he saw himself served in that fashion? Let no more be said than this: that it was such that he rose again in his stirrups, and gripping his sword harder in both hands, he brought it down on the Basque with such fury, catching him squarely on the cushion and on the head, that, so good a defence being of no use, it was as if a mountain had fallen on him; and he began to pour blood from his nose and his mouth and his ears, and to look like falling off the mule, as he certainly would have done if he had not thrown his arms round its neck. But for all that his feet came out of the stirrups and then his arms let go; and the mule, terrified by that fearful blow, went galloping across the field, and after a few bucks brought its master to the ground.

Don Quixote sat watching him with great composure, and when he saw him fall he leapt off his horse and went up to him very nimbly, and putting the point of his sword between his eyes told him to surrender, or he would cut off his head. The Basque was so dazed that he could not answer a word, and it would have gone badly with him, blind with rage as Don Quixote was, if the ladies of the coach, who until then had watched the fight in a swoon of terror, had not come to where he was and begged him most earnestly to do them the great kindness and favour of sparing this squire of theirs his life. To which Don Quixote answered, with great haughtiness and gravity:

"Certainly, fair ladies, I am very content to do what you ask; but it must be on one condition and agreement, which is that this knight shall promise me to go to the town of El Toboso and present himself on my behalf before the peerless Doña Dulcinea, that she may do with him whatever she pleases."

The frightened and disconsolate lady, without stopping to consider what Don Quixote was asking, and without asking who Dulcinea might be, promised him that the squire would do everything he was ordered to do on his behalf.

"Then on the faith of that word I shall do him no further harm, though he had well deserved it of me."

Chapter 10: Of the Amusing Conversation That Passed Between Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, His Squire

By this time Sancho Panza had got up, rather knocked about by the friars' servants, and had been watching his master Don Quixote's battle, praying to God in his heart that He might be pleased to give him the victory, and that in it he might win some isle to make him governor of, as he had promised. Seeing the quarrel over at last, and his master getting back up on Rocinante, he came to hold the stirrup; and before he mounted, Sancho went down on his knees in front of him and, taking his hand, kissed it and said:

"May it please your worship, my lord Don Quixote, to give me the government of the isle that has been won in this fierce quarrel; for however big it may be, I feel I have the strength to govern it as well as anybody who ever governed an isle in this world."

To which Don Quixote answered:

"Take note, brother Sancho, that this adventure and others like it are not adventures of isles, but of crossroads, in which nothing is won but a broken head or an ear the less. Have patience, for adventures will come along in which I can make you not only a governor but something better still."

Sancho thanked him warmly, and kissing his hand again and the skirt of his mail-coat, helped him up onto Rocinante; and he got on his own donkey and set off after his master, who, at a smart pace and without taking leave of the people in the coach or saying anything more to them, rode into a wood that was close by. Sancho followed at his ass's full trot, but Rocinante went so fast that, finding himself left behind, he had to shout to his master to wait for him. Don Quixote did so, reining Rocinante in until his tired squire came up, and when he arrived Sancho said:

"It seems to me, sir, that it would be a good idea for us to take sanctuary in some church; because, considering the state that man you fought with was left in, it wouldn't be at all surprising if they reported the business to the Holy Brotherhood and had us arrested. And upon my word, if they do, we shall sweat for it before we get out of gaol."

"Be quiet," said Don Quixote. "And where have you ever seen, or read, that a knight errant has been brought before a judge, however many homicides he may have committed?"

"I know nothing about homicides," answered Sancho, "and I never tasted one in my life. All I know is that the Holy Brotherhood has a say about people who fight out in the country, and I don't meddle in the other business."

"Then don't worry, my friend," answered Don Quixote, "for I would get you out of the hands of the Chaldeans, let alone the Brotherhood. But tell me, on your life: have you seen a more valiant knight than I am in all the known world? Have you read in any history of another who has, or ever had, more spirit in attacking, more staying power in persevering, more skill in wounding or more knack in bringing men down?"

"The truth is," answered Sancho, "that I have never read any history at all, because I can neither read nor write. But what I'll dare to bet is that I have never in all the days of my life served a bolder master than your worship, and please God these bold doings may not be paid for where I said. What I do beg of your worship is to see to yourself, for a great deal of blood is coming out of that ear; and I have lint here and a little white ointment in the saddlebags."

"All that could very well have been spared," answered Don Quixote, "if I had only remembered to make a flask of the balm of Fierabrás, for with a single drop of it we should save both time and medicines."

"What flask and what balm is that?" said Sancho Panza.

"It is a balm," answered Don Quixote, "the recipe for which I have by heart, and with it there is no need to fear death or to think of dying of any wound. And so, when I have made it and given it to you, all you have to do is this: when you see that in some battle they have cut me in half through the middle — as very often happens — neatly take the part of my body that has fallen to the ground, and with great delicacy, before the blood congeals, put it back on the other half that is left in the saddle, taking care to fit it on evenly and exactly. Then you will give me just two swallows of the balm I have mentioned, and you will see me come out sounder than an apple."

"If that's so," said Panza, "here and now I give up the government of the promised isle, and I want nothing else in payment of my many good services but that your worship should give me the recipe for that surpassing liquor. For I reckon that an ounce of it would be worth more than two reals anywhere, and I need nothing more than that to get through this life in comfort and respectability. But the thing to know now is whether it costs much to make."

"Three gallons of it can be made for less than three reals," answered Don Quixote.

"Sinner that I am!" said Sancho. "Then what is your worship waiting for, to make it and to teach it to me?"

"Quiet, my friend," answered Don Quixote. "I mean to teach you greater secrets than that and to do you greater favours. And for the present let us see to ourselves, for my ear hurts more than I could wish."

Sancho took the lint and the ointment out of the saddlebags. But when Don Quixote came to see his helmet broken he thought he would go out of his mind, and putting his hand on his sword and raising his eyes to heaven he said:

"I make a vow to the Creator of all things, and to the four holy Gospels where they are most fully written, to lead the life the great Marquis of Mantua led when he swore to avenge the death of his nephew Valdovinos — which was to eat no bread off a tablecloth, nor take his pleasure with his wife, and other things which, though I do not remember them, I here declare expressed — until I have taken full vengeance on the man who did me such an outrage."

Hearing this, Sancho said:

"Consider, your worship, my lord Don Quixote, that if the knight has carried out what he was ordered, and gone to present himself before my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, then he will have done his duty and deserves no further punishment unless he commits some fresh offence."

"You have spoken and hit the point very well," answered Don Quixote; "and so I annul the vow as far as taking fresh vengeance on him is concerned. But I make it and confirm it afresh, to lead the life I have described, until I take by force another helmet as good as this one from some knight. And do not think, Sancho, that I do this idly, for I have a good model to follow in it: this very same thing happened, word for word, over the helmet of Mambrino, which cost Sacripante so dear."

"Your worship can send such vows to the devil, sir," replied Sancho; "they are very bad for the health and very hard on the conscience. Just tell me now: if by any chance we don't meet a man in a helmet for many days, what are we to do? Is the vow to be kept, in spite of all the inconveniences and discomforts — sleeping in your clothes, and not sleeping in any town, and a thousand other penances that were in the vow of that mad old Marquis of Mantua that your worship wants to renew now? Look properly, your worship: no armed men go along these roads, only carriers and carters, who not only don't wear helmets but very likely have never heard one mentioned in the whole of their lives."

"You are wrong there," said Don Quixote, "because we shall not have been two hours at these crossroads before we see more men in armour than went against Albraca for the conquest of Angelica the Fair."

"All right, then, so be it," said Sancho, "and please God it may go well with us, and the time may come at last for winning this isle that is costing me so dear, and then let me die."

"I have told you already, Sancho, not to let that trouble you at all; for if an isle is not to be had, there is the kingdom of Denmark or of Sobradisa, which will fit you like a ring on your finger. And what is more, being on the mainland, you ought to be all the better pleased. But let us leave that for its own time, and see whether you have anything in those saddlebags for us to eat, because afterwards we must go and look for some castle to lodge in tonight and make the balm I told you of; for I swear to God this ear of mine is hurting a great deal."

"I have an onion here, and a bit of cheese and I don't know how many crusts of bread," said Sancho; "but they aren't dishes fit for so valiant a knight as your worship."

"How little you understand it!" answered Don Quixote. "I would have you know, Sancho, that it is an honour to knights errant not to eat for a month; and when they do eat, to eat whatever comes first to hand. And this would be plain to you if you had read as many histories as I have; for although there have been a great many, in none of them have I found any account of knights errant eating, except by chance and at some sumptuous banquets given for them, and the rest of the days they spent on flowers. And although it is to be understood that they could not get on without eating and without doing all the other natural offices — because, after all, they were men like ourselves — it is also to be understood that, spending most of their lives in forests and wildernesses and without a cook, their most usual food would be rustic fare of the sort you are offering me now. So, Sancho my friend, do not distress yourself over what pleases me. And do not go trying to make a new world, or knocking knight-errantry off its hinges."

"Forgive me, your worship," said Sancho; "for as I can neither read nor write, as I have said before, I don't know and haven't grasped the rules of the knightly profession. And from now on I'll stock the saddlebags with every kind of dried fruit for your worship, since you are a knight; and for myself, since I am not, I'll stock them with other things that fly and have more substance to them."

"I do not say, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "that knights errant are obliged to eat nothing but those fruits you speak of, only that their most ordinary sustenance must have been those, and certain herbs they found in the fields, which they knew and which I know too."

"It's a virtue," answered Sancho, "to know those herbs; for the way I imagine things going, one of these days we shall need to make use of that knowledge."

And bringing out what he had said he was carrying, the two of them ate in good peace and fellowship. But being anxious to find somewhere to lodge that night, they made very short work of their poor dry meal. They mounted at once and hurried to reach some inhabited place before dark; but the sun failed them, and with it the hope of getting what they wanted, when they were near some goatherds' huts, and so they decided to spend the night there. And as much as it grieved Sancho not to reach a town, so much did it please his master to sleep under the open sky, since it seemed to him that every time this happened to him he was performing an act of possession that made the proof of his knighthood easier.

Chapter 11: Of What Happened to Don Quixote with Some Goatherds

He was made welcome by the goatherds with a good will; and Sancho, having settled Rocinante and his donkey as best he could, made straight for the smell given off by certain pieces of salted goat that were bubbling over the fire in a pot. And although he would have liked at that very moment to see whether they were ready to be transferred from the pot to his stomach, he did not, because the goatherds took them off the fire; and spreading some sheepskins on the ground they laid their rustic table in great haste and invited the two of them, with every sign of goodwill, to share what they had.

Six of them sat down round the skins — all there were at the fold — having first, with clumsy ceremony, begged Don Quixote to sit on a trough they turned upside down for him. Don Quixote sat down, and Sancho remained standing to serve him the cup, which was made of horn. Seeing him on his feet, his master said:

"So that you may see, Sancho, the good that knight-errantry has in it, and how near those who follow any office in it are to coming quickly to be honoured and esteemed by the world, I want you to sit here at my side and in the company of these good people, and to be one and the same thing with me, who am your master and natural lord: eat off my plate and drink where I drink. For the same may be said of knight-errantry as is said of love: that it makes all things equal."

"Many thanks!" said Sancho. "But I can tell your worship that so long as I have plenty to eat, I would eat it as well or better standing up and by myself as sitting beside an emperor. And in fact, if the truth is to be told, what I eat in my own corner without airs and graces, even if it is bread and an onion, tastes far better to me than the turkeys at other tables where I have to chew slowly, drink little, wipe my mouth often, and not sneeze or cough if I want to, or do other things that being alone and free bring with them. So, sir, these honours that your worship wants to do me for being a servant and hanger-on of knight-errantry, as I am, being your worship's squire — turn them into something else of more comfort and profit to me; for these, though I take them as received in full, I renounce from now until the end of the world."

"For all that, you shall sit down; because God exalts him who humbles himself."

And taking him by the arm, he forced him to sit beside him.

The goatherds understood nothing of this jargon about squires and knights errant, and did nothing but eat and hold their tongues and stare at their guests, who with great relish and appetite were stowing away pieces of salt goat the size of your fist. When the meat course was over they spread a great quantity of dried acorns on the sheepskins, and along with them set out half a cheese harder than if it had been made of mortar. The drinking-horn was not idle all this while, for it went round so often — now full, now empty, like the bucket of a waterwheel — that it easily emptied one of the two wineskins that were on show.

When Don Quixote had thoroughly satisfied his stomach, he took up a handful of acorns and, looking at them attentively, let his voice run out into words like these:

"Happy the age and happy the centuries that the ancients called golden — and not because gold, which in this iron age of ours is so highly valued, was got in that fortunate one without any labour, but because those who lived then did not know these two words, thine and mine. In that holy age all things were held in common. To get his ordinary food no man had to take any trouble but to reach up his hand and take it from the sturdy oaks, which stood generously inviting him with their sweet ripe fruit. The clear springs and running rivers offered him, in magnificent abundance, delicious and transparent water. In the clefts of the rocks and the hollows of the trees the diligent and prudent bees set up their republic, offering to any hand, without asking anything in return, the fertile harvest of their sweetest labour. The noble cork trees shed of themselves, with no other artifice than their own courtesy, their broad light bark, with which men began to roof their houses, propped on rough stakes, only as a defence against the weather.

"All was peace then, all friendship, all concord. The heavy blade of the crooked plough had not yet dared to open or violate the merciful bowels of our first mother, for she of her own accord, without being forced, offered from every part of her fertile and spacious breast whatever could satisfy and sustain and delight the children who then possessed her. Then indeed the simple and lovely shepherdesses went from valley to valley and hillock to hillock, with their hair in a plait or loose, in no more clothing than was needed to cover decently what decency requires, and always has required, to be covered; and their ornaments were not those in use now, on which the purple of Tyre and silk tortured in so many ways are lavished, but a few green leaves of burdock and ivy woven together — with which they went about, perhaps, as grand and as well turned out as our court ladies go now with the rare and outlandish inventions that idle curiosity has taught them.

"In those days the loving thoughts of the soul were dressed simply and plainly, in the very way and manner the soul conceived them, without hunting for an artificial roundabout of words to set them off. Fraud, deceit and malice had not yet mixed themselves with truth and plain dealing. Justice kept within her own bounds, and neither favour nor self-interest dared disturb or offend her, as they so much diminish and disturb and persecute her now. The law of a judge's whim had not yet planted itself in his understanding, because then there was nothing to judge and nobody to be judged. Maidens and modesty went about, as I have said, wherever they pleased, alone and their own mistresses, without fear that another's licence or lustful intent would harm them; and if they came to ruin it was of their own liking and their own free will.

"And now, in these detestable ages of ours, no woman is safe, even if another labyrinth like the one in Crete hides her and shuts her in; because there, through the chinks or on the air, with the zeal of accursed importunity, the pestilence of love gets in and wrecks her whole seclusion. For the protection of these, as time went on and wickedness increased, the order of knights errant was instituted: to defend maidens, protect widows and succour orphans and the needy. Of this order am I, brother goatherds; and I thank you for the entertainment and the good welcome you give me and my squire. For although by natural law all living men are obliged to favour knights errant, still, knowing that without knowing this obligation you took me in and made much of me, it is only right that with all the goodwill I have I should thank you for yours."

Our knight made this whole long harangue — which might very well have been spared — because the acorns they gave him brought the Golden Age to his mind, and he took it into his head to deliver that useless discourse to the goatherds, who listened without answering him a word, thoroughly bemused and open-mouthed. Sancho too kept quiet, and ate acorns, and paid very frequent visits to the second wineskin, which they had hung from a cork tree to keep the wine cool.

Don Quixote was longer talking than they were finishing supper; at the end of which one of the goatherds said:

"So that your worship may say with more truth, sir knight errant, that we entertained you with a prompt and hearty goodwill, we should like to give you some pleasure and diversion by getting a mate of ours to sing, who will not be long in getting here. He is a very sharp lad and very much in love, and, above all, he can read and write and is such a player on the rebec that there is nothing left to wish for."

Hardly had the goatherd finished saying this when the sound of the rebec reached them, and shortly afterwards the player arrived: a young man of about twenty-two, very good-looking. His mates asked him whether he had eaten, and when he said yes the one who had made the offer said:

"In that case, Antonio, you can do us the pleasure of singing a little, so that this gentleman our guest may see that there are people in the hills and woods too who know something about music. We have told him about your accomplishments and we want you to show them and prove us right. So on your life, sit down and sing the ballad of your love that your uncle the prebendary wrote for you, which they thought so well of in the village."

"With pleasure," answered the young man.

And without waiting to be asked twice he sat down on the stump of a lopped oak, and tuning his rebec he presently began to sing, very gracefully, in this manner:

Antonio

	I know you love me, Olalla,
	although you have never said so,
	not even with your eyes,
	those silent tongues of love.
	Because I know you have your wits,
	I hold it that you want me;
	for love was never wretched
	that was once acknowledged.
	It is true enough that sometimes,
	Olalla, you have given me signs
	that you have a soul of bronze
	and a white breast of flint.
	But there, among your scoldings
	and your most virtuous refusals,
	hope will sometimes show me
	the hem of her skirt.
	My faith throws itself at the lure —
	faith that has never been able
	to shrink for not being called
	or swell for being chosen.
	If love is a courtesy,
	then from the courtesy you have
	I gather that the end of my hopes
	must be the one I imagine.
	And if attentions count for anything
	towards making a heart kind,
	some of those I have paid you
	strengthen my case.
	For if you have taken note of it,
	you must have seen more than once
	that I have worn on a Monday
	the clothes that did me honour on Sunday.
	Since love and fine clothes
	travel the same road,
	I have wanted at all times
	to look well in your eyes.
	I leave out the dancing I gave up for you,
	and I say nothing of the music
	you have heard at unlikely hours
	and at the first cock-crow.
	I do not count the praises
	I have spoken of your beauty;
	which, though they were true,
	have made me disliked by some.
	Teresa of the Berrocal,
	when I was praising you, said to me:
	"There is a man who thinks he adores an angel
	and comes to adore an ape;
	thanks to a lot of trinkets
	and to false hair,
	and to hypocritical beauties
	that would deceive Love himself."
	I gave her the lie and she was angry;
	her cousin took her part;
	he challenged me, and you know
	what I did and what he did.
	I do not want you by the bushel,
	nor court you and serve you
	for the sake of keeping you;
	my design is a better one.
	The Church has yokes
	that are bows of silk;
	put your neck in the collar
	and you will see me put in mine.
	And if not, I swear from this moment,
	by the most blessed saint there is,
	never to come out of these mountains
	except to be a friar.

With that the goatherd made an end of his song; and although Don Quixote begged him to sing some more, Sancho Panza would not have it, being more disposed for sleep than for listening to songs. And so he said to his master:

"Your worship might do well to settle now where you are to spend the night, for the work these good men do all day does not allow them to spend their nights singing."

"I understand you, Sancho," Don Quixote answered him; "for it is quite clear to me that those visits to the wineskin call for repayment in sleep rather than in music."

"It tastes good to all of us, God be praised," answered Sancho.
