"I do not deny it," replied Don Quixote; "but settle yourself where you like. Men of my profession look better watching than sleeping. But all the same, Sancho, it would be as well if you dressed this ear of mine again, for it is hurting more than it need."

Sancho did as he was told; and one of the goatherds, seeing the wound, told him not to worry, for he would put something on it that would heal it easily. Taking some leaves of rosemary, of which there was plenty about, he chewed them and mixed them with a little salt, and applying them to the ear he bandaged it up very well, assuring him that no other medicine was needed; and so it proved.

Chapter 12: Of What a Goatherd Told Those Who Were with Don Quixote

While this was going on, another of the lads who brought them their supplies from the village arrived, and said:

"Do you know what's happening down in the village, mates?"

"How could we know?" answered one of them.

"Then you must know," the lad went on, "that this morning that famous shepherd-scholar called Grisóstomo died, and it is whispered that he died of love for that bedevilled girl Marcela, rich Guillermo's daughter, the one who goes about these wilds dressed as a shepherdess."

"For Marcela, you mean," said one.

"That's who I mean," answered the goatherd. "And the best of it is that he ordered in his will that they were to bury him out in the country, as though he were a Moor, and at the foot of the crag where the cork-tree spring is; because, so they say, and they say he said it himself, that is the place where he first saw her. And he ordered other things too, of such a kind that the priests of the village say they must not be carried out, and it is not right that they should be, because they look like heathen practices. To all of which that great friend of his, Ambrosio the scholar, who also dressed himself as a shepherd along with him, answers that everything must be carried out without a single thing missing, exactly as Grisóstomo left orders; and the whole village is in an uproar over it. But from what they say, in the end it will be done as Ambrosio and all the shepherds who are his friends want; and tomorrow they are coming to bury him with great pomp where I have said. And I reckon it will be very well worth seeing; at any rate I shan't miss going to see it, even if I knew I couldn't get back to the village tomorrow."

"We'll all do the same," answered the goatherds, "and we'll draw lots for who is to stay behind and look after everybody's goats."

"You're right, Pedro," said one; "though there'll be no need to take that trouble, for I'll stay for the lot of you. And don't put it down to virtue or to any want of curiosity in me, but to the fact that I can't walk for that stake that went through my foot the other day."

"For all that, we thank you," answered Pedro.

And Don Quixote begged Pedro to tell him who the dead man was and who the shepherdess; to which Pedro answered that all he knew was that the dead man was a rich gentleman, from a village up in those mountains, who had been a student for many years at Salamanca, at the end of which he had come home with the reputation of being very learned and very well read.

"They said in particular that he knew the science of the stars, and of what the sun and the moon get up to away in the sky; because he could tell us the exact cripse of the sun and the moon."

"It is called an eclipse, my friend, not a cripse, when those two great luminaries go dark," said Don Quixote.

But Pedro, not stopping over trifles, went on with his tale:

"He could tell too whether the year was going to be plentiful or sterrile."

"Sterile is what you mean, my friend," said Don Quixote.

"Sterile or sterrile," answered Pedro, "it all comes out the same in the end. And I tell you that with what he said his father and his friends, who believed him, grew very rich, because they did what he advised them, when he told them: 'Sow barley this year, not wheat; this year you can sow chickpeas and not barley; next year will be a good one for oil; the three after it you won't get a drop.'"

"That science is called astrology," said Don Quixote.

"I don't know what it's called," replied Pedro, "but I know he knew all that, and more besides. Anyhow, not many months went by after he came home from Salamanca before he turned up one day dressed as a shepherd, with his crook and his sheepskin, having taken off the long gown he wore as a scholar; and along with him another great friend of his called Ambrosio, who had been his fellow-student, dressed as a shepherd too. I was forgetting to say that Grisóstomo, the dead man, was a great hand at writing verses; so much so that he wrote the carols for Christmas Eve and the plays for Corpus Christi that the lads of our village used to act, and everyone said they were first-rate.

"When the villagers saw the two scholars turned shepherds so suddenly, they were amazed, and could not guess what had moved them to make so strange a change. By this time Grisóstomo's father was dead, and he was left the heir to a great deal of property, both goods and land, and no small quantity of stock, large and small, and a great deal of money — of all of which the young man was left absolute master; and to tell the truth he deserved it all, for he was a very good companion, and charitable, and a friend to good men, and he had a face like a blessing. Afterwards it came to be understood that he had changed his clothes for no other reason than to go about these wild places after that shepherdess Marcela our lad mentioned just now, with whom the poor dead Grisóstomo had fallen in love.

"And now I want to tell you, because it is right you should know it, who this girl is. Perhaps — and there is no perhaps about it — you will never have heard the like of it in all the days of your life, even if you live more years than sorrow."

"Say Sarah," put in Don Quixote, unable to bear the goatherd's swapping of words.

"Sorrow lives long enough," answered Pedro; "and if you are going to keep picking me up on my words at every step, sir, we shall not be finished in a year."

"Forgive me, my friend," said Don Quixote; "I only said it because there is such a difference between sorrow and Sarah. But you answered very well, because sorrow does live longer than Sarah. Go on with your story, and I will not interrupt you again in anything."

"Well then, my dear good sir," said the goatherd, "in our village there was a farmer even richer than Grisóstomo's father, whose name was Guillermo, and to whom God gave, besides his many and great riches, a daughter, at whose birth her mother died — the most respected woman there was in all these parts. I seem to see her now, with that face of hers that had the sun on one side of it and the moon on the other; and above all a good manager and a friend to the poor, for which I believe her soul must be enjoying God in the next world at this very hour. Of grief at the death of so good a wife her husband Guillermo died, leaving his daughter Marcela, a young girl and rich, in the charge of an uncle of hers who is a priest and holds a benefice in our village.

"The girl grew up so beautiful that she made us remember her mother's beauty, which was very great; and even so it was reckoned that the daughter's would go beyond it. And so it did, for when she got to be fourteen or fifteen nobody looked at her without blessing God for having made her so lovely, and most of them fell in love and were lost for her. Her uncle kept her very carefully and very much shut up; but for all that the fame of her great beauty spread so far that, as much for it as for her great riches, her uncle was begged and solicited and pestered to give her in marriage, not only by the men of our own village but by men from many leagues round, and the best of them at that. But he — who is an upright good Christian — although he would have liked to marry her off as soon as he saw she was of age, would not do it without her consent, and never had an eye to the profit and advantage that holding the girl's property while he put off her marriage offered him. And upon my word this was said in more than one gossiping circle in the village, to the good priest's credit."

For I want you to know, sir knight errant, that in these little places everything is talked about and everything is gossiped over; and take it from me, as I take it from myself, that a clergyman must be uncommonly good to make his parishioners speak well of him, particularly in the villages.

"That is the truth," said Don Quixote, "and go on, for the tale is a very good one, and you, good Pedro, tell it with a very good grace."

"May the Lord's grace not fail me, for that is the one that matters. And for the rest, you must know that although her uncle put the suitors before his niece and told her the qualities of each one in particular, of the many who asked for her, and begged her to marry and to choose to her own liking, she never answered anything but that for the present she did not want to marry, and that being so young she did not feel fit to bear the burden of matrimony. With these excuses, which seemed reasonable enough, her uncle left off pestering her and waited for her to get on a little in years and know how to choose a companion to her own taste. For he used to say, and said very rightly, that parents ought not to settle their children against their will.

"But lo and behold, when nobody was expecting it, one day the fastidious Marcela turns up as a shepherdess; and with her uncle and the whole village powerless against it, all advising her not to, she took to going out into the fields with the other village girls and to minding her own flock. And once she came out in public and her beauty was seen openly, I could not properly tell you how many rich young men, gentlemen and farmers, have taken to Grisóstomo's costume and go courting her about these fields. One of them, as has been said already, was our dead friend, of whom they said that he had stopped loving her and had begun to worship her.

"And nobody should think that because Marcela put herself into that free way of living, so unconstrained and with so little or no seclusion in it, she has therefore given any sign, or the shadow of one, that could damage her modesty and her good name. On the contrary, such and so great is the vigilance with which she looks after her honour that of all who court and solicit her not one has boasted, or could truthfully boast, that she has given him the smallest hope of getting what he wants. For although she does not run away or shun the company and conversation of the shepherds, and treats them courteously and in a friendly way, the moment any one of them comes to declare his intentions to her — even if they are as proper and holy as marriage — she flings him off as though from a catapult.

"And with this turn of temper she does more damage in this country than if the plague had come into it; because her friendliness and her beauty draw the hearts of those who deal with her into serving her and loving her, but her disdain and her plain speaking drive them to the point of despair. And so they do not know what to call her, but shout after her that she is cruel and ungrateful, with other titles of the same kind, which show plainly enough what her disposition is like. If you were to be here some day, sir, you would hear these hills and valleys ringing with the laments of the disappointed men who follow her.

"Not far from here there is a place where there are almost two dozen tall beeches, and there is not one of them that has not the name of Marcela carved and written on its smooth bark; and over some of them a crown carved in the same tree, as though the lover were saying more plainly that Marcela wears it and deserves it out of all human beauty. Here one shepherd sighs, there another complains; over there you hear love songs, over here despairing dirges. There is one who spends all the hours of the night sitting at the foot of some oak or rock, and there, without once closing his weeping eyes, sunk and carried away in his own thoughts, the sun finds him in the morning; and there is another who, without giving his sighs a moment's rest or truce, in the middle of the burning heat of the most oppressive summer afternoon, stretched out on the scorching sand, sends his complaints up to merciful heaven. And over this one and that one, and over those and these, the beautiful Marcela triumphs, free and unconcerned; and all of us who know her are waiting to see what her pride will come to, and who is to be the lucky man who will come and tame so terrible a nature and enjoy so extraordinary a beauty.

"Since everything I have told you is such well-established truth, I am inclined to believe that what our lad said about the cause of Grisóstomo's death is true too. And so I advise you, sir, not to fail to be at his burial tomorrow, which will be well worth seeing, for Grisóstomo has many friends, and it is not half a league from this place to the one where he has ordered himself to be buried."

"I shall bear it in mind," said Don Quixote, "and I thank you for the pleasure you have given me with the telling of so delicious a tale."

"Oh!" replied the goatherd, "I don't know the half of what has happened to Marcela's lovers; but it may be that tomorrow we shall run into some shepherd on the road who will tell us. And for now it will be as well if you go and sleep under a roof, because the night air might do your wound harm — though the medicine you have had put on it is such that there is nothing to fear from any accident."

Sancho Panza, who by now was consigning the goatherd's endless talking to the devil, urged for his part that his master should go inside and sleep in Pedro's hut. He did so, and spent most of the rest of the night in memories of his lady Dulcinea, in imitation of Marcela's lovers. Sancho Panza settled himself between Rocinante and his donkey and slept, not like a rejected lover, but like a man who had been kicked to a pulp.

Chapter 13: In Which the Tale of the Shepherdess Marcela Is Concluded, with Other Events

Hardly had day begun to show itself on the balconies of the east when five of the six goatherds got up and went to wake Don Quixote, and to ask him whether he was still minded to go and see Grisóstomo's famous funeral, and to say that they would keep him company. Don Quixote, who wanted nothing better, got up and told Sancho to saddle and pack at once, which he did with great dispatch, and with the same dispatch they all took the road.

They had not gone a quarter of a league when, at a crossing of paths, they saw coming towards them some six shepherds dressed in black sheepskins and with their heads crowned with garlands of cypress and bitter oleander. Each of them carried a stout holly staff in his hand. With them came two gentlemen on horseback, very well fitted out for travelling, with three servants on foot accompanying them. When they met they greeted each other courteously, and asking one another where they were going they learned that they were all bound for the place of the burial; and so they all began to travel together.

One of the horsemen, speaking to his companion, said:

"It seems to me, Señor Vivaldo, that we shall count the delay we make in seeing this famous funeral well spent; and famous it cannot fail to be, judging by the extraordinary things these shepherds have told us, both about the dead shepherd and about the murderous shepherdess."

"So it seems to me too," answered Vivaldo; "and I would delay not one day but four for the sake of seeing it."

Don Quixote asked them what they had heard about Marcela and Grisóstomo. The traveller said that early that morning they had met these shepherds, and that seeing them in such mournful dress they had asked them the reason for it; that one of them had told the story, describing the strangeness and the beauty of a shepherdess called Marcela, and the love of the many who courted her, and the death of that Grisóstomo whose funeral they were going to. In short, he told everything that Pedro had told Don Quixote.

This talk ended and another began, the man called Vivaldo asking Don Quixote what it was that moved him to go armed in that fashion through so peaceful a country. To which Don Quixote answered:

"The profession I follow neither allows nor permits me to go about in any other way. Easy living, luxury and repose were invented for soft courtiers; but toil, unrest and arms were invented and made only for those whom the world calls knights errant, of whom I, though unworthy, am the least of all."

The moment they heard this they all took him for a madman; and to make sure of it and see what sort of madness his was, Vivaldo asked him again what he meant by "knights errant".

"Have your worships not read," answered Don Quixote, "the annals and histories of England, which deal with the famous exploits of King Arthur, whom in our Castilian speech we constantly call King Artús — of whom there is an ancient and common tradition throughout that kingdom of Great Britain that this king did not die, but that by the art of enchantment he was turned into a crow, and that in the course of time he is to come back and reign and recover his kingdom and his sceptre? For which reason it cannot be proved that from that time to this any Englishman has ever killed a crow. Well, in the time of that good king that famous order of chivalry of the Knights of the Round Table was instituted, and there took place, exactly as they are told, the loves of Sir Lancelot of the Lake and Queen Guinevere, with that most honourable lady Quintañona as their go-between and confidante — from which came that ballad so well known and so much sung in our Spain:

	Never was a knight
	so well waited on by ladies
	as Lancelot was
	when he came from Britain —

with that sweet and gentle progress of his amorous and valiant deeds. From then on, passing from hand to hand, that order of chivalry went spreading and extending through many and various parts of the world; and famous in it and known for their deeds were the valiant Amadís of Gaul, with all his sons and grandsons down to the fifth generation, and the valorous Felixmarte of Hyrcania, and the never-sufficiently-praised Tirant lo Blanc; and almost in our own days we saw and conversed with and heard the invincible and valiant knight Don Belianís of Greece. This, then, gentlemen, is what it is to be a knight errant, and what I have described is the order of his chivalry; in which, as I have said before, I, sinner though I am, have made my profession, and I profess the very thing those knights professed. And so I go through these solitudes and wildernesses looking for adventures, with my mind made up to offer my arm and my person to the most dangerous that fortune may send me, in aid of the weak and the needy."

By these words the travellers were finally satisfied that Don Quixote was out of his wits, and what kind of madness had the mastery of him; at which they felt the same astonishment that everyone felt on first coming to know of it. And Vivaldo, who was a very shrewd man of a cheerful disposition, so as to get through the little of the road they said was left without tedium, and to bring them to the mountain where the burial was, wanted to give him occasion to go further with his absurdities. And so he said:

"It seems to me, sir knight errant, that your worship has professed one of the strictest professions on earth, and I reckon that even that of the Carthusian friars is not so strict."

"As strict it may very well be," answered our Don Quixote, "but that it is as necessary to the world I am within two fingers of doubting. Because, if the truth is to be told, the soldier who carries out what his captain orders does no less than the captain who gives the order. What I mean is that religious men, in all peace and quiet, ask heaven for the good of the earth; but we soldiers and knights put into execution what they ask for, defending it with the valour of our arms and the edges of our swords — not under a roof, but under the open sky, set up as a target for the unbearable rays of the sun in summer and the bristling frosts of winter. So we are God's ministers on earth, and the arms by which His justice is carried out on it. And since matters of war and everything touching and concerning them cannot be put into execution without sweating and struggling and labouring, it follows that those who profess it undoubtedly have greater labour than those who in quiet peace and repose are praying God to favour those who can do little for themselves.

"I do not mean to say, and it does not even cross my mind, that the state of a knight errant is as good as that of a cloistered religious; I only want to infer, from what I suffer, that it is undoubtedly more laborious and more belaboured, and hungrier and thirstier, more wretched, more ragged and more louse-ridden. Because there is no doubt that the knights errant of the past went through a great deal of misfortune in the course of their lives. And if some of them rose to be emperors by the valour of their arms, upon my word it cost them a good deal of their blood and their sweat; and if those who rose to that rank had gone without enchanters and sages to help them, they would have been thoroughly cheated of their desires and thoroughly deceived in their hopes."

"I am of that opinion," replied the traveller; "but one thing among many others strikes me very badly in knights errant, and it is that when they find themselves on the point of undertaking some great and dangerous adventure, in which there is plain danger of losing their lives, they never at that instant of attacking remember to commend themselves to God, as every Christian is obliged to do in such dangers; on the contrary, they commend themselves to their ladies with as much eagerness and devotion as if the ladies were their God — a thing that seems to me to smell somewhat of heathenism."

"Sir," answered Don Quixote, "that cannot possibly be otherwise, and the knight errant who did anything else would be in a bad way; for it is already the use and custom in knight-errantry that a knight errant who, on undertaking some great feat of arms, has his lady before him, should turn his eyes on her softly and lovingly, as though asking her with them to favour and protect him in the doubtful pass he is entering; and even if nobody hears him, he is obliged to say a few words under his breath commending himself to her with all his heart. And of this we have countless examples in the histories. Nor is it to be understood from this that they are to leave off commending themselves to God; there is time and place for that in the course of the business."

"For all that," replied the traveller, "I still have a scruple; which is that I have often read that words pass between two knights errant, and one thing leading to another their anger takes fire, and they wheel their horses and take a good stretch of ground, and then, without more ado, at full gallop they come at each other again; and in the middle of the charge they commend themselves to their ladies. And what usually comes of the encounter is that one of them goes over his horse's crupper, run through and through with his opponent's lance, and it goes so with the other too that if he did not hold on to his horse's mane he could not help coming to the ground. And I do not see how the dead man had any time to commend himself to God in the course of so headlong a business. It would have been better if the words he spent in the charge commending himself to his lady had been spent on what he owed and was bound to as a Christian. What is more, I reckon that not all knights errant have ladies to commend themselves to, because not all of them are in love."

"That cannot be," answered Don Quixote. "I say it cannot be that there should be a knight errant without a lady, because it is as proper and natural for such men to be in love as it is for the sky to have stars; and you may be quite sure that no history has ever been seen in which a knight errant is found without a love. And by the very fact of his being without one he would not be held a legitimate knight, but a bastard, and one who got into the fortress of the said chivalry not by the door but over the wall, like a robber and a thief."

"For all that," said the traveller, "it seems to me, if I remember rightly, that I have read that Don Galaor, brother of the valiant Amadís of Gaul, never had a particular lady to commend himself to; and for all that he was thought none the less of, and was a very valiant and famous knight."

To which our Don Quixote answered:

"Sir, one swallow does not make a summer. What is more, I know that in secret that knight was very much in love. Besides, his liking every woman who took his fancy was a natural failing that he could not keep a hand on. But in short, it is very well established that he had one alone whom he had made mistress of his will, and to her he commended himself very often and very secretly, because he prided himself on being a discreet knight."

"Then if it is of the essence that every knight errant must be in love," said the traveller, "your worship may well be believed to be so, being of the profession. And unless your worship prides yourself on being as discreet as Don Galaor, I beg you as earnestly as I can, in the name of the whole of this company and my own, to tell us the name, the country, the rank and the beauty of your lady; for she would count herself fortunate to have the whole world know that she is loved and served by such a knight as your worship appears to be."

At this Don Quixote gave a great sigh and said:

"I cannot say whether my sweet enemy is pleased or not that the world should know I serve her. I can only say, in answer to what is asked of me with such courtesy, that her name is Dulcinea; her country El Toboso, a village of La Mancha; her rank must be at the least that of a princess, since she is my queen and my lady; her beauty superhuman, since in her are made true all the impossible and chimerical attributes of beauty that the poets give their ladies — that her hair is gold, her forehead the Elysian fields, her eyebrows the rainbow, her eyes suns, her cheeks roses, her lips coral, her teeth pearls, her neck alabaster, her breast marble, her hands ivory, her whiteness snow; and the parts that modesty has hidden from human sight are such, as I think and believe, that discreet consideration can only prize them and not compare them."

"We should like to know her lineage, race and family," said Vivaldo.

To which Don Quixote answered:

"She is not of the ancient Roman Curtii, Caii and Scipios, nor of the modern Colonnas and Orsinis; nor of the Moncadas and Requesenes of Catalonia, still less of the Rebellas and Villanovas of Valencia; nor the Palafoxes, Nuzas, Rocabertis, Corellas, Lunas, Alagones, Urreas, Foces and Gurreas of Aragon; nor the Cerdas, Manriques, Mendozas and Guzmanes of Castile; nor the Alencastros, Pallas and Meneses of Portugal. But she is of the Tobosos of La Mancha — a line which, though modern, is such that it may give a noble beginning to the most illustrious families of the centuries to come. And let nobody argue with me about this, except on the conditions Cervino set at the foot of the trophy of Roland's arms, which said:

	let no man move them
	who cannot prove himself against Roland."

"Although mine is of the Cachopines of Laredo," answered the traveller, "I shall not dare set it beside the Tobosos of La Mancha — though, to tell the truth, that surname has never reached my ears until now."

"As if it would not have reached them!" replied Don Quixote.

All the rest were listening with great attention to the conversation of the two, and even the goatherds and shepherds themselves recognised how utterly wanting in wits our Don Quixote was. Only Sancho Panza thought that everything his master said was true, knowing who he was and having known him since his birth; and what he had some doubts about was believing that business of the lovely Dulcinea of El Toboso, because no such name and no such princess had ever come to his notice, though he lived so near El Toboso.

They were going along in this talk when they saw, coming down through the gap between two high mountains, some twenty shepherds, all dressed in black woollen skins and crowned with garlands which, as it turned out afterwards, were of yew and of cypress. Six of them were carrying a bier, covered with a great variety of flowers and branches. Seeing which, one of the goatherds said:

"Those coming there are the men carrying Grisóstomo's body, and the foot of that mountain is the place where he ordered them to bury him."

So they hurried to get there, and arrived just as those coming had set the bier down on the ground; and four of them with sharp mattocks were digging the grave beside a hard rock.

The two parties greeted each other courteously; and then Don Quixote and those who had come with him fell to looking at the bier, and on it they saw, covered with flowers, a dead body dressed as a shepherd, of about thirty years old to look at; and although he was dead, he showed that in life he had had a handsome face and a gallant bearing. Round about him on the bier itself were some books and a great many papers, some open and some folded. And all who were looking at this, and those who were opening the grave, and everybody else who was there, kept a wonderful silence, until one of the men who had carried the dead man said to another:

"Look carefully, Ambrosio, whether this is the place Grisóstomo spoke of, since you want what he left ordered in his will to be carried out so exactly."

"This is it," answered Ambrosio; "for many a time in this place my unhappy friend told me the story of his misfortune. Here he told me he first saw that mortal enemy of the human race; here too it was that he first declared to her a passion as honourable as it was loving; and here it was, the last time, that Marcela finished undeceiving and disdaining him, so that she put an end to the tragedy of his miserable life. And here, in memory of so many misfortunes, he wanted to be laid in the bowels of eternal oblivion."

And turning to Don Quixote and the travellers, he went on:

"That body, gentlemen, which you are looking at with pitying eyes, was the storehouse of a soul in which heaven had placed an infinite share of its riches. That is the body of Grisóstomo, who was unique in wit, alone in courtesy, extreme in gentleness, a phoenix in friendship, generous without measure, grave without presumption, cheerful without vulgarity, and, in short, first in everything that goes to being good, and without a second in everything that went to being unfortunate. He loved well, and was hated; he adored, and was disdained; he pleaded with a wild beast, he importuned a piece of marble, he ran after the wind, he shouted into the wilderness, he served ingratitude — from which he got for his reward the spoils of death in the middle of the course of his life, which was ended by a shepherdess whom he was trying to make immortal, so that she might live in people's memory, as those papers you are looking at would very well show, if he had not ordered me to give them to the fire as soon as I had given his body to the earth."

"You would be using greater severity and cruelty with them," said Vivaldo, "than their owner himself; for it is neither just nor right that the will of a man should be carried out when what he orders goes outside all reasonable sense. Augustus Caesar would not have had a good name if he had allowed what the divine Mantuan left ordered in his will to be put into execution. So, Señor Ambrosio, now that you are giving your friend's body to the earth, do not go giving his writings to oblivion; for if he ordered it as an injured man, it is not right that you should carry it out as an unwise one. On the contrary, by giving these papers life, see that Marcela's cruelty has life for ever, so that it may serve as an example in the times to come to the living, to keep away and flee from falling down such precipices as this. For I already know, and so do all of us who come here, the story of this loving and desperate friend of yours; and we know of your friendship, and the occasion of his death, and what he left ordered at the end of his life. From which lamentable history one may gather how great was Marcela's cruelty, and Grisóstomo's love, and the faith of your friendship, and the end that waits for those who gallop with a loose rein down the path that raving love sets before their eyes. Last night we heard of Grisóstomo's death, and that he was to be buried in this place; and so, out of curiosity and pity, we left the direct road we were on and agreed to come and see with our eyes what had so grieved us in the hearing. And in payment for this pity, and for the wish that was born in us to remedy it if we could, we beg you, wise Ambrosio — at least I beg it of you for my own part — that instead of burning these papers you will let me carry off a few of them."

And without waiting for the shepherd to answer, he put out his hand and took some of those that were nearest; seeing which, Ambrosio said:

"Out of courtesy I shall let you keep the ones you have already taken, sir; but to imagine that I shall leave off burning the rest is an idle thought."

Vivaldo, who was anxious to see what the papers said, opened one of them at once and saw that it was headed: Song of Despair. Ambrosio heard him and said:

"That is the last paper the unhappy man wrote; and so that you may see, sir, the pass his misfortunes had brought him to, read it out so as to be heard; for the time they take to open the grave will give you room enough for it."

"I shall do it very willingly," said Vivaldo.

And as all the bystanders had the same wish, they gathered round him; and reading in a clear voice, he saw that it went like this:

Chapter 14: In Which Are Set Down the Despairing Verses of the Dead Shepherd, with Other Unlooked-For Events

Grisóstomo's Song

	Since you insist, cruel one, that the force
	of your harsh severity be published abroad
	from tongue to tongue and from one people to another,
	I shall make hell itself lend my sad breast
	a note of grief, to wrench the ordinary
	use of my voice out of its course.
	And matching my desire, which strains
	to tell my pain and your exploits,
	the terrible voice shall carry the sound,
	and mixed with it, for greater torment,
	pieces of my own wretched entrails.
	Listen, then, and lend an attentive ear
	not to any ordered music but to the noise
	that comes up out of the depths of my bitter heart,
	driven by a raving I cannot help,
	for my own relief and your annoyance.
	The roaring of the lion, the terrifying howl
	of the fierce wolf, the horrible hiss
	of the scaly serpent, the appalling
	bellow of some monster, the ominous
	croaking of the crow, the uproar
	of the wind fought over an unquiet sea;
	the implacable bellow of the beaten bull,
	the pitiable cooing of the widowed dove,
	the mournful song of the envied owl,
	together with the weeping
	of all the black infernal crew —
	let them all come out with my grieving soul,
	mixed into one sound, in such a way
	that all the senses are confounded;
	for the cruel pain that is in me
	demands new methods to be told.
	The sands of father Tagus shall not hear
	the sad echoes of so much confusion,
	nor the olives of the famous Betis:
	for my hard sorrows shall be scattered
	on high crags and in deep hollows,
	with a dead tongue and with living words;
	or in dark valleys, or on lonely
	beaches stripped of human dealing,
	or where the sun has never shown its light,
	or among the venomous multitude
	of beasts that the Libyan plain feeds.
	For although in the desert wastes
	the hoarse and uncertain echoes of my hurt
	may sound with your unmatched severity,
	by the privilege of my short destiny
	they shall be carried through the wide world.
	Disdain kills; patience is brought down
	by a suspicion, true or false;
	jealousy kills with a harsher rigour;
	long absence throws a life out of order;
	against a fear of being forgotten
	firm hope of good fortune is no use.
	In all of them there is certain, unavoidable death;
	but I — a miracle never seen! — live on,
	jealous, absent, disdained and certain
	of the suspicions that have killed me;
	and in the forgetting that feeds my fire,
	and among so many torments, my sight
	never manages to see hope even as a shadow,
	nor do I, in my despair, look for her;
	rather, to go to the extreme in my complaint,
	I swear to be without her for ever.
	Can a man, by any chance, in one instant
	hope and fear, or is it right to do it,
	when the grounds for fear are the more certain?
	Ought I, with harsh jealousy standing before me,
	to shut these eyes, when I must see it
	through a thousand wounds opened in my soul?
	Who would not throw the doors wide open
	to mistrust, when he sees
	disdain uncovered, and his suspicions —
	oh, bitter conversion! — turned into truths,
	and clean truth turned into a lie?
	Oh, in the kingdom of love you fierce tyrants,
	jealousies, put a blade into these hands!
	Give me, disdain, a twisted rope.
	But, alas for me, with a cruel victory
	your memory smothers even my suffering.
	I die, then; and so as never to hope
	for good fortune in death or in life,
	I shall be obstinate in my fancy.
	I shall say that the man who loves well is right,
	and that the freest soul is the one most surrendered
	to love's ancient tyranny.
	I shall say that my perpetual enemy
	has a soul as beautiful as her body,
	and that her forgetfulness is born of my own fault,
	and that, by the harms he does us, love
	keeps his empire in a just peace.
	And with this opinion and a hard noose,
	hastening the wretched hour
	that her disdain has brought me to,
	I shall offer body and soul to the winds,
	with no laurel or palm of good to come.
	You, who by so many wrongs show me
	the reason that forces me to do this wrong
	to the weary life I loathe —
	since you see already the plain proof
	that this deep wound in my heart gives you
	of how gladly I offer myself to your severity —
	if by any chance you think I deserve
	that the clear sky of your beautiful eyes
	should cloud over at my death, do not let it:
	for I want no reparation from you
	for making you a present of my soul's spoils.
	Rather, laughing at the funeral,
	show that my end was your holiday;
	though it is great simplicity to advise you of it,
	since I know your glory stands
	in my life reaching its end so soon.
	Let them come, for it is time, out of the deep abyss —
	Tantalus with his thirst; let Sisyphus come
	with the terrible weight of his stone;
	let Tityus bring his vulture, and likewise
	let Ixion not hold back with his wheel,
	nor the sisters who labour so hard;
	and let them all together transfer
	their mortal anguish into my breast, and in low voices —
	if such things are owed to a man in despair —
	sing sad, sorrowing obsequies
	over a body that is denied even a shroud.
	And let the three-faced porter of hell,
	with a thousand other chimeras and monsters,
	carry the mournful counterpoint;
	for no better pomp seems to me
	to be deserved by a lover who is dead.
	Song of despair, do not complain
	when you leave my sad company;
	rather, since the cause that gave you birth
	increases her good fortune by my misery,
	be not sad even in the grave.

Those who had listened thought well of Grisóstomo's song, although the man who read it said it did not seem to him to square with the account he had heard of Marcela's modesty and goodness, because in it Grisóstomo complained of jealousy and suspicion and absence, all to the prejudice of Marcela's good name and reputation. To which Ambrosio, as one who knew his friend's most hidden thoughts, answered:

"So that you may satisfy yourself on that doubt, sir, you should know that when the unhappy man wrote this song he was away from Marcela, having gone away from her of his own accord, to see whether absence would use its ordinary powers on him. And as there is nothing that does not torment an absent lover, and no fear that does not overtake him, so Grisóstomo was tormented by imagined jealousies and dreaded suspicions as though they had been real. And with that, the truth that fame proclaims of Marcela's goodness stands where it did; for apart from being cruel, and a little arrogant, and a great deal disdainful, envy itself neither ought nor is able to find any fault in her."

"That is the truth," answered Vivaldo.

And as he was about to read another of the papers he had saved from the fire, he was stopped by a marvellous vision — for that is what it seemed — which suddenly presented itself to their eyes. For on top of the rock where they were digging the grave there appeared the shepherdess Marcela, so beautiful that her beauty went beyond her reputation. Those who had never seen her before looked at her in wonder and silence, and those who were used to seeing her were left no less astonished than those who never had. But hardly had Ambrosio seen her when, with every sign of an indignant spirit, he said:

"Have you come, by any chance, fierce basilisk of these mountains, to see whether the wounds of this poor wretch whose life your cruelty took will bleed at your presence? Or have you come to gloat over the cruel exploits of your nature, or to watch from that height, like another pitiless Nero, the burning of his Rome in flames, or to trample arrogantly on this unhappy corpse, as Tarquin's ungrateful daughter trampled on her father's? Tell us quickly what you have come for, or what it is that pleases you most; for since I know that Grisóstomo's thoughts never failed to obey you in life, I shall see to it that, now he is dead, the thoughts of all those who called themselves his friends obey you too."

"I come, Ambrosio, for none of the things you have said," answered Marcela, "but to speak up for myself and to make plain how unreasonable are all those who blame me for their sufferings and for Grisóstomo's death. And so I beg all of you who are here to listen to me, for it will not take much time or many words to persuade sensible people of a truth.

"Heaven made me beautiful, you say, and so beautiful that my beauty moves you to love me whether you will or no; and for the love you show me, you say — and even demand — that I am obliged to love you back. By the natural understanding that God has given me I know that everything beautiful is lovable; but I cannot see that, merely by being loved, a thing that is loved for being beautiful is obliged to love whoever loves it. What is more, it might happen that the lover of the beautiful thing was ugly; and since ugliness deserves to be shunned, it comes very badly to say, 'I love you because you are beautiful; you must love me although I am ugly.'

"But even supposing the beauty is equal on both sides, it does not follow that the desires must be equal too; for not all beauties fall in love. Some of them delight the eye without conquering the will. If every beauty made men fall in love and conquered them, our wills would go wandering about confused and lost, not knowing where they were to stop; for the beautiful objects being infinite, the desires would have to be infinite too. And from what I have heard, true love is not divided, and must be voluntary and not forced. This being so, as I believe it is, why do you want me to surrender my will by force, obliged by nothing but your saying that you love me?

"If not, tell me this: if heaven had made me ugly instead of beautiful, would it have been just for me to complain of you for not loving me? What is more, you must consider that I did not choose the beauty I have; such as it is, heaven gave it me freely, without my asking for it or choosing it. And just as the viper does not deserve to be blamed for the poison it carries, although it kills with it, since nature gave it, so neither do I deserve to be reproved for being beautiful. For beauty in a virtuous woman is like a distant fire or a sharp sword: the one does not burn, and the other does not cut, anybody who does not come near them. Honour and virtue are ornaments of the soul, without which the body, even if it is beautiful, ought not to look so. Then if modesty is one of the virtues that most adorn and beautify body and soul, why should a woman who is loved for being beautiful lose it, in order to fall in with the intention of a man who, for his own pleasure alone, uses all his strength and cunning to make her lose it?

"I was born free, and in order to be able to live free I chose the solitude of the fields. The trees of these mountains are my company, the clear waters of these streams my mirrors; with the trees and the waters I share my thoughts and my beauty. I am a distant fire and a sword laid far off. Those I have made fall in love by the sight of me I have undeceived with my words. And if desires are kept alive by hopes, then since I gave no hope to Grisóstomo or to anyone else, it may fairly be said of the end of any of them that he was killed by his own obstinacy rather than by my cruelty.

"And if I am charged with his intentions having been honourable, and that for that reason I was obliged to meet them, I say that when, in this very place where they are now digging his grave, he declared to me the goodness of his intention, I told him that mine was to live in perpetual solitude, and that the earth alone should enjoy the fruit of my seclusion and the spoils of my beauty. And if, with all that plain speaking, he chose to persist against hope and to sail against the wind, is it any wonder that he drowned in mid-ocean of his own folly? If I had led him on, I should have been false; if I had contented him, I should have gone against my own better intention and purpose. He persisted after being undeceived; he despaired without being hated. Consider now whether it is reasonable that I should be blamed for his pain.

"Let the man who is deceived complain; let the man who has been cheated of promised hopes despair; let the man I call to trust me, and the man I accept take pride in it. But let no man call me cruel or a murderer whom I do not promise, deceive, call or accept.

"Heaven has not so far willed that I should love by destiny, and to think that I am going to love by choice is a waste of time. Let this general undeceiving serve each of those who court me for his own particular profit; and let it be understood from now on that if anybody dies for me, he does not die of jealousy or of being scorned, since a woman who loves nobody can give nobody cause for jealousy; and plain speaking is not to be counted as disdain.

"Let the man who calls me a wild beast and a basilisk leave me alone as a harmful and evil thing; let the man who calls me ungrateful not serve me; the man who calls me unapproachable not approach me; the man who calls me cruel not follow me. For this wild beast, this basilisk, this ungrateful, cruel and unapproachable woman will not seek them out or serve them or approach them or follow them in any way whatever.

"If Grisóstomo was killed by his impatience and his headlong desire, why should my decent conduct and my reserve be blamed for it? If I keep my purity in the company of the trees, why should a man who wants me to keep it in the company of men want me to lose it? I have, as you know, property of my own, and I do not covet other people's; I have a free nature and I do not care to be subject to anyone. I neither love nor hate anybody. I do not deceive this man or solicit that one, I do not trifle with one or amuse myself with another. The decent conversation of the village girls hereabouts and the care of my goats are my amusement. My desires have these mountains for their boundary; and if they go beyond them, it is to contemplate the beauty of the sky — steps by which the soul travels towards its first dwelling."

And saying this, without waiting for any answer, she turned her back and went into the thickest part of a wood that was near, leaving everyone there astonished as much by her good sense as by her beauty. And some of them — those who had been wounded by the powerful arrow of the rays of her lovely eyes — showed signs of wanting to follow her, taking no advantage of the plain undeceiving they had just heard. Seeing which, and thinking that here was a good opportunity to make use of his chivalry in succouring maidens in distress, Don Quixote laid his hand on the hilt of his sword and said, in a loud and distinct voice:

"Let no person, of whatever state and condition, dare to follow the beautiful Marcela, on pain of falling under my furious indignation. She has shown, with clear and sufficient arguments, how little or no blame she has had in Grisóstomo's death, and how far she is from consenting to the desires of any of her lovers; for which reason it is only just that, instead of being followed and persecuted, she should be honoured and esteemed by all the good people of the world, since she shows that in it she is the only woman who lives with so honourable an intention."

Whether it was because of Don Quixote's threats, or because Ambrosio told them to finish what they owed their good friend, not one of the shepherds stirred or moved from there until, the grave being finished and Grisóstomo's papers burned, they laid his body in it, not without many tears from the bystanders. They closed the grave with a heavy stone until a slab should be finished which, Ambrosio said, he meant to have made, with an epitaph that was to read like this:

	Here lies the wretched frozen body
	of a lover who was a shepherd of flocks,
	and lost for want of love.
	He died at the hands of the severity
	of a shy, beautiful, ungrateful girl,
	through whom the tyranny of love
	spreads out its empire.

Then they scattered a great many flowers and branches over the grave, and all offering their condolences to his friend Ambrosio, they took their leave of him. Vivaldo and his companion did the same, and Don Quixote took leave of his hosts and of the travellers, who begged him to come with them to Seville, it being so convenient a place for finding adventures that in every street and round every corner more of them offer themselves than anywhere else. Don Quixote thanked them for the information and for the goodwill they showed in wanting to do him a kindness, and said that for the present he neither wished nor ought to go to Seville until he had cleared all those mountains of the thieving scoundrels that they were said to be full of. Seeing his firm resolve, the travellers would not press him any further, but taking their leave again they left him and went on their road; on which they did not lack for things to talk about, both the story of Marcela and Grisóstomo and the madnesses of Don Quixote. And he made up his mind to go and look for the shepherdess Marcela and offer her everything he could in her service. But things did not turn out as he expected, as is told in the course of this true history, the second part ending here.

Chapter 15: In Which Is Told the Unlucky Adventure That Don Quixote Ran Into When He Ran Into Some Heartless Yangüesan Carriers

Part Three of the Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha

The wise Cide Hamete Benengeli relates that as soon as Don Quixote had taken leave of his hosts and of everyone who had been at the shepherd Grisóstomo's burial, he and his squire went into the same wood they had seen the shepherdess Marcela go into. And having spent more than two hours going about in it, looking for her everywhere without being able to find her, they came to a stop in a meadow full of fresh grass, beside which ran a quiet, cool stream — so inviting that it tempted, and indeed compelled, them to spend the hours of the afternoon heat there, which was by now beginning to come on in earnest.

Don Quixote and Sancho dismounted, and leaving the donkey and Rocinante at their liberty to crop the abundant grass, they ransacked the saddlebags; and without any ceremony, in good peace and fellowship, master and man ate what they found in them.

Sancho had not troubled to hobble Rocinante, being confident that he knew him for so meek an animal and so little given to lust that all the mares in the pastures of Córdoba would not have led him into mischief. But fate — and the devil, who does not sleep all the time — arranged matters so that a herd of Galician ponies belonging to some Yangüesan carriers happened to be grazing in that valley; for it is these men's custom to take their midday rest with their string of animals in places where there is grass and water, and the spot Don Quixote had chanced upon suited them exactly. Now it so happened that a desire came upon Rocinante to disport himself with the lady ponies. And the moment he caught their scent he abandoned his natural pace and habit and, without asking his master's leave, broke into a brisk little trot and went off to communicate his need to them. But they, who to all appearances were keener on grazing than on anything else, received him with their hoofs and their teeth in such a way that in no time at all his girths were broken and he was left saddleless and stripped. But what he must have felt still more was that the carriers, seeing the violence being done to their mares, came running with their staves and gave him so many blows that they brought him down in a bad way on the ground.

By this time Don Quixote and Sancho, who had watched Rocinante's beating, came up panting; and Don Quixote said to Sancho:

"From what I can see, friend Sancho, these are no knights, but low fellows of base breeding. I say it because you may perfectly well help me to take due vengeance for the injury that has been done to Rocinante before our very eyes."

"What the devil sort of vengeance are we to take," answered Sancho, "when there are more than twenty of them and no more than two of us — and perhaps not even two, but one and a half?"

"I count for a hundred," replied Don Quixote.

And without any more discussion he laid his hand on his sword and charged the Yangüesans; and Sancho Panza did the same, urged and moved by his master's example. And at the first stroke Don Quixote dealt one of them a slash that opened the leather jerkin he was wearing, along with a good part of the shoulder inside it. The Yangüesans, seeing themselves roughly handled by two men alone when there were so many of them, ran to their staves, and getting the pair of them in the middle they began to lay on with great energy and enthusiasm. The truth is that at the second stroke they had Sancho on the ground, and the same happened to Don Quixote, for all his skill and his good courage; and it was his luck to come down at the feet of Rocinante, who had not yet got up — from which one may judge the fury with which staves smash away when they are in rustic and angry hands.

The Yangüesans, seeing the mess they had made, loaded up their string of animals with all the speed they could and went on their way, leaving the two adventurers in a bad state and in a worse temper.

The first to come round was Sancho Panza; and finding himself next to his master, he said in a sick and pitiful voice:

"Señor Don Quixote! Oh, Señor Don Quixote!"

"What do you want, brother Sancho?" answered Don Quixote in the same feeble and doleful tone as Sancho.

"I should like, if it were possible," answered Sancho Panza, "for your worship to give me two swallows of that drink of Fiery Brass, if your worship happens to have it there to hand. Perhaps it will be as good for broken bones as it is for wounds."

"If I had it here, unlucky man that I am, what more should we need?" answered Don Quixote. "But I swear to you, Sancho Panza, on the word of a knight errant, that before two days are out — unless fortune orders otherwise — I shall have it in my possession, or my hands will have failed me badly."

"And in how many days does your worship reckon we shall be able to move our feet?" replied Sancho Panza.

"For my own part," said the battered knight, "I could not put a limit to those days. But I am to blame for the whole thing, because I had no business to lay my hand on my sword against men who were not knights like myself. And so I believe that the god of battles has allowed this punishment to be given me as a penalty for breaking the laws of chivalry. For which reason, Sancho Panza, it is as well that you should be warned of what I am now going to tell you, because it matters a great deal to the health of us both. And it is this: when you see rabble of that kind doing us some injury, do not wait for me to lay my hand on my sword against them, because I shall do no such thing; instead, put your own hand to your sword and punish them entirely to your taste. And if knights come to their aid and defence, I shall be able to defend you and set about them with all my might; for you must have seen by a thousand signs and proofs how far the valour of this strong arm of mine extends."

Such was the arrogance the poor gentleman was left in by his victory over the valiant Basque. But his master's advice did not strike Sancho Panza as good enough for him to let it pass without an answer, so he said:

"Sir, I am a peaceable man, a quiet one, an easy one, and I know how to swallow any injury, because I have a wife and children to keep and bring up. So let it be a piece of advice to your worship too — since it cannot be an order — that on no account will I lay a hand on my sword, either against a peasant or against a knight; and that from this moment, before God, I forgive every injury that has been done me and that ever will be done me, whether it was done, or is being done, or is to be done, by a person high or low, rich or poor, gentleman or commoner, without excepting any rank or condition whatever."

Hearing which, his master answered him:

"I wish I had breath enough to speak a little more comfortably, and that this pain I have in my rib would let up just enough for me to make you understand, Panza, the mistake you are in. Come here, sinner: if the wind of fortune, so contrary to us until now, should turn in our favour, filling the sails of our desire so that we come safely and without any check into port on one of the isles I have promised you — what would become of you, if, having won it, I made you lord of it? Are you going to make that impossible by not being a knight, and not wanting to be one, and having neither the courage nor the intention to avenge your injuries and defend your dominion? For you must know that in kingdoms and provinces newly conquered the tempers of the natives are never so settled, nor so much on the new lord's side, that there is not something to fear from their making some new move to upset things again and, as they say, try their luck once more. And so the new possessor needs understanding, to know how to govern, and courage, to attack and defend himself whatever happens."

"In this business that has just happened to us," answered Sancho, "I wish I had had that understanding and that courage your worship speaks of. But I swear to you, on the word of a poor man, that I am fitter for plasters than for parleys. See whether your worship can get up, and we will help Rocinante, though he doesn't deserve it, since he was the chief cause of all this pounding. I would never have believed such a thing of Rocinante; I took him for a chaste person and as peaceable as myself. Well, they are right when they say it takes a long time to get to know people, and that there is nothing certain in this life. Who would have said that after those tremendous sword-slashes your worship gave that unlucky knight errant, there would come, express and hot on their heels, this great tempest of sticks that has broken over our backs?"

"Yours, at least, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "must be used to squalls of that sort. But mine, brought up between fine linen and Holland cloth, will obviously feel the pain of this misfortune more keenly. And if it were not that I imagine — imagine, do I say? I know for a certainty — that all these discomforts are inseparable from the exercise of arms, I would let myself die here of sheer vexation."

To this the squire replied:

"Sir, since these misfortunes are part of chivalry's own harvest, tell me, your worship: do they come round very often, or have they set seasons when they happen? Because it seems to me that after two such harvests we shall be no use for the third, unless God in his infinite mercy comes to our help."

"You must know, friend Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "that the life of knights errant is subject to a thousand dangers and misfortunes; and neither more nor less, it is in the immediate power of knights errant to become kings and emperors, as experience has shown in the case of many and various knights whose histories I know in full. And I could tell you now, if the pain would let me, of some who by the valour of their arm alone have risen to the high positions I have mentioned; and these same men were seen, before and after, in all sorts of calamities and miseries. For the valorous Amadis of Gaul found himself in the power of his mortal enemy Archelaus the enchanter, of whom it is taken as an established fact that, having him prisoner, he tied him to a pillar in a courtyard and gave him more than two hundred lashes with his horse's reins. And there is even a secret author, and one of no small credit, who says that the Knight of the Sun was caught in a certain castle by a trapdoor that gave way under his feet, and in falling found himself in a deep pit underground, bound hand and foot, and there they gave him one of those things they call a clyster, of snow-water and sand, which very nearly finished him; and if he had not been helped in that great trouble by a wise man who was a great friend of his, it would have gone very badly with the poor knight. So I may well pass among such good company, for the affronts those men suffered were greater than the one we are suffering now. Because I want you to be informed, Sancho, that wounds given with whatever instruments happen to be in a man's hand are no affront; and this stands in the law of duelling, written in express words: that if a shoemaker hits another man with the last he has in his hand, although it is genuinely made of wood, it will not therefore be said that the man he hit with it has been cudgelled. I say this so that you shall not think that, because we have come out of this brawl pounded, we have come out of it affronted; because the weapons those men carried, the ones they mashed us with, were nothing but their staves, and not one of them, so far as I recollect, had a rapier, a sword or a dagger."

"They gave me no chance," answered Sancho, "to look into it that far. Because I had hardly laid a hand on my trusty blade when they crossed my shoulders with their pine-staves in such a way that they took the sight out of my eyes and the strength out of my feet and laid me down where I am now lying; and where it gives me no trouble at all to wonder whether the business of the staves was an affront or not, but a great deal of trouble to feel the pain of the blows, which are going to stay printed on my memory as firmly as on my back."

"For all that, I would have you know, brother Panza," replied Don Quixote, "that there is no memory time does not put an end to, and no pain death does not carry off."

"And what greater misfortune can there be," replied Panza, "than one that has to wait for time to put an end to it and death to carry it off? If this trouble of ours were the kind that is cured with a couple of plasters, it wouldn't be so bad; but I can see that all the poultices in a hospital won't be enough to get us even into a decent state."

"Leave off that and draw strength out of weakness, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "for that is what I mean to do. And let us see how Rocinante is, for it seems to me the poor beast has not had the smallest share in this misfortune."

"There is nothing to wonder at in that," answered Sancho, "he being so good a knight errant. What I wonder at is that my donkey should have got off free and without costs, where we have come out without ribs."

"Fortune always leaves one door open in misfortunes, to give a remedy for them," said Don Quixote. "I say it because that little beast can now make up for the lack of Rocinante and carry me from here to some castle where I may be cured of my wounds. What is more, I shall not count such a mount a dishonour, because I remember reading that the good old Silenus, tutor and schoolmaster to the merry god of laughter, entered the city of the hundred gates riding very comfortably on a very handsome ass."

"It may well be true that he rode, as your worship says," answered Sancho, "but there is a great difference between riding and going slung across like a sack of rubbish."

To which Don Quixote answered:

"Wounds received in battle give honour rather than take it away. So, friend Panza, do not argue with me any more; but as I have told you already, get up as best you can and put me on top of your donkey in whatever way pleases you most, and let us get away from here before night comes and catches us in this wilderness."

"But I have heard your worship say," said Panza, "that it is very much a knight errant's business to sleep out on moors and in deserts for most of the year, and that they count it a great piece of luck."

"That is," said Don Quixote, "when they cannot do otherwise, or when they are in love. And this is so true that there has been a knight who stayed on a rock, in sun and shade and in all the inclemencies of heaven, for two years without his lady knowing anything about it. And one of these was Amadis, when, calling himself Beltenebros, he lodged on the Poor Rock — for eight years or eight months, I am not sure which, because I am not very good on the reckoning. Enough that he was there doing penance for some vexation or other that the lady Oriana had caused him. But let us leave this now, Sancho, and get it over before some other misfortune happens to the donkey, as it did to Rocinante."

"Even that would be the devil's own work," said Sancho.

And letting off thirty groans, and sixty sighs, and a hundred and twenty curses and damnations on whoever had brought him there, he got up, sticking halfway like a Turkish bow, unable to finish straightening himself. And with all this labour he harnessed his ass, which had also gone somewhat astray with the excessive freedom of that day. Then he got Rocinante up; and if that animal had had a tongue to complain with, it is safe to say that neither Sancho nor his master would have outdone him.

In the end Sancho settled Don Quixote on the ass and tied Rocinante on behind; and leading the ass by the halter, he set off, more or less, towards where he thought the high road might be. And fortune, which was guiding his affairs from good to better, had not let him go a short league before it brought him to the road, on which he made out an inn that, to his annoyance and to Don Quixote's satisfaction, was bound to be a castle. Sancho insisted it was an inn and his master that it was not, but a castle; and the argument lasted so long that they had time to reach it without finishing it, and Sancho went straight in with his whole train, without any further inquiry.

Chapter 16: Of What Happened to the Ingenious Gentleman in the Inn That He Imagined to Be a Castle

The innkeeper, seeing Don Quixote slung across the ass, asked Sancho what was wrong with him. Sancho answered that it was nothing, only that he had had a fall down off a rock and his ribs were somewhat bruised. The innkeeper had for a wife a woman not of the sort usually found in that trade, because she was naturally kind-hearted and felt for the troubles of her neighbours; and so she came at once to see to Don Quixote, and made a daughter of hers — a girl, unmarried and very good-looking — help her to nurse their guest.

There was also a servant at the inn, a girl from Asturias, broad in the face, flat at the back of the head, snub-nosed, blind in one eye and not very sound in the other. It is true that the elegance of her figure made up for the rest of her shortcomings: she did not stand five foot from her feet to her head, and her shoulders, which weighed on her somewhat, made her look at the ground rather more than she would have liked. This graceful young woman, then, helped the daughter, and between them they made Don Quixote a very bad bed in a garret which gave clear signs of having served for many years, in earlier times, as a hayloft. A carrier was also lodged in it, whose bed was made up a little way beyond our Don Quixote's; and although it was put together out of the pack-saddles and blankets of his mules, it had a great advantage over Don Quixote's, which consisted only of four badly planed boards laid on two trestles of unequal height; a mattress so thin it might have been a quilt, full of lumps which, if they had not shown through some of the holes that they were made of wool, would to the touch have been taken for pebbles, given how hard they were; two sheets made of the leather they use for shields; and a blanket whose threads, if anyone had wanted to count them, could have been counted without losing one.

In this accursed bed Don Quixote lay down, and the innkeeper's wife and her daughter plastered him from top to toe, with Maritornes — for that was the Asturian's name — holding the light for them. And as she was putting on the poultices, the innkeeper's wife saw Don Quixote so bruised in places that she said it looked more like a beating than a fall.

"They were not blows," said Sancho; "it was just that the rock had a lot of points and knobs on it, and each one had made its own bruise."

And he added:

"Manage it, madam, so that there are a few pieces of tow left over, for there will be no lack of somebody who needs them; my own back aches a bit too."

"In that case," answered the innkeeper's wife, "you must have had a fall as well."

"I did not fall," said Sancho Panza; "but with the shock I got at seeing my master fall, my body aches in such a way that I feel as if I had been given a thousand strokes with a stick."

"That could very well be," said the daughter; "for it has often happened to me to dream I was falling from the top of a tower and never getting to the ground, and when I woke up out of the dream I found myself as bruised and battered as if I really had fallen."

"That's just the point, madam," answered Sancho Panza: "that I, without dreaming anything at all — being wider awake than I am now — find myself with hardly fewer bruises than my master Don Quixote."

"What is this knight called?" asked Maritornes the Asturian.

"Don Quixote of La Mancha," answered Sancho Panza; "and he is a knight adventurer, and one of the best and strongest that the world has seen this long while."

"And what is a knight adventurer?" asked the girl.

"Are you so new in the world that you don't know?" answered Sancho Panza. "Then let me tell you, sister, that a knight adventurer is a thing that in two shakes is thrashed and is an emperor. Today he is the most wretched creature in the world and the most in need, and tomorrow he will have two or three kingdoms' crowns to give away to his squire."

"Then how is it that you, being squire to so good a master," said the innkeeper's wife, "have not so much as an earldom, by the look of you?"

"It is still early days," answered Sancho; "we have only been out looking for adventures for a month, and so far we have not run into any that is one. And sometimes it happens that you look for one thing and find another. The truth is that if my master Don Quixote recovers from this wound, or fall, and I am not left crippled by it, I would not change my prospects for the best title in Spain."

Don Quixote had been listening to all this talk very attentively, and sitting up in bed as best he could and taking the innkeeper's wife by the hand, he said to her:

"Believe me, beauteous lady, you may call yourself fortunate for having lodged my person in this castle of yours — which person is such that, if I do not praise it, it is because of what they say, that self-praise debases. But my squire will tell you who I am. I say only that I shall keep the service you have rendered me eternally written in my memory, to be grateful to you for it as long as my life lasts. And would to high heaven that love did not hold me so surrendered and so subject to his laws, and to the eyes of that beautiful ingrate whose name I say between my teeth; for then the eyes of this fair maiden would be the masters of my liberty."

The innkeeper's wife and her daughter and good Maritornes were bewildered to hear the knight errant's speeches, which they understood about as well as if he had been talking Greek, although they gathered clearly enough that the whole of it was aimed at compliments and gallantry. Being unused to language of the sort, they looked at him and marvelled, and he seemed to them a different kind of man from the ones in ordinary use; and thanking him in innkeeperly phrases for his offers, they left him. And Maritornes the Asturian saw to Sancho, who needed it no less than his master.

Now the carrier had arranged with her that they should enjoy themselves together that night, and she had given him her word that once the guests were quiet and her employers asleep she would come and look for him and satisfy him in whatever he asked. And it is told of this good girl that she never gave a promise of that kind that she did not keep, even if she gave it on a mountainside and with no witness at all; because she prided herself greatly on being a gentlewoman, and did not consider it any disgrace to be in service at an inn, since it was misfortunes and bad luck, she said, that had brought her to that condition.

Don Quixote's hard, narrow, mean and treacherous bed stood first, in the middle of that star-lit stable; and next to it Sancho made up his own, which consisted only of a rush mat and a blanket that looked more like sheared canvas than wool. Beyond these two beds came the carrier's, put together, as has been said, out of the pack-saddles and the whole harness of the two best mules he had with him, although there were twelve of them, sleek, fat and famous; for he was one of the rich carriers of Arévalo, according to the author of this history, who makes particular mention of this carrier because he knew him very well, and some will even have it that he was some sort of relation of his. Besides which, Cide Mahamate Benengeli was a most inquisitive historian and most exact in everything; which can be plainly seen, since the details set down here, minute and trivial as they are, he was unwilling to pass over in silence. From which the solemn historians might take an example — the ones who tell us of great actions so briefly and so scantily that we barely get a taste of them, leaving in the inkwell, whether through carelessness or malice or ignorance, the most substantial part of the work. A thousand blessings on the author of Tablante de Ricamonte, and on the author of that other book which tells the deeds of Count Tomillas, and on the exactness with which they describe everything!

To go on, then: after the carrier had visited his string of mules and given them their second feed, he stretched himself out on his pack-saddles and settled down to wait for his most punctual Maritornes. Sancho was by now poulticed and lying down, and although he did his best to sleep, the pain in his ribs would not let him; and Don Quixote, with the pain in his own, lay with his eyes as wide open as a hare's. The whole inn was silent, and in the whole of it there was no other light than what came from a lamp that hung burning in the middle of the entry.

This marvellous stillness, and the thoughts our knight always carried about with him of the incidents that are related at every turn in the books that had caused his misfortune, brought to his imagination one of the strangest pieces of madness that can readily be imagined. Which was that he fancied he had arrived at a famous castle — for, as has been said, every inn he lodged in was a castle to his mind — and that the innkeeper's daughter was the daughter of the lord of the castle, and that she, conquered by his gallantry, had fallen in love with him and promised that she would come that night, unknown to her parents, to lie with him for a good while. And holding this whole chimera he had built himself for firm and valid, he began to be troubled and to think about the perilous pass in which his chastity was about to be put; and he resolved in his heart to commit no treachery against his lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, even if Queen Guinevere herself and her lady Quintañona were to present themselves in front of him.

While he was thinking about this nonsense, the time and the hour arrived — an unlucky one for him — of the Asturian's coming. In her shift and barefoot, with her hair caught up in a fustian net, she came into the room where the three of them were lodged with silent, careful steps, looking for the carrier. But she had hardly reached the door when Don Quixote heard her; and sitting up in bed, in spite of his poultices and the pain in his ribs, he stretched out his arms to receive his beauteous maiden. The Asturian, drawn in on herself and saying nothing, going along with her hands out in front of her feeling for her beloved, ran into Don Quixote's arms; and he seized her tightly by one wrist, and pulling her towards him — she not daring to say a word — made her sit down on the bed.

He felt her shift next, and although it was made of sacking, to him it seemed to be of the finest and thinnest silk. On her wrists she wore some glass beads, but to him they gave off the gleam of precious oriental pearls. Her hair, which was something in the nature of a horse's mane, he set down for threads of the most brilliant Arabian gold, whose brightness put out the light of the sun itself. And her breath, which without any doubt smelt of yesterday's salad left standing overnight, seemed to him to give off from her mouth a soft and aromatic fragrance. In short, he painted her in his imagination in exactly the shape and manner he had read about in his books of that other princess who came to see the sorely wounded knight, conquered by her love for him, with all the ornaments that are set down here. And so great was the poor gentleman's blindness that neither the touch of her, nor her breath, nor other things the good girl had about her undeceived him — things that would have made anybody vomit who was not a carrier. On the contrary, it seemed to him that he had the goddess of beauty in his arms. And holding her fast, he began to say to her in a low and loving voice:

"I could wish I were in a condition, beautiful and noble lady, to be able to repay so great a favour as the one you have done me with the sight of your great beauty. But fortune, which never tires of persecuting good men, has been pleased to put me in this bed, where I lie so pounded and broken that even if my will wanted to satisfy yours it would be impossible. And what is more, there is added to this impossibility another and a greater one, which is the pledged faith I have given to the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso, sole lady of my most hidden thoughts. If it were not for that standing in the way, I should not be so witless a knight as to let slip the fortunate opportunity that your great goodness has put me in."
