Maritornes was in an agony and sweating at finding herself gripped like this by Don Quixote, and without understanding or paying attention to a word he was saying, she was trying to get herself free without speaking. The good carrier, whom his bad desires were keeping awake, had heard his mistress from the moment she came in at the door. He had listened attentively to everything Don Quixote said, and, jealous that the Asturian should have broken her word to him for somebody else, he came closer to Don Quixote's bed and stood still, to see what all this talk he could not understand would come to. But when he saw that the girl was struggling to get loose and Don Quixote labouring to hold her, he did not think much of the joke; and raising his arm high he let fall so terrible a punch on the enamoured knight's narrow jaws that he bathed his whole mouth in blood. And not content with that, he climbed on top of his ribs and at more than a trot walked up and down the whole length of them.

The bed, which was a little frail and on no firm foundations, being unable to bear the addition of the carrier, came down on the floor; and at the great noise of it the innkeeper woke, and immediately imagined it must be some brawl of Maritornes', because when he shouted for her she did not answer. With this suspicion he got up, and lighting a lamp went towards where he had heard the scuffle. The girl, seeing her master coming, and knowing what a terrible temper he had, all frightened and flustered took refuge in Sancho Panza's bed, where he was still asleep, and there she huddled down and rolled herself into a ball. The innkeeper came in saying:

"Where are you, you whore? I'll be bound this is your doing."

At this Sancho woke up, and feeling that weight almost on top of him, thought he had the nightmare, and began throwing punches in every direction; and among others he landed I do not know how many on Maritornes, who, stung by the pain, threw modesty out of the window and gave Sancho back so many in return that in spite of himself she woke him thoroughly. And he, finding himself handled in that fashion and not knowing by whom, hauled himself up as best he could and closed with Maritornes, and between the two of them there began the hardest-fought and funniest skirmish in the world.

The carrier, then, seeing by the light of the innkeeper's lamp how his lady was faring, left Don Quixote and ran to give her the help she needed. The innkeeper did the same, but with a different intention, because he went to punish the girl, believing beyond a doubt that she alone was the cause of all that harmony. And so, as the saying goes — the cat to the rat, the rat to the rope, the rope to the stick — the carrier laid into Sancho, Sancho into the girl, the girl into him, the innkeeper into the girl, and all of them pounded away so busily that they never gave themselves a moment's rest. And the best of it was that the innkeeper's lamp went out; and as they were left in the dark, they all set about one another so pitilessly and so blindly that wherever they put a hand they left nothing sound.

It happened that there was lodging at the inn that night an officer of the sort they call the Old Holy Brotherhood of Toledo, who, hearing the extraordinary uproar of the fight, took hold of his staff of office and the tin box with his warrants in it and came into the room in the dark, calling out:

"Hold, in the name of the law! Hold, in the name of the Holy Brotherhood!"

And the first person he ran into was the battered Don Quixote, who was lying on his back on his collapsed bed, entirely senseless; and getting his hand by chance on his beard, he went on shouting:

"Help for the law!"

But seeing that the man he had hold of did not stir or move, he took it into his head that he was dead and that the people in the room were his murderers; and on this suspicion he raised his voice, calling out:

"Shut the inn door! Take care nobody gets out — there's a man been killed in here!"

This shout startled everybody, and each of them dropped the fight at the point the shout caught them. The innkeeper withdrew to his room, the carrier to his pack-saddles, the girl to her corner; only the unfortunate Don Quixote and Sancho could not move from where they were. At this the officer let go of Don Quixote's beard and went out to look for a light so as to find the criminals and arrest them; but he did not find one, because the innkeeper had deliberately put out the lamp when he retired to his room, and the officer was obliged to go to the fireplace, where with a great deal of trouble and time he lit another lamp.

Chapter 17: In Which Are Continued the Innumerable Hardships That the Brave Don Quixote and His Good Squire Sancho Panza Went Through in the Inn Which, to His Misfortune, He Took for a Castle

By this time Don Quixote had come round out of his swoon; and in the same tone of voice with which he had called his squire the day before, when he was stretched out in the valley of the staves, he began calling him now:

"Friend Sancho, are you asleep? Are you asleep, friend Sancho?"

"How am I supposed to sleep, curse it," answered Sancho, full of misery and resentment, "when it looks for all the world as if every devil in hell had been at me tonight?"

"You may well believe it," answered Don Quixote, "because either I know very little, or this castle is enchanted. Because you must know — but what I am going to tell you now, you must swear to me you will keep secret until after my death."

"I swear it," answered Sancho.

"I say it," replied Don Quixote, "because I am an enemy to taking away anybody's good name."

"I say I swear it," Sancho said again, "and that I'll keep quiet about it until after your worship's days are over — and please God I may be able to let it out tomorrow."

"Do I treat you so badly, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "that you would like to see me dead as soon as that?"

"It isn't for that," answered Sancho, "but because I'm an enemy to keeping things too long, and I shouldn't like them to go rotten on me from being kept."

"Let it be for whatever reason it likes," said Don Quixote. "I trust more to your affection and your courtesy. And so you must know that tonight there has happened to me one of the strangest adventures that I could ever find words for. To tell it you shortly: a little while ago there came to me the daughter of the lord of this castle, who is the neatest and fairest maiden to be found over a great part of the earth. What could I tell you about the ornament of her person? What about her gallant understanding? What about other hidden things which, to keep the faith I owe my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, I shall let pass untouched and in silence? I will only tell you that heaven, envious of so great a good as fortune had put in my hands — or perhaps, and this is the more likely, because as I have said this castle is enchanted — while I was with her in the sweetest and most loving conversation, there came, without my seeing her or knowing where it came from, a hand fixed to the arm of some monstrous giant, and planted such a punch on my jaws that I have them all bathed in blood; and afterwards it pounded me in such a way that I am worse off than I was yesterday, when the Yangüesans, on account of Rocinante's excesses, did us the injury you know of. From which I gather that the treasure of this maiden's beauty must be guarded by some enchanted Moor, and cannot be meant for me."

"Nor for me either," answered Sancho, "because more than four hundred Moors have been thumping me, in such a way that the pounding with the staves was cakes and ale by comparison. But tell me, sir: how do you come to call this a good and rare adventure, when it has left us in the state it has? Your worship at least came off less badly, since you had that incomparable beauty you speak of in your hands; but what did I get except the greatest hammering I expect to get in the whole of my life? Unlucky me, and unlucky the mother that bore me, for I am no knight errant and never mean to be one, and the largest share of all the disasters falls to me!"

"So you were beaten too?" answered Don Quixote.

"Haven't I told you I was, curse my ancestry?" said Sancho.

"Don't distress yourself, my friend," said Don Quixote; "I shall make the precious balm now, and we shall be cured with it in the twinkling of an eye."

By this time the officer had finished lighting his lamp and came in to look at the man he thought was dead. And as soon as Sancho saw him come in — seeing him arrive in his shirt, with a cloth round his head and a lamp in his hand, and with a very ugly face on him — he asked his master:

"Sir, could this by any chance be the enchanted Moor, coming back to punish us in case he left anything in the inkwell?"

"It cannot be the Moor," answered Don Quixote, "because those under enchantment let themselves be seen by nobody."

"If they don't let themselves be seen, they let themselves be felt," said Sancho; "and if they don't, my back can speak to it."

"So could mine," answered Don Quixote, "but that is not evidence enough to believe that this man we can see is the enchanted Moor."

The officer came up; and finding them talking in such a peaceable conversation, he was taken aback. It is true that Don Quixote was still lying on his back, unable to move for being so thoroughly pounded and plastered. The officer went over to him and said:

"Well, how goes it, my good man?"

"I would speak with better breeding," answered Don Quixote, "if I were you. Is it the custom in this country to talk in that fashion to knights errant, you blockhead?"

The officer, finding himself so badly treated by a man of such a bad appearance, could not stand it; and lifting the lamp, oil and all, he brought it down on Don Quixote's head in such a way that he left him very well cracked indeed. And as everything was left in the dark, he went straight out; and Sancho Panza said:

"There's no doubt about it, sir, this is the enchanted Moor; and he must be keeping the treasure for other people, and for us he keeps nothing but the punches and the lamp-blows."

"That is how it is," answered Don Quixote, "and there is no need to take any notice of these matters of enchantment, or any reason to lose our temper or get angry over them; for since they are invisible and imaginary, we shall find nobody to take our revenge on, however hard we try. Get up, Sancho, if you can, and call the governor of this fortress, and try to get me a little oil, wine, salt and rosemary to make the health-giving balm; for indeed I think I have great need of it now, because a great deal of blood is running out of the wound this phantom has given me."

Sancho got up with a good deal of pain in his bones and went off in the dark to where the innkeeper was; and running into the officer, who was listening to hear how his enemy was getting on, he said:

"Sir, whoever you may be, do us the favour and the kindness of giving us a little rosemary, oil, salt and wine, which is needed to cure one of the best knights errant on earth, who is lying in that bed there, sorely wounded by the hands of the enchanted Moor who is in this inn."

When the officer heard that, he took him for a man out of his wits; and as it was already beginning to get light he opened the inn door and, calling the innkeeper, told him what this good fellow wanted. The innkeeper supplied him with everything he asked for, and Sancho carried it to Don Quixote, who was lying with his hands on his head, complaining of the pain of the blow with the lamp, which had done him no more harm than to raise two rather large lumps; and what he thought was blood was nothing but the sweat he was sweating in the anguish of the past storm.

To be brief, he took his simples, out of which he made a compound, mixing them all together and boiling them for a good while, until it seemed to him they were exactly right. He then asked for some flask to pour it into, and as there was none in the inn, he settled on putting it into a tin oil-can that the innkeeper made him a free gift of. Next he said over the can more than eighty Our Fathers, and as many Hail Marys, Salves and Creeds, accompanying every word with a cross by way of a blessing; at all of which Sancho, the innkeeper and the officer were present, the carrier by now being quietly about the business of looking after his mules.

This done, he decided to make trial at once, on himself, of the virtue of that precious balm as he imagined it; and so he drank down what would not go into the can and was left over in the pot it had been boiled in — very nearly a quart. And he had hardly finished drinking it when he began to vomit in such a way that there was nothing left in his stomach; and with the retching and heaving of the vomit an enormous sweat broke out on him, so he gave orders that they should wrap him up and leave him alone. They did so, and he stayed asleep for more than three hours; at the end of which he woke up and felt his body enormously relieved, and so much better of his battering that he considered himself cured. And he genuinely believed he had hit on the balm of Fierabrás, and that with that remedy he could from then on take on any wreck, battle or brawl whatever, however dangerous, without any fear at all.

Sancho Panza, who also took his master's recovery for a miracle, begged him to give him what was left in the pot, which was no small quantity. Don Quixote granted it, and taking it in both hands, in good faith and better spirits, Sancho tipped it down his throat and got very little less inside him than his master had. Now the fact is that poor Sancho's stomach cannot have been as delicate as his master's, and so, before he could vomit, he was seized with such gripings and heavings, with such sweats and faintings, that he thought good and truly that his last hour had come; and finding himself so afflicted and distressed, he cursed the balm and the thief who had given it to him. Seeing him in that state, Don Quixote said:

"I believe, Sancho, that all this trouble comes on you from not being a dubbed knight; because it is my opinion that this liquor cannot be any good to those who are not."

"If your worship knew that," replied Sancho, "bad luck to me and all my kin! — then why did you let me taste it?"

At this the brew did its work, and the poor squire began to empty himself at both ends with such urgency that neither the rush mat he had lain down on again nor the canvas blanket he was covering himself with were of any further use. He sweated and sweated again with such spasms and seizures that not only he but everybody thought his life was ending. This squall and bad passage lasted him nearly two hours, at the end of which he was not left as his master had been, but so pounded and broken that he could not hold himself up.

But Don Quixote, who, as has been said, felt relieved and well, wanted to set off at once in search of adventures, since it seemed to him that all the time he was delaying there was being taken away from the world and from those in it who needed his favour and protection — the more so given the confidence and assurance his balm gave him. And so, forced on by this desire, he saddled Rocinante himself and put the pack-saddle on his squire's donkey, and helped him to dress too and to get up on the ass. Then he mounted; and going over to a corner of the inn, he took hold of a pike that was standing there, to serve him as a lance.

Everybody in the inn was watching him — there were more than twenty people. The innkeeper's daughter was watching him too, and he for his part never took his eyes off her, and every now and then let out a sigh that seemed to be torn from the depths of his entrails; and they all supposed it must be from the pain he felt in his ribs — at any rate, that is what those supposed who had seen him being poulticed the night before.

When the two of them were mounted, standing at the inn door, he called the innkeeper and said to him in a very calm and solemn voice:

"Many and very great, sir governor, are the favours I have received in this castle of yours, and I remain under the deepest obligation to be grateful to you for them all the days of my life. If I can repay you for them by making you avenged on some arrogant person who has done you an injury, know that my office is nothing else but to help those who can do little for themselves, to avenge those who receive wrongs, and to punish treachery. Search your memory, and if you find anything of that sort to commend to me, you have only to say so; for I promise you, by the order of knighthood I have received, to have you satisfied and paid to the full extent of your wishes."

The innkeeper answered him with the same composure:

"Sir knight, I have no need for your worship to avenge me for any injury, because I know how to take whatever revenge I think fit when they are done me. All I need is for your worship to pay me the bill you have run up in the inn tonight — for the straw and barley for your two beasts as well as for the supper and the beds."

"So this is an inn?" replied Don Quixote.

"And a very respectable one," answered the innkeeper.

"I have lived in error until now," answered Don Quixote, "for I truly thought it was a castle, and not a bad one. But since it turns out that it is not a castle but an inn, what can be done for the moment is that you should excuse me the payment; for I cannot go against the order of knights errant, of whom I know for certain — never having read anything to the contrary until now — that they never paid for lodging or anything else at any inn they stayed at, because whatever good welcome is given them is owed to them by custom and by right, in payment for the unbearable hardship they suffer looking for adventures night and day, in winter and in summer, on foot and on horseback, in thirst and in hunger, in heat and in cold, exposed to all the inclemencies of heaven and to all the discomforts of earth."

"That has very little to do with me," answered the innkeeper. "Pay me what is owing to me, and let us have no more tales or chivalries; the only account I keep is the one for collecting what belongs to me."

"You are a fool and a bad innkeeper," answered Don Quixote.

And putting his legs to Rocinante and levelling his pike, he rode out of the inn without anybody stopping him; and without looking to see whether his squire was following, he got a good distance off.

The innkeeper, who saw him go without paying, went to collect from Sancho Panza; who said that since his master had refused to pay, he would not pay either, because, being squire to a knight errant as he was, the same rule and reason held for him as for his master about not paying anything in inns and taverns. The innkeeper was very much annoyed at this, and threatened him that if he did not pay he would collect it in a way he would be sorry for. To which Sancho answered that, by the law of chivalry his master had received, he would not pay a single copper if it cost him his life; because he was not going to let the good old custom of knights errant be lost on his account, nor were the squires of such knights who were still to come into the world going to complain of him and reproach him with breaking so just a privilege.

It was poor Sancho's bad luck that among the people in the inn there happened to be four wool-carders from Segovia, three needle-makers from the Colt quarter of Córdoba, and two men from the Fair district of Seville — a merry crowd, well-meaning, mischievous and playful; who, almost as if they had been prompted and moved by one and the same spirit, came up to Sancho and pulled him off the ass. One of them went in for the blanket off the innkeeper's bed, and tipping Sancho into it they looked up and saw that the ceiling was rather lower than they needed for their work, and decided to go out into the yard, which had the sky for its ceiling. And there, with Sancho in the middle of the blanket, they began to toss him up in the air and to amuse themselves with him as people do with a dog at carnival time.

The shouts the wretched blanketed man let out were so many that they reached his master's ears; who, deciding to stop and listen carefully, believed some new adventure was coming his way — until he plainly recognised that the man shouting was his squire. And turning his reins, he came up to the inn at a laboured gallop; and finding it shut, he rode round it to see whether he could find any way in. But he had not got as far as the walls of the yard, which were not very high, when he saw the bad game they were playing with his squire. He saw him go up and down through the air with such grace and quickness that, if his anger had let him, I am inclined to think he would have laughed. He tried to climb from the horse onto the top of the wall, but he was so pounded and broken that he could not even dismount; and so, from on top of the horse, he began to hurl so many insults and abuses at the men who were tossing Sancho that it is not possible to write them down. But for all that they did not stop laughing or stop their work, nor did the flying Sancho leave off his complaints, mixed now with threats and now with entreaties; but it was all of very little use, and no use at all, until out of sheer weariness they let him be.

They brought his ass over to him and helped him up on it, and wrapped him in his coat. And Maritornes, who was a compassionate soul, seeing him so exhausted, thought it right to help him out with a jug of water, and so she fetched him one from the well, it being colder there. Sancho took it and was raising it to his mouth when he stopped at the shouts his master was giving him:

"Sancho, my son, don't drink water! My son, don't drink it, it will kill you! Look — I have the most holy balm here" — and he showed him the can of the brew — "and with two drops of that you will be cured beyond a doubt."

At these shouts Sancho turned his eyes sideways at him and said, in louder ones still:

"Has your worship forgotten, by any chance, that I am not a knight? Or do you want me to finish bringing up what is left of my insides from last night? Keep your liquor and all the devils along with it, and leave me alone."

And to finish saying this and to begin drinking were all one; but as at the first swallow he saw that it was water, he did not want to go any further with it, and begged Maritornes to bring him some wine, which she did with a very good will, and paid for it out of her own money. For it is said of her that, although she was in that line of work, she had certain shades and distant hints of a Christian about her.

As soon as Sancho had drunk, he dug his heels into his ass; and the inn door being thrown wide open for him, he rode out of it very well pleased at not having paid anything and at having got his own way, even though it had been at the expense of his usual sureties, which were his shoulders. It is true that the innkeeper kept his saddlebags in payment of what was owing; but Sancho never missed them, he came out in such a state. The innkeeper wanted to bar the door properly as soon as he saw him outside, but the blanket-men would not have it — a crowd who, even if Don Quixote had genuinely been one of the knights errant of the Round Table, would not have valued him at two farthings.

Chapter 18: In Which Are Set Down the Words That Passed Between Sancho Panza and His Master Don Quixote, with Other Adventures Worth Relating

Sancho reached his master so wilted and faint that he could not urge his donkey along. When Don Quixote saw him in that state he said:

"Now, my good Sancho, I am finally convinced that that castle, or inn, is enchanted beyond a doubt; because those men who amused themselves with you so outrageously — what could they be but phantoms and people from the other world? And I confirm it by the fact that when I was at the wall of the yard watching the acts of your sad tragedy, it was not possible for me to climb it, nor could I even get down off Rocinante, because they must have had me under an enchantment. For I swear to you, on the faith of what I am, that if I could have climbed up or got down I would have avenged you in such a way that those villains and scoundrels would have remembered the joke for ever — even if in doing it I had knowingly gone against the laws of chivalry, which, as I have often told you already, do not allow a knight to lay a hand on a man who is not one, except in defence of his own life and person in a case of urgent and great necessity."

"I would have avenged myself too if I could, knight or no knight; but I couldn't. Though it's my belief that those men who had their fun with me were not phantoms or enchanted men, as your worship says, but men of flesh and bone like ourselves. And every one of them, from what I heard them called while they were tossing me, had his own name: one of them was called Pedro Martínez and another Tenorio Hernández, and I heard that the innkeeper was called Juan Palomeque the Left-handed. So, sir, your not being able to get over the yard wall or down off your horse was something other than enchantments. And what I get clear out of all this is that these adventures we go about looking for are going to bring us, in the end, to so many misadventures that we shan't know which is our right foot. And what would be better and more sensible, according to my poor understanding, would be for us to go back to our village, now it's harvest time and there's the farm to see to, and give up gadding about from pillar to post and from ditch to bucket, as they say."

"How little you know, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "about the business of chivalry! Be quiet and have patience, for the day will come when you will see with your own eyes what an honourable thing it is to follow this calling. If not, tell me: what greater satisfaction can there be in the world, or what pleasure can equal that of winning a battle and triumphing over one's enemy? None, beyond any doubt."

"That must be so," answered Sancho, "although I know nothing about it. All I know is that since we became knights errant — or your worship did, for there's no reason to count me in so honourable a number — we have never won a single battle except the one with the Basque, and even out of that your worship came with half an ear and half a helmet the less. From then till now it has been all sticks and more sticks, punches and more punches, with me getting the blanket-tossing on top of it, and having it done to me by enchanted persons I can't take revenge on — so that I might find out how far the pleasure of beating your enemy goes, as your worship says."

"That is the grief I have, and the one you ought to have, Sancho," answered Don Quixote. "But from now on I shall try to get hold of a sword made with such mastery that no kind of enchantment can be worked on the man who carries it. And it might even be that fortune would bring me the one belonging to Amadis when he called himself the Knight of the Burning Sword, which was one of the best swords any knight in the world ever had; because, besides having the virtue I have mentioned, it cut like a razor, and there was no armour, however strong or however enchanted, that could stand in its way."

"I am so lucky," said Sancho, "that when that happened and your worship did come to find a sword like that, it would turn out to serve and benefit dubbed knights only, like the balm; and the squires can go hang."

"Don't be afraid of that, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "heaven will do better than that by you."

Don Quixote and his squire were going along in this conversation when Don Quixote saw a great thick cloud of dust coming towards them along the road they were on; and seeing it, he turned to Sancho and said:

"This is the day, Sancho, on which the good fortune my luck has in store for me is to be seen. This is the day, I say, on which the valour of my arm is to be shown as much as on any other, and on which I am to do deeds that will stay written in the book of Fame for all the centuries to come. Do you see that cloud of dust rising over there, Sancho? Well, the whole of it is thick with an enormous army made up of various and innumerable peoples, marching along that way."

"By that reckoning there must be two," said Sancho, "because over here on the opposite side there's another cloud of dust just like it going up."

Don Quixote turned to look at it and saw that it was true; and being extraordinarily pleased, he concluded without a shadow of doubt that they were two armies coming to attack and meet each other in the middle of that broad plain. For at every hour and every moment his fancy was full of those battles, enchantments, incidents, absurdities, loves and challenges that are told of in the books of chivalry, and everything he said or thought or did was directed towards things of that kind. And the cloud of dust he had seen was being raised by two great flocks of sheep and rams coming along that same road from two different directions, which, because of the dust, could not be made out until they came close. And Don Quixote insisted so vehemently that they were armies that Sancho came to believe it and to say to him:

"Sir, what are we to do, then?"

"Do?" said Don Quixote. "Favour and help the needy and the defenceless. And you must know, Sancho, that the one coming towards our front is led and commanded by the great emperor Alifanfarón, lord of the great island of Taprobana; this other one marching at my back belongs to his enemy, the king of the Garamantes, Pentapolin of the Rolled-up Sleeve, because he always goes into battle with his right arm bare."

"But why do these two lords dislike each other so much?" asked Sancho.

"They dislike each other," answered Don Quixote, "because this Alifanfarón is a raging pagan and is in love with Pentapolin's daughter, who is a very beautiful and moreover very charming lady, and a Christian; and her father will not hand her over to the pagan king unless he first gives up the law of his false prophet Mohammed and comes over to hers."

"By my beard," said Sancho, "if Pentapolin isn't doing exactly right, and I mean to help him all I can!"

"In that you will be doing what you ought, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "because to go into battles of this kind it is not required that a man be a dubbed knight."

"I understand that well enough," answered Sancho; "but where are we to put this ass so that we can be sure of finding him again when the scuffle is over? Because I don't believe going into one mounted on that sort of steed has been the custom up to now."

"That is true," said Don Quixote. "What you can do with him is leave him to his own adventures, whether he gets lost or not; because we shall have so many horses after we come out victorious that even Rocinante is in danger of my exchanging him for another. But listen to me carefully and look, for I want to give you an account of the chief knights coming in these two armies. And so that you may see them and note them better, let us withdraw to that little rise over there, from which the two armies must be visible."

They did so, and stationed themselves on a hillock from which the two flocks that Don Quixote had made into armies would have been perfectly visible if the clouds of dust they were raising had not blurred and blinded the view. But for all that, seeing in his imagination what he neither saw nor was there, he began to say in a raised voice:

"That knight you see over there in the yellow armour, who carries on his shield a crowned lion lying at a maiden's feet, is the valorous Laurcalco, lord of the Silver Bridge. The other one in the armour with gold flowers, who carries on his shield three silver crowns on a blue field, is the dreaded Micocolembo, grand duke of Quirocia. The other one with the giant limbs on his right hand is the never-frightened Brandabarbarán of Boliche, lord of the three Arabias, who comes armed in that serpent's skin and has for a shield a door which, by all report, is one of those of the temple Samson pulled down when with his own death he took vengeance on his enemies.

"But turn your eyes this other way and you will see, in front of and at the head of this other army, the always victorious and never vanquished Timonel of Carcajona, prince of New Biscay, who comes armed in armour quartered blue, green, white and yellow, and carries on his shield a gold cat on a tawny field, with a motto that says Miau, which is the beginning of the name of his lady, who is said to be the peerless Miulina, daughter of the duke Alfeñiquén of the Algarve. The other one, who loads and weighs down the loins of that powerful mare and comes in armour as white as snow with a white shield and no device at all, is a new knight, French by nation, called Pierres Papin, lord of the baronies of Utrique. The other one, who is beating the flanks of that dappled, nimble zebra with his iron heels and carries the arms of the blue vairs, is the mighty duke of Nerbia, Espartafilardo of the Wood, who has for a device on his shield an asparagus plant, with a motto in Castilian that says: My fortune creeps."

And in this way he went on naming a great many knights of the one squadron and the other that he was imagining, and gave every one of them his arms, colours, devices and mottoes off the top of his head, carried away by the imagination of that madness of his such as was never seen before. And without stopping he went on:

"This squadron in front of us is formed and made up of people of various nations. Here are those who drank the sweet waters of the famous Xanthus; the mountain men who tread the Massylian fields; those who sift the finest and smallest gold in happy Arabia; those who enjoy the famous cool banks of the clear Thermodon; those who bleed golden Pactolus by many and various channels; the Numidians, unreliable in their promises; the Persians, famous for bows and arrows; the Parthians and the Medes, who fight as they run away; the Arabs, whose houses move; the Scythians, as cruel as they are fair-skinned; the Ethiopians with their pierced lips; and infinite other nations whose faces I know and see, although I cannot recall their names.

"In this other squadron come those who drink the crystal streams of the olive-bearing Betis; those who smooth and polish their faces with the liquor of the ever rich and golden Tagus; those who enjoy the profitable waters of the divine Genil; those who tread the fields of Tartessos, abundant in pasture; those who take their pleasure in the Elysian meadows of Jerez; the men of La Mancha, rich and crowned with golden ears of corn; those clothed in iron, ancient relics of the Gothic blood; those who bathe in the Pisuerga, famous for the gentleness of its current; those who pasture their flocks in the wide meadows of the winding Guadiana, celebrated for its hidden course; those who shiver with the cold of the wooded Pyrenees and with the white flakes of the lofty Apennine; in short, all that Europe holds and encloses within itself."

Good God, how many provinces he named, how many nations he called over, giving each one, with marvellous quickness, the attributes that belonged to it — wholly absorbed and steeped in what he had read in his lying books! Sancho Panza hung on his words without saying any of his own, and every now and then turned his head to see whether he could catch sight of the knights and giants his master was naming; and as he could make out none of them, he said:

"Sir, I commend to the devil any man, or giant, or knight of all the ones your worship is talking about that shows up anywhere in all this — at least, I can't see them. Perhaps it's all enchantment, like the phantoms last night."

"How can you say that?" answered Don Quixote. "Can't you hear the neighing of the horses, the sounding of the trumpets, the noise of the drums?"

"I hear nothing," answered Sancho, "except a great deal of bleating of sheep and rams."

And that was the truth, because the two flocks were coming close by now.

"The fear you are in," said Don Quixote, "is making you neither see nor hear straight, Sancho; because one of the effects of fear is to confuse the senses and make things seem other than they are. And if you are so much afraid, get away to one side and leave me alone; alone I am enough to give the victory to whichever side I give my help to."

And saying this he put spurs to Rocinante, and with his lance in the rest went down the slope like a thunderbolt. Sancho shouted after him:

"Come back, your worship, Señor Don Quixote! I swear to God they're rams and sheep you're going to charge! Come back — cursed be the father that begot me! What madness is this? Look, there isn't a giant or a knight, or cats, or armour, or shields quartered or whole, or blue vairs or devilish ones. What are you doing? Sinner that I am before God!"

Not even for that did Don Quixote turn back; instead he went on shouting at the top of his voice:

"Now then, knights, all of you who follow and serve under the banners of the valorous emperor Pentapolin of the Rolled-up Sleeve — follow me, all of you! You shall see how easily I give him his revenge on his enemy Alifanfarón of Taprobana!"

Saying this, he charged into the middle of the squadron of sheep and began to spear them with as much courage and daring as if he were really spearing his mortal enemies. The shepherds and drovers who were with the flock shouted at him to stop; but seeing that it was no use, they unfastened their slings and began to salute his ears with stones the size of your fist. Don Quixote paid no attention to the stones; instead, riding about in all directions, he was saying:

"Where are you, arrogant Alifanfarón? Come out to me. I am a single knight, and I want to try your strength man to man and take your life from you, in payment for the life you are taking from the valorous Pentapolin of the Garamantes."

At this moment a pebble came along from the brook — one of the smooth white ones they call sugared almonds — and hitting him in the side, buried two of his ribs in his body. Finding himself so badly handled, he was sure he was dead or mortally wounded; and remembering his liquor, he pulled out his can and put it to his mouth and began to pour the liquor into his stomach. But before he had finished getting down what seemed to him enough, along came another almond and hit him so squarely on the hand and on the can that it smashed the can to pieces, taking three or four teeth and molars out of his mouth on its way and badly crushing two fingers of his hand.

Such was the first blow, and such the second, that the poor knight had no choice but to come down off the horse. The shepherds came up to him and believed they had killed him; and so, in great haste, they rounded up their flock and loaded up the dead beasts, of which there were more than seven, and without looking into anything further they went off.

All this time Sancho was up on the slope watching the mad things his master was doing, tearing at his beard and cursing the hour and the moment fortune had introduced him to the man. Seeing him, then, fallen on the ground and the shepherds gone by now, he came down off the slope and went over to him, and found him in a very bad way, though he had not lost consciousness, and said to him:

"Didn't I tell you, Señor Don Quixote, to come back, and that what you were going to attack were not armies but flocks of rams?"

"That is how that thieving enchanter, my enemy, can make things disappear and counterfeit them. You must know, Sancho, that it is a very easy matter for such people to make us see whatever they like; and this malignant creature who persecutes me, envious of the glory he saw I was going to win from this battle, has turned the squadrons of enemies into flocks of sheep. If you don't believe it, do one thing for me, Sancho, on my life, so that you may be undeceived and see that what I tell you is true. Get up on your ass and follow them quietly, and you will see how, when they have gone a little way from here, they turn back into what they were at first, and stop being rams and become men, whole and upright, exactly as I described them to you before. But don't go now, because I need your help and support. Come here to me and look how many teeth and molars I am missing, for it seems to me I haven't one left in my mouth."

Sancho came so close that he almost put his eyes into his mouth — and it was just at the moment when the balm had done its work in Don Quixote's stomach. And at the very instant Sancho got there to look into his mouth, he shot out everything he had inside him, harder than out of a musket, and landed the whole of it in the compassionate squire's beard.

"Holy Mary!" said Sancho. "And what is this that's happened to me? There's no doubt the poor sinner is wounded to death, since he's vomiting blood out of his mouth."

But looking into it a little more closely, he made out by the colour, taste and smell that it was not blood but the balm out of the can that he had seen him drink; and he was so disgusted that his stomach turned over and he vomited his insides up all over his own master, and the pair of them were left as fine as pearls. Sancho went to his ass to get something out of the saddlebags to clean himself with and to see to his master; and when he could not find them he came near to losing his wits. He cursed himself all over again, and resolved in his heart to leave his master and go home, even if he lost the wages for what he had served and his hopes of the government of the promised isle.

At this Don Quixote got up, and putting his left hand over his mouth so that the rest of his teeth should not fall out, he took hold with the other of Rocinante's reins — for the horse had never stirred from his master's side, so loyal and well-conditioned was he — and went over to where his squire was, leaning on his ass with his hand against his cheek, looking like a man deep in thought. And seeing him in that condition, with every sign of such sadness, Don Quixote said to him:

"You must know, Sancho, that one man is no more than another unless he does more than another. All these squalls that come on us are signs that the weather will soon clear and things will go well for us; because it is not possible for either the bad or the good to last, and it follows from this that, the bad having lasted a long time, the good must be close. So you ought not to distress yourself over the misfortunes that happen to me, since you get no share of them."

"How do I not?" answered Sancho. "Was the man they tossed in a blanket yesterday, by any chance, anybody but my father's son? And the saddlebags I'm missing today, with all my valuables in them — do they belong to anybody but the same man?"

"You are missing the saddlebags, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"That I am," answered Sancho.

"In that case we have nothing to eat today," replied Don Quixote.

"That would be so," answered Sancho, "if there were none of those herbs to be found in these meadows that your worship says he knows, the ones that knights errant as unlucky as your worship generally make up such shortages with."

"For all that," answered Don Quixote, "I would rather have at this moment a quarter-loaf of bread, or a whole loaf and two heads of salt herring, than all the herbs Dioscorides describes, even in the edition illustrated by Doctor Laguna. But in spite of everything, get up on your donkey, my good Sancho, and come along after me; for God, who provides for all things, will not fail us, the more so as we are so much about his service as we are — since he does not fail the gnats in the air, or the little worms in the earth, or the tadpoles in the water; and he is so merciful that he makes his sun rise on the good and on the wicked, and sends his rain on the unjust and the just."

"Your worship," said Sancho, "would have made a better preacher than a knight errant."

"Knights errant knew about everything and have to know about everything, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "because in past ages there was a knight errant who would stop and deliver a sermon or a discourse in the middle of an army camp as though he had taken his degree at the University of Paris; from which it may be inferred that the lance never blunted the pen, nor the pen the lance."

"Very well then, let it be as your worship says," answered Sancho. "Let us get away from here now and try to find somewhere to lodge tonight; and please God it may be in a place where there are no blankets, nor blanket-men, nor phantoms, nor enchanted Moors — because if there are, I'll give the whole business to the devil, bag and baggage."

"Ask God for it yourself, my son," said Don Quixote, "and lead on wherever you like, for this time I want to leave our lodging to your choice. But give me your hand here and feel with your finger, and look carefully at how many teeth and molars I am missing on this right side of the upper jaw, which is where I feel the pain."

Sancho put his fingers in, and while he was feeling about he said:

"How many molars did your worship use to have on this side?"

"Four," answered Don Quixote, "not counting the wisdom tooth, all of them whole and very sound."

"Your worship should think carefully about what you're saying, sir," answered Sancho.

"I say four, if it was not five," answered Don Quixote; "because in the whole of my life I have never had a tooth or a molar pulled out of my mouth, nor has one fallen out or been eaten away by decay or by any rheum."

"Well, on this lower part," said Sancho, "your worship has no more than two molars and a half; and on the upper, not half a one nor any at all — it's as smooth up there as the palm of my hand."

"Unlucky man that I am!" said Don Quixote, hearing the sad news his squire gave him. "I would rather they had cut off an arm, as long as it was not my sword arm; because I would have you know, Sancho, that a mouth without molars is like a mill without a millstone, and a tooth is to be prized far above a diamond. But we who profess the strict order of chivalry are subject to all this. Mount up, my friend, and lead on, and I will follow you at whatever pace you like."

Sancho did so, and set off towards where he thought he might find shelter, without leaving the high road, which ran very straight along there. Going along little by little, then — because the pain in Don Quixote's jaws would not let him settle or attend to making any speed — Sancho decided to entertain him and take his mind off it by telling him something; and among the other things he said was what will be told in the following chapter.

Chapter 19: Of the Sensible Remarks Sancho Exchanged with His Master, and of the Adventure That Happened to Him with a Dead Body, and Other Famous Events

"It seems to me, sir, that all these misfortunes that have been happening to us these last few days have without any doubt been a punishment for the sin your worship committed against the order of your chivalry, in not keeping the oath you swore not to eat bread off a tablecloth or take your pleasure with the queen, and all the rest of it that goes with that and that your worship swore to keep, until you took that helmet of Malandrino's, or whatever the Moor's name is — I don't remember it properly."

"You are quite right, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "but to tell you the truth, it had gone clean out of my memory. And you may also take it as certain that the business of the blanket happened to you through your own fault in not reminding me of it in time. But I shall make amends, for there are ways of composition in the order of chivalry for everything."

"But did I swear anything, by any chance?" answered Sancho.

"It does not matter that you have not sworn," said Don Quixote. "It is enough that I understand you are not very safe from being an accessory; and one way or the other, it will do no harm to provide ourselves with a remedy."

"Well, if that's how it is," said Sancho, "mind your worship doesn't go and forget this too, the way you forgot about the oath. Perhaps the phantoms will get the urge to amuse themselves with me all over again — and with your worship too, if they see you so stubborn."

They were in this and other talk when night caught them in the middle of the road, without their having or being able to find anywhere to take shelter that night. And what was worse about it was that they were dying of hunger; for with the loss of the saddlebags they had lost the whole of their larder and provisions. And to complete this misfortune, an adventure happened to them which, without any contrivance at all, genuinely looked like one.

It came about like this. Night closed in with some darkness; but for all that they kept going, Sancho believing that since this was the high road he would in all reason find some inn on it within a league or two. Going along, then, in this fashion — the night dark, the squire hungry and the master with an appetite for his dinner — they saw coming towards them along the very road they were on a great multitude of lights, which looked like nothing so much as moving stars. Sancho was thunderstruck at the sight of them, and Don Quixote was not entirely at his ease. The one pulled at his ass's halter and the other at his hack's reins, and they stood still, watching attentively to see what this might be; and they saw that the lights kept getting nearer, and the nearer they came the bigger they looked. At which sight Sancho began to shake like a man with quicksilver in him, and Don Quixote's hair stood on end; and Don Quixote, plucking up a little courage, said:

"This, Sancho, must without any doubt be a very great and very dangerous adventure, in which it will be necessary for me to show all my valour and my strength."

"Unlucky me!" answered Sancho. "If this adventure should happen to be one of phantoms, as it is beginning to look to me, where are the ribs to be found that can put up with it?"

"However much they may be phantoms," said Don Quixote, "I shall not let them touch a thread of your clothing. If they made a joke of you the other time, it was because I could not get over the walls of the yard; but now we are out in open country, where I can wield my sword exactly as I please."

"And if they enchant you and stiffen you up as they did the other time," said Sancho, "what good will it do to be in open country or not?"

"For all that," replied Don Quixote, "I beg you, Sancho, to keep your courage up; experience will show you the courage I have."

"I will keep it up, if it please God," answered Sancho.

And the two of them drew off to one side of the road and went back to watching attentively to see what all this business of the travelling lights could be. And very shortly afterwards they made out a great many men in white robes, whose fearful appearance finished off Sancho Panza's courage altogether: he began to knock his teeth together like a man shivering with the ague, and the knocking and chattering got worse when they saw clearly what it was. For they made out as many as twenty of the white-robed men, all on horseback, with lighted torches in their hands; behind whom came a litter draped in mourning, followed by another six riders in mourning down to the feet of their mules — which they could tell were not horses by the quiet way they went. The white-robed men were murmuring among themselves in a low, pitying voice.

This strange vision, at such an hour and in such a lonely place, was quite enough to put fear into Sancho's heart, and even into his master's; and so it would have been in Don Quixote's case — for Sancho's courage had already gone to pieces. The opposite happened to his master: at that moment it presented itself vividly to his imagination that this was one of the adventures out of his books. He fancied that the litter was a bier carrying some sorely wounded or dead knight whose vengeance was reserved for him alone; and without any further reasoning he levelled his pike, settled himself firmly in the saddle, and with a fine spirit and bearing placed himself in the middle of the road along which the white-robed men had to pass. And when he saw them close by, he raised his voice and said:

"Halt, knights, or whoever you may be, and give me an account of who you are, where you come from, where you are going, and what it is you are carrying on that bier. For by all appearances either you have done, or somebody has done to you, some outrage; and it is fitting and necessary that I should know of it, either to punish you for the wrong you have done, or to avenge you for the injury that has been done to you."

"We are in a hurry," answered one of the white-robed men, "and the inn is a long way off, and we cannot stop to give as long an account as you ask for."

And spurring his mule, he went on past. Don Quixote took this answer very much amiss, and grabbing the bridle he said:

"Halt, and be better bred, and give me an account of what I have asked you; if not, you are all in battle with me."

The mule was a nervous one, and on being seized by the bridle it took such fright that it reared up and threw its master to the ground over its hindquarters. A servant who was going along on foot, seeing the white-robed man come down, began to abuse Don Quixote; who, thoroughly angry by now, levelled his pike without waiting for any more and charged one of the mourners, and brought him down badly wounded on the ground. And wheeling round on the rest of them, it was a thing worth seeing, the speed with which he attacked and scattered them; it looked for all the world as if wings had sprouted on Rocinante at that instant, so lightly and so proudly did he go.

The white-robed men were all timid people and unarmed, and so they easily left the fight in a moment and set off running across that field with their lighted torches, looking exactly like masqueraders running about on a night of merrymaking and festival. The mourners, for their part, were so tangled and wrapped up in their long skirts and gowns that they could not move; and so, in complete safety, Don Quixote cudgelled the lot of them and made them quit the place very much against their will — because they all thought this was no man but a devil out of hell, come out to take from them the dead body they were carrying in the litter. Sancho watched the whole thing, marvelling at his master's fire, and said to himself:

"There is no doubt about it, this master of mine is as brave and as strong as he says he is."

There was a torch burning on the ground next to the first man the mule had thrown, by whose light Don Quixote was able to see him; and coming up to him, he put the point of his pike in his face, telling him to surrender or he would kill him. To which the fallen man answered:

"I am surrendered enough already, since I cannot move — I have a broken leg. I beg your worship, if you are a Christian knight, not to kill me; you would be committing a great sacrilege, for I am a licentiate and I have taken minor orders."

"Then who the devil brought you here," said Don Quixote, "since you are a churchman?"

"Who, sir?" replied the fallen man. "My bad luck."

"Then a worse one is threatening you," said Don Quixote, "unless you satisfy me on everything I asked you before."

"Your worship shall be satisfied easily," answered the licentiate. "And so your worship must know that although I said just now that I was a licentiate, I am only a bachelor of arts, and my name is Alonso López. I come from the city of Baeza with eleven other priests, the ones who ran off with the torches. We are going to the city of Segovia, accompanying a dead body which is in that litter — that of a gentleman who died in Baeza, where he was left for the time being; and now, as I say, we were taking his bones to his tomb, which is in Segovia, where he was born."

"And who killed him?" asked Don Quixote.

"God, by means of a pestilential fever he caught," answered the bachelor.

"In that case," said Don Quixote, "Our Lord has taken from me the trouble I should have had in avenging his death, if anybody else had killed him. But since the one who killed him did kill him, there is nothing for it but to keep quiet and shrug my shoulders, because I should do the same if he killed me myself. And I should like your reverence to know that I am a knight of La Mancha, called Don Quixote, and that my office and calling is to travel the world putting the crooked straight and undoing injuries."

"I don't know how that can be about putting the crooked straight," said the bachelor, "since you have turned me from straight to crooked, leaving me with a broken leg that will never be seen straight again as long as it lives. And the injury you have undone in me has been to leave me injured in such a way that I shall stay injured for ever. And it has been misfortune enough to run into you, who go about looking for adventures."

"Not all things," answered Don Quixote, "happen in the same way. The damage lay, Señor Bachelor Alonso López, in your coming as you did, by night, dressed in those surplices, with lighted torches, praying, covered in mourning — so that you looked exactly like something evil out of the other world. And so I could not fail to do my duty by attacking you, and I would have attacked you even if I had known for certain that you were the actual satans of hell, which is what I judged and always took you for."

"Since my luck has willed it so," said the bachelor, "I beg your worship, sir knight errant — who have given me such a bad turn — to help me get out from under this mule, which has my leg caught between the stirrup and the saddle."

"I might have gone on talking till tomorrow!" said Don Quixote. "And how long were you going to wait before telling me your trouble?"

He at once shouted to Sancho Panza to come; but Sancho did not trouble to come, because he was busy stripping a pack-mule those good gentlemen had brought along with them, very well stocked with things to eat. Sancho made a sack out of his coat, and gathering up everything he could get and everything that would fit into the bag, he loaded his donkey; and then he answered his master's shouts and helped to get the bachelor out from the weight of the mule. And putting him up on it, they gave him his torch; and Don Quixote told him to follow the track of his companions and to beg their pardon on his behalf for the injury, which it had not been in his power to avoid doing them. And Sancho said to him too:

"If those gentlemen should happen to want to know who the valiant man was who put them in that state, your worship may tell them it was the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha, who by another name is called the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance."

With that the bachelor went off; and Don Quixote asked Sancho what had moved him to call him the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance just then rather than at any other time.

"I'll tell you," answered Sancho. "It's because I have been looking at you for a while by the light of that torch that poor unfortunate is carrying, and your worship really does have the worst-looking face I have ever seen in my life — the worst lately, at any rate. And it must have been caused either by the exhaustion of this fight or by the lack of the teeth and molars."

"It is not that," answered Don Quixote, "but that the wise man whose business it is to write the history of my deeds must have thought it well that I should take some sort of by-name, as all the knights of the past used to do. One called himself the Knight of the Burning Sword; another, the Knight of the Unicorn; that one, the Knight of the Maidens; this one, the Knight of the Phoenix; another, the Knight of the Griffin; another again, the Knight of Death — and by these names and emblems they were known all over the round world. And so I say that the wise man I have mentioned must have put it on your tongue and into your thoughts just now to call me the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, which is what I intend to call myself from today on. And so that the name may suit me better, I mean to have a very sorrowful figure painted on my shield when I get the chance."

"There's no need to spend time and money on having that figure painted," said Sancho. "What ought to be done is for your worship to uncover your own and show your face to the people who look at you; and without anything more and without any other picture or shield they'll call you the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance. And believe me, I'm telling you the truth, because I promise your worship — and let this be said in fun — that hunger and the missing molars give you such a bad face that, as I've said already, the sorrowful painting can very well be spared."

Don Quixote laughed at Sancho's wit, but for all that he resolved to call himself by that name as soon as he could have his shield, or buckler, painted as he had imagined it.

At this the bachelor came back and said to Don Quixote:

"I was forgetting to tell you: your worship should be aware that you are excommunicated for having laid violent hands on a holy thing — juxta illud: Si quis suadente diabolo, and so on."

"I do not understand that Latin," answered Don Quixote, "but I know very well that I did not lay hands on you, only this pike. What is more, I did not think I was assaulting priests or things belonging to the Church, which I respect and adore as the Catholic and faithful Christian I am, but phantoms and monsters from the other world. And even if that were how it was, I have in my memory what happened to the Cid Ruy Díaz when he smashed the chair of that king's ambassador in front of His Holiness the Pope, for which the Pope excommunicated him — and that day the good Rodrigo de Vivar went about as a very honourable and valiant knight."

On hearing this the bachelor went off, as has been said, without answering him a word. Don Quixote wanted to look and see whether the body in the litter was bones or not, but Sancho would not have it, saying:

"Sir, your worship has finished this dangerous adventure more safely than any of the ones I have seen. These people, although they were beaten and scattered, might just possibly realise that it was one man alone who beat them, and, ashamed and embarrassed about it, get themselves together again and come looking for us and give us something to think about. The donkey is as he ought to be, the hills are close, hunger is pressing, and there is nothing to do but retire in good order; and, as they say, let the dead go to the grave and the living to the loaf."

And driving his ass in front of him, he asked his master to follow; who, thinking Sancho was right, followed him without arguing any further. And after they had gone a little way between two small hills they found themselves in a wide, hidden valley, where they dismounted. Sancho unloaded the donkey, and stretched out on the green grass, with hunger for their sauce, they breakfasted, lunched, had their tea and had their supper all at the same time, satisfying their stomachs with more than one cold pie that the dead man's reverend gentlemen — who rarely let themselves go short — had been carrying on their pack-mule of supplies.

But another misfortune befell them, which Sancho considered the worst of the lot: they had no wine to drink, nor even any water to put to their lips. And, harried by thirst, Sancho — seeing that the meadow they were in was thick with fine green grass — said what will be told in the following chapter.

Chapter 20: Of the Unheard-Of and Unparalleled Adventure Achieved by the Valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha with Less Danger Than Any Ever Achieved by Any Famous Knight in the World

"It isn't possible, my dear sir, but that this grass is evidence that there must be some spring or stream close by that keeps it damp. So it would be a good idea for us to go a little further on, and we shall come across somewhere to relieve this terrible thirst that is wearing us out — which without any doubt causes more suffering than hunger does."

Don Quixote thought the advice good; and taking Rocinante by the rein, and Sancho his ass by the halter after loading onto him the leavings of the supper, they began to make their way up the meadow by touch, because the darkness of the night let them see nothing at all. But they had not gone two hundred paces when there came to their ears a great noise of water, as though it were falling from some great high crags. The noise delighted them enormously; and stopping to listen and make out which direction it was coming from, they heard all at once another din that watered down their pleasure at the water — Sancho's especially, since he was naturally timid and of small courage.

What they heard, I say, was blows being struck in a steady rhythm, with a certain creaking of iron and chains, which, accompanied by the furious din of the water, would have put terror into any heart other than Don Quixote's. The night, as has been said, was dark, and they happened to have got in among some tall trees whose leaves, moved by the soft wind, made a low and frightening sound. So that the loneliness, the place, the darkness, the noise of the water and the whispering of the leaves — all of it caused horror and dread, especially when they found that the blows did not stop, and the wind did not sleep, and the morning did not come; with the addition to all this of not knowing where they were. But Don Quixote, with his intrepid heart for company, leapt onto Rocinante, and bracing his buckler on his arm and levelling his pike, he said:

"Friend Sancho, you must know that I was born, by heaven's will, in this iron age of ours in order to bring back to life in it the age of gold, or the golden age as it is usually called. I am the man for whom are reserved the dangers, the great exploits, the valorous deeds. I am, I say again, the man who is to bring back the Knights of the Round Table, the Twelve Peers of France and the Nine Worthies, and who is to consign to oblivion the Platirs, the Tablantes, the Olivantes and Tirantes, the Phoebuses and Belianises, along with the whole crowd of the famous knights errant of the past, doing in this age I find myself in such great things, such strange things and such feats of arms as shall darken the brightest of theirs.

"You mark well, faithful and loyal squire, the darkness of this night, its strange silence, the muffled and confused noise of these trees, the fearful sound of that water we came looking for, which seems to be falling and hurling itself down from the high mountains of the moon, and that ceaseless hammering that wounds and hurts our ears. All of which things, together and each one on its own, are enough to instil fear, dread and terror in the breast of Mars himself, let alone in a man not used to incidents and adventures of the kind. Well, all this that I am painting for you is fuel and a spur to my courage, which is already making my heart burst in my breast with the desire it has to take on this adventure, however difficult it shows itself to be.

"So tighten Rocinante's girths a little, and God be with you, and wait for me here three days and no more; and if I have not come back within them, you may go back to our village, and from there, as a favour and a good turn to me, you will go to El Toboso, where you will tell my incomparable lady Dulcinea that her captive knight died attempting things that might make him worthy of being able to call himself hers."

When Sancho heard his master's words he began to weep with the greatest tenderness in the world and to say to him:

"Sir, I don't know why your worship wants to take on this terrifying adventure. It's night now, nobody can see us here, we can very well turn aside and get out of the danger even if we don't drink for three days; and since there's nobody to see us, there'll be nobody to mark us down as cowards. What's more, I've heard the priest of our village preach — the one your worship knows well — that whoever looks for danger dies in it. So it isn't right to tempt God by taking on such a monstrous business, where a man can't get out except by a miracle. And it's enough of them that heaven has worked for your worship already, in saving you from being tossed in a blanket as I was, and in bringing you out the winner, free and safe, from among all those enemies who were with the dead man.

"And if none of this moves or softens that hard heart, let it be moved by thinking and believing that your worship will hardly have got away from here before I, out of pure fright, give up my soul to whoever wants to carry it off. I left my own country and left children and wife to come and serve your worship, thinking I'd be worth more and not less; but as greed bursts the sack, so it has torn my hopes apart. Just when I had them liveliest, of getting that wretched, ill-starred isle your worship has promised me so many times, I find that in payment and exchange for it you now want to leave me in a place as far from human company as this. For the love of the one God, sir, let no such wrong be done me. And if your worship will not give up attempting this business altogether, at least put it off till the morning. For by what the science I learnt when I was a shepherd shows me, it can't be three hours from now to daybreak, because the mouth of the Horn is over our heads and midnight is on the line of the left arm."

"How can you tell, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "where that line falls, or where that mouth or that nape of the neck you speak of is, when the night is so dark that not a single star appears in the whole sky?"

"That's so," said Sancho; "but fear has a great many eyes and sees things underneath the ground, let alone up above in the sky. Besides which, by good reasoning it can easily be worked out that it isn't long from here to daylight."

"Let it be as long or as short as it likes," answered Don Quixote. "It shall not be said of me, now or at any time, that tears and entreaties turned me aside from doing what I owed to my knightly style. And so I beg you, Sancho, to be quiet; for God, who has put it into my heart to attempt this unheard-of and terrifying adventure now, will take care to look after my safety and to comfort your sorrow. What you have to do is tighten Rocinante's girths properly and stay here, for I shall be back soon, alive or dead."

Sancho, then, seeing his master's final resolve and how little his tears, advice and entreaties were worth with him, decided to make use of his own ingenuity and get him to wait for daylight if he could. And so, while he was tightening the horse's girths, quietly and without being noticed he tied Rocinante's two feet together with his ass's halter, so that when Don Quixote tried to set off he could not, because the horse could only move by jumping. Seeing the success of his trick, Sancho Panza said:

"There you are, sir: heaven, moved by my tears and my prayers, has ordained that Rocinante can't stir. And if you insist and spur him and beat him, it will be putting fortune out of temper and kicking, as they say, against the pricks."

Don Quixote was in despair at this; and the more he put his legs to the horse, the less he could move him. And without seeing through to the tying, he thought it best to calm down and wait either for daybreak or for Rocinante to move, believing beyond a doubt that this came from somewhere other than Sancho's ingenuity; and so he said to him:

"Since this is how it is, Sancho, and Rocinante cannot move, I am content to wait for the dawn to smile, even though I weep at how long she takes to come."

"There's no need to weep," answered Sancho, "for I'll keep your worship entertained by telling stories from now till daybreak — unless you want to get down and sleep a little on the green grass, the way knights errant do, so as to be more rested when the day comes and the moment for taking on this altogether extraordinary adventure that's waiting for you."

"What do you mean, get down? What do you mean, sleep?" said Don Quixote. "Am I by any chance one of those knights who take their rest in the middle of dangers? Sleep yourself, since you were born to sleep, or do whatever you like; I shall do what I see best fits my purpose."

"Don't be angry, my dear sir," answered Sancho, "I didn't mean anything by it."

And going up to him, he put one hand on the front of the saddle and the other on the back, so that he was left hugging his master's left thigh, not daring to move a finger's breadth away from him: such was the fear he had of the blows, which were still sounding away at their intervals. Don Quixote told him to tell some story to entertain him, as he had promised; to which Sancho said he would if the terror of what he was hearing would let him.

"But for all that, I'll make an effort to tell a story which, if I manage to tell it and nobody stops me, is the best of all stories. And let your worship pay attention, because I'm starting now.

"Once upon a time there was what there was, and may the good that comes be for everybody and the harm for whoever goes looking for it. And your worship should note, sir, that the beginning the ancients gave their tales was not just anything, but a saying of Cato the Senseless, the Roman, which goes: 'and the harm for whoever goes looking for it' — which fits here like a ring on a finger, so that your worship will keep still and not go looking for harm anywhere, and we'll go back by another road, since nobody is forcing us to follow this one where so many frights come over us."

"Get on with your story, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and leave the road we are to follow to me."

"I say, then," Sancho went on, "that in a village in Extremadura there was a shepherd who kept goats — I mean he was a goatherd — and this shepherd or goatherd, as I say, of my story was called Lope Ruiz; and this Lope Ruiz was in love with a shepherdess called Torralba, and this shepherdess called Torralba was the daughter of a rich stockman, and this rich stockman —"

"If you tell your story like that, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "saying everything twice over, you will not be finished in two days. Tell it straight through and tell it like a man of sense; and if not, don't tell it at all."

"The way I'm telling it," answered Sancho, "is the way all tales are told where I come from, and I don't know how to tell it any other way, and it isn't right for your worship to ask me to take up new customs."

"Tell it however you like," answered Don Quixote; "since fate wills that I cannot help listening to you, go on."

"So then, dear sir of my soul," Sancho went on, "as I've said already, this shepherd was in love with Torralba the shepherdess, who was a strapping girl, hard to handle and rather on the mannish side, because she had a bit of a moustache — I can see her now."

"So you knew her, then?" said Don Quixote.

"I didn't know her," answered Sancho, "but the man who told me this story told me it was so certain and true that when I told it to somebody else I could safely swear I'd seen the whole thing myself. So then, as the days came and the days went, the devil, who never sleeps and who tangles everything up, arranged it so that the love the shepherd had for the shepherdess turned into hatred and ill will. And the cause of it, according to spiteful tongues, was a certain quantity of little jealousies she gave him, of the kind that go past the line and get into forbidden country. And from then on the shepherd loathed her so much that, to avoid seeing her, he decided to get out of that part of the country and go where his eyes would never see her again. Torralba, finding herself scorned by Lope, straight away loved him better than she ever had before."

"That is women's nature," said Don Quixote: "to scorn the man who loves them and love the man who loathes them. Go on, Sancho."

"It so happened," said Sancho, "that the shepherd carried out what he'd decided; and driving his goats in front of him, he set off across the fields of Extremadura to cross over into the kingdom of Portugal. Torralba, who got to hear of it, went after him, and followed him on foot and barefoot a long way behind, with a staff in her hand and saddlebags round her neck, in which she carried — so it's said — a piece of a mirror and a bit of a comb and some little pot or other of face paint. But whatever she was carrying, which I don't mean to go into now, all I'll say is that they say the shepherd came with his flock to cross the river Guadiana, and at that season it was swollen and almost over its banks; and at the place where he arrived there was no boat or barge, and nobody to take him or his flock over to the other side. Which distressed him a great deal, because he could see Torralba coming up very close now and she'd give him a lot of grief with her pleading and her tears.

"But he went on looking about until he saw a fisherman who had a boat beside him — such a small one that only one person and one goat could fit in it. Even so, he spoke to him and settled with him to carry him and the three hundred goats he had with him across. The fisherman got into the boat and took one goat over; he came back and took another; he came back again and took another over."

And Sancho added: "Let your worship keep count of the goats the fisherman is taking over; because if you lose track of one of them, the story is finished and it won't be possible to tell another word of it.

"To go on, then, and I say that the landing place on the other side was full of mud and slippery, and the fisherman took a long time going and coming. For all that, he came back for another goat, and another, and another —"

"Take it that he has taken them all over," said Don Quixote. "Don't go coming and going like that, or you will not have got them across in a year."

"How many have gone over so far?" said Sancho.

"How the devil should I know?" answered Don Quixote.

"There you are, that's just what I said: that you should keep a good count. Well, by God, the story's finished, because there's no going on with it."

"How can that be?" answered Don Quixote. "Is knowing the exact number of goats that have gone over so essential to the story that if one of them is got wrong you cannot go on with it?"

"No, sir, not at all," answered Sancho. "But at the very instant I asked your worship to tell me how many goats had gone over and you answered that you didn't know, everything I had left to tell went clean out of my memory. And upon my word, there was a lot of virtue and enjoyment in it."

"So the story," said Don Quixote, "is finished already?"

"As finished as my own mother," said Sancho.

"I tell you truly," answered Don Quixote, "that you have told one of the newest tales, stories or histories that anybody in the world could have thought of; and that such a way of telling it and of leaving off will never be seen and can never have been seen in anyone's whole life — though I expected nothing else from your good sense. But I am not surprised, since perhaps these blows, which do not stop, must have got your understanding into a muddle."

"That may well be," answered Sancho, "but I know that where my story's concerned there's no more to say: it ends right where the mistake in counting the goats' crossing begins."

"Let it end where it likes, and welcome," said Don Quixote, "and let us see whether Rocinante can move."

He put his legs to him again, and again the horse gave a jump and stood still: he was tied that thoroughly.
