At this point it appears that either the cold of the morning, which was coming on, or something loosening that Sancho had eaten at supper, or that it was simply nature — which is what one ought most to believe — brought upon him the will and the desire to do what nobody else could do for him. But so much fear had got into his heart that he did not dare move the black of a fingernail away from his master. And to think of not doing what he needed to do was not possible either. So what he did, for the sake of peace, was to let go with his right hand, which he had hold of the back of the saddle with; and with it, quietly and without any noise at all, he undid the running knot his breeches were held up by, without help from any other; and once it was off, they came down at once and stayed round him like fetters. After this he lifted his shirt as best he could and put both his buttocks out into the air, which were not very small ones.

This done — and he thought it was the most he had to do to get out of that terrible strait and distress — another and a greater one came over him, which was that it seemed to him he could not relieve himself without making a racket and a noise. And he began to clench his teeth and hunch his shoulders, gathering in his breath as much as he possibly could. But with all these efforts he was so unlucky that in the end he came to make a little noise, quite different from the one that was frightening him so much. Don Quixote heard it and said:

"What sound is that, Sancho?"

"I don't know, sir," he answered. "It must be something new; adventures and misadventures never begin small."

He tried his luck again, and it went so well for him that with no more noise or disturbance than the last, he found himself free of the load that had given him so much trouble. But as Don Quixote had as lively a sense of smell as of hearing, and Sancho was so close and stitched to him that the vapours went up almost in a straight line, it could not be helped that some of them reached his nostrils. And they had hardly got there when he went to their rescue, pinching them between two fingers; and in a somewhat nasal tone he said:

"It seems to me, Sancho, that you are very much afraid."

"So I am," answered Sancho; "but how does your worship see it now more than at any other time?"

"In that now more than at any other time you smell, and not of amber," answered Don Quixote.

"That may well be," said Sancho, "but it isn't my fault, it's your worship's, for dragging me about at unearthly hours and along these unaccustomed ways."

"Move three or four of them off over there, my friend," said Don Quixote — all this without taking his fingers from his nose — "and from now on take more care of your own person and of what you owe to mine. It is the great deal of conversation I have with you that has bred this disrespect."

"I'll bet," replied Sancho, "that your worship thinks I've done something with my person that I shouldn't have."

"Stirring it only makes it worse, friend Sancho," answered Don Quixote.

In this conversation and others like it master and man passed the night. But seeing that morning was coming on fast, Sancho very carefully untied Rocinante and did up his breeches. As soon as Rocinante found himself free, although he was not in the least spirited by nature, it seems he felt it, and began to paw the ground — because as for curvetting, with all due respect to him, he did not know how.

Seeing, then, that Rocinante was moving at last, Don Quixote took it for a good sign, and believed it was a sign that he should attempt that terrifying adventure.

By this time the dawn had finished breaking and things could be made out distinctly, and Don Quixote saw that he was among some tall trees — chestnuts, which cast a very dark shade. He noticed too that the hammering had not stopped, but he could not see what might be causing it. And so, without delaying any longer, he made Rocinante feel his spurs; and taking leave of Sancho again, he ordered him to wait there for three days at the most, as he had told him once before, and that if he had not come back by the end of them he should take it for certain that God had been pleased to let his days come to an end in that dangerous adventure. He repeated the message and embassy he was to carry on his behalf to his lady Dulcinea; and told him that as far as the payment for his services went he need not worry, because he had left his will made before he came away from his village, in which he would find himself paid everything to do with his wages, pro rata, for the time he had served. But that if God brought him out of that danger safe and sound and without a scratch, he could count the promised isle as far more than certain.

Sancho began to weep all over again, hearing his good master's pitiful words all over again, and he made up his mind not to leave him until the very last passage and end of the business.

From these tears and this honourable resolution of Sancho Panza's the author of this history concludes that he must have been well born, and at the very least an Old Christian. His feeling softened his master somewhat, but not so much that he showed any weakness; instead, hiding it as best he could, he began to ride towards the direction from which it seemed to him the noise of the water and of the hammering came.

Sancho followed him on foot, leading his donkey by the halter as he usually did — that perpetual companion of his good fortunes and his bad. And having gone a good way among those chestnuts and shady trees, they came out into a little meadow that lay at the foot of some high rocks, down which an enormous head of water came hurling itself. At the foot of the rocks stood some badly made houses, more like the ruins of buildings than houses, out of which they made out that the noise and din of that hammering, which still had not stopped, was coming.

Rocinante was upset by the din of the water and of the blows; and Don Quixote, quieting him, went on getting closer to the houses little by little, commending himself with all his heart to his lady, begging her to favour him in that terrifying journey and enterprise, and on the way commending himself to God as well, that he would not forget him. Sancho never left his side, stretching his neck and his gaze out as far as he could between Rocinante's legs to see whether he could make out yet what was keeping him in such suspense and such dread.

Another hundred paces or so they went, when, on turning a corner, there appeared plain and open the very cause — it could be nothing else — of that horrible and, to them, terrifying noise that had kept them so suspended and so frightened all night long. And it was — take it, reader, without grief and annoyance — six fulling hammers, which with their alternating blows made all that din.

When Don Quixote saw what it was, he went dumb and stiffened from head to foot. Sancho looked at him and saw that he had his head bent down on his chest, with every sign of being mortified. Don Quixote looked at Sancho too, and saw that he had his cheeks blown out and his mouth full of laughter, with evident signs of being about to burst with it; and his melancholy could not do so much with him that at the sight of Sancho he could keep from laughing himself. And when Sancho saw that his master had begun, he let go of the dam in such a way that he had to hold his sides in with his fists to keep from bursting with laughter. Four times he quieted down, and four times he went back to his laughing with the same violence as the first; at which Don Quixote was already giving himself to the devil — and the more so when he heard him say, by way of mockery:

"You must know, friend Sancho, that I was born, by heaven's will, in this iron age of ours in order to bring back to life in it the golden age, or the age of gold. I am the man for whom are reserved the dangers, the great exploits, the valorous deeds..."

And in this fashion he went on repeating all or most of the speeches Don Quixote had made the first time they heard the terrifying blows.

Seeing, then, that Sancho was making fun of him, Don Quixote was so mortified and so angry that he lifted his pike and gave him two blows with it such that, if he had taken them on the head as he took them on the back, Don Quixote would have been free of paying him any wages, except to his heirs. Seeing that he was drawing such earnest out of his own joking, and afraid his master might carry it further, Sancho said to him very humbly:

"Calm down, your worship; before God, I'm only joking."

"Well, because you are joking, I am not," answered Don Quixote. "Come here, my merry gentleman: does it seem to you that if these had been not fulling hammers but some other dangerous adventure, I would not have shown the spirit needed to undertake it and finish it? Am I obliged, by any chance, being a knight as I am, to know and distinguish sounds and tell which are fulling hammers and which are not? Especially when it might be — as it is the truth — that I have never seen them in my life, whereas you will have seen them, low peasant that you are, bred and born among them. If not, make these six hammers turn into six giants and throw them at my beard one by one, or all together; and if I do not lay every one of them heels up, make whatever mockery of me you like."

"That's enough, my dear sir," replied Sancho. "I confess I've been a bit too free with my laughing. But tell me, your worship, now that we're at peace — and so may God bring you out of every adventure that happens to you as safe and sound as he has brought you out of this one — hasn't it been a thing to laugh at, and isn't it a thing to tell, the great fright we've had? At least the one I had; for as for your worship, I know already that you don't know it and don't know what fear or dread is."

"I do not deny," answered Don Quixote, "that what has happened to us is a thing worth laughing at; but it is not a thing worth telling, because not everybody is discerning enough to put things in their proper place."

"At least," answered Sancho, "your worship knew how to put the pike in its proper place, aiming at my head and hitting me on the back — thanks be to God and to the trouble I took to dodge sideways. But there, it'll all come out in the wash; and I've heard it said, 'He loves you well who makes you cry.' Besides which, great lords generally give a servant a pair of breeches straight after a bad word; though I don't know what they generally give him after giving him a beating, unless it's that knights errant give isles after beatings, or kingdoms on the mainland."

"The dice might well fall in such a way," said Don Quixote, "that everything you say would come true. And forgive what is past, since you are a man of sense and know that a man's first impulses are not in his own hands. And be warned from now on about one thing, so that you may hold back and restrain yourself from talking too much with me: in all the books of chivalry I have read — and they are infinite — I have never found any squire who talked as much with his lord as you do with yours. And truly I count it a great fault, in you and in me: in you, in that you esteem me too little; in me, in that I do not let myself be esteemed more. Why, Gandalín, squire to Amadis of Gaul, was count of the Firm Isle, and one reads of him that he always spoke to his lord with his cap in his hand, his head bent and his body doubled over more turquesco. And what shall we say of Gasabal, squire to Don Galaor, who was so silent that, to make the excellence of his marvellous silence clear to us, his name is mentioned only once in the whole of that history, great as it is and true as it is? From all I have said you are to infer, Sancho, that it is necessary to make a difference between master and man, between lord and servant, and between knight and squire. So from today onwards we must treat one another with more respect and without teasing each other; because however I may come to be angry with you, it will be the worse for the pitcher. The favours and benefits I have promised you will arrive in their own time; and if they do not arrive, at least the wages are not to be lost, as I have told you already."

"Everything your worship says is all very well," said Sancho; "but I'd like to know, in case the time for the favours doesn't come and it's necessary to fall back on the time for the wages, how much a knight errant's squire earned in those days, and whether they were hired by the month or by the day, like bricklayers' labourers."

"I do not believe," answered Don Quixote, "that such squires were ever on wages, but on favour. And if I have now assigned you one in the sealed will I left at home, it was for what might happen; because I still do not know how chivalry will turn out in these calamitous times of ours, and I would not have my soul suffer in the next world for small matters. Because I want you to know, Sancho, that in this world there is no more dangerous condition than that of the adventurers."

"That's true enough," said Sancho, "since the mere noise of the hammers of a fulling mill could disturb and unsettle the heart of so valorous a wandering adventurer as your worship. But you may be quite sure that from now on I won't open my lips to make fun of your worship's affairs, but only to honour you, as my master and natural lord."

"In that way," replied Don Quixote, "you will live long on the face of the earth; because after our parents, our masters are to be respected as if they were."

Chapter 21: Which Treats of the High Adventure and Rich Prize of Mambrino's Helmet, with Other Things That Happened to Our Invincible Knight

At this it began to rain a little, and Sancho would have liked them to go inside the fulling mill; but Don Quixote had taken such a loathing to it, on account of the heavy joke, that he would on no account go in. And so, turning off the road to the right hand, they came out on another like the one they had travelled the day before.

A little further on, Don Quixote made out a man on horseback with something on his head that shone as though it were gold; and he had hardly caught sight of him when he turned to Sancho and said:

"It seems to me, Sancho, that there is no proverb that is not true, because they are all maxims drawn from experience itself, the mother of all the sciences — and especially the one that says, 'Where one door shuts, another opens.' I say it because if last night fortune shut on us the door of the thing we were looking for, deceiving us with the fulling hammers, now she throws another wide open for us, on a better and more certain adventure; and if I fail to get in through it, the fault will be mine, without my being able to lay it on knowing little about fulling mills or on the darkness of the night. I say this because, if I am not mistaken, there is a man coming towards us with Mambrino's helmet on his head — the one I swore that oath about, as you know."

"Your worship should be careful what you say, and more careful what you do," said Sancho; "I shouldn't like it to be another lot of fulling mills that finished off the fulling and pounding of our wits."

"The devil take you for a man!" replied Don Quixote. "What has a helmet to do with fulling mills?"

"I know nothing about it," answered Sancho; "but upon my word, if I were allowed to talk as much as I used to, perhaps I'd give such reasons that your worship would see he was mistaken in what he says."

"How can I be mistaken in what I say, you scrupulous traitor?" said Don Quixote. "Tell me, don't you see that knight coming towards us on a dappled grey horse, with a golden helmet on his head?"

"What I see and make out," answered Sancho, "is nothing but a man on a grey ass like mine, with something on his head that shines."

"Well, that is Mambrino's helmet," said Don Quixote. "Get off to one side and leave me alone with him. You shall see how, without saying a word, to save time, I finish this adventure, and the helmet I have wanted so long is left mine."

"I'll take care to get off to one side," replied Sancho; "but please God, I say again, it may be marjoram and not fulling mills."

"I have told you already, brother, not to mention that business of the fulling mills to me again, not even in thought," said Don Quixote; "for I vow — and I say no more — to full your soul for you."

Sancho shut up, afraid his master might carry out the oath he had hurled at him, round as a cannonball.

Now the fact of the matter about the helmet and the horse and the knight Don Quixote could see is this. In that district there were two villages, one so small that it had neither an apothecary nor a barber, and the other, which was next to it, had both. And so the barber of the larger one served the smaller, where a sick man had need of being bled and another of getting a shave; and it was for these that the barber was coming, and he had a brass basin with him. And luck would have it that just as he was coming along it began to rain; and so that his hat, which must have been new, should not be spoiled, he put the basin on his head — and as it was clean, it shone from half a league off. He was riding a grey ass, as Sancho said, and this was why Don Quixote took it for a dappled grey horse and a knight and a helmet of gold; because everything he saw he fitted very easily to his deranged chivalries and his ill-starred fancies.

And when he saw the poor knight getting close, without stopping to argue with him at all he lowered his pike and charged at full stretch of Rocinante's gallop, meaning to run him through from side to side; but as he reached him, without checking the fury of his charge, he shouted:

"Defend yourself, wretched creature, or hand over to me of your own free will what is so justly owed me!"

The barber, who without thinking of it or fearing it saw that phantom coming down on him, had no other way of saving himself from the blow of the lance than to let himself drop off the ass; and he had not touched the ground before he was up again, nimbler than a fallow deer, and running off across that plain so fast that the wind could not have caught him. He left the basin on the ground, and Don Quixote was satisfied with that, and said the pagan had shown good sense and had imitated the beaver, which, finding itself pressed by the hunters, bites and tears off with its own teeth the thing it knows by natural instinct it is being hunted for. He ordered Sancho to pick up the helmet; who, taking it in his hands, said:

"By God, it's a good basin, and it's worth a piece of eight as surely as a maravedi."

And handing it to his master, Don Quixote put it straight on his head, turning it this way and that, looking for the visor; and when he could not find it he said:

"There is no doubt that the pagan this famous helmet was originally forged to fit must have had an enormous head; and the worst of it is that half of it is missing."

When Sancho heard him call the basin a helmet he could not hold in his laughter; but his master's temper came into his mind and he stopped in the middle of it.

"What are you laughing at, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"I'm laughing," he answered, "at the thought of the great head the pagan owner of this headpiece had, because the thing is the spitting image of a barber's basin and nothing else."

"Do you know what I imagine, Sancho? That this famous piece, this enchanted helmet, must by some strange accident have come into the hands of somebody who did not know how to recognise or value it; and that, without knowing what he was doing, seeing it was of the purest gold, he must have melted down the other half to make use of the price, and out of this half he made this thing, which looks like a barber's basin, as you say. But be that as it may: to me, who know what it is, its transmutation makes no difference. I shall get it seen to in the first place where there is a blacksmith, and in such a way that the one the god of the smithies made and forged for the god of battles will not have the advantage of it, or even come near it. And in the meantime I shall wear it as best I can, for something is better than nothing — the more so as it will certainly be enough to protect me from a stone."

"That will be so," said Sancho, "if it isn't thrown with a sling, as they threw them in that fight between the two armies, when they blessed your worship's molars for you and broke the can with that most blessed brew in it that made me vomit up my insides."

"I am not much grieved at having lost it," said Don Quixote, "because as you know, Sancho, I have the recipe by heart."

"So do I," answered Sancho, "but if I ever make it or taste it again in my life, may my hour come here and now. What's more, I don't mean to put myself in the way of needing it, because I mean to guard myself with all five of my senses against being wounded or wounding anybody. As for being tossed in a blanket again, I say nothing, because misfortunes of that kind can hardly be prevented; and if they come, there's nothing to do but hunch your shoulders, hold your breath, shut your eyes and let yourself go wherever luck and the blanket take you."

"You are a bad Christian, Sancho," said Don Quixote, hearing this, "because you never forget an injury once it has been done you. Let me tell you that it is the mark of noble and generous breasts to take no notice of childish things. What foot did you come away lame on, what rib broken, what head cracked, that you cannot forget that joke? For when the thing is properly weighed up, it was a joke and a piece of fun; and if I did not understand it so, I would have gone back there long ago and done more damage in your revenge than the Greeks did for the stolen Helen. Who, if she had been alive in this age, or my Dulcinea in that one, could be sure she would not have the reputation for beauty that she has."

And here he gave a sigh and sent it up to the clouds. And Sancho said:

"Let it pass for a joke, then, since the revenge can't pass for earnest. But I know what quality the earnest and the joking were of, and I know too that they'll never fall out of my memory, any more than they'll come off my back. But leaving that aside, tell me, your worship: what are we to do about this dappled grey horse that looks like a grey ass, which that Martino your worship knocked down has left abandoned here? Because by the way he took to his heels and made off like a shot, he doesn't look likely to come back for it ever. And by my beard, the grey is a good one!"

"It is not my custom," said Don Quixote, "to strip those I defeat, nor is it a practice of chivalry to take their horses and leave them on foot — unless it were that the victor had lost his own in the fight, in which case it is lawful to take the loser's, as won in lawful war. So, Sancho, leave that horse, or ass, or whatever you want it to be; because as soon as its owner sees us a good way off from here, he will come back for it."

"God knows I'd like to take it," replied Sancho, "or at least swap it for this one of mine, which doesn't seem to me as good. Truly the laws of chivalry are narrow ones, if they don't stretch as far as letting a man swap one ass for another; and I'd like to know whether I could at least swap the harness."

"On that I am not very certain," answered Don Quixote; "and in a case of doubt, until I am better informed, I say that you may swap them, if you are in extreme need of them."

"So extreme," answered Sancho, "that if they had been for my own person I couldn't have needed them more."

And then, empowered by that permission, he performed a mutatio caparum and turned his donkey out beyond all beauty, leaving him improved by a third and a fifth. This done, they breakfasted on the remains of the camp supplies they had stripped off the pack-mule and drank the water of the fulling-mill stream, without turning their faces to look at the mills: such was the loathing they had for them on account of the fright they had put them in.

Their hunger cut short, then, and their gloom along with it, they mounted; and without taking any set road — since it is very much the way of knights errant not to take a fixed one — they set off riding wherever Rocinante's will took them, which carried his master's along with it, and the donkey's too, since the donkey always followed wherever the horse led, in good love and fellowship. For all that, they came back to the high road and followed it at a venture, with no other plan at all.

Going along like this, Sancho said to his master:

"Sir, will your worship give me leave to talk with you a little? Since you laid that harsh commandment of silence on me, more than four things have gone rotten in my stomach, and there's one I have on the tip of my tongue now that I shouldn't like to see spoiled."

"Say it," said Don Quixote, "and be brief in your speeches, for none of them is enjoyable if it is long."

"I say, then, sir," answered Sancho, "that these last few days I've been thinking how little there is to be won or gained by going about looking for these adventures your worship looks for in these wildernesses and crossroads, where, even when the most dangerous ones are won and finished, there's nobody to see them or hear about them. And so they'll have to stay in everlasting silence, to the harm of your worship's purpose and of what they deserve. And so it seems to me it would be better — saving your worship's better judgement — if we went to serve some emperor, or some other great prince who has a war on, in whose service your worship could show the valour of his person, his great strength and his greater understanding. Which being seen by the lord we served, he'd be bound to reward us, each according to his deserts; and there'd be no lack of somebody there to put your worship's exploits into writing, for a lasting memorial. Of mine I say nothing, since they're not to go outside the limits proper to a squire; though I can tell you that if it's the custom in chivalry to write down squires' exploits, I don't think mine will be left out between the lines."

"You do not speak badly, Sancho," answered Don Quixote; "but before it comes to that, it is necessary to go about the world, as it were on probation, looking for adventures, so that by finishing some of them a man may acquire such a name and fame that when he comes to the court of some great monarch the knight is already known by his deeds. And so that hardly will the boys have seen him come in at the city gate before they will all follow and surround him, shouting and saying, 'This is the Knight of the Sun,' or of the Serpent, or of whatever other emblem it was under which he had performed great exploits. 'This,' they will say, 'is the man who defeated in single combat the huge giant Brocabruno of the Great Strength; the man who freed the Great Mameluke of Persia from the long enchantment he had been under for almost nine hundred years.'

"And so, from mouth to mouth, they will go proclaiming your deeds; and then, at the uproar of the boys and the rest of the people, the king of that kingdom will come to the windows of his royal palace, and as soon as he sees the knight and recognises him by his arms or by the device on his shield, he cannot help saying, 'Come now! Let all my knights who are in my court go out to receive the flower of chivalry, who is arriving!' At which command they will all go out, and the king will come as far as the middle of the staircase and embrace him very closely and give him the kiss of peace on the cheek; and then he will lead him by the hand to the lady queen's apartment, where the knight will find her with her daughter the princess, who is bound to be one of the loveliest and most perfect maidens that could be found, with a great deal of trouble, over a great part of the discovered earth.

"After this, immediately and directly, it will come about that she sets her eyes on the knight and he on hers, and each will seem to the other something more divine than human; and without knowing how or why, they will be left caught and tangled in the intricate net of love, and in great distress in their hearts at not knowing how they are to speak to one another and reveal their longings and their feelings.

"From there they will take him, no doubt, to some room of the palace, richly furnished, where, having taken his armour off him, they will bring him a rich scarlet cloak to cover himself with; and if he looked well in armour, he is bound to look as well and better in his doublet. Night coming on, he will have supper with the king, the queen and the princess, where he will never take his eyes off her, looking at her by stealth from the people around; and she will do the same with the same shrewdness, because, as I have said, she is a very discerning maiden.

"The tables will be cleared, and all at once there will come in at the door of the hall an ugly little dwarf with a beautiful lady, who comes behind the dwarf between two giants, with a certain adventure devised by a most ancient sage, and whoever finishes it will be held to be the best knight in the world. The king will then command that all those present should try it, and none of them will bring it to a finish and a conclusion but the guest knight, greatly to the profit of his fame — at which the princess will be perfectly delighted, and will count herself contented and repaid besides for having placed and settled her thoughts in so high a quarter.

"And the good of it is that this king, or prince, or whatever he is, has a very hard-fought war on with another as powerful as himself; and the guest knight asks him, after some days he has been at his court, for leave to go and serve him in that war. The king will give it him with a very good will, and the knight will kiss his hands courteously for the favour he does him.

"And that night he will take leave of his lady the princess through the grille of a garden that gives onto the room where she sleeps, through which he had already spoken to her many other times, with a lady-in-waiting the princess trusted a great deal as go-between and party to it all. He will sigh, she will faint, the lady will fetch water, she will be very distressed because morning is coming and she would not have them discovered, for her mistress's honour's sake. In the end the princess will come to herself and give her white hands through the grille to the knight, who will kiss them a thousand times over and bathe them in tears. It will be settled between the two of them how they are to let each other know their good or bad fortunes, and the princess will beg him to stay away as little as he can; he will promise it her with many oaths; he kisses her hands again and takes his leave with such feeling that he comes near to ending his life.

"He goes from there to his room, throws himself on his bed, cannot sleep for the pain of the parting, gets up very early in the morning, goes to take leave of the king and the queen and the princess. He is told, after taking leave of the two of them, that the lady princess is unwell and cannot receive a visit; the knight thinks it is from grief at his going, his heart is pierced through, and he comes near to giving an open sign of his pain. The go-between lady is standing there and has to notice it all, and goes off to tell her mistress, who receives her with tears and tells her that one of the greatest griefs she has is not knowing who her knight is, and whether or not he is of a line of kings. The lady assures her that so much courtesy, breeding and valour as her knight's could not be contained except in a royal and lofty subject; the poor girl comforts herself with this; she does her best to be comforted, so as not to give her parents a bad impression of her; and at the end of two days she comes out in public.

"The knight has gone by now. He fights in the war, defeats the king's enemy, wins many cities, triumphs in many battles, comes back to court, sees his lady in the usual place, and it is arranged that he shall ask her father for her as his wife in payment for his services. The king will not give her to him, because he does not know who he is; but for all that, either by carrying her off or by some other means whatever, the princess comes to be his wife and her father comes to count it a great piece of luck, because it turns out on inquiry that the knight is the son of a valorous king of some kingdom or other — I believe it cannot be on the map. The father dies, the princess inherits, the knight is king in two words. Here comes in at once the doing of favours to his squire and to all those who helped him rise to so high an estate: he marries his squire to a lady-in-waiting of the princess's, who will no doubt be the one who was the go-between in his love affair, and who is the daughter of a very great duke."

"That's what I ask, and fair play," said Sancho. "That's what I'm holding to, because the whole of it is bound to happen to your worship to the letter, now you're calling yourself the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance."

"Do not doubt it, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "because by the same road and the same steps I have described, knights errant rise and have risen to be kings and emperors. All that remains now is to look about and see which king of the Christians or of the pagans has a war on and has a beautiful daughter. But there will be time to think of this, since, as I have told you, one must first win fame elsewhere before going to court.

"There is another thing I lack, too. Supposing a king is found with a war and a beautiful daughter, and that I have won incredible fame throughout the universe, I do not see how it could be found that I am of a line of kings, or at least second cousin to an emperor; because the king will not give me his daughter to wife unless he is first thoroughly satisfied on this, however much my famous deeds may deserve it. So through this defect I am afraid of losing what my arm has well deserved. It is quite true that I am a gentleman of a known house, holding property in my own right and entitled to the five-hundred-sueldo indemnity; and it might be that the sage who writes my history would trace out my kindred and descent in such a way that he would find me the fifth or sixth in descent from a king.

"Because I would have you know, Sancho, that there are two kinds of lineage in the world. Some trace and bring down their descent from princes and monarchs, whom time has little by little undone, and they have finished in a point like a pyramid stood upside down. Others had their beginning in low people and go climbing step by step until they come to be great lords. So that the difference is that some were what they are no longer, and others are what they were not. And I might be one of these — that after inquiry my beginning would prove to have been great and famous, with which the king my father-in-law-to-be ought to be satisfied. And if not, the princess is bound to love me in such a way that in spite of her father, even if she knew clearly that I was the son of a water-carrier, she will take me for her lord and her husband. And if not, here comes in carrying her off and taking her wherever I like best; because time or death will put an end to her parents' anger."

"Here comes in nicely too," said Sancho, "what some unscrupulous people say: 'Don't ask as a favour what you can take by force.' Though it fits better to say: 'A leap over the hedge is worth more than good men's prayers.' I say it because if the lord king, your worship's father-in-law, won't be brought round to handing over my lady the princess, there's nothing for it, as your worship says, but to carry her off and spirit her away. But the trouble is that until peace is made and the kingdom is enjoyed in quiet, the poor squire may go hungry as far as the favours are concerned — unless the go-between lady, who's to be his wife, comes away with the princess and he shares his bad luck with her until heaven ordains otherwise; because I suppose his master could give her to him for his lawful wife straight away."

"There is nobody to prevent that," said Don Quixote.

"Well, if that's how it is," answered Sancho, "there's nothing for it but to commend ourselves to God and let luck run wherever it can best direct things."

"May God do it," answered Don Quixote, "as I desire and as you, Sancho, need. And let him be mean who thinks himself mean."

"Let it be so, in God's name," said Sancho, "for I'm an Old Christian, and that's enough for me to be a count with."

"It is more than enough," said Don Quixote; "and even if you were not, it would make no difference, because, since I shall be king, I can very well give you nobility without your buying it or serving me with anything for it. Because once I make you a count, there you are a gentleman, and let them say what they like — for upon my word they will have to call you 'your lordship', however much it annoys them."

"And I'll be bound I'd know how to carry off the tittle!" said Sancho.

"Title you should say, not tittle," said his master.

"So be it," answered Sancho Panza. "I say I'd know how to manage it well enough; because upon my life, I was beadle of a confraternity once, and the beadle's robes sat so well on me that everybody said I had the presence to be steward of the same confraternity. So what will it be when I put a duke's gown on my back, or dress myself in gold and pearls like a foreign count? It's my belief they'll come a hundred leagues to see me."

"You will look well," said Don Quixote, "but it will be necessary for you to shave your beard often; because, thick, tangled and untidy as you keep it, if you do not take a razor to it every two days at the least, they will see what you are from a musket shot away."

"What is there to it," said Sancho, "except to take a barber and keep him on wages in the house? And if it's necessary I'll even make him walk behind me like a grandee's master of horse."

"But how do you know," asked Don Quixote, "that grandees have their masters of horse walk behind them?"

"I'll tell you," answered Sancho. "Some years ago I spent a month at court, and there I saw a very small gentleman walking about, who they said was a very great one, with a man following him on horseback at every turn he took, so that he looked like nothing so much as his tail. I asked why that man didn't come alongside the other one instead of always walking behind him. They answered me that he was his master of horse, and that it was the custom of grandees to have such men behind them. I've known it so well ever since that I've never forgotten it."

"I say you are right," said Don Quixote, "and that in the same way you may have your barber behind you. Customs did not all come in together, nor were they invented all at once, and you may be the first count to have his barber behind him. And in fact shaving a man is a matter of greater trust than saddling a horse."

"Let the business of the barber be my responsibility," said Sancho, "and let your worship's be to try to come to be king and to make me a count."

"So it shall be," answered Don Quixote.

And raising his eyes, he saw what will be told in the following chapter.

Chapter 22: Of the Liberty Don Quixote Gave to a Number of Unfortunates Who Were Being Taken, Against Their Will, Where They Had No Wish to Go

Cide Hamete Benengeli, Arab author and Manchegan, relates in this most grave, high-sounding, minute, sweet and imagined history that after the words related at the end of chapter twenty-one had passed between the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha and Sancho Panza his squire, Don Quixote raised his eyes and saw coming along the road he was on some twelve men on foot, strung like beads by the neck on a great iron chain, and all of them with manacles on their hands. There were also two men on horseback and two on foot with them: those on horseback with wheel-lock muskets, and those on foot with javelins and swords. And as soon as Sancho Panza saw them he said:

"That's a chain of galley slaves, people forced by the king, on their way to the galleys."

"What do you mean, forced?" asked Don Quixote. "Is it possible that the king uses force on anybody?"

"I don't say that," answered Sancho, "but that they're people who for their crimes have been condemned to serve the king in the galleys by force."

"In short," replied Don Quixote, "however it may be, these people are being taken by force and not of their own will."

"That's so," said Sancho.

"Then in that case," said his master, "here comes in the exercise of my office: to undo violence and to help and succour the wretched."

"Your worship should note," said Sancho, "that justice, which is the king himself, is not using force or doing injury to people of this kind, but punishing them for their crimes."

At this the chain of galley slaves came up, and Don Quixote in very courteous terms asked those who were guarding them to be good enough to inform him and tell him the reason, or reasons, why they were taking these people along in that fashion. One of the mounted guards answered that they were galley slaves, people belonging to His Majesty on their way to the galleys, and that there was nothing more to say, nor did he have anything more to know.

"For all that," replied Don Quixote, "I should like to learn from each one of them in particular the cause of his misfortune."

He added to these such other and such polite terms, to move them to tell him what he wanted, that the other mounted guard said to him:

"Although we have the register and the certificate of each of these unfortunates' sentences here with us, this is no time to stop and get them out and read them. Your worship may go up and ask the men themselves, and they will tell you if they choose — and choose they will, because they are people who take pleasure in doing and telling knaveries."

With this permission, which Don Quixote would have taken even if it had not been given him, he went up to the chain and asked the first man for what sins he was going along in so bad a fashion. He answered that it was for being in love that he was going along in that way.

"For that and no more?" replied Don Quixote. "Why, if they send men to the galleys for being in love, I might have been rowing in them long ago."

"The love isn't the kind your worship thinks," said the galley slave. "Mine was that I was so fond of a washing basket crammed with white linen that I hugged it to me so tightly that if the law hadn't taken it off me by force, I wouldn't have let go of it of my own will even now. It was caught in the act, there was no room for torture, the case was concluded, they fitted out my shoulders with a hundred, and three straight in the gurapas by way of an extra, and the job was done."

"What are gurapas?" asked Don Quixote.

"Gurapas are galleys," answered the galley slave.

He was a young fellow of about twenty-four, and he said he was from Piedrahíta. Don Quixote asked the same of the second, who did not answer a word, so downcast and gloomy did he look; but the first answered for him, and said:

"This one, sir, is going as a canary — I mean, as a musician and a singer."

"How is that?" repeated Don Quixote. "Do musicians and singers go to the galleys too?"

"Yes, sir," answered the galley slave, "for there's nothing worse than singing under pressure."

"On the contrary," said Don Quixote, "I have heard it said that he who sings frightens away his troubles."

"Here it's the other way about," said the galley slave: "he who sings once weeps for the rest of his life."

"I do not understand it," said Don Quixote.

But one of the guards said to him:

"Sir knight, 'singing under pressure' means, among these unholy people, confessing under torture. They gave this sinner the torture and he confessed his crime, which was being a rustler, that is a thief of livestock; and because he confessed they sentenced him to six years in the galleys, besides the two hundred lashes he is already carrying on his back. And he goes along thoughtful and sad all the time, because the other thieves who stayed behind and the ones who are here abuse him and grind him down and make a mock of him and think nothing of him, because he confessed and hadn't the courage to say no. Because they say that a no has as many letters in it as a yes, and that a criminal is lucky enough when his life or his death lies on his own tongue and not on the witnesses and the evidence; and to my mind they are not very far off the road."

"And that is how I understand it too," answered Don Quixote.

Passing on to the third, he asked what he had asked the others; who answered at once and with a great deal of coolness, and said:

"I'm going for five years to the lady gurapas for being short of ten ducats."

"I would give twenty with a very good will," said Don Quixote, "to get you out of that trouble."

"That strikes me," answered the galley slave, "like a man who has money in the middle of the ocean and is dying of hunger with nowhere to buy what he needs. I say it because if I'd had at the right moment those twenty ducats your worship is offering me now, I'd have greased the clerk's quill with them and sharpened up the attorney's wits, in such a way that today I'd have found myself in the middle of the Zocodover square in Toledo and not on this road, leashed like a greyhound. But God is great: patience, and enough said."

Don Quixote passed on to the fourth, a man with a venerable face and a white beard that came down below his chest; who, on hearing himself asked the reason he was there, began to cry and did not answer a word. But the fifth condemned man served him as a tongue, and said:

"This honourable man is going for four years to the galleys, after having paraded the usual streets dressed up in state and on horseback."

"That is," said Sancho Panza, "as it seems to me, having been put to public shame."

"That's it," replied the galley slave; "and the offence they gave him this penalty for is having been a broker of ears — and of the whole body too. What I mean, in fact, is that this gentleman is going as a pimp, and for likewise having his touch and trimming of sorcery."

"If they had not added that touch and trimming," said Don Quixote, "then for pure pimping alone he would not deserve to go and row in the galleys, but to command them and be their admiral. For the office of pimp is not just anything: it is an office for people of discernment and absolutely necessary in a well-ordered state, and it ought to be practised only by people very well born. And indeed there ought to be an inspector and examiner of them, as there is of the other trades, with a fixed and known number of them, like the brokers on the exchange. And in this way a great many evils would be avoided that are caused by this office and occupation being in the hands of stupid people of little understanding — such as women of small account, pages and rascals of few years and little experience, who at the most necessary moment, when it is a question of laying a plan that matters, let the crumbs freeze between the mouth and the hand and do not know which is their right hand.

"I should like to go further and give the reasons why it is proper to make a careful choice of those who are to hold so necessary an office in the state, but this is not the right place for it; some day I shall tell it to somebody who can see to it and put it right. I only say now that the pain caused me by seeing these white hairs and this venerable face in such distress, for pimping, has been taken away by the addition of his being a sorcerer — although I know very well that there are no spells in the world that can move or force the will, as some simple people think. Our will is free, and there is no herb or enchantment that can force it. What certain simple women and certain knavish tricksters generally do is to make up some mixtures and poisons that drive men mad, giving people to understand that they have the power to make them love — which is, as I say, an impossibility, to force the will."

"That's the truth," said the good old man; "and in fact, sir, in the matter of sorcery I was not to blame; in the matter of pimping I couldn't deny it. But I never thought I was doing any harm by it: my whole intention was that everybody should enjoy themselves and live in peace and quiet, without quarrels or troubles. But this good intention has been no use at all to me in keeping me from going where I don't expect to come back from, considering the weight of my years and a trouble with my water that doesn't let me rest for a moment."

And here he went back to his weeping as before; and Sancho felt so much pity for him that he took a four-real piece out of his shirt and gave it to him as alms.

Don Quixote went on and asked another his offence, who answered with no less, but with a great deal more, style than the last one:

"I'm here because I carried my games too far with two first cousins of mine, and with two other sisters who weren't mine. In the end I carried the game so far with all of them that the result of it was the family growing so tangled that there's no devil can sort it out. Everything was proved against me, there was no favour to be had, I had no money, I was on the point of losing my gullet, they sentenced me to six years in the galleys, and I agreed to it: it's the punishment for my fault. I'm young, let life last, for with it everything can be got. If your worship, sir knight, has anything to relieve us poor wretches with, God will repay you in heaven, and we on earth will take care to pray to God in our prayers for your worship's life and health, and may it be as long and as good as your fine appearance deserves."

This one was in a student's dress, and one of the guards said he was a great talker and a very fine Latinist.

Behind all these came a man of very good appearance, about thirty years old, except that when he looked at you he squinted one eye a little into the other. He was tied differently from the rest, because he had a chain on his leg so long that it wound right round his body, and two rings at his throat, one on the chain and the other one of the kind they call a keep-friend or a foot-friend, from which two irons came down to his waist, and to these were fastened two manacles holding his hands, shut with a heavy padlock; so that he could not raise his hands to his mouth, nor lower his head to reach his hands.

Don Quixote asked why this man was going along with so many more irons than the others. The guard answered him that it was because this one man had more crimes on him than all the rest put together, and that he was so daring and such a great scoundrel that even taking him along in that fashion they were not safe from him, but were afraid he would escape from them.

"What crimes can he have," said Don Quixote, "if they have deserved no greater penalty than being sent to the galleys?"

"He is going for ten years," replied the guard, "which is the same as civil death. There is no need to know more than that this good man is the famous Ginés de Pasamonte, who by another name is called Ginesillo de Parapilla."

"Señor commissary," said the galley slave then, "go gently, and let us not start sorting out names and surnames now. Ginés is my name and not Ginesillo, and Pasamonte is my family and not Parapilla, as your worship says. And let everybody take a turn around himself, and he will not be doing badly."

"Speak with less swagger, my lord thief above the ordinary size," replied the commissary, "unless you want me to shut you up in a way you won't like."

"It is plain to see," answered the galley slave, "that a man goes along as God is pleased to have him; but one day somebody will find out whether my name is Ginesillo de Parapilla or not."

"Well, isn't that what they call you, you liar?" said the guard.

"They do," answered Ginés, "but I'll see to it that they don't call me it — or I'd tear them out somewhere I'm saying between my teeth. Sir knight, if you have anything to give us, give it us now and go with God; you're becoming a nuisance with all this wanting to know about other people's lives. And if you want to know mine, know that I am Ginés de Pasamonte, whose life is written by these thumbs."

"He speaks the truth," said the commissary: "he has written his own history himself, and there is nothing to touch it, and he leaves the book in pawn in the prison for two hundred reals."

"And I mean to redeem it," said Ginés, "even if it were pledged for two hundred ducats."

"Is it as good as that?" said Don Quixote.

"It is so good," answered Ginés, "that it's a bad year for Lazarillo de Tormes and for everything of that kind that has been written or ever will be. What I can tell your worship is that it deals in truths, and truths so fine and so entertaining that no lies can equal them."

"And what is the book called?" asked Don Quixote.

"The Life of Ginés de Pasamonte," answered the man himself.

"And is it finished?" asked Don Quixote.

"How can it be finished," he answered, "when my life isn't finished yet? What is written is from my birth up to the moment they sent me to the galleys this last time."

"So you have been in them before?" said Don Quixote.

"In the service of God and the king I was in them another four years, and I know already what the ship's biscuit and the whip taste like," answered Ginés. "And it doesn't grieve me much to be going to them, because there I'll have the chance to finish my book. I've a great many things left to say, and in the galleys of Spain there's more leisure than a man needs — though I don't need much more for what I have to write, since I know it by heart."

"You seem clever," said Don Quixote.

"And unlucky," answered Ginés, "because misfortunes always persecute good wits."

"They persecute scoundrels," said the commissary.

"I have told you already, Señor commissary," answered Pasamonte, "to go gently. Those gentlemen didn't give you that staff to ill-treat us poor wretches who are going along here, but to guide us and take us where His Majesty commands. If not — by the life of — enough! It might be that one day the stains that were made at the inn will come out in the wash. And let everybody hold his tongue, and live well and speak better, and let us get on our way, for this is a great deal too much amusement."

The commissary raised his staff high to strike Pasamonte in answer to his threats; but Don Quixote put himself in between and begged him not to ill-treat the man, since it was not much that a man whose hands were tied so tightly should have his tongue a little loose. And turning to all those on the chain, he said:

"From everything you have told me, dearest brothers, I have gathered clearly that although they have punished you for your faults, the penalties you are going to suffer give you very little pleasure, and that you are going to them very unwillingly and very much against your own will; and that it might be that the small courage that man had under torture, and this one's lack of money, and the other's lack of influence, and finally the judge's crooked judgement, may have been the cause of your ruin and of your not having got the justice that was on your side.

"All of which presents itself to my mind in such a way that it is telling me, persuading me and even forcing me to show in your case the purpose for which heaven threw me into the world and made me profess in it the order of chivalry that I profess, and the vow I made in it to favour the needy and those oppressed by the powerful. But because I know that one part of prudence is that what can be done by fair means should not be done by foul, I want to beg these gentlemen the guards and the commissary to be good enough to untie you and let you go in peace; there will be no lack of others to serve the king on better occasions. For it seems to me a hard case to make slaves of those whom God and nature made free.

"What is more, gentlemen guards," Don Quixote added, "these poor men have committed nothing against you. Let each of them settle it with his own sin. There is a God in heaven who does not neglect to punish the wicked or to reward the good, and it is not right that honourable men should be executioners of other men when nothing in it concerns them. I ask this with this gentleness and calm, so that I may have something to thank you for if you carry it out; and if you will not do it willingly, this lance and this sword, with the valour of my arm, will make you do it by force."

"A pretty piece of foolery!" answered the commissary. "That's a fine joke he has come out with after all this time! He wants us to let the king's convicts go, as though we had authority to release them or he had any to order us to! Your worship had better get on your way, sir, and good luck to you, and straighten that basin you have on your head, and don't go looking for three feet on a cat."

"You are the cat, and the rat, and the rascal!" answered Don Quixote.

And saying and doing, he charged him so suddenly that, without giving him time to put himself on his guard, he brought him down on the ground badly wounded by a thrust of the lance; and it turned out well for him, because this was the one with the musket. The other guards were astonished and taken aback by the unlooked-for event; but recovering themselves, those on horseback put their hands to their swords and those on foot to their javelins and charged Don Quixote, who waited for them with great calm.

And no doubt it would have gone badly for him if the galley slaves, seeing the chance that offered itself of getting their liberty, had not gone after it and set about breaking the chain they were strung on. The confusion was such that the guards — now running to the galley slaves, who were getting themselves loose, now attacking Don Quixote, who was attacking them — did nothing of any use.

Sancho for his part helped to free Ginés de Pasamonte, who was the first to leap out into the open free and unencumbered; and, charging at the fallen commissary, he took his sword and his musket from him, with which, aiming at one and marking down another without ever firing it, he left not a guard in the whole field, because they all fled — as much from Pasamonte's musket as from the many stones the loosed galley slaves were throwing at them.

Sancho was much saddened by this business, because it came into his mind that the men who were running away were bound to report the affair to the Holy Brotherhood, who would come out with the alarm bell ringing to look for the offenders. And he said so to his master, and begged him that they should get away from there at once and take cover in the mountains, which were near.

"That is all very well," said Don Quixote, "but I know what it is proper to do now."

And calling all the galley slaves, who were milling about in an uproar and had stripped the commissary down to the skin, they all gathered round him to hear what he would order them, and he said to them:

"It is the mark of well-born people to be grateful for the benefits they receive, and one of the sins that most offends God is ingratitude. I say it because you have already seen, gentlemen, by plain experience, the benefit you have received from me. In payment for it I should like — and it is my will — that, loaded with that chain I took off your necks, you should set out at once and go to the city of El Toboso, and there present yourselves before the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso and tell her that her knight, he of the Sorrowful Countenance, sends her his greetings, and give her a point-by-point account of everything that has taken place in this famous adventure, up to your being set at the liberty you wanted. And this done, you may go wherever you like and good luck go with you."

Ginés de Pasamonte answered for them all, and said:

"What your worship orders us, sir and our deliverer, is impossible with every kind of impossibility to carry out; because we can't go along the roads together, but only singly and separately, each one his own way, trying to get into the bowels of the earth so as not to be found by the Holy Brotherhood, who without any doubt are bound to come out looking for us. What your worship can do, and it's right that you should, is to change that service and toll to the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso into a certain quantity of Hail Marys and Creeds, which we'll say for your worship's intention; and that's a thing that can be done by night and by day, running away or resting, in peace or in war. But to think that we're going back now to the fleshpots of Egypt — I mean, to take up our chain and set out on the road to El Toboso — is to think that it's night now when it isn't yet ten in the morning, and it's asking us for that the way you'd ask an elm tree for pears."

"Then I swear by all that's holy," said Don Quixote, in a temper by now, "Don son of a whore, Don Ginesillo de Paropillo, or whatever you call yourself, that you shall go alone, tail between your legs, with the whole chain on your back!"

Pasamonte, who was not in the least long-suffering, and who by now had made out that Don Quixote was not very sane — since he had committed such an absurdity as wanting to give them their freedom — seeing himself treated in that fashion, winked at his companions; and drawing off to one side, they began to rain such a quantity of stones on Don Quixote that he could not get his hands going fast enough to cover himself with his buckler, and poor Rocinante took no more notice of the spur than if he had been made of bronze. Sancho got behind his ass and with him defended himself from the cloud and hailstorm that was raining down on the pair of them.

Don Quixote could not shield himself so well but that any number of pebbles hit him about the body, with such force that they brought him down on the ground; and he had hardly fallen when the student was on top of him and took the basin off his head and gave him three or four blows with it on the back and as many more on the ground, with which he smashed it to pieces. They took off him a jerkin he was wearing over his armour, and they would have taken his stockings if the greaves had not got in the way. They took Sancho's coat, and leaving him stripped to his shirt and sharing out among themselves the rest of the spoils of the battle, they each went their own way, with more care about escaping the Brotherhood they were afraid of than about loading themselves with the chain and going to present themselves before the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso.

The donkey and Rocinante, Sancho and Don Quixote were left alone: the donkey with his head down and thoughtful, shaking his ears every now and then, thinking the storm of stones that was still troubling his ears had not stopped; Rocinante stretched out beside his master, for he had come down to the ground too from another stone; Sancho in his shirt and afraid of the Holy Brotherhood; and Don Quixote in the deepest gloom at finding himself so badly used by the very men he had done so much good to.

Chapter 23: Of What Happened to the Famous Don Quixote in the Sierra Morena, Which Was One of the Rarest Adventures Related in This True History

Finding himself so badly used, Don Quixote said to his squire:

"I have always heard it said, Sancho, that doing good to low fellows is throwing water into the sea. If I had believed what you told me, I should have avoided this trouble; but it is done now: patience, and let it be a lesson from here on."

"Your worship will learn that lesson," answered Sancho, "about as much as I'm a Turk. But since you say that if you had believed me you'd have avoided this damage, believe me now and you'll avoid a greater one; because I can tell you that with the Holy Brotherhood there's no using chivalry — they don't give two maravedis for all the knights errant there are. And I tell you I fancy I can hear their arrows humming past my ears already."

"You are a coward by nature, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "but so that you shall not say I am obstinate and never do what you advise, this once I mean to take your advice and get away from the fury you are so afraid of. But it must be on one condition: that never, in life or in death, are you to tell anybody that I withdrew and got away from this danger out of fear, but only to satisfy your entreaties. And if you say anything else, you will be lying in it; and from now for then, and from then for now, I give you the lie, and say that you lie and will lie every time you think it or say it. And do not argue with me any more; because at the mere thought of my withdrawing and retiring from any danger — especially this one, which seems to carry some sort of a hint of a shadow of fear about it — I am ready to stay here and wait, alone, not only for the Holy Brotherhood you speak of and are afraid of, but for the brothers of the twelve tribes of Israel, and the seven Maccabees, and Castor and Pollux, and all the brothers and brotherhoods there are in the world."

"Sir," answered Sancho, "retreating isn't running away, and waiting isn't good sense when the danger is bigger than the hope; and it's for wise men to keep themselves today for tomorrow and not stake everything on one day. And let me tell you that although I'm a clumsy peasant, I still understand something about what they call good management. So don't be sorry for having taken my advice: get up on Rocinante if you can — and if you can't, I'll help you — and follow me, for my wits tell me we have more need of our feet now than of our hands."

Don Quixote mounted without answering him another word; and with Sancho leading the way on his ass, they went into one side of the Sierra Morena, which was close by. Sancho meant to cross the whole of it and come out at El Viso or Almodóvar del Campo, and hide for some days in those wild places so as not to be found if the Brotherhood came looking for them. What encouraged him in this was having seen that the store of provisions carried on his ass had come free out of the fight with the galley slaves — a thing he judged a miracle, considering what the galley slaves carried off and searched for.

As soon as Don Quixote got into those mountains his heart lifted, those places seeming to him well suited for the adventures he was looking for. There came back into his memory the marvellous things that had happened to knights errant in solitudes and wild places of that kind. He rode along thinking about all this, so absorbed and carried away by it that he thought of nothing else. Nor did Sancho have any other care — once it seemed to him that they were travelling somewhere safe — than to satisfy his stomach with what was left of the clerical spoils. And so he went along behind his master, sitting side-saddle on his donkey, taking things out of a sack and stowing them in his belly; and he would not have given a farthing to run across another adventure while he was going along like that.

At this he raised his eyes and saw that his master had stopped and was trying with the point of his pike to lift some bundle or other that was lying on the ground; so he hurried up to help him if it were needed. And when he arrived it was just as his master was raising on the point of his pike a saddle cushion with a portmanteau attached to it, half rotten, or altogether rotten and falling apart; but it weighed so much that it was necessary for Sancho to get down to pick them up, and his master told him to see what was in the portmanteau.

Sancho did it very smartly; and although the portmanteau was fastened with a chain and its padlock, through the torn and rotted parts of it he could see what was inside, which was four shirts of fine Holland linen and other linen things, no less remarkable than clean; and in a handkerchief he found a good little pile of gold crowns. And as soon as he saw them he said:

"Blessed be all heaven, that has thrown us an adventure with some profit in it!"

And searching further, he found a little pocket-book, richly bound. Don Quixote asked for this, and told him to keep the money and take it for himself. Sancho kissed his hands for the favour, and stripping the bag of its linen, he put it into the provisions sack. All of which Don Quixote saw, and said:

"It seems to me, Sancho — and it is not possible that it should be anything else — that some traveller who had lost his way must have passed through these mountains, and been set on by robbers and killed, and that they brought him to bury him in this out-of-the-way place."

"That can't be," answered Sancho, "because if they were robbers they wouldn't have left this money here."

"You are right," said Don Quixote; "and so I cannot guess or make out what this can be. But wait: we shall see whether there is anything written in this little pocket-book by which we can pick up the trail and come to know what we want."

He opened it, and the first thing he found written in it, as in a rough draft though in a very good hand, was a sonnet; which, reading it aloud so that Sancho should hear it too, he found went like this:

	Either Love lacks understanding,
	or he has cruelty to spare, or my pain
	is not equal to the cause that condemns me
	to the harshest kind of torment.
	But if Love is a god, it follows
	that he is ignorant of nothing; and it is very good reasoning
	that a god should not be cruel. Then who ordains
	the terrible grief that I adore and feel?
	If I say it is you, Fili, I am wrong;
	so much evil does not fit inside so much good,
	nor does this ruin come to me from heaven.
	I shall have to die soon, which is the surest thing;
	for when the cause of the trouble is not known,
	it is a miracle to hit on the medicine.

"There's nothing to be learnt from that ballad," said Sancho, "unless we can ride that filly there to the end of the road."

"What filly is here?" said Don Quixote.

"It seemed to me," said Sancho, "that your worship named a filly there."

"I said Fili, not filly," answered Don Quixote; "and this, without any doubt, is the name of the lady the author of this sonnet is complaining about. And upon my word he must be a reasonable poet, or I know little of the art."

"So your worship understands verses as well?" said Sancho.

"And more than you think," answered Don Quixote; "and you shall see it when you carry a letter, written in verse from top to bottom, to my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso. Because I want you to know, Sancho, that all, or most, of the knights errant of the past age were great versifiers and great musicians; for these two accomplishments, or graces rather, go with wandering lovers. It is true that the verses of the knights of the past have more spirit than polish in them."

"Read some more, your worship," said Sancho; "you'll find something to satisfy us."

Don Quixote turned the page and said:

"This is prose, and it looks like a letter."

"A letter to be sent, sir?" asked Sancho.

"By the beginning it looks like nothing but a love letter," answered Don Quixote.

"Then read it out loud, your worship," said Sancho, "for I greatly enjoy these matters of love."

"With pleasure," said Don Quixote.

And reading it aloud, as Sancho had asked him to, he found it went like this:

Your false promise and my certain misfortune are carrying me to a place from which the news of my death will come back to your ears sooner than the words of my complaints. You threw me over, ungrateful woman, for a man who has more, not for a man who is worth more, than I am; but if virtue were a wealth that people valued, I should not envy other men's good fortune or weep for my own bad. What your beauty raised up, your actions have pulled down: by the one I understood you were an angel, and by the others I know you are a woman. Stay in peace, you who caused my war, and may heaven grant that your husband's deceits stay hidden for ever, so that you may not be left repenting what you did and I may not take a revenge I do not want.

Having finished reading the letter, Don Quixote said:

"Less can be got out of this than out of the verses — except that whoever wrote it is some rejected lover."

And leafing through almost the whole of the little book, he found other verses and letters, some of which he could read and some not; but what all of them contained was complaints, laments, mistrust, pleasures and displeasures, favours and disdains, some of them celebrated and others wept over.

While Don Quixote was going through the book, Sancho was going through the portmanteau, not leaving a corner of the whole of it, nor of the cushion, that he did not search, examine and investigate; nor a seam that he did not unpick, nor a tuft of wool that he did not pull apart, so that nothing should be left for want of diligence or through carelessness — such an appetite had the crowns he had found awakened in him, and there were more than a hundred of them. And although he found nothing more than what he had found, he counted the flights in the blanket, the vomiting of the brew, the blessings of the staves, the carrier's punches, the loss of the saddlebags, the theft of his coat and all the hunger, thirst and weariness he had gone through in his good master's service as well spent, since it seemed to him he was more than very well paid by the favour he had received in being given what they had found.

The Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance was left with a great desire to know who the owner of the portmanteau might be, guessing from the sonnet and the letter, from the gold money and from the very good shirts, that he must be some person of standing who was in love, and whom his lady's disdain and bad treatment must have driven to some desperate extremity. But as no living person appeared anywhere in that uninhabitable and rugged place from whom he could get information, he thought of nothing but going on, taking no other road than the one Rocinante wanted, which was wherever he could get along, always with the notion that some strange adventure could not fail to turn up among those thickets.

Going along, then, with this thought, he saw a man leaping over the top of a little hill that came into view in front of him, going from crag to crag and from bush to bush with extraordinary agility. He seemed to be half naked, with a thick black beard, a great deal of tangled hair, bare feet and nothing at all on his legs; his thighs were covered by a pair of breeches, apparently of tawny velvet, but so torn to pieces that his flesh showed through in many places. He had nothing on his head; and although he went past with the quickness that has been described, the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance saw and noted all these particulars. And although he tried, he could not follow him, because it was not given to Rocinante's weakness to go over that rough ground, especially as he was naturally short-stepped and phlegmatic.

Don Quixote immediately imagined that this was the owner of the cushion and the portmanteau, and he resolved in himself to look for him, even if he had to spend a year going about those mountains until he found him. And so he ordered Sancho to get down off the ass and cut across one side of the mountain, while he would go along the other, and it might be that with this effort they would come across the man who had got away from them in such a hurry.

"I can't do that," answered Sancho, "because the moment I get away from your worship, fear is on me at once and attacks me with a thousand kinds of frights and visions. And let what I say serve as notice that from now on I shall not move a finger's breadth from your presence."

"So be it," said the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance; "and I am very glad you want to make use of my courage, which will not fail you even if the courage of your body fails. Come along after me now, little by little or however you can, and make lanterns of your eyes. We shall go round this little sierra; perhaps we shall come across the man we saw, who without any doubt is none other than the owner of our find."

To which Sancho answered:

"It would be a good deal better not to look for him; because if we find him and he happens to be the owner of the money, it's clear I'll have to give it back. So it would have been better, without going to this useless trouble, for me to keep it in good faith until its true owner turned up by some other way that was less inquisitive and less industrious — and perhaps it would have been at a time when I'd have spent it, and then the king would have let me off."

"You are mistaken there, Sancho," answered Don Quixote; "since we have already fallen into a suspicion of who the owner is, and have him almost in front of us, we are obliged to look for him and give it back to him. And even if we did not look for him, the strong suspicion we have that he is the man puts us as much in the wrong as if he were. So, friend Sancho, do not be distressed at looking for him, considering the distress it will take away from me if I find him."

And so he spurred Rocinante, and Sancho followed him with his usual donkey. And having gone round part of the mountain, they found in a stream, fallen and dead and half eaten by dogs and pecked at by crows, a mule with its saddle and bridle on — all of which confirmed them still further in the suspicion that the man who had run away was the owner of the mule and of the cushion.

While they were looking at it they heard a whistle like that of a shepherd looking after his flock, and all at once, on their left hand, there appeared a good number of goats, and behind them, on top of the mountain, appeared the goatherd who was looking after them, who was an old man. Don Quixote shouted to him and asked him to come down to where they were. He answered at the top of his voice, asking what had brought them to that place, which was seldom or never trodden except by the feet of goats or of wolves and other wild beasts that went about there. Sancho answered him that he should come down and they would give him a full account of everything. The goatherd came down, and on reaching where Don Quixote was, he said:

"I'll wager you're looking at the hired mule that's lying dead in that hollow. Well, upon my word, it's been in that spot six months now. Tell me: have you come across its owner anywhere about?"

"We have come across nobody," answered Don Quixote, "except a cushion and a little portmanteau that we found not far from this place."

"I found it too," answered the goatherd, "but I never wanted to pick it up or go near it, being afraid of some mishap and of their claiming it off me as stolen goods; for the devil is subtle, and things come up under a man's feet for him to trip and fall over without his knowing how or why."

"That's exactly what I say," answered Sancho: "I found it too, and I wouldn't go within a stone's throw of it. There I left it and there it stays as it was — I don't want a dog with a bell on it."

"Tell me, my good man," said Don Quixote, "do you know who the owner of these things may be?"

"What I can tell you," said the goatherd, "is that about six months ago, more or less, there arrived at a shepherds' hut some three leagues from this place a young man of fine build and bearing, riding that very mule that's lying dead there, and with the same cushion and portmanteau you say you found and didn't touch. He asked us which part of this sierra was the wildest and most hidden; we told him it was this one where we are now — and that's the truth of it, because if you go half a league further in, you may not manage to find your way out. And I'm amazed at how you've been able to get here, for there's no road or path that leads to this place.
