"I say, then, that on hearing our answer the young man turned his reins and headed for the place we'd pointed out, leaving us all pleased with his fine appearance and astonished at his question and at the haste with which we saw him ride off and turn towards the sierra. And from then on we never saw him again, until some days later he came out on the road at one of our shepherds and, without saying anything to him, went up to him and gave him a great many punches and kicks, and then went to the flock's she-ass and took all the bread and cheese she was carrying; and this done, he went back into the sierra with extraordinary quickness.

"When some of us goatherds learnt of this, we went looking for him for nearly two days through the thickest part of this sierra, at the end of which we found him lodged in the hollow of a thick and mighty cork tree. He came out to us very meekly, his clothes torn by now and his face disfigured and burnt by the sun in such a way that we hardly knew him; except that his clothes, torn as they were, along with what we knew of them, gave us to understand he was the man we were looking for.

"He greeted us courteously, and in a few very well-chosen words he told us not to be surprised at seeing him going about in that way, because it was necessary for him so as to carry out a certain penance that had been laid on him for his many sins. We begged him to tell us who he was, but we could never get it out of him. We also asked him that when he needed food, which he could not do without, he'd tell us where we could find him, because we'd bring it to him with a great deal of love and care; and that if this too was not to his liking, he should at least come out and ask for it, and not take it from the shepherds. He thanked us for our offer, asked pardon for the past attacks, and promised to ask for it from then on for the love of God, without giving anybody any trouble. As for where he lived, he said he had no dwelling but whatever chance offered him wherever night caught him.

"And he ended his talk with such tender weeping that we who had listened to him would have been made of stone if we hadn't joined him in it, thinking how we'd seen him the first time and what we saw him now. Because, as I've said, he was a very fine, well-favoured young man, and in his courteous and well-ordered speech he showed himself to be well born and a very courtly person; for even though we who were listening to him were rustics, his breeding was such that it was enough to make itself known to rusticity itself.

"And in the middle of the best of his talk he stopped and went dumb; he fixed his eyes on the ground for a good while, during which we all stood still and in suspense, waiting to see what that trance would come to, with no small pity at seeing it. Because from the way he opened his eyes and stared fixedly at the ground for a long time without moving an eyelash, and other times shut them, pressing his lips together and arching his eyebrows, we easily saw that some fit of madness had come over him.

"But he soon gave us to understand that what we thought was true, because he leapt up in a great fury from the ground where he'd thrown himself and attacked the first man he found next to him with such spirit and rage that if we hadn't pulled him off him he'd have killed him with his fists and his teeth. And all the time he was doing it he was saying: 'Ah, treacherous Fernando! Here, here you shall pay me for the wrong you did me: these hands shall pull out your heart, where every wickedness together has its lodging and its lair, and above all fraud and deceit!' And to these he added other speeches, all aimed at speaking ill of this Fernando and branding him a traitor and a false man.

"We got him off, then, with no small trouble; and he, without saying another word, went away from us and dived into these thickets and brambles at a run, in such a way that he made it impossible for us to follow him. From this we conclude that his madness comes on him in fits, and that somebody called Fernando must have done him some bad turn, as heavy a one as the state it has brought him to shows. And all of this has been confirmed since then by the times — and there have been many of them — that he has come out on the road, sometimes to ask the shepherds to give him some of what they are carrying to eat, and other times to take it from them by force; because when he is in his fit of madness, even if the shepherds offer it him willingly, he won't accept it but takes it with his fists; and when he is in his senses he asks for it for the love of God, courteously and politely, and gives a great many thanks for it, and not without tears.

"And I tell you truly, gentlemen," the goatherd went on, "that yesterday I and four lads — two of them servants and two friends of mine — made up our minds to look for him until we find him; and once he is found, whether by force or willingly, we mean to take him to the town of Almodóvar, which is eight leagues from here, and there we'll cure him if his trouble has any cure, or we'll find out who he is when he's in his senses, and whether he has relations we can give news of his misfortune to.

"This, gentlemen, is what I can tell you about what you've asked me; and understand that the owner of the things you found is the same man you saw go past as fast as he was naked" — for Don Quixote had already told him how he had seen that man leaping across the sierra.

Don Quixote was astonished at what he had heard from the goatherd, and was left with an even greater desire to know who the unfortunate madman was; and he resolved in himself what he had already been thinking: to look for him over the whole mountain, without leaving a corner or a cave in it unexamined, until he found him. But luck did better than he thought or hoped, because at that very instant there appeared, out of a ravine in a mountainside that came out where they were, the young man he was looking for, who was talking to himself about things that could not be understood close to, let alone from a distance. His clothes were as they have been described, except that when he came near, Don Quixote saw that a jerkin torn to pieces that he was wearing was scented with amber; from which he finally understood that a person who wore clothes of that kind could not be of the lowest quality.

On reaching them, the young man greeted them in a harsh, unmusical voice, but with a great deal of courtesy. Don Quixote returned his greetings with no less politeness, and dismounting from Rocinante, with a fine bearing and grace he went to embrace him and held him a good while tightly in his arms, as though he had known him a long time. The other — whom we may call the Ragged One of the Sorry Countenance, as we call Don Quixote he of the Sorrowful — after letting himself be embraced, pushed him a little away from himself, and putting his hands on Don Quixote's shoulders, stood looking at him as though he wanted to see whether he knew him — no less astonished, perhaps, at seeing Don Quixote's figure, build and armour than Don Quixote was at seeing him. In short, the first to speak after the embracing was the Ragged One, and he said what will be told further on.

Chapter 24: In Which the Adventure of the Sierra Morena Is Continued

The history says that Don Quixote listened to the ragged Knight of the Sierra with the very closest attention; who, going on with his talk, said:

"Certainly, sir, whoever you may be — for I do not know you — I thank you for the signs of goodwill and the courtesy you have shown me. And I could wish I were in a condition to repay with more than the will the kindness you have shown me in the good welcome you have given me; but my luck will not give me anything else to answer the good turns that are done me with, except a good desire to repay them."

"Mine," answered Don Quixote, "are desires to serve you — so much so that I had made up my mind not to leave these mountains until I had found you and learnt from you whether some kind of remedy could be found for the grief that the strangeness of your life shows you to be suffering; and if it were necessary to look for it, to look for it with all possible diligence. And if your misfortune were of the kind that has its doors shut against every sort of consolation, I meant to help you weep and lament over it as best I could, since it is still a consolation in misfortunes to find somebody who is sorry for them.

"And if my good intention deserves to be repaid with any kind of courtesy, I beg you, sir, by the great courtesy I see is shut up in you — and at the same time I conjure you by the thing you have most loved or most love in this life — to tell me who you are and the cause that has brought you to live and die in these solitudes like a brute beast, since you dwell among them so far from your own self, as your dress and person show. And I swear," Don Quixote added, "by the order of chivalry I received, unworthy and sinner though I am, and by the profession of knight errant, that if in this you gratify me, sir, I will serve you with all the earnestness that being who I am obliges me to: either by remedying your misfortune, if it has a remedy, or by helping you to weep over it, as I have promised you."

The Knight of the Wood, hearing the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance talk in this way, did nothing but look at him, and look at him again, and look him up and down once more; and after he had had a good look at him, he said:

"If you have anything to give me to eat, for the love of God give it me; and once I have eaten I will do everything I am told, in gratitude for the good wishes that have been shown me here."

Sancho at once got something out of his sack, and the goatherd out of his pouch, and with them the Ragged One satisfied his hunger, eating what they gave him like a man in a daze, so fast that he left no space between one mouthful and the next — for he bolted them rather than swallowed them. And while he was eating, neither he nor those who were watching him said a word. When he had finished eating he signed to them to follow him, which they did, and he took them to a little green meadow that lay round the turn of a rock not far from there. On reaching it he stretched himself out on the ground, on the grass, and the rest did the same; and all this without anybody speaking, until the Ragged One, having settled himself in his place, said:

"If it is your pleasure, gentlemen, that I should tell you in a few words the immensity of my misfortunes, you must promise me that you will not interrupt the thread of my sad history with any question or with anything else; because the moment you do, whatever I am telling will stop there."

These words of the Ragged One's brought to Don Quixote's memory the tale his squire had told him, when he got the number of goats that had crossed the river wrong and the story was left hanging. But to come back to the Ragged One, he went on to say:

"I make this stipulation because I would like to get quickly past the tale of my misfortunes; for bringing them back to mind serves no other purpose than to add fresh ones. And the less you ask me, the sooner I shall have finished telling them — though I shall not leave anything untold that is of any importance for satisfying your curiosity completely."

Don Quixote promised it in the name of the rest, and with this assurance the man began like this:

"My name is Cardenio; my birthplace, one of the best cities of this Andalusia; my family, noble; my parents, rich; my misfortune, so great that my parents must have wept over it and my family felt it, without being able to relieve it with their wealth — for the goods of fortune are generally worth little for putting right the sorrows heaven sends.

"There lived in this same country a heaven, in which love placed all the glory I could ever have wished for myself: such is the beauty of Luscinda, a young lady as noble and as rich as I am, but with more good fortune and less constancy than was owing to my honourable love for her. This Luscinda I loved, wanted and worshipped from my earliest and tenderest years, and she loved me with that simplicity and good will her few years allowed. Our parents knew what we intended and were not sorry about it, because they could see clearly that if it went further it could have no other end than our marrying, a thing which the equality of our families and wealth almost arranged of itself.

"Our ages grew, and with them the love of us both — so much so that Luscinda's father thought that for the sake of appearances he was obliged to refuse me the entry of his house, imitating in this almost exactly the parents of that Thisbe the poets have made so much of. And this refusal was adding flame to flame and desire to desire; because although they put silence on our tongues, they could not put it on our pens, which, with more freedom than tongues, generally give whoever they like to understand what is shut up in the soul — for very often the presence of the thing we love disturbs and strikes dumb the most determined intention and the boldest tongue.

"Oh heavens, how many notes I wrote her! How many charming and modest answers I had! How many songs I composed and how many love poems, in which the soul declared and set down its feelings, painted its burning desires, dwelt on its memories and gave itself pleasure!

"In the end, finding myself at my wits' end and my soul consuming itself with the desire to see her, I decided to put into practice and finish off in a moment the thing that seemed to me most likely to bring me the reward I wanted and deserved. And this was to ask her father for her as my lawful wife, which I did; to which he answered that he thanked me for the goodwill I showed in honouring him and in wanting to honour myself with something of his, but that since my father was alive it was for him by right to make that request; because if it were not done with his full goodwill and pleasure, Luscinda was not a woman to be taken or given by stealth.

"I thanked him for his good intention, thinking he was right in what he said, and that my father would come round to it as soon as I told him. And with this intention, at that very instant, I went to tell my father what I wanted. And just as I went into a room where he was, I found him with an open letter in his hand, which, before I could say a word to him, he gave me, saying: 'By that letter, Cardenio, you will see how ready Duke Ricardo is to do you a favour.'"

This Duke Ricardo, as you gentlemen must already know, is a grandee of Spain who has his estate in the best part of this Andalusia.

"I took the letter and read it, and it was couched in such pressing terms that even I thought it wrong of my father not to do what it asked, which was to send me at once to where the duke was; because he wanted me to be a companion, not a servant, to his eldest son, and he took it on himself to put me in a position that would match the esteem he had for me. I read the letter and went dumb as I read it, and more so when I heard my father saying to me: 'In two days from now, Cardenio, you will set off to do the duke's will; and give thanks to God that he is opening a road for you along which you may reach what I know you deserve.' To these he added other fatherly words of advice.

"The time for my departure came. I spoke to Luscinda one night and told her everything that was happening, and I did the same to her father, begging him to wait some days and put off giving her in marriage until I saw what Ricardo wanted of me. He promised me it, and she confirmed it with a thousand oaths and a thousand faintings.

"I came, in the end, to where Duke Ricardo was. I was so well received and treated by him that from the first envy began to do its work, the old servants feeling it towards me, since it seemed to them that the signs the duke gave of favouring me were bound to be to their disadvantage. But the one who was most delighted with my coming was a second son of the duke's called Fernando, a dashing young man, a gentleman, generous and amorous; who in a short time wanted me to be so much his friend that it gave everybody something to talk about. And although the eldest was fond of me and did me kindnesses, he did not go to the lengths that Don Fernando loved and treated me with.

"Now the fact is that, as among friends there is no secret that is not shared, and the favour I was in with Don Fernando had stopped being favour and become friendship, he told me all his thoughts — especially one love affair which was giving him a certain amount of unease. He was in love with a farmer's daughter, one of his father's vassals — and her parents were very rich — and she was so beautiful, modest, sensible and virtuous that nobody who knew her could decide which of these things she excelled in most.

"These very good qualities of the beautiful country girl brought Don Fernando's desires to such a pass that he decided, in order to get his way and conquer her integrity, to give her his word to be her husband — because any other way was attempting the impossible. I, obliged by his friendship, tried with the best arguments I knew and the most vivid examples I could to stop him and turn him away from such a purpose. But seeing it was no use, I decided to tell the business to Duke Ricardo his father. But Don Fernando, being shrewd and sharp, suspected and feared this, since it seemed to him that I was obliged, as a good servant, not to keep hidden a thing that was so much to the injury of my lord the duke's honour.

"And so, to distract and deceive me, he told me he could find no better remedy for driving out of his memory the beauty that had him so much in its power than going away for some months; and that he wanted the going away to be that the two of us should come to my father's house, with the excuse they would give the duke that he was coming to see and bargain for some very good horses in my city, which is the mother of the best in the world.

"I had hardly heard him say this when, moved by my own love, I would have approved his decision as one of the soundest imaginable even if it had not been so good a one, since I saw what a fine chance and opportunity it offered me of seeing my Luscinda again. With this thought and this desire I approved his idea and encouraged his purpose, telling him to put it into practice as quickly as possible, because in fact absence does its work in spite of the firmest attachments. By the time he came to tell me this, as was found out afterwards, he had already enjoyed the country girl on the strength of being her husband, and was waiting for a chance to declare himself in safety, afraid of what the duke his father would do when he found out about his folly.

"It happened, then, that as love in young men is for the most part not love but appetite — which, since it has pleasure for its final end, comes to an end on reaching it, and what looked like love has to go back the way it came, because it cannot go past the limit nature set it, a limit nature never set on what is true love — I mean that as soon as Don Fernando had enjoyed the country girl, his desires were quieted and his eagerness cooled. And if at first he had pretended to want to go away in order to cure them, now he genuinely tried to go so as not to have to carry them out.

"The duke gave him leave and ordered me to go with him. We came to my city; my father received him as the man he was; I saw Luscinda again straight away, and my desires came back to life, though they had never been dead or deadened. Of these I gave an account, to my cost, to Don Fernando, since it seemed to me that by the law of the great friendship he was showing I ought to hide nothing from him. I praised Luscinda's beauty, charm and good sense in such a way that my praises stirred up in him the desire to see a young lady adorned with so many good qualities. I satisfied him in it, by my short-sighted luck, showing her to him one night by the light of a candle, through a window where the two of us used to talk to each other. He saw her in a house-gown, and such that all the beauties he had seen up to then were put out of his mind. He was struck dumb, lost his senses, was left entranced and, in the end, as much in love as you will see in the course of the tale of my misfortune.

"And to inflame his desire further — which he hid from me and revealed only to heaven when he was alone — fortune willed that he should find one day a note of hers asking me to ask her father for her as my wife, so sensible, so modest and so loving that on reading it he told me that in Luscinda alone were shut up all the graces of beauty and understanding that were shared out among the rest of the women in the world.

"It is quite true, and I want to confess it now, that although I could see how justly Don Fernando was praising Luscinda, it grieved me to hear those praises out of his mouth; and I began to be afraid and suspicious of him, because no moment went past in which he did not want us to talk about Luscinda, and he would start the conversation even if he had to drag it in by the hair — a thing that woke a certain something of jealousy in me. Not that I feared any reverse in Luscinda's goodness and faith; but for all that, my luck made me afraid of the very thing she was assuring me of. Don Fernando always contrived to read the papers I sent Luscinda and the ones she answered me with, on the grounds that he greatly enjoyed the good sense of us both.

"It happened, then, that Luscinda having asked me for a book of chivalry to read, which she was very fond of, and it being the one about Amadis of Gaul —"

Don Quixote had hardly heard him name a book of chivalry when he said:

"If your worship had told me at the beginning of your history that her worship the lady Luscinda was fond of books of chivalry, no other exaggeration would have been needed to give me to understand the loftiness of her understanding; because she would not have had so good a one as you, sir, have painted her with, if she had lacked a taste for such delicious reading. So as far as I am concerned, there is no need to spend any more words in declaring her beauty, worth and understanding to me; simply from having understood her taste, I confirm her as the most beautiful and most intelligent woman in the world.

"And I could wish, sir, that your worship had sent her, along with Amadis of Gaul, the excellent Don Rugel of Greece; for I know the lady Luscinda would greatly enjoy Daraida and Geraya, and the wise sayings of the shepherd Darinel, and those admirable verses of his pastorals, sung and performed by him with all charm, discretion and ease. But a time may come when that omission can be made good, and the making good of it need take no longer than your worship's being pleased to come with me to my village; for there I can give you more than three hundred books, which are the delight of my soul and the entertainment of my life — although it is my belief that I have none left at all, thanks to the malice of wicked and envious enchanters.

"And your worship must forgive me for having gone against what we promised about not interrupting your talk; for on hearing of matters of chivalry and of knights errant, it is as much in my power to stop talking about them as it is in the power of the sun's rays to stop giving heat, or the moon's to stop bringing damp. So: your pardon, and go on, which is what most matters now."

While Don Quixote was saying what has just been set down, Cardenio's head had fallen on his chest, with every sign of his being deep in thought. And although Don Quixote told him twice to go on with his history, he neither raised his head nor answered a word; but at the end of a good while he raised it and said:

"There is no getting it out of my mind, nor will there be anybody in the world who can get it out, or make me understand anything else — and the man who understood or believed the contrary would be a blockhead — but that that great villain Master Elisabat was living in sin with Queen Madásima."

"That he was not, I swear it!" answered Don Quixote in a great temper — and he hurled his usual oath at him. "And that is a very great piece of malice, or knavery rather. Queen Madásima was a very great lady, and it is not to be supposed that so high a princess would live in sin with a quack surgeon; and whoever understands the contrary is lying like a very great scoundrel. And I shall give him to understand it, on foot or on horseback, armed or unarmed, by night or by day, or however it best pleases him."

Cardenio was looking at him very attentively — the fit of his madness having come on him by now, and he was in no state to go on with his history; nor would Don Quixote have listened to it, so much had what he had heard about Madásima disgusted him. A strange business: that he should take her part as though she had genuinely been his own true and natural lady — that is what his excommunicated books had brought him to.

I say, then, that as Cardenio was mad by now, and heard himself called a liar and a scoundrel with other insults of the same kind, he did not think much of the joke, and he picked up a stone he found next to him and struck Don Quixote such a blow on the chest with it that he knocked him over on his back. Sancho Panza, seeing his master brought to that pass, went for the madman with his fist clenched; and the Ragged One received him in such a way that with one punch he laid him at his feet, and then got on top of him and pounded his ribs entirely to his own satisfaction. The goatherd, who tried to defend him, ran the same risk. And after he had them all beaten and pounded, he left them and went off with perfect calm to hide himself in the mountain.

Sancho got up, and with the rage he was in at finding himself thrashed so undeservedly, he went to take his revenge on the goatherd, telling him that it was his fault for not having warned them that this man's madness took him in fits; because if they had known that, they would have been on their guard and able to look out for themselves. The goatherd answered that he had said so already, and that if Sancho had not heard it, it was not his fault. Sancho Panza answered back, and the goatherd answered back again, and the end of the answering back was that they caught each other by the beard and exchanged such punches that if Don Quixote had not made peace between them they would have torn each other to pieces. Sancho, grappling with the goatherd, was saying:

"Let me be, your worship, Sir Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance; with this man, who is a peasant like myself and hasn't been dubbed a knight, I can perfectly safely get satisfaction for the injury he's done me, fighting him hand to hand like an honourable man."

"That is so," said Don Quixote, "but I know that he is not at all to blame for what has happened."

With this he calmed them down; and Don Quixote went back to asking the goatherd whether it would be possible to find Cardenio, because he was left with an enormous desire to know the end of his history. The goatherd told him what he had told him at first, which was that he did not know his hiding place for certain; but that if he went about much in that district, he could not fail to find him, either sane or mad.

Chapter 25: Which Treats of the Strange Things That Happened to the Brave Knight of La Mancha in the Sierra Morena, and of His Imitation of Beltenebros' Penance

Don Quixote took his leave of the goatherd, and getting up on Rocinante again, he ordered Sancho to follow him, which Sancho did with his donkey, very much against his will. They went further and further, little by little, into the roughest part of the mountain; and Sancho was dying to talk with his master and wanted him to begin the conversation, so as not to go against what he had been ordered. But being unable to put up with so much silence, he said to him:

"Señor Don Quixote, will your worship give me your blessing and my leave? I want to go home from here, to my wife and children, with whom at any rate I shall talk and hold forth as much as I like. Because for your worship to want me to go about with him through these lonely places by day and by night and not talk to him when I feel like it is burying me alive. If only luck had it that the animals talked, as they used to talk in old Isop's day, it wouldn't be so bad, because then I'd discuss whatever came into my head with my donkey and get through my bad luck that way. It's a hard thing, and one a man can't bear patiently, to go about looking for adventures all your life and find nothing but kicks and blanket-tossings, brickbats and punches — and on top of all that we've got to sew up our mouths and not dare say what a man has in his heart, as though we were dumb."

"I understand you, Sancho," answered Don Quixote. "You are dying for me to lift the ban I have laid on your tongue. Take it as lifted, and say what you like, on condition that this lifting is to last no longer than while we are going about these mountains."

"So be it," said Sancho. "Let me talk now, for afterwards God knows what will happen. And starting to enjoy this safe-conduct, I say: what did it matter to your worship to stand up so hard for that Queen Magimasa, or whatever her name is? Or what did it signify whether that abbot was her friend or not? For if your worship had let it pass, since you weren't her judge, I really believe the madman would have gone on with his story, and we'd have saved the blow with the stone, and the kicks, and more than half a dozen cuffs besides."

"Upon my word, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "if you knew as I know what an honourable and distinguished lady Queen Madásima was, I know you would say I showed a great deal of patience, since I did not break the mouth such blasphemies came out of. Because it is a very great blasphemy to say or think that a queen was living in sin with a surgeon. The truth of the story is that this Master Elisabat the madman spoke of was a very prudent man of very sound advice, and served the queen as tutor and physician; but to think she was his mistress is an absurdity that deserves very heavy punishment. And so that you may see that Cardenio did not know what he was saying, you must note that when he said it he was already out of his senses."

"That's what I say," said Sancho: "that there was no call to take any account of a madman's words. Because if good luck hadn't helped your worship and steered the stone at your chest instead of your head, we'd have been in a fine state for standing up for that lady of mine, God confound her. And I'll bet Cardenio wouldn't have got off on grounds of madness!"

"Against the sane and against the mad alike, every knight errant is obliged to stand up for the honour of women, whoever they may be — much more so for queens of such high rank and worth as Queen Madásima was, for whom I have a particular affection on account of her good qualities. Because besides having been beautiful, she was moreover very prudent and very patient in her calamities, and she had a great many; and Master Elisabat's advice and company were of a great deal of use and relief to her in being able to bear her troubles with prudence and patience. And from this the ignorant and ill-meaning common people took occasion to say and think that she was his mistress; and they lie, I say it again, and will lie another two hundred times, all who think or say such a thing."

"I neither say it nor think it," answered Sancho. "Let them settle it themselves; let them eat it with their own bread. Whether they were living in sin or not, they'll have given God the account. I come from my own vineyards, I know nothing; I'm no friend to knowing about other people's lives; a man who buys and lies feels it in his own purse. What's more, naked I was born and naked I find myself: I neither lose nor gain. And supposing they were — what's it to me? Plenty of people think there's bacon hanging when there isn't even a hook. But who can put gates on an open field? Besides which, they said things about God himself."

"God help me," said Don Quixote, "what a string of foolish things you are threading together, Sancho! What have the proverbs you are stringing on got to do with what we are discussing? On your life, Sancho, be quiet; and from now on busy yourself with spurring your ass and leave off busying yourself with what does not concern you. And understand with all five of your senses that everything I have done, am doing and shall do is very much founded on reason and very much in accordance with the rules of chivalry, which I know better than all the knights who ever professed them in the world."

"Sir," answered Sancho, "and is it a good rule of chivalry that we should go about lost in these mountains, with no path or road, looking for a madman who, once we've found him, may take it into his head to finish what he left half done — not of his story, but of your worship's head and my ribs, and break them completely?"

"Be quiet, I tell you again, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "for I would have you know that what brings me to these parts is not so much the desire to find the madman as the desire to perform here a deed by which I shall win everlasting name and fame throughout the whole of the discovered earth; and it will be such a deed that I shall set the seal with it on everything that can make a knight errant perfect and famous."

"And is it a very dangerous deed, this?" asked Sancho Panza.

"No," answered the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, "although the dice might fall in such a way that we threw a losing cast instead of a winning one. But the whole thing will depend on your diligence."

"On my diligence?" said Sancho.

"Yes," said Don Quixote, "because if you come back quickly from where I mean to send you, my suffering will quickly be over and my glory will quickly begin. And since it is not right that I should keep you in suspense any longer, waiting to see what my words are coming to, I want you to know, Sancho, that the famous Amadis of Gaul was one of the most perfect knights errant. I have not put it well when I say one of them: he was the only one, the first, the unique one, the lord of all who were in the world in his time. A bad year and a bad month to Don Belianis and to all those who say he equalled him in anything, because they are mistaken, I swear it.

"I say likewise that when a painter wants to come out famous in his art, he tries to imitate the originals of the most singular painters he knows; and this same rule holds for all the other trades and callings of any account that serve for the adornment of nations. And so it must be done, and is done, by the man who wants to win a name for prudence and endurance, imitating Ulysses, in whose person and labours Homer paints us a living portrait of prudence and endurance — as Virgil likewise showed us, in the person of Aeneas, the valour of a dutiful son and the shrewdness of a brave and understanding captain, not painting or revealing them as they were but as they ought to have been, so as to leave their virtues as an example to the men who came after.

"In this same way Amadis was the north star, the morning star, the sun of brave and loving knights, whom all of us who serve under the banner of love and chivalry ought to imitate. This being so, as it is, I find, friend Sancho, that the knight errant who imitates him most closely will be nearest to attaining the perfection of chivalry. And one of the things in which this knight most showed his prudence, worth, courage, endurance, constancy and love was when he withdrew, scorned by the lady Oriana, to do penance on the Poor Rock, changing his name to Beltenebros — a name, certainly, that was significant and proper to the life he had chosen of his own free will.

"So that it is easier for me to imitate him in this than in cleaving giants, beheading serpents, killing dragons, routing armies, wrecking fleets and undoing enchantments. And since these places are so well suited for effects of the kind, there is no reason to let the opportunity go by that now offers me its forelock so conveniently."

"In short," said Sancho, "what is it your worship means to do in this out-of-the-way place?"

"Have I not told you already," answered Don Quixote, "that I want to imitate Amadis, playing here the man in despair, the idiot and the madman — imitating at the same time the brave Don Roland, when he found in a spring the evidence that Angelica the Fair had done a base thing with Medoro, and out of grief at it went mad and tore up the trees, muddied the waters of the clear springs, killed shepherds, destroyed flocks, burnt huts, pulled down houses, dragged mares about and did a hundred thousand other outrages worthy of everlasting name and record?

"And although I do not intend to imitate Roland, or Orlando, or Rotolando — for he had all three of these names — point by point in all the mad things he did and said and thought, I shall make a sketch of them, as best I can, in those that seem to me the most essential. And it may be that I shall come to be satisfied with the imitation of Amadis alone, who without doing any mad things that caused damage, but only weeping and grieving, won as much fame as the best of them."

"It seems to me," said Sancho, "that the knights who did such things were provoked and had a cause for those follies and penances. But your worship — what cause have you for going mad? What lady has scorned you, or what evidence have you found to give you to understand that the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso has done anything childish with Moor or Christian?"

"That is just the point," answered Don Quixote, "and that is the fine thing about my business. For a knight errant to go mad with a cause deserves neither thanks nor gratitude: the touch of it is to go out of my wits without any occasion, and give my lady to understand that if I do this dry, what would I do wet? What is more, I have occasion enough in the long absence I have kept from my ever-lady Dulcinea of El Toboso; for as you heard that shepherd Ambrosio say the other day, whoever is absent has all the ills and fears them all.

"So, friend Sancho, do not waste time advising me to give up so rare, so happy and so unheard-of an imitation. Mad I am, and mad I must be until you come back with the answer to a letter I mean to send by you to my lady Dulcinea. And if it is such as my faithfulness deserves, my idiocy and my penance will be over; and if it is the opposite, I shall be mad in earnest, and being so, I shall feel nothing. So that whichever way she answers, I shall come out of the struggle and the labour you leave me in, either enjoying the good news you bring me, as a sane man, or not feeling the bad news you bring me, as a madman.

"But tell me, Sancho: have you got Mambrino's helmet safely put away? For I saw that you picked it up off the ground when that ungrateful fellow tried to smash it to pieces. But he could not — from which one may see the fineness of its temper."

To which Sancho answered:

"By the living God, Sir Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, I can't stand or bear patiently some of the things your worship says. They make me start imagining that everything you tell me about chivalries and winning kingdoms and empires, about giving away isles and doing other favours and grand things the way knights errant do — that the whole of it must be so much wind and lies, and all humbug, or humbuggery, or whatever we call it. Because when a man hears your worship say that a barber's basin is Mambrino's helmet, and doesn't come out of that error in more than four days, what's he to think except that whoever says and maintains such a thing must be addled in his judgement? I've got the basin in the sack, all battered, and I'm taking it to have it seen to at home and shave myself in it, if God ever gives me the grace to see my wife and children again one day."

"Look, Sancho, by the same one you swore by just now I swear to you," said Don Quixote, "that you have the shortest understanding any squire in the world has or ever had. Is it possible that in all the time you have gone about with me you have not noticed that all the things belonging to knights errant look like fantasies, follies and absurdities, and that they are all done the wrong way round? And not because it is really so, but because there is always a crowd of enchanters going about among us who change and alter all our affairs and turn them about according to their taste, and according to whether they feel like favouring us or destroying us. And so what looks to you like a barber's basin looks to me like Mambrino's helmet, and will look like something else to somebody else.

"And it was rare foresight in the sage who is on my side to make what really and truly is Mambrino's helmet look like a basin to everybody; because it being of such value, the whole world would persecute me to take it from me. But since they see it is nothing more than a barber's basin, they do not trouble to go after it — as was well shown by the man who tried to break it and left it lying on the ground without taking it away. Upon my word, if he had recognised it he would never have left it. Keep it, my friend, for I do not need it at present; on the contrary, I am about to take off all this armour and be left as naked as when I was born, if I decide to follow Roland rather than Amadis in my penance."

Talking like this, they came to the foot of a high mountain that stood alone, almost like a sheer crag, among many others that surrounded it. A gentle little stream ran along its skirt, and all round it there was a meadow so green and so lush that it was a pleasure to the eyes that looked at it. There were a great many wild trees about, and some plants and flowers that made the place a peaceful one. This site the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance chose for doing his penance; and so, on seeing it, he began to say in a loud voice, as though he were out of his senses:

"This is the place, O heavens, that I appoint and choose for weeping over the misfortune you yourselves have put me in! This is the spot where the moisture of my eyes shall swell the waters of this little stream, and my continual and deep sighs shall set the leaves of these mountain trees continually moving, in testimony and token of the pain my harried heart suffers!

"O you, whoever you may be, rustic gods who have your dwelling in this uninhabitable place, hear the complaints of this unhappy lover, whom a long absence and some imagined jealousies have brought to lament among these wild places and to complain of the hard nature of that beautiful and ungrateful woman, the limit and end of all human beauty!

"O you wood nymphs and dryads, who have the custom of living in the thickets of the mountains — so may the nimble and lustful satyrs, by whom you are loved, though in vain, never disturb your sweet peace — help me to lament my misfortune, or at least do not grow tired of hearing it!

"O Dulcinea of El Toboso, day of my night, glory of my pain, north star of my roads, star of my fortune — so may heaven give you good fortune in whatever you may see fit to ask of it — consider the place and the state to which your absence has brought me, and answer with the proper return what my faithfulness deserves!

"O solitary trees, who from today on are to keep my solitude company, give some sign, by the soft movement of your branches, that my presence does not displease you!

"O you, my squire, agreeable companion in my more prosperous and my more adverse fortunes, take careful note of what you shall see me do here, so that you may tell and recite it to the total cause of it all!"

And saying this, he got down off Rocinante, and in a moment took off his bridle and his saddle; and giving him a slap on the hindquarters, he said to him:

"Freedom is given you by one who is left without it, O horse as outstanding for your deeds as you are unlucky in your fortune. Go where you like, for you carry it written on your forehead that neither Astolfo's hippogriff nor the famous Frontino, who cost Bradamante so dear, could equal you in speed."

Seeing this, Sancho said:

"Bless the man who has spared us the trouble of unsaddling the grey; because upon my word there'd have been no lack of little pats to give him and things to say in his praise. Though if he were here I wouldn't let anybody unsaddle him, since there'd be no call for it — the general rules for the man in love or the man in despair had nothing to do with him, seeing that his master, who was me while God willed it, was neither. And truly, Sir Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, if it's the case that my going and your worship's madness are meant in earnest, it'll be as well to saddle Rocinante again to make up for the lack of the grey, because it'll save time on my going and coming; for if I do it on foot, I don't know when I'll get there or when I'll be back, since when it comes down to it I'm a bad walker."

"I say, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "let it be as you like, for your plan does not seem bad to me. And I say that you shall set off three days from now, because in that time I want you to see what I do and say for her, so that you can tell her about it."

"But what more have I got to see," said Sancho, "than what I've seen?"

"You are well up in the tale!" answered Don Quixote. "I have still to tear my clothes, scatter my armour about and knock my head against these rocks, along with other things of that sort that are bound to astonish you."

"For the love of God," said Sancho, "let your worship be careful how you give yourself those knocks on the head; because you might come to such a rock, and at such a point, that with the very first one the whole machinery of this penance would be finished. And I'd be of the opinion that since your worship thinks the knocks on the head are necessary here and that this business can't be done without them, you might be satisfied — seeing that the whole thing is pretended and a made-up affair and a joke — you might be satisfied, I say, with giving them to yourself in the water, or on something soft like cotton wool; and leave the rest to me, for I'll tell my lady that your worship was giving them to yourself on the point of a rock harder than a diamond."

"I am grateful for your good intention, friend Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "but I want you to be informed that all these things I am doing are not done in joke but very much in earnest; because otherwise it would be going against the orders of chivalry, which command us not to tell any lie, on pain of being treated as relapsed heretics — and doing one thing for another is the same as lying. So my knocks on the head must be genuine, solid and valid, without anything sophistical or fanciful about them. And it will be necessary for you to leave me some lint to dress myself with, since fortune willed that we should lose the balm we lost."

"It was worse losing the ass," answered Sancho, "since the lint and everything else was lost along with him. And I beg your worship not to remember that accursed brew again; just to hear it mentioned turns my soul over, let alone my stomach. And I beg you further: reckon that the three days you gave me as a term for watching the mad things you do are over already, because I take them as seen and as settled beyond appeal, and I'll tell my lady marvels. So write the letter and send me off at once, because I have a great desire to come back and get your worship out of this purgatory I'm leaving you in."

"Purgatory, do you call it, Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "You would have done better to call it hell, and worse than that, if there is anything worse."

"For him that hath hell," answered Sancho, "nulla is retentio, as I've heard it said."

"I do not understand what retentio means," said Don Quixote.

"Retentio," answered Sancho, "means that whoever's in hell never comes out of it and can't. Which will be the other way round for your worship, or my feet will be doing badly by me, so long as I've got spurs to liven up Rocinante with. Just put me once and for all in El Toboso and in front of my lady Dulcinea, and I'll tell her such things about the follies and mad tricks — which are all one — that your worship has done and is still doing, that I'll get her softer than a glove, even if I find her harder than a cork tree; and with her sweet, honeyed answer I'll come back through the air like a witch and get your worship out of this purgatory, which looks like hell and isn't, since there's hope of getting out of it — which, as I've said, the people who are in hell haven't got, and I don't think your worship will say otherwise."

"That is the truth," said the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance; "but how shall we manage about writing the letter?"

"And the donkey-warrant as well," added Sancho.

"It shall all be included," said Don Quixote; "and it would be a good thing, since there is no paper, if we wrote it as the ancients did, on tree leaves or on little wax tablets — though that would be as hard to find now as paper. But it has just come into my memory where it will be well, and more than well, to write it: in the little pocket-book that was Cardenio's. And you will take care to have it copied onto paper, in a good hand, in the first place you come to where there is a schoolmaster; and if not, any parish clerk will copy it for you. And do not give it to any notary to copy, for they write a legal hand that Satan himself could not read."

"But what is to be done about the signature?" said Sancho.

"Amadis's letters are never signed," answered Don Quixote.

"That's all very well," answered Sancho, "but the warrant has to be signed of necessity; and if that's copied, they'll say the signature is a forgery and I'll be left without any donkeys."

"The warrant shall go in the same little book, signed; and when my niece sees it she will make no difficulty about carrying it out. And as far as the love letter goes, you will put as the signature: 'Yours until death, the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance.' And it will make very little difference that it goes in another hand, because as far as I can recall, Dulcinea cannot write or read, and in the whole of her life she has never seen my handwriting or a letter of mine; for my love and hers have always been platonic, going no further than a modest look. And even that so seldom that I could truthfully swear that in the twelve years I have loved her more than the light of these eyes that the earth will one day eat, I have not seen her four times — and it might even be that of those four times she never once noticed I was looking at her: such is the seclusion and confinement her father, Lorenzo Corchuelo, and her mother, Aldonza Nogales, have brought her up in."

"Well, well!" said Sancho. "So Lorenzo Corchuelo's daughter is the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, otherwise called Aldonza Lorenzo?"

"That is she," said Don Quixote, "and she is the one who deserves to be lady of the whole universe."

"I know her well," said Sancho, "and I can tell you she throws the bar as well as the strongest lad in the whole village. Praise the Giver, she's a girl with some go in her, straight up and down and hair on her chest, and she can pull the beard out of the mud for any knight errant, or knight to be, who has her for his lady. Oh, the son of a bitch, what a pair of lungs she's got, and what a voice! I can tell you that one day she got up on top of the village bell tower to call some lads of her father's who were out in a fallow field, and although they were more than half a league off, they heard her as clearly as if they'd been standing at the foot of the tower. And the best thing about her is that she's not a bit prim, because she's got a lot of the courtier in her: she jokes with everybody and makes a laugh and a game out of everything.

"Now I say, Sir Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, that not only can and should your worship do mad things for her, but you can with perfect justice despair and hang yourself as well; and nobody who hears of it will fail to say you did extremely well, even if the devil carries you off for it. And I'd like to see myself on the road now, just to look at her, because it's a long time since I saw her and she must be changed by now, for it wears a woman's face out a great deal to be always out in the fields, in the sun and the wind.

"And I'll confess a truth to your worship, Señor Don Quixote: up till now I've been in a great ignorance, because I thought, in good faith and sincerity, that the lady Dulcinea must be some princess your worship was in love with, or some such person as would deserve the rich presents your worship has sent her — the Basque and the galley slaves and a good many others there must be, seeing how many victories your worship must have won and did win in the time when I wasn't yet your squire. But when you think about it properly, what is it to the lady Aldonza Lorenzo — I mean the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso — that the men your worship sends her and is going to send her should go and kneel down in front of her? Because it might be that at the moment they arrived she'd be scutching flax or threshing on the threshing floor, and they'd be embarrassed to see her, and she'd laugh and be annoyed at the present."

"I have told you many times before now, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that you are a very great talker, and that although your wit is blunt, you often manage a sharp point. But so that you may see how foolish you are and how discerning I am, I want you to listen to a short story.

"You must know that a beautiful widow, young, free and rich, and above all easy-going, fell in love with a lay brother, a plump, well-set-up young fellow. His superior came to hear of it, and one day said to the good widow, by way of brotherly reproof: 'I am astonished, madam, and not without a great deal of cause, that a woman as distinguished, as beautiful and as rich as your worship should have fallen in love with a man as coarse, as low and as stupid as so-and-so, when there are in this house so many masters, so many licentiates and so many theologians among whom your worship might pick as though among pears, saying "I'll have this one, I won't have that one".' But she answered him with a great deal of grace and ease: 'Your worship, my dear sir, is very much mistaken, and thinks in a very old-fashioned way, if you think I have chosen badly in so-and-so, idiot as he seems to you; because for what I want him for, he knows as much philosophy as Aristotle, and more.'

"So, Sancho, for what I want Dulcinea of El Toboso for, she is worth as much as the highest princess on earth. Why, not all the poets who praise ladies under a name they give them at their own pleasure really have such ladies. Do you suppose that the Amaryllises, the Phyllises, the Silvias, the Dianas, the Galateas, the Alidas and the rest of them that the books, the ballads, the barbers' shops and the playhouses are full of were genuinely ladies of flesh and blood, and belonged to the men who celebrate them and celebrated them? Certainly not: most of them are invented, to give a subject for their verses and so that people should take them for men in love and for men with spirit enough to be so.

"And so it is enough for me to think and believe that the good Aldonza Lorenzo is beautiful and virtuous; and as far as family goes it matters little, since nobody is going to make inquiries into it in order to give her some order of knighthood, and I reckon to myself that she is the highest princess in the world. Because you must know, Sancho, if you do not know it, that two things alone stir a man to love more than any others, and they are great beauty and a good name; and these two things are found perfectly in Dulcinea, because in being beautiful no woman equals her, and in a good name few come near her.

"And to have done with the whole thing: I imagine that everything I say is exactly so, with nothing over and nothing lacking; and I paint her in my imagination as I want her, both in beauty and in rank. Helen does not come near her, nor does Lucretia reach her, nor any other of the famous women of ages past, Greek, barbarian or Latin. And let each man say what he likes; for if I am reproved for this by the ignorant, I shall not be punished by the strict."

"I say your worship is right in everything," answered Sancho, "and that I am an ass. Though I don't know why I put the word ass in my mouth, since you're not to mention rope in the house of a man who's been hanged. But let's have the letter, and goodbye — I'm off."

Don Quixote took out the pocket-book, and going off to one side, with great calm he began to write the letter; and on finishing it he called Sancho and told him he wanted to read it to him so that he could learn it by heart, in case he lost it on the road, because with his bad luck anything might be feared. To which Sancho answered:

"Let your worship write it two or three times there in the book and give it me, and I'll carry it safe; because to think that I'm going to learn it by heart is nonsense — my memory is so bad that I often forget my own name. But for all that, say it to me, your worship, for I'd very much like to hear it, since it must go like something out of a mould."

"Listen, this is how it goes," said Don Quixote:

Don Quixote's Letter to Dulcinea of El Toboso

Sovereign and lofty lady:

He that is wounded by the point of absence and pierced to the very tissues of the heart, sweetest Dulcinea of El Toboso, sendeth thee that health which he himself hath not. If thy beauty scorn me, if thy worth be not to my profit, if thy disdain be my undoing, then, howbeit I be a man of much sufferance, ill shall I be able to hold out in this affliction, which, besides being grievous, is very long-lasting. My good squire Sancho shall give thee full report, O fair ingrate, my beloved enemy, of the state in which I am left for thy sake. If it please thee to succour me, I am thine; and if not, do that which liketh thee, for by the ending of my life I shall have satisfied thy cruelty and my own desire.

Thine until death,

The Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance

"By my father's life," said Sancho when he had heard the letter, "that's the loftiest thing I ever heard. Bless me, how your worship says everything you want to say in there, and how well the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance fits into the signature! I tell you truly that your worship is the very devil, and there's nothing you don't know."

"Everything is needed," answered Don Quixote, "for the office I follow."

"Come on, then," said Sancho, "put the order for the three donkeys on the other side, and sign it very clearly so that they'll know it when they see it."

"With pleasure," said Don Quixote.

And having written it, he read it to him; and it went like this:

Your worship will please, by this first of donkeys, my dear niece, to deliver to Sancho Panza, my squire, three of the five I left at home and which are in your worship's charge. Which three donkeys I hereby order to be made over and paid for as against as many received here in cash, which is duly evidenced; and on his receipt they shall be well delivered. Done in the bowels of the Sierra Morena, the twenty-second of August of the present year.

"That's fine," said Sancho. "Let your worship sign it."

"There is no need to sign it," said Don Quixote, "only to put my flourish, which is the same thing as a signature; and for three asses, or even for three hundred, it would be enough."

"I trust your worship," answered Sancho. "Let me be — I'll go and saddle Rocinante, and your worship get ready to give me your blessing; because I mean to set off at once, without watching the idiocies your worship is going to perform. I'll say I saw you do so many that she won't want any more."

"At the very least I want you, Sancho — and because it is necessary that it should be so, I say I want you — to see me stripped, and to do a dozen or two mad things, which I shall do in less than half an hour; because having seen them with your own eyes, you may safely swear to any others you care to add. And I assure you that you will not tell as many as I mean to do."

"For the love of God, my dear sir, don't let me see your worship stripped; it will give me a great deal of grief and I shan't be able to help crying. And my head is in such a state from the weeping I did last night over the grey that I'm in no condition to get into fresh weeping. And if it's the case that your worship wants me to see some mad things, do them with your clothes on, briefly, and the ones that come handiest.

"What's more, none of it was needed as far as I'm concerned; and as I've said already, it would save the road for my coming back, which is to be with the news your worship wants and deserves. And if not, let the lady Dulcinea look out; because if she doesn't answer as she ought to, I make a solemn vow to whoever I can that I'll get the right answer out of her stomach with kicks and slaps. Because where is it to be borne that a knight errant as famous as your worship should go mad, without rhyme or reason, over a — ? Don't make me say it, madam, for by God I'll let fly and sell the whole lot at twelve, even if it never sells. I'm a fine one for that! She little knows me! Well, upon my word, if she knew me she'd keep my day as a fast!"

"Upon my word, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "by the look of it you are no saner than I am."

"I'm not so mad," answered Sancho, "but I'm more hot-tempered. But leaving that aside, what is your worship going to eat while I'm away? Are you going to go out on the road like Cardenio and take it off the shepherds?"

"Do not let that trouble you," answered Don Quixote, "because even if I had food I should eat nothing but the herbs and fruits this meadow and these trees may give me; for the fine point of my business lies in not eating and in performing other equivalent austerities."

"Goodbye, then. But do you know what I'm afraid of, your worship? That I shan't manage to find my way back to this place where I'm leaving you now, it's so hidden away."

"Take your bearings carefully; I shall try not to move away from this district," said Don Quixote, "and I shall even take care to climb up on these higher crags to see whether I can make you out when you come back. What is more, the surest thing, so that you do not miss me and get lost, will be for you to cut some of the broom that grows plentifully about here and go on putting it down at intervals until you come out on the open ground; and it will serve you as landmarks and signs for finding me when you come back, in imitation of the thread in Theseus's labyrinth."

"I'll do that," answered Sancho Panza.

And cutting some, he asked his master for his blessing; and not without a great many tears on both sides, he took his leave of him. And getting up on Rocinante, whom Don Quixote earnestly commended to him, telling him to look after the horse as he would his own person, he set off on the road down to the plain, scattering the broom branches at intervals as his master had advised him. And so he went off, although Don Quixote still kept pressing him to watch him do at least two mad things. But he had not gone a hundred paces when he came back and said:

"I say, sir, your worship spoke very well: so that I can swear without any burden on my conscience that I've seen you do mad things, it'll be as well if I see at least one — although I've seen a very big one in your worship's staying behind."

"Did I not tell you so?" said Don Quixote. "Wait, Sancho; I shall do them in the time it takes to say a creed."

And stripping off his breeches in all haste, he was left in his skin and his shirt-tails; and then, without any more ado, he cut two capers in the air and turned two somersaults, head down and heels up, revealing things which, so as not to see them a second time, made Sancho turn Rocinante's rein and hold himself content and satisfied that he could swear his master was left mad. And so we shall leave him to go on his way until he comes back, which was soon.

Chapter 26: In Which Are Continued the Refinements That Don Quixote Performed as a Lover in the Sierra Morena

Coming back to tell what the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance did once he found himself alone, the history says that as soon as Don Quixote had finished turning his somersaults, naked from the waist down and clothed from the waist up, and saw that Sancho had gone without choosing to wait and see any more idiocies, he climbed up onto the point of a high rock, and there went back to thinking about what he had thought about many times before without ever settling it. And this was which would be better and would suit his case more: to imitate Roland in the outrageous mad things he did, or Amadis in the melancholy ones. And talking to himself, he said:

"If Roland was as good a knight and as brave as they all say, what is there to wonder at? After all, he was enchanted and nobody could kill him except by sticking a farthing pin through the sole of his foot, and he always wore shoes with seven iron soles. Although the tricks did him no good against Bernardo del Carpio, who saw through them and choked him to death in his arms at Roncesvalles.

"But leaving the matter of his courage aside, let us come to his losing his wits — which he certainly did, because of the evidence he found at the spring and the news the shepherd gave him that Angelica had slept more than two siestas with Medoro, a curly-headed little Moor and page to Agramante. And if he understood this to be true and that his lady had done him a wrong, it was no great thing for him to go mad.

"But I — how can I imitate him in the mad things if I do not imitate him in the occasion for them? Because I would dare to swear that my Dulcinea of El Toboso has not seen a single Moor in the whole of her life, in his own dress and as he really is, and that she stands today as her mother bore her; and I should be doing her a plain injury if, imagining anything else about her, I went mad with that particular kind of madness of Roland the furious.

"On the other hand, I see that Amadis of Gaul, without losing his wits and without doing mad things, won as great a fame as a lover as the best of them; because what he did, according to his history, was no more than this: finding himself scorned by his lady Oriana, who had ordered him not to appear in her presence until it should be her will, he withdrew to the Poor Rock in the company of a hermit, and there he wept his fill and commended himself to God, until heaven came to his help in the middle of his greatest distress and need.

"And if this is true, as it is, why should I want to take the trouble now of stripping myself completely, or of upsetting these trees, which have done me no harm? Nor have I any reason to muddy the clear water of these streams, which are to give me drink when I am thirsty. Long live the memory of Amadis, and let him be imitated by Don Quixote of La Mancha in everything he can; of whom it shall be said what was said of the other, that if he did not achieve great things, he died attempting them. And if I am not cast off or scorned by Dulcinea of El Toboso, it is enough for me, as I have said already, to be absent from her.

"Come then, to work! Come into my memory, deeds of Amadis, and show me where I must begin to imitate you. But I know already that the most he did was to pray and commend himself to God. Yet what shall I do about a rosary, having none?"

At this it came into his mind how he would make one; and it was that he tore a great strip off the tail of his shirt, which was hanging loose, and put eleven knots in it, one of them fatter than the rest, and this served him as a rosary the whole time he was there, in which he said a million Hail Marys. And what wearied him a great deal was not finding another hermit thereabouts to hear his confession and be a comfort to him.

And so he entertained himself walking about the little meadow, writing and carving on the bark of the trees and in the fine sand a great many verses, all of them fitted to his sadness and some in praise of Dulcinea. But those that could be found entire and could still be read after they had found him there were no more than these that follow:

	Trees and grasses and plants
	that grow about this place,
	so tall, so green and so many,
	if you take no pleasure in my hurt,
	hear my holy complaints.
	Let my grief not upset you,
	however terrible it may be;
	for, to pay you his share of the reckoning,
	here Don Quixote wept
	for the absence of Dulcinea
	of El Toboso.
	This is the place where
	the most loyal lover there is
	hides himself from his lady,
	and has come to such a bad pass
	without knowing how or by which road.
	Love drags him about by the ears,
	being of a very bad breed;
	and so, till he has filled a cask,
	here Don Quixote wept
	for the absence of Dulcinea
	of El Toboso.
	Looking for adventures
	among the hard rocks,
	cursing hard hearts,
	for it is among crags and thickets
	that the sad man finds misfortunes,
	love struck him with his whip,
	not with his soft strap;
	and, catching him on the back of the neck,
	here Don Quixote wept
	for the absence of Dulcinea
	of El Toboso.

The addition of "of El Toboso" to Dulcinea's name caused no small amount of laughter in those who found the verses just given, because they supposed Don Quixote must have supposed that if, on naming Dulcinea, he did not also say "of El Toboso", the stanza could not be understood; and that was the truth of it, as he afterwards admitted. He wrote a great many others, but as has been said, no more than these three stanzas could be made out clearly or found entire.

With this, and with sighing and calling on the fauns and satyrs of those woods, on the nymphs of the rivers, on the sorrowful and moist Echo, to answer him and comfort him and hear him, he passed his time — and with looking for a few herbs to keep himself alive on until Sancho came back. And if Sancho had taken three weeks instead of the three days he did take, the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance would have been left so disfigured that the mother who bore him would not have known him.

And it will be as well to leave him wrapped up in his sighs and his verses, and tell what happened to Sancho Panza on his errand. Which was that on coming out on the high road he set off in search of El Toboso; and the next day he reached the inn where the misfortune of the blanket had happened to him. And he had hardly caught sight of it when it seemed to him that he was going through the air again, and he did not want to go inside — although he arrived at an hour when he could and should have done so, it being dinner time and his having a longing to taste something hot, since for days on end everything had been cold.

This necessity forced him to go up close to the inn, still uncertain whether he would go in or not. And while he was in this state, two people came out of the inn who recognised him at once; and one of them said to the other:

"Tell me, Señor Licentiate, that man on the horse — isn't that Sancho Panza, the one our adventurer's housekeeper said had gone off with his master as his squire?"

"So it is," said the licentiate; "and that is our Don Quixote's horse."

And they recognised him as well as they did because they were the curate and the barber of his own village, the very ones who had held the scrutiny and general trial of the books. As soon as they had finished recognising Sancho Panza and Rocinante, being eager for news of Don Quixote, they went up to him; and the curate called him by his name, saying:

"Friend Sancho Panza, where is your master?"

Sancho Panza recognised them at once, and made up his mind to conceal the place and the state in which and how he had left his master; and so he answered them that his master was busy in a certain place on a certain matter of great importance to him, which he could not reveal for the eyes in his head.

"No, no," said the barber, "Sancho Panza. If you don't tell us where he is, we shall imagine — as we are already imagining — that you have killed and robbed him, since you are riding on his horse. Upon my word, you must produce the owner of the hack, or it will be the worse for you."

"There's no call for threats with me; I'm not a man who robs or kills anybody. Let every man be killed by his own luck, or by God who made him. My master is doing penance in the middle of that mountain, entirely to his own satisfaction."

And then, all in a rush and without stopping, he told them the state he had left him in, the adventures that had happened to them, and how he was carrying the letter to the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, who was Lorenzo Corchuelo's daughter, and that his master was in love with her up to his liver.

The two of them were astonished at what Sancho Panza told them; and although they already knew about Don Quixote's madness and the kind it was, every time they heard about it they were astonished all over again. They asked Sancho Panza to show them the letter he was carrying to the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso. He said it was written in a pocket-book, and that his master's order was that he should have it copied onto paper at the first place he came to; to which the curate said he should show it him and he would copy it in a very good hand.

Sancho Panza put his hand into his shirt looking for the little book, but he did not find it, nor could he have found it if he had gone on looking until now, because Don Quixote had kept it and had not given it him, nor had Sancho remembered to ask him for it.

When Sancho saw he could not find the book, his face went the colour of death; and feeling all over his body again in a great hurry, he saw again that he could not find it. And without any more ado he put both fists to his beard and pulled half of it out, and then, quickly and without stopping, gave himself half a dozen punches on the face and on the nose, so that he bathed the whole of it in blood. Seeing which, the curate and the barber asked him what had happened to him, that he was in such a state.

"What should have happened to me," answered Sancho, "except that I have lost three donkeys from one hand to the other in a single moment, and every one of them was like a castle?"

"How is that?" asked the barber.

"I've lost the pocket-book," answered Sancho, "with the letter for Dulcinea in it and a warrant signed by my master, ordering his niece to give me three donkeys out of the four or five that were at home."

And with this he told them about the loss of the grey. The curate comforted him, and told him that when he found his master he would have him confirm the gift and make out the warrant again on paper, as was the use and custom, because warrants made out in pocket-books were never accepted or honoured.

Sancho was comforted at this, and said that if that was so, the loss of Dulcinea's letter did not trouble him much, because he knew it almost by heart, and it could be copied down from him wherever and whenever they liked.

"Say it, then, Sancho," said the barber, "and we'll copy it out afterwards."

Sancho Panza stopped and scratched his head to bring the letter back to mind, and stood now on one foot and now on the other; sometimes he looked at the ground, sometimes at the sky; and after he had gnawed away half the tip of one finger, keeping in suspense those who were waiting for him to say it at last, he said, after an enormously long while:

"By God, Señor Licentiate, the devil take the thing I can remember of the letter — although at the beginning it said: 'Lofty and sodden lady.'"

"It wouldn't have said sodden," said the barber, "but superhuman, or sovereign lady."

"That's it," said Sancho. "Then, if I don't remember it wrong, it went on — if I don't remember it wrong — 'the wounded by the pint of absence and the pierced in the tassels of the heart kisses your worship's hands, ungrateful and very unknown beauty'; and there was something I don't know about health and sickness that he was sending her; and then it went slipping along that way until it finished up with 'Yours until death, the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance.'"

The two of them were not a little pleased to see how good Sancho Panza's memory was, and praised it highly, and asked him to say the letter another two times so that they too could learn it by heart and copy it out in due course. Sancho said it another three times, and another three times said another three thousand absurdities.

After this he likewise told them his master's affairs, but did not say a word about the blanket-tossing that had happened to him at that inn, which he refused to go into. He also said that as soon as he brought his master a good dispatch from the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, he was to set off to see about becoming an emperor, or at the very least a monarch; for they had settled it so between the two of them, and it was a very easy thing to become one, considering the valour of his person and the strength of his arm. And that once he was one, he was to marry Sancho off, because by then he would be a widower — it could not be otherwise — and was to give him for a wife one of the empress's ladies, heiress to a rich, great estate on the mainland, with no isles or islets about it, for he did not want them any more.

Sancho said all this so composedly, wiping his nose every now and then, and with so little sense, that the two of them were astonished all over again, considering how violent Don Quixote's madness must have been, since it had carried this poor man's judgement away with it. They did not want to take the trouble of getting him out of the error he was in, since it seemed to them that as it did his conscience no harm it was better to leave him in it, and it would be more entertaining for them to listen to his foolishness. And so they told him to pray to God for his master's health, since it was a contingent and very achievable thing that in the course of time he should come to be an emperor as he said, or at the very least an archbishop, or hold some equivalent dignity. To which Sancho answered:

"Gentlemen, if fortune turned things about in such a way that my master took it into his head not to be an emperor but to be an archbishop, I'd like to know now what wandering archbishops generally give their squires."

"They generally give them," answered the curate, "some benefice, either a simple one or one with a cure of souls, or some post as sacristan, which brings them in a good settled income, besides the altar dues, which are generally reckoned at as much again."

"For that it will be necessary," replied Sancho, "for the squire not to be married and to know how to serve at Mass, at the very least. And if that's so, unlucky me, for I'm married and I don't know the first letter of the ABC! What will become of me if my master takes a fancy to being an archbishop and not an emperor, as is the use and custom of knights errant?"

"Don't distress yourself, friend Sancho," said the barber; "we'll beg your master here, and advise him, and even put it to him as a matter of conscience, that he should be an emperor and not an archbishop — because it will be easier for him, on the grounds that he's more of a fighter than a scholar."

"That's how it has seemed to me," answered Sancho, "although I can tell you he has the ability for everything. What I mean to do on my side is to pray to Our Lord to throw him into whichever line he can serve him best in and do me the most favours in."
