"You say it like a man of sense," said the curate, "and you'll do it like a good Christian. But what has to be done now is to make arrangements for getting your master out of that useless penance you say he's doing. And to think of the way we're to go about it, and to have dinner, since it's time for it, we had better go into this inn."

Sancho told them to go in themselves, and that he would wait outside and afterwards tell them the reason why he was not going in and why it was not advisable for him to; but that he begged them to bring him something to eat out there that was hot, and likewise some barley for Rocinante. They went in and left him; and shortly afterwards the barber brought him something to eat.

Afterwards, having thought over carefully between them the way they were to go about getting what they wanted, the curate hit on an idea very well fitted to Don Quixote's taste and to their own purpose. And it was that he told the barber that what he had thought of was that he himself would dress up as a damsel errant, and that the barber should do his best to get himself up as a squire; and that they would go like that to where Don Quixote was, pretending that she was a distressed and needy damsel, and would ask him for a boon, which he could not refuse to grant her, being a valorous knight errant.

And the boon she meant to ask him for was that he should come with her wherever she took him, to undo a wrong that a wicked knight had done her; and that she likewise begged him not to order her to take off her veil, or ask her anything about her affairs, until he had got her justice against that wicked knight. And that he should be in no doubt that Don Quixote would agree to everything she asked him on those terms; and that in this way they would get him out of there and take him to his village, where they would see whether his strange madness had any remedy.

Chapter 27: Of How the Curate and the Barber Carried Out Their Plan, with Other Things Worthy of Being Told in This Great History

The curate's idea did not strike the barber as a bad one — so far from it that they put it into practice at once. They asked the innkeeper's wife for a skirt and a headdress, leaving her a new cassock of the curate's as a pledge. The barber made a great beard out of a grey or reddish oxtail that the innkeeper kept his comb hanging on. The innkeeper's wife asked them what they wanted these things for. The curate told her in a few words about Don Quixote's madness, and how this disguise was needed for getting him down out of the mountain, where he was at that moment.

The innkeeper and his wife immediately realised that the madman was their guest, the one with the balm and the master of the blanketed squire, and they told the curate everything that had happened to them with him, not keeping quiet about the thing Sancho kept so quiet about.

In short, the innkeeper's wife dressed the curate up in a way that was a sight to see. She put on him a cloth skirt with bands of black velvet a hand's breadth wide all over it, all slashed, and a bodice of green velvet trimmed with edging of white satin, which — bodice and skirt alike — must have been made in the time of King Wamba. The curate would not let them put a headdress on him, but put on his head a little quilted linen cap that he wore for sleeping at night, and bound a garter of black taffeta round his forehead, and with another garter made a mask with which he covered his beard and face very thoroughly. He rammed his hat down on top, which was so big that it could have served him as a sunshade; and wrapping himself in his cloak, he got up sideways on his mule, and the barber on his, with his beard that came down to his waist, half red and half white — being made, as has been said, out of the tail of a reddish ox.

They took their leave of everybody, and of good Maritornes, who promised to say a rosary, sinner though she was, so that God should give them good success in so arduous and so Christian a business as the one they had undertaken.

But he had hardly got out of the inn when a thought came to the curate: that he was doing wrong to have got himself up like that, it being an unbecoming thing for a priest to dress that way however much depended on it. And telling this to the barber, he begged him to change clothes with him, since it was more proper that the barber should be the distressed damsel and he would play the squire, and in that way his own dignity would be less profaned; and that if the barber would not do it, he had made up his mind not to go any further, even if the devil carried Don Quixote off.

At this Sancho arrived, and at the sight of the two of them in that dress he could not hold in his laughter. In the end the barber agreed to everything the curate wanted; and changing the plan round, the curate went on instructing him in the manner he was to adopt and the words he was to say to Don Quixote to move and force him to come away with him and leave off his fondness for the place he had chosen for his empty penance. The barber answered that without being given any lesson he would manage it perfectly. He did not want to dress up just then, until they were near where Don Quixote was; and so he folded up his clothes, and the curate stowed his beard, and they went on their way, with Sancho Panza guiding them. And Sancho told them as they went about what had happened to them with the madman they had found in the sierra — keeping quiet, however, about the finding of the portmanteau and everything in it; because, dolt though he was, the lad was a little on the greedy side.

The next day they came to the place where Sancho had left the branches as signs to find the spot where he had left his master; and on recognising it he told them this was the way in, and that they might as well dress up if that really had anything to do with his master's deliverance. For they had told him beforehand that going in that way and dressing in that fashion was the whole essential thing for getting his master out of that bad life he had chosen; and they charged him earnestly not to tell his master who they were or that he knew them; and that if his master asked him — as he was bound to ask him — whether he had given the letter to Dulcinea, he was to say yes, and that as she could not read she had answered him by word of mouth, saying that she ordered him, on pain of her displeasure, to come and see her that very moment, because it was a matter of great importance to her. For with this, and with what they meant to say to him, they took it as certain that they would bring him round to a better life, and get him to set out at once to go and be an emperor or a monarch — for as far as being an archbishop went, there was nothing to fear.

Sancho listened to it all and took it very well into his memory, and thanked them warmly for their intention of advising his master to be an emperor and not an archbishop, because it was his own opinion that for doing favours to their squires, emperors could do more than wandering archbishops. He also told them that it would be as well if he went ahead to find him and give him his lady's answer, since that would be enough on its own to get him out of that place without their putting themselves to so much trouble. What Sancho Panza said seemed good to them, and so they decided to wait for him until he came back with news of finding his master.

Sancho went in among those ravines of the sierra, leaving the two of them in one along which ran a small, quiet stream, agreeably and coolly shaded by other rocks and some trees that stood about there. The heat, and the day they arrived there, was one of those of the month of August, when in those parts the burning heat is usually very great; the hour, three in the afternoon: all of which made the place more agreeable and made it an invitation to wait there for Sancho's return, which is what they did.

The two of them being there, then, at their ease and in the shade, there came to their ears a voice which, without the accompaniment of any instrument, sounded sweetly and delightfully — at which they were not a little astonished, since it seemed to them that this was no place where there could be anybody who sang so well. Because although it is often said that shepherds with extraordinary voices are to be found in the woods and fields, this is more the exaggeration of poets than the truth; and the more so when they noticed that what they heard being sung were verses, not of rustic herdsmen but of well-bred courtiers. And this truth was confirmed by the verses they heard, which were these:

	What is it wears my fortunes down?
		Disdain.
	And what is it swells my griefs?
		Jealousy.
	And what is it tries my patience?
		Absence.
	So in this sickness of mine
	no remedy is to be had,
	since my hope is killed outright
	by disdain, jealousy and absence.
	Who is it causes me this pain?
		Love.
	And who is it grudges me my glory?
		Fortune.
	And who consents to my grieving?
		Heaven.
	So I am afraid I shall die
	of this strange complaint of mine,
	since they combine to do me harm —
	love, fortune and heaven.
	Who will make my luck any better?
		Death.
	And the good of love, who reaches it?
		Change.
	And its ills, who cures them?
		Madness.
	So it is no sense at all
	to want to cure the passion
	when the remedies are
	death, change and madness.

The hour, the season, the loneliness, the voice and the skill of the singer caused astonishment and delight in the two who heard it, and they stayed still, waiting to hear whether anything more would come. But finding that the silence lasted some while, they decided to go out and look for the musician who sang with so good a voice. And just as they were about to do it, the same voice made them stay where they were, coming again to their ears singing this sonnet:

	Holy friendship, who on light wings,
	leaving your outward likeness here on earth,
	went up in gladness among the blessed souls
	to the halls of heaven,
	from up there, when you choose, you show us
	the just peace covered over with a veil,
	through which there sometimes shows the zeal
	for good works that are, in the end, bad.
	Leave heaven, O friendship, or else do not allow
	deceit to put on your livery,
	which it uses to destroy sincere intention;
	for if you do not take your appearance from it,
	the world will soon find itself in the struggle
	of that first discordant confusion.

The song ended with a deep sigh, and the two of them listened carefully and went back to waiting to hear whether any more would be sung. But finding that the music had turned into sobs and pitiful groans, they decided to find out who the sad man was, as remarkable in his voice as he was sorrowful in his groaning; and they had not gone far when, on turning the point of a rock, they saw a man of the same build and figure that Sancho Panza had described to them when he told them Cardenio's story. And this man, when he saw them, did not start, but stayed still with his head bent on his chest like a man deep in thought, without raising his eyes to look at them any more than the first time, when they came up unexpectedly.

The curate, who was a well-spoken man — being one who already knew about his misfortune, since he had recognised him by the description — went up to him, and in brief but very well-judged words begged and urged him to leave that wretched life, so that he should not lose it there, which would be the greatest misfortune of all misfortunes.

Cardenio was at that moment in his full senses, free of that furious fit that so often carried him out of himself; and so, seeing the two of them in a dress so unusual among people who went about those solitudes, he could not help being somewhat astonished — and the more so when he heard them speak about his business as about a thing already known, since the curate's words gave him to understand that. And so he answered in this way:

"I can see plainly, gentlemen, whoever you may be, that heaven, which takes care to help the good, and often the wicked too, is sending me, without my deserving it, in these remote places so far removed from the common dealings of men, certain people who, setting before my eyes with vivid and various arguments how unreasonable I am in living the life I live, have tried to get me out of it into a better condition. But since they do not know that I know that on coming out of this trouble I am bound to fall into a greater one, perhaps they must take me for a man of feeble reasoning — or, what would be worse, for a man of no judgement at all.

"And it would be no wonder if that were so, because I can see for myself that the force of my imagination of my misfortunes is so intense and has such power over my ruin that, without my being able to do anything to stop it, I end up like a stone, without any good sense or awareness. And I come to see the truth of this when some people tell me and show me evidence of the things I have done while that terrible fit has me in its power; and I can do no more than grieve to no purpose and curse my luck to no profit, and give as an excuse for my mad acts the telling of the cause of them to anybody who wants to hear it. Because when sane people see what the cause is, they will not be astonished at the effects; and if they cannot give me a remedy, at least they will not blame me, and their annoyance at my violence will turn into pity for my misfortunes.

"And if it is the case, gentlemen, that you come with the same intention that others have come with, before you go any further with your judicious persuasions I beg you to listen to the tale — which has no end — of my misfortunes; because perhaps, once you have understood it, you will save yourselves the trouble you would take in comforting a hurt that is incapable of any comfort."

The two of them, who wanted nothing else than to know the cause of his trouble from his own mouth, begged him to tell it, offering to do nothing but what he wanted himself, in the way of remedy or comfort. And with this the sad gentleman began his pitiful history, almost in the same words and following the same course as when he had told it to Don Quixote and the goatherd a few days before, when, on account of Master Elisabat and Don Quixote's exactness in keeping up the proprieties of chivalry, the tale had been left unfinished, as the history has related. But now good luck willed that the fit of madness held off and gave him room to tell it to the end.

And so, coming to the passage about the note Don Fernando had found in the copy of Amadis of Gaul, Cardenio said he had it well by heart, and that it went like this:

Luscinda to Cardenio

Every day I discover in you qualities that oblige and compel me to esteem you more highly; and so, if you wish to get me out of this debt without executing judgement on my honour, you may very well do it. I have a father who knows you and who is fond of me, and who, without forcing my will, will fall in with whatever it will be right for you to want, if you value me as you say and as I believe.

"It was this note that moved me to ask for Luscinda as my wife, as I have already told you; and it was on account of this that Luscinda was left in Don Fernando's opinion as one of the most sensible and quick-witted women of her time; and this note was what put into him the desire to destroy me before mine could be carried out.

"I told Don Fernando what Luscinda's father was insisting on, which was that my father should ask him for her, and that I did not dare tell my own father, being afraid he would not agree to it — not because he did not thoroughly know Luscinda's quality, goodness, virtue and beauty, and that she had qualities enough to ennoble any other line in Spain, but because I understood from him that he wanted me not to marry so soon, until he saw what Duke Ricardo would do for me. In short, I told him that I did not venture to say it to my father, both because of that obstacle and because of a great many others that made me afraid, without my knowing what they were, except that it seemed to me that what I wanted was never going to come about.

"To all this Don Fernando answered that he would undertake to speak to my father and get him to speak to Luscinda's. O ambitious Marius, O cruel Catiline, O criminal Sulla, O lying Ganelon, O treacherous Vellido, O vengeful Julian, O covetous Judas! Traitor, cruel, vengeful and lying — what disservice had this poor wretch done you, who with such openness revealed to you the secrets and the joys of his heart? What offence did I do you? What words did I say to you, or what advice did I give you, that was not all aimed at increasing your honour and your profit?

"But what am I complaining of, unlucky man that I am? Since it is a certain thing that when misfortunes are brought on by the current of the stars, coming as they do from high to low, hurling themselves down with fury and violence, there is no force on earth that can stop them and no human contrivance that can foresee them. Who could have imagined that Don Fernando — an illustrious, intelligent gentleman, under obligation to me for my services, and with power enough to get whatever his amorous desire asked for wherever it settled — should have grown so bitter, as they say, over taking from me one single ewe lamb that I did not even yet possess?

"But let these reflections be left aside as useless and unprofitable, and let us knot up the broken thread of my unhappy history.

"I say, then, that it seemed to Don Fernando that my presence was an obstacle to putting his false and wicked plan into effect, and so he decided to send me to his elder brother on the excuse of asking him for some money to pay for six horses which he had deliberately bought — and solely for this purpose of getting me out of the way, so that he could better succeed in his corrupt intention — on the very day he offered to speak to my father; and he wanted me to go for the money.

"Could I have foreseen this treachery? Could I, by any chance, have hit on imagining it? Certainly not; on the contrary, I offered with the greatest pleasure to set off at once, delighted with the good purchase that had been made. That night I spoke to Luscinda and told her what had been settled with Don Fernando, and that she should have firm hope that our good and just desires would come about. She, as unsuspecting as I was of Don Fernando's treachery, told me to try to come back soon, because she thought the fulfilment of our wishes would take no longer than my father took to speak to hers. I do not know what came over her, but on finishing saying this her eyes filled with tears and a knot came into her throat that would not let her say a word of the many others she seemed to me to be trying to say to me.

"I was astonished at this new turn, never before seen in her; because we always talked to each other, the times good fortune and my own diligence allowed it, with complete cheerfulness and pleasure, without mixing tears, sighs, jealousies, suspicions or fears into our conversation. It was all a matter of my magnifying my good luck at heaven's having given her to me as my lady: I exaggerated her beauty, I marvelled at her worth and understanding. She gave me back the exchange, praising in me whatever, being in love, seemed to her worth praising. With this we told each other a hundred thousand trifles and pieces of news about our neighbours and acquaintances, and the furthest my boldness ever went was to take, almost by force, one of her lovely white hands and raise it to my mouth, as far as the narrowness of a low grille that separated us allowed.

"But the night before the sad day of my departure, she wept and moaned and sighed, and went away and left me full of confusion and alarm, appalled at having seen such new and such sad signs of grief and feeling in Luscinda. But so as not to destroy my hopes, I put it all down to the strength of the love she had for me and to the pain that absence usually causes in those who love each other well.

"In the end I went away sad and thoughtful, my soul full of fancies and suspicions, without knowing what I suspected or fancied: clear signs showing me the sad event and the misfortune that was in store for me.

"I reached the place I was sent to. I gave the letters to Don Fernando's brother. I was well received, but not quickly dispatched, because he ordered me to wait — very much against my liking — for eight days, and in a place where the duke his father would not see me, because his brother wrote to him that he should send him a certain sum of money without his father's knowledge. And it was all the invention of that false Don Fernando, since his brother did not lack money to send me off at once. This was an order and a command that put me in a position to disobey it, since it seemed to me impossible to keep myself alive for so many days in Luscinda's absence — and the more so, having left her in the sadness I have told you of. But for all that I obeyed, like a good servant, although I could see that it was bound to be at the cost of my health.

"But four days after I got there, a man came looking for me with a letter, which he gave me and which I knew by the address to be from Luscinda, because the writing on it was hers. I opened it, afraid and alarmed, believing it must be something grave that had moved her to write to me while I was away, since even when I was there she seldom did it.

"Before reading it I asked the man who had given it him and how long he had taken on the road. He told me that as it happened, going along a street in the city at midday, a very beautiful lady had called him from a window with her eyes full of tears, and had said to him in a great hurry: 'Brother, if you are a Christian, as you look to be, for the love of God I beg you to get this letter at once, at once, to the place and the person named on the address, both of which are well known; and in doing it you will do a great service to our Lord. And so that you shall not lack the means to do it, take what is in this handkerchief.'

"'And saying this,' he said, 'she threw me a handkerchief out of the window, with a hundred reals tied up in it and this gold ring I have here, along with the letter I have given you. And then, without waiting for any answer from me, she left the window — though first she saw how I took the letter and the handkerchief, and I signed to her that I would do what she asked. And so, finding myself so well paid for the trouble I might take in bringing it to you, and knowing by the address that you were the man it was being sent to — because I know you very well, sir — and being moved besides by that beautiful lady's tears, I decided not to trust anybody else but to come myself and give it you; and in the sixteen hours since it was given me I have done the journey, which as you know is eighteen leagues.'

"While the grateful and newly-made courier was telling me this, I hung on his words, my legs trembling in such a way that I could hardly hold myself up. In the end I opened the letter and saw that it contained these words:

The word Don Fernando gave you, to speak to your father so that your father should speak to mine, he has kept more to his own pleasure than to your profit. Know, sir, that he has asked for me as his wife, and my father, carried away by the advantage he thinks Don Fernando has over you, has agreed to what he wants, and so much in earnest that the betrothal is to take place two days from now, so secretly and so privately that the only witnesses are to be the heavens and some of the household. Imagine the state I am in. Whether it is worth your coming, you must see; and whether I love you or not, the outcome of this business will give you to understand. Please God this may reach your hands before mine finds itself in a position to be joined with the hand of a man who knows so badly how to keep the faith he promises.

"These, in short, were the words the letter contained, and the ones that made me set off at once, without waiting for any other answer or any other money; for I saw plainly enough by then that it was not the buying of horses but the buying of his own pleasure that had moved Don Fernando to send me to his brother.

"The anger I conceived against Don Fernando, together with the fear of losing the treasure I had won with so many years of service and longing, put wings on me; for almost as though I flew, the next day I was in my own town, at exactly the point and hour that was right for going to speak to Luscinda. I went in secretly, and left the mule I had come on at the house of the good man who had brought me the letter; and luck willed that at that moment it should be so good to me that I found Luscinda standing at the grille, the witness of our love. Luscinda knew me at once, and I knew her; but not as she ought to have known me and I ought to have known her. But who is there in the world who can boast that he has penetrated and understood the confused thinking and changeable nature of a woman? Nobody, certainly.

"I say, then, that as soon as Luscinda saw me she said to me: 'Cardenio, I am dressed for a wedding. Don Fernando the traitor and my father the covetous man are already waiting for me in the hall with other witnesses, who will be witnesses of my death sooner than of my betrothal. Do not be alarmed, my friend, but try to be present at this sacrifice; and if it cannot be prevented by my words, I have a dagger hidden about me that can prevent more determined forces, putting an end to my life and a beginning to your knowing the love I have had for you and still have.'

"I answered her in alarm and haste, afraid I should have no time to answer her at all: 'Lady, may your deeds make your words come true; for if you are carrying a dagger to prove yourself with, here I am carrying a sword to defend you with, or to kill myself with if fortune goes against us.'

"I do not think she could hear all these words, because I heard that they were calling her in a hurry, because the bridegroom was waiting. With this the night of my sorrow closed in and the sun of my happiness went down: I was left without light in my eyes and without reasoning in my understanding. I could not manage to go into her house, nor could I move anywhere at all; but considering how much my presence mattered for whatever might happen in that case, I took as much courage as I could and went into the house. And as I already knew all its ways in and out very well, and the more so with the commotion that was secretly going on in it, nobody noticed me. So that, without being seen, I had a chance to place myself in the recess made by a window of that same hall, which was covered by the ends and fringes of two tapestries, between which I could see, without being seen, everything that was going on in the hall.

"Who could describe now the shocks that hit my heart while I was there, the thoughts that came to me, the reflections I made? They were so many and such that they cannot be told, and it is not even right that they should be. Enough that you should know that the bridegroom came into the hall with no other adornment than the same ordinary clothes he usually wore. He brought as his best man a first cousin of Luscinda's, and there was nobody from outside in the whole hall except the servants of the house.

"A little later Luscinda came out of a dressing room, accompanied by her mother and two of her maids, as well dressed and got up as her rank and beauty deserved, and as befitted one who was the perfection of courtly elegance and splendour. My suspense and rapture gave me no room to look at and note in detail what she had on; I could only take in the colours, which were flesh-pink and white, and the glints thrown out by the stones and jewels of her headdress and of the whole gown — all of which was surpassed by the singular beauty of her lovely fair hair, so that in competition with the precious stones and the light of four torches that were in the hall, hers offered more brilliance to the eye.

"O memory, mortal enemy of my rest! What is the use of representing to me now the incomparable beauty of that adored enemy of mine? Would it not be better, cruel memory, that you should remind me and represent to me what she did then, so that, moved by so plain a wrong, I might try — if not for revenge — at least to lose my life?"

"Do not grow tired, gentlemen, of hearing these digressions I make; for my suffering is not of the kind that can or should be told briefly and in passing, since every circumstance of it seems to me to deserve a long discourse."

To this the curate answered that not only were they not tired of hearing him, but that the small particulars he was telling gave them a great deal of pleasure, being such that they deserved not to be passed over in silence, and deserved the same attention as the main part of the tale.

"I say, then," Cardenio went on, "that everybody being in the hall, the parish priest came in; and taking the two of them by the hand to do what is required in such an act, at the words 'Do you, lady Luscinda, take the lord Don Fernando, here present, for your lawful husband, as Holy Mother Church commands?' I put my whole head and neck out from between the tapestries, and with the most attentive ears and a soul in turmoil I set myself to listen to what Luscinda would answer, expecting from her answer the sentence of my death or the confirmation of my life.

"Oh, if only I had dared to come out then, crying aloud: 'Ah, Luscinda, Luscinda, look what you are doing! Consider what you owe me! See that you are mine and cannot be another's! Be warned that your saying yes and the ending of my life must happen at one and the same instant. Ah, treacherous Don Fernando, robber of my glory, death of my life! What do you want? What are you after? Consider that you cannot as a Christian reach the end of your desires, because Luscinda is my wife and I am her husband.'

"Ah, madman that I am — now that I am absent and far from the danger, I say I ought to have done what I did not do! Now that I let my dear treasure be stolen, I curse the robber, on whom I could have taken revenge if I had had the heart for it as I have the heart for complaining! In short, since I was a coward and a fool then, it is no great matter that I should die now mortified, repentant and mad.

"The priest was waiting for Luscinda's answer, which she was a good while in giving; and when I thought she was pulling out the dagger to prove herself, or loosening her tongue to say some truth or undeceiving that would come out to my advantage, I hear her say in a faint, weak voice: 'I do.' And Don Fernando said the same; and giving her the ring, they were left bound in an indissoluble knot. The bridegroom came up to embrace his wife, and she, putting her hand over her heart, fell fainting into her mother's arms.

"It remains now to say the state I was left in, seeing in the yes I had heard my hopes mocked, Luscinda's words and promises false, and myself made incapable of ever recovering the good I had lost in that instant. I was left without counsel, abandoned — as it seemed to me — by all heaven, made an enemy of the earth that held me up, the air denying me breath for my sighs and the water moisture for my eyes; only fire increased, in such a way that I was all burning with rage and jealousy.

"Everybody was thrown into confusion by Luscinda's faint; and when her mother unfastened her bodice to let the air get to her, a folded paper was found in it, which Don Fernando took at once and set himself to read by the light of one of the torches. And on finishing reading it, he sat down in a chair and put his hand to his cheek, with every sign of a man deep in thought, without attending to the remedies that were being applied to his wife to bring her out of her faint.

"Seeing the whole household in an uproar, I ventured to come out, whether I was seen or not, with the resolve that if they did see me I would do such a wild thing that everybody would come to understand the just indignation of my breast in the punishment of the false Don Fernando, and even of the changeable heart of the fainting traitress. But my luck — which must be keeping me for greater evils, if it is possible that there are any — arranged that at that moment I should have more understanding than I have had ever since. And so, without wanting to take revenge on my greatest enemies, which would have been easy since they were so far from thinking about me, I chose to take it on myself and to carry out on myself the punishment they deserved — and perhaps with more severity than would have been used on them if I had killed them then, since a death that comes suddenly soon ends the pain, but one that is drawn out with torments is always killing without ever ending the life.

"In the end I left that house and came to the house of the man where I had left the mule. I had him saddle her, and without taking leave of him I mounted and rode out of the city, not daring, like another Lot, to turn my face and look at it. And when I found myself alone in the open country, and the darkness of the night hid me and its silence invited me to complain, without any respect or fear of being heard or recognised, I let out my voice and loosed my tongue in so many curses against Luscinda and Don Fernando, as though with them I were making good the wrong they had done me.

"I gave her the titles of cruel, of ungrateful, of false and thankless; but above all of covetous, since my enemy's wealth had closed the eyes of her affection, to take her from me and hand her to the man fortune had shown itself more generous and open-handed with. And in the middle of the flood of these curses and reproaches, I made excuses for her, saying that it was no great thing that a girl brought up quietly in her parents' house, made and used always to obey them, should have chosen to fall in with their wishes, since they were giving her for a husband a gentleman so distinguished, so rich and so well-bred that if she had refused to accept him it might be thought either that she had no sense or that her affections were somewhere else — a thing that would work so much to the harm of her good name and reputation.

"Then I would turn round and say that if she had said I was her husband, they would have seen that she had not made so bad a choice in choosing me that they could not have excused her; because before Don Fernando offered himself, they could not themselves have hit on wishing for a better husband for their daughter than me, if they had measured their wishes by reason. And that she could very well, before putting herself in the last and unavoidable pass of giving her hand, have said that I had already given her mine; for I would have come forward and agreed with everything she might have thought of inventing in the case.

"In the end I concluded that little love, little judgement, great ambition and a desire for grandeur had made her forget the words with which she had deceived me, kept me going and sustained me in my firm hopes and honourable desires.

"With these cries and this restlessness I travelled what was left of that night, and at dawn I came to one of the ways into these mountains, along which I travelled another three days, with no path or road, until I came to a stop at some meadows which lie I do not know which way from these mountains; and there I asked some herdsmen which way the wildest part of these sierras lay. They told me it was this way. I set off for it at once, with the intention of ending my life here; and on getting in among these wild places, my mule fell dead of weariness and hunger, or — what I am more inclined to believe — in order to shake off so useless a burden as she was carrying in me. I was left on foot, worn out by nature, pierced through with hunger, with nobody to help me and no thought of looking for anybody.

"In that state I lay stretched out on the ground for I do not know how long, at the end of which I got up without hunger, and found beside me some goatherds who must without doubt have been the ones who relieved my need, because they told me the state they had found me in, and how I was saying so many mad and absurd things that they were clear evidence of my having lost my wits. And I have felt in myself ever since that I do not have them whole all the time, but so damaged and feeble that I do a thousand mad things — tearing my clothes, shouting through these solitudes, cursing my luck and repeating in vain the beloved name of my enemy, with no other thought or purpose at those times than to try to end my life by shouting. And when I come to myself, I find myself so tired and pounded that I can hardly move.

"My most usual dwelling is in the hollow of a cork tree, big enough to cover this wretched body. The cowherds and goatherds who go about these mountains, moved by charity, keep me alive, putting food for me along the paths and on the rocks where they suppose I might chance to pass and find it. And so, even when my wits fail me at the time, natural need makes me recognise food and wakes in me the desire to want it and the will to take it. Other times they tell me, when they meet me in my senses, that I come out on the roads and take it by force, even when they give it me willingly, from the shepherds who are bringing it from the village to the sheepfolds.

"In this way I get through my wretched, extreme life, until heaven is pleased either to bring it to its final end or to put it into my memory to make me not remember Luscinda's beauty and treachery and Don Fernando's wrong; for if he does this without taking my life, I shall turn my thoughts to better reasoning. And if not, there is nothing for it but to beg him to have mercy on my soul outright, for I feel in myself neither courage nor strength to get my body out of the straits I have chosen to put it in of my own free will."

"This, gentlemen, is the bitter story of my misfortune. Tell me whether it is such that it can be attended with less feeling than what you have seen in me. And do not tire yourselves out persuading me or advising me what reason may tell you might be good for my remedy; because it will do as much good with me as a medicine prescribed by a famous doctor does for a sick man who will not take it. I do not want health without Luscinda; and since she chose to belong to another, being — or having been bound to be — mine, let me choose to belong to misfortune, when I might have belonged to good luck.

"She chose, by her change, to make my ruin permanent; I shall choose, by contriving to lose myself, to make her wish come true; and it will be an example to those to come that I alone lacked what all other unfortunate men have to spare. For to them the impossibility of comfort is usually a comfort, and in me it is the cause of greater sufferings and evils, because I believe that even death will not put an end to them."

Here Cardenio brought to an end his long speech and his history, as unhappy as it was full of love. And just as the curate was preparing to say a few words of comfort to him, he was stopped by a voice that came to his ears, saying in sorrowful tones what will be told in the fourth part of this narrative — for at this point the wise and cautious historian Cide Hamete Benengeli brought the third to an end.

Chapter 28: Which Treats of the New and Agreeable Adventure That Befell the Curate and the Barber in the Same Sierra

Part Four of the Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha

Most happy and most fortunate were the times in which the boldest of knights, Don Quixote of La Mancha, was launched upon the world; for it is because he took so honourable a decision as wanting to bring back to life and restore to the world the already lost and almost dead order of knight-errantry that we now enjoy, in this age of ours which is so in want of cheerful entertainment, not only the sweetness of his true history but also the tales and episodes in it, which are in part no less agreeable, no less artfully made and no less true than the history itself.

Which history, going on with its carded, twisted and wound thread, relates that just as the curate was beginning to prepare himself to comfort Cardenio, he was prevented by a voice that came to his ears saying in sad tones:

"Oh God! Can it be possible that I have found at last a place that can serve as a hidden grave for the heavy burden of this body I keep going so much against my will? Yes, it can, if the solitude these mountains promise does not lie to me. Ah, wretched woman, and how much more agreeable company these crags and thickets will be to my purpose than any human being's — since they will give me room to communicate my misfortune to heaven in complaints! For there is nobody on earth from whom one can hope for counsel in doubts, relief in troubles or remedy in evils."

The curate and those with him heard and took in all these words; and as it seemed to them, as it was, that they were being said close by, they got up to look for the speaker. And they had not gone twenty paces when, behind a boulder, they saw sitting at the foot of an ash tree a young fellow dressed as a farm labourer, whose face they could not see for the moment because he had it bent down, being engaged in washing his feet in the stream that ran along there.

And they came up so silently that he did not notice them, nor was he attending to anything except washing his feet, which were such that they seemed nothing but two pieces of white crystal born among the other stones of the stream. The whiteness and beauty of the feet took them aback, since it seemed to them that they were not made for treading clods or for going about behind the plough and the oxen, as their owner's dress suggested. And so, seeing that they had not been noticed, the curate, who was in front, signed to the other two to crouch down or hide behind some pieces of rock that were there, and they all did so, watching attentively what the young man did.

He had on a short brown two-skirted jacket, belted close to the body with a white towel. He wore likewise breeches and gaiters of brown cloth, and on his head a brown cap. He had the gaiters pushed up to halfway up his leg, which without any doubt looked like white alabaster. He finished washing his beautiful feet, and then dried them with a head-cloth he pulled out from under the cap; and on going to take the cap off he raised his face, and those who were watching him had the chance to see an incomparable beauty — such that Cardenio said to the curate in a low voice:

"Since this is not Luscinda, this is no human being but a divine one."

The young man took off the cap, and shaking his head from side to side, there began to loosen and spread out a head of hair that the sun's rays might have envied. By this they knew that the one who seemed a labourer was a woman, and a delicate one, and even the most beautiful the eyes of the other two had seen up to then — and Cardenio's too, if he had not looked at and known Luscinda; for he afterwards declared that only Luscinda's beauty could compete with hers.

The long fair hair not only covered her shoulders but hid the whole of her under it all round; so that except for the feet, no other part of her body showed: so long and so much of it there was. And in this her hands served her as a comb; and if the feet in the water had looked like pieces of crystal, the hands in the hair seemed like pieces of packed snow — all of which put the three who were watching her into greater astonishment and a greater desire to know who she was.

For this reason they decided to show themselves; and at the movement they made in getting to their feet, the beautiful girl raised her head, and pushing the hair away from in front of her eyes with both hands, she looked at those who were making the noise. And she had hardly seen them when she got to her feet, and without waiting to put on her shoes or gather up her hair, she snatched up very quickly a bundle that looked like clothes which she had beside her, and tried to take to flight, full of alarm and fright. But she had not gone six steps when, her delicate feet being unable to bear the roughness of the stones, she came down on the ground.

Which the three of them seeing, they came out to her, and the curate was the first to say to her:

"Stop, madam, whoever you may be; the men you see here have no other intention than to serve you. There is no reason for you to put yourself to such unnecessary flight, because your feet will not be able to bear it and we will not allow it."

To all this she answered not a word, astonished and confused. So they came up to her, and the curate, taking her by the hand, went on to say:

"What your dress denies us, madam, your hair reveals to us: clear signs that the causes must be of no small moment which have disguised your beauty in dress as unworthy as this and brought you into a solitude as great as this — in which it has been good fortune to have found you, if not to give a remedy for your troubles, at least to give them counsel. For no trouble, so long as it does not end the life, can weary a person so much or come so near to the extreme of being one that the sufferer should refuse even to listen to advice that is given with good intentions. So, madam — or sir, or whatever you may choose to be — put off the alarm the sight of us has caused you and tell us your good or bad fortune; for in us together, or in each of us, you will find somebody to help you feel your misfortunes."

While the curate was saying all this, the disguised girl stood as though entranced, looking at them all without moving her lips or saying a single word, exactly like some country rustic who is suddenly shown rare things he has never seen before. But when the curate went back to saying other words directed to the same purpose, she gave a deep sigh and broke her silence and said:

"Since the solitude of these mountains has not been enough to hide me, and the loosening of my untidy hair has not allowed my tongue to be a liar, it would be useless for me to pretend all over again now what, if it were believed, would be believed more out of courtesy than for any other reason. This being granted, I say, gentlemen, that I thank you for the offer you have made me, which has put me under an obligation to satisfy you in everything you have asked — although I am afraid the account I give you of my misfortunes will cause you distress as much as pity, because you will find no remedy to remedy them and no comfort to lighten them.

"But for all that, so that my honour may not go on wavering in your minds, since you have already recognised me for a woman and see me young, alone and in this dress — all of them things together, and each one on its own, which can throw any honest reputation to the ground — I shall have to tell you what I would rather keep quiet if I could."

All this she said without stopping, this person who looked so beautiful a woman, with so ready a tongue and so soft a voice that her good sense astonished them no less than her beauty. And when they had made her new offers and new entreaties to keep her promise, she, without making them beg any further, put on her shoes with complete modesty and gathered up her hair, and settled herself on the seat of a stone; and with the three of them placed around her, forcing herself to hold back some tears that came into her eyes, she began the history of her life in a calm, clear voice, like this:

"In this Andalusia there is a place from which a duke takes his title, which makes him one of those they call grandees of Spain. This man has two sons: the elder, heir to his estate and, by the look of it, to his good habits; and the younger, I do not know what he is the heir of, unless it is of Vellido's treacheries and Ganelon's lies.

"My parents are this lord's vassals, humble in family but so rich that if the goods of their birth had matched the goods of their fortune, they would have had nothing more to wish for and I should not have had to fear finding myself in the misfortune I am in. Because perhaps my lack of good fortune comes from the lack of it they had in not being born distinguished. It is quite true that they are not so low that they need be ashamed of their condition, nor so high that they take away from me the notion I have that my misfortune comes from their humble station.

"They are, in short, farmers, plain people, with no admixture of any ill-sounding blood, and, as they say, Old Christians of the oldest vintage — but so rich that their wealth and handsome way of living is little by little winning them the name of gentlefolk, and even of gentry. Although the greatest wealth and nobility they prided themselves on was having me for their daughter; and so, both because they had no other daughter or son to inherit from them and because they were fond parents, I was one of the most indulged daughters that parents ever indulged.

"I was the mirror they looked at themselves in, the staff of their old age, and the object towards which — measuring them by heaven's will — they directed all their wishes; from which, they being so good, mine did not depart a hair's breadth. And in the same way that I was mistress of their hearts, so I was of their property. Through me the servants were taken on and dismissed; the reckoning and account of what was sown and gathered passed through my hands; the olive mills, the wine presses, the number of the large and small livestock, the number of the beehives — in short, of everything that so rich a farmer as my father can have and does have, I kept the account and was the steward and mistress, with so much care on my part and so much pleasure on theirs that I honestly cannot find words for it.

"The hours of the day I had left over, after giving out what was needed to the foremen, the overseers and the other day labourers, I spent on those occupations that are as proper as they are necessary for young women, such as the needle and the lace-cushion offer, and often the distaff. And if I sometimes left these occupations aside to refresh my spirits, I took refuge in the entertainment of reading some devotional book, or of playing a harp — because experience showed me that music settles unsettled minds and relieves the troubles that are born in the spirit.

"This, then, was the life I led in my parents' house; and if I have told it in such detail, it has not been out of ostentation or to make it understood that I am rich, but so that it may be noticed how blamelessly I have come from that good condition I have described to the unhappy one I now find myself in.

"The case, then, is this. Passing my life in so many occupations and in a seclusion that might have been compared to a convent's, being seen — as I thought — by no other person than the servants of the house, since on the days I went to Mass it was so early in the morning, and I was so much accompanied by my mother and other maidservants, and so veiled and so careful, that my eyes hardly saw more ground than the piece I set my feet on; and yet in spite of all this, the eyes of love — or of idleness rather, which the eyes of the lynx cannot match — saw me, in the shape of the attentions of Don Fernando, that being the name of the duke's younger son that I have told you about."

The woman who was telling the tale had hardly named Don Fernando when the colour changed in Cardenio's face and he began to sweat, with such a great disturbance that the curate and the barber, who noticed it, were afraid he was having that fit of madness they had heard came on him from time to time. But Cardenio did nothing except sweat and stay still, staring hard at the country girl, guessing who she was; and she, without noticing Cardenio's movements, went on with her history, saying:

"And they had hardly seen me when, according to what he said afterwards, he was as much taken captive by love of me as his behaviour gave everyone to understand. But to get quickly to the end of the tale of my misfortunes, which has none, I want to pass over in silence the efforts Don Fernando made to declare his intentions to me. He bribed the whole household; he gave and offered gifts and favours to my relatives. The days were all holidays and rejoicing in my street; at night the music let nobody sleep. The notes that came into my hands, I do not know how, were endless, full of loving words and offers, with fewer letters in them than promises and oaths.

"All of which not only did not soften me but hardened me, as though he had been my mortal enemy and everything he did to bring me round to his wishes had been done for the opposite effect. Not that Don Fernando's good looks displeased me, or that I thought his attentions excessive; because it gave me a certain something of pleasure to see myself so much loved and esteemed by so distinguished a gentleman, and it did not grieve me to see my own praises in his papers — for in this, however plain we women may be, it seems to me that we always take pleasure in being called beautiful.

"But against all this stood my sense of honour and the constant advice my parents gave me, who by now knew Don Fernando's intentions quite openly, because by then he did not care in the least that the whole world should know them. My parents told me that they left and deposited their honour and good name in my virtue and goodness alone, and that I should consider the inequality there was between me and Don Fernando, and that from this I should see that his thoughts, whatever he might say to the contrary, were aimed more at his own pleasure than at my good. And that if I wanted to put some kind of obstacle in the way so that he should give up his unjust pretensions, they would marry me at once to whoever I most liked, either from the most distinguished people of our own village or from all those round about — since everything could be hoped for from their great property and my good name.

"With these firm promises, and with the truth of what they told me, I fortified my integrity, and I never chose to answer Don Fernando with a word that could show him, even from a great way off, any hope of getting what he wanted.

"All this reserve of mine, which he must have taken for disdain, must have been what sharpened his lustful appetite further — for that is the name I want to give the affection he showed me; which, if it had been what it ought to have been, you would not be hearing about it now, because there would have been no occasion to tell you.

"In the end Don Fernando learnt that my parents were about to marry me off, in order to take away from him the hope of possessing me, or at least so that I should have more guards to guard me; and this news, or suspicion, was the cause of his doing what you shall now hear.

"And it was that one night, when I was in my room with only the company of a maid who served me, having the doors well shut for fear that through carelessness my honour should find itself in danger, without my knowing or imagining how, in the middle of all these precautions and preventions and in the loneliness of that silence and confinement, I found him in front of me. The sight of him confused me in such a way that it took away the sight of my eyes and struck my tongue dumb; and so I was not able to cry out, nor do I think he would have let me, because he came up to me at once, and taking me in his arms — for I, as I say, had no strength to defend myself, disturbed as I was — he began to say such things to me that I do not know how it is possible for a lie to have such skill that it can put them together in a way that makes them seem so true. The traitor made his tears give credit to his words and his sighs to his intentions. I, poor creature, alone among my own people and little practised in cases of the kind, began, I do not know how, to take so many falsehoods for truths — but not in such a way that his tears and sighs moved me to any more than a proper compassion.

"And so, that first shock passing off, I came somewhat to recover my lost spirits, and with more courage than I thought I could have, I said to him: 'If, sir, as I am in your arms, I were between the paws of a fierce lion, and freeing myself from them were assured me on condition that I did or said something to the harm of my honour, it would be as possible for me to do it or say it as it is possible for what has already happened not to have happened. So that if you have my body encircled with your arms, I have my soul bound with my good intentions, which are as different from yours as you will see if you try to go further with them by using force on me.

"'I am your vassal, but not your slave; nor has the nobility of your blood, nor ought it to have, any power to dishonour and think little of the humbleness of mine. And I value myself as much, peasant and countrywoman as I am, as you do yourself, lord and gentleman as you are. With me your force is to have no effect, nor are your riches to have any worth, nor are your words to be able to deceive me, nor your sighs and tears to soften me. If I saw any one of all these things I have mentioned in the man my parents gave me for a husband, my will would fall in with his and would not depart from his; so that, being left with my honour even if I were left without pleasure, I would give up willingly what you, sir, are now trying to get with so much force. I have said all this because there is no thinking that any man shall get anything at all from me who is not my lawful husband.'

"'If that is all you are troubled about, most beautiful Dorotea' — for that is this unfortunate woman's name — said the disloyal gentleman, 'see, here I give you my hand to be yours; and let the witnesses of this truth be the heavens, from whom nothing is hidden, and this image of Our Lady that you have here.'"

When Cardenio heard her say that her name was Dorotea, he went back to his agitation and finally confirmed his first opinion as true; but he did not want to interrupt the tale, so as to see how the thing he already almost knew would come out. He only said:

"So Dorotea is your name, madam? I have heard of another of the same name, who perhaps runs neck and neck with you in misfortunes. Go on, for a time will come when I can tell you things that will appal you to the same degree that they grieve you."

Dorotea took notice of Cardenio's words and of his strange, ruined dress, and begged him that if he knew anything about her affairs he would tell her at once; because if fortune had left her anything good, it was the courage she had to bear any disaster that might come on her, being certain that, as it seemed to her, none could come that would increase the one she had by a hair's breadth.

"I would not lose the chance, madam," answered Cardenio, "of telling you what I think, if what I imagine were true; and so far there is no opportunity lost, and it matters nothing to you to know it."

"Be it as it may," answered Dorotea. "What happened in my story was that Don Fernando took an image that was in that room and set it up as a witness to our betrothal. With the most forceful words and extraordinary oaths he gave me his word to be my husband — although before he had finished saying them I told him he should look carefully at what he was doing and consider the anger his father would feel at seeing him married to a peasant woman, one of his own vassals; that he should not be blinded by my beauty, such as it was, since it was not enough to find an excuse in it for his mistake; and that if he wanted to do me any good at all, for the love he bore me, it should be to let my luck run at the level my quality could reach, because marriages as unequal as that are never enjoyed and never last long in the pleasure they begin with.

"All these arguments I have set down here I said to him, and a great many others I do not remember; but they were not enough to make him give up his intention, exactly like a man who does not mean to pay and therefore, when the bargain is being struck, does not stick at difficulties.

"At this point I made a short argument with myself, and said to myself: 'Well, I shall not be the first who by way of marriage has risen from a humble to a great condition, nor will Don Fernando be the first whom beauty — or blind infatuation, which is more likely — has made take a partner unequal to his greatness. Since, then, I am not making a new world or a new custom, it is as well to accept this honour that luck is offering me, even if in this man the affection he shows me lasts no longer than the satisfaction of his desire; because in the end, in God's eyes, I shall be his wife. And if I try to send him away with disdain, I can see he is in such a state that, not using the means he ought to, he will use force, and I shall be left dishonoured and without any excuse for the blame that might be put on me by anyone who did not know how blamelessly I had come to this pass. Because what arguments would be enough to persuade my parents, and others, that this gentleman came into my room without my consent?'

"All these questions and answers I turned over in my imagination in an instant; and above all, what began to press on me and incline me to what was, without my thinking it, my ruin, were Don Fernando's oaths, the witnesses he called on, the tears he shed and, finally, his figure and good looks, which, accompanied by so many signs of true love, could have conquered any heart as free and as guarded as mine.

"I called my maid, so that she should join the witnesses of heaven on earth. Don Fernando went back to repeating and confirming his oaths; he added new saints as witnesses to the first ones; he called down on himself a thousand curses to come if he did not keep what he promised me; he moistened his eyes again and increased his sighs; he held me tighter in his arms, out of which he had never let me go. And with this, and with my maid going out of the room again, I ceased to be a maiden and he finished becoming a traitor and a false man.

"The day that followed the night of my ruin came, I think, not as quickly as Don Fernando wanted; because once the thing appetite asks for has been had, the greatest pleasure that can come is to get away from where it was got. I say this because Don Fernando was in a hurry to get away from me; and by the contrivance of my maid, who was the same one who had brought him there, he found himself in the street before daybreak.

"And on taking leave of me — although not with so much eagerness and vehemence as when he came — he told me to be assured of his faith and that his oaths were firm and true. And to confirm his word further, he took a rich ring off his finger and put it on mine.

"In short, he went and I was left, I do not know whether sad or glad. This I can say for certain: that I was left confused and thoughtful and almost out of myself with what had just happened, and I had not the spirit — or it did not occur to me — to scold my maid for the treachery she had committed in shutting Don Fernando into my own room, because I still could not decide whether what had happened to me was good or bad. On his going I told Don Fernando that by the same road as that night he could see me on other nights, since I was his already, until, whenever he chose, the thing should be made public.

"But he did not come on any other, except the next one; nor could I see him in the street or at church for more than a month. I wore myself out in vain trying to see him, although I knew he was in the town and that most days he went hunting, an exercise he was very fond of.

"Those days and those hours I know well were ill-starred and unlucky for me, and I know well that in them I began to doubt, and even to disbelieve, Don Fernando's good faith. And I know too that my maid heard then the words of reproof for her boldness that she had not heard before; and I know that I was obliged to keep an account of my tears and of the composure of my face, so as not to give my parents occasion to ask me what I was so unhappy about and force me to look for lies to tell them.

"But all this came to an end in a moment, when a moment came in which all considerations were trampled down and honourable reasoning was finished, and patience was lost and my secret thoughts came out into the open. And this was because, a few days later, it was said in the village that in a city near there Don Fernando had married a young lady altogether extremely beautiful and of very distinguished parents, although not so rich that on the strength of her dowry she could have aspired to so noble a marriage. It was said that she was called Luscinda, along with other things that had happened at the betrothal that were worth wondering at."

Cardenio heard the name Luscinda, and did nothing but hunch his shoulders, bite his lips, arch his eyebrows and, shortly afterwards, let two fountains of tears fall from his eyes. But Dorotea did not stop going on with her tale for that, and said:

"This sad news reached my ears; and instead of my heart freezing when I heard it, so much anger and rage caught fire in it that it was very little short of my going out into the streets shouting, publishing the treachery and betrayal that had been done to me. But this fury was calmed for the time being by the thought of putting into practice that same night what I did put into practice: which was to put on this dress that was given me by one of those they call farm-lads in a farmer's house, who was a servant of my father's, to whom I revealed my whole misfortune and begged him to go with me as far as the city where I understood my enemy was. He, after reproving my boldness and calling my decision an ugly one, seeing me settled in my opinion, offered to keep me company, as he put it, to the end of the world.

"Then, at once, I shut up in a linen pillowcase a woman's dress and some jewels and money, for whatever might happen. And in the silence of that night, without telling my treacherous maid, I left my house, accompanied by my servant and by a great many imaginings, and set out on the road to the city on foot, carried along in flight by the desire to arrive — if not to prevent what I took to be already done, at least to make Don Fernando tell me with what soul he had done it.

"I got where I wanted in two and a half days; and on going into the city I asked for the house of Luscinda's parents, and the first man I put the question to answered me with more than I would have wanted to hear. He told me the house and everything that had happened at his daughter's betrothal, a thing so public in the city that people gathered in knots all over it to tell it.

"He told me that on the night Don Fernando was betrothed to Luscinda, after she had given her yes to being his wife, she had been seized by a violent faint; and that when her husband came to unfasten her bodice to let the air get to her, he found in it a paper written in Luscinda's own hand, in which she said and declared that she could not be Don Fernando's wife, because she was Cardenio's — who, from what the man told me, was a very distinguished gentleman of that same city — and that if she had given her yes to Don Fernando, it was so as not to depart from obedience to her parents.

"In short, such things did he say the paper contained that it gave people to understand that she had meant to kill herself as soon as the betrothal was over, and gave there the reasons why she had taken her life. All of which they say was confirmed by a dagger they found on her in some part of her clothing.

"All of which Don Fernando seeing, and thinking that Luscinda had made a mock and a fool of him and thought little of him, he went for her before she came out of her faint, and with the same dagger they had found on her he tried to stab her; and he would have done it if her parents and those who were present had not stopped him.

"They said further that Don Fernando immediately went away, and that Luscinda did not come out of her fit until the next day, when she told her parents that she was the true wife of that Cardenio I have mentioned. I learnt more: that this Cardenio, so they said, had been present at the betrothal, and that on seeing her betrothed — a thing he had never expected — he left the city in despair, first writing her a letter in which he gave her to understand the wrong Luscinda had done him, and how he was going where people would not see him.

"All this was public and notorious in the whole city, and everybody was talking about it; and they talked more when they learnt that Luscinda had disappeared from her parents' house and from the city, since they could not find her anywhere in it — at which her parents were out of their wits and did not know what course to take to find her.

"What I learnt put my hopes back in play, and I thought it better not to have found Don Fernando than to find him married, since it seemed to me that the door to my remedy was not yet entirely shut. I gave myself to understand that it might be that heaven had put that obstacle in the way of the second marriage in order to bring him to recognise what he owed to the first, and to realise that he was a Christian and was more bound to his own soul than to human considerations. All these things I turned over in my fancy, and comforted myself without having any comfort, inventing long, faint hopes so as to keep going the life I now loathe.

"Being in the city, then, without knowing what to do with myself, since I could not find Don Fernando, there came to my ears a public proclamation offering a great reward to whoever should find me, giving a description of my age and of the very dress I was wearing. And I heard it said that people were saying that the young man who came with me had taken me from my parents' house — a thing that went to my very soul, seeing how far down my reputation had gone, since it was not enough to lose it by my coming away, but the question of who with had to be added, and he so low a person and so unworthy of my honourable intentions.

"The moment I heard the proclamation I left the city with my servant, who was by then beginning to show signs of wavering in the faithfulness he had promised me; and that night we went into the thick of this mountain, in fear of being found. But as they usually say that one evil calls up another, and that the end of one misfortune is generally the beginning of a greater, so it happened to me. Because my good servant, faithful and trustworthy until then, as soon as he saw me in this solitude, urged on by his own knavery rather than by my beauty, chose to take advantage of the opportunity that these wastes seemed to him to offer; and with little shame and less fear of God or respect for me, he made love to me. And seeing that I answered the shamelessness of his proposals with ugly and just words, he left aside the entreaties he had first meant to make use of and began to use force.

"But just heaven, which seldom or never fails to look at and favour just intentions, favoured mine in such a way that with my small strength and with little trouble I sent him over a precipice, where I left him, I do not know whether dead or alive. And then, with more speed than my fright and weariness called for, I went into these mountains, with no other thought or plan than to hide myself in them and to escape from my father and from those who were looking for me on his behalf.

"With this wish I came into them I do not know how many months ago, and there I found a stockman who took me as a servant to a place in the very bowels of this sierra, whom I have served as a shepherd boy all this time, trying always to be out in the fields so as to hide this hair which now, so unexpectedly, has revealed me.

"But all my industry and all my care was and has been of no use, since my master came to know that I was not a man, and the same wicked thought was born in him that had been born in my servant. And as fortune does not always give the remedy along with the trouble, I found no precipice or ravine to throw the master down and put him out of his pain, as I found for the servant; and so I thought it the lesser difficulty to leave him and hide myself all over again among these wild places, rather than try my strength or my arguments on him.

"I say, then, that I went back into hiding, and to looking for somewhere where without any hindrance I could beg heaven with sighs and tears to take pity on my misfortune and give me the means and the help to get out of it, or else to leave my life among these solitudes — with no memory left of this unhappy woman, who so blamelessly will have given people something to talk and gossip about in her own country and in other people's."

Chapter 29: Which Treats of the Amusing Device and Method Used to Get Our Enamoured Knight Out of the Very Harsh Penance He Had Imposed on Himself

"This, gentlemen, is the true history of my tragedy. Look and judge now whether the sighs you heard, the words you listened to and the tears that came out of my eyes had cause enough to show themselves in greater abundance. And when you have considered the nature of my misfortune, you will see that comfort will be useless, since the remedy for it is impossible.

"I only beg you — a thing you can easily and ought to do — to advise me where I can spend my life without being finished off by the fear and alarm I have of being found by those who are looking for me. Because although I know that the great love my parents have for me assures me that I shall be well received by them, so much shame comes over me at the mere thought that I must appear before them not as they thought I would, that I count it better to exile myself for ever from being seen than to see their faces, thinking that they are looking at mine as one that has none of the modesty they must have promised themselves in me."

She fell silent on saying this, and her face was covered by a colour that showed very plainly the feeling and the shame in her soul. In their own souls those who had listened to her felt as much pity as astonishment at her misfortune; and although the curate wanted to comfort and advise her at once, Cardenio spoke first, saying:

"So, madam, you are the beautiful Dorotea, the only daughter of the rich Clenardo."

Dorotea was astonished when she heard her father's name, and at seeing how poor a creature it was who named him — for it has already been said what a bad state Cardenio's clothes were in. And so she said to him:

"And who are you, brother, that you know my father's name like this? Because up to now, if I do not remember wrong, in the whole course of the tale of my misfortune I have not named him."

"I am," answered Cardenio, "that luckless man who, as you have said, madam, Luscinda said was her husband. I am the unhappy Cardenio, whom the wicked conduct of the same man who has put you in the state you are in has brought to the state you see me in: ragged, half naked, without any human comfort and — what is worst of all — without my wits, since I only have them when heaven takes a fancy to give them me for some brief space.

"I, madam, am the man who was present at Don Fernando's outrages and who waited to hear the yes Luscinda pronounced to being his wife. I am the man who had not the courage to see what her faint came to, or what came of the paper that was found in her bosom, because my soul had not the endurance to see so many misfortunes at once. And so I left the house and my patience, and a letter which I left with a man I was staying with, whom I begged to put it into Luscinda's hands, and I came away to these solitudes with the intention of ending in them the life I have loathed from that moment as my mortal enemy.

"But fate has not chosen to take it from me, being content with taking my wits — perhaps to keep me for the good fortune I have had in finding you. For if what you have told here is true, as I believe it is, it might still be that heaven has kept a better outcome to our disasters in store for us both than we think. Because, granted that Luscinda cannot marry Don Fernando, being mine, nor Don Fernando marry her, being yours, and that she has declared it so plainly, we may well hope that heaven will give us back what is ours, since it still exists and has not been made over to anybody or destroyed.

"And since we have this comfort, born not of a very remote hope nor founded on wild imaginings, I beg you, madam, to take another resolution in your honourable thoughts, since I mean to take one in mine, adjusting yourself to expect better fortune. For I swear to you, on the faith of a gentleman and a Christian, not to abandon you until I see you in Don Fernando's power; and that when I cannot bring him by argument to recognise what he owes you, then to use the freedom that being a gentleman gives me, and to be able with just title to challenge him for the injustice he does you — without remembering my own wrongs, whose vengeance I shall leave to heaven so as to attend on earth to yours."

Dorotea was left utterly astonished by what Cardenio said; and not knowing what thanks to give for such great offers, she tried to take hold of his feet to kiss them. But Cardenio would not allow it, and the licentiate answered for them both, and approved Cardenio's good reasoning; and above all he begged, advised and urged them to go with him to his village, where they could make good the things they lacked, and that there they would arrange how to look for Don Fernando, or how to take Dorotea to her parents, or do whatever else should seem best to them.

Cardenio and Dorotea thanked him and accepted the kindness that was offered them. The barber, who had been all this time in suspense and silent, also made his own good speech, and offered himself with no less goodwill than the curate to everything that might be of service to them. He likewise told them briefly the reason that had brought them there, along with the strangeness of Don Quixote's madness, and how they were waiting for his squire, who had gone to look for him. There came into Cardenio's memory, as though in a dream, the quarrel he had had with Don Quixote, and he told the others about it — but he could not say what the reason for their argument had been.

At this they heard shouts, and knew that the man shouting was Sancho Panza, who, not having found them in the place where he had left them, was calling for them at the top of his voice. They went out to meet him; and asking him about Don Quixote, he told them how he had found him half naked in his shirt, thin, yellow and dying of hunger, and sighing for his lady Dulcinea; and that although he had told him she ordered him to leave that place and go to El Toboso, where she was waiting for him, he had answered that he was determined not to appear before her beauty until he had performed deeds that made him worthy of her favour. And that if this went on, he was in danger of not coming to be an emperor, as he was bound to be, or even an archbishop, which was the least he could be. And so they should consider what was to be done to get him out of there.

The licentiate answered that he should not distress himself, for they would get him out of there whether he liked it or not. He then told Cardenio and Dorotea what they had thought of as a remedy for Don Quixote, or at least for taking him home.
