To which Dorotea said that she would make a better distressed damsel than the barber, and what was more, that she had clothes there to do it to the life; and that they should leave it in her hands to know how to act out everything that was needed for carrying out their plan, because she had read a great many books of chivalry and knew well the style that distressed damsels used when they asked their boons of knights errant.

"Then nothing more is needed," said the curate, "except that it should be put into practice at once. Without any doubt good luck is showing itself in our favour, since so unexpectedly a door has begun to open for you, my friends, towards your remedy, and the one we needed has been made easy for us."

Dorotea then took out of her pillowcase a whole skirt of a certain rich stuff and a short cloak of another showy green material, and out of a little box a necklace and other jewels, with which in an instant she adorned herself in such a way that she looked like a rich, great lady. All this, and more, she said she had brought from home for whatever might come up, and that until then she had had no occasion to need it. Her great grace, charm and beauty pleased everybody extremely, and confirmed Don Fernando in their opinion as a man of little judgement, since he threw so much beauty aside.

But the one who marvelled most was Sancho Panza, because it seemed to him — as was indeed the truth — that in all the days of his life he had never seen so beautiful a creature. And so he asked the curate very earnestly to tell him who that beautiful lady was, and what she was looking for in those out-of-the-way parts.

"This beautiful lady, brother Sancho," answered the curate, "is — as though it were nothing at all — the heiress in the direct male line to the great kingdom of Micomicón, who comes looking for your master to ask him a boon, which is that he should undo a wrong or injury that a wicked giant has done her; and it is on the fame your master has as a good knight throughout the discovered world that this princess has come from Guinea to look for him."

"A lucky search and a lucky find," said Sancho Panza at this, "and more so if my master is fortunate enough to undo that injury and put that wrong right by killing that son of a bitch of a giant your worship speaks of — and kill him he will if he meets him, unless he happens to be a phantom, because against phantoms my master has no power at all.

"But one thing I want to beg your worship, among others, Señor Licentiate; and it's that, so that my master doesn't get the urge to be an archbishop, which is what I'm afraid of, your worship should advise him to marry this princess at once. And then he'll be made incapable of taking archbishop's orders and will easily come into his empire, and I to the end of my wishes. Because I've looked at it carefully and I find by my reckoning that it doesn't suit me for my master to be an archbishop, since I'm no use to the Church, being married; and to go about now getting dispensations so as to be able to hold a Church income, having a wife and children as I have, would be a never-ending business. So, sir, the whole point of it is that my master should marry this lady at once — whose name I don't know yet, and so I don't call her by it."

"She is called," answered the curate, "the Princess Micomicona; because her kingdom being called Micomicón, it is plain that she must be called that."

"There's no doubt about that," answered Sancho, "for I've seen a lot of people take their surname and family name from the place where they were born, calling themselves Pedro of Alcalá, Juan of Úbeda and Diego of Valladolid; and this same custom must be used over there in Guinea, the queens taking the names of their kingdoms."

"That must be it," said the curate; "and as for your master's marrying, I shall do everything in my power about it."

At which Sancho was as pleased as the curate was astonished at his simplicity, and at seeing how firmly the very same absurdities as his master's were fixed in his fancy, since without any doubt he gave himself to understand that his master would come to be an emperor.

By this time Dorotea had got up on the curate's mule and the barber had fitted the oxtail beard to his face, and they told Sancho to guide them to where Don Quixote was; and they warned him not to say that he knew the licentiate or the barber, because the whole point of his master's coming to be an emperor lay in his not knowing them. Neither the curate nor Cardenio chose to go with them — Cardenio so that Don Quixote should not remember the quarrel he had had with him, and the curate because his presence was not needed just then. And so they let them go ahead, and followed them on foot, little by little.

The curate did not fail to advise Dorotea what she had to do; to which she said that they need not worry, and that everything should be done without missing a point, exactly as the books of chivalry required and described it.

They must have gone three quarters of a league when they made out Don Quixote among some tangled rocks, dressed by now, though not in armour. And as soon as Dorotea saw him and was informed by Sancho that this was Don Quixote, she whipped up her palfrey, with the well-bearded barber following her. And on getting up to him, the squire threw himself off his mule and went to take Dorotea in his arms; and she, dismounting with great ease, went and knelt down before Don Quixote's feet. And although he struggled to raise her, she, without getting up, spoke to him in this manner:

"From here I shall not rise, O valorous and mighty knight, until your goodness and courtesy grant me a boon, which shall redound to the honour and glory of your person and to the good of the most disconsolate and injured maiden the sun has looked upon. And if it is so that the valour of your strong arm answers to the report of your immortal fame, you are bound to favour this unfortunate woman who comes from lands so far off, drawn by the scent of your famous name, seeking you as the remedy of her misfortunes."

"I shall not answer you a word, fair lady," answered Don Quixote, "nor hear anything more of your affairs, until you rise from the ground."

"I shall not rise, sir," answered the afflicted maiden, "unless first, by your courtesy, the boon I ask is granted me."

"I grant and concede it to you," answered Don Quixote, "provided that it need not be fulfilled to the harm or diminishment of my king, of my country, or of her who holds the key of my heart and my liberty."

"It shall not be to the harm or the diminishment of any of those you name, my good lord," replied the sorrowing maiden.

And while this was going on, Sancho Panza got close to his master's ear and said to him very quietly:

"Your worship can perfectly well grant her the boon she asks, sir, for it's nothing at all: it's only killing a great big giant; and the one who's asking it is the high princess Micomicona, queen of the great kingdom of Micomicón in Ethiopia."

"Let her be whoever she may," answered Don Quixote, "for I shall do what I am bound to do and what my conscience dictates to me, in accordance with what I have professed."

And turning to the maiden, he said:

"Let your great beauty rise, for I grant you the boon you may wish to ask of me."

"Then the one I ask," said the maiden, "is that your magnanimous person should come with me at once wherever I take you, and should promise me not to get involved in any other adventure or undertaking whatever until you have given me vengeance on a traitor who, against all divine and human law, has usurped my kingdom from me."

"I say that I grant it," answered Don Quixote, "and so, madam, you may from today on throw off the melancholy that is wearing you out and make your fainting hope take on new spirit and strength. For with God's help and my arm's, you shall soon see yourself restored to your kingdom and seated on the throne of your ancient and great estate, in spite and in defiance of the villains who may wish to gainsay it. And to work — for they say that danger generally lies in delay."

The distressed maiden struggled very insistently to kiss his hands, but Don Quixote, who was in everything a courteous and well-bred knight, would never allow it; instead he made her get up and embraced her with great courtesy and good breeding, and ordered Sancho to see to Rocinante's girths and arm him that very moment. Sancho took down the armour, which was hanging from a tree like a trophy, and, seeing to the girths, armed his master in a moment; and Don Quixote, finding himself armed, said:

"Let us go from here, in God's name, to favour this great lady."

The barber was still on his knees, taking great care to hide his laughter and to keep his beard from falling off — with whose falling everybody might perhaps have been left without achieving their good intention. And seeing that the boon had now been granted and how briskly Don Quixote was getting himself ready to go and fulfil it, he got up and took his lady by the other hand, and between the two of them they got her up on the mule. Then Don Quixote got up on Rocinante, and the barber settled himself on his mount, with Sancho left on foot — at which the loss of the grey came back to him afresh, with how much he wanted him now. But he bore it all cheerfully, since it seemed to him that his master was now on the road, and very near, to being an emperor; for he supposed without any doubt that he would marry that princess and be at the very least king of Micomicón.

The only thing that grieved him was the thought that that kingdom was in the land of the blacks, and that the people they would give him as his vassals would all be black. To which he at once found a good remedy in his imagination, and said to himself:

"What do I care if my vassals are black? Is there anything more to it than loading them up and bringing them to Spain, where I'll be able to sell them and where they'll pay me for them in cash, and with the money I'll be able to buy some title or some post to live comfortably on all the days of my life? Go on, then — go to sleep, and have no wit or ability for managing things and for selling thirty or ten thousand vassals in the time it takes to say knife! By God I'll shift the lot of them, small along with great, or however I can; and black as they may be, I'll turn them into white ones or yellow ones. Come along — do you think I suck my thumb?"

With this he went along so busy and so pleased that he forgot the trouble of walking on foot.

Cardenio and the curate were watching all this from among some thickets, and did not know what to do to join up with them. But the curate, who was a great contriver, immediately thought of what they should do to get what they wanted; and it was that with a pair of scissors he carried in a case he very smartly took off Cardenio's beard, and dressed him in a brown jacket of his own and gave him a black cloak, and he himself was left in his breeches and doublet. And Cardenio was left so different from what he had looked before that he would not have known himself, even if he had looked in a mirror.

This done — and although the others had gone on ahead while the two of them were disguising themselves — they easily came out on the high road before them, because the thickets and bad going of those places did not allow those on horseback to travel as fast as those on foot. In fact they placed themselves on the flat, at the way out of the sierra; and as soon as Don Quixote and his companions came out of it, the curate set himself to look at him very slowly, giving signs that he was gradually recognising him. And after he had been looking at him for a good while, he went up to him with open arms, saying at the top of his voice:

"Well met, mirror of chivalry, my good fellow-countryman Don Quixote of La Mancha, the flower and cream of gentility, the shelter and remedy of the needy, the quintessence of knights errant!"

And saying this, he had hold of Don Quixote round the knee of his left leg; and Don Quixote, appalled at what he was seeing and hearing this man say and do, set himself to look at him carefully, and finally recognised him and was left as though appalled at seeing him, and made a great effort to dismount. But the curate would not allow it, so that Don Quixote said:

"Let me be, your worship, Señor Licentiate; there is no reason why I should be on horseback and a person as reverend as your worship on foot."

"That I shall not allow on any account," said the curate. "Let your greatness stay on horseback, since it is on horseback that you perform the greatest exploits and adventures that have been seen in our age. As for me, unworthy priest that I am, it will be enough for me to get up behind on one of these gentlemen's mules who are travelling with your worship, if they do not take it amiss. And I shall even reckon that I am riding on the horse Pegasus, or on the zebra or mare that famous Moor Muzaraque rode, who to this day lies enchanted on the great hill of Zulema, not far from the great Compluto."

"I had not thought so far, my lord Licentiate," answered Don Quixote; "and I know that my lady the princess will be pleased, for love of me, to order her squire to give your worship the saddle of his mule, and he can settle himself behind, if the mule will stand it."

"She will stand it, I believe," answered the princess; "and I know too that there will be no need to order my lord the squire, for he is so courteous and so courtly that he will not allow a churchman to go on foot when he can go on horseback."

"That is so," answered the barber.

And dismounting in a moment, he invited the curate to take the saddle, and he took it without needing much asking. And the trouble was that when the barber was getting up behind, the mule — which was, after all, a hired one, and to say that it was a bad one that is enough — lifted its hindquarters a little and let fly two kicks in the air, which, if they had caught Master Nicolás in the chest or on the head, would have made him wish the devil had the whole expedition after Don Quixote. Even so, they startled him in such a way that he came down on the ground, with so little care for his beard that it fell off on the ground. And finding himself without it, he had no other remedy than to hurry to cover his face with both hands and to complain that they had knocked his teeth out.

Don Quixote, seeing that whole bundle of beard, with no jaws and no blood, a long way from the fallen squire's face, said:

"By the living God, this is a great miracle! It has knocked the beard off him and torn it off his face, as if it had been taken off on purpose!"

The curate, who saw the danger his invention ran of being discovered, ran at once for the beard and went with it to where Master Nicolás was lying, still shouting away; and with one movement, pulling his head against his own chest, he stuck it back on him, muttering over him some words which he said were a certain charm proper for sticking on beards, as they would see. And when he had it on him, he stood back, and the squire was left as well bearded and as sound as before — at which Don Quixote was extraordinarily astonished, and begged the curate to teach him that charm when he had a chance; for he understood that its power must extend to more than sticking on beards, since it was clear that where a beard was pulled off the flesh must be left raw and injured, and since it healed all that, it was good for more than beards.

"That is so," said the curate, and promised to teach it him at the first opportunity.

They arranged that for the moment the curate should ride, and that the three of them should change about at intervals until they reached the inn, which must be about two leagues from there. The three of them being mounted — that is to say, Don Quixote, the princess and the curate — and the three of them on foot — Cardenio, the barber and Sancho Panza — Don Quixote said to the maiden:

"Let your greatness, my lady, lead wherever it most pleases you."

And before she could answer, the licentiate said:

"Towards what kingdom does your ladyship mean to lead? Is it, by any chance, towards that of Micomicón? It must be, or I know little about kingdoms."

She, who was well up in everything, understood that she should answer yes; and so she said:

"Yes, sir, my road lies towards that kingdom."

"If that is so," said the curate, "we shall have to pass through the middle of my village, and from there your worship will take the route to Cartagena, where you can take ship with good luck. And if there is a favourable wind, a calm sea and no storms, in a little less than nine years you may be in sight of the great Lake Pissabed — I mean Maeotis — which is a little more than a hundred days' journey this side of your greatness's kingdom."

"Your worship is mistaken, my dear sir," she said, "because it is not two years since I left it; and truly I never had good weather, and in spite of that I have arrived at seeing what I so much wanted, which is my lord Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose fame reached my ears as soon as I set foot in Spain, and which moved me to look for him, so as to commend myself to his courtesy and trust my just cause to the valour of his unconquerable arm."

"No more: let my praises cease," said Don Quixote at this point, "because I am an enemy to every kind of flattery; and although this is not flattery, still such talk offends my chaste ears. What I can say, my lady, is that whether I have valour or not, whatever I have or have not is to be employed in your service to the point of losing my life. And so, leaving this for its own time, I beg the lord licentiate to tell me what the reason is that has brought him to these parts, so alone and with so few servants and so lightly equipped that it appals me."

"To that I shall answer briefly," answered the curate; "because your worship must know, Señor Don Quixote, that Master Nicolás, our friend and our barber, and I were going to Seville to collect a certain sum of money that a relative of mine who went over to the Indies many years ago had sent me — and not so few of them that they do not come to more than sixty thousand assayed pesos, which is something. And passing through these places yesterday, four highwaymen came out at us and took from us even the beards off our faces; and they took them in such a way that it was as well for the barber to put on false ones. And even this young man here" — pointing to Cardenio — "they left looking like a new man.

"And the good of it is that it is common report all over this district that the men who robbed us are some galley slaves who they say were set free, almost on this very spot, by a man so brave that in spite of the commissary and the guards he loosed the whole lot of them. And without any doubt he must have been out of his wits, or he must be as great a scoundrel as they are, or some man without a soul or a conscience, since he chose to loose the wolf among the sheep, the fox among the hens, the fly among the honey. He chose to defraud justice, to go against his king and natural lord, since he went against his just commands. He chose, I say, to take from the galleys their oarsmen, to throw the Holy Brotherhood into an uproar when it had been resting many years; he chose, in short, to do a deed by which his soul may be lost without his body's gaining anything."

Sancho had told the curate and the barber about the adventure of the galley slaves, which his master had brought off with so much glory to himself; and this was why the curate laid the colours on so thick in relating it, to see what Don Quixote would do or say. And Don Quixote's colour changed at every word, and he did not dare say that he had been the deliverer of those good people.

"These, then," said the curate, "were the men who robbed us; and God in his mercy pardon the man who kept them from being taken to the punishment they deserved."

Chapter 30: Which Treats of the Good Sense of the Beautiful Dorotea, with Other Very Entertaining and Amusing Matters

The curate had hardly finished when Sancho said:

"Well, upon my faith, Señor Licentiate, the man who did that exploit was my master; and not for want of my telling him beforehand and warning him to look at what he was doing, and that it was a sin to give them their freedom, because every one of them was going along there for being an enormous scoundrel."

"You blockhead!" said Don Quixote at this. "It is no business or concern of knights errant to inquire whether the afflicted, chained and oppressed people they meet on the roads are going along in that fashion, or are in that distress, through their faults or through their merits. It is only their business to help them as people in need, setting their eyes on their sufferings and not on their villainies. I came upon a rosary and string of miserable and unfortunate people, and I did with them what my religion requires of me, and let the rest settle itself. And to whoever has thought ill of it — saving the holy dignity of the lord licentiate and his honourable person — I say that he knows little about the business of chivalry, and that he lies like a son of a bitch and a base-born man; and this I shall give him to understand with my sword, where it is set down at greater length."

And he said this while settling himself in his stirrups and pulling down his morion — because the barber's basin, which by his reckoning was Mambrino's helmet, he was carrying hung from the front of his saddle until he could get it mended from the bad treatment the galley slaves had given it.

Dorotea, who was quick-witted and full of humour, and who by now knew Don Quixote's deranged temper and that everybody was making fun of him except Sancho Panza, did not want to be behind the rest; and seeing him so angry, she said to him:

"Sir knight, may your worship remember the boon you have promised me, and that in accordance with it you cannot get involved in any other adventure, however urgent. Let your worship calm your breast, for if the lord licentiate had known that the galley slaves had been set free by that unconquered arm, he would have put three stitches in his mouth and even bitten his tongue three times over rather than have said a word that would work to your worship's displeasure."

"That I certainly swear to," said the curate, "and I would even have pulled out one of my moustaches."

"I shall be quiet, my lady," said Don Quixote, "and I shall hold back the just anger that had already risen in my breast, and shall go along quiet and peaceable until I have fulfilled the promised boon for you. But in payment for this good intention, I beg you to tell me, if it is not disagreeable to you, what your trouble is, and how many, who and what sort are the persons on whom I am to give you due, satisfying and complete vengeance."

"That I shall do gladly," answered Dorotea, "if it does not weary you to hear of griefs and misfortunes."

"It will not weary me, my lady," answered Don Quixote.

To which Dorotea answered:

"Then since that is so, let your worships give me your attention."

She had hardly said this when Cardenio and the barber placed themselves at her side, eager to see how the quick-witted Dorotea would invent her history; and Sancho did the same, being as much taken in by her as his master was. And she, after settling herself well in the saddle and preparing herself with a cough and other gestures, began very gracefully to speak in this way:

"First of all, I want your worships to know, my dear sirs, that I am called —"

And she stopped a little here, because she had forgotten the name the curate had given her. But he came to the rescue, because he understood what she was stuck on, and said:

"It is no wonder, my lady, that your greatness should be confused and embarrassed in telling your misfortunes; for they are generally such that they very often take away the memory of those they ill-treat, in such a way that they do not even remember their own names — as they have done with your great ladyship, who has forgotten that she is called the Princess Micomicona, lawful heiress to the great kingdom of Micomicón. And with this prompting your greatness can now easily bring back to your injured memory everything you wish to tell."

"That is the truth," answered the maiden, "and from now on I believe there will be no need to prompt me with anything, for I shall bring my true history into good harbour.

"Which is that the king my father, who is called Tinacrio the Knowing, was very learned in this thing they call the magic art, and found out by his science that my mother, whose name was Queen Jaramilla, was to die before him, and that shortly afterwards he too was to pass out of this life and I was to be left an orphan of father and mother.

"But he used to say that this did not weary him so much as what threw him into confusion, which was knowing for a very certain thing that a monstrous giant, lord of a great isle that almost borders on our kingdom, called Pandafilando of the Gloomy Eye — because it is an established fact that although he has his eyes in their place and straight, he always looks the wrong way as though he were cross-eyed, and he does this out of wickedness and to put fear and terror into those he looks at — I say that he learnt that this giant, on hearing that I was orphaned, was to come over my kingdom with a great force and take the whole of it from me, without leaving me one small village to take refuge in; but that I could avoid all this ruin and misfortune if I would marry him. But as far as he understood, he never expected that I should feel inclined to make so unequal a marriage; and in this he told the plain truth, because it has never crossed my mind to marry that giant — nor any other, however great and monstrous he might be.

"My father also said that after he was dead, and I saw Pandafilando beginning to come over my kingdom, I was not to wait to put myself in a state of defence, because that would be my destruction; but that I should freely leave the kingdom clear for him, if I wanted to avoid the death and total destruction of my good and loyal vassals, because it would not be possible to defend myself against the giant's devilish strength. But that I should at once set off with some of my people on the road to the Spains, where I should find the remedy of my troubles in finding a knight errant whose fame would by that time be spread throughout that whole kingdom, and who was to be called, if I do not remember wrong, Don Quickset or Don Kickshaw."

"Don Quixote she means, madam," said Sancho Panza at this point, "or, by another name, the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance."

"That is the truth," said Dorotea. "He said further that he was to be tall of body, dry in the face, and that on the right side, under the left shoulder, or somewhere about there, he was to have a dark mole with certain hairs on it like bristles."

Hearing this, Don Quixote said to his squire:

"Come here, Sancho my son, help me undress; I want to see whether I am the knight that wise king left prophesied."

"But what does your worship want to undress for?" said Dorotea.

"To see whether I have that mole your father spoke of," answered Don Quixote.

"There is no need to undress," said Sancho; "I know that your worship has a mole of that description in the middle of your backbone, which is a sign of being a strong man."

"That is enough," said Dorotea, "because among friends one is not to look at small matters; and whether it is on the shoulder or on the backbone matters little. It is enough that there should be a mole, and let it be where it likes, since it is all the same flesh. And without a doubt my good father was right in everything, and I have been right in commending myself to Señor Don Quixote, for he is the man my father spoke of, since the marks of his face agree with those of the great fame this knight has not only in Spain but in the whole of La Mancha. For I had hardly disembarked at Osuna when I heard so many of his exploits told that my soul told me at once that he was the very man I had come to look for."

"But how did your worship disembark at Osuna, my lady," asked Don Quixote, "when it is not a seaport?"

But before Dorotea could answer, the curate took the matter in hand and said:

"The lady princess must mean that after she disembarked at Málaga, the first place where she heard news of your worship was Osuna."

"That is what I meant to say," said Dorotea.

"And that makes sense," said the curate; "and let your majesty go on."

"There is nothing more to go on with," answered Dorotea, "except that in the end my luck has been so good in finding Señor Don Quixote that I already count and hold myself as queen and mistress of my whole kingdom, since he, out of his courtesy and magnanimity, has promised me the boon of going with me wherever I take him — which will be nowhere but to set him in front of Pandafilando of the Gloomy Eye, so that he may kill him and give me back what he has so unreasonably usurped from me. For all this is bound to happen exactly to order, since Tinacrio the Knowing, my good father, left it so prophesied. He also left it said and written in Chaldean, or Greek, letters — for I cannot read them — that if this knight of the prophecy, after having cut the giant's throat, should wish to marry me, I was to give myself over to him at once and without any argument as his lawful wife, and give him possession of my kingdom along with the possession of my person."

"What do you think of that, friend Sancho?" said Don Quixote at this point. "Do you hear what is going on? Did I not tell you so? See whether we have a kingdom to rule and a queen to marry."

"I'll swear to that!" said Sancho. "And damn the man who doesn't marry her the moment he's slit Señor Pandafiddle's little gullet! Why, it isn't as if the queen were a bad one! May the fleas in my bed turn out as good!"

And saying this, he cut two capers in the air with every sign of the greatest delight, and then went to take the reins of Dorotea's mule; and making her stop, he knelt down before her, begging her to give him her hands to kiss as a sign that he took her for his queen and mistress. Which of the bystanders could have kept from laughing, seeing the master's madness and the servant's simplicity? In fact Dorotea gave them to him, and promised to make him a great lord in her kingdom when heaven should do her so much good as to let her recover it and enjoy it. Sancho thanked her in such words that he set them all laughing again.

"This, gentlemen," Dorotea went on, "is my history. It only remains to tell you that of all the escort I brought out of my kingdom, nobody is left me but this good bearded squire, because all the rest were drowned in a great storm we had in sight of the port; and he and I came to land on two planks, as though by a miracle. And so the whole course of my life is miracle and mystery, as you will have noticed. And if in anything I have gone too far, or been less exact than I should, put the blame on what the lord licentiate said at the beginning of my tale: that constant and extraordinary hardships take away the memory of the one who suffers them."

"They shall not take away mine, O high and valorous lady," said Don Quixote, "however many I go through in serving you, and however great and unheard-of they may be. And so I confirm afresh the boon I have promised you, and swear to go with you to the end of the world until I face that fierce enemy of yours, whose arrogant head I mean, with God's help and my arm's, to cut off with the edge of this — I do not want to say good sword, thanks to Ginés de Pasamonte, who took mine."

This he said between his teeth, and he went on to say:

"And after I have cut it off and put you in peaceful possession of your estate, it will be left to your own will to do with your person whatever comes best to your liking; because as long as I have my memory occupied and my will held captive, and my understanding lost, to that — and I say no more — it is not possible that I should face, even in thought, the idea of marrying, even if it were the phoenix itself."

What his master said at the last about not wanting to marry struck Sancho so badly that in great anger he raised his voice and said:

"I swear by me, and vow by me, that your worship, Señor Don Quixote, has not got a whole set of wits. Why, how is it possible that your worship should have any doubt about marrying so high a princess as this one? Do you think fortune is going to offer you good luck like this behind every corner? Is my lady Dulcinea more beautiful, by any chance? No, she certainly is not, nor by half; and I'm even ready to say she doesn't come up to the shoe of the one who's standing in front of you. So bad luck to the earldom I'm hoping for, if your worship goes about asking for truffles in the middle of the sea. Marry her, marry her at once, in Satan's name, and take that kingdom that's dropping into your hands as a free gift; and once you're a king, make me a marquis or a governor, and after that the devil can carry off the lot for all I care."

Don Quixote, hearing such blasphemies spoken against his lady Dulcinea, could not bear it; and raising his pike, without saying a word to Sancho and without so much as opening his mouth, he gave him two such blows that he brought him down on the ground. And if Dorotea had not shouted to him not to give him any more, he would certainly have taken his life then and there.

"Do you think," he said to him after a while, "you low peasant, that there is always to be room for you to put your hand in my crotch, and that it is all to be your going wrong and my forgiving you? Do not think it, you excommunicated scoundrel — for excommunicated you certainly are, since you have set your tongue on the peerless Dulcinea. And do you not know, you clodhopper, you porter, you rogue, that if it were not for the valour she pours into my arm, I should not have enough of it to kill a flea? Tell me, you sly fellow with a viper's tongue: who do you think has won this kingdom and cut off this giant's head and made you a marquis — for I count all this as done already and as a thing settled beyond appeal — if it is not Dulcinea's valour, taking my arm as the instrument of her exploits? She fights in me and conquers in me, and I live and breathe in her, and have life and being. Oh, you son of a bitch and a scoundrel, how ungrateful you are: you see yourself raised from the dust of the earth to be a titled lord, and you answer so good a turn by speaking ill of the woman who did it for you!"

Sancho was not in so bad a state that he did not hear everything his master said to him; and getting up with a fair amount of speed, he went and put himself behind Dorotea's palfrey, and from there said to his master:

"Tell me, sir: if your worship has made up your mind not to marry this great princess, it's clear that the kingdom won't be yours; and it not being yours, what favours can you do me? That's what I'm complaining about. Marry this queen once and for all, your worship, now we've got her here as though she'd rained down out of the sky, and afterwards you can go back to my lady Dulcinea. There must have been kings in the world who kept a mistress. As for the beauty, I don't meddle in it; because in truth, if it must be said, they both seem good to me — though I've never seen the lady Dulcinea."

"What do you mean, you have never seen her, you blaspheming traitor?" said Don Quixote. "Have you not just this minute brought me a message from her?"

"I say I haven't seen her at leisure enough," said Sancho, "to have taken particular note of her beauty and her good points one by one; but taken all in a lump, she seems good to me."

"Now I excuse you," said Don Quixote, "and forgive me the anger I have given you, for a man's first impulses are not in his own hands."

"I can see that," answered Sancho; "and so with me the urge to talk is always a first impulse, and I can't help saying, at least once, whatever comes to my tongue."

"For all that," said Don Quixote, "look out what you say, Sancho, because the pitcher goes so often to the well — and I say no more."

"Very well then," answered Sancho, "God is in heaven and sees the tricks, and he will be the judge of which of us does more harm: me for not speaking well, or your worship for not acting well."

"Let there be no more of it," said Dorotea. "Run, Sancho, and kiss your master's hand and ask his pardon; and from now on be more careful in your praise and your blame, and do not speak ill of that lady of El Toboso, whom I do not know except to serve her. And have confidence in God, for you shall not go without an estate to live in like a prince."

Sancho went with his head down and asked his master for his hand, and he gave it him with a composed bearing; and after he had kissed it, he gave him his blessing, and told Sancho that they should go on a little way ahead, because he had things to ask him and matters of great importance to discuss with him. Sancho did so, and the two of them drew off somewhat ahead, and Don Quixote said to him:

"Since you came back I have had no time or room to ask you many things in particular about the embassy you carried and the answer you brought. And now, since fortune has granted us the time and the place, do not deny me the happiness you can give me with such good news."

"Let your worship ask what you like," answered Sancho, "for I'll get as well out of it all as I got into it. But I beg your worship, my dear sir, not to be so vengeful from now on."

"Why do you say that, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"I say it," he answered, "because these blows just now were more for the quarrel the devil stirred up between the two of us the other night than for what I said against my lady Dulcinea, whom I love and revere like a holy relic — although there's nothing of the kind about her — simply because she belongs to your worship."

"Do not go back to that sort of talk, Sancho, on your life," said Don Quixote, "for it distresses me. I forgave you then, and you know well what they usually say: for a new sin, a new penance."

While the two of them were in this conversation, the curate said to Dorotea that she had shown great skill both in the tale itself and in its shortness, and in the resemblance it had to those in the books of chivalry. She said she had often amused herself with reading them, but that she did not know where the provinces and seaports were, and so had said at random that she had disembarked at Osuna.

"I understood that," said the curate, "and that is why I hurried to say what I said, and everything was put right. But is it not a strange thing to see how easily this unfortunate gentleman believes all these inventions and lies, simply because they have the style and manner of the follies in his books?"

"It is," said Cardenio, "and so rare and unheard-of a thing that I do not know whether, if a man wanted to invent it and make it up out of his head, there would be a wit sharp enough to hit on it."

"Well, there is another thing about it," said the curate: "that apart from the simplicities this good gentleman says that touch on his madness, if you talk to him about other things he reasons with excellent good sense and shows he has a clear and equable understanding in everything. So that as long as you do not touch him on his chivalries, nobody would judge him to be anything but a man of very good understanding."

While they were in this conversation, Don Quixote went on with his own, and said to Sancho:

"Let us throw our quarrels into the sea, friend Panza, and tell me now, without any regard to anger or resentment: where, how and when did you find Dulcinea? What was she doing? What did you say to her? What did she answer you? What face did she make while she read my letter? Who copied it out for you? And everything else that you see is worth knowing, asking and answering in this case — without adding anything or lying to please me, and without cutting it short either so as not to take my pleasure away."

"Sir," answered Sancho, "if the truth is to be told, nobody copied the letter out for me, because I didn't carry any letter."

"It is exactly as you say," said Don Quixote, "because I found the little pocket-book I wrote it in still in my possession two days after you left, which caused me the greatest distress, since I did not know what you would do when you found yourself without the letter; and I always believed you would come back from the place where you missed it."

"So I would have," answered Sancho, "if I hadn't got it by heart when your worship read it to me — so that I said it over to a parish clerk, who copied it out of my head so exactly, point by point, that he said that in all the days of his life, although he had read a great many letters of excommunication, he had never seen or read so fine a letter as that one."

"And have you still got it by heart, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"No, sir," answered Sancho, "because after I'd given it, as I saw it was going to be no further use, I set about forgetting it. And if I remember anything, it's that bit about the sodden — I mean the sovereign lady — and the last bit: 'Yours until death, the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance.' And in between those two things I put in more than three hundred souls, and lives, and eyes of mine."

Chapter 31: Of the Delightful Conversation That Passed Between Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, His Squire, with Other Incidents

"None of that displeases me; go on," said Don Quixote. "You arrived — and what was that queen of beauty doing? I am certain you found her threading pearls, or embroidering some device with gold thread for this captive knight of hers."

"I found her doing nothing of the kind," answered Sancho, "but winnowing two bushels of wheat in a yard at her house."

"Then reckon," said Don Quixote, "that the grains of that wheat were grains of pearl, since her hands had touched them. And did you notice, my friend, whether the wheat was white or spring wheat?"

"It was neither: it was red," answered Sancho.

"Then I assure you," said Don Quixote, "that winnowed by her hands it made white bread, beyond any doubt. But go on: when you gave her my letter, did she kiss it? Did she put it on top of her head? Did she perform any ceremony worthy of such a letter — or what did she do?"

"When I was going to give it her," answered Sancho, "she was in the full swing of shaking a good lot of wheat she had in the sieve, and she said to me: 'Put that letter down on that sack, my friend; I can't read it until I've finished sifting all that's here.'"

"Discerning lady!" said Don Quixote. "That must have been so as to read it at her leisure and take pleasure in it. Go on, Sancho: and while she was about her business, what conversation did she have with you? What did she ask you about me? And what did you answer her? Finish, tell me all of it; do not leave the smallest thing in the inkwell."

"She asked me nothing," said Sancho; "but I told her how your worship, for her sake, was doing penance, stripped from the waist up, buried among these mountains as though you were a savage, sleeping on the ground, not eating bread off a tablecloth or combing your beard, weeping and cursing your fortune."

"In saying that I cursed my fortune you spoke wrongly," said Don Quixote, "because on the contrary I bless it, and shall bless it all the days of my life, for having made me worthy to deserve to love so high a lady as Dulcinea of El Toboso."

"She's high, all right," answered Sancho: "upon my word she's a good six inches taller than me."

"But how is that, Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "Have you measured yourself against her?"

"I measured myself this way," answered Sancho: "going up to help her put a sack of wheat on a donkey, we got so close together that I could see she had a good hand's breadth on me."

"But is it not true," replied Don Quixote, "that she accompanies and adorns that height with a thousand millions of graces of the soul? But you will not deny me one thing, Sancho: when you got close to her, did you not smell a Sabaean scent, an aromatic fragrance, a certain something good that I cannot manage to give a name to? I mean, a savour or a breath as if you were in the shop of some elegant glove-maker?"

"What I can say," said Sancho, "is that I smelt a bit of a mannish smell; and it must have been because with all that exercise she was sweaty and a bit leathery."

"It cannot have been that," answered Don Quixote, "but you must have had a cold in the head, or you must have been smelling yourself; because I know well what that rose among thorns smells of, that lily of the field, that dissolved amber."

"It may all be so," answered Sancho, "for often enough that smell comes off me that seemed to me then to be coming off her worship the lady Dulcinea; but there's nothing to be surprised at in that, since one devil is like another."

"Well then," Don Quixote went on, "here she has finished cleaning her wheat and sending it to the mill. What did she do when she read the letter?"

"The letter," said Sancho, "she didn't read, because she said she couldn't read or write. Instead she tore it up and made small pieces of it, saying she didn't want to give it to anybody to read, so that her secrets shouldn't be known in the village; and that what I'd told her by word of mouth about the love your worship had for her and the extraordinary penance you were doing on her account was enough.

"And finally she told me to tell your worship that she kissed your hands, and that she was left there with more desire to see you than to write to you; and that so she begged and ordered you that, on sight of the present, you should come out of those thickets and leave off doing absurd things, and set out that very moment on the road to El Toboso, unless something more important came up — because she had a great desire to see your worship. She laughed a great deal when I told her that your worship called yourself the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance. I asked her whether the Basque from the other day had been there; she told me yes, and that he was a very decent man. I asked her about the galley slaves too, but she told me she hadn't seen any of them so far."

"So far everything goes well," said Don Quixote. "But tell me: what jewel was it she gave you on your leaving, for the news you carried her of me? Because it is an old and established custom among knights and ladies errant to give the squires, damsels or dwarfs who bring them news — of their ladies to them, and of their knights errant to the ladies — some rich jewel as a reward, in gratitude for their message."

"That may very well be so, and I hold it a good custom; but it must have been in times past, because now the custom must only be to give a piece of bread and cheese, which was what my lady Dulcinea gave me over the wall of a yard when I took my leave of her. And for a further mark of it, the cheese was sheep's cheese."

"She is generous in the extreme," said Don Quixote, "and if she did not give you a jewel of gold, it must without doubt have been because she did not have one there to hand to give you. But sleeves are welcome after Easter: I shall see her, and everything shall be put right.

"Do you know what I am amazed at, Sancho? That it seems to me you went and came back through the air, since you have taken little more than three days to go and come from here to El Toboso, there being more than thirty leagues from here to there. From which I give myself to understand that that wise necromancer who takes an interest in my affairs and is my friend — because there must be one, and there has to be one, on pain of my not being a good knight errant — I say that this person must have helped you along without your noticing it.

"For there are sages of this kind who take a knight errant sleeping in his bed and, without his knowing how or in what manner, he wakes next morning more than a thousand leagues from where he went to sleep. And if it were not for this, knights errant could not help one another in their dangers, as they do at every turn. For it happens that one of them is fighting in the mountains of Armenia with some dragon, or some fierce monster, or with another knight, and he is getting the worst of the battle and is already at the point of death — and when you least expect it, there appears over there, on top of a cloud or on a chariot of fire, another knight who is a friend of his, and who a little before was in England, and he helps him and saves him from death; and at night he is at home in his lodgings, having supper very comfortably. And it is often two or three thousand leagues from the one place to the other. And all this is done by the ingenuity and knowledge of these wise enchanters who look after these valorous knights.

"So, friend Sancho, I find no difficulty in believing that in so short a time you have gone and come back from this place to El Toboso, since, as I have said, some friendly sage must have carried you along without your noticing it."

"That must be it," said Sancho, "because upon my word Rocinante went along as if he had been a gypsy's donkey with quicksilver in his ears."

"Quicksilver, indeed!" said Don Quixote. "And a legion of devils besides, who are a people who travel and make others travel, without getting tired, as far as they take a fancy to.

"But leaving this aside: what do you think I ought to do now about my lady's ordering me to go and see her? Because although I see that I am obliged to carry out her command, I also see that I am prevented by the boon I have promised the princess who is travelling with us; and the law of chivalry forces me to keep my word before my own pleasure. On the one hand the desire to see my lady harries and wearies me; on the other, my pledged word and the glory I am to win in this enterprise urge and call me.

"But what I mean to do is to travel fast and get quickly to where this giant is; and on arriving I shall cut off his head and settle the princess peacefully in her estate, and at that very moment I shall turn back to see the light that lights my senses — to whom I shall make such excuses that she will come to think well of my delay, since she will see that it all works to the increase of her glory and fame. For all that I have won, win and shall win by arms in this life comes to me from the favour she gives me and from my being hers."

"Oh dear," said Sancho, "how damaged your worship is in the brainpan! Why, tell me, sir: does your worship mean to travel this whole road for nothing, and to let pass and lose so rich and distinguished a marriage as this, where they give you a kingdom for a dowry — a kingdom which upon my word I've heard is more than twenty thousand leagues round, and abounds in every one of the things that are needed to keep human life going, and is bigger than Portugal and Castile put together?

"Be quiet, for the love of God, and be ashamed of what you've said; and take my advice, and forgive me, and marry at once in the first place where there's a priest. And if not, there's our licentiate here, who'd do it beautifully. And note that I'm old enough now to give advice, and that this advice I'm giving fits your case like a mould; and that a bird in the hand is worth a vulture on the wing, because whoever has a good thing and chooses badly may be as angry as he likes but he'll get no satisfaction."

"Look, Sancho," answered Don Quixote: "if the advice you are giving me to marry is so that I shall be a king at once on killing the giant, and have the means to do you favours and give you what I promised, I would have you know that without marrying I shall be able to satisfy your wish very easily. Because before going into battle I shall stipulate, as a bonus, that if I come out the winner, then even if I do not marry they are to give me a part of the kingdom so that I can give it to whoever I like; and when they give it me, who do you want me to give it to except you?"

"That's clear enough," answered Sancho, "but let your worship take care to choose it towards the sea, because if the living doesn't suit me I can ship my black vassals off and do with them what I've said already. And your worship needn't trouble to go and see my lady Dulcinea for the present, but go and kill the giant and let's get this business finished; for by God, it's settled in my mind that it's going to be a very honourable and a very profitable one."

"I tell you, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that you are right, and that I shall have to take your advice as far as going with the princess before going to see Dulcinea. And I warn you not to say anything to anybody, nor to those who are travelling with us, of what we have discussed and settled here; for since Dulcinea is so reserved that she does not want her thoughts known, it will not be right for me, or anybody else on my behalf, to reveal them."

"Well, if that's so," said Sancho, "how is it that your worship makes everybody he beats with his arm go and present themselves before my lady Dulcinea, which is as good as your signature that you love her and are in love with her? And since those who go are bound to go and kneel down in her presence and say they come on your worship's behalf to give her their obedience, how can the thoughts of the pair of you be kept hidden?"

"Oh, what a fool and what a simpleton you are!" said Don Quixote. "Do you not see, Sancho, that all that works to her greater exaltation? Because you must know that in this style of chivalry of ours it is a great honour for a lady to have many knights errant serving her, without their thoughts going any further than to serve her, simply because she is who she is, and expecting no other reward for their many good desires than that she should be content to accept them as her knights."

"With that kind of love," said Sancho, "I've heard it preached that we're to love Our Lord — for himself alone, without being moved by hope of glory or fear of punishment. Though I'd rather love and serve him for what I could get out of it."

"The devil take you for a peasant," said Don Quixote, "and what shrewd things you say sometimes! Anybody would think you had studied."

"Well, upon my word I can't read," answered Sancho.

At this Master Nicolás shouted to them to wait a little, as they wanted to stop and drink at a little spring that was there. Don Quixote stopped, to Sancho's no small pleasure, since he was tired by now of telling so many lies and was afraid his master would catch him out in his words; because although he knew that Dulcinea was a country girl of El Toboso, he had never seen her in his life.

Cardenio had by this time put on the clothes Dorotea had been wearing when they found her, which, although not very good, were a great improvement on the ones he was leaving off. They dismounted beside the spring, and with what the curate had provided himself with at the inn they satisfied — though only a little — the great hunger they were all carrying.

While they were doing this, a boy who was travelling that way happened to pass; and stopping to look very attentively at the people who were at the spring, a little later he rushed at Don Quixote and, throwing his arms round his legs, began to cry in good earnest, saying:

"Oh, my dear sir! Doesn't your worship know me? Look at me properly — I'm that boy Andrés that your worship untied from the oak tree where I was tied up."

Don Quixote recognised him, and taking him by the hand, he turned to those who were there and said:

"So that your worships may see how important it is to have knights errant in the world to undo the wrongs and injuries done in it by the insolent and wicked men who live in it, your worships must know that some days ago, passing through a wood, I heard some cries and some very pitiful shouts, as of an afflicted and needy person. I hurried at once, carried by my duty, towards the quarter where it seemed to me the lamentable voices were sounding, and I found tied to an oak tree this boy who is now standing here — at which I am delighted in my soul, because he will be a witness who will not let me lie in anything.

"I say he was tied to the oak, stripped from the waist up, and a peasant, who I afterwards learnt was his master, was flaying him with lashes from a mare's reins. And as soon as I saw him I asked the reason for so brutal a beating. The lout answered that he was whipping him because he was his servant, and that certain acts of carelessness he was guilty of came more from thieving than from stupidity. At which this child said: 'Sir, he's only whipping me because I ask him for my wages.' The master answered with I do not know what harangues and excuses, which although they were heard by me were not accepted. In short, I made him untie the boy, and took an oath from the peasant that he would take him along with him and pay him one real on top of another, and perfumed into the bargain.

"Is not all this true, Andrés my son? Did you not notice with what authority I ordered it, and with what humility he promised to do everything I laid on him and stated and required? Answer; do not be shy or hesitate over anything: tell these gentlemen what happened, so that it may be seen and considered how useful it is, as I say, to have knights errant on the roads."

"Everything your worship has said is perfectly true," answered the boy, "but the end of the business turned out completely the opposite of what your worship imagines."

"What do you mean, the opposite?" replied Don Quixote. "So the peasant did not pay you?"

"Not only did he not pay me," answered the boy, "but as soon as your worship had got out of the wood and we were left alone, he tied me up to the same oak again and gave me so many more lashes that I was left like Saint Bartholomew flayed. And at every lash he gave me he made some witty crack about your worship that would have made me laugh if I hadn't been in so much pain. In fact he left me in such a state that up to now I've been getting cured in a hospital of the harm the wicked peasant did me then.

"And your worship is to blame for the whole of it; because if you'd gone on your way and not come where nobody called you, and hadn't meddled in other people's business, my master would have been satisfied with giving me a dozen or two lashes and would then have let me go and paid me what he owed me. But as your worship dishonoured him so pointlessly and said so many insulting things to him, his temper caught fire; and as he couldn't take it out on your worship, when he found himself alone the storm burst on me, in such a way that I don't think I'll ever be a man again as long as I live."

"The trouble," said Don Quixote, "lay in my going away; for I should not have gone until I had left you paid, because I ought to have known well by long experience that there is no peasant who keeps the word he has given, if he sees that keeping it does not suit him. But you remember, Andrés, that I swore that if he did not pay you I would go and look for him, and that I would find him even if he hid himself in the belly of the whale."

"That's the truth," said Andrés, "but it was no use at all."

"Now you shall see whether it is any use," said Don Quixote.

And saying this, he got up in a great hurry and ordered Sancho to bridle Rocinante, who was grazing while they ate.

Dorotea asked him what it was he meant to do. He answered that he meant to go and look for the peasant and punish him for such wicked conduct, and get Andrés paid to the last maravedi, in spite and to the annoyance of every peasant in the world. To which she answered that he should note that, in accordance with the promised boon, he could not get involved in any undertaking until he had finished hers; and that since he knew this better than anybody, he should calm his breast until he came back from her kingdom.

"That is true," answered Don Quixote, "and Andrés must have patience until the return, as you say, madam. And I swear and promise him again afresh not to stop until I have him avenged and paid."

"I don't believe in those oaths," said Andrés. "I'd rather have something now to get me to Seville than all the vengeances in the world. Give me, if you've got any there, something to eat and take with me — and God be with your worship and with all knights errant, and may they go as well errant for themselves as they've gone for me."

Sancho took a piece of bread and another of cheese out of his store and, giving it to the lad, said to him:

"Here you are, brother Andrés, for a share of your misfortune falls on all of us."

"And what share falls on you?" asked Andrés.

"This share of bread and cheese I'm giving you," answered Sancho, "and God knows whether I'll be short of it or not; because I'd have you know, my friend, that we squires of knights errant are subject to a great deal of hunger and bad luck, and to other things besides that are better felt than told."

Andrés took hold of his bread and cheese, and seeing that nobody was giving him anything else, he bent his head and took the road in his hands, as they say. But it is quite true that on leaving he said to Don Quixote:

"For the love of God, sir knight errant, if you ever meet me again, even if you see them tearing me to pieces, don't help me or come to my rescue, but leave me to my misfortune; because it won't be so great that it isn't smaller than what will come to me from your worship's help — and God curse you, and all the knights errant that were ever born into the world."

Don Quixote was getting up to punish him, but the boy set off running in such a way that nobody dared follow him. Don Quixote was left utterly mortified by Andrés's story, and it was necessary for the others to take great care not to laugh, so as not to mortify him completely.

Chapter 32: Which Treats of What Happened to All Don Quixote's Party at the Inn

Their good meal being over, they saddled at once; and without anything happening to them worth telling, they reached the inn the next day — the terror and dread of Sancho Panza; and although he would have liked not to go into it, there was no escaping it.

The innkeeper's wife, the innkeeper, his daughter and Maritornes, who saw Don Quixote and Sancho coming, came out to receive them with every sign of great delight; and he received them with a grave bearing and approval, and told them to get him ready a better bed than the last time. To which their hostess answered that if he paid better than the other time, she would give him one fit for a prince. Don Quixote said he would; and so they got him a reasonable one ready in the same garret as before, and he lay down at once, because he came in very much battered and short of wits.

He had hardly shut himself in when the hostess flew at the barber and, seizing him by the beard, said:

"By all that's holy, you shan't make any more use of my tail for your beard, and you'll give me my tail back; because my husband's thing is going about all over the floor, which is a shame — I mean the comb, that I used to hang from my good tail."

The barber would not give it her, however hard she pulled, until the licentiate told him to give it her, because there was no longer any need to make use of that device but he should uncover himself and show himself in his own shape, and tell Don Quixote that when the thieving galley slaves had stripped them they had come to that inn in flight; and that if he asked about the princess's squire, they would tell him that she had sent him on ahead to give notice to the people of her kingdom that she was coming and was bringing with her the deliverer of them all. With this the barber willingly gave the tail back to the innkeeper's wife, and they likewise returned all the other accessories she had lent for Don Quixote's deliverance.

Everybody at the inn was amazed at Dorotea's beauty, and even at the fine build of the shepherd lad Cardenio. The curate had them prepare a meal for them from whatever there was in the inn, and the host, in hopes of better payment, promptly prepared them a reasonable dinner. And all this while Don Quixote slept, and they were of the opinion that he should not be woken, because sleeping would do him more good just then than eating.

Over dinner, with the innkeeper, his wife, his daughter, Maritornes and all the travellers there, they discussed Don Quixote's strange madness and the state they had found him in. The hostess told them what had happened to her and to the carrier with him, and looking round in case Sancho happened to be there and not seeing him, she told them the whole story of his blanketing — at which they got no small amount of pleasure. And when the curate said that the books of chivalry Don Quixote had read had turned his brain, the innkeeper said:

"I don't know how that can be; because in truth, as far as I understand, there's no better reading in the world. I've got two or three of them there myself, along with some other papers, and they've genuinely given me new life — not only me but a lot of other people. Because at harvest time a lot of reapers gather here on holidays, and there are always some who can read; and one of them picks up one of these books, and more than thirty of us gather round him, and we listen to him with such pleasure that it takes a thousand grey hairs off us. At least I can say for myself that when I hear about those furious, terrible blows the knights lay on, it makes me want to do the same, and I could go on listening to them night and day."

"And I'm no different," said the innkeeper's wife, "because I never have a good moment in my house except the one when you're listening to the reading — you're so besotted then that you forget to quarrel."

"That's the truth," said Maritornes; "and upon my word I greatly enjoy hearing those things too, they're very lovely. Especially when they tell how one lady or another is under some orange trees with her arms round her knight, and a duenna is standing guard for them, dying of envy and in a great fright. I say the whole of it is like honey."

"And what do you think, mistress?" said the curate, speaking to the innkeeper's daughter.

"I don't know, sir, upon my soul," she answered. "I listen to it as well, and in truth, although I don't understand it, I get pleasure from hearing it. But I don't take pleasure in the blows my father takes pleasure in, but in the laments the knights make when they're away from their ladies — for in truth they sometimes make me cry out of the pity I feel for them."

"So you would have given them relief, mistress," said Dorotea, "if they had wept for you?"

"I don't know what I'd have done," answered the girl; "I only know that some of those ladies are so cruel that their knights call them tigers and lions and a thousand other filthy things. And, Jesus! I don't know what sort of people they are, so heartless and so unfeeling, that rather than look at an honourable man they let him die or go mad. I don't know what all that prudishness is for: if they do it out of respectability, let them marry the men, for that's the very thing the men want."

"Be quiet, child," said the innkeeper's wife, "for you seem to know a great deal about these things, and it isn't right for young girls to know or say so much."

"As this gentleman asked me," she answered, "I couldn't help answering him."

"Very well then," said the curate; "bring me those books, my good host, for I want to see them."

"With pleasure," he answered.

And going into his room, he brought out of it an old little portmanteau fastened with a little chain; and opening it, he found in it three large books and some papers in a very good hand, written by hand. The first book he opened he saw was Don Cirongilio of Thrace, and the second Felixmarte of Hircania, and the other the History of the Great Captain Gonzalo Hernández de Córdoba, with the Life of Diego García de Paredes. As soon as the curate read the first two titles, he turned his face to the barber and said:

"What we need here now is my friend's housekeeper and his niece."

"We don't," answered the barber; "I know how to carry them off to the yard or the chimney myself — and upon my word there's a very good fire in it."

"So your worship wants to burn more books?" said the innkeeper.

"No more," said the curate, "than these two: the Don Cirongilio and the Felixmarte."

"But are my books heretics or phlegmatics, by any chance," said the innkeeper, "that you want to burn them?"

"Schismatics you mean, my friend," said the barber, "not phlegmatics."

"That's it," replied the innkeeper; "but if you want to burn one, let it be that one about the Great Captain and that Diego García; because I'd sooner let them burn a child of mine than let them burn either of the others."

"My dear brother," said the curate, "these two books are lying books and are full of absurdities and ravings; and this one about the Great Captain is true history, and contains the deeds of Gonzalo Hernández de Córdoba, who for his many great exploits deserved to be called by the whole world the Great Captain — a famous and glorious name, and deserved by him alone. And this Diego García de Paredes was a distinguished gentleman, a native of the city of Trujillo in Extremadura, a most valiant soldier, and of such natural strength that he stopped a millwheel with one finger in the middle of its spin; and, standing with a two-handed sword at the entrance to a bridge, he held back a whole innumerable army from crossing it; and he did other such things that — since he tells them and writes them himself, with the modesty of a gentleman writing his own chronicle — if somebody else, free and unbiased, had written them, they would have consigned to oblivion those of your Hectors, Achilleses and Rolands."

"Get along with you!" said the said innkeeper. "Look what he's astonished at — stopping a millwheel! By God, your worship ought to read now what Felixmarte of Hircania did, who with one back-handed stroke split five giants through the middle as if they'd been made of beans, like the little friars children make. And another time he charged an enormous and most powerful army, where he had more than a million six hundred thousand soldiers against him, all armed from foot to head, and he scattered the whole lot of them as if they'd been flocks of sheep.

"And what will they tell me about the excellent Don Cirongilio of Thrace, who was so brave and spirited, as will be seen in the book, where it tells how, sailing along a river, a fiery serpent came out at him from the middle of the water; and he, as soon as he saw it, threw himself on it and got astride its scaly back and gripped its throat with both hands so hard that, the serpent seeing that he was strangling it, it had no other way out but to let itself sink to the bottom of the river, carrying the knight with it, because he would never let go? And when they got down there he found himself in palaces and gardens so lovely that it was a marvel; and then the serpent turned into an ancient old man, who told him so many things that there's nothing more to hear. Be quiet, sir; if you heard this you'd go mad with pleasure. Two figs for the Great Captain and for that Diego García you talk about!"

Hearing this, Dorotea said quietly to Cardenio:

"Our host is not far off making a second part to Don Quixote."

"So it seems to me," answered Cardenio; "because, by the signs he gives, he takes it for certain that everything these books tell happened exactly as they write it, and barefoot friars would not make him believe anything else."

"Look, my friend," the curate said again, "there never was in the world a Felixmarte of Hircania, or a Don Cirongilio of Thrace, or other such knights as the books of chivalry tell of; because the whole thing is the invention and fiction of idle wits, who composed them for the purpose you speak of, of passing the time, as your reapers pass it reading them. Because I genuinely swear to you that such knights never existed in the world, and that such exploits and absurdities never happened in it."

"Tell that to another dog with that bone!" answered the innkeeper. "As if I didn't know how many make five and where my shoe pinches! Don't imagine your worship can feed me pap, because by God I'm not so green. It's a fine thing that your worship should want to give me to understand that everything these good books say is absurdity and lies — printed as they are with the licence of the gentlemen of the Royal Council, as though they were the sort of people who'd let so many lies be printed all together, and so many battles and so many enchantments that they take your wits away!"

"I have told you already, my friend," replied the curate, "that this is done to entertain our idle thoughts. And just as in well-ordered states it is allowed that there should be games of chess, ball and billiards to entertain those who have no work and ought not and cannot work, so it is allowed to print and to have such books, in the belief — as is the truth — that there could be nobody so ignorant as to take any of these books for true history.

"And if it were permitted me now, and the company required it, I would say some things about what books of chivalry ought to have in them if they are to be good ones, which would perhaps be of profit and even of pleasure to some people. But I hope a time will come when I can communicate it to somebody who can put it right; and in the meantime believe what I have told you, master innkeeper, and take your books, and settle it with their truths or their lies for yourself, and much good may they do you — and God grant that you may not come to limp on the same foot your guest Don Quixote limps on."

"Not I," answered the innkeeper. "I shan't be so mad as to make myself a knight errant; for I can see plainly that what was the custom in that time, when they say those famous knights went about the world, isn't the custom now."

Halfway through this conversation Sancho arrived, and he was left very confused and thoughtful at having heard it said that knights errant were not the custom nowadays, and that all the books of chivalry were foolishness and lies. And he resolved in his heart to wait and see what his master's journey came to; and that if it did not turn out with the happiness he expected, he was determined to leave him and go back to his wife and children and his usual work.

The innkeeper was carrying off the portmanteau and the books, but the curate said to him:

"Wait; I want to see what those papers are that are written in such a good hand."

The host took them out, and giving them to him to read, he saw some eight sheets of manuscript, and at the beginning they had a large title that said: The Tale of Reckless Curiosity. The curate read three or four lines to himself and said:

"Certainly the title of this tale does not strike me badly, and it makes me want to read the whole of it."

To which the innkeeper answered:

"Then your reverence may well read it; because I can tell you that some guests who have read it here have been very much pleased with it and have asked me for it very insistently. But I haven't wanted to give it them, meaning to give it back to whoever left this portmanteau forgotten here with these books and those papers; for it may well be that its owner will come back this way some time. And although I know I shall miss the books, upon my word I mean to give them back to him: for innkeeper though I am, I am still a Christian."

"You are quite right, my friend," said the curate; "but for all that, if the tale pleases me, you must let me copy it out."

"Very willingly," answered the innkeeper.

While the two of them were saying this, Cardenio had taken up the tale and begun to read in it; and thinking the same as the curate, he begged him to read it in a way that everybody could hear.

"I would read it," said the curate, "if it were not better to spend this time in sleeping than in reading."

"It will be rest enough for me," said Dorotea, "to pass the time hearing some tale, since my spirit is not yet so quiet that it lets me sleep when I ought to."

"Well then," said the curate, "I shall read it, if only out of curiosity; perhaps there will be something enjoyable in it."

Master Nicolás hurried to beg him the same, and Sancho too; which the curate seeing, and understanding that he would give everybody pleasure and would get some himself, he said:

"Then since that is so, let everybody give me their attention, for the tale begins like this."

Chapter 33: In Which Is Told the Tale of Reckless Curiosity

In Florence, a rich and famous city of Italy in the province they call Tuscany, there lived Anselmo and Lotario, two rich and distinguished gentlemen, and such friends that by way of pre-eminence and by antonomasia they were called the two friends by everybody who knew them. They were unmarried, young men of the same age and the same habits — all of which was cause enough for the two of them to answer each other with a reciprocal friendship.

It is quite true that Anselmo was rather more inclined to the pastimes of love than Lotario, whose taste ran to hunting; but when the occasion came, Anselmo would give up going after his own pleasures to follow Lotario's, and Lotario would leave his to attend on Anselmo's. And in this way their wills went so exactly together that no well-regulated clock kept time with them.

Anselmo was head over ears in love with a distinguished and beautiful young lady of the same city, the daughter of such good parents and so good in herself that he decided — with the approval of his friend Lotario, without which he did nothing — to ask her parents for her as his wife; and so he put it into effect. And the man who carried the message was Lotario, and the man who concluded the business so much to his friend's liking that in a short time he found himself put in possession of what he wanted; and Camila was so pleased at having got Anselmo for a husband that she never stopped giving thanks to heaven, and to Lotario, by whose means so great a good had come to her.

The first few days — as all wedding days are usually cheerful — Lotario went on frequenting his friend Anselmo's house as he used to, doing his best to honour him, entertain him and give him pleasure in every way he could. But once the wedding was over and the frequency of visits and congratulations had settled down, Lotario began carefully to be careless about going to Anselmo's house, since it seemed to him — as it is reasonable that it should seem to all people of judgement — that a man ought not to visit and frequent the houses of his married friends in the same way as when they were single. Because although good and true friendship neither can nor ought to be suspect in anything, still, a married man's honour is so delicate a thing that it seems it can be offended even by his own brothers, let alone by his friends.

Anselmo noticed Lotario's slackness and complained bitterly about it, telling him that if he had known that getting married was going to prevent him from associating with him as he used to, he would never have done it; and that if, by the good understanding the two of them had while he was single, they had earned so sweet a name as being called the two friends, he should not allow so famous and so agreeable a name to be lost simply for the sake of playing the man of discretion, with no other occasion at all.
