And so he begged him — if it was permissible for such a way of speaking to be used between them — to be master of his house again and to come in and out of it as before, assuring him that his wife Camila had no other pleasure and no other wish than the one he wanted her to have, and that having learnt how truly the two of them loved each other, she was puzzled to see so much aloofness in him.

To all these and a great many other arguments that Anselmo made to Lotario to persuade him to come back to his house as he used to, Lotario answered with so much prudence, judgement and good sense that Anselmo was satisfied of his friend's good intentions; and they agreed together that on two days a week and on holidays Lotario should come and eat with him. And although this was settled between them, Lotario resolved to do no more than what he saw was best suited to his friend's honour, whose good name he valued more than his own.

He used to say, and said rightly, that a married man whom heaven had granted a beautiful wife should take as much care about what men friends he brought into his house as about seeing what women friends his wife associated with; because what is not done and arranged in the squares, in the churches, at public festivals or on pilgrimages — things husbands cannot always refuse their wives — is arranged and made easy in the house of the woman friend or relative who is most trusted.

Lotario also used to say that married men needed to have some friend each who would warn them of the mistakes in their conduct; because it often happens that, with the great love a husband has for his wife, he either does not warn her or does not tell her, so as not to annoy her, that she should do or leave off doing certain things which, done or not done, would work to his honour or his discredit. And being warned of this by his friend, he could easily put everything right.

But where is a friend to be found as judicious and as loyal and true as Lotario asks for here? I certainly do not know: only Lotario was such a man, who with all diligence and care looked after his friend's honour and contrived to trim, shave and shorten the days of the agreement about going to his house, so that the coming and going of a rich young man, well-bred and well-born, and with the good qualities he believed he had, into the house of so beautiful a woman as Camila, should not look bad to the idle common people and to wandering, malicious eyes. Because although her goodness and worth could put a bridle on any slandering tongue, still he did not want to put her good name or his friend's in any doubt; and for this reason he spent and occupied most of the agreed days on other things, which he gave out were unavoidable. And so, in complaints from the one and excuses from the other, a great many hours and parts of the day were passed.

It happened, then, that one day when the two of them were walking about a meadow outside the city, Anselmo said to Lotario something like this:

"You supposed, friend Lotario, that for the favours God has done me in making me the son of such parents as mine were, and in giving me, with no sparing hand, the goods both of nature and of fortune, I cannot answer with a gratitude that comes up to the good I have received — and above all to the good he did me in giving me you for a friend and Camila for my own wife: two treasures which I value, if not to the degree I ought, at least to the degree I can.

"Well, with all these things, which are generally the whole of what men live contented with and can live contented with, I live the most distressed and the most miserable man in the whole universe. Because for I do not know how many days a desire has been wearying and pressing on me so strange and so far outside the common way of other men that I am astonished at myself, and blame myself and scold myself when I am alone, and try to keep quiet about it and hide it even from my own thoughts. And it has been about as possible for me to come out with this secret as if I had deliberately tried to tell it to the whole world. And since in fact it has to come out into the open, I want it to be into the open of the archive of your secrecy; trusting that with it, and with the effort you will make, as my true friend, to put me right, I shall soon find myself free of the distress it causes me, and my happiness through your care will come up to the level my unhappiness has reached through my own madness."

Anselmo's words held Lotario in suspense, and he did not know what such a long preparation or preamble would come to; and although he kept turning over in his imagination what that desire could be that was wearying his friend so much, he always fell a long way wide of the mark of the truth. And to get quickly out of the agony that suspense caused him, he told him that he was doing a plain injury to their great friendship by going about looking for roundabout ways to tell him his most hidden thoughts, since he could certainly count on getting from him either advice for keeping them in check or help for carrying them out.

"That is the truth," answered Anselmo, "and with that confidence I let you know, friend Lotario, that the desire that wearies me is wondering whether Camila, my wife, is as good and as perfect as I think she is; and I cannot be certain of this truth except by testing her in such a way that the test shows the carats of her goodness, as fire shows those of gold.

"Because it is my opinion, my friend, that a woman is no better than she is or is not solicited, and that only that woman is strong who does not bend to the promises, the gifts, the tears and the constant importunities of eager lovers. For what is there to be thankful for," he said, "in a woman's being good, if nobody tells her to be bad? What is so great about a woman's being quiet and modest when she is given no opportunity to break out, and when she knows that she has a husband who, catching her in her first indiscretion, will take her life? So the woman who is good out of fear or for want of opportunity, I am not prepared to hold in the esteem in which I shall hold the woman who is solicited and pursued and comes out with the crown of victory.

"So that for these reasons, and for a great many others I could tell you to give credit and strength to the opinion I hold, I want Camila my wife to pass through these difficulties and be refined and assayed in the fire of finding herself courted and solicited — and by a man of enough worth to set his desires on her. And if she comes out of this battle, as I believe she will, with the palm, I shall count my good fortune unequalled; I shall be able to say that the emptiness of my desires is filled; I shall say that the strong woman fell to my lot, of whom the Wise Man says: who shall find her? And if this turns out the opposite of what I expect, then with the pleasure of seeing that I was right in my opinion I shall bear without pain the pain that my very costly experiment may reasonably cause me.

"And granted that nothing you may say to me against my wish is to be of any use in making me give up carrying it out, I want you, friend Lotario, to make yourself ready to be the instrument that works this piece of business I want; and I shall give you the opportunity to do it, and shall not fail to give you everything I see is needed for soliciting a modest, honourable, retiring and disinterested woman.

"And what moves me, among other things, to entrust so hard an enterprise to you is seeing that if Camila is conquered by you, the conquest is not to be pushed to the last extremity, but only to counting as done what is to be done, out of proper respect. And so I shall not be injured except in intention, and my injury will stay hidden in the virtue of your silence, which I know very well will be as everlasting as death's in anything that touches me. So that if you want me to have a life I can call one, you must from this moment enter this battle of love, not lukewarmly or lazily but with the eagerness and diligence my desire requires, and with the confidence our friendship assures me of."

These were the words Anselmo said to Lotario, to all of which he listened so attentively that except for the ones already written that he said to him, he did not open his lips until Anselmo had finished. And seeing that he was saying no more, after he had looked at him for a good while, as though he were looking at some other thing he had never seen before that caused him astonishment and dread, he said to him:

"I cannot persuade myself, friend Anselmo, that the things you have said to me are not a joke; for if I had thought you were saying them in earnest, I would not have let you get so far, since by refusing to listen to you I would have prevented your long harangue. Without a doubt I imagine either that you do not know me or that I do not know you. But no: I know very well that you are Anselmo, and you know that I am Lotario. The trouble is that I think you are not the Anselmo you used to be, and you must have thought that I am not the Lotario I ought to be either. Because the things you have said to me are not the things of that Anselmo my friend, nor are the things you ask of me to be asked of that Lotario you know.

"For good friends are to test their friends and make use of them, as a poet said, usque ad aras — which meant that they were not to make use of their friendship in things that were against God. Well, if a heathen felt this about friendship, how much better ought a Christian to feel it, who knows that for no human friendship is he to lose the divine one? And when a friend throws the bar so far as to set aside the claims of heaven in order to attend to his friend's, it ought not to be for light matters of small moment but for those on which his friend's honour and life depend.

"Then tell me now, Anselmo: which of these two things of yours is in danger, that I should venture to gratify you and do a thing as detestable as the one you are asking? Neither of them, certainly; on the contrary, you are asking me, as I understand it, to try and set about taking away your honour and your life, and taking away mine along with them. Because if I am to try to take away your honour, it is clear that I am taking away your life, since a man without honour is worse than a dead man; and I, being the instrument — as you want me to be — of so much harm to you, do I not come to be left dishonoured and, by the same reasoning, without a life?

"Listen, friend Anselmo, and have the patience not to answer me until I have finished telling you what occurs to me about what your desire has asked of you; for there will be time enough for you to reply and for me to listen."

"With pleasure," said Anselmo. "Say what you like."

And Lotario went on to say:

"It seems to me, Anselmo, that you have your wits at this moment in the state the Moors are always in, who cannot be given to understand the error of their sect by quotations from Holy Scripture, or by arguments that consist in the speculation of the understanding, or that are founded on articles of faith; but they must be brought palpable, easy, intelligible, demonstrative, indubitable examples, with mathematical demonstrations that cannot be denied — as when they say, 'If from two equal parts we take away equal parts, those that are left are equal too.' And when they do not understand this in words, as in fact they do not, it has to be shown them with the hands and put in front of their eyes; and even then nobody is able to persuade them of the truths of my sacred religion.

"And I shall have to use this same procedure and method with you; because the desire that has been born in you goes so far astray and so far outside anything that has a shadow of reason in it that it seems to me the time I spend giving you to understand your simplicity — for at present I do not want to give it another name — will be time wasted. And I am even inclined to leave you in your folly, as a punishment for your wicked wish; but the friendship I have for you does not let me use such severity, and does not allow me to leave you standing in such an obvious danger of ruining yourself.

"And so that you may see it clearly, tell me, Anselmo: have you not told me that I am to solicit a woman who keeps herself to herself, to persuade a modest woman, to make offers to a disinterested woman, to court a prudent woman? Yes, you have told me so. Well, if you know that you have a wife who keeps to herself, who is modest, disinterested and prudent, what are you looking for? And if you think that she is bound to come out the winner from all my assaults, as she will without a doubt, what better titles do you think you can give her afterwards than the ones she has now, or what will she be afterwards more than she is now? Either you do not hold her to be what you say, or you do not know what you are asking.

"If you do not hold her to be what you say, then why do you want to test her, instead of doing with her whatever comes best to your liking, as with a bad woman? But if she is as good as you believe, it will be an impertinent thing to make an experiment on the truth itself, since once it is made it will be left with the same estimation it had before.

"So that it is a conclusive argument that attempting things from which harm can come to us sooner than profit is the mark of unreasoning and reckless judgements — and the more so when people want to attempt things they are neither forced nor compelled to, and which show from a long way off that attempting them is plain madness.

"Difficult things are attempted for God, or for the world, or for both together. Those attempted for God are the ones the saints attempted, attempting to live the life of angels in human bodies. Those attempted out of respect for the world are those of the men who cross such an infinity of water, such a diversity of climates, such strangeness of peoples, in order to get these things they call the goods of fortune. And those attempted for God and for the world together are those of brave soldiers, who have hardly seen a gap opened in the enemy's wall as wide as a round cannonball could make when, putting aside all fear and without reasoning or noticing the plain danger that threatens them, carried on the wings of the desire to stand up for their faith, their nation and their king, they throw themselves fearlessly into the middle of a thousand opposing deaths that are waiting for them.

"These are the things that are usually attempted, and it is honour, glory and profit to attempt them, however full they may be of drawbacks and dangers. But the thing you say you want to attempt and put into practice will get you neither glory from God, nor goods of fortune, nor fame among men. Because supposing you come out of it as you want, you will be left no prouder, no richer and no more honoured than you are now; and if you do not come out of it, you will find yourself in the greatest misery that can be imagined. For it will be no use to you then to think that nobody knows the disaster that has happened to you, because it will be enough to afflict you and undo you that you know it yourself.

"And to confirm this truth I want to tell you a stanza that the famous poet Luigi Tansillo made at the end of the first part of his Tears of Saint Peter, which goes like this:

	The grief grows, and the shame grows too,
	in Peter, when the day has shown itself;
	and although he sees nobody there, he is ashamed
	of himself, at seeing that he had sinned.
	For a great heart needs more than being looked at
	to move it to feel shame:
	it is ashamed of itself when it goes wrong,
	even if it sees nobody but heaven and earth.

"So that you will not escape your pain by secrecy; on the contrary, you will have to weep continually — if not tears from your eyes, then tears of blood from your heart, as that simple-minded doctor wept whom our poet tells us made the test of the cup, which the prudent Rinaldo, reasoning better, excused himself from making. And granted that that is a poetical fiction, it has shut up inside it moral secrets worth noting and understanding and imitating.

"What is more, with what I mean to tell you now you will finally come to recognise the great mistake you want to make. Tell me, Anselmo: if heaven or good luck had made you the lord and lawful possessor of a most perfect diamond, of whose quality and carats every jeweller who saw it was satisfied, and if they all with one voice and by common opinion said that in carats, quality and fineness it came up to everything the nature of such a stone could reach, and if you yourself believed it so, knowing nothing to the contrary — would it be right for you to take it into your head to take that diamond and put it between an anvil and a hammer, and there, by sheer force of blows and arms, test whether it is as hard and as fine as they say? And still more so if you actually did it? For supposing the stone resisted so foolish a test, it would not get any more value or any more fame from it; and if it broke, which it might well do, would not everything be lost? Certainly it would, leaving its owner in everybody's opinion as a simpleton.

"Then reckon, friend Anselmo, that Camila is a most perfect diamond, both in your estimation and in other people's, and that it is not right to put her in a position where she may be broken; since even if she is left whole, she cannot rise to any greater value than she has now, and if she failed and did not resist, consider from now on what state you would be left in without her, and how rightly you could blame yourself for having been the cause of her ruin and of your own.

"See that there is no jewel in the world worth as much as a chaste and honourable woman, and that the whole honour of women consists in the good opinion people have of them; and since your wife's is such that it reaches the extreme of goodness you know, why do you want to put this truth in doubt?

"Look, my friend, woman is an imperfect animal, and one ought not to put obstacles in her way to trip her up and make her fall, but to take them out and clear her road of every hindrance, so that without difficulty she may run lightly to attain the perfection she lacks, which consists in being virtuous.

"The naturalists tell us that the ermine is a little animal with an extremely white coat, and that when they want to hunt it, the hunters use this device: knowing the places it usually passes and comes to, they block them off with mud; and then, driving it, they head it towards that place; and as soon as the ermine reaches the mud it stands still and lets itself be taken and caught, rather than pass through the mire and lose and dirty its whiteness, which it values more than liberty and life.

"The modest and chaste woman is an ermine, and the virtue of modesty is whiter and cleaner than snow; and whoever wants her not to lose it, but rather to keep and preserve it, must use a different method from the one used with the ermine — because they are not to put in front of her the mire of the gifts and attentions of importunate lovers; since perhaps, and even without the perhaps, she has not enough virtue and natural strength to trample and pass through those obstacles by herself, and it is necessary to take them away and to put in front of her the cleanness of virtue and the beauty that a good name contains in itself.

"The good woman is likewise like a mirror of bright, clear glass; but it is liable to be misted over and darkened by any breath that touches it. With the modest woman one must use the method one uses with holy relics: worship them and do not touch them. A good woman is to be guarded and prized as a beautiful garden full of flowers and roses is guarded and prized, whose owner allows nobody to walk in it or handle it; it is enough that from a distance, and through the iron railings, people should enjoy its fragrance and its beauty.

"Finally, I want to tell you some verses that have come into my memory, which I heard in a modern play and which seem to me to be to the purpose of what we are discussing. A prudent old man was advising another, the father of a young girl, to keep her in, guard her and shut her up; and among other arguments he said this to him:"

	Woman is made of glass;
	but one is not to test
	whether she can break or not,
	because anything might be.
	And breaking is the easier thing,
	and it is no sense to put
	at risk of being broken
	what cannot be soldered again.
	And let everybody hold
	this opinion, and I found it on reason:
	that if there are Danaës in the world,
	there are showers of gold as well.

"Everything I have said to you so far, Anselmo, has been about what concerns you; and now it is right that something should be heard about what concerns me. And if it is long, forgive me, for the labyrinth you have got into and want me to get you out of requires all of it.

"You take me for your friend and want to take away my honour, a thing that is against all friendship; and you not only aim at this but try to get me to take yours away from you. That you want to take mine away from me is clear, since when Camila sees that I am soliciting her, as you ask, it is certain that she must take me for a man without honour and without decency, seeing that I am attempting and doing a thing so far outside what being who I am and your friendship oblige me to. That you want me to take yours away from you there is no doubt, because Camila, seeing that I am soliciting her, is bound to think that I have seen in her some lightness that gave me the boldness to reveal my wicked desire to her; and her holding herself dishonoured, her dishonour touches you, as a thing belonging to you.

"And from this arises what is commonly discussed: that the husband of an adulterous wife, even though he does not know it and has given no occasion for his wife not to be what she ought, and even though it has not been in his hands, or through his carelessness and want of caution, to prevent his misfortune — for all that, they call him and name him by a name of reproach and contempt; and in a certain way those who know his wife's wickedness look at him with eyes of scorn, instead of looking at him with eyes of pity, seeing that it is not through his own fault but through the pleasure of his wicked partner that he is in that misfortune.

"But I want to tell you the reason why the husband of a bad wife is with just cause dishonoured, even though he does not know she is bad, and is not at fault, and has had no part in it and given no occasion for her being so. And do not grow tired of hearing me, for it will all work to your profit.

"When God created our first father in the earthly Paradise, Holy Scripture says that God poured sleep on Adam, and that while he was sleeping he took a rib out of his left side, from which he formed our mother Eve; and as soon as Adam woke and looked at her, he said: 'This is flesh of my flesh and bone of my bones.' And God said: 'For this shall a man leave his father and mother, and they shall be two in one same flesh.' And then the divine sacrament of matrimony was instituted, with such bonds that death alone can untie them. And this miraculous sacrament has such force and virtue that it makes two different persons one same flesh; and it does more still in good married couples, who, although they have two souls, have no more than one will.

"And from this it comes about that, the wife's flesh being one and the same with the husband's, the stains that fall on it, or the defects she brings on herself, work back on the husband's flesh, even though he has not, as has been said, given occasion for that harm. Because just as the pain of the foot, or of any limb of the human body, is felt by the whole body, since it is all of one same flesh, and the head feels the injury to the ankle although it did not cause it, so the husband shares in his wife's dishonour, being one same thing with her. And since the honours and dishonours of the world all are and are born of flesh and blood, and those of the bad wife are of that kind, it necessarily follows that the husband gets a share of them and is held dishonoured without knowing it.

"See, then, Anselmo, what danger you are putting yourself in by wanting to disturb the peace your good wife lives in. See out of what an empty and impertinent curiosity you want to stir up the humours that are now settled in your chaste wife's breast. Notice that what you are risking to gain is little, and that what you will lose will be so much that I shall leave it where it is, because I have no words to describe it.

"But if everything I have said is not enough to move you from your wicked purpose, you may well look for another instrument of your dishonour and misfortune, for I do not mean to be it, even if I lose your friendship for it — which is the greatest loss I can imagine."

Having said this, the virtuous and prudent Lotario fell silent; and Anselmo was left so confused and thoughtful that for a good while he could not answer him a word. But at last he said to him:

"With the attention you have seen, friend Lotario, I have listened to everything you wanted to say to me; and in your arguments, examples and comparisons I have seen the great good sense you have and the height of true friendship you have reached. And likewise I see and confess that if I do not follow your opinion and go after my own, I am running away from good and running after evil.

"This granted, you must consider that I am now suffering from the illness some women have, who take a fancy to eat earth, plaster, charcoal and other things that are worse — disgusting even to look at, let alone to eat. So that it is necessary to use some artifice for me to be cured; and this could easily be done, simply by your beginning, however lukewarmly and pretendingly, to solicit Camila. She will not be so soft as to lay her modesty on the ground at the first encounters; and with this beginning alone I shall be content, and you will have done what you owe to our friendship — not only giving me my life but persuading me that I am not without honour.

"And you are obliged to do this for one reason alone; and it is that, since I am, as I am, determined to put this test into practice, you are not to allow me to give an account of my folly to any other person, by which I would put in jeopardy the honour you are trying to keep me from losing. And if your own is not at the point it ought to be in Camila's opinion while you are soliciting her, it matters little or nothing, since shortly, seeing in her the integrity we expect, you will be able to tell her the plain truth of our device, and your reputation will go back to what it was.

"And since you are risking so little and can give me so much satisfaction by taking the risk, do not fail to do it, however many objections may be put in front of you; since, as I have said already, simply by your beginning I shall count the case as closed."

Lotario, seeing Anselmo's settled will, and not knowing what further examples to bring him or what further arguments to show him so that he should not follow it, and seeing that he was threatening to give an account of his wicked desire to somebody else, decided, to avoid a greater evil, to satisfy him and do what he asked — with the purpose and intention of steering the business in such a way that, without disturbing Camila's mind, Anselmo should be satisfied. And so he answered him that he should not communicate his idea to anybody else, and that he took that enterprise upon himself and would begin it whenever it best pleased Anselmo.

Anselmo embraced him tenderly and affectionately and thanked him for his offer as though he had done him some great favour; and it was agreed between the two of them that the work should begin the very next day. Anselmo said he would give him place and time to speak to Camila alone, and would likewise give him money and jewels to give her and to offer her. He advised him to give her music and to write verses in her praise; and that if he did not want to take the trouble of making them, he would make them himself. Lotario offered to do it all — with a very different intention from the one Anselmo supposed.

And with this arrangement they went back to Anselmo's house, where they found Camila anxious and worried, waiting for her husband, because that day he was later than usual in coming.

Lotario went off to his own house, and Anselmo stayed in his, as pleased as Lotario was thoughtful, not knowing what plan to lay so as to come well out of that impertinent business. But that night he thought of the way he would take to deceive Anselmo without offending Camila; and the next day he came to eat with his friend, and was well received by Camila, who received him and made much of him very willingly, understanding the goodwill her husband had for him.

They finished eating, the cloth was cleared, and Anselmo told Lotario to stay there with Camila while he went to see about a necessary piece of business, and that he would be back within an hour and a half. Camila begged him not to go, and Lotario offered to keep him company; but nothing was any use with Anselmo. On the contrary, he pressed Lotario to stay and wait for him, because he had a matter of great importance to discuss with him. He also told Camila not to leave Lotario alone until he came back. In fact he knew so well how to feign the necessity — or the foolishness — of his going away that nobody could have understood it was feigned.

Anselmo went, and Camila and Lotario were left alone at the table, because the rest of the household had all gone off to eat. Lotario saw himself put into the lists his friend had wanted, and with the enemy in front of him who could have conquered a squadron of armed knights with her beauty alone: consider whether it was reasonable that Lotario should be afraid of her.

But what he did was to put his elbow on the arm of his chair and his open hand against his cheek, and, begging Camila's pardon for the discourtesy, said that he wanted to rest a little until Anselmo came back. Camila answered that he would rest better on the sofa than in the chair, and so begged him to come and sleep on it. Lotario would not, and stayed there asleep until Anselmo came back; who, finding Camila in her own room and Lotario asleep, believed that as he had been away so long the two of them had by now had time to talk, and even to sleep, and could not wait for the hour when Lotario should wake so as to go out with him again and ask him about his fortunes.

Everything turned out as he wanted: Lotario woke, and the two of them left the house at once, and so he asked him what he wanted to know. And Lotario answered him that it had not seemed to him a good idea to reveal himself completely the first time; and so he had done nothing but praise Camila for her beauty, telling her that in the whole city there was no other subject of talk than her beauty and good sense; and that this had seemed to him a good beginning for making a start on winning her goodwill, and disposing her to listen to him another time with pleasure — using in this the device the devil uses when he wants to deceive somebody who is standing on the watchtower looking out for himself: he transforms himself into an angel of light, being an angel of darkness, and putting good appearances in front of him, at the end reveals who he is and gets his way, if his trick is not found out at the beginning.

All this pleased Anselmo greatly, and he said he would give him the same opportunity every day, even without going out of the house, because he would occupy himself in it with things that would keep Camila from finding out about their device.

It happened, then, that a great many days went by in which, without Lotario's saying a word to Camila, he answered Anselmo that he was speaking to her and could never get out of her the smallest sign of agreeing to anything that was wrong, or even give a sign of the shadow of hope; on the contrary, he said, she threatened him that if he did not get rid of that wicked thought, she would tell her husband.

"Very good," said Anselmo. "So far Camila has resisted words; we must see how she resists deeds. Tomorrow I shall give you two thousand gold crowns to offer her, and even to give her, and as many again to buy jewels to bait her with. For women are usually fond — and the more so if they are beautiful, however chaste they may be — of this business of turning themselves out well and going about elegantly. And if she resists this temptation, I shall be satisfied and shall trouble you no further."

Lotario answered that since he had begun, he would carry that enterprise through to the end, although he expected to come out of it worn out and beaten. The next day he received the four thousand crowns, and with them four thousand confusions, because he did not know what to say by way of a new lie. But in the end he decided to tell him that Camila stood as firm against gifts and promises as against words, and that there was no reason to weary himself any further, because all the time was being spent for nothing.

But fortune, which was steering things another way, arranged that, having left Lotario and Camila alone as he used to do at other times, Anselmo shut himself in a room and through the keyhole watched and listened to what the two of them were doing. And he saw that in more than half an hour Lotario did not say a word to Camila, and would not have said one if he had been there for a century; and he realised that everything his friend had told him about Camila's answers was fiction and lies.

And to see whether this was so, he came out of the room and, calling Lotario aside, asked him what news there was and what temper Camila was in. Lotario answered him that he did not mean to take another stitch in that business, because she answered so harshly and coldly that he had not the courage to say anything more to her.

"Ah, Lotario, Lotario!" said Anselmo. "How badly you answer what you owe me and the great trust I put in you! I have just been watching you through the opening this keyhole gives, and I have seen that you have not said a word to Camila — from which I give myself to understand that you have still to say her the first ones. And if this is so, as it certainly is, why do you deceive me, or why do you want to take away by your contrivance the means I might find of getting what I want?"

Anselmo said no more, but what he had said was enough to leave Lotario mortified and confused; who, almost as though taking it as a point of honour to have been caught out in a lie, swore to Anselmo that from that moment he took it so much upon himself to satisfy him and not to lie to him that he would see it for himself if he spied on him carefully — and what was more, that there would be no need to take any such trouble, because the trouble he meant to take to satisfy him would put him beyond all suspicion.

Anselmo believed him; and to give him a safer and less alarming opportunity, he decided to be away from his house for eight days, going to that of a friend of his who lived in a village not far from the city; with which friend he arranged that he should send for him very urgently, so as to have an excuse to give Camila for his going.

Unhappy and ill-advised Anselmo! What is it you are doing? What is it you are contriving? What is it you are arranging? See that you are working against yourself, contriving your own dishonour and arranging your own ruin. Your wife Camila is good; you possess her quietly and peacefully; nobody troubles your pleasure; her thoughts do not go beyond the walls of her house; you are her heaven on earth, the target of her desires, the fulfilment of her pleasures and the measure by which she measures her will, fitting it in everything to yours and to heaven's.

Well, if the mine of her honour, beauty, modesty and reserve gives you without any labour all the wealth it holds and all you could desire, why do you want to dig into the ground and look for new veins of new and never-before-seen treasure, putting yourself in danger that the whole thing may come down — since, after all, it rests on the weak supports of her frail nature? Consider that whoever looks for the impossible deserves to be denied the possible, as a poet said better, saying:

	I look for life in death,
	for health in sickness,
	for liberty in prison,
	for a way out of what is shut,
	and for loyalty in the traitor.
	But my luck, from which
	I never hope for any good,
	has laid it down with heaven
	that since I ask for the impossible,
	they shall not give me even the possible.

The next day Anselmo went off to the village, leaving word with Camila that during the time he was away Lotario would come to look after his house and to eat with her, and that she should take care to treat him as she would his own person. Camila, being a sensible and honourable woman, was distressed at the orders her husband was leaving her, and told him that he should note that it was not right for anybody, in his absence, to occupy the chair at his table; and that if he was doing it because he had no confidence that she could manage his house, he should try her this once and would see by experience that she was equal to greater responsibilities. Anselmo replied that this was his pleasure, and that she had nothing more to do than bow her head and obey him. Camila said she would do so, though against her will.

Anselmo left, and the next day Lotario came to the house, where he was received by Camila with a loving and modest welcome. She never put herself in a place where Lotario could see her alone, because she always went about surrounded by her menservants and maids — especially by a maid of hers called Leonela, whom she was very fond of, the two of them having been brought up together from childhood in Camila's parents' house, and when she married Anselmo she had brought her with her.

For the first three days Lotario never said anything to her, although he could have done, when the cloth was cleared and the household went off to eat in a great hurry, because Camila had ordered it so. And Leonela even had orders to eat before Camila did and never to move from her side. But she, having her thoughts set on other matters that pleased her, and needing those hours and that room to occupy them with her own satisfactions, did not always carry out her mistress's command; on the contrary, she left them alone as though that had been what she was ordered. But Camila's modest presence, the gravity of her face and the composure of her person was such that it put a bridle on Lotario's tongue.

But the good that Camila's many virtues did, in putting silence on Lotario's tongue, worked out more to the harm of them both. Because if his tongue was silent, his thoughts ran on and had room to contemplate, point by point, all the extremes of goodness and beauty that Camila had, which were enough to make a marble statue fall in love, let alone a heart of flesh.

Lotario looked at her in the room and the space where he ought to have been speaking to her, and considered how worthy she was of being loved; and this consideration began little by little to make assaults on the respect he had for Anselmo. And a thousand times he wanted to leave the city and go where Anselmo would never see him nor he see Camila; but the pleasure he found in looking at her got in the way and held him back. He forced himself and fought with himself to throw off and not to feel the pleasure that drew him to look at Camila. When he was alone he blamed himself for his folly, called himself a bad friend and even a bad Christian; he made arguments and comparisons between himself and Anselmo, and they all stopped at saying that Anselmo's madness and misplaced confidence had been greater than his own want of loyalty, and that if he had as good an excuse before God as before men for what he meant to do, he would not fear any punishment for his fault.

In the end Camila's beauty and goodness, together with the opportunity the ignorant husband had put into his hands, laid Lotario's loyalty on the ground. And without looking at anything except what his own pleasure inclined him to, at the end of three days of Anselmo's absence — during which he was in a continual battle to resist his desires — he began to make love to Camila, with so much agitation and with such loving words that Camila was taken aback, and did nothing except get up from where she was and go into her own room without answering him a word.

But Lotario's hope was not dismayed by this coldness — hope, which is always born together with love; on the contrary, he thought the more of Camila. And she, having seen in Lotario what she had never expected, did not know what to do with herself. And thinking it neither a safe nor a proper thing to give him occasion or opportunity to speak to her again, she decided to send that same night — as she did — a servant of hers with a note to Anselmo, in which she wrote these words:

Chapter 34: In Which the Tale of Reckless Curiosity Is Continued

Just as they say that an army looks wrong without its general and a castle without its governor, so I say that a young married woman looks far more wrong without her husband, when the justest of reasons do not prevent it. I find myself so badly off without you, and so incapable of putting up with this absence, that if you do not come soon I shall have to go and stay at my parents' house, even if I leave yours without a guard; because the one you left me, if he was left with that title, seems to me to be looking after his own pleasure more than after what concerns you. And since you are a man of sense, I have no more to say to you — nor is it right that I should say more.

Anselmo received this letter, and understood from it that Lotario had already begun the enterprise and that Camila must have answered as he wanted. And, extremely pleased at such news, he sent back word to Camila by mouth that she should on no account move out of his house, because he would be back very shortly.

Camila was astonished at Anselmo's answer, which put her into more confusion than before, because she neither dared to stay in her house nor to go to her parents'; for by staying her modesty ran into danger, and by going she went against her husband's command.

In the end she settled on what was worst for her, which was staying, and resolved not to run away from Lotario's presence, so as not to give her servants anything to talk about. And by now she was sorry she had written what she wrote to her husband, afraid he would think Lotario had seen some looseness in her that had moved him not to keep up the respect he owed her. But, relying on her own goodness, she trusted in God and in her own good intentions, with which she meant to resist in silence everything Lotario might want to say to her, without giving any further account to her husband, so as not to put him to some quarrel and trouble. And she was even looking for some way to excuse Lotario to Anselmo when he should ask her what had moved her to write him that note.

With these thoughts, more honourable than sound or useful, she spent another day listening to Lotario; who pressed so hard that Camila's firmness began to waver, and her modesty had a great deal of work to do to keep to her eyes so that they should not show some sign of the loving compassion that Lotario's tears and words had woken in her breast. All this Lotario noticed, and all of it inflamed him.

Finally it seemed to him that it was necessary, in the room and the time Anselmo's absence gave him, to tighten the siege round that fortress. And so he attacked her self-esteem with praises of her beauty, because there is nothing that more quickly brings down and levels the embattled towers of a beautiful woman's vanity than that same vanity, set on the tongue of flattery. In fact, with all diligence, he mined the rock of her integrity with such engines that even if Camila had been made entirely of bronze, she would have come to the ground. He wept, he begged, he offered, he flattered, he insisted and he pretended with so much feeling and with such signs of being in earnest that he broke through Camila's guard and came to triumph over what he had least expected and most desired.

Camila surrendered; Camila surrendered. But what wonder, if Lotario's friendship did not stay standing? A clear example that shows us that the passion of love is only conquered by running away from it, and that nobody should come to grips with so powerful an enemy, because divine strength is needed to conquer his human strength.

Only Leonela knew her mistress's weakness, because the two bad friends and new lovers could not hide it from her. Lotario did not want to tell Camila about Anselmo's plan, or that Anselmo had given him the opportunity to reach that point, so that she should not think less of his love and suppose that he had solicited her like that, by chance and without meaning it, and not on purpose.

A few days later Anselmo came back to his house, and did not notice what was missing in it, which was the thing he valued least and prized most. He went at once to see Lotario, and found him at home. They embraced each other, and the one asked for the news of his life or his death.

"The news I can give you, friend Anselmo," said Lotario, "is that you have a wife who can deservedly be the example and the crown of all good women. The words I have said to her the wind has carried off; my offers have been thought little of; my gifts have not been accepted; some pretended tears of mine have been notably laughed at. In short, just as Camila is the sum of all beauty, she is the storehouse where modesty resides and where good breeding and reserve live, along with every virtue that can make an honourable woman praiseworthy and fortunate.

"Take back your money, my friend, for I have it here without having had any need to touch it; Camila's integrity does not surrender to things as low as gifts and promises. Be content, Anselmo, and do not want to make any more tests than the ones you have made. And since you have crossed dry-shod the sea of the difficulties and suspicions men may and do have about women, do not choose to go into the deep ocean of new troubles all over again, or to make trial with another pilot of the soundness and strength of the ship heaven gave you as your lot to cross the sea of this world in. Instead, reckon that you are already in a safe harbour, and grapple yourself with the anchors of good sense, and let yourself lie there until they come to ask you for the debt that no human nobility excuses a man from paying."

Anselmo was extremely pleased with Lotario's words, and believed them exactly as though they had been spoken by some oracle. But for all that, he begged him not to give up the enterprise, even if it were only out of curiosity and for entertainment, and even if he did not from then on employ such urgent efforts as he had until then. And he said he only wanted him to write some verses in her praise under the name of Chloris, because he would give Camila to understand that he was in love with a lady to whom he had given that name so as to be able to celebrate her with the propriety her modesty deserved; and that if Lotario did not want to take the trouble of writing the verses, he would write them himself.

"That will not be necessary," said Lotario, "since the Muses are not such enemies of mine that they do not visit me for some hours in the year. Tell Camila what you have said about my pretended love affair; the verses I shall make, and if they are not as good as the subject deserves, they will at least be the best I can do."

On this the impertinent man and the treacherous friend agreed. And Anselmo, going back to his house, asked Camila the thing she was already surprised he had not asked her: which was to tell him the reason why she had written him the note she sent. Camila answered that it had seemed to her that Lotario looked at her a little more freely than when he was at home; but that she had been undeceived now and believed it had been her own imagination, because by now Lotario avoided seeing her and being alone with her.

Anselmo told her she could be perfectly easy about that suspicion, because he knew that Lotario was in love with a distinguished young lady of the city, whom he celebrated under the name of Chloris; and that even if he were not, there was nothing to fear from Lotario's honesty and from the great friendship between the two of them. And if Camila had not been warned by Lotario that that love affair with Chloris was a pretence, and that he had told Anselmo so in order to spend a few hours on Camila's own praises, she would without any doubt have fallen into the despairing net of jealousy; but being forewarned, she got through that alarm without distress.

The next day, the three of them being at table, Anselmo begged Lotario to say something of what he had composed to his beloved Chloris; since Camila did not know her, he could safely say whatever he liked.

"Even if she did know her," answered Lotario, "I would hide nothing; because when a lover praises his lady for being beautiful and reproaches her for being cruel, he does no discredit to her good name. But be that as it may, what I can say is that yesterday I made a sonnet on this Chloris's ingratitude, which goes like this:

	In the silence of the night, when
	sweet sleep takes possession of mortals,
	I am giving to heaven and to my Chloris
	the poor account of my rich sufferings.
	And at the time when the sun begins to show
	through the rosy gates of the east,
	with sighs and broken-off words
	I go over the old complaint again.
	And when the sun, from its starred seat,
	sends its rays straight down to the earth,
	the weeping grows and I double my groans.
	Night comes back, and I go back to the sad tale,
	and always I find, in this mortal struggle of mine,
	heaven deaf, and Chloris without ears."

Camila thought well of the sonnet, but Anselmo better, since he praised it and said that the lady who did not answer such plain truths was excessively cruel. To which Camila said:

"So everything that lovesick poets say is true?"

"As poets, they do not speak the truth," answered Lotario; "but as lovers, they always fall as short as they are truthful."

"There is no doubt of that," replied Anselmo — all of it to back up and give credit to Lotario's ideas with Camila, who was as unaware of Anselmo's contrivance as she was by now in love with Lotario.

And so, with the pleasure she took in anything of his, and the more so since she understood that his desires and his writings were aimed at her, and that she was the real Chloris, she begged him that if he knew another sonnet or other verses, he should say them.

"I do know one," answered Lotario, "but I do not think it is as good as the first — or, to put it better, less bad. And you can judge for yourselves, for here it is:

	I know that I am dying; and if I am not believed,
	dying is the more certain, as it is more certain
	that I shall be seen dead at your feet, beautiful ingrate,
	sooner than repenting of adoring you.
	I may find myself in the country of oblivion,
	stripped of life and glory and favour,
	and there it will be possible to see, in my opened breast,
	how your lovely face is carved there.
	For I keep this relic for the hard
	passage my own persistence threatens me with,
	which draws its strength from your very severity.
	Pity the man who sails, with the sky dark,
	over an unknown sea and a dangerous course,
	where neither pole star nor harbour offers itself."

Anselmo praised this second sonnet too, as he had done the first; and in this way he went on adding link after link to the chain with which his dishonour was being fastened and bound. For the more Lotario dishonoured him, the more he told him he was being honoured; and with this, every step Camila went down towards the centre of her disgrace, she went up, in her husband's opinion, towards the summit of virtue and of her good name.

It happened at this time that Camila, finding herself once — among other times — alone with her maid, said to her:

"I am mortified, Leonela my friend, to see how little I have known how to value myself, since I did not even make Lotario buy with time the complete possession of my will that I gave him so quickly. I am afraid he will think of my quickness, or my lightness, without noticing the force he used on me so that I could not resist him."

"Do not let that trouble you, my lady," answered Leonela, "for it is no argument, and no reason for the value to go down, that a thing should be given quickly — if what is given is good and worth valuing in itself. And it is even a common saying that whoever gives at once gives twice."

"They also say," said Camila, "that what costs little is valued at less."

"That argument does not apply to you," answered Leonela; "because love, as I have heard tell, sometimes flies and sometimes walks, runs with this man and goes slowly with that one, cools some and burns up others, wounds some and kills others; at one and the same moment it begins the race of its desires and at that same moment it finishes and concludes it; in the morning it will lay siege to a fortress and by night it has it surrendered, because there is no strength that resists it.

"And this being so, what are you frightened at, or what are you afraid of, if the same thing must have happened to Lotario, since love took my master's absence as the instrument for conquering us? And it necessarily followed that within that absence what love had determined should be brought to a conclusion, without giving time to time for Anselmo to have any of it to come back in, and for the work to be left unfinished by his presence. Because love has no better minister for carrying out what it wants than opportunity: it makes use of opportunity in all its doings, and chiefly at the beginnings. I know all this very well, more from experience than from hearsay; and one day I shall tell you about it, my lady, for I too am flesh and young blood.

"What is more, my lady Camila, you did not give yourself up or surrender so quickly that you had not first seen in Lotario's eyes, in his sighs, in his words and in his promises and gifts, the whole of his soul, seeing in it and in his virtues how worthy Lotario was of being loved. So if this is so, do not let those scrupulous and squeamish thoughts assault your imagination, but be assured that Lotario values you as you value him, and live contented and satisfied that, since you have fallen into love's snare, the man who has you tight is a man of worth and value.

"And that he not only has the four S's that they say good lovers must have, but a whole ABC from beginning to end. If you do not believe me, listen and you will see how I say it to you by heart. He is, from what I see and as it seems to me, appreciative, blameless, chivalrous, devoted, enamoured, firm, gallant, honourable, illustrious, just, kind, loyal, manly, noble, open-hearted, princely, quick-witted, rich, and the S's they talk about; and then tactful, and veracious. The X does not fit him, because it is a harsh letter; the Y I have said already with the I; and the Z — zealous guardian of your honour."

Camila laughed at her maid's ABC, and thought her better practised in the affairs of love than she said; and Leonela admitted it, revealing to Camila that she was carrying on a love affair with a well-born young man of the same city. At which Camila was disturbed, fearing that this was the road along which her own honour might run into danger. She pressed her to say whether their conversations went further than being conversations. Leonela, with little shame and a great deal of freedom, answered her that they did; because it is a certain thing by now that the carelessness of mistresses takes away the shame of their maids, who, when they see their mistresses stumble, think nothing of limping themselves, or of its being known.

Camila could do nothing but beg Leonela to say nothing about her own doings to the man she said was her lover, and to conduct her affairs in secret, so that they should not come to the knowledge of Anselmo or of Lotario. Leonela answered that she would do so, but she kept her word in such a way that she made good Camila's fear that she would lose her reputation through her. Because the immodest and impudent Leonela, once she saw that her mistress's conduct was not what it used to be, made bold to bring her lover into the house and lodge him there, confident that even if her mistress saw him she would not dare to expose him. For this is one of the harms, among others, that the sins of mistresses bring: that they make themselves slaves of their own maids and are obliged to cover up their immodesties and vile behaviour, as happened with Camila. For although she saw once and many times that her Leonela was with her gallant in a room of her house, not only did she not dare scold her, but she gave her the chance to shut him in there, and took away all the obstacles so that he should not be seen by her husband.

But she could not take them away enough to keep Lotario from seeing him come out once, at the break of dawn; who, not knowing who it was, thought at first that it must be some phantom. But when he saw him walk off, muffle himself up and cover himself with care and caution, he came down from his simple idea and fell into another, which would have been the ruin of everybody if Camila had not put it right.

Lotario thought that this man he had seen come out of Anselmo's house at such an hour had not gone into it on Leonela's account; he did not even remember that Leonela existed in the world. He only believed that Camila, in the same way as she had been easy and light with him, was so for somebody else. For these are the additions that a bad woman's wickedness brings with it: that she loses the credit of her honour with the very man she gave herself up to after being begged and persuaded, and he believes she gives herself up to others still more easily, and gives infallible credit to any suspicion that comes to him about it.

And it looks as though at this point Lotario's whole good understanding failed him, and every one of his prudent arguments went out of his memory; since without making a single one that was good, or even reasonable, without any more ado, before Anselmo got up, impatient and blinded by the jealous rage that was gnawing at his entrails, and dying to take revenge on Camila, who had offended him in nothing at all, he went to Anselmo and said to him:

"Know, Anselmo, that for many days I have been fighting with myself, forcing myself not to tell you what it is no longer possible or right for me to hide from you any longer. Know that Camila's fortress is now surrendered and subject to anything I may want to do with it.

"And if I have been slow to reveal this truth to you, it has been to see whether it was some light fancy of hers, or whether she was doing it to test me and see whether the love-making I began with her, with your leave, was carried on with a settled purpose. I likewise believed that if she had been what she ought to be, and what we both took her for, she would already have given you an account of my soliciting her; but having seen that she is slow about it, I recognise that the promises she has given me are true — that when you next go away from your house she will talk with me in the storeroom where your valuables are kept." And it was true that Camila used to talk with him there. "And I do not want you to run headlong to take some revenge, since the sin has not yet been committed except in thought, and it might be that between now and the time for putting it into practice Camila's thought would change and repentance be born in its place.

"And so, since you have always followed my advice in whole or in part, follow and keep one piece of advice I shall give you now, so that without any deception and with cautious forethought you may satisfy yourself of whatever you see best suits you. Pretend to go away for two or three days, as you do at other times, and arrange to stay hidden in your storeroom — since the tapestries that are there and other things you can hide behind offer you a great deal of convenience. And then you will see with your own eyes, and I with mine, what Camila wants; and if it is the wickedness that is more to be feared than hoped for, then with silence, shrewdness and discretion you may be the executioner of your own injury."

Anselmo was left absorbed, taken aback and astonished by Lotario's words, because they caught him at a time when he least expected to hear them; for he already took Camila to be the conqueror of Lotario's pretended assaults, and was beginning to enjoy the glory of the victory. He stayed silent for a good while, looking at the ground without moving an eyelash, and at last he said:

"You have done it, Lotario, as I expected of your friendship. In everything I shall follow your advice: do as you like and keep that secrecy you see is proper in a case as unexpected as this."

Lotario promised it him; and on leaving him, he repented entirely of everything he had told him, seeing how foolishly he had behaved, since he could have taken revenge on Camila, and not by so cruel and so dishonourable a road. He cursed his own understanding, called his hasty decision ugly, and did not know what course to take to undo what was done, or to find some reasonable way out of it. In the end he decided to give Camila a full account of it all; and as there was no lack of opportunity for doing so, he found her alone that same day, and she, as soon as she saw she could speak to him, said:

"Know, friend Lotario, that I have a grief in my heart which presses on it in such a way that it seems it wants to burst in my breast — and it will be a wonder if it does not. For Leonela's shamelessness has come to such a pitch that every night she shuts a gallant of hers into this house and stays with him until daylight, so much at the cost of my reputation that whoever sees him come out of my house at such extraordinary hours will be left an open field for judging it. And what wearies me is that I cannot punish her or scold her: her being the secretary of our own dealings has put a bridle on my mouth to keep quiet about hers, and I am afraid that some bad business will come of it."

When Camila first said this, Lotario believed it was a device to mislead him into thinking that the man he had seen come out was Leonela's and not hers; but seeing her weep and grieve, and beg him for a remedy, he came to believe the truth, and believing it, he was left completely confused and repentant. But for all that, he answered Camila that she should not distress herself, for he would arrange a remedy to put a stop to Leonela's insolence.

He also told her what, urged on by the furious rage of jealousy, he had said to Anselmo, and how it was arranged that he should hide in the storeroom to see plainly from there how little loyalty she kept for him. He begged her pardon for this madness, and asked her advice about how to remedy it and get well out of so tangled a labyrinth as his bad reasoning had put him into.

Camila was appalled to hear what Lotario told her, and with great anger and with many well-judged arguments she scolded him and called his wicked thought and the foolish, wicked decision he had taken ugly. But since a woman naturally has a quicker wit than a man both for good and for evil — although it begins to fail her when she deliberately sets herself to reason things out — Camila at that very instant found the way to remedy a business that seemed so past remedy. And she told Lotario to arrange that Anselmo should hide the next day where he had said, because she meant to make his hiding into a convenience by which from then on the two of them could enjoy each other without any alarm. And without declaring her whole plan to him, she warned him to be careful that once Anselmo was hidden he should come when Leonela called him, and that to everything she said to him he should answer as he would have answered if he had not known that Anselmo was listening. Lotario insisted that she should finish declaring her intention to him, so that he could keep to everything he saw was necessary with more safety and forethought.

"I say," said Camila, "that there is nothing more to keep to, except to answer me as I shall ask you." Camila did not want to give him a prior account of what she meant to do, being afraid that he would not want to follow the plan that seemed so good to her, and would follow or look for others that could not be as good.

With this Lotario went off; and Anselmo, the next day, with the excuse of going to that village of his friend's, left and came back to hide himself — which he was able to do conveniently, because Camila and Leonela deliberately gave him the opportunity.

Anselmo being hidden, then, with the sort of alarm one may imagine in a man who was expecting to see with his own eyes an anatomy made of the entrails of his honour, he was on the point of losing the highest good he thought he possessed in his beloved Camila. Camila and Leonela, being by now safe and certain that Anselmo was hidden, came into the storeroom; and Camila had hardly set foot in it when, giving a great sigh, she said:

"Ah, Leonela my friend! Would it not be better, before I come to carry out the thing I do not want you to know about — so that you may not try to prevent it — that you should take Anselmo's dagger, which I have asked you for, and run it through this shameful breast of mine? But do not do such a thing, for it will not be right that I should bear the penalty of another's fault. First I want to know what it was that Lotario's bold and immodest eyes saw in me that was the cause of giving him the boldness to reveal to me a desire as wicked as the one he has revealed, in contempt of his friend and to my dishonour. Go to that window, Leonela, and call him, for beyond any doubt he must be in the street waiting to put his wicked intention into effect. But my own intention shall be put into effect first, cruel as it is honourable."

"Ah, my lady!" answered the shrewd and forewarned Leonela. "What is it you want to do with this dagger? Do you by any chance want to take your own life, or to take Lotario's? For either of these things you may want must work out to the loss of your reputation and good name. It is better for you to hide the injury done you, and not to let this wicked man come into this house now and find us alone. Look, my lady, we are weak women and he is a man, and a determined one; and coming as he does with that wicked purpose, blind and full of passion, perhaps before you carry out yours he will do the thing that would be worse for you than taking your life. A curse on my lord Anselmo, for having given this shameless creature so much run of his house! And supposing, my lady, that you kill him, as I think you mean to do — what are we to do with him afterwards, once he is dead?"

"What, my friend?" answered Camila. "We shall leave him for Anselmo to bury; for it will be only right that he should count as a rest the labour he takes in putting his own infamy underground. Call him, and be quick; for all the time I delay in taking due vengeance for my injury, it seems to me that I am offending against the loyalty I owe my husband."

Anselmo was listening to all this, and at every word Camila said his thoughts changed. But when he understood that she was resolved to kill Lotario, he wanted to come out and reveal himself so that such a thing should not be done; but he was held back by the desire to see what all this gallantry and honourable resolution would come to, meaning to come out in time to prevent it.

At this Camila was taken by a violent faint, and throwing herself down on a bed that was there, Leonela began to weep very bitterly and to say:

"Ah, unlucky woman that I am, if I were unfortunate enough to have dying here in my arms the flower of the world's modesty, the crown of good women, the example of chastity —!"

And other things like these, so that nobody who heard her would not have taken her for the most grief-stricken and loyal maid in the world, and her mistress for another new and persecuted Penelope. Camila was not long in coming out of her faint; and on coming to herself, she said:

"Why do you not go, Leonela, and call the most loyal friend to a friend that ever the sun looked on or the night covered? Be quick, run, hurry, go — do not let the fire of the anger I have blow itself out with delay, and the just vengeance I am waiting for turn into threats and curses."

"I am going to call him now, my lady," said Leonela; "but you must first give me that dagger, so that while I am away you shall not do something with it that will leave everybody who loves you with cause to weep all their lives."

"Go without any fear, Leonela my friend, for I shall not," answered Camila. "Because although I may be bold and simple in your opinion in standing up for my honour, I shall not be as much so as that Lucretia they say killed herself without having committed any fault at all, and without first having killed the man who was the cause of her misfortune. I shall die, if I die, but it must be avenged and satisfied on the man who has given me cause to come to this pass and weep over his boldness, which was born so blamelessly on my side."

Leonela had to be begged a great deal before she would go out and call Lotario; but at last she went. And while she was away, Camila was left saying, as though she were talking to herself:

"God help me! Would it not have been more sensible to have sent Lotario away, as I have done many other times, instead of putting him in the position I have now put him in, of taking me for immodest and wicked, at least for the time I shall take to undeceive him? It would certainly have been better; but then I would not be avenged, nor my husband's honour satisfied, if he could get out again with clean hands and at an easy walk from where his wicked thoughts got him in.

"Let the traitor pay with his life for what he attempted with so lustful a desire. Let the world know, if it ever comes to know it, that Camila not only kept her loyalty to her husband but gave him vengeance on the man who dared to offend him.

"But for all that, I believe it would have been better to give an account of this to Anselmo. Yet I did point it out to him in the letter I wrote him at the village; and I believe that his not coming to remedy the harm I indicated to him there must have been because, out of pure goodness and trustfulness, he neither would nor could believe that in the breast of so firm a friend of his there could be room for any kind of thought against his honour. Nor did I believe it myself afterwards, for many days, nor would I ever have believed it if his insolence had not gone so far that the open gifts and the lavish promises and the constant tears made it plain to me.

"But why am I making these speeches now? Does a gallant resolution have any need of advice, by any chance? Certainly not. Away, then, with traitors — here, vengeance! Let the false man come in; let him come, let him arrive, let him die and be finished, and let what happens happen. I came clean into the power of the man heaven gave me for my own; clean I mean to come out of it — and at the most I shall come out bathed in my own chaste blood, and in the impure blood of the falsest friend that friendship ever saw in the world."

And saying this, she walked about the room with the dagger drawn, taking such wild and extravagant steps and making such gestures that she looked for all the world as if she had lost her wits, and were no delicate woman but some bravo in despair.

Anselmo was watching all of it, covered by some tapestries where he had hidden himself, and was astonished at all of it; and it already seemed to him that what he had seen and heard was satisfaction enough for greater suspicions than his, and by now he could have wished the test of Lotario's coming might not happen, being afraid of some sudden bad turn. And when he was just about to reveal himself and come out, to embrace his wife and undeceive her, he stopped, because he saw that Leonela was coming back leading Lotario by the hand.

And as soon as Camila saw him, she drew a great line on the floor in front of her with the dagger and said:

"Lotario, take note of what I say to you: if by any chance you dare to cross this line you see, or even to come up to it, at the moment I see you attempting it I shall run this dagger I have in my hands through my own breast. And before you answer me a word to this, I want you to listen to some others of mine; afterwards you shall answer whatever pleases you best.

"First, Lotario, I want you to tell me whether you know Anselmo my husband, and in what opinion you hold him; and secondly, I want to know as well whether you know me. Answer me this, and do not be alarmed, and do not think much about what you have to answer, for they are no difficult questions I am asking you."

Lotario was not so slow-witted that from the first moment Camila told him to have Anselmo hidden he had not realised what she meant to do; and so he fell in with her intention so cleverly and so promptly that between the two of them they would have made that lie pass for more than certain truth. And so he answered Camila in this way:

"I did not think, beautiful Camila, that you were calling me to ask me things so far outside the purpose I have come here with. If you are doing it to put off the favour you promised me, you could have kept it at a distance from further off; because the good we desire torments us more the nearer hope is to possessing it. But so that you may not say I do not answer your questions, I say that I know your husband Anselmo, and that the two of us have known each other since our earliest years; and I do not want to speak of what you know so well about our friendship, so as not to make myself a witness of the wrong love is making me do him — a powerful excuse for greater errors than this. You I know, and hold in the same possession that he holds you in; for if it were not so, for lesser charms than yours I would not have gone against what I owe to being who I am and against the sacred laws of true friendship, now broken and violated by me for so powerful an enemy as love."

"If you confess that," answered Camila, "mortal enemy of everything that justly deserves to be loved, with what face do you dare appear before one who you know is the mirror in which the man you ought to be looking at looks at himself — so that you might see with how little cause you injure him? But now, ah, unhappy woman that I am, I realise who it is that has made you take so little care of what you owe to yourself: it must have been some freedom of mine, which I will not call immodesty, since it will not have come from any deliberate decision but from one of those pieces of carelessness that women who think they have nobody to be on their guard against are apt to commit without noticing.

"If not, tell me: when, you traitor, did I answer your entreaties with any word or sign that could wake in you the shadow of a hope of fulfilling your shameful desires? When were your loving words not undone and rebuked by mine with severity and harshness? When were your many promises and your greater gifts believed by me, or accepted?

"But since it seems to me that nobody can persevere a long time in a purpose of love unless he is kept up by some hope, I choose to lay on myself the blame for your impertinence — since without a doubt some carelessness of mine has kept your attentions going so long. And so I mean to punish myself and give myself the penalty your fault deserves.

"And so that you might see that, being so inhuman to myself, it was not possible that I should be otherwise to you, I chose to bring you here to be a witness of the sacrifice I mean to make to the offended honour of my so honourable husband — wronged by you with the greatest care you were capable of, and by me as well, with the little caution I have kept about avoiding the occasion, if I gave you any, to favour and canonise your wicked intentions.

"I say again that the suspicion I have that some carelessness of mine bred such deranged thoughts in you is what wearies me most, and what I most want to punish with my own hands; because if another executioner punished me, perhaps my fault would be more public. But before I do this, I mean to kill as I die, and to take with me the man who will finally satisfy the desire for vengeance I hope for and have — seeing there, wherever I may go, the penalty imposed by that justice which is disinterested and does not bend for the man who has put me in such desperate straits."

And saying these words, with an incredible force and quickness she rushed at Lotario with the drawn dagger, with such signs of wanting to drive it into his breast that he was almost in doubt whether those demonstrations were false or true; for he was obliged to use both his ingenuity and his strength to prevent Camila from striking him. And she acted that strange deceit and villainy so vividly that, to give it the colour of truth, she chose to tint it with her own blood. For seeing that she could not get at Lotario — or pretending that she could not — she said:

"Since fortune will not satisfy my so just desire completely, at least it will not be powerful enough to keep me from satisfying it in part."

And forcing her dagger hand free, which Lotario had hold of, she pulled it out; and guiding its point to a place where it could not wound deeply, she drove it in and buried it above the hollow of her left side, close to the shoulder, and then let herself fall to the ground as though in a faint.

Leonela and Lotario were left taken aback and astonished at such an event, and still doubted the truth of the thing, seeing Camila stretched on the ground and bathed in her own blood. Lotario ran very quickly, terrified and out of breath, to pull out the dagger; and on seeing how small the wound was, he came out of the fear he had been in until then, and marvelled all over again at the shrewdness, prudence and great cleverness of the beautiful Camila. And to play his own part, he began to make a long, sad lamentation over Camila's body, as though she were dead, calling down a great many curses not only on himself but on the man who had been the cause of putting him in that position. And as he knew his friend Anselmo was listening to him, he said things that would have made anybody who heard him feel far more pity for him than for Camila, even judging her to be dead.

Leonela took her in her arms and put her on the bed, begging Lotario to go and look for somebody who would treat Camila secretly. She also asked his advice and opinion about what they should tell Anselmo about her mistress's wound if he happened to come before she was better. He answered that they should say whatever they liked, since he was in no state to give advice that would be of any use. He only told her to try to stop the bleeding, because he was going off where people would not see him. And with every sign of great grief and feeling, he left the house.

And when he found himself alone and in a place where nobody could see him, he never stopped crossing himself, marvelling at Camila's ingenuity and at Leonela's so entirely convincing gestures.
