He thought how thoroughly convinced Anselmo would now be that he had a second Portia for a wife, and he wanted to be with him so that the two of them could celebrate the most artfully hidden lie and truth that could ever have been imagined.

Leonela stopped her mistress's blood, as has been said, which was no more than was enough to give credit to their deceit; and washing the wound with a little wine, she bound it up as best she knew how, saying such things while she was dressing it that even if there had been nothing else before them, they would have been enough to make Anselmo believe he had in Camila an image of modesty itself.

To Leonela's words were joined others of Camila's, calling herself a coward and a poor-spirited creature, since courage had failed her at the moment when it was most needed for taking the life she so much loathed. She asked her maid's advice on whether or not she should tell her beloved husband about the whole affair; and Leonela told her not to tell him, because it would put him under an obligation to take revenge on Lotario, which could not happen without a great deal of risk to himself; and that a good wife was bound not to give her husband any occasion to quarrel, but to take away from him all those she possibly could.

Camila answered that his advice seemed very good to her and that she would follow it, but that in any case they would have to find something to tell Anselmo about the cause of that wound, which he could not fail to see. To which Leonela answered that she did not know how to tell a lie, even in fun.

"And what am I to know, my dear," replied Camila, "when I would not dare to forge or keep up a lie if my life depended on it? And if we cannot manage to find a way out of this, it will be better to tell him the naked truth than to have him catch us out in a lying account."

"Do not distress yourself, my lady," answered Leonela. "Between now and tomorrow I shall think what we are to tell him; and perhaps, the wound being where it is, you will be able to hide it without his seeing it, and heaven will be pleased to favour our so just and so honourable intentions. Calm yourself, my lady, and try to calm your agitation, so that my master shall not find you in a fright; and leave the rest to me and to God, who always comes to the help of good intentions."

Anselmo had been listening most attentively, and watching them act out the tragedy of the death of his honour — which the characters in it acted with such strange and effective feeling that it seemed they had been transformed into the very truth of what they were pretending. He was longing for night, and for the chance to get out of his house and go to see his good friend Lotario, so as to congratulate himself with him on the precious pearl he had found in the undeceiving proof of his wife's goodness. The two women took care to give him room and opportunity to get out, and he, not losing it, went out and then went to look for Lotario.

And when he had found him, it is not easy to tell the embraces he gave him, the things he said to him about his own happiness, the praises he gave Camila. All of which Lotario listened to without being able to show any sign of gladness, because it came into his memory how deceived his friend was and how unjustly he was wronging him. And although Anselmo could see that Lotario was not glad, he believed the cause was his having left Camila wounded and having been the cause of it himself; and so, among other things, he told him not to distress himself about what had happened to Camila, because without doubt the wound was slight, since the two of them had agreed to hide it from him. And that, this being so, there was nothing to fear, but that from then on he should take pleasure and be glad with him, since by Lotario's ingenuity and by his means he found himself raised to the highest happiness that could be wished for; and that he wanted their only entertainment to be making verses in praise of Camila, to make her eternal in the memory of the ages to come. Lotario praised his good resolution and said that for his part he would help to raise so illustrious a building.

With this Anselmo was left the most deliciously deceived man there could be in the world. He himself led home by the hand, believing he was leading the instrument of his glory, the whole ruin of his good name. Camila received him with a face that seemed put out, though with a soul that was laughing. This deception lasted some days, until, at the end of a few months, Fortune turned her wheel and the wickedness that had been covered up until then with so much artifice came out into the open, and Anselmo's reckless curiosity cost him his life.

Chapter 35: In Which Is Brought to an End the Tale of Reckless Curiosity, and Which Treats of the Fierce and Monstrous Battle Don Quixote Had with Some Skins of Red Wine

There was not much left of the tale to read when out of the garret where Don Quixote was resting came Sancho Panza in a great commotion, shouting:

"Come, gentlemen, quickly, and help my master, who is in the middle of the hardest-fought and closest battle my eyes have ever seen! By the living God, he has dealt such a slash at the giant, the lady Princess Micomicona's enemy, that he has cut his head clean off, as though it had been a turnip!"

"What are you saying, brother?" said the curate, leaving off reading what was left of the tale. "Are you in your senses, Sancho? How the devil can what you say be so, when the giant is two thousand leagues from here?"

At this they heard a great noise in the room, and Don Quixote shouting:

"Hold, thief, villain, scoundrel! I have you here, and your scimitar shall not save you!"

And it seemed he was dealing great slashes at the walls. And Sancho said:

"There's no call to stop and listen: go in and separate the fight, or help my master — though there won't be any need now, because beyond a doubt the giant is dead by this time and giving God an account of his past and wicked life. I saw the blood running along the floor, and the head cut off and fallen to one side, and it's as big as a great wineskin."

"Strike me dead," said the innkeeper at this, "if Don Quixote — or Don Devil — hasn't dealt a slash at one of the skins of red wine that were standing full at the head of his bed, and the spilt wine must be what looks like blood to this good fellow."

And with this he went into the room, and everybody after him, and they found Don Quixote in the strangest costume in the world. He was in his shirt, which was not long enough to finish covering his thighs in front, and behind it was six fingers shorter. His legs were very long and thin, covered with hair and not in the least clean. On his head he had a little red cap, greasy, which belonged to the innkeeper. Round his left arm he had wound the bed-blanket, which Sancho had a grudge against — and he knew very well why. And in his right hand he had his drawn sword, with which he was dealing slashes in every direction, saying things as though he were genuinely fighting some giant.

And the best of it is that he did not have his eyes open, because he was asleep and dreaming that he was in battle with the giant; for so intense was his imagination of the adventure he was going to bring to an end that it made him dream he had already arrived in the kingdom of Micomicón and was already in the fight with his enemy. And he had dealt so many slashes at the wineskins, believing he was dealing them at the giant, that the whole room was full of wine.

Which the innkeeper seeing, he took such offence that he flew at Don Quixote and with his closed fist began to give him so many blows that if Cardenio and the curate had not pulled him off him, he would have finished the war of the giant himself. And in spite of all that, the poor knight did not wake up, until the barber brought a great cauldron of cold water from the well and threw it all over his body at one go, with which Don Quixote woke — but not with enough awareness to notice the state he was in.

Dorotea, who saw how short and thin his clothing was, would not come in to watch the battle of her champion and her enemy.

Sancho was going about looking for the giant's head all over the floor; and as he could not find it, he said:

"I know already that everything in this house is enchantment; because the other time, in this same place where I am standing now, they gave me a great many cuffs and blows without my knowing who was giving them me, and I could never see anybody. And now this head doesn't turn up that I saw cut off with my very own eyes, and the blood was running out of the body like out of a fountain."

"What blood and what fountain are you talking about, enemy of God and of his saints?" said the innkeeper. "Don't you see, you thief, that the blood and the fountain are nothing but these wineskins here that have been punctured and the red wine that's swimming about this room? — and may I see the soul of whoever punctured them swimming in hell!"

"I know nothing about it," answered Sancho. "All I know is that I'm going to be so unlucky that, for not finding this head, my earldom will melt away like salt in water."

And Sancho awake was in a worse state than his master asleep, so much had his master's promises done for him. The innkeeper was in despair at the squire's stolidity and the master's mischief, and swore it should not be like the last time, when they got away without paying; and that this time the privileges of his chivalry should not be any good to him for getting out of paying for the one thing and the other — down to the cost of the patches that would have to be put on the burst skins.

The curate had hold of Don Quixote's hands; and he, believing that the adventure was over now and that he was in the presence of the Princess Micomicona, knelt down in front of the curate, saying:

"Your greatness, high and famous lady, may well live from today on secure against any harm this base-born creature can do you; and I too, from today on, am released from the word I gave you, since with the help of God on high and with the favour of her for whom I live and breathe, I have kept it so well."

"Didn't I say so?" said Sancho, hearing this. "So I wasn't drunk after all! Just look whether my master hasn't got the giant salted down already! The bulls are as good as in the ring — my earldom is cast and moulded!"

Who could have kept from laughing at the absurdities of the two of them, master and man? Everybody laughed except the innkeeper, who was giving himself to Satan. But at last the barber, Cardenio and the curate did so much that with no small trouble they got Don Quixote into bed, and he fell asleep with every sign of enormous exhaustion.

They let him sleep, and went out into the porch of the inn to comfort Sancho Panza for not having found the giant's head; although they had more to do in calming the innkeeper, who was in despair at the sudden death of his wineskins. And the innkeeper's wife was saying at the top of her voice:

"In an evil moment and at an unlucky hour this knight errant came into my house — I wish my eyes had never seen him, for he costs me dear enough. The last time he went off with the reckoning for one night, for supper, bed, straw and barley for himself and his squire and a hack and a donkey, saying he was a knight adventurer — and may God give bad adventures to him and to every adventurer in the world — and that for this reason he was not obliged to pay anything, because that was how it stood written in the tariffs of knight-errantry.

"And now, on his account, this other gentleman came and carried off my tail, and has given it me back with more than two farthings' worth of damage, all bare, so that it can't serve for what my husband wants it for. And to finish and crown it all, bursting my wineskins and spilling my wine — and may I see his blood spilt! Well, don't let him imagine anything: by my father's bones and by my mother's memory, if they don't pay me for it farthing by farthing, my name isn't what my name is and I'm not my own father's daughter!"

These and other such speeches the innkeeper's wife made in great anger, and her good servant Maritornes helped her. The daughter said nothing, and smiled from time to time. The curate settled it all, promising to make good their loss as best he could, both of the wineskins and of the wine, and above all of the damage to the tail, which they made so much account of.

Dorotea comforted Sancho Panza by telling him that whenever it should appear to have been true that his master had beheaded the giant, she promised him, as soon as she found herself peacefully settled in her kingdom, to give him the best earldom in it. Sancho was comforted at this, and assured the princess that she could take it for certain that he had seen the giant's head, and that for a further mark of it, it had a beard that came down to its waist; and that if it did not turn up, it was because everything that happened in that house went by way of enchantment, as he had proved another time when he had lodged in it. Dorotea said she believed it, and that he should not distress himself, for everything would come out well and would turn out exactly to order.

Everybody being settled, the curate wanted to finish reading the tale, because he saw that there was not much of it left. Cardenio, Dorotea and all the rest begged him to finish it. He, wanting to give everybody pleasure — and because of the pleasure he took in it himself — went on with the tale, which went like this:

It happened, then, that through the satisfaction Anselmo felt about Camila's goodness, he lived a contented and carefree life; and Camila deliberately put on a cold face for Lotario, so that Anselmo should take the opposite view of the affection she had for him. And to confirm the thing further, Lotario asked leave not to come to the house any more, since the annoyance Camila got from the sight of him was so plainly shown; but the deceived Anselmo told him on no account to do such a thing. And in this way, in a thousand ways, Anselmo was the manufacturer of his own dishonour, believing he was the manufacturer of his own happiness.

At this point Leonela's own pleasure at finding herself given a free hand in her love affair went so far that, without looking at anything else, she went after it at full gallop, trusting that her mistress would cover for her — and would even advise her how she could go about it with little risk. In the end, one night Anselmo heard footsteps in Leonela's room, and wanting to go in and see who was making them, he found that the door was being held against him — a thing that gave him more determination to open it. And he forced it so hard that he opened it and got inside just in time to see a man jumping out of the window into the street; and hurrying to catch him or recognise him, he could do neither the one nor the other, because Leonela threw her arms round him, saying:

"Calm yourself, my dear master, and do not make a disturbance or go after the man who jumped out of here. It is my own affair, and so much so that he is my husband."

Anselmo would not believe it; on the contrary, blind with anger, he pulled out his dagger and tried to stab Leonela, telling her to tell him the truth or he would kill her. She, in her fright, not knowing what she was saying, said to him:

"Do not kill me, sir, for I shall tell you things of more importance than you can imagine."

"Tell them at once," said Anselmo; "if not, you are a dead woman."

"For the moment it will be impossible," said Leonela, "the state of confusion I am in. Leave me until tomorrow, and then you shall learn from me what will astonish you; and be assured that the man who jumped out of this window is a young man of this city who has given me his hand to be my husband."

Anselmo was calmed at this and was willing to wait the time he was asked for, because he did not expect to hear anything that was against Camila, being so satisfied and so sure of her goodness. And so he went out of the room and left Leonela shut up in it, telling her that she would not come out of there until she had told him what she had to tell him.

He then went to see Camila and to tell her, as he did tell her, everything that had passed between him and her maid, and the promise she had given him to tell him great and important things. Whether Camila was disturbed or not there is no need to say; because such fear came over her, genuinely believing — and it was to be believed — that Leonela was bound to tell Anselmo everything she knew about her want of good faith, that she had not the courage to wait and see whether her suspicion turned out false or not.

And that same night, when it seemed to her that Anselmo was asleep, she gathered together the best jewels she had and some money, and without being noticed by anybody she left the house and went to Lotario's, and told him what was happening and begged him to put her somewhere safe, or that the two of them should go off together where they could be safe from Anselmo. The confusion Camila put Lotario into was such that he could not answer her a word, nor could he settle what to do.

In the end he decided to take Camila to a convent where a sister of his was prioress. Camila consented to it; and with the speed the case demanded, Lotario took her and left her at the convent, and he likewise went away from the city at once, without telling anybody about his going.

When day broke, without noticing that Camila was missing from his side, in his eagerness to know what Leonela wanted to tell him, Anselmo got up and went to where he had left her shut in. He opened the door and went into the room, but did not find Leonela in it: he only found some sheets knotted together and tied to the window, a sign and mark that she had let herself down that way and gone.

He came back at once, very sad, to tell Camila about it; and not finding her in bed or anywhere in the house, he was appalled. He asked the servants of the house about her, but nobody could give him an account of what he asked for.

It happened by chance, as he was going about looking for Camila, that he saw her chests open and most of her jewels missing from them; and with this he finally realised his misfortune, and that Leonela was not the cause of his ruin. And exactly as he was, without finishing dressing, sad and thoughtful, he went to give an account of his misery to his friend Lotario. But when he did not find him, and his servants told him that he had been missing from the house that night and had taken with him all the money he had, he thought he would go out of his mind. And to finish and conclude it all, going back to his own house, he found in it not one of all the menservants and maidservants he had, but the house deserted and empty.

He did not know what to think, what to say or what to do, and little by little his wits were leaving him. He looked at himself and saw himself in an instant without a wife, without a friend and without servants; abandoned, as it seemed to him, by the sky that covered him; and above all without honour, because in Camila's absence he saw his own ruin.

He resolved at last, after a long while, to go to the village of his friend where he had been when he gave the opportunity for the whole of that misfortune to be contrived. He shut the doors of his house, got on his horse, and with fainting spirits set off. And he had hardly gone halfway when, harried by his own thoughts, he was obliged to dismount and tie his horse to a tree, at whose trunk he let himself drop, giving tender, sorrowful sighs; and there he stayed until it was almost dark.

And at that hour he saw a man coming on horseback from the city, and after greeting him he asked him what news there was in Florence. The citizen answered:

"The strangest that has been heard in it for many a day; because it is publicly said that Lotario, that great friend of Anselmo the rich man who lived by St John's, carried off Camila, Anselmo's wife, last night — and Anselmo has disappeared too. All this has been told by a maid of Camila's, whom the governor found last night letting herself down by a sheet from the windows of Anselmo's house. In fact I do not know exactly how the business went; I only know that the whole city is astonished at it, because such a thing was not to be expected from the great and familiar friendship of the two of them, which they say was so great that people used to call them the two friends."

"Is it known, by any chance," said Anselmo, "which road Lotario and Camila have taken?"

"Not in the least," said the citizen, "although the governor has been very diligent in looking for them."

"God go with you, sir," said Anselmo.

"And stay with you," answered the citizen, and went off.

With such disastrous news, Anselmo came very nearly to the point not only of losing his wits but of ending his life. He got up as best he could and reached his friend's house, who did not yet know his misfortune. But when he saw him arrive yellow, wasted and dried up, he understood that he was suffering under some grave trouble. Anselmo at once asked to be put to bed and to be given writing materials. It was done so, and they left him lying down and alone, because he wanted it so, and even asked them to shut the door.

Finding himself alone, then, he began to load his imagination so heavily with his misfortune that he plainly recognised that his life was coming to an end; and so he arranged to leave a record of the cause of his strange death. And beginning to write, before he had finished setting down everything he wanted to say, his breath failed him and he left his life in the hands of the grief his reckless curiosity had caused him.

The master of the house, seeing that it was late and that Anselmo did not call, decided to go in and find out whether his indisposition was getting worse; and he found him stretched out face downwards, half his body on the bed and the other half on the writing table, on which lay the paper written and open, and he still had the pen in his hand. The host went up to him, having called him first; and taking him by the hand, seeing that he did not answer and finding him cold, he saw that he was dead.

He was astonished and greatly distressed, and called the household to see the misfortune that had happened to Anselmo; and finally he read the paper, which he recognised as being written in Anselmo's own hand, and which contained these words:

A foolish and reckless desire has taken away my life. If the news of my death should reach Camila's ears, let her know that I forgive her, because she was not obliged to work miracles, nor did I have any need to want her to work them; and since I was the manufacturer of my own dishonour, there is no reason why —

This far Anselmo wrote, by which it could be seen that at that point, without being able to finish the sentence, his life finished.

The next day his friend gave notice of his death to Anselmo's relatives, who already knew of his misfortune, and to the convent where Camila was — who was almost at the point of keeping her husband company on that unavoidable journey, not because of the news of her dead husband but because of what she learnt about the absent friend. It is said that although she found herself a widow, she would not leave the convent, nor take her vows as a nun either, until, not many days later, news came to her that Lotario had died in a battle which at that time Monsieur de Lautrec fought against the Great Captain Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba in the kingdom of Naples, where the too late repentant friend had gone. Which Camila learning, she took her vows, and within a few days ended her life at the harsh hands of sorrow and melancholy. This was the end they all came to, born of so senseless a beginning.

"This tale," said the curate, "seems good to me; but I cannot persuade myself that it is true. And if it is invented, the author invented it badly, because it cannot be imagined that there is a husband so foolish as to want to make so costly an experiment as Anselmo's. If this case had been put between a gallant and a lady, it might have passed; but between husband and wife it has something of the impossible about it. And as far as the way of telling it goes, that does not displease me."

Chapter 36: Which Treats of Other Rare Events That Happened at the Inn

While they were at this, the innkeeper, who was standing at the door of the inn, said:

"This lot coming is a fine troop of guests: if they stop here, we shall have a gaudeamus."

"What sort of people are they?" said Cardenio.

"Four men," answered the innkeeper, "come riding short-stirruped in the Moorish fashion, with lances and shields, and all of them with black masks on. And along with them comes a woman dressed in white, on a side-saddle, with her face covered too, and two more lads on foot."

"Are they very close?" asked the curate.

"So close," answered the innkeeper, "that they are here now."

Hearing this, Dorotea covered her face and Cardenio went into Don Quixote's room; and they had hardly had time for this when there came into the inn everybody the innkeeper had described. The four on horseback, who were of very fine build and bearing, dismounted and went to help down the woman who was riding on the side-saddle; and one of them, taking her in his arms, set her down in a chair that stood at the door of the room where Cardenio had hidden himself.

In all this time neither she nor they had taken off their masks or said a single word — only that, on sitting down in the chair, the woman gave a deep sigh and let her arms fall, like a person ill and fainting. The lads on foot took the horses to the stable.

Seeing this, the curate, eager to know who these people were who went about in such dress and such silence, went to where the lads were and asked one of them what he wanted to know; who answered him:

"By God, sir, I couldn't tell you who these people are. All I know is that they look very distinguished, especially the one who went and took that lady you've seen in his arms; and I say this because all the rest treat him with respect, and nothing is done except what he orders and commands."

"And the lady — who is she?" asked the curate.

"I couldn't tell you that either," answered the lad, "because in the whole of the journey I haven't seen her face. Sigh I have heard her many times, and give such groans that with every one of them she seems to want to give up her soul. And it's no wonder we know no more than we've said, because my companion and I have only been with them two days; for having met them on the road, they begged us and persuaded us to come with them as far as Andalusia, offering to pay us very well for it."

"And have you heard any of them named?" asked the curate.

"Certainly not," answered the lad, "because they all travel with such silence that it's a marvel; there's nothing to be heard among them but the sighs and sobs of the poor lady, which move us to pity. And without a doubt we're convinced that she's being taken by force wherever she's going; and, from what you can gather from her dress, she's a nun, or is going to be one, which is the likelier; and perhaps because the convent must not be coming to her of her own will, she goes along sad, as she seems to be."

"It might all be so," said the curate.

And leaving them, he went back to where Dorotea was, who, having heard the muffled woman sigh, and moved by natural compassion, went up to her and said:

"What are you suffering from, my lady? See whether it is one of the things women generally have practice and experience in curing; for on my side I offer you a good will to serve you."

To all this the grief-stricken lady said nothing; and although Dorotea came back with greater offers, she still kept her silence, until the masked gentleman came up — the one the lad said the others obeyed — and said to Dorotea:

"Do not weary yourself, madam, in offering anything to that woman, because it is her custom not to be grateful for anything that is done for her; and do not try to get her to answer you, unless you want to hear some lie from her mouth."

"I have never told one," said the woman who until then had been silent. "On the contrary, it is because I am so truthful and so incapable of lying devices that I find myself now in such misfortune. And of this I want you yourself to be the witness, since my pure truth is what makes you false and a liar."

Cardenio heard these words very plainly and distinctly, being so close to the one who was saying them that only the door of Don Quixote's room stood between them; and as soon as he heard them, giving a great cry, he said:

"God help me! What is this I am hearing? What voice is this that has reached my ears?"

That lady turned her head at these shouts, thoroughly startled; and not seeing who was giving them, she stood up and went to go into the room. Which the gentleman seeing, he held her back without letting her move a step. In her agitation and distress the taffeta with which she had her face covered fell off, and revealed an incomparable beauty and a miraculous face — although colourless and terrified, because she was going about with her eyes searching every place her sight could reach, so eagerly that she looked like a person out of her senses; and these signs, without anybody's knowing why she made them, put great pity into Dorotea and into everybody who was looking at her.

The gentleman held her strongly by the shoulders; and being so busy holding her, he could not put a hand to lift the mask that was slipping down, as in fact it slipped off altogether. And raising her eyes, Dorotea, who was holding the lady in her arms, saw that the man who was also holding her was her own husband, Don Fernando; and she had hardly recognised him when, hurling out from the depths of her being a long and most sorrowful "Ah!" she let herself fall backwards in a faint; and if the barber had not been standing right there, who caught her in his arms, she would have come down on the ground.

The curate ran at once to take her mask off so as to throw water on her face; and as soon as he uncovered her, Don Fernando recognised her — for he was the one who was holding the other woman — and he was left as though dead at the sight of her. But not that he let go for all that of Luscinda, who was the one trying to get free of his arms; and she had recognised Cardenio by his cry, and he had recognised her. Cardenio likewise heard the "Ah!" that Dorotea gave when she fell fainting; and believing it was his Luscinda, he came out of the room in terror, and the first thing he saw was Don Fernando, holding Luscinda in his arms. Don Fernando also recognised Cardenio at once; and all three of them, Luscinda, Cardenio and Dorotea, were left dumb and taken aback, hardly knowing what had happened to them.

They were all silent and they all looked at each other: Dorotea at Don Fernando, Don Fernando at Cardenio, Cardenio at Luscinda and Luscinda at Cardenio. But the first to break the silence was Luscinda, speaking to Don Fernando in this way:

"Let me go, Señor Don Fernando, by what you owe to being who you are, since you will not do it for any other consideration. Let me get to the wall I am the ivy of, to the support they have not been able to part me from — not your importunities, or your threats, or your promises, or your gifts. Notice how heaven, by unusual roads and roads hidden from us, has put my true husband in front of me. And you know well, by a thousand costly experiences, that death alone would have been enough to rub him out of my memory. Let such plain undeceiving, then, be enough to make you turn — since you can do nothing else — your love into rage, your affection into resentment, and end my life with it; for if I give it up in front of my good husband I shall count it well spent. Perhaps by my death he will be satisfied of the faith I kept for him until the last extremity of my life."

Dorotea had meanwhile come to herself, and had been listening to all the words Luscinda said, by which she came to know who she was; and seeing that Don Fernando still did not let her out of his arms and did not answer her words, she forced herself as much as she could, got up and went and knelt at his feet; and shedding a great quantity of lovely and pitiable tears, she began to say to him:

"Unless it is, my lord, that the rays of this sun you hold eclipsed in your arms take away and dazzle those of your eyes, you will have seen by now that the woman kneeling at your feet is the luckless — until you choose otherwise — and unfortunate Dorotea.

"I am that humble country girl whom you, out of your goodness or your pleasure, chose to raise to the height of being able to call herself yours. I am the one who, shut inside the limits of modesty, lived a contented life until, at the sound of your importunities and your apparently just and loving protestations, she opened the doors of her reserve and handed you the keys of her liberty — a gift so ill repaid by you, as it plainly shows that I have been obliged to find myself in the place where you find me, and to see you in the state in which I see you.

"But for all this, I would not have it fall into your imagination to think that I have come here by the roads of my own dishonour, when I have been brought here only by those of the pain and grief of finding myself forgotten by you. You wanted me to be yours, and you wanted it in such a way that, although you may now want me not to be, it will not be possible for you to stop being mine.

"Consider, my lord, that the incomparable love I bear you may be some recompense for the beauty and nobility for which you are leaving me. You cannot belong to the beautiful Luscinda, because you are mine; nor can she be yours, because she is Cardenio's. And it will be easier for you, if you look at it, to bring your affections round to loving one who adores you than to bring one who loathes you round to loving you well.

"You solicited my carelessness; you begged my integrity; you were not ignorant of my rank; you know very well how I gave myself up to your whole will. You are left no room or refuge to call yourself deceived. And if this is so, as it is, and you are as much a Christian as you are a gentleman, why do you delay by so many roundabout ways to make me happy at the end, as you made me happy at the beginning?

"And if you will not have me for what I am, which is your true and lawful wife, have me at least and take me as your slave; for as long as I am in your power I shall count myself fortunate and well off. Do not allow, by leaving and abandoning me, that people should gather in knots over my dishonour; do not give my parents so bad an old age, since the loyal services they have always done yours as good vassals do not deserve it.

"And if it seems to you that you will be ruining your blood by mixing it with mine, consider that there is little or no nobility in the world that has not gone along that road, and that the blood taken from women is not what counts in illustrious descents; the more so as true nobility consists in virtue, and if that is lacking in you by denying me what you so justly owe me, then I shall be left with a better claim to nobility than the one you have.

"In the end, my lord, the last thing I say to you is that whether you will or not, I am your wife. Witnesses are your own words, which neither are nor ought to be lies, if it is the case that you pride yourself on the very thing you despise me for. A witness will be the signature you made, and a witness heaven, which you yourself called on as witness of what you promised me. And if all this fails, your own conscience will not fail to cry out silently in the middle of your happiness, standing up for this truth I have told you and disturbing your best pleasures and satisfactions."

These and other words the grief-stricken Dorotea said, with so much feeling and so many tears that the very men who came with Don Fernando, and all the rest who were present, joined her in them. Don Fernando listened to her without answering her a word, until she made an end of hers and a beginning of so many sobs and sighs that it would have had to be a heart of bronze that was not softened by such signs of grief.

Luscinda was looking at her, no less grieved by her suffering than astonished at her great good sense and beauty; and although she wanted to go to her and say some words of comfort to her, Don Fernando's arms would not let her, holding her tight. And he, full of confusion and dread, after a good while spent looking attentively at Dorotea, opened his arms and, setting Luscinda free, said:

"You have conquered, beautiful Dorotea, you have conquered; for it is not possible to have the heart to deny so many truths together."

With the faint Luscinda had had, as soon as Don Fernando let her go she was about to fall to the ground; but Cardenio being right there — who had placed himself behind Don Fernando's back so as not to be recognised — putting all fear aside and risking everything, ran to hold Luscinda up; and taking her in his arms, he said to her:

"If merciful heaven is pleased and willing that you should have some rest at last, my loyal, faithful and beautiful lady, nowhere do I believe you will have it more safely than in these arms that now receive you, and that received you once before, when fortune was willing that I could call you mine."

At these words Luscinda set her eyes on Cardenio; and having begun to recognise him, first by his voice, and making sure it was he by the sight of him, almost out of her senses and without regard for any decorum at all, she threw her arms round his neck, and putting her face against Cardenio's, said to him:

"You indeed, my lord, are the true master of this captive of yours, however much contrary fortune may prevent it, and however many threats are made against this life that is kept alive by yours."

This was a strange spectacle for Don Fernando and for all the bystanders, who marvelled at so unheard-of an event. It seemed to Dorotea that Don Fernando's face had lost its colour and that he was making as though to take revenge on Cardenio, because she saw him move his hand to put it on his sword; and as soon as she thought it, with unheard-of quickness she clasped him round the knees, kissing them and holding him so tight that she would not let him move; and without stopping her tears for a moment, she said to him:

"What is it you mean to do, my only refuge, in this so unexpected pass? At your feet you have your wife, and the woman you want to be your wife is in her husband's arms. Consider whether it will be right for you, or whether it will even be possible for you, to undo what heaven has done; or whether it will suit you to want to raise up and set level with yourself the woman who, setting aside every obstacle, confirmed in her truth and her constancy, has her own eyes before your eyes, and her face and breast bathed in the moisture of her love for her true husband.

"By the God who is, I beg you, and by who you yourself are I entreat you, that this so plain undeceiving should not only not increase your anger but diminish it in such a way that with quiet and calm you allow these two lovers to have theirs, without any hindrance from you, for all the time heaven may be pleased to grant it them. And in this you will show the generosity of your illustrious and noble breast, and the world will see that with you reason has more force than appetite."

While Dorotea was saying this, although Cardenio held Luscinda in his arms he did not take his eyes off Don Fernando, resolved that if he saw him make any movement to his disadvantage, he would try to defend himself and to set about, as best he could, everybody who showed themselves against him, even if it cost him his life.

But at this point Don Fernando's friends came up, and the curate and the barber, who had been present at all of it — and good Sancho Panza was not missing either. And they all surrounded Don Fernando, begging him to be good enough to look at Dorotea's tears; and that, what she had said in her speech being true — as they without doubt believed it was — he should not allow her to be cheated of such just hopes. That he should consider that it was not by chance, as it seemed, but by the particular providence of heaven that they had all come together in a place where none of them had least expected it.

And he should note, said the curate, that death alone could part Luscinda from Cardenio; and even if they were divided by the edge of some sword, they would count their death as the greatest happiness. And that in knots that cannot be undone it was the height of good sense, by forcing and conquering oneself, to show a generous spirit, allowing the two of them by his own will alone to enjoy the good that heaven had already granted them.

That he should likewise set his eyes on Dorotea's beauty, and would see that few or none could equal her, let alone have any advantage over her; and that to her beauty he should add her humility and the extreme of the love she bore him. And above all, that he should note that if he prided himself on being a gentleman and a Christian, he could do nothing else but keep the word he had given; and that by keeping it he would fulfil his duty to God and satisfy sensible people, who know and recognise that it is the prerogative of beauty, even in a humble subject, provided it goes with modesty, to be able to raise itself and be made equal to any height, without any note of degradation to the man who raises it and makes it equal to himself; and that when the strong laws of desire are obeyed, so long as no sin comes into it, the man who follows them ought not to be blamed.

In short, to these arguments they all added others, such and so many that Don Fernando's valiant breast — being, after all, nourished with illustrious blood — was softened and let itself be conquered by the truth, which he could not have denied even if he had wanted to. And the sign he gave of having surrendered and given himself over to the good opinion that had been put to him was to bend down and embrace Dorotea, saying to her:

"Get up, my lady; it is not right that the woman I hold in my soul should be kneeling at my feet. And if until now I have given no signs of what I say, perhaps it has been by heaven's arrangement, so that, seeing in you the faith with which you love me, I might know how to value you as you deserve. What I beg of you is that you should not reproach me with my bad conduct and my great carelessness; for the same occasion and force that moved me to accept you as mine was the very thing that drove me to try not to be yours. And that this is true, turn and look at the eyes of the now contented Luscinda, and in them you will find an excuse for all my errors. And since she has found and got what she wanted, and I have found in you everything I need, let her live safe and contented long and happy years with her Cardenio; for I shall pray to heaven to let me live them with my Dorotea."

And saying this, he embraced her again and put his face against hers with so tender a feeling that he had to take great care that the tears should not go on to give unmistakable signs of his love and his repentance. Luscinda's and Cardenio's did not do the same, nor did those of almost everybody who was there present; because they began to shed so many, some out of their own happiness and others out of other people's, that it seemed for all the world as if some grave and dreadful case had befallen the lot of them. Even Sancho Panza wept — although he afterwards said that he was only weeping because he saw that Dorotea was not, as he had thought, the queen Micomicona, from whom he was expecting so many favours.

The astonishment, along with the weeping, lasted some while in all of them; and then Cardenio and Luscinda went and knelt down before Don Fernando, thanking him for the kindness he had done them in such courteous words that Don Fernando did not know how to answer them; and so he raised them up and embraced them with signs of great love and great courtesy.

He then asked Dorotea to tell him how she had come to that place so far from her own. She, in short and well-judged words, told everything she had told Cardenio before; which Don Fernando and those who came with him enjoyed so much that they could have wished the tale had lasted longer — such was the charm with which Dorotea told her misfortunes.

And as soon as she had finished, Don Fernando told what had happened to him in the city after he found the paper in Luscinda's bosom, in which she declared that she was Cardenio's wife and could not be his. He said he had wanted to kill her, and would have done it if he had not been prevented by her parents; and that he had left her house in that state, furious and mortified, resolved to take revenge more conveniently. And that the next day he learnt that Luscinda had gone from her parents' house, without anybody's being able to say where she had gone; and that in the end, at the end of some months, he came to learn that she was in a convent, meaning to stay in it all her life if she could not spend it with Cardenio.

And that as soon as he learnt it, choosing those three gentlemen to go with him, he came to the place where she was; and that he had not wanted to speak to her, being afraid that once it was known he was there, the convent would be more closely guarded. And so, waiting for a day when the gate was open, he left the two of them to guard the door, and he with the other had gone into the convent looking for Luscinda, whom they found in the cloister talking to a nun; and snatching her up, without giving her room to do anything else, they had come away with her to a place where they got what they needed for bringing her along. All of which they had been able to do in complete safety, because the convent was out in the country, a good way outside the town.

He said that as soon as Luscinda saw herself in his power, she lost all her senses; and that after coming to herself she had done nothing but weep and sigh, without saying a word; and that in this way, accompanied by silence and tears, they had come to that inn — which for him was like having come to heaven, where all the misfortunes of earth are cancelled and come to an end.

Chapter 37: In Which Is Continued the Story of the Famous Princess Micomicona, with Other Amusing Adventures

Sancho was listening to all this with no small grief in his soul, seeing that his hopes of a title were disappearing and going up in smoke, and that the lovely Princess Micomicona had turned into Dorotea and the giant into Don Fernando, while his master was sleeping soundly away, quite unaware of everything that had happened.

Dorotea could not be sure that the good fortune she now had was not a dream. Cardenio was in the same state of mind, and Luscinda's ran on the same account. Don Fernando gave thanks to heaven for the favour he had received and for having brought him out of that tangled labyrinth where he had been so near to losing his good name and his soul. And in the end, everybody in the inn was contented and delighted at the good outcome of such knotted and desperate affairs.

The curate, being a man of judgement, set it all in order and congratulated each of them on the good they had got. But the one who most rejoiced and was most contented was the innkeeper's wife, because of the promise Cardenio and the curate had made her to pay her for all the damages and expenses that had come to her on Don Quixote's account.

Only Sancho, as has been said, was the afflicted, the unlucky and the sad one; and so, with a melancholy face, he went in to his master, who had just woken up, and said to him:

"Your worship, Sir Sorrowful Countenance, may perfectly well sleep as much as you like, without troubling to kill any giant or to give the princess back her kingdom, for it is all done and finished."

"That I well believe," answered Don Quixote, "because I have had with the giant the most monstrous and enormous battle I expect to have in all the days of my life; and with one backhand stroke — smack! — I brought his head down on the ground, and so much blood came out of him that the streams of it ran along the ground as though they had been water."

"As though they had been red wine, your worship might better have said," answered Sancho; "because I want your worship to know, if you don't know it already, that the dead giant is a punctured wineskin, and the blood is six gallons of red wine that it was carrying in its belly, and the cut-off head is the whore that bore me — and Satan take the lot of it."

"And what is this you are saying, madman?" replied Don Quixote. "Are you in your senses?"

"Get up, your worship," said Sancho, "and you'll see the fine job you've done and what we've got to pay; and you'll see the queen turned into a private lady called Dorotea, along with other events that will astonish you if you take them in."

"I should not be surprised at any of that," replied Don Quixote; "because, if you remember rightly, the last time we were here I told you that everything that happened here was a matter of enchantment, and it would be no great thing if it were the same now."

"I'd believe all of it," answered Sancho, "if my blanketing had been a thing of the same kind; but it wasn't, it was real and true. And I saw that the innkeeper who's here today had hold of one corner of the blanket and was pushing me up towards the sky with a great deal of charm and energy, and with as much laughing as strength; and where it comes to recognising people, it's my belief, simpleton and sinner though I am, that there's no enchantment at all in it, but a great deal of pounding and a great deal of bad luck."

"Very well, God will put it right," said Don Quixote. "Give me my clothes and let me go out there, for I want to see the events and transformations you speak of."

Sancho gave him his clothes; and while he was dressing, the curate told Don Fernando and the rest about Don Quixote's madness, and about the device they had used to get him off the Poor Rock, where he imagined he was on account of his lady's scorn. He likewise told them almost all the adventures Sancho had told, at which they were not a little astonished and amused, since it seemed to them what it seemed to everybody: that it was the strangest kind of madness that could enter a deranged mind.

The curate said further that, since the lady Dorotea's good fortune now prevented their going on with their plan, it was necessary to invent and find another for being able to get him back to his own country. Cardenio offered to carry on with what they had begun, and said that Luscinda would take and act Dorotea's part.

"No," said Don Fernando, "it shall not be so; I want Dorotea to go on with her own invention. As long as this good gentleman's village is not very far from here, I shall be glad to have his cure seen to."

"It is not more than two days' journey from here."

"Well, even if it were more, I should be pleased to travel them for the sake of doing so good a work."

At this point Don Quixote came out, armed at all points, with Mambrino's helmet — battered as it was — on his head, his buckler braced on his arm and leaning on his trunk of a pike. Don Fernando and the rest were taken aback by Don Quixote's strange appearance: seeing his face half a league long, dry and yellow, the mismatched pieces of his armour, and his solemn bearing, they stayed silent until they should see what he would say. And he, with great gravity and calm, setting his eyes on the beautiful Dorotea, said:

"I am informed, beautiful lady, by this squire of mine that your greatness has been annihilated and your being undone, since from the queen and great lady you used to be you have turned into a private young woman. If this has been by order of the necromancer king your father, out of fear that I would not give you the necessary and proper help, I say that he did not know and does not know the half of the Mass, and that he was little versed in the histories of chivalry; because if he had read them and gone through them as attentively and as thoroughly as I have gone through and read them, he would have found at every step how other knights of less fame than mine have brought off harder things — since it is no great matter to kill a little giant, however arrogant he may be. Because it is not many hours since I was face to face with him, and — I will say no more, so that they may not tell me I am lying; but time, the revealer of all things, will tell it when we least expect it."

"It was two wineskins you were face to face with, and no giant," said the innkeeper at this point.

Don Fernando ordered him to be quiet and on no account to interrupt Don Quixote's talk; and Don Quixote went on to say:

"I say, in short, high and disinherited lady, that if for the reason I have given your father has worked this metamorphosis on your person, you should give it no credit at all; because there is no danger on earth through which my sword will not open a road — with which, by laying your enemy's head on the ground, I shall put the crown of your own kingdom on your head within a few days."

Don Quixote said no more, and waited for the princess to answer him; and she, since she already knew Don Fernando's decision that the deception should be carried on until Don Quixote was taken back to his own country, answered him with a great deal of charm and gravity:

"Whoever told you, valorous Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, that I had changed and altered my being did not tell you the truth; because I am today the same woman I was yesterday. It is true that certain fortunate events have made some change in me, and have given me the best fortune I could have wished myself; but I have not for that reason stopped being what I was before, or stopped having the same intention I have always had of making use of the valour of your valiant and invincible arm.

"So, my lord, let your goodness give back his honour to the father who begot me, and hold him for a wise and prudent man, since with his science he found so easy and so true a road for remedying my misfortune. For I believe that if it had not been for you, sir, I should never have managed to have the good fortune I have; and in this I speak as much truth as most of these gentlemen who are present are good witnesses of. What remains is that tomorrow we should set out, because today not much of a journey could be made; and for the rest of the good outcome I hope for, I shall leave it to God and to the valour of your breast."

This the quick-witted Dorotea said; and on hearing it, Don Quixote turned to Sancho and, with every sign of great anger, said to him:

"Now I tell you, little Sancho, that you are the biggest little scoundrel there is in Spain. Tell me, you vagabond thief: did you not just now finish telling me that this princess had turned into a girl called Dorotea, and that the head which I know I cut off a giant was the whore that bore you, along with other absurdities that put me in the greatest confusion I have ever been in in all the days of my life? I swear —" and he looked up at the sky and clenched his teeth "— that I am ready to make such havoc of you as will put salt in the brainpan of every lying squire of knights errant there may be in the world from this day on!"

"Let your worship calm down, my dear sir," answered Sancho. "It might well be that I was mistaken as far as the change of the lady Princess Micomicona goes; but as far as the giant's head goes — or at least the puncturing of the wineskins and the blood's being red wine — I am not mistaken, by the living God! Because the wineskins are there wounded, at the head of your worship's bed, and the red wine has made a lake of the room. And if not, you'll see it when the eggs are frying — I mean you'll see it when his worship the innkeeper here asks you for the damage on the lot of it. As for the rest, that the lady queen is as she was, I rejoice in my soul, because my share is in it, like everybody else's."

"Now I tell you, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that you are an idiot; and forgive me, and enough of it."

"Enough," said Don Fernando, "and let no more be said about it. And since the lady princess says we are to travel tomorrow, because today it is late, let it be so; and tonight we can spend in good conversation until the coming day, when we shall all accompany Señor Don Quixote, because we want to be witnesses of the valorous and unheard-of exploits he is to perform in the course of this great enterprise he has taken on."

"It is I who am to serve you and go with you," answered Don Quixote; "and I am very grateful for the kindness done me and for the good opinion held of me, which I shall try to make come true, or it will cost me my life — and even more, if more can cost me."

Many words of politeness and many offers passed between Don Quixote and Don Fernando; but silence was put on all of it by a traveller who came into the inn at that moment, whose dress showed him to be a Christian newly come from the land of the Moors. For he came dressed in a short-skirted coat of blue cloth, with half sleeves and no collar; his breeches were likewise of blue linen, with a cap of the same colour; he wore date-coloured buskins and a Moorish scimitar hung from a baldric that crossed his chest.

Behind him came in, on a donkey, a woman dressed in the Moorish fashion, her face covered with a veil on her head; she wore a little brocade cap, and was dressed in a robe that covered her from her shoulders to her feet. The man was of a strong, well-favoured build, a little over forty years old, somewhat dark in the face, with long moustaches and a very well kept beard. In short, his bearing showed that if he had been well dressed people would have judged him to be a person of quality and well born.

On coming in he asked for a room; and when they told him there was none in the inn, he showed himself put out; and going up to the woman who by her dress appeared to be a Moor, he lifted her down in his arms. Luscinda, Dorotea, the innkeeper's wife, her daughter and Maritornes, drawn by the new dress they had never seen before, gathered round the Moorish woman; and Dorotea, who was always charming, polite and quick-witted, thinking that both she and the man who had brought her were distressed at the lack of a room, said to her:

"Do not let the lack of comfort here trouble you too much, my lady, for it is the nature of inns not to have any; but for all that, if you would like to come in with us" — pointing to Luscinda — "perhaps in the course of this journey you have found other welcomes not as good."

The veiled woman answered nothing to this, and did nothing but get up from where she had sat down; and putting both hands crossed on her breast and bending her head, she bowed her body as a sign that she was grateful. By her silence they supposed that without any doubt she must be a Moor and could not speak Christian.

At this the captive came up, having been busy with something else until then; and seeing that they had all gathered round the woman who came with him, and that she was silent at everything they said to her, he said:

"My ladies, this young woman hardly understands my language, and does not know how to speak any except the one of her own country; and that is why she must not have answered, and does not answer, what she is asked."

"She is asked nothing at all," answered Luscinda, "except to be offered our company for tonight and a share of the place where we shall settle ourselves, where she will be made as comfortable as the accommodation allows, with the goodwill that obliges us to serve all strangers who have need of it — especially when it is a woman one serves."

"On her behalf and my own," answered the captive, "I kiss your hands, my lady, and value very highly, and as it deserves, the kindness you offer; for on such an occasion, and from people of the sort your looks show you to be, it is easy to see that it must be very great."

"Tell me, sir," said Dorotea, "is this lady a Christian or a Moor? Because her dress and her silence make us think she is what we would not wish her to be."

"A Moor she is in her dress and in her body, but in her soul she is very much a Christian, because she has the greatest desire to be one."

"So she is not baptised?" asked Luscinda.

"There has been no opportunity for it," answered the captive, "since she left Algiers, her country and her home; and up to now she has not found herself in such immediate danger of death as to make it necessary to baptise her before she knew all the ceremonies our Mother the Holy Church requires. But God will be pleased that she shall soon be baptised with the propriety her quality deserves, which is more than her dress and mine show."

With these words he put a longing into everybody who was listening to know who the Moorish woman and the captive were; but nobody wanted to ask them just then, seeing that this was more a moment for getting them some rest than for asking them about their lives.

Dorotea took her by the hand and led her to sit down beside her, and asked her to take off her veil. She looked at the captive, as though asking him to tell her what they were saying and what she should do. He told her in Arabic that they were asking her to take off her veil, and that she should do it. And so she took it off, and revealed a face so beautiful that Dorotea thought her more beautiful than Luscinda, and Luscinda thought her more beautiful than Dorotea; and all the bystanders recognised that if any face could be set level with those two, it was the Moorish woman's, and there were even some who gave hers the advantage in something. And as beauty has the prerogative and grace of reconciling minds and drawing wills to itself, they all at once surrendered to the desire to serve and make much of the beautiful Moor.

Don Fernando asked the captive what the Moorish woman was called, and he answered Lela Zoraida; and as soon as she heard this she understood what they had asked the Christian, and said in a great hurry, full of distress and charm:

"No, no Zoraida: María, María!" — giving them to understand that she was called María and not Zoraida.

These words, and the great feeling with which the Moorish woman said them, made more than one tear fall from some of those who heard her, especially from the women, who by their nature are tender and compassionate. Luscinda embraced her very lovingly, saying to her:

"Yes, yes: María, María."

To which the Moorish woman answered:

"Yes, yes: María; Zoraida macange!" — which means no.

By now night was coming on, and by order of those who had come with Don Fernando the innkeeper had been busy and careful in getting them the best supper he possibly could. The hour arriving, then, they all sat down at a long table like a servants' hall table, because there was no round or square one in the inn; and they gave the head and chief place — although he refused it — to Don Quixote, who wanted the lady Micomicona to be at his side, since he was her protector. Then Luscinda and Zoraida sat down, and opposite them Don Fernando and Cardenio, and then the captive and the other gentlemen, and beside the ladies the curate and the barber.

And so they had supper very contentedly, and their contentment was increased when they saw that Don Quixote, leaving off eating and moved by the same sort of spirit that had moved him to talk as much as he did when he had supper with the goatherds, began to say:

"Truly, gentlemen, if it is properly considered, those who profess the order of knight-errantry see great and unheard-of things. If not — which of the living in the world, coming in now through the gate of this castle and seeing us in the state we are in, would judge and believe that we are who we are? Who could say that this lady at my side is the great queen we all know her to be, and that I am that Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance who goes about in the mouth of fame? There is no doubting it now: this art and calling exceeds all those that men have invented, and it is to be held in the greater esteem the more dangers it is subject to.

"Let them get out of my sight who say that letters have the advantage of arms; for I shall tell them, whoever they may be, that they do not know what they are saying. Because the reason such people generally give, and the one they chiefly rely on, is that the labours of the spirit exceed those of the body, and that arms are exercised with the body alone — as if it were a porter's trade, for which nothing is needed but good strength; or as if in this thing we call arms there were not shut up, for those of us who profess it, the acts of fortitude, which demand a great deal of understanding to carry out; or as if the spirit of the warrior who has charge of an army, or of the defence of a besieged city, did not work as hard with the spirit as with the body.

"If not, let it be seen whether by bodily strength a man can find out and guess the enemy's intention, his designs, his stratagems, his difficulties, or how to forestall the harm that is feared — for all these things are actions of the understanding, in which the body has no part at all.

"This being so, then, that arms require the spirit as much as letters do, let us see now which of the two spirits, the scholar's or the warrior's, works harder. And this will come to be known by the end and purpose each one is directed to, because that intention is to be valued higher which has the nobler end for its object.

"The end and purpose of letters — and I am not speaking now of divine letters, whose aim is to carry and guide souls to heaven, for no other can be set level with an end as endless as that; I speak of human letters — their end is to set distributive justice at its proper point and to give each man what is his, to understand and to see that good laws are kept. An end, certainly, generous and lofty and worthy of great praise, but not of so much as the one arms attend to, which have for their object and end peace, which is the greatest good men can desire in this life.

"And so the first good news the world had and men had were the news the angels gave on the night that was our day, when they sang in the air: 'Glory be in the highest, and peace on earth to men of good will.' And the salutation that the best master of earth and heaven taught his intimates and his favoured ones was to tell them that when they went into any house they should say: 'Peace be on this house.' And many other times he told them: 'My peace I give you, my peace I leave you; peace be with you' — like a jewel and a pledge given and left by such a hand; a jewel without which there can be no good at all, on earth or in heaven.

"This peace is the true end of war, for to say arms is the same thing as to say war. Granting this truth, then, that the end of war is peace, and that in this it has the advantage of the end of letters, let us come now to the bodily labours of the scholar and to those of the professor of arms, and let it be seen which are the greater."

Don Quixote went on with his talk in such a way, and in such good terms, that he obliged none of those who were listening to him to take him for a madman just then. On the contrary, as most of them were gentlemen, to whom arms belong, they listened to him very willingly; and he went on to say:

"I say, then, that the student's labours are these: chiefly poverty — not because they are all poor, but so as to put the case in the extremest terms it can have. And having said that he suffers poverty, it seems to me there was nothing more to say about his bad luck, because whoever is poor has nothing good. This poverty he suffers in all its parts, now in hunger, now in cold, now in nakedness, now in all of them together; but with all that, it is not so great that he does not eat, even if it is a little later than the usual hour, even if it is off the leavings of the rich — for the greatest wretchedness of the student is what they call among themselves going for the soup. And they do not lack somebody else's brazier or fireside, which if it does not warm them at least takes the edge off their cold, and in the end they sleep the night under a roof.

"I do not want to come to other small matters — that is, the lack of shirts and the shortage of shoes, the thinness and threadbareness of the coat, or that stuffing themselves with so much pleasure when good luck sends them some feast. By this road I have described, rough and difficult, tripping here, falling there, getting up further on, falling again here, they arrive at the rank they want. And having reached it, we have seen many of them who, having passed through these Syrtes and these Scyllas and Charybdises, as though carried on the wings of favourable fortune — I say we have seen them ruling and governing the world from a chair, their hunger changed into fullness, their cold into comfort, their nakedness into fine clothes, and their sleeping on a rush mat into resting between Holland sheets and damask: a reward justly deserved by their virtue.

"But set against and compared with the labours of the soldier, theirs are left a long way behind in everything, as I shall now say."

Chapter 38: Which Treats of Don Quixote's Curious Discourse on Arms and Letters

Going on, Don Quixote said:

"Since we began with the student's poverty and its parts, let us see whether the soldier is any richer. And we shall see that there is nobody poorer in poverty itself, because he depends on the miserableness of his pay, which comes either late or never, or on whatever he can scrape together with his own hands, at notable danger to his life and his conscience. And sometimes his nakedness is such that a slashed jerkin serves him for finery and for a shirt; and in the middle of winter, out in the open country, he generally repairs himself against the inclemency of the sky with nothing but the breath of his mouth — which, since it comes out of an empty place, I take it as established must come out cold, against all nature.

"Well, wait for him to wait for night to come so as to restore himself from all these discomforts in the bed that is waiting for him, which, unless it is his own fault, will never sin by being too narrow; for he may measure out on the ground as many feet as he likes, and turn over in it as he pleases, without any fear that the sheets will shrink on him.

"Let there come now, on top of all this, the day and the hour of taking his degree in his calling; let there come a day of battle, when they will put the doctor's cap on his head — made of lint, to dress some bullet wound which will perhaps have gone through his temples, or will leave him crippled of an arm or a leg. And when this does not happen, but merciful heaven guards him and keeps him alive and whole, it may be that he will be left in the same poverty he was in before, and that it will be necessary for one encounter after another, one battle after another, to happen, and for him to come out of them all the winner, in order to get on at all. But these miracles are seldom seen.

"But tell me, gentlemen, if you have thought about it: how many fewer are those rewarded by war than those who have perished in it? Without any doubt you must answer that there is no comparison, and that the dead cannot be brought to an account, while the living who have been rewarded could be counted in three figures.

"All this is the other way round with scholars, because out of their gowns' skirts — I will not say out of their sleeves — they all have something to keep themselves going with. So that although the soldier's labour is greater, his reward is a great deal less.

"But to this it can be answered that it is easier to reward two thousand scholars than thirty thousand soldiers, because the first are rewarded by giving them posts, which must of necessity be given to men of their profession, and the second cannot be rewarded except out of the very property of the lord they serve; and this impossibility strengthens my argument further. But let us leave this aside, for it is a labyrinth very hard to get out of, and come back to the pre-eminence of arms over letters — a matter which is still to be settled, considering the arguments each side puts forward for itself.

"Among the ones I have mentioned, letters say that without them arms could not be kept up, because war too has its laws and is subject to them, and laws fall under what letters and scholars are. To this arms answer that laws could not be kept up without them, because it is with arms that states are defended, kingdoms preserved, cities guarded, roads made safe and seas cleared of pirates; and in the end, if it were not for arms, states, kingdoms, monarchies, cities and the roads by sea and land would be subject to the severity and the confusion that war brings with it while it lasts and has licence to use its privileges and its forces.

"And it is a settled truth that the thing that costs most is valued, and ought to be valued, most highly. To reach eminence in letters costs a man time, sleepless nights, hunger, nakedness, dizziness, indigestion and other things attached to these, some of which I have already mentioned. But for a man to come by the proper steps to be a good soldier costs him everything it costs the student, in so much greater a degree that there is no comparison, because at every step he stands to lose his life.

"And what fear of want and poverty can reach or weary the student that comes up to the one a soldier has, who, finding himself besieged in some stronghold and standing at his post or on guard in some ravelin or cavalier, hears that the enemy are mining towards the place where he is, and cannot on any account move away from there or run away from the danger that threatens him so close at hand? The only thing he can do is to give his captain notice of what is happening, so that he can remedy it with a countermine, and to stay where he is himself, fearing and expecting the moment when he shall suddenly go up to the clouds without wings and come down to the depths against his will.

"And if this seems a small danger, let us see whether it is matched or bettered by that of two galleys ramming each other prow to prow in the middle of the wide sea, which, being locked and grappled together, leave the soldier no more space than the two feet of plank on the beak-head. And in spite of this, seeing that he has in front of him as many ministers of death threatening him as there are guns trained on him from the other side, not a lance-length from his body; and seeing that at the first slip of his feet he would go to visit the deep bosom of Neptune — in spite of all this, with an intrepid heart, carried by the honour that urges him on, he sets himself up as a target for all that musketry and tries to get across so narrow a passage to the enemy vessel.

"And what is most to be marvelled at is that one man has hardly fallen where he will not be able to get up again until the end of the world before another takes his very place; and if this one too falls into the sea, which is waiting for him like an enemy, another and another follows him without giving time to time for their deaths: the greatest courage and daring that can be found in all the passages of war.

"Blessed be those happy ages that were without the appalling fury of these devilish instruments of artillery, whose inventor is at this moment, I am convinced, being given in hell the reward of his diabolical invention — with which he made it possible for a base and cowardly arm to take the life of a valiant knight; and for a stray ball, without his knowing how or from where, in the middle of the courage and spirit that fires and animates brave breasts, fired off by a man who perhaps ran away and was frightened by the flash the powder made in going off in that accursed machine, to come and cut short and end in an instant the thoughts and the life of a man who deserved to enjoy them for long ages.

"And so, considering this, I am ready to say that it grieves me in my soul to have taken up this calling of knight errant in an age as detestable as this one we now live in. Because although no danger frightens me, still it makes me uneasy to think that powder and lead may take away from me the chance of making myself famous and known, by the valour of my arm and the edge of my sword, throughout the whole of the discovered earth. But let heaven do what it is pleased to do; for I shall be all the more esteemed, if I come out with what I am after, in proportion as I have exposed myself to greater dangers than the knights errant of past ages exposed themselves to."

All this long preamble Don Quixote made while the others were having supper, forgetting to lift a mouthful to his own mouth, although Sancho Panza had told him several times to eat his supper, for there would be time afterwards to say everything he wanted.

In those who had listened to him there came a fresh pity at seeing that a man who apparently had a good understanding and reasoned well about everything he discussed should have lost it so completely when it came to that black and pitch-dark chivalry of his. The curate told him that he was quite right in everything he had said in favour of arms, and that he himself, although a scholar and a graduate, was of the same opinion.

They finished supper and the cloth was cleared; and while the innkeeper's wife, her daughter and Maritornes were getting ready Don Quixote of La Mancha's garret, where they had decided that the women should shut themselves up alone that night, Don Fernando begged the captive to tell them the course of his life, because it could not fail to be strange and enjoyable, judging by the signs he had begun to give in coming in Zoraida's company.

To which the captive answered that he would very willingly do what he was asked, and that he was only afraid the tale would not be such as to give them the pleasure he wanted to; but that for all that, so as not to fail in obeying him, he would tell it. The curate and all the rest thanked him and begged him again; and he, seeing himself begged by so many, said that there was no need for begging where commanding had so much force.

"And so, let your worships give me your attention, and you will hear a true account, which perhaps the lying ones that are generally put together with careful and studied artifice could not come up to."

With this he made them all settle themselves and lend him a great silence; and he, seeing that they were quiet by now and waiting for whatever he might want to say, began to speak in a pleasant, calm voice in this way:

Chapter 39: In Which the Captive Tells His Life and Adventures

"My family had its beginning in a place in the mountains of León, with whom nature was more grateful and generous than fortune — although, in the narrow circumstances of those villages, my father still had the reputation of being rich, and he would genuinely have been so if he had been as clever at keeping his property as he was at spending it. And this disposition of his, of being open-handed and a spender, came from having been a soldier in the years of his youth; for soldiering is a school where the mean man becomes generous and the generous man a spendthrift. And if a few miserly soldiers are to be found, they are like monsters, seldom seen.
