"My father went past the limits of generosity and came close to those of being a spendthrift — a thing that is of no use at all to a married man who has children to succeed him in his name and his condition. The ones my father had were three, all sons and all old enough to choose their walk in life.

"Seeing, then, that he could not, as he put it, hold his own hand back against his own disposition, my father chose to deprive himself of the instrument and cause that made him a spender and a giver — which was to deprive himself of his property, without which Alexander himself would have looked close-fisted.

"And so, calling the three of us alone into a room one day, he said something like what I shall now say: 'My sons, to tell you that I love you well, it is enough to know and to say that you are my sons; and to understand that I love you badly, it is enough to know that I do not hold my hand back where keeping your property is concerned. So that you may understand from now on that I love you as a father, and that I do not want to destroy you like a stepfather, I want to do a thing with you that I have had in mind for a long time and have arranged after mature consideration.

"'You are now of an age to take up a condition in life, or at least to choose a calling such that, when you are older, it will bring you honour and profit. And what I have thought of is to make four parts of my property: three of them I shall give you, to each what falls to him, without exceeding in anything; and the other I shall keep for myself, to live and keep myself the days heaven is pleased to give me of life.

"'But I should like each one of you, once he has in his own hands the part of the property that falls to him, to follow one of the roads I shall name. There is a proverb in our Spain which is, in my opinion, a very true one, as they all are, being brief maxims drawn from long and judicious experience; and the one I mean says: "The Church, or the sea, or the king's house" — as if it said more plainly: "Whoever wants to get on and be rich, let him either follow the Church, or go to sea and practise the art of trade, or go and serve kings in their households"; because they say: "A crumb from a king is worth more than a favour from a lord."

"'I say this because I should like — and it is my will — that one of you should follow letters, another trade, and the other serve the king in war, since it is hard to get into his service in his household; for although war does not give a man much wealth, it usually gives him a great deal of worth and a great deal of fame. Within eight days I shall give you the whole of your share in money, without cheating you of a farthing, as you will see by the fact. Tell me now whether you mean to follow my opinion and my advice in what I have put to you.'

"And ordering me, as the eldest, to answer, after telling him not to get rid of his property but to spend as much as he chose, since we were young enough to know how to earn it, I ended by concluding that I would fall in with what he wanted, and that mine was to follow the calling of arms, serving God and my king in it. The second brother made the same offers, and chose to go to the Indies, taking the property that fell to him invested in goods. The youngest, and, I believe, the wisest, said he wanted to follow the Church, or to go and finish the studies he had begun at Salamanca.

"As soon as we had finished agreeing and choosing our callings, my father embraced us all; and with the promptness he had promised, he carried out everything he had promised us. And giving each one his share, which as far as I remember was three thousand ducats each in money — because an uncle of ours bought the whole property and paid for it in cash, so that it should not go out of the family stock — on one and the same day the three of us took our leave of our good father.

"And on that same day, since it seemed to me an inhumanity that my father should be left old and with so little property, I got him to take two thousand ducats out of my three thousand, because the rest was enough for me to fit myself out with what a soldier needs. My two brothers, moved by my example, each gave him a thousand ducats: so that my father was left with four thousand in money, and three thousand more, which was apparently the value of the property that fell to him, which he would not sell but chose to keep as land.

"I say, in short, that we took our leave of him and of that uncle of ours I have mentioned, not without a great deal of feeling and tears from everybody; charging us to let them know, every time there was a chance of doing it, how we fared, well or badly. We promised it; and embracing us and giving us his blessing, one of us took the road to Salamanca, the other to Seville and I to Alicante, where I had news that there was a Genoese ship taking on a cargo of wool for Genoa.

"It will be twenty-two years this year since I left my father's house, and in all of them, although I have written some letters, I have had no news of him or of my brothers. And what I have gone through in this stretch of time I shall tell briefly.

"I took ship at Alicante, arrived at Genoa on a prosperous voyage, went from there to Milan, where I fitted myself out with arms and with some soldierly finery, and from there I meant to go and enlist in Piedmont; and being already on the road to Alessandria della Paglia, I had news that the great Duke of Alba was going over to Flanders. I changed my plan, went with him and served him in the campaigns he made; I was present at the deaths of the Counts of Egmont and Horn; I got to be ensign to a famous captain from Guadalajara called Diego de Urbina.

"And some time after I arrived in Flanders, news came of the league which His Holiness Pope Pius the Fifth, of happy memory, had made with Venice and with Spain against the common enemy, which is the Turk — who at that same time had won with his fleet the famous island of Cyprus, which was under Venetian rule: a lamentable and unfortunate loss. It was known for certain that the most serene Don John of Austria, natural brother of our good King Philip, was coming as general of this league. The enormous preparation for war that was being made was published abroad. All of which stirred me and moved my spirit and my desire to see myself in the campaign that was expected; and although I had hints, and almost certain promises, that at the first opportunity that offered I should be promoted to captain, I chose to leave it all and come, as I did come, to Italy.

"And my good luck willed that my lord Don John of Austria had just arrived at Genoa, on his way to Naples to join up with the Venetian fleet, as he afterwards did at Messina.

"I say, in short, that I found myself in that most fortunate campaign, made a captain of infantry by then, to which honourable rank my good luck raised me rather than my deserts. And on that day, which was so happy a one for Christendom — because on it the world and all the nations were undeceived of the error they were in, believing that the Turks were unbeatable at sea — on that day, I say, on which Ottoman pride and arrogance was broken, among all the fortunate men who were there (for the Christians who died there had more good fortune than those who were left alive and victorious), I alone was the unlucky one; since instead of being able to expect, if it had been in Roman times, some naval crown, I found myself on the night that followed so famous a day with chains on my feet and manacles on my hands.

"And it happened like this. Uchalí, king of Algiers, a bold and successful corsair, having attacked and taken the Maltese flagship — only three knights being left alive on her, and those badly wounded — Gian Andrea's flagship came up to help her, and I was on board with my company. And doing what I ought to on such an occasion, I leapt onto the enemy galley, which, sheering off from the one that had run against her, prevented my soldiers from following me; and so I found myself alone among my enemies, whom I could not resist because there were so many of them. In the end they overpowered me, covered with wounds. And as you gentlemen will have heard that Uchalí got away with his whole squadron, I came to be left a captive in his power, and I alone was the sad man among so many glad ones and the captive among so many free ones; for fifteen thousand Christians got the liberty they had longed for that day, all of whom had been at the oar in the Turkish fleet.

"They took me to Constantinople, where the Grand Turk Selim made my master general of the sea, because he had done his duty in the battle, having carried off the standard of the Order of Malta as a token of his valour.

"The second year, which was the year seventy-two, I found myself at Navarino, rowing in the flagship with the three lanterns. I saw and noted the opportunity that was lost there of catching the whole Turkish fleet in the harbour; because all the levantines and janissaries who were in it took it for certain that they would be attacked inside the harbour itself, and had their kit and their pasamaques — which are their shoes — ready to run away overland at once without waiting to be fought: such was the fear they had come to have of our fleet. But heaven ordered it otherwise — not through the fault or carelessness of the general who commanded our men, but through the sins of Christendom, and because God wills and allows that we should always have executioners to punish us.

"In fact Uchalí withdrew to Modon, which is an island next to Navarino; and putting his men ashore, he fortified the mouth of the harbour and stayed quiet until my lord Don John went back.

"On this voyage the galley called The Prize was taken, whose captain was a son of that famous corsair Barbarossa. She was taken by the flagship of Naples, called The She-Wolf, commanded by that thunderbolt of war, that father of soldiers, that fortunate and never-conquered captain Don Álvaro de Bazán, Marquis of Santa Cruz.

"And I do not want to leave out what happened at the taking of The Prize. Barbarossa's son was so cruel, and treated his captives so badly, that as soon as the men at the oar saw that the galley She-Wolf was coming up on them and overhauling them, they all let go of the oars at the same moment and seized their captain, who was standing on the gangway shouting to them to row faster; and passing him from bench to bench, from stern to bow, they gave him such bites that a little past the mast his soul had already passed to hell: such was, as I have said, the cruelty with which he treated them and the hatred they had for him.

"We went back to Constantinople; and the next year, which was seventy-three, it was learnt there how my lord Don John had taken Tunis and had taken that kingdom from the Turks and put Muley Hamet in possession of it, cutting off the hopes Muley Hamida had of reigning in it again — the cruellest and the bravest Moor the world ever had.

"The Grand Turk felt this loss deeply; and using the shrewdness they all have in his house, he made peace with the Venetians, who wanted it a great deal more than he did. And the next year, seventy-four, he attacked the Goletta and the fort which my lord Don John had left half built beside Tunis. In all these passages I was at the oar, without any hope of liberty — at least I did not hope to have it by ransom, because I had made up my mind not to write the news of my misfortune to my father.

"The Goletta was lost, in the end, and the fort was lost; against which two places there were seventy-five thousand paid Turkish soldiers, and of Moors and Arabs from all Africa more than four hundred thousand — this enormous number of men accompanied by so much ammunition and so many engines of war, and by so many pioneers, that with their hands and by handfuls of earth they could have buried the Goletta and the fort.

"The Goletta was lost first, held until then to be impregnable; and it was not lost through the fault of its defenders, who did in its defence everything they ought and could, but because experience showed how easily trenches could be raised in that desert sand — since at two hand-breadths water was found, and the Turks did not find it at two yards. And so with a great many sacks of sand they raised the trenches so high that they overtopped the walls of the fort; and firing down on it from above, nobody could stand there or attend to the defence.

"It was the general opinion that our men should not have shut themselves into the Goletta but should have waited for the landing out in the open; and those who say this speak from a distance and with little experience of such cases. Because if in the Goletta and the fort there were hardly seven thousand soldiers, how could so small a number, however brave they might be, come out into the open and hold the fortifications at the same time against so great a number as the enemy's? And how is it possible for a fortress not to be lost when it is not relieved, and the more so when it is besieged by enemies who are many and obstinate, and in their own country?

"But to many it seemed, and so it seemed to me, that it was a particular grace and favour that heaven did Spain in allowing that workshop and cloak of wickedness to be razed — that glutton or sponge and moth of the endless sums of money that were spent there to no purpose, serving no other end than to keep alive the memory of its having been won by the most fortunate and unconquered Charles the Fifth; as though it were necessary, to make that memory eternal — as it is and will be — that those stones should hold it up.

"The fort was lost too; but the Turks won it foot by foot, because the soldiers who defended it fought so valiantly and so strongly that they killed more than twenty-five thousand of the enemy in twenty-two general assaults they made on them. Of the three hundred who were left alive, not one was taken prisoner unwounded — a certain and clear sign of their effort and valour, and of how well they had defended and held their positions.

"A small fort or tower in the middle of the lagoon surrendered on terms, in the charge of Don Juan Zanoguera, a Valencian gentleman and a famous soldier. They took prisoner Don Pedro Puertocarrero, general of the Goletta, who did everything possible to defend his fortress; and he felt the loss of it so much that he died of grief on the road to Constantinople, where they were taking him captive.

"They likewise took prisoner the general of the fort, who was called Gabrio Cervellón, a Milanese gentleman, a great engineer and a most valiant soldier. Many people of note died in these two fortresses, one of whom was Pagán de Oria, a knight of the habit of St John, of a generous disposition, as was shown by the extreme liberality he used towards his brother, the famous Gian Andrea de Oria. And what made his death more pitiful was his having died at the hands of some Arabs he trusted, seeing the fort already lost, who offered to take him in Moorish dress to Tabarca, which is a little port or station the Genoese who work at coral-fishing have on those shores. These Arabs cut off his head and brought it to the general of the Turkish fleet, who fulfilled on them our Castilian proverb, 'Though the treason pleases, the traitor is loathed'; for they say the general ordered the men who brought him the present to be hanged, because they had not brought the man alive.

"Among the Christians who were lost in the fort was one called Don Pedro de Aguilar, a native of I do not know what place in Andalusia, who had been an ensign in the fort, a soldier of great account and of rare understanding: he had a particular gift in what they call poetry. I say this because his luck brought him to my galley and to my bench, and to being a slave of my own master. And before we left that harbour, this gentleman made two sonnets by way of epitaphs, one to the Goletta and the other to the fort. And truly I must say them, because I know them by heart and I think they will cause pleasure rather than distress."

The moment the captive named Don Pedro de Aguilar, Don Fernando looked at his companions, and all three of them smiled; and when he came to speak of the sonnets, one of them said:

"Before your worship goes any further, I beg you to tell me what became of this Don Pedro de Aguilar you have mentioned."

"What I know," answered the captive, "is that at the end of two years he spent in Constantinople he escaped in Albanian dress with a Greek spy; and I do not know whether he got to freedom, although I believe he did, because a year later I saw the Greek in Constantinople, and I could not ask him how that journey turned out."

"Well, he did," answered the gentleman; "because that Don Pedro is my brother, and he is now at home in our village, well and rich, married and with three children."

"Thanks be to God," said the captive, "for so many favours as he did him; because there is no happiness on earth, to my mind, that comes up to gaining a lost liberty."

"And what is more," replied the gentleman, "I know the sonnets my brother made."

"Then say them, your worship," said the captive, "for you will know how to say them better than I do."

"With pleasure," answered the gentleman; "and the one about the Goletta went like this."

Chapter 40: In Which the Captive's Story Is Continued

	Blessed souls, who from the mortal veil
	free and released, by the good you did,
	rose up from the low earth
	to the highest and best part of heaven,
	and, burning with anger and with honourable zeal,
	exercised the strength of your bodies,
	so that with your own blood and other men's you coloured
	the neighbouring sea and the sandy ground:
	life failed before courage did
	in your weary arms, which, dying,
	carry the victory in being defeated.
	And this mortal, sad fall of yours
	between the wall and the sword is winning you
	fame that the world gives you, and heaven glory.

"That is exactly the way I know it," said the captive.

"Then the one about the fort, if I do not remember it wrong," said the gentleman, "goes like this:

	Out of this barren, ruined ground,
	out of these clods thrown down on the floor,
	the holy souls of three thousand soldiers
	rose living to a better dwelling,
	the strength of their sturdy arms
	having first been exercised in vain,
	until at last, being few and weary,
	they gave up their lives to the edge of the sword.
	And this is the ground that has continually
	been full of a thousand lamentable memories
	in the ages past and present.
	But no juster souls than these
	will ever have risen from its hard bosom to the clear sky,
	nor did it ever hold up bodies as brave."

The sonnets were thought well of, and the captive was glad at the news they gave him of his comrade; and going on with his tale, he said:

"The Goletta and the fort having surrendered, then, the Turks gave orders for the Goletta to be dismantled — because the fort was left in such a state that there was nothing to level. And to do it more quickly and with less labour, they mined it in three places; but with none of them could they blow up what seemed the weakest part, which were the old walls; while everything that was left standing of the new fortification the Fratín had built came down very easily.

"In short, the fleet went back to Constantinople triumphant and victorious; and a few months later my master Uchalí died — the man they called Uchalí Fartax, which means, in the Turkish language, the scabby renegade, because that is what he was. And it is the custom among the Turks to take names from some defect they have or some good quality they possess. And this is because there are among them only four surnames of families, which descend from the Ottoman house, and the rest, as I have said, take their name and surname either from the blemishes of the body or the virtues of the mind.

"And this Scabby Man rowed at the oar as a slave of the Grand Signor for fourteen years, and at more than thirty-four years of age he turned renegade, out of spite because a Turk, while he was at the oar, gave him a slap in the face; and to be able to revenge himself he gave up his faith. And his ability was so great that, without rising by the disgusting means and roads by which most of the Grand Turk's favourites rise, he came to be king of Algiers and afterwards general of the sea, which is the third highest office in that dominion.

"He was a Calabrian by nation, and morally he was a decent man, and treated his captives with a great deal of humanity; he came to have three thousand of them, who after his death were shared out, as he left it in his will, between the Grand Signor — who is also the inheriting son of everybody who dies, and comes in for a share along with the rest of the children the dead man leaves — and his own renegades.

"And I fell to a Venetian renegade whom Uchalí, when he was a ship's boy on a vessel, had taken prisoner, and had loved so much that he was one of his most indulged favourites; and he came to be the cruellest renegade that has ever been seen. He was called Hassan Aga, and came to be very rich and to be king of Algiers; and it was with him that I came from Constantinople, somewhat pleased at being so near Spain — not because I meant to write to anybody about my unfortunate case, but to see whether luck was more favourable to me in Algiers than in Constantinople, where I had already tried a thousand ways of escaping and none of them had come off or come out well. And I meant in Algiers to look for other means of getting what I so much wanted; because hope never abandoned me of having my liberty, and when what I contrived and planned and put into practice did not have an outcome that answered to the intention, then, without abandoning myself, I would invent and look for another hope to keep me going, however weak and feeble it might be.

"With this I kept life going, shut up in a prison or house that the Turks call a bagnio, where they shut up the Christian captives — both the king's and those belonging to private persons; and those they call the store captives, which is like saying captives of the town council, who serve the city in the public works it carries out and in other jobs. And these particular captives have very great difficulty in getting their liberty; for as they belong to the community and have no particular master, there is nobody with whom to arrange their ransom, even if they have one.

"To these bagnios, as I have said, some private people of the town generally bring their captives, chiefly when they are for ransom, because there they keep them at their ease and in safety until their ransom comes. The king's captives who are for ransom likewise do not go out to work with the rest of the gang, except when their ransom is slow in coming; and then, to make them write for it more urgently, they make them work and go for firewood with the others, which is no small labour.

"I, then, was one of the ransom men; because as soon as it was known that I was a captain, although I stated my small means and my lack of property, it was of no use in keeping them from putting me in the number of the gentlemen and the ransom people. They put a chain on me, more as a mark of ransom than to keep me by it; and so I passed my life in that bagnio with a great many other gentlemen and people of standing, marked and held to be for ransom.

"And although hunger and nakedness might weary us at times, and indeed almost always, nothing wearied us so much as hearing and seeing, at every turn, the never-before-seen or heard-of cruelties my master practised on the Christians. Every day he hanged his man, impaled that one, cut off this one's ears; and this on so little occasion, and with so little of any, that the Turks recognised he did it for no other reason than to do it, and because it was his natural disposition to be the murderer of the whole human race.

"The only man who came off well with him was a Spanish soldier called something de Saavedra; who, although he had done things that will stay in the memory of those people for many years, and all of them to get his liberty, was never given a blow by him, or ordered to be given one, or spoken a bad word to. And for the least of the many things he did, we were all afraid he would be impaled, and he was afraid of it himself more than once. And if time allowed it, I would say something now of what this soldier did, which would be enough to entertain you and astonish you a great deal better than the tale of my own history.

"I say, then, that over the courtyard of our prison came the windows of the house of a rich and distinguished Moor; which, as the Moors' windows generally are, were more holes than windows, and even these were covered with very thick, tight lattices.

"It happened, then, that one day, being on a terrace of our prison with three other companions, having jumping matches in our chains to pass the time, and being alone, because all the other Christians had gone out to work, I happened to raise my eyes and saw that out of those closed little windows I have mentioned there appeared a cane, and at the end of it a cloth tied on; and the cane was swaying and moving about, almost as though it were making signs for us to come and take it.

"We looked at it, and one of the men who were with me went and put himself under the cane, to see whether they would let it go, or what they would do; but as soon as he arrived they raised the cane and moved it from side to side, as though they were saying no with the head. The Christian came back, and they lowered it again and made the same movements as before. Another of my companions went, and the same thing happened to him as to the first. Finally the third went, and it went with him as with the first and the second.

"Seeing this, I did not want to leave off trying my luck; and as soon as I came and put myself under the cane, they let it drop, and it fell at my feet inside the bagnio. I hurried to untie the cloth, in which I saw a knot, and inside it came ten cianíis, which are coins of low-grade gold the Moors use, each one worth ten of our reals. Whether I was pleased with the find there is no need to say, since my delight was as great as my astonishment at thinking where that good could come to us from — especially to me, since the signs of their not having wanted to let the cane go except to me plainly said that the favour was being done to me.

"I took my good money, broke the cane, went back to the little terrace, looked at the window, and saw that out of it there came a very white hand, which they opened and shut very quickly. From this we understood, or imagined, that some woman who lived in that house must have done us that kindness; and as a sign that we were grateful for it, we made salaams in the Moorish fashion, bending the head, bowing the body and putting our arms on our breasts.

"A little later they put out of the same window a small cross made of canes, and then took it in again. This sign confirmed us in the belief that some Christian woman must be a captive in that house, and that she was the one who was doing us this kindness; but the whiteness of the hand and the bracelets we saw on it undid this idea, although we supposed she must be a Christian turned renegade, whom their own masters generally take as their lawful wives, and even count it good luck, because they value them more highly than the women of their own nation.

"In all our reasoning we fell a long way wide of the truth of the case; and so all our entertainment from then on was watching and taking our bearings from the window where the star of the cane had appeared to us. But a good fortnight went by in which we did not see it, or the hand either, or any other sign.

"And although in this time we tried with all diligence to find out who lived in that house, and whether there was any Christian renegade woman in it, there was never anybody who could tell us anything except that a distinguished, rich Moor lived there called Hadji Morato, who had been governor of La Pata, which is an office of high standing among them.

"But when we were least expecting any more cianíis to rain from that quarter, we suddenly saw the cane appear, and another cloth on it with a bigger knot; and this was at a time when the bagnio, as the last time, was empty and without people. We made the usual test, each of the same three of us going before I did; but the cane surrendered to nobody but me, for on my arriving they let it fall.

"I untied the knot and found forty Spanish gold crowns and a paper written in Arabic, and at the end of the writing a great cross drawn. I kissed the cross, took the crowns, went back to the terrace, we all made our salaams, the hand appeared again, I made signs that I would read the paper, they shut the window.

"We were all left confused and delighted with what had happened; and as none of us understood Arabic, our desire to understand what the paper contained was great, and greater still was the difficulty of finding somebody to read it.

"In the end I made up my mind to trust a renegade, a native of Murcia, who had declared himself a great friend of mine, and had given pledges between the two of us that obliged him to keep any secret I entrusted to him. Because some renegades, when they mean to go back to Christian country, are apt to bring with them signed papers from important captives, in which they certify, in the form they can, that such-and-such a renegade is a decent man, and that he has always done good to Christians, and that he means to escape at the first opportunity that offers.

"Some men get these certificates with a good intention, others make use of them by chance and by design: for on coming to raid the Christian country, if by any chance they are wrecked or taken prisoner, they pull out their signed papers and say that by those papers it will be seen with what purpose they were coming, which was to stay in the Christian country, and that this was why they had come out privateering with the rest of the Turks. With this they escape that first onslaught and are reconciled to the Church without any harm being done them; and when they see their chance they go back to Barbary to be what they were before. Others there are who use these papers, and get them, with a good intention and do stay in Christian country.

"Well, one of the renegades I have described was this friend of mine, who had certificates from all our companions in which we vouched for him as much as we possibly could; and if the Moors had found these papers on him they would have burnt him alive.

"I learnt that he knew Arabic very well, and not only how to speak it but how to write it; but before revealing myself to him completely, I told him to read me that paper, which I had happened to find in a hole in my quarters. He opened it and stayed a good while looking at it and construing it, muttering between his teeth. I asked him whether he understood it; he told me very well, and that if I wanted him to give it me word for word, I should give him ink and pen so that he could do it better. We at once gave him what he asked for, and he translated it little by little; and on finishing, he said: 'Everything that is here in Spanish, without a letter missing, is what this Moorish paper contains; and it must be noted that where it says Lela Marién it means Our Lady the Virgin Mary.'

"We read the paper, and it went like this:

When I was a little girl, my father had a slave woman who taught me the Christian prayer in my own language, and told me many things about Lela Marién. The Christian woman died, and I know she did not go to the fire but to Allah, because afterwards I saw her twice, and she told me to go to the country of the Christians to see Lela Marién, who loved me very much. I do not know how to go: many Christians have I seen through this window, and none of them has seemed to me a gentleman but you. I am very beautiful and young, and I have a great deal of money to take with me: see whether you can arrange how we may go, and you shall be my husband there if you like; and if you do not like, it will not matter to me, for Lela Marién will give me somebody to marry. I wrote this: look who you give it to to read; do not trust any Moor, because they are all treacherous. This grieves me a great deal: I could wish you would not reveal yourself to anybody, because if my father knows it he will throw me at once into a well and cover me with stones. On the cane I shall put a thread: tie the answer there; and if you have nobody to write Arabic for you, tell me by signs, for Lela Marién will make me understand you. May she and Allah keep you, and that cross which I kiss many times, for so the captive woman told me to do.

"Consider, gentlemen, whether it was reasonable that the words of this paper should astonish us and delight us. And they did so, both of them, in such a way that the renegade realised that this paper had not been found by chance but had really been written to one of us; and so he begged us that, if what he suspected was true, we should trust him and tell him, and he would risk his life for our liberty.

"And saying this, he pulled out of his breast a metal crucifix and with many tears swore by the God that image represented — in whom he, sinner and wicked man though he was, believed well and faithfully — to keep loyalty and secrecy with us in everything we might want to reveal to him. Because it seemed to him, and he almost prophesied, that by means of the woman who had written that paper, he and all of us were to have our liberty, and he was to see himself in the state he so much desired, which was to be brought back into the bosom of Holy Church, his mother, from whom he was cut off and separated like a rotten limb through his ignorance and his sin.

"The renegade said this with so many tears and with signs of so much repentance that we all agreed, and came round to declaring the truth of the case to him; and so we gave him an account of everything, hiding nothing from him. We showed him the little window where the cane appeared, and he marked the house from there, and undertook to take particular and great care to find out who lived in it.

"We agreed likewise that it would be well to answer the Moorish girl's note; and as we had somebody who knew how to do it, the renegade immediately wrote down the words I dictated to him, which were exactly the ones I shall say — because of all the substantial points that happened to me in this affair, not one has gone out of my memory, nor will it go while I have life.

"In fact, what was answered to the Moorish girl was this:

May the true Allah keep you, my lady, and that blessed Marién, who is the true mother of God and is the one who has put it into your heart to go to the Christian country, because she loves you well. Pray to her to be pleased to give you to understand how you may put into practice what she commands you, for she is so good that she will do it. On my part and on the part of all these Christians who are with me, I offer to do everything we can for you, to the death. Do not fail to write to me and let me know what you mean to do, for I shall always answer you; because the great Allah has given us a Christian captive who can speak and write your language as well as you will see by this paper. So that without any fear you may let us know everything you wish. As for what you say, that if you go to the Christian country you are to be my wife, I promise it you as a good Christian; and know that the Christians keep what they promise better than the Moors do. May Allah and Marién his mother be in your keeping, my lady.

"This paper being written and closed, I waited two days for the bagnio to be empty as it usually was, and then went out to the usual place on the little terrace to see whether the cane appeared, which was not long in showing itself. As soon as I saw it, although I could not see who was putting it out, I showed the paper, as though giving them to understand that they should put out the thread; but it was already put on the cane, and I tied the paper to it. And a little later our star appeared again, with the white flag of peace of the little bundle. They let it drop, and I picked it up, and found in the cloth, in coin of every kind of silver and gold, more than fifty crowns — which fifty times over doubled our delight and confirmed our hope of getting our liberty.

"That same night our renegade came back and told us he had learnt that in that house lived the very Moor we had been told was called Hadji Morato, extremely rich in every way, who had one daughter only, heiress to the whole of his property; and that it was the general opinion throughout the city that she was the most beautiful woman in Barbary. And that many of the viceroys who came there had asked for her as a wife, and she had never wanted to marry. And he also learnt that she had had a Christian slave woman, who was already dead. All of which agreed with what came in the paper.

"We at once went into council with the renegade about what plan should be adopted for getting the Moorish girl away and coming, all of us, to Christian country; and in the end it was agreed for the time being that we should wait for Zoraida's next word — for that was the name of the woman who now wants to be called María — because we saw plainly that she, and nobody else, was the one who was to find a way through all those difficulties. When we had settled this, the renegade said we should not be distressed, for he would either lose his life or set us at liberty.

"For four days the bagnio was full of people, which was why the cane was four days in appearing; at the end of which, in the usual emptiness of the bagnio, it appeared with the cloth so pregnant that it promised a most fortunate delivery. The cane and the cloth bent down to me, and I found in it another paper and a hundred gold crowns, with no other money at all. The renegade was there; we gave him the paper to read inside our quarters, and he said it went like this:

I do not know, my lord, how to arrange for us to go to Spain, nor has Lela Marién told me, although I have asked her. What can be done is that I shall give you through this window a great deal of gold money: ransom yourself with it, and your friends, and let one of you go to Christian country and buy a boat there and come back for the rest. And I shall be found in my father's garden, which is at the Bab Azoun gate, near the shore, where I am to be all this summer with my father and my servants. From there, by night, you can get me out without any fear and take me to the boat. And remember that you are to be my husband, because if not I shall ask Marién to punish you. If you trust nobody to go for the boat, ransom yourself and go, for I know that you will come back better than another, since you are a gentleman and a Christian. Try to find out where the garden is; and when you walk that way I shall know that the bagnio is empty, and I shall give you a great deal of money. Allah keep you, my lord.

"This is what the second paper said and contained. Which everybody seeing, each one offered to be the one who was ransomed, and promised to go and come back with complete punctuality; and I offered to do the same. To all of which the renegade objected, saying that on no account would he consent to any one of them going free until they all went together, because experience had shown him how badly free men kept the promises they made in captivity.

"For a great many times some important captives had used that remedy, ransoming one man to go to Valencia or Majorca with money to be able to fit out a boat and come back for the men who had ransomed him, and they had never come back; because the liberty they had got and the fear of losing it again rubbed out of their memories every obligation in the world. And in confirmation of the truth he was telling us, he told us briefly a case that had happened at almost that same time to some Christian gentlemen, the strangest that ever happened in those parts, where at every turn things of great terror and astonishment happen.

"In fact he came round to saying that what could and ought to be done was that the money that was to be given for ransoming the Christian should be given to him to buy a boat there in Algiers, on the pretext of setting up as a merchant and trader at Tetuan and on that coast; and that once he was master of the boat, a plan would easily be found for getting them out of the bagnio and putting them all aboard.

"The more so as, if the Moorish girl gave money to ransom them all, as she said, then once they were free it would be the easiest thing in the world to take ship even in the middle of the day. And that the greatest difficulty that presented itself was that the Moors do not allow any renegade to buy or own a boat, unless it is a big vessel for going privateering, because they are afraid that a man who buys a boat — especially if he is a Spaniard — only wants it to go to the Christian country. But that he would smooth over this obstacle by getting a Tagarin Moor to go partners with him in the ownership of the boat and in the profits of the merchandise; and under this cover he would come to be master of the boat, with which he counted everything else as done.

"And although it had seemed better to me and my companions to send for the boat to Majorca, as the Moorish girl said, we did not dare contradict him, being afraid that if we did not do what he said he would give us away and put us in danger of losing our lives if he revealed Zoraida's dealings — for whose life we would all have given our own.

"And so we decided to put ourselves in God's hands and in the renegade's; and at that same moment an answer was sent to Zoraida, telling her that we would do everything she advised, because she had thought it out as well as if Lela Marién had told her, and that it lay with her alone to put the business off or to put it into practice at once. I offered myself afresh to be her husband. And with this, another day when the bagnio happened to be empty, at different times, with the cane and the cloth, she gave us two thousand gold crowns and a paper in which she said that on the first jumá — which is Friday — she was going to her father's garden, and that before she went she would give us more money; and that if that was not enough we should let her know, and she would give us as much as we asked for, because her father had so much that he would not miss it — the more so as she had the keys of everything.

"We at once gave five hundred crowns to the renegade to buy the boat. With eight hundred I ransomed myself, giving the money to a Valencian merchant who happened to be in Algiers at the time, who ransomed me from the king by taking me on his word, giving his own word that with the first vessel that came from Valencia he would pay my ransom. Because if he had handed over the money at once, it would have given the king grounds for suspecting that my ransom had been in Algiers for a long time and that the merchant had kept quiet about it for his own profit. In fact my master was so full of quibbles that on no account did I dare have the money paid out at once.

"On the Thursday before the Friday when the beautiful Zoraida was to go to the garden, she gave us another thousand crowns and let us know she was going, begging me that if I was ransomed I should find out at once where her father's garden was, and that in any case I should look for an occasion to go there and see her. I answered her in a few words that I would do so, and that she should take care to commend us to Lela Marién with all those prayers the captive woman had taught her.

"This done, they arranged for our three companions to be ransomed, so as to make it easier to get out of the bagnio, and because, seeing me ransomed and themselves not, when there was money, they might be upset and the devil might persuade them to do something to Zoraida's harm. For although their being who they were might have made me safe from this fear, still I did not want to put the business at risk; and so I had them ransomed by the same arrangement as I ransomed myself, handing all the money to the merchant so that he could stand surety with certainty and safety — to whom we never revealed our dealings and our secret, because of the danger there was."

Chapter 41: In Which the Captive Still Continues His Story

"Not a fortnight went by before our renegade had bought a very good boat, big enough for more than thirty people; and to make his business safe and give it a colour, he decided to make — as he did make — a voyage to a place called Sargel, which is thirty leagues from Algiers towards Oran, where there is a great trade in dried figs. Two or three times he made this voyage in the company of the Tagarin I have mentioned. Tagarins is what they call in Barbary the Moors of Aragon, and the ones from Granada they call Mudéjares; and in the kingdom of Fez they call the Mudéjares elches, who are the people that king most makes use of in war.

"I say, then, that every time he passed with his boat he anchored in a little cove that was not two crossbow shots from the garden where Zoraida was waiting; and there the renegade would station himself very deliberately with the young Moors who pulled at the oar, either to say his prayers or as though rehearsing in play what he meant to do in earnest. And so he would go to Zoraida's garden and ask her father for fruit, and her father would give it him without knowing him.

"And although he would have liked to speak to Zoraida, as he afterwards told me, and to tell her that he was the man who by my orders was to take her to the Christian country, and that she should be contented and easy in her mind, it was never possible for him — because Moorish women do not let themselves be seen by any Moor or Turk unless their husband or their father orders it. With Christian captives they let themselves be dealt with and talked to, even more than would be reasonable; and I should have been sorry if he had spoken to her, for perhaps he would have alarmed her by letting her see that her business was in the mouths of renegades.

"But God, who was ordering it another way, gave no opportunity for our renegade's good intention. And he, seeing how safely he came and went to Sargel, and that he anchored when and how and where he liked, and that the Tagarin his companion had no will but what his own ordered, and that I was already ransomed, and that all that was lacking was to find some Christians to pull at the oar, told me to look out which men I wanted to bring with me apart from the ransomed ones, and to have them spoken to for the coming Friday, which he had settled on for our departure.

"Seeing this, I spoke to twelve Spaniards, all of them strong men at the oar, and of the sort who could get out of the city most freely; and it was no small matter to find so many at that juncture, because there were twenty vessels out privateering and they had taken all the oar-men away — and these would not have been found either if their master had not stayed that summer without going out privateering, to finish a galliot he had on the stocks.

"To these men I said nothing except that on the coming Friday afternoon they should go out one by one, without being noticed, and make their way towards Hadji Morato's garden, and wait there for me until I came. I gave this instruction to each of them separately, with orders that even if they saw other Christians there, they should tell them nothing except that I had ordered them to wait in that place.

"This done, I had another thing to do, which was the one that mattered most to me: and that was to let Zoraida know the point the business had reached, so that she should be forewarned and on her guard, and should not be startled if we came on her suddenly before the time when she could imagine the Christians' boat could be back. And so I decided to go to the garden and see whether I could speak to her; and on the pretext of gathering some herbs, one day before my departure I went there.

"And the first person I met was her father, who said to me, in a language which throughout Barbary, and even in Constantinople, is found between captives and Moors — which is neither Moorish nor Castilian nor of any other nation, but a mixture of all the languages, with which we all understand each other — I say, then, that in this manner of speech he asked me what I was looking for in that garden of his, and whose man I was. I answered him that I was a slave of Arnaute Mamí — and this because I knew very well that he was a great friend of his — and that I was looking for all sorts of herbs to make a salad. He asked me next whether I was a man for ransom or not, and how much my master was asking for me.

"While we were in all these questions and answers, the beautiful Zoraida came out of the garden house, who had seen me a long while before; and as Moorish women make no scruple at all about showing themselves to Christians, nor do they avoid them, as I have said, she thought nothing of coming to where her father was with me. Indeed, as soon as her father saw her coming, and coming slowly, he called her and told her to come up.

"It would be too much for me to describe now the great beauty, the elegance, the splendid and rich adornment with which my beloved Zoraida showed herself to my eyes. I shall only say that more pearls hung from her lovely neck, ears and hair than she had hairs on her head. On her ankles, which she wore bare in their fashion, she wore two carcajes — for that is what the bangles or anklets are called in Moorish — of the purest gold, with so many diamonds set in them that she afterwards told me her father valued them at ten thousand doubloons; and the ones she wore on her wrists were worth as much again.

"The pearls were in great quantity and very fine, because the greatest finery and splendour of Moorish women is to adorn themselves with rich pearls and seed-pearl; and so there are more pearls and seed-pearl among the Moors than among all the other nations. And Zoraida's father had the reputation of having a great many, and the best in Algiers, and of likewise having more than two hundred thousand Spanish crowns — of all of which she was mistress who is now mistress of me.

"Whether with all this adornment she could then look beautiful or not may be guessed from what is left of her after so many hardships, and what she must have been in her prosperity. Because it is well known that some women's beauty has its days and its seasons, and requires circumstances to lessen it or increase it; and it is a natural thing that the passions of the mind should raise it or lower it, though most often they destroy it.

"I say, in short, that she came then dressed to the height and beautiful to the height — or at least she seemed to me the most beautiful I had seen until then. And with this, seeing the obligations she had put me under, it seemed to me that I had before me a deity from heaven, come down to earth for my delight and my rescue.

"As soon as she came up, her father told her in their language that I was a captive of his friend Arnaute Mamí and had come to look for salad herbs. She took it up, and in that mixture of languages I have described she asked me whether I was a gentleman and what the reason was that I did not ransom myself. I answered her that I was already ransomed, and that from the price she could see what my master valued me at, since he had been given fifteen hundred zoltanís for me.

"To which she answered: 'Truly, if you had belonged to my father, I would have made him refuse twice that for you; because you Christians always lie in everything you say, and make yourselves out poor in order to cheat the Moors.'

"'That may well be, my lady,' I answered her, 'but truly I have dealt honestly with my master, and I deal honestly, and shall deal honestly, with everybody in the world.'

"'And when do you go?' said Zoraida.

"'Tomorrow, I think,' I said, 'because there is a French vessel here that sails tomorrow, and I mean to go in her.'

"'Would it not be better,' replied Zoraida, 'to wait until ships come from Spain, and go with them instead of with the French, who are no friends of yours?'

"'No,' I answered; 'although if it is true, as there is news, that a Spanish ship is on its way, I would still wait for her, except that it is more certain I shall be leaving tomorrow. Because the desire I have to see myself in my own country, and with the people I love, is so great that it will not let me wait for another opportunity, however much better, if it is slow in coming.'

"'You must without doubt be married in your own country,' said Zoraida, 'and that is why you want to go and be with your wife.'

"'I am not married,' I answered, 'but I have given my word to marry as soon as I get there.'

"'And is the lady beautiful to whom you gave it?' said Zoraida.

"'So beautiful,' I answered, 'that to describe her and tell you the truth, she is very like you.'

"At this her father laughed heartily and said: 'By Allah, Christian, she must be very beautiful indeed if she is like my daughter, who is the most beautiful woman in this whole kingdom. If you do not believe it, look at her carefully and you will see that I am telling you the truth.'

"Zoraida's father served us as interpreter for most of these words and speeches, being the better linguist; because although she spoke the bastard language which, as I have said, is used there, she made her meaning clearer by signs than by words.

"While we were in these and a great many other exchanges, a Moor came running up and said at the top of his voice that four Turks had jumped over the hedges or walls of the garden and were picking the fruit, although it was not ripe. The old man was startled, and so was Zoraida; because the fear the Moors have of the Turks is common and almost natural, especially of the soldiers, who are so insolent and have so much power over the Moors who are subject to them that they treat them worse than if they were their own slaves.

"I say, then, that her father said to Zoraida: 'Daughter, get back to the house and shut yourself in, while I go and speak to these dogs; and you, Christian, look for your herbs and go, and good luck to you, and may Allah take you safely to your own country.'

"I bowed, and he went off to look for the Turks, leaving me alone with Zoraida, who began to make as though to go where her father had ordered her. But her father had hardly been hidden by the trees of the garden when she turned to me with her eyes full of tears and said: 'Ámexi, Christian, ámexi?' — which means: 'Are you going, Christian, are you going?'

"I answered her: 'Yes, my lady, but on no account without you. Expect me on the first jumá, and do not be alarmed when you see us; for beyond any doubt we shall go to the Christian country.'

"I said this to her in such a way that she understood very well all the words that passed between us; and putting one arm round my neck, she began to walk towards the house with fainting steps. And luck willed — and it might have been very bad luck if heaven had not ordered it otherwise — that as the two of us were going along in the manner and posture I have described, with one arm round my neck, her father, who was already coming back from sending off the Turks, saw us in the state and manner we were going in, and we saw that he had seen us.

"But Zoraida, being alert and quick-witted, would not take her arm off my neck; on the contrary, she came closer to me and put her head on my breast, bending her knees a little, giving clear signs and appearances of fainting; and I likewise gave it to be understood that I was holding her up against my will.

"Her father came running to where we were, and seeing his daughter in that state, asked her what was the matter; but as she did not answer him, her father said: 'Without any doubt she has fainted with the shock of these dogs coming in.' And taking her from mine, he leaned her against his own breast; and she, giving a sigh and with her eyes not yet dry of tears, said again: 'Ámexi, Christian, ámexi' — 'Go, Christian, go.'

"To which her father answered: 'It does not matter, daughter, that the Christian should go; he has done you no harm, and the Turks have gone now. Let nothing alarm you, for there is nothing that can distress you, since, as I have told you, the Turks went back the way they came at my request.'

"'They alarmed her, sir, as you say,' I said to her father; 'but since she says I am to go, I do not want to distress her. Stay in peace, and with your leave I shall come back, if it should be necessary, for herbs to this garden; for according to my master there are none better for salad anywhere than here.'

"'You may come back for as many as you like,' answered Hadji Morato; 'for my daughter does not say this because you or any of the Christians annoyed her, but because in meaning to say that the Turks should go, she said that you should go — or because it was time for you to look for your herbs.'

"With this I took my leave of the two of them at once; and she, her soul being torn out of her by the look of it, went off with her father. And I, on the pretext of looking for herbs, went thoroughly and at my leisure round the whole garden: I looked carefully at the ways in and out, and at the strength of the house, and at the conveniences that might offer for making the whole of our business easier. This done, I came away and gave the renegade and my companions an account of everything that had happened; and by now I could not wait for the hour of seeing myself enjoying without alarm the good fortune that luck was offering me in the beautiful and lovely Zoraida.

"In the end the time passed and the day and hour we so much wanted came; and all of us following the order and plan we had many times settled on with careful consideration and long discussion, we had the good outcome we wanted. Because on the Friday that followed the day I talked with Zoraida in the garden, our renegade at nightfall anchored the boat almost opposite where the most beautiful Zoraida was.

"The Christians who were to pull at the oar were already prepared and hidden in various places all round about there. They were all in suspense and excitement, waiting for me, eager by now to attack the vessel they had in front of their eyes; because they did not know about the renegade's arrangement, but thought that they had to get and win their liberty by strength of arm, taking the lives of the Moors who were in the boat.

"It happened, then, that as soon as I showed myself, and my companions, all the rest who were hidden and saw us came up to us. This was at an hour when the city was already shut and nobody appeared anywhere in that whole stretch of country.

"When we were together, we were in doubt whether it would be better to go first for Zoraida or to overpower first the Moorish rowers who pulled at the oar in the boat. And while we were in this doubt, our renegade came up to us asking what we were waiting for, since it was time now and all his Moors were off their guard and most of them asleep. We told him what we were hesitating over, and he said that the thing that mattered most was to take the vessel first, which could be done with the greatest ease and without any danger, and that then we could go for Zoraida.

"What he said seemed good to all of us; and so, without delaying any further, with him leading, we came to the vessel; and jumping in first, he put his hand to a scimitar and said in Moorish: 'Let none of you move from here unless he wants it to cost him his life.' By this time almost all the Christians had got in. The Moors, who were of little spirit, hearing their captain speak in that fashion, were appalled; and without a single one of them putting a hand to his weapons — for they had few or almost none — they let themselves be tied hand and foot by the Christians without saying a word; which the Christians did very quickly, threatening the Moors that if they raised their voices in any way whatever, they would put the whole lot of them to the sword on the spot.

"This being done, half of our men staying behind to guard them, the rest of us, with the renegade again leading the way, went to Hadji Morato's garden; and good luck willed that on getting there to open the gate, it opened as easily as if it had not been shut. And so, with great quietness and silence, we got to the house without being heard by anybody.

"The most beautiful Zoraida was waiting for us at a window; and as soon as she heard people, she asked in a low voice whether we were nizarani — as much as to say or to ask whether we were Christians. I answered her that we were, and that she should come down. When she recognised me she did not hesitate a moment, but without answering me a word came down in an instant, opened the door and showed herself to us all, so beautiful and so richly dressed that I cannot manage to describe it.

"As soon as I saw her I took one of her hands and began to kiss it, and the renegade did the same, and my two comrades; and the rest, who did not know the case, did what they saw us do, so that it looked for all the world as if we were thanking her and acknowledging her as the mistress of our liberty.

"The renegade asked her in the Moorish language whether her father was in the garden. She answered that he was, and that he was asleep.

"'Then it will be necessary to wake him,' replied the renegade, 'and to take him with us, and everything of value there is in this beautiful garden.'

"'No,' she said. 'My father is not to be touched on any account, and there is nothing else in this house except what I am taking, which is so much that there will be plenty for you all to be left rich and contented; and wait a little and you shall see.'

"And saying this she went in again, saying she would be back very soon and that we should stay still without making any noise. I asked the renegade what had passed between them, and he told me; and I told him that in nothing was more to be done than what Zoraida wanted.

"And just as she was coming back loaded with a little chest full of gold crowns — so many that she could hardly hold it up — bad luck would have it that her father woke in the meantime and heard the noise going on in the garden. And leaning out of the window, he immediately recognised that all the people in it were Christians; and giving a great many loud, wild shouts, he began to cry in Arabic: 'Christians, Christians! Thieves, thieves!' At which shouts we were all thrown into the greatest and most fearful confusion.

"But the renegade, seeing the danger we were in and how much it mattered to him to succeed in that enterprise before we were heard, went up very quickly to where Hadji Morato was, and some of us went up along with him; for I did not dare to leave Zoraida, who had let herself fall into my arms as though in a faint.

"In short, those who went up managed so well that in a moment they came down with Hadji Morato, bringing him with his hands tied and a handkerchief put in his mouth, which did not let him say a word, threatening him that speaking would cost him his life. When his daughter saw him she covered her eyes so as not to see him, and her father was appalled, not knowing how willingly she had put herself into our hands. But feet being what was most needed then, with diligence and speed we got into the boat, where those who had stayed in her were waiting for us, afraid of some bad turn happening to us.

"Hardly two hours of the night could have gone by when we were all in the boat, in which the tying was taken off Zoraida's father's hands and the cloth out of his mouth; but the renegade told him again not to say a word, or they would take his life. He, seeing his daughter there, began to sigh most tenderly, and more so when he saw that I was holding her tightly in my arms and that she, without defending herself or complaining or drawing away, stayed still. But for all that he kept quiet, so that they should not carry out the many threats the renegade was making him.

"Seeing herself in the boat, then, and that we were about to put the oars in the water, and seeing her father there and the other Moors who were tied up, Zoraida told the renegade to ask me to do her the kindness of loosing those Moors and giving her father his liberty, because she would throw herself into the sea sooner than see before her eyes, and on her account, a father who had loved her so much taken away captive.

"The renegade told me; and I answered that I was very willing. But he answered that it was not advisable, because if they were left there they would raise the alarm in the countryside at once and rouse the city, and would be the cause of light frigates coming out to look for them and cutting them off by land and sea, so that we should not be able to escape; and that what could be done was to give them their liberty on reaching the first Christian land. We were all of this opinion; and Zoraida, who was given an account of it with the reasons that moved us not to do at once what she wanted, was also satisfied.

"And then, with joyful silence and glad diligence, each of our brave rowers took his oar, and we began, commending ourselves to God with all our hearts, to steer for the islands of Majorca, which is the nearest Christian land.

"But because of the north wind blowing a little and the sea being somewhat rough, it was not possible to hold the course for Majorca, and we were obliged to let ourselves go along the coast towards Oran, not without a great deal of distress on our part, for fear of being spotted from the town of Sargel, which lies on that coast sixty miles from Algiers. And we were likewise afraid of meeting in that stretch one of the galliots that ordinarily come with merchandise from Tetuan — although each of us on his own, and all of us together, presumed that if we met a merchant galliot, so long as it was not one of those that go privateering, not only should we not be lost but we should take a vessel in which we could finish our voyage more safely.

"While we were sailing, Zoraida kept her head between my hands so as not to see her father, and I felt that she was calling on Lela Marién to help us.

"We must have sailed a good thirty miles when day broke on us, about three musket shots off the land, all of which we saw was deserted and with nobody to spot us. But for all that, by strength of arm we worked our way a little further out to sea, which was somewhat calmer by now; and having got out almost two leagues, orders were given for the men to row in watches while we ate something, for the boat was well provisioned. But the rowers said this was no time to take any rest, and that those who were not rowing should give them something to eat, since they would not let go of the oars on any account.

"It was done so; and at this a steady wind began to blow, which obliged us to make sail at once and leave the oar and head for Oran, it being impossible to make any other voyage. It was all done with the greatest speed; and so, under sail, we ran more than eight miles an hour, with no other fear at all except that of meeting a vessel that was out privateering."

"We gave the Moorish rowers something to eat, and the renegade comforted them by telling them that they were not being taken away as captives, and that at the first opportunity they would be given their liberty. The same was said to Zoraida's father, who answered:

"'Any other thing I might expect and believe of your generosity and good conduct, Christians; but as for giving me my liberty, do not take me for so simple as to imagine it. For you never put yourselves in danger to take it from me in order to give it back so generously — especially knowing who I am, and the profit that can come to you from giving it me. Which profit, if you will name it, I offer you here and now whatever you may want for me and for that unfortunate daughter of mine; or, if not, for her alone, who is the greatest and the better part of my soul.'

"On saying this he began to weep so bitterly that he moved us all to compassion and forced Zoraida to look at him; and she, seeing him weep, was so softened that she got up from my feet and went to embrace her father; and putting her face against his, the two of them began such tender weeping that a great many of us who were there joined them in it.

"But when her father saw her dressed as if for a feast and with so many jewels on her, he said to her in their language: 'What is this, daughter? Yesterday at nightfall, before this terrible misfortune we are in came upon us, I saw you in your ordinary house clothes; and now, without your having had time to dress, and without any glad news having been given you to celebrate by adorning and beautifying yourself, I see you turned out in the best clothes I knew how and was able to give you when fortune was more favourable to us. Answer me this, for it holds me more in suspense and astonishment than the very misfortune I find myself in.'

"Everything the Moor said to his daughter the renegade translated for us, and she answered him not a word. But when he saw at one side of the boat the little chest where she used to keep her jewels — which he well knew he had left in Algiers and had not brought to the garden — he was still more bewildered, and asked her how that chest had come into our hands and what was inside it.

"To which the renegade, without waiting for Zoraida to answer him, answered: 'Do not weary yourself, sir, in asking Zoraida your daughter so many things, because with one answer of mine I shall satisfy you on all of them. And so I want you to know that she is a Christian, and that she has been the file for our chains and the liberty of our captivity. She is here of her own free will, as glad — as far as I can imagine — to see herself in this state as a man who comes out of darkness into light, out of death into life, and out of pain into glory.'

"'Is what this man says true, daughter?' said the Moor.

"'It is,' answered Zoraida.

"'So in fact,' replied the old man, 'you are a Christian, and the one who has put her father into the power of his enemies?'

"To which Zoraida answered: 'The one who is a Christian I am; but not the one who has put you in this position, because my wish never went so far as to leave you or to do you harm, but to do myself good.'

"'And what good is it that you have done yourself, daughter?'

"'That,' she answered, 'you must ask of Lela Marién, for she will be able to tell you better than I can.'

"The Moor had hardly heard this when with incredible speed he threw himself headfirst into the sea, where without any doubt he would have drowned if the long, encumbering robe he was wearing had not held him up a little on the water. Zoraida cried out for them to get him out, and so we all hurried up; and taking hold of him by his robe, we pulled him out half drowned and unconscious — at which Zoraida was so distressed that, as though he were already dead, she made a tender and sorrowful lament over him.

"We turned him face downwards, he brought up a great deal of water, and he came to himself at the end of two hours; during which, the wind having changed, it suited us to turn back towards land and to pull hard at the oars so as not to run aground on it. But our good luck willed that we came to a cove that lies beside a little promontory or cape which the Moors call La Cava Rumía, which in our language means the wicked Christian woman; and it is a tradition among the Moors that the Cava, through whom Spain was lost, is buried in that place, because cava in their language means wicked woman and rumía Christian. And they even count it a bad omen to come and anchor there when necessity forces them to it, because they never anchor there without it — although for us it was no shelter of a wicked woman but a safe harbour of rescue, the sea being as rough as it was.

"We put our sentries ashore and never let go of the oars; we ate some of what the renegade had provided, and prayed to God and to Our Lady with all our hearts to help us and favour us so that we might come happily to the end of so fortunate a beginning. Orders were given, at Zoraida's entreaty, that we should put her father ashore and all the other Moors who came tied up there, because she had not the heart, and her tender feelings could not bear, to see her father tied up before her eyes and those people of her own country prisoners. We promised her to do so at the time of our leaving, since there was no danger in leaving them in that place, which was uninhabited.

"Our prayers were not so empty that they were not heard by heaven; for in our favour the wind then changed, the sea grew calm, and invited us to go back cheerfully to going on with the voyage we had begun.

"Seeing this, we untied the Moors and put them ashore one by one, at which they were astonished. But on coming to put Zoraida's father ashore, who was by now fully in his senses, he said:

"'Why do you think, Christians, that this wicked female is glad that you should give me my liberty? Do you think it is out of pity for me? Certainly not, but she does it because of the obstacle my presence will be to her when she wants to put her wicked desires into practice. And do not think that what has moved her to change her religion is her understanding that yours has the advantage of ours, but her knowing that in your country immodesty is practised more freely than in ours.'

"And turning to Zoraida — while I and another Christian held him fast by both arms, so that he should not do something wild — he said to her: 'Oh, shameless girl and ill-advised child! Where are you going, blind and out of your wits, in the power of these dogs, our natural enemies? Cursed be the hour in which I begot you, and cursed be the indulgences and pleasures I have brought you up in!'

"But seeing that he looked like not finishing so quickly, I hurried to put him ashore; and from there he went on at the top of his voice with his curses and laments, praying to Mohammed to pray to Allah to destroy us, confound us and finish us. And when, having made sail, we could no longer hear his words, we saw his actions, which were tearing at his beard, pulling out his hair and rolling on the ground. But once he raised his voice in such a way that we could make out that he was saying: 'Come back, beloved daughter, come back to land, for I forgive you everything. Hand those men that money, which is theirs now, and come back and comfort this poor sad father of yours, who will leave his life on this deserted sand if you leave him!'

"All of which Zoraida heard, and felt all of it, and wept over it; and she could not manage to say or answer him a word except: 'May it please Allah, my father, that Lela Marién, who has been the cause of my being a Christian, may comfort you in your sorrow. Allah knows well that I could not do anything other than what I have done, and that these Christians owe nothing to my will; for even if I had wanted not to come with them and to stay at home, it would have been impossible for me, so hard did my soul press me to carry out this thing which seems to me as good as you, beloved father, judge it wicked.'

"This she said at a time when her father could not hear her, and we could not see him any more. And so, comforting Zoraida, we all attended to our voyage, which the wind itself made so easy for us that we took it as certain that at daybreak the next day we should see ourselves on the shores of Spain.

"But as good fortune seldom or never comes pure and simple, without being accompanied or followed by some evil that disturbs it or startles it, our luck willed — or perhaps the curses the Moor had thrown at his daughter, which are always to be feared, whatever father they come from — our luck willed, I say, that when we were well out to sea, and almost three hours of the night had gone by, going along with the sail spread from top to bottom and the oars lashed, because the favourable wind saved us the labour of needing them, by the light of the moon, which was shining clearly, we saw close to us a round ship which, with all her sails spread and her helm a little to windward, was crossing in front of us — and this so close that we were obliged to strike sail so as not to run into her, and they likewise put their helm hard over to give us room to pass.

"They had come to the ship's side to ask us who we were and where we were sailing and where we came from. But because they asked us this in French, our renegade said: 'Let nobody answer; for these are certainly French corsairs, who prey on everything.'

"Because of this warning, nobody answered a word; and having gone a little way ahead, so that the ship was now to leeward, they suddenly let off two pieces of artillery, and by the look of it both of them were loaded with chain-shot, because with one they cut our mast through the middle and brought it down along with the sail into the sea; and immediately, firing off another piece, the ball came and struck the middle of our boat, so that it opened her right up, without doing any other harm. But as we saw ourselves going to the bottom, we all began to shout for help and to beg the men in the ship to take us in, because we were sinking.

"They then struck sail; and putting the skiff or boat into the sea, as many as twelve Frenchmen got into it, well armed with their muskets and their matches lit, and so came alongside ours. And seeing how few we were and how the boat was sinking, they took us in, saying that this had happened to us for having used the discourtesy of not answering them. Our renegade took the chest with Zoraida's riches and dropped it into the sea, without anybody's noticing what he did.

"In short, we all went over to the French, who, after informing themselves of everything they wanted to know about us, as though they had been our chief enemies, stripped us of everything we had; and from Zoraida they took even the anklets she wore on her feet. But what they did to Zoraida did not distress me as much as the fear I had that they would pass from taking her most rich and precious jewels to taking the jewel that was worth most and that she prized most. But the desires of those people do not extend beyond money, and their greed never sees itself satisfied with that; which then went so far that they would even have taken the captives' clothes off us if they had been of any use to them.

"And there was an opinion among them that we should all be thrown into the sea wrapped in a sail, because they meant to trade at some ports in Spain under the name of Bretons, and if they took us alive they would be punished when their theft was discovered. But the captain, who was the one who had stripped my beloved Zoraida, said he was satisfied with the prize he had, and that he did not want to touch at any Spanish port but to pass the straits of Gibraltar by night, or as best he could, and to go to La Rochelle, which he had sailed from. And so they agreed to give us the skiff of their ship, and everything needed for the short voyage we had left — which they did the next day, in sight of the land of Spain; at which sight all our distresses and poverties were completely forgotten, as though they had never happened to us: such is the pleasure of getting back a lost liberty.

"It could have been about midday when they put us into the boat, giving us two barrels of water and some ship's biscuit.
