And the captain, moved by I do not know what compassion, as the most beautiful Zoraida was getting in, gave her as much as forty gold crowns, and would not let his soldiers take from her these same clothes she now has on.

"We got into the boat; we thanked them for the kindness they were doing us, showing ourselves more grateful than aggrieved. They stood out to sea, holding their course for the straits; and we, without looking to any other pole star than the land that showed in front of us, rowed so hard that at sunset we were so close that we could easily, as it seemed to us, have got there before it was quite dark. But as the moon did not appear that night and the sky showed dark, and as we did not know the district we were in, it did not seem to us a safe thing to run ashore, as many of us thought we should — saying that we ought to make for it even if it was among rocks and far from any town, because in that way we should settle the fear it was reasonable to have that corsair vessels from Tetuan might be about in those parts: men who spend the night in Barbary and the dawn on the coasts of Spain, and generally take a prize and go home to sleep again. But of the conflicting opinions, the one adopted was that we should approach little by little and, if the calmness of the sea allowed it, land wherever we could.

"So it was done; and it must have been a little before midnight when we came to the foot of an enormous, high mountain, not so close to the sea that it did not leave a little space for landing comfortably. We ran onto the sand, went ashore, kissed the ground, and with tears of the gladdest happiness we all gave thanks to God, our Lord, for the incomparable good he had done us.

"We got the provisions out of the boat, hauled her up on land and went a great way up the mountain; because even there we were still, and we still could not settle our hearts, nor could we quite believe that it was Christian land that was now holding us up.

"Day broke later, in my opinion, than we would have wished. We finished climbing the whole mountain to see whether any settlement could be made out from up there, or any shepherds' huts; but however far we stretched our eyes, we made out neither settlement nor person nor path nor road. For all that, we decided to go inland, since it could not fail to happen that we should soon find somebody to give us news of the country.

"But what wearied me most was seeing Zoraida going on foot over those rough places; for although I once put her on my shoulders, my weariness tired her more than her rest rested her; and so she would never again let me take that labour on. And with a great deal of patience and signs of cheerfulness, I always leading her by the hand, we must have gone a little less than a quarter of a league when there came to our ears the sound of a small bell — a clear sign that there was a flock somewhere near.

"And all of us looking carefully to see whether anybody appeared, we saw at the foot of a cork tree a young shepherd, who with great calm and unconcern was carving a stick with a knife. We shouted; and he, raising his head, sprang lightly to his feet; and, as we afterwards learnt, the first people who came into his view were the renegade and Zoraida. And as he saw them in Moorish dress, he thought that the whole of Barbary was down on him; and diving into the wood ahead with extraordinary speed, he began to give the loudest shouts in the world, saying: 'Moors, there are Moors in the country! Moors, Moors! To arms, to arms!'

"At these shouts we were all left in confusion, and did not know what to do with ourselves. But considering that the shepherd's shouts were bound to raise the countryside, and that the coastguard cavalry were bound to come at once to see what it was, we decided that the renegade should take off his Turkish clothes and put on a captive's jacket that one of us gave him at once, although he was left in his shirt. And so, commending ourselves to God, we went by the same road we had seen the shepherd take, expecting all the time that the coastguard cavalry would come down on us.

"And our expectation did not deceive us; because two hours had not gone by when, having come out of those thickets onto a plain, we made out as many as fifty horsemen coming towards us at great speed at a half-gallop. And as soon as we saw them we stood still waiting for them. But when they came up and saw, instead of the Moors they were looking for, so many poor Christians, they were bewildered; and one of them asked us whether we were by any chance the reason why a shepherd had called to arms.

"'Yes,' I said; and I was about to begin telling him my story, and where we came from and who we were, when one of the Christians who came with us recognised the horseman who had asked us the question, and said, without letting me say another word: 'Thanks be to God, gentlemen, who has brought us to so good a place! Because if I am not mistaken, the ground we are treading is that of Vélez Málaga — unless the years of my captivity have taken from my memory the recollection that you, sir, who are asking us who we are, are Pedro de Bustamante, my uncle.'

"The Christian captive had hardly said this when the horseman threw himself off his horse and came to embrace the young man, saying: 'Nephew of my soul and my life, I know you now; and I have wept for you as dead, I and my sister your mother and all your family, who are still alive; and God has been pleased to give them life so that they may enjoy the pleasure of seeing you. We knew already that you were in Algiers, and by the signs and appearance of your clothes and those of everybody in this company, I understand that you have had a miraculous deliverance.'

"'So it is,' answered the young man, 'and there will be time left for us to tell you all about it.'

"As soon as the horsemen understood that we were Christian captives, they got down off their horses, and each of them offered us his own to take us to the city of Vélez Málaga, which was a league and a half from there. Some of them went back to fetch the boat to the city, when we told them where we had left it; others took us up behind them, and Zoraida rode behind the Christian's uncle.

"The whole town came out to receive us, having already heard the news of our coming from somebody who had gone on ahead. They were not astonished at seeing freed captives or captive Moors, because all the people of that coast are used to seeing both the one and the other; but they were astonished at Zoraida's beauty, which at that instant and season was at its height, both with the weariness of the journey and with the gladness of finding herself at last in Christian country without the alarm of being lost. And this had brought such colour into her face that, unless my love was deceiving me then, I shall dare to say that there was no lovelier creature in the world — at least that I had ever seen.

"We went straight to the church to give thanks to God for the favour we had received; and as soon as Zoraida came into it, she said that there were faces there that looked like Lela Marién's. We told her they were images of her, and as best he could the renegade gave her to understand what they meant, so that she might worship them as if each one of them were really the same Lela Marién who had spoken to her. She, who has a good understanding and a quick, clear nature, at once understood everything that was said to her about the images.

"From there they took us and shared us out in different houses of the town; but the renegade, Zoraida and I were taken by the Christian who had come with us to his parents' house, who were moderately well off in the goods of fortune, and they made much of us with as much love as of their own son.

"Six days we stayed at Vélez, at the end of which the renegade, having made whatever declaration he needed, went off to the city of Granada to be brought back by means of the Holy Inquisition into the most holy bosom of the Church. The other freed Christians each went wherever seemed best to them, and Zoraida and I were left alone, with nothing but the crowns the Frenchman's courtesy gave Zoraida — with which I bought this animal she rides on. And I, serving her up to now as a father and a squire and not as a husband, we go with the intention of seeing whether my father is alive, or whether either of my brothers has had more prosperous luck than mine — although, since heaven has made me Zoraida's companion, it seems to me that no other lot could come to me, however good, that I should value more highly.

"The patience with which Zoraida bears the discomforts poverty brings with it, and the desire she shows to see herself a Christian at last, is so great and such that it astonishes me and moves me to serve her all the time of my life — although the pleasure I have in seeing myself hers and in her being mine is disturbed and undone by not knowing whether I shall find in my own country some corner to shelter her in, and whether time and death may have made such a change in the property and lives of my father and my brothers that I shall hardly find anybody who knows me, if they are gone.

"I have no more, gentlemen, to tell you of my history; whether it is agreeable and out of the ordinary, let your own good judgements decide. For my own part I can say that I could have wished to tell it you more briefly — although the fear of boring you has taken more than four circumstances off my tongue."

Chapter 42: Which Treats of What Further Happened at the Inn, and of Many Other Things Worth Knowing

The captive fell silent on saying this, and Don Fernando said to him:

"Certainly, captain, the manner in which you have told this strange affair has been such that it matches the novelty and strangeness of the case itself. The whole of it is out of the ordinary and rare, and full of incidents that astonish and hold in suspense whoever hears them. And the pleasure we have got in listening to it is such that even if tomorrow's daylight found us still entertained with the same tale, we should be glad to have it begun all over again."

And on saying this, Don Fernando and all the rest offered him everything in their power for his service, in words and terms so affectionate and so genuine that the captain thought himself very well repaid by their goodwill. In particular Don Fernando offered him that if he would go back with him, he would get the marquis his brother to be godfather at Zoraida's baptism, and that for his own part he would fit him out in such a way that he could enter his own country with the standing and the comfort that were due to his person. For all of which the captive thanked him most courteously, but he would not accept any of his generous offers.

At this point night was coming on; and as it closed in, a coach arrived at the inn with some men on horseback. They asked for lodging; to whom the innkeeper's wife answered that there was not a hand's breadth free in the whole inn.

"Well, even if that is so," said one of the men on horseback who had come in, "there is bound to be room for his lordship the judge who is here."

At this title the hostess was flustered, and said:

"Sir, the fact of the matter is that I have no beds; if his worship the judge brings one, as he must do, let him come in and welcome, and my husband and I will get out of our own room to make his worship comfortable."

"Very well then," said the squire.

But by this time a man had got out of the coach whose dress at once showed the office and rank he held; because the long gown with the ruffled sleeves he was wearing showed that he was a judge, as his servant had said. He was leading by the hand a young girl of about sixteen, dressed for travelling, so smart, so beautiful and so graceful that the sight of her put everybody into admiration — so much so that if they had not seen Dorotea and Luscinda and Zoraida, who were at the inn, they would have believed that another beauty like this girl's could hardly be found.

Don Quixote was present when the judge and the girl came in, and as soon as he saw him he said:

"Your worship may safely come in and take your ease in this castle; for although it is narrow and badly furnished, there is no narrowness and no discomfort in the world that does not make room for arms and letters — and the more so if arms and letters bring beauty as their guide and leader, as your worship's letters bring in this fair maiden, before whom not only should castles be opened and thrown wide, but crags should divide and mountains split and bow down to make her welcome. Come in, your worship, I say, to this paradise, for here you will find stars and suns to keep company with the heaven your worship brings with you. Here you will find arms at their height and beauty at its extreme."

The judge was astonished at Don Quixote's speech, and set himself to look at him very deliberately, and his figure astonished him no less than his words. And without finding any words to answer him with, he was astonished all over again when he saw before him Luscinda, Dorotea and Zoraida, who at the news of the new guests, and at what the innkeeper's wife had told them of the girl's beauty, had come to see her and welcome her. But Don Fernando, Cardenio and the curate made him plainer and more courtly offers. In fact his lordship the judge came in bewildered, both at what he saw and at what he heard, and the beauties of the inn gave the beautiful girl their welcome.

In short, the judge saw plainly that all the people who were there were people of standing; but Don Quixote's figure, face and bearing baffled him. And courteous offers having passed among them all, and the accommodation of the inn having been reckoned up, what had already been arranged was arranged: that all the women should go into the garret already mentioned and that the men should stay outside, as though on guard over them. And so the judge was content that his daughter — for that was who the girl was — should go with those ladies, which she did very willingly. And with part of the innkeeper's narrow bed and half of the one the judge had brought, they settled themselves that night better than they had expected.

The captive, whose heart had been leaping from the moment he saw the judge with a suspicion that this was his brother, asked one of the servants who came with him what his name was and whether he knew what part of the country he came from. The servant answered him that he was called Licentiate Juan Pérez de Viedma, and that he had heard he came from a place in the mountains of León. With this account, and with what he had seen, he was finally confirmed in the belief that this was his brother, who had followed letters on their father's advice. And in excitement and delight, calling Don Fernando, Cardenio and the curate aside, he told them what was happening, assuring them that this judge was his brother.

The servant had also told him that he was going out as a judge to the Indies, to the High Court of Mexico. He learnt too that the girl was his daughter, at whose birth her mother had died, and that he had been left very rich by the dowry which stayed in the house with the daughter. He asked their advice as to how he should reveal himself, or how to find out first whether, once he had revealed himself, his brother would be ashamed at seeing him poor or would receive him warmly.

"Leave the making of that trial to me," said the curate; "the more so as there is no thinking otherwise than that you, captain, will be very well received. Because the worth and prudence that your brother's good face reveals give no signs of his being arrogant or ungracious, or of his not knowing how to set the accidents of fortune at their proper value."

"For all that," said the captain, "I would like to make myself known to him not suddenly but by roundabout ways."

"I tell you again," answered the curate, "that I shall manage it in a way that will leave us all satisfied."

By this time supper was ready, and they all sat down at the table except the captive and the ladies, who had supper by themselves in their room. In the middle of supper the curate said:

"Of your worship's very name, my lord judge, I had a comrade in Constantinople, where I was a captive for some years; which comrade was one of the bravest soldiers and captains in the whole Spanish infantry — but as much as he had of courage and worth, so much he had of bad luck."

"And what was this captain called, my dear sir?" asked the judge.

"He was called," answered the curate, "Ruy Pérez de Viedma, and he was a native of a place in the mountains of León; and he told me a thing that had happened to his father with his brothers which, if it had not been told me by a man as truthful as he was, I should have taken for one of those tales old women tell by the fire in winter.

"Because he told me that his father had divided his property among the three sons he had, and had given them certain pieces of advice, better than Cato's. And I can tell you that the choice he made of coming to the wars had turned out so well for him that in a few years, by his own worth and effort, with no arm to help him but his own great virtue, he rose to be a captain of infantry and to see himself in the way and in the standing to be soon a colonel. But fortune was against him; for where he might have expected to find it good, there he lost it, along with his liberty, in that most fortunate day when so many recovered theirs — which was the battle of Lepanto. I lost mine at the Goletta, and afterwards, by different turns, we found ourselves comrades in Constantinople. From there he went to Algiers, where I know that one of the strangest cases that have ever happened in the world happened to him."

From here the curate went on, and with brief compression told what had happened to his brother with Zoraida; to all of which the judge listened so attentively that never had he been so much of a hearer — which is what his title of oidor means — as he was then. The curate only went as far as the point when the French stripped the Christians who were in the boat, and the poverty and want in which his comrade and the beautiful Moorish woman had been left; of whom he had not learnt what had become of them, nor whether they had reached Spain or whether the French had carried them off to France.

The captain was listening to everything the curate said, standing a little way off, and was noting every movement his brother made. And seeing that the curate had now come to the end of his tale, he gave a great sigh, and with his eyes filling with water, said:

"Oh, sir, if you knew what news it is you have told me, and how nearly it touches me — so nearly that I am forced to give signs of it with these tears which, against all my discretion and reserve, are coming out of my eyes! That valorous captain you speak of is my elder brother, who, being stronger and of loftier thoughts than I or another younger brother of mine, chose the honourable and worthy calling of war, which was one of the three roads our father put to us, as your comrade told you in the tale you thought you heard from him.

"I followed letters, in which God and my own diligence have put me in the position you see. My youngest brother is in Peru, so rich that with what he has sent my father and me he has fully made good the share he took, and has even put into my father's hands the means to satisfy his natural generosity; and I likewise have been able to keep myself with more decency and standing in my studies and to reach the post you see me in.

"My father is still alive, dying with the longing to hear of his eldest son, and asking God with continual prayers that death may not close his eyes until he sees his son's alive. About whom I am amazed that, being so sensible a man, in so many hardships and afflictions, or in prosperous turns, he should have neglected to send his father news of himself; because if he or any of us had known, he would have had no need to wait for the miracle of the cane to get his ransom.

"But what I am afraid of now is wondering whether those Frenchmen may have given him his liberty, or may have killed him to cover up their theft. All this will mean that I shall go on with my journey, not with the pleasure I began it with but with nothing but melancholy and sadness.

"Oh, my good brother, if only I knew now where you were! For I would go and look for you and free you from your hardships, even if it were at the cost of my own. Oh, if only somebody would take news to our old father that you were alive, even if you were in the most hidden dungeons of Barbary — for his riches, and my brother's and mine, would get you out of them! Oh Zoraida, beautiful and generous, if only somebody could repay the good you did a brother of mine! If only somebody could be present at the new birth of your soul, and at the wedding, which would give us all so much happiness!"

These and other such words the judge said, so full of compassion at the news he had been given of his brother that everybody who heard him joined him in showing the feeling they had for his grief.

The curate, then, seeing how well he had come out with his plan and with what the captain wanted, did not want to keep them all sad any longer; and so he got up from the table and went into where Zoraida was, and took her by the hand, and after her came Luscinda, Dorotea and the judge's daughter. The captain was waiting to see what the curate meant to do, which was that, taking him too by the other hand, he went with the two of them to where the judge and the other gentlemen were, and said:

"Let your tears cease, my lord judge, and let your wish be filled with all the good that could be wished for; since you have before you your good brother and your good sister-in-law. This man you see here is Captain Viedma, and this is the beautiful Moorish woman who did him so much good. The Frenchmen I told you of put them in the straits you see, so that you might show the generosity of your good heart."

The captain ran to embrace his brother, and his brother put both hands on his chest so as to look at him a little further off; but when he had finished recognising him, he embraced him so tightly, shedding such tender tears of happiness, that most of those who were present had to join him in them. The words the two brothers said to each other, the feelings they showed, I hardly think can be imagined, let alone written down.

There, in a few words, they gave each other an account of their fortunes; there the good friendship of two brothers was shown at its height; there the judge embraced Zoraida; there he offered her his property; there he made his daughter embrace her; there the beautiful Christian girl and the most beautiful Moorish girl set everybody's tears going again.

There Don Quixote stood attentive, without saying a word, considering these very strange events and putting them all down to the chimeras of knight-errantry.

There it was arranged that the captain and Zoraida should go back with his brother to Seville and let their father know of his being found and of his freedom, so that he might come as best he could to be present at Zoraida's wedding and baptism — since it was not possible for the judge to leave the journey he was on, because he had news that in a month's time the fleet would sail from Seville to New Spain, and it would be a great inconvenience to him to lose the passage.

In short, everybody was contented and glad at the captive's good fortune; and as the night had now gone almost two thirds of its journey, they agreed to go to bed and rest for what was left of it. Don Quixote offered to keep watch over the castle, so that they should not be attacked by some giant or other wandering scoundrel, greedy for the great treasure of beauty that castle held. Those who knew him thanked him for it, and gave the judge an account of Don Quixote's strange humour, which he found not a little entertaining.

Only Sancho Panza was in despair at how long they were taking to go to bed; and he alone settled himself better than any of them, lying down on his donkey's harness, which was to cost him as dear as will be told further on.

The ladies having gone to their room, then, and the rest having settled themselves as best they could, Don Quixote went out of the inn to stand sentry over the castle, as he had promised.

It happened, then, that a little before dawn came, there reached the ladies' ears a voice so tuneful and so good that it obliged them all to give it their attention — especially Dorotea, who was awake, and at whose side slept Doña Clara de Viedma, for that was the name of the judge's daughter. Nobody could imagine who the person was who sang so well; and it was a single voice, without any instrument to accompany it. Sometimes it seemed to them that the singing was in the yard, sometimes that it was in the stable; and while they were in this confusion, listening very attentively, Cardenio came to the door of the room and said:

"Whoever is not asleep, listen; you will hear the voice of a muleteer's boy who sings in such a way that he enchants."

"We are already listening to it, sir," answered Dorotea.

And with this Cardenio went away; and Dorotea, giving it all the attention she could, made out that what was being sung was this.

Chapter 43: In Which Is Related the Agreeable Story of the Muleteer's Boy, with Other Strange Events That Happened at the Inn

	A sailor of love am I,
	and on his deep ocean
	I sail without any hope
	of reaching any harbour.
	I go on following a star
	that I make out from far off,
	lovelier and more shining
	than any Palinurus saw.
	I do not know where it guides me,
	and so I sail in confusion,
	my soul intent on watching it,
	careful and careless at once.
	Impertinent reserves,
	a modesty beyond the custom,
	are clouds that hide her from me
	when I most try to see her.
	O clear and shining star,
	in whose light I burn myself away:
	the moment you hide from me
	will be the moment of my death.

The singer having got to this point, it seemed to Dorotea that it would not be right for Clara to miss hearing so good a voice; and so, shaking her one way and the other, she woke her, saying:

"Forgive me, child, for waking you, since I do it so that you may have the pleasure of hearing the best voice you will perhaps have heard in the whole of your life."

Clara woke up thoroughly drowsy, and the first time did not understand what Dorotea was saying to her; and asking her again, Dorotea told her again, at which Clara paid attention. But she had hardly heard two lines that the singer was going on with when such a strange trembling took her, as though she were ill with some grave attack of the ague; and hugging Dorotea tightly, she said to her:

"Oh, lady of my soul and my life, why did you wake me? For the greatest good fortune that could come to me just now was to have my eyes and my ears shut, so as not to see or hear that unhappy musician."

"What is this you say, child? They tell me the man who is singing is a muleteer's boy."

"He is nothing of the kind: he is the lord of villages," answered Clara, "and of the place he holds in my soul so securely that if he does not choose to leave it, it will not be taken from him for ever."

Dorotea was astonished at the girl's feeling words, thinking that they went a long way beyond the good sense her few years promised; and so she said to her:

"You speak in such a way, Señora Clara, that I cannot understand you: explain yourself more, and tell me what you mean about a soul and villages and this musician, whose voice has left you in such distress. But do not tell me anything just now, for I do not want to lose, by attending to your alarm, the pleasure I get from listening to the singer; for it seems to me that he is going back to his song with new verses and a new tune."

"Very well," answered Clara.

And so as not to hear him she stopped up both her ears with her hands, at which Dorotea was astonished too; and Dorotea, listening to what was being sung, found that it went on in this way:

	Sweet hope of mine,
	who, breaking through impossibilities and thickets,
	go steadily on the road
	that you yourself invent and prepare:
	do not lose heart at seeing yourself
	at every step beside the step of your own death.
	Lazy men do not attain
	honourable triumphs or any victory,
	nor can those be happy
	who, not standing up against fortune,
	surrender, helpless,
	all their senses to soft idleness.
	That love should sell his glories
	dear is very reasonable, and is fair dealing;
	for there is no richer treasure
	than the one that is assayed by his own pleasure,
	and it is a plain thing
	that what costs little is not valued.
	Persistence in love
	sometimes attains impossible things;
	and so, although with mine
	I follow the hardest roads of love,
	I do not for that reason despair
	of reaching heaven from the earth.

Here the voice came to an end, and Clara made a beginning of fresh sobs. All of which inflamed Dorotea's desire to know the cause of such sweet singing and such sad weeping. And so she asked her again what it was she had meant to tell her before. Then Clara, afraid that Luscinda might hear her, hugging Dorotea tightly, put her mouth so close to Dorotea's ear that she could safely speak without being heard by anybody else, and said to her:

"This man who is singing, my lady, is the son of a gentleman, a native of the kingdom of Aragon, the lord of two villages, who lived opposite my father's house at Court. And although my father had the windows of his house covered with cloths in winter and lattices in summer, I do not know how it was or was not, but this gentleman, who was at his studies, saw me — and I do not know whether it was at church or somewhere else.

"In the end he fell in love with me, and gave me to understand it from the windows of his house with so many signs and so many tears that I had to believe him, and even love him, without knowing what it was he wanted of me. Among the signs he made me was one of putting his two hands together, giving me to understand that he would marry me; and although I should have been very glad if it had been so, being alone and without a mother I did not know who to talk it over with, and so I let it be without giving him any other favour except that, when my father was out of the house and his was too, I would raise the cloth or the lattice a little and let myself be seen at full length — at which he made such a festival that he gave signs of going out of his mind.

"At this the time of my father's departure came on, which he learnt about, and not from me, since I could never tell him. He fell ill, as I understand it, of grief; and so on the day we left I could never see him to say goodbye to him, even with my eyes.

"But after two days of travelling, on going into an inn at a place a day's journey from here, I saw him at the door of the inn, dressed as a muleteer's boy, so to the life that if I had not carried him so well painted in my soul it would have been impossible to recognise him. I recognised him, I was astonished and I was glad. He looked at me by stealth from my father, whom he always hides from when he crosses in front of me on the roads and at the inns we come to. And as I know who he is, and consider that for love of me he comes on foot and with so much hardship, I am dying of distress; and where he puts his feet I put my eyes.

"I do not know with what intention he comes, or how he has been able to escape from his father, who loves him extraordinarily, because he has no other heir and because he deserves it, as your worship will see when you see him. And I can tell you more: that everything he sings he gets out of his own head, for I have heard it said that he is a very great scholar and poet. And there is more: that every time I see him or hear him sing, I tremble all over and start with fright, afraid my father will recognise him and come to know of what we want.

"In my life I have never spoken a word to him, and for all that I love him in such a way that I shall not be able to live without him. This, my lady, is all I can tell you about this musician whose voice has pleased you so much; from which alone you may see plainly that he is no muleteer's boy, as you say, but the lord of souls and villages, as I have told you."

"Say no more, Señora Doña Clara," said Dorotea at this point, and this while kissing her a thousand times; "say no more, I say, and wait for the new day to come, for I hope in God so to direct your affairs that they may have the happy end so honourable a beginning deserves."

"Oh, my lady," said Doña Clara, "what end can be hoped for, if his father is so distinguished and so rich that he will think I cannot even be his son's servant, much less his wife? And as for marrying without my father's knowledge, I would not do it for anything in the world. All I could wish is that this young man would go back and leave me; perhaps by not seeing him, and with the great distance of the road we are going, the pain I feel now would be eased — although I can tell you that this remedy I am imagining will do me very little good.

"I do not know what the devil this has been, or how this love I have for him got in, seeing that I am such a girl and he such a boy; for truly I believe we are of the very same age, and I am not sixteen yet — for my father says I shall be sixteen on Saint Michael's day coming."

Dorotea could not help laughing to hear how like a child Doña Clara talked, and said to her:

"Let us rest, madam, for what little I think is left of the night, and God will send the morning and we shall prosper — or my hands will serve me badly."

With this they settled down, and a great silence was kept throughout the inn. The only people who were not asleep were the innkeeper's daughter and Maritornes her servant; who, since they already knew the humour Don Quixote sinned by, and that he was outside the inn armed and on horseback keeping watch, decided between them to play some joke on him, or at least to pass a little time listening to his absurdities.

Now the fact is that in the whole inn there was no window that looked out onto the fields except a hole in a hayloft, through which they threw the straw out. To this hole the two half-maidens came, and saw that Don Quixote was on horseback, leaning on his pike, giving from time to time such sorrowful, deep sighs that with each one his soul seemed to be torn out of him. And they likewise heard him say in a soft, delicate, loving voice:

"O my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, extreme of all beauty, end and completion of good sense, storehouse of the best charm, treasury of modesty, and finally the very idea of everything profitable, honourable and delightful there is in the world! And what may your grace be doing now? Have you by any chance your thoughts on your captive knight, who has of his own will chosen to expose himself to so many dangers simply to serve you?

"Give me news of her, O luminary of the three faces! Perhaps out of envy of hers you are looking at her now; either walking about some gallery of her sumptuous palaces, or leaning on some balcony, considering how, without loss to her modesty and her greatness, she is to calm the storm this troubled heart of mine suffers for her sake; what glory she is to give my pains, what quiet to my anxiety and, in the end, what life to my death and what reward to my services.

"And you, sun, who must by now be saddling your horses in haste so as to get up early and go out to see my lady — as soon as you see her, I beg you to greet her on my behalf; but take care that on seeing her and greeting her you do not give her the kiss of peace on her face, for I shall be more jealous of you than you were of that swift ingrate who made you sweat and run so hard over the plains of Thessaly, or along the banks of the Peneus — for I do not properly remember where you ran that time, jealous and in love."

Don Quixote had got to this point in his sorrowful speech when the innkeeper's daughter began to hiss at him and to say:

"My dear sir, will your worship please come over here?"

At which signs and voice Don Quixote turned his head, and saw by the light of the moon — which was then at its full brightness — that he was being called from the hole which seemed to him a window, and one with gilded bars at that, as befits the windows of such rich castles as he imagined that inn to be. And at that instant it presented itself to his mad imagination that once again, as the last time, the fair maiden, daughter of the lady of that castle, conquered by her love for him, was coming back to solicit him. And with this thought, so as not to show himself discourteous and ungrateful, he turned Rocinante's reins and came up to the hole; and as soon as he saw the two girls, he said:

"I pity you, fair lady, for having set your loving thoughts in a quarter where it is not possible to answer you as your great worth and gentility deserve; for which you must not blame this wretched knight errant, whom love has made incapable of surrendering his affections to any woman but the one who, at the moment his eyes saw her, made her the absolute mistress of his soul.

"Forgive me, good lady, and get you back to your room, and do not, by declaring your desires to me any further, oblige me to show myself more ungrateful. And if out of the love you bear me you find in me anything else with which to satisfy you, so long as it is not that same love, ask it of me; for I swear to you, by that absent sweet enemy of mine, to give it you on the spot, even if you asked me for a lock of Medusa's hair, which was all snakes, or for the very rays of the sun shut up in a phial."

"My lady has need of nothing of the sort, sir knight," said Maritornes at this point.

"Then what has your lady need of, discerning duenna?" answered Don Quixote.

"Only one of your beautiful hands," said Maritornes, "so as to relieve with it the great longing that has brought her to this hole, so much at the risk of her honour that if her lord father had heard her, the smallest slice of her would have been her ear."

"I should have liked to see that!" answered Don Quixote. "But he will take good care not to, unless he wants to make the most disastrous end that any father in the world ever made, for having laid hands on the delicate limbs of his lovesick daughter."

It seemed to Maritornes that Don Quixote would certainly give the hand they had asked for; and settling in her mind what she was going to do, she got down from the hole and went to the stable, where she took the halter of Sancho Panza's donkey and came back to her hole very quickly, just as Don Quixote had got to his feet on Rocinante's saddle so as to reach the barred window where he imagined the wounded maiden to be. And on giving her his hand, he said:

"Take, madam, this hand — or rather, this executioner of the world's evildoers; take this hand, I say, which no other woman's has touched, not even hers who has complete possession of the whole of my body. I do not give it you to kiss, but so that you may look at the fabric of its sinews, the linking of its muscles, the width and roominess of its veins; from which you may gather what the strength must be of the arm that has such a hand."

"Now we shall see," said Maritornes.

And making a running noose in the halter, she threw it round his wrist; and getting down from the hole, she tied what was left very tightly to the bolt of the hayloft door. Don Quixote, feeling the roughness of the cord on his wrist, said:

"It seems more as though your worship were grating my hand than caressing it; do not treat it so badly, for it is not to blame for the harm my will does you; nor is it right that you should take out the whole of your annoyance on so small a part of me. Consider that whoever loves well does not revenge herself so ill."

But nobody was listening to any of these speeches of Don Quixote's by now, because as soon as Maritornes had tied him, she and the other girl went off dying of laughter, and left him held in such a way that it was impossible for him to get free.

He was, then, as has been said, standing on his feet on Rocinante, with his whole arm through the hole and tied by the wrist to the bolt of the door, in the greatest fear and anxiety — for if Rocinante moved to one side or the other, he would be left hanging by the arm. And so he did not dare make any movement at all, although from Rocinante's patience and quietness one might well expect that he would stay without moving for a whole century.

In short, seeing himself tied and that the ladies had gone away, Don Quixote set himself to imagine that all this was being done by way of enchantment, as the last time, when in that same castle that enchanted Moor of a carrier had pounded him. And he cursed to himself his own want of judgement and reasoning; since, having come out of that castle so badly the first time, he had ventured to go into it a second, it being an established maxim among knights errant that when they have tried an adventure and not succeeded in it, it is a sign that it is not reserved for them but for others, and so they have no need to try it a second time.

For all that, he pulled at his arm to see whether he could get free; but he was so well tied that all his attempts were in vain. It is quite true that he pulled cautiously, so that Rocinante should not move; and although he would have liked to sit down and settle himself in the saddle, he could do nothing but stand up, or tear his hand off.

There was the wishing for Amadis's sword, against which no enchantment had any power; there was the cursing of his fortune; there was the exaggerating of the loss the world would suffer by his absence for as long as he stayed there enchanted — for he had beyond any doubt come to believe that he was; there was the remembering all over again of his beloved Dulcinea of El Toboso; there was the calling for his good squire Sancho Panza, who, buried in sleep and stretched out on his donkey's pack-saddle, at that moment did not remember the mother that bore him; there he called on the sages Lirgandeo and Alquife to help him; there he invoked his good friend Urganda to come to his rescue; and finally, there the morning caught him, so desperate and bewildered that he bellowed like a bull. Because he did not expect that daylight would put his trouble right, since he took it to be everlasting, believing himself to be enchanted. And what made him believe it was seeing that Rocinante moved neither much nor little; and he believed that in that fashion, without eating or drinking or sleeping, he and his horse would have to stay until that evil influence of the stars was past, or until some wiser enchanter disenchanted him.

But he was very much deceived in his belief; because dawn had hardly begun to break when four men on horseback arrived at the inn, very well turned out and equipped, with their muskets across their saddlebows. They knocked with great blows at the inn door, which was still shut; which Don Quixote seeing from where he still did not leave off keeping sentry, he said in an arrogant, loud voice:

"Knights, or squires, or whoever you may be: you have no reason to knock at the gates of this castle; for it is plain enough that at such an hour either those within are asleep, or it is not the custom of fortresses to be opened until the sun is spread over the whole ground. Draw off outside, and wait for the day to grow light, and then we shall see whether it is right or not that they should open to you."

"What the devil sort of fortress or castle is this," said one of them, "to oblige us to keep such ceremonies? If you are the innkeeper, order them to open to us; for we are travellers who want no more than to give our mounts some barley and go on, because we are in a hurry."

"Do I look to you, gentlemen, as if I had the build of an innkeeper?" answered Don Quixote.

"I do not know what you have the build of," answered the other, "but I know that you talk nonsense in calling this inn a castle."

"A castle it is," replied Don Quixote, "and one of the best in this whole province; and it has people inside it who have had a sceptre in their hand and a crown on their head."

"It would be better the other way round," said the traveller: "the sceptre on the head and the crown in the hand. And it will be, if it comes to it, that there must be some company of players inside, who often have those crowns and sceptres you speak of; because in an inn as small as this, and where such silence is kept, I do not believe people worthy of a crown and sceptre are lodged."

"You know little of the world," replied Don Quixote, "since you are ignorant of the things that generally happen in knight-errantry."

The companions who came with the questioner were getting tired of the conversation he was having with Don Quixote, and so they went back to knocking with great fury; and it was in such a way that the innkeeper woke up, and everybody else in the inn as well; and so he got up to ask who was knocking.

It happened at this time that one of the mounts the four men who were knocking had come on came up to smell Rocinante, who, melancholy and sad, with his ears drooping, was holding up his stretched-out master without moving. And as after all he was made of flesh, although he looked as if he were made of wood, he could not help responding and turning to smell the one who was coming to caress him. And so he had hardly moved at all when Don Quixote's joined feet slipped apart, and, sliding off the saddle, he would have come down on the ground if he had not been left hanging by the arm — a thing that caused him so much pain that he believed either that they were cutting off his wrist or that his arm was being torn off. Because he was left so close to the ground that with the very tips of his toes he kissed the earth; which was to his own harm, because, feeling how little he lacked to put the soles of his feet on the ground, he wore himself out and stretched as far as he could to reach it: exactly like men who are given the torture of the pulley, hung at just-touching and not-touching, who are themselves the cause of increasing their own pain by the eagerness they put into stretching, deceived by the hope that presents itself to them that with a very little more stretching they will reach the ground.

Chapter 44: In Which Are Continued the Unheard-Of Events at the Inn

In fact Don Quixote gave so many shouts that the innkeeper, quickly opening the inn doors, came out in a fright to see who was giving such cries, and those who were outside did the same. Maritornes, who had already woken at the same shouts, imagining what it might be, went to the hayloft and untied, without anybody's seeing her, the halter that was holding Don Quixote up; and he immediately came down on the ground in sight of the innkeeper and the travellers, who, coming up to him, asked him what was the matter with him that he was giving such shouts. He, without answering a word, took the cord off his wrist and, getting to his feet, mounted Rocinante, braced his shield, levelled his pike, and, taking a good stretch of ground, came back at a half gallop, saying:

"Whoever shall say that I have been enchanted with any just title — provided my lady the Princess Micomicona gives me leave for it — I give him the lie, I challenge him and defy him to single combat."

The new travellers were astonished at Don Quixote's words, but the innkeeper took them out of that astonishment by telling them that this was Don Quixote and that there was no need to take any notice of him, because he was out of his mind.

They asked the innkeeper whether by any chance a boy of about fifteen had come to that inn, dressed as a muleteer's lad, with such-and-such a description — giving exactly the description of Doña Clara's lover. The innkeeper answered that there were so many people at the inn that he had not noticed the one they were asking about. But one of them, having seen the coach the judge had come in, said:

"He must certainly be here, because this is the coach they say he is following. Let one of us stay at the door and the rest go in and look for him; and it would be as well too if one of us went right round the inn, so that he does not get away over the yard walls."

"That is what we will do," answered one of them.

And two of them going inside, one stayed at the door and the other went off to go round the inn — all of which the innkeeper watched, and could not make out what all these measures were being taken for, although he well believed they were looking for the lad whose description they had given him.

By this time day was breaking; and for that reason as well as because of the noise Don Quixote had made, everybody was awake and getting up — especially Doña Clara and Dorotea, who, the one in alarm at having her lover so close and the other in her eagerness to see him, had been able to sleep very badly that night.

Don Quixote, who saw that none of the four travellers took any notice of him or answered his challenge, was dying and raging with vexation and fury. And if he had found in the ordinances of his chivalry that a knight errant might lawfully take on and undertake another enterprise when he had given his word and faith not to enter on any until he had finished the one he had promised, he would have attacked the lot of them and made them answer him whether they liked it or not. But since it seemed to him neither proper nor becoming to begin a new enterprise until he had put Micomicona in her kingdom, he had to keep quiet and stay still, waiting to see what those travellers' measures would come to.

One of them found the young man he was looking for asleep beside a muleteer's boy, quite unaware that anybody was looking for him, let alone that anybody would find him. The man took him by the arm and said to him:

"Certainly, Señor Don Luis, the clothes you have on answer well to who you are, and the bed I find you in speaks well of the indulgence your mother brought you up with."

The young man rubbed his sleepy eyes and looked slowly at the man who had hold of him, and then recognised that he was a servant of his father's, at which he got such a shock that he could not manage, or was not able, to say a word to him for a good while. And the servant went on to say:

"There is nothing else to be done here, Señor Don Luis, but to be patient and go back home — unless your worship would like your father and my master to go to the other world; because nothing else is to be expected from the grief he is left in through your being away."

"But how did my father know," said Don Luis, "that I was coming this road and in this dress?"

"A student," answered the servant, "whom you told about your plans was the one who revealed it, moved by pity at what he saw your father doing the moment he missed you. And so he sent off four of his servants to look for you, and we are all here at your service, more delighted than can be imagined at the good errand we shall go back on, taking you to the eyes that love you so much."

"That will be as I choose, or as heaven ordains," answered Don Luis.

"What can you choose, or what can heaven ordain, except to agree to your going back? For nothing else is going to be possible."

All these words that passed between the two of them were heard by the muleteer's boy beside whom Don Luis had been lying; and getting up from there, he went to tell Don Fernando and Cardenio and the rest — who had dressed by now — what was going on. He told them how that man called this boy "Don", and what words were passing, and how he wanted to take him back to his father's house and the boy did not want to go. And with this, and with what they knew of him from the fine voice heaven had given him, they were all seized with a great desire to know more particularly who he was, and even to help him if anybody tried to use force on him. And so they went towards the quarter where he was still talking and arguing with his servant.

At this Dorotea came out of her room, and behind her Doña Clara in great distress; and Dorotea, calling Cardenio aside, told him in a few words the story of the musician and Doña Clara. And he told her too what was happening about his father's servants coming to look for him, and he did not say it so quietly that Clara failed to hear it; at which she was so far out of herself that if Dorotea had not come to hold her, she would have come down on the floor. Cardenio told Dorotea that they should go back to their room, and that he would try to put everything right; and they did so.

By now all four of the men who had come looking for Don Luis were inside the inn and gathered round him, urging him to go back at once, without a moment's delay, to comfort his father. He answered that he could on no account do it until he had finished a business in which his life, his honour and his soul were at stake. The servants then pressed him, saying that on no account would they go back without him, and that they would take him whether he liked it or not.

"That you will not do," replied Don Luis, "unless you take me dead — although whatever way you take me, it will be taking me without my life."

By this time everybody else in the inn had come up to the argument, especially Cardenio, Don Fernando, his companions, the judge, the curate, the barber and Don Quixote, who by now thought there was no further need to guard the castle. Cardenio, who already knew the young man's story, asked those who wanted to take him what moved them to want to take that boy away against his will.

"What moves us," answered one of the four, "is to give his father back his life, which through this gentleman's absence is in danger of being lost."

To this Don Luis said:

"There is no need to give an account of my affairs here: I am free, and I shall go back if I choose to, and if not, none of you is going to force me."

"Reason will force your worship," answered the man; "and when reason is not enough with your worship, it will be enough with us to do what we came for and what we are bound to do."

"Let us know what all this is at bottom," said the judge at this point.

But the man, who knew him as a neighbour of his house, answered:

"Does your worship not know, my lord judge, this gentleman, who is your neighbour's son, and who has got away from his father's house in dress as unbecoming to his rank as your worship can see?"

The judge then looked at him more attentively and recognised him; and embracing him, he said:

"What childishness is this, Señor Don Luis, or what causes so powerful that they have moved you to come in this way, and in this dress, which so ill becomes your quality?"

Tears came into the young man's eyes, and he could not answer a word. The judge told the four men to calm down, for it would all be settled properly; and taking Don Luis by the hand, he drew him aside and asked him what this coming had been about.

And while he was asking him this and other questions, they heard great shouts at the door of the inn; and the cause of them was that two guests who had lodged there that night, seeing everybody busy finding out what the four men were after, had tried to go without paying what they owed. But the innkeeper, who attended more to his own business than to other people's, caught them as they came out of the door and asked for his money, and reproached them for their bad intentions in such words that he moved them to answer him with their fists; and so they began to lay into him in such a way that the poor innkeeper had to shout and call for help.

The innkeeper's wife and daughter could see nobody less occupied and able to help him than Don Quixote, to whom the innkeeper's daughter said:

"Help my poor father, sir knight, by the power God gave you; for two wicked men are pounding him like grain."

To which Don Quixote answered very slowly and with great composure:

"Fair maiden, there is no place for your petition at present, because I am prevented from getting involved in another adventure while I have not brought to a head one that my word has committed me to. But what I can do to serve you is this, as I shall now tell you: run and tell your father to keep up that battle as best he can and on no account to let himself be beaten, while I ask the Princess Micomicona's leave to be able to help him in his distress; for if she gives it me, take it as certain that I shall get him out of it."

"Sinner that I am!" said Maritornes, who was standing there. "Before your worship gets that leave you speak of, my master will already be in the other world."

"Only let me get the leave I speak of, madam," answered Don Quixote; "for once I have it, it will make very little difference that he should be in the other world, for I shall get him out of there in spite of the whole world's gainsaying it — or at the very least I shall give you such revenge on those who have sent him there that you will be more than moderately satisfied."

And without saying any more he went and knelt down before Dorotea, asking her in knightly and errant words that her greatness might be pleased to give him leave to succour and help the governor of that castle, who was in grave straits. The princess gave it him with a good will, and he at once, bracing his shield and putting his hand to his sword, hurried to the door of the inn, where the two guests were still handling the innkeeper roughly. But as soon as he arrived he stopped short and stayed still, although Maritornes and the innkeeper's wife kept asking him what he was waiting for, and telling him to help their master and husband.

"I hold back," said Don Quixote, "because it is not lawful for me to put my hand to my sword against people of squirely rank; but call my squire Sancho here to me, for this defence and vengeance is his affair and concern."

This was going on at the door of the inn, and there the punches and cuffs were flying in fine style, all to the harm of the innkeeper and to the fury of Maritornes, the innkeeper's wife and her daughter, who were in despair at seeing Don Quixote's cowardice and at how badly things were going for their husband, master and father.

But let us leave him here, for there will be no lack of somebody to help him; and if not, let the man who takes on more than his strength promises suffer and hold his tongue. And let us go back fifty paces to see what Don Luis answered the judge, whom we left aside asking him the reason for his coming on foot and dressed in such vile clothes. To which the young man, taking hold of his hands tightly, as a sign that some great grief was pressing on his heart, and shedding tears in great abundance, said to him:

"My dear sir, I can tell you nothing else except that from the moment heaven willed it and our being neighbours made it easy for me to see my lady Doña Clara, your daughter and my mistress, from that instant I made her the mistress of my will. And if yours, my true lord and father, does not prevent it, this very day she is to be my wife.

"For her I left my father's house, and for her I put on this dress, so as to follow her wherever she went, like the arrow to its target or the sailor to the pole star. She knows no more of my feelings than what she has been able to gather from the times she has seen my eyes weeping from a distance. You know already, sir, my parents' wealth and nobility, and that I am their only heir: if it seems to you that these are qualities enough for you to venture to make me happy in everything, receive me at once as your son. For if my father, carried away by other designs of his own, should not approve of this good fortune I have managed to find for myself, time has more power to undo and change things than human wills have."

The lovesick young man fell silent on saying this; and the judge was left, on hearing him, taken aback, bewildered and astonished, both at having heard the manner and the good sense with which Don Luis had revealed his feelings, and at finding himself at a point where he did not know what course to take in so sudden and unexpected a business. And so he answered nothing except that he should be easy for the present and keep his servants occupied so that they should not take him back that day, so that there might be time to consider what would be best for everybody. Don Luis kissed his hands by force, and even bathed them in tears — a thing that might have softened a heart of marble, let alone the judge's, who, being a man of sense, had already recognised how good that marriage was for his daughter, although, if it were possible, he would have wanted to bring it about with the consent of Don Luis's father, who he knew meant to get his son a title.

By this time the guests had made peace with the innkeeper, having paid him everything he asked, more through Don Quixote's persuasion and good arguments than through threats; and Don Luis's servants were waiting for the end of the judge's talk and their master's decision, when the devil, who never sleeps, arranged that at that very moment there came into the inn the barber from whom Don Quixote had taken Mambrino's helmet and Sancho Panza the ass's harness, which he had exchanged for his own. And this barber, taking his donkey to the stable, saw Sancho Panza mending something or other on the pack-saddle; and as soon as he saw it he recognised it, and made bold to rush at Sancho, saying:

"Ah, you thief, I have you here! Give me back my basin and my pack-saddle, along with all the harness you stole from me!"

Sancho, seeing himself attacked so suddenly and hearing the abuse being flung at him, with one hand took hold of the pack-saddle and with the other gave the barber such a cuff that he bathed his teeth in blood; but the barber did not for that let go of the hold he had on the pack-saddle. On the contrary, he raised his voice in such a way that everybody in the inn came running at the noise and the quarrel, and he was saying:

"Help, in the name of the king and the law! On top of my getting my own property back, this thieving highwayman wants to kill me!"

"You lie," answered Sancho, "for I am no highwayman: my master Don Quixote won these spoils in fair war."

Don Quixote was there by now, very pleased at seeing how well his squire both defended and attacked; and from then on he counted him a man of worth, and resolved in his heart to dub him a knight at the first chance that offered, thinking that the order of chivalry would be well bestowed on him.

Among other things the barber said in the course of the quarrel, he came to say:

"Gentlemen, this pack-saddle is as much mine as the death I owe to God, and I know it as well as if I had given birth to it; and there is my ass in the stable, who will not let me lie. If not, try it on him, and if it does not fit him to a hair I shall stand as a liar. And there is more: that the same day it was taken from me, they also took from me a new brass basin that had never been used, which was worth a crown of anybody's money."

Here Don Quixote could not hold himself in without answering; and putting himself between the two of them and separating them, and depositing the pack-saddle on the ground so that it should stay in plain sight until the truth came out, he said:

"So that your worships may see clearly and plainly the error this good squire is in, since he calls a basin what was, is and shall be Mambrino's helmet, which I took from him in fair war and made myself lord of by lawful and legitimate possession! As for the pack-saddle, I do not meddle in it; all I can say about it is that my squire Sancho asked my leave to take the trappings off this defeated coward's horse and adorn his own with them. I gave it him and he took them; and as for their having turned from trappings into a pack-saddle, I can give no other explanation than the ordinary one: that transformations of that sort are seen in the events of chivalry. In confirmation of which, run, Sancho my son, and bring out here the helmet this good man says is a basin."

"By God, sir," said Sancho, "if we have no other proof of our case than the one your worship gives, that Malbrino helmet is as much a basin as this good man's trappings are a pack-saddle!"

"Do as I tell you," replied Don Quixote; "for not everything in this castle is to be guided by enchantment."

Sancho went to where the basin was and brought it; and as soon as Don Quixote saw it, he took it in his hands and said:

"Let your worships look with what face this squire could say that this is a basin and not the helmet I have described. And I swear by the order of chivalry I profess that this is the same helmet I took from him, without anything having been added to it or taken away."

"There is no doubt about that," said Sancho at this, "because from the time my master won it until now he has only fought one battle with it, when he set free those unlucky men in chains; and if it hadn't been for this basinhelm, he wouldn't have come off very well that time either, because there was a great deal of stone-throwing in that engagement."

Chapter 45: In Which the Doubt About Mambrino's Helmet and the Pack-Saddle Is Finally Cleared Up, with Other Adventures That Genuinely Happened

"What do your worships think, gentlemen," said the barber, "of what these fine gentlemen maintain, since they still insist that this is not a basin but a helmet?"

"And whoever says the contrary," said Don Quixote, "I shall make him see that he lies, if he is a knight; and if a squire, that he lies a thousand times over."

Our own barber, who was present at all of it, knowing Don Quixote's humour so well, chose to encourage his nonsense and carry the joke further so that everybody should laugh; and he said, speaking to the other barber:

"Master barber, or whoever you are, know that I too am of your trade, and have had my certificate of examination these twenty years and more, and I know very well every one of the instruments of barbering, without missing one. And neither more nor less, I was for a time in my youth a soldier, and I know too what a helmet is, and what a morion, and a close casque, and other things belonging to soldiering — I mean to the kinds of arms soldiers carry. And I say, saving a better opinion, and always deferring to a better understanding, that this piece which is here in front of us and which this good gentleman has in his hands is not only not a barber's basin, but is as far from being one as white is from black and truth from lies. I also say that this, although it is a helmet, is not a whole helmet."

"Certainly not," said Don Quixote, "because it is missing half of it, which is the beaver."

"That is so," said the curate, who had already understood his friend the barber's intention.

And Cardenio confirmed the same, and Don Fernando and his companions; and even the judge would have helped on the joke for his part if he had not been so preoccupied with Don Luis's business; but the earnest of what he was thinking about held him so much in suspense that he attended little or not at all to those pleasantries.

"God help me!" said the outwitted barber at this. "Is it possible that so many honourable people should say that this is not a basin but a helmet? This looks like a thing that could astonish a whole university, however learned it is. Enough: if this basin is a helmet, then this pack-saddle must be a horse's trappings too, as this gentleman has said."

"It looks like a pack-saddle to me," said Don Quixote, "but I have already said that I do not meddle in that."

"Whether it is a pack-saddle or trappings," said the curate, "depends on nothing more than Señor Don Quixote's saying so; for in these matters of chivalry all these gentlemen and I give him the advantage."

"By God, my dear sirs," said Don Quixote, "the things that have happened to me in this castle, in the two times I have lodged in it, are so many and so strange that I do not dare to say anything positively about whatever may be asked concerning what is contained in it, because I imagine that everything that goes on here goes by way of enchantment. The first time an enchanted Moor who is in it wearied me a great deal, and it went not much better for Sancho with certain followers of his. And last night I hung by this arm for nearly two hours, without knowing how or why I came to fall into that misfortune. So that for me now to put myself into a thing of so much confusion and give my opinion would be falling into rash judgement.

"As for what they say, that this is a basin and not a helmet, I have already answered; but as for declaring whether that is a pack-saddle or trappings, I do not dare to give a definitive sentence: I simply leave it to your worships' good judgement. Perhaps, since you are not dubbed knights as I am, the enchantments of this place will have nothing to do with your worships, and your understandings will be free, and you will be able to judge the things of this castle as they really and truly are, and not as they seemed to me."

"There is no doubt," Don Fernando answered to this, "that Señor Don Quixote has spoken very well today in saying that the settling of this case belongs to us. And so that it may go on a better footing, I shall take these gentlemen's votes in secret, and shall give full and clear notice of the result."

For those who knew about Don Quixote's humour, all this was matter for the greatest laughter; but to those who did not know about it, it seemed the greatest absurdity in the world — especially to Don Luis's four servants, and to Don Luis neither more nor less, and to three other travellers who had happened to come to the inn and who looked as if they were officers of the Holy Brotherhood, as in fact they were.

But the one who was most in despair was the barber, whose basin, there in front of his eyes, had turned into Mambrino's helmet, and whose pack-saddle he had no doubt at all was about to turn into a rich horse's trappings. And both sides laughed to see how Don Fernando went about taking the votes of one man after another, speaking to them in the ear so that they might declare in secret whether that jewel they had fought so much over was a pack-saddle or trappings. And after he had taken the votes of those who knew Don Quixote, he said aloud:

"The case is, my good man, that I am tired by now of taking so many opinions; because I see that there is nobody I ask what I want to know who does not tell me that it is nonsense to say this is a donkey's pack-saddle, and that it is a horse's trappings, and of a thoroughbred horse at that. And so you will have to be patient; because in spite of you and of your ass, this is trappings and not a pack-saddle, and you have argued and proved your side very badly."

"May I have no share in heaven," said the out-barbered barber, "if all your worships are not mistaken; and may my soul appear before God as this appears to me to be a pack-saddle and not trappings. But there, laws go where kings will — and so on; and I say no more. And truly I am not drunk, for I have not broken my fast — unless it is with sinning."

The foolish things the barber said caused no less laughter than Don Quixote's absurdities; and Don Quixote at this point said:

"There is nothing more to do here but that each man should take what is his own; and whom God gave it to, may Saint Peter bless it for him."

One of the four servants said:

"Unless this is a heavy joke, I cannot persuade myself that men of as good an understanding as all these people here are, or seem to be, would dare to say and maintain that this is not a basin and that not a pack-saddle. But since I see that they maintain it and say it, I give myself to understand that there is some mystery in insisting on a thing so contrary to what truth itself and experience itself show us. Because I swear by all that's holy" — and he hurled out a round oath — "that everybody alive in the world today shall not persuade me otherwise than that this is a barber's basin and that a donkey's pack-saddle."

"It might well be a she-donkey's," said the curate.

"It comes to the same," said the servant, "for the case does not turn on that, but on whether it is or is not a pack-saddle, as your worships say."

Hearing this, one of the officers who had come in, who had heard the quarrel and dispute, full of anger and annoyance said:

"It is as much a pack-saddle as my father is; and whoever has said or shall say anything else must be drunk as a grape."

"You lie like a base-born scoundrel," answered Don Quixote.

And raising his pike, which he never let out of his hands, he was going to bring it down on his head with such a blow that if the officer had not got out of the way he would have left him stretched out there. The pike went to pieces on the ground, and the other officers, who saw their companion badly used, raised their voices calling for help in the name of the Holy Brotherhood.

The innkeeper, who was of the company, ran at once for his staff of office and his sword and placed himself at his companions' side. Don Luis's servants gathered round Don Luis so that he should not get away from them in the uproar. The barber, seeing the house in confusion, took hold of his pack-saddle again, and Sancho did the same. Don Quixote put his hand to his sword and charged the officers. Don Luis shouted to his servants to leave him and go to the help of Don Quixote, and of Cardenio and Don Fernando, who were all supporting Don Quixote.

The curate shouted, the innkeeper's wife screamed, her daughter was distressed, Maritornes wept, Dorotea was bewildered, Luscinda taken aback and Doña Clara in a faint. The barber pounded Sancho, Sancho ground the barber. Don Luis, when one of his servants dared to take him by the arm so that he should not get away, gave him a punch that bathed his teeth in blood; the judge defended him; Don Fernando had an officer under his feet and was measuring his body with them entirely to his own satisfaction. The innkeeper raised his voice again, calling for help in the name of the Holy Brotherhood — so that the whole inn was wailing, shouting, screaming, confusion, fears, alarms, disasters, sword-strokes, cuffs, blows, kicks and effusion of blood.

And in the middle of this chaos, machine and labyrinth of things, it presented itself to Don Quixote's memory that he saw himself plunged head and heels into the discord of Agramante's camp; and so he said in a voice that made the inn thunder:

"Hold, all of you! Let everybody sheathe his sword! Let everybody be calm! Let everybody listen to me, if everybody wants to be left alive!"

At which great shout everybody stopped, and he went on to say:

"Did I not tell you, gentlemen, that this castle was enchanted, and that some region of devils must live in it? In confirmation of which, I want you to see with your own eyes how the discord of Agramante's camp has been transferred and moved here among us. See how over there they fight for the sword, here for the horse, over yonder for the eagle, over here for the helmet; and we are all fighting, and none of us understands one another. Come, then, your worship, my lord judge, and your worship, master curate, and let one of you act as King Agramante and the other as King Sobrino, and make peace among us; because by God Almighty it is great knavery that so many people of standing as we are here should kill one another for such trifling causes."

The officers, who did not understand Don Quixote's phrases and saw themselves badly handled by Don Fernando, Cardenio and their companions, would not calm down; the barber would, because in the quarrel he had had both his beard and his pack-saddle undone. Sancho, at his master's slightest word, obeyed like a good servant. Don Luis's four servants also stayed still, seeing how little they gained by not doing so. Only the innkeeper insisted that the insolences of that madman must be punished, who at every turn threw his inn into an uproar.

In the end the noise was quieted for the time being, the pack-saddle stayed trappings till the day of judgement, and the basin stayed a helmet and the inn a castle in Don Quixote's imagination.

Everybody being quiet, then, and made friends at the urging of the judge and the curate, Don Luis's servants went back to insisting that he should come away with them that moment. And while he was dealing with them, the judge consulted with Don Fernando, Cardenio and the curate about what he ought to do in that case, telling them the arguments Don Luis had put to him. In the end it was agreed that Don Fernando should tell Don Luis's servants who he was, and that it was his wish that Don Luis should go with him to Andalusia, where he would be valued by his brother the marquis as Don Luis's worth deserved; because in this way it was known from Don Luis's own intention that he would not for the present go back to his father's eyes if they tore him to pieces. So the four of them, understanding Don Fernando's rank and Don Luis's intention, decided between them that three of them should go back to tell his father what was happening, and that the other should stay to serve Don Luis and not to leave him until they came back for him, or until he saw what his father ordered.

In this way that whole machine of quarrels was quieted by Agramante's authority and King Sobrino's prudence. But the enemy of concord and the rival of peace, seeing himself despised and made a fool of, and how little fruit he had got out of putting them all into so confused a labyrinth, decided to try his hand again, raising up new quarrels and disturbances.

The fact is that the officers had quieted down, having overheard the rank of the men they had been fighting, and had withdrawn from the quarrel, since it seemed to them that whatever way it turned out they were bound to get the worst of the battle. But one of them — the one who had been pounded and trampled by Don Fernando — remembered that among some warrants he carried for arresting certain criminals, he carried one against Don Quixote, whom the Holy Brotherhood had ordered to be arrested for the freedom he had given the galley slaves, and as Sancho had very reasonably feared.

Thinking of this, then, he wanted to make certain whether the description he carried of Don Quixote fitted; and pulling a parchment out of his shirt, he came upon the one he was looking for. And setting himself to read it slowly, because he was not a good reader, at every word he read he set his eyes on Don Quixote and went on comparing the description in the warrant with Don Quixote's face; and he found that beyond any doubt this was the man the warrant spoke of. And he had hardly made certain when, gathering up his parchment, he took the warrant in his left hand and with his right seized Don Quixote by the neck so tightly that he did not let him breathe, and said at the top of his voice:

"Help, in the name of the Holy Brotherhood! And so that it may be seen that I ask it in earnest, let this warrant be read, in which it is set down that this highwayman is to be arrested."

The curate took the warrant and saw that everything the officer said was true, and how it agreed with Don Quixote's description; and Don Quixote, seeing himself badly treated by that villainous scoundrel, with his temper at its height and the very bones of his body cracking, as best he could seized the officer by the throat with both hands — so that if he had not been rescued by his companions, he would have left his life there before Don Quixote let go his hold.

The innkeeper, who was bound to support men of his own office, ran at once to help him.
