The innkeeper's wife, seeing her husband in a quarrel again, raised her voice again, whose note was taken up at once by Maritornes and her daughter, calling for help from heaven and from those who were there. Sancho, seeing what was going on, said:

"By the living Lord, everything my master says about the enchantments of this castle is true, since it is not possible to live one hour in it in peace!"

Don Fernando separated the officer and Don Quixote, and, to the satisfaction of both, unlocked their hands, which had the one a firm hold on the collar of the other's coat and the other on the other's throat. But the officers did not for this stop demanding their prisoner, and that people should help them to hand him over tied up and delivered entirely to their will, because that was what the service of the king and of the Holy Brotherhood required; on whose behalf they again asked for help and support in making that arrest of that robber and highwayman of paths and highways.

Don Quixote laughed to hear these words; and with great calm he said:

"Come here, you low and base-born people: do you call it robbery on the highway to give liberty to men in chains, to loose prisoners, to help the wretched, to raise up the fallen, to relieve the needy? Ah, infamous people, deserving by your low and vile understanding that heaven should not communicate to you the worth that is shut up in knight-errantry, nor give you to understand the sin and ignorance you are in in not reverencing the shadow, let alone the presence, of any knight errant!

"Come here, you gang of thieves and not officers of the gang, highway robbers with the licence of the Holy Brotherhood; tell me: who was the ignorant man who signed a warrant of arrest against such a knight as I am? Who was the man who did not know that knights errant are exempt from every court of law, and that their law is their sword, their statutes their courage, their ordinances their own will?

"Who was the idiot, I say again, who does not know that there is no patent of gentility with as many privileges and exemptions as the one a knight errant acquires on the day he is dubbed a knight and gives himself up to the hard exercise of chivalry? What knight errant ever paid poll tax, sales tax, the queen's shoe-money, the royal levy, road toll or ferry? What tailor ever charged him for making a suit of clothes? What governor of a castle took him in and made him pay his share of the reckoning? What king did not seat him at his table? What maiden did not take a fancy to him and surrender herself to him, at his whole liking and pleasure? And, in the end, what knight errant has there been, is there, or ever shall be in the world, who has not the spirit to give, single-handed, four hundred blows to four hundred officers who set themselves in front of him?"

Chapter 46: Of the Notable Adventure of the Officers of the Holy Brotherhood, and of the Great Ferocity of Our Good Knight Don Quixote

While Don Quixote was saying this, the curate was persuading the officers that Don Quixote was out of his wits, as they could see by his deeds and his words, and that there was no reason to carry the business further, since even if they arrested him and took him away, they would have to let him go again as a madman. To which the man with the warrant answered that it was not his business to judge Don Quixote's madness but to do what his superior had ordered him; and that once he was arrested, they could let him go three hundred times for all he cared.

"For all that," said the curate, "this time you are not to take him — nor will he let himself be taken, as far as I can see."

In fact the curate knew so much to say to them, and Don Quixote knew how to do so many mad things, that the officers would have been madder than he was if they had not recognised Don Quixote's failing; and so they thought it best to calm down, and even to act as mediators in making peace between the barber and Sancho Panza, who were still keeping up their quarrel with great bitterness.

Finally, as officers of the law, they mediated the case and were arbitrators in it, in such a way that both parties were left, if not completely contented, at least somewhat satisfied — because the pack-saddles were exchanged but not the girths and headstalls. And as for the business of Mambrino's helmet, the curate, on the sly and without Don Quixote's knowing about it, gave him eight reals for the basin, and the barber made out a receipt for it and an undertaking not to claim he had been cheated, then or for ever after, amen.

These two quarrels being quieted, then, which were the chief and weightiest ones, it remained for Don Luis's servants to agree that three should go back and one should stay to go with him where Don Fernando wanted to take him. And as good luck and better fortune had already begun to break lances and smooth away difficulties in favour of the lovers at the inn and the brave men in it, it chose to carry it through and give everything a happy outcome; for the servants agreed to everything Don Luis wanted. At which Doña Clara was so delighted that nobody who looked at her face at that moment could have failed to see the joy of her soul.

Zoraida, although she did not properly understand all the things she had seen, grew sad and glad by guesswork, according to what she saw and noted in each person's face — especially her Spaniard's, on whom she always had her eyes fixed and her soul hanging.

The innkeeper, who had not failed to notice the gift and payment the curate had made the barber, asked for Don Quixote's reckoning, together with the damage to his wineskins and the loss of his wine, swearing that neither Rocinante nor Sancho's donkey should leave the inn until he was paid to the last farthing. The curate quieted it all and Don Fernando paid it — although the judge had also very willingly offered the payment. And they were all left in such peace and quiet that the inn no longer seemed the discord of Agramante's camp, as Don Quixote had called it, but the very peace and quiet of the time of Octavian; for all of which it was the general opinion that thanks were due to the good intentions and great eloquence of the curate and to Don Fernando's incomparable generosity.

Finding himself free and clear, then, of so many quarrels, his squire's as well as his own, it seemed to Don Quixote that it would be as well to go on with the journey he had begun and put an end to that great adventure he had been called and chosen for. And so with settled determination he went and knelt down before Dorotea, who would not let him say a word until he got up; and he, to obey her, got to his feet and said to her:

"It is a common proverb, fair lady, that diligence is the mother of good fortune, and in many and grave matters experience has shown that the promptness of the man of business brings a doubtful suit to a good end. But in nothing is this truth better shown than in matters of war, where speed and quickness forestall the enemy's plans and win the victory before the opponent puts himself on his guard.

"All this I say, high and precious lady, because it seems to me that our staying in this castle is by now without profit, and might do us so much harm that we should see it one day. For who knows whether by hidden and diligent spies your enemy the giant may already have learnt that I am going to destroy him, and, time allowing him, may fortify himself in some impregnable castle or fortress against which my efforts and the strength of my untiring arm would be of little use? So, my lady, let us forestall his designs, as I have said, with our own diligence, and let us set off at once and good fortune go with us; for your greatness's having your fortune as you wish it depends on nothing more than my not being slow in coming face to face with your opponent."

Don Quixote fell silent and said no more, and waited with great composure for the fair princess's answer; who, with a lordly manner suited to Don Quixote's style, answered him in this way:

"I thank you, sir knight, for the desire you show to favour me in my great distress, exactly as befits a knight, whose business and concern it is to favour orphans and the needy; and may heaven grant that your desire and mine be fulfilled, so that you may see that there are grateful women in the world. And as for my departure, let it be at once; for I have no will but yours: dispose of me entirely as you like and please, for she who once handed you the defence of her person and put in your hands the restoring of her dominions is not going to want to go against whatever your prudence may ordain."

"In God's hands be it," said Don Quixote. "Since it is so that a lady humbles herself before me, I do not want to lose the chance of raising her up and setting her on her inherited throne. Let the departure be at once, because what they usually say — that danger lies in delay — is putting spurs to my desire and to the road. And since heaven has not created, nor hell seen, anybody who could frighten me or make me a coward, saddle Rocinante, Sancho, and get your donkey ready and the queen's palfrey; and let us take our leave of the governor and of these gentlemen and go from here this very moment."

Sancho, who was present at all of it, said, shaking his head from side to side:

"Ah, sir, sir, there's more mischief in the little village than is talked about — saving the respect due to the honourable ladies present."

"What mischief can there be in any village, or in all the cities in the world, that can be talked about to my discredit, peasant?"

"If your worship gets angry," answered Sancho, "I'll be quiet, and leave off saying what I'm bound to say as a good squire, and as a good servant ought to say to his master."

"Say what you like," replied Don Quixote, "so long as your words are not aimed at making me afraid; for if you are afraid, you are behaving as who you are, and if I am not, I am behaving as who I am."

"It isn't that — sinner that I was before God!" answered Sancho. "It's that I take it as certain and settled that this lady who says she is queen of the great kingdom of Micomicón is no more so than my mother; because if she were what she says, she wouldn't go about nuzzling with one of the people in this company at every turn of the head and every time our backs are turned."

Dorotea turned red at Sancho's words, because it was true that her husband Don Fernando had once or twice, by stealth from other eyes, gathered with his lips part of the reward his desires deserved; which Sancho had seen, and it had seemed to him that such freedom was more the mark of a court lady than of the queen of so great a kingdom. And she neither could nor would answer Sancho a word, but let him go on with his talk; and he went on to say:

"I say this, sir, because if, after we have travelled roads and highways and gone through bad nights and worse days, the man who is enjoying himself at this inn is to come and pick the fruit of our labours, there is no reason for me to hurry and saddle Rocinante and put the pack-saddle on the donkey and get the palfrey ready; for it would be better for us to stay still, and let every whore spin her own flax, and let's eat."

God help me, how great the anger was that Don Quixote felt on hearing his squire's unseemly words! I say it was so great that with a stumbling voice and a stammering tongue, shooting live fire out of his eyes, he said:

"Oh, you villainous scoundrel, ill-mannered, unseemly, ignorant, ineloquent, foul-tongued, insolent, back-biting and slanderous creature! Have you dared to say such words in my presence and in that of these illustrious ladies, and dared to put such indecencies and impudences into your muddled imagination? Get out of my presence, monster of nature, treasury of lies, cupboard of falsehoods, granary of knaveries, inventor of wickednesses, publisher of stupidities, enemy of the respect due to royal persons! Go; do not appear before me, on pain of my anger!"

And saying this, he arched his eyebrows, blew out his cheeks, looked all round him and gave the ground a great stamp with his right foot — all signs of the anger shut up in his entrails. At which words and furious gestures Sancho was left so shrunken and frightened that he would have been glad if at that instant the earth had opened under his feet and swallowed him. And he did not know what to do with himself but to turn his back and get away from his master's angry presence.

But the quick-witted Dorotea, who by now understood Don Quixote's humour so well, said, to soften his anger:

"Do not be vexed, Sir Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, at the foolish things your good squire has said, because perhaps he must not say them without some occasion; nor can it be suspected of his good understanding and Christian conscience that he would bear false witness against anybody. And so it must be believed, without putting any doubt on it, that since in this castle, as you say yourself, sir knight, everything goes and happens by way of enchantment, it might be — I say — that Sancho saw by this devilish means what he says he saw, so much to the offence of my modesty."

"By omnipotent God I swear," said Don Quixote at this, "that your greatness has hit the point, and that some evil vision must have been put before this poor sinner Sancho, which made him see what it would have been impossible to see except by way of enchantments; for I know well from this unfortunate man's goodness and innocence that he does not know how to bear false witness against anybody."

"So it is and so it shall be," said Don Fernando; "for which reason your worship, Señor Don Quixote, ought to forgive him and bring him back into the fold of your favour, sicut erat in principio, before such visions took his wits away."

Don Quixote answered that he did forgive him; and the curate went for Sancho, who came very humbly, and, kneeling down, asked his master for his hand. And he gave it him, and after letting him kiss it he gave him his blessing, saying:

"Now you will finally recognise, Sancho my son, that what I have told you many other times is true — that everything in this castle is done by way of enchantment."

"That is what I believe," said Sancho, "except that business of the blanket, which really happened in the ordinary way."

"Do not believe it," answered Don Quixote; "for if it had been so, I would have avenged you then, and even now. But neither then nor now could I, or did I see, anybody on whom to take vengeance for your injury."

They all wanted to know what this business of the blanket was, and the innkeeper told them, point by point: the aerial flights of Sancho Panza, at which they all laughed not a little, and at which Sancho would have been no less mortified if his master had not assured him all over again that it was an enchantment — although Sancho's foolishness never went so far that he believed it was not the plain and settled truth, with no mixture of deception in it, that he had been tossed in a blanket by people of flesh and blood, and not by phantoms dreamed or imagined, as his master believed and maintained.

Two days had now gone by since that distinguished company had been at the inn; and thinking it was now time to leave, they made arrangements so that, without Dorotea and Don Fernando putting themselves to the trouble of going back with Don Quixote to his village on the pretext of Queen Micomicona's deliverance, the curate and the barber might take him away, as they wanted, and try to have his madness cured in his own country.

And what they arranged was that they came to terms with an ox-carter who happened to pass that way, so that he should carry him in this fashion. They made a kind of cage of barred timbers, big enough for Don Quixote to fit comfortably inside it; and then Don Fernando and his companions, with Don Luis's servants and the officers, together with the innkeeper, all by the curate's arrangement and advice, covered their faces and disguised themselves, some one way and some another, so that Don Quixote should think they were different people from the ones he had seen in that castle.

This done, with the greatest silence they went in to where he was sleeping and resting after the past scuffles. They came up to him, sleeping free and safe from any such event; and taking a firm hold on him, they tied his hands and feet very securely, so that when he woke with a start he could not stir, or do anything except be astonished and taken aback at seeing such strange faces in front of him.

And at once he fell into the notion his continual, deranged imagination presented him with, and believed that all those figures were phantoms of that enchanted castle, and that without any doubt he was now enchanted, since he could neither move nor defend himself — exactly as the curate, the contriver of this machine, had thought it would happen.

Sancho alone, of everybody present, was in his own right senses and in his own right figure; who, although he wanted very little of having the same disease as his master, did not fail to recognise who all those counterfeit figures were. But he did not dare unstitch his mouth until he saw what that assault on and imprisonment of his master would come to — and his master did not say a word either, waiting to see the end of his misfortune. Which was that, bringing the cage there, they shut him inside it and nailed the timbers so firmly that they could not have been broken with two good pulls.

They then took him on their shoulders; and as they went out of the room there was heard a fearful voice, as fearful as the barber knew how to make it — not the pack-saddle one but the other — which said:

"O Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance! Let not the imprisonment thou goest in cause thee any affliction, for so it behoveth, that thou mayest the sooner finish the adventure wherein thy great valour hath placed thee. Which shall be finished when the furious Manchegan lion and the white Tobosan dove shall lie together in one, after their high necks have been bowed to the soft matrimonical yoke; from which unheard-of union there shall come forth into the light of the world brave whelps, who shall imitate the rampant claws of their valiant father. And this shall be before the pursuer of the fleeing nymph shall twice make his visit to the shining signs in his swift and natural course.

"And thou, O most noble and obedient squire that ever had sword at his belt, beard on his face and smell in his nostrils, be not dismayed or discontented to see carried off thus before thine own eyes the flower of knight-errantry; for soon, if it please the fashioner of the world, thou shalt see thyself so lofty and so exalted that thou shalt not know thyself, and the promises thy good master hath made thee shall not go unfulfilled. And I assure thee, on the part of the wise Lady Liarina, that thy wages shall be paid thee, as thou shalt see by the deed. And follow the footsteps of the valiant and enchanted knight, for it is fitting that thou shouldst go where ye both shall stop. And since it is not lawful for me to say more, God be with you; for I return to where I myself know."

And on finishing the prophecy he raised his voice to a high pitch and then lowered it, with such a tender note that even those who were in on the joke came near to believing that what they heard was true.

Don Quixote was left comforted by the prophecy he had heard, because he immediately gathered its meaning entire; and he saw that they were promising him that he would be joined in holy and lawful matrimony with his beloved Dulcinea of El Toboso, from whose happy womb would come the whelps, who were his children, for the everlasting glory of La Mancha. And believing this thoroughly and firmly, he raised his voice, and, giving a great sigh, said:

"O you, whoever you may be, who have prophesied so much good to me! I beg you to ask on my behalf the wise enchanter who has charge of my affairs not to let me perish in this prison where they are now taking me, until I have seen fulfilled such glad and incomparable promises as the ones that have been made to me here. For once this is so, I shall count the pains of my prison a glory, and these chains that gird me a relief, and this bed they lay me on not a hard field of battle but a soft couch and a happy bridal bed.

"And as far as the comfort of Sancho Panza my squire goes, I trust in his goodness and good conduct that he will not leave me in good luck or in bad; because even if it should not come about, through his short fortune or mine, that I can give him the isle, or something equivalent that I have promised him, at least his wages cannot be lost, for in my will, which is already made, I have set down what is to be given him — not in proportion to his many good services but to my own means."

Sancho Panza bowed to him with great politeness and kissed both his hands — because he could not have kissed one, both being tied together.

Then those apparitions took the cage on their shoulders and settled it on the ox-cart.

Chapter 47: Of the Strange Manner in Which Don Quixote of La Mancha Was Enchanted, with Other Famous Events

When Don Quixote saw himself caged in that fashion and up on the cart, he said:

"I have read many and very grave histories of knights errant, but I have never read, or seen, or heard that enchanted knights are carried off in this way and at the pace these lazy, slow animals promise. Because they generally carry them off through the air, with extraordinary speed, shut up in some grey dark cloud, or in some chariot of fire, or else on some hippogriff or other such beast. But that they should now be carrying me on an ox-cart — by the living God, it puzzles me!

"But perhaps the chivalry and the enchantments of these times of ours must follow a different road from the one the ancients followed. And it might also be that, as I am a new knight in the world and the first to have brought back to life the now forgotten calling of adventuring chivalry, other kinds of enchantment and other ways of carrying off the enchanted may also have been newly invented. What do you think of this, Sancho my son?"

"I don't know what I think," answered Sancho, "not being as well read as your worship in errant writings. But for all that, I'd dare to state and swear that these apparitions going about here are not altogether Catholic."

"Catholic? My father!" answered Don Quixote. "How can they be Catholic when they are all devils who have taken on phantom bodies in order to come and do this and put me in this state? And if you want to see the truth of it, touch them and feel them, and you will find that they have no body but of air, and that they consist of nothing but the appearance."

"By God, sir," replied Sancho, "I've touched them already; and this devil going about here so busily is plump with flesh, and has another property very different from the one I've heard say devils have. Because, according to what people say, they all smell of brimstone and other bad smells; but this one smells of amber half a league off."

Sancho said this about Don Fernando, who, being such a great lord, must have smelt of what Sancho said.

"Do not be surprised at that, friend Sancho," answered Don Quixote; "for I would have you know that devils know a great deal, and although they carry smells about with them, they themselves smell nothing, because they are spirits; and if they do smell, they cannot smell good things but only bad and stinking ones. And the reason is that, since wherever they are they carry hell with them, and cannot receive any kind of relief in their torments, and since a good smell is a thing that delights and pleases, it is not possible that they should smell anything good. And if it seems to you that this devil you speak of smells of amber, either you are deceiving yourself or he wants to deceive you by making you not take him for a devil."

All this conversation passed between master and man. And Don Fernando and Cardenio, afraid that Sancho might come to see all the way through their invention — which he was already very close on the heels of — decided to cut it short by leaving; and calling the innkeeper aside, they ordered him to saddle Rocinante and put the pack-saddle on Sancho's donkey, which he did very quickly.

By this time the curate had come to terms with the officers to accompany him as far as his village, giving them so much a day. Cardenio hung on the pommel of Rocinante's saddle the shield on one side and the basin on the other, and by signs ordered Sancho to get up on his ass and take Rocinante's reins, and stationed the two officers with their muskets on the two sides of the cart.

But before the cart moved, the innkeeper's wife, her daughter and Maritornes came out to say goodbye to Don Quixote, pretending that they were weeping with grief at his misfortune; to whom Don Quixote said:

"Do not weep, my good ladies, for all these misfortunes go with those who profess what I profess; and if these calamities did not happen to me, I should not count myself a famous knight errant. Because to knights of little name and fame such things never happen, since there is nobody in the world who remembers them. To the valorous, yes; for they have many princes and many other knights envying their virtue and their courage, who try by wicked means to destroy the good. But for all that, virtue is so powerful that by itself alone, in spite of all the necromancy known to its first inventor Zoroaster, it will come out victorious from every trial and will give light to the world, as the sun gives it in the sky.

"Forgive me, fair ladies, if through any carelessness of mine I have done you any wrong; for wilfully and knowingly I never did any to anybody. And pray to God to get me out of these prisons where some ill-intentioned enchanter has put me; for if I see myself free of them, the favours you have done me in this castle will not fall out of my memory, that I may repay them and serve them and reward them as they deserve."

While the ladies of the castle were doing this with Don Quixote, the curate and the barber took their leave of Don Fernando and his companions, and of the captain and his brother and all those contented ladies, especially Dorotea and Luscinda. They all embraced and agreed to send each other news of how they fared, Don Fernando telling the curate where he should write to him so as to let him know how Don Quixote ended, assuring him that there would be nothing that would give him more pleasure than to know it; and that he likewise would let him know about everything he saw might give him pleasure, both about his marriage and about Zoraida's baptism, and how Don Luis turned out, and Luscinda's return home. The curate promised to do everything he was asked, with complete punctuality. They embraced again, and again made fresh offers.

The innkeeper came up to the curate and gave him some papers, telling him he had found them in the lining of the portmanteau where the Tale of Reckless Curiosity had been found; and that since their owner had never come back that way, he should take the lot of them, for as he could not read he did not want them. The curate thanked him; and opening them at once, he saw that at the beginning of the writing it said: The Tale of Rinconete and Cortadillo — from which he understood it was some story, and gathered that since the Reckless Curiosity had been good, this one would be too, since they might all be by the same author. And so he kept it, meaning to read it when he had the chance.

He got on his horse, and his friend the barber too, with their masks on so that they should not be immediately recognised by Don Quixote, and they set off riding behind the cart. And the order they went in was this: the cart went first, driven by its owner; on the two sides went the officers, as has been said, with their muskets; then came Sancho Panza on his ass, leading Rocinante by the rein. Behind all this came the curate and the barber on their powerful mules, with their faces covered as has been said, with a grave, composed bearing, travelling no faster than the slow pace of the oxen allowed. Don Quixote went along seated in the cage, his hands tied, his feet stretched out and leaning against the bars, with as much silence and as much patience as though he had not been a man of flesh but a statue of stone.

And so, at that pace and in that silence, they travelled a good two leagues, until they came to a valley which seemed to the ox-driver a suitable place to rest and give the oxen some grazing. And discussing it with the curate, the barber was of the opinion that they should go on a little further, because he knew that behind a rise that showed close by there was a valley with more grass, and much better than the one where they wanted to stop. The barber's opinion was taken, and so they went on with their journey.

At this the curate turned his head and saw that behind them were coming some six or seven men on horseback, well turned out and equipped, by whom they were soon overtaken, because they were travelling not with the phlegm and calm of oxen but like men riding canons' mules and eager to get quickly to the inn for their midday rest, which showed less than a league from there. The busy men came up to the lazy ones and greeted each other courteously; and one of those who were coming — who was, in short, a canon of Toledo and master of the rest who were with him — seeing the orderly procession of cart, officers, Sancho, Rocinante, curate and barber, and above all Don Quixote caged and imprisoned, could not help asking what it meant to be taking that man along in that way; although he had already given himself to understand, seeing the officers' insignia, that he must be some villainous highwayman, or some other criminal whose punishment belonged to the Holy Brotherhood. One of the officers, to whom the question was put, answered like this:

"Sir, what it means for this gentleman to be going along in this fashion, let him say himself, because we do not know."

Don Quixote heard the conversation and said:

"Are your worships by any chance, sir knights, versed and expert in this matter of knight-errantry? Because if you are, I shall tell you my misfortunes; and if not, there is no reason for me to weary myself in telling them."

And by this time the curate and the barber had come up, seeing that the travellers were in conversation with Don Quixote of La Mancha, so as to answer in such a way that their contrivance should not be discovered.

The canon answered what Don Quixote had said:

"Truly, brother, I know more about books of chivalry than about Villalpando's Compendium of Logic. So that if it depends on nothing more than that, you may safely tell me whatever you like."

"In God's hands be it," replied Don Quixote. "Since that is so, I want you to know, sir knight, that I go enchanted in this cage through the envy and fraud of wicked enchanters; for virtue is more persecuted by the wicked than loved by the good. A knight errant I am, and not one of those whose names Fame never remembered to make everlasting in her memory, but one of those who, in spite and to the vexation of envy itself, and of all the magi Persia bred, the brahmins India and the gymnosophists Ethiopia, shall set his name in the temple of immortality, to serve as an example and a model in the ages to come, where knights errant may see the steps they must follow if they wish to reach the summit and honourable height of arms."

"Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha speaks the truth," said the curate at this point; "for he goes enchanted in this cart, not through his own faults and sins but through the ill will of those whom virtue annoys and courage angers. This, sir, is the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, if you have ever heard him named, whose valorous exploits and great deeds shall be written on hard bronze and in everlasting marble, however much envy may weary itself in darkening them and malice in hiding them."

When the canon heard the prisoner and the free man speak in such a style, he came near to crossing himself in astonishment, and could not make out what had happened to him; and all those who came with him fell into the same astonishment.

At this Sancho Panza, who had come close to hear the conversation, said, to patch everything up:

"Now, gentlemen, love me or hate me for what I say, the fact of the matter is that my master Don Quixote is as much enchanted as my mother is. He has his wits whole, he eats and drinks and does his necessities like other men, and as he did them yesterday, before they caged him. This being so, how do they want to make me understand that he goes enchanted? For I have heard a great many people say that the enchanted neither eat nor sleep nor talk, and my master, if nobody stops him, will talk more than thirty attorneys."

And turning to look at the curate, he went on to say:

"Ah, master curate, master curate! Did your worship think I don't know you, and do you suppose I don't fathom and guess what these new enchantments are aiming at? Well, let me tell you I know you, however much you cover your face, and let me tell you I understand you, however much you disguise your tricks. In the end, where envy reigns virtue cannot live, nor generosity where there is meanness.

"Devil take it! For if it hadn't been for your reverence, this would be the hour when my master was married to the Princess Micomicona and I was a count at the very least — for nothing else was to be expected, both from the goodness of my master, the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, and from the greatness of my services. But I see now that what they say is true: that the wheel of Fortune goes round faster than a millwheel, and that those who were riding high yesterday are on the floor today. It grieves me for my children and my wife, because when they could and should have expected to see their father come in at their door made a governor or viceroy of some isle or kingdom, they will see him come in made a stable-boy.

"All this I have said, master curate, is nothing more than to urge on your paternity to make a matter of conscience of the bad treatment my master is being given, and to look out that God does not call you to account in the next life for this imprisonment of my master, and charge you with all those rescues and good deeds my master Don Quixote is failing to do in this time he is a prisoner."

"Mend me those lamps!" said the barber at this point. "So you too, Sancho, are of your master's brotherhood? By the living Lord, I am beginning to see that you will have to keep him company in the cage, and that you will end as enchanted as he is, for as much as you have caught of his humour and his chivalry! In an evil hour you got yourself pregnant with his promises, and in an evil hour that isle you so much want got into your brainpan."

"I am not pregnant by anybody," answered Sancho, "nor am I a man to let myself be got pregnant, not by the king himself; and poor as I am, I am an Old Christian and I owe nothing to anybody. And if I want isles, other men want worse things; and every man is the son of his own deeds. And, being a man, I might come to be Pope, let alone governor of an isle — the more so as my master may win so many that he will be short of people to give them to.

"Let your worship look how you talk, master barber; for there is more to it than shaving beards, and there is a difference between one Peter and another. I say this because we all know one another, and no loaded dice are to be thrown at me. And as for this business of my master's enchantment, God knows the truth; and let it stay there, because stirring it only makes it worse."

The barber did not want to answer Sancho, in case with his simplicities he should reveal what he and the curate were so anxious to conceal. And for this same fear the curate had told the canon to ride on a little ahead, and he would tell him the mystery of the caged man, along with other things that would entertain him. The canon did so and went on ahead with his servants and with him; and he listened attentively to everything the curate chose to tell him about Don Quixote's character, life, madness and habits, telling him briefly the beginning and the cause of his derangement and the whole progress of his adventures, up to his having been put in that cage, and the plan they had of taking him to his own country to see whether by some means they could find a remedy for his madness.

The servants and the canon were astonished all over again at hearing Don Quixote's extraordinary history; and on finishing hearing it, he said:

"Truly, master curate, I find by my own reckoning that these things they call books of chivalry are harmful to the state. And although, carried away by an idle and false taste, I have read almost the beginning of most of those that are in print, I have never been able to bring myself to read a single one from beginning to end — because it seems to me that, more or less, they are all one and the same thing, and this one has no more in it than that, nor that one than the other.

"And as it seems to me, this kind of writing and composition comes under the head of those fables they call Milesian, which are nonsensical tales that aim only at giving pleasure and not at teaching: the opposite of what the apologue fables do, which give pleasure and teach at the same time. And granting that the chief purpose of such books is to give pleasure, I do not know how they can achieve it, being full of so many and such outrageous absurdities. For the pleasure the soul conceives must come from the beauty and harmony it sees or contemplates in the things that sight or imagination sets before it; and everything that has ugliness and disorder in it can cause us no contentment at all.

"Then what beauty can there be, or what proportion of the parts to the whole and of the whole to the parts, in a book or fable where a lad of sixteen deals a slash at a giant like a tower and divides him into two halves, as if he were made of sugar-paste? Or where, when they want to paint us a battle, after saying that on the enemy side there are a million combatants, so long as the hero of the book is against them we must of necessity, however it displeases us, understand that this knight won the victory by the valour of his strong arm alone?

"Then what shall we say of the readiness with which a queen or an heiress empress lets herself be carried off in the arms of a wandering and unknown knight? What mind, unless it is altogether barbarous and uncultivated, can be satisfied with reading that a great tower full of knights goes sailing over the sea like a ship with a favourable wind, and tonight is in Lombardy and tomorrow morning in the lands of Prester John of the Indies, or in others that neither Ptolemy discovered nor Marco Polo saw?

"And if it were answered to me that the men who compose such books write them as things of fiction, and that so they are not obliged to look at niceties or truths, I would answer them that a lie is the better the more it looks like truth, and pleases the more the more it has of the doubtful and the possible about it. Lying fables must be married to the understanding of those who read them, being written in such a way that, making impossibilities easy, levelling out great things, holding minds in suspense, they may astonish, hold, excite and entertain, so that wonder and delight go along at one and the same pace. And none of these things can be done by a man who runs away from likeness to truth and from imitation, in which the perfection of what is written consists.

"I have never seen any book of chivalry that makes a whole body of a fable with all its limbs, so that the middle corresponds to the beginning and the end to the beginning and the middle; instead they compose them with so many limbs that it looks more as if they meant to form a chimera or a monster than to make a well-proportioned figure. Besides this, they are harsh in style, incredible in their exploits, lascivious in their love affairs, ill-mannered in their courtesies, long in their battles, foolish in their arguments, absurd in their journeys; and finally, they are strangers to all judicious craft, and for this reason deserve to be banished from the Christian commonwealth as a useless people."

The curate listened to him with great attention, and thought him a man of good understanding and that he was right in everything he said; and so he told him that, being of the same opinion himself and having a grudge against books of chivalry, he had burnt all Don Quixote's, which were a great many. And he told him about the scrutiny he had made of them, and which he had condemned to the fire and which he had left alive — at which the canon laughed not a little, and said that for all the ill he had spoken of such books, he found one good thing in them: that they were a subject on which a good mind could show itself, because they gave a long, broad field over which the pen could run without any hindrance.

There it could describe shipwrecks, storms, encounters and battles; painting a valorous captain with all the qualities required to be one, showing himself prudent in forestalling the tricks of his enemies, and an eloquent orator in persuading or dissuading his soldiers, mature in counsel, quick in decision, as brave in waiting as in attacking; painting now a lamentable and tragic event, now a glad and unexpected happening; there a most beautiful lady, modest, clever and reserved; here a Christian knight, brave and courteous; over there an outrageous barbarian braggart; over here a courteous prince, valorous and well-mannered; representing the goodness and loyalty of vassals, the greatness and favours of lords.

Now he can show himself an astrologer, now an excellent cosmographer, now a musician, now well informed in matters of state, and sometimes the chance will come to him to show himself a necromancer, if he likes. He can show the cunning of Ulysses, the piety of Aeneas, the courage of Achilles, the misfortunes of Hector, the treacheries of Sinon, the friendship of Euryalus, the generosity of Alexander, the valour of Caesar, the clemency and truthfulness of Trajan, the fidelity of Zopyrus, the prudence of Cato; and, in the end, all those actions that can make an illustrious man perfect — now putting them in one man alone, now dividing them among many.

"And this being done with a pleasant style and with an ingenious invention that comes as close as possible to the truth, he will without doubt weave a web of various and beautiful threads which, once finished, will show such perfection and beauty that it will achieve the best end that is aimed at in writing, which is to teach and give pleasure at the same time, as I have said already. Because the loose form of writing in these books gives the author room to show himself epic, lyric, tragic, comic, with all those parts that the sweetest and most agreeable arts of poetry and rhetoric hold in themselves; for the epic can be written in prose as well as in verse."

Chapter 48: In Which the Canon Continues the Subject of the Books of Chivalry, with Other Matters Worthy of His Wit

"It is exactly as your worship says, master canon," said the curate; "and for this reason those who up to now have composed such books deserve more blame, for having taken no notice of any good reasoning, or of the art and rules by which they might have guided themselves and become as famous in prose as the two princes of Greek and Latin poetry are in verse."

"I, at least," replied the canon, "have had a certain temptation to write a book of chivalry, keeping in it all the points I have mentioned. And if I am to confess the truth, I have more than a hundred pages written. And to make trial of whether they came up to my own estimate of them, I have shown them to men passionately fond of this kind of reading, learned and judicious, and to others who are ignorant and attend only to the pleasure of hearing absurdities; and from all of them I have found an agreeable approval.

"But for all that, I have not gone on with it, both because it seems to me I am doing a thing outside my profession and because I see that the number of the simple is greater than that of the prudent; and although it is better to be praised by the few who are wise than laughed at by the many who are fools, I do not want to submit myself to the muddled judgement of the conceited common crowd, whose business it is for the most part to read such books.

"But what most took it out of my hands, and even out of my thoughts, to finish it was an argument I made with myself, drawn from the plays that are performed nowadays, saying: 'If those that are in use now, both the invented ones and those from history, all or most of them are known absurdities and things without head or tail — and in spite of that the crowd hears them with pleasure and holds them and approves them as good, when they are so far from being so; and the authors who compose them and the actors who perform them say that they have to be so because that is how the crowd wants them and not otherwise; and that the ones which have a plan and follow the fable as art requires serve for nothing but four judicious men who understand them, while all the rest are left with no notion of their craftsmanship; and that it suits them better to earn a living from the many than a reputation from the few — in that case my book, after I have singed my eyebrows keeping the rules I have mentioned, will end by leaving me like the tailor on the corner, who sewed for nothing and found the thread himself.'

"And although I have sometimes tried to persuade the actors that they are deceived in the opinion they hold, and that they will draw more people and win more fame by performing plays that follow the art than with the absurd ones, they are so tied and welded to their own opinion that there is no argument or evidence that will get them out of it.

"I remember that one day I said to one of these obstinate men: 'Tell me, do you not remember that a few years ago three tragedies were performed in Spain, composed by a famous poet of these kingdoms, which were such that they astonished, delighted and held in suspense everybody who heard them, simple and prudent alike, the crowd and the select alike — and those three alone gave the players more money than thirty of the best that have been made since?'

"'No doubt,' answered the manager I speak of, 'your worship must mean La Isabela, La Filis and La Alejandra.'

"'Those are the ones I mean,' I replied; 'and see whether they kept the precepts of the art well, and whether by keeping them they failed to appear what they were and to please everybody. So the fault does not lie with the crowd, who ask for absurdities, but with those who do not know how to put anything else on. Why, La ingratitud vengada was no absurdity, nor did La Numancia have any in it, nor was any to be found in El mercader amante, nor in La enemiga favorable either, nor in certain others that have been composed by some poets of understanding, for their own fame and renown and for the profit of those who have performed them.'

"And I added other things to these, with which, in my opinion, I left him somewhat confused but neither satisfied nor convinced enough to be got out of his mistaken idea."

"Your worship has touched on a matter, master canon," said the curate at this point, "that has woken in me an old grudge I have against the plays that are in use now — such a grudge that it matches the one I have against the books of chivalry. Because, the play having to be, as Cicero thinks, a mirror of human life, an example of manners and an image of truth, the ones that are performed now are mirrors of absurdity, examples of foolishness and images of lasciviousness.

"For what greater absurdity can there be in the matter we are discussing than for a baby in swaddling clothes to come on in the first scene of the first act, and in the second to come on already a bearded man? And what greater than to paint us a brave old man and a cowardly young one, a rhetorical footman, a page giving counsel, a king turned porter and a princess turned scullery maid?

"What shall I say, then, of the care they take over the times in which the actions they perform can or could have happened, except that I have seen a play whose first act began in Europe, whose second was in Asia and whose third finished in Africa — and if it had been in four acts, the fourth would have finished in America, and so it would have been done in all four quarters of the world?

"And if imitation is the chief thing a play must have, how is it possible to satisfy any moderate understanding when, inventing an action that takes place in the time of King Pepin and Charlemagne, the very man who plays the leading part in it is said to have been the Emperor Heraclius who entered Jerusalem with the Cross, and the man who won the Holy Sepulchre like Godfrey of Bouillon, when there are endless years between the one and the other? And when, the play being founded on an invented thing, they attribute historical truths to it and mix in with it pieces of other events that happened to different people at different times — and this not with likely contrivances but with plain errors, altogether inexcusable?

"And the bad thing is that there are ignorant men who say that this is what perfection is, and that anything else is looking for dainties. And what if we come to religious plays? What false miracles they invent in them, what apocryphal and ill-understood things, attributing to one saint the miracles of another! And even in secular plays they dare to work miracles, with no more respect or consideration than their thinking that such a miracle and stage effect, as they call it, will go down well there, so that ignorant people may be astonished and come to the play. All of which is to the prejudice of truth and to the damage of history, and even to the disgrace of the Spanish wits; because foreigners, who keep the laws of drama with great exactness, take us for barbarians and ignoramuses when they see the absurdities and follies of the plays we make.

"And it would not be enough excuse for this to say that the chief purpose well-ordered states have in allowing public plays to be performed is to entertain the community with some honest recreation and to divert it at times from the bad humours that idleness generally breeds; and that since this is achieved with any play, good or bad, there is no need to lay down laws or to oblige those who compose and perform them to make them as they ought to be made, since, as I have said, what is aimed at in them is achieved with any of them.

"To which I would answer that this end would be achieved a great deal better, beyond all comparison, with good plays than with those that are not good. Because after hearing a play that is well made and well ordered, the listener would come away cheered by the comic parts, taught by the serious ones, astonished by the events, made wiser by the arguments, forewarned by the deceptions, made shrewd by the examples, angry against vice and in love with virtue; for all these effects a good play must wake in the mind of whoever listens to it, however rustic and dull he may be. And it is impossible with every impossibility that a play which has all these qualities should fail to cheer and entertain, satisfy and content, a great deal more than one which lacks them — as for the most part these do that are ordinarily performed nowadays.

"And the poets who compose them are not to blame for it, because there are some among them who know very well where they go wrong and know extremely well what they ought to do; but as plays have become a saleable commodity, they say, and they say truly, that the players would not buy them if they were not of that stamp. And so the poet tries to fall in with what the player who is to pay him for his work asks of him.

"And that this is true may be seen by the many and endless plays composed by a most fortunate wit of these kingdoms, with so much elegance, so much charm, such graceful verse, such good arguments, such weighty maxims, and, in the end, so full of eloquence and loftiness of style that his fame fills the world. And through his wanting to fit in with the players' taste, they have not all reached — as some of them have reached — the point of perfection they require.

"Others compose them with so little care for what they are doing that after they have been performed the players have to run away and go into hiding, afraid of being punished — as they often have been — for having performed things to the prejudice of certain kings and to the dishonour of certain families.

"And all these troubles would stop, and a great many more that I do not mention, if there were at Court some intelligent and judicious person to examine all plays before they were performed — not only those that were put on at Court but all that people wanted to perform in Spain — and without whose approval, seal and signature no magistrate in his own district would allow any play to be performed. And in this way the players would take care to send their plays to Court and could perform them in safety; and those who compose them would look at what they were doing with more care and study, being afraid of having to put their works through the strict examination of somebody who understands. And in this way good plays would be made and what is aimed at in them would be most happily achieved: the entertainment of the people, the reputation of the wits of Spain, the profit and safety of the players and the saving of the trouble of punishing them.

"And if the same man, or another, were given the charge of examining the books of chivalry that were newly composed, without doubt some might come out with the perfection your worship has described, enriching our language with the agreeable and precious treasure of eloquence, and giving occasion for the old books to be darkened by the light of the new ones that came out, for the honest pastime not only of the idle but of the busiest people; for it is not possible for the bow to be always bent, nor can human nature and weakness keep going without some lawful recreation."

The canon and the curate had got to this point in their conversation when the barber, riding ahead, came up to them and said to the curate:

"Here, sir licentiate, is the place I said would be a good one for us to take our midday rest while the oxen have fresh and plentiful grazing."

"So it seems to me too," answered the curate.

And on telling the canon what he meant to do, he too wanted to stay with them, invited by the site of a beautiful valley that offered itself to their sight. And both to enjoy it and to enjoy the curate's conversation, of whom he had by now grown fond, and to learn in more detail about Don Quixote's exploits, he ordered some of his servants to go to the inn, which was not far from there, and to bring from it whatever there was to eat, for all of them, because he had decided to take his midday rest in that place that afternoon. To which one of his servants answered that the pack-mule with the supplies, which must be at the inn by now, was carrying provisions enough to make it unnecessary to take anything from the inn but barley.

"Well, if that is so," said the canon, "let all the mounts be taken over there, and have the pack-mule brought back."

While this was going on, Sancho, seeing that he could speak to his master without the constant attendance of the curate and the barber, whom he regarded as suspect, came up to the cage where his master was and said to him:

"Sir, to unburden my conscience I want to tell you how things stand about this enchantment of yours; and it is that these two who are coming along here with their faces covered are the curate of our village and the barber. And I imagine they have hit on this plan of carrying you off like this out of pure envy at your worship's getting ahead of them in doing famous deeds. This truth being granted, it follows that you do not go enchanted but hoodwinked and made a fool of. As proof of which I want to ask you one thing; and if you answer me as I believe you are bound to answer, you will touch this trick with your hand and will see that you do not go enchanted but with your judgement upside down."

"Ask what you like, Sancho my son," answered Don Quixote, "and I shall satisfy you and answer entirely as you wish. And as for your saying that those men who are coming and going with us are the curate and the barber, our fellow-countrymen and acquaintances, it may well be that they seem to be the very men; but that they really and in fact are, do not believe that on any account.

"What you have to believe and understand is that if they look like them, as you say, it must be that those who have enchanted me will have taken that appearance and likeness; because it is easy for enchanters to take whatever shape they fancy, and they will have taken those of these friends of ours to give you occasion to think what you are thinking and to put you in a labyrinth of fancies from which you could not manage to get out, even if you had Theseus's thread.

"And they will also have done it so that I should waver in my understanding and not be able to make out where this injury comes to me from. Because if on the one hand you tell me that the barber and the curate of our village are with me, and on the other I see myself caged, and know of myself that human strength, unless it were supernatural, would not be enough to cage me — what do you want me to say or think, except that the manner of my enchantment goes beyond every one I have read of in all the histories that treat of knights errant who have been enchanted? So you may set your mind at peace and rest about believing that they are the men you say, because they are as much those men as I am a Turk. And as for your wanting to ask me something, say on, and I shall answer you even if you go on asking me from now till tomorrow."

"Our Lady help me!" answered Sancho, giving a great shout. "And is it possible that your worship is so thick in the skull and so short of brains that you do not see that what I am telling you is the plain truth, and that in this imprisonment and misfortune of yours malice has a larger part than enchantment? But since it is so, I mean to prove to you plainly that you do not go enchanted. If not, tell me — and so may God get you out of this storm, and so may you find yourself in my lady Dulcinea's arms when you least expect it —"

"Have done with conjuring me," said Don Quixote, "and ask what you like; for I have told you already that I shall answer you with complete punctuality."

"That is what I ask," replied Sancho; "and what I want to know is that you should tell me, without adding or taking away anything at all but with the whole truth, as it is expected that all those who profess arms should tell it and do tell it — as your worship professes them, under the title of knights errant —"

"I say that I shall not lie in anything," answered Don Quixote. "Do finish asking, for truly you weary me with so many safeguards, entreaties and preambles, Sancho."

"I say that I am sure of my master's goodness and truthfulness; and so, because it bears on our case, I ask, speaking with all respect, whether by any chance since your worship has been caged and, in your own opinion, enchanted in this cage, you have felt the wish and the need to do the greater or the lesser waters, as they say."

"I do not understand that about doing waters, Sancho; make yourself clearer if you want me to answer you straight."

"Is it possible that your worship does not understand about doing the lesser or the greater waters? Why, at school they wean the boys on it. Well, let me tell you that what I mean is whether you have felt the need to do the thing that cannot be got out of."

"Ah, now, now I understand you, Sancho! And many times; and I have the need even now. Get me out of this danger, for things are not altogether clean here!"

Chapter 49: Which Treats of the Judicious Conversation Sancho Panza Had with His Master Don Quixote

"Ah," said Sancho, "I have you now! This is what I wanted to know as I want my own soul and my own life. Come here, sir: could you deny what they commonly say hereabouts when a person is out of sorts — 'I don't know what is the matter with so-and-so, he neither eats nor drinks nor sleeps nor answers to the point what he is asked; you would think he was enchanted'? From which it comes out that those who do not eat or drink or sleep or do the natural acts I speak of are the ones who are enchanted — but not those who have the need your worship has, and who drinks when he is given drink, and eats when he has food, and answers everything he is asked."

"You speak the truth, Sancho," answered Don Quixote; "but I have told you already that there are many kinds of enchantment, and it might be that with time they have changed from one kind to another, and that the custom now is for the enchanted to do everything I do, although they did not do it before. So that against the custom of the times there is no arguing and no drawing conclusions. I know and am convinced that I go enchanted, and this is enough for the safety of my conscience — which I should burden very heavily if I thought I was not enchanted and let myself stay in this cage, idle and cowardly, cheating of my help all those needy and distressed people who at this very hour must have a pressing and extreme need of my aid and protection."

"For all that," replied Sancho, "I say that for greater abundance and satisfaction it would be as well if your worship tried to get out of this prison — which I undertake with all my power to make easy, and even to get you out of it — and tried once more to get up on your good Rocinante, who also seems to go enchanted, so melancholy and sad is he. And this done, let us try our luck again at looking for more adventures; and if it does not turn out well for us, we still have time to come back to the cage, in which I promise, on the word of a good and loyal squire, to shut myself up along with your worship, if by any chance your worship should be so unlucky, or I so simple, as not to manage to bring off what I say."

"I am content to do as you say, brother Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "and when you see an opening for putting my liberty into effect, I shall obey you in everything and through everything. But you, Sancho, will see how mistaken you are in your understanding of my misfortune."

In this talk the knight errant and the ill-erring squire entertained themselves until they arrived where the curate, the canon and the barber, already dismounted, were waiting for them.

The ox-driver at once unyoked the oxen from the cart and let them go at their ease about that green and pleasant spot, whose coolness invited people to enjoy it — not people as enchanted as Don Quixote but as alert and judicious as his squire; who begged the curate to allow his master to come out of the cage for a while, because if they did not let him come out, that prison would not travel as clean as the decency of such a knight as his master required.

The curate understood him and said he would very willingly do what he asked if he were not afraid that as soon as his master found himself at liberty he would be up to his old tricks and go off where nobody would ever see him again.

"I stand surety against his running away," answered Sancho.

"And I too," said the canon, "and the more so if he gives me his word as a knight not to leave us until it is our wish."

"I do give it," answered Don Quixote, who was listening to all of it; "the more so as a man who is enchanted, as I am, is not free to do with his person what he likes, because the one who enchanted him can make him not stir from one spot for three centuries; and if he should have run away, he will bring him back through the air."

And since this was so, they might very well let him loose, especially as it was so much to everybody's advantage; and if they would not let him loose, he warned them that he could not help troubling their sense of smell, unless they got out of the way.

The canon took him by the hand, although he had them tied, and on his good faith and word they let him out of the cage — at which he was infinitely and enormously glad to find himself outside it. And the first thing he did was to stretch his whole body, and then he went to where Rocinante was, and, giving him two pats on the hindquarters, said:

"I still hope in God and in his blessed Mother, flower and mirror of horses, that we shall soon see ourselves both as we would wish: you with your master on your back, and I on top of you, exercising the office God threw me into the world for."

And saying this, Don Quixote went off with Sancho to a remote place, from which he came back much relieved and with more eagerness to put into practice whatever his squire should decide.

The canon watched him, and marvelled at the strangeness of his great madness, and at the fact that in everything he said and answered he showed himself to have an excellent understanding, only losing his stirrups — as has been said other times — when he was talked to about chivalry. And so, moved by compassion, after they had all sat down on the green grass to wait for the canon's supplies, he said to him:

"Is it possible, sir gentleman, that the bitter and idle reading of books of chivalry can have had so much power over your worship as to turn your judgement in such a way that you come to believe that you go enchanted, along with other things of that stamp, as far from being true as lying itself is from the truth?

"And how is it possible that there should be a human understanding that gives itself to believe that there have been in the world that infinity of Amadises, and that mob of so many famous knights, so many emperors of Trebizond, so many Felixmartes of Hircania, so many palfreys, so many wandering damsels, so many serpents, so many dragons, so many giants, so many unheard-of adventures, so many kinds of enchantment, so many battles, so many outrageous encounters, so much splendour of costume, so many princesses in love, so many squires made counts, so many amusing dwarfs, so many love-notes, so much wooing, so many valiant women — and, in the end, so many and such nonsensical things as the books of chivalry contain?

"For my own part I can say that when I read them, so long as I do not set my imagination on thinking that they are all lies and frivolity, they give me some pleasure; but when I realise what they are, I throw the best of them against the wall, and would even throw it into the fire if I had one near or in front of me — as deserving such a punishment for being false and deceitful and outside the dealings common nature calls for, and as inventors of new sects and a new way of life, and as giving occasion for the ignorant crowd to come to believe and hold as true all the foolishness they contain.

"And they even have such daring that they dare to disturb the wits of judicious and well-born gentlemen, as may be plainly seen from what they have done with your worship, since they have brought you to such a pass that it is necessary to shut you in a cage and carry you about on an ox-cart, like a man who takes or carries a lion or a tiger from place to place to make money out of letting people see it.

"Come, Señor Don Quixote, have pity on yourself, and come back into the fold of good sense, and learn to use the great share of it heaven was pleased to give you, employing the most fortunate talent of your mind on some other reading that may work to the profit of your conscience and the increase of your honour!

"And if, still carried away by your natural inclination, you want to read books of exploits and of chivalry, read in Holy Scripture the book of Judges; for there you will find grand truths and deeds as true as they are brave. Lusitania had a Viriathus; Rome a Caesar; Carthage a Hannibal; Greece an Alexander; Castile a Count Fernán González; Valencia a Cid; Andalusia a Gonzalo Fernández; Extremadura a Diego García de Paredes; Jerez a Garci Pérez de Vargas; Toledo a Garcilaso; Seville a Don Manuel de León — the reading of whose valorous deeds can entertain, teach, delight and astonish the loftiest minds that read them.

"This indeed will be reading worthy of your worship's good understanding, my dear Señor Don Quixote; out of which you will come learned in history, in love with virtue, taught in goodness, improved in your habits, brave without rashness, bold without cowardice — and all this for the honour of God, your own profit and the fame of La Mancha, from where, as I have learnt, your worship takes your beginning and origin."

Don Quixote listened most attentively to the canon's arguments; and when he saw that he had made an end of them, after looking at him for a good while he said to him:

"It seems to me, sir gentleman, that your worship's talk has been aimed at wanting to give me to understand that there have been no knights errant in the world, and that all the books of chivalry are false, lying, harmful and useless to the state; and that I have done wrong in reading them, and worse in believing them, and worse still in imitating them, having set myself to follow the very hard profession of knight-errantry that they teach — denying to me that there have been in the world any Amadises, of Gaul or of Greece, or any of the other knights the writings are full of."

"It is all exactly to the letter as your worship goes on relating it," said the canon at this.

To which Don Quixote answered:

"Your worship added too, saying that such books had done me a great deal of harm, since they had turned my judgement and put me in a cage, and that it would be better for me to mend my ways and change my reading, reading other books that are truer and that give more pleasure and teach better."

"That is so," said the canon.

"Then I," replied Don Quixote, "find by my own reckoning that the man out of his senses and enchanted is your worship, since you have set yourself to speak so many blasphemies against a thing so accepted in the world and held to be so true that whoever denied it, as your worship denies it, would deserve the same punishment your worship says you give the books when you read them and they annoy you.

"Because to try to give anybody to understand that Amadis never existed in the world, or any of the other adventuring knights the histories are packed with, will be to try to persuade them that the sun does not give light, or ice cold, or the earth support. For what mind can there be in the world that could persuade another that the business of the princess Floripes and Guy of Burgundy was not true, and the business of Fierabrás at the bridge of Mantible, which happened in the time of Charlemagne — which I swear is as true as it is now daylight?

"And if that is a lie, then it must be a lie too that there was ever a Hector, or an Achilles, or the war of Troy, or the Twelve Peers of France, or King Arthur of England, who to this day goes about turned into a crow and is expected back in his kingdom at any moment. And they will also make bold to say that the history of Guarino Mezquino is a lie, and that of the quest of the Holy Grail, and that the loves of Sir Tristram and Queen Iseult are apocryphal, like those of Guinevere and Lancelot — when there are people who can almost remember having seen the duenna Quintañona, who was the best pourer of wine that Great Britain ever had.

"And this is so much the case that I remember a grandmother of mine on my father's side saying to me, when she saw some duenna in a venerable headdress: 'That one, grandson, is like the duenna Quintañona' — from which I argue that she must have known her, or at least must have managed to see some portrait of her.

"And who could deny that the history of Pierres and the fair Magalona is true, since even to this day one may see in the royal armoury the peg with which the valiant Pierres steered the wooden horse he rode through the air on, which is a little bigger than a cart shaft? And beside the peg is Babieca's saddle, and at Roncesvalles is Roland's horn, as big as a great beam; from which it is to be inferred that there were Twelve Peers, that there was a Pierres, that there were Cids and other such knights,

	the sort of men that people say
	go riding to their adventures.

"If not, let them also tell me that it is not true that the valiant Portuguese Juan de Merlo was a knight errant, who went to Burgundy and fought in the city of Arras with the famous lord of Charny, called Monsieur Pierres, and afterwards in the city of Basle with Monsieur Henri de Remestán, coming out of both enterprises victorious and full of honourable fame; and the adventures and challenges likewise carried through in Burgundy by the valiant Spaniards Pedro Barba and Gutierre Quijada — from whose family I descend in the direct male line — defeating the sons of the Count of St Pol.

"Let them deny me too that Don Fernando de Guevara did not go looking for adventures in Germany, where he fought Messer George, a knight of the house of the Duke of Austria. Let them say that the jousts of Suero de Quiñones at the Pass were a joke; and the enterprises of Monsieur Luis de Falces against Don Gonzalo de Guzmán, a Castilian knight — along with a great many other exploits performed by Christian knights, both of these kingdoms and of foreign ones, so authentic and true that I say again that whoever denied them would be wanting in all reason and good sense."

The canon was astonished to hear the mixture Don Quixote made of truths and lies, and to see the knowledge he had of all those things touching and concerning the deeds of his errant chivalry; and so he answered him:

"I cannot deny, Señor Don Quixote, that some of what your worship has said is true, especially as far as the Spanish knights errant go; and likewise I am willing to grant that there were Twelve Peers of France, but I am not willing to believe that they did all the things Archbishop Turpin writes of them. Because the truth of it is that they were knights chosen by the kings of France, whom they called peers because they were all equal in worth, in quality and in valour — at least, if they were not, it was reasonable that they should be; and it was like one of the religious orders in use now, of Santiago or of Calatrava, in which it is assumed that those who profess it must be, or ought to be, valorous, brave and well-born knights. And as they now say knight of St John, or of Alcántara, in those days they said knight of the Twelve Peers, because twelve equals were chosen for that military order.

"As for there having been a Cid there is no doubt, nor about Bernardo del Carpio either; but that they did the exploits people speak of, I believe there is a very great deal of doubt. As for that other matter of the peg your worship speaks of belonging to Count Pierres, and that it stands beside Babieca's saddle in the royal armoury, I confess my sin: I am so ignorant, or so short-sighted, that although I have seen the saddle I have not noticed the peg — and it being as big as your worship says."

"Well, it is there, without any doubt," replied Don Quixote; "and for a further mark of it, they say it is kept in a leather case so that it does not get rusty."

"That may all be," answered the canon; "but by the orders I have taken, I do not remember having seen it. Yet even granting that it is there, I do not for that undertake to believe the histories of so many Amadises, or those of that mob of knights people tell us about; nor is it right that a man like your worship, so honourable and of such good qualities and endowed with so good an understanding, should give himself to believe that so many and such strange follies as those written in the nonsensical books of chivalry are true."

Chapter 50: Of the Shrewd Arguments Don Quixote Had with the Canon, and Other Events

"That is a fine thing!" answered Don Quixote. "Books that are printed with the licence of kings and with the approval of those they were submitted to, and that are read and celebrated with general pleasure by the great and the small, by the poor and the rich, by the learned and the ignorant, by commoners and gentlemen — in short, by every kind of person, of whatever rank and condition — are these to be lies? And especially when they carry so much appearance of truth, since they tell us the father, the mother, the country, the relatives, the age, the place and the exploits, point by point and day by day, that such a knight performed or such knights performed.

"Be quiet, your worship, do not say such a blasphemy — and believe me, in this I am advising you what you ought to do as a man of sense — but read them, and you will see the pleasure you get from that reading.

"If not, tell me: is there any greater delight than to see, as we might put it, a great lake of boiling pitch showing itself here in front of us now, bubbling away, with a great many serpents, snakes and lizards and many other kinds of fierce and appalling animals swimming and crossing about in it; and out of the middle of the lake there comes a most sorrowful voice, saying: 'Thou, knight, whoever thou art, who art looking on this fearful lake, if thou wouldst attain the treasure hidden beneath these black waters, show the valour of thy strong breast and throw thyself into the middle of its black and burning liquor; for if thou dost not so, thou shalt not be worthy to see the high marvels that are shut up and contained in the seven castles of the seven fays that lie beneath this blackness'?

"And that the knight has hardly finished hearing the fearful voice when, without going into any further reckoning with himself, without stopping to consider the danger he is putting himself in, and even without stripping off the weight of his heavy armour, commending himself to God and to his lady, he throws himself into the middle of the boiling lake; and when he least expects it and does not know where he is to stop, he finds himself among flowering fields, with which the Elysian ones have nothing to do at all?

"There it seems to him that the sky is more transparent, and that the sun shines with a newer brightness. There is offered to his eyes a pleasant wood made up of trees so green and leafy that their greenness gladdens the sight, while the sweet, unlearned song of the small, endless, painted birds that go crossing among the tangled branches entertains the ears. Here he discovers a little stream whose cool waters, which look like liquid crystal, run over fine sands and white pebbles that resemble sifted gold and pure pearls. Over there he sees a cunningly made fountain of variegated jasper and smooth marble; over here he sees another decorated in the grotesque style, where the small shells of mussels, with the twisted white and yellow houses of the snail, set in a disordered order with pieces of shining crystal and counterfeit emeralds mixed in among them, make a varied work, so that art, imitating nature, seems there to beat her.

"Over yonder there suddenly discovers itself to him a strong castle or splendid palace, whose walls are of solid gold, whose battlements are of diamonds, whose gates are of jacinth; in short, it is of such admirable workmanship that, the material it is made of being no less than diamonds, carbuncles, rubies, pearls, gold and emeralds, the making of it is worth still more.
