"And is there anything more to see, after seeing this, than to see coming out of the castle gate a good number of maidens, whose elegant and splendid costumes, if I set myself now to describe them as the histories tell them to us, would be a never-ending business? And then to see the one who seemed the chief of them all take by the hand the daring knight who threw himself into the boiling lake, and lead him, without saying a word to him, into the rich palace or castle, and have him stripped as naked as his mother bore him, and bathed with warm waters, and then anointed all over with scented ointments, and dressed in a shirt of the finest silk, all scented and perfumed; and another maiden come and throw over his shoulders a cloak which, at the very least, they say is generally worth a city, and even more?

"What a thing it is, then, when they tell us that after all this they take him to another hall, where he finds the tables laid with such order that he is taken aback and astonished! What, to see them pour water on his hands, all of it distilled from amber and scented flowers! What, to have him seated on an ivory chair! What, to see all the maidens serve him, keeping a marvellous silence! What, to have brought to him such a variety of dishes, so tastily cooked that his appetite does not know which to stretch out a hand to! What must it be to hear the music that plays while he eats, without anybody's knowing who sings it or where it sounds from!

"And, the meal being over and the tables cleared, for the knight to be left leaning back in his chair, and perhaps picking his teeth as the custom is, and all at once there comes in at the door of the hall another maiden far more beautiful than any of the first ones, and sits down at the knight's side, and begins to give him an account of what castle that is, and how she is held enchanted in it, along with other things that hold the knight in suspense and astonish the readers who go on reading his history?

"I do not want to go on any longer about this, since it may be gathered from it that any part one reads, of any history of a knight errant, is bound to cause pleasure and wonder in anybody who reads it. And believe me, your worship, and, as I have told you before, read these books, and you will see how they banish whatever melancholy you have and improve your temper, if by any chance it is a bad one.

"For my own part I can say that since I have been a knight errant I have been brave, courteous, generous, well-bred, open-handed, polite, daring, gentle, patient, an endurer of hardships, of imprisonments, of enchantments. And although it is so short a time since I saw myself shut in a cage like a madman, I expect, by the valour of my arm, heaven favouring me and fortune not being against me, in a few days to see myself king of some kingdom, where I may show the gratitude and generosity my breast holds.

"For upon my word, sir, the poor man is incapable of showing the virtue of generosity to anybody, however completely he possesses it; and gratitude that consists only in the wish is a dead thing, as faith without works is dead. For this reason I could wish that fortune would soon offer me some occasion to make me an emperor, so as to show my heart by doing good to my friends — especially to this poor Sancho Panza, my squire, who is the best man in the world; and I should like to give him an earldom I have promised him this long while, except that I am afraid he will not have the ability to govern his estate."

Sancho heard almost these last words of his master's, and said to him:

"Do your best, Señor Don Quixote, to give me that earldom, as much promised by your worship as it is hoped for by me; for I promise you that I shall not be short of ability to govern it. And when I am short of it, I have heard it said that there are men in the world who take lords' estates on lease and give them so much a year, and they take care of the governing themselves, and the lord sits with his legs stretched out enjoying the income they give him without troubling about anything else. And that is what I shall do, and I shall not stick at so much more or so much less, but shall get out of the whole thing at once and enjoy my income like a duke, and let them settle it among themselves."

"That, brother Sancho," said the canon, "holds good as far as enjoying the income goes; but as for administering justice, the lord of the estate must attend to it, and here comes in ability and good judgement, and above all the honest intention of getting it right. If this is missing at the beginning, the middle and the end will always go wrong; and so God generally helps the good intention of the simple man as much as he withholds his favour from the bad intention of the clever one."

"I know nothing about those philosophies," answered Sancho Panza; "all I know is that I would know how to govern the earldom as soon as I had it. For I have as much soul as anybody else and as much body as the biggest, and I should be as much king of my estate as anybody else is of his. And being so, I should do what I liked; and doing what I liked, I should do as I pleased; and doing as I pleased, I should be contented; and when a man is contented, he has nothing more to want; and having nothing more to want, that is the end of it. So let the estate come, and God be with you and let us see each other, as one blind man said to another."

"Those are not bad philosophies, as you call them, Sancho; but for all that, there is a great deal to be said on this matter of earldoms."

To which Don Quixote replied:

"I do not know that there is any more to be said; I simply guide myself by the example the great Amadis of Gaul gives me, who made his squire count of the Firm Isle. And so I can, without any scruple of conscience, make Sancho Panza a count, who is one of the best squires any knight errant ever had."

The canon was astonished at the well-ordered absurdities Don Quixote had spoken, at the manner in which he had painted the adventure of the Knight of the Lake, at the impression the deliberate lies of the books he had read had made on him — and finally he was astonished at Sancho's foolishness, in wanting so eagerly to get the earldom his master had promised him.

By this time the canon's servants were coming back, having gone to the inn for the pack-mule with the supplies; and making a table of a carpet and of the green grass of the meadow, they sat down in the shade of some trees and ate there, so that the ox-driver should not lose the convenience of that spot, as has been said.

And while they were eating, they suddenly heard a loud crashing and the sound of a bell that came from among some brambles and thick bushes that were nearby; and at the same instant they saw coming out from among those thickets a beautiful goat, her whole coat mottled with black, white and brown. Behind her came a goatherd shouting at her and saying the words they use to her to make her stop or come back to the flock. The runaway goat, frightened and terrified, came to the company as though to take refuge with them, and stopped there. The goatherd came up, and taking her by the horns, said to her as though she were capable of reasoning and understanding:

"Ah, wanderer, wanderer, Spotty, Spotty, how lame you have been going these last few days! What wolves frighten you, my girl? Won't you tell me what this is, my beauty? But what can it be except that you are female and cannot keep still? A curse on your nature and on the nature of all those you take after! Come back, come back, my friend; for if not as contented, at least you will be safer in your own fold or with your companions. For if you, who are to guard them and lead them, go about so unguided and so far off the road, what will become of them?"

The goatherd's words gave pleasure to those who heard them, especially to the canon, who said to him:

"On your life, brother, take it easy for a while and do not be in such a hurry to get this goat back to her flock; for since she is female, as you say, she must follow her natural instinct, however much you set yourself to prevent it. Take this mouthful and have a drink, and you will cool your temper down, and meanwhile the goat can rest."

And to say this and to give him the loins of a cold rabbit on the point of his knife were all one. The goatherd took it and thanked him; he drank and calmed down, and then said:

"I should not like your worships to take me for a simpleton because I have talked to this animal so seriously; for truly the words I said to her are not without a meaning. A rustic I am, but not so much of one that I do not understand how a man must deal with men and with beasts."

"That I well believe," said the curate; "for I know by experience that the mountains breed scholars and the shepherds' huts hold philosophers."

"At least, sir," replied the goatherd, "they take in men who have learnt their lesson. And so that you may believe this truth and touch it with your hand — although it may look as if I were inviting myself without being asked — if you do not object to it and would like, gentlemen, to lend me an attentive ear for a short while, I shall tell you a true story that will bear out what that gentleman" — pointing to the curate — "has said, and what I have said."

To this Don Quixote answered:

"Since I see that this case has a certain something of the shadow of an adventure of chivalry about it, I for my part will listen to you very willingly, brother; and so will all these gentlemen, for as much as they are people of good sense and lovers of curious novelties that hold, gladden and entertain the senses — as I have no doubt your tale will do. Begin, then, my friend, and we shall all listen."

"I take mine out," said Sancho; "I am going off to that stream there with this pie, where I mean to stuff myself for three days. Because I have heard my master Don Quixote say that a knight errant's squire is to eat, when the chance offers, until he can eat no more, on the grounds that they are apt to happen into a wood so tangled that they cannot manage to get out of it in six days; and if a man does not go in full, or with his saddlebags well provided, he may stay there — as many a man does stay — turned into mummy-meat."

"You are quite right, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Go where you like and eat what you can; for I have had enough, and all I have left is to give my soul its refreshment, as I shall by listening to this good man's tale."

"So shall we all give ours theirs," said the canon.

And then he asked the goatherd to begin what he had promised. The goatherd gave two pats on the back to the goat, which he had by the horns, saying to her:

"Lie down beside me, Spotty; there is still time for us to get back to our fold."

It seems the goat understood him, because as soon as her master sat down she stretched herself out beside him very quietly, and, looking him in the face, gave him to understand that she was attending to what he was saying. And he began his history like this.

Chapter 51: Which Treats of What the Goatherd Told All Those Who Were Carrying Don Quixote Away

"Three leagues from this valley there is a village which, although small, is one of the richest anywhere in this district; and in it there was a very honourable farmer — so much so that, although being honoured goes with being rich, he was more honoured for the virtue he had than for the wealth he possessed.

"But what made him happiest, as he used to say, was having a daughter of such extraordinary beauty, rare good sense, charm and virtue that anybody who knew her and looked at her was astonished to see the extraordinary qualities heaven and nature had enriched her with. As a little girl she was beautiful, and she went on growing in beauty, and at the age of sixteen she was most beautiful of all.

"The fame of her beauty began to spread through all the villages round about — and why do I say through the villages round about only, when it spread to distant cities and even got into the halls of kings and into the ears of every kind of person, who came from all quarters to see her as a rare thing or as an image that works miracles? Her father guarded her, and she guarded herself; for there are no padlocks, guards or locks that guard a young girl better than those of her own reserve.

"The father's wealth and the daughter's beauty moved a great many people, both from the village and from outside it, to ask for her as a wife. But he, as the man whose business it was to dispose of so rich a jewel, went about bewildered, unable to decide which of the endless number who pestered him he would hand her to. And among the many who had that good wish I was one, and I was given many great hopes of success by knowing that her father knew who I was: that I was a native of the same village, clean in blood, in the flower of my age, very rich in property and no less finished in my wits.

"With all these same qualities another man of the same village asked for her too, which was the reason for suspending and putting into the balance her father's inclination — since it seemed to him that his daughter would be well bestowed on either of us. And to get out of this difficulty, he decided to tell Leandra about it, for that is the name of the rich girl who has put me in this misery, noting that since the two of us were equal, it was right to leave the choosing to his beloved daughter's own liking — a thing worth imitating by all fathers who want to settle their children in life. I do not say they should let them choose in low and wicked matters, but that they should put good ones before them, and of the good ones let them choose as they like.

"I do not know what Leandra's liking was; I only know that her father put us both off with his daughter's youth and with general words, which neither bound him nor released us either. My rival is called Anselmo and I Eugenio, so that you may have the names of the people this tragedy contains — whose ending is still hanging in the balance, though it can easily be understood that it will be a disastrous one.

"At this time there came to our village a certain Vicente de la Rosa, the son of a poor farmer of the same place; which Vicente came from Italy and from various other parts, where he had been a soldier. A captain who happened to pass through with his company had taken him away from our village when he was a boy of about twelve, and the lad came back twelve years later dressed as a soldier, painted with a thousand colours, covered with a thousand glass trinkets and fine steel chains. Today he put on one piece of finery and tomorrow another, but all of them flimsy, painted, of little weight and less substance.

"The country people, who are naturally spiteful, and who when idleness gives them the chance are spite itself, noticed it and counted his finery and ornaments point by point, and found that the outfits were three, of different colours, with their garters and stockings; but he made so many combinations and inventions out of them that if they had not been counted, there would have been people ready to swear he had shown off more than ten changes of clothing and more than twenty sets of plumes. And do not let what I am telling you about the clothes seem impertinent and excessive, because they make a good part of this story.

"He used to sit on a stone bench under a great poplar that stands in our square, and there he kept us all open-mouthed, hanging on the exploits he went on telling us about. There was no country in the whole globe he had not seen, nor any battle he had not been in. He had killed more Moors than Morocco and Tunis hold, and had fought more single combats — according to him — than Gante and Luna, Diego García de Paredes and a thousand others he named; and he had come out of all of them victorious, without their having shed a single drop of his blood.

"On the other hand, he showed the marks of wounds which, although they could not be made out, he gave us to understand were musket shots got in different skirmishes and actions. And finally, with unheard-of arrogance, he addressed his equals — and the very men who knew him — with the familiar 'you', and said that his father was his own arm, his family his own deeds, and that as a soldier he owed nothing even to the king himself.

"Added to these arrogances was his being a bit of a musician and playing a guitar with a strumming style, so that some people said he made it talk. But his gifts did not stop there, for he also had the gift of poetry; and so out of every trifle that happened in the village he composed a ballad a league and a half long.

"This soldier, then, that I have painted here — this Vicente de la Rosa, this bravo, this dandy, this musician, this poet — was seen and looked at many times by Leandra from a window of her house that looked onto the square. The tinsel of his showy clothes made her fall in love; his ballads enchanted her, for of every one he composed he handed round twenty copies; the exploits he had recounted of himself came to her ears; and finally — as the devil must have arranged it so — she came to fall in love with him before any notion of courting her had been born in him.

"And as in matters of love there is none that is more easily brought off than the one that has the lady's own wish on its side, Leandra and Vicente easily came to an understanding; and before any of her many suitors had realised what she wanted, she had already got it — having left the house of her dear and beloved father, for a mother she has none, and gone away from the village with the soldier, who came out of this enterprise with more triumph than out of all the many he laid claim to.

"The event astonished the whole village, and everybody who heard of it. I was left taken aback, Anselmo appalled, her father grief-stricken, her relatives shamed, the law busy, the officers of the Brotherhood alert. The roads were watched, the woods were searched and everything else there was; and at the end of three days they found the capricious Leandra in a cave in a mountain, stripped to her shift, without a great deal of money and the most precious jewels she had taken from her home.

"They brought her back into her injured father's presence; they asked her about her misfortune; she confessed without any pressing that Vicente de la Rosa had deceived her, and under his word to be her husband had persuaded her to leave her father's house; that he would take her to the richest and most delightful city there was in the whole universe, which was Naples; and that she, badly advised and worse deceived, had believed him; and, robbing her father, had given herself up to him the very night she disappeared; and that he had taken her to a rough mountain and shut her up in that cave where they had found her.

"She also told how the soldier, without taking her honour, had robbed her of everything she had, and had left her in that cave and gone away — an event that astonished everybody all over again.

"It was hard for us to believe the young man's continence, but she maintained it so earnestly that it was enough to comfort the disconsolate father, who made no account of the wealth they had taken from him, since they had left him his daughter with the jewel which, once lost, leaves no hope of ever being recovered again.

"The same day Leandra reappeared, her father made her disappear from our eyes and took her away to shut her up in a convent in a town near here, hoping that time would wear away some part of the bad opinion his daughter had put herself in. Leandra's few years served as an excuse for her fault, at least with those who had no interest in her being bad or good; but those who knew her good sense and great understanding did not put her sin down to ignorance, but to her forwardness and to the natural inclination of women, which for the most part is generally headstrong and ill-ordered.

"Leandra being shut up, Anselmo's eyes were left blind — or at least with nothing to look at that gave him any pleasure; and mine in darkness, with no light to guide them to anything enjoyable. With Leandra's absence our sadness grew and our patience shrank; we cursed the soldier's finery and abominated Leandra's father's want of caution.

"Finally Anselmo and I agreed to leave the village and come to this valley, where he, pasturing a great quantity of sheep of his own and I a numerous flock of goats, also mine, pass our lives among the trees, giving vent to our passions, either singing together the praises or the reproaches of the beautiful Leandra, or sighing alone and communicating our complaints to the sky by ourselves.

"In imitation of us, a great many others of Leandra's suitors have come to these rough mountains, following the same occupation as ours; and there are so many of them that it seems this place has been turned into pastoral Arcadia, so full is it of shepherds and folds, and there is no part of it where the name of the beautiful Leandra is not heard. This man curses her and calls her capricious, changeable and immodest; that one condemns her as easy and light; another absolves her and forgives her; another arraigns her and reproaches her; one celebrates her beauty, another disowns her character; and in the end they all dishonour her and they all adore her.

"And the madness of them all goes so far that there are men who complain of her disdain without ever having spoken to her, and even men who lament and feel the raging disease of jealousy, which she never gave anybody cause for — because, as I have said already, her sin was known before her wish was. There is no hollow in a rock, no bank of a stream, no shade of a tree that is not occupied by some shepherd telling his misfortunes to the air. Echo repeats the name of Leandra wherever it can be formed: Leandra the mountains ring with, Leandra the streams murmur, and Leandra keeps us all in suspense and enchanted, hoping without hope and fearing without knowing what we fear.

"Among all these deranged men, the one who shows himself to have the least and the most judgement is my rival Anselmo, who, having so many other things to complain of, complains only of absence; and to the sound of a rebeck, which he plays admirably, he makes his complaint in singing, with verses that show his good understanding. I follow another and easier road, and to my mind the sounder one, which is to speak ill of the lightness of women, of their inconstancy, of their double dealing, of their dead promises, of their broken faith and, in the end, of the little judgement they have in knowing where to place their thoughts and intentions.

"And this, gentlemen, was the reason for the words and arguments I made to this goat when I got here; for because she is female I think little of her, although she is the best in my whole fold. This is the story I promised to tell you; and if I have been long-winded in telling it, I shall not be short in serving you: near here I have my hut, and in it I have fresh milk and very tasty cheese, along with various ripe fruits no less agreeable to the sight than to the taste."

Chapter 52: Of the Quarrel Don Quixote Had with the Goatherd, with the Rare Adventure of the Penitents, Which He Brought to a Happy Conclusion by the Sweat of His Brow

The goatherd's tale gave general pleasure to everybody who had listened to it; and it was particularly well received by the canon, who with unusual curiosity noted the manner in which he had told it — as far from seeming a rustic goatherd as it was close to showing him a well-bred courtier. And so he said the curate had spoken very well in saying that the mountains bred scholars.

They all made offers to Eugenio; but the one who showed himself most generous in this was Don Quixote, who said to him:

"Certainly, brother goatherd, if I found myself in a position to be able to begin any adventure, I would set out this very moment so that you might come well out of yours. For I would get Leandra out of the convent — where she must without any doubt be against her will — in spite of the abbess and of anybody who tried to prevent it, and would put her in your hands, so that you might do with her entirely as you liked and pleased, keeping, however, the laws of chivalry, which command that no wrong whatever shall be done to any maiden. Although I hope in God Our Lord that the power of a malicious enchanter will not be so great that the power of another better-intentioned enchanter cannot be greater; and for that time I promise you my favour and help, as my profession obliges me to — which is nothing else than to favour the helpless and the needy."

The goatherd looked at him; and seeing Don Quixote in such bad condition and of such an appearance, he was astonished and asked the barber, who was near him:

"Sir, who is this man, who has such a build and talks in such a way?"

"Who should he be," answered the barber, "but the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha, undoer of injuries, righter of wrongs, the shelter of maidens, the terror of giants and the winner of battles?"

"That sounds to me," answered the goatherd, "like what one reads in the books of knights errant, who did all that your worship says of this man; though it is my opinion either that your worship is joking or that this fine gentleman must have the rooms of his head empty."

"You are an enormous scoundrel," said Don Quixote at this; "and it is you who are empty and short of brains, for I am fuller than the very great whore of a bitch who bore you ever was."

And saying and doing, he snatched up a loaf that was near him and hit the goatherd full in the face with it, with such fury that he flattened his nose. But the goatherd, who did not understand jokes, seeing how much in earnest they were ill-treating him, without any respect for the carpet or the cloths or all those who were eating, leapt on Don Quixote; and seizing him by the neck with both hands, he would not have hesitated to strangle him if Sancho Panza had not come up at that moment and taken hold of him by the shoulders and thrown him down on top of the table, breaking plates, smashing cups and spilling and scattering everything that was on it.

Don Quixote, finding himself free, ran to get on top of the goatherd; who, with his face covered in blood and pounded with Sancho's kicks, was going about on all fours looking for one of the knives from the table so as to take some bloody revenge — but the canon and the curate prevented him. The barber, however, so arranged it that the goatherd got Don Quixote underneath him, on whom he rained such a number of blows that as much blood rained from the poor knight's face as from his own.

The canon and the curate were bursting with laughter, the officers were leaping with joy, and both sides were egging them on as people do with dogs when they are locked in a fight. Only Sancho Panza was in despair, because he could not shake off one of the canon's servants, who was preventing him from helping his master.

In short, everybody being in merriment and festival except the two pounding men who were clawing at each other, they heard the sound of a trumpet so sad that it made them turn their faces towards where it seemed to be sounding. But the one who was most excited at hearing it was Don Quixote, who, although he was underneath the goatherd, very much against his will and rather more than moderately pounded, said to him:

"Brother devil — for it is not possible that you should not be one, since you have had the strength and the force to subdue mine — I beg you that we may make a truce, for no more than an hour; because the sorrowful sound of that trumpet that reaches our ears seems to me to be calling me to some new adventure."

The goatherd, who was tired by now of pounding and being pounded, let him go at once; and Don Quixote got to his feet, likewise turning his face to where the sound was heard, and suddenly saw coming down a slope a great many men dressed in white, in the manner of penitents.

The case was that that year the clouds had refused their dew to the earth, and in all the places of that district processions, prayers and penances were being made, asking God to open the hands of his mercy and send them rain. And to this end the people of a village that was nearby were coming in procession to a hermitage of devotion that stood on a rise in that valley.

Don Quixote, seeing the strange clothes of the penitents, without its crossing his mind how many times he must have seen them before, imagined that this was a matter of adventure and that it belonged to him alone, as a knight errant, to undertake it. And he was further confirmed in this fancy by thinking that an image they were carrying covered in mourning must be some great lady whom those villains and discourteous scoundrels were carrying off by force.

And as soon as this fell into his mind, he ran with great speed to Rocinante, who was grazing about, and took the bridle and the shield off the saddlebow, and bridled him in a moment; and asking Sancho for his sword, he mounted Rocinante and braced his shield and said in a loud voice to everybody who was present:

"Now, valorous company, you shall see how much it matters that there should be knights in the world who profess the order of knight-errantry. Now, I say, you shall see, in the setting free of that good lady who is being carried off captive there, whether knights errant are to be valued."

And on saying this he squeezed his thighs against Rocinante, because spurs he had none; and at full gallop — because a flat-out charge is not read of anywhere in this whole true history as ever having been made by Rocinante — he went to meet the penitents, although the curate and the canon and the barber went to stop him. But it was not possible for them, nor did the shouts Sancho gave him stop him either, saying:

"Where are you going, Señor Don Quixote? What devils have you in your breast, urging you to go against our Catholic faith? Take notice — bad luck to me — that that is a procession of penitents, and that the lady they are carrying on the platform is the most blessed image of the spotless Virgin. Look what you are doing, sir, for this once it may be said that it is not what you know about."

Sancho wearied himself in vain, because his master was so set on reaching the sheeted men and on freeing the mourning lady that he did not hear a word; and even if he had heard it, he would not have turned back if the king had ordered him to.

He got to the procession, then, and pulled up Rocinante, who by then was wanting to rest a little, and in a disturbed, hoarse voice said:

"You who, perhaps because you are not good men, hide your faces: attend and listen to what I want to say to you."

The first to stop were those who were carrying the image; and one of the four priests who were singing the litanies, seeing Don Quixote's strange appearance, Rocinante's thinness and other laughable details he noticed and made out in Don Quixote, answered him, saying:

"Brother, if you want to tell us anything, tell it quickly, because these brothers are opening their own flesh, and we cannot — nor is it reasonable that we should — stop to hear anything at all, unless it is so short that it can be said in two words."

"In one I shall say it," replied Don Quixote, "and it is this: that you should this instant set free that beautiful lady, whose tears and sad face give clear signs that you are carrying her off against her will and that you have done her some notorious wrong. And I, who was born into the world to undo such injuries, shall not allow her to go one step further without giving her the liberty she wants and deserves."

At these words, everybody who heard them realised that Don Quixote must be some madman, and they set to laughing very heartily — whose laughter was putting powder to Don Quixote's anger, for without saying another word he drew his sword and charged at the litter. One of those who were carrying it, leaving the load to his companions, came out to meet Don Quixote, brandishing a forked prop or stave with which he supported the litter while he rested; and taking on it a great slash Don Quixote dealt him, which cut it in two, with the last third that was left in his hand he gave Don Quixote such a blow on top of one shoulder, on the sword side, that his shield could not cover him against such peasant force, and poor Don Quixote came to the ground in a very bad way.

Sancho Panza, who was panting along at his heels, seeing him fallen, shouted to his pounder not to give him another blow, because he was a poor enchanted knight who had never done harm to anybody in all the days of his life. But what stopped the countryman was not Sancho's shouts but seeing that Don Quixote did not stir hand or foot; and so, believing that he had killed him, he quickly pulled his tunic up to his belt and set off running across the country like a fallow deer.

By this time everybody in Don Quixote's company had come up to where he was; and the people of the procession, who saw them coming at a run, and with them the officers with their crossbows, feared some evil turn, and they all made a ring round the image; and, with their hoods raised, gripping their scourges — and the priests their candlesticks — they waited for the assault, determined to defend themselves and even to attack their assailants if they could. But fortune managed it better than was expected, because Sancho did nothing but throw himself on his master's body, making over him the most sorrowful and the most laughable lament in the world, believing that he was dead.

The curate was recognised by another curate who was in the procession, whose recognition put the two squadrons' conceived fear to rest. The first curate gave the second, in a couple of sentences, an account of who Don Quixote was; and so both he and the whole crowd of penitents went to see whether the poor knight was dead, and they heard Sancho Panza saying with tears in his eyes:

"Oh flower of chivalry, who with one blow of a stave brought to an end the course of your so well-spent years! Oh honour of your family, honour and glory of all La Mancha and even of the whole world, which, with you gone out of it, will be left full of evildoers with no fear of being punished for their evil deeds! Oh generous beyond all the Alexanders, since for only eight months of service you had given me the best isle the sea girds and surrounds! Oh humble with the arrogant and arrogant with the humble, attempter of dangers, endurer of insults, in love without a cause, imitator of the good, scourge of the wicked, enemy of the base — in short, a knight errant, which is everything that can be said!"

At Sancho's shouts and groans, Don Quixote came back to life, and the first word he said was:

"The man who lives absent from you, sweetest Dulcinea, is subject to greater miseries than these. Help me, friend Sancho, to get onto the enchanted cart, for I am in no state to press Rocinante's saddle, since this whole shoulder of mine is smashed to pieces."

"That I shall do very willingly, my dear sir," answered Sancho; "and let us go back to my village in the company of these gentlemen, who wish you well, and there we shall arrange to make another sally that may bring us more profit and fame."

"You speak well, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "and it will be great prudence to let this evil influence of the stars that is now running blow itself out."

The canon, the curate and the barber told him he would do very well to do as he said; and so, having taken great pleasure in Sancho Panza's simplicities, they put Don Quixote on the cart as he had come before.

The procession formed up again and went on its way. The goatherd took his leave of everybody. The officers would not go any further, and the curate paid them what was owing to them. The canon asked the curate to let him know how Don Quixote turned out, whether he was cured of his madness or went on in it; and with this he took his leave to go on with his journey. In the end they all separated and parted, leaving alone the curate and the barber, Don Quixote and Panza, and the good Rocinante, who through everything he had seen had been as patient as his master.

The ox-driver yoked his oxen and settled Don Quixote on a bundle of hay, and with his usual phlegm followed the road the curate wanted; and at the end of six days they arrived at Don Quixote's village, which they entered in the middle of the day, which happened to be a Sunday, and the people were all in the square, through the middle of which Don Quixote's cart passed.

They all ran to see what was coming in the cart; and when they recognised their fellow-countryman they were amazed, and a boy ran off to give the news to his housekeeper and his niece that their uncle and master was coming thin and yellow, stretched out on a heap of hay on an ox-cart. It was a pitiful thing to hear the cries the two good women raised, the slaps they gave themselves, the curses they hurled all over again at the accursed books of chivalry — all of which broke out afresh when they saw Don Quixote come in at their doors.

At the news of Don Quixote's arrival, Sancho Panza's wife came running, who had already learnt that he had gone off with him serving as his squire; and as soon as she saw Sancho, the first thing she asked him was whether the ass had come back well. Sancho answered that he had come back better than his master.

"Thanks be to God," she replied, "who has done me so much good. But now tell me, my friend: what good have you got out of your squiring? What skirt do you bring me? What little shoes for your children?"

"I bring none of that, wife," said Sancho, "although I bring other things of more moment and consideration."

"That gives me a great deal of pleasure," answered his wife. "Show me those things of more consideration and more moment, my dear; I want to see them, so as to cheer up this heart of mine, which has been so sad and discontented in all the ages of your absence."

"I shall show you them at home, wife," said Panza; "and for now be content, for if God is pleased that we should go out on another journey to look for adventures, you will soon see me a count or governor of an isle — and not one of the ones about here, but the best that can be found."

"May heaven grant it, husband, for we have great need of it. But tell me: what is this about isles? I do not understand it."

"Honey is not for the ass's mouth," answered Sancho. "In due time you will see, wife, and you will even be astonished to hear yourself called Your Ladyship by all your vassals."

"What is this you are saying, Sancho, about ladyships and isles and vassals?" answered Juana Panza — for that was Sancho's wife's name, although they were not related, but because in La Mancha it is the custom for wives to take their husbands' surname.

"Do not be in such a hurry, Juana, to know all this so fast; it is enough that I am telling you the truth, and sew up your mouth. I shall only tell you, just in passing, that there is nothing more delightful in the world than for an honourable man to be squire to a knight errant who goes looking for adventures. It is quite true that most of the ones you find do not turn out as much to your liking as a man would want, because out of a hundred you meet, ninety-nine generally come out crooked and awry. I know it by experience, because out of some of them I have come blanketed and out of others pounded. But for all that, it is a fine thing to be waiting for what will happen, crossing mountains, searching woods, treading rocks, visiting castles, putting up at inns entirely as you please, without paying — the devil take it — a maravedi."

All this talk passed between Sancho Panza and Juana Panza his wife, while Don Quixote's housekeeper and niece received him and undressed him and stretched him out in his old bed. He looked at them with squinting eyes and could not manage to understand where he was.

The curate charged the niece to take great care to look after her uncle, and to be on the alert that he did not escape from them again, telling her what it had been necessary to do to bring him home. Here the two of them raised their cries to heaven again; there the curses on the books of chivalry broke out afresh; there they begged heaven to confound in the centre of the abyss the authors of so many lies and absurdities. Finally they were left bewildered and afraid that they would find themselves without their master and uncle the moment he had any improvement; and it turned out just as they imagined it.

But the author of this history, although he has searched with curiosity and diligence for the deeds Don Quixote performed on his third sally, has not been able to find any account of them, at least in authentic writings. Only fame has kept, in the memories of La Mancha, that Don Quixote, the third time he left his house, went to Saragossa, where he was present at some famous jousts that were held in that city, and that things happened to him there worthy of his valour and good understanding.

Nor could he learn anything at all about his end and death, nor would he have learnt it or known it if good luck had not sent him an ancient physician who had in his possession a leaden box which, as he said, had been found in the pulled-down foundations of an ancient hermitage that was being rebuilt. In which box some parchments had been found, written in Gothic letters but in Castilian verse, which contained many of his exploits and gave an account of the beauty of Dulcinea of El Toboso, of Rocinante's figure, of Sancho Panza's faithfulness and of the burial of Don Quixote himself, with various epitaphs and eulogies of his life and habits.

And the ones that could be read and made out clearly were those the trustworthy author of this new and never-before-seen history sets down here. Which author asks those who read it, as a reward for the immense labour it cost him to inquire and search all the archives of La Mancha in order to bring it to light, nothing except that they should give it the same credit that judicious people usually give to the books of chivalry that are so much in favour in the world; for with this he will count himself well paid and satisfied, and will be encouraged to bring out and look for others, if not as truthful, at least of as much invention and entertainment.

The first words written on the parchment that was found in the leaden box were these:

	The Academicians of Argamasilla,
	a Place in La Mancha,
	on the Life and Death of the Valorous
	Don Quixote of La Mancha,
	hoc scripserunt:
	Monicongo, Academician of Argamasilla,
	on the Tomb of Don Quixote

Epitaph

	The madcap who adorned La Mancha
	with more spoils than Jason of Crete;
	the judgement that had its weathervane
	sharp where it would have been better broad;
	the arm whose strength stretched so far
	that it reached from Cathay to Gaeta;
	the most appalling and most discerning muse
	that ever graved verses on a plate of bronze;
	the man who left the Amadises behind
	and thought very little of the Galaors,
	resting on his own love and gallantry;
	the man who silenced the Belianises,
	the man who went erring on Rocinante,
	lies beneath this cold stone.
	Paniaguado, Academician of Argamasilla,
	in laudem Dulcineae del Toboso

Sonnet

	This woman you see with the beefy face,
	high in the bosom and spirited in her bearing,
	is Dulcinea, queen of El Toboso,
	whom the great Quixote was in love with.
	For her he trod the one side and the other
	of the great Black Sierra, and the famous
	field of Montiel, as far as the grassy
	plain of Aranjuez, on foot and weary.
	Rocinante's fault — oh, hard star! — that this
	Manchegan lady and this unconquered
	knight errant, in their tender years:
	she, by dying, left off being beautiful,
	and he, though he stands written in marble,
	could not escape love, angers and deceits.
	Capricioso, Most Judicious Academician of Argamasilla,
	in Praise of Rocinante, Don Quixote of La Mancha's Horse

Sonnet

	On the proud diamond throne
	that Mars treads with bloody feet,
	the frenzied Manchegan flies his standard
	with an unheard-of effort.
	He hangs up his arms and the fine steel
	with which he wrecks, levels, splits and cleaves:
	new exploits! But art invents
	a new style for the new paladin.
	And if Gaul prides itself on its Amadis,
	by whose brave descendants Greece
	triumphed a thousand times and spreads her fame,
	today the hall where Bellona presides
	crowns Quixote; and lofty La Mancha prides itself
	on him more than Greece or Gaul on theirs.
	Never does oblivion stain his glories,
	since even Rocinante, in being gallant,
	surpasses Brigliadoro and Bayard.
	Burlador, Academician of Argamasilla,
	to Sancho Panza

Sonnet

	Sancho Panza is this man, small in body
	but great in worth: a strange miracle!
	The simplest and most guileless squire
	the world ever had, I swear and certify.
	He was within a hair's breadth of being a count,
	if there had not conspired to do him harm
	the insolence and the injuries of this stingy
	age, which does not spare even a donkey.
	On one of those he rode — begging pardon for the word —
	this meek squire, behind the meek
	horse Rocinante and behind his master.
	Oh, empty hopes of mankind!
	How you go past with your promise of rest,
	and end at last in shadow, in smoke, in a dream!
	Cachidiablo, Academician of Argamasilla,
	on the Tomb of Don Quixote

Epitaph

	Here lies the knight,
	well pounded and ill-erring,
	whom Rocinante carried
	along one road and another.
	Sancho Panza the blockhead
	lies beside him too,
	the most faithful squire
	that the squire's trade ever saw.
	Tiquitoc, Academician of Argamasilla,
	on the Tomb of Dulcinea of El Toboso

Epitaph

	Here rests Dulcinea;
	and although she was plump of flesh,
	she was turned to dust and ashes
	by appalling and ugly death.
	She was of pure-bred stock,
	and had some hints of a lady about her;
	she was the great Quixote's flame,
	and she was the glory of her village.

These were the verses that could be read; the rest, the lettering being worm-eaten, were handed to an academician so that he might make them out by guesswork. It is understood that he has done it, at the cost of many sleepless nights and a great deal of labour, and that he means to bring them out, in hopes of Don Quixote's third sally.

Forsi altro canterà con miglior plettro.

The End

Prologue to the Reader

God help me, how eagerly you must be waiting now, illustrious reader — or common reader, whichever you are — for this prologue, believing you will find in it revenges, quarrels and abuse of the author of the second Don Quixote; I mean the man they say was begotten at Tordesillas and born at Tarragona.

Well, in truth I am not going to give you that satisfaction; for although injuries wake anger in the humblest breasts, in mine this rule shall have its exception. You would like me to call him an ass, an idiot and an impudent fellow, but it does not cross my mind: let his own sin punish him, let him eat it with his own bread, and let him settle it himself.

What I have not been able to help feeling is that he marks me down as old and one-handed — as though it had been in my power to hold back time so that it should not pass over me, or as though my maiming had been got in some tavern, and not on the highest occasion that past ages ever saw, or present ages see, or ages to come can hope to see.

If my wounds do not shine in the eyes of whoever looks at them, they are valued at least in the esteem of those who know where they were got; for a soldier looks better dead in the battle than free in flight. And this is so much the case with me that if they were to put an impossibility before me now and make it easy for me, I would rather have been in that prodigious action than be whole of my wounds now without having been in it. The wounds a soldier shows in his face and on his breast are stars that guide others to the heaven of honour and to the wish for a just praise. And it must be noted that a man does not write with his grey hairs but with his understanding, which generally improves with the years.

I have also felt his calling me envious, and describing to me, as though I were ignorant, what a thing envy is; when in plain fact, of the two kinds there are, I know only the holy kind, the noble and well-intentioned one. And this being so, as it is, I am not likely to persecute any priest, and the more so if he has in addition the rank of familiar of the Holy Office. And if he said it on behalf of the man he seems to have said it for, he was mistaken from beginning to end; for I worship that man's genius, and admire his works and his continual and virtuous industry.

But in fact I am grateful to this gentleman the author for saying that my Exemplary Novels are more satirical than exemplary — but that they are good; and they could not be good if they did not have a bit of everything in them.

It seems to me you are telling me that I am keeping myself very much in bounds and holding myself well within the limits of my own modesty, knowing that affliction should not be added to the afflicted, and that the affliction this gentleman must be feeling is certainly great, since he does not dare to appear in the open field and under a clear sky, hiding his name and inventing his birthplace, as though he had committed some treason against his sovereign.

If by any chance you should come to know him, tell him from me that I do not count myself injured; for I know very well what the devil's temptations are, and that one of the greatest of them is to put it into a man's understanding that he can compose and print a book, and get as much fame by it as money, and as much money as fame. And in confirmation of this, I want you, with your good humour and charm, to tell him this story:

There was in Seville a madman who fell into the most amusing absurdity and obsession that any madman in the world ever fell into. And it was that he made a tube out of a cane, sharpened at the end; and on catching some dog in the street, or anywhere else, he would hold one of its hind feet down with one of his own and lift the other with his hand, and as best he could he would fit the tube into the place where, by blowing into it, he made the dog round as a ball. And when he had it in that state he would give it two little pats on the belly and let it go, saying to the bystanders, who were always many: "Do your worships suppose it is a small labour to blow up a dog?"

Does your worship suppose now that it is a small labour to make a book?

And if this story does not fit him, you may tell him this one, my friend the reader, which is also about a madman and a dog:

There was in Córdoba another madman, who had the habit of carrying on top of his head a piece of marble slab, or a stone that was not very light; and on coming upon some dog that was off its guard, he would go up close to it and drop the weight plumb down on it. The dog would be furious, and, barking and howling, would not stop for three streets.

Now it happened that among the dogs he let the load down on was a dog belonging to a cap-maker, whom his master was very fond of. The stone came down, hit him on the head, the pounded dog set up a howl, his master saw it and felt it, seized a measuring rod and came out at the madman and did not leave a whole bone in him. And at every blow he gave him he said: "You thieving dog — my pointer? Didn't you see, you cruel man, that my dog was a pointer?" And repeating the word "pointer" over and over, he sent the madman away beaten to a pulp.

The madman took the lesson to heart and withdrew, and for more than a month he did not come out into the square. At the end of which time he came back with his invention and with a heavier load. He would go up to where a dog was and, looking at it very carefully and fixedly, and without wanting or daring to let the stone down, he would say: "This is a pointer — look out!" In fact every dog he came upon, even if they were mastiffs or lapdogs, he said was a pointer; and so he never let the stone go again.

Perhaps something of the sort may happen to this historian: that he will not dare to let the weight of his wit down again on books which, when they are bad, are harder than rocks.

Tell him too that as for the threat he makes me, that his book is going to take my profits away, I do not care a farthing; and, borrowing from the famous interlude of La Perendenga, I answer him: long live my lord the Alderman, and Christ be with us all.

Long live the great Count of Lemos, whose Christian spirit and generosity, well known as they are, keep me on my feet against all the blows of my short fortune; and long live the supreme charity of the most illustrious Archbishop of Toledo, Don Bernardo de Sandoval y Rojas — and let there be no printing presses in the world for all I care, and let them print more books against me than there are letters in the Coplas de Mingo Revulgo.

These two princes, without any flattery of mine or any other kind of applause soliciting them, out of their goodness alone have taken it on themselves to do me kindness and favour me; and in this I count myself happier and richer than if fortune had set me on its summit by the ordinary road. A poor man may have honour, but not a vicious man; poverty may cloud nobility over, but it cannot darken it altogether; and since virtue gives off some light of itself, even through the obstacles and the chinks of straitened means, it comes to be valued by lofty and noble spirits, and consequently favoured.

And say no more to him — nor do I want to say any more to you, except to warn you to consider that this second part of Don Quixote which I am offering you is cut by the same craftsman and out of the same cloth as the first, and that in it I give you Don Quixote at greater length, and, in the end, dead and buried, so that nobody may dare to bring fresh testimonies against him — for those we have are enough, and it is enough too that an honourable man should have given an account of these judicious follies without wanting to go into them all over again. For the abundance of things, even good ones, makes them cease to be valued, and their scarcity, even of bad ones, counts for something.

I was forgetting to tell you to expect the Persiles, which I am now finishing, and the second part of the Galatea.

Dedication: To the Count of Lemos

When I sent Your Excellency my plays some days ago, printed before they were performed, if I remember rightly I said that Don Quixote was standing with his spurs on, ready to go and kiss Your Excellency's hands. And now I say that he has put them on and set off; and if he gets there, it seems to me I shall have done Your Excellency some service, because I am being pressed very hard from endless quarters to send him, so as to take away the queasiness and the nausea that another Don Quixote has caused, who under the name of a second part has gone about the world in disguise.

And the man who has shown most eagerness for him has been the great emperor of China; for a month ago he wrote me a letter in the Chinese language by a special courier, asking me — or rather begging me — to send him one, because he wanted to found a college where the Castilian language should be taught, and he wanted the book they read to be the history of Don Quixote. And along with this he told me that I should come and be the rector of that college.

I asked the messenger whether His Majesty had given him any money towards my expenses for me. He answered that it had not so much as crossed his mind. "Well then, brother," I answered him, "you may go back to your China at your ten leagues a day, or your twenty, or whatever rate you were dispatched at; for I am not in health to set out on so long a journey, and besides being ill I am very short of money. And emperor for emperor and monarch for monarch, in Naples I have the great Count of Lemos, who, without so many little titles of colleges and rectorships, keeps me, protects me and does me more kindness than I can manage to wish for."

With this I sent him off, and with this I take my leave, offering Your Excellency The Labours of Persiles and Sigismunda, a book I shall finish within four months, Deo volente; and which must be either the worst or the best that has been composed in our language — I mean of the books of entertainment. And I say that I repent of having said the worst, because according to my friends' opinion it is bound to reach the highest degree of goodness possible.

May Your Excellency come back in the health that is wished for you; for Persiles will by then be ready to kiss your hands, and I your feet, as the servant I am of Your Excellency's. From Madrid, the last day of October of sixteen hundred and fifteen.

Your Excellency's servant,

Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra

Part Two (1615)

Chapter 1: Of What the Curate and the Barber Discussed with Don Quixote About His Illness

Cide Hamete Benengeli relates, in the second part of this history and the third sally of Don Quixote, that the curate and the barber went almost a month without seeing him, so as not to bring back and put into his mind the things that had happened. But they did not for that leave off visiting his niece and his housekeeper, charging them to take care to look after him, giving him comforting things to eat that were suitable for the heart and the brain, from which, by all good reasoning, his whole misfortune proceeded.

The women said that this was what they were doing, and what they would go on doing with all possible goodwill and care, because they could see that from moment to moment their master was giving signs of being in his full senses; at which the two men were greatly pleased, since it seemed to them they had done right in bringing him home enchanted on the ox-cart, as was told in the first part of this history — as great as it is exact — in its last chapter.

And so they decided to visit him and make trial of his improvement, although they held it almost impossible that he should have any; and they agreed not to touch him on any point of knight-errantry, so as not to run the risk of unstitching the stitches of the wound, which were still so tender.

They visited him, then, and found him sitting up in bed dressed in a green baize jacket, with a red Toledo cap; and he was so dried up and shrivelled that he looked like nothing but a thing made of mummy-flesh. He received them very well; they asked him about his health, and he gave an account of himself and of it with great good sense and in very elegant words.

And in the course of their talk they came to discuss this thing they call statecraft and forms of government, correcting this abuse and condemning that, reforming one custom and banishing another, each of the three of them making himself a new legislator, a modern Lycurgus or a brand-new Solon; and they so remade the state that it seemed as though they had put it in a forge and taken out a different one from the one they put in. And Don Quixote spoke with so much judgement on all the subjects that were touched on that the two examiners believed beyond any doubt that he was completely well and in his full senses.

The niece and the housekeeper were present at the conversation, and could not stop giving thanks to God at seeing their master with so good an understanding. But the curate, changing his first plan, which was not to touch him on anything to do with chivalry, wanted to make a complete trial of whether Don Quixote's soundness was false or true; and so, by one step and another, he came to relate some news that had come from the court. And among other things he said that it was held for certain that the Turk was coming down with a powerful fleet, and that his design was not known, nor where so great a storm-cloud would burst; and that with this fear, which almost every year sounds the alarm on us, the whole of Christendom was under arms, and His Majesty had had the coasts of Naples and Sicily and the island of Malta provided for. To this Don Quixote answered:

"His Majesty has acted like a most prudent warrior in providing for his states in time, so that the enemy should not find him unprepared. But if my advice were taken, I would advise him to use a precaution which His Majesty at this hour must be very far from thinking of."

The curate had hardly heard this when he said to himself:

"God hold you in his hand, poor Don Quixote; for it seems to me that you are hurling yourself down from the high summit of your madness into the deep abyss of your simplicity."

But the barber, who had already hit on the same thought as the curate, asked Don Quixote what this precaution was that he said it would be well to take; perhaps it might be such that it should go on the list of the many impertinent pieces of advice that are generally given to princes.

"Mine, master shaver," said Don Quixote, "will not be impertinent but pertinent."

"I do not say it in that sense," replied the barber, "but because experience has shown that all or most of the schemes that are put to His Majesty are either impossible, or absurd, or to the harm of the king or the kingdom."

"Well, mine," answered Don Quixote, "is neither impossible nor absurd, but the easiest, the justest and the handiest and quickest that could come into any schemer's head."

"Your worship is slow in telling it, Señor Don Quixote," said the curate.

"I should not like," said Don Quixote, "to tell it here now and have it in the ears of the gentlemen of the Council tomorrow morning, and somebody else carry off the thanks and the reward for my labour."

"For my part," said the barber, "I give my word, here and before God, not to say what your worship may tell us to king or knave or any earthly man — an oath I learnt from the ballad about the curate who in the preamble told the king about the thief who had stolen his hundred doubloons and his fast-trotting mule."

"I know no stories," said Don Quixote, "but I know that this is a good oath, on the strength of my knowing that master barber is a decent man."

"And even if he were not," said the curate, "I stand security and answer for him that in this case he will say no more than a dumb man, on pain of paying whatever is judged and sentenced against him."

"And who stands security for your worship, master curate?" said Don Quixote.

"My profession," answered the curate, "which is to keep secrets."

"Body of me!" said Don Quixote at this. "Is there anything more to it than for His Majesty to order by public proclamation that all the knights errant who are wandering about Spain should gather at the court on a set day? For even if no more than half a dozen came, there might come among them one who would be enough on his own to destroy the whole power of the Turk.

"Give me your attention, your worships, and follow me. Is it by any chance a new thing for a single knight errant to undo an army of two hundred thousand men, as though they all together had one single throat, or were made of sugar-paste? If not, tell me: how many histories are full of these marvels? If only — in an unlucky hour for me, I will not say for anybody else — the famous Don Belianis were alive today, or one of the countless line of Amadis of Gaul! For if any one of these were alive today and came face to face with the Turk, upon my word I would not want to be the Turk. But God will look after his people, and will provide somebody who, if not as fierce as the knights errant of the past, at least will not be inferior to them in spirit. And God understands me, and I say no more."

"Oh!" said the niece at this point. "Kill me if my master does not want to be a knight errant again!"

To which Don Quixote said:

"A knight errant I shall die; and let the Turk come down or go up when he pleases and with as much power as he can muster. I say again that God understands me."

At this point the barber said:

"I beg your worships to give me leave to tell a short story that happened in Seville, which fits so exactly here that it makes me want to tell it."

Don Quixote gave him leave, and the curate and the rest gave him their attention, and he began in this way:

"In the madhouse at Seville there was a man whom his relatives had put there for want of wits. He was a graduate in canon law from Osuna; but even if he had been one from Salamanca, in many people's opinion he would still have been mad.

"This graduate, after some years of confinement, gave himself to understand that he was sane and in his full senses; and with this notion he wrote to the archbishop, begging him earnestly and in very well-ordered terms to order him to be got out of the misery he was living in, since by God's mercy he had now recovered his lost wits — but that his relatives, so as to enjoy their share of his property, were keeping him there, and in spite of the truth wanted him to be mad until his death.

"The archbishop, persuaded by many well-ordered and judicious notes, ordered a chaplain of his to find out from the warden of the house whether what that licentiate wrote him was true, and likewise to talk with the madman, and if he thought he had his wits, to take him out and set him at liberty.

"The chaplain did so; and the warden told him that the man was still mad — that although he often talked like a person of great understanding, in the end he would let fly with so many foolish things that in number and in size they matched his earlier displays of good sense, as could be tested by talking to him. The chaplain wanted to test it; and being put with the madman, he talked with him for an hour and more, and in all that time the madman never said a crooked or absurd word. On the contrary, he spoke so carefully that the chaplain was obliged to believe that the madman was sane.

"And among other things the madman told him was that the warden had a grudge against him, so as not to lose the presents his relatives made him for saying that he was still mad and had only lucid intervals; and that the greatest enemy he had in his misfortune was his own large property, since his enemies, so as to enjoy it, played false and cast doubt on the favour Our Lord had done him in turning him from a beast back into a man.

"In the end he spoke in such a way that he made the warden suspect, his relatives greedy and heartless, and himself so sensible that the chaplain determined to take him away with him so that the archbishop might see him and touch with his hand the truth of that business.

"With this good faith the good chaplain asked the warden to have the clothes the licentiate had come in given back to him. The warden said again that he should consider what he was doing, because without any doubt the licentiate was still mad. The warden's warnings and cautions were of no use at all in stopping the chaplain from taking him away; the warden obeyed, seeing that it was the archbishop's order.

"They put the licentiate's own clothes on him, which were new and decent; and when he saw himself dressed like a sane man and stripped of the madman's dress, he begged the chaplain out of charity to give him leave to go and say goodbye to his companions the madmen. The chaplain said he wanted to go with him and see the madmen who were in the house.

"They went up, in fact, along with some others who happened to be there; and the licentiate, coming to a cage where there was a furious madman — though at that moment quiet and calm — said to him: 'My brother, see whether you have any commands for me, because I am going home; for God has been pleased, out of his infinite goodness and mercy and without my deserving it, to give me back my wits. I am well now and sane; for with regard to God's power nothing is impossible. Have great hope and trust in Him; for since He has brought me back to my former state, He will bring you back to yours too if you trust in Him. I shall take care to send you some good things to eat, and eat them in any case; because I would have you know that it is my belief, as a man who has been through it, that all our madness comes from having empty stomachs and brains full of air. Take heart, take heart; for weakening under misfortunes wears down the health and brings on death.'

"All these words of the licentiate's were heard by another madman who was in another cage opposite the furious one's; and getting up from an old rush mat where he was lying stark naked, he asked at the top of his voice who it was that was going away well and sane. The licentiate answered: 'It is I, brother, who am going; for I have no need to stay here any longer, for which I give endless thanks to heaven, that has done me so great a favour.'

"'Look what you say, licentiate; do not let the devil deceive you,' replied the madman. 'Rest your feet and stay quietly at home, and you will save yourself the journey back.'

"'I know I am well,' replied the licentiate, 'and there will be no need to go round the stations again.'

"'You well?' said the madman. 'Very good, we shall see; go with God. But I swear to you by Jupiter, whose majesty I represent on earth, that for this sin alone which Seville is committing today, in taking you out of this house and holding you for sane, I mean to inflict such a punishment on it that the memory of it shall last for ever and ever, amen. Do you not know, you wretched little licentiate, that I can do it — since, as I say, I am Jupiter the Thunderer, and hold in my hands the burning bolts with which I can and do threaten and destroy the world? But with one thing only do I mean to punish this ignorant town, and that is by not raining on it or on its whole district and neighbourhood for three whole years, which are to be counted from the day and moment this threat has been made. You free, you well, you sane — and I mad, and I sick, and I tied up? I shall think of raining about as soon as I think of hanging myself.'

"The bystanders were attentive to the madman's shouts and words; but our licentiate, turning to our chaplain and taking him by the hands, said to him: 'Do not distress yourself, my dear sir, or take any notice of what this madman has said; for if he is Jupiter and will not rain, I, who am Neptune, the father and god of the waters, will rain as often as I take a fancy to and as often as it is needed.'

"To which the chaplain answered: 'For all that, Señor Neptune, it will not be well to annoy Señor Jupiter. Let your worship stay at home, and another day, when there is more convenience and more time, we shall come back for your worship.'

"The warden and the bystanders laughed, at whose laughter the chaplain was half mortified; they took the licentiate's clothes off him, he stayed in the house, and that is the end of the story."

"So this is the story, master barber," said Don Quixote, "that fitted so exactly here that you could not help telling it? Ah, master shaver, master shaver, how blind is the man who cannot see through a sieve! And is it possible that your worship does not know that comparisons made between one wit and another, one valour and another, one beauty and another and one family and another are always odious and badly received?

"I, master barber, am not Neptune the god of the waters, nor do I try to get anybody to hold me for sensible when I am not. I only weary myself with giving the world to understand the error it is in in not bringing back to itself that most happy time when the order of knight-errantry was in the field. But our depraved age is not worthy to enjoy so great a good as the ages enjoyed when the knights errant took on themselves and threw on their own shoulders the defence of kingdoms, the protection of maidens, the succouring of orphans and wards, the punishment of the arrogant and the reward of the humble.

"Most of the knights who are in use now hear the rustle of the damasks, the brocades and the other rich stuffs they dress in sooner than the mail they arm themselves with. There is no knight now who sleeps in the open fields, exposed to the severity of the sky, armed at all points from feet to head. There is nobody now who, without taking his feet out of the stirrups and leaning on his lance, merely tries to snatch a little sleep, as the knights errant did.

"There is nobody now who, coming out of this wood, goes into that mountain, and from there treads a barren, deserted seashore, most often stormy and rough; and, finding on it and at its edge a small boat with no oars, sail, mast or rigging at all, throws himself into it with an intrepid heart, giving himself up to the merciless waves of the deep sea, which now carry him up to the sky and now bring him down to the abyss; and he, setting his breast against the irresistible storm, when he least expects it finds himself three thousand leagues and more from the place where he embarked; and, leaping onto a remote and unknown shore, things happen to him worthy of being written not on parchment but on bronze.

"But now idleness triumphs over diligence, laziness over labour, vice over virtue, arrogance over courage, and the theory of arms over the practice of them — which lived and shone only in the ages of gold and in the knights errant.

"If not, tell me: who more virtuous and more valiant than the famous Amadis of Gaul? Who more judicious than Palmerin of England? Who more accommodating and handy than Tirant lo Blanc? Who more elegant than Lisuarte of Greece? Who more slashed and more slashing than Don Belianis? Who more intrepid than Perion of Gaul, or who more given to attempting dangers than Felixmarte of Hircania, or who more sincere than Esplandián? Who more headlong than Don Cirongilio of Thrace? Who fiercer than Rodomonte? Who more prudent than King Sobrino? Who more daring than Rinaldo? Who more unconquerable than Roland? And who more gallant and more courteous than Ruggiero, from whom the dukes of Ferrara are descended today, according to Turpin in his Cosmography?

"All these knights, and a great many others I could name, master curate, were knights errant, the light and glory of chivalry. It is of these, or of such men as these, that I could have wished the men of my scheme to be; and if they were, His Majesty would find himself well served and would save a great deal of expense, and the Turk would be left tearing his beard. And so I do not want to stay at home, since the chaplain does not take me out of it; and if his Jupiter, as the barber has said, will not rain, here am I, who will rain whenever I take a fancy to. I say this so that Master Basin may know that I understand him."

"Truly, Señor Don Quixote," said the barber, "I did not mean it in that sense; and so God help me as my intention was a good one, and your worship ought not to take offence."

"Whether I can take offence or not," answered Don Quixote, "I know myself."

To this the curate said:

"Well, I have hardly said a word so far, and I should not like to be left with a scruple that gnaws and scratches at my conscience, arising from what Señor Don Quixote has said here."

"For greater things than that," answered Don Quixote, "master curate has leave; and so he may say his scruple, because it is no pleasure to go about with a scrupulous conscience."

"Then with that permission," answered the curate, "I say that my scruple is that I cannot on any account persuade myself that the whole crowd of knights errant your worship has mentioned, Señor Don Quixote, were really and truly people of flesh and blood in the world; on the contrary, I imagine that the whole of it is fiction, fable and lies, and dreams told by men who are awake — or rather half asleep."

"That is another error," answered Don Quixote, "that many people have fallen into, who do not believe there were ever such knights in the world; and many times, with different people and on different occasions, I have tried to bring this almost universal delusion into the light of truth. Sometimes I have not succeeded in my purpose and other times I have, supporting it on the shoulders of truth — which truth is so certain that I am ready to say that with my own eyes I saw Amadis of Gaul, who was a tall man, white in the face, with a well-set beard, though a black one, with a look between mild and severe, short in speech, slow to anger and quick to put anger aside.

"And in the way I have outlined Amadis I could, in my opinion, paint and describe every knight errant who goes about the histories in the world; for from the notion I have that they were as their histories relate, and from the exploits they performed and the dispositions they had, their features, colouring and heights can be worked out by good philosophy."

"How big does your worship think, my dear Señor Don Quixote," asked the barber, "the giant Morgante must have been?"

"On this matter of giants," answered Don Quixote, "there are different opinions as to whether there have been any in the world or not; but Holy Scripture, which cannot fail by an atom in the truth, shows us that there were, telling us the history of that great Philistine Goliath, who was seven and a half cubits high, which is an outrageous size. Also in the island of Sicily leg-bones and shoulder-blades have been found so large that their size shows that their owners were giants, and as big as great towers; geometry puts this truth beyond doubt.

"But for all that, I could not say with certainty what size Morgante was, although I imagine he cannot have been very tall. And what moves me to be of this opinion is finding in the history where his exploits are particularly mentioned that he often slept under a roof; and since he found a house he could fit into, it is clear that his size was not outrageous."

"That is so," said the curate.

And, enjoying hearing him say such great absurdities, he asked him what he thought about the faces of Rinaldo of Montalban and of Roland and of the other Twelve Peers of France, since they had all been knights errant.

"Of Rinaldo," answered Don Quixote, "I dare to say that he was broad in the face, ruddy in colour, with dancing and somewhat prominent eyes, touchy and excessively hot-tempered, a friend of thieves and of lost characters. Of Roland — or Rotolando, or Orlando, for the histories call him by all these names — I am of the opinion, and I maintain, that he was of middling height, broad-shouldered, somewhat bow-legged, dark in the face and red-bearded, hairy in the body and threatening in his look; short of speech, but very polite and well-bred."

"If Roland was no more of a gentleman than your worship has said," replied the curate, "it is no wonder that the lady Angelica the Fair scorned him and left him for the elegance, spirit and charm the downy-bearded young Moor must have had that she gave herself to; and she was judicious in loving Medoro's softness rather than Roland's roughness."

"That Angelica, master curate," answered Don Quixote, "was a girl who went astray, a wanderer and something of a capricious creature, and she left the world as full of her improprieties as of the fame of her beauty. She despised a thousand lords, a thousand brave men and a thousand men of sense, and was satisfied with a smooth-faced little page with no property or name except what the friendship he kept for his friend could give him as a grateful man.

"The great singer of her beauty, the famous Ariosto, either not daring or not wanting to sing what happened to that lady after her base surrender — which cannot have been things overly virtuous — left her where he said:

	And how she received the sceptre of Cathay,
	perhaps another will sing with a better plectrum.
