"And no doubt this was like a prophecy; for poets are also called vates, which means prophets. This truth is seen clearly, because since then a famous Andalusian poet has wept and sung her tears, and another famous and unique Castilian poet has sung her beauty."

"Tell me, Señor Don Quixote," said the barber at this point, "has there been no poet who has written a satire on that lady Angelica, among so many as have praised her?"

"I well believe," answered Don Quixote, "that if Sacripante or Roland had been poets, they would have given the girl a soaping by now; because it is proper and natural to poets who are scorned and not accepted by their ladies — invented ladies, or ladies invented after all by the men who chose them as the mistresses of their thoughts — to revenge themselves with satires and libels: a revenge, certainly, unworthy of generous hearts. But up to now no defamatory verse against the lady Angelica, who turned the world upside down, has come to my notice."

"A miracle!" said the curate.

And at this they heard the housekeeper and the niece, who had left the conversation by now, giving great shouts in the yard, and they all hurried to the noise.

Chapter 2: Which Treats of the Notable Quarrel Sancho Panza Had with Don Quixote's Niece and Housekeeper, with Other Amusing Matters

The history relates that the shouts Don Quixote, the curate and the barber heard came from the niece and the housekeeper, who were making them at Sancho Panza, who was struggling to get in and see Don Quixote while they blocked the door against him:

"What does this stray creature want in this house? Get off to your own, brother; for it is you and nobody else who leads my master astray and coaxes him away and takes him off along those byways."

To which Sancho answered:

"You housekeeper of Satan's, the man who is coaxed away and led astray and taken off along those byways is me, not your master. He took me off round the world, and you are cheating yourselves by half the just price: he got me out of my house with tricks, promising me an isle that I am waiting for to this day."

"May bad isles choke you, you accursed Sancho," answered the niece. "And what are isles? Are they something to eat, you greedy glutton that you are?"

"They are not to eat," replied Sancho, "but to govern and rule — and better than four cities and four magistrates of the court."

"For all that," said the housekeeper, "you shall not come in here, you sack of wickedness and bag of malice. Go and govern your own house and till your own patches of land, and give up trying for isles or islets."

The curate and the barber got great pleasure from hearing the three of them talk; but Don Quixote, afraid that Sancho would come unstitched and blurt out a heap of malicious foolishness and touch on points that would not do his own reputation any good, called him, and made the two women be quiet and let him in.

Sancho came in, and the curate and the barber took their leave of Don Quixote, of whose health they despaired, seeing how fixed he was in his deranged notions and how steeped in the simplicity of his ill-erring chivalries. And so the curate said to the barber:

"You will see, neighbour, how when we least expect it our gentleman will be off again to fly along the riverbank."

"I do not doubt it," answered the barber; "but I am not so much amazed at the knight's madness as at the squire's simplicity, who has that business of the isle so firmly believed in that I do not think all the undeceivings that can be imagined will get it out of his skull."

"God help them," said the curate; "and let us keep watch and see what all this machine of absurdities of such a knight and such a squire comes to — for it seems they were forged, the two of them, in one and the same mould, and that the master's madnesses without the servant's foolishnesses would not be worth a farthing."

"That is so," said the barber, "and I should very much like to know what the two of them will be discussing now."

"I am certain," answered the curate, "that the niece or the housekeeper will tell us afterwards, for they are not of the sort to leave off listening."

Meanwhile, Don Quixote shut himself up with Sancho in his room; and, being alone, he said to him:

"It grieves me a great deal, Sancho, that you have said and go on saying that I was the man who got you out of your own little house — knowing that I did not stay in my own houses either. We came out together, we went together and we wandered together: one and the same fortune and one and the same luck has run for the two of us. If they tossed you in a blanket once, they have pounded me a hundred times, and this is the advantage I have over you."

"That stands to reason," answered Sancho, "because, according to what your worship says, misfortunes belong more properly to knights errant than to their squires."

"You are mistaken, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Following the maxim, quando caput dolet — and so on."

"I understand no language but my own," answered Sancho.

"I mean," said Don Quixote, "that when the head aches, all the limbs ache; and so, being your master and lord, I am your head and you are a part of me, since you are my servant. And for this reason the harm that touches me, or shall touch me, must hurt you, and yours must hurt me."

"So it ought to have been," said Sancho; "but when they were tossing me as a limb, my head was standing behind the wall watching me fly through the air without feeling any pain at all. And since the limbs are bound to feel the head's pain, the head ought to be bound to feel theirs."

"Do you mean to say now, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "that I did not feel pain when they were tossing you? And if you do say it, do not say it or think it; for I felt more pain then in my spirit than you did in your body.

"But let us leave this aside for now, for there will be a time when we can weigh it up and set it in its proper place. And tell me, friend Sancho: what do they say about me in the village? What opinion do the common people hold of me, what the gentry and what the gentlemen? What do they say about my courage, what about my exploits and what about my courtesy? What is being said about the task I have taken on of bringing back to life and restoring to the world the now forgotten order of chivalry?

"In short, Sancho, I want you to tell me what has come to your ears about this; and you are to tell me this without adding anything to the good or taking anything from the bad. For it is the part of loyal vassals to tell their lords the truth in its own shape and figure, without flattery's enlarging it or any other empty consideration diminishing it.

"And I want you to know, Sancho, that if the naked truth reached the ears of princes, without the clothes of flattery, other centuries would run and other ages would be counted more of iron than ours — which I take to be, of all the ages now in use, the golden one. Let this warning serve you, Sancho, so that judiciously and with good intentions you may put into my ears the truth of what you know about what I have asked you."

"That I shall do very willingly, my dear sir," answered Sancho, "on condition that your worship is not to be angry at what I say, since you want me to say it naked, without dressing it in any other clothes than the ones it came to my knowledge in."

"On no account shall I be angry," answered Don Quixote. "You may well speak freely, Sancho, and without any beating about the bush."

"Well, the first thing I say," he said, "is that the common people hold your worship for an enormous madman, and me for no less of an idiot. The gentry say that, not keeping himself within the limits of the gentry, your worship has put a 'Don' on himself and rushed into being a gentleman with four vine-stocks and two acres of land and a rag behind and another in front. The gentlemen say they would rather the gentry did not set themselves up against them — especially those squirely gentry who blacken their shoes with smoke and darn the holes in their black stockings with green silk."

"That," said Don Quixote, "has nothing to do with me, since I always go well dressed and never patched. Torn, that may well be — and torn more by my armour than by time."

"As for your worship's courage, courtesy, exploits and undertaking," Sancho went on, "there are different opinions. Some say: 'mad, but amusing'; others, 'brave, but unlucky'; others, 'courteous, but impertinent' — and so they run on through so many things that they leave neither your worship nor me a whole bone."

"Look, Sancho," said Don Quixote: "wherever virtue is at a high degree, it is persecuted. Few or none of the famous men of the past escaped being slandered by malice.

"Julius Caesar, that most spirited, most prudent and most valiant captain, was set down as ambitious and somewhat unclean, both in his dress and in his habits. Alexander, whose exploits earned him the name of the Great, they say of him that he had his certain touch of the drunkard. Of Hercules, the man of the many labours, it is told that he was lascivious and soft. Of Don Galaor, Amadis of Gaul's brother, it is whispered that he was more than excessively lustful; and of his brother, that he was a weeper.

"So that, Sancho, among so many slanders on good men, mine may well pass, so long as they are no more than the ones you have said."

"There's the rub, body of my father!" replied Sancho.

"Why, is there more?" asked Don Quixote.

"The tail is still to be skinned," said Sancho. "Everything so far is cakes and ale; but if your worship wants to know all there is about the calumnies they lay on you, I shall bring you here this very moment somebody who will tell you all of them without a crumb missing.

"Because last night Bartolomé Carrasco's son arrived, who is coming from his studies at Salamanca made a bachelor of arts; and when I went to give him welcome, he told me that your worship's history is going about in books now, under the title of The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha. And he says they mention me in it under my own name of Sancho Panza, and the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, along with other things that passed between us two when we were alone — so that I crossed myself in fright at how the historian who wrote them could have known them."

"I assure you, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that the author of our history must be some wise enchanter; for nothing they want to write about is hidden from such men."

"And how could he help being wise and an enchanter," said Sancho, "when — according to Bachelor Sansón Carrasco, for that is the name of the man I have mentioned — the author of the history is called Cide Hamete Aubergine!"

"That name is a Moorish one," answered Don Quixote.

"That will be it," answered Sancho, "because I have generally heard it said that the Moors are fond of aubergines."

"You must be mistaking, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "the surname of this Cide, which in Arabic means lord."

"That may well be," replied Sancho; "but if your worship would like me to bring him here, I shall go for him on wings."

"You will do me a great pleasure, my friend," said Don Quixote; "for what you have told me holds me in suspense, and I shall not eat a mouthful that tastes good to me until I am informed of it all."

"Then I am off for him," answered Sancho.

And leaving his master, he went to look for the bachelor, with whom he came back a little while later; and between the three of them there passed a most amusing conversation.

Chapter 3: Of the Ridiculous Conversation That Passed Between Don Quixote, Sancho Panza and the Bachelor Sansón Carrasco

Don Quixote was left extremely thoughtful, waiting for the bachelor Carrasco, from whom he expected to hear the news of himself put into a book, as Sancho had said. And he could not persuade himself that such a history existed, since the blood of the enemies he had killed was not yet dry on the blade of his sword, and already they wanted his lofty chivalries to be going about in print.

For all that, he imagined that some sage, either friend or enemy, must have put them into print by art of enchantment: if a friend, to magnify them and set them above the most distinguished deeds of any knight errant; if an enemy, to annihilate them and put them below the vilest ever written of any vile squire — although, he said to himself, squires' exploits were never written. And if it were true that such a history existed, it being of a knight errant, it must of necessity be grandiloquent, lofty, distinguished, magnificent and true.

With this he comforted himself somewhat; but he was discomforted by thinking that its author was a Moor, judging by that name of Cide; and from the Moors no truth at all was to be expected, because they are all cheats, forgers and fantasists. He was afraid the man might have treated his love affairs with some indecency that would work to the discredit and injury of his lady Dulcinea of El Toboso's modesty; he wished he had declared his faithfulness and the respect he had always kept for her, scorning queens, empresses and maidens of every quality and holding in check the impulses of natural movements.

And so, wrapped and rewrapped in these and a great many other fancies, Sancho and Carrasco found him, and Don Quixote received them with great courtesy.

The bachelor, although he was called Sansón, was not very big in body, though a very great joker; sallow in colour but of very good understanding. He must have been about twenty-four, round-faced, with a flat nose and a big mouth — all signs of his being of a mischievous disposition and a lover of jokes and fun, as he showed on seeing Don Quixote by putting himself on his knees in front of him and saying:

"Give me your greatness's hands, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha; for by the habit of St Peter that I wear — although I have taken no orders but the first four — your worship is one of the most famous knights errant that there has been, or ever will be, in the whole round world. A blessing on Cide Hamete Benengeli, who left the history of your great deeds written; and a double blessing on the man of curiosity who took care to have them translated from Arabic into our common Castilian, for the universal entertainment of the people."

Don Quixote made him get up and said:

"So it is true that there is a history of me, and that the man who composed it was a Moor and a sage?"

"It is so true, sir," said Sansón, "that it is my belief that more than twelve thousand copies of this history are in print today. And if not, let Portugal, Barcelona and Valencia say so, where they have been printed; and there is even a report that it is being printed at Antwerp, and I have an inkling that there is not going to be a nation or a language it will not be translated into."

"One of the things," said Don Quixote at this, "that must most content a virtuous and eminent man is to see himself, while still alive, going about on people's tongues with a good name, printed and in type. I said with a good name, because if it were the other way about, no death would come up to it."

"If it is a question of a good reputation and a good name," said the bachelor, "your worship alone carries off the palm from all knights errant; because the Moor in his language and the Christian in his took care to paint us to the life your worship's gallantry, your great spirit in facing dangers, your patience in adversities and your endurance both of misfortunes and of wounds, and the modesty and continence of the so platonic love between your worship and my lady Doña Dulcinea of El Toboso."

"I have never," said Sancho Panza at this point, "heard my lady Dulcinea called Doña, but only the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso; and so the history is already wrong in this."

"That is not an objection of any importance," answered Carrasco.

"Certainly not," answered Don Quixote. "But tell me, master bachelor: which of my exploits are the most valued in this history?"

"On that," answered the bachelor, "there are different opinions, as there are different tastes. Some stick to the adventure of the windmills, which seemed to your worship to be Briareuses and giants; others to the fulling mills; this man to the description of the two armies, which afterwards turned out to be two flocks of sheep; that man makes much of the one about the dead man they were taking to be buried at Segovia; one says that the freeing of the galley slaves is better than all of them; another that none comes up to the one about the two Benedictine giants, along with the quarrel with the valorous Basque."

"Tell me, master bachelor," said Sancho at this point: "does the adventure of the Yangüesans come into it, when our good Rocinante took it into his head to ask for truffles in the middle of the sea?"

"The sage left nothing in the inkwell," answered Sansón. "He says everything and notes everything, down to the capers good Sancho cut in the blanket."

"I cut no capers in the blanket," answered Sancho; "in the air, yes — and more of them than I would have liked."

"As far as I can imagine," said Don Quixote, "there is no human history in the world that does not have its ups and downs, especially those that treat of chivalry, which can never be full of prosperous events."

"For all that," answered the bachelor, "some who have read the history say they would have been glad if the authors of it had forgotten a few of the endless beatings that Señor Don Quixote was given in various encounters."

"That is where the truth of the history comes in," said Sancho.

"They could also have kept quiet about them in fairness," said Don Quixote; "since the actions that neither change nor alter the truth of the history there is no reason to write, if they are bound to work to the contempt of the hero of the history. Upon my word, Aeneas was not as pious as Virgil paints him, nor Ulysses as prudent as Homer describes him."

"That is so," replied Sansón, "but it is one thing to write as a poet and another as a historian: the poet may tell or sing things not as they were but as they ought to have been, and the historian must write them not as they ought to have been but as they were, without adding to the truth or taking anything from it."

"Well, if that Moorish gentleman is going in for telling truths," said Sancho, "then among my master's beatings mine are sure to be found; because they never took the measure of his worship's shoulders without taking mine of my whole body. But there is nothing to wonder at in that, since, as my master himself says, the limbs must share in the head's pain."

"You are a sly one, Sancho," answered Don Quixote. "Upon my word, you are not short of memory when you choose to have it."

"Even if I wanted to forget the blows they have given me," said Sancho, "the bruises would not allow it, and they are still fresh on my ribs."

"Be quiet, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and do not interrupt master bachelor, whom I beg to go on telling me what is said about me in the history you speak of."

"And about me," said Sancho, "for they say too that I am one of the chief carackters in it."

"Characters, not carackters, friend Sancho," said Sansón.

"Have we got another reprover of vokibles here?" said Sancho. "Well, if they take to that, we shall never finish in our whole lives."

"God give me a bad one, Sancho," answered the bachelor, "if you are not the second person in the history; and there are people who would rather hear you talk than the finest-drawn character in the whole of it — although there are also those who say you were excessively credulous in believing that the government of that isle offered you by Señor Don Quixote, who is here present, could be real."

"There is still sun on the wall," said Don Quixote; "and the further Sancho goes on in years, the fitter and abler he will be to be a governor, with the experience the years bring, than he is now."

"By God, sir," said Sancho, "the isle I would not govern at the age I am now, I shall not govern at the age of Methuselah. The trouble is that the said isle is hanging about somewhere or other, and not that I am short of the wits to govern it."

"Commend it to God, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and it will all turn out well, and perhaps better than you think; for the leaf does not stir on the tree without God's will."

"That is true," said Sansón; "for if God wills it, Sancho shall not be short of a thousand isles to govern, let alone one."

"I have seen governors about," said Sancho, "who to my mind do not come up to the sole of my shoe, and for all that they are called Your Lordship and are served on silver."

"Those are not governors of isles," replied Sansón, "but of other and easier governments; for those who govern isles must at the very least know grammar."

"I could deal with the gram well enough," said Sancho, "but as for the mar, I neither draw nor pay, because I do not understand it. But leaving this business of the government in God's hands, to send me wherever he can best be served by me, I say, master bachelor Sansón Carrasco, that it has given me endless pleasure that the author of the history has spoken of me in such a way that the things told of me are not annoying. For on the word of a good squire, if he had said things about me that were not very much those of an Old Christian, as I am, the deaf would have heard us."

"That would be working miracles," answered Sansón.

"Miracles or no miracles," said Sancho, "let every man look how he talks or how he writes about persons, and not set down at random the first thing that comes into his head."

"One of the faults they find with this history," said the bachelor, "is that its author put into it a tale called The Reckless Curiosity — not for being bad or badly reasoned, but for not belonging in that place, and having nothing to do with the history of his worship Señor Don Quixote."

"I would bet," replied Sancho, "that the son of a dog has mixed cabbages with baskets."

"Now I say," said Don Quixote, "that the author of my history has not been a sage but some ignorant chatterer who set himself to write it at random and with no reasoning at all, come what may — like Orbaneja, the painter of Úbeda, who, on being asked what he was painting, answered: 'Whatever comes out.' Once he painted a cock in such a fashion and so ill-favoured that it was necessary to write beside it in Gothic letters: 'This is a cock.' And so it must be with my history, which will need a commentary to be understood."

"Not at all," answered Sansón, "because it is so clear that there is nothing in it to puzzle over. Children handle it, young men read it, grown men understand it and old men praise it. And, in short, it is so thumbed and so read and so well known to every kind of person that people have hardly seen a thin hack before they say: 'There goes Rocinante.'

"And those who have taken most to reading it are the pages: there is no lord's antechamber where a Don Quixote is not to be found; some pick it up as others put it down; these pounce on it and those ask for it. In short, this history is the most enjoyable and least harmful entertainment that has been seen up to now, because in the whole of it there is not to be discovered, even by a hint, one immodest word or one thought that is less than Catholic."

"To write in any other way," said Don Quixote, "would not be writing truths but lies; and historians who make use of lies ought to be burnt like men who make counterfeit money. And I do not know what moved the author to make use of other people's tales and stories when there was so much to write about in mine: no doubt he must have gone by the proverb, 'With straw or with hay —' and so on.

"For truly, in setting out my thoughts alone, my sighs, my tears, my good desires and my undertakings, he could have made a volume bigger than, or as big as, all El Tostado's works put together. In fact, what I make out, master bachelor, is that to compose histories and books, of whatever sort they may be, a great judgement and a mature understanding are needed. To say witty things and to write amusing ones is the work of great minds: the most judicious character in a play is the fool, because the man who wants to give people to understand that he is simple must not be so. History is like a sacred thing, because it must be true; and where truth is, God is, in so far as truth goes. But in spite of this there are some who compose and hurl books out of themselves as if they were fritters."

"There is no book so bad," said the bachelor, "that it has not something good in it."

"There is no doubt of that," replied Don Quixote; "but it often happens that men who had deservedly earned and won great fame by their writings lost it altogether, or diminished it somewhat, on giving them to the press."

"The cause of that," said Sansón, "is that as printed works are looked at slowly, their faults are easily seen, and they are scrutinised the more closely the greater the fame of the man who composed them. Men famous for their wits, the great poets, the illustrious historians, are always — or most often — envied by those whose pleasure and particular entertainment is to judge other people's writings without having given any of their own to the light of the world."

"That is nothing to wonder at," said Don Quixote, "because there are many theologians who are no good for the pulpit and are extremely good at seeing the faults or the excesses of those who preach."

"All this is so, Señor Don Quixote," said Carrasco; "but I could wish that such censurers were more merciful and less scrupulous, and did not fix on the specks in the very bright sun of the work they are finding fault with. For if aliquando bonus dormitat Homerus, let them consider how much he was awake, so as to give his work its light with the least shadow he could. And perhaps it might be that what looks bad to them are beauty-spots, which sometimes increase the beauty of the face that has them. And so I say that the risk a man runs who prints a book is enormous, since it is impossible with every impossibility to compose one such that it will satisfy and content everybody who reads it."

"The one that treats of me," said Don Quixote, "must have contented very few."

"On the contrary; since stultorum infinitus est numerus, endless are those who have enjoyed that history. And some have found fault and dishonesty in the author's memory, since he forgets to tell who the thief was who stole Sancho's grey — for it is not stated there, and it is only to be inferred from what is written that he was stolen, and shortly afterwards we see Sancho on horseback on the same donkey, without its having turned up.

"They also say he forgot to put in what Sancho did with those hundred crowns he found in the portmanteau in the Sierra Morena, which are never mentioned again; and there are many who want to know what he did with them, or what he spent them on, which is one of the substantial points missing from the work."

Sancho answered:

"I, Señor Sansón, am in no state at the moment to get into accounts or stories; for I have been taken with a faintness of the stomach which, if I do not repair it with two swallows of the old stuff, will put me on Saint Lucy's thorn. I have it at home; my missus is waiting for me; when I have finished eating I shall come back and satisfy your worship and the whole world about anything they want to ask, both about the loss of the donkey and about the spending of the hundred crowns."

And without waiting for an answer or saying another word, he went off home.

Don Quixote asked and begged the bachelor to stay and take pot luck with him. The bachelor took up the invitation; he stayed, a couple of pigeons were added to the ordinary fare, chivalry was discussed at table, Carrasco fell in with his humour, the banquet ended, they slept through the afternoon heat, Sancho came back and the earlier talk was taken up again.

Chapter 4: In Which Sancho Panza Satisfies the Bachelor Sansón Carrasco on His Doubts and Questions, with Other Events Worth Knowing and Telling

Sancho came back to Don Quixote's house, and going back to the earlier discussion, said:

"As for what Señor Sansón said about wanting to know who, or how, or when my donkey was stolen from me, in answer I say that the very night when, running away from the Holy Brotherhood, we went into the Sierra Morena — after the luckless adventure of the galley slaves and the one about the dead man they were taking to Segovia — my master and I got into a thicket, where my master, leaning on his lance, and I on my grey, pounded and worn out from the past scuffles, set ourselves to sleep as though it had been on four feather mattresses.

"I especially slept with such a heavy sleep that whoever it was had time to come up and prop me on four stakes he set at the four corners of the pack-saddle, so that he left me sitting on it as though on horseback and got the grey out from under me without my feeling it."

"That is an easy thing, and no new occurrence; for the same thing happened to Sacripante when, at the siege of Albracca, that famous thief called Brunello got his horse out from between his legs by that very same device," said Don Quixote.

"Day came," Sancho went on, "and I had hardly given a shiver when, the stakes going, I came down on the ground with a great fall. I looked for the donkey and did not see him; tears came into my eyes, and I made such a lamentation that if the author of our history did not put it in, he may reckon he put in nothing good. At the end of I do not know how many days, as we were coming along with the lady Princess Micomicona, I recognised my ass, and that riding on him in gypsy dress was that Ginés de Pasamonte, that trickster and enormous scoundrel that my master and I got off the chain."

"That is not where the mistake lies," replied Sansón, "but in the fact that before the donkey had turned up, the author says that Sancho was riding on the same grey."

"To that," said Sancho, "I do not know what to answer, except that the historian was mistaken, or it must have been the printer's carelessness."

"That is certainly it," said Sansón; "but what became of the hundred crowns? Did they melt away?"

Sancho answered:

"I spent them for the good of my own person and my wife's and my children's, and they have been the reason my wife bears patiently with the roads and highways I have gone along serving my master Don Quixote. Because if at the end of all this time I had come home without a farthing and without the donkey, a black fortune would have been waiting for me.

"And if there is anything more to know about me, here I am, and I shall answer the king himself in person; and nobody has any business meddling in whether I brought them or did not bring them, whether I spent them or did not spend them. For if the beatings they gave me on those journeys were to be paid for in money, even if they were only valued at four maravedis apiece, another hundred crowns would not be enough to pay me half of it. And let every man put his hand on his own breast and not set himself to judge white for black and black for white; for every man is as God made him, and often a good deal worse."

"I shall take care," said Carrasco, "to charge the author of the history that if he prints it again he must not forget this that good Sancho has said, which will raise it a good span higher than it stands."

"Is there anything else to correct in this book, master bachelor?" asked Don Quixote.

"There must be," he answered, "but none of it can be of the importance of the ones already mentioned."

"And by any chance," said Don Quixote, "does the author promise a second part?"

"He does promise one," answered Sansón; "but he says he has not found it and does not know who has it, and so we are in doubt whether it will come out or not. And both for this reason and because some say, 'Second parts were never any good,' and others, 'What is written about Don Quixote's affairs is enough,' it is doubted that there is to be a second part — although some who are more jovial than saturnine say: 'Let us have more Quixotries: let Don Quixote charge and Sancho Panza talk, and be it what it may, we shall be satisfied with that.'"

"And what is the author's intention?"

"That," answered Sansón, "as soon as he finds the history he is looking for with extraordinary diligence, he will put it in print at once, moved more by the profit that will come to him from giving it out than by any other praise."

To which Sancho said:

"Money and profit is what the author has his eye on? It will be a marvel if he gets it right, because he will do nothing but botch and botch, like a tailor on the eve of Easter; and works that are done in a hurry are never finished with the perfection they require. Let that Moorish gentleman, or whatever he is, mind what he is doing; for my master and I will give him so much rubble to hand in the matter of adventures and different happenings that he will be able to put together not only a second part but a hundred.

"The good man must think, no doubt, that we are asleep here on the straw; but let him hold our foot while he shoes us and he will see which one we limp on. What I can say is that if my master would take my advice, we should be out in those fields by now undoing injuries and putting wrongs right, as is the use and custom of good knights errant."

Sancho had hardly finished saying this when there came to their ears the neighing of Rocinante; which neighing Don Quixote took for a most fortunate omen, and he decided to make another sally three or four days from then. And declaring his intention to the bachelor, he asked his advice as to which quarter he should begin his journey in.

The bachelor answered that it was his opinion he should go to the kingdom of Aragon and to the city of Saragossa, where in a few days' time some most solemn jousts were to be held for the feast of St George, in which he could win fame above all the knights of Aragon — which would be to win it above all the knights in the world. He praised his decision as most honourable and most valiant, and warned him to go more cautiously in facing dangers, on the grounds that his life was not his own but belonged to all those who needed him to protect them and rescue them in their misfortunes.

"That is the very thing I complain about, Señor Sansón," said Sancho at this point; "for my master goes at a hundred armed men the way a greedy boy goes at half a dozen melons. Body of the world, master bachelor! Surely there are times to attack and times to retreat; surely it cannot all be 'St James, and at them, Spain!'

"And what is more, I have heard it said — and I believe by my master himself, if I remember rightly — that between the extremes of cowardice and rashness lies the middle point of courage. And if this is so, I do not want him to run away when there is no reason to, or to attack when going too far calls for something else.

"But above all, I warn my master that if he is to take me with him, it must be on condition that he does all the fighting himself, and that I am not to be obliged to anything except looking after his person in what concerns his cleanness and his comfort. In that I shall dance attendance on him; but to suppose that I am going to put a hand to my sword, even against low scoundrels with axe and helmet, is to think of what will not happen.

"I, Señor Sansón, do not mean to win a reputation for bravery, but for being the best and most loyal squire that ever served a knight errant. And if my master Don Quixote, obliged by my many good services, should want to give me some isle out of the many his worship says he is bound to come across, I shall receive a great favour in it; and if he does not give me one, I was born anyway, and a man must not live in dependence on anybody but God. And what is more, bread will taste as good to me, and perhaps better, out of a government as in it.

"And how do I know but that in these governments the devil has got some trip-up prepared for me, where I may stumble and fall and knock my teeth out? Sancho I was born and Sancho I mean to die. But if for all that, quietly and easily, without much trouble and without much risk, heaven should send me some isle or something of the sort, I am not such a fool as to throw it away; for they also say: 'When they give you the heifer, run with the halter'; and 'When good fortune comes, get it into your house.'"

"Brother Sancho," said Carrasco, "you have spoken like a professor; but for all that, trust in God and in Señor Don Quixote, who is bound to give you a kingdom, let alone an isle."

"The more is the same as the less," answered Sancho; "although I can tell Señor Carrasco that my master would not be throwing the kingdom he gave me into a torn sack, for I have taken my own pulse and I find myself in health to rule kingdoms and govern isles; and I have told my master this other times already."

"Take care, Sancho," said Sansón, "for office changes manners, and it might be that on seeing yourself a governor you would not know the mother that bore you."

"That is to be understood," answered Sancho, "of those who were born in the mallows, and not of those who have four fingers of Old Christian fat on their souls, as I have. Just come and try my disposition, and see whether it will use ingratitude to anybody!"

"God grant it," said Don Quixote, "and it will show itself when the government comes; for I fancy I have it in front of my eyes already."

This said, he begged the bachelor that if he were a poet he would do him the kindness of composing him some verses that should treat of the leave-taking he meant to make of his lady Dulcinea of El Toboso; and that he should note that at the beginning of each line he was to put a letter of her name, so that at the end of the verses, putting the first letters together, one should read: Dulcinea of El Toboso.

The bachelor answered that although he was not one of the famous poets of Spain — of whom, they said, there were no more than three and a half — he would not fail to compose such verses, although he found a great difficulty in composing them, because the letters that made up the name were seventeen. And that if he made four Castilian stanzas of four lines each, there would be one letter left over; and if of five lines each, which they call ten-liners or roundels, three letters would be missing. But that for all that he would try to swallow one letter as best he could, so that in the four Castilian stanzas the name of Dulcinea of El Toboso should be included.

"It must be so in any case," said Don Quixote; "for if the name is not there plain and manifest, there is no woman who would believe that the verses were made for her."

They settled on this, and that the departure should be a week from then. Don Quixote charged the bachelor to keep it secret, especially from the curate and from Master Nicolás, and from his niece and the housekeeper, so that they should not hinder his honourable and valorous decision. Carrasco promised it all.

With this he took his leave, charging Don Quixote to let him know of all his good or bad fortunes when there was an opportunity. And so they parted, and Sancho went to put in order what was needed for their journey.

Chapter 5: Of the Judicious and Amusing Conversation That Passed Between Sancho Panza and Teresa Panza His Wife, and Other Events Worthy of Happy Memory

(On coming to write this fifth chapter, the translator of this history says that he holds it to be apocryphal, because in it Sancho Panza talks in a different style from the one that could be expected of his short wit, and says things so subtle that he does not think it possible he could have known them. But that he did not want to leave off translating it, so as to fulfil what he owed to his office; and so he went on, saying:)

Sancho reached his house so delighted and cheerful that his wife saw his cheerfulness a crossbow shot away — so much so that it obliged her to ask him:

"What have you got, Sancho my friend, that you come so cheerful?"

To which he answered:

"Wife, if God had willed it, I should be very glad not to be as pleased as I look."

"I do not understand you, husband," she replied, "and I do not know what you mean by that about your being glad, if God had willed it, not to be pleased; for silly as I am, I do not know who takes pleasure in not having any."

"Look, Teresa," answered Sancho, "I am cheerful because I have decided to go back to serving my master Don Quixote, who means to go out for the third time to look for adventures; and I am going out with him again, because my need requires it, along with the hope — which cheers me — of thinking that I may find another hundred crowns like the ones already spent. Although it makes me sad to have to part from you and my children.

"And if God would give me my food dry-shod and at home, without dragging me over rough ground and crossroads — for he could do it at little cost and by no more than wanting to — it is clear that my cheerfulness would be firmer and sounder, since the cheerfulness I have goes mixed with the sadness of leaving you. So I was right to say I would be glad, if God had willed it, not to be pleased."

"Look, Sancho," replied Teresa, "ever since you made yourself a limb of a knight errant you talk in such a roundabout way that nobody can understand you."

"It is enough that God understands me, wife," answered Sancho, "for He is the understander of all things; and let this stop here. And note, my dear, that you must take care over these three days with the grey, so that he is fit to take up arms: double his feed, see to the pack-saddle and the rest of the tackle, because we are not going to a wedding but to go round the world and to have givings and takings with giants, with dragons and with monsters, and to hear hissings, roarings, bellowings and howlings — and even all this would be lavender-water if we did not have to deal with Yangüesans and enchanted Moors."

"I well believe, husband," replied Teresa, "that squires errant do not eat their bread for nothing; and so I shall stay behind praying to Our Lord to get you out of so much bad fortune soon."

"I tell you, wife," answered Sancho, "that if I did not expect before very long to see myself governor of an isle, I should drop down dead here."

"Not that, my husband," said Teresa; "let the hen live, even with her pip. Live you, and let the devil take all the governments there are in the world. Without a government you came out of your mother's belly, without a government you have lived till now, and without a government you will go — or they will carry you — to the grave when God is pleased. There are plenty of people in the world like that who live without a government, and they do not for that stop living and being counted in the number of the people. The best sauce in the world is hunger; and as the poor are never short of that, they always eat with pleasure.

"But look, Sancho: if by any chance you find yourself with some government, do not forget me and your children. Note that Sanchico is a full fifteen now, and it is right that he should go to school, if his uncle the abbot is to make a churchman of him. Note too that Mari Sancha your daughter will not die if we marry her off; for she is giving me hints that she wants a husband as much as you want to find yourself with a government. And after all, a badly married daughter looks better than a well-kept mistress."

"Upon my word," answered Sancho, "if God brings me to have anything in the way of a government, I mean to marry Mari Sancha off so high, wife, that they will not be able to reach her without calling her My Lady."

"Not that, Sancho," answered Teresa. "Marry her to her equal, which is the soundest thing; because if you take her out of clogs and into high shoes, and out of a brown fourteen-thread skirt into a hooped one and silk gowns, and out of a 'Marica' and a plain 'you' into a 'Doña So-and-so' and a 'Your Ladyship', the girl will not know herself, and at every turn she will fall into a thousand blunders, showing the yarn of her coarse, common cloth."

"Be quiet, you fool," said Sancho; "it will only be a matter of getting used to it for two or three years, and after that the ladyship and the dignity will fit her as though they were moulded. And if not, what does it matter? Let her be Your Ladyship, and come what may."

"Measure yourself by your own condition, Sancho," answered Teresa; "do not try to raise yourself higher, and note the proverb that says: 'Wipe your neighbour's son's nose and take him into your house.' Certainly it would be a fine thing to marry our María to some great count or lordly gentleman who, whenever the fancy took him, would give her a fresh coat of paint, calling her a peasant girl, the daughter of a clod-splitter and a distaff-scraper! Not in my lifetime, husband! Is that, indeed, what I have brought up my daughter for?

"You bring the money, Sancho, and leave the marrying of her to me. For there is Lope Tocho, Juan Tocho's son, a plump, healthy lad, and we know him, and I know he does not look on the girl with a bad eye. And with him, who is our equal, she will be well married, and we shall always have her under our eyes, and we shall all be one — parents and children, grandchildren and sons-in-law — and God's peace and blessing will go about among us all. And do not you go marrying her off now in those courts and those great palaces, where they will neither understand her nor she understand herself."

"Come here, you beast and wife of Barabbas," replied Sancho. "Why do you want now, without rhyme or reason, to stop me marrying my daughter to somebody who will give me grandchildren that are called Your Lordship? Look, Teresa: I have always heard my elders say that the man who does not know how to enjoy good luck when it comes to him ought not to complain when it passes him by. And it would not be right that now, when it is knocking at our door, we should shut it in its face. Let us let ourselves be carried by this favourable wind that is blowing for us."

(It is by this way of talking, and by what Sancho says further on, that the translator of this history said he held this chapter to be apocryphal.)

"Does it not seem to you, you animal," Sancho went on, "that it will be a good thing to drop my body into some profitable government that will get our foot out of the mud? And let Mari Sancha be married to whoever I like, and you will see how they call you Doña Teresa Panza, and how you sit in church on a carpet and cushions and hangings, in spite and to the annoyance of the gentlewomen of the village! And if not, stay always in the same state, without growing or shrinking, like a figure in a tapestry! And let us say no more about this, for Sanchica is to be a countess whatever you may say to me."

"Do you see all you are saying, husband?" answered Teresa. "Well, for all that, I am afraid that this earldom of my daughter's is going to be her ruin. You do what you like, whether you make her a duchess or a princess, but I can tell you that it will not be with my will or my consent.

"I was always a friend to equality, brother, and I cannot bear to see people give themselves airs with no grounds for it. Teresa they put on me at my baptism, a plain, bare name, with no additions or trimmings or the fringes of Dons and Doñas. Cascajo my father was called; and me, for being your wife, they call Teresa Panza, when by good reason they ought to call me Teresa Cascajo. But there, laws go where kings will; and I am content with this name without their putting a Don on top of it that weighs so much I cannot carry it.

"And I do not want to give people anything to talk about when they see me go about dressed like a countess or a governor's wife, for they will say at once: 'Just look how airily the slattern goes! Yesterday she could not get her fill of pulling at a tuft of tow, and went to Mass with her head covered by the tail of her skirt instead of a mantle, and today she goes with a hooped skirt and brooches and airs, as though we did not know her.'

"If God keeps me my seven — or my five — senses, or whichever ones I have, I do not mean to give anybody the chance to see me in such a fix. You go off, brother, and be a government or an isle, and give yourself airs to your heart's content; but my daughter and I, by my mother's memory, are not going to move a step out of our village. The honourable woman has a broken leg and stays at home; and for the modest girl, doing something is her holiday.

"Go off with your Don Quixote to your adventures, and leave us to our misfortunes, for God will improve them for us if we are good. And I certainly do not know who put a Don on him, when neither his parents nor his grandparents had one."

"Now I say," replied Sancho, "that you have some familiar spirit in that body of yours. God help you, woman, and what a lot of things you have strung together, one on another, with neither head nor tail! What have Cascajo and the brooches and the proverbs and the airs to do with what I am saying?

"Come here, you idiot and ignorant woman — for I can call you that, since you do not understand my arguments and go running away from good luck. If I were saying that my daughter should throw herself down from a tower, or go wandering about the world as the princess Doña Urraca wanted to do, you would be right not to fall in with my wishes. But if in two shakes, and in less than the opening and shutting of an eye, I clap a Don and a Ladyship on her back, and take her out of the stubble and put her under a canopy and on a dais, on a platform with more velvet cushions on it than the Almohads of Morocco had Moors in their line — why should you not consent and want what I want?"

"Do you know why, husband?" answered Teresa. "Because of the proverb that says: 'The man who covers you uncovers you.' People run their eyes over the poor man as though in passing, and rest them on the rich one; and if that rich man was once poor, that is where the muttering and the ill-speaking begins, and worse still the persevering of the ill-speakers, who are about these streets in heaps, like swarms of bees."

"Look, Teresa," answered Sancho, "and listen to what I want to tell you now; perhaps you will never have heard it in all the days of your life, and I am not now speaking off my own bat, for everything I mean to say is maxims from the preaching father who preached in this village last Lent — who, if I remember rightly, said that all present things the eyes are looking at present themselves and stand and remain in our memory far better and with more force than things past."

(All these arguments that Sancho goes on making here are the second reason the translator gives for holding this chapter to be apocryphal, since they go beyond Sancho's capacity. And he went on to say:)

"From which it comes about that when we see some person well turned out and dressed in rich clothes and with a train of servants, it seems that it forces us and invites us to have respect for that person, even though our memory at that instant may present to us some low condition we once saw that same person in. Which shame, whether it was of poverty or of birth, since it has passed, is not; and only what we see before us is.

"And if this man, whom fortune has taken out of the rough draft of his low condition — for it was in these very words that the father said it — to the height of his prosperity, is well-bred, generous and courteous with everybody, and does not set himself up in competition with those who are noble by long descent, take it as certain, Teresa, that there will be nobody who remembers what he was, but they will reverence what he is — unless it is the envious, from whom no prosperous fortune is safe."

"I do not understand you, husband," replied Teresa. "Do what you like, and do not break my head any more with your harangues and rhetorics. And if you are revolved on doing what you say —"

"Resolved you should say, wife," said Sancho, "and not revolved."

"Do not set yourself to argue with me, husband," answered Teresa. "I speak as God is pleased to have me, and I do not go into any finer drawing. And I say that if you are persisting in having a government, take your son Sancho with you, so that you may teach him from now on how to have a government; for it is right that children should inherit and learn their fathers' trades."

"As soon as I have a government," said Sancho, "I shall send for him by the post, and I shall send you money, which I shall not be short of; for there is never any lack of people to lend it to governors when they have none. And dress him so as to hide what he is and make him look like what he is going to be."

"You send the money," said Teresa, "and I shall dress him up like a palm-shoot."

"So we are agreed, then," said Sancho, "that our daughter is to be a countess."

"The day I see her a countess," answered Teresa, "that is the day I shall reckon I am burying her. But I tell you again to do what pleases you, for we women are born with this burden of being obedient to our husbands, even if they are blockheads."

And at this she began to weep as truly as though she already saw Sanchica dead and buried. Sancho comforted her by telling her that although he would have to make her a countess, he would make her one as late as he possibly could. With this their talk came to an end, and Sancho went back to see Don Quixote to make arrangements for their departure.

Chapter 6: Of What Passed Between Don Quixote and His Niece and Housekeeper, Which Is One of the Most Important Chapters in the Whole History

While Sancho Panza and his wife Teresa Cascajo were having the irrelevant conversation just related, Don Quixote's niece and housekeeper were not idle; for by a thousand signs they were gathering that their uncle and master meant to break out for the third time and go back to the practice of his — as they saw it — ill-erring chivalry. They tried by every possible means to turn him away from so bad an idea, but it was all preaching in the desert and hammering cold iron.

For all that, among many other things they said to him, the housekeeper said:

"Truly, my dear sir, if your worship does not plant your feet flat and stay quietly at home, and leave off going about the mountains and the valleys like a soul in torment looking for those things they call adventures — which I call disasters — I shall have to complain aloud and at the top of my voice to God and to the king, so that they may put a stop to it."

To which Don Quixote answered:

"Housekeeper, what God will answer to your complaints I do not know, nor what His Majesty will answer either. I only know that if I were king I would excuse myself from answering the endless infinity of impertinent petitions that are given him every day; for one of the greatest labours kings have, among many others, is being obliged to listen to everybody and answer everybody. And so I would not want affairs of mine to give him any trouble."

To which the housekeeper said:

"Tell us, sir: are there no knights at His Majesty's court?"

"Yes," answered Don Quixote, "and a great many; and it is right that there should be, to adorn the greatness of princes and to display the royal majesty."

"Then would your worship not be one of those," she replied, "who serve their king and lord standing still, staying at court?"

"Look, my friend," answered Don Quixote: "not all knights can be courtiers, nor can or should all courtiers be knights errant. There have to be all kinds in the world; and although we are all knights, there is a great deal of difference between the one sort and the other. Because courtiers, without going out of their rooms or over the threshold of the court, travel all over the world by looking at a map, without its costing them a farthing or their suffering heat or cold, hunger or thirst.

"But we, the true knights errant, in the sun, in the cold, in the wind, in the inclemencies of the sky, by night and by day, on foot and on horseback, measure the whole earth with our own feet. And we know our enemies not only in paintings but in their own being, and we attack them at every pass and on every occasion, without looking at trifles or at the laws of duelling: whether or not the other man's lance or sword is shorter; whether he carries relics on him, or some hidden trick; whether or not the sun is to be divided and shared out, along with other ceremonies of that stamp that are used in private duels between one man and another, which you do not know about and I do.

"And you must know something more: that the good knight errant, even if he sees ten giants whose heads not only touch but go past the clouds, and each of whom has two enormous towers for legs, and whose arms are like the masts of great, powerful ships, and each eye like a great millwheel and burning hotter than a glass furnace, must not be frightened by them in any way at all. On the contrary, with a fine bearing and an intrepid heart he must go at them and charge them, and if it is possible defeat and rout them in a small instant, even if they came armed in the shells of a certain fish which they say are harder than if they were of diamond, and carried instead of swords sharp knives of Damascus steel, or iron-shod clubs with points of steel on them too, as I have seen more than twice.

"All this I have said, my good housekeeper, so that you may see the difference there is between one kind of knight and another. And it would be reasonable that there should be no prince who did not value more highly this second — or rather this first — species of knights errant; for, as we read in their histories, there have been men among them who have been the salvation not of one kingdom only but of many."

"Ah, my dear sir!" said the niece at this point. "Let your worship note that everything you say about knights errant is fable and lies, and their histories, if they were not to be burnt, deserve to have a penitent's smock put on each of them, or some mark by which it would be known as infamous and as a destroyer of good morals."

"By the God who sustains me," said Don Quixote, "if you were not directly my niece, as my own sister's daughter, I would inflict such a punishment on you for the blasphemy you have spoken that it would ring through the whole world. How is it possible that a chit of a girl who hardly knows how to work a dozen lace bobbins should dare to set her tongue to censuring the histories of knights errant?

"What would Señor Amadis say if he heard such a thing? But I am quite sure he would forgive you, because he was the humblest and most courteous knight of his time, and moreover a great protector of maidens. But somebody else might have heard you who would have done you no good by it; for they are not all courteous or well-mannered: there are some villains and boors among them.

"Nor are all those who call themselves knights knights through and through: some are of gold and others of alchemy, and they all look like knights, but not all of them can stand the touchstone of truth. There are low men who burst themselves trying to look like knights, and there are lofty knights who seem to be dying on purpose to look like low men; the first raise themselves either by ambition or by virtue, the second lower themselves either by slackness or by vice. And we need to make use of a discerning judgement to tell apart these two kinds of knights, so alike in their names and so far apart in their actions."

"God help me!" said the niece. "That your worship should know so much, uncle, that if it were needed at a pinch you could get up in a pulpit and go and preach in the streets — and that with all this you should fall into so great a blindness and so plain a foolishness that you give yourself to understand that you are brave when you are old, that you have strength when you are ill, and that you set wrongs right when you are bowed down by age; and, above all, that you are a knight when you are not — because although gentlefolk may be knights, poor men are not!"

"You are quite right, niece, in what you say," answered Don Quixote, "and I could tell you things about lineages that would astonish you; but so as not to mix the divine with the human, I shall not say them.

"Look, my friends: all the lineages there are in the world — and listen to me carefully — can be reduced to four kinds, which are these. Some had humble beginnings and went on spreading and extending until they reached the greatest greatness. Others had great beginnings and went on preserving them, and preserve and maintain them in the condition they began in. Others, although they had great beginnings, ended in a point like a pyramid, having diminished and annihilated their beginning until it stopped at nothing at all — as the point of a pyramid is, which compared with its base or foundation is nothing. And there are others, and these are the most numerous, who neither had a good beginning nor a reasonable middle, and so will have an end without a name, like the lineage of the common and ordinary people.

"Of the first, who had a humble beginning and rose to the greatness they now preserve, let the Ottoman house serve you as an example, which from a humble and lowly shepherd who gave it its beginning stands at the height where we see it. Of the second lineage, which had its beginning in greatness and preserves it without increasing it, many princes will be an example who are princes by inheritance and keep themselves so without increasing or diminishing it, holding themselves peacefully within the limits of their states.

"Of those who began great and ended in a point there are thousands of examples; for all the Pharaohs and Ptolemies of Egypt, the Caesars of Rome, along with the whole crowd — if one may give them that name — of endless princes, monarchs and lords, Medes, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks and barbarians, all these lineages and lordships have ended in a point and in nothing at all, both they and those who gave them their beginning; since it would not be possible now to find any of their descendants, and if we did find one, it would be in a low and humble condition.

"Of the plebeian lineage I have nothing to say, except that it serves only to increase the number of those who are alive, without their greatness deserving any other fame or any other praise.

"From all I have said I want you to gather, my silly girls, that there is great confusion among lineages, and that only those seem great and illustrious that show it in the virtue and in the riches and generosity of their owners. I said virtues, riches and generosity, because the great man who is vicious will be a great vicious man, and the rich man who is not generous will be a miserly beggar; for it is not the having of riches that makes their owner happy but the spending of them — and not the spending of them anyhow, but knowing how to spend them well.

"To the poor knight no other road is left for showing that he is a knight but the road of virtue: being affable, well-bred, courteous, polite and obliging; not proud, not arrogant, not a back-biter, and above all charitable. For with two maravedis that he gives a poor man with a cheerful heart he will show himself as generous as the man who gives alms to the ringing of a bell; and there will be nobody who sees him adorned with the virtues I have mentioned who, even without knowing him, will not judge him and hold him to be of good stock — and his not being so would be a miracle. And praise was always the reward of virtue, and the virtuous cannot fail to be praised.

"There are two roads, my daughters, by which men can go to come to be rich and honoured: one is that of letters, the other that of arms. I have more of arms than of letters, and I was born, judging by my inclination to arms, under the influence of the planet Mars; so that I am almost forced to follow its road, and along it I must go in spite of the whole world. And it will be useless to weary yourselves in persuading me not to want what the heavens want, fortune ordains, reason requires and, above all, my own will desires.

"For knowing as I do the countless labours that go with knight-errantry, I also know the endless goods that are attained by it; and I know that the path of virtue is very narrow and the road of vice broad and spacious; and I know that their ends and destinations are different, because the road of vice, wide and spacious, ends in death, and the road of virtue, narrow and laborious, ends in life — and not in a life that comes to an end but in the one that will have no end. And I know, as our great Castilian poet says, that

	It is along these rough places that the road runs
	to the high seat of immortality,
	which nobody reaches who turns aside from it."

"Oh, unlucky me!" said the niece. "So my master is a poet as well! He knows everything, he can do everything: I would bet that if he wanted to be a bricklayer he would know how to build a house as well as he would build a cage."

"I promise you, niece," answered Don Quixote, "that if these chivalric thoughts did not carry all my senses along with them, there would be nothing I could not do, and no piece of craftsmanship that would not come out of my hands — especially cages and toothpicks."

At this moment there was a knock at the door; and on their asking who was knocking, Sancho Panza answered that it was he. And the housekeeper had hardly recognised him when she ran off to hide so as not to see him, so much did she loathe him. The niece opened the door, his master Don Quixote came out to receive him with open arms, and the two of them shut themselves up in his room, where they had another conversation that the last one does not surpass.

Chapter 7: Of What Passed Between Don Quixote and His Squire, with Other Most Famous Events

The housekeeper had hardly seen Sancho Panza shutting himself up with her master when she realised what they were up to; and imagining that out of that consultation would come the decision on his third sally, she took her cloak and, full of distress and grief, went to look for the bachelor Sansón Carrasco, thinking that as he was well spoken and a new friend of her master's he might persuade him to give up so deranged a plan.

She found him walking about the courtyard of his house; and on seeing him she let herself drop at his feet, sweating and distressed. When Carrasco saw her with such signs of grief and alarm, he said to her:

"What is this, mistress housekeeper? What has happened to you, that it looks as though your soul were being torn out of you?"

"It is nothing, my dear Señor Sansón, except that my master is coming out — he is coming out, and no doubt about it!"

"And where is he coming out at, madam?" asked Sansón. "Has some part of his body burst?"

"He is not coming out anywhere," she answered, "except at the door of his madness. I mean, master bachelor of my soul, that he wants to go out again — and with this it will be the third time — to look about the world for what he calls good fortunes, when I cannot understand how he gives them that name.

"The first time they brought him back to us slung across a donkey, pounded with blows. The second he came on an ox-cart, put away and shut up in a cage, where he gave himself to understand that he was enchanted; and the poor creature came in such a state that the mother who bore him would not have known him: thin, yellow, his eyes sunk into the topmost garrets of his brain — so that to bring him round somewhat I got through more than six hundred eggs, as God knows and everybody knows, and my hens, who will not let me lie."

"That I well believe," answered the bachelor; "for they are so good, so fat and so well brought up that they would not say one thing for another if they burst. In fact, mistress housekeeper: is there nothing else, and has no other mishap happened, but this that is feared Señor Don Quixote wants to do?"

"No, sir," she answered.

"Then do not distress yourself," answered the bachelor; "but go home and good luck to you, and have something hot ready for my breakfast, and on the way go and say the prayer of St Apollonia, if you know it; for I shall come along presently and you shall see marvels."

"Wretched me!" replied the housekeeper. "Your worship says I am to say the prayer of St Apollonia? That would be if my master had it in his teeth, but he has it in nothing but his skull."

"I know what I am saying, mistress housekeeper. Go, and do not set yourself to argue with me; for you know I am a bachelor of Salamanca, and there is no more bachelling to be done," answered Carrasco.

And with this the housekeeper went off, and the bachelor went straight away to look for the curate, to discuss with him what will be told in its own time.

During the time Don Quixote and Sancho were shut up together, there passed the words that the history relates with great exactness and truthful report.

Sancho said to his master:

"Sir, I have got my wife reclined to letting me go with your worship wherever you like to take me."

"Reconciled you should say, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "not reclined."

"Once or twice," answered Sancho, "if I remember rightly, I have begged your worship not to correct my words, so long as you understand what I mean by them; and that when you do not understand them you should say, 'Sancho, or devil, I do not understand you'; and if I do not make myself clear, then you may correct me. For I am so fossil —"

"I do not understand you, Sancho," said Don Quixote at once, "since I do not know what 'I am so fossil' means."

"'So fossil' means," answered Sancho, "I am so like that."

"I understand you less than ever now," replied Don Quixote.

"Well, if you cannot understand me," answered Sancho, "I do not know how to put it: I know no more, and God be with me."

"Ah, now, now I see it," answered Don Quixote: "you mean to say that you are so docile, mild and manageable that you will take whatever I tell you and go along with whatever I teach you."

"I would bet," said Sancho, "that from the very beginning you fathomed me and understood me, and only wanted to muddle me so as to hear me say another two hundred blunders."

"That may be," replied Don Quixote. "And in fact, what does Teresa say?"

"Teresa says," said Sancho, "that I should tie my finger tight to your worship, and that papers should speak and beards keep quiet; because whoever cuts does not shuffle, and one 'take this' is worth more than two 'I'll give you'. And I say that a woman's advice is little, and the man who does not take it is mad."

"And I say so too," answered Don Quixote. "Speak on, friend Sancho; go ahead, for you are talking pearls today."

"The case is," replied Sancho, "that, as your worship knows better than I do, we are all subject to death, and today we are and tomorrow we are not, and the lamb goes as quickly as the sheep, and nobody can promise himself in this world more hours of life than God chooses to give him — because death is deaf, and when she comes to knock at the doors of our life she is always in a hurry, and neither prayers nor force nor sceptres nor mitres will make her stop, according to common report and fame and according to what they tell us from those pulpits."

"All that is true," said Don Quixote, "but I do not know where you are getting to."

"I am getting to this," said Sancho: "that your worship should fix me a set wage of what you are to give me each month for the time I serve you, and that the said wage should be paid me out of your property. For I do not want to be at the mercy of favours, which come late, or badly, or never; God help me with what is my own.

"In short, I want to know what I am earning, be it little or much; for the hen lays on one egg, and many littles make a much, and while something is being earned nothing is being lost. It is true that if it should happen — which I neither believe nor expect — that your worship gave me the isle you have promised me, I am not so ungrateful, nor do I take things so to the last hair, as not to want the income of that isle to be valued and deducted from my wages pro cat-a."

"Friend Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "sometimes a cat may serve as well as a rat."

"I understand," said Sancho: "I would bet you were going to say rata and not cata; but it does not matter at all, since your worship has understood me."

"And so well understood," answered Don Quixote, "that I have penetrated to the bottom of your thoughts, and I know the target you are shooting at with the innumerable arrows of your proverbs.

"Look, Sancho: I would readily fix you a wage if I had found in any of the histories of the knights errant an example that revealed and showed me, through some small chink, what they used to earn each month or each year. But I have read all, or most, of their histories, and I do not remember having read that any knight errant ever fixed a set wage for his squire. I only know that they all served on favour, and that when they least expected it, if their lords' luck had run well, they found themselves rewarded with an isle or with something equivalent, and at the very least were left with a title and a lordship.

"If on these hopes and terms you, Sancho, care to come back and serve me, so be it and good luck to you; for to think that I am going to take the ancient usage of knight-errantry off its hinges and out of its bounds is to think of what will not happen. So, my Sancho, go back to your house and declare my intention to your Teresa; and if she is willing and you are willing to be on favour with me, bene quidem; and if not, we are as good friends as before. For if the dovecote is not short of food, it will not be short of doves.

"And note, my son, that a good hope is worth more than a poor possession, and a good grievance than a bad payment. I speak in this way, Sancho, to give you to understand that I too, like you, know how to hurl proverbs as though they rained.

"And, in short, I mean to say, and I do say, that if you do not want to come on favour with me and run the same luck as I run, God be with you and make a saint of you; for I shall not be short of squires who are more obedient, more attentive and not as awkward or as talkative as you."

When Sancho heard his master's firm resolution, the sky clouded over for him and the wings fell off his heart, because he had believed that his master would not go without him for all the wealth in the world. And so, while he was standing there in suspense and thoughtful, Sansón Carrasco came in with the niece, eager to hear with what arguments he would persuade his master not to go back to looking for adventures.

Sansón came up, that famous joker; and embracing him as he had the first time, he said to him in a raised voice:

"O flower of knight-errantry! O shining light of arms! O honour and mirror of the Spanish nation! May it please God Almighty, where it is more fully set down, that whatever person or persons put an obstacle in the way of and hinder your third sally may never find their way out of the labyrinth of their own desires, and may never have their wicked wishes fulfilled."

And turning to the housekeeper, he said:

"Mistress housekeeper may perfectly well leave off saying the prayer of St Apollonia; for I know that it is a settled decision of the spheres that Señor Don Quixote should go back to carrying out his lofty new intentions. And I should be greatly burdening my own conscience if I did not urge and persuade this knight not to keep the strength of his valorous arm and the goodness of his most valiant spirit any longer shrunk up and held back — because by his delay he is cheating the righting of wrongs, the protection of orphans, the honour of maidens, the support of widows and the prop of married women, along with other things of that stamp that touch, concern, depend on and belong to the order of knight-errantry.

"Come, my dear Señor Don Quixote, handsome and brave: let your worship and your greatness set out today rather than tomorrow; and if anything is lacking for putting it into effect, here am I to supply it with my person and my property. And if it should be necessary to serve your magnificence as a squire, I shall count it the greatest good fortune!"

At this Don Quixote said, turning to Sancho:

"Did I not tell you, Sancho, that I should have squires to spare? See who offers himself to be one: none other than the unheard-of bachelor Sansón Carrasco, perpetual jester and merrymaker of the courtyards of the Salamanca schools, sound in his person, agile in his limbs, silent, an endurer of heat as well as of cold, of hunger as well as of thirst, with all those qualities that are required for being a knight errant's squire.

"But heaven forbid that, to follow my own pleasure, I should hamstring and break the pillar of letters and the vessel of the sciences, and cut down the eminent palm of the good and liberal arts. Let the new Samson stay in his own country and, honouring it, honour along with it the grey hairs of his aged parents; for I shall be content with any squire at all, since Sancho does not deign to come with me."

"I do deign," answered Sancho, softened and with his eyes full of tears; and he went on: "It shall not be said of me, my dear sir, 'the bread eaten and the company broken up.' No, I do not come of any ungrateful stock; for the whole world knows, and especially my village, who the Panzas were that I descend from. And what is more, I have recognised and fathomed by many good deeds, and by more good words, the wish your worship has to do me favours.

"And if I have got into reckonings of so much more and so much less about my wages, it has been to please my wife; who, when she takes it into her head to press for a thing, there is no mallet that tightens the hoops of a cask as hard as she presses for what she wants to be done. But in the end a man must be a man and a woman a woman; and since I am a man wherever I am, which I cannot deny, I mean to be one in my own house too, whoever it may displease.

"And so there is nothing more to do but for your worship to draw up your will with its codicil, in such a way that it cannot be revolted, and let us set off at once, so that Señor Sansón's soul may not suffer, since he says his conscience diktates him to persuade your worship to go out into the world a third time. And I offer myself afresh to serve your worship faithfully and loyally, as well as and better than all the squires who have served knights errant in past and present times."

The bachelor was astonished to hear Sancho Panza's manner and way of talking; for although he had read the first history of his master, he had never believed he was as amusing as they paint him there. But hearing him now say "a will and codicil that cannot be revolted", instead of "a will and codicil that cannot be revoked", he believed everything he had read about him, and confirmed him as one of the most solemn idiots of our times; and he said to himself that two such madmen as master and man had never been seen in the world.

Finally Don Quixote and Sancho embraced and stayed friends; and with the advice and approval of the great Carrasco, who was for the time being their oracle, it was arranged that their departure should be three days from then, in which time there would be room to get ready what was needed for the journey and to look for a close helmet, which Don Quixote said he must in any case take with him. Sansón offered him one, because he knew a friend of his who had one would not refuse it him — although it was darker with rust and mould than it was bright and clean with polished steel.
