The curses the two women, housekeeper and niece, hurled at the bachelor were beyond counting: they tore their hair, they scratched their faces, and in the manner of the hired mourners of those days they lamented the departure as though it were their master's death. The design Sansón had in persuading him to go out again was to do what the history relates further on, all on the advice of the curate and the barber, with whom he had discussed it beforehand.

In short, in those three days Don Quixote and Sancho provided themselves with what they thought suited them; and Sancho having pacified his wife and Don Quixote his niece and his housekeeper, at nightfall, without anybody's seeing them except the bachelor, who wanted to go half a league out of the village with them, they set out on the road to El Toboso: Don Quixote on his good Rocinante and Sancho on his old grey, his saddlebags provided with things belonging to the commissariat and his purse with money that Don Quixote gave him for whatever might come up.

Sansón embraced him and begged him to send him news of his good or bad luck, so as to be glad at the one or sorry at the other, as the laws of their friendship required. Don Quixote promised it him, Sansón turned back to his village, and the two of them took the road to the great city of El Toboso.

Chapter 8: Which Relates What Happened to Don Quixote on His Way to See His Lady Dulcinea of El Toboso

"Blessed be the mighty Allah!" says Hamete Benengeli at the beginning of this eighth chapter. "Blessed be Allah!" he repeats three times; and he says that he gives these blessings because he sees that he now has Don Quixote and Sancho out in the field, and that the readers of his agreeable history may reckon that from this point Don Quixote's exploits and pleasantries and his squire's begin.

He urges them to forget the ingenious gentleman's past chivalries and set their eyes on the ones that are to come, which now begin on the road to El Toboso as the others began on the plains of Montiel; and it is not much that he asks for so much as he promises. And so he goes on, saying:

Don Quixote and Sancho were left alone; and Sansón had hardly gone off when Rocinante began to neigh and the grey to sigh, which was taken by both of them, knight and squire, for a good sign and a most fortunate omen — although, if the truth is to be told, the grey's sighs and brayings were more numerous than the hack's neighing, from which Sancho gathered that his own fortune was bound to overtop his master's and set itself above it. He founded this on I do not know what judicial astrology he happened to know, although the history does not explain it; they only heard him say that when he stumbled or fell he was glad he had not come out of the house, because from stumbling or falling nothing came but a torn shoe or broken ribs. And, fool though he was, he was not very far off the road in this.

Don Quixote said to him:

"Friend Sancho, night is coming down on us fast, and with more darkness than we needed to be able to see El Toboso by daylight — where I have decided to go before I put myself into any other adventure; and there I shall receive the blessing and the kind leave of the peerless Dulcinea, with which leave I expect and hold it certain that I shall finish and bring to a happy end every dangerous adventure. Because nothing in this life makes knights errant braver than seeing themselves favoured by their ladies."

"So I believe," answered Sancho; "but I think it will be difficult for your worship to speak to her or be with her in any place, at least, where you can receive her blessing — unless she throws it down to you from the wall of the yard, which is where I saw her the first time, when I took her the letter with the news of the follies and mad things your worship was doing in the heart of the Sierra Morena."

"Was it the wall of a yard that you took that for, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "where or through which you saw that never sufficiently praised gentility and beauty? It cannot have been anything but the galleries or corridors, or the arcades, or whatever they call them, of rich and royal palaces."

"It might all have been so," answered Sancho, "but it looked like a wall to me — unless I am short of memory."

"For all that, let us go there, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "for so long as I see her, it makes no difference to me whether it is over a wall or through windows, or through chinks or garden railings; for any ray from the sun of her beauty that reaches my eyes will light my understanding and strengthen my heart, so that I shall be left unique and unequalled in good sense and in courage."

"Well, truly, sir," answered Sancho, "when I saw that sun of the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, it was not so bright that it could throw off any rays at all; and it must have been that, as her worship was winnowing that wheat I mentioned, the great deal of dust she was raising settled like a cloud in front of her face and darkened it."

"Do you still persist, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "in saying, in thinking, in believing and in insisting that my lady Dulcinea was winnowing wheat — when that is a task and an occupation far removed from everything that people of standing do and ought to do, who are set up and kept for other occupations and pastimes that show their standing from a crossbow shot away?

"How badly you remember, Sancho, those verses of our poet where he paints for us the work those four nymphs were doing in their dwellings of crystal, who put their heads out of the beloved Tagus and sat down in the green meadow to work those rich webs the ingenious poet describes to us there, which were all of gold and silk and pearls woven and worked in together. And in this way my lady's work must have been when you saw her; except that the envy some wicked enchanter must have for my affairs changes and turns everything that is to give me pleasure into shapes different from their own.

"And so I am afraid that in that history of my exploits they say is going about in print, if by any chance its author has been some sage who is an enemy of mine, he will have put one thing for another, mixing a thousand lies with one truth and amusing himself with telling other actions outside what the continuity of a true history requires. Oh envy, root of endless evils and canker of the virtues! All the other vices, Sancho, bring a certain something of pleasure with them, but envy brings nothing but disgusts, bitternesses and rages."

"That is what I say too," answered Sancho; "and I think that in that book or history the bachelor Carrasco told us he had seen about us, my honour must be going about dragged this way and that, all over the place, sweeping the streets. Well, on the word of a good man, I have never spoken ill of any enchanter, nor have I so many good things that I could be envied.

"It is quite true that I am somewhat malicious and that I have my certain hints of a rogue about me; but it is all covered and hidden by the great cloak of my simplicity, which is always natural and never contrived. And even if I had nothing else but believing, as I always do believe, firmly and truly in God and in everything the Holy Roman Catholic Church holds and believes, and being, as I am, a mortal enemy of the Jews, the historians ought to have mercy on me and treat me well in their writings. But let them say what they like; for naked I was born and naked I find myself: I neither lose nor gain. Though, seeing myself put into books and going about the world from hand to hand, I do not care a fig what they say about me."

"That seems to me, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "like what happened to a famous poet of these times, who, having written a malicious satire against all the ladies of the court, did not put in or name one lady about whom it might be doubted whether she was one or not. And she, seeing that she was not on the list with the rest, complained to the poet, asking him what he had seen in her that he had not put her in the number of the others, and telling him to lengthen the satire and put her in the enlargement — and if not, to look out for what he was born for. The poet did it, and put her in in terms not fit for duennas to repeat; and she was satisfied at finding herself with a reputation, even an infamous one.

"With this too goes what they tell of that shepherd who set fire to and burnt down the famous temple of Diana, counted one of the seven wonders of the world, only so that his name should stay alive in the ages to come. And although it was ordered that nobody should name him or make mention of his name by word or in writing, so that he should not achieve the end of his desire, still it came to be known that his name was Herostratus.

"To this also belongs what happened to the great Emperor Charles the Fifth with a gentleman in Rome. The emperor wanted to see that famous temple of the Rotunda, which in ancient times was called the temple of all the gods and now, with a better dedication, is called the temple of all the saints; and it is the building that has been left most entire of those the heathen raised in Rome, and the one that best preserves the fame of the grandeur and magnificence of its founders. It is made in the shape of half an orange, enormously great, and is very light, with no other light coming into it than what is allowed by one window — or rather a round skylight — that stands at its top.

"And the emperor was looking at the building from there, and with him and at his side was a Roman gentleman, explaining to him the beauties and subtleties of that great machine and memorable architecture. And when they had come away from the skylight, he said to the emperor: 'A thousand times, Sacred Majesty, the wish came to me to take hold of your Majesty and throw myself down from that skylight, so as to leave an eternal fame of myself in the world.'

"'I thank you,' answered the emperor, 'for not having put so wicked a thought into effect; and from now on I shall not put you in the way of testing your loyalty again. And so I order you never to speak to me, or to be anywhere where I am.' And after these words he did him a great favour.

"I mean, Sancho, that the desire to attain fame is extremely active. Who do you suppose it was that threw Horatius down from the bridge, armed at all points, into the depths of the Tiber? Who burnt Mucius's arm and hand? Who drove Curtius to hurl himself into the deep burning chasm that opened in the middle of Rome? Who, against all the omens that had been shown against it, made Caesar cross the Rubicon? And, with more modern examples, who scuttled the ships and left high and dry and cut off the valorous Spaniards led by that most courteous Cortés in the New World?

"All these and other great and various exploits are, were and shall be the works of fame, which mortals desire as rewards and as part of the immortality their famous deeds deserve — although we Christians, Catholics and knights errant must attend more to the glory of the ages to come, which is everlasting in the ethereal and heavenly regions, than to the vanity of the fame that is won in this present and perishable age; which fame, however long it lasts, must in the end come to an end with the world itself, which has its own appointed end.

"So, Sancho, our works must not go outside the limit the Christian religion we profess has set for us. We have to kill pride in the giants; envy, by generosity and a good heart; anger, by a calm bearing and quietness of mind; gluttony and sleep, by the little we eat and the long watches we keep; lust and lasciviousness, by the loyalty we keep to those we have made the ladies of our thoughts; sloth, by going about all the parts of the world looking for the occasions that may make us, and do make us, famous knights as well as Christians. See here, Sancho, the means by which are reached the highest praises that a good name brings with it."

"Everything your worship has told me up to now," said Sancho, "I have understood very well; but for all that, I should like your worship to absorb me a doubt that has just come into my memory at this moment."

"Absolve, you mean, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Say on and welcome, and I shall answer what I know."

"Tell me, sir," Sancho went on: "those Julys or Augusts, and all those valiant knights you have mentioned, who are dead by now — where are they now?"

"The heathen," answered Don Quixote, "are without doubt in hell; the Christians, if they were good Christians, are either in purgatory or in heaven."

"Very good," said Sancho; "but let us know now: those graves where the bodies of those great gentlemen lie — have they silver lamps in front of them, or are the walls of their chapels hung with crutches, with shrouds, with wigs, with legs and eyes of wax? And if not with that, what are they hung with?"

To which Don Quixote answered:

"The tombs of the heathen were for the most part sumptuous temples: the ashes of Julius Caesar's body were set on a stone pyramid of outrageous size, which today in Rome they call St Peter's Needle. The emperor Hadrian had for his tomb a castle as big as a good-sized village, which they called Moles Hadriani, and which is now the castle of Sant' Angelo in Rome. Queen Artemisia buried her husband Mausolus in a tomb that was held to be one of the seven wonders of the world. But none of these tombs, nor many others the heathen had, was hung with shrouds or with other offerings and signs that showed those buried in them to be saints."

"That is what I am coming to," replied Sancho. "And tell me now: which is more — to raise a dead man, or to kill a giant?"

"The answer is at hand," answered Don Quixote: "raising a dead man is more."

"I have you now," said Sancho. "Then the fame of the man who raises the dead, gives sight to the blind, straightens the lame and gives health to the sick — and in front of whose tombs lamps burn, and whose chapels are full of devout people who kneel and worship his relics — will be a better fame, for this world and for the next, than the fame all the heathen emperors and knights errant there have ever been in the world left or ever shall leave."

"I confess that truth too," answered Don Quixote.

"Well, this fame, these graces, these prerogatives — as they call this," answered Sancho, "belong to the bodies and the relics of the saints, who, with the approval and licence of our holy mother the Church, have lamps, candles, shrouds, crutches, paintings, wigs, eyes and legs, by which they increase devotion and enlarge their Christian fame. Kings carry the bodies of the saints, or their relics, on their own shoulders; they kiss the pieces of their bones; they adorn and enrich their oratories and their most treasured altars with them —"

"What do you want me to infer, Sancho, from all you have said?" said Don Quixote.

"I mean," said Sancho, "that we should set about being saints, and we shall get the good fame we are after a great deal sooner. And note, sir, that yesterday or the day before — for one may put it that way, it is so short a time ago — they canonised or beatified two little barefoot friars, whose iron chains that they used to gird and torment their bodies with people now count it a great piece of luck to kiss and touch; and they are held in more veneration than, as I said, Roland's sword in the armoury of the king our lord, whom God keep.

"So, my dear sir, it is better to be a humble little friar of whatever order it may be than a valiant knight errant; two dozen scourgings do more with God than two thousand lance-thrusts, whether they give them to giants or to monsters or to drakins."

"All that is so," answered Don Quixote, "but we cannot all be friars, and many are the roads by which God takes his own to heaven: chivalry is a religion, and there are knights who are saints in glory."

"Yes," answered Sancho, "but I have heard it said that there are more friars in heaven than knights errant."

"That is," answered Don Quixote, "because the number of religious is greater than that of knights."

"There are many knights errant," said Sancho.

"Many," answered Don Quixote, "but few who deserve the name of knights."

In these and other such talk that night and the following day went by for them, without anything happening to them worth telling, which grieved Don Quixote not a little.

At last, the next day at nightfall, they made out the great city of El Toboso, at whose sight Don Quixote's spirits were gladdened and Sancho's saddened — because he did not know Dulcinea's house, nor had he ever in his life seen her, any more than his master had seen her. So that the one because he wanted to see her, and the other because he had never seen her, were both agitated; and Sancho could not imagine what he was to do when his master sent him to El Toboso.

Finally Don Quixote arranged to go into the city after nightfall; and while the hour was coming on they stayed among some oak trees that stood near El Toboso. And when the appointed moment came they went into the city, where things happened to them that come to something indeed.

Chapter 9: Which Relates What Will Be Seen There

It was exactly midnight, more or less, when Don Quixote and Sancho left the hill and went into El Toboso. The town was in a peaceful silence, because all its inhabitants were asleep and resting with their legs stretched out, as they say. The night was half clear, although Sancho would have liked it to be altogether dark, so as to find in its darkness an excuse for his own foolishness.

Nothing was to be heard in the whole place but the barking of dogs, which thundered in Don Quixote's ears and troubled Sancho's heart. From time to time a donkey brayed, pigs grunted, cats miaowed; and these voices of different sounds were made louder by the silence of the night — all of which the enamoured knight took for a bad omen. But for all that, he said to Sancho:

"Sancho my son, lead the way to Dulcinea's palace: it might be that we shall find her awake."

"To what palace am I to lead the way, body of the sun," answered Sancho, "when the one I saw her greatness in was nothing but a very small house?"

"She must have withdrawn at the time," answered Don Quixote, "into some small apartment of her castle, taking her pleasure alone with her maidens, as is the use and custom of great ladies and princesses."

"Sir," said Sancho, "since your worship insists, in spite of me, that my lady Dulcinea's house is a castle, is this by any chance an hour to find the door open? And will it be right for us to give great knocks so that they may hear us and open to us, throwing all the people into an uproar and a commotion? Are we by any chance going to knock at the door of our kept women, as men do who keep mistresses, who come and knock and go in at whatever hour it may be, however late?"

"Let us first of all find the castle once and for all," replied Don Quixote, "and then I shall tell you, Sancho, what it will be well for us to do. And note, Sancho, that either I see badly or that great bulk and shadow that shows from here must be Dulcinea's palace."

"Then let your worship lead the way," answered Sancho: "perhaps it is so — although I shall see it with my eyes and touch it with my hands, and then I shall believe it as much as I believe it is now daylight."

Don Quixote led the way; and having gone about two hundred paces, he came upon the bulk that was casting the shadow, and saw a great tower, and then recognised that this building was no castle but the chief church of the town. And he said:

"We have come upon the church, Sancho."

"So I see," answered Sancho; "and please God we do not come upon our own graves, for it is no good sign to be going about among cemeteries at such hours — and the more so as I told your worship, if I remember rightly, that this lady's house must be up a little blind alley."

"God's curse on you, you idiot!" said Don Quixote. "Where have you found it laid down that castles and royal palaces are built up blind alleys?"

"Sir," answered Sancho, "every country has its own custom: perhaps here in El Toboso it is the custom to build palaces and great buildings up alleys. And so I beg your worship to let me look about these streets or alleys that offer themselves: it might be that in some corner I should come across this castle — and may I see it eaten by dogs, for it has us running about and worn out like this."

"Speak with respect, Sancho, of my lady's affairs," said Don Quixote; "and let us keep the peace and not throw the rope after the bucket."

"I shall restrain myself," answered Sancho; "but with what patience can I bear it that your worship should expect me, from one single time when I saw our mistress's house, to know it for ever and to find it at midnight — when your worship cannot find it, and must have seen it thousands of times?"

"You will drive me to despair, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Come here, you heretic: have I not told you a thousand times that in all the days of my life I have never seen the peerless Dulcinea, nor ever crossed the threshold of her palace, and that I am in love only by hearsay and by the great reputation she has for beauty and good sense?"

"Now I hear it," answered Sancho; "and I say that since your worship has never seen her, neither have I —"

"That cannot be," replied Don Quixote; "for at the very least you have told me yourself that you saw her winnowing wheat, when you brought me the answer to the letter I sent her by you."

"Do not go by that, sir," answered Sancho, "for I would have you know that the sight of her and the answer I brought you were by hearsay too; because I know who the lady Dulcinea is about as well as I could hit the sky with my fist."

"Sancho, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "there are times for joking and times when jokes fall flat and look bad. Just because I say that I have neither seen nor spoken to the lady of my soul, you are not to say too that you have neither spoken to her nor seen her, when it is quite the other way about, as you know."

While the two of them were in this conversation, they saw a man coming past where they were with two mules; and from the noise the plough made as it dragged along the ground they judged he must be a labourer who had got up before daylight to go to his ploughing — and so it turned out. The labourer came along singing that ballad that goes:

	It went ill with you, Frenchmen,
	in that hunt at Roncesvalles.

"May they kill me, Sancho," said Don Quixote on hearing it, "if anything good is going to happen to us tonight. Do you not hear what that countryman is singing?"

"I do hear it," answered Sancho; "but what has the hunt at Roncesvalles to do with our business? He might just as well have been singing the ballad of Calaínos, for all the difference it would make to whether things go well or badly for us in our affair."

At this the labourer came up, and Don Quixote asked him:

"Could you tell me, my good friend — and may God give you good fortune — whereabouts here are the palaces of the peerless princess Doña Dulcinea of El Toboso?"

"Sir," answered the lad, "I am a stranger here and have only been a few days in this town, working for a rich farmer at the field labour. In that house opposite live the curate and the sacristan of the place; either of them, or both, will be able to give your worship an account of this lady princess, because they have the list of all the inhabitants of El Toboso — although it is my belief that there is no princess at all living in the whole of it. A great many ladies of standing, yes; and each of them may be a princess in her own house."

"Then among those, my friend," said Don Quixote, "must be the one I am asking you about."

"That may be," answered the lad; "and goodbye, for the dawn is coming."

And whipping up his mules, he waited for no more questions.

Sancho, who saw his master in suspense and thoroughly discontented, said to him:

"Sir, the day is coming on fast, and it would not be sensible to let the sun find us in the street. It will be better for us to get outside the city, and for your worship to hide in some wood near here; and I shall come back by day, and shall not leave a nook in this whole place where I do not look for my lady's house, castle or palace — and I should be unlucky indeed if I did not find it. And when I have found it, I shall speak to her worship and tell her where and how your worship is left waiting for her to give you an arrangement and a plan for seeing her, without any damage to her honour and reputation."

"You have spoken, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "a thousand maxims shut up in the circle of a few words: the advice you have now given me I like and receive most willingly. Come, my son, and let us go and look for somewhere for me to hide; and you shall come back, as you say, to look for, to see and to speak to my lady, from whose good sense and courtesy I expect more than miraculous favours."

Sancho was frantic to get his master out of the town, so that he should not find out the lie about the answer he had taken him from Dulcinea in the Sierra Morena; and so he hurried their going, which took place at once. And two miles from the place they found a wood or grove, where Don Quixote hid himself while Sancho went back to the city to speak to Dulcinea — on which embassy things happened to him that call for fresh attention and fresh belief.

Chapter 10: Which Relates the Trick Sancho Used in Enchanting the Lady Dulcinea, and Other Events as Ridiculous as They Are True

On coming to relate what he relates in this chapter, the author of this great history says that he would have liked to pass it over in silence, for fear it would not be believed; because Don Quixote's mad acts here reached the limit and boundary of the greatest that can be imagined, and even went two crossbow shots beyond the greatest. Finally, although with this fear and misgiving, he wrote them exactly as Don Quixote did them, without adding to the history or taking from it one atom of the truth, and without caring at all about the objections that might be raised against him as a liar. And he was right, because truth may be worn thin but does not break, and always floats on top of lies as oil does on water.

And so, going on with his history, he says that as soon as Don Quixote had hidden himself in the grove, oak wood or forest beside the great El Toboso, he ordered Sancho to go back to the city, and not to come back into his presence without having first spoken to his lady on his behalf, begging her that she would be pleased to let herself be seen by her captive knight and would deign to give him her blessing, so that he might hope through it for the most fortunate outcomes to all his undertakings and difficult enterprises. Sancho undertook to do it exactly as he was ordered and to bring him back as good an answer as he had brought him the first time.

"Go, my son," replied Don Quixote, "and do not be alarmed when you find yourself before the light of the sun of beauty you are going to look for. Happy you, above all the squires in the world!

"Have your memory ready, and do not let it slip how she receives you: whether she changes colour while you are giving her my message; whether she becomes uneasy and agitated on hearing my name; whether she cannot keep still on her cushion, if you happen to find her seated on the rich dais of her authority. And if she is standing, watch whether she shifts now onto one foot and now onto the other; whether she repeats the answer she gives you two or three times; whether she changes it from mild to harsh, from sour to loving; whether she raises a hand to her hair to tidy it even when it is not untidy.

"In short, my son, watch all her actions and movements; because if you report them to me as they were, I shall work out what she has hidden in the secret of her heart about the matter of my love. For you must know, Sancho, if you do not know it, that among lovers the outward actions and movements they show, when their love affairs are in question, are the most certain couriers, bringing the news of what is going on inside the soul. Go, my friend, and may a better fortune than mine guide you, and may a better outcome bring you back than the one I am left fearing and hoping for in this bitter solitude where you leave me."

"I shall go and come back quickly," said Sancho; "and let your worship widen out that little heart of yours, my dear sir, for it must be no bigger than a hazelnut just now. And consider that they say a stout heart breaks bad luck, and that where there is no bacon there are no hooks; and they also say: the hare jumps up where nobody expects it. I say this because if we did not find my lady's palaces or castles last night, now that it is daylight I mean to find them when I least expect it — and once they are found, leave me alone with her."

"Truly, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "you always bring in your proverbs as much to the point of what we are discussing as God may give me better luck in what I want."

This said, Sancho turned his back and switched up his grey; and Don Quixote stayed on horseback, resting on his stirrups and on the support of his lance, full of sad and confused fancies. And there we shall leave him and go with Sancho Panza, who left his master no less confused and thoughtful than his master was left — so much so that he had hardly got out of the wood when, turning his head and seeing that Don Quixote was out of sight, he got down off the donkey and, sitting at the foot of a tree, began to talk to himself and to say:

"Now let us know, brother Sancho, where your worship is going. Are you going to look for some donkey that has got lost? 'Certainly not.' Then what are you going to look for? 'I am going to look for — as though it were nothing at all — a princess, and in her the sun of beauty and the whole sky put together.' And where do you expect to find this thing you speak of, Sancho? 'Where? In the great city of El Toboso.'

"Very well: and on whose behalf are you going to look for her? 'On behalf of the famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, who rights wrongs, and gives food to the man who is thirsty and drink to the man who is hungry.' All that is very well. And do you know her house, Sancho? 'My master says it must be royal palaces or splendid castles.' And have you by any chance ever seen it? 'Neither I nor my master have ever seen it.'

"And does it seem to you that it would be sensible and well done if the people of El Toboso, learning that you were here meaning to coax their princesses away and unsettle their ladies, were to come and pound your ribs with sticks and not leave a whole bone in you? 'Truly they would be quite right, unless they considered that I am under orders, and that "a messenger you are, my friend, no blame belongs to you, not you."'

"Do not rely on that, Sancho, because the people of La Mancha are as hot-tempered as they are honourable, and they will not stand being tickled by anybody. By the living God, if they get wind of you I promise you bad luck. 'Get away, you rogue! Strike somewhere else, lightning! No, indeed — am I to go looking for three feet on a cat for somebody else's pleasure? And what is more, looking for Dulcinea in El Toboso will be like looking for Marica in Ravenna, or for the bachelor in Salamanca. The devil, the devil has got me into this, and nobody else!'"

This soliloquy Sancho had with himself, and what he got out of it was that he went on to say to himself:

"Very well: everything has a remedy except death, under whose yoke we must all pass, however it displeases us, at the end of our lives. This master of mine, by a thousand signs, I have seen is a madman fit to be tied — and I am not far behind him either, since I am more of an idiot than he is, seeing that I follow him and serve him, if the proverb is true that says: 'Tell me who you go about with and I shall tell you who you are,' and the other one: 'Not who you are born with but who you graze with.'

"Well, he being mad as he is, and with a madness that most often takes one thing for another and judges white for black and black for white — as appeared when he said the windmills were giants, and the friars' mules dromedaries, and the flocks of sheep armies of enemies, and a great many other things in the same key — it will not be very difficult to make him believe that a country girl, the first I come across here, is the lady Dulcinea. And if he does not believe it, I shall swear to it; and if he swears, I shall swear back; and if he insists, I shall insist harder, in such a way that I shall always have my end of the plank on top, come what may.

"Perhaps with this insisting I shall get him to stop sending me on such errands again, seeing how badly I come back from them; or perhaps he will think, as I imagine, that some wicked enchanter of the ones he says wish him harm will have changed her shape so as to do him harm and injury."

With this thought Sancho Panza's spirit was calmed, and he counted his business well finished; and he stayed there until the afternoon, so as to give Don Quixote time to think he had taken it to go to El Toboso and back. And it all turned out so well for him that when he got up to mount the grey, he saw three country girls coming from El Toboso towards where he was, on three young asses — or she-asses, for the author does not state it, although it is more to be believed that they were she-asses, that being the usual mount of village women. But as not much depends on it, there is no need for us to stop and settle it.

In short: as soon as Sancho saw the country girls, he went off at a smart pace to look for his master Don Quixote, and found him sighing and making a thousand loving laments. As soon as Don Quixote saw him, he said:

"What is it, friend Sancho? Am I to mark this day with a white stone or a black one?"

"It will be better," answered Sancho, "for your worship to mark it with red ochre, like the notices on professors' chairs, so that people who see it may see it plainly."

"In that case," replied Don Quixote, "you bring good news."

"So good," answered Sancho, "that your worship has nothing more to do than to spur Rocinante and come out into the open to see the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, who with two other maidens of hers is coming to see your worship."

"Holy God! What is this you are saying, friend Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "Take care not to deceive me, and do not try with false joys to cheer my genuine sorrows."

"What should I get out of deceiving your worship," answered Sancho, "especially when you are so near discovering my truth? Spur on, sir, and come, and you will see our mistress the princess coming, dressed and adorned — in short, as befits who she is. Her maidens and she are all one blaze of gold, all clusters of pearls, all diamonds, all rubies, all cloth of brocade more than ten thicknesses deep; their hair loose over their shoulders, which are so many rays of the sun playing with the wind; and, above all, they come riding on three dappled canaanies, which are a thing to see."

"Hackneys you mean, Sancho."

"There is little difference," answered Sancho, "between canaanies and hackneys; but let them come on what they may, they come the most splendid ladies anybody could wish for — especially the princess Dulcinea, my lady, who stuns the senses."

"Let us go, Sancho my son," answered Don Quixote; "and as a reward for this news, as unexpected as it is good, I give you the best spoils I win in the first adventure I have. And if this does not satisfy you, I give you the foals my three mares are to give me this year, which as you know are out in the common meadow of our village waiting to foal."

"I shall stick to the foals," answered Sancho, "because it is not very certain that the spoils of the first adventure will be good ones."

By this time they came out of the wood and made out the three village women close by. Don Quixote ran his eyes all along the road to El Toboso, and as he saw nothing but the three country girls, he was thoroughly upset and asked Sancho whether he had left them outside the city.

"Outside the city?" he answered. "Has your worship got eyes in the back of your head, that you do not see that these women coming here are the ones, shining like the sun itself at midday?"

"I see nothing, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "but three country girls on three donkeys."

"Now God deliver me from the devil!" answered Sancho. "And is it possible that three hackneys — or whatever they are called — as white as driven snow should look like donkeys to your worship? By the living Lord, may they pull this beard off me if that were true!"

"Well, I tell you, friend Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that it is as true that they are donkeys, or she-donkeys, as that I am Don Quixote and you Sancho Panza — at least, they look so to me."

"Be quiet, sir," said Sancho; "do not say such a thing, but wipe those eyes of yours and come and pay your respects to the lady of your thoughts, who is coming close now."

And saying this, he went forward to receive the three village women; and getting down off the grey, he took the halter of one of the three country girls' donkeys, and, going down on both knees, said:

"Queen and princess and duchess of beauty, may your loftiness and greatness be pleased to receive into your favour and good graces your captive knight, who stands there turned to marble, thoroughly disturbed and pulseless at finding himself in your magnificent presence. I am Sancho Panza, his squire, and he is the much-harried knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, called by another name the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance."

By this time Don Quixote had gone down on his knees beside Sancho, and was looking with starting eyes and a troubled gaze at the woman Sancho was calling queen and lady. And as he could make out nothing in her but a village girl, and not one with a very good face — because she was round-faced and flat-nosed — he was taken aback and astonished, and did not dare to unstitch his lips.

The country women were likewise astonished at seeing those two men, so different from each other, kneeling down and not letting their companion go past. But the one who was being held up broke the silence, and, thoroughly graceless and cross, said:

"Get out of the way, bad luck to you, and let us pass; we are in a hurry."

To which Sancho answered:

"O princess and universal lady of El Toboso! How is it that your magnanimous heart is not softened at seeing kneeling before your exalted presence the pillar and support of knight-errantry?"

Hearing which, another of the two said:

"Whoa there, I'm currying you down, my father-in-law's donkey! Just look at these young gentlemen coming to make fun of village girls, as though we didn't know how to fling taunts as well as they do! Go your way, and let us go ours, and it will be healthier for you."

"Get up, Sancho," said Don Quixote at this point; "for I see now that Fortune, not satisfied with the harm she has done me, has taken possession of all the roads by which any contentment might come to this wretched soul I have in my flesh.

"And you, O highest worth that can be desired, limit of human gentility, sole remedy of this afflicted heart that adores you: now that the malignant enchanter persecutes me and has put clouds and cataracts on my eyes, and for them alone and for no others has changed and transformed your unequalled beauty and face into that of a poor country girl — if he has not also changed mine into that of some monster, so as to make it loathsome in your eyes — do not fail to look at me mildly and lovingly, seeing in this submission and kneeling that I make to your counterfeited beauty the humility with which my soul adores you."

"Take that, grandad!" answered the village girl. "I'm a fine one for listening to flatterations! Get out of the way and let us go, and we shall be grateful to you."

Sancho got out of the way and let her go, extremely pleased at having come well out of his entanglement.

The village girl who had played the part of Dulcinea had hardly found herself free when, spurring her canaany with a goad she carried on a stick, she set off at a run across the meadow. And as the she-ass felt the point of the goad, which hurt her more than usual, she began to buck, so that she brought the lady Dulcinea to the ground. Which Don Quixote seeing, he ran to lift her up, and Sancho to straighten and tighten the pack-saddle, which had also slipped under the donkey's belly.

The pack-saddle being settled, then, and Don Quixote wanting to lift his enchanted lady in his arms onto the she-ass, the lady got up off the ground and saved him the trouble; because, drawing back a little, she took a short run and, putting both hands on the she-ass's hindquarters, dropped her body, lighter than a falcon, onto the pack-saddle and sat astride like a man. And then Sancho said:

"By St Roque, our mistress is lighter than a hobby-hawk, and she could teach the most skilful Cordoban or Mexican rider how to mount short-stirruped! She cleared the back of the saddle in one jump, and without spurs she makes the hackney run like a zebra. And her maidens are not far behind her: they all run like the wind."

And it was the truth, because as soon as Dulcinea was on horseback they all whipped up after her and set off at a run, without turning their heads back for more than half a league. Don Quixote followed them with his eyes; and when he saw they were out of sight, he turned to Sancho and said:

"Sancho, what do you think — how much am I hated by enchanters? And see how far their malice goes and the grudge they have against me, since they have wanted to deprive me of the pleasure it would have given me to see my lady in her own being. In fact I was born to be an example of the unfortunate, and to be the target and the butt at which the arrows of bad fortune take aim and are levelled.

"And you must also note, Sancho, that these traitors were not content with having turned and transformed my Dulcinea, but they transformed and turned her into a shape as low and as ugly as that village girl's; and along with it they took from her what is so much a mark of great ladies, which is a good smell, since they go about always among ambergris and among flowers. Because I would have you know, Sancho, that when I came to help Dulcinea up onto her hackney — as you say it was, though it seemed a she-ass to me — she gave off a smell of raw garlic that turned my head and poisoned my soul."

"Oh, the rabble!" shouted Sancho at this. "Oh, you ill-starred and ill-meaning enchanters, and if only somebody could see the lot of you strung up by the gills like sardines on a string! You know a great deal, you can do a great deal and you do a great deal more.

"It should have been enough for you, you scoundrels, to have changed the pearls of my lady's eyes into cork-oak galls and her hair of the purest gold into the bristles of a red ox's tail, and, in short, all her features from good to bad, without touching her smell; for by that at least we might have made out what was hidden under that ugly rind — although, to tell the truth, I never saw her ugliness but her beauty, which was raised to a higher point and a higher carat by a mole she had over her right lip, in the manner of a moustache, with seven or eight fair hairs like threads of gold and more than a hand's breadth long."

"As for that mole," said Don Quixote, "considering the correspondence there is between the moles of the face and those of the body, Dulcinea must have another on the flat of the thigh on the side that corresponds to where she has the one on her face. But hairs of the size you have described are very long for moles."

"Well, I can tell your worship," answered Sancho, "that they looked as though they had been born there."

"I believe it, my friend," replied Don Quixote, "because nature put nothing in Dulcinea that was not perfect and well finished; and so, if she had a hundred moles like the one you speak of, in her they would not be moles but shining moons and stars. But tell me, Sancho: that thing that looked to me like a pack-saddle, which you were straightening — was it a plain saddle or a lady's saddle?"

"It was neither," answered Sancho, "but a short-stirruped saddle, with a field-covering worth half a kingdom, so rich is it."

"And that I should not have seen all that, Sancho!" said Don Quixote. "Now I say again, and I shall say it a thousand times, that I am the unluckiest of men."

That sly fellow Sancho had all he could do to hide his laughter, hearing the foolish things his master said, so delicately deceived. Finally, after many other things had passed between the two of them, they got back on their beasts and followed the road to Saragossa, where they expected to arrive in time to be present at some solemn festivals that are held every year in that distinguished city. But before they got there, things happened to them which, for being many, great and new, deserve to be written and read, as will be seen further on.

Chapter 11: Of the Strange Adventure That Befell the Valorous Don Quixote with the Cart or Wagon of the Parliament of Death

Don Quixote went along the road extremely thoughtful, considering the wicked trick the enchanters had played on him in turning his lady Dulcinea into the bad shape of the village girl, and he could not imagine what remedy he could find for turning her back into her first being. And these thoughts carried him so far out of himself that without noticing it he let go of Rocinante's reins; who, feeling the freedom he was given, stopped at every step to graze the green grass those fields were full of. Sancho Panza brought him back from his trance, saying to him:

"Sir, sorrows were not made for beasts but for men; but if men feel them too much they turn into beasts. Let your worship pull yourself together and come to yourself, and take up Rocinante's reins, and liven up and wake up, and show that gallantry that it is proper for knights errant to have. What the devil is this? What kind of collapse is this? Are we here, or in France? May Satan carry off all the Dulcineas there are in the world, for the health of one single knight errant is worth more than all the enchantments and transformations on earth."

"Be quiet, Sancho," answered Don Quixote in a voice that was not very faint; "be quiet, I say, and do not speak blasphemies against that enchanted lady, for I alone am to blame for her misfortune and ill luck: her bad fortune has been born of the envy the wicked have for me."

"That is what I say," answered Sancho: "whoever saw her then and sees her now — what heart would not weep?"

"You may well say that, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "since you saw her in the whole entirety of her beauty; for the enchantment did not go so far as to disturb your sight or to hide her beauty from you: it is against me alone and against my eyes that the force of its poison is aimed.

"But for all that, Sancho, I have noticed one thing, which is that you described her beauty badly to me; because, if I remember rightly, you said she had eyes like pearls, and eyes that look like pearls belong more to a sea-bream than to a lady. And to my belief Dulcinea's must be of green emeralds, wide-set, with two heavenly arches serving them as eyebrows. And take those pearls away from her eyes and move them to her teeth; for you certainly got it the wrong way about, Sancho, taking the eyes for the teeth."

"It might all be so," answered Sancho, "because her beauty confused me as much as her ugliness did your worship. But let us commend it all to God, who is the knower of the things that are to happen in this valley of tears, in this wicked world of ours, where hardly anything is to be found that is without a mixture of wickedness, trickery and knavery.

"One thing grieves me, my dear sir, more than others, and that is thinking what plan is to be adopted when your worship defeats some giant or some other knight and orders him to go and present himself before the beauty of the lady Dulcinea: where is this poor giant, or this poor wretched defeated knight, to find her? I fancy I can see them going about El Toboso like a lot of dummies looking for my lady Dulcinea; and even if they meet her in the middle of the street they will know her no better than they know my father."

"Perhaps, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "the enchantment will not go so far as to take away the recognition of Dulcinea from the defeated giants and knights I send to present themselves. And with one or two of the first I defeat and send to her we shall make the experiment of whether they see her or not, ordering them to come back and give me an account of what has happened to them about it."

"I say, sir," replied Sancho, "that what your worship has said seems good to me, and that by this device we shall come to know what we want to know. And if it is the case that she is hidden from your worship alone, the misfortune will be your worship's rather than hers. But so long as the lady Dulcinea has health and contentment, we shall manage here and get through it as best we can, looking for our adventures and leaving time to do its own work; for time is the best doctor for these and for greater illnesses."

Don Quixote was about to answer Sancho Panza, but he was prevented by a cart that came out across the road, loaded with the most various and strange characters and figures that could be imagined. The man who was driving the mules and serving as carter was an ugly devil. The cart came uncovered to the open sky, without any awning or hurdle.

The first figure that offered itself to Don Quixote's eyes was that of Death herself, with a human face; next to her came an angel with great painted wings; on one side there was an emperor with a crown, apparently of gold, on his head; at Death's feet was the god they call Cupid, without a bandage over his eyes but with his bow, quiver and arrows. There came too a knight armed at all points, except that he wore no morion or close helmet but a hat full of feathers of various colours; and with these came other people in different dress and with different faces.

All of which, seen suddenly, somewhat startled Don Quixote and put fear into Sancho's heart. But Don Quixote was soon delighted, believing that some new and dangerous adventure was offering itself; and with this thought, and with a mind prepared to face any danger, he placed himself in front of the cart and said in a loud, threatening voice:

"Carter, coachman, or devil, or whatever you are, do not delay in telling me who you are, where you are going and who the people are you are carrying in your wagon, which looks more like Charon's boat than the carts that are in use."

To which the Devil answered mildly, stopping the cart:

"Sir, we are players of Angulo the Bad's company. This morning, which is the octave of Corpus Christi, we performed in a village behind that hill the mystery play of The Parliament of Death, and we are to perform it this afternoon in that village you can see from here. And as it is so close, and to save ourselves the trouble of undressing and dressing again, we are travelling in the very clothes we perform in.

"That lad goes as Death; the other as the Angel; that woman, who is the manager's wife, goes as the Queen; the other as the Soldier; that one as the Emperor; and I as the Devil, and I am one of the chief figures in the play, because in this company I take the leading parts. If your worship wants to know anything else about us, ask me and I shall be able to answer you with complete exactness; for, being a devil, I know everything."

"On the faith of a knight errant," answered Don Quixote, "as soon as I saw this cart I imagined that some great adventure was offering itself to me; and now I say that one must touch appearances with the hand to give room for undeceiving. Go with God, good people, and put on your festival; and see whether you have any commands in which I can be of use to you, for I shall carry them out with a good will and a good heart, because from a boy I was fond of the mask, and in my youth my eyes ran after the strolling players."

While they were in this talk, luck willed that one of the company should come up who was dressed as a mummer, with a great many little bells, and who carried on the end of a stick three inflated cow-bladders. This clown, coming up to Don Quixote, began to fence with the stick and to beat the ground with the bladders and to take great leaps, ringing his bells; whose ugly appearance so startled Rocinante that, without Don Quixote's being able to hold him in, he took the bit between his teeth and set off running across the field with more lightness than the bones of his skeleton had ever promised.

Sancho, who considered the danger his master was in of being thrown, jumped off the grey and hurried at full speed to help him; but when he got to him he was already on the ground, and beside him Rocinante, who had come down with his master — the usual end and finish of Rocinante's high spirits and his boldness.

But Sancho had hardly left his own mount to go to Don Quixote when the dancing devil with the bladders jumped onto the grey and thumped him with them; and the fear and the noise, more than the pain of the blows, made him fly across the country towards the village where they were going to hold the festival.

Sancho watched his grey's flight and his master's fall, and did not know which of the two needs to attend to first. But in fact, as a good squire and a good servant, love for his master weighed more with him than fondness for his donkey — although every time he saw the bladders rise in the air and come down on his grey's hindquarters they were agonies and mortal frights to him, and he would sooner have had those blows given him on the apples of his eyes than on the smallest hair of his ass's tail.

In this perplexed distress he came to where Don Quixote was, a great deal more knocked about than he would have liked; and helping him up onto Rocinante, he said to him:

"Sir, the Devil has carried off the grey."

"What devil?" asked Don Quixote.

"The one with the bladders," answered Sancho.

"Then I shall get him back," replied Don Quixote, "even if he shuts himself up with him in the deepest and darkest dungeons of hell. Follow me, Sancho, for the cart goes slowly, and with its mules I shall make good the loss of the grey."

"There is no need to take that trouble, sir," answered Sancho. "Let your worship cool your anger, for by the look of it the Devil has left the grey already and is coming back to his home ground."

And so it was; because the Devil had come down with the grey, in imitation of Don Quixote and Rocinante, and had gone off to the village on foot, while the donkey came back to his master.

"For all that," said Don Quixote, "it will be as well to punish that devil's rudeness on one of the people in the cart, even if it is the emperor himself."

"Let your worship get that out of your head," replied Sancho, "and take my advice, which is never to meddle with players, for they are a favoured sort of people. I have seen a player in prison for two murders and come out free and without costs. Let your worship know that as they are cheerful people who give pleasure, everybody favours them, everybody protects them, helps them and thinks well of them — and the more so if they belong to one of the royal or licensed companies, all or most of whom, in their dress and get-up, look like princes."

"For all that," answered Don Quixote, "that play-acting devil shall not get away boasting, even if the whole human race favours him."

And saying this he turned back to the cart, which by now was close to the village. He went along shouting:

"Stop, wait, you merry and rejoicing crowd; for I want to give you to understand how the donkeys and beasts that serve as mounts for the squires of knights errant are to be treated."

So loud were Don Quixote's shouts that the people in the cart heard and understood them; and judging by his words the intention of the man who was saying them, in an instant Death jumped down out of the cart, and after her the Emperor, the Devil-carter and the Angel — nor did the Queen or the god Cupid stay behind. And they all loaded themselves with stones and drew up in a line, waiting to receive Don Quixote on the points of their pebbles.

Don Quixote, seeing them drawn up in so gallant a squadron with their arms raised in the attitude of letting fly their stones with force, reined in Rocinante and set himself to think in what way he could attack them with least danger to his person. While he was pausing, Sancho came up; and seeing him in the posture of attacking that well-formed squadron, said to him:

"It would be plain madness to attempt such an enterprise. Consider, my dear sir, that against brook-soup and hold-your-hat there is no defensive armour in the world, unless it is to stuff yourself and shut yourself into a bronze bell.

"And it must also be considered that it is more rashness than courage for one man alone to attack an army where Death is, and where emperors fight in person, and which is helped by the good angels and the bad. And if this consideration does not move you to keep still, let it move you to know for certain that among all those people standing there, although they look like kings, princes and emperors, there is not one knight errant."

"Now indeed," said Don Quixote, "you have hit, Sancho, on the point that can and ought to change me from my settled intention. I neither can nor ought to draw my sword, as I have told you many other times, against anybody who is not a dubbed knight. It is for you, Sancho, if you want to take vengeance for the injury done to your grey; and I shall help you from here with shouts and salutary advice."

"There is no need, sir," answered Sancho, "to take vengeance on anybody, since it is not the part of good Christians to take it for injuries. What is more, I shall settle it with my ass to put his grievance in the hands of my will, which is to live peacefully the days heaven may give me of life."

"Since that is your decision," replied Don Quixote, "good Sancho, judicious Sancho, Christian Sancho and sincere Sancho, let us leave these phantoms and go back to looking for better and more distinguished adventures; for I see this country is of a sort where there cannot fail to be many, and very miraculous ones."

He turned his reins at once, Sancho went to get his grey, Death with her whole flying squadron went back to their cart and went on with their journey; and this was the happy end of the fearful adventure of the Cart of Death, thanks be given to the salutary advice Sancho Panza gave his master — to whom, the next day, another adventure happened with a lovesick knight errant, of no less suspense than the last.

Chapter 12: Of the Strange Adventure That Befell the Valiant Don Quixote with the Brave Knight of the Mirrors

Don Quixote and his squire spent the night that followed the day of their encounter with Death under some tall, shady trees, Don Quixote having eaten, at Sancho's urging, some of what was carried in the grey's store. And in the middle of supper Sancho said to his master:

"Sir, what a fool I should have looked if I had chosen as my reward the spoils of the first adventure your worship finished, instead of the foals of the three mares! In fact, in fact, a bird in the hand is worth more than a vulture on the wing."

"All the same," answered Don Quixote, "if you, Sancho, had let me attack as I wanted, there would have fallen to you as spoils at the very least the Empress's gold crown and Cupid's painted wings; for I would have pulled them off against the grain and put them into your hands."

"The sceptres and crowns of play-acting emperors," answered Sancho Panza, "were never of pure gold but of tinsel or tinplate."

"That is true," replied Don Quixote, "because it would not be right that the trappings of a play should be genuine rather than pretended and merely apparent, as the play itself is — with which I want you to be on good terms, Sancho, keeping it in your favour, and by the same token those who act plays and those who compose them, because they are all instruments of doing a great good to the state, holding a mirror up before us at every step in which the actions of human life are seen to the life. And there is no comparison that shows us more to the life what we are and what we must be than plays and players.

"If not, tell me: have you never seen a play acted where kings, emperors and pontiffs are brought in, and knights and ladies and various other characters? One plays the ruffian, another the trickster, this one the merchant, that one the soldier, another the wise fool, another the foolish lover; and when the play is over and they take off the clothes belonging to it, all the players are left equal."

"Yes, I have seen it," answered Sancho.

"Well, the same thing," said Don Quixote, "happens in the comedy and business of this world, where some play emperors, others pontiffs, and, in short, all the characters that can be brought into a play; but on coming to the end, which is when life is over, death takes off them all the clothes that made them different, and they are left equal in the grave."

"A brave comparison!" said Sancho, "although not so new that I have not heard it many and various times — like the one about the game of chess, where, while the game lasts, each piece has its own particular office; and when the game is over they are all mixed and put together and shuffled, and thrown into a bag, which is like throwing a life into the grave."

"Every day, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "you are becoming less simple and more judicious."

"Yes, some of your worship's good sense is bound to rub off on me," answered Sancho; "for lands that are barren and dry in themselves come to give good fruit when they are manured and cultivated. I mean that your worship's conversation has been the manure that has fallen on the barren land of my dry wits, and the cultivating has been the time I have served you and dealt with you; and with this I hope to give fruits of myself that shall be a blessing, such that they will not fall away or slip from the paths of the good breeding your worship has worked into my parched understanding."

Don Quixote laughed at Sancho's affected speech, and it seemed to him that what he said about his improvement was true; because from time to time he talked in a way that astonished him — although all or most of the times Sancho tried to talk in the formal, courtly manner he ended his speech by hurling himself down from the mountain of his simplicity into the depths of his ignorance. And where he showed himself most elegant and most retentive was in bringing in proverbs, whether or not they came to the point of what he was discussing, as will have been seen and noticed in the course of this history.

In this and other talk a great part of the night went by for them, and Sancho took it into his head to let the floodgates of his eyes fall, as he used to put it when he wanted to sleep; and, unharnessing the grey, he gave him plentiful and free pasture. He did not take the saddle off Rocinante, because it was his master's express command that during the time they were in the field, or were not sleeping under a roof, he should not unharness Rocinante: an ancient usage established and kept by knights errant, to take the bridle off and hang it from the saddlebow — but take the saddle off the horse? Look out for that!

And so Sancho did it, and gave him the same freedom as the grey; whose friendship with Rocinante was so unique and so close that there is a report, by tradition from fathers to sons, that the author of this true history wrote particular chapters about it, but that, to keep the decency and decorum owing to so heroic a history, he did not put them into it — although sometimes he forgets this resolution of his and writes that as soon as the two beasts came together they set to scratching each other; and that afterwards, tired and satisfied, Rocinante would lay his neck across the grey's — with more than half a yard of it left over on the other side — and the two of them, looking attentively at the ground, would generally stay like that for three days, or at least all the time they were left alone and hunger did not compel them to look for food.

I say that they say the author left it written that he had compared them in friendship to the friendship of Nisus and Euryalus, and of Pylades and Orestes; and if this is so, one may see, to universal astonishment, how firm the friendship of these two peaceable animals must have been — and to the confusion of men, who know so badly how to keep friendship with one another. For this reason it was said:

	There is no friend for a friend:
	the reeds turn into lances;

and by the other man who sang:

	Between friend and friend, the bug — and so on.

And let nobody think the author went somewhat off the road in having compared the friendship of these animals to that of men; for men have received many hints from beasts and learnt many important things from them — such as, from the storks, the clyster; from dogs, vomiting and gratitude; from cranes, watchfulness; from ants, foresight; from elephants, modesty; and from the horse, loyalty.

Finally Sancho fell asleep at the foot of a cork tree, and Don Quixote dozed at the foot of a sturdy oak. But a very short space of time had gone by when he was woken by a noise he heard behind him; and getting up with a start, he set himself to look and listen for where the noise was coming from, and saw that it was two men on horseback, and that one of them, letting himself drop out of the saddle, said to the other:

"Get down, my friend, and take the bridles off the horses; for to my mind this place is well provided with grass for them, and with the silence and solitude my loving thoughts need."

To say this and to stretch himself out on the ground were all one moment; and as he threw himself down, the armour he was wearing rang, a plain sign by which Don Quixote knew he must be a knight errant. And going up to Sancho, who was asleep, he took him by the arm, and with no small trouble brought him round to his senses, and said to him in a low voice:

"Brother Sancho, we have an adventure."

"God send us a good one," answered Sancho; "and where is her worship this lady adventure, my dear sir?"

"Where, Sancho?" replied Don Quixote. "Turn your eyes and look, and you will see stretched out there a knight errant who, as far as I can make out, cannot be excessively cheerful; because I saw him throw himself off his horse and stretch out on the ground with certain signs of vexation, and as he fell his armour rang."

"Then how does your worship find," said Sancho, "that this is an adventure?"

"I do not mean to say," answered Don Quixote, "that this is a whole adventure, but the beginning of one; for this is how adventures begin. But listen; for by the sound of it he is tuning a lute or a guitar, and, judging by the way he spits and clears his chest, he must be getting ready to sing something."

"Upon my word it is so," answered Sancho, "and he must be a knight in love."

"There is not one of the knights errant who is not," said Don Quixote. "And let us listen to him, for by the thread we shall get at the ball of his thoughts, if he does sing; because out of the abundance of the heart the tongue speaks."

Sancho was about to answer his master, but he was prevented by the voice of the Knight of the Wood, which was neither very bad nor very good. And while the two of them stood astonished, they heard that what he sang was this sonnet:

	Give me, my lady, some rule that I may follow,
	cut to the pattern of your own will;
	for it will be so valued by mine
	that I shall never depart a point from it.
	If it is your pleasure that I should die
	keeping my suffering silent, count me finished already;
	if you want me to tell it you in some unusual
	way, I shall make love himself tell it.
	I am made proof against opposites,
	of soft wax and of hard diamond,
	and I fit my soul to the laws of love.
	Soft as it is, or strong, I offer you my breast:
	carve on it or stamp on it whatever pleases you,
	for I swear to keep it there for ever.

With an "Ah!" that seemed to be torn from the depths of his heart, the Knight of the Wood made an end of his song; and a little later, in a sorrowful, grieving voice, he said:

"O most beautiful and most ungrateful woman in the world! How can it be possible, most serene Casildea de Vandalia, that you should allow this captive knight of yours to wear himself out and finish in continual wanderings and in rough, hard labours? Is it not enough by now that I have made all the knights of Navarre, all those of León, all those of Tartessus, all the Castilians and, in short, all the knights of La Mancha confess you to be the most beautiful woman in the world?"

"Not that," said Don Quixote at this point; "for I am of La Mancha and I have never confessed any such thing, nor could I nor ought I to confess a thing so damaging to my lady's beauty. And you see for yourself, Sancho, that this knight is raving. But let us listen: perhaps he will explain himself further."

"He will, indeed," replied Sancho; "for he looks like going on complaining for a month at a stretch."

But it was not so, because the Knight of the Wood, having half heard that there were people talking near him, without going any further with his lament, got to his feet and said in a sonorous, well-bred voice:

"Who goes there? What sort of people? Are you by any chance of the number of the contented, or of the afflicted?"

"Of the afflicted," answered Don Quixote.

"Then come to me," answered the Knight of the Wood, "and you may reckon that you are coming to sadness itself and to affliction itself."

Don Quixote, finding himself answered so tenderly and so courteously, went up to him, and Sancho neither more nor less.

The lamenting knight took Don Quixote by the arm, saying:

"Sit down here, sir knight; for to understand that you are one, and one of those who profess knight-errantry, it is enough for me to have found you in this place, where solitude and the night air keep you company — the natural beds and proper dwellings of knights errant."

To which Don Quixote answered:

"A knight I am, and of the profession you name; and although sadnesses, misfortunes and disasters have their own seat in my soul, that has not driven out of it the compassion I feel for other men's troubles. From what you were saying a little while ago I gathered that yours are the troubles of love — I mean of the love you bear that beautiful ingrate you named in your laments."

By the time this was going on they were seated together on the hard ground, in good peace and fellowship, as though at daybreak they were not going to break each other's heads.

"By any chance, sir knight," the Knight of the Wood asked Don Quixote, "are you in love?"

"By misfortune I am," answered Don Quixote; "although the harms that are born of well-placed affections ought to be counted graces rather than misfortunes."

"That is true," replied the Knight of the Wood, "if disdains did not disturb our reason and our understanding — disdains which, when they are many, look like acts of revenge."

"I have never been disdained by my lady," answered Don Quixote.

"Certainly not," said Sancho, who was standing right there; "because my lady is like a tame ewe: she is softer than butter."

"Is this your squire?" asked the Knight of the Wood.

"He is," answered Don Quixote.

"I have never seen a squire," replied the Knight of the Wood, "who dares to speak where his master is speaking. At least there is that one of mine, who is as big as his father, and it will not be proved that he has ever unstitched his lips where I am talking."

"Well, upon my word," said Sancho, "I have talked and I can talk in front of somebody as — but let it stay there, for stirring it only makes it worse."

The Knight of the Wood's squire took Sancho by the arm, saying to him:

"Let the two of us go off where we can talk squire-fashion as much as we like, and leave these gentlemen our masters to lock horns telling each other the histories of their loves; for it is a safe bet that daylight will catch them at it and they will not have finished."

"So be it and welcome," said Sancho; "and I shall tell your worship who I am, so that you may see whether I can be counted in the dozen of the most talkative squires."

With this the two squires drew off, and there passed between them a conversation as amusing as the one that passed between their masters was grave.

Chapter 13: In Which the Adventure of the Knight of the Wood Is Continued, with the Judicious, New and Agreeable Conversation That Passed Between the Two Squires

Knights and squires were divided, the latter telling each other their lives and the former their loves; but the history relates first the conversation of the men and then goes on with that of the masters. And so it says that, drawing off a little from them, the Knight of the Wood's squire said to Sancho:

"It is a laborious life we lead and live, my dear sir, we who are squires to knights errant: truly we eat our bread in the sweat of our faces, which is one of the curses God laid on our first parents."

"One might also say," added Sancho, "that we eat it in the frost of our bodies; for who has more heat and more cold than the wretched squires of knight-errantry? And it would be less bad if we did eat, since with bread sorrows are less; but sometimes a day or two goes by without our breakfasting on anything but the wind that blows."

"All this can be borne and put up with," said the Knight of the Wood's squire, "for the hope we have of the reward; because unless the knight errant a squire serves is excessively unlucky, at the very least after a few passes he will find himself rewarded with a handsome government of some isle or other, or with a good-looking earldom."

"I," replied Sancho, "have already told my master that I shall be satisfied with the government of some isle; and he is so noble and so generous that he has promised it me many and various times."

"I," said the other, "shall be satisfied for my services with a canonry, and my master has already made it over to me — and such a one!"

"Your worship's master," said Sancho, "must be a knight of the ecclesiastical sort, and can do such favours for his good squires; but mine is merely a layman — although I remember when discerning people, though ill-intentioned to my mind, wanted to advise him to try to be an archbishop. But he would have nothing but being an emperor, and I was trembling all that time in case it came into his head to go into the Church, because I did not find myself fit to hold benefices in it; for I would have your worship know that although I look like a man, I am a beast where the Church is concerned."

"Well, truly your worship is mistaken," said the Knight of the Wood's squire, "on the grounds that island governments are not all of good quality. Some are crooked, some are poor, some are gloomy; and finally the most upright and best appointed of them brings with it a heavy load of anxieties and discomforts, which the unlucky man whose lot it falls to puts on his own shoulders.

"It would be a great deal better if we who profess this accursed servitude withdrew to our own homes and entertained ourselves there with gentler occupations — such as, let us say, hunting or fishing; for what squire is there so poor in the world who is short of a hack and a couple of greyhounds and a fishing rod to entertain himself with in his village?"

"I am short of none of that," answered Sancho. "It is true that I have no hack, but I have an ass that is worth twice as much as my master's horse. May God give me a bad Easter, and let it be the very next one that comes, if I would swap him for it, even if they gave me four bushels of barley on top. Your worship will take it for a joke, the value of my grey — for grey is the colour of my donkey. And I should not be short of greyhounds either, since there are plenty to spare in my village; and what is more, hunting is most enjoyable when it is done at somebody else's cost."

"Really and truly, master squire," answered the other, "I have proposed and determined to give up these drunken follies of these knights and to withdraw to my village and bring up my little children, for I have three like three oriental pearls."

"I have two," said Sancho, "who could be presented to the Pope in person — especially a girl I am bringing up to be a countess, if God is pleased, though in spite of her mother."

"And what age is this lady who is being brought up to be a countess?" asked the Knight of the Wood's squire.

"Fifteen, two more or less," answered Sancho; "but she is as tall as a lance, and as fresh as an April morning, and she has the strength of a porter."

"Those are qualities," answered the other, "not only for being a countess but for being a nymph of the green wood. Oh, the whoreson little whore, what a pair of loins the hussy must have!"

To which Sancho answered, somewhat put out:

"She is no whore, nor was her mother one, nor will either of the two of them be one, God willing, as long as I live. And speak more decently; for considering that your worship has been brought up among knights errant, who are courtesy itself, those words do not strike me as very well arranged."

"Oh, how little your worship understands about the business of praise, master squire!" replied the other. "How is it you do not know that when some knight gives the bull a good lance-thrust in the ring, or when somebody does something well done, the common people generally say: 'Oh, the whoreson rogue, how well he has done it!'? And what looks like abuse is, on those terms, notable praise. And you may disown, sir, the sons and daughters who do not do things that deserve their parents' being given such praises."

"I do disown them," answered Sancho; "and in that way and by that same reasoning your worship might throw a whole whoredom over me and my children and my wife, because everything they do and say is extreme enough to deserve such praises. And to see them again I pray God to get me out of mortal sin — which will be the same thing as getting me out of this dangerous office of squire, which I have fallen into for the second time, baited and taken in by a purse with a hundred ducats in it that I found one day in the heart of the Sierra Morena.

"And the devil sets before my eyes here, there, no, not here but over yonder, a bag full of doubloons, so that I fancy at every step I am touching it with my hand and hugging it and carrying it home and taking out mortgages and setting up rents and living like a prince. And while I am thinking of this, all the labours I suffer with this idiot of a master of mine become easy and bearable — and I know he has more of the madman about him than of the knight."

"That is why they say," answered the other, "that greed bursts the sack; and if we are to talk of madmen, there is no greater one in the world than my master, because he is one of those they mean when they say, 'Other men's cares kill the ass.' For to get another knight to recover the wits he has lost, he plays the madman himself, and goes about looking for something which, once found, may blow up in his face — I do not know."

"And is he in love, by any chance?"

"He is," said the Knight of the Wood's squire: "with a certain Casildea de Vandalia, the rawest and the most roasted lady to be found in the whole world.
