But it is not on the foot of rawness that he limps; other and greater tricks are rumbling in his belly, and it will show before many hours are out."

"There is no road so smooth," replied Sancho, "that it has not some stumble or ditch in it. In other houses they cook beans, and in mine by the cauldron. Madness must have more companions and hangers-on than good sense has. But if it is true, as people commonly say, that having companions in one's troubles serves as a relief in them, I may console myself with your worship, since you serve another master as foolish as mine."

"Foolish, but brave," answered the other; "and more of a rogue than of a fool or a brave man."

"Mine is not that," answered Sancho: "I mean he has nothing of the rogue about him. On the contrary, he has a soul like a pitcher; he does not know how to do harm to anybody, but good to everybody, nor has he any malice: a child could make him believe it was night in the middle of the day. And for this simplicity I love him like the strings of my heart, and I cannot bring myself to leave him, whatever absurdities he commits."

"For all that, brother and sir," said the Knight of the Wood's squire, "if the blind man leads the blind, they are both in danger of falling into the ditch. It is better for us to retire in good order and go back to our own home ground; for those who look for adventures do not always find good ones."

Sancho was spitting often, apparently a certain kind of sticky and rather dry saliva; which the charitable woodland squire seeing and noticing, he said:

"It seems to me that with all this talking our tongues are sticking to our palates; but I have an unsticker hanging from my horse's saddlebow which is as good as they come."

And getting up, he came back a little later with a great wineskin and a pie half a yard long — and this is no exaggeration, because it was made of a white rabbit so big that Sancho, on touching it, took it to be made of a full-grown goat, not a kid. Which Sancho seeing, he said:

"And your worship carries this about with you, sir?"

"Well, what did you suppose?" answered the other. "Am I by any chance some squire of water and wool? I carry better stores on my horse's hindquarters than a general takes with him when he goes on the march."

Sancho ate without needing to be begged, and in the dark swallowed mouthfuls the size of the knots in a hobble-rope. And he said:

"Your worship is indeed a faithful and lawful squire, running and grinding, magnificent and great, as this banquet shows — which, if it has not come here by art of enchantment, at least looks as if it had. And not like me, poor wretched creature, who carry in my saddlebags nothing but a little cheese so hard that a giant's head could be broken with it, along with four dozen carob beans and as many hazelnuts and walnuts, thanks to my master's stinginess and to the opinion he holds and the rule he keeps that knights errant must keep themselves and live on nothing but dried fruit and the herbs of the field."

"Upon my word, brother," replied the other, "my stomach is not made for golden thistles or wild pears or mountain roots. Let our masters settle it with their opinions and their chivalric laws, and eat whatever they order. I carry cold pies and this wineskin hanging from my saddlebow, just in case; and it is so devoted to me and I love it so much that few moments go by without my giving it a thousand kisses and a thousand embraces."

And saying this, he put it into Sancho's hands; and Sancho, tipping it up and setting it to his mouth, stood looking at the stars for a quarter of an hour; and on finishing his drink he let his head fall to one side, and, giving a great sigh, said:

"Oh, the whoreson rogue, and what a good Catholic it is!"

"There, you see," said the Knight of the Wood's squire, hearing Sancho's "whoreson", "how you have praised this wine by calling it a whoreson?"

"I say," answered Sancho, "that I confess I recognise it is no dishonour to call anybody a son of a whore when it comes under the head of praising him. But tell me, sir, by the memory of what you love most: is this wine from Ciudad Real?"

"A fine taster!" answered the other. "Truly it is from nowhere else, and it has some years of age on it."

"Tell me another!" said Sancho. "Do not think otherwise than that it would be beyond me to hit on knowing it. Is it not a fine thing, master squire, that I have so great and so natural an instinct in this matter of knowing wines that, if you give me any at all to smell, I can hit on its country, its family, its flavour and how long it will keep and the changes it will go through, with every circumstance belonging to the wine?

"But there is nothing to wonder at in it, since I had in my family on my father's side the two most excellent wine-tasters La Mancha has known for many years past. As a proof of which, this is what happened to them.

"They were both given some wine out of a cask to try, and were asked their opinion on the condition, quality, goodness or badness of the wine. One of them tried it with the tip of his tongue; the other did no more than put it to his nose. The first said the wine tasted of iron; the second said it tasted more of Cordovan leather. The owner said the cask was clean and that the wine had had nothing put in it that could have given it a taste of iron or of leather. For all that, the two famous tasters stood by what they had said. Time went on, the wine was sold, and on cleaning out the cask they found in it a small key hanging from a strap of Cordovan leather.

"So your worship may see whether a man who comes of this stock can give his opinion in such cases."

"That is why I say," said the Knight of the Wood's squire, "that we should give up going about looking for adventures; and since we have loaves, let us not go looking for cakes, and let us get back to our huts, for God will find us there if he chooses."

"I shall serve my master until he gets to Saragossa; and after that we shall all come to an understanding."

Finally the two good squires talked so much and drank so much that sleep had to tie up their tongues and take the edge off their thirst — for to quench it would have been impossible. And so, both of them clutching the now almost empty wineskin, with their mouthfuls half chewed in their mouths, they fell asleep; where we shall leave them for the present, to tell what passed between the Knight of the Wood and the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance.

Chapter 14: In Which the Adventure of the Knight of the Wood Is Carried Further

Among many things that passed between Don Quixote and the Knight of the Wood, the history says that the Knight of the Wood said to Don Quixote:

"In short, sir knight, I want you to know that my destiny — or rather my own choice — brought me to fall in love with the peerless Casildea de Vandalia. I call her peerless because she has no peer, either in the size of her body or in the height of her rank and her beauty.

"This Casildea, then, that I am telling you about, repaid my honourable thoughts and respectful desires by making me busy myself, as Hercules's stepmother made him, in many and various dangers, promising me at the end of each one that at the end of the next the end of my hopes would come. But my labours have gone on linking themselves together in such a way that they are beyond counting, and I do not know which is to be the last one that will make a beginning to the fulfilling of my good desires.

"Once she ordered me to go and challenge that famous giantess of Seville called the Giralda, who is as strong and valiant as though she were made of bronze, and who, without moving from one place, is the most movable and changeable woman in the world. I went, I saw her and I conquered her, and I made her stand still and keep in her place — because for more than a week nothing blew but north winds.

"There was also a time when she ordered me to go and weigh in my hands the ancient stones of the mighty Bulls of Guisando, an enterprise fitter to be entrusted to porters than to knights. Another time she ordered me to hurl myself down and sink into the chasm of Cabra — an unheard-of and fearful danger — and to bring her a particular account of what is shut up in that dark depth.

"I stopped the Giralda's movement, I weighed the Bulls of Guisando, I threw myself into the chasm and brought to light what was hidden in its abyss; and my hopes were as dead as dead, and her commands and her disdains as alive as alive.

"In short, she has now finally ordered me to travel through all the provinces of Spain and to make all the knights errant who wander through them confess that she alone is the most excellent in beauty of all the women alive today, and that I am the bravest and most truly enamoured knight in the world. On which demand I have now travelled the greater part of Spain, and in it I have defeated many knights who have dared to contradict me.

"But what I most pride and plume myself on is having defeated in single combat that so famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, and having made him confess that my Casildea is more beautiful than his Dulcinea; and in this one victory alone I reckon I have defeated all the knights in the world, because this Don Quixote I speak of has defeated them all — and, having defeated him, his glory, his fame and his honour have been transferred and passed over to my person;

	and the conqueror is honoured the more,
	the more the conquered man is esteemed.

"So that the innumerable exploits of the said Don Quixote now stand to my account and are mine."

Don Quixote was astonished to hear the Knight of the Wood, and a thousand times he was on the point of telling him he lied, and he already had the "you lie" on the tip of his tongue; but he restrained himself as best he could, so as to make him confess his lie out of his own mouth. And so he said to him calmly:

"That your worship, sir knight, may have defeated most of the knights errant in Spain, and even in the whole world, I say nothing about; but that you should have defeated Don Quixote of La Mancha, I put in doubt. It might have been some other man who looked like him — although there are few who look like him."

"How, not?" replied the Knight of the Wood. "By the sky that covers us, I fought with Don Quixote and I beat him and overcame him; and he is a tall man, dry in the face, with long, lean, wiry limbs, going grey, with an aquiline and somewhat hooked nose, and with big black drooping moustaches. He campaigns under the name of the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, and has for a squire a farmer called Sancho Panza; he presses the back and rules the bridle of a famous horse called Rocinante; and, in short, he has for the lady of his affections a certain Dulcinea of El Toboso, at one time called Aldonza Lorenzo — as mine, being called Casilda and being from Andalusia, I call Casildea de Vandalia. If all these details are not enough to prove my truth, here is my sword, which will make incredulity itself believe it."

"Calm yourself, sir knight," said Don Quixote, "and listen to what I want to say to you. You must know that this Don Quixote you speak of is the greatest friend I have in this world — so much so that I could say I hold him in the place of my own person; and by the details you have given me of him, so exact and so certain, I cannot think anything but that he is the very man you defeated.

"On the other hand, I see with my eyes and touch with my hands that it is not possible that he should be the same man — unless it were that, as he has many enchanters for enemies, and one in particular who ordinarily persecutes him, one of them may have taken his shape and let himself be beaten, so as to cheat him of the fame his lofty chivalries have won and earned him throughout the whole of the discovered earth.

"And in confirmation of this I want you to know too that these enchanters who are his enemies not two days ago transformed the shape and person of the beautiful Dulcinea of El Toboso into a low and coarse country girl; and in this same way they must have transformed Don Quixote. And if all this is not enough to satisfy you of this truth I am telling, here is Don Quixote himself, who will maintain it with his arms on foot, or on horseback, or in whatever way pleases you."

And saying this he got to his feet and gripped his sword, waiting to see what decision the Knight of the Wood would take; who, in a voice equally calm, answered and said:

"A good payer does not mind giving pledges: the man who was once able to defeat you transformed, Señor Don Quixote, may well hope to overcome you in your own being. But since it is not right that knights should do their feats of arms in the dark, like highwaymen and ruffians, let us wait for daylight, so that the sun may see our deeds. And it must be a condition of our battle that the loser is to remain at the winner's will, so that he may do with him whatever he likes, provided that what is laid on him is fitting for a knight."

"I am more than content with that condition and agreement," answered Don Quixote.

And on saying this, they went to where their squires were and found them snoring, and in the same posture they had been in when sleep took them by surprise. They woke them and ordered them to have the horses ready, because at sunrise the two of them were to fight a bloody, single and unequal battle. At which news Sancho was appalled and thunderstruck, fearing for his master's safety on account of the brave deeds he had heard the Knight of the Wood's squire tell of his own master. But without saying a word, the two squires went off to look for their beasts, for by now all three horses and the grey had smelt one another and were all standing together.

On the way the Knight of the Wood's squire said to Sancho:

"You must know, brother, that the fighting men of Andalusia have a custom, when they are seconds in some quarrel, of not standing idle with their hands folded while their principals fight it out. I say this so that you may be warned that while our masters fight, we too are to fight and knock each other to splinters."

"That custom, master squire," answered Sancho, "may hold and pass among the ruffians and fighting men you speak of, but among the squires of knights errant, not in a hundred years. At least I have never heard my master speak of any such custom, and he knows by heart all the ordinances of knight-errantry.

"What is more, I am willing to grant that it is true and an express ordinance that squires must fight while their masters fight; but I do not want to keep it — I would rather pay the penalty laid down for such peaceable squires, which I am sure comes to no more than two pounds of wax. And I would rather pay those two pounds, which I know will cost me less than the lint I might spend on doctoring my head, which I already count as split and divided into two parts. And there is more: that I am made incapable of fighting by having no sword, since I have never worn one in my life."

"For that I know a good remedy," said the Knight of the Wood's squire. "I have here two linen sacks of the same size: you shall take one and I the other, and we shall fight with sack-blows, with equal arms."

"In that way, so be it and welcome," answered Sancho, "because such a fight will serve rather to dust us down than to wound us."

"It must not be like that," replied the other; "because we must put inside the sacks, so that the wind does not carry them off, half a dozen nice smooth pebbles, weighing the same on both sides; and in this way we shall be able to sack each other without doing ourselves any harm or damage."

"Just look, body of my father," answered Sancho, "what onion-sables, or what flakes of carded cotton he is putting in the sacks so that our skulls should not be pounded and our bones ground to powder! But even if they were filled with silk cocoons, let me tell you, my dear sir, that I am not going to fight. Let our masters fight and let them settle it, and let us drink and live; for time takes care to take our lives away without our going about looking for appetisers to make them end before their proper season and term and before they fall ripe of themselves."

"For all that," replied the Knight of the Wood's squire, "we must fight for half an hour at least."

"Not that," answered Sancho. "I shall not be so discourteous or so ungrateful as to pick any quarrel at all, however small, with a man I have eaten and drunk with. What is more, being without anger or annoyance, who the devil is going to bring himself to fight cold?"

"For that," said the Knight of the Wood's squire, "I shall provide a sufficient remedy: which is that before we begin the fight I shall come up quietly to your worship and give you three or four slaps that will lay you at my feet; with which I shall wake up your anger even if you are sleepier than a dormouse."

"Against that stroke I know another," answered Sancho, "which is not a whit behind it: I shall pick up a cudgel, and before your worship comes to wake up my anger I shall put yours to sleep with such blows that it will not wake up except in the other world — where it is known that I am not a man who lets anybody handle his face.

"And let every man look to his own arrow, although the soundest thing would be for each man to let his own anger sleep, for nobody knows anybody else's soul; and many a man goes for wool and comes back shorn. And God blessed peace and cursed quarrels; because if a cat, hunted and shut in and squeezed, turns into a lion, God knows what I, who am a man, might turn into. And so from now on I give your worship notice, master squire, that all the harm and damage that comes of our quarrel is to be on your account."

"Very well," replied the Knight of the Wood's squire. "God will send the morning and we shall get on."

At this a thousand kinds of painted little birds were beginning to warble in the trees, and in their various cheerful songs they seemed to be greeting and welcoming the fresh dawn, who was already showing the beauty of her face at the doors and balconies of the east, shaking from her hair an endless number of liquid pearls; in whose sweet liquor the grasses bathed themselves and seemed likewise to be sprouting and raining fine white seed-pearl. The willows dripped a savoury manna, the springs laughed, the streams murmured, the woods grew glad and the meadows grew rich at her coming.

But the light of day had hardly given room to see and tell things apart when the first thing that offered itself to Sancho Panza's eyes was the nose of the Knight of the Wood's squire, which was so big that it almost cast a shadow over his whole body. It is related, in fact, that it was of excessive size, hooked in the middle and all covered with warts, of a purplish colour like an aubergine; it came down two fingers below his mouth; and its size, colour, warts and hooking so disfigured his face that on seeing him Sancho began to kick with his feet and beat with his hands, like a child in a fit, and resolved in his heart to let himself be given two hundred slaps rather than wake his anger to fight with that monster.

Don Quixote looked at his opponent and found that he had already put on his helmet and closed it, so that he could not see his face; but he noticed that he was a well-built man and not very tall. Over his armour he wore a surcoat or tunic of a stuff apparently of the finest gold, sown all over with a great many little moons of shining mirrors, which made him extremely elegant and showy. Over his helmet there floated a great quantity of green, yellow and white plumes; the lance, which he had leaning against a tree, was enormous and thick, with a steel head more than a hand's breadth long.

Don Quixote looked at it all and noted it all, and judged from what he had seen and looked at that this knight must be a man of great strength. But he was not for that afraid, as Sancho Panza was; on the contrary, with a fine boldness he said to the Knight of the Mirrors:

"If your great eagerness to fight, sir knight, has not used up your courtesy, by that courtesy I beg you to raise your visor a little, so that I may see whether the gallantry of your face answers to that of your build."

"Whether you come out of this enterprise beaten or victorious, sir knight," answered the Knight of the Mirrors, "you will have time and room enough to see me; and if I do not satisfy your wish now, it is because I think I am doing a notable wrong to the beautiful Casildea de Vandalia in wasting the time it would take me to raise my visor without making you confess what you know already I am after."

"Well, while we are mounting," said Don Quixote, "you may perfectly well tell me whether I am that Don Quixote you said you had defeated."

"To that we answer you," said the Knight of the Mirrors, "that you look like the very knight I defeated as one egg looks like another; but since you say he is persecuted by enchanters, I shall not dare to state whether you are the man in question or not."

"That is enough for me," answered Don Quixote, "to make me believe you are deceived. But to get you out of it altogether, let our horses be brought; for in less time than it would have taken you to raise your visor, if God and my lady and my arm stand by me, I shall see your face, and you will see that I am not the beaten Don Quixote you suppose."

With this, cutting short their words, they mounted; and Don Quixote turned Rocinante's reins to take the necessary ground for coming back and meeting his opponent, and the Knight of the Mirrors did the same. But Don Quixote had not gone twenty paces when he heard the Knight of the Mirrors calling him; and the two of them dividing the distance, the Knight of the Mirrors said to him:

"Note, sir knight, that the condition of our battle is that the loser, as I have said before, is to be at the winner's discretion."

"I know it already," answered Don Quixote, "provided that what is laid on and ordered the loser is something that does not go outside the limits of chivalry."

"That is understood," answered the Knight of the Mirrors.

At this the squire's strange nose came into Don Quixote's view, and he was no less astonished at seeing it than Sancho had been — so much so that he judged him to be some monster, or a new kind of man of a sort not in use in the world.

Sancho, who saw his master ride off to take his run, would not stay alone with the man with the nose, being afraid that with one single flick of that nose against his own his quarrel would be finished, and he would be left stretched on the ground either by the blow or by the fright. And he went after his master, hanging on to one of Rocinante's stirrup-leathers; and when it seemed to him that it was time for his master to turn back, he said to him:

"I beg your worship, my dear sir, that before you go back to meet him you will help me up onto that cork tree, from where I shall be able to see the gallant encounter your worship is going to have with this knight more to my liking and better than from the ground."

"I rather think, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that you want to perch and climb onto a scaffold to watch the bulls without danger."

"To tell the truth," answered Sancho, "that squire's outrageous nose has me appalled and full of terror, and I do not dare to stay near him."

"It is such," said Don Quixote, "that if I were not who I am, it would appal me too. So come: I shall help you up where you say."

While Don Quixote was delayed getting Sancho up the cork tree, the Knight of the Mirrors took as much ground as he thought necessary; and believing Don Quixote had done the same, without waiting for the sound of a trumpet or any other signal to warn them, he turned his horse's reins — which was no lighter or better-looking than Rocinante — and at his full gallop, which was a middling trot, went to meet his enemy.

But seeing him busy getting Sancho up, he pulled up his reins and stopped in the middle of his run — at which his horse was extremely grateful, on the grounds that it could not move any longer. Don Quixote, who thought his enemy was coming at him on wings, dug his spurs hard into Rocinante's shrunken flanks and made him get on in such a way that the history relates this was the only time he was known to have run at all, because all the rest of the time it was always plain trotting. And with this unheard-of fury he came to where the Knight of the Mirrors was digging his spurs into his horse up to the rowel-buttons, without being able to move him a single finger's breadth from the place where he had brought his charge to a standstill.

At this good moment and juncture Don Quixote found his opponent hampered with his horse and busy with his lance, which he either never managed or never had time to set in its rest. Don Quixote, who was not looking at these difficulties, safely and without any danger at all met the Knight of the Mirrors with such force that, much against his will, he brought him down to the ground over his horse's hindquarters, with such a fall that, without stirring hand or foot, he gave signs of being dead.

Sancho had hardly seen him fall when he slid down from the cork tree and came in all haste to where his master was; who, dismounting from Rocinante, went over to the Knight of the Mirrors and undid the laces of his helmet to see whether he was dead and to let the air get to him if he happened to be alive.

And he saw — who could tell what he saw without causing astonishment, wonder and dread in those who hear it? He saw, says the history, the very face, the very figure, the very aspect, the very physiognomy, the very effigy, the very perspecktive of the bachelor Sansón Carrasco. And as soon as he saw it he said in a loud voice:

"Come here, Sancho, and see what you are to see and not to believe! Hurry, my son, and mark what magic can do, what wizards and enchanters can do!"

Sancho came; and when he saw the bachelor Carrasco's face, he began to cross himself a thousand times and to bless himself as many. In all this the fallen knight gave no signs of being alive, and Sancho said to Don Quixote:

"I am of the opinion, my dear sir, that just in case, your worship should stick and drive your sword into the mouth of this man who looks like the bachelor Sansón Carrasco: perhaps in him you will kill one of your enemies the enchanters."

"You do not speak badly," said Don Quixote, "because of enemies, the fewer the better."

And drawing his sword to put Sancho's advice into effect, up came the Knight of the Mirrors' squire, without the nose that had made him so ugly, and said in a loud voice:

"Look what you are doing, Señor Don Quixote; for that man you have at your feet is the bachelor Sansón Carrasco, your friend, and I am his squire."

And Sancho, seeing him without that first ugliness, said to him:

"And the nose?"

To which he answered:

"I have it here, in my pocket."

And putting his hand to the right one, he pulled out a nose of pasteboard and varnish, of the masquerade kind, of the make already described. And Sancho, looking at him more and more, said in a loud, wondering voice:

"Holy Mary help me! Is this not Tomé Cecial, my neighbour and my gossip?"

"That I am indeed!" answered the now unnosed squire. "Tomé Cecial I am, gossip and friend Sancho Panza; and presently I shall tell you the channels, tricks and tangles by which I have come here. And meanwhile, ask and beg your master not to touch, ill-treat, wound or kill the Knight of the Mirrors he has at his feet; because beyond any doubt he is that rash and ill-advised bachelor Sansón Carrasco, our fellow-countryman."

At this the Knight of the Mirrors came to himself; which Don Quixote seeing, he put the naked point of his sword over his face and said to him:

"You are a dead man, knight, unless you confess that the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso excels your Casildea de Vandalia in beauty. And besides this you must promise, if you come alive out of this contest and fall, to go to the city of El Toboso and present yourself before her on my behalf, so that she may do with you whatever she pleases; and if she leaves you at your own disposal, you must likewise come back and look for me — the trail of my exploits will serve you as a guide to bring you where I am — and tell me what has passed between you and her: conditions which, in accordance with those we laid down before our battle, do not go outside the terms of knight-errantry."

"I confess," said the fallen knight, "that the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso's unstitched and dirty shoe is worth more than Casildea's badly combed, though clean, beard; and I promise to go and to come back from her presence to yours, and to give you a full and particular account of what you ask me."

"You must also confess and believe," added Don Quixote, "that the knight you defeated was not and could not have been Don Quixote of La Mancha, but some other man who looked like him — as I confess and believe that you, although you look like the bachelor Sansón Carrasco, are not he but another man who looks like him, and that my enemies have put him here in front of me in his shape, so as to hold back and cool the force of my anger and so that I may use the glory of my victory mildly."

"I confess, judge and feel it all as you believe, judge and feel it," answered the battered knight. "Let me get up, I beg you, if the blow of my fall allows it, for it has left me in a bad enough state."

Don Quixote helped him up, along with Tomé Cecial, his squire, from whom Sancho never took his eyes, asking him things whose answers gave him plain signs that he really was the Tomé Cecial he said he was. But the notion his master's words had put into Sancho — that the enchanters had changed the shape of the Knight of the Mirrors into that of the bachelor Carrasco — did not let him give credit to the truth he was looking at with his own eyes.

Finally master and man stayed with this delusion; and the Knight of the Mirrors and his squire, downcast and out of luck, went off away from Don Quixote and Sancho, meaning to look for some place where they could plaster and splint his ribs. Don Quixote and Sancho went back to their road to Saragossa, where the history leaves them, so as to give an account of who the Knight of the Mirrors and his big-nosed squire were.

Chapter 15: In Which Is Told and Made Known Who the Knight of the Mirrors and His Squire Were

Don Quixote went along extremely contented, proud and boastful at having won a victory over so valiant a knight as he imagined the Knight of the Mirrors to be — from whose knightly word he expected to learn whether his lady's enchantment was still going on, since that defeated knight was obliged, on pain of not being one, to come back and give him an account of what had happened to him with her. But Don Quixote was thinking one thing and the Knight of the Mirrors another, since for the moment his only thought was to look for somewhere to be plastered, as has been said.

The history says, then, that when the bachelor Sansón Carrasco advised Don Quixote to go back to his abandoned chivalries, it was because he had first gone into council with the curate and the barber about what means might be taken to bring Don Quixote round to staying quietly and peacefully at home, without his badly sought adventures upsetting him.

Out of which consultation there came, by the common vote of them all and the particular opinion of Carrasco, that they should let Don Quixote go out, since holding him back seemed impossible; and that Sansón should come out on the road as a knight errant and pick a fight with him — there would be no lack of grounds — and defeat him, holding this to be an easy matter; and that it should be an agreed compact that the loser should stay at the winner's mercy.

And so, Don Quixote being defeated, the bachelor knight was to order him to go back to his village and his house and not to leave it for two years, or until such time as he should be ordered otherwise by him; which it was clear that Don Quixote, once defeated, would undoubtedly carry out, so as not to go against and fail the laws of chivalry. And it might be that in the time of his confinement he would forget his vain notions, or there would be room to look for some suitable remedy for his madness.

Carrasco accepted it, and Tomé Cecial, Sancho Panza's gossip and neighbour, offered himself as his squire — a cheerful man with a slippery skull. Sansón armed himself as has been related, and Tomé Cecial fitted over his own natural nose the false masquerade one already described, so that he should not be recognised by his gossip when they met.

And so they followed the same road Don Quixote was taking, and came near to being present at the adventure of the Cart of Death. And finally they came upon them in the wood, where everything happened to them that the prudent reader has read. And if it had not been for Don Quixote's extraordinary notions, in giving himself to understand that the bachelor was not the bachelor, the master bachelor would have been made incapable for ever of taking his licentiate's degree, for having found no nests where he thought he would find birds.

Tomé Cecial, seeing how badly he had achieved what he wanted and what a bad end his journey had come to, said to the bachelor:

"Certainly, Señor Sansón Carrasco, we have got what we deserved: an enterprise is thought of and undertaken easily, but most often a man gets out of it with difficulty. Don Quixote mad, we sane: he goes off sound and laughing, your worship is left pounded and sad. Now let us know which is the greater madman: the man who is mad because he cannot help it, or the man who is mad by his own choice?"

To which Sansón answered:

"The difference between those two madmen is that the one who is mad by necessity will always be so, and the one who is mad of his own accord will leave off being so whenever he likes."

"Then since that is so," said Tomé Cecial, "I was mad of my own accord when I chose to make myself your worship's squire, and by the same accord I choose to leave off being one and to go back home."

"That is your affair," answered Sansón; "but to think that I am going back to mine before I have pounded Don Quixote with a stick is to think of what will not happen. And what will take me to look for him now is not the wish that he should recover his wits but the wish for revenge; for the great pain in my ribs does not let me make any more merciful reflections."

In this talk the two of them went along until they came to a village where they had the good luck to find a bone-setter, who treated the unfortunate Sansón. Tomé Cecial went back and left him, and he was left planning his revenge; and the history will speak of him again in its own time, so as not to leave off making merry now with Don Quixote.

Chapter 16: Of What Happened to Don Quixote with a Judicious Gentleman of La Mancha

Don Quixote went on his journey with the gladness, contentment and pride that has been described, imagining himself, on account of his late victory, to be the bravest knight errant the world had in that age. He counted as finished and brought to a happy end all the adventures that might happen to him from then on; he thought little of enchantments and enchanters; he did not remember the innumerable beatings he had been given in the course of his chivalries, or the stone that knocked out half his teeth, or the ingratitude of the galley slaves, or the boldness and hail of staves of the Yangüesans.

In short, he said to himself that if he could only find the art, the way or the means of disenchanting his lady Dulcinea, he would not envy the greatest good fortune the most fortunate knight errant of past ages ever attained or could have attained. He was wholly taken up with these fancies when Sancho said to him:

"Is it not a fine thing, sir, that I still have in front of my eyes the outrageous nose, and above regulation size, of my gossip Tomé Cecial?"

"And do you believe, Sancho, by any chance, that the Knight of the Mirrors was the bachelor Carrasco, and his squire Tomé Cecial your gossip?"

"I do not know what to say to that," answered Sancho; "I only know that the details he gave me about my house and my wife and children nobody but he himself could have given me. And his face, once the nose was off, was the very face of Tomé Cecial, as I have seen it many times in my village and with one wall between our two houses; and the tone of his voice was all one."

"Let us be reasonable, Sancho," replied Don Quixote. "Come here: on what consideration can it be supposed that the bachelor Sansón Carrasco should come as a knight errant, armed with offensive and defensive arms, to fight with me? Have I by any chance been his enemy? Have I ever given him occasion to bear me a grudge? Am I his rival, or does he profess arms, so as to be envious of the fame I have won by them?"

"Well, what are we to say, sir," answered Sancho, "about that knight's being so like the bachelor Carrasco, whoever he may be, and his squire like Tomé Cecial my gossip? And if it is enchantment, as your worship has said, were there no other two men in the world for them to look like?"

"It is all contrivance and design," answered Don Quixote, "of the malignant magicians who persecute me; who, foreseeing that I was going to come out the winner of the contest, provided that the defeated knight should show the face of my friend the bachelor, so that the friendship I bear him should set itself between the edge of my sword and the force of my arm and should cool the just anger of my heart, and in this way the man who by tricks and falsehoods was trying to take my life should be left alive.

"As a proof of which you know already, Sancho, by an experience that will not let you lie or be deceived, how easy it is for enchanters to change one face into another, making the beautiful ugly and the ugly beautiful; since not two days ago you saw with your own eyes the beauty and gallantry of the peerless Dulcinea in her whole entirety and natural form, and I saw her in the ugliness and lowness of a coarse country girl, with cataracts on her eyes and a bad smell in her mouth.

"And what is more, since the perverse enchanter dared to work so wicked a transformation, it is no great matter that he should have worked that of Sansón Carrasco and that of your gossip, so as to take the glory of the victory out of my hands. But for all that, I comfort myself; because in the end, in whatever shape it was, I have come out the winner over my enemy."

"God knows the truth of it all," answered Sancho.

And as he knew that Dulcinea's transformation had been his own contrivance and trick, his master's chimeras did not satisfy him; but he did not want to argue back, in case he should say some word that would reveal his deception.

They were in this talk when they were overtaken by a man who was coming behind them along the same road on a very handsome dapple-grey mare, dressed in a coat of fine green cloth panelled with tawny velvet, with a cap of the same velvet. The mare's harness was of the field sort and short-stirruped, likewise in purple and green. He wore a Moorish scimitar hanging from a broad baldric of green and gold, and his buskins were of the same work as the baldric. His spurs were not gilded but coated with a green varnish, so smooth and burnished that, matching the whole of the rest of his dress, they looked better than if they had been of pure gold.

When he came up to them the traveller greeted them courteously, and, spurring his mare, was going on past; but Don Quixote said to him:

"Fine sir, if your worship is going our road and is not in a hurry, I should take it as a kindness if we might travel together."

"Truly," answered the man on the mare, "I would not go past like this if it were not for fear that the company of my mare might excite that horse."

"You may perfectly well, sir," answered Sancho at this, "you may perfectly well hold in your mare, because our horse is the most virtuous and best-behaved in the world: he has never done anything base on such occasions, and the one time he broke out to do it my master and I paid for it sevenfold. I say again that your worship may stop if you like; for even if they served her to him between two plates, it is a safe bet that the horse would not face her."

The traveller reined in, marvelling at Don Quixote's bearing and face — for he was riding without his helmet, which Sancho was carrying like a bag on the front of the grey's pack-saddle. And if the man in green looked hard at Don Quixote, Don Quixote looked far harder at the man in green, thinking him a man of substance. He seemed to be about fifty years old; his grey hairs were few and his face aquiline; his look was between cheerful and grave; in short, in his dress and bearing he gave one to understand that he was a man of good qualities.

What the man in green judged of Don Quixote of La Mancha was that he had never seen such a manner or such an appearance of a man. He marvelled at the length of his horse, the size of his body, the thinness and yellowness of his face, his armour, his bearing and his composure: a figure and portrait not seen in that country for long ages past.

Don Quixote noticed clearly the attention with which the traveller was looking at him, and read his wish in his suspense; and, being so courteous and so fond of pleasing everybody, before he could ask him anything he met him halfway, saying:

"This figure your worship has seen in me, being so new and so far outside the ones that are commonly in use, I should not be surprised if it had surprised you. But your worship will stop being surprised when I tell you, as I do tell you, that I am a knight —

	the sort of men that people say
	go riding to their adventures.

"I left my own country, mortgaged my estate, gave up my comforts and threw myself into Fortune's arms to carry me wherever she was best pleased. I chose to bring back to life the now dead order of knight-errantry, and for many days now, stumbling here, falling there, hurling myself down in this place and getting up in that, I have carried out a great part of my wish, helping widows, protecting maidens and favouring married women, orphans and wards — the proper and natural office of knights errant.

"And so, by my valorous, many and Christian exploits I have deserved to go about in print by now in almost all, or most, of the nations of the world. Thirty thousand copies of my history have been printed, and it is on the way to being printed thirty thousand thousand times, if heaven does not put a stop to it.

"In short, to shut it all up in a few words, or in one: I say that I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, otherwise called the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance. And although self-praise debases, I am sometimes forced to speak my own — and this is to be understood as when nobody is present to speak it for me. So that, sir gentleman, neither this horse, nor this lance, nor this shield, nor my squire, nor all these arms together, nor the yellowness of my face, nor my wasted thinness can astonish you from now on, since you know now who I am and the profession I follow."

Having said this, Don Quixote fell silent; and the man in green, by the time he took to answer him, seemed unable to manage it. But after a good while he said to him:

"You hit rightly, sir knight, on knowing my wish from my suspense; but you have not hit on taking away the wonder that having seen you causes in me. For although, as you say, sir, my knowing who you are might take it away, it has not been so; on the contrary, now that I know it, I am left more taken aback and more full of wonder.

"How is it possible that there are knights errant in the world today, and that there are printed histories of genuine chivalries? I cannot persuade myself that there is anybody on earth today who favours widows, protects maidens, honours married women or helps orphans; and I would not have believed it if I had not seen it with my own eyes in your worship.

"Blessed be heaven! For by that history your worship says is in print of your lofty and truthful chivalries, the innumerable ones of the invented knights errant that the world was full of will have been consigned to oblivion — so harmful to good morals and so much to the prejudice and discredit of good histories."

"There is a great deal to say," answered Don Quixote, "on the question of whether the histories of knights errant are invented or not."

"Why, is there anybody who doubts," answered the man in green, "that such histories are false?"

"I doubt it," answered Don Quixote, "and let it stay there; for if our journey lasts, I hope in God to give your worship to understand that you have done wrong to go with the current of those who hold it certain that they are not true."

From this last speech of Don Quixote's the traveller got an inkling that Don Quixote must be some sort of idiot, and waited for him to confirm it with more of the same. But before they got on to other conversation, Don Quixote begged him to tell him who he was, since he had told him about his own condition and his life. To which the man in the Green Coat answered:

"I, Sir Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, am a gentleman, a native of a village where we shall go and dine today, if God is pleased. I am more than moderately rich and my name is Don Diego de Miranda. I pass my life with my wife and my children and my friends; my pastimes are hunting and fishing, but I keep neither hawk nor greyhounds, only a tame decoy-partridge or a bold ferret.

"I have some six dozen books, some in Spanish and some in Latin, some of history and others of devotion; books of chivalry have not yet come over the thresholds of my doors. I look through the secular ones more than the devotional, so long as they are decent entertainment, delighting with their language and astonishing and holding one with their invention — although there are very few of these in Spain.

"Sometimes I eat with my neighbours and friends, and often I invite them; my invitations are clean and neat and not at all mean. I have no taste for backbiting, nor do I allow backbiting in front of me; I do not pry into other men's lives, nor am I a lynx for other people's doings; I hear Mass every day; I share my goods with the poor, without making a display of my good works, so as not to give hypocrisy and vainglory an entry into my heart — enemies that gently take possession of the most guarded heart. I try to make peace between those I know are at odds; I am devoted to Our Lady; and I always trust in the infinite mercy of God our Lord."

Sancho was most attentive to the account of the gentleman's life and pastimes; and thinking it good and holy, and that the man who led it must work miracles, he threw himself off the grey and in great haste went and seized his right stirrup, and with a devout heart and almost in tears kissed his feet again and again. Which the gentleman seeing, he asked him:

"What are you doing, brother? What kisses are these?"

"Let me kiss," answered Sancho, "because your worship seems to me the first saint in the saddle I have seen in all the days of my life."

"I am no saint," answered the gentleman, "but a great sinner. You are the one, brother, who must be good, as your simplicity shows."

Sancho went back to his pack-saddle, having brought his master's deep melancholy out into laughter and caused fresh astonishment in Don Diego. Don Quixote asked him how many children he had, and told him that one of the things in which the ancient philosophers, who lacked the true knowledge of God, placed the highest good was in the goods of nature, in those of fortune, in having many friends and in having many good children.

"I, Señor Don Quixote," answered the gentleman, "have one son who, if I did not have him, would perhaps make me judge myself happier than I am — and not because he is bad, but because he is not as good as I would like.

"He must be about eighteen; six of those years he has been at Salamanca learning the Latin and Greek languages. And when I wanted him to go on to study other sciences, I found him so steeped in that of poetry — if that can be called a science — that it is not possible to make him face the science of law, which I would have liked him to study, or the queen of them all, theology.

"I would have liked him to be the crown of his family, since we live in an age when our kings highly reward virtuous and good letters; for letters without virtue are pearls on a dunghill. He spends the whole day settling whether Homer said well or badly in such a line of the Iliad; whether Martial was indecent or not in such an epigram; whether such and such lines of Virgil are to be understood in one way or another. In short, all his conversation is with the books of the poets I have mentioned, and with those of Horace, Persius, Juvenal and Tibullus; for of the modern writers in Spanish he takes little account.

"And with all the ill will he shows towards poetry in Spanish, his mind is now taken up with making a gloss on four lines that have been sent him from Salamanca, and I think they are for a literary competition."

To all which Don Quixote answered:

"Children, sir, are pieces of their parents' entrails, and so they must be loved, good or bad as they may be, as we love the souls that give us life. It is for parents to guide them from small children along the steps of virtue, of good breeding and of good Christian habits, so that when they are grown they may be the staff of their parents' old age and the glory of their posterity.

"And as for forcing them to study this or that science, I do not hold it sound — although persuading them will do no harm. And when a man does not have to study pane lucrando, the student being fortunate enough that heaven gave him parents who can leave him something, I should be of the opinion that they should let him follow whatever science they see him most inclined to. And although poetry is less useful than delightful, it is not one of those that generally dishonour the man who possesses them.

"Poetry, sir gentleman, is in my opinion like a tender young girl, extremely beautiful, whom a great many other girls take care to enrich, polish and adorn — and these are all the other sciences; and she must make use of them all, and they must all get their authority from her. But this girl does not want to be handled, or dragged through the streets, or published at the street corners of the squares or in the corners of palaces.

"She is made of an alchemy of such virtue that whoever knows how to treat her will turn her into the purest gold of inestimable price. Whoever has her must keep her within bounds, not letting her run into filthy satires or soulless sonnets; she must not be for sale in any way at all, unless it is in heroic poems, in lamentable tragedies or in cheerful, skilfully made comedies; she must not let herself be handled by clowns or by the ignorant crowd, incapable of knowing or valuing the treasures shut up in her.

"And do not think, sir, that I am calling only the low and humble people the crowd here; for everybody who does not know, even if he is a lord and a prince, may and must be counted in the number of the crowd. And so the man who handles and keeps poetry with the requirements I have described will be famous, and his name esteemed in all the civilised nations of the world.

"And as for what you say, sir, that your son does not think much of poetry in Spanish, I give myself to understand that he is not very sound in it, and the reason is this: the great Homer did not write in Latin, because he was a Greek, nor did Virgil write in Greek, because he was a Latin. In short, all the ancient poets wrote in the language they sucked in with their milk, and did not go looking for foreign ones to declare the loftiness of their ideas.

"And this being so, it would be reasonable that this custom should spread through all the nations, and that the German poet should not be undervalued because he writes in his own language, nor the Castilian, nor even the Basque who writes in his.

"But your son, as I imagine, sir, must be out of temper not with poetry in Spanish but with poets who are mere Spanish versifiers, without knowing other languages or other sciences to adorn and rouse and help their natural impulse. And even in this there may be a mistake; because, according to true opinion, the poet is born — meaning that the natural poet comes out of his mother's womb a poet, and with that inclination heaven gave him, without any more study or contrivance, composes things that make the man true who said: est Deus in nobis, and so on.

"I say too that the natural poet who helps himself with art will be far better and will have the advantage over the poet who wants to be one merely by knowing the art. The reason is that art does not go beyond nature but perfects it; so that, nature and art being mixed together, and art with nature, they will produce a most perfect poet.

"Let this, then, be the conclusion of my talk, sir gentleman: that your worship should let your son travel where his star calls him. For being as good a student as he must be, and having already happily climbed the first step of the sciences, which is that of the languages, with them he will by himself climb to the summit of humane letters — which look as well in a gentleman of cloak and sword, and adorn, honour and dignify him as much, as mitres do bishops or robes do learned lawyers.

"Let your worship scold your son if he writes satires that damage other people's honour, and punish him and tear them up; but if he writes discourses in the manner of Horace, where he reproves the vices in general, as he did it so elegantly, then praise him. Because it is lawful for a poet to write against envy and to speak ill of the envious in his verses, and so of the other vices, provided he does not point at any particular person. But there are poets who, for the sake of saying one malicious thing, will risk being banished to the islands of Pontus.

"If the poet is chaste in his habits, he will be chaste in his verses too: the pen is the tongue of the soul; as the ideas are that are conceived in it, so will his writings be. And when kings and princes see the miraculous science of poetry in prudent, virtuous and grave subjects, they honour them, esteem them and enrich them, and even crown them with the leaves of the tree that lightning does not harm — as a sign that those whose brows they see honoured and adorned with such crowns are not to be harmed by anybody."

The man in the Green Coat was astonished at Don Quixote's discourse — so much so that he began to lose the opinion he had of him as an idiot. But halfway through this talk Sancho, as it was not much to his taste, had turned off the road to ask for a little milk from some shepherds who were milking sheep nearby.

And at this the gentleman was going to take up the conversation again, extremely satisfied with Don Quixote's good sense and good reasoning, when Don Quixote, raising his head, saw coming along the road they were travelling a cart full of royal flags. And believing that it must be some new adventure, he called Sancho at the top of his voice to come and give him his helmet. And Sancho, hearing himself called, left the shepherds and in all haste whipped up the grey and came to where his master was — to whom there happened a terrifying and preposterous adventure.

Chapter 17: Where the Highest Point Don Quixote's Unheard-of Courage Reached or Could Reach Is Shown, with the Happily Finished Adventure of the Lions

The history tells that when Don Quixote was shouting to Sancho to bring him his helmet, Sancho was buying some curds that the shepherds were selling him; and, harried by his master's great haste, he did not know what to do with them or what to carry them in, and, so as not to lose them, since he had already paid for them, he decided to throw them into his master's helmet. And with this good provision made, he came back to see what was wanted of him; and when he arrived his master said to him:

"Give me that helmet, my friend; for either I know little about adventures, or what I make out over there is one that will oblige me — and does oblige me — to take up my arms."

The man in the Green Coat, hearing this, cast his eyes all around, and made out nothing but a cart coming towards them with two or three little flags on it, which gave him to understand that the cart must be carrying money belonging to His Majesty; and he said so to Don Quixote. But Don Quixote gave him no credit, always believing and thinking that whatever happened to him must be adventures and more adventures; and so he answered the gentleman:

"A man forewarned is half the battle fought: nothing is lost by my arming myself, for I know by experience that I have visible and invisible enemies, and I do not know when, or where, or at what time, or in what shapes they will attack me."

And turning to Sancho, he asked him for the helmet; and Sancho, as he had had no chance to get the curds out, was forced to hand it over as it was. Don Quixote took it, and, without noticing what was inside, jammed it on his head in all haste. And as the curds were squeezed and pressed, the whey began to run down all over Don Quixote's face and beard; at which he took such a fright that he said to Sancho:

"What can this be, Sancho? It seems as if my skull were going soft, or my brains were melting, or as if I were sweating from my feet to my head. And if I am sweating, it is truly not from fear; no doubt I believe the adventure that is about to happen to me now is a terrible one. Give me something to wipe myself with, if you have it, for this copious sweat is blinding my eyes."

Sancho said nothing and gave him a cloth, and along with it gave thanks to God that his master had not tumbled to the case. Don Quixote wiped himself and took off his helmet to see what the thing was that, as it seemed to him, was making his head cold; and, seeing that white porridge inside the helmet, he put it to his nose, and, smelling it, said:

"By the life of my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, those are curds you have put in here, you traitor, you rascal, you ill-mannered squire!"

To which, with great coolness and dissimulation, Sancho answered:

"If they are curds, let your worship give them to me and I shall eat them... But no, let the devil eat them, for it must have been he who put them there. Was I likely to have the impudence to dirty your worship's helmet? You have hit on the impudent man, haven't you! Upon my word, sir, by what God gives me to understand, I too must have enchanters persecuting me as a creature and a limb of your worship, and they will have put that filth there to move your patience to anger and to make you grind my ribs as you generally do. Well, truly this time they have jumped short, because I trust the good sense of my master, who will have considered that I have no curds, nor milk, nor anything else worth as much; and that if I had, I should have put it in my stomach sooner than in the helmet."

"It may all be," said Don Quixote.

The gentleman watched it all and marvelled at it all — especially when, after Don Quixote had cleaned his head, face, beard and helmet, he jammed it on again; and, settling himself firmly in the stirrups, feeling for his sword and gripping his lance, said:

"Now, let come what may come; for here I stand with a mind to take on Satan himself in person."

At this the cart with the flags came up, in which there were no people but the carter, on the mules, and a man sitting on the front. Don Quixote placed himself in front of it and said:

"Where are you going, brothers? What cart is this, what are you carrying in it, and what flags are these?"

To which the carter answered:

"The cart is mine; what is going in it is two brave caged lions that the governor of Oran is sending to court as a present to His Majesty; the flags are the king our lord's, as a sign that something of his is travelling here."

"And are the lions big?" asked Don Quixote.

"So big," answered the man who was riding at the door of the cart, "that bigger ones, or as big, have never crossed from Africa to Spain. I am the lion-keeper, and I have brought over others, but none like these. They are a male and a female; the male is in this first cage and the female in the one behind. And they are hungry at the moment, because they have not eaten today. So your worship had better get out of the way, for we must reach our stage quickly and feed them."

To which Don Quixote said, smiling a little:

"Lion cubs to me? To me, lion cubs, and at such an hour? Well, by God, those gentlemen who are sending them here shall see whether I am a man to be frightened by lions! Get down, my good fellow, and, since you are the lion-keeper, open those cages and throw those beasts out here; for in the middle of this open country I shall let them know who Don Quixote of La Mancha is, in spite and in defiance of the enchanters who are sending them to me."

"Ha, ha!" said the gentleman to himself at this. "Our good knight has given a sign of what he is: the curds have certainly softened his skull and ripened his brains."

At this Sancho came up to him and said:

"Sir, for the love of God, will your worship manage it somehow so that my master Don Quixote does not take on these lions? Because if he does, they will tear us all to pieces here."

"Why, is your master so mad," answered the gentleman, "that you are afraid of it and believe he will take on such savage animals?"

"He is not mad," answered Sancho, "he is reckless."

"I shall see to it that he is not," replied the gentleman.

And going up to Don Quixote, who was urging the lion-keeper to open the cages, he said to him:

"Sir knight, knights errant should undertake the adventures that hold out some hope of coming well out of them, not those that take that hope away altogether; because valour that trespasses into the jurisdiction of rashness has more of madness in it than of fortitude. What is more, these lions are not coming against your worship, nor do they dream of it: they are being carried as a present to His Majesty, and it will not be right to hold them up or hinder them on their journey."

"Let your worship go, sir gentleman," answered Don Quixote, "and see to your tame decoy-partridge and your bold ferret, and let each man do his own office. This is mine, and I know whether these gentlemen the lions are coming at me or not."

And turning to the lion-keeper, he said:

"I swear, you scoundrel, that if you do not open the cages this instant, I shall pin you to the cart with this lance!"

The carter, seeing the determination of that armed apparition, said to him:

"My dear sir, may it please your worship, out of charity, to let me unyoke the mules and get myself to safety with them before the lions are unsheathed; because if they kill them I am ruined for the rest of my life, since I have no other property but this cart and these mules."

"O man of little faith!" answered Don Quixote. "Get down and unyoke and do whatever you like, for you will soon see that you have worked for nothing and might have saved yourself the trouble."

The carter got down and unyoked in great haste, and the lion-keeper said in a loud voice:

"Let all here present be my witnesses that against my will and under compulsion I am opening the cages and letting the lions loose, and that I protest to this gentleman that all the harm and damage these beasts may do will run and go to his account, together with my wages and my dues. Your worships, gentlemen, get yourselves under cover before I open, for I am safe enough that they will do me no harm."

Once more the gentleman urged him not to commit such a folly, for it was tempting God to undertake such an absurdity. To which Don Quixote answered that he knew what he was doing. The gentleman answered him that he should think it over carefully, for he was of the opinion that he was deceiving himself.

"Now, sir," replied Don Quixote, "if your worship does not care to be a spectator of what in your view is going to be a tragedy, spur the dapple mare and get yourself to safety."

Which Sancho hearing, he begged him with tears in his eyes to give up such an enterprise, in comparison with which the windmills, and the fearful business of the fulling-mills, and, in short, all the exploits he had undertaken in the whole course of his life, had been cakes and fancy bread.

"Look, sir," said Sancho, "there is no enchantment here nor anything like it; because I have seen through the bars and chinks of the cage a real lion's claw, and I gather from it that the lion whose claw it must be is bigger than a mountain."

"Fear, at any rate," answered Don Quixote, "will make him look to you bigger than half the world. Withdraw, Sancho, and leave me; and if I die here, you know our old agreement: you will go to Dulcinea, and I say no more to you."

To these he added other arguments, by which he took away any hope that he would leave off pursuing his deranged intention. The man in the Green Coat would have liked to oppose him, but he saw himself unequal in arms, and it did not seem to him good sense to take on a madman, which was what Don Quixote had by now seemed to him at every point. And Don Quixote, going back to urging the lion-keeper and repeating his threats, gave the gentleman occasion to spur his mare, and Sancho his grey, and the carter his mules, all of them trying to get as far away from the cart as they could before the lions were unbasketed.

Sancho was weeping for the death of his master, which this time he undoubtedly believed was coming to him in the lions' claws; he cursed his luck and called it a wretched hour when it came into his head to go back into his service; but for all his weeping and lamenting he did not leave off drubbing the grey to get him away from the cart. The lion-keeper, then, seeing that the runaways were now a good way off, went back to putting to Don Quixote and formally notifying him of what he had already put to him and notified him of; to which he answered that he heard him, and that he need not trouble with any more notifications and formalities, since they would all bear little fruit, and that he should hurry up.

In the space of time the lion-keeper took to open the first cage, Don Quixote was considering whether it would be better to do the battle on foot rather than on horseback; and in the end he decided to do it on foot, fearing that Rocinante would take fright at the sight of the lions. For this reason he leapt off the horse, threw down his lance, gripped his shield and, drawing his sword, step by step, with marvellous boldness and a valiant heart, went and planted himself in front of the cart, commending himself to God with his whole heart and then to his lady Dulcinea.

And it is to be noted that at this point the author of this true history breaks out and says: "O strong and, beyond all extolling, spirited Don Quixote of La Mancha, mirror in which all the brave men of the world may look at themselves, second and new Don Manuel de León, who was the glory and honour of Spanish knights! With what words shall I tell this so astounding exploit, or with what arguments shall I make it credible to the ages to come, or what praises will there be that do not befit and suit you, though they be hyperboles above all hyperboles? You on foot, you alone, you fearless, you great-souled, with only a sword — and not one of the sharp ones with the little dog on the blade — with a shield of no very bright and clean steel, standing there waiting and watching for the two fiercest lions the African forests ever bred. Let your own deeds be the ones to praise you, valiant Manchegan, for I leave them here at their height for want of words to extol them."

Here the author's outburst just quoted stopped, and he went on, knotting up the thread of the history, saying that the lion-keeper, seeing Don Quixote already in position, and that he could not avoid loosing the male lion on pain of falling into the bad graces of the indignant and daring knight, threw the first cage wide open, in which, as has been said, was the lion, who turned out to be of extraordinary size and of a frightful and hideous aspect.

The first thing he did was to roll over in the cage, where he had been lying, and put out his claw and stretch himself all over. Then he opened his mouth and yawned very slowly, and with nearly a foot and a half of tongue that he put out, he dusted his eyes and washed his face. That done, he put his head out of the cage and looked in every direction with eyes like live coals — a sight and a bearing to strike terror into rashness itself. Only Don Quixote was watching him attentively, longing for him to jump down from the cart at last and come to grips with him, between which he expected to tear him to pieces.

Up to this point went the extreme of his never-before-seen madness. But the generous lion, more well-bred than arrogant, taking no notice of childishness or of bravado, after looking one way and the other as has been said, turned his back and showed his hindquarters to Don Quixote, and with great coolness and calm went and lay down again in the cage. Which Don Quixote seeing, he ordered the lion-keeper to beat him with a stick and provoke him to bring him out.

"That I will not do," answered the lion-keeper, "because if I goad him, the first man he will tear to pieces will be myself. Let your worship, sir knight, be satisfied with what has been done — which is everything that can be said in the way of valour — and not try a second fortune. The lion has his door open: it is in his own hands to come out or not to come out; but since he has not come out so far, he will not come out all day. Your worship's greatness of heart is well enough declared: no brave fighter, as far as I understand it, is obliged to more than to challenge his enemy and wait for him in the field; and if his opponent does not turn up, the disgrace stays with him, and the man who waited wins the crown of victory."

"That is true," answered Don Quixote. "Shut the door, my friend, and give me a certificate, in the best form you can, of what you have seen me do here — namely, how you opened to the lion, I waited for him, he did not come out; I waited for him again, he again did not come out and went and lay down. I am obliged to no more; and enchantments be gone, and God help right and truth, and true chivalry. And shut the door, as I have said, while I make signs to the runaways and absentees, so that they may learn of this exploit from your own mouth."

The lion-keeper did so, and Don Quixote, putting on the point of his lance the cloth with which he had wiped his face after the shower of curds, began to call to those who had not stopped running and looking back at every step, all in a body with the gentleman at their head. But Sancho, happening to see the signal of the white cloth, said:

"May they kill me if my master has not beaten the savage beasts, since he is calling us."

They all stopped, and recognised that the man making the signals was Don Quixote; and, losing some part of their fear, little by little they came nearer until they could plainly hear Don Quixote's shouts as he called them. Finally they came back to the cart, and when they arrived Don Quixote said to the carter:

"Go back, brother, to yoking your mules and carrying on with your journey; and you, Sancho, give him two gold crowns, for him and for the lion-keeper, in recompense for the time they have been held up on my account."

"I shall give them very willingly," answered Sancho; "but what has become of the lions? Are they dead or alive?"

Then the lion-keeper, in detail and with his own pauses, told the end of the contest, exaggerating as best he could and knew how the valour of Don Quixote, at the sight of whom the lion, turned coward, would not and dared not come out of the cage, although the cage door had stood open for a good while; and how, because he had told that knight that it was tempting God to provoke the lion into coming out by force, as he wanted him provoked, he had — much against his own grain and against his whole will — allowed the door to be shut.

"What do you think of that, Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "Are there any enchantments that can prevail against true valour? The enchanters may well take my luck away from me, but my strength and my spirit will be impossible."

Sancho handed over the crowns, the carter yoked up, the lion-keeper kissed Don Quixote's hands for the bounty he had received, and promised him to tell that valorous exploit to the king himself when he found himself at court.

"Well, if His Majesty should happen to ask who did it, tell him it was the Knight of the Lions; for from now on I want the name I have had until now, of the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, to be traded, changed, turned and altered into this one. And in this I am following the ancient usage of knights errant, who changed their names whenever they liked, or whenever it suited them."

The cart went on its way, and Don Quixote, Sancho and the man in the Green Coat went on theirs.

In all this time Don Diego de Miranda had not spoken a word, being wholly intent on watching and noting Don Quixote's deeds and words, and thinking that he was a sane madman and a madman veering towards sane. The first part of his history had not yet come to his notice; for if he had read it, the astonishment his deeds and words put him into would have ceased, since he would already have known the kind of his madness. But as he did not know it, he took him now for sane and now for mad, because what he said was orderly, elegant and well put, and what he did was preposterous, foolhardy and stupid. And he said to himself:

"What greater madness can there be than putting on a helmet full of curds and giving oneself to understand that the enchanters were softening one's skull? And what greater rashness and absurdity than wanting to fight lions by main force?"

Out of these imaginings and out of this soliloquy he was drawn by Don Quixote, who said to him:

"Who doubts, Señor Don Diego de Miranda, that your worship holds me in your own opinion to be an absurd and mad man? And it would be no great wonder if it were so, because my works can bear witness to nothing else. Well, for all that, I should like your worship to notice that I am not so mad or so wanting as I must have seemed to you.

"A gallant knight makes a fine show in the eyes of his king, in the middle of a great square, driving his lance home with a happy stroke into a brave bull; a knight makes a fine show, armed in glittering arms, passing down the lists in cheerful jousts before the ladies; and all those knights make a fine show who in military exercises, or in what look like them, entertain and gladden and, if one may say so, honour the courts of their princes.

"But better than all these is the show made by a knight errant who, through the deserts, through the solitudes, through the crossroads, through the forests and over the mountains, goes about looking for dangerous adventures, meaning to bring them to a happy and well-fortuned end, and all only to win glorious and lasting fame. Better, I say, is the show made by a knight errant helping a widow in some unpeopled place than by a courtier knight paying compliments to a young lady in the cities.

"All knights have their particular exercises: let the courtier serve the ladies; let him give lustre to his king's court with liveries; let him keep poor knights going with the splendid dishes on his table; let him arrange jousts, hold tournaments and show himself great, generous and magnificent, and a good Christian above all — and in this way he will meet his exact obligations.

"But let the knight errant search out the corners of the world; let him get into the most tangled labyrinths; let him attempt the impossible at every step; let him endure on the unpeopled wastes the burning rays of the sun in the middle of summer, and in winter the hard inclemency of the winds and the frosts; let no lions dismay him, no phantoms frighten him, no monsters terrify him — since to look for these, to attack those and to conquer them all are his chief and truest exercises.

"I, then, since it fell to my lot to be one of the number of knight-errantry, cannot leave off attempting everything that seems to me to fall under the jurisdiction of my exercises; and so, attacking the lions I attacked just now was directly my business, even though I knew it was exorbitant rashness. Because I know very well what valour is: it is a virtue set between two vicious extremes, which are cowardice and rashness; but it will be less bad for the man who is brave to touch and rise to the point of rashness than for him to sink and touch the point of cowardice. For just as it is easier for the spendthrift to become generous than it is for the miser, so it is easier for the rash man to end in true bravery than for the coward to rise to true valour. And in this business of attempting adventures, believe me, your worship, Señor Don Diego: it is better to lose by a card too many than by a card too few, because it sounds better in the ears of those who hear it that 'such and such a knight is rash and daring' than that 'such and such a knight is timid and cowardly'."

"I say, Señor Don Quixote," answered Don Diego, "that everything your worship has said and done is levelled by the pointer of reason itself, and that in my view, if the ordinances and laws of knight-errantry were lost, they would be found in your worship's breast as in their own strongroom and archive. And let us hurry, for it is getting late, and let us reach my village and my house, where your worship will rest from the labour you have been through — which, if it has not been of the body, has been of the spirit, and that sometimes overflows into a weariness of the body."

"I take the offer as a great favour and kindness, Señor Don Diego," answered Don Quixote.

And, spurring on harder than they had until then, it must have been about two in the afternoon when they reached the village and the house of Don Diego, whom Don Quixote called the Knight of the Green Coat.

Chapter 18: Of What Happened to Don Quixote in the Castle or House of the Knight of the Green Coat, with Other Extravagant Matters

Don Quixote found Don Diego de Miranda's house to be roomy, in the village way; the coat of arms, though of rough stone, over the street door; the wine-store in the courtyard; the cellar under the entry, and a great many earthenware jars standing round it — which, being from El Toboso, brought back to him the memory of his enchanted and transformed Dulcinea. And sighing, and without looking at what he was saying or at whose presence he was in, he said:

	O sweet tokens, found to my sorrow,
	sweet and joyful when God was willing!

"O Tobosan jars, you have brought back to my memory the sweet token of my greatest bitterness!"

The student poet, Don Diego's son, heard him say this, having come out with his mother to receive him; and mother and son were left astonished at the sight of Don Quixote's strange figure. And Don Quixote, dismounting from Rocinante, went with great courtesy to ask for her hands to kiss them, and Don Diego said:

"Receive, my lady, with your usual graciousness, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, who is the man you have before you: a knight errant, and the bravest and the most judicious the world has."
