The lady, who was called Doña Cristina, received him with signs of much affection and much courtesy, and Don Quixote offered himself to her service in quite enough judicious and well-turned phrases. Almost the same civilities passed with the student, who, on hearing Don Quixote speak, took him for a judicious and sharp-witted man.

Here the author paints all the circumstances of Don Diego's house, painting for us in them what a rich farming gentleman's house contains; but the translator of this history thought it best to pass over these and other such small details in silence, because they did not fit well with the main purpose of the history, which has more of its force in the truth than in cold digressions.

They brought Don Quixote into a hall, Sancho unarmed him, and he was left in his wide breeches and a chamois doublet, all greasy with the grime of his armour. His collar was a plain student's falling band, without starch and without lace; his buskins were date-coloured and his shoes were waxed. He belted on his good sword, which hung from a baldric of sealskin — for it is held that he was for many years troubled with his kidneys; he threw on a short cloak of good grey cloth. But before all this, with five buckets of water, or six — for on the number of buckets there is some difference of opinion — he washed his head and face, and even so the water was left the colour of whey, thanks to Sancho's greediness and to the buying of those black curds of his that turned his master so white.

With the said finery, and with a graceful, gallant air, Don Quixote went out into another hall, where the student was waiting for him to entertain him while the tables were being laid; for on the coming of so noble a guest the lady Doña Cristina wanted to show that she knew how, and was able, to make much of those who came to her house.

While Don Quixote was being unarmed, Don Lorenzo — for that was the name of Don Diego's son — had the chance to say to his father:

"What are we to say this knight is, sir, that your worship has brought home to us? For his name, his figure and his saying that he is a knight errant have my mother and me astonished."

"I do not know what to tell you, my son," answered Don Diego. "All I shall know how to say to you is that I have seen him do things belonging to the greatest madman in the world, and say things so judicious that they rub out and undo his deeds. Talk to him yourself and feel the pulse of what he knows; and, since you are judicious, judge of his good sense or his silliness whichever seems most reasonable — although, to tell the truth, I take him for mad rather than sane."

With this Don Lorenzo went to entertain Don Quixote, as has been said; and, among other talk that passed between the two of them, Don Quixote said to Don Lorenzo:

"Señor Don Diego de Miranda, your worship's father, has given me notice of the rare ability and subtle intelligence your worship has, and, above all, that your worship is a great poet."

"A poet, that may well be," answered Don Lorenzo, "but great, not by any stretch of thought. It is true that I am somewhat fond of poetry and of reading the good poets, but not in such a way that I can be given the name of great, as my father says."

"That modesty does not strike me badly," answered Don Quixote, "because there is no poet who is not arrogant and does not think of himself that he is the greatest poet in the world."

"There is no rule without an exception," answered Don Lorenzo, "and there will be somebody who is one and does not think so."

"Few," answered Don Quixote. "But tell me, your worship: what verses are these you have in hand at the moment, that your father tells me are making you somewhat restless and thoughtful? And if it is some gloss, I understand something in the matter of glosses, and I should be glad to hear them; and if they are for a literary competition, let your worship try to carry off the second prize, because the first is always carried off by favour or by the great rank of the person, the second is carried off by plain justice, and the third comes to be the second, and the first, on this reckoning, will be the third — after the manner of the degrees they give in the universities. But for all that, the name of first is a great personage."

"So far," Don Lorenzo said to himself, "I shall not be able to judge you a madman. Let us go on."

And he said to him:

"It seems to me that your worship has been through the schools: what sciences have you attended?"

"That of knight-errantry," answered Don Quixote, "which is as good as that of poetry, and a couple of finger-widths better."

"I do not know what science that may be," replied Don Lorenzo, "and up to now it has not come to my notice."

"It is a science," replied Don Quixote, "that shuts up in itself all the sciences in the world, or most of them — on the grounds that the man who professes it has to be a jurist, and know the laws of distributive and commutative justice, so as to give each man what is his and what belongs to him; he has to be a theologian, so as to know how to give an account of the Christian law he professes, clearly and distinctly, wherever he may be asked for it; he has to be a physician, and chiefly a herbalist, so as to recognise in the middle of unpeopled places and deserts the herbs that have the virtue of healing wounds, since the knight errant cannot go looking at every turn for somebody to cure them for him; he has to be an astronomer, so as to know by the stars how many hours of the night have gone by, and in what part and in what climate of the world he finds himself; he has to know mathematics, because at every step he will find himself needing them.

"And, leaving aside that he has to be adorned with all the theological and cardinal virtues and coming down to other small matters, I say that he has to know how to swim as they say the fish Nicholas swam; he has to know how to shoe a horse and to mend a saddle and a bridle. And, coming back to what was said above, he has to keep faith with God and with his lady; he has to be chaste in his thoughts, decent in his words, generous in his works, valiant in his deeds, patient in hardships, charitable to the needy, and, finally, an upholder of the truth, though defending it should cost him his life.

"Of all these great and least parts a good knight errant is made up. So let your worship see, Señor Don Lorenzo, whether it is a snivelling science that the knight learns who studies it and professes it, and whether it can be set level with the loftiest ones taught in the colleges and the schools."

"If that is so," replied Don Lorenzo, "I say that this science has the advantage over all of them."

"What do you mean, if it is so?" answered Don Quixote.

"What I mean to say," said Don Lorenzo, "is that I doubt whether there have been, or whether there are now, knights errant adorned with so many virtues."

"Many times I have said what I say again now," answered Don Quixote: "that the greater part of the people of the world are of the opinion that there have never been knights errant in it. And since it seems to me that unless heaven miraculously gives them to understand the truth that there were such men and that there are such men, any labour a man takes on must be in vain — as experience has shown me many times — I do not want to stop now to draw your worship out of the error you share with the many. What I mean to do is to pray heaven to draw you out of it, and to give you to understand how profitable and how necessary knights errant were to the world in the past ages, and how useful they would be in the present if they were in use. But what triumph now, for the sins of the people, are sloth, idleness, gluttony and self-indulgence."

"Our guest has got away from us," Don Lorenzo said to himself at this. "But for all that, he is a splendid madman, and I should be a slack-witted fool if I did not believe so."

Here they made an end of their talk, because they were called to dinner. Don Diego asked his son what he had got clear about the guest's wits; to which he answered:

"All the doctors and good clerks in the world will not get him out of the rough draft of his madness: he is a streaky madman, full of lucid intervals."

They went in to dinner, and the dinner was such as Don Diego had said on the road that he generally gave his guests: clean, plentiful and tasty. But what most contented Don Quixote was the marvellous silence there was throughout the house, which was like a Carthusian monastery.

The cloth being taken away, then, and thanks given to God and water given for the hands, Don Quixote pressed Don Lorenzo hard to say the verses for the literary competition; to which he answered that, so as not to look like one of those poets who refuse their verses when they are begged for them and vomit them up when nobody asks —

"— I shall say my gloss, for which I expect no prize at all, since I made it only to exercise my wits."

"A judicious friend of mine," answered Don Quixote, "was of the opinion that nobody ought to wear himself out glossing verses; and the reason, he said, was that the gloss could never come up to the text, and that many times, or most times, the gloss went wide of the intention and purpose of what the glossed lines called for; and, what is more, that the laws of the gloss were excessively narrow, since they allow no questions, no 'said he' and no 'shall I say', no turning verbs into nouns, no shifting of the sense, along with other bindings and tightnesses that those who gloss go tied up in — as your worship must know."

"Truly, Señor Don Quixote," said Don Lorenzo, "I keep wanting to catch your worship out in one sustained piece of bad Latin, and I cannot, because you slip out of my hands like an eel."

"I do not understand," answered Don Quixote, "what your worship says or means to say in that about my slipping."

"I shall make myself understood," answered Don Lorenzo; "and for the moment let your worship be attentive to the glossed verses and to the gloss, which go in this way:

	If only my "was" turned back into "is,"
	without waiting for more "will be" —
	or if the time would come already
	of what is to be hereafter!

Gloss

	In the end, since everything passes,
	the good that Fortune gave me passed —
	Fortune, no niggard at that time —
	and she never gave it back to me,
	neither in plenty nor by measure.
	Centuries now you have seen me,
	Fortune, laid here at your feet;
	turn me back into a lucky man,
	for my being will be a happy one
	if only my "was" turned back into "is."
	I want no other pleasure or glory,
	no other palm or conquest,
	no other triumph, no other victory,
	but to go back to that contentment
	which is a grief in my memory.
	If you take me back there,
	Fortune, then all the fierceness
	of my fire is tempered —
	and the more so if this good comes at once,
	without waiting for more "will be."
	I am asking for impossible things,
	since to make time be again
	after it has once been
	is a thing no power on earth
	has ever stretched itself so far as.
	Time runs, it flies, it goes
	light-footed, and it will not come back,
	and he would be wrong who asked
	either that the time were gone already
	or that the time would come back already.
	I live a perplexed life,
	now hoping, now fearing:
	it is a death I know well,
	and it is far better, by dying,
	to look for a way out of the pain.
	It would be to my own advantage
	to make an end; but it is not,
	since, by better reasoning,
	what keeps me alive is the fear
	of what is to be hereafter.

When Don Lorenzo had finished saying his gloss, Don Quixote stood up, and in a raised voice that was more like a shout, gripping Don Lorenzo's right hand in his own, said:

"By the highest heavens there are, generous young man, you are the best poet in the world, and you deserve to be crowned with laurel, not by Cyprus or by Gaeta, as a certain poet said, God forgive him, but by the academies of Athens, if they were alive today, and by those that are alive today in Paris, Bologna and Salamanca! May it please heaven that the judges who take the first prize from you should be shot through by Phoebus, and that the Muses should never cross the thresholds of their houses. Say me some longer verses, sir, if you will be so good; for I want to take the whole pulse of your admirable wit from end to end."

Is it not a fine thing that they say Don Lorenzo was pleased at hearing himself praised by Don Quixote, even though he took him for mad? O power of flattery, how far you stretch, and how wide are the limits of your agreeable jurisdiction! Don Lorenzo bore this truth out, since he agreed to Don Quixote's request and wish, saying him this sonnet on the fable or history of Pyramus and Thisbe:

Sonnet

	The beautiful maiden breaks the wall
	that opened the gallant breast of Pyramus:
	Love sets out from Cyprus and goes straight
	to see the narrow and prodigious crack.
	Silence speaks there, because the voice
	does not dare go in by so narrow a narrows;
	but souls do — for love is used, in fact,
	to making easy the most difficult thing.
	Desire went out of all measure, and the step
	of the imprudent girl solicits,
	for her own pleasure, her own death: see what a story —
	that both of them in one instant, oh strange case,
	are killed, are hidden and are brought back to life
	by one sword, one tomb, one memory.

"Blessed be God!" said Don Quixote, having heard Don Lorenzo's sonnet, "that among the infinite consumptive poets there are, I have seen one consummate poet, as your worship is, my dear sir; which is what the workmanship of this sonnet gives me to understand."

Four days Don Quixote spent, most royally entertained, in Don Diego's house, at the end of which he asked leave to go, telling him that he thanked him for the kindness and good treatment he had received in his house; but that, since it did not look well for knights errant to give many hours to leisure and comfort, he wanted to go and fulfil his office by looking for the adventures that he was informed that country abounded in, where he hoped to pass the time until the day of the jousts at Saragossa came, which was the straight line of his course. And that first he had to go into the cave of Montesinos, of which so many and such wonderful things were told in those parts, finding out and inquiring at the same time about the birth and true springs of the seven lagoons commonly called the Lagoons of Ruidera.

Don Diego and his son praised his honourable determination, and told him to take from their house and their estate anything that suited him, for they would serve him with all possible good will, since the worth of his person and his honourable profession obliged them to it.

The day of his departure came at last, as glad for Don Quixote as it was sad and ill-starred for Sancho Panza, who found himself very well off with the abundance of Don Diego's house and refused to go back to the hunger that is customary in the woods and the unpeopled places, and to the tightness of his badly provided saddlebags. So he filled them and heaped them up with the most necessary things he could think of; and on taking his leave Don Quixote said to Don Lorenzo:

"I do not know whether I have told your worship before, and if I have told you I say it again: that whenever your worship wants to save roads and labour in reaching the inaccessible summit of the temple of Fame, you have nothing else to do but to leave the path of poetry to one side, which is somewhat narrow, and take the very narrowest one of knight-errantry, which is enough to make you an emperor in the time it takes to say so."

With these arguments Don Quixote finished closing the case for his madness, and still more with the ones he added, saying:

"God knows whether I should like to take Señor Don Lorenzo with me, to teach him how the humble are to be pardoned and the proud trampled and put underfoot — virtues attached to the profession I profess. But since his few years do not call for it, and his praiseworthy exercises will not want to allow it, I content myself only with pointing out to your worship that, being a poet, you will be able to be famous if you are guided more by other people's opinion than by your own; because there is no father or mother to whom their own children look ugly, and in the children of the understanding this deception runs stronger still."

Father and son marvelled afresh at Don Quixote's interlarded speeches, now judicious and now preposterous, and at the theme and the doggedness with which he kept to going out at all costs in search of his unfortunate adventures, which he held to be the end and the target of his desires. The offers and civilities were repeated, and, with the good leave of the lady of the castle, Don Quixote and Sancho set off on Rocinante and the grey.

Chapter 19: Where the Adventure of the Lovesick Shepherd Is Told, with Other Truly Amusing Events

Don Quixote had gone only a short stretch away from Don Diego's village when he came upon two men who looked like priests or like students, and two farm labourers, all four mounted on donkeys. One of the students was carrying, done up in a piece of green buckram like a portmanteau, what looked like a little white cloth and two pairs of ribbed woollen stockings; the other was carrying nothing but two blunt fencing swords, new, with their buttons on. The labourers were carrying other things which gave a sign and an indication that they were coming from some large town where they had bought them, and were taking them home to their village.

And students and labourers alike fell into the same astonishment that everybody fell into who saw Don Quixote for the first time, and they were dying to know what sort of man this was, so far outside the use of other men.

Don Quixote greeted them, and, after learning the road they were taking, which was the same one he was making, he offered them his company and asked them to hold back their pace, because their she-donkeys walked faster than his horse. And, to oblige them, in a few words he told them who he was, and his office and profession, which was that of a knight errant who went about looking for adventures in all the parts of the world. He told them that his own name was Don Quixote of La Mancha, and his by-name the Knight of the Lions.

All this, for the labourers, was talking to them in Greek or in thieves' cant; but not for the students, who saw at once the weakness of Don Quixote's brain. Even so, they looked at him with wonder and with respect, and one of them said to him:

"If your worship, sir knight, is not taking any settled road — as those who look for adventures generally do not — let your worship come along with us: you will see one of the best and richest weddings that has been celebrated to this day in La Mancha, or for a great many leagues round about it."

Don Quixote asked him whether it was some prince's, that he made so much of it.

"It is not," answered the student, "but a farmer's and a farmer's daughter's: he the richest in all this country, and she the most beautiful that men have seen. The show they are to be made with is out of the ordinary and new, because they are to be celebrated in a meadow next to the bride's village — she is called, by way of eminence, Quiteria the Beautiful, and the bridegroom is called Camacho the Rich. She is eighteen years old and he twenty-two; both a match for each other, although some inquisitive people who have all the world's pedigrees by heart will have it that beautiful Quiteria's family is a step above Camacho's. But nobody looks at that any more, since riches have the power to solder over a great many cracks.

"In fact this Camacho is open-handed, and he has taken a fancy to roofing over the whole meadow with branches, in such a way that the sun will have his work cut out if he wants to come in and visit the green grass the ground is covered with. He has also got up dances, both sword dances and little-bell dances, since there are men in his village who can ring them and shake them out to perfection; of clog-dancers I say nothing, for the crowd of them he has mustered is a judgement. But none of the things I have mentioned, nor a great many others I have left unmentioned, will make this wedding more memorable than what I imagine the despairing Basilio will do at it.

"This Basilio is a young fellow from the same place as Quiteria, whose house stood a wall and a half from the house of Quiteria's parents — from which love took the occasion to make the world over again the by now forgotten loves of Pyramus and Thisbe. Because Basilio fell in love with Quiteria from his tender first years, and she went on answering his desire with a thousand honourable favours, so much so that the loves of the two children Basilio and Quiteria were told as an entertainment in the village.

"Their years went on growing, and Quiteria's father decided to block Basilio's ordinary entry into his house; and, to save himself from going about wary and full of suspicions, he arranged to marry his daughter to the rich Camacho, since it did not seem to him a good thing to marry her to Basilio, who did not have as many of fortune's goods as he had of nature's. For if the truth is to be told without envy, he is the nimblest young man we know: a great thrower of the bar, an outstanding wrestler and a great pelota player; he runs like a fallow deer, jumps better than a goat and knocks down the skittles as if by enchantment; he sings like a lark and plays a guitar until he makes it talk, and, above all, he handles a sword with the best of them."

"For that one accomplishment alone," said Don Quixote at this point, "that young man would deserve to marry not merely the beautiful Quiteria but Queen Guinevere herself, if she were alive today, in spite of Lancelot and of all those who might want to prevent it."

"Try that on my wife!" said Sancho Panza, who up to then had been going along silent and listening. "She will have nothing but that everybody should marry his equal, holding to the proverb that says 'every ewe to her own mate'. What I should like is that this good Basilio, whom I am beginning to take a fancy to, should marry that lady Quiteria; and may they have a good long life and a good rest — I was going to say it the other way round — those who stop the marriage of people who love each other well."

"If all those who love each other well had to marry," said Don Quixote, "the choice and jurisdiction of marrying their children to whom and when they should would be taken away from parents. And if the choosing of husbands were left to the will of daughters, there would be one who would choose her father's servant, and one who would choose a man she saw going past in the street and thought dashing and well set up, even if he were a broken-down swashbuckler. For love and fondness easily blind the eyes of the understanding, which are so necessary for choosing one's state; and the state of matrimony is in great danger of being got wrong, and it needs great care and a particular favour from heaven to get it right.

"A man means to take a long journey, and if he is prudent, before setting out he looks for some safe and agreeable company to travel with. Well then, why should not the same be done by the man who has to travel all his life, right to the stopping-place of death — and the more so if the company is to keep him company in bed, at table and everywhere, as a wife's does her husband's? A man's own wife is not merchandise that, once bought, can be given back or traded or exchanged, because she is an inseparable accident that lasts as long as life lasts: she is a noose that, once you have put it round your neck, turns into the Gordian knot, and unless death's scythe cuts it there is no untying it. A great many more things I could say on this matter, if I were not stopped by my wish to know whether the licentiate has anything more to say about Basilio's history."

To which the bachelor student — or licentiate, as Don Quixote had called him — answered:

"Of the whole business I have nothing more to say except that from the moment Basilio learned that the beautiful Quiteria was marrying Camacho the Rich, nobody has ever seen him laugh again or say a sensible word, and he goes about always thoughtful and sad, talking to himself, by which he gives certain and clear signs that his wits have turned. He eats little and sleeps little, and what he eats is fruit, and where he sleeps, if he sleeps, is out in the fields on the hard ground, like a brute animal. Every now and then he looks at the sky, and other times he fixes his eyes on the ground with such a trance on him that he looks like nothing but a dressed statue whose clothes are moved by the air. In short, he gives such signs of having a heart in torment that all of us who know him are afraid that beautiful Quiteria's saying yes tomorrow will be the sentence of his death."

"God will manage it better," said Sancho. "For God, who gives the wound, gives the medicine. Nobody knows what is to come: between now and tomorrow there are a great many hours, and in one of them, and even in a moment, a house falls down. I have seen it rain and shine at one and the same instant; a man goes to bed healthy at night and cannot move the next day. And tell me: is there by any chance anybody who can boast that he has driven a nail into Fortune's wheel? Certainly not. And between a woman's yes and her no I would not dare to put the point of a pin, because it would not fit. Only give me Quiteria loving Basilio with a good heart and a good will, and I shall give him a sackful of good luck; for love, as I have heard it said, looks through a pair of spectacles that make copper seem gold, poverty riches and gummy eyes pearls."

"Where are you going to end up, Sancho, curse you?" said Don Quixote. "When you start threading proverbs and tales together, there is nobody who can wait for you but Judas himself, and may he carry you off. Tell me, animal, what do you know about nails, or wheels, or anything else at all?"

"Oh! Well, if they do not understand me," answered Sancho, "it is no wonder that my judgements are taken for nonsense. But it does not matter: I understand myself, and I know I have not said many foolish things in what I have said. It is only that your worship, my dear sir, is always the persecutor of my sayings, and even of my doings."

"Prosecutor you should say," said Don Quixote, "and not persecutor, you perverter of good language, and God confound you."

"Do not go setting on me, your worship," answered Sancho, "since you know I was not brought up at Court and have not studied at Salamanca, so as to know whether I am adding or taking away a letter from my words. Why, God bless me, there is no call to oblige a man from the back country to talk like a man of Toledo; and there may be men of Toledo who are no great hands at this business of polished speech either."

"That is so," said the licentiate, "because those who are brought up in the Tanneries and in the Zocodover market cannot speak as well as those who walk up and down almost all day in the cloister of the cathedral, and they are all men of Toledo. Pure language, proper, elegant and clear, is found in judicious men of the court, even though they were born in Majalahonda. I said judicious, because there are many who are not; and judiciousness is the grammar of good language, which goes along with usage. I, gentlemen, for my sins, have studied canon law at Salamanca, and I pride myself a little on saying what I mean in clear, plain, meaningful words."

"If you did not pride yourself more on knowing how to wave about those black swords you are carrying than on your tongue," said the other student, "you would have come out first in your licentiate examinations instead of coming out last."

"Look here, bachelor," answered the licentiate, "you hold the most mistaken opinion in the world about swordsmanship, in taking it for an empty thing."

"For me it is not an opinion but a settled truth," replied Corchuelo. "And if you want me to show you so by experience, you have the swords, there is room, I have wrists and strength, which, backed by my spirit — and that is not small — will make you confess that I am not deceiving myself. Get down and use your footwork and your circles and your angles and your science; for I expect to make you see stars at midday with my modern, clumsy skill, in which, after God, I trust that the man is still to be born who will make me turn my back, and that there is nobody in the world I cannot make give ground."

"As to turning your back or not, I do not go into that," replied the fencer. "Though it might well be that in the very place where you first planted your foot, there they would dig your grave — I mean that you would be left dead there by the swordsmanship you despise."

"We shall see about that now," answered Corchuelo.

And, getting off his donkey with great quickness, he furiously snatched one of the swords the licentiate was carrying on his.

"It must not be like this," said Don Quixote at this instant, "for I mean to be the master of this fencing bout and the judge of this many times unsettled question."

And, dismounting from Rocinante and gripping his lance, he planted himself in the middle of the road, just as the licentiate, with a graceful carriage of his body and neat footwork, was going at Corchuelo, who came at him throwing, as the saying goes, fire out of his eyes. The other two labourers of the party, without getting down off their donkeys, served as spectators of the mortal tragedy.

The slashes, thrusts, downstrokes, backhands and two-handed cuts that Corchuelo let fly were beyond counting: thicker than liver and finer than hail. He charged like an angry lion, but out to meet him would come a shut-your-mouth from the button of the licentiate's sword, which stopped him in the middle of his fury and made him kiss it as if it were a relic — though not with as much devotion as relics ought to be and generally are kissed.

Finally the licentiate counted him out, thrust by thrust, all the buttons of a short cassock he was wearing, making ribbons of its skirts like octopus tails; he knocked his hat off twice, and wore him out to such a degree that out of spite, choler and rage Corchuelo seized the sword by the hilt and flung it through the air with such force that one of the labourers there, who was a notary, went after it and afterwards gave it in his official testimony that he had thrown it nearly three-quarters of a league from himself — which testimony serves and has served to make it known and seen in all truth how force is beaten by art.

Corchuelo sat down, tired out, and Sancho, coming up to him, said:

"Upon my faith, master bachelor, if your worship takes my advice, from now on you should not challenge anybody to fence, but to wrestle or to throw the bar, since you have the years and the strength for it. Because of these men they call fencers, I have heard it said that they will put the point of a sword through the eye of a needle."

"I am content," answered Corchuelo, "to have fallen off my donkey, and to have had experience show me the truth I was so far from."

And, getting up, he embraced the licentiate, and they were left better friends than before; and, not wanting to wait for the notary, who had gone after the sword, since it seemed to them he would be a long time, they decided to go on, so as to get early to Quiteria's village, which was where they all came from.

For what was left of the road, the licentiate went on telling them about the excellences of the sword, with so many demonstrative arguments and so many mathematical figures and demonstrations that they were all convinced of the goodness of the science, and Corchuelo was brought round from his obstinacy.

Night had fallen; but before they arrived it seemed to all of them that there was a sky full of innumerable shining stars in front of the village. They also heard confused, soft sounds of various instruments — flutes, little drums, psalteries, pipes, tabors and jingles. And when they got near they saw that the trees of an arbour that had been set up by hand at the entrance to the village were all full of lamps, which the wind did not trouble, for it was not blowing then but so gently that it had no strength to move the leaves of the trees.

The musicians were the merrymakers of the wedding, who were going about that pleasant place in various parties, some dancing, others singing and others playing the diversity of the instruments already named. In fact it looked like nothing but gladness running and contentment leaping all over that meadow.

A great many others were busy putting up stands from which, the next day, they could conveniently see the plays and dances that were to be performed in that place set aside for solemnising the wedding of Camacho the Rich and the funeral rites of Basilio. Don Quixote would not go into the place, though both the labourer and the bachelor asked him to; but he gave as his excuse, sufficient enough in his own view, that it was the custom of knights errant to sleep in the fields and the woods rather than in inhabited places, even under gilded roofs. And with this he turned a little off the road, much against Sancho's will, the memory coming back to him of the good lodging he had had in Don Diego's castle or house.

Chapter 20: Where the Wedding of Camacho the Rich Is Told, with What Happened to Basilio the Poor

Hardly had the white dawn given shining Phoebus room to dry the liquid pearls out of her golden hair with the heat of his warm rays, when Don Quixote, shaking the sloth out of his limbs, got to his feet and called his squire Sancho, who was still snoring. Which Don Quixote seeing, before he woke him he said to him:

"O you, more blessed than any who live on the face of the earth, since without envying or being envied you sleep with a quiet spirit, and no enchanters persecute you and no enchantments startle you! Sleep, I say again, and I shall say it another hundred times, with no jealousy over your lady keeping you in perpetual watchfulness, and no thought of paying the debts you owe keeping you awake, nor of what you must do to feed yourself and your small, distressed family tomorrow.

"Ambition does not disturb you, and the vain pomp of the world does not tire you, since the limits of your desires do not stretch any further than to thinking about your donkey — for the thinking about your person you have laid on my shoulders: a counterweight and a load that nature and custom have laid on masters. The servant sleeps and the master lies awake, thinking how he is to keep him, better him and do him favours. The anguish of seeing the sky turn to bronze and not come to the earth with the dew it needs does not afflict the servant but the master, who must keep in barrenness and hunger the man who served him in fertility and abundance."

To all this Sancho made no answer, because he was asleep, nor would he have woken up so soon if Don Quixote had not brought him round with the butt of his lance. He woke at last, sleepy and lazy, and, turning his face in every direction, said:

"From over by that arbour, if I am not mistaken, there comes a whiff and a smell a great deal more of grilled bacon than of rushes and thyme. Weddings that begin with smells like that, by my blessed self, must be plentiful and open-handed ones."

"Have done, glutton," said Don Quixote. "Come, we shall go and see this wedding, to see what the scorned Basilio does."

"Let him do whatever he likes," answered Sancho. "He should not have been poor, and then he would have married Quiteria. Is there nothing more to it than having not a farthing and wanting to raise yourself up above the clouds? Upon my word, sir, I am of the opinion that a poor man should be content with what he finds, and not go asking for oysters up a tree.

"I would bet an arm that Camacho could bury Basilio in silver; and if that is so, as it must be, Quiteria would be a great fool to throw away the finery and the jewels Camacho must have given her and can still give her, and choose instead Basilio's bar-throwing and his play with the black sword. They will not give you a quarter-pint of wine in the tavern for a good throw of the bar or a fine pass with a sword. Talents and gifts that are not saleable — let Count Dirlos have them and welcome; but when such gifts fall on a man who has good money, may my life be as good as they look. On a good foundation you can raise a good building, and the best foundation and trench in the world is money."

"For God's sake, Sancho," said Don Quixote at this, "make an end of your harangue. It is my belief that if you were let go on with the ones you start at every step, you would have no time left for eating or for sleeping, since you would spend it all in talking."

"If your worship had a good memory," replied Sancho, "you would remember the articles of our agreement before we came out of the house this last time. One of them was that you were to let me talk as much as I liked, so long as it was not against my neighbour or against your worship's authority; and up to now I do not think I have gone against that article."

"I do not remember, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "any such article. And granting that it is so, I want you to be quiet and to come along; for the instruments we heard last night are beginning to gladden the valleys again, and no doubt the wedding will be celebrated in the cool of the morning and not in the heat of the afternoon."

Sancho did as his master ordered him, and, putting the saddle on Rocinante and the pack-saddle on the grey, the two of them mounted and went at a walking pace in under the arbour.

The first thing that offered itself to Sancho's sight was a whole young bullock spitted on a whole elm tree; and in the fire where it was to be roasted a middling mountain of wood was burning. Six pots that stood round the bonfire had not been cast in the common mould of the rest of the world's pots, because they were six half-jars, each one of which would hold a whole slaughterhouse of meat: they soaked up and shut inside themselves whole sheep without its showing, as though they were pigeons. The skinned hares and the plucked hens hanging from the trees to be buried in the pots were beyond number; the birds and game of various sorts were infinite, hanging from the trees so that the air could cool them.

Sancho counted more than sixty wineskins of over sixteen gallons each, and all of them full, as it later turned out, of generous wines. There were stacks of the whitest bread, like the heaps of wheat there generally are on the threshing floors; the cheeses, laid up like lattice-work bricks, made a wall; and two cauldrons of oil, bigger than a dyer's, served for frying things of batter, which they lifted out fried with two stout paddles and plunged into another cauldron of prepared honey that stood alongside.

The cooks, men and women, came to more than fifty: all clean, all busy and all contented. In the swollen belly of the bullock were twelve tender little sucking pigs, sewn up inside, which served to give it flavour and make it tender. The spices of various kinds looked as though they had been bought not by the pound but by the hundredweight, and they were all on show in a great chest. In short, the show made by the wedding was rustic, but so abundant that it could have fed an army.

Sancho Panza looked at it all and contemplated it all and took a fancy to it all. First the pots captured and conquered his desire, out of which he would very willingly have taken a middling stewpot; then the wineskins won over his good will; and last of all the fritters, if such round-bellied cauldrons could be called frying pans. And so, unable to bear it and unable to help himself, he went up to one of the busy cooks and, with courteous and hungry words, begged him to let him dip a crust of bread in one of those pots. To which the cook answered:

"Brother, this day is not one of those over which hunger has any jurisdiction, thanks to the rich Camacho. Get down and see whether there is a ladle about, and skim off a hen or two, and much good may it do you."

"I do not see one," answered Sancho.

"Wait," said the cook. "Sinner that I am, what a squeamish, useless creature you must be!"

And saying this he seized a small cauldron, and, plunging it into one of the half-jars, brought up in it three hens and two geese, and said to Sancho:

"Eat, my friend, and breakfast on this skimming while the dinner hour comes round."

"I have nothing to put it in," answered Sancho.

"Then take the ladle and all," said the cook; "Camacho's riches and Camacho's contentment make up for everything."

While this was happening to Sancho, then, Don Quixote was watching some twelve labourers coming in at one side of the arbour on twelve most beautiful mares, with rich and showy country harness and a great many little bells on their breast-bands, all dressed in their merrymaking and holiday clothes. In an ordered troop they ran not one but a great many courses across the meadow, with a merry uproar and shouting, calling out:

"Long live Camacho and Quiteria: he as rich as she is beautiful, and she the most beautiful in the world!"

Which Don Quixote hearing, he said to himself:

"It is plain enough that these men have never seen my Dulcinea of El Toboso, because if they had seen her they would hold their hands in praising this Quiteria of theirs."

A little after that, many and various dances began to come in at different parts of the arbour, among them a sword dance of some twenty-four young men of gallant looks and spirit, all dressed in fine, very white linen with their head-cloths worked in various colours of fine silk. And one of the men on the mares asked the young fellow leading them, who was a nimble lad, whether any of the dancers had been wounded.

"So far, blessed be God, nobody has been wounded: we are all going sound."

And at once he began to weave in and out with the rest of his companions, with so many turns and so much skill that, although Don Quixote was used to seeing dances of the sort, none had ever pleased him as much as that one.

He was also pleased by another that came in, of the most beautiful girls, so young that to look at them none was under fourteen or over eighteen, all dressed in fine green cloth, their hair partly braided and partly loose, but all of it so fair that it could have competed with the sun's; and over it they wore garlands made up of jasmine, roses, amaranth and honeysuckle. A venerable old man and an elderly matron led them, but nimbler and more loose-limbed than their years promised. A Zamoran bagpipe made the music for them; and they, carrying decency in their faces and their eyes and nimbleness in their feet, showed themselves the best dancers in the world.

After this one came in another dance, one of the contrived sort and of those they call spoken dances. It was of eight nymphs, divided into two files. Of one file the god Cupid was the leader, and of the other Self-Interest — Cupid decked out with wings, bow, quiver and arrows, Self-Interest dressed in rich and various colours of gold and silk.

The nymphs who followed Love carried their names written on their backs on white parchment in large letters: the title of the first was poetry, that of the second good sense, that of the third good birth and that of the fourth valour. In the same way those who followed Self-Interest came labelled: the title of the first said liberality, that of the second largesse, that of the third treasure and that of the fourth peaceful possession.

In front of them all came a wooden castle drawn by four wild men, all dressed in ivy and in hemp dyed green, so much to the life that they came near frightening Sancho. On the front of the castle and on all four sides of it was written: the castle of modesty. Four skilled players of the tabor and pipe made the music for them.

Cupid began the dance, and, having made two figures, he raised his eyes and drew his bow at a girl who placed herself between the battlements of the castle, to whom he spoke in this way:

	I am the god who is powerful
	in the air and on the earth
	and in the wide and billowing sea,
	and in everything the abyss shuts up
	in its terrifying pit.
	I have never known what fear is;
	whatever I want, I can do,
	even when I want the impossible,
	and in everything that is possible
	I command, take away, set up and forbid.

He finished the stanza, shot an arrow over the top of the castle and withdrew to his place. Then Self-Interest came out and made two more figures; the little drums fell silent, and he said:

	I am the one who can do more than Love,
	and it is Love who guides me;
	I am of the best stock
	that heaven breeds on earth,
	the best known and the greatest.
	I am Self-Interest, in whom
	few are used to doing well,
	and to do anything without me is a great miracle;
	and such as I am, I consecrate myself to you
	for ever and ever, amen.

Self-Interest withdrew and Poetry came forward, who, after making her figures like the rest, fixed her eyes on the girl on the castle and said:

	In the sweetest of conceits,
	the sweetest Poetry,
	lofty, grave and judicious,
	sends you her soul, my lady,
	wrapped up in a thousand sonnets.
	If my insistence does not
	trouble you, then your fortune,
	envied by a great many others,
	will be lifted up by me
	above the circle of the moon.

Poetry moved off, and from Self-Interest's side came Liberality, and, having made her figures, said:

	They give the name of Liberality
	to the giving that runs from the extreme
	of prodigality,
	and from the opposite one, which argues
	a lukewarm and slack will.
	But I, to make you great,
	mean from today on to be prodigal;
	for though it is a vice, it is an honourable vice
	and the vice of a heart in love,
	which shows itself in giving.

In this way all the figures of the two squadrons came out and withdrew, and each one made his figures and said his verses, some of them elegant and some of them ridiculous; and Don Quixote took down by heart — and his memory was a great one — only the ones already given. Then they all mixed together, making and unmaking knots with graceful ease and freedom; and when Love went past in front of the castle he shot his arrows over the top, but Self-Interest broke gilded money-pots against it.

Finally, after they had danced a good while, Self-Interest brought out a large purse made from the skin of a great tabby cat, which looked as if it were full of money, and, throwing it at the castle, the boards were knocked out of their sockets with the blow and fell down, leaving the girl uncovered and without any defence at all. Self-Interest came up with the figures of his party, and, throwing a great gold chain round her neck, they made a show of seizing her, conquering her and carrying her off captive. Which Love and his supporters seeing, they made as if to take her from him; and all the demonstrations they made were in time to the little drums, dancing and stepping in order. The wild men made peace between them, who with great quickness set the boards of the castle up and fitted them together again, and the girl shut herself up in it as before; and with this the dance ended, to the great contentment of those who were watching it.

Don Quixote asked one of the nymphs who had composed and arranged it. She answered that it was a beneficed priest of that village, who had a fine head for inventions of the kind.

"I would bet," said Don Quixote, "that this bachelor or beneficed priest must be more Camacho's friend than Basilio's, and that he must have more of the satirist in him than of the vespers-singer. He has fitted Basilio's talents and Camacho's riches into the dance very neatly!"

Sancho Panza, who was listening to all of it, said:

"My money's on the king: I stand by Camacho."

"In short," said Don Quixote, "it is plain enough, Sancho, that you are a peasant and one of those who say, 'Long live the winner!'"

"I do not know which sort I am," answered Sancho, "but I do know that I shall never take such elegant skimmings out of Basilio's pots as this that I have taken out of Camacho's."

And he showed him the cauldron full of geese and hens, and, seizing one of them, began to eat with great charm and appetite, and said:

"In the teeth of Basilio's talents! You are worth as much as you have, and you have as much as you are worth. There are only two families in the world, as a grandmother of mine used to say — the Haves and the Have-nots — although she stood by the Haves. And these days, my lord Don Quixote, they take the pulse of the purse sooner than of the person: a donkey covered in gold looks better than a horse under a pack-saddle. So I say again that I stand by Camacho, out of whose pots the skimmings are plentiful geese and hens, hares and rabbits; while out of Basilio's, if it comes to hand, and even if it only comes to foot, they will be dishwater."

"Have you finished your harangue, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"I shall have finished it," answered Sancho, "because I see that your worship takes it heavily; for if that did not come in between, I had work cut out here for three days."

"Please God, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "that I may see you dumb before I die."

"At the rate we are going," answered Sancho, "before your worship dies I shall be chewing earth, and then it may be that I shall be so dumb that I shall not speak a word until the end of the world, or at least until the day of Judgement."

"Even if that should happen so, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "your silence will never come up to what you have talked, are talking and are going to talk in your lifetime. And besides, it is very much in the order of nature that the day of my death should come before the day of yours; and so I never expect to see you dumb, not even when you are drinking or sleeping, which is as far as I can go."

"Upon my faith, sir," answered Sancho, "there is no trusting the fleshless lady — I mean death, who eats lamb as readily as mutton. And I have heard our curate say that she treads with an equal foot on the high towers of kings and on the humble huts of the poor. This lady has more of power about her than of squeamishness: she is not at all fussy, she eats everything and makes do with anything, and she stuffs her saddlebags with people of every sort, age and rank. She is no reaper who sleeps through the noonday, for she reaps at all hours and cuts the dry grass along with the green; and she does not seem to chew but to bolt and swallow whatever is put in front of her, because she has a dog's hunger that is never satisfied. And although she has no belly, she gives you to understand that she is dropsical and thirsty enough to drink down the lives of all who live, the way a man drinks down a jug of cold water."

"No more, Sancho," said Don Quixote at this point. "Hold yourself at your best and do not let yourself fall; for truly what you have said about death in your rustic terms is what a good preacher could have said. I tell you, Sancho, that if along with the good nature and good sense you have you could take a pulpit in hand, you might go about this world preaching fine things."

"He preaches well who lives well," answered Sancho, "and I know no other 'ologies."

"Nor do you need any," said Don Quixote; "but I cannot for the life of me understand or make out how, the fear of God being the beginning of wisdom, you, who are more afraid of a lizard than of Him, know so much."

"Let your worship judge of your chivalries, sir," answered Sancho, "and not go meddling in judging other people's fears or bravery; for I am as fine a fearer of God as anybody's son in the parish. And let your worship let me polish off this skimming, since all the rest is idle words that they will call us to account for in the other life."

And saying this he began afresh to storm his cauldron, with such good appetite that he woke Don Quixote's; and he would no doubt have helped him, if he had not been stopped by what must of necessity be told further on.

Chapter 21: Where Camacho's Wedding Is Carried Further, with Other Delightful Events

While Don Quixote and Sancho were in the talk reported in the last chapter, loud shouts and a great noise were heard; and the men on the mares were making them and causing it, going at full gallop and shouting to meet the bride and bridegroom, who came surrounded by a thousand kinds of instruments and contrivances, accompanied by the curate and by the relations of both, and by all the most distinguished people of the neighbouring places, everybody dressed for the holiday.

And as soon as Sancho saw the bride he said:

"Upon my faith, she does not come dressed as a farm girl but as a fine court lady! By God, as far as I can make out, the medallions she was to have worn are rich coral, and the green cloth of Cuenca is thirty-pile velvet! And I'll be bound the trimming is strips of white linen — I swear it is satin! And take a look at her hands, decked out with jet rings: strike me down if they are not gold rings, and very gold, and set with pearls as white as curds, each one of which must be worth an eye out of your head. Oh, the whoreson, and what hair! If it is not false, I have never seen it longer or fairer in all my life. No, go on, find a fault in her spirit or in her figure, and don't compare her to a palm tree swaying loaded down with clusters of dates — because that is just what the trinkets look like that she has hanging from her hair and her throat. I swear on my soul she is a fine, well-built girl, and she could sail past the shoals of Flanders and come through."

Don Quixote laughed at Sancho Panza's rustic praises; but it seemed to him that, apart from his lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, he had never seen a more beautiful woman. Beautiful Quiteria came along somewhat pale, and it must have been from the bad night that brides always spend getting themselves up for the coming day of their wedding.

They were drawing near a platform that stood at one side of the meadow, decked out with carpets and boughs, where the marriage was to be made and from where they were to watch the dances and the contrivances. And just as they were reaching the place, they heard great shouting behind them, and a voice saying:

"Wait a little, you people, as thoughtless as you are in a hurry."

At which shouts and words they all turned their heads, and saw that the man making them was dressed, by the look of it, in a black tunic slashed with crimson in the shape of flames. He came crowned — as was seen at once — with a crown of funereal cypress, and in his hands he carried a great staff.

As he came nearer he was recognised by everybody as the gallant Basilio, and they were all left in suspense, waiting to see where his shouts and his words were going to end, and fearing some bad outcome from his coming at such a moment.

He arrived at last, tired and out of breath; and, planting himself in front of the couple, driving his staff into the ground — for it had a steel point at the end of it — with his colour changed and his eyes fixed on Quiteria, in a trembling and hoarse voice he said these words:

"You know very well, ungrateful Quiteria, that by the holy law we profess, while I am alive you cannot take a husband; and at the same time you are not ignorant that, because I was waiting for time and my own efforts to improve the goods of my fortune, I never chose to stop keeping the decorum your honour called for. But you, throwing behind you all the obligations you owe to my honest desire, want to make another man lord of what is mine — a man whose riches serve him not only as good fortune but as the very best of luck.

"And so that he may have it in full measure, and not as I think he deserves it but as the heavens choose to give it him, I shall with my own hands undo the impossibility or the obstacle that could stand in its way, by taking myself out from between. Long live, long live the rich Camacho with the ungrateful Quiteria, for long and happy ages; and let him die, let him die, poor Basilio, whose poverty cut the wings of his happiness and put him in the grave!"

And saying this he seized the staff he had driven into the ground; and, half of it staying in the earth, he showed that it served as the sheath of a middling rapier that was hidden inside it. And, setting what might be called the hilt on the ground, with a light unconcern and a settled purpose he threw himself upon it, and in an instant showed the bloody point coming out at his back, with half the steel blade — the wretched man left bathed in his own blood and stretched on the ground, run through by his own weapon.

His friends ran up at once to help him, grieved by his misery and pitiful misfortune; and Don Quixote, leaving Rocinante, ran to help him and took him in his arms, and found that he had not yet expired. They wanted to draw the rapier out, but the curate, who was there, was of the opinion that they should not draw it out before confessing him, because drawing it out and his expiring would be all in one moment. But Basilio, coming round a little, said in a pained and fainting voice:

"If you would only, cruel Quiteria, in this last and forced extremity give me your hand as my wife, I should still think my rashness had some excuse, since in it I attained the good of being yours."

The curate, hearing this, told him to attend to the health of his soul before the pleasures of the body, and to ask God very earnestly for pardon for his sins and for his desperate decision. To which Basilio answered that on no account would he confess unless Quiteria first gave him her hand as his wife: that this contentment would set his will to rights and give him breath to confess.

As soon as Don Quixote heard the wounded man's request, he said in a loud voice that Basilio was asking a thing that was very just and reasonable, and, besides, very easily done; and that Señor Camacho would be left just as honoured in receiving the lady Quiteria as the widow of the valorous Basilio as if he had received her from her father's side.

"Here there need be no more than a single yes, which will have no other effect than the pronouncing of it, since the marriage bed of this wedding is to be the grave."

Camacho heard it all, and it all left him bewildered and confused, not knowing what to do or what to say. But the voices of Basilio's friends were so many, begging him to consent to Quiteria's giving him her hand so that his soul should not be lost by departing this life in despair, that they moved him and even forced him to say that if Quiteria wanted to give it, he was content, since it was all only putting off the fulfilling of his desires for a moment.

Then they all turned to Quiteria, and some with entreaties, and others with tears, and others with forcible arguments, urged her to give her hand to poor Basilio; and she, harder than marble and more motionless than a statue, showed that she neither knew how, nor was able, nor wanted to answer a word — and she would not have answered if the curate had not told her to make up her mind quickly about what she was going to do, because Basilio already had his soul between his teeth and there was no room to wait for undecided decisions.

Then the beautiful Quiteria, without answering a single word, troubled, and to all appearances sad and sorry, came to where Basilio was lying with his eyes already turned up, his breath short and hurried, murmuring Quiteria's name between his teeth and giving signs of dying like a pagan and not like a Christian. Quiteria came, then, and, going down on her knees, asked him for his hand by signs and not by words. Basilio unfixed his eyes, and, looking at her attentively, said to her:

"O Quiteria, you have come to be merciful at a moment when your mercy must serve as the knife that finishes taking my life away, since I no longer have the strength to bear the glory you give me in choosing me for your own, or to hold off the pain that is so quickly covering my eyes with the terrible shadow of death! What I beg of you is this, O fatal star of mine: that the hand you ask of me and want to give me should not be for form's sake, nor to deceive me all over again, but that you should confess and say that, with no force put on your will, you hand it over and give it to me as to your lawful husband. For it is not reasonable that at a moment like this you should deceive me, or use any pretence with a man who has dealt in so many truths with you."

In the middle of these words he kept fainting away, so that all who were present thought that each faint was going to carry his soul off with it. Quiteria, all decency and all modesty, taking Basilio's hand in her right hand, said to him:

"No force would be enough to twist my will; and so, with the freest will I have, I give you my hand as your lawful wife and take yours — if it is that you give it me of your own free choice, without its being troubled or crossed by the calamity your hasty reasoning has put you in."

"I do give it," answered Basilio, "not troubled or confused, but with the clear understanding heaven chose to give me; and so I give myself and hand myself over as your husband."

"And I as your wife," answered Quiteria, "whether you live long years or whether they carry you out of my arms to the grave."

"For a young man as badly wounded as this," said Sancho Panza at this point, "he does a great deal of talking. Make him leave off the sweet nothings and attend to his soul, which to my mind he has more in his tongue than between his teeth."

Basilio and Quiteria being joined hand in hand, then, the curate, tender and in tears, gave them his blessing and asked heaven to give a good rest to the soul of the newly married man — who, as soon as he had received the blessing, jumped nimbly to his feet and with unheard-of coolness pulled out the rapier that had his own body for a sheath.

All the bystanders were left astonished, and some of them, simpler than they were curious, began to cry out at the tops of their voices:

"A miracle, a miracle!"

But Basilio answered:

"Not 'a miracle, a miracle', but a trick, a trick!"

The curate, disconcerted and thunderstruck, ran up with both hands to feel the wound, and found that the blade had gone not through Basilio's flesh and ribs but through a hollow iron tube, full of blood, that he had fitted neatly in that place — the blood, as was learnt afterwards, prepared in such a way that it would not congeal.

In short, the curate and Camacho and all the rest of the bystanders held themselves to have been fooled and made game of. The bride gave no sign of being sorry about the trick; on the contrary, hearing it said that the marriage, having been a deception, could not hold good, she said that she confirmed it afresh. From which they all gathered that the whole business had been arranged by the agreement and knowledge of the two of them — at which Camacho and his supporters were left so put out that they referred their revenge to their hands, and, drawing a great many swords, charged at Basilio, in whose favour almost as many were drawn in an instant.

And Don Quixote, taking the lead on horseback with his lance on his arm and well covered by his shield, made everybody give way to him. Sancho, who never took any pleasure or delight in doings of the kind, took refuge among the jars where he had drawn off his agreeable skimmings, that place seeming to him a sanctuary that ought to be held in respect. Don Quixote was saying in a loud voice:

"Hold, gentlemen, hold; for there is no reason for you to take revenge for the wrongs love does us. And note that love and war are one and the same thing; and just as in war it is lawful and customary to use tricks and stratagems to overcome the enemy, so in the contests and rivalries of love the deceits and dodges that are worked to get the end desired are held to be good, provided they are not to the damage and dishonour of the thing loved.

"Quiteria was Basilio's, and Basilio Quiteria's, by the just and favourable disposition of the heavens. Camacho is rich, and will be able to buy his pleasure when, where and how he likes. Basilio has nothing but this one ewe, and nobody is going to take her from him, however powerful he may be; for those two whom God has joined, man cannot separate — and whoever tries it must first come past the point of this lance."

And with that he brandished it so strongly and so skilfully that he struck terror into all who did not know him. And Quiteria's slight fixed itself so deeply in Camacho's imagination that it rubbed her out of his memory in an instant; and so the persuasions of the curate, who was a prudent and well-meaning man, took effect with him, by which Camacho and those of his party were left peaceable and quiet. In sign of which they put their swords back in their places, blaming Quiteria's readiness more than Basilio's trickery — Camacho reasoning that if Quiteria loved Basilio as a girl, she would love him as a married woman too, and that he ought to give thanks to heaven more for having taken her from him than for having given her.

Camacho and his troop being consoled and pacified, then, all those of Basilio's side quieted down; and the rich Camacho, to show that he did not feel the trick and set no store by it, wanted the festivities to go on as though he were really being married. But Basilio and his wife and their followers would not stay for them, and so they went off to Basilio's village — for the virtuous and judicious poor also have people to follow them, honour them and stand by them, as the rich have people to flatter them and keep them company.

They took Don Quixote away with them, valuing him as a man of worth and with hair on his chest. Sancho alone had his soul darkened, at seeing himself unable to wait for Camacho's splendid dinner and festivities, which lasted until night. And so, worn out and sad, he followed his master, who was going along with Basilio's party, and so he left behind him the fleshpots of Egypt — though he carried them in his soul, the by now nearly finished and used-up skimming he had in his cauldron standing for the glory and abundance of the good thing he was losing. And so, distressed and thoughtful, though not hungry, without getting down off the grey he followed in Rocinante's tracks.

Chapter 22: Where an Account Is Given of the Great Adventure of the Cave of Montesinos, in the Heart of La Mancha, Which the Valorous Don Quixote of La Mancha Brought to a Happy Conclusion

Great and many were the attentions the newly married couple paid Don Quixote, feeling themselves obliged by the show he had made in defending their cause; and along with his valour they rated his good sense, holding him for a Cid in arms and a Cicero in eloquence. Good Sancho took his ease for three days at the bride and bridegroom's expense, from whom it was learnt that the mock wounding had not been a plan arranged with the beautiful Quiteria but a device of Basilio's, expecting from it exactly the outcome that had been seen. It is true, though, that he confessed he had let some of his friends into his idea, so that at the necessary moment they might back up his intention and warrant his deception.

"They cannot and should not be called deceptions," said Don Quixote, "when they have virtuous ends in view."

And he said that the marrying of two people in love was the most excellent of ends, pointing out that the greatest enemy love has is hunger and continual need, because love is all gladness, merriment and contentment, and the more so when the lover is in possession of the thing loved, against which need and poverty are opposed and declared enemies. And he said all this with the intention that Señor Basilio should leave off practising the talents he had, which, though they gave him fame, did not give him money, and should attend to getting himself an estate by lawful and industrious means, which are never wanting to the prudent and hard-working.

"The honourable poor man — if a poor man can be honourable — has a treasure in having a beautiful wife; and when she is taken from him, his honour is taken from him and killed. The beautiful and honourable woman whose husband is poor deserves to be crowned with the laurels and palms of conquest and triumph. Beauty by itself draws the good will of all who look at it and know it, and the royal eagles and the high-flying birds swoop down on it as on a delicious lure; but if need and hardship are joined to such beauty, then the crows and the kites and the other birds of prey attack it too — and the woman who stands firm against so many assaults well deserves to be called her husband's crown.

"Look here, judicious Basilio," Don Quixote added. "It was the opinion of some wise man or other that there was only one good woman in the whole world, and he gave it as his advice that every man should think and believe that this one good woman was his own, and in that way he would live contented. I am not married, nor has it come into my mind so far to be so; and, for all that, I should venture to give advice to any man who asked me for it about the way he ought to look for the woman he meant to marry.

"First of all, I should advise him to look more at her reputation than at her property, because a good woman does not attain a good reputation merely by being good but by seeming so; for public forwardness and freedom do a great deal more damage to women's honour than secret wickednesses. If you bring a good woman into your house, it will be an easy thing to keep her, and even improve her, in that goodness; but if you bring in a bad one, you will have your work cut out mending her — for it is not very easily done to pass from one extreme to the other. I do not say it is impossible, but I hold it to be difficult."

Sancho was listening to all this, and he said to himself:

"This master of mine, when I talk about things with pith and substance in them, generally says that I might take a pulpit in my hands and go about the world preaching fine things; and I say of him that when he starts threading judgements together and giving advice, he could take not only one pulpit in his hands but two on every finger, and go about the market squares saying whatever he pleased. The devil take you for a knight errant, and all the things you know! I thought, upon my soul, that he could only know what had to do with his chivalries; but there is nothing he does not peck at and stick his spoon into."

Sancho was muttering this a little out loud, and his master half heard him, and asked him:

"What are you muttering, Sancho?"

"I am not saying anything or muttering about anything," answered Sancho. "I was only saying to myself that I wish I had heard what your worship has said here before I married, for perhaps I should be saying now: 'the ox that is loose licks himself best'."

"Is your Teresa as bad as that, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"She is not very bad," answered Sancho, "but she is not very good; at least she is not as good as I should like."

"You do wrong, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "in speaking ill of your wife, who is, after all, the mother of your children."

"We owe each other nothing," answered Sancho, "because she speaks ill of me too whenever she takes it into her head — especially when she is jealous, and then Satan himself may put up with her."

Finally they spent three days with the newly married couple, where they were entertained and served like royal persons. Don Quixote asked the licentiate swordsman to give him a guide to take him to the cave of Montesinos, because he had a great desire to go into it and see with his own eyes whether the marvels that were told of it all through those parts were true.

The licentiate told him he would give him a cousin of his, a famous student and very fond of reading books of chivalry, who would very willingly put him at the mouth of the cave itself and would show him the Lagoons of Ruidera, likewise famous through all La Mancha and even through all Spain. And he told him he would find pleasant entertainment in him, since he was a young man who knew how to make books for printing and for dedicating to princes.

At last the cousin came on a pregnant she-ass whose pack-saddle was covered with a bright striped rug or piece of sacking. Sancho saddled Rocinante and got the grey ready, provided his saddlebags — which were joined by the cousin's, likewise well provided — and, commending themselves to God and taking their leave of everybody, they set out, taking the road to the famous cave of Montesinos.

On the way Don Quixote asked the cousin what kind and quality his pursuits, his profession and his studies were; to which he answered that his profession was to be a humanist, and his pursuits and studies to compose books for the press, all of them of great profit and no less entertainment to the commonwealth. That one of them was called The Book of Liveries, in which he painted seven hundred and three liveries with their colours, mottoes and devices, out of which courtier knights could pick and take whichever they liked at times of festival and merrymaking, without going about begging them from anybody or distilling their brains, as they say, to get them to fit their wishes and intentions.

"Because I give to the jealous man, to the scorned man, to the forgotten man and to the absent man the ones that suit them, and they will fit them better than their own skins. I have another book too, which I mean to call The Metamorphoses, or the Spanish Ovid, of a new and rare invention; because in it, imitating Ovid in the burlesque style, I paint who the Giralda of Seville was, and the Angel of the Magdalen, who the Vecinguerra Conduit of Cordova was, who the Bulls of Guisando were, and the Sierra Morena, and the fountains of Leganitos and Lavapiés in Madrid, not forgetting the Louse Fountain, the Gilded Spout and the Prioress — and this with their allegories, metaphors and transferences, so that they gladden, astonish and instruct all at once.

"I have another book that I call A Supplement to Polydore Vergil, which deals with the invention of things and is of great erudition and study, on the grounds that the things of great substance Polydore left unsaid, I find out and set forth in a graceful style. Vergil forgot to declare to us who was the first man in the world to have a cold, and the first to take the mercury cure for the French disease; and I declare it to the letter and back it up with more than twenty-five authors — so your worship may see whether I have worked well and whether such a book will be useful to all the world."

Sancho, who had been very attentive to the cousin's account, said to him:

"Tell me, sir, and so may God give you good luck in the printing of your books: could you tell me — and of course you could, since you know everything — who was the first man to scratch his head? For I hold for my own part that it must have been our father Adam."

"It must have been," answered the cousin, "because there is no doubt that Adam had a head and hair; and, this being so, and his being the first man in the world, he would have scratched himself at some time."

"So I believe," answered Sancho. "But tell me now: who was the first tumbler in the world?"

"Truly, brother," answered the cousin, "I shall not be able to settle that for the moment, until I have studied it. I shall study it when I get back to where my books are, and I shall satisfy you next time we see each other, for this must not be the last."

"Well look, sir," replied Sancho, "do not put yourself to any trouble over it, because I have just this minute hit on the answer to what I asked you. Know that the first tumbler in the world was Lucifer, when they threw him or hurled him out of heaven, and he came tumbling all the way down to the pit."

"You are right, my friend," said the cousin.

And Don Quixote said:

"That question and that answer are not yours, Sancho: you have heard somebody else say them."

"Be quiet, sir," replied Sancho, "for upon my faith, if I take to asking and answering, I shall not have finished between now and tomorrow. Why, to ask foolish questions and answer nonsense I have no need to go about looking for help from the neighbours."

"You have said more, Sancho, than you know," said Don Quixote; "for there are some men who wear themselves out learning and establishing things which, once learnt and established, are not worth a farthing to the understanding or to the memory."

In these and other pleasant conversations that day went by for them, and at night they lodged in a small village, where the cousin told Don Quixote that from there to the cave of Montesinos was no more than two leagues, and that if he had made up his mind to go into it, it would be necessary to provide themselves with ropes to tie himself with and let himself down into its depths.

Don Quixote said that even if it went down to the abyss, he had to see where it ended; and so they bought nearly a hundred fathoms of rope, and the next day at two in the afternoon they reached the cave, whose mouth is spacious and wide but full of thorn bushes and wild fig trees, of brambles and undergrowth so thick and tangled that they altogether blind and cover it.

On seeing it, the cousin, Sancho and Don Quixote dismounted, and the two of them at once tied Don Quixote very tightly with the ropes; and while they were swathing and girding him, Sancho said to him:

"Look what you are doing, my dear sir. Do not go burying yourself alive, or put yourself where you will look like a bottle being let down into a well to cool. Why, it is nothing to do with your worship and none of your business to be the explorer of this place, which must be worse than a dungeon."

"Tie and be quiet," answered Don Quixote; "for an undertaking like this one, Sancho my friend, was reserved for me."

And then the guide said:

"I beg your worship, Señor Don Quixote, to look hard and to examine with a hundred eyes what is down there: perhaps there will be things I can put into my book of Transformations."

"The tambourine is in the hands of a man who knows how to play it," answered Sancho Panza.

This said, and the tying of Don Quixote finished — which was not over his armour but over his arming doublet — Don Quixote said:

"We have been careless in not providing ourselves with some small cowbell, which could have been tied next to me on this same rope, and by whose sound it would be understood that I was still going down and was still alive. But since that is not possible now, into the hand of God, who will guide me."

And then he went down on his knees and said a prayer in a low voice to heaven, asking God to help him and give him good success in that apparently dangerous and untried adventure; and then he said in a loud voice:

"O lady of my actions and my movements, most illustrious and peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso! If it is possible for the pleas and prayers of this fortunate lover of yours to reach your ears, by your unheard-of beauty I beg you to hear them, which are nothing but a prayer that you should not deny me your favour and protection, now that I have such need of it. I am about to hurl myself down, to sink myself and to plunge into the abyss that is opening here in front of me, only so that the world may know that if you favour me, there is no impossibility I shall not attempt and carry through."
