And, saying this, he went up to the chasm and saw that it was not possible to let himself down or to make room for the entry except by main force or by sword-strokes; and so, laying his hand on his sword, he began to knock down and cut away the undergrowth at the mouth of the cave. At whose noise and racket there came out of it an infinite number of enormous crows and jackdaws, so thick and in such haste that they knocked Don Quixote to the ground; and if he had been as much of a believer in omens as he was a Catholic Christian, he would have taken it for a bad sign and excused himself from shutting himself up in such a place.

Finally he got up, and, seeing that no more crows were coming out, nor other night birds such as the bats that had come out among the crows, with the cousin and Sancho paying out the rope he let himself sink to the bottom of the terrible cavern. And as he went in, Sancho gave him his blessing and made a thousand crosses over him, saying:

"God guide you, and Our Lady of the Rock of France along with the Trinity of Gaeta, flower and cream and froth of knights errant! There you go, champion of the world, heart of steel, arms of bronze! God guide you again, and bring you back free, sound and without a scratch to the light of this life you are leaving to bury yourself in this darkness you are looking for!"

Almost the same prayers and supplications were made by the cousin.

Don Quixote went down calling out for them to give him rope and more rope, and they gave it to him little by little; and when the shouts, coming out channelled up the cave, stopped being heard, they had already paid out the hundred fathoms of rope, and were of the opinion that they should haul Don Quixote up again, since they could give him no more line.

Even so, they waited about half an hour, at the end of which space they set to hauling in the rope again — with great ease and with no weight at all, a sign that made them imagine that Don Quixote was staying down there. And believing so, Sancho wept bitterly and hauled away in a great hurry to find out the truth; but, coming to a little over eighty fathoms as far as they could judge, they felt a weight, at which they were extremely glad. Finally, at ten fathoms, they saw Don Quixote distinctly, and Sancho called out to him, saying:

"Very welcome back, my dear sir, for we were already thinking you were staying down there for breeding stock."

But Don Quixote did not answer a word; and, getting him right out, they saw that he had his eyes shut, with every sign of being asleep. They laid him out on the ground and untied him, and even so he did not wake; but they turned him and rolled him and shook him and shifted him about so much that at the end of a good while he came to himself, stretching, exactly as if he were waking from some heavy, deep sleep. And, looking one way and the other, as if terrified, he said:

"God forgive you, my friends; for you have taken me away from the sweetest and most agreeable life and sight that any human being has ever seen or passed through. In fact I now know for certain that all the contentments of this life pass like a shadow and a dream, or wither like the flower of the field. O unfortunate Montesinos! O sorely wounded Durandarte! O luckless Belerma! O weeping Guadiana, and you unhappy daughters of Ruidera, who show in your waters the tears your beautiful eyes have wept!"

The cousin and Sancho listened to Don Quixote's words, which he said as though he were dragging them out of his entrails with immense pain. They begged him to give them to understand what he was saying, and to tell them what he had seen in that hell.

"Do you call it a hell?" said Don Quixote. "Well, do not call it that, because it does not deserve the name, as you will see presently."

He asked them to give him something to eat, for he was extremely hungry. They spread the cousin's sacking on the green grass, went to the store in their saddlebags and, all three of them sitting down in good love and fellowship, took their tea and their supper all at once. The sacking taken up, Don Quixote of La Mancha said:

"Let nobody get up, and all of you, my sons, be attentive to me."

Chapter 23: Of the Wonderful Things the Matchless Don Quixote Said He Had Seen in the Deep Cave of Montesinos, Whose Impossibility and Magnitude Make This Adventure Pass for Apocryphal

It must have been four in the afternoon when the sun, covered over among the clouds, with scanty light and tempered rays, gave Don Quixote room to tell his two most distinguished listeners, without heat and discomfort, what he had seen in the cave of Montesinos. And he began in the following way:

"About twelve or fourteen times a man's height down in this dungeon, on the right-hand side, there opens a hollow and a space big enough to hold a great cart with its mules. A little light comes into it through some chinks or holes that answer to it a long way off, opening on the surface of the earth. I saw this hollow and this space at a time when I was already tired and vexed at finding myself hanging and dangling from the rope, travelling down through that dark region without any certain or settled road; and so I decided to go into it and rest a little.

"I shouted, asking you not to let down any more rope until I told you to, but you must not have heard me. I went on gathering in the rope you were sending down and, making a coil or a heap of it, I sat down on it, deep in thought, considering what I ought to do to get down to the bottom, having nobody to hold me up. And while I was in this thought and confusion, suddenly and without my seeking it, a very deep sleep came over me. And when I least expected it, without knowing how or why, I woke out of it and found myself in the middle of the most beautiful, pleasant and delightful meadow that nature can breed or the most judicious human imagination imagine.

"I opened my eyes wide, I rubbed them, and I saw that I was not asleep but was really awake. For all that, I felt my head and my chest to make certain whether it was I myself who was there, or some empty and counterfeit phantom; but the touch, the feeling, the ordered reasoning I was doing inside me, all made me certain that I was there then the same man that I am here now.

"Then there offered itself to my sight a royal and sumptuous palace or castle whose walls seemed to be built of transparent, clear crystal; and, two great doors of it opening, I saw a venerable old man coming out through them and towards me, dressed in a long cloak of purple baize that trailed on the ground. Over his shoulders and his chest ran a collegiate sash of green satin; his head was covered with a black Milanese cap, and his beard, snow-white, came down past his waist. He carried no weapon at all, only a rosary in his hand with beads larger than middling walnuts, and its every tenth bead like a middling ostrich egg. His bearing, his walk, his gravity and his enormously broad presence, each thing by itself and all of them together, astonished me and filled me with wonder.

"He came up to me, and the first thing he did was to embrace me tightly, and then to say to me: 'For long ages now, valorous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, those of us who are enchanted in these solitudes have been waiting to see you, so that you might give the world notice of what is shut up and covered by the deep cave you have come into, called the cave of Montesinos: an exploit reserved to be undertaken by nothing but your invincible heart and your stupendous spirit. Come with me, most illustrious sir, for I want to show you the marvels this transparent castle hides, of which I am the governor and perpetual chief warden — because I am Montesinos himself, from whom the cave takes its name.'

"Hardly had he told me that he was Montesinos when I asked him whether it was true what was told in the world up here: that he had cut the heart out of the middle of the breast of his great friend Durandarte with a small dagger, and carried it to the lady Belerma, as Durandarte had ordered him at the point of his death. He answered me that they told the truth in everything except about the dagger, because it was no dagger, nor small, but a keen-pointed poniard, sharper than an awl."

"The poniard must have been," said Sancho at this point, "one of Ramón de Hoces's, the Sevillian's."

"I do not know," Don Quixote went on, "but it would not be that dagger-maker's, because Ramón de Hoces was yesterday, and the business at Roncesvalles, where this misfortune happened, was many years ago. And this point is of no importance, and it neither disturbs nor alters the truth and the tenor of the history."

"That is so," answered the cousin. "Go on, your worship, Señor Don Quixote, for I am listening to you with the greatest pleasure in the world."

"And with no less do I tell it," answered Don Quixote. "And so I say that the venerable Montesinos took me into the crystal palace, where in a low chamber, extremely cool and all of alabaster, there was a marble tomb, made with great craftsmanship, on which I saw a knight stretched out at full length — not made of bronze, or of marble, or of jasper, as they generally are on other tombs, but of pure flesh and pure bone. He had his right hand — which to my mind is somewhat hairy and sinewy, a sign that its owner had great strength — laid over the region of his heart.

"And before I could ask Montesinos anything, seeing me hanging astonished over the man on the tomb, he said to me: 'This is my friend Durandarte, the flower and mirror of the loving and valiant knights of his time. Merlin holds him enchanted here, as he holds me and a great many other men and women — Merlin, that French enchanter who they say was the devil's son; and what I believe is that he was not the devil's son, but that he knew, as they say, one point more than the devil. How or why he enchanted us nobody knows, and time will tell — and it is not very far off, as I imagine.

"'What astonishes me is that I know, as surely as I know it is day now, that Durandarte ended the days of his life in my arms, and that after he was dead I took out his heart with my own hands; and truly it must have weighed two pounds, because, according to the naturalists, the man who has the bigger heart is endowed with more valour than the man whose heart is small. Well then, this being so, and this knight having really died, how is it that he now complains and sighs from time to time as if he were alive?'

"This said, the wretched Durandarte, giving a great cry, said:

	O my cousin Montesinos!
	The last thing that I begged of you
	was that when I should be dead
	and my soul torn out of me,
	you would carry off my heart
	to where Belerma was,
	cutting it out of my breast
	with a poniard or a dagger.

"Which hearing, the venerable Montesinos went down on his knees before the grieving knight, and with tears in his eyes said to him: 'Long ago, Señor Durandarte, dearest cousin of mine, long ago I did what you ordered me on the ill-starred day of our loss. I took out your heart as best I could, without leaving the least part of it in your breast; I cleaned it with a lace handkerchief; I set off with it at a gallop for France, having first laid you in the bosom of the earth with tears enough to wash my hands and clean off with them the blood they had on them from having been about in your entrails.

"'And, for still better proof, cousin of my soul, at the first place I came to on the way out of Roncesvalles I put a little salt on your heart, so that it should not smell badly and should come, if not fresh then at least cured, into the presence of the lady Belerma — whom, along with you, and me, and Guadiana your squire, and the duenna Ruidera and her seven daughters and two nieces, and a great many others of your acquaintances and friends, the wise Merlin has kept enchanted here these many years. And though more than five hundred have gone by, not one of us has died. Only Ruidera and her daughters and nieces are missing, whom Merlin, out of the compassion he must have felt for their weeping, turned into as many lagoons, which now, in the world of the living and in the province of La Mancha, they call the Lagoons of Ruidera. Seven of them belong to the kings of Spain, and the two nieces to the knights of a most holy order they call the Order of Saint John.

"'Guadiana your squire, likewise lamenting your misfortune, was turned into a river called by his own name; and when he reached the surface of the earth and saw the sun of that other sky, the grief he felt at seeing that he was leaving you was so great that he plunged into the bowels of the earth. But since it is impossible not to follow his natural current, from time to time he comes out and shows himself where the sun and the people can see him. The lagoons I have named keep feeding him with their waters, and with these and a great many others that join him he goes into Portugal, grand and pompous. But for all that, wherever he goes he shows his sadness and melancholy, and he does not pride himself on breeding fine and valuable fish in his waters, but coarse and unpalatable ones, very different from those of the golden Tagus.

"'And what I am telling you now, my cousin, I have told you many times; and, since you do not answer me, I imagine that you do not believe me, or do not hear me, at which I take as much pain as God knows. Some news I want to give you now which, even if it does not serve to relieve your grief, will not increase it in any way. Know that you have here in your presence — and open your eyes and you will see him — that great knight of whom the wise Merlin has prophesied so many things: that Don Quixote of La Mancha, I mean, who has brought the by now forgotten order of knight-errantry back to life in the present age, freshly and with greater advantages than in the ages past; and by whose means and favour it might be that we should be disenchanted, for great exploits are reserved for great men.'

"'And if it should not be so,' answered the grieving Durandarte in a faint, low voice, 'if it should not be so, cousin, I say: patience, and shuffle the cards.'

"And, turning on his side, he went back to his accustomed silence without speaking another word.

"At this there were heard great howls and weeping, along with deep groans and anguished sobs. I turned my head, and saw through the crystal walls that a procession was passing through another chamber, in two files of the most beautiful girls, all dressed in mourning, with white turbans on their heads in the Turkish fashion. At the very end of the files came a lady — for so her gravity made her look — likewise dressed in black, with white veils so long and flowing that they kissed the ground. Her turban was twice as big as the biggest of any of the others'. Her eyebrows met, and her nose was somewhat flat; her mouth was large, but her lips were red; her teeth, when she now and then let them show, proved to be thin-set and badly arranged, though they were as white as peeled almonds. In her hands she carried a fine cloth, and in it, as far as I could make out, a heart of mummified flesh, so dried and cured did it come.

"Montesinos told me that all those people in the procession were the servants of Durandarte and Belerma, who were enchanted there with their two masters, and that the last, who carried the heart in the cloth in her hands, was the lady Belerma, who with her maidens made that procession four days a week and sang — or, better said, wept — laments over the body and over the grieving heart of her cousin. And that if she had seemed to me somewhat ugly, or not as beautiful as her fame made her, the cause was the bad nights and the worse days she went through in that enchantment, as I could see by the great rings under her eyes and by her broken colour.

"'And her sallowness and the rings under her eyes,' he said, 'do not come from her being in the monthly trouble that is ordinary in women, because it is many months, and even years, since she has had it or since it has looked in at her door; they come from the pain her heart feels for the one she has in her hands all the time, which renews and brings back to her memory the misfortune of her ill-fated lover. If it were not for that, the great Dulcinea of El Toboso, so celebrated in all these parts and even in all the world, would scarcely come up to her in beauty, grace and spirit.'

"'Hold hard there!' I said then. 'Señor Don Montesinos, let your worship tell his history as he ought; for you know very well that all comparison is odious, and so there is no call to compare anybody with anybody. The peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso is who she is, and the lady Doña Belerma is who she is and who she has been, and let it stay there.'

"To which he answered me: 'Señor Don Quixote, forgive me, for I confess I did wrong, and I did not speak well in saying that the lady Dulcinea would scarcely come up to the lady Belerma; since it was enough for me to have gathered, from certain hints or other, that your worship is her knight, for me to bite my tongue before comparing her with anything but heaven itself.'

"With this satisfaction the great Montesinos gave me, my heart quieted down from the shock I received at hearing my lady compared with Belerma."

"And I do wonder," said Sancho, "how your worship did not get on top of the old fellow and grind all his bones with kicking and pluck his beard until there was not a hair left in it."

"No, Sancho my friend," answered Don Quixote, "it would not have been becoming in me to do that, because we are all obliged to have respect for the old, even if they are not knights, and chiefly for those who are knights and are under enchantment. I know very well that in a great many other questions and answers that passed between the two of us, neither of us was left owing the other anything."

At this point the cousin said:

"I do not know, Señor Don Quixote, how in as little time as your worship has been down there, you can have seen so many things and talked and answered so much."

"How long ago did I go down?" asked Don Quixote.

"A little over an hour," answered Sancho.

"That cannot be," replied Don Quixote, "because down there night fell on me and day broke, and night fell and day broke again, three times over; so that by my reckoning I have been three days in those remote parts, hidden from our sight."

"My master must be telling the truth," said Sancho; "for since everything that has happened to him is by enchantment, perhaps what seems to us an hour must seem three days and nights down there."

"That will be it," answered Don Quixote.

"And has your worship eaten in all this time, my dear sir?" asked the cousin.

"I have not broken my fast with a mouthful," answered Don Quixote, "and I have not even been hungry, or thought about it."

"And do the enchanted eat?" said the cousin.

"They do not eat," answered Don Quixote, "nor have they any of the grosser needs of the body; although it is held that their nails, their beards and their hair go on growing."

"And do the enchanted sleep, by any chance, sir?" asked Sancho.

"Certainly not," answered Don Quixote; "at least in these three days I have been with them, none of them has shut an eye, and neither have I."

"Here the proverb fits well," said Sancho: "'tell me who you go with and I will tell you who you are'. Your worship goes about with the enchanted, who are fasters and wakers — no wonder if you neither eat nor sleep while you are about with them. But forgive me, my dear sir, if I tell you that of everything you have said here, God take me — I was going to say the devil — if I believe a single thing."

"How not?" said the cousin. "Was Señor Don Quixote going to lie? Why, even if he had wanted to, he has not had time to compose and imagine so many million lies."

"I do not believe my master lies," answered Sancho.

"Then what do you believe?" Don Quixote asked him.

"I believe," answered Sancho, "that that Merlin, or those enchanters who enchanted the whole crew your worship says you saw and dealt with down there, jammed into your fancy or your memory this whole machine you have told us, and everything else you have left to tell."

"All that might be, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "but it is not so, because what I have told I saw with my own eyes and touched with my own hands.

"But what will you say when I tell you now how, among an infinite number of other things and marvels Montesinos showed me — which, at leisure and in their own good time, I shall go on telling you in the course of our journey, since they do not all belong in this place — he showed me three country girls who were going about those most delightful fields skipping and jumping like goats? And hardly had I seen them when I knew that one of them was the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso, and the other two those very country girls who were coming with her, whom we spoke to on the way out of El Toboso.

"I asked Montesinos whether he knew them; he answered me that he did not, but that he imagined they must be some great ladies under enchantment who had appeared in those meadows a few days before, and that I should not wonder at it, because there were a great many other ladies there of the past and present ages, enchanted in different and strange shapes, among whom he recognised Queen Guinevere and her duenna Quintañona, pouring out the wine for Lancelot

	when he came from Britain."

When Sancho Panza heard his master say this, he thought he would lose his wits or die laughing; for as he knew the truth about the pretended enchantment of Dulcinea, of which he himself had been the enchanter and the raiser of the false witness, he came to know beyond any doubt that his master was out of his senses and mad at every point. And so he said to him:

"In an unlucky conjunction and in a worse season and on an ill-starred day did your worship go down, my dear patron, to the other world, and in a bad moment did you meet with Señor Montesinos, who has sent you back to us like this. You were very well off up here with your whole judgement such as God had given it to you, speaking judgements and giving advice at every step, and not as you are now, telling the greatest absurdities that can be imagined."

"As I know you, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "I take no notice of your words."

"Nor I of your worship's," replied Sancho, "even if you wound me, even if you kill me for the ones I have said to you, or for the ones I mean to say if you do not correct and mend your own. But tell me, your worship, now that we are at peace: how, or by what, did you recognise our lady and mistress? And if you spoke to her, what did you say, and what did she answer you?"

"I recognised her," answered Don Quixote, "by her wearing the same clothes she was wearing when you showed her to me. I spoke to her, but she did not answer me a word; on the contrary, she turned her back on me and went off in flight so fast that an arrow would not have caught her. I wanted to follow her, and I should have done it if Montesinos had not advised me not to wear myself out over it, because it would be in vain, and the more so because the hour was coming round when it was proper for me to come out of the chasm again. He told me too that in the course of time I should be given notice how he, and Belerma and Durandarte, with all who were there, were to be disenchanted.

"But what gave me the most pain of all I saw and noted there was this: that while Montesinos was saying these things to me, one of the two companions of the luckless Dulcinea came up to me at my side, without my seeing her come, and, her eyes full of tears, said to me in a troubled, low voice: 'My lady Dulcinea of El Toboso kisses your worship's hands, and begs your worship to do her the kindness of letting her know how you are; and, being in great need, she likewise begs your worship, as earnestly as she can, to be so good as to lend her, on the security of this new cotton petticoat I have here, half a dozen reals, or whatever your worship may have; and she gives her word to give them back to you very shortly.'

"This message astonished and amazed me, and, turning to Señor Montesinos, I asked him: 'Is it possible, Señor Montesinos, that the enchanted people of quality suffer want?' To which he answered me: 'Believe me, your worship, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, that this thing they call want is in use everywhere, and stretches over everything, and reaches everybody, and does not spare even the enchanted. And since the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso sends to ask for those six reals, and the pledge is a good one by the look of it, there is nothing for it but to give them to her; for without doubt she must be in some great strait.'

"'A pledge I shall not take,' I answered him, 'nor shall I give her what she asks, because I have only four reals' — which I gave her (and they were the ones you gave me the other day, Sancho, to give in alms to the poor I met on the roads) — and I said to her: 'Tell your lady, my friend, that her troubles grieve me to the soul, and that I wish I were a Fugger to put them right; and let her know that I neither can nor ought to have any health while I go without the sight of her and her judicious conversation; and that I beg her, as earnestly as I can, that her worship be pleased to let herself be seen and dealt with by this captive servant of hers and worn-out knight.

"'You shall tell her too that when she least expects it she will hear how I have made an oath and a vow, in the manner of the one the Marquis of Mantua made to avenge his nephew Baldwin when he found him at the point of death in the middle of the mountain — which was not to eat bread off a tablecloth, with the other odds and ends he added there, until he had avenged him. And so I shall make mine, not to rest, and to travel the seven parts of the world more punctually than the Infante Don Pedro of Portugal travelled them, until I have disenchanted her.'

"'All that and more your worship owes to my lady,' the girl answered me. And, taking the four reals, instead of making me a curtsey she cut a caper and sprang two full measuring-yards into the air."

"O holy God!" said Sancho at this, letting out a great shout. "Is it possible that there is such a thing in the world, and that enchanters and enchantments have such force in it that they have turned my master's good judgement into so preposterous a madness? Oh sir, sir, for God's sake, let your worship look to yourself and stand up for your honour, and give no credit to these emptinesses that have left your senses short and out of true!"

"You talk that way, Sancho, because you love me," said Don Quixote; "and, since you are not experienced in the things of the world, everything that has any difficulty in it seems impossible to you. But time will go on, as I have said before, and I shall tell you some of the things I have seen down there that will make you believe the ones I have told here, whose truth admits of neither reply nor dispute."

Chapter 24: Where a Thousand Trifles Are Told, as Impertinent as They Are Necessary to the True Understanding of This Great History

The man who translated this great history from the original written by its first author, Cide Hamete Benengeli, says that when he came to the chapter of the adventure of the cave of Montesinos, there were written in the margin of it, in Hamete's own hand, these very words:

"I cannot bring myself to understand, nor can I persuade myself, that everything written in the foregoing chapter happened exactly so to the valorous Don Quixote. The reason is that all the adventures that have happened up to here have been possible and probable; but for this one of the cave I can find no way in to holding it for true, since it goes so far outside the bounds of reason.

"For me to think that Don Quixote lied, he being the most truthful gentleman and the noblest knight of his time, is not possible: he would not have told a lie if they had shot him full of arrows. On the other hand, I consider that he told it and said it with all the circumstances given, and that he could not have manufactured so great a machine of absurdities in so short a space. And if this adventure seems apocryphal, the fault is not mine; and so, without affirming it to be false or true, I write it down.

"You, reader, since you are prudent, judge whatever seems best to you; for I neither ought nor am able to do more — although it is held for certain that at the time of his end and death they say he took it back, and said he had invented it because it seemed to him to fit and square well with the adventures he had read in his histories."

And then he goes on, saying:

The cousin was astonished, both at Sancho Panza's boldness and at his master's patience, and judged that the mild temper Don Quixote was showing just then was born of the contentment he felt at having seen his lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, even under enchantment; because if it had not been so, Sancho had said him words and arguments that deserved a beating with a stick, since it really seemed to the cousin that he had been getting a little bold with his master, to whom he said:

"I, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, count the day I have spent with your worship as most excellently well spent, because in it I have gained four things. The first, to have come to know your worship, which I hold to be a great piece of happiness. The second, to have learnt what is shut up in this cave of Montesinos, along with the transformations of the Guadiana and of the Lagoons of Ruidera, which will serve me for the Spanish Ovid I have in hand.

"The third, to have made out the antiquity of playing cards, which were at least already in use in the time of the emperor Charlemagne, as may be gathered from the words your worship says Durandarte spoke when, at the end of that long space Montesinos spent talking to him, he woke up saying: 'Patience, and shuffle the cards.' And that expression and manner of speaking he cannot have learnt while he was enchanted, but when he was not, in France and in the time of the said emperor Charlemagne. And this discovery comes to me exactly to the pattern for that other book I am composing, which is the Supplement to Polydore Vergil on the invention of antiquities; and I believe that in his he forgot to put in the invention of playing cards, which I shall put in now, and it will be of great importance, and the more so when I cite an author as grave and as truthful as Señor Durandarte. The fourth is to have learnt with certainty the source of the river Guadiana, until now unknown to the world."

"Your worship is right," said Don Quixote; "but I should like to know, granting that God does you the favour of giving you licence to print these books of yours — which I doubt — whom you mean to dedicate them to."

"There are lords and grandees in Spain they can be dedicated to," said the cousin.

"Not many," answered Don Quixote; "and not because they do not deserve it, but because they do not want to accept them, so as not to be obliged to the recompense that seems to be owing to their authors' labour and courtesy. I know one prince who can make up for the failure of all the rest, with so many advantages that if I dared to name them I should perhaps wake envy in more than four generous breasts. But let this stay here for another and more convenient time, and let us go and look for somewhere to shelter tonight."

"Not far from here," answered the cousin, "there is a hermitage where a hermit makes his dwelling, who they say has been a soldier, and who is held to be a good Christian and very judicious and charitable besides. Next to the hermitage he has a small house he has built at his own expense; but for all that, small though it is, it can take in guests."

"Does this hermit by any chance keep hens?" asked Sancho.

"Few hermits are without them," answered Don Quixote, "because the ones in use nowadays are not like those of the deserts of Egypt, who dressed in palm leaves and ate roots out of the ground. And it is not to be understood that by speaking well of those I do not speak well of these; I only mean that the penances of the present ones do not come up to the rigour and hardness of those days. But that does not stop them all from being good men; at least I judge them for good; and, when everything is running murky, the hypocrite who pretends to be good does less harm than the open sinner."

While they were at this, they saw a man coming on foot towards where they were, walking fast and beating with a stick at a mule loaded with lances and halberds. When he came up to them he greeted them and passed straight on. Don Quixote said to him:

"Good man, stop; for it looks as if you are going faster than that mule needs."

"I cannot stop, sir," answered the man, "because the arms you see I am carrying here are to be used tomorrow; and so I am forced not to stop, and God be with you. But if you want to know what I am carrying them for, I mean to lodge tonight at the inn that is above the hermitage; and if you are taking this same road, you will find me there, and I shall tell you marvels. And God be with you again."

And he prodded the mule on in such a way that Don Quixote had no chance to ask him what marvels these were that he meant to tell them; and, as he was somewhat curious and was always worn down by his desire to know new things, he ordered that they should set off at once and go and spend the night at the inn, without touching at the hermitage, where the cousin would have liked them to stay.

So it was done: they mounted, and all three followed the straight road to the inn, which they reached a little before nightfall. The cousin told Don Quixote they should call at the hermitage to drink a draught. As soon as Sancho Panza heard this he turned the grey towards the hermitage, and Don Quixote and the cousin did the same; but Sancho's bad luck seems to have arranged that the hermit should not be at home, for that was what an under-hermit they found at the hermitage told them. They asked her for some of the good stuff; she answered that her master had none, but that if they wanted cheap water, she would give it them very willingly.

"If it were water I was thirsty for," answered Sancho, "there are wells on the road where I could have satisfied myself. Oh, Camacho's wedding and the abundance of Don Diego's house, how many times am I going to miss you!"

With this they left the hermitage and spurred on towards the inn; and a little way along they came upon a young lad who was walking ahead of them, not in any great hurry, so that they caught him up. He was carrying his sword over his shoulder, with a bundle or wrapper on it, apparently of his clothes — which, by the look of it, must have been his breeches or wide trousers, and a short cloak and a shirt or two, because he had on a velvet jerkin with a few glimmers of satin about it, and his shirt was hanging out. His stockings were of silk and his shoes square-toed in the court fashion; his age must have come to eighteen or nineteen; his face was cheerful and to all appearances he was nimble on his feet. He was going along singing seguidillas to lighten the labour of the road. When they came up to him he had just finished singing one that the cousin took down by heart, which they say went:

	To the wars I am carried
	by my own need;
	if I had any money,
	I would not go, in truth.

The first to speak to him was Don Quixote, saying:

"You travel very light, sir gallant. And where away? Let us know, if it is your pleasure to say."

To which the lad answered:

"Travelling so light is caused by the heat and by poverty, and where I am going is to the wars."

"How poverty?" asked Don Quixote. "For as to the heat, that may well be."

"Sir," replied the young man, "in this bundle I am carrying a pair of velvet trousers, the companions of this jerkin. If I wear them out on the road, I shall not be able to do myself honour with them in the city, and I have nothing to buy others with. And so, both for that reason and to air myself, I go about in this way, until I can catch up with some companies of infantry that are not twelve leagues from here, where I shall enlist; and there will be no lack of baggage animals to travel on from then on, as far as the port of embarkation, which they say is to be Cartagena. And I would sooner have the king for my master and lord, and serve him in the wars, than some threadbare wretch at court."

"And does your worship carry any special allowance, by any chance?" asked the cousin.

"If I had served some grandee of Spain, or some person of quality," answered the lad, "I should be sure to be carrying one, for that is what comes of serving good masters: out of the servants' hall men generally come out to be ensigns or captains, or with some good pension. But I, unfortunate creature, always served hunters after places and newcomers, on board and wages so wretched and so thin that half of it went in paying to have a collar starched. And it would be counted a miracle if a page out to make his fortune ever attained even a reasonable one."

"And tell me, on your life, my friend," asked Don Quixote, "is it possible that in the years you served you could not get hold of even one livery?"

"They have given me two," answered the page; "but just as, when a man leaves a religious house before taking his vows, they take back the habit and give him back his own clothes, so my masters gave me back mine. When the business they had come to court for was finished, they went back to their houses and took in the liveries they had given out for show and nothing else."

"A notable piece of spilorceria, as the Italian says," said Don Quixote; "but for all that, count it good fortune that you have come out of the court with as good an intention as you carry. Because there is nothing on earth more honourable or more profitable than to serve God first of all, and then your king and natural lord, especially in the exercise of arms, by which a man attains, if not more riches, at least more honour than by letters — as I have said many times. For although letters have founded more great estates than arms, still there is a something about the men of arms over the men of letters, with a certain I-know-what of splendour to be found in them that puts them ahead of everybody.

"And what I want to tell you now, carry in your memory, for it will be of great profit and relief to you in your hardships. And it is this: put aside the imagining of the adverse things that may come to you, of which the worst of all is death; and, so long as that death is a good one, the best of all is dying. They asked Julius Caesar, that valorous Roman emperor, which was the best death; he answered: the unthought-of, the sudden, the unforeseen. And although he answered as a pagan and a stranger to the knowledge of the true God, for all that he spoke well, so as to spare himself human feeling.

"For supposing they kill you in the first action and skirmish, either by a shot from a cannon or blown up by a mine — what does it matter? It is all dying, and the work is finished. And, according to Terence, the soldier who is dead in the battle makes a better show than the one who is alive and safe in flight. And the good soldier attains as much fame as he has obedience to his captains and to those who have the right to command him.

"And note, my son, that it becomes a soldier better to smell of gunpowder than of civet; and that if old age catches you in this honourable exercise, even though it be full of wounds and crippled or lame, at least it cannot catch you without honour — and with an honour that poverty cannot lessen. And the more so since orders are now being given for the keeping and relief of old and crippled soldiers; for it is not right that they should be treated the way some men treat the black people they hold enslaved, freeing them and giving them their liberty when they are already old and can no longer serve, and, turning them out of the house under the title of free men, making them the slaves of hunger, from which they can expect no freeing but by death.

"And for the present I do not want to tell you any more, except that you should get up behind me on this horse of mine as far as the inn, and there you shall have supper with me; and in the morning you shall follow your road, and may God give you as good a one as your intentions deserve."

The page did not accept the invitation to ride behind him, though he did accept the one to have supper with him at the inn; and at this moment, they say, Sancho said to himself:

"God bless you for a master! And is it possible that a man who knows how to say such things, and so many of them, and such good ones as he has said here, should say that he has seen the impossible absurdities he tells about the cave of Montesinos? Well now, time will tell."

And with this they came to the inn, just as night was falling, and not without pleasure to Sancho at seeing that his master judged it a real inn and not a castle as he usually did. They had hardly got in when Don Quixote asked the innkeeper about the man with the lances and halberds; who answered him that he was in the stable settling his mule. The cousin and Sancho did the same with their donkeys, giving Rocinante the best manger and the best place in the stable.

Chapter 25: Where the Adventure of the Braying Is Noted, and the Amusing One of the Puppet-Master, with the Memorable Divinations of the Soothsaying Ape

Don Quixote's bread would not bake, as the saying goes, until he had heard and learnt the marvels promised by the man who was carrying the arms. He went to look for him where the innkeeper had said he was, and found him, and told him that he must at all costs tell him now what he was going to tell him later, about what he had asked him on the road. The man answered him:

"The tale of my marvels has to be taken more at leisure, and not standing up. Let your worship, my good sir, let me finish seeing to my beast, and I shall tell you things to astonish you."

"Let there be no delay for that," answered Don Quixote, "for I shall help you with everything."

And so he did, sifting the barley for him and cleaning out the manger — a humility that obliged the man to tell him with good will what he was asking. And, sitting down on a stone bench with Don Quixote beside him, and having as his senate and audience the cousin, the page, Sancho Panza and the innkeeper, he began to speak in this way:

"Your worships must know that in a village that is four and a half leagues from this inn it happened that one of its aldermen, through the contrivance and trickery of a girl who was his servant — and this is a long story — lost a donkey. And although the alderman made every possible effort to find it, it was not possible.

"A fortnight must have gone by, according to public voice and report, since the donkey went missing, when the alderman who had lost it was standing in the market square and another alderman of the same village said to him: 'Pay me for the good news, my friend, for your donkey has turned up.' 'I promise you good payment, my friend,' answered the other, 'but let us know where it has turned up.' 'On the mountain,' answered the finder. 'I saw him this morning, without a pack-saddle and without any harness at all, and so thin it was a misery to look at him. I tried to drive him ahead of me and bring him to you, but he has gone so wild and so shy that when I got up to him he ran away and got into the most hidden part of the mountain. If you want the two of us to go back and look for him, let me put this she-ass of mine in my house, and I shall come straight back.' 'You will do me a great pleasure,' said the man who had lost the donkey, 'and I shall try to pay you back in the same coin.'

"With all these circumstances, and in the very way I am telling it, everybody tells it who is informed about the truth of this business. In short, the two aldermen went off on foot side by side to the mountain, and, coming to the place and spot where they thought they would find the donkey, they did not find him; nor did he appear anywhere in those parts, however hard they looked for him.

"Seeing, then, that he did not appear, the alderman who had seen him said to the other: 'Look, my friend: a plan has come into my head by which without any doubt we shall be able to find this animal, even if he has got into the bowels of the earth and not merely of the mountain. And it is that I know how to bray marvellously; and if you know anything at all about it, hold the business as concluded.' 'Anything at all, do you say, my friend?' said the other. 'By God, I would not give way to anybody at it, not even to the donkeys themselves.'

"'We shall see about that now,' answered the second alderman, 'because I have determined that you shall go by one part of the mountain and I by another, so that we go round it and cover the whole of it, and every so often you shall bray and I shall bray, and it cannot be otherwise but that the donkey will hear us and answer us, if he is on the mountain.' To which the owner of the donkey answered: 'I say, my friend, that the plan is excellent and worthy of your great wit.'

"And, the two of them dividing according to the agreement, it happened that they brayed at almost the same time; and each of them, deceived by the other's braying, came running to look for him, thinking the donkey had turned up. And, on seeing each other, the man who had lost him said: 'Is it possible, my friend, that it was not my donkey that brayed?' 'No, it was not; it was I,' answered the other. 'Now I say,' said the owner, 'that between you and a donkey, my friend, there is no difference at all as far as braying goes, because in all my life I have never seen or heard anything more to the life.'

"'Those praises and that extolling,' answered the man with the plan, 'belong and apply better to you than to me, my friend; for by the God who made me, you could give two brays' start to the greatest and most expert brayer in the world. Because the tone you have is high; the sustaining of the voice is in its right time and measure; the dying falls are many and quick; and, in short, I give myself up as beaten and hand you the palm and the standard of this rare accomplishment.' 'Now I say,' answered the owner, 'that from here on I shall hold and value myself more, and shall think I know something, since I have some gift; for although I thought I brayed well, I never understood I came up to the extreme you say.'

"'I shall say too, now,' answered the second, 'that there are rare accomplishments lost in the world, and that they are badly bestowed on those who do not know how to make use of them.' 'Ours,' answered the owner, 'except in cases like the one we have in hand, cannot serve us in others — and even in this one, please God they may be of some use.'

"This said, they divided again and went back to their braying, and at every step they deceived each other and came together again, until they settled it between them as a countersign that, so as to be understood as themselves and not the donkey, they should bray twice, one bray after the other. With this, doubling the brays at every step, they went round the whole mountain without the lost donkey answering, even by signs. But how was the poor unlucky creature to answer, when they found him in the most hidden part of the wood, eaten by wolves?

"And, on seeing him, his owner said: 'I was already wondering why he did not answer; for if he had not been dead he would have brayed if he had heard us, or he would not have been a donkey. But in exchange for having heard you bray with such grace, my friend, I count as well spent the labour I have had in looking for him, even though I have found him dead.' 'The credit is in a good hand, my friend,' answered the other, 'for if the abbot sings well, the altar boy is not far behind him.'

"With this, disconsolate and hoarse, they went back to their village, where they told their friends, neighbours and acquaintances everything that had happened to them in the search for the donkey, each of them exaggerating the other's grace in braying — all of which was learnt and spread through the neighbouring places.

"And the devil, who never sleeps, being a friend to sowing and scattering quarrels and discord everywhere, raising squabbles on the wind and great fights out of nothing, arranged and brought it about that the people of the other villages, on seeing anybody from ours, would bray, as though throwing our aldermen's braying in their faces. The boys took it up, which was to fall into the hands and the mouths of all the devils in hell; and the braying went spreading from one village to another, so that the natives of the village of the bray are known as easily as black people are known and told apart from white. And this joke has gone so far in its bad luck that many times, with armed hands and in formed squadrons, the mocked have gone out against the mockers to give them battle, and neither king nor rook, neither fear nor shame, could put a stop to it.

"I believe that tomorrow or the next day the men of my village, who are the men of the bray, are going to take the field against another place two leagues from ours, which is one of those that persecute us most; and, so as to come out well prepared, I have bought these lances and halberds you have seen.

"And these are the marvels I said I would tell you, and if they have not seemed marvels to you, I know no others."

And with this the good man made an end of his talk; and at this moment there came in at the inn door a man dressed all in chamois — stockings, wide breeches and doublet — who said in a loud voice:

"Master host, is there lodging? For here comes the soothsaying ape and the puppet play of the setting free of Melisendra."

"Body of me," said the innkeeper, "here is Master Pedro! We are in for a good night."

I was forgetting to say that this Master Pedro had his left eye and nearly half his cheek covered with a patch of green taffeta, a sign that all that side must have been diseased. And the innkeeper went on, saying:

"Very welcome, your worship, Master Pedro. Where is the ape and the puppet stage, that I do not see them?"

"They are coming up close," answered the man all in chamois, "except that I have come ahead to find out whether there is lodging."

"I would take it from the Duke of Alba himself to give it to Master Pedro," answered the innkeeper. "Let the ape and the stage come up, for there are people in the inn tonight who will pay to see it and to see the ape's accomplishments."

"So be it and welcome," answered the man with the patch, "and I shall bring the price down and count myself well paid with my costs alone. And I shall go back and make the cart come on that the ape and the stage are travelling in."

And with that he went out of the inn again.

Don Quixote then asked the innkeeper what Master Pedro this was, and what puppet stage and what ape he was bringing. To which the innkeeper answered:

"This is a famous puppet-master who has been going about this Aragonese Mancha for a good while now, showing a play of Melisendra set free by the famous Don Gaiferos, which is one of the best and best-performed stories to be seen in this kingdom for many years past. He also brings with him an ape of the rarest ability ever seen among apes or imagined among men; because if they ask him something, he pays attention to what they are asking him and then jumps on his master's shoulder, and, putting his mouth to his ear, tells him the answer to what they are asking, and Master Pedro declares it at once. And he says a great deal more about things past than about those to come; and although he does not hit it right every time in everything, he goes wrong in very few, so that he makes us believe he has the devil in him.

"Two reals he charges for every question, if the ape answers — I mean if the master answers for him after he has spoken in his ear; and so it is believed that this Master Pedro is extremely rich. And he is a gallant fellow, as they say in Italy, and bon compaño, and gives himself the best life in the world; he talks more than six men and drinks more than twelve, all at the cost of his tongue and his ape and his puppet stage."

At this Master Pedro came back, and in a cart came the stage, and the ape — big and without a tail, with a felt behind, but not bad-faced. And hardly had Don Quixote seen him when he asked him:

"Tell me, your worship, Sir Soothsayer: what fish do we catch? What is to become of us? And here you have my two reals."

And he ordered Sancho to give them to Master Pedro, who answered for the ape and said:

"Sir, this animal does not answer or give any notice about things that are to come; about things past he knows something, and about present ones a certain amount."

"Body of me," said Sancho, "I would not give a farthing to have anybody tell me what has happened to me! Because who can know it better than I do myself? And to pay to have somebody tell me what I know would be a great foolishness. But since he knows present things, here are my two reals, and let his lordship the Most Monkeyish tell me what my wife Teresa Panza is doing at this moment, and what she is busy with."

Master Pedro would not take the money, saying:

"I do not care to take the rewards in advance, without the services having come first."

And, giving two slaps with his right hand on his left shoulder, the ape sprang up on it in one leap; and, putting his mouth to his ear, he chattered his teeth very fast. And, having kept up this performance for about the space of a creed, with another leap he was down on the floor. And on the instant, in the greatest haste, Master Pedro went and knelt down in front of Don Quixote, and, embracing his legs, said:

"These legs I embrace as though I were embracing the two pillars of Hercules, O distinguished reviver of the by now forgotten knight-errantry! O never-sufficiently-praised knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, courage of the fainthearted, prop of the falling, arm of the fallen, staff and comfort of all the unfortunate!"

Don Quixote was left thunderstruck, Sancho dumbfounded, the cousin bewildered, the page astonished, the man of the braying gaping, the innkeeper confused and, finally, all who heard the puppet-master's words amazed; and he went on, saying:

"And you, O good Sancho Panza, the best squire and squire to the best knight in the world, be glad, for your good wife Teresa is well; and this is the very hour when she is combing a pound of flax, and, for a further sign, she has at her left side a broken-lipped jug that holds a good drop of wine, with which she entertains herself at her work."

"That I believe very well," answered Sancho, "because she is a blessed creature; and if she were not jealous, I would not swap her for the giantess Andandona, who, according to my master, was a very complete and worthy woman. And my Teresa is one of those who will not let themselves go short, even if it is at their heirs' expense."

"Now I say," said Don Quixote at this point, "that the man who reads much and travels much sees much and knows much. I say this because what persuasion would have been enough to persuade me that there are apes in the world who can tell fortunes, as I have now seen with my own eyes? Because I am that very Don Quixote of La Mancha this good animal has named — although he has stretched himself out somewhat in my praises. But whatever I may be, I give thanks to heaven that endowed me with a soft and compassionate spirit, always inclined to do good to everybody and harm to nobody."

"If I had money," said the page, "I would ask the ape what is to happen to me on the journey I am making."

To which Master Pedro answered, having by now got up from Don Quixote's feet:

"I have already said that this little beast does not answer about what is to come; for if he did, it would not matter that there was no money, since for the service of Señor Don Quixote here present I would give up all the profits in the world. And now, because I owe it to him, and to give him pleasure, I mean to set up my stage and give pleasure to everybody in the inn, without any payment at all."

Which the innkeeper hearing, and being extremely glad, he showed the place where the stage could be set up, and it was done in a moment.

Don Quixote was not very happy about the ape's divinations, since it did not seem to him proper that an ape should tell fortunes, either about things to come or about things past. And so, while Master Pedro was setting up the stage, Don Quixote withdrew with Sancho to a corner of the stable, where, without being heard by anybody, he said to him:

"Look, Sancho, I have thought hard about this ape's strange ability, and I find by my reckoning that without doubt this Master Pedro, his master, must have made a pact, tacit or express, with the devil."

"If the packet is expressed and the devil's," said Sancho, "no doubt it must be a very dirty packet; but what use are these packets to Master Pedro?"

"You do not understand me, Sancho. I only mean that he must have made some agreement with the devil to pour that ability into the ape, so that he may earn his living by it; and afterwards, when he is rich, he will give him his soul, which is what this universal enemy is after. And what makes me believe this is seeing that the ape only answers about things past or present, and the devil's knowledge cannot stretch further than that, since he does not know things to come except by conjecture, and not always then; because it is reserved to God alone to know the times and the moments, and for Him there is no past and no future, for everything is present.

"And this being so, as it is, it is clear that this ape talks in the devil's style; and I marvel that they have not denounced him to the Holy Office and examined him and dragged out of him by whose power he divines. Because it is certain that this ape is no astrologer, and neither he nor his master casts, or knows how to cast, these figures they call judicial, which are so much in use now in Spain that there is not a wretched little woman, or a page, or a cobbler who does not presume to cast a figure, as though it were a jack of cards off the floor — ruining with their lies and their ignorance the marvellous truth of the science.

"I know of one lady who asked one of these figure-casters whether a small lapdog she had would get with pup and litter, and how many and of what colour the pups would be that she littered. To which the gentleman astrologer, after having cast the figure, answered that the little bitch would get with pup and would litter three little dogs, one green, another red and the other mottled, on condition that the said bitch should be covered between eleven and twelve o'clock in the day or in the night, and that it should be on a Monday or a Saturday. And what happened was that two days later the bitch died of overeating, and the gentleman caster was left with the credit in the place of being a most infallible astrologer, as all or most casters are."

"For all that," said Sancho, "I should like your worship to tell Master Pedro to ask his ape whether what happened to your worship in the cave of Montesinos is true; for I hold for myself, with your worship's pardon, that it was all humbug and lies, or at the least things dreamed."

"It could all be," answered Don Quixote, "but I shall do what you advise, although a certain I-know-not-what of scruple will stay with me."

While they were at this, Master Pedro came looking for Don Quixote to tell him that the stage was in order now, and that his worship should come and see it, because it deserved it. Don Quixote told him what was on his mind, and begged him to ask his ape at once to tell him whether certain things that had happened to him in the cave of Montesinos had been dreamed or true, because to him they seemed to have something of both. To which Master Pedro, without answering a word, brought the ape back and, setting him in front of Don Quixote and Sancho, said:

"Look, Sir Ape: this gentleman wants to know whether certain things that happened to him in a cave called the cave of Montesinos were false or true."

And, making him the accustomed signal, the ape climbed up on his left shoulder, and, apparently speaking in his ear, Master Pedro said at once:

"The ape says that part of the things your worship saw or went through in the said cave are false, and part probable; and that this is what he knows, and nothing else, as far as this question goes. And that if your worship wants to know more, next Friday he will answer everything he is asked, because for now his power has run out and will not come to him until Friday, as he has said."

"Did I not say so?" said Sancho. "That I could not settle it in my mind that all your worship said, my dear sir, about the goings-on in the cave was true — no, nor even half of it?"

"Events will tell, Sancho," answered Don Quixote; "for time, the discoverer of all things, leaves nothing that it does not bring out into the light of the sun, even if it is hidden in the bosom of the earth. And for now let this be enough, and let us go and see good Master Pedro's stage, for I hold for myself that it must have something new about it."

"Something?" answered Master Pedro. "Sixty thousand somethings this stage of mine holds inside it. I tell your worship, my lord Don Quixote, that it is one of the most worth-seeing things the world has today; and operibus credite, et non verbis; and now to work, for it is getting late and we have a great deal to do and to say and to show."

Don Quixote and Sancho obeyed him and came to where the stage was already set up and uncovered, full on every side of lighted wax tapers that made it showy and shining. On arriving, Master Pedro got inside it, since he was the one who had to work the figures of the contrivance; and outside there stood a boy, Master Pedro's servant, to serve as interpreter and expounder of the mysteries of that stage: he had a little wand in his hand with which he pointed out the figures as they came on.

All the people in the inn being placed, then, some of them standing, facing the stage, and Don Quixote, Sancho, the page and the cousin settled in the best seats, the interpreter began to say what will be heard and seen by anyone who hears or sees the next chapter.

Chapter 26: Where the Amusing Adventure of the Puppet-Master Is Carried Further, with Other Things That Are Truly Very Good

They all fell silent, Tyrians and Trojans alike — I mean that everybody who was watching the stage was hanging on the mouth of the man who declared its marvels — when there was heard sounding inside the stage a quantity of kettledrums and trumpets, and a great deal of artillery going off; whose noise passed in a short time, and then the boy raised his voice and said:

"This true history that is here performed before your worships is taken word for word out of the French chronicles and out of the Spanish ballads that are in the mouths of the people and of the boys about these streets. It deals with the setting free by Señor Don Gaiferos of his wife Melisendra, who was held captive in Spain, in the power of the Moors, in the city of Sansueña — for that was the name then of the city that today is called Saragossa. And your worships may see there how Don Gaiferos is playing at tables, according to what is sung:

	Don Gaiferos sits playing at tables,
	and Melisendra is forgotten now.

"And that personage who looks out there, with a crown on his head and a sceptre in his hands, is the emperor Charlemagne, the reputed father of this Melisendra, who, vexed at seeing the idleness and carelessness of his son-in-law, comes out to scold him. And notice with what vehemence and eagerness he scolds him, so that it looks as if he wants to give him half a dozen raps on the head with the sceptre — and there are even authors who say he gave them to him, and gave them well. And, after having said him a great many things about the danger his honour was running in not seeing to his wife's freedom, they say he said to him:

"'I have said enough to you: look to it.'

"Let your worships also observe how the emperor turns his back and leaves Don Gaiferos in a rage; who, as you now see, impatient with fury, hurls the board and the pieces far away from him and asks in haste for his arms, and asks his cousin Don Roland for the loan of his sword Durindana, and how Don Roland will not lend it him, offering him his company in the difficult enterprise he is undertaking. But the valorous angry man will not accept it; on the contrary, he says that he alone is enough to bring his wife out, even if she were shut away in the deepest centre of the earth. And with this he goes in to arm himself, so as to set out at once.

"Turn your worships' eyes to that tower that appears there, which is supposed to be one of the towers of the castle of Saragossa that they now call the Aljafería; and that lady who appears on that balcony, dressed in the Moorish fashion, is the peerless Melisendra, who from there would often set herself to look at the road to France and, setting her imagination on Paris and on her husband, would console herself in her captivity.

"Look too at a new turn of events that is happening now, perhaps never seen before. Do you not see that Moor who, hushed and step by step, with his finger on his lips, is coming up behind Melisendra? Well, look how he gives her a kiss right on the lips, and the haste she makes to spit and to wipe them with the white sleeve of her shift, and how she laments and tears out her beautiful hair for grief, as though it had the blame for the mischief.

"Look too at that grave Moor there in those galleries, who is King Marsilio of Sansueña; who, having seen the Moor's insolence — although he was a relation of his and a great favourite — ordered him to be arrested on the spot and given two hundred lashes, taking him through the usual streets of the city,

	with the criers going in front
	and the constables' staves behind;

"and here you see them coming out to carry out the sentence, when the offence has hardly been carried out at all; because among Moors there is no 'notice to the other party' or 'let it stand to proof', as there is among us."

"Boy, boy," said Don Quixote at this point in a loud voice, "keep to your history in a straight line, and do not go off into curves and cross-cuts; for to get a truth out clean a great many proofs and re-provings are needed."

Master Pedro said from inside as well:

"Boy, do not go in for fancy work, but do as this gentleman orders you, and that will be the surest way. Keep to your plainsong and do not go in for counterpoints, for they generally break from being too fine."

"I shall do so," answered the boy; and he went on, saying: "This figure that appears here on horseback, wrapped in a Gascon cloak, is Don Gaiferos himself, whose wife, now avenged of the amorous Moor's boldness, with a better and quieter countenance has set herself at the tower windows and is talking with her husband, believing him to be some traveller — with whom she went through all those words and speeches of the ballad that says:

	Sir knight, if to France ye go,
	ask there for Gaiferos —

"which I do not say now, because from long-windedness tedium is usually bred. It is enough to see how Don Gaiferos discovers himself, and how by the glad gestures Melisendra makes we are given to understand that she has recognised him, and the more so now that we see she is letting herself down from the balcony to place herself on the crupper of her good husband's horse.

"But — oh, unlucky lady! — a corner of her petticoat has caught on one of the irons of the balcony, and she is hanging in the air unable to reach the ground. But you see how merciful heaven comes to the rescue in the greatest necessities: for Don Gaiferos arrives, and, without looking to see whether the rich petticoat will tear or not, he seizes hold of her and brings her down to the ground in spite of it, and then at one leap sets her on his horse's crupper, astride like a man, and tells her to hold on tight and to throw her arms round his back so as to cross them over his chest, so that she may not fall — because the lady Melisendra was not used to horsemanship of the kind.

"You see too how the horse's neighing gives signs that he is content with the valiant and beautiful burden he carries in his lord and his lady. You see how they turn their backs and leave the city and, glad and merry, take the road to Paris. Go in peace, O peerless pair of true lovers! May you come safe to your longed-for country, without fortune putting any obstacle in the way of your happy journey! May the eyes of your friends and your relations see you enjoy in quiet peace the days that are left you of your life — and may they be the days of Nestor!"

Here Master Pedro raised his voice again and said:

"Plainness, boy; do not soar; all affectation is bad."

The interpreter answered nothing; on the contrary, he went on, saying:

"There were not wanting some idle eyes, which generally see everything, that did not see Melisendra's coming down and getting up, and they gave notice of it to King Marsilio, who at once ordered the alarm to be sounded. And look how quickly, for the city is already sinking under the noise of the bells sounding from all the towers of the mosques."

"Not that!" said Don Quixote at this. "In this matter of the bells Master Pedro is going very wide of the mark, because bells are not used among Moors, but kettledrums and a kind of shawm like our own reed-pipes; and this business of bells ringing in Sansueña is beyond any doubt a great absurdity."

Which Master Pedro hearing, he left off ringing and said:

"Do not look at trifles, your worship, Señor Don Quixote, or want to carry things so far that you never find the end of them. Are there not a thousand plays performed about here, almost every day, full of a thousand improprieties and absurdities, and for all that they run their course most happily and are listened to not merely with applause but with admiration and everything else? Go on, boy, and let them talk; for so long as I fill my bag, let there be more improprieties in it than the sun has atoms."

"That is the truth," replied Don Quixote.

And the boy said:

"Look how much and how splendid a body of horse comes out of the city in pursuit of the two Catholic lovers, how many trumpets sounding, how many shawms playing and how many kettledrums and side drums thundering. I fear they will catch them up and bring them back tied to the tail of their own horse, which would be a horrible spectacle."

Seeing and hearing so much Moorishness and so much uproar, then, it seemed to Don Quixote a good thing to give help to the fugitives; and, standing up, he said in a loud voice:

"I shall not consent, in my days and in my presence, that so famous a knight and so daring a lover as Don Gaiferos should be treated with such foul play. Stop, you baseborn rabble! Do not follow him or pursue him, or you have me to fight with!"

And, saying and doing, he drew his sword and at one bound placed himself next to the stage, and with a headlong and never-before-seen fury began to rain sword-strokes down on the puppet Moorishness, knocking some over, beheading others, maiming this one, shattering that one; and, among many other blows, he let fly one downstroke such that if Master Pedro had not ducked, shrunk and crouched, it would have sheared his head off more easily than if it had been made of marzipan paste. Master Pedro was shouting, saying:

"Stop, your worship, Señor Don Quixote, and note that these you are knocking down and shattering and killing are not real Moors but figures made of paste. Look — sinner that I am! — you are destroying me and ruining my whole livelihood!"

But for all that Don Quixote did not stop dealing out sword-strokes, two-handed cuts, slashes and backhands as if it were raining them. Finally, in less than the time it takes to say two creeds, he had the whole stage on the ground, with all its gear and its figures smashed to pieces and crumbled: King Marsilio badly wounded, and the emperor Charlemagne with his crown and his head split in two.

The senate of listeners was thrown into an uproar, the ape fled over the roofs out of the window, the cousin was frightened, the page lost his nerve, and even Sancho Panza himself was in enormous terror, because, as he swore when the storm was over, he had never seen his master in such a headlong rage.

The general destruction of the stage being accomplished, then, Don Quixote quieted down a little and said:

"I should like to have here in front of me at this moment all those who do not believe, and do not want to believe, how much use knights errant are in the world. Look — if I had not been present here, what would have become of good Don Gaiferos and the beautiful Melisendra? It is a safe bet that by this hour those dogs would have caught them and done them some outrage. In short, long live knight-errantry over everything alive on earth today!"

"Long live it and welcome," said Master Pedro at this in a sickly voice, "and let me die, since I am so unfortunate that I can say with King Rodrigo:

	Yesterday I was lord of Spain,
	and today I have not one battlement
	that I can call my own.

"Not half an hour ago, nor even a middling moment, I saw myself lord of kings and emperors, my stables and my chests and my bags full of infinite horses and innumerable finery; and now I see myself desolate and cast down, poor and a beggar, and, above all, without my ape — for upon my word my teeth will sweat before I get him back into my hands. And all through the ill-considered fury of this gentleman knight, of whom it is said that he protects orphans and rights wrongs and does other charitable works; and in me alone has his generous intention come to fail — blessed and praised be the heavens, up there where they have their loftiest seats. In short, the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance was bound to be the one to disfigure my figures."

Sancho Panza was moved by Master Pedro's words, and said to him:

"Do not weep, Master Pedro, and do not lament, for you break my heart. Because I let you know that my master Don Quixote is so Catholic and so scrupulous a Christian that if he grasps that he has done you some wrong, he will know it and will want to pay you and satisfy you with a great deal over."

"If Señor Don Quixote would only pay me some part of the workmanship he has unworked, I should be content, and his worship would set his conscience at rest — because no man can be saved who holds what belongs to another against its owner's will and does not restore it."

"That is so," said Don Quixote; "but so far I do not know that I have anything of yours, Master Pedro."

"How not?" answered Master Pedro. "And these relics lying on this hard and barren ground — who scattered them and annihilated them but the invincible force of that powerful arm? And whose were their bodies but mine? And what did I keep myself on but them?"

"Now I finally believe," said Don Quixote at this point, "what I have believed a great many other times: that these enchanters who persecute me do nothing but set the figures in front of my eyes as they really are, and then change them and swap them for whatever ones they please. Really and truly I tell you, gentlemen who hear me, that everything that has happened here seemed to me to be happening to the letter: that Melisendra was Melisendra, Don Gaiferos Don Gaiferos, Marsilio Marsilio and Charlemagne Charlemagne. That is why my choler rose; and, to fulfil my profession as a knight errant, I wanted to give help and favour to those who were fleeing, and with this good purpose I did what you have seen. If it has come out backwards, it is not my fault but the fault of the wicked ones who persecute me; and, for all that, for this mistake of mine, though it did not come out of malice, I mean to condemn myself in costs. Let Master Pedro see what he wants for the broken figures, and I offer to pay it him at once in good current Castilian money."

Master Pedro bowed to him, saying:

"I expected no less from the unheard-of Christian charity of the valorous Don Quixote of La Mancha, true helper and protector of all needy and destitute vagabonds. And here the master innkeeper and the great Sancho shall be mediators and appraisers between your worship and me of what the now broken figures are worth or might be worth."

The innkeeper and Sancho said they would do so, and then Master Pedro picked up off the ground King Marsilio of Saragossa, with his head gone, and said:

"It can be seen how impossible it is to restore this king to his first condition; and so it seems to me, saving a better judgement, that I should be given for his death, end and finish four reals and a half."

"Go on," said Don Quixote.

"Well, for this split from top to bottom," Master Pedro went on, taking the halved emperor Charlemagne in his hands, "it would not be too much if I asked five reals and a quarter."

"That is not little," said Sancho.

"Nor much," replied the innkeeper. "Split the difference and set him down five reals."

"Let him have the whole five and a quarter," said Don Quixote, "for the sum of this notable misfortune does not stand on a quarter more or less; and let Master Pedro finish quickly, for supper time is coming on and I have certain forebodings of hunger."

"For this figure," said Master Pedro, "which is without a nose and short of one eye, and is the beautiful Melisendra, I want — and I am setting it fairly — two reals and twelve maravedís."

"The devil would be in it," said Don Quixote, "if Melisendra were not by now with her husband, at the very least, on the borders of France; because the horse they were riding seemed to me to be flying rather than running. And so there is no call to sell me the cat for a hare by presenting me here with a noseless Melisendra, when the other one, if it comes to that, is at this moment taking her ease in France with her husband with her legs stretched out. God help every man with what is his own, Master Pedro, and let us all walk on level ground and with sound intentions. And go on."

Master Pedro, who saw that Don Quixote was heeling over and going back to his first theme, did not want him to get away; and so he said to him:

"This must not be Melisendra but one of the girls who waited on her; and so, with sixty maravedís given me for her I shall be content and well paid."

In this way he went on putting a price on a great many other shattered figures, which the two arbitrating judges afterwards moderated to the satisfaction of both parties, and which came to forty reals and three quarters; and besides this, which Sancho paid out at once, Master Pedro asked for two reals for the trouble of catching the ape.

"Give them to him, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "not for catching the ape but for catching himself a drink; and I would give two hundred now as a reward to anybody who could tell me with certainty that the lady Doña Melisendra and Señor Don Gaiferos were already in France and among their own people."

"Nobody could tell us better than my ape," said Master Pedro, "but there is no devil that could catch him now — though I imagine that affection and hunger will force him to come looking for me tonight; and God will send the morning and we shall see each other."
