In short, the storm of the puppet stage came to an end, and they all had supper in peace and good company at Don Quixote's expense, for he was generous in the last degree.

Before daybreak the man with the lances and the halberds went off; and after it was light the cousin and the page came to take their leave of Don Quixote, the one to go back to his own country and the other to go on with his journey, towards which Don Quixote gave him a dozen reals. Master Pedro did not want to get into any more chopping and changing of words with Don Quixote, whom he knew very well; and so he was up before the sun and, gathering up the relics of his stage and his ape, went off to look for his own adventures too.

The innkeeper, who did not know Don Quixote, was as astonished by his madnesses as by his generosity. Finally Sancho paid him very well by his master's orders, and, taking their leave of him, at about eight in the morning they left the inn and set out on their road — where we shall leave them going, for that is what is needed to make room for telling other things that belong to the setting out of this famous history.

Chapter 27: Where an Account Is Given of Who Master Pedro and His Ape Were, with the Bad Outcome Don Quixote Had in the Adventure of the Braying, Which He Did Not End as He Wished or as He Had Planned

Cide Hamete, the chronicler of this great history, comes into this chapter with these words: "I swear as a Catholic Christian..." — to which his translator says that Cide Hamete's swearing as a Catholic Christian, he being a Moor, as he undoubtedly was, meant nothing else but this: that just as the Catholic Christian, when he swears, swears — or ought to swear — the truth, and to tell it in whatever he says, so he was telling the truth, as though he were swearing as a Catholic Christian, in what he meant to write about Don Quixote, and especially in saying who Master Pedro was and who the soothsaying ape was that had all those villages marvelling with his divinations.

He says, then, that anybody who has read the first part of this history will remember that Ginés de Pasamonte to whom, among other galley slaves, Don Quixote gave freedom in the Sierra Morena — a kindness that was afterwards ill thanked and worse repaid by that malignant and badly brought up crew.

This Ginés de Pasamonte, whom Don Quixote called Ginesillo de Parapilla, was the man who stole Sancho Panza's grey; and, since the how and the when of it were not put into the first part through the printers' fault, it has given a great many people something to puzzle over, who put the missing passage down to the author's short memory. But in short, Ginés stole him while Sancho Panza was sleeping on his back, using the trick and the method Brunello used when, while Sacripante was at Albraca, he drew the horse out from between his legs; and afterwards Sancho got him back, as has been told.

This Ginés, then, afraid of being found by the law, which was looking for him to punish him for his infinite villainies and crimes — which were so many and such that he himself composed a great volume telling them — decided to cross over into the kingdom of Aragon and cover his left eye, taking up the trade of puppet-master; for this and sleight of hand he could do to perfection.

It happened, then, that from some Christians who had been set free and were coming from Barbary he bought that ape, whom he taught that on being given a certain signal he should climb up on his shoulder and murmur — or seem to murmur — in his ear. This done, before he went into any place where he was going with his stage and his ape, he would find out at the nearest place, or from whoever he best could, what particular things had happened in that place, and to what people. And, carrying them well in his memory, the first thing he did was to show his stage, which was sometimes of one story and sometimes of another, but all of them cheerful and merry and well known.

The show over, he would announce his ape's abilities, telling the people that he divined all things past and present, but that in the matter of things to come he had no skill. For the answer to each question he asked two reals, and for some he cut the price, according to how he took the pulse of the questioners. And since he sometimes came to the houses of people whose doings he knew, even if they asked him nothing so as not to have to pay him, he would give the ape the signal and then say that he had told him such and such a thing, which fitted the facts to a mould. With this he got himself an unspeakable credit, and everybody went trooping after him. Other times, being so shrewd, he would answer in such a way that the answers fitted the questions well; and, as nobody pressed him or pushed him to say how his ape divined, he made monkeys of them all and filled his pouches.

As soon as he came into the inn he recognised Don Quixote and Sancho, and through recognising them it was easy for him to fill Don Quixote and Sancho Panza with wonder, and everybody else who was there. But it would have cost him dear if Don Quixote had brought his hand down a little lower when he cut off King Marsilio's head and destroyed all his cavalry, as has been told in the foregoing chapter.

This is what there is to say about Master Pedro and his ape.

And, coming back to Don Quixote of La Mancha, I say that after leaving the inn he decided to see first the banks of the river Ebro and all those parts, before going into the city of Saragossa, since the great deal of time that was left from then until the jousts gave him room for everything. With this intention he followed his road, along which he travelled two days without anything happening to him worth putting in writing, until on the third, coming up a rise, he heard a great noise of drums, trumpets and harquebuses.

At first he thought some regiment of soldiers was passing that way, and to see them he spurred Rocinante up the rise. And when he was at the top he saw at the foot of it, as far as he could judge, more than two hundred men armed with different kinds of arms — that is to say, long spears, crossbows, partisans, halberds and pikes, and a few harquebuses, and a great many bucklers.

He came down the slope and got near enough to the squadron to see the flags distinctly, judge their colours and note the devices they carried on them — especially one that came on a standard or pennant of white satin, on which was painted very much to the life a donkey like a little Sardinian ass, its head raised, its mouth open and its tongue out, in the act and posture of a beast in the middle of braying. Around it were written in large letters these two lines:

	Our two good magistrates, 'tis plain,
	did not stand and bray in vain.

By this ensign Don Quixote gathered that these people must be from the village of the bray, and he said so to Sancho, explaining to him what was written on the standard. He told him too that the man who had given them notice of the business had been wrong in saying that it was two aldermen who had brayed; but that, according to the lines on the standard, they had been magistrates. To which Sancho Panza answered:

"Sir, there is nothing to stick at in that, for it may very well be that the aldermen who brayed then came in time to be magistrates of their village, and so they can be called by both titles; and what is more, it makes no difference to the truth of the history whether the brayers were magistrates or aldermen, so long as they brayed one way or the other — because a magistrate is as likely to bray as an alderman."

Finally they learnt and made out that the mocked village was coming out to fight another that mocked it more than was just and more than was owing to good neighbourliness.

Don Quixote went up to them, to Sancho's no small distress, for he was never fond of finding himself in expeditions of the sort. The men of the squadron took him into their midst, believing he was one of their own party. Don Quixote, raising his visor with a fine spirit and bearing, came up to the standard of the donkey, and there all the chief men of the army gathered round him to look at him, filled with the usual astonishment that everybody fell into who looked at him for the first time.

Don Quixote, seeing them so intent on looking at him without anybody speaking to him or asking him anything, decided to make use of that silence, and, breaking his own, raised his voice and said:

"Good gentlemen, as earnestly as I can I beg you not to interrupt an argument I want to make you, until you find that it displeases and annoys you; for if that happens, at the least sign you make me I shall put a seal on my mouth and clap a gag on my tongue."

They all told him to say whatever he liked, for they would listen to him gladly. With this licence Don Quixote went on, saying:

"I, my dear sirs, am a knight errant, whose exercise is that of arms and whose profession is to favour those in need of favour and to come to the help of the destitute. Some days ago I learnt of your misfortune and of the cause that moves you to take up arms at every turn to avenge yourselves on your enemies; and, having gone over your business once and many times in my understanding, I find, according to the laws of duelling, that you are mistaken in holding yourselves affronted, because no single man can affront a whole community, unless it is by challenging all of it together for treason, since he does not know in particular who committed the treason he is challenging it for.

"An example of this we have in Don Diego Ordóñez de Lara, who challenged the whole people of Zamora because he did not know that Vellido Dolfos alone had committed the treason of killing his king; and so he challenged them all, and the vengeance and the answer concerned them all — although it is quite true that Señor Don Diego went somewhat too far, and even went a long way past the limits of the challenge, because he had no call to challenge the dead, the waters, the loaves of bread, those who were still unborn, and the other trifles that are set out there. But let it pass; for when choler bursts its banks, the tongue has no father, tutor or bridle to check it.

"This being so, then — that one man alone cannot affront a kingdom, a province, a city, a commonwealth or a whole community — it comes out clean that there is no call to go out to avenge the challenge of such an affront, since it is none. Because it would be a fine thing if the people of Clock-town killed each other at every turn with whoever called them by that name, and so with the stew-pot men, the aubergine men, the whale men, the soap men, and all the other names and nicknames that go about here in the mouths of boys and of people of no great account! It would be a fine thing, certainly, if all these distinguished towns took offence and revenged themselves and went about with their swords for ever sliding out like sackbuts at every quarrel, however small!

"No, no, and God neither permit it nor wish it. Prudent men and well-ordered commonwealths have to take up arms and draw their swords and put their persons, lives and estates at risk for four things: the first, to defend the Catholic faith; the second, to defend their own lives, which is a law of nature and of God; the third, in defence of their honour, their family and their property; the fourth, in the service of their king in a just war. And if we want to add a fifth, which can be counted as second, it is in defence of their country. To these five causes, as the chief ones, some others may be added that are just and reasonable and that make it right to take up arms; but to take them up for childishness and for things that are matter for laughter and entertainment rather than for affront, looks as if the man who takes them up is short of all reasonable judgement.

"What is more, taking unjust revenge — and there can be none that is just — goes directly against the holy law we profess, in which we are commanded to do good to our enemies and to love those who hate us; a commandment which, though it looks somewhat difficult to keep, is not so except for those who have less of God in them than of the world, and more of the flesh than of the spirit. Because Jesus Christ, true God and true man, who never lied and could not and cannot lie, being our lawgiver, said that his yoke was easy and his burden light; and so he would not command us anything that it was impossible to carry out. And so, my dear sirs, your worships are bound by divine and human laws to quiet down."

"The devil take me," said Sancho to himself at this, "if this master of mine is not a 'ologian; and if he is not one, he is as like one as one egg is to another."

Don Quixote took a little breath, and, seeing that they were still lending him silence, wanted to go further with his talk — as he would have done if Sancho's sharpness had not got in the way; for Sancho, seeing that his master had stopped, took over from him, saying:

"My master Don Quixote of La Mancha, who at one time was called the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance and is now called the Knight of the Lions, is a very well-advised gentleman who knows Latin and Spanish like a bachelor of arts, and in everything he deals with and advises on he goes about it like a very good soldier, and he has all the laws and ordinances of what they call duelling at his fingertips. And so there is nothing to do but let yourselves be led by whatever he says, and it is on my head if you go wrong.

"And besides, it stands said already that it is foolishness to take offence merely at hearing a bray; because I remember, when I was a boy, that I brayed whenever I felt like it, without anybody stopping me, and with such grace and truth to life that when I brayed all the donkeys in the village brayed too. And I was none the less for that the son of my parents, who were most honourable people; and although for this ability I was envied by more than four of the stiff-necked men of my village, I did not care two farthings. And, so that you may see I am telling the truth, wait and listen — for this science is like swimming: once learnt, it is never forgotten."

And then, putting his hand to his nose, he began to bray so lustily that all the nearby valleys rang with it. But one of the men standing next to him, believing he was making fun of them, raised a long stick he had in his hand and gave him such a blow with it that, without being able to help himself, Sancho Panza went down on the ground.

Don Quixote, who saw Sancho in such bad case, charged at the man who had struck him with his lance couched; but so many got in the way that it was not possible to avenge him. On the contrary, seeing that a stormcloud of stones was raining down on him and that a thousand levelled crossbows and no fewer harquebuses were threatening him, he turned Rocinante's reins and, at the fastest gallop he could manage, got out from among them, commending himself with all his heart to God to deliver him from that danger, fearing at every step that some bullet would come in at his back and out at his chest; and every moment he took in his breath to see whether it failed him.

But the men of the squadron were satisfied with seeing him run, and did not shoot at him. They put Sancho on his donkey, hardly come round yet, and let him go after his master — not because he had his senses about him to steer it, but because the grey followed Rocinante's tracks, without whom he could not be a moment at ease. Don Quixote, then, having got a good way off, turned his head and saw Sancho coming, and waited for him, seeing that nobody was following.

The men of the squadron stayed there until night; and, their opponents not having come out to battle, they went back to their village, merry and glad; and if they had known the ancient custom of the Greeks, they would have raised a trophy in that place.

Chapter 28: Of Things That Benengeli Says Whoever Reads Him Will Know, If He Reads Them with Attention

When the brave man flees, foul play has been discovered, and it is the part of prudent men to keep themselves for a better occasion. This truth was borne out in Don Quixote, who, giving way to the fury of the village and to the bad intentions of that indignant squadron, took to his heels; and, without remembering Sancho or the danger he was leaving him in, he got as far off as seemed to him enough to be safe. Sancho followed him, laid across his donkey, as has been related.

He arrived at last, come round to his senses by now, and on arriving he let himself fall off the grey at Rocinante's feet, all anguish, all bruises and all beating. Don Quixote dismounted to look at his wounds; but, finding him sound from head to foot, he said to him with a good deal of choler:

"In an evil hour did you know how to bray, Sancho! And where did you find it good to name the rope in the hanged man's house? To music of brays, what counterpoint was to be expected but of cudgels? And give thanks to God, Sancho, that since they crossed you with a stick they did not make the sign of the cross over you with a scimitar."

"I am not up to answering," answered Sancho, "because I feel as if I were talking out of my shoulder blades. Let us mount and get away from here, and I shall put silence on my brays — but not on saying that knights errant run away and leave their good squires ground like henna, or like chaff, in the power of their enemies."

"He does not flee who retires," answered Don Quixote; "because you must know, Sancho, that valour which is not founded on the base of prudence is called rashness, and the exploits of the rash man are put down more to good luck than to his spirit. And so I confess that I have retired but have not fled; and in this I have imitated a great many brave men who have kept themselves for better times, and the histories are full of it — which, since they would be of no profit to you or of any pleasure to me, I do not report to you now."

By this time Sancho was on his beast, helped by Don Quixote, who likewise got up on Rocinante; and little by little they went to take cover in a poplar grove that showed itself about a quarter of a league from there. From time to time Sancho let out some very deep "ohs" and some sorrowful groans; and when Don Quixote asked him the cause of such bitter feeling, he answered that from the end of his backbone to the nape of his skull it hurt him in such a way that it took his senses away.

"The cause of that pain," said Don Quixote, "must without doubt be that, as the stick they struck you with was long and full-length, it caught you all across the back, where all those parts come in that are hurting you; and if it had caught more of you, more would be hurting."

"By God," said Sancho, "your worship has got me out of a great doubt, and has cleared it up for me in fine terms! Body of me! Was the cause of my pain so hidden that it needed telling me that everything hurts that the stick reached? If my ankles were hurting, there might still be some guessing about why they hurt; but for what has been pounded to hurt me is not much of a guess.

"Upon my word, sir our master, another man's trouble hangs by a hair; and every day I am sighting more land of how little I can expect from the company I keep with your worship. Because if this time you have let me be cudgelled, another time and another hundred times we shall go back to the blanket-tossings of long ago and to other childishnesses — which, if this time they have come out on my back, next time will come out at my eyes.

"I should do a great deal better — except that I am a barbarian and shall never do anything good in all my life — I should do a great deal better, I say again, to go back home and to my wife and to my children, and to keep her and bring them up on what God was pleased to give me, and not go trailing after your worship along roads that are no roads and by paths and highways that are neither, drinking badly and eating worse.

"And then take sleeping! Count out seven feet of earth, brother squire, and if you want more, take as many again, for it is in your own hand to dish it out; and stretch yourself out to your heart's content. May I see burnt and turned to powder the first man who put a stitch into knight-errantry, or at least the first man who wanted to be squire to such fools as all the past knights errant must have been. Of the present ones I say nothing, since your worship is one of them, and I have respect for them, and because I know that your worship knows one point more than the devil in everything you say and everything you think."

"I would make a good bet with you, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that now that you go along talking with nobody to stop you, nothing at all hurts you anywhere in your body. Talk, my son, everything that comes into your mind and to your mouth; for in exchange for nothing hurting you, I shall count as a pleasure the annoyance your impertinences give me. And if you so much want to go back to your house with your wife and children, God forbid that I should stop you: you have money of mine. Look how long it is since this third time we came out of our village, and look what you can and ought to earn each month, and pay yourself with your own hand."

"When I served Tomé Carrasco," answered Sancho, "the father of the bachelor Sansón Carrasco, whom your worship knows well, I earned two ducats a month, besides my food. With your worship I do not know what I can earn, although I know that the squire of a knight errant has more work than the man who serves a farmer. Because, in short, those of us who serve farmers, however much we work by day and however badly things go, at night we have a stew for supper and sleep in a bed — which I have not slept in since I have been serving your worship. Except for the short time we were at Don Diego de Miranda's house, and the feast I had with the skimmings I took out of Camacho's pots, and what I ate and drank and slept at Basilio's house, all the rest of the time I have slept on the hard ground in the open air, subject to what they call the inclemencies of heaven, keeping myself going on scraps of cheese and crusts of bread, and drinking water, sometimes from brooks and sometimes from springs, out of whatever we come across in these out-of-the-way places where we go about."

"I confess," said Don Quixote, "that everything you say is true, Sancho. How much do you think I ought to give you over and above what Tomé Carrasco gave you?"

"To my mind," said Sancho, "with two reals more that your worship added each month, I should count myself well paid. That is as to the wages of my labour; but as to satisfying me over the word and promise your worship has made me of giving me the government of an isle, it would be just for another six reals to be added, which in all would come to thirty."

"That is very good," replied Don Quixote; "and, according to the wages you have set yourself, it is twenty-three days since we came out of our village. Reckon it up, Sancho, pro rata, and see what I owe you, and pay yourself, as I have told you, with your own hand."

"Oh, body of me!" said Sancho. "Your worship goes very wide in this reckoning, because in the matter of the promise of the isle it has to be counted from the day your worship promised it me until the present hour we are in."

"Well then, how long is it, Sancho, since I promised it you?" said Don Quixote.

"If I remember rightly," answered Sancho, "it must be more than twenty years, three days more or less."

Don Quixote gave himself a great slap on the forehead and began to laugh very heartily, and said:

"Why, I was hardly two months in the Sierra Morena, or in the whole course of our sallies — and you say, Sancho, that it is twenty years since I promised you the isle? Now I say that you want the money of mine that you have to be eaten up in your wages; and if that is so and it pleases you, from here I give it you, and much good may it do you; for in exchange for seeing myself rid of so bad a squire, I shall be glad to be left poor and without a farthing.

"But tell me, you perverter of the squirely ordinances of knight-errantry: where have you seen or read that any squire of a knight errant ever set himself to bargain with his master about 'so much more must you give me every month for serving you'? Go in, go in, you villain, poltroon and monster — for you look like all of them; go in, I say, into the mare magnum of their histories, and if you find that any squire ever said, or thought, what you have said here, I want you to nail him on my forehead and, into the bargain, give me four good flicks on the nose, sealed and delivered.

"Turn the grey's reins, or his halter, and go back home, because not one step further from here shall you go on with me. O bread ill-acknowledged! O promises badly placed! O man who has more of the beast in him than of the person! Now, when I was thinking of setting you up in such a station that in spite of your wife they would call you 'your lordship' — now you take your leave? Now you go, when I was coming with a firm and binding intention of making you lord of the best isle in the world? In short, as you have said at other times, honey is not for the mouth of... and so forth. An ass you are, and an ass you have to be, and you will end an ass when the course of your life runs out; for I hold for myself that your life will come to its last term before you tumble to it and grasp that you are a beast."

Sancho was looking hard at Don Quixote while he was saying him these abuses, and he was so stricken that the tears came into his eyes, and in a pained and sickly voice he said to him:

"My dear sir, I confess that to be an ass altogether I lack nothing but the tail. If your worship wants to put one on me, I shall count it well put on, and shall serve you as a donkey all the days that are left me of my life. Let your worship forgive me and pity my green years, and note that I know little, and that if I talk a lot it comes more from a disease than from malice; but he who errs and mends commends himself to God."

"I should have been astonished, Sancho, if you had not mixed some little proverb into your talk. Well now, I forgive you, provided that you mend yourself and that from now on you do not show yourself such a friend of your own interest, but try to broaden your heart, and take heart and courage to wait for the fulfilling of my promises — which, though it is late, is not made impossible."

Sancho answered that he would do so, even if he had to draw strength out of weakness.

With this they went into the poplar grove, and Don Quixote settled himself at the foot of an elm and Sancho at the foot of a beech; for trees of that kind, and others like them, always have feet and never hands. Sancho spent the night painfully, because the cudgelling made itself felt more in the night air. Don Quixote spent it in his usual memories; but for all that they gave their eyes up to sleep, and at daybreak they followed their road, looking for the banks of the famous Ebro — where there happened to them what will be told in the coming chapter.

Chapter 29: Of the Famous Adventure of the Enchanted Boat

By their measured steps, and by steps still to be measured, two days after leaving the poplar grove Don Quixote and Sancho came to the river Ebro; and the sight of it was a great pleasure to Don Quixote, because he contemplated and looked at the pleasantness of its banks, the clearness of its waters, the quietness of its course and the abundance of its liquid crystal, whose glad sight renewed a thousand loving thoughts in his memory. Above all he went back and forth over what he had seen in the cave of Montesinos; for although Master Pedro's ape had told him that part of those things were true and part lies, he held more by the true ones than by the lying ones — quite the other way from Sancho, who held them all for the very truth of lying.

Going along in this way, then, there offered itself to his sight a small boat without oars or any other tackle, tied up on the bank to the trunk of a tree that stood on the shore. Don Quixote looked in every direction and saw nobody at all; and then, without any more ado, he got down off Rocinante and ordered Sancho to do the same off the grey, and to tie both beasts very securely together to the trunk of a poplar or willow that stood there. Sancho asked him the cause of this sudden dismounting and this tying up. Don Quixote answered:

"You must know, Sancho, that this boat here is directly — and it cannot possibly be otherwise — calling me and inviting me to get into it and go in it to bring help to some knight, or to some other person of quality in need, who must be laid under some great affliction. Because this is the manner of the books of chivalrous histories and of the enchanters who meddle and talk in them: when some knight is laid under some hardship out of which he cannot be delivered except by the hand of another knight, even though they are two or three thousand leagues apart, and even more, either they snatch him up in a cloud or they furnish him with a boat to get into, and in less than the opening and shutting of an eye they carry him, either through the air or over the sea, wherever they like and wherever his help is needed. And so, Sancho, this boat is put here for that same purpose; and this is as true as it is now day. And before this one is over, tie the grey and Rocinante together, and into the hand of God, who will guide us; for I would not give up embarking if barefoot friars begged me to."

"Well, since that is so," answered Sancho, "and your worship means to run at every step into these things — I do not know whether to call them absurdities — there is nothing for it but to obey and bow my head, keeping to the proverb 'do what your master tells you and sit down at table with him'. But for all that, for the discharge of my conscience, I want to warn your worship that to my mind this boat is not one of the enchanted ones but belongs to some fishermen on this river, because the best shad in the world are caught in it."

This is what Sancho was saying while he tied up the beasts, leaving them to the protection and shelter of the enchanters with a good deal of pain to his soul. Don Quixote told him not to grieve over the abandoning of those animals, since the one who was going to carry them along such longinquous roads and regions would see to feeding them.

"I do not understand that about 'longwinkyous'," said Sancho, "and I have never heard such a word in all the days of my life."

"Longinquous," answered Don Quixote, "means far off; and it is no wonder that you do not understand it, for you are not obliged to know Latin, like some who presume they know it and are ignorant of it."

"They are tied up now," replied Sancho. "What are we to do next?"

"What?" answered Don Quixote. "Cross ourselves and weigh anchor — I mean, embark and cut the cable this boat is tied by."

And, giving a leap into it, with Sancho after him, he cut the cord, and the boat began to draw away little by little from the bank. And when Sancho saw himself a matter of two yards out into the river, he began to shake, fearing he was lost; but nothing gave him more pain than hearing the grey braying and seeing Rocinante struggling to get himself loose, and he said to his master:

"The grey is braying, grieved at our being gone, and Rocinante is trying to get free to throw himself after us. O dearest friends, stay in peace, and may the madness that takes us away from you, turned into a coming to our senses, bring us back into your presence!"

And with that he began to weep so bitterly that Don Quixote, vexed and choleric, said to him:

"What are you afraid of, you cowardly creature? What are you weeping about, you heart of butter? Who is chasing you, or who is hunting you, you spirit of a house mouse? Or what do you lack, you destitute man in the very bowels of abundance? Are you by any chance travelling on foot and barefoot over the Riphaean mountains, instead of sitting on a plank like an archduke on the smooth course of this pleasant river, out of which in a short space we shall come to the wide sea? But we must have come out already, and travelled at least seven or eight hundred leagues; and if I had an astrolabe here to take the height of the pole with, I would tell you how many we have travelled — although either I know very little, or we have already passed, or shall soon pass, the equinoctial line, which divides and cuts the two opposite poles at equal distance."

"And when we get to that line your worship talks about," asked Sancho, "how far shall we have travelled?"

"A long way," replied Don Quixote; "because of the three hundred and sixty degrees the globe contains, of water and of land, according to the computation of Ptolemy, who was the greatest cosmographer known, we shall have travelled half when we reach the line I have named."

"By God," said Sancho, "your worship brings me a fine sort of person as a witness for what he says — a Toll-and-Lousy, with 'pee' tacked on the front of him, or 'pee-oh', or I do not know what."

Don Quixote laughed at the interpretation Sancho had given to the name and to the computation and reckoning of the cosmographer Ptolemy, and said to him:

"You must know, Sancho, that among the Spaniards and those who embark at Cadiz to go to the East Indies, one of the signs they have for knowing they have passed the equinoctial line I have told you about is that all the lice die on everybody in the ship, without one being left, and you would not find one in the whole vessel if you paid its weight in gold. And so, Sancho, you may run a hand over a thigh; and if you come across anything alive, we shall be out of this doubt, and if not, we have passed it."

"I do not believe any of that," answered Sancho, "but for all that I shall do what your worship orders me — although I do not see what need there is for these experiments, since I see with my own eyes that we have not got five yards from the bank, and we have not slipped two yards from where the beasts are, because there are Rocinante and the grey in the very place where we left them. And taking a sight of it, as I am taking one now, I swear we are not moving or going along at an ant's pace."

"Make the test I have told you, Sancho, and do not trouble about any other; for you know nothing about what colures, lines, parallels, zodiacs, ecliptics, poles, solstices, equinoxes, planets, signs, points and measures are, of which the celestial and terrestrial spheres are composed. If you knew all these things, or part of them, you would see clearly how many parallels we have cut, how many signs we have seen and how many constellations we have left behind and are leaving behind now. And I tell you again to feel and fish about, for I hold for myself that you are cleaner than a sheet of smooth white paper."

Sancho felt himself, and, bringing his hand round nicely and carefully towards the back of his left knee, he raised his head, looked at his master and said:

"Either the experiment is false, or we have not got to where your worship says, not by many leagues."

"Why, what is it?" asked Don Quixote. "Have you come across something?"

"Something, and somethings!" answered Sancho.

And, shaking his fingers, he washed his whole hand in the river, down the middle of whose current the boat was quietly gliding, moved by no secret intelligence and by no hidden enchanter, but by the very course of the water, gentle and smooth just then.

At this they made out some great water mills that stood in the middle of the river; and hardly had Don Quixote seen them when he said to Sancho in a loud voice:

"Do you see, my friend? There is the city, castle or fortress where there must be some knight held down, or some queen, princess or infanta come to grief, for whose rescue I have been brought here."

"What the devil city, fortress or castle is your worship talking about, sir?" said Sancho. "Do you not see that those are water mills standing in the river, where they grind the wheat?"

"Be quiet, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "for although they look like water mills, they are not; and I have told you before that enchantments turn everything about and change it out of its natural being. I do not mean that they really change one being into another, but that they seem to — as experience showed in the transformation of Dulcinea, the only refuge of my hopes."

At this the boat, having got into the middle of the river's current, began to travel less slowly than it had until then. The millers at the mills, who saw that boat coming down the river and going to run into the millrace, came out in a hurry, a great many of them with long poles to stop it; and, as they came out floured, with their faces and their clothes covered in the dust of the flour, they made an ugly sight. They shouted at the tops of their voices, saying:

"Devils of men! Where are you going? Have you come here to kill yourselves? What do you want — to drown and be torn to pieces on these wheels?"

"Did I not tell you, Sancho," said Don Quixote at this point, "that we had come to where I must show how far the valour of my arm reaches? Look what villains and poltroons come out to meet me, look how many monsters set themselves against me, look how many hideous faces are pulling grimaces at us... Well, now you shall see, you rascals!"

And, standing up in the boat, he began to threaten the millers in a loud voice, saying to them:

"Wicked and worse-advised rabble, set at liberty and at their own free will the person you hold oppressed in that fortress or prison of yours, high or low, of whatever sort or quality he may be; for I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, called by another name the Knight of the Lions, to whom, by the order of high heaven, it is reserved to bring this adventure to a happy end."

And, saying this, he laid his hand on his sword and began to fence with it in the air against the millers; who, hearing and not understanding that nonsense, set themselves with their poles to stop the boat, which was already going into the race and channel of the wheels.

Sancho went down on his knees, devoutly asking heaven to deliver him from so plain a danger — as it did, through the skill and quickness of the millers, who, putting their poles against the boat, stopped it, but not in such a way as to keep from capsizing it and pitching Don Quixote and Sancho into the water. But it turned out well for Don Quixote, who could swim like a goose, although the weight of his armour took him to the bottom twice; and if it had not been for the millers, who threw themselves into the water and pulled the pair of them out almost bodily, it would have been Troy for them both.

Set on land, then, more wet than dying of thirst, Sancho went down on his knees, his hands together and his eyes fixed on heaven, and asked God in a long and devout prayer to deliver him from then on from the bold desires and undertakings of his master.

At this the fishermen who owned the boat arrived, whose boat the wheels of the mills had smashed to pieces; and, seeing it broken, they set about stripping Sancho and asking Don Quixote to pay for it. And he, with great calm, as though nothing at all had happened to him, told the millers and the fishermen that he would pay for the boat most willingly, on condition that they gave up, freely and without any trickery, the person or persons who were held down in that castle of theirs.

"What persons or what castle are you talking about," answered one of the millers, "you man without any sense? Do you by any chance want to carry off the women who come to grind wheat at these mills?"

"Enough!" said Don Quixote to himself. "Here it would be preaching in the desert to try to bring this rabble round to doing any virtuous thing for the asking. And in this adventure two mighty enchanters must have met, and one of them blocks what the other tries: one furnished me with the boat and the other pitched me over the side. God set it right, for this whole world is machinery and contrivances, one against another. I can do no more."

And, raising his voice, he went on, looking at the mills:

"My friends, whoever you may be, who are left shut up in that prison, forgive me; for by my misfortune and by yours, I cannot bring you out of your affliction. This adventure must be kept and reserved for some other knight."

Having said this, he came to terms with the fishermen and paid fifty reals for the boat, which Sancho handed over most unwillingly, saying:

"With two boat-fares like this we shall have the whole capital at the bottom."

The fishermen and millers were astonished, looking at those two figures so far outside the use of other men, and they could not make out at all where the arguments and questions Don Quixote was putting to them were leading; and, taking them for madmen, they left them and went back to their mills, and the fishermen to their huts. Don Quixote and Sancho went back to their beasts, and to being beasts; and this was the end of the adventure of the enchanted boat.

Chapter 30: Of What Befell Don Quixote with a Beautiful Huntress

Knight and squire got back to their animals melancholy enough and in a bad humour, and especially Sancho, whom it went to the soul to touch the stock of their money, since it seemed to him that everything taken out of it was being taken out of the pupils of his own eyes. Finally, without a word passing between them, they mounted and went away from the famous river — Don Quixote buried in the thoughts of his love and Sancho in those of his advancement, which just then seemed to him to be a long way off. Because, dolt though he was, he grasped well enough that his master's actions, all or most of them, were absurdities, and he was looking for a chance when, without going into accounts or leave-takings with his master, he might one day break away and go off home. But fortune arranged things quite the other way from what he feared.

It happened, then, that the next day, at sunset and on coming out of a wood, Don Quixote cast his eyes over a green meadow, and at the far end of it he saw people; and, coming nearer, he made out that they were a hawking party. He came nearer still, and among them he saw a splendid lady on a snow-white palfrey or hackney, decked out with green harness and a silver saddle. The lady likewise came dressed in green, and so gallantly and richly that gallantry itself seemed transformed into her. On her left hand she carried a goshawk, a sign that gave Don Quixote to understand that this was some great lady, and that she must be the mistress of all those hunters — as was the truth. And so he said to Sancho:

"Run, Sancho my son, and tell that lady of the palfrey and the goshawk that I, the Knight of the Lions, kiss the hands of her great beauteousness; and that if her greatness gives me leave, I shall go and kiss them, and serve her in whatever my strength can and her highness may command me. And mind how you speak, Sancho, and take care not to jam any proverb of yours into your embassy."

"You have found your jammer, have you not?" answered Sancho. "Try that on me! Why, this is not the first time in my life that I have carried embassies to high and lofty ladies!"

"Unless it was the one you carried to the lady Dulcinea," replied Don Quixote, "I do not know that you have carried any other, at least in my service."

"That is true," answered Sancho, "but a good payer does not mind pledges, and in a full house supper is soon cooked. I mean that there is no need to tell me or warn me about anything, because I have something for everything and I know a little about it all."

"I believe it, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Go, and good luck, and God guide you."

Sancho set off at a gallop, driving the grey out of his usual pace, and came to where the beautiful huntress was; and, dismounting and going down on his knees in front of her, he said to her:

"Beautiful lady, that knight who appears over there, called the Knight of the Lions, is my master, and I am a squire of his who at home is called Sancho Panza. This same Knight of the Lions, who not long ago was called the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, sends by me to ask your greatness to be pleased to give him leave so that, with your purpose and good pleasure and consent, he may put his desire into practice — which is nothing else, as he says and as I think, but to serve your soaring high-flyingness and beauteousness. In giving it, your ladyship will do a thing that redounds to your own good, and he will receive a most signal favour and contentment."

"Certainly, good squire," answered the lady, "you have delivered your embassy with all the circumstances such embassies call for. Get up off the ground, for it is not right that the squire of so great a knight as the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance — of whom we already have a great deal of news here — should be on his knees. Get up, my friend, and tell your master that he is very welcome to come and make use of me and of the duke my husband, at a country house we have here."

Sancho got up, astonished as much at the good lady's beauty as at her great breeding and courtesy, and still more at what she had said about having news of his master the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance; and if she had not called him the Knight of the Lions, it must have been because he had taken the name so recently. The duchess, whose title is still not known, asked him:

"Tell me, brother squire: this master of yours, is he not one about whom there goes a printed history called The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha, who has for the lady of his soul a certain Dulcinea of El Toboso?"

"That is the very man, my lady," answered Sancho; "and that squire of his who goes about, or ought to go about, in that history, whom they call Sancho Panza, is me — unless they swapped me in the cradle, I mean unless they swapped me in the printing."

"I am very glad of all this," said the duchess. "Go, brother Panza, and tell your master that he is well arrived and welcome to my estates, and that nothing could come to me that would give me greater contentment."

Sancho, with this most agreeable answer, went back to his master with the greatest pleasure, and told him everything the great lady had said, praising her great beauteousness, her great grace and courtesy to the skies in his rustic terms. Don Quixote drew himself up gallantly in the saddle, settled himself well in the stirrups, adjusted his visor, spurred Rocinante and with a fine boldness went to kiss the duchess's hands.

The duchess, having sent for the duke her husband, told him the whole of Don Quixote's embassy while Don Quixote was coming up; and the two of them, having read the first part of this history and having understood from it the preposterous humour of Don Quixote, waited for him with the greatest pleasure and with a desire to know him, having settled it beforehand to fall in with his humour and to agree with him in whatever he said, treating him as a knight errant for as long as he stayed with them, with all the ceremonies customary in the books of chivalry, which they had read and were even very fond of.

At this Don Quixote came up with his visor raised; and, making as if to dismount, Sancho ran up to hold his stirrup for him. But he was so unlucky that, in getting off the grey, he caught one foot in a rope of the pack-saddle in such a way that it was not possible to untangle him, and instead he was left hanging from it with his mouth and his chest on the ground.

Don Quixote, who was not in the habit of dismounting without somebody holding his stirrup, thinking that Sancho had already got there to hold it, threw the weight of his body down all at once, and brought Rocinante's saddle with him — for it must have been badly girthed — and the saddle and he came to the ground, not without shame to him and with a great many curses that he muttered between his teeth at the wretched Sancho, who still had his foot in the shackle.

The duke ordered his hunters to go to the knight and the squire, who lifted up Don Quixote, badly used by his fall; and, limping and as best he could, he went to bend his knees before the two nobles. But the duke would not allow it on any account; on the contrary, dismounting from his own horse, he went and embraced Don Quixote, saying to him:

"It grieves me, Sir Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, that the first thing your worship has done in my country should have been as bad as we have just seen; but the carelessness of squires is often the cause of worse things than this."

"The thing I have had happen in meeting you, valorous prince," answered Don Quixote, "cannot possibly be bad, even if my fall had not stopped until the bottom of the abyss, since the glory of having seen you would have lifted me and brought me out of it. My squire, God curse him, is better at untying his tongue to say malicious things than at tying and girthing a saddle so that it will hold. But however I may find myself, fallen or standing, on foot or on horseback, I shall always be at your service and at that of my lady the duchess, your worthy consort, worthy lady of beauty and universal princess of courtesy."

"Gently, my lord Don Quixote of La Mancha!" said the duke. "For where my lady Doña Dulcinea of El Toboso is, it is not reasonable that other beauties should be praised."

By this time Sancho Panza was free of the noose; and, finding himself close by, before his master could answer he said:

"It cannot be denied, but must be affirmed, that my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso is very beautiful; but where you least expect it, up jumps the hare. Because I have heard it said that this thing they call nature is like a potter who makes clay pots, and the man who makes one beautiful pot can make two, and three, and a hundred. I say it because upon my word my lady the duchess is not one step behind my mistress the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso."

Don Quixote turned to the duchess and said:

"Your greatness may imagine that no knight errant in the world ever had a more talkative or a more amusing squire than the one I have; and he will bear me out if your great loftiness cares to make use of me for a few days."

To which the duchess answered:

"That good Sancho is amusing I value highly, because it is a sign that he is judicious; for wit and drollery, Señor Don Quixote, as your worship knows very well, do not settle on dull minds. And, since good Sancho is amusing and droll, from this moment I confirm him as judicious."

"And talkative," added Don Quixote.

"So much the better," said the duke, "because a great deal of drollery cannot be said in a few words. And, so that we may not lose our time in them, let the great Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance come..."

"Of the Lions your highness should say," said Sancho, "for there is no Sorrowful Countenance now, nor any countenance at all."

"Let it be the Knight of the Lions," the duke went on. "I say let the Knight of the Lions come to a castle of mine that is nearby, where he shall be given the welcome that is justly owed to so lofty a person, and the one that the duchess and I generally give to all the knights errant who come to it."

By this time Sancho had put Rocinante's saddle to rights and girthed it properly; and, Don Quixote getting up on him and the duke on a handsome horse, they set the duchess between them and made for the castle. The duchess ordered Sancho to ride beside her, because she took infinite pleasure in hearing his judicious sayings. Sancho did not need asking twice, and wove himself in among the three of them and made a fourth in the conversation, to the great pleasure of the duchess and the duke, who counted it a great piece of luck to take into their castle so errant a knight and so errand-run a squire.

Chapter 31: Which Deals with Many and Great Matters

Extreme was the gladness Sancho carried about with him at seeing himself, as he thought, in the duchess's favour; because he imagined he was going to find in her castle what he had found in Don Diego's house and in Basilio's, being always fond of the good life. And so he took the chance by the forelock in this matter of treating himself well, whenever and wherever it offered.

The history relates, then, that before they reached the country house or castle, the duke rode on ahead and gave orders to all his servants about the way they were to treat Don Quixote; who, as soon as he came with the duchess to the castle gates, was met by two footmen or grooms who came out of it dressed to their feet in what they call morning gowns, of the finest crimson satin; and, catching Don Quixote up in their arms, without his being heard or seen, they said to him:

"Let your greatness go and help my lady the duchess down."

Don Quixote did so, and there were great civilities between the two of them over the business; but in the end the duchess's insistence won, and she would not come down off the palfrey except in the duke's arms, saying that she did not find herself worthy of giving so great a knight so useless a burden. Finally the duke came out to help her down; and, on going into a great courtyard, two beautiful maidens came up and threw over Don Quixote's shoulders a great cloak of the finest scarlet, and in an instant all the galleries of the courtyard were crowned with the menservants and maidservants of those nobles, calling out at the tops of their voices:

"Welcome to the flower and cream of knights errant!"

And all of them, or most, sprinkled flasks of scented waters over Don Quixote and over the duke and duchess; at all of which Don Quixote marvelled. And that was the first day when he wholly knew and believed himself to be a true knight errant and not a fanciful one, seeing himself treated in the very way he had read that such knights were treated in the ages past.

Sancho, abandoning the grey, stitched himself to the duchess and went into the castle; and, his conscience biting him for leaving the donkey alone, he went up to a reverend duenna who had come out with others to receive the duchess, and said to her in a low voice:

"Señora González, or whatever your worship's name may be..."

"I am called Doña Rodríguez de Grijalba," answered the duenna. "What is it you want, brother?"

To which Sancho answered:

"I should like your worship to do me the kindness of going out to the castle gate, where you will find a grey donkey of mine. Let your worship be so good as to order him to be put — or to put him — in the stable, because the poor little creature is a little timid, and will not be able to bear being alone on any account."

"If the master is as judicious as the man," answered the duenna, "we are in a fine way! Be off with you, brother, and much bad luck to you and to whoever brought you here, and see to your own donkey; for we duennas of this house are not accustomed to business of that kind."

"Well, truly," answered Sancho, "I have heard my master say — and he is a diviner of the histories — telling that one about Lancelot,

	when he came from Britain,
	for ladies waited on him,
	and duennas on his horse;

"and as far as my donkey in particular goes, I would not swap him for Sir Lancelot's nag."

"Brother, if you are a jester," replied the duenna, "keep your drolleries for where they will look like drolleries and be paid for; for from me you will get nothing but a fig."

"Well and good," answered Sancho, "and it will be a good ripe one, since your worship will not lose the trick of her years by a single point!"

"Son of a whore," said the duenna, all fired up with choler by now, "whether I am old or not I shall account for to God and not to you, you rascal stuffed with garlic."

And she said this in such a loud voice that the duchess heard it; and, turning and seeing the duenna so upset and her eyes so bloodshot, she asked her who she was quarrelling with.

"With this good man here," answered the duenna, "who has earnestly asked me to go and put a donkey of his that is at the castle gate into the stable, bringing it up as an example that they did so I do not know where — that some ladies waited on a certain Lancelot and some duennas on his nag — and, above all, by way of good manners, he has called me old."

"That I should take as an affront," answered the duchess, "beyond anything anybody could say to me."

And, speaking to Sancho, she said:

"Note, Sancho my friend, that Doña Rodríguez is very young, and that she wears that headdress more for authority and for custom than for her years."

"May the years I have left to live be bad ones," answered Sancho, "if I said it for that. I only said it because I have such affection for my donkey that it seemed to me I could not commend him to a more charitable person than the lady Doña Rodríguez."

Don Quixote, who was hearing it all, said to him:

"Are these conversations for this place, Sancho?"

"Sir," answered Sancho, "every man must talk about his own business wherever he may be. Here I remembered the grey, and here I spoke of him; and if I had remembered him in the stable, there I should have spoken of him."

To which the duke said:

"Sancho is quite right, and there is nothing to blame him for. The grey shall be given all he could ask for, and let Sancho not worry, for he shall be treated like Sancho's own person."

With these speeches, agreeable to everybody but Don Quixote, they came up to the top of the house and brought Don Quixote into a hall hung with the richest cloths of gold and brocade. Six maidens unarmed him and served him as pages, all of them coached and instructed by the duke and duchess about what they had to do and how they had to treat Don Quixote, so that he might imagine and see that they were treating him as a knight errant.

Don Quixote, once unarmed, was left in his narrow wide breeches and his chamois doublet — dry, tall, stretched out, with his jaws kissing each other on the inside; a figure such that, if the maidens who were serving him had not taken care to hide their laughter, which was one of the strict orders their master and mistress had given them, they would have burst laughing.

They asked him to let himself be undressed for a shirt, but he would never consent, saying that decency looked as well in knights errant as valour. Still, he said they should give the shirt to Sancho; and, shutting himself up with him in a chamber where there was a rich bed, he undressed and put on the shirt. And, finding himself alone with Sancho, he said to him:

"Tell me, you modern clown and ancient blockhead: does it seem to you a good thing to dishonour and affront a duenna as venerable and as worthy of respect as that one? Were those times to be remembering the grey, or are these nobles the sort to let the beasts go badly when they treat their owners so handsomely? For God's sake, Sancho, restrain yourself, and do not show the coarse thread in such a way that they tumble to it that you are woven of villainous and common cloth.

"Look, you sinner, that a lord is held in higher esteem the more honourable and well-born servants he has; and that one of the greatest advantages princes have over other men is that they are served by servants as good as themselves. Do you not see, distressed man that you are and unlucky man that I am, that if they see you are a coarse peasant or a droll idiot, they will think that I am some charlatan or some sham knight? No, no, Sancho my friend, run, run from these dangers; for the man who trips into being a talker and a wit falls at the first kick and comes down a wretched buffoon.

"Bridle your tongue, consider and chew over your words before they come out of your mouth, and note that we have arrived at a place where, with God's favour and the valour of my arm, we must come out bettered by a third and a fifth in fame and in fortune."

Sancho promised him very earnestly that he would sew up his mouth, or bite his tongue, before speaking a word that was not very much to the point and well considered, as his master ordered him; and that he should not worry about it, for it would never be through him that anybody found out who they were.

Don Quixote dressed, put on his baldric with his sword, threw the scarlet cloak over his shoulders, put on a cap of green satin the maidens gave him, and with this adornment went out into the great hall, where he found the maidens drawn up in a line, as many on one side as on the other, and all of them with the wherewithal to give him water for his hands, which they did with a great many bows and ceremonies.

Then came twelve pages with the steward to take him in to dinner, for the duke and duchess were already waiting for him. They took him into their midst and, full of pomp and majesty, led him to another hall, where a rich table was laid with only four covers. The duchess and the duke came out to the door of the hall to receive him, and with them a grave churchman, one of those who govern the houses of princes; one of those who, not being born princes, never manage to teach those who are how they ought to be so; one of those who want the greatness of the great to be measured by the narrowness of their own minds; one of those who, meaning to teach those they govern to be moderate, make them mean. Of such as these, I say, must have been the grave churchman who came out with the duke and duchess to receive Don Quixote.

A thousand courteous civilities were exchanged, and, finally, taking Don Quixote into their midst, they went and sat down at the table.

The duke invited Don Quixote to take the head of the table; and although he refused it, the duke's importunities were so many that he had to take it. The churchman sat opposite him, and the duke and the duchess on the two sides.

Sancho was present at all of it, gaping and astonished at seeing the honour those princes were paying his master; and, seeing the many ceremonies and entreaties that passed between the duke and Don Quixote to make him sit at the head of the table, he said:

"If your worships give me leave, I shall tell you a story that happened in my village about this business of seats."

Hardly had Sancho said this when Don Quixote trembled, believing beyond any doubt that he was going to say some foolish thing. Sancho looked at him and understood him, and said:

"Do not be afraid, my dear sir, that I shall let myself go, or that I shall say anything that does not come very much to the point; for I have not forgotten the advice your worship gave me a little while ago about talking much or little, or well or badly."

"I do not remember any of it, Sancho," answered Don Quixote. "Say what you like, so long as you say it quickly."

"Well, what I want to say," said Sancho, "is so true that my master Don Quixote here present will not let me lie."

"For my part," replied Don Quixote, "lie as much as you like, Sancho, for I shall not stop you; but look to what you are going to say."

"I have looked and looked at it again so much that the man who rings the alarm is safe enough, as will be seen by the deed."

"It would be as well," said Don Quixote, "if your greatnesses ordered this fool thrown out of here, for he will say a thousand pieces of nonsense."

"By the duke's life," said the duchess, "Sancho shall not leave my side a moment. I am very fond of him, because I know he is very judicious."

"Judicious days may your holiness live," said Sancho, "for the good opinion you have of me, even if there is nothing of it in me. And the story I want to tell is this. A gentleman of my village, very rich and of good family — because he came of the Álamos of Medina del Campo, and married Doña Mencía de Quiñones, who was the daughter of Don Alonso de Marañón, a knight of the Order of Santiago, who was drowned at the Herradura, over whom there was that quarrel in our village years ago in which, as I understand it, my master Don Quixote took a part, and out of which Tomasillo the Rascal, the son of Balbastro the blacksmith, came out wounded... Is not all this true, sir our master? Say so, on your life, so that these gentlefolk may not take me for some lying chatterer."

"So far," said the churchman, "I take you more for a chatterer than a liar; but from now on I do not know what I shall take you for."

"You give so many witnesses, Sancho, and so many particulars, that I cannot help saying that you must be telling the truth. Get on, and shorten the story, for you are on the road not to finish in two days."

"He shall not shorten it at all," said the duchess, "if he means to please me; on the contrary, he shall tell it in the way he knows how, even if he does not finish it in six days — and if they were so many, they would be for me the best days I ever spent in my life."

"I say, then, my dear sirs," Sancho went on, "that this same gentleman, whom I know like my own hands, because it is not a crossbow-shot from my house to his, invited a farmer, poor but honourable —"

"Get on, brother," said the churchman at this point, "for you are on the road not to stop with your story before the next world."

"I shall stop short of halfway, if God is pleased," answered Sancho. "And so I say that, this same farmer coming to the house of the said gentleman who had invited him — God rest his soul, for he is dead now, and for a further sign they say he died the death of an angel, though I was not there myself, having gone off at that time to reap at Tembleque —"

"On your life, my son, come back quickly from Tembleque, and, without burying the gentleman, unless you want to hold any more funerals, finish your story."

"The fact is, then," replied Sancho, "that as the two of them were about to sit down at table — and I seem to see them now more than ever —"

The duke and duchess were taking great pleasure in the displeasure the good churchman was showing at the delays and pauses with which Sancho was telling his story, and Don Quixote was eating himself up with choler and rage.

"I say, then," said Sancho, "that, the two of them being, as I have said, about to sit down at table, the farmer kept insisting that the gentleman should take the head of the table, and the gentleman kept insisting too that the farmer should take it, because in his house what he ordered was to be done. But the farmer, who prided himself on being courteous and well brought up, would never do it, until the gentleman, vexed, put both hands on his shoulders and made him sit down by force, saying to him: 'Sit down, you blockhead, for wherever I sit will be the head of the table for you.' And that is the story, and truly I believe it has not been brought in here beside the point."

Don Quixote turned a thousand colours, which marbled his brown skin and showed through it. The duke and duchess hid their laughter, so that Don Quixote should not be utterly put out of countenance, having understood Sancho's malice; and, to change the conversation and stop Sancho going on with other absurdities, the duchess asked Don Quixote what news he had of the lady Dulcinea, and whether he had sent her any presents of giants or villains in the last few days, since he could not have failed to conquer a great many. To which Don Quixote answered:

"My lady, my misfortunes, though they had a beginning, will never have an end. Giants I have conquered, and poltroons and villains I have sent her; but where were they to find her, if she is enchanted and turned into the ugliest peasant girl that can be imagined?"

"I do not know," said Sancho Panza. "To me she seems the most beautiful creature in the world; at least in nimbleness and in jumping I know well enough that she would not give a tumbler any odds. Upon my word, my lady duchess, she leaps from the ground onto a she-ass as if she were a cat."

"Have you seen her enchanted, Sancho?" asked the duke.

"Have I seen her!" answered Sancho. "Why, who the devil but me was the first to hit on the business of the enchantment? She is about as enchanted as my father is!"

The churchman, who heard talk of giants, poltroons and enchantments, tumbled to it that this must be Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose history the duke read regularly, and which he had rebuked him for many times, telling him that it was an absurdity to read such absurdities. And, making certain that what he suspected was true, with great choler he said to the duke:

"Your Excellency, my lord, will have to give an account to Our Lord of what this good man does. This Don Quixote, or Don Fool, or whatever he is called, I imagine cannot be as much of an idiot as Your Excellency wants him to be, when you put chances into his hand so that he may carry his nonsense and emptiness further."

And, turning the conversation to Don Quixote, he said to him:

"And you, soul of a pitcher, who has jammed it into your brain that you are a knight errant and that you conquer giants and take villains prisoner? Be off with you, and much good may it do you: go back home, and bring up your children if you have any, and see to your property, and leave off wandering about the world gaping at the wind and giving everybody who knows you and does not know you something to laugh at. Where in the world have you found that there ever were, or are now, knights errant? Where are there giants in Spain, or villains in La Mancha, or enchanted Dulcineas, or all the herd of simplicities that are told about you?"

Don Quixote listened attentively to the arguments of that venerable man; and, seeing that he had fallen silent, with no respect for the duke and duchess, with an angry expression and a face in an uproar, he got to his feet and said...

But this answer deserves a chapter to itself.

Chapter 32: Of the Answer Don Quixote Gave His Reprover, with Other Grave and Amusing Events

Don Quixote, then, being on his feet and trembling from head to foot like a man dosed with quicksilver, said in a hurried and troubled voice:

"The place where I am, and the presence I find myself in, and the respect I have always had and still have for the calling your worship professes, hold and tie the hands of my just anger. And so, both for what I have said and because everybody knows that the weapons of gowned men are the same as women's, which are the tongue, I shall enter with mine into an equal battle with your worship — from whom good advice was rather to be expected than shameful abuse.

"Holy and well-meaning reproofs call for other circumstances and require other conditions. At the very least, having reproved me in public and so harshly has gone past all the limits of good reproof, since the first sort settle better on gentleness than on harshness; and it is not right, without having any knowledge of the sin one is reproving, to call the sinner an idiot and a fool without any more ado.

"If not, tell me, your worship: for which of the idiocies you have seen in me do you condemn and abuse me, and order me to go home and see to the government of my house and my wife and my children, without knowing whether I have any? Is there nothing more to it than to walk helter-skelter into other people's houses and govern their owners — and, some of you having been brought up in the narrowness of some boarding school, without having seen more of the world than can be contained in twenty or thirty leagues of territory, to burst in and lay down laws for chivalry and pass judgement on knights errant?

"Is it by any chance a vain undertaking, or time badly spent, that is spent wandering about the world, not looking for its comforts but for the rough places by which the good climb to the seat of immortality? If knights held me for a fool, or the magnificent, or the generous, or the highly born, I should count it an irreparable affront; but that students who never entered or set foot on the paths of chivalry should hold me for a simpleton, I do not care a farthing. A knight I am and a knight I shall die, if it please the Almighty.

"Some go by the broad field of proud ambition; others by that of servile and base flattery; others by that of deceitful hypocrisy; and some by that of true religion. But I, inclined by my star, go by the narrow path of knight-errantry, for the exercise of which I despise property but not honour. I have made satisfaction for wrongs, righted injustices, punished insolences, conquered giants and trampled monsters. I am in love, only because it is necessary that knights errant should be; and, being so, I am not one of the vicious lovers but of the continent Platonic ones. My intentions I always direct to good ends, which are to do good to everybody and harm to nobody. Whether the man who understands this, who does this, who deals in this deserves to be called a dolt, let your greatnesses say — excellent duke and duchess."

"Well said, by God!" said Sancho. "Do not say another word in your own defence, my lord and master, because there is nothing more to say, or to think, or to keep on with in the world. And besides, when this gentleman denies, as he has denied, that there have been any knights errant in the world or that there are any now, what wonder is it that he knows nothing of the things he has been talking about?"

"By any chance," said the churchman, "are you, brother, that Sancho Panza they speak of, to whom your master has promised an isle?"

"I am," answered Sancho, "and I am one who deserves it as well as anybody else. I am one of those who say 'keep company with the good and you will be one of them', and I am one of those 'not who you are born with, but who you graze with', and one of those 'he who leans against a good tree is covered by a good shade'. I have leaned against a good master, and I have been many months in his company, and I mean to be another like him, God willing; and long life to him and long life to me — for he will not run short of empires to command, nor I of isles to govern."

"No, certainly not, Sancho my friend," said the duke at this point. "For I, in Señor Don Quixote's name, grant you the government of one I have going spare, and of no small quality."

"Down on your knees, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and kiss His Excellency's feet for the favour he has done you."

Sancho did so; which the churchman seeing, he got up from the table extremely vexed, saying:

"By the habit I wear, I am half inclined to say that Your Excellency is as much of a simpleton as these sinners are. Look whether they are not bound to be mad, when the sane canonise their madnesses! Your Excellency may stay with them; for as long as they are in the house, I shall be in mine, and shall excuse myself from reproving what I cannot remedy."

And, without saying any more or eating any more, he went off, without the duke and duchess's entreaties being able to stop him — although the duke did not say much to him, prevented by the laughter his impertinent choler had caused him. He finished laughing and said to Don Quixote:

"Your worship, Sir Knight of the Lions, has answered so loftily for yourself that there is nothing left for you to make good over this business, which, though it looks like a wrong, is no wrong at all; because, just as women cannot inflict a wrong, neither can churchmen, as your worship knows better than I."

"That is so," answered Don Quixote, "and the reason is that the man who cannot be wronged cannot wrong anybody. Women, children and churchmen, since they cannot defend themselves, cannot be affronted even though they are offended; because between a wrong and an affront there is this difference, as Your Excellency knows better: the affront comes from a party who can inflict it, and does inflict it, and stands by it; the wrong can come from any quarter without affronting.

"Take an example. A man is in the street, off his guard; ten come up with armed hands and, beating him with sticks, he lays hand to his sword and does his duty, but the multitude of his opponents stands against him and does not let him carry out his intention, which is to avenge himself. This man is left wronged but not affronted. And another example will confirm the same thing. A man is standing with his back turned; another comes up and beats him with a stick, and, having beaten him, runs off and does not wait, and the first follows and does not catch him. The man who took the blows received a wrong but not an affront, because the affront must be stood by. If the man who gave him the blows, though he gave them by a treacherous stroke, had laid hand to his sword and stood his ground, facing his enemy, then the beaten man would be left wronged and affronted at the same time: wronged, because he was struck by treachery; affronted, because the man who struck him stood by what he had done, without turning his back and standing his ground.

"And so, according to the laws of that accursed duelling, I may be wronged but not affronted; because children have no feeling in the matter, nor women, and they cannot run away, and they have no call to stand their ground — and the same holds of those set apart in holy religion, because these three kinds of people lack offensive and defensive weapons; and so, although they are naturally obliged to defend themselves, they are not obliged to offend anybody. And although a little while ago I said I might be wronged, I now say that I may not, on any account; because the man who cannot receive an affront can still less give one.

"For which reasons I ought not to feel, and do not feel, the things that good man has said to me. I only wish he had waited a little, so that I could have given him to understand the error he is in, in thinking and saying that there have never been and are not now any knights errant in the world; for if Amadís had heard such a thing, or one of the infinite number of his line, I know it would not have gone well with his worship."

"That I would swear to," said Sancho: "they would have given him such a slash as would have split him from top to bottom like a pomegranate, or like a very ripe melon. They were fine ones for putting up with ticklings of that sort! Upon my blessed self, I hold it for certain that if Reinaldos de Montalbán had heard those arguments from the little man, he would have given him such a smack across the mouth that he would not have spoken for three years. No, let him just take them on and see how he got out of their hands!"

The duchess was dying of laughter at hearing Sancho talk, and in her opinion she held him for more amusing and more mad than his master; and there were many in that time who were of this same opinion.

Finally Don Quixote quieted down, and the dinner came to an end; and, as the cloth was taken away, four maidens came in, one with a silver basin, another with a silver ewer, another with two of the whitest and richest towels over her shoulder, and the fourth with her arms bared to the elbow and in her white hands — which were undoubtedly white — a round ball of Naples soap.

The one with the basin came up, and with a fine grace and ease fitted the basin under Don Quixote's beard; and he, without saying a word, astonished at such a ceremony, believing that it must be the custom of that country to wash the beard instead of the hands, stretched his out as far as he could. And at the same moment the ewer began to rain, and the maiden with the soap worked his beard over in great haste, raising flakes of snow — for the soapsuds were no less white — not only on the beard but all over the face and the eyes of the obedient knight, so much so that they made him shut them by force.

The duke and the duchess, who knew nothing about any of this, were waiting to see where such an extraordinary washing was going to end.
