The barber maiden, when she had him a hand's breadth deep in lather, pretended that the water had run out and ordered the one with the ewer to go and fetch some, saying that Señor Don Quixote would wait. She did so, and Don Quixote was left the strangest figure, and the most calculated to raise laughter, that could be imagined.

Everybody present was looking at him, and there were a good many of them; and, seeing him with half a yard of neck, more than moderately brown, his eyes shut and his beard full of soap, it was a great marvel and a great piece of discretion that they could hide their laughter. The maidens who were playing the trick kept their eyes lowered, not daring to look at their master and mistress, in whose bodies choler and laughter were tumbling over each other, so that they did not know which to attend to: punishing the girls' boldness or rewarding them for the pleasure they were getting from seeing Don Quixote in that state.

Finally the maiden with the ewer came, and they finished washing Don Quixote; and then the one who had the towels wiped him and dried him very deliberately, and, all four making him a great and deep bow and curtsey together, they were about to go. But the duke, so that Don Quixote should not tumble to the joke, called the maiden with the basin, saying to her:

"Come and wash me, and mind that the water does not run out on you."

The girl, sharp and quick, came and set the basin on the duke as on Don Quixote, and, hurrying, they washed him and soaped him very well; and, leaving him dried and clean, they went off with curtseys. Afterwards it was learnt that the duke had sworn that if they had not washed him as they washed Don Quixote, he would have punished their impudence — which they had judiciously put right by soaping him too.

Sancho was watching the ceremonies of that washing attentively, and he said to himself:

"God bless me! Can it be the custom in this country to wash squires' beards as well as knights'? Because in God and in my soul I have great need of it, and even if they shaved mine off with a razor I should count it a further kindness."

"What are you saying to yourself, Sancho?" asked the duchess.

"I say, my lady," he answered, "that in the courts of other princes I have always heard it said that when the cloth is taken away they give water for the hands, but not lye for the beard; and that this is why it is good to live a long time, so as to see a great deal. Although they also say that the man who lives a long life has to go through a great deal of trouble — although going through a washing of this kind is more of a pleasure than a labour."

"Do not be uneasy, Sancho my friend," said the duchess, "for I shall have my maidens wash you, and even put you in the wash-tub if need be."

"With the beard I shall be content," answered Sancho, "for now at least; for as time goes on, God has said what will be."

"See, steward," said the duchess, "to what good Sancho asks, and carry out his wishes to the letter."

The steward answered that Señor Sancho should be served in everything, and with that he went off to his dinner and took Sancho with him, leaving the duke and duchess and Don Quixote at the table talking about many different things, but all of them touching on the exercise of arms and of knight-errantry.

The duchess begged Don Quixote to sketch out and describe for her — since he seemed to have a happy memory — the beauty and the features of the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso; for, from what fame proclaimed about her beauty, she took it for understood that she must be the loveliest creature on the globe, and even in all La Mancha. Don Quixote sighed at hearing what the duchess asked of him, and said:

"If I could take out my heart and set it before your greatness's eyes, here on this table and on a plate, it would save my tongue the labour of saying what can hardly be thought — because Your Excellency would see her in it, painted entire. But what is the use of my setting myself now to sketch and describe point by point and part by part the beauty of the peerless Dulcinea, when it is a load worthy of other shoulders than mine, an enterprise on which the brushes of Parrhasius, Timanthes and Apelles ought to be employed, and the chisels of Lysippus, to paint her and grave her on panels, on marble and on bronze, and Ciceronian and Demosthenic rhetoric to praise her?"

"What does Demosthenic mean, Señor Don Quixote?" asked the duchess. "For it is a word I have never heard in all the days of my life."

"Demosthenic rhetoric," answered Don Quixote, "is the same as saying the rhetoric of Demosthenes, as Ciceronian is that of Cicero — who were the two greatest rhetoricians in the world."

"That is so," said the duke, "and you have been caught out in asking such a question. But for all that, Señor Don Quixote would give us great pleasure if he would paint her for us; for it is a safe bet that even in a rough sketch and outline she would come out such that the most beautiful women would envy her."

"I would do it, certainly," answered Don Quixote, "if the misfortune that happened to her a little while ago had not rubbed her out of my mind — a misfortune such that I am more in a state to weep over it than to describe it. Because your greatnesses must know that, going a few days ago to kiss her hands and to receive her blessing, her good pleasure and her leave for this third sally, I found a different woman from the one I was looking for. I found her enchanted and turned from a princess into a peasant, from beautiful into ugly, from an angel into a devil, from fragrant into stinking, from well-spoken into rustic, from composed into a leaper, from light into darkness and, finally, from Dulcinea of El Toboso into a country wench from Sayago."

"God bless me!" said the duke at this instant, letting out a great shout. "Who has been the man who has done the world so much harm? Who has taken from it the beauty that gladdened it, the grace that entertained it and the decency that did it credit?"

"Who?" answered Don Quixote. "Who can it be but some malignant enchanter, of the many envious ones who persecute me? That accursed race, born into the world to darken and annihilate the exploits of the good and to give light and raise up the doings of the wicked. Enchanters have persecuted me, enchanters persecute me and enchanters will persecute me until they have thrown me and my high chivalries into the deep abyss of oblivion; and they hurt me and wound me in the place where they see I feel it most, because to take away a knight errant's lady is to take away the eyes he sees with, and the sun that gives him light, and the food that keeps him alive. Many other times I have said it, and now I say it again: that a knight errant without a lady is like a tree without leaves, a building without foundations and a shadow without a body to cast it."

"There is no more to be said," said the duchess. "But if, for all that, we are to give credit to the history of Señor Don Quixote that has come out into the light of the world a few days since, with the general applause of the people, it is gathered from it — if I remember rightly — that your worship has never seen the lady Dulcinea, and that this lady does not exist in the world but is a fanciful lady whom your worship engendered and gave birth to in your understanding, and painted with all the graces and perfections you pleased."

"There is a great deal to say about that," answered Don Quixote. "God knows whether there is a Dulcinea in the world or not, or whether she is fanciful or not fanciful; and these are not the kind of things whose investigation is to be carried to the end. I neither engendered nor gave birth to my lady, although I contemplate her as a lady ought to be who contains in herself the qualities that can make her famous in all the parts of the world: beautiful without a blemish, grave without pride, loving with decency, grateful because courteous, courteous because well brought up, and, finally, high by lineage — since on good blood beauty shines out and shows itself with more degrees of perfection than in beautiful women humbly born."

"That is so," said the duke; "but Señor Don Quixote must give me leave to say what the history of his exploits that I have read forces me to say — from which it is inferred that, granting there is a Dulcinea, in El Toboso or out of it, and that she is beautiful in the highest degree in which your worship paints her for us, in the matter of the height of her lineage she does not run level with the Orianas, the Alastrajareas, the Madásimas or others of that stamp, of whom the histories are full that your worship knows so well."

"To that I can say," answered Don Quixote, "that Dulcinea is the daughter of her own works, and that virtues improve the blood, and that a humble man who is virtuous is to be esteemed and held higher than a vicious man who has been raised up. And what is more, Dulcinea has a strip of quality about her that can carry her to being a queen with a crown and a sceptre; for the merit of a beautiful and virtuous woman stretches to working greater miracles, and, though not formally, still virtually she has greater fortunes shut up inside her."

"I say, Señor Don Quixote," said the duchess, "that in everything your worship says you go with a leaden foot and, as the saying is, with the sounding line in your hand; and that from now on I shall believe, and make everybody in my house believe — and even the duke my lord, if it should be necessary — that there is a Dulcinea in El Toboso, and that she is alive today, and beautiful, and nobly born, and worthy that such a knight as Señor Don Quixote should serve her, which is the most I can say or know how to say.

"But I cannot help forming one scruple, and having a certain I-do-not-know-what of a grudge against Sancho Panza. The scruple is that the history I mentioned says that this Sancho Panza found this lady Dulcinea, when he carried her a letter on your worship's behalf, winnowing a sack of wheat — and, for a further sign, it says it was red wheat: a thing that makes me doubt the height of her lineage."

To which Don Quixote answered:

"My lady, your greatness must know that all or most of the things that happen to me go outside the ordinary bounds of the things that happen to other knights errant, whether they are directed by the inscrutable will of the fates or whether they come directed by the malice of some envious enchanter. And since it is by now an established thing that all or most famous knights errant have some grace or other — one the grace of not being able to be enchanted, another that of having flesh so impenetrable that he cannot be wounded, as the famous Roland was, one of the Twelve Peers of France, of whom it is told that he could not be wounded except through the sole of his left foot, and that this had to be with the point of a stout pin and with no other kind of weapon at all; so that when Bernardo del Carpio killed him at Roncesvalles, seeing that he could not gash him with iron, he lifted him off the ground in his arms and strangled him, remembering then the death Hercules gave to Antaeus, that fierce giant who they said was the son of Earth.

"I want to infer from all this that I might have some grace of the kind — not that of not being able to be wounded, because experience has shown me many times that I am of soft flesh and not at all impenetrable, nor that of not being able to be enchanted, since I have already seen myself shut in a cage, into which all the world would not have had the power to shut me if it had not been by the force of enchantments. But since I got free of that one, I want to believe that there will be no other that can hurt me. And so, these enchanters, seeing that they cannot use their evil arts on my person, take their revenge on the things I love most, and want to take away my life by ill-treating Dulcinea's, by whom I live.

"And so I believe that when my squire carried her my embassy, they turned her into a country wench busy at so low an occupation as winnowing wheat. But I have already said that that wheat was neither red nor wheat, but grains of oriental pearl. And as proof of this truth I want to tell your magnitudes how, coming through El Toboso a little while ago, I could never find Dulcinea's palaces; and how the next day, Sancho my squire having seen her in her own shape, which is the loveliest on the globe, she seemed to me a coarse, ugly country girl, and not at all well-spoken, when she is the very discretion of the world. And since I am not enchanted, and cannot be, by any sound reasoning, it is she who is the enchanted one, the injured one, the changed and swapped and turned-about one; and in her my enemies have taken their revenge on me, and for her I shall live in perpetual tears until I see her in her first state.

"All this I have said so that nobody should stick at what Sancho said about Dulcinea's sifting or winnowing; for since they changed her for me, it is no wonder that they swapped her for him. Dulcinea is of good family and well born, and of the gentle lineages there are in El Toboso — which are many, ancient and very good — it is a safe bet that no small part belongs to the peerless Dulcinea, through whom her place will be famous and named in the ages to come, as Troy has been through Helen and Spain through la Cava, though with a better title and a better fame.

"On the other hand, I want your ladyships to understand that Sancho Panza is one of the most amusing squires who ever served a knight errant. Sometimes he has simplicities so sharp that the wondering whether he is simple or sharp gives no small pleasure. He has malices that condemn him for a rogue, and carelessnesses that confirm him for a dolt. He doubts everything and believes everything; when I think he is about to throw himself over the cliff of foolishness, he comes out with judgements that lift him to the sky. In short, I would not swap him for any other squire, even if they gave me a city into the bargain; and so I am in doubt whether it will be a good thing to send him to the government your greatness has favoured him with — although I see in him a certain aptitude for this business of governing, so that with his understanding trimmed up a little he would carry off any government as the king carries off his taxes.

"And what is more, we already know by many experiences that a man needs neither much ability nor much learning to be a governor, since there are a hundred about who can hardly read and who govern like gerfalcons. The touchstone is that they should have good intentions and want to get everything right; for they will never lack somebody to advise them and set them on the road in what they have to do — like those governors who are knights and not lawyers, and give judgement with an assessor. I would advise him to take no bribe and lose no right, and other little things I still have in my stomach, which will come out in their own time for Sancho's use and the profit of the isle he governs."

The duke, the duchess and Don Quixote had reached this point in their conversation when they heard a great many voices and a great noise of people in the palace; and all at once Sancho came into the hall in a great fright, with a lye-cloth for a bib, and behind him a great many lads — or, better said, kitchen scullions and other small fry — and one came with a little trough of water which by its colour and its lack of cleanness showed itself to be washing-up water. The one with the trough was following him and chasing him, and was doing his best to get it into place and fit it under his beard, while another scullion made as if he wanted to wash it.

"What is this, brothers?" asked the duchess. "What is this? What do you want with this good man? How is it you do not consider that he is a governor elect?"

To which the scullion barber answered:

"This gentleman will not let himself be washed, as the custom is, and as the duke my lord was washed and his master the gentleman."

"I will indeed," answered Sancho with a great deal of choler, "but I should like it to be with cleaner towels, with clearer lye and with hands not so dirty. There is not so much difference between me and my master that they should wash him with angels' water and me with devils' lye. The customs of countries and of princes' palaces are good just so far as they do not cause distress; but the custom of washing that is used here is worse than a flogging by penitents. I am clean about the beard and have no need of refreshments of that kind; and whoever comes to wash me, or to touch a hair of my head — I mean of my beard, speaking with all due respect — I shall give him such a punch that I shall leave my fist set in his skull; for these ceremonies and soapings look more like tricks than the entertaining of guests."

The duchess was dying of laughter, seeing Sancho's choler and hearing his arguments; but it did not give Don Quixote much pleasure to see him so badly got up with the marbled towel and so surrounded by so many kitchen entertainers. And so, making the duke and duchess a deep bow, as though asking their leave to speak, in a composed voice he said to the rabble:

"Here, gentlemen knights! Let your worships leave the young man alone and go back the way you came, or by some other way if you feel like it; for my squire is as clean as anybody else, and those little troughs are cramping little pots for him. Take my advice and leave him, because neither he nor I know anything about the business of jokes."

Sancho took the words out of his mouth and went on, saying:

"No, let them just come and make fun of the stray — I shall put up with it about as well as it is now night! Bring a comb here, or whatever they like, and curry-comb this beard of mine; and if they get anything out of it that offends cleanliness, let them shear me in crosses."

At this point, without leaving off laughing, the duchess said:

"Sancho Panza is right in everything he has said, and he will be right in everything he says. He is clean, and, as he says, he has no need to wash; and if our custom does not please him, his soul is in his own palm. And besides, you ministers of cleanliness have been excessively slack and careless — and I do not know whether to say impudent — in bringing to such a personage and to such a beard, instead of basins and ewers of pure gold and towels of German linen, little troughs and wooden bowls and sideboard dishcloths. But in short, you are bad men and badly born, and you cannot help, villains that you are, showing the grudge you bear the squires of knights errant."

The rascally ministers, and even the steward who had come with them, believed that the duchess was speaking in earnest; and so they took the lye-cloth off Sancho's chest, and all of them, confused and almost put out of countenance, went off and left him. And he, seeing himself out of what to his mind was an extreme danger, went and knelt down before the duchess and said:

"From great ladies, great favours are to be expected; this one that your worship has done me today cannot be paid for with less than wishing to see myself dubbed a knight errant, so as to spend all the days of my life in serving so lofty a lady. A labourer I am, Sancho Panza is my name, married I am, children I have and as a squire I serve. If with any of these things I can serve your greatness, I shall be quicker to obey than your ladyship to command."

"It is plain enough, Sancho," answered the duchess, "that you have learnt to be courteous in the school of courtesy itself; it is plain enough, I mean, that you have been brought up at the breast of Señor Don Quixote, who must be the cream of civilities and the flower of ceremonies — or cirrymonies, as you say. Blessings on such a master and such a servant: the one for the pole star of knight-errantry and the other for the star of squirely faithfulness. Get up, Sancho my friend, for I shall repay your courtesies by making the duke my lord fulfil, as soon as he can, the promised favour of the government."

With this the conversation stopped, and Don Quixote went off to take his siesta; and the duchess asked Sancho that if he was not very anxious to sleep, he should come and spend the afternoon with her and her maidens in a very cool room. Sancho answered that although it was true that he was in the habit of sleeping four or five hours during the summer siestas, still, to serve her goodness, he would try with all his strength not to sleep at all that day, and would come obediently at her order; and off he went. The duke gave fresh orders that Don Quixote should be treated as a knight errant, without departing a point from the manner in which they tell that the knights of old were treated.

Chapter 33: Of the Delightful Conversation the Duchess and Her Maidens Had with Sancho Panza, Worth Reading and Worth Noting

The history relates, then, that Sancho did not sleep that siesta, but, to keep his word, came as soon as he had eaten to see the duchess; who, with the pleasure she took in hearing him, made him sit down next to her on a low chair — although Sancho, out of pure good breeding, did not want to sit. But the duchess told him to sit as a governor and talk as a squire, since for both things together he deserved the very bench of the Cid Ruy Díaz the Champion.

Sancho shrugged his shoulders, obeyed and sat down; and all the duchess's maidens and duennas gathered round her, attentive and in the deepest silence to hear what he would say. But the duchess was the one who spoke first, saying:

"Now that we are alone and nobody is listening to us here, I should like the lord governor to resolve certain doubts I have, born of the history of the great Don Quixote that is already in print. One of these doubts is that, since good Sancho never saw Dulcinea — I mean the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso — and never took her Señor Don Quixote's letter, because it was left behind in the notebook in the Sierra Morena, how did he dare to invent the answer, and all that about finding her winnowing wheat, when the whole thing was a trick and a lie, and so much to the damage of the good name of the peerless Dulcinea, and all of it so ill-suited to the quality and faithfulness of good squires?"

At these words, without answering any of them, Sancho got up out of his chair and, with quiet steps, his body bent over and his finger on his lips, went all round the room lifting the hangings; and then, this done, he sat down again and said:

"Now, my lady, that I have seen that nobody is listening to us on the sly, apart from the people present, I shall answer without fear or start what I have been asked and everything else I may be asked. And the first thing I say is that I hold my master Don Quixote for a downright madman — although sometimes he says things that, to my mind and to the minds of all who hear him, are so judicious and so well set on the right track that Satan himself could not say them better. But for all that, truly and without any scruple, it has settled in me that he is an idiot. And since I have this in my noddle, I make bold to make him believe things with neither head nor feet to them, like that business of the answer to the letter, and the business of six or eight days ago, which is not in the history yet: that is to say, the enchantment of my lady Doña Dulcinea, whom I have given him to understand is enchanted, when it is no more true than the hills of Úbeda."

The duchess begged him to tell her about that enchantment or trick, and Sancho told it to her all just as it had happened, at which the listeners took no small pleasure. And, going on with her talk, the duchess said:

"From what good Sancho has told me, a scruple goes leaping about in my soul, and a certain whisper comes to my ears saying: 'Since Don Quixote of La Mancha is mad, wanting and an idiot, and Sancho Panza his squire knows it, and for all that serves him and follows him and goes along relying on his empty promises, then without any doubt he must be madder and more foolish than his master. And this being so, as it is, it will be counted against you, my lady duchess, if you give this Sancho Panza an isle to govern; for the man who does not know how to govern himself, how will he know how to govern others?'"

"By God, my lady," said Sancho, "that scruple comes straight to the birth. But tell it, your worship, to speak plainly, or however it likes, for I know it is telling the truth: if I were judicious, I should have left my master days ago. But this was my luck and this my ill fortune; I can do no more, I have to follow him. We are from the same place, I have eaten his bread, I am fond of him, he is grateful, he gave me his ass-colts and, above all, I am faithful; and so it is impossible for anything to part us except the spade and the mattock.

"And if your high-flyingness does not want the promised government given to me, God made me out of less, and it might be that not giving it me would redound to the good of my conscience; for though I am a fool, I understand that proverb 'the ant grew wings to her own harm'. And it might even be that Sancho the squire would get to heaven quicker than Sancho the governor. They bake as good bread here as in France; and at night all cats are grey; and wretched enough is the man who has not breakfasted by two in the afternoon; and there is no stomach a hand's breadth bigger than another, and it can be filled, as they say, with straw and hay; and the little birds of the field have God for their provider and steward; and four yards of Cuenca cloth keep you warmer than another four of fine Segovia stuff; and when we leave this world and go down into the earth, the prince travels by as narrow a path as the day-labourer, and the Pope's body takes up no more feet of ground than the sexton's, even if the one is taller than the other; because when we go into the hole we all fit ourselves in and shrink, or they make us fit and shrink, however little we like it — and good night to us.

"And I say again that if your ladyship will not give me the isle because I am a fool, I shall know how to not care a bit about it because I am judicious. And I have heard it said that behind the cross stands the devil, and that all is not gold that glitters, and that from among the oxen and the ploughs and the yokes they took the ploughman Wamba to be king of Spain, and from among the brocades and the pastimes and the riches they took Rodrigo to be eaten by snakes — if the verses of the old ballads are not lying."

"And of course they are not lying!" said Doña Rodríguez the duenna at this point, who was one of the listeners. "For there is a ballad that says they put King Rodrigo alive, alive, into a tomb full of toads, snakes and lizards, and that two days later the king said from inside the tomb, in a pained and low voice:

	Now they are eating me, now they are eating me
	there where I had most sinned;

"and, going by that, this gentleman is quite right to say that he would rather be a ploughman than a king, if he is to be eaten by vermin."

The duchess could not hold her laughter at hearing her duenna's simplicity, nor did she stop marvelling at hearing Sancho's arguments and proverbs, and she said to him:

"Good Sancho knows already that whatever a knight once promises he tries to carry out, even if it costs him his life. The duke, my lord and husband, although he is not one of the errant sort, is a knight none the less for that; and so he will keep his word about the promised isle, in spite of the envy and the malice of the world. Let Sancho be of good heart, for when he least expects it he will find himself sitting in the chair of his isle and of his estate, and taking his government in hand, and he shall throw it over for another of three-pile brocade. What I charge him with is to look how he governs his vassals, noting that they are all loyal and well born."

"As for governing them well," answered Sancho, "there is no need to charge me with that, because I am charitable by nature and have compassion for the poor; and don't steal a loaf from the man who bakes and kneads; and by my blessed self they shall not load the dice on me. I am an old dog and understand every 'here, boy'; and I know how to wake myself up at the right times, and I do not let cobwebs get in front of my eyes, because I know where the shoe pinches me. I say it because the good will find a hand and a hold with me, and the bad neither foot nor entrance. And it seems to me that in this business of governments it is all a matter of beginning, and it might be that after a fortnight of being a governor I should be licking my fingers after the office and know more about it than about working in the fields, where I was brought up."

"You are right, Sancho," said the duchess, "for nobody is born taught, and bishops are made out of men and not out of stones. But, coming back to the talk we were having a little while ago about the enchantment of the lady Dulcinea, I hold it for a certain and more than established thing that the notion Sancho had of playing a trick on his master and giving him to understand that the country girl was Dulcinea — and that if his master did not recognise her it must be because she was enchanted — was all the invention of one of the enchanters who persecute Señor Don Quixote. Because really and truly I know from a good source that the country wench who leapt up onto the she-ass was and is Dulcinea of El Toboso, and that good Sancho, thinking he was the deceiver, is the deceived; and there is no more doubting this truth than there is about things we never saw.

"And let Señor Sancho Panza know that we have enchanters here too who are fond of us and tell us what goes on in the world, plainly and simply, without tangles and machinery. And let Sancho believe me that the leaping country wench was and is Dulcinea of El Toboso, who is as enchanted as the mother who bore her; and when we least expect it we shall see her in her own shape, and then Sancho will come out of the deception he is living in."

"All that may very well be," said Sancho Panza. "And now I am willing to believe what my master tells about what he saw in the cave of Montesinos, where he says he saw the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso in the same dress and habit as I said I had seen her in when I enchanted her purely to please myself. And it must all have been the other way round, as your worship says, my lady; because from my poor wits it neither can nor ought to be presumed that I could build so sharp a piece of humbug in an instant, nor do I believe my master is so mad that with so feeble and thin a persuasion as mine he would believe a thing so far outside all bounds.

"But, my lady, your goodness should not for this reason take me for ill-meaning, since a blockhead like me is not obliged to bore through the thoughts and malices of those wretched enchanters. I made that up to escape my master Don Quixote's scoldings, and not with any intention of offending him; and if it has come out backwards, God is in heaven and judges hearts."

"That is the truth," said the duchess; "but tell me now, Sancho, what is this you say about the cave of Montesinos? For I should like to know it."

Then Sancho Panza told her point by point what has been said about that adventure. Which the duchess hearing, she said:

"From this business it can be inferred that, since the great Don Quixote says he saw there the very country girl Sancho saw on the way out of El Toboso, it is undoubtedly Dulcinea, and the enchanters are going about here very sharp and excessively inquisitive."

"That is what I say," said Sancho Panza. "For if my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso is enchanted, so much the worse for her; I am not going to take on my master's enemies, who must be many and bad. The truth is that the woman I saw was a country girl, and I took her for a country girl and judged her for such a country girl; and if that was Dulcinea, it is not to be put down to my account, nor is it to run at my charge, or there will be a fight over it.

"No — but let them keep coming at me at every turn with a 'say-you and say-I', 'Sancho said it, Sancho did it, Sancho went off and Sancho came back', as though Sancho were some whoever-you-please and not the very Sancho Panza who goes about in books now all over the world, according to what Sansón Carrasco told me — and he is at least a person bachelored at Salamanca, and such people cannot lie except when they feel like it or when it suits them very well. So there is no call for anybody to take me on; and, since I have a good name, and, as I heard my master say, a good name is worth more than great riches, jam that government on me and you shall see wonders; for a man who has been a good squire will be a good governor."

"Everything good Sancho has said here," said the duchess, "is a set of Catonian judgements, or at least drawn from the very entrails of Micael Verino himself, florentibus occidit annis. In short, in short, to speak in his own manner: under a bad cloak there is often a good drinker."

"Truly, my lady," answered Sancho, "in my life I have never drunk out of malice; out of thirst it may well be, because I have nothing of the hypocrite about me. I drink when I feel like it, and when I do not feel like it and when they give it me, so as not to look either squeamish or badly brought up; for at a friend's toast, what heart could be so much of marble as not to pledge him back? But though I put them on, I do not dirty them; and what is more, the squires of knights errant almost always drink water, because they are always going about through woods, forests and meadows, mountains and crags, without finding a drop of mercy of wine even if they would give an eye for it."

"So I believe," answered the duchess. "And for now, let Sancho go and rest, and afterwards we shall talk at more length and give orders about his going quickly to have that government jammed on him, as he puts it."

Sancho kissed the duchess's hands again, and begged her to do him the favour of having good care taken of his grey, because he was the light of his eyes.

"What grey is this?" asked the duchess.

"My donkey," answered Sancho; "and so as not to name him by that name, I generally call him the grey. And I asked this lady duenna, when I came into this castle, to take care of him, and she flew up as if I had told her she was ugly or old — when it ought to be more proper and natural for duennas to look after donkeys than to lend authority to drawing rooms. God bless me, how badly a gentleman of my village got on with these ladies!"

"He must have been some peasant," said Doña Rodríguez the duenna, "for if he had been a gentleman and well born he would have set them above the horn of the moon."

"Well now," said the duchess, "let there be no more of it. Let Doña Rodríguez be quiet and let Señor Panza calm himself, and let the treatment of the grey be my charge; for since he is a jewel of Sancho's, I shall set him above the pupils of my eyes."

"It will be enough for him to be in the stable," answered Sancho; "for as to being above the pupils of your greatness's eyes, neither he nor I is worthy to be there for a single moment, and I should consent to it about as readily as to being stabbed. For although my master says that in courtesies it is better to lose by a card too many than by too few, in donkeyish ones — and eye-pupilish ones — you have to go with the dividers in your hand and by measured limits."

"Let Sancho take him to the government," said the duchess, "and there he can treat him as he likes, and even pension him off from work."

"Do not think your worship, my lady duchess, that you have said anything very much," said Sancho; "for I have seen more than two asses go off to governments, and my taking mine would be nothing new."

Sancho's arguments renewed the duchess's laughter and her contentment; and, sending him off to rest, she went to give the duke an account of what had passed between them, and between the two of them they laid out and arranged a trick to play on Don Quixote that should be a famous one and should fit the chivalric style — in which style they played him a great many, so apt and so judicious that they are the best adventures this great history contains.

Chapter 34: Which Tells of the News That Came of How the Peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso Was to Be Disenchanted, Which Is One of the Most Famous Adventures in This Book

Great was the pleasure the duke and duchess took in Don Quixote's conversation and in Sancho Panza's; and, confirming themselves in their intention of playing them some tricks that should carry the glimmerings and appearance of adventures, they took as their starting point the adventure of the cave of Montesinos that Don Quixote had already told them, so as to play him one that should be famous. (But what most astonished the duchess was that Sancho's simplicity should be so great that he had come to believe it an infallible truth that Dulcinea of El Toboso was enchanted, when he himself had been the enchanter and the humbug of that business.)

And so, having given their servants orders about everything they had to do, six days later they took him out boar hunting, with as great an apparatus of huntsmen and beaters as a crowned king could have taken. They gave Don Quixote a hunting suit and Sancho another, green, of the finest cloth; but Don Quixote would not put his on, saying that the next day he had to go back to the hard exercise of arms and could not carry wardrobes and stores about with him. Sancho did take the one they gave him, with the intention of selling it at the first chance he could get.

The expected day having come, then, Don Quixote armed himself, Sancho dressed himself, and, on his grey, which he would not leave although they offered him a horse, he got in among the troop of huntsmen. The duchess came out splendidly turned out, and Don Quixote, out of pure courtesy and civility, took the rein of her palfrey, although the duke would not have consented to it. And finally they came to a wood that lay between two very high mountains, where, the stands, hides and paths being taken and the people distributed to different positions, the hunt began with a great uproar, shouting and hallooing, so that they could not hear one another, what with the barking of the dogs and the sound of the horns.

The duchess dismounted, and with a sharp boar spear in her hands took up a stand where she knew boars generally came. The duke dismounted too, and Don Quixote, and they placed themselves at her sides. Sancho placed himself behind all of them without getting off the grey, whom he would not have dared to abandon in case some mishap befell him.

And they had hardly set foot and drawn up in a line with a great many other servants of theirs when, harried by the dogs and followed by the hunters, they saw an enormous boar coming at them, gnashing its teeth and tusks and throwing foam out of its mouth. And, on seeing it, gripping his shield and laying his hand on his sword, Don Quixote went forward to receive it. The duke did the same with his boar spear; and the duchess would have gone ahead of them all if the duke had not stopped her.

Only Sancho, on seeing the valiant animal, abandoned the grey and ran for it as fast as he could, and, trying to climb up a tall oak, found it impossible. On the contrary, being halfway up and gripping a branch, struggling to get to the top, he was so short of luck and so unfortunate that the branch broke off; and, on his way to the ground, he was left hanging in the air, caught on a stump of the oak and unable to reach the ground.

And, seeing himself like that, and that the green coat was tearing, and thinking that if that fierce animal came up there it could reach him, he began to shout so much and to call for help so earnestly that everybody who heard him and could not see him believed he was between the teeth of some wild beast.

Finally the tusked boar was left run through with the blades of the many boar spears that were put in front of it; and Don Quixote, turning his head at Sancho's shouts — for by them he had recognised him by now — saw him hanging from the oak head downwards, with the grey next to him, for he had not abandoned him in his calamity. And Cide Hamete says that he seldom saw Sancho Panza without seeing the grey, or the grey without seeing Sancho: such was the friendship and good faith the two of them kept with each other.

Don Quixote came and unhooked Sancho; who, seeing himself free and on the ground, looked at the tear in his hunting coat and it grieved him to the soul, for he had thought he had an entailed estate in that suit. At this they laid the mighty boar across a pack mule and, covering it with sprigs of rosemary and branches of myrtle, carried it, as though in sign of victorious spoils, to some great field tents that were pitched in the middle of the wood, where they found the tables laid in order and the dinner ready — so sumptuous and grand that the greatness and magnificence of the man who gave it could be plainly seen in it. Sancho, showing the duchess the wounds in his torn suit, said:

"If this hunt had been for hares or little birds, my coat would have been safe from coming to this pass. I do not know what pleasure there is in waiting for an animal that, if it reaches you with one tusk, can take your life. I remember having heard an old ballad sung that says:

	May you be eaten by the bears,
	like Favila the renowned."

"That was a Gothic king," said Don Quixote, "who, going out to hunt boar, was eaten by a bear."

"That is what I say," answered Sancho: "that I would not have princes and kings put themselves into dangers of the kind for the sake of a pleasure that ought not to be one, since it consists in killing an animal that has committed no crime at all."

"On the contrary, you are mistaken, Sancho," answered the duke, "because the exercise of hunting big game is more suitable and necessary for kings and princes than any other. Hunting is an image of war: there are stratagems in it, tricks and ambushes for overcoming the enemy in safety; extreme colds and intolerable heats are borne in it; idleness and sleep are cut down, the strength is built up, the limbs of the man who practises it are made nimble; and, in short, it is an exercise that can be carried out without harm to anybody and with pleasure to many. And the best thing about it is that it is not for everybody, as the other kinds of hunting are — except hawking, which is likewise only for kings and great lords. So, Sancho, change your opinion; and when you are a governor, busy yourself with hunting and you will see how it repays you a hundredfold."

"Not that," answered Sancho. "The good governor, a broken leg and at home. It would be a fine thing if people with business came looking for him worn out and he were up in the hills enjoying himself! The government would go finely then! Upon my word, sir, hunting and pastimes are more for idlers than for governors. What I mean to entertain myself with is playing trumps for stakes at the holidays and skittles on Sundays and feast days; for those hunts, or hunt-pots either, do not go with my nature or agree with my conscience."

"Please God, Sancho, that it may be so, for from saying to doing is a long way."

"Let it be what it may," replied Sancho, "for a good payer does not mind pledges, and the man God helps is better off than the man who rises early, and guts carry feet and not feet guts. I mean that if God helps me, and I do what I ought with good intentions, I shall undoubtedly govern better than a gerfalcon. No — just put a finger in my mouth and see whether I bite or not!"

"God curse you and all his saints curse you, cursed Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and when will the day come — as I have said so many other times — when I shall see you speak one connected and orderly sentence without proverbs! Let your greatnesses leave this fool alone, my dear sirs, for he will grind your souls not merely between two but between two thousand proverbs, brought in as seasonably and as timely as God may give him health, or give it me if I should ever want to listen to them."

"Sancho Panza's proverbs," said the duchess, "although they are more than the Greek Commander's, are not for that reason less to be valued, because of the shortness of the judgements in them. For my own part I can say that they give me more pleasure than others, however much better brought in and more seasonably fitted."

With these and other entertaining conversations they came out of the tent into the wood, and in going round some of the hides the day went by and night came on them — and not as clear or as calm as the season of the year called for, which was midsummer; but a certain half-light it brought with it helped the duke and duchess's plan a great deal.

And so, as soon as it began to grow dark, a little after twilight, all at once it seemed that the whole wood was on fire on all four sides; and then there were heard here and there, and this way and that, infinite bugles and other instruments of war, as of many troops of cavalry going through the wood. The light of the fire and the sound of the warlike instruments almost blinded and deafened the eyes and ears of the bystanders, and of everybody else in the wood.

Then there were heard infinite battle cries in the Moorish fashion, as they raise them when they go into battle; trumpets and clarions sounded, drums thundered, fifes shrilled, almost all at once, so continuously and so fast that the man would have had no senses who did not lose them at the confused sound of so many instruments. The duke was struck dumb, the duchess dumbfounded, Don Quixote amazed, Sancho Panza trembling; and, in the end, even those who knew the cause were frightened. Fear brought silence on them, and a courier who went past in front of them in the dress of a devil, blowing on a huge hollow horn in place of a bugle, which gave out a hoarse and terrible sound.

"Hey there, brother courier!" said the duke. "Who are you, where are you going, and what men of war are these who seem to be crossing this wood?"

To which the courier answered in a hideous and unabashed voice:

"I am the Devil. I am going to look for Don Quixote of La Mancha. The people coming this way are six troops of enchanters, who are bringing the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso on a triumphal car. She comes enchanted, with the gallant Frenchman Montesinos, to give Don Quixote his orders about how this lady is to be disenchanted."

"If you were the devil, as you say and as your figure shows, you would already have recognised this knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, since you have him in front of you."

"In God and in my conscience," answered the Devil, "I was not looking at that, because I carry my thoughts scattered over so many things that I was forgetting the main one I came for."

"Without any doubt," said Sancho, "this demon must be a decent man and a good Christian; because if he were not, he would not swear in God and in my conscience. Now I hold for myself that even in hell itself there must be good people."

Then the Demon, without dismounting, turned his eyes to Don Quixote and said:

"To you, Knight of the Lions — and may I see you between their claws — the unfortunate but valiant knight Montesinos sends me, ordering me to tell you on his behalf that you are to wait for him in the very place where I find you, because he brings with him the lady they call Dulcinea of El Toboso, with orders to give you what is needed for disenchanting her. And, since my coming was for nothing more, my stay shall be no longer: demons like me be with you, and the good angels with these ladies and gentlemen."

And, saying this, he blew the monstrous horn, turned his back and went off without waiting for an answer from anybody.

Astonishment was renewed in everyone, and especially in Sancho and Don Quixote: in Sancho, at seeing that in the teeth of the truth they wanted Dulcinea to be enchanted; in Don Quixote, at not being able to make certain whether what had happened to him in the cave of Montesinos was true or not. And, while he was raised up in these thoughts, the duke said to him:

"Does your worship mean to wait, Señor Don Quixote?"

"Why not?" he answered. "Here I shall wait, fearless and strong, even if all hell should come to attack me."

"Well, if I see another devil and hear another horn like the last one, I shall wait here about as much as I shall in Flanders," said Sancho.

At this the night closed in more, and a great many lights began to run about through the wood, exactly as the dry exhalations of the earth run about the sky, which look to our eyes like running stars. There was heard likewise a terrible noise, of the kind made by the solid wheels that ox carts generally have, from whose harsh and continuous screech they say the wolves and the bears run away, if there are any where they pass.

To all this tempest there was added another that increased them all, which was that it really seemed as though four encounters or battles were being fought at one and the same time on the four sides of the wood: for over there sounded the hard uproar of terrifying artillery, over yonder infinite muskets were being fired, close by sounded almost the voices of the combatants, far off the Moorish battle cries were repeated.

Finally the bugles, the horns, the hunting horns, the clarions, the trumpets, the drums, the artillery, the harquebuses and, above all, the fearful noise of the carts, all together made a sound so confused and so horrible that Don Quixote needed all his heart to bear it; but Sancho's came to the ground, and he fell in a faint into the duchess's lap. She received him there, and in great haste ordered water to be thrown in his face. It was done, and he came round to his senses just as one of the carts with the screeching wheels was arriving at that place.

It was drawn by four sluggish oxen, all covered with black trappings; on each horn they carried a great wax torch tied and lit; and on top of the cart was made a high seat, on which sat a venerable old man with a beard whiter than snow itself, and so long that it came down past his waist. His dress was a long gown of black buckram; and, since the cart came full of infinite lights, everything on it could be well made out and discerned. It was guided by two hideous demons dressed in the same buckram, with such hideous faces that Sancho, having seen them once, shut his eyes so as not to see them twice.

The cart coming level with the place, then, the venerable old man got up from his high seat and, standing on his feet, said in a great voice:

"I am the wise Lirgandeo."

And the cart passed on without another word. Behind this one there passed another cart in the same fashion, with another old man enthroned; who, making the cart stop, said in a voice no less grave than the other's:

"I am the wise Alquife, the great friend of Urganda the Unknown."

And he passed on.

Then, in the same manner, another cart arrived; but the man sitting on the throne was not old like the others, but a big robust fellow with an ugly look about him, who, on arriving, standing up like the others, said in a hoarser and more devilish voice:

"I am Arcaláus the enchanter, mortal enemy of Amadís of Gaul and of all his kindred."

And he passed on. A little way off from there these three carts halted, and the tiresome noise of their wheels stopped; and then there was heard another — not a noise, but a sound made up of a soft and ordered music, at which Sancho was glad, and he took it for a good sign. And so he said to the duchess, from whom he never moved a point or a step:

"My lady, where there is music there can be nothing bad."

"Nor where there are lights and brightness," answered the duchess.

To which Sancho replied:

"Fire gives light and bonfires give brightness, as we see in the ones that surround us — and they might very well burn us up; but music is always a sign of merrymaking and festivity."

"Time will tell," said Don Quixote, who was listening to it all.

And he was right, as is shown in the following chapter.

Chapter 35: Where the News Don Quixote Had of Dulcinea's Disenchantment Is Carried Further, with Other Wonderful Events

In time to the agreeable music they saw coming towards them one of the carts they call triumphal, drawn by six dun mules covered over with white linen; and on each one rode a torch-bearing penitent, likewise dressed in white, with a great lighted wax torch in his hand. The cart was twice, and even three times, bigger than the ones before, and the sides of it and the top were taken up by twelve more penitents as white as snow, all with their torches lit — a sight that filled them with wonder and terror together.

And on a raised throne there sat a nymph dressed in a thousand veils of silver tissue, with infinite leaves of gold spangling shining through them all, which made her, if not richly, at least showily dressed. She had her face covered with a transparent and delicate gauze, so that, without its threads getting in the way, there could be made out through them a most beautiful maiden's face; and the many lights gave room to distinguish her beauty and her years, which to look at did not reach twenty nor fall short of seventeen.

Beside her came a figure dressed in one of those trailing gowns, down to the feet, its head covered with a black veil. But the moment the cart came face to face with the duke and duchess and Don Quixote, the music of the shawms stopped, and then that of the harps and lutes that were playing on the cart. And, the figure in the gown getting to its feet, it parted the gown to both sides, and, taking the veil off its face, showed itself plainly to be the very figure of death, fleshless and hideous — at which Don Quixote felt distress and Sancho fear, and the duke and duchess made some show of being frightened.

This living death, raised up and standing, in a rather sleepy voice and with a not very wide-awake tongue, began to speak in this way:

	I am Merlin, the one the histories
	say had the devil for a father
	(a lie made authoritative by the ages),
	prince of Magic and monarch
	and archive of the Zoroastrian science,
	rival of the ages and the centuries
	that try to cover over the exploits
	of the brave and errant knights
	for whom I have had and still have great affection.
	And although the condition of enchanters,
	of magi or of magicians, is always
	hard, harsh and unyielding,
	mine is tender, soft and loving,
	and a friend to doing good to all people.
	In the gloomy caverns of Dis,
	where my soul was busying itself
	in forming certain rhombs and characters,
	there came the grieving voice of the beautiful
	and peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso.
	I learnt of her enchantment and her misfortune,
	and her transformation from a gentle lady
	into a rustic village girl; I was moved to pity,
	and, shutting my spirit in the hollow
	of this terrible and fierce skeleton,
	after turning over a hundred thousand books
	of this devilish and clumsy science of mine,
	I come to give the remedy that suits
	so great a grief, so great an ill.
	O you, the glory and honour of all who wear
	the tunics of steel and of diamond,
	light and lantern, path, pole star and guide
	of those who, leaving behind dull sleep
	and the idle feather bed, set themselves
	to practise the intolerable exercise
	of bloody and heavy arms!
	To you I speak — O man, as you deserve,
	never sufficiently praised — to you, valiant
	and judicious together, Don Quixote,
	splendour of La Mancha, star of Spain:
	that for the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso
	to recover her first estate,
	it is needful that Sancho, your squire,
	should give himself three thousand lashes
	and three hundred, upon both his valiant buttocks,
	bared to the air, and in such a way
	that they smart him, sting him and vex him.
	And in this all those are agreed
	who have been the authors of her misfortune,
	and this is what my coming is for, my lords and ladies.

"By all that's holy!" said Sancho at this. "Never mind three thousand lashes — I would as soon give myself three as three stabs. The devil take you for a way of disenchanting! I do not see what my backside has to do with enchantments! By God, if Señor Merlin has found no other way of disenchanting the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, she can go to her grave enchanted!"

"I shall take you," said Don Quixote, "you villain stuffed with garlic, and tie you to a tree as naked as your mother bore you; and I shall give you not three thousand three hundred lashes but six thousand six hundred, so well laid on that they will not come off at three thousand three hundred tugs. And do not answer me a word, or I shall tear the soul out of you."

Hearing which, Merlin said:

"It must not be like that, because the lashes good Sancho has to receive must be of his own free will and not by force, and at whatever time he likes; no fixed term is set for him. But he is allowed, if he wants to buy off his suffering by half of this whipping, to let them be given him by somebody else's hand, even if it is a rather heavy one."

"Neither somebody else's nor my own, neither heavy nor weighing," replied Sancho. "No hand at all is going to touch me. Did I by any chance give birth to the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, that my backside should pay for what her eyes sinned? My lord and master, now — yes, he is a party to her, since he calls her at every turn 'my life', 'my soul', his food and his prop — he can and should whip himself for her and take all the steps necessary for her disenchantment. But whipping myself...? Abernuncio!"

Sancho had hardly finished saying this when the silvered nymph who came beside Merlin's spirit got to her feet, and, taking the fine veil off her face, showed it to be such that it seemed to everybody more than excessively beautiful; and, with a manly unconcern and in a voice that was not very ladylike, speaking straight at Sancho Panza, she said:

"O wretched squire, soul of a pitcher, heart of cork, with entrails of pebble and flint! If you were ordered, you thieving face-flayer, to throw yourself down to the ground from a high tower; if you were asked, enemy of the human race, to eat a dozen toads, two dozen lizards and three dozen snakes; if you were urged to kill your wife and your children with some cruel, sharp scimitar — it would be no wonder if you showed yourself squeamish and unwilling. But to make a fuss about three thousand three hundred lashes, when there is no charity-school boy, however poor a creature, who does not take that many every month, astonishes, stuns and terrifies all the merciful hearts of those who hear it, and even the hearts of all those who come to learn of it in the course of time.

"Set, O miserable and hardened animal, set, I say, those skittish little mule's eyes of yours on the pupils of these of mine, which have been compared to shining stars, and you shall see them weep thread by thread and skein by skein, making furrows, tracks and paths across the beautiful fields of my cheeks. Let it move you, you sly and evil-minded monster, that my age, so full of flower — still in the teen-and-something of my years, for I am nineteen and have not reached twenty — is being consumed and withered under the rind of a rustic peasant girl. And if I do not look like her now, it is a particular favour that Señor Merlin here present has done me, only so that my beauty may soften you; for the tears of an afflicted beauty turn crags into cotton wool and tigers into sheep.

"Lay it on, lay it on that great carcass of yours, you untamed brute, and rouse that spirit out of its sloth — the spirit that inclines you to nothing but eating and more eating — and set free the smoothness of my flesh, the gentleness of my nature and the beauty of my face. And if you will not soften for my sake or bring yourself round to any reasonable terms, do it for that poor knight you have at your side — for your master, I mean, whose soul I can see stuck crosswise in his throat, not ten fingers from his lips, waiting for nothing but your hard or soft answer, either to come out at his mouth or to go back down to his stomach."

Hearing this, Don Quixote felt his throat and said, turning to the duke:

"By God, sir, Dulcinea has told the truth, for here I have my soul stuck crosswise in my throat like the nut of a crossbow."

"What do you say to this, Sancho?" asked the duchess.

"I say, my lady," answered Sancho, "what I have said: as for the lashes, abernuncio."

"Abrenuncio you should say, Sancho, and not as you say it," said the duke.

"Let your greatness let me be," answered Sancho, "for I am not in a state now to look at subtleties or at a letter more or less; because these lashes they are going to give me, or that I am going to give myself, have me so troubled that I do not know what I am saying or what I am doing.

"But I should like to know from the lady my lady Doña Dulcina of El Toboso where she learnt the manner of begging she has. She comes to ask me to open up my flesh with lashes, and she calls me a soul of a pitcher and an untamed brute, with a whole string of bad names that the devil may put up with. Is my flesh made of bronze, by any chance, or is it anything to me whether she is disenchanted or not? What basket of white linen, of shirts, of headcloths and of socks — even though I do not wear them — does she bring along in front of her to soften me, instead of one piece of abuse after another? For she knows the proverb they say about here, that a donkey loaded with gold climbs a mountain lightly, and that gifts break rocks, and 'pray to God and keep hammering', and that one 'here you are' is worth more than two 'I'll give you'.

"And my lord and master, who ought to have stroked my hair the right way and coaxed me into turning myself into wool and carded cotton, says that if he catches me he will tie me naked to a tree and double the stake on the lashes. And these afflicted gentlefolk ought to consider that they are asking not only a squire to whip himself but a governor — as who should say, 'and cherries with it'. Let them learn, let them learn, much good may it do them, how to beg and how to ask and how to have some breeding; for all times are not alike, and men are not always in a good humour. I am bursting with grief just now over seeing my green coat torn, and they come and ask me to whip myself of my own free will, when my will is about as far from it as from turning me into a cacique in the Indies."

"Well truly, Sancho my friend," said the duke, "if you do not soften more than a ripe fig, you shall not take that government in hand. It would be a fine thing if I sent my islanders a cruel governor with flinty entrails, who will not bend to the tears of afflicted maidens or to the pleas of judicious, imperious and ancient enchanters and sages! In short, Sancho, either you must be whipped, or they must whip you, or you must not be a governor."

"Sir," answered Sancho, "would they not give me two days' grace to think about what suits me best?"

"No, on no account," said Merlin. "Here, in this instant and in this place, it must be settled what is to become of this business. Either Dulcinea will go back to the cave of Montesinos and to her first state as a peasant girl, or else, in the state she is in, she will be carried to the Elysian Fields, where she will be waiting until the tale of the whipping is complete."

"Come, good Sancho," said the duchess, "good courage, and a good return for the bread you have eaten of Señor Don Quixote's — whom we must all serve and please for his good nature and for his high chivalries. Say yes to this whipping, my son, and let the devil go to the devil and fear to the mean-spirited; for a good heart breaks bad luck, as you know very well."

To these arguments Sancho answered with these preposterous ones, saying to Merlin:

"Tell me, your worship, Señor Merlin: when the devil courier arrived here and gave my master a message from Señor Montesinos, ordering him on his behalf to wait for him here because he was coming to give orders for the lady Doña Dulcinea of El Toboso to be disenchanted — and up to now we have not seen Montesinos, or anything like him."

To which Merlin answered:

"The Devil, Sancho my friend, is an ignorant fellow and a very great rogue. I sent him to look for your master, but not with a message from Montesinos, but with one from me; because Montesinos is in his cave attending to — or, better said, waiting for — his own disenchantment, which still has the tail left to skin. If he owes you anything, or you have any business to do with him, I shall bring him to you and set him down wherever you like best. And for now, finish saying yes to this discipline; and believe me, it will do you a great deal of good, both for the soul and for the body: for the soul, because of the charity with which you will do it; for the body, because I know you are of a sanguine complexion, and taking a little blood out of you can do you no harm."

"There are a great many doctors in the world — even the enchanters are doctors," replied Sancho. "But since everybody tells me so, though I do not see it myself, I say I am content to give myself the three thousand three hundred lashes, on condition that I am to give them to myself whenever and however I like, without any limit being set on the days or on the time; and I shall try to get out of the debt as soon as possible, so that the world may enjoy the beauty of the lady Doña Dulcinea of El Toboso, since, by the look of it, she really is beautiful, the other way round from what I thought.

"It must also be a condition that I am not to be obliged to draw blood with the discipline, and that if any of the lashes are fly-flicks, they are to be counted in. Item, that if I make a mistake in the number, Señor Merlin, since he knows everything, is to take care to count them and to let me know how many I am short of or over."

"About the ones over there will be no need to give notice," answered Merlin, "because on reaching the exact number the lady Dulcinea will at once and suddenly be disenchanted, and she will come looking for good Sancho, like a grateful woman, to give him thanks and even rewards for the good work. So there is nothing to have any scruples about, over or under; and heaven forbid that I should cheat anybody, even by a hair of the head."

"Well then, into the hand of God!" said Sancho. "I consent to my own bad luck; I say I accept the penance on the conditions set down."

Sancho had hardly said these last words when the music of the shawms sounded again and infinite harquebuses were let off again, and Don Quixote hung on Sancho's neck, giving him a thousand kisses on the forehead and on the cheeks. The duchess and the duke and all the bystanders showed signs of having received the greatest contentment, and the cart began to move off; and, as she passed, the beautiful Dulcinea bowed her head to the duke and duchess and made Sancho a great curtsey.

And by now the dawn was coming on apace, glad and smiling: the little flowers of the fields were lifting themselves up and standing straight, and the liquid crystal of the streams, murmuring between white and grey pebbles, was going to pay its tribute to the rivers that waited for it. The glad earth, the clear sky, the clean air, the serene light, each by itself and all together, gave plain signs that the day, which came treading on the skirts of the dawn, was going to be calm and bright. And the duke and duchess, satisfied with the hunt and with having carried out their intention so judiciously and so successfully, went back to their castle, with the intention of following up their tricks — for there was no earnest that could give them more pleasure.

Chapter 36: Where the Strange and Never-Imagined Adventure of the Distressed Duenna, Alias the Countess Trifaldi, Is Told, with a Letter Sancho Panza Wrote to His Wife Teresa Panza

The duke had a steward of a very playful and easy wit, who had taken the part of Merlin and arranged all the apparatus of the adventure just described, composed the verses and got a page to play Dulcinea. Finally, with his master and mistress taking a hand in it, he arranged another of the most amusing and strangest contrivance that can be imagined.

The duchess asked Sancho the next day whether he had begun the task of the penance he had to perform for Dulcinea's disenchantment. He said he had, and that the night before he had given himself five lashes. The duchess asked him what he had given them to himself with. He answered that it was with his hand.

"That," replied the duchess, "is giving yourself pats rather than lashes. I hold for myself that the wise Merlin will not be content with such gentleness. It will be necessary for good Sancho to make himself some scourge of thorns, or of knotted cords, that will let themselves be felt; because learning enters with blood, and the freedom of so great a lady as Dulcinea is not to be given away so cheaply for so small a price. And let Sancho note that works of charity done lukewarmly and slackly have no merit and are worth nothing."

To which Sancho answered:

"Let your ladyship give me some suitable scourge or lash, and I shall give it myself so long as it does not hurt too much; because I would have your worship know that although I am a rustic, my flesh has more of cotton in it than of esparto grass, and it would not be a good thing for me to waste myself away for somebody else's profit."

"So be it," answered the duchess. "Tomorrow I shall give you a scourge that will fit you exactly and will suit the tenderness of your flesh as though they were its own sisters."

To which Sancho said:

"Your highness must know, my lady of my soul, that I have a letter written to my wife Teresa Panza, giving her an account of everything that has happened to me since I left her. I have it here in my bosom, and it needs nothing but the address on it. I should like your judiciousness to read it, because it seems to me that it goes in the governor style — I mean, in the way governors ought to write."

"And who dictated it?" asked the duchess.

"Who was to dictate it but me, sinner that I am?" answered Sancho.

"And did you write it yourself?" said the duchess.

"Not by a long way," answered Sancho, "because I cannot read or write, although I can sign my name."

"Let us see it," said the duchess, "for it is a safe bet that you show in it the quality and sufficiency of your wits."

Sancho took an open letter out of his bosom, and, the duchess taking it, she saw that it went in this way:

Letter from Sancho Panza to Teresa Panza, His Wife

If they gave me good lashes, I was riding well mounted; if I have a good government, it is costing me good lashes. You will not understand this, my Teresa, for the present; another time you will know it. You must know, Teresa, that I have decided that you are to travel in a coach, which is what matters, because every other way of travelling is going on all fours. You are a governor's wife — see whether anybody is going to gnaw at your heels now!

I am sending you a green hunting suit here that my lady the duchess gave me; alter it so that it will serve for a skirt and a bodice for our daughter. Don Quixote, my master, from what I have heard said in this country, is a sane madman and an amusing idiot, and I am not far behind him. We have been in the cave of Montesinos, and the wise Merlin has laid hold of me for the disenchanting of Dulcinea of El Toboso, who is called Aldonza Lorenzo over there. With three thousand three hundred lashes, less five, that I have to give myself, she will be left as disenchanted as the mother who bore her. You are not to say anything about this to anybody, because put your business to the council and some will say it is white and others that it is black.

In a few days from now I shall set off for the government, where I go with the greatest desire to make money, because they have told me that all new governors go with this same desire. I shall feel its pulse and let you know whether you are to come and be with me or not. The grey is well, and sends you his best regards; and I do not mean to leave him even if they carried me off to be the Great Turk.

My lady the duchess kisses your hands a thousand times; send her back two thousand, for there is nothing that costs less or comes cheaper, as my master says, than good manners. It has not pleased God to furnish me with another portmanteau with another hundred crowns in it, like the one of the other day; but do not let that grieve you, my Teresa, for safe is the man who rings the alarm, and it will all come out in the wash of the government. Only it has grieved me a great deal that they tell me if I once get a taste of it, I shall be licking my fingers after it; and if that were so, it would not come cheap to me — although the crippled and maimed have their own canonry in the alms they beg. So one way or another you are going to be rich and in luck. God give it you, as He can, and keep me to serve you. From this castle, the twentieth of July 1614.

Your husband the governor,

Sancho Panza.

When the duchess had finished reading the letter she said to Sancho:

"In two things the good governor goes a little off the road. One is in saying, or giving to understand, that this government has been given him for the lashes he has to give himself — when he knows, and cannot deny, that when the duke my lord promised it him, there was no dreaming that there were lashes in the world. The other is that he shows himself very greedy in it, and I should not like that to turn out ill; for greed bursts the sack, and a greedy governor makes justice ungoverned."

"I do not mean it in that way, my lady," answered Sancho; "and if it seems to your worship that this letter does not go as it should, there is nothing for it but to tear it up and make a new one — and it might well be worse, if it is left to my noddle."

"No, no," replied the duchess, "this one is good, and I want the duke to see it."

With this they went out to a garden where they were to dine that day. The duchess showed the duke Sancho's letter, at which he received the greatest pleasure. They dined; and after the cloth had been taken away, and after they had entertained themselves a good while with Sancho's delicious conversation, all at once there was heard the very mournful sound of a fife and that of a hoarse and untuned drum. Everybody showed themselves disturbed by the confused, martial and mournful harmony, and especially Don Quixote, who could not keep still in his seat for pure agitation. Of Sancho there is nothing to say except that fear carried him to his usual refuge, which was the side or the skirts of the duchess, because really and truly the sound they were hearing was extremely mournful and melancholy.

And, while they were all in this suspense, they saw coming into the garden two men dressed in mourning, so long and trailing that it dragged on the ground. These came beating two great drums, likewise covered with black. At their side came the fife player, black and pitch-dark like the rest. Following the three came a personage of gigantic body, mantled rather than dressed in a gown of the deepest black, whose skirt was likewise outrageously large. Over the gown he was girt and crossed with a broad baldric, also black, from which there hung an enormous scimitar with black fittings and scabbard. He came with his face covered by a transparent black veil, through which there half showed an extremely long beard, white as snow. He moved his steps in time to the drums with great gravity and composure. In short, his greatness, his swagger, his blackness and his attendants could have astonished — and did astonish — everybody who looked at him without knowing him.

He came, then, with the deliberation and pomp described, and knelt down before the duke, who was standing waiting for him with the rest of those there. But the duke would on no account allow him to speak until he got up. The prodigious scarecrow did so; and, standing on his feet, he lifted the mask off his face and made plain the most horrifying, the longest, the whitest and the thickest beard that human eyes had until then ever seen; and then he unfixed and dragged out of his broad, deep chest a grave and sonorous voice, and, fixing his eyes on the duke, said:

"Most high and mighty lord, I am called Trifaldin of the White Beard. I am squire to the Countess Trifaldi, otherwise called the Distressed Duenna, on whose behalf I bring your greatness an embassy — which is that your magnificence should be pleased to give her the power and the leave to come in and tell you her trouble, which is one of the strangest and most astonishing that the most troubled mind in the world could ever have thought of.

"And first she wishes to know whether the valorous and never-conquered knight Don Quixote of La Mancha is in this castle of yours; in search of whom she has come on foot and without breakfasting from the kingdom of Candaya to this estate of yours — a thing that can and ought to be held for a miracle or for the force of enchantment. She is waiting at the gate of this fortress or country house, and waits for nothing but your good pleasure to come in. I have spoken."

And then he coughed and stroked his beard from top to bottom with both hands, and with great composure stood waiting for the duke's answer, which was:

"Good squire Trifaldin of the White Beard, we have had news these many days now of the misfortune of my lady the Countess Trifaldi, whom the enchanters have made them call the Distressed Duenna. You may very well tell her, stupendous squire, to come in, and that the valiant knight Don Quixote of La Mancha is here, from whose generous nature she may safely promise herself all protection and all help. And you may likewise tell her on my behalf that if my favour should be necessary to her, it shall not be wanting, since being a knight already obliges me to give it — a knight being bound and concerned to favour all sorts of women, and especially widowed, ruined and distressed duennas, as her ladyship must be."

Hearing which, Trifaldin bent his knee to the ground; and, making a sign to the fife and the drums to play, at the same sound and at the same pace as he had come in, he went out of the garden again, leaving everybody astonished at his presence and his bearing. And the duke, turning to Don Quixote, said to him:

"In short, famous knight, the darkness of malice and of ignorance cannot cover and dim the light of valour and of virtue. I say this because your goodness has hardly been six days in this castle when already they come looking for you from far-off and distant lands, and not in coaches or on dromedaries but on foot and fasting — the sad and the afflicted, trusting that they will find in that mighty arm the remedy for their troubles and hardships, thanks to your great exploits, which run and travel round the whole discovered surface of the earth."

"I could wish, lord duke," answered Don Quixote, "that that blessed churchman were here present who at table the other day showed himself in such an ill temper and with such a grudge against knights errant, so that he might see with his own eyes whether such knights are necessary in the world.
