He would at least put his hand on it, that people who are extraordinarily afflicted and disconsolate, in great cases and in enormous misfortunes, do not go looking for their remedy to the houses of lawyers, or to that of the village sacristans, or to the gentleman who has never managed to get outside the boundaries of his own place, or to the idle courtier who is sooner looking for news to report and tell than trying to do deeds and exploits for others to tell and write about.

"The remedy for troubles, the succour of needs, the protection of maidens, the consolation of widows are found in no kind of persons better than in knights errant; and for being one I give infinite thanks to heaven, and I count as very well spent any mishap and hardship that may come to me in this so honourable exercise. Let this duenna come and ask whatever she likes, for I shall make out her remedy for her in the strength of my arm and in the fearless resolution of my courageous spirit."

Chapter 37: Where the Famous Adventure of the Distressed Duenna Is Carried Further

The duke and duchess were extremely glad to see how well Don Quixote was answering to their design; and at this point Sancho said:

"I should not like this lady duenna to put any stumbling block in the way of the promise of my government, because I have heard a Toledo apothecary say — and he talked like a goldfinch — that wherever duennas came into it, nothing good could happen. God bless me, how badly that apothecary got on with them! From which I gather that, since all duennas are tiresome and impertinent, of whatever quality and condition they may be, what will the distressed ones be like — such as they say this Countess Three-Skirts, or Three-Tails, is? For in my country skirts and tails, tails and skirts, are all one."

"Be quiet, Sancho my friend," said Don Quixote; "for since this lady duenna comes from such far-off lands to look for me, she cannot be one of those the apothecary had in his reckoning — and what is more, this one is a countess; and when countesses serve as duennas, it must be in the service of queens and empresses, since in their own houses they are the greatest of ladies and are served by other duennas."

To this Doña Rodríguez, who happened to be there, answered:

"My lady the duchess has duennas in her service who could have been countesses if fortune had wished it; but laws go where kings wish. And let nobody speak ill of duennas, and especially of the old ones and the unmarried; for although I am not one myself, I understand very well and can see clearly the advantage an unmarried duenna has over a widowed one — and whoever sheared us was left with the scissors in his hand."

"For all that," replied Sancho, "there is so much to shear off duennas, according to my barber, that it will be better not to stir the rice even if it sticks."

"Squires are always our enemies," answered Doña Rodríguez; "for, since they are the goblins of the anterooms and see us at every turn, the times they are not praying — which are many — they spend in gossiping about us, digging up our bones and burying our good name. Well, I consign them to the walking logs; for whether they like it or not we shall go on living in the world, and in the great houses, even if we die of hunger and cover our delicate or not-so-delicate flesh with a black widow's gown, as a man covers or hides a dunghill with a tapestry on a procession day. Upon my word, if it were given to me and the occasion called for it, I would make it plain, not only to those present but to the whole world, that there is no virtue that is not shut up in a duenna."

"I believe," said the duchess, "that my good Doña Rodríguez is right, and very much so; but she had better wait for a proper time to stand up for herself and for the rest of the duennas, so as to confound the bad opinion of that bad apothecary and root out the one the great Sancho Panza has in his breast."

To which Sancho answered:

"Ever since I have had the fumes of a governor about me, the dizzy spells of a squire have left me, and I do not care a wild fig for all the duennas there are."

They would have gone further with their duenna-ish talk if they had not heard the fife and the drums beginning to sound again, from which they understood that the Distressed Duenna was coming in. The duchess asked the duke whether it would be right to go out and receive her, since she was a countess and a person of quality.

"For what she has of countess about her," answered Sancho, before the duke could answer, "I am quite content that your greatnesses should go out and receive her; but for the duenna part of her, my opinion is that you should not stir a step."

"Who brings you into this, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"Who, sir?" answered Sancho. "I bring myself in, and I may bring myself in, as a squire who has learnt the terms of courtesy in your worship's school — you being the most courteous and best brought-up knight there is in all courteousness. And in these things, as I have heard your worship say, a man loses as much by a card too many as by a card too few; and a word to the wise."

"It is as Sancho says," said the duke. "We shall see the cut of the countess, and by that we shall measure out the courtesy that is owing to her."

At this the drums and the fife came in, as they had the first time.

And here, with this short chapter, the author made an end, and began the next, carrying on the same adventure, which is one of the most notable in the history.

Chapter 38: Where the Distressed Duenna Gives an Account of Her Ill Fortune

Behind the mournful musicians there began to come into the garden as many as twelve duennas, divided into two files, all dressed in wide widow's gowns of what looked like fulled serge, with white headdresses of fine cotton so long that they showed nothing of the gown but its hem.

After them came the Countess Trifaldi, led by the hand by the squire Trifaldin of the White Beard, dressed in the finest black baize, unnapped — for had it been napped, every grain of it would have shown as big as one of the good chickpeas of Martos. The tail, or skirt, or whatever they may like to call it, ended in three points, which were held up in the hands of three pages, likewise dressed in mourning, making a showy and mathematical figure with the three acute angles that the three points formed. From which everybody who looked at the pointed skirt gathered that she must be called the Countess Trifaldi for that reason, as who should say the Countess of the Three Skirts.

And Benengeli says that it was true, and that by her own family name the countess was called Lobuna, on the grounds that a great many wolves were bred in her county; and that if they had been foxes instead of wolves she would have been called Zorruna, it being the custom in those parts for lords to take the style of their names from the thing or things their estates are richest in. But this countess, to favour the novelty of her skirt, dropped the Lobuna and took up the Trifaldi.

The twelve duennas and their lady came at a procession pace, their faces covered with black veils — not transparent like Trifaldin's, but so close-woven that nothing at all showed through.

As soon as the duennaish squadron had finished appearing, the duke, the duchess and Don Quixote got to their feet, and so did all those who were watching that deliberate procession. The twelve duennas halted and made an aisle, down the middle of which the Distressed Lady came forward, with Trifaldin still holding her by the hand. Seeing which, the duke, the duchess and Don Quixote came forward some twelve paces to receive her. She, going down on her knees on the ground, said in a voice coarse and hoarse rather than fine and delicate:

"Let your greatnesses be pleased not to pay so much courtesy to this servant of yours — I mean this servingwoman of yours; because, distressed as I am, I shall not manage to answer as I ought, on account of my strange and never-before-seen misfortune having carried off my understanding I do not know where, and it must be very far off, since the more I look for it the less I find it."

"He would be without his own, my lady countess," answered the duke, "who did not discover your worth from your person, which without anything more to see deserves all the cream of courtesy and all the flower of well-bred ceremony."

And, raising her by the hand, he led her to sit down in a chair next to the duchess, who received her likewise with a great deal of civility.

Don Quixote said nothing, and Sancho was dying to see the face of the Trifaldi and of some of her many duennas; but it was not possible until they uncovered themselves of their own free will and pleasure.

Everybody having settled down and fallen silent, they were waiting to see who would break the silence, and it was the Distressed Duenna, with these words:

"I am confident, most powerfullest lord, most beautifullest lady and most judiciousest bystanders, that my most afflictedest trouble will find in your most valorousest breasts a reception no less pleasant than it is generous and sorrowful; because it is such a trouble as is enough to move marble to tenderness, and to soften diamonds, and to make pliable the steel of the hardest hearts in the world. But before it comes out into the square of your hearings — not to say your ears — I should like to be made knowing whether there is in this gathering, ring and company the most refinedest knight Don Quixote of La Manchissima and his squirissimo Panza."

"The Panza," said Sancho, before anybody else could answer, "is here, and the Don Quixotissimo likewise; and so you may, most dolorousest duennissima, say whatever you likissimost, for we are all ready and most preparedest to be your most servantissimous."

At this Don Quixote got up, and, directing his words to the Distressed Duenna, said:

"If your troubles, afflicted lady, can promise themselves any hope of remedy from the valour or the strength of any knight errant, here are mine, which, weak and brief though they are, will all be employed in your service. I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose business it is to come to the help of all sorts of needy people; and, this being so, as it is, you have no need, my lady, to seek anybody's good will or to look for preambles, but plainly and without going round about to tell your ills — for there are ears listening to you that will know how to grieve over them, if not how to remedy them."

Hearing which, the Distressed Duenna made as if to throw herself at Don Quixote's feet, and indeed threw herself down; and, struggling to embrace them, she said:

"Before these feet and legs I throw myself, O unconquered knight, since they are the bases and pillars of knight-errantry. These feet I want to kiss, on whose steps hangs and depends the whole remedy of my misfortune, O valorous errant, whose true exploits leave behind and outshine the fabulous ones of the Amadíses, Esplandiáns and Belianíses!"

And, leaving Don Quixote, she turned to Sancho Panza, and, taking him by the hands, said to him:

"O you, the most loyal squire who ever served a knight errant in the present or in the past ages, longer in goodness than the beard of Trifaldin my attendant, who is here present! You may well pride yourself that in serving the great Don Quixote you serve in shorthand the whole herd of knights who have handled arms in the world. I conjure you, by what you owe to your most faithful goodness, to be a good intercessor for me with your master, so that he may at once favour this most humble and most unfortunate countess."

To which Sancho answered:

"That my goodness should be as long and as great as your squire's beard, my ladyship, matters very little to me. Let my soul have its beard and moustaches on it when I go out of this life, which is what matters; for about the beards down here I care little or nothing. But without all these wheedlings and entreaties I shall beg my master — who I know is fond of me, and the more so now that he needs me for a certain piece of business — to favour and help your worship in everything he can. Let your worship unpack your trouble and tell it to us, and leave it to us, for we shall all understand one another."

The duke and duchess were bursting with laughter at all this, as the people who had felt the pulse of that adventure, and they praised between themselves the sharpness and the play-acting of the Trifaldi, who, sitting down again, said:

"Of the famous kingdom of Candaya, which lies between the great Taprobana and the South Sea, two leagues beyond Cape Comorin, the lady was Queen Doña Maguncia, widow of King Archipiela her lord and husband, of which marriage they had and procreated the Infanta Antonomasia, heiress of the kingdom; which said Infanta Antonomasia was brought up and grew up under my tutelage and teaching, since I was the most senior and the chief duenna of her mother.

"It happened, then, that with days going and days coming, the child Antonomasia reached the age of fourteen with such great perfection of beauty that nature could not have raised her a point higher. And are we to say that her good sense was a snivelling little thing? She was as judicious as she was beautiful, and she was the most beautiful in the world — and is so still, unless by now the envious fates and the hardened Parcae have cut the thread of her life. But they will not have, for the heavens will not permit so great a harm to be done to the earth as it would be to carry off unripe the cluster of the loveliest vine in the world.

"With this beauty — and not praised as it deserves by my clumsy tongue — an infinite number of princes fell in love, both native and foreign; among whom a private gentleman who was at court dared to raise his thoughts to the heaven of so much beauty, trusting in his youth and his gallantry and in his many abilities and graces and in the ease and happiness of his wit. Because I would have your greatnesses know, if you do not take it amiss, that he played a guitar until he made it talk; and, what is more, he was a poet and a great dancer, and he knew how to make a birdcage, so that merely by making them he could have earned his living if he had found himself in extreme need — and all these parts and graces are enough to bring down a mountain, let alone a delicate maiden.

"But all his gentility and his fine grace and all his graces and abilities would have counted for little or nothing in reducing the fortress of my girl, if the thieving face-flayer had not used the remedy of reducing me first. First the villain and soulless vagabond wanted to get my good will and bribe my liking, so that I, a bad governor, should hand him the keys of the fortress I was guarding. In short: he flattered my understanding and reduced my will with I do not know what trinkets and toys he gave me; but what most laid me low and brought me down on the ground were some verses I heard him sing one night from a grating that looked out on a little alley where he was standing — which, if I remember rightly, went:

	From my sweet enemy there comes
	a hurt that wounds the soul,
	and, for greater torment still, it wills
	that it be felt and not be told.

"The verses seemed to me of pearl, and his voice of syrup; and ever since — I mean from that time on, seeing the ill I fell into through these and other such verses — I have thought that from good and well-ordered commonwealths the poets ought to be banished, as Plato advised; at least the lascivious ones, because they write verses that are not like those of the Marquis of Mantua, which entertain and make children and women weep, but sharp things that, like soft thorns, run through your soul and, like lightning, wound you inside it, leaving your clothes untouched. And another time he sang:

	Come, death, so hidden away
	that I may not feel you coming,
	so that the pleasure of dying
	may not give me back my life.

"And other little verses and tail-pieces of the same stamp, which sung enchant and written hold you spellbound. And then, what about when they stoop to composing a kind of verse that was in use in Candaya at that time, which they called seguidillas? Then there was the leaping of souls, the frisking of laughter, the restlessness of bodies and, in short, the quicksilver of all the senses. And so I say, my dear sirs, that such versifiers ought by a just title to be banished to the Isles of the Lizards.

"But it is not their fault, but the fault of the simpletons who praise them and the fools who believe them; and if I had been the good duenna I ought to have been, their stale-brewed conceits would not have moved me, and I should not have believed it true when they say: 'I live dying, I burn in the ice, I shiver in the fire, I hope without hope, I go away and I stay,' along with other impossibilities of that breed that their writings are full of. And then what about when they promise the phoenix of Arabia, the crown of Ariadne, the horses of the Sun, the pearls of the South, the gold of Tibar and the balsam of Panchaia? Here is where they stretch out their pens furthest, since it costs them little to promise what they never intend and are not able to fulfil.

"But where am I straying to? Ah, wretched me! What madness or what folly carries me off to tell other people's faults when I have so much to say about my own? Ah, luckless me again! It was not the verses that reduced me but my own simplicity; it was not the music that softened me but my own frivolity. My great ignorance and my small caution opened the road and cleared the path for the steps of Don Clavijo — that being the name of the said gentleman.

"And so, with me as the go-between, he found himself once and a great many times in the chamber of Antonomasia, who was deceived by me and not by him, under the title of her true husband; for, sinner though I am, I would never have consented to his coming, without being her husband, as near as the welt of the sole of her slippers. No, no, not that: matrimony must come first in any business of this kind that is handled by me!

"There was only one harm in this business, which was the inequality of it, Don Clavijo being a private gentleman and the Infanta Antonomasia the heiress, as I have said, of the kingdom. For some days this tangle stayed hidden and covered up by the shrewdness of my caution, until it seemed to me that a certain swelling of Antonomasia's belly was uncovering it at a great rate; the fear of which made the three of us go into council, out of which it came that, before the bad business came out into the light, Don Clavijo should apply to the vicar for Antonomasia as his wife, on the strength of a written promise the infanta had made him of being his wife, drawn up by my wits with such force that not even Samson's strength could have broken it.

"The steps were taken, the vicar saw the promise, this same vicar took the lady's confession, she confessed straight out, and he ordered her to be lodged in the house of a very honourable officer of the court..."

At this point Sancho said:

"So there are officers of the court in Candaya too, and poets and seguidillas — from which I can swear that I imagine all the world is one and the same. But let your worship hurry up, Señora Trifaldi, for it is late and I am already dying to know the end of this very long story."

"I shall," answered the countess.

Chapter 39: Where the Trifaldi Carries On Her Stupendous and Memorable History

Every word Sancho said gave the duchess as much pleasure as it drove Don Quixote to despair; and, ordering him to be quiet, the Distressed Lady went on, saying:

"In short, after a great many questions and answers, the infanta staying always at her thirteen, without going back on or varying from her first declaration, the vicar gave sentence in favour of Don Clavijo and handed her over to him as his lawful wife — at which Queen Doña Maguncia, the mother of the Infanta Antonomasia, took such offence that within three days we buried her."

"She must have died, no doubt about it," said Sancho.

"Obviously!" answered Trifaldin. "In Candaya they do not bury living people, but dead ones."

"It has been known, sir squire," replied Sancho, "for a person in a faint to be buried in the belief that they were dead; and it seemed to me that Queen Maguncia was more obliged to faint than to die. With life a great many things are put right, and the infanta's folly was not so great as to deserve being felt so much. If that lady had married some page of hers, or some other servant of her household, as a great many others have done, from what I have heard, the harm would have been past remedy; but her having married a gentleman as much of a gentleman and as well-informed as they have painted him here for us — truly and truly, though it was a piece of foolishness, it was not so great a one as people think. Because, according to my master's rules — and he is here present and will not let me lie — just as bishops are made out of learned men, so out of knights, and especially errant ones, can be made kings and emperors."

"You are right, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "because a knight errant, so long as he has a couple of fingers of good luck, is in the immediate potentiality of being the greatest lord in the world. But let the Distressed Lady go on, for I can see through it that she still has the bitter part to tell of this history that has been sweet so far."

"And how bitter the bitter part is!" answered the countess. "So bitter that beside it colocynth is sweet and oleander tasty.

"The queen being dead, then — and not in a faint — we buried her; and hardly had we covered her with the earth and hardly had we said her the last farewell, when —

	quis talia fando temperet a lachrymis? —

"mounted on a wooden horse, there appeared above the queen's grave the giant Malambruno, first cousin to Maguncia, who along with being cruel was an enchanter. And he, by his arts, in revenge for his cousin's death, and as a punishment for Don Clavijo's boldness, and out of spite at Antonomasia's excess, left the two of them enchanted on the grave itself: her turned into a bronze she-ape, and him into a terrifying crocodile of some unknown metal; and between the two of them stands a pillar, likewise of metal, and on it, written in the Syriac tongue, some letters which, having been set out in the Candayan and now in the Castilian, hold this sentence: 'These two bold lovers shall not recover their first shape until the valorous Manchegan comes to grips with me in single battle; for the fates keep this never-before-seen adventure for his great valour alone.'

"This done, he drew from its scabbard a broad and enormous scimitar and, seizing me by the hair, made a feint of wanting to cut my throat and slice my head clean off. I was thrown into confusion, my voice stuck in my throat, I was cast down in the last degree; but for all that I made the greatest effort I could, and in a trembling, pained voice I said him so many things and such things that they made him suspend the carrying out of so severe a punishment.

"Finally he had all the palace duennas brought before him, who were these here present; and, after having enlarged on our guilt and abused the nature of duennas, their bad habits and worse contrivances, and loading them all with the guilt that was mine alone, he said he did not want to punish us with capital punishment but with other, drawn-out punishments that would give us a civil and continuous death. And in that very moment and instant when he finished saying this, we all felt the pores of our faces opening, and pricking all over them as if with the points of needles. We put our hands at once to our faces and found ourselves in the state you shall now see."

And then the Distressed Lady and the other duennas lifted the masks they had come covered with, and uncovered their faces, all thickly grown with beards — some fair, some black, some white and some grizzled. At the sight of which the duke and duchess showed themselves astonished, Don Quixote and Sancho thunderstruck, and all those present dumbfounded.

And the Trifaldi went on:

"In this way that poltroon and evil-minded Malambruno punished us, covering the softness and smoothness of our faces with the roughness of these bristles. Would to heaven he had rather struck our heads off with his enormous scimitar than shadowed the light of our faces with this fleece that covers us! Because if we go into the reckoning, my dear sirs — and what I am going to say now I should have liked to say with my eyes turned to fountains; but the thought of our misfortune, and the seas they have rained until now, have left them without moisture and dry as beards of corn, and so I shall say it without tears — I say, then: where can a duenna with a beard go? What father or what mother will grieve for her? Who will give her any help? For even when she has a smooth skin and a face martyred with a thousand kinds of paints and washes, she can hardly find anybody to love her; what will she do when she uncovers a face turned into a forest? O duennas and companions of mine, we were born at an unlucky moment, in an ill-starred hour our parents engendered us!"

And, saying this, she gave signs of fainting away.

Chapter 40: Of Things That Belong and Pertain to This Adventure and to This Memorable History

Really and truly, everybody who enjoys histories like this one ought to show themselves grateful to Cide Hamete, its first author, for the care he took in telling us the smallest quavers of it, without leaving anything, however minute, that he did not bring distinctly into the light: he paints the thoughts, uncovers the imaginings, answers the unspoken questions, clears up the doubts, resolves the arguments; in short, he makes plain the very atoms of the most inquisitive desire. O most celebrated author! O fortunate Don Quixote! O famous Dulcinea! O amusing Sancho Panza! All together and each one of you singly, may you live infinite ages, for the pleasure and the general entertainment of the living.

The history says, then, that as soon as Sancho saw the Distressed Lady in a faint, he said:

"By the faith of an honest man, I swear, and by the memory of all my ancestors the Panzas, that I have never heard or seen such an adventure as this, nor has my master ever told me of one, nor has it ever fitted into his imagination. May a thousand Satans take you — not to curse you as an enchanter and a giant, Malambruno — and could you find no other kind of punishment to give these poor sinners but bearding them? How much better would it not have been, and how much more to their purpose, to take away the upper halves of their noses, even if they talked through them, than to put beards on them? I would wager they have not the means to pay anybody to shave them."

"That is the truth, sir," answered one of the twelve; "we have not the means to trim ourselves. And so some of us have taken as a thrifty remedy the use of certain plasters or sticking patches, and, applying them to our faces and pulling them off all at once, we are left as bare and smooth as the bottom of a stone mortar. Because although there are women in Candaya who go from house to house to take off the down and shape the eyebrows and do other cosmetic offices belonging to women, we duennas of my lady's household would never let them in — because most of them smell of being third parties, having left off being first ones. And if we are not relieved by Señor Don Quixote, they will carry us to the grave with beards."

"I would have my own plucked out in the land of the Moors," said Don Quixote, "if I did not put an end to yours."

At this point the Trifaldi came out of her faint and said:

"The ring of that promise, valorous knight, reached my ears in the middle of my faint, and has been the means of my coming out of it and recovering all my senses. And so I beg you again, illustrious errant and indomitable lord, that your gracious promise may turn into a deed."

"It shall not be held up by me," answered Don Quixote. "See, my lady, what it is I have to do, for my spirit is very ready to serve you."

"The case is," answered the Distressed Lady, "that from here to the kingdom of Candaya, if you go by land, is five thousand leagues, two more or less; but if you go by air and in a straight line, it is three thousand two hundred and twenty-seven. It is also to be known that Malambruno told me that when fortune furnished me with the knight who was to set us free, he would send him a mount a great deal better and with fewer vices than the ones you hire; because it is to be that same wooden horse on which the valorous Pierres carried off the fair Magalona.

"This horse is steered by a peg he has in his forehead, which serves him for a bridle, and he flies through the air with such lightness that it looks as if the devils themselves were carrying him. This horse, according to ancient tradition, was made by that wise Merlin; he lent him to Pierres, who was his friend, and with him Pierres made great journeys and carried off, as has been said, the fair Magalona, taking her on the crupper through the air and leaving everybody who looked at them from the ground gaping. And he lent him to nobody but the man he chose, or the man who paid best for him; and from the great Pierres until now we know of nobody who has got up on him.

"Malambruno has taken him from there by his arts and has him in his power, and makes use of him in his journeys, which he makes at every moment to various parts of the world; and today he is here and tomorrow in France and the next day in Potosí. And the good of it is that this horse neither eats nor sleeps nor wears out horseshoes, and goes at an amble through the air without having wings, so that the man on his back can carry a cup full of water in his hand without spilling a drop of it, so smoothly and quietly does he travel — for which reason the fair Magalona was very glad to ride on him."

To this Sancho said:

"For travelling quietly and smoothly, my grey — even though he does not travel through the air; but on the ground I would match him against all the ambling horses in the world."

They all laughed, and the Distressed Lady went on:

"And this horse, if Malambruno means to put an end to our misfortune, will be in our presence before half an hour of the night has gone; because he gave me to understand that the sign he would give me by which I should know that he had found the knight I was looking for would be to send me the horse, wherever I was, conveniently and quickly."

"And how many will that horse hold?" asked Sancho.

The Distressed Lady answered:

"Two people: one in the saddle and the other on the crupper; and for the most part these two people are a knight and a squire, when there is no stolen maiden."

"I should like to know, Señora Distressed Lady," said Sancho, "what name that horse has."

"His name," answered the Distressed Lady, "is not like Bellerophon's horse, which was called Pegasus, or like Alexander the Great's, called Bucephalus, or like the furious Orlando's, whose name was Brigliadoro, still less Bayard, which was Reinaldos de Montalbán's, or Frontino, like Ruggiero's, or Boötes or Pyrois, as they say the horses of the Sun are called; nor is he called Orelia either, like the horse on which the unfortunate Rodrigo, the last king of the Goths, went into the battle where he lost his life and his kingdom."

"I would wager," said Sancho, "that since they have not given him any of those famous names of such well-known horses, they will not have given him my master's either — Rocinante, which for fitness beats all the ones that have been named."

"That is so," answered the bearded countess, "but still his name suits him very well, because he is called Clavileño the Swift — a name that agrees with his being made of wood, and with the peg he carries in his forehead, and with the lightness with which he travels; for in our tongue the peg is the clavija and the wood the leño. And so, as far as the name goes, he may well compete with the famous Rocinante."

"The name does not displease me," replied Sancho, "but with what bridle or with what halter is he steered?"

"I have already said," answered the Trifaldi, "that it is with the peg; for by turning it one way or the other the knight on his back makes him travel as he likes, whether through the air, or skimming and almost sweeping the ground, or by the middle way, which is the one to be looked for and to be kept to in all well-ordered actions."

"I should like to see it," answered Sancho; "but to think that I have to get up on him, either in the saddle or on the crupper, is asking pears of an elm tree. It is a fine thing that I can hardly keep my seat on my grey, and on a pack-saddle softer than silk itself, and now they want me to keep my seat on a wooden crupper without any cushion or padding at all! By God, I do not intend to pound myself to bits to take the beards off anybody. Let everybody shave as best suits him, for I do not intend to keep my master company on such a long journey. What is more, I cannot be as much to the point for the shaving of these beards as I am for the disenchantment of my lady Dulcinea."

"Yes you are, my friend," answered the Trifaldi, "and so much so that without your presence I understand we shall do nothing."

"Help, in the king's name!" said Sancho. "What have squires got to do with their masters' adventures? Are they to carry off the fame of the ones they finish, and are we to carry the labour? Body of me! If only the historians would say: 'Such and such a knight finished such and such an adventure, but with the help of so-and-so his squire, without whom it would have been impossible to finish it.' But they write bare and dry, 'Don Paralipomenon of the Three Stars finished the adventure of the six monsters,' without naming the person of his squire, who was present at the whole of it, as though he had never been in the world!

"Now, gentlemen, I say again that my master may go alone, and much good may it do him; and I shall stay here in the company of the duchess my lady, and it might be that when he came back he would find my lady Dulcinea's cause improved by a third and a fifth — because in my idle and unoccupied moments I mean to give myself a round of lashes that no hair shall cover."

"For all that, you must go with him if it is necessary, good Sancho, because good people will beg you to; and the faces of these ladies must not be left so thickly grown for your useless fear. That would certainly be a bad business."

"Help, in the king's name, again!" replied Sancho. "If this charity were being done for some sheltered maidens or for some charity-school girls, a man might venture on any labour; but to bear it for taking the beards off duennas — bad luck to it! I would sooner see them all bearded, from the greatest to the least, and from the most affected to the primmest."

"You get on badly with duennas, Sancho my friend," said the duchess. "You are following the Toledo apothecary's opinion very closely. But upon my word you are wrong; for there are duennas in my house who could be a model for duennas, and here is my Doña Rodríguez, who will not let me say otherwise."

"Let your excellency say it if you like," said Rodríguez; "for God knows the truth of everything, and good or bad, bearded or smooth as we duennas may be, our mother bore us like the other women; and since God threw us into the world, He knows why, and I hold by His mercy and not by anybody's beard."

"Well now, Señora Rodríguez," said Don Quixote, "and Señora Trifaldi and company: I trust in heaven that it will look with kind eyes on your troubles, and that Sancho will do what I order him — let Clavileño only come and let me only find myself face to face with Malambruno. For I know there would be no razor that could shave your worships as easily as my sword would shave Malambruno's head off his shoulders; for God suffers the wicked, but not for ever."

"Ah!" said the Distressed Lady at this. "May all the stars of the celestial regions look with kindly eyes on your greatness, valorous knight, and pour into your spirit all prosperity and valour, so that you may be the shield and protection of the abused and downtrodden duennaish race, abominated by apothecaries, gossiped about by squires and wheedled at by pages. Cursed be the wretched girl who in the flower of her years did not go and be a nun sooner than a duenna! Unfortunate creatures that we duennas are — for even if we came down in a straight line, man from man, from Hector the Trojan himself, our ladies would still not leave off throwing a 'you there' at us, if they thought it would make them queens by it. O giant Malambruno, who, enchanter though you are, are most certain in your promises! Send us the peerless Clavileño now, so that our misfortune may come to an end; for if the hot weather sets in and these beards of ours last, woe to our luck!"

The Trifaldi said this with so much feeling that she drew the tears out of the eyes of all the bystanders, and even flooded Sancho's; and he resolved in his heart to go with his master to the furthest parts of the world, if the taking of the wool off those venerable faces depended on it.

Chapter 41: Of the Coming of Clavileño, with the End of This Long-Drawn-Out Adventure

Night came on at this, and with it the appointed moment when the famous horse Clavileño should arrive; whose lateness was already wearing at Don Quixote, since it seemed to him that, Malambruno being slow in sending him, either he was not the knight for whom that adventure was reserved or Malambruno did not dare to come to single battle with him.

But see here: all at once there came into the garden four wild men dressed all in green ivy, carrying a great wooden horse on their shoulders. They set him with his feet on the ground, and one of the wild men said:

"Let the man who has the spirit for it get up on this machine."

"I do not get up here," said Sancho, "because I have neither the spirit nor the knighthood."

And the wild man went on, saying:

"And let the squire take the crupper, if there is one; and let him trust the valorous Malambruno, for he shall be harmed by no sword but Malambruno's own and by no other malice. And there is nothing to do but turn this peg he has set on his neck, and he will carry them through the air to where Malambruno is waiting for them. But so that the height and loftiness of the road may not give them vertigo, they must have their eyes covered until the horse neighs, which will be the sign that their journey is over."

This said, leaving Clavileño, with a graceful bearing they went back the way they had come. The Distressed Lady, as soon as she saw the horse, said to Don Quixote almost in tears:

"Valorous knight, Malambruno's promises have proved certain. The horse is in the house, our beards are growing, and every one of us and with every hair of them begs you to shave us and shear us; since there is nothing more to it but for you to get up on him with your squire and give a happy beginning to your new journey."

"That I shall do, Señora Countess Trifaldi, most willingly and with the best will in the world, without stopping to take a cushion or put on my spurs, so as not to lose time: so great is my desire to see you, my lady, and all these duennas smooth and bare."

"That I shall not do," said Sancho, "either with a bad will or with a good one, on any account. And if this shaving cannot be done without my getting up on the crupper, my master may well look for another squire to go with him, and these ladies for another way of smoothing their faces; for I am no witch, to take pleasure in going about through the air. And what will my islanders say when they learn that their governor goes about taking walks on the winds?

"And another thing: there being three thousand and so many leagues from here to Candaya, if the horse gets tired or the giant gets annoyed we shall take half a dozen years to get back, and by then there will be neither isle nor isler in the world that knows me. And since it is commonly said that in delay lies danger, and that when they give you the heifer you should run with the halter, let these ladies' beards forgive me, but Saint Peter is well enough off in Rome — I mean I am well enough off in this house, where so much kindness is done me and from whose master I look for so great a benefit as seeing myself a governor."

To which the duke said:

"Sancho my friend, the isle I have promised you is not movable or fugitive: it has roots so deep, thrown down into the depths of the earth, that they will not pull it up or shift it from where it is at three tugs. And since you know that I know that there is no kind of office of any great value that is not got by some sort of bribe, one more and another less, the bribe I mean to take for this government is that you should go with your master Don Quixote to bring this memorable adventure to its top and its end. And whether you come back on Clavileño with the speed his lightness promises, or whether contrary fortune brings you back on foot, turned pilgrim from inn to inn and from tavern to tavern, whenever you come back you will find your isle where you left it, and your islanders with the same desire to receive you as their governor that they have always had, and my will shall be the same. And do not put this truth in doubt, Señor Sancho, for it would be doing a plain wrong to the desire I have to serve you."

"No more, sir," said Sancho. "I am a poor squire and I cannot carry so many courtesies on my back. Let my master mount, let them cover these eyes of mine and commend me to God; and let them tell me whether, when we are going through those high places, I may commend myself to Our Lord or call on the angels to favour me."

To which the Trifaldi answered:

"Sancho, you may very well commend yourself to God or to whomever you like; for Malambruno, though he is an enchanter, is a Christian, and works his enchantments with a great deal of shrewdness and a great deal of care, without meddling with anybody."

"Well then," said Sancho, "God help me, and the Most Holy Trinity of Gaeta!"

"Since the memorable adventure of the fulling mills," said Don Quixote, "I have never seen Sancho in such terror as now; and if I were as much of a believer in omens as some, his faint-heartedness would tickle my spirit a little. But come here, Sancho, for with these ladies' and gentlemen's leave I want to have two words with you apart."

And, drawing Sancho aside among some trees in the garden and taking both his hands, he said to him:

"You see now, brother Sancho, the long journey that is waiting for us, and that God knows when we shall come back from it, or what convenience and leisure our business will give us. And so I should like you to withdraw now to your room, as though you were going to look for something necessary for the road, and in the twinkling of an eye give yourself, on account of the three thousand three hundred lashes you are bound to, five hundred at least — which will be so many given; and to begin things is to have them half finished."

"By God," said Sancho, "your worship must be out of your mind! This is like what they say: 'You see me in a hurry and you ask me for my maidenhead!' Now, when I have to go and sit on a bare board, does your worship want me to hurt my backside? Truly and truly, your worship is not being reasonable. Let us go now and shave these duennas, and on the way back I promise your worship, as sure as I am who I am, to make such haste to get out of my obligation that your worship will be content; and I say no more."

And Don Quixote answered:

"Well, with that promise, good Sancho, I go consoled; and I believe you will keep it, because in fact, though a fool, you are a man of true colours."

"I am not of any colour, I am brown," said Sancho; "but even if I were of mixed cloth, I would keep my word."

And with this they went back to mount Clavileño, and as he mounted Don Quixote said:

"Cover yourself, Sancho, and mount, Sancho; for a man who sends for us from such far-off lands will not be one to deceive us, for the little glory that can come to him from deceiving somebody who trusts him. And, granting that everything turned out backwards from what I imagine, no malice can dim the glory of having undertaken this exploit."

"Let us go, sir," said Sancho, "for these ladies' beards and tears I have nailed into my heart, and I shall not eat a mouthful that tastes good to me until I see them in their first smoothness. Let your worship mount and cover yourself first; for if I am to go on the crupper, it is plain that the man in the saddle mounts first."

"That is the truth," replied Don Quixote.

And, taking a handkerchief out of his pocket, he asked the Distressed Lady to cover his eyes very well; and, having had them covered, he uncovered them again and said:

"If I remember rightly, I have read in Virgil that business of the Palladium of Troy, which was a wooden horse the Greeks presented to the goddess Pallas, and which went pregnant with armed knights who were afterwards the total ruin of Troy. And so it will be as well to see first what Clavileño has in his stomach."

"There is no call for it," said the Distressed Lady, "for I answer for him and know that Malambruno has nothing malicious or treacherous about him. Let your worship, Señor Don Quixote, mount without any dread, and on my head be it if any harm comes to you."

It seemed to Don Quixote that anything he might say about his own safety would be to the detriment of his valour; and so, without arguing any more, he got up on Clavileño and tried the peg, which turned easily. And, as he had no stirrups and his legs hung down, he looked like nothing so much as a figure in a Flemish tapestry, painted or woven into some Roman triumph.

Unwillingly and little by little Sancho got himself up; and, settling as best he could on the crupper, he found it rather hard and not at all soft, and asked the duke whether, if it were possible, they could let him have some cushion or some pillow, even if it were from my lady the duchess's drawing room or from some page's bed, because that horse's crupper seemed more of marble than of wood.

To this the Trifaldi said that Clavileño would suffer no harness or any kind of adornment on him; that what he could do was to sit sidesaddle, and then he would not feel the hardness so much. Sancho did so, and, saying goodbye, let himself be blindfolded; and then, after being blindfolded, he uncovered himself again, and, looking tenderly and with tears at everybody in the garden, asked them to help him in this pass with a paternoster and an ave apiece, so that God might furnish somebody to say them for them when they found themselves in the same pass. To which Don Quixote said:

"You thief, are you on the gallows by any chance, or at the last term of your life, to use prayers of that kind? Are you not, you soulless and cowardly creature, in the very place the fair Magalona occupied, from which she came down not to the grave but to be queen of France, if the histories are not lying? And I, who am at your side, may I not set myself beside the valorous Pierres, who pressed this very place I am pressing now? Cover yourself, cover yourself, you disheartened animal, and do not let the fear you feel come out at your mouth, at least in my presence."

"Cover me up," answered Sancho; "and since they will not have me commend myself to God or be commended, what wonder is it if I am afraid there may be some region of devils about here who will land us in the criminals' field?"

They covered themselves; and Don Quixote, feeling that he was as he ought to be, tried the peg. And he had hardly put his fingers on it when all the duennas and everybody present raised their voices, saying:

"God guide you, valorous knight!"

"God be with you, fearless squire!"

"Now, now you are going through the air, cutting through it faster than an arrow!"

"Now you are beginning to astonish and amaze everybody watching you from the ground!"

"Hold on, valorous Sancho, you are swaying! Mind you do not fall, for your fall will be worse than that of the bold young man who wanted to drive the chariot of the Sun, his father!"

Sancho heard the voices, and, squeezing up against his master and gripping him with his arms, said to him:

"Sir, how can these people say we are going so high, if their voices reach us here, and it sounds for all the world as if they were talking right next to us?"

"Do not stick at that, Sancho; for since these things and these flights go outside the ordinary courses, from a thousand leagues off you will see and hear whatever you like. And do not squeeze me so tight, for you are pulling me over. And truly I do not know what you are troubled or frightened about, for I would dare to swear that in all the days of my life I have never got up on a mount with a smoother pace: it seems for all the world as though we were not moving from one place. Banish fear, my friend, for in fact the thing is going as it ought and we have the wind behind us."

"That is the truth," answered Sancho, "for on this side there comes such a strong wind at me that it seems as if they were blowing on me with a thousand bellows."

And so it was, for some great bellows were making the air on him: so well was that adventure laid out by the duke and the duchess and their steward that it lacked nothing that could make it perfect.

Feeling himself blown on, then, Don Quixote said:

"Without any doubt, Sancho, we must be arriving now at the second region of the air, where the hail and the snows are engendered; the thunder, the lightning and the thunderbolts are engendered in the third region; and if we go on climbing in this way, we shall soon strike the region of fire, and I do not know how to temper this peg so that we do not climb to where we shall be burnt up."

At this, with some tow that lit and went out easily, hanging from a cane, they were warming their faces from a distance. Sancho, feeling the heat, said:

"May they kill me if we are not in the place of fire already, or very near it; because a good part of my beard has been singed, and I am half inclined, sir, to uncover myself and see what part of the world we are in."

"Do no such thing," answered Don Quixote, "and remember the true story of the licentiate Torralba, whom the devils carried off through the air, riding on a cane with his eyes shut, and in twelve hours he arrived in Rome and got down at the Torre di Nona, which is a street of the city, and saw the whole disaster and assault and the death of Bourbon; and by morning he was back in Madrid, where he gave an account of everything he had seen. He said too that when he was going through the air the devil ordered him to open his eyes, and he opened them and saw himself so close, as it seemed to him, to the body of the moon that he could have grasped it with his hand; and that he did not dare to look at the earth for fear of growing dizzy.

"So, Sancho, there is no call for us to uncover ourselves; for the man who has charge of us will answer for us, and perhaps we are circling up and climbing high so as to drop at one swoop on the kingdom of Candaya, as the saker or the peregrine does on the heron to catch her, however high she soars. And, although it seems to us that it is not half an hour since we set off from the garden, believe me, we must have come a long way."

"I do not know how it is," answered Sancho Panza. "I can only say that if the lady Magellan, or Magalona, was satisfied with this crupper, she cannot have been very tender of flesh."

All this talk of the two brave men was heard by the duke and the duchess and the people in the garden, from which they took extraordinary pleasure; and, wanting to bring the strange and well-made adventure to a close, they set fire to Clavileño's tail with some tow. And at once, the horse being full of thundering rockets, he flew through the air with a strange noise and pitched Don Quixote and Sancho Panza to the ground, half singed.

By this time the whole bearded squadron of duennas and the Trifaldi and all had disappeared out of the garden, and the people in the garden were left stretched out on the ground as if in a faint. Don Quixote and Sancho got up in a bad way, and, looking in every direction, were astounded to find themselves in the very garden they had set out from, and to see so many people stretched out on the ground.

And their astonishment grew still greater when at one side of the garden they saw a great lance driven into the ground, and hanging from it by two green silk cords a smooth white parchment, on which, in great gold letters, was written the following:

The illustrious knight Don Quixote of La Mancha has finished and completed the adventure of the Countess Trifaldi, otherwise called the Distressed Duenna, and company, merely by attempting it.

Malambruno declares himself content and satisfied to the full of his desire; the duennas' beards are now smooth and bare, and King Don Clavijo and Antonomasia are restored to their first estate. And when the squirely whipping has been completed, the white dove shall find herself free of the pestilent gerfalcons who persecute her and in the arms of her beloved and cooing mate; for so it is ordained by the wise Merlin, arch-enchanter of enchanters.

Don Quixote, then, having read the letters on the parchment, clearly understood that they were speaking of Dulcinea's disenchantment; and, giving many thanks to heaven that with so little danger he had finished so great a feat, restoring to their former complexion the faces of the venerable duennas, who were no longer to be seen, he went to where the duke and duchess had still not come round, and, taking the duke by the hand, said to him:

"Come, good sir, good courage; good courage, for it is all nothing! The adventure is over now, and without harm to anybody, as the writing set up on that pillar plainly shows."

The duke, little by little, and like a man waking from a heavy sleep, came round to himself; and in the same manner the duchess and everybody else who had fallen down about the garden, with such signs of wonder and terror that they could almost have given it to be understood that what they knew so well how to feign in play had really happened to them. The duke read the notice with his eyes half shut, and then with open arms went to embrace Don Quixote, telling him that he was the best knight who had ever been seen in any age.

Sancho was looking about for the Distressed Lady, to see what face she had without the beard, and whether she was as beautiful without it as her splendid figure promised; but they told him that as soon as Clavileño came down burning through the air and struck the ground, the whole squadron of duennas with the Trifaldi had disappeared, and that they were already shaved and without a stubble. The duchess asked Sancho how he had got on during that long journey. To which Sancho answered:

"I, my lady, felt that we were flying, as my master told me, through the region of fire, and I wanted to uncover my eyes a little; but my master, of whom I asked leave to uncover them, would not allow it. But I, having I do not know what shreds of curiosity in me and of wanting to know what is kept from me and blocked off, quietly and without anybody seeing, right beside my nose, moved aside just so much of the handkerchief that was covering my eyes, and looked out that way towards the earth; and it seemed to me that the whole of it was no bigger than a grain of mustard seed, and the men walking about on it a little bigger than hazelnuts — so you may see how high we must have been going then."

To this the duchess said:

"Sancho my friend, look at what you are saying; for by the sound of it you did not see the earth but the men walking about on it. And it is plain that if the earth looked to you like a grain of mustard seed and every man like a hazelnut, one man alone would have covered the whole earth."

"That is true," answered Sancho, "but for all that I uncovered it from one little side and saw the whole of it."

"Look, Sancho," said the duchess, "for from one little side you cannot see the whole of what you are looking at."

"I do not know about those ways of looking," replied Sancho. "I only know that your ladyship had better understand that, since we were flying by enchantment, by enchantment I could see the whole earth and all the men wherever I looked at them. And if this is not believed of me, neither will your worship believe how, uncovering myself right by my eyebrows, I saw myself so close to heaven that there was not a hand and a half between me and it; and by what I can swear, my lady, it is very big indeed.

"And it happened that we were going through the part where the seven little goats are — the Pleiades, that is. And in God and in my soul, since in my childhood I was a goatherd in my own country, as soon as I saw them such a longing came over me to amuse myself with them for a while! And if I had not satisfied it, I think I should have burst. So I come along and I take and — what do I do? Without saying anything to anybody, or to my master either, quietly and gently I got down off Clavileño and amused myself with the little goats, which are like gillyflowers and like flowers, for nearly three quarters of an hour; and Clavileño never stirred from his place or went on."

"And while good Sancho was amusing himself with the goats," asked the duke, "what was Señor Don Quixote amusing himself with?"

To which Don Quixote answered:

"Since all these things and these events go outside the natural order, it is no great matter that Sancho says what he says. For myself I can say that I neither uncovered myself above nor below, and I saw neither the sky nor the earth, nor the sea nor the sands. It is quite true that I felt I was passing through the region of the air, and even that I was touching that of fire; but that we passed beyond that I cannot believe, since, the region of fire being between the heaven of the moon and the last region of the air, we could not have reached the heaven where the seven little goats Sancho speaks of are without being burnt up. And, since we were not scorched, either Sancho is lying or Sancho is dreaming."

"I am neither lying nor dreaming," answered Sancho. "If you doubt it, ask me for the marks of those goats, and by them you will see whether I am telling the truth or not."

"Say them, then, Sancho," said the duchess.

"They are," answered Sancho, "two green, two red, two blue, and one mottled."

"That is a new kind of goat," said the duke, "and in this region of ours on the ground such colours are not in use — I mean goats of such colours."

"That is plain enough," said Sancho. "Why, there has to be some difference between the goats of the sky and the goats of the ground."

"Tell me, Sancho," asked the duke: "did you see any he-goat up there among those goats?"

"No, sir," answered Sancho, "but I have heard it said that none of them ever goes past the horns of the moon."

They would not ask him anything more about his journey, because it seemed to them that Sancho had the thread in hand for strolling through all the heavens and bringing news of everything that went on up there, without having stirred from the garden.

In short, this was the end of the adventure of the Distressed Duenna, which gave the duke and duchess something to laugh about, not only at that time but for the whole of their lives, and gave Sancho something to tell for centuries, if he had lived them. And Don Quixote, going up to Sancho, said in his ear:

"Sancho, since you want people to believe you about what you saw in the sky, I want you to believe me about what I saw in the cave of Montesinos; and I say no more to you."

Chapter 42: Of the Advice Don Quixote Gave Sancho Panza Before He Went to Govern the Isle, with Other Well-Considered Matters

With the happy and amusing outcome of the adventure of the Distressed Lady, the duke and duchess were left so pleased that they decided to go further with their tricks, seeing what a convenient subject they had for having them taken for earnest. And so, having laid out the plan and the orders their servants and their vassals were to keep with Sancho in the government of the promised isle, the next day — which was the one after Clavileño's flight — the duke told Sancho to smarten himself up and get ready to go and be governor, for his islanders were already waiting for him like the rain in May. Sancho bowed to him and said:

"Ever since I came down from the sky, and ever since from its high summit I looked at the earth and saw it so small, the great longing I had to be a governor has cooled in me somewhat; because what greatness is there in ruling over a grain of mustard seed, or what dignity or empire in governing half a dozen men the size of hazelnuts — which, to my mind, was all there were in the whole earth? If your lordship would be pleased to give me a tiny little piece of the sky, even if it were no more than half a league, I would take it more willingly than the biggest isle in the world."

"Look, Sancho my friend," answered the duke, "I cannot give a piece of the sky to anybody, not even a piece the size of a fingernail, for those favours and graces are reserved to God alone. What I can give you I do give: an isle ready-made and proper, round and well proportioned and extremely fertile and rich, where if you know how to manage yourself you can, with the riches of earth, gain those of heaven."

"Well now," answered Sancho, "let this isle come; for I shall struggle to be such a governor that in spite of rascals I shall go to heaven. And this is not out of any greed I have to get above myself or to raise myself higher, but out of the desire I have to try what being a governor tastes like."

"If you once taste it, Sancho," said the duke, "you will be licking your fingers after the government, since it is the sweetest thing to command and be obeyed. It is a safe bet that when your master gets to be an emperor — which he undoubtedly will, the way his affairs are heading — they will not tear it away from him easily, and it will hurt and grieve him in the middle of his soul for the time he has spent without being one."

"Sir," replied Sancho, "I imagine it is a good thing to be in command, even if it is only of a flock of sheep."

"Let them bury me with you, Sancho, for you know about everything," answered the duke; "and I hope you will be as good a governor as your judgement promises. And let this rest here; and note that tomorrow, on that very day, you are to go to the government of the isle, and this afternoon they will fit you out with the proper clothes you are to wear and with all the things necessary for your departure."

"Let them dress me," said Sancho, "however they like; for whatever way I go dressed I shall be Sancho Panza."

"That is true," said the duke; "but the clothes have to fit the office or the dignity a man professes, for it would not be right for a jurist to dress like a soldier, or a soldier like a priest. You, Sancho, shall go dressed partly as a lawyer and partly as a captain; because in the isle I am giving you, arms are as necessary as letters, and letters as arms."

"Letters," answered Sancho, "I have few, because I do not even know my A B C; but it is enough for me to have the Christ-cross by heart to be a good governor. Of arms I shall handle whichever they give me until I drop, and God before us."

"With such a good memory," said the duke, "Sancho cannot go wrong in anything."

At this Don Quixote arrived; and, learning what was afoot and the speed with which Sancho was to set off to his government, with the duke's leave he took him by the hand and went with him to his own room, meaning to advise him how he was to conduct himself in his office.

Having gone into his room, then, he shut the door behind him and made Sancho sit down beside him almost by force; and in a composed voice he said to him:

"Infinite thanks I give heaven, Sancho my friend, that before and ahead of my coming across any good fortune of my own, good fortune has come out to receive and meet you. I, who had made over the payment of your services to my own good luck, find myself only at the beginnings of getting ahead; and you, ahead of time and against the law of reasonable expectation, find yourself rewarded in your desires.

"Others bribe, importune, solicit, get up early, beg, insist, and do not attain what they are after; and along comes another, and without knowing how or why finds himself with the charge and office that a great many others were after; and here it comes in and fits well to say that there is good and bad fortune in ambitions. You, who to my mind are without any doubt a blockhead, without getting up early or staying up late and without taking any pains at all, merely with the breath of knight-errantry that has touched you, find yourself, without any more ado, governor of an isle, as though it were nothing.

"All this I say, Sancho, so that you should not put down to your own deserts the favour you have received, but should give thanks to heaven, which disposes things gently — and afterwards you shall give them to the greatness that the profession of knight-errantry contains in itself. Your heart being disposed, then, to believe what I have told you, be attentive, my son, to this Cato of yours, who wants to advise you and to be the pole star and the guide to set you on your road and bring you out at a safe harbour from this stormy sea you are about to put out into; for offices and great charges are nothing but a deep gulf of confusions.

"First of all, my son, you must fear God, because in fearing him lies wisdom; and being wise you cannot go wrong in anything.

"Second, you must set your eyes on who you are, trying to know yourself — which is the most difficult knowledge that can be imagined. From knowing yourself will come your not puffing yourself up like the frog who wanted to make himself equal to the ox; for if you do that, the thought of having kept pigs in your own country will come to be the ugly feet to the spread tail of your folly."

"That is true," answered Sancho, "but it was when I was a boy; afterwards, when I was something of a young man, it was geese I kept and not pigs. But this seems to me beside the point, for not everybody who governs comes of the stock of kings."

"That is true," replied Don Quixote, "for which reason those who are not of noble beginnings must accompany the gravity of the charge they exercise with a mild gentleness which, guided by prudence, may free them from the malicious gossip that no station escapes.

"Make a display, Sancho, of the humbleness of your family, and do not be ashamed to say that you come of farm labourers; because, seeing that you are not put out of countenance, nobody will set about putting you out of countenance. And take more pride in being a virtuous humble man than a proud sinner. Innumerable are those who, born of low stock, have risen to the highest papal and imperial dignity; and of this truth I could bring you so many examples that they would tire you.

"Look, Sancho: if you take virtue as your means and pride yourself on doing virtuous deeds, there is no call to envy those who have princes and lords for parents; because blood is inherited and virtue is acquired, and virtue is worth by itself what blood is not worth.

"This being so, as it is, then if by any chance some relation of yours should come to see you when you are in your isle, do not turn him away or affront him; on the contrary, you must receive him, make much of him and entertain him. In doing so you will satisfy heaven, which is pleased that nobody should despise what it made, and you will answer to what you owe to a well-ordered nature.

"If you bring your wife with you — for it is not right that those who attend governments for a long time should be without their own wives — teach her, instruct her and rub off her natural roughness, because everything a judicious governor generally gains, a rustic and foolish woman generally loses and spills.

"If by any chance you should be widowed — a thing that can happen — and with your office should better yourself in a consort, do not take one of the kind who will serve you as a hook and a fishing rod, and as the 'no thank you — but drop it in my hood'; because in truth I tell you that for everything the judge's wife receives, the husband must give an account at the universal reckoning, where in death he shall pay fourfold the entries he did not charge himself with in life.

"Never be guided by the law of your own fancy, which generally finds a great deal of favour with ignorant men who presume to be sharp.

"Let the tears of the poor man find more compassion in you, but no more justice, than the depositions of the rich. Try to uncover the truth through the rich man's promises and gifts as much as through the poor man's sobs and importunities.

"When equity can and should have a place, do not lay all the rigour of the law on the offender, for the reputation of the severe judge is no better than that of the compassionate one.

"If you should happen to bend the rod of justice, let it not be with the weight of a gift but with that of mercy.

"When it falls to you to judge some case of an enemy of yours, take your mind off your own injury and set it on the truth of the case.

"Do not let your own passion blind you in another man's cause, for the mistakes you make in it will most often be past remedy; and if they are not, it will be at the cost of your credit and even of your property.

"If some beautiful woman comes to ask you for justice, take your eyes off her tears and your ears off her sighs, and consider at leisure the substance of what she is asking for, unless you want your reason to be drowned in her weeping and your goodness in her sighs.

"The man you have to punish in deeds, do not treat badly in words; for the pain of the punishment is enough for the wretched man, without the addition of hard words.

"Consider the guilty man who falls under your jurisdiction to be a miserable man, subject to the conditions of our depraved nature; and in everything that lies with you, without doing a wrong to the other party, show yourself merciful and clement to him. Because although all God's attributes are equal, to our eyes the attribute of mercy shines and shows itself more than that of justice.

"If you follow these precepts and these rules, Sancho, your days will be long, your fame will be everlasting, your rewards heaped up, your happiness beyond telling; you will marry your children as you like, they and your grandchildren will have titles, you will live in peace and in the good pleasure of the people, and in the last steps of your life the step of death will reach you, in a gentle and ripe old age, and the tender, delicate hands of your great-great-grandchildren will close your eyes.

"What I have told you so far are precepts that are to adorn your soul; listen now to those that are to serve for the adornment of the body."

Chapter 43: Of the Second Set of Advice Don Quixote Gave Sancho Panza

Who could have heard Don Quixote's last speech without taking him for a very sane person and a very well-meaning one? But, as has been said many times in the course of this great history, he only went off the rails when they touched him on chivalry, and in all his other talk he showed himself to have a clear and unencumbered understanding — so that at every step his deeds discredited his judgement and his judgement his deeds. But in this second set of precepts he gave Sancho, he showed great charm and set his judiciousness and his madness at a very high pitch.

Sancho listened to him most attentively, and tried to keep his advice in his memory, like a man who meant to hold on to it and to come by it to a good delivery from the pregnancy of his government. Don Quixote went on, then, and said:

"As to how you are to govern your own person and household, Sancho, the first thing I charge you with is to be clean, and to cut your nails and not let them grow, as some do, whose ignorance has given them to understand that long nails make their hands beautiful — as if that excrement and outgrowth they leave uncut were a nail, when it is rather the claws of a lizard-hunting kestrel: a filthy and monstrous abuse.

"Do not go about ungirt and slack, Sancho, for disordered clothes are a sign of a feeble spirit — unless the disorder and the slackness come under the head of slyness, as was judged in Julius Caesar's case.

"Take the pulse with discretion of what your office may be worth; and if it will run to giving liveries to your servants, give them decent and useful ones rather than showy and gallant ones, and share them out between your servants and the poor. I mean that if you are to dress six pages, dress three and another three poor men, and then you will have pages for heaven and pages for the ground; and this new way of giving liveries is beyond the reach of the vainglorious.

"Do not eat garlic or onions, so that they may not find out your rusticity by the smell.

"Walk slowly; speak with composure, but not in such a way that you seem to be listening to yourself, for all affectation is bad.

"Eat little and sup even less, for the health of the whole body is forged in the workshop of the stomach.

"Be temperate in drinking, considering that too much wine keeps no secret and holds to no promise.

"Take care, Sancho, not to chew on both sides of your mouth, and not to eructate in front of anybody."

"That business of eructating I do not understand," said Sancho.

And Don Quixote said to him:

"To eructate, Sancho, means to belch; and this is one of the coarsest words the Castilian tongue has, although it is very expressive. And so people of taste have taken refuge in Latin, and for belching say eructating, and for belches, eructations. And if some people do not understand these terms, it matters little; usage will bring them in with time, so that they are easily understood — and this is enriching the language, over which the common people and usage have power."

"Truly, sir," said Sancho, "one of the pieces of advice and warning I mean to carry in my memory will be that of not belching, because I generally do it very often."

"Eructating, Sancho, not belching," said Don Quixote.

"Eructating I shall say from now on," answered Sancho, "and upon my word I shall not forget it."

"Also, Sancho, you must not mix into your talk the multitude of proverbs you generally do; for although proverbs are short judgements, you often drag them in so much by the hair that they look more like nonsense than judgements."

"God can put that right," answered Sancho, "because I know more proverbs than a book, and so many of them come into my mouth together when I talk that they fight one another to get out; but my tongue goes on throwing out the first ones it comes across, even if they are not to the point. But I shall take care from now on to say the ones that suit the gravity of my charge; for in a full house supper is soon cooked, and he who cuts the pack does not shuffle, and safe is the man who rings the alarm, and giving and holding needs some brains."

"That is it, Sancho!" said Don Quixote. "Jam them in, thread them, string them together, for there is nobody to hold you back! 'My mother beats me and I spin my top!' I am telling you to leave off proverbs, and in an instant you have thrown out a whole litany of them here, which fit what we are talking about about as well as the hills of Úbeda do. Look, Sancho, I am not telling you that a proverb brought in to the point looks bad; but to load and thread proverbs on helter-skelter makes conversation feeble and low.

"When you get on horseback, do not go throwing your body over the hind saddlebow, or carry your legs stiff and straight out and away from the horse's belly; nor go so slack that it looks as if you were on the grey. For riding makes some men horsemen and others horse-boys.

"Let your sleep be moderate, for the man who does not get up with the sun does not enjoy the day. And note, Sancho, that diligence is the mother of good fortune, and that laziness, her opposite, never reached the goal a good wish asks for.

"This last piece of advice I want to give you now, although it does not serve for the adornment of the body, I want you to carry very much in your memory, for I believe it will be of no less use to you than the ones I have given you so far. And it is that you should never set yourself to argue about lineages, at least by comparing them with each other; because of necessity, among those compared one has to be the better, and by the one you cast down you will be hated and by the one you raise up you will in no way be rewarded.

"Your dress shall be full hose, a long jerkin and a cloak a little longer; wide breeches, not by any means, for they suit neither knights nor governors.

"For now this is what has occurred to me, Sancho, to advise you. Time will go on, and according to the occasions so shall my precepts be, so long as you take care to let me know the state you find yourself in."

"Sir," answered Sancho, "I see well enough that everything your worship has told me is good and holy and profitable; but what use will it be if I remember none of it? It is true that the business of not letting my nails grow and of marrying again if it should happen will not slip out of my noddle; but all those other hotchpotches and tangles and jumbles, I do not remember them and shall remember them no more than last year's clouds. And so it will be necessary for them to be given me in writing; for although I cannot read or write, I shall give them to my confessor so that he can drive them into me and go over them with me when it is needed."

"Ah, sinner that I am," answered Don Quixote, "how badly it looks in governors not to be able to read or write! Because you must know, Sancho, that a man's not knowing how to read, or his being left-handed, argues one of two things: either that he was the son of parents who were excessively humble and low, or that he was so mischievous and bad that no good habits or good teaching could get into him. It is a great fault you carry about with you, and so I should like you to learn at least to sign your name."

"I know very well how to sign my name," answered Sancho; "for when I was steward of the confraternity in my village I learnt to make some letters like the mark on a bale, which they said made my name. And besides, I shall pretend that my right hand is crippled and get somebody else to sign for me; for there is a remedy for everything except death, and, having the command and the staff, I shall do what I like. What is more, the man whose father is mayor — and I being a governor, which is more than being a mayor, come along and see!

"No — let them jeer at me and slander me, and they will come for wool and go back shorn; and whom God loves, his house smells sweet; and a rich man's follies pass for wise judgements in this world; and, being one myself, being a governor and generous into the bargain, as I mean to be, no fault of mine will show. No — make yourself honey and the flies will eat you; you are worth as much as you have, a grandmother of mine used to say; and of a man with roots you will never get your revenge."

"Oh, God curse you, Sancho!" said Don Quixote at this. "May sixty thousand Satans carry you off and your proverbs with you! For an hour now you have been stringing them together and giving me a swallow of torment with each one.
