I assure you that these proverbs will take you to the gallows one day; because of them your vassals will take the government away from you, or there will be risings among them. Tell me, where do you find them, ignoramus, or how do you apply them, idiot? For me to say one and apply it properly, I sweat and labour as though I were digging."

"By God, sir our master," replied Sancho, "your worship complains about very small things. Why the devil do you fret about my making use of my own property, when I have no other and no other capital but proverbs and more proverbs? And now four occur to me that came in here exactly to the pattern, or like pears in a basket; but I shall not say them, because good silence they call Sancho."

"That Sancho is not you," said Don Quixote, "because you are not only not good silence, but bad speech and bad insisting. All the same, I should like to know what four proverbs came into your memory just now that were to the point here; for I am going over my own, which is a good one, and none occurs to me."

"What better," said Sancho, "than 'never put your thumbs between two wisdom teeth', and 'to "get out of my house" and "what do you want with my wife" there is no answering', and 'whether the pitcher hits the stone or the stone the pitcher, it goes badly for the pitcher' — all of which come to the point? Because nobody should take on his governor or the man who commands him, since he will come off hurt, like the man who puts his finger between two wisdom teeth; and even if they are not wisdom teeth, so long as they are teeth it does not matter. And to whatever the governor says there is no answering, as with 'get out of my house' and 'what do you want with my wife'. And as for the stone and the pitcher, a blind man would see it. So it is necessary that the man who sees the mote in his neighbour's eye should see the beam in his own, so that it may not be said of him: 'the dead woman was frightened of the one with her throat cut'; and your worship knows very well that a fool knows more in his own house than a wise man in another's."

"Not that, Sancho," answered Don Quixote; "for the fool knows nothing, either in his own house or in another's, since on the foundation of foolishness no judicious building will stand. And let us leave this here, Sancho; for if you govern badly, the fault will be yours and the shame mine. But I console myself that I have done what I ought in advising you with all the earnestness and judgement possible to me: with this I discharge my obligation and my promise. God guide you, Sancho, and govern you in your government, and get me out of the scruple I am left with that you are going to turn the whole isle upside down — a thing I could avoid by disclosing to the duke who you are, telling him that all that fat and that little person of yours is nothing but a sack full of proverbs and mischief."

"Sir," replied Sancho, "if it seems to your worship that I am not fit for this government, I release you from it here and now; for I care more for a single black speck of my soul's fingernail than for my whole body. And I shall keep myself alive as plain Sancho on bread and onions as well as as a governor on partridges and capons; and what is more, while we are asleep we are all equal, the great and the small, the poor and the rich. And if your worship looks into it, you will see that it was your worship alone who put me into this business of governing; for I know no more about governing isles than a vulture does. And if you imagine that because I am a governor the devil will carry me off, I would rather go to heaven as Sancho than to hell as a governor."

"By God, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "for these last words alone that you have said, I judge that you deserve to be governor of a thousand isles. You have a good nature, without which there is no learning worth anything. Commend yourself to God, and try not to go wrong in your first intention — I mean that you should always have the aim and firm purpose of getting things right in whatever business comes to you, because heaven always favours good desires. And let us go in to dinner, for I believe these ladies and gentlemen are waiting for us."

Chapter 44: How Sancho Panza Was Taken to His Government, and of the Strange Adventure That Befell Don Quixote in the Castle

They say that in the very original of this history it is read that when Cide Hamete came to write this chapter, his interpreter did not translate it as he had written it — which was a kind of complaint the Moor made against himself for having taken in hand a history as dry and as limited as this one of Don Quixote, since it seemed to him that he always had to talk about him and about Sancho, without daring to spread himself into other digressions and episodes graver and more entertaining.

And he said that to have the understanding, the hand and the pen always tied to writing about a single subject and speaking through the mouths of a few people was an unbearable labour whose fruit did not redound to its author; and that, to escape this drawback, he had used in the first part the device of certain tales, such as The Ill-Advised Curiosity and that of the Captive Captain, which stand as though separate from the history, since the rest that are told there are cases that happened to Don Quixote himself and could not be left unwritten.

He also thought, as he says, that many people, carried away by the attention Don Quixote's exploits demand, would not give it to the tales and would pass over them either in a hurry or in annoyance, without noticing the elegance and craftsmanship they contain in themselves — which would show itself plainly in the open when they came out into the light on their own, without leaning on Don Quixote's madnesses or on Sancho's foolishness.

And so in this second part he did not want to insert loose or stuck-on tales but some episodes that should look like them, born of the very events that the truth provides — and even these limitedly, and with only the words that are enough to set them out. And since he holds and shuts himself within the narrow limits of the narrative, having the ability, sufficiency and understanding to deal with the whole universe, he asks that his labour should not be despised, and that he should be given praise not for what he writes but for what he has left unwritten.

And then the history goes on, saying that when Don Quixote had finished dinner on the day he gave Sancho his advice, that afternoon he gave it him in writing, so that he could look for somebody to read it to him. But hardly had he given it him when it fell out of his hands and came into the duke's, who shared it with the duchess; and the two of them marvelled afresh at Don Quixote's madness and his wit. And so, carrying their tricks further, that afternoon they sent Sancho with a great retinue to the place that was to be his isle.

It happened, then, that the man who had charge of him was a steward of the duke's, very judicious and very amusing — for there can be no amusement where there is no judgement — who had played the part of the Countess Trifaldi with the grace already described; and with this, and with being coached by his master and mistress on how he was to conduct himself with Sancho, he carried out his purpose marvellously.

I say, then, that it happened that as soon as Sancho saw this steward, he seemed to see the very face of the Trifaldi in his; and, turning to his master, he said to him:

"Sir, either the devil must carry me off from where I stand here, in justice and in belief, or your worship must admit to me that this face of the duke's steward here is the same as the Distressed Lady's."

Don Quixote looked attentively at the steward, and, having looked at him, said to Sancho:

"There is no call for the devil to carry you off, Sancho, either in justice or in belief — for I do not know what you mean. The Distressed Lady's face is the steward's, but that does not make the steward the Distressed Lady; for if it did, it would imply a very great contradiction. And this is not the time to make these investigations, for it would be getting ourselves into intricate labyrinths. Believe me, my friend, it is necessary to pray to Our Lord very earnestly to deliver the two of us from bad sorcerers and bad enchanters."

"It is no joke, sir," replied Sancho, "for a little while ago I heard him speak, and it sounded for all the world as though the Trifaldi's voice were ringing in my ears. Well now, I shall be quiet; but I shall not leave off going about on the watch from now on, to see whether I can find another sign that confirms or undoes my suspicion."

"That is what you must do, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and you shall give me notice of everything you find out in this business and of everything that happens to you in the government."

Sancho set off at last, attended by a great many people, dressed as a lawyer, and over that a very wide coat of tawny watered camlet with a cap of the same, riding a mule with short stirrups; and behind him, by the duke's orders, went the grey with harness and donkeyish trappings of silk and brand new. Sancho turned his head from time to time to look at his donkey, in whose company he went so contented that he would not have swapped with the emperor of Germany.

On taking his leave of the duke and duchess he kissed their hands, and took his master's blessing, which he gave him in tears; and Sancho received it with a pouting lip.

Let good Sancho go in peace and good luck, kind reader, and expect two bushels of laughter from learning how he conducted himself in his charge; and meanwhile attend to learning what happened to his master that night — at which, if you do not laugh, at least you will part your lips in an ape's grin, since Don Quixote's doings must be celebrated either with wonder or with laughter.

It is told, then, that Sancho had hardly set off when Don Quixote felt his loneliness; and if it had been possible for him to revoke his commission and take away his government, he would have done it. The duchess noticed his melancholy and asked him what he was sad about; and that if it was Sancho's absence, there were squires, duennas and maidens in her house who would serve him quite to the satisfaction of his wishes.

"It is true, my lady," answered Don Quixote, "that I feel Sancho's absence; but that is not the chief cause that makes me seem sad. And of the many offers your excellency makes me, I accept and choose only the good will with which they are made; and for the rest I beg Your Excellency to consent and permit that within my own room I alone should be the one to serve myself."

"Truly," said the duchess, "Señor Don Quixote, it must not be so: four of my maidens, as beautiful as flowers, shall serve you."

"For me," answered Don Quixote, "they will not be like flowers but like thorns to pierce my soul. They shall come into my room, or anything like it, about as soon as they can fly. If your greatness wants to go on doing me favours I do not deserve, let me be alone with myself and serve myself inside my own doors; let me put a wall between my desires and my chastity. And I do not want to lose this habit because of the generosity your highness wants to show me. In short, I would sooner sleep in my clothes than let anybody undress me."

"No more, no more, Señor Don Quixote," replied the duchess. "For my part I say that I shall give orders that not so much as a fly shall come into your chamber, let alone a maiden. I am not the person to spoil Señor Don Quixote's decency; for, as far as I can see, the virtue that shows most among his many virtues is that of chastity. Let your worship undress and dress by yourself and in your own way, how and when you like, for there will be nobody to stop you; and inside your room you will find the vessels needed by a man who sleeps behind a shut door, so that no natural necessity may oblige him to open it. Long live the great Dulcinea of El Toboso for a thousand ages, and let her name be spread over the whole round of the earth, since she has deserved to be loved by so valiant and so chaste a knight; and may the kindly heavens pour into the heart of Sancho Panza, our governor, a desire to finish his disciplines quickly, so that the world may go back to enjoying the beauty of so great a lady."

To which Don Quixote said:

"Your loftiness has spoken like the woman you are; for in the mouth of good ladies there can be nothing bad. And Dulcinea will be more fortunate and better known in the world for your greatness's having praised her than for all the praises the most eloquent men on earth could give her."

"Well now, Señor Don Quixote," replied the duchess, "the supper hour is coming on, and the duke must be waiting. Let your worship come and let us have supper, and you shall go to bed early; for the journey you made yesterday from Candaya was not so short that it will not have caused you some aching."

"I feel none, my lady," answered Don Quixote, "because I would venture to swear to Your Excellency that in all my life I have never got up on a quieter beast or one of a better pace than Clavileño; and I do not know what could have moved Malambruno to get rid of so light and so fine a mount, and burn it up like that without any more ado."

"It may be imagined about that," answered the duchess, "that, repenting of the harm he had done the Trifaldi and company and other people, and of the wickednesses he must have committed as a sorcerer and an enchanter, he wanted to make an end of all the instruments of his trade; and, as the chief one and the one that most kept him restless, wandering from land to land, he burned Clavileño. And with his burnt ashes and with the trophy of the notice, the valour of the great Don Quixote of La Mancha is made everlasting."

Don Quixote gave the duchess fresh thanks again; and after supper he withdrew alone to his room, without allowing anybody to come in with him to serve him — so much did he fear meeting with occasions that might move or force him to lose the chaste decorum he kept for his lady Dulcinea, always keeping in his imagination the goodness of Amadís, the flower and mirror of knights errant. He shut the door behind him, and by the light of two wax candles undressed; and as he was taking off his stockings — O disaster unworthy of such a person! — there escaped him not sighs or anything else that might discredit the cleanness of his manners, but as many as two dozen stitches of one stocking, which was left like a lattice.

The good gentleman was distressed in the extreme, and he would have given an ounce of silver to have a scruple of green silk there — I say green silk because the stockings were green.

Here Benengeli broke out and, writing, said: "O poverty, poverty! I do not know with what reason that great poet of Cordova was moved to call you

	holy gift ungratefully received!

"I, although a Moor, know very well, through the dealings I have had with Christians, that holiness consists in charity, humility, faith, obedience and poverty; but for all that, I say that a man must have a great deal of God in him who can come to be content with being poor — unless it is with that kind of poverty of which one of their greatest saints says: 'Have all things as though you had them not'; and this they call poverty of spirit. But you, second poverty — and it is you I am talking about — why do you want to dash yourself against gentlemen and the well born rather than against other people? Why do you oblige them to give their shoes a lick of lampblack, and to have the buttons on their jerkins some of silk, some of horsehair and some of glass? Why must their collars, for the most part, always be crimped and not spread open with a mould?"

And in this it will be seen that the use of starch and open collars is an old one. And he went on: "Wretched is the well-born man who goes about feeding his honour with thin broth, eating badly and behind a closed door, making a hypocrite of the toothpick he goes out into the street with after eating nothing that obliged him to clean his teeth! Wretched, I say, is the man who has a skittish honour and thinks that from a league off people can see the patch on his shoe, the sweat stains on his hat, the threadbare place on his cloak and the hunger in his stomach!"

All this was renewed for Don Quixote in the running of his stitches; but he consoled himself with seeing that Sancho had left him a pair of travelling boots, which he meant to put on the next day. Finally he lay down thoughtful and grieved, as much for the loss Sancho was to him as for the irreparable disaster of his stockings, whose stitches he would have taken up even with silk of another colour — which is one of the greatest signs of poverty a gentleman can give in the course of his long-drawn-out hardship.

He put out the candles; it was hot and he could not sleep; he got up from the bed and opened a little the window of a grating that looked out on a beautiful garden, and, on opening it, he felt and heard that there were people walking and talking in the garden. He set himself to listen attentively. The people below raised their voices enough for him to hear these words:

"Do not press me, Emerencia, to sing; for you know that from the moment this stranger came into this castle and my eyes looked at him, I do not know how to sing but only how to weep. What is more, my lady's sleep is lighter rather than heavy, and I should not want her to find us here for all the treasure in the world. And supposing she were asleep and did not wake, my song would be in vain if this new Aeneas, who has come to my regions to leave me mocked, sleeps and does not wake to hear it."

"Do not think so, Altisidora my friend," they answered. "For without any doubt the duchess and everybody in this house is asleep, except the lord of your heart and the awakener of your soul; because I heard just now that he was opening the window of the grating in his chamber, and no doubt he must be awake. Sing, my wounded one, in a low and gentle tone to the sound of your harp; and if the duchess hears us, we shall blame the heat."

"That is not the point of it, Emerencia," answered Altisidora, "but that I should not like my song to uncover my heart and have me judged by those who know nothing of the mighty power of love as a whimsical and light girl. But come what may, for a blush on the face is better than a stain on the heart."

And with this she heard a harp very sweetly played. Hearing which, Don Quixote was thunderstruck, because in that instant there came into his memory the infinite adventures like this one — of windows, gratings and gardens, music, love-making and swoonings — that he had read in his empty-headed books of chivalry.

Then he imagined that some maiden of the duchess's was in love with him, and that modesty forced her to keep her feeling secret. He was afraid she might overcome him, and he resolved in his mind not to let himself be conquered; and, commending himself with all good courage and good will to his lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, he determined to listen to the music. And, to give it to be understood that he was there, he gave a pretended sneeze, at which the maidens were not a little glad, for they wanted nothing else but that Don Quixote should hear them. The harp being run over, then, and tuned, Altisidora began this ballad:

	O you who lie in your bed
	between sheets of finest linen,
	sleeping with your legs stretched out
	from the night until the morning,
	the most valiant knight
	that La Mancha has ever produced,
	more chaste and more blessed
	than the fine gold of Arabia!
	Hear a sorrowful maiden,
	well grown and badly used,
	who in the light of your two suns
	feels her soul burning up.
	You go looking for your adventures
	and you find other people's misfortunes;
	you deal out the wounds and you deny
	the remedy that would heal them.
	Tell me, valorous young man
	— and God prosper your longings —
	whether you were raised in Libya
	or in the mountains of Jaca;
	whether serpents gave you milk;
	whether, by chance, your nurses were
	the roughness of the forests
	and the horror of the mountains.
	Dulcinea may very well,
	that plump and healthy girl,
	pride herself on having tamed
	a tigress and a fierce wild beast.
	For this she will be famous
	from Henares to Jarama,
	from the Tagus to Manzanares,
	from Pisuerga as far as Arlanza.
	I would trade myself for her,
	and give a petticoat on top,
	one of the gayest ones I have,
	with fringes trimmed with gold.
	Oh, to find myself in your arms,
	or if not, beside your bed,
	scratching your head for you
	and killing off your dandruff!
	I ask too much, and I am not worthy
	of so signal a favour:
	I should like to rub your feet,
	which is enough for a humble girl.
	Oh, what caps I would give you,
	what socks worked with silver,
	what hose of damask,
	what cloaks of the finest linen!
	What most excellent pearls,
	each one the size of an oak gall,
	which, if they had no companions,
	would be called the Peerless Ones!
	Do not look from your Tarpeian rock
	on this fire that burns me up,
	Manchegan Nero of the world,
	and do not fan it with your fury.
	I am a girl, a tender maiden;
	my age does not pass fifteen:
	I am fourteen and three months,
	I swear to you by God and my soul.
	I am not lame and I am not crippled,
	and I have nothing withered about me;
	my hair is like lilies,
	and, standing up, it trails on the ground.
	And though my mouth is aquiline
	and my nose is rather flat,
	my teeth being of topaz
	exalts my beauty to the sky.
	My voice, as you can hear if you listen,
	is a match for the sweetest;
	and I am of a figure
	something less than middling.
	These and my other graces
	are the spoils of your quiver;
	I am a maiden of this house,
	and Altisidora they call me.

Here the song of the sorely wounded Altisidora came to an end, and the dismay of the courted Don Quixote began; who, giving a great sigh, said to himself:

"That I must be such an unfortunate errant that there is no maiden who looks at me and does not fall in love with me...! That the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso must be so short of luck that they will not leave her alone to enjoy my incomparable constancy...! What do you want with her, you queens? Why do you persecute her, you empresses? Why do you harry her, you maidens of fourteen and fifteen? Leave her, leave the poor girl to triumph and rejoice and take pride in the lot Love chose to give her in surrendering my heart to her and handing over my soul.

"See, you enamoured crew, that for Dulcinea alone I am of dough and sugar paste, and for all the rest I am of flint; for her I am honey and for you aloes; for me Dulcinea alone is the beautiful, the judicious, the chaste, the gallant and the well born, and the rest are the ugly, the foolish, the light and the worst born. Nature threw me into the world to be hers and no other woman's. Let Altisidora weep or sing; let the lady despair for whom they beat me in the castle of the enchanted Moor; for I have to be Dulcinea's, boiled or roast, clean, well brought up and chaste, in spite of all the sorcerous powers on earth."

And with this he shut the window with a bang; and, put out and grieved, as though some great misfortune had befallen him, he lay down on his bed, where we shall leave him for now, because the great Sancho Panza is calling us, wanting to make a beginning of his famous government.

Chapter 45: Of How the Great Sancho Panza Took Possession of His Isle, and of the Manner in Which He Began to Govern

O perpetual discoverer of the antipodes, torch of the world, eye of heaven, sweet swayer of the water coolers, Thymbraeus here, Phoebus there, archer this way and physician that, father of Poetry, inventor of Music — you who always rise and, though it looks like it, never set! To you I speak, O sun, by whose help man begets man; to you I speak, that you may favour me and light up the darkness of my wits, so that I may go point by point through the narration of the great Sancho Panza's government; for without you I feel myself lukewarm, feeble and confused.

I say, then, that with all his retinue Sancho came to a town of about a thousand inhabitants, which was one of the best the duke had. They gave him to understand that it was called the isle of Barataria — either because the place was called Baratario, or because of the bargain rate at which the government had been given him. On reaching the gates of the town, which was walled, the town council came out to receive him; the bells were rung, and all the inhabitants gave signs of general gladness, and with a great deal of pomp they took him to the chief church to give thanks to God. And then, with some ridiculous ceremonies, they handed him the keys of the town and admitted him as perpetual governor of the isle of Barataria.

The dress, the beard, the fatness and the shortness of the new governor astonished all the people who did not know the crux of the joke, and even all those who did, and they were many. Finally, on bringing him out of the church, they took him to the judgement seat and sat him down in it; and the duke's steward said to him:

"It is an ancient custom in this isle, my lord governor, that whoever comes to take possession of this famous isle is obliged to answer a question that is put to him, which shall be somewhat intricate and difficult; and by his answer the people take and feel the pulse of their new governor's wits, and so are either glad or sorry at his coming."

While the steward was saying this to Sancho, he was looking at some large and numerous letters written on the wall opposite his seat; and, as he could not read, he asked what those paintings on the wall were. He was answered:

"Sir, there is written and noted the day on which Your Lordship took possession of this isle, and the inscription says: Today, on such and such a day of such and such a month and year, Señor Don Sancho Panza took possession of this isle: may he enjoy it many years."

"And who do they call Don Sancho Panza?" asked Sancho.

"Your lordship," answered the steward; "for no other Panza has come into this isle but the one sitting in that chair."

"Then note, brother," said Sancho, "that I have no Don, and there has never been one in my whole family. Plain Sancho Panza they call me, and Sancho my father was called, and Sancho my grandfather, and they were all Panzas without any additions of Dons or Doñas. And I imagine that in this isle there must be more Dons than stones. But enough: God understands me; and it may be that if the government lasts me four days I shall weed out these Dons, which by their numbers must be as annoying as gnats. Let the steward go on with his question, and I shall answer as best I know how, whether the people are sorry or not sorry."

At this moment two men came into the court, one dressed as a farmer and the other as a tailor, since he carried a pair of scissors in his hand; and the tailor said:

"My lord governor, I and this farmer come before your worship because this good man came to my shop yesterday — for I, saving the presence of those here, am a licensed tailor, God be blessed — and, putting a piece of cloth in my hands, asked me: 'Sir, would there be enough cloth in this to make me a cap?' I, measuring the cloth by eye, answered that there would. He must have imagined, as I imagine, and I imagined rightly, that I no doubt wanted to steal some part of the cloth off him, going on his own bad conscience and on the bad name of tailors; and he came back at me and asked me to see whether there would be enough for two. I guessed his thought and told him there would. And he, riding on his damaging first intention, went on adding caps and I went on adding yeses, until we got to five caps; and just now, at this minute, he has come for them. I give them to him, and he will not pay me for the making; on the contrary, he wants me to pay him or give him back his cloth."

"Is all this so, brother?" asked Sancho.

"Yes, sir," answered the man; "but let your worship make him show the five caps he has made me."

"Willingly," answered the tailor.

And, pulling his hand out from under his cloak on the instant, he showed on it five caps set on the five tips of the fingers of his hand, and said:

"Here are the five caps this good man is asking me for; and in God and in my conscience I have nothing left over of the cloth, and I shall submit the work to the inspectors of the trade."

Everybody present laughed at the multitude of caps and at the novel lawsuit. Sancho set himself to think a little, and said:

"It seems to me that in this suit there is no call for long delays, but for judging straight away by the judgement of a good man. And so I give it as my sentence that the tailor should lose his making and the farmer his cloth, and that the caps should be taken to the prisoners in the gaol, and there is an end of it."

If his other sentences moved the bystanders to wonder, this one provoked them to laughter; but in the end what the governor ordered was done. And before him there presented themselves two old men, one of whom carried a giant fennel stalk for a staff; and the one without a staff said:

"Sir, some days ago I lent this good man ten gold crowns in gold, to do him a pleasure and a good turn, on condition that he should give them back to me when I asked for them. Many days went by without my asking him for them, so as not to put him in greater difficulty over giving them back than he was in when I lent them. But, since it seemed to me that he was being slack about paying, I have asked him for them once and many times; and not only does he not give them back, he denies them and says that I never lent him any such ten crowns, and that if I did lend them him he has already given them back. I have no witnesses either to the loan or to the return, because he has not returned them. I should like your worship to put him on his oath; and if he swears he has given them back, I forgive him them here and before God."

"What do you say to this, good old man with the staff?" said Sancho.

To which the old man said:

"I, sir, confess that he lent them me; and let your worship lower that rod of yours. And since he leaves it to my oath, I shall swear that I have given them back and paid them really and truly."

The governor lowered the rod; and meanwhile the old man with the staff gave the staff to the other old man to hold for him while he swore, as if it were much in his way, and then laid his hand on the cross of the rod, saying that it was true that those ten crowns he was being asked for had been lent to him, but that he had given them back out of his own hand into the other's, and that, not realising this, the other kept asking for them again and again.

Which the great governor seeing, he asked the creditor what he answered to what his opponent said; and he said that without any doubt his debtor must be telling the truth, because he took him for an honest man and a good Christian, and that he himself must have forgotten how and when he had given them back, and that from then on he would never ask him for anything again. The debtor took his staff again and, bowing his head, went out of the court.

Seeing which, and that he was going off without any more ado, and seeing too the patience of the plaintiff, Sancho bowed his head over his chest and, putting the forefinger of his right hand over his eyebrows and his nose, stayed as though in thought for a short space; and then he raised his head and ordered them to call back the old man with the staff, who had already gone. They brought him back, and, seeing him, Sancho said:

"Give me that staff, good man, for I need it."

"Very willingly," answered the old man. "Here it is, sir."

And he put it into his hand. Sancho took it and, giving it to the other old man, said to him:

"Go, and God be with you, for now you are paid."

"I, sir?" answered the old man. "Why, is this fennel stalk worth ten gold crowns?"

"Yes," said the governor; "or if not, I am the greatest blockhead in the world. And now it will be seen whether I have the headpiece to govern a whole kingdom."

And he ordered that there, in front of everybody, the cane should be broken open. It was done, and in the heart of it they found ten crowns in gold. Everybody was amazed, and they held their governor for a new Solomon.

They asked him how he had gathered that those ten crowns were in that fennel stalk, and he answered that it was from having seen the old man who was swearing give his opponent that staff while he made his oath, and swear that he had really and truly given them to him; and then, on finishing the oath, ask him for the staff back again. From this it came into his imagination that inside it was the payment they were arguing about. From which it could be gathered that those who govern, even if they are fools, are sometimes set on the right road by God in their judgements. And besides, he had heard the curate of his village tell another case like that one; and he had such a great memory that if it were not for his forgetting everything he wanted to remember, there would not be such a memory in the whole isle.

Finally, the one old man shamefaced and the other paid, they went off; and the bystanders were left amazed, and the man who was writing down Sancho's words, deeds and movements could not settle whether he should hold him and set him down for a fool or for a judicious man.

Then, this suit being over, there came into the court a woman gripping tightly to a man dressed as a rich herdsman, and she came shouting loudly and saying:

"Justice, my lord governor, justice! And if I do not find it on earth, I shall go and look for it in heaven! My lord governor of my soul, this wicked man caught me in the middle of that field and has used my body as if it were a badly washed rag; and, wretched creature that I am, he has taken from me what I had kept for more than twenty-three years, defending it from Moors and Christians, from natives and foreigners; and I always as hard as a cork tree, keeping myself as whole as the salamander in the fire or as wool among the brambles — only for this good man to come along now with his clean hands to handle me."

"That still has to be found out — whether this gallant has clean hands or not," said Sancho.

And, turning to the man, he asked him what he said and what he answered to that woman's complaint. And he, all confused, answered:

"Gentlemen, I am a poor herdsman of pigs, and this morning I was leaving this place after selling — saving your presence — four pigs, and what they took off me in excise and extortions came to little less than they were worth. I was going back to my village, and on the road I came across this good dame; and the devil, who mixes everything up and cooks everything, made us lie together. I paid her enough, and she, not content, laid hold of me and has not let me go until she had brought me to this place. She says I forced her, and she lies, by the oath I make or mean to make; and this is the whole truth, without a mite missing."

Then the governor asked him whether he had any silver money on him; he said he had about twenty ducats in his bosom in a leather purse. He ordered him to take it out and hand it over, just as it was, to the complainant; he did it trembling. The woman took it and, making a thousand bows to everybody and praying God for the life and health of the lord governor, who looked after needy orphans and maidens in this way, went out of the court holding the purse gripped in both hands — although first she looked to see whether the money she was carrying inside it was silver.

She had hardly gone out when Sancho said to the herdsman, whose tears were already starting and whose eyes and heart were going after his purse:

"Good man, go after that woman and take the purse from her whether she wants it or not, and come back here with her."

And he did not say it to a fool or a deaf man, for he set off at once like lightning and went to do what he was told. Everybody present was in suspense, waiting for the end of that suit; and a little later the man and the woman came back gripping and gripped tighter than the first time: she with her skirt lifted up and the purse held in her lap, and the man struggling to get it off her — but it was not possible, so well did the woman defend it, and she was calling out:

"Justice of God and of the world! Look, your worship, my lord governor, at the shamelessness and the little fear of this soulless man, who in the middle of a town and in the middle of the street has tried to take away from me the purse your worship ordered to be given me."

"And has he taken it from you?" asked the governor.

"Taken it?" answered the woman. "I would sooner let them take my life than take the purse. A fine thing that would be! They will have to throw other cats than this wretched, disgusting creature in my face! Pincers and hammers, mallets and chisels would not be enough to get it out of my nails, nor even lions' claws: they would sooner have my soul out of the middle of the middle of my flesh!"

"She is right," said the man, "and I give myself up beaten and out of strength, and I confess that mine are not enough to take it from her; and I leave it."

Then the governor said to the woman:

"Show me that purse, honourable and valiant lady."

She gave it him at once, and the governor gave it back to the man and said to the woman who had used force and had none used on her:

"Sister of mine, if you had shown the same spirit and courage in defending your body that you have shown in defending this purse — and even half as much — the strength of Hercules could not have forced you. Go, and God be with you, and much bad luck; and do not stop anywhere in this whole isle or within six leagues around it, on pain of two hundred lashes. Go at once, I say, you brazen, shameless cheat!"

The woman was frightened and went off with her head down and ill contented; and the governor said to the man:

"Good man, go with God to your village with your money; and from now on, if you do not want to lose it, see that you do not take a fancy to lying with anybody."

The man thanked him as badly as he knew how, and went off; and the bystanders were left amazed all over again at their new governor's judgements and sentences. All of which, noted by his chronicler, was written at once to the duke, who was waiting for it with great eagerness.

And let good Sancho stay here, for his master is pressing us hard, being greatly stirred by Altisidora's music.

Chapter 46: Of the Terrifying Bell-and-Cat Fright Don Quixote Received in the Course of the Enamoured Altisidora's Courtship

We left the great Don Quixote wrapped up in the thoughts the music of the enamoured maiden Altisidora had caused him. He went to bed with them; and, as though they were fleas, they did not let him sleep or rest a moment, and the ones he had lost out of his stockings joined them. But since time is swift and there is no gully that holds it up, it went riding on the hours, and the morning hour arrived very quickly.

Which Don Quixote seeing, he left the soft feathers and, in no way sluggish, put on his chamois suit and pulled on his travelling boots, to hide the disaster of his stockings; he threw his scarlet cloak over him and set on his head a cap of green velvet trimmed with silver braid; he hung his baldric over his shoulders with his good cutting sword, took up a great rosary he always carried with him, and with great pomp and swagger went out into the antechamber, where the duke and duchess were already dressed and apparently waiting for him.

And, as he was passing along a gallery, Altisidora and the other maiden her friend were waiting for him on purpose; and as soon as Altisidora saw Don Quixote she pretended to faint, and her friend caught her in her lap and in great haste began to unfasten her bodice. Don Quixote, seeing it, came up to them and said:

"I know very well what these attacks come from."

"I do not know what they come from," answered the friend, "because Altisidora is the healthiest maiden in this whole house, and I have never heard so much as an 'ah' out of her in all the time I have known her. A curse on all the knights errant there are in the world, if they are all as ungrateful as this. Go away, your worship, Señor Don Quixote, for this poor girl will not come round while your worship is here."

To which Don Quixote answered:

"Let your worship see, madam, that a lute is put in my room tonight, and I shall console this wounded maiden as best I can; for in the beginnings of love, prompt disenchantment is generally a well-approved remedy."

And with this he went off, so as not to be noticed by anybody who might see him there. He had hardly got away when the fainting Altisidora, coming round, said to her companion:

"It will be necessary for the lute to be put there; for no doubt Don Quixote means to give us some music, and it will not be bad, since it is his."

They went at once to tell the duchess what was afoot and about the lute Don Quixote was asking for; and she, extremely glad, arranged with the duke and with her maidens to play him a trick that should be more laughable than harmful, and they waited for the night with great pleasure. And the night came on as quickly as the day had come, which the duke and duchess spent in delicious talk with Don Quixote.

And the duchess that day really and truly sent off a page of hers — the one who had played the enchanted figure of Dulcinea in the wood — to Teresa Panza, with the letter from her husband Sancho Panza and with the bundle of clothes he had left to be sent to her, charging him to bring back a good account of everything that passed between them.

This done, and eleven o'clock at night having come, Don Quixote found a guitar in his room. He tuned it, opened the grating and heard that there were people about in the garden; and, having run over the frets of the guitar and tuned it as best he knew how, he spat and cleared his chest, and then, in a slightly hoarse but tuneful voice, sang the following ballad, which he had himself composed that day:

	The forces of love are apt
	to knock souls off their hinges,
	taking for their instrument
	a careless idleness.
	Sewing and needlework,
	and being always busy,
	are apt to be the antidote
	to the poison of love's longings.
	For sheltered young women
	who hope to be married,
	modesty is the dowry
	and the voice of their praises.
	Knights errant,
	and those who go about the court,
	pay their compliments to the loose
	and marry the modest.
	There are loves of the sunrise
	that pass between guests at an inn,
	which come quickly to their sunset,
	because they end in the parting.
	Love newly arrived,
	that came today and goes tomorrow,
	does not leave its images
	well printed on the soul.
	Painting laid over painting
	neither shows nor marks;
	and where there is a first beauty
	the second wins no trick.
	Dulcinea of El Toboso
	I have painted on the blank
	tablet of my soul in such a way
	that it is impossible to rub her out.
	Constancy in lovers
	is the part most to be prized,
	by which love works its miracles
	and by which it raises them up.

Don Quixote had got this far in his song — and the duke and duchess, Altisidora and almost all the people of the castle were listening to him — when all at once, from the top of a gallery that hung plumb over Don Quixote's grating, they let down a cord with more than a hundred cowbells tied to it; and then, after them, they emptied out a great sack of cats, which likewise had smaller bells tied to their tails.

So great was the noise of the bells and the yowling of the cats that, although the duke and duchess had been the inventors of the trick, it still startled them; and Don Quixote was left thunderstruck with fear. And it so happened that two or three cats got in through the grating of his chamber, and, dashing from one side to the other, it looked as though a region of devils were about the room. They put out the candles that were burning in the room, and went about looking for a way to escape. The letting down and pulling up of the cord of great bells did not stop; most of the people in the castle, who did not know the truth of the business, were bewildered and astonished.

Don Quixote got to his feet, and, laying his hand on his sword, began to lunge through the grating and to say in a loud voice:

"Away, malignant enchanters! Away, you sorcerous rabble; for I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, against whom your evil intentions have neither strength nor power!"

And, turning to the cats that were about the room, he let fly a great many sword-strokes at them. They made for the grating and got out that way — except one which, seeing itself so hard pressed by Don Quixote's slashes, sprang at his face and seized his nose with its claws and its teeth; at the pain of which Don Quixote began to shout as loudly as he could.

Hearing which, the duke and duchess, and guessing what it might be, ran with great haste to his chamber; and, opening it with a master key, they saw the poor knight struggling with all his strength to tear the cat off his face. They came in with lights and saw the unequal fight; the duke ran up to part it, and Don Quixote said loudly:

"Let nobody take him off me! Leave me hand to hand with this demon, with this sorcerer, with this enchanter, and I shall give him to understand between him and me who Don Quixote of La Mancha is!"

But the cat, taking no notice of these threats, growled and held on. In the end, though, the duke tore him loose and threw him out through the grating.

Don Quixote was left with his face riddled and his nose in no very sound state, though very put out that they had not let him finish the battle he had so well joined with that villainous enchanter. They had Aparicio's oil brought, that costly balm for wounds, and Altisidora herself with her snow-white hands put bandages over everything that was hurt. And, as she put them on, she said to him in a low voice:

"All these misadventures happen to you, you hard-hearted knight, for the sin of your hardness and obstinacy; and please God that your squire Sancho may forget to whip himself, so that this so beloved Dulcinea of yours may never come out of her enchantment, and you may never enjoy her or come to the marriage bed with her — at least while I am alive, who adore you."

To all this Don Quixote answered not a word, but only gave a deep sigh; and then he stretched himself out on his bed, thanking the duke and duchess for their kindness — not because he had any fear of that catty, enchanting, cowbell-ringing rabble, but because he had recognised the good intention with which they had come to help him. The duke and duchess left him to rest and went off, sorry at the bad outcome of the trick; for they had not believed that that adventure would turn out so heavy and so costly for Don Quixote, whom it cost five days of being shut up in bed, where another adventure happened to him more agreeable than the last — which his historian does not want to tell now, so as to attend to Sancho Panza, who was going about very busily and very amusingly in his government.

Chapter 47: Where the Account of How Sancho Panza Conducted Himself in His Government Is Carried Further

The history tells that from the court they took Sancho Panza to a sumptuous palace, where in a great hall a royal and spotless table was laid; and, as soon as Sancho came into the hall, shawms sounded and four pages came out to give him water for his hands, which Sancho received with a great deal of gravity.

The music stopped, and Sancho sat down at the head of the table, because there was no other seat and no other cover on the whole of it. At his side there stood a personage who afterwards proved to be a doctor, with a whalebone wand in his hand. They lifted a very rich white cloth that was covering the fruit and a great variety of dishes of different foods; a man who looked like a student said grace, and a page put a laced bib on Sancho; another, who did the office of steward, set a dish of fruit in front of him.

But he had hardly eaten a mouthful when the man with the wand touched the dish with it, and it was taken away from in front of him with the greatest speed; but the steward brought him another with different food on it. Sancho was going to try it; but before he could reach it or taste it, the wand had touched it and a page had taken it up as quickly as he had the fruit. Which Sancho seeing, he was left bewildered; and, looking at everybody, he asked whether this dinner was to be eaten like a conjuring trick. To which the man with the wand answered:

"It is not to be eaten, my lord governor, except as is the use and custom in other isles where there are governors. I, sir, am a doctor, and I am salaried in this isle to be doctor to its governors; and I look after their health a great deal more than after my own, studying night and day and taking the measure of the governor's constitution, so as to get his cure right when he falls ill. And the chief thing I do is to attend his dinners and suppers, and to let him eat what seems to me suitable for him, and to take away from him what I imagine will do him harm and be noxious to his stomach.

"And so I ordered the dish of fruit taken away, for being excessively moist; and the dish of the other food I ordered taken away too, for being excessively hot and having a great many spices in it, which increase thirst; and the man who drinks a great deal kills and consumes the radical moisture, in which life consists."

"In that case, that dish of partridges over there, which are roasted and, to my mind, well seasoned, will do me no harm."

To which the doctor answered:

"Those the lord governor shall not eat as long as I have life in me."

"Well, why not?" said Sancho.

And the doctor answered:

"Because our master Hippocrates, the pole star and the light of medicine, says in an aphorism of his: Omnis saturatio mala, perdices autem pessima — which means, 'All surfeit is bad, but surfeit of partridges is the worst of all.'"

"If that is so," said Sancho, "let the doctor see, of all the dishes on this table, which will do me most good and least harm, and let me eat of it without his cudgelling it away from me; because, by the governor's life — and so may God let me enjoy it — I am dying of hunger; and denying me my food, however it may grieve the doctor and whatever more he may say to me, will sooner be taking my life away from me than adding to it."

"Your worship is right, my lord governor," answered the doctor; "and so it is my opinion that your worship should not eat any of those stewed rabbits over there, because it is a hairy sort of food. Of that veal, if it had not been roasted and pickled, one might still have tried it; but there is no call for it."

And Sancho said:

"That great dish over there that is steaming further along seems to me to be an olla podrida — that great mixed stew; and, given the variety of things there are in such stews, I cannot fail to come across something in it that will be to my taste and to my profit."

"Absit!" said the doctor. "Let so bad a thought go far from us: there is nothing in the world worse to live on than an olla podrida. Away with the mixed stews to the canons, or to the rectors of colleges, or to peasant weddings, and let them leave the tables of governors free, where all niceness and all refinement must be present. And the reason is that always and everywhere and by everybody simple medicines are more esteemed than compound ones, because in simple ones you cannot go wrong and in compound ones you can, by altering the quantity of the things they are compounded of. But what I know the lord governor must eat now, to preserve his health and strengthen it, is a hundred little rolled wafers and some thin little slices of quince paste, which will settle his stomach and help his digestion."

Hearing this, Sancho leaned back against the back of his chair and looked hard at this doctor, and in a grave voice asked him what he was called and where he had studied. To which he answered:

"I, my lord governor, am called Doctor Pedro Recio de Agüero, and I am a native of a place called Tirteafuera, which is between Caracuel and Almodóvar del Campo, on the right-hand side; and I have my doctor's degree from the university of Osuna."

To which Sancho answered, all fired up with choler:

"Well, Doctor Pedro Recio de Mal Agüero — Pedro Recio of Ill Omen — native of Get-You-Gone, a place that lies on the right-hand side as you go from Caracuel to Almodóvar del Campo, graduated at Osuna: get out of my sight this instant, or I swear by the sun that I shall take up a cudgel and that, beginning with you, there will not be a doctor left in the whole isle — at least of those I understand to be ignorant ones; for the wise, prudent and judicious doctors I shall set on top of my head and honour like divine persons.

"And I say again, Pedro Recio, be off with you from here; if not, I shall take this chair I am sitting in and smash it over your head. And let them ask me for it at my audit: I shall clear myself by saying that I did God a service in killing a bad doctor, who is the hangman of the commonwealth. And give me something to eat, or else take back your government; for an office that does not feed the man who holds it is not worth two beans."

The doctor was thrown into a fright at seeing the governor so choleric, and he wanted to do a get-you-gone out of the hall — except that at that instant a post horn sounded in the street; and the steward, leaning out of the window, came back saying:

"A courier is coming from the duke my lord; he must be bringing some despatch of importance."

The courier came in sweating and alarmed, and, taking a packet out of his bosom, put it into the governor's hands; and Sancho put it into the steward's, ordering him to read the address, which went thus: To Don Sancho Panza, governor of the isle of Barataria, into his own hand or into his secretary's. Hearing which, Sancho said:

"Who here is my secretary?"

And one of those present answered:

"I, sir, because I know how to read and write, and I am a Biscayan."

"With that addition," said Sancho, "you could very well be secretary to the emperor himself. Open that packet and see what it says."

The newborn secretary did so; and, having read what it said, he said that it was business to be dealt with in private. Sancho ordered the hall cleared, and that nobody should stay in it but the steward and the head steward; and the rest, and the doctor, went off. And then the secretary read the letter, which went like this:

It has come to my notice, Señor Don Sancho Panza, that certain enemies of mine and of that isle are to make a furious assault on it, I do not know on what night. It will be well to keep watch and be on the alert, so that they may not take you unprepared. I know too, from true spies, that four disguised persons have come into that place to take your life, because they are afraid of your wits. Keep your eye open, and look to who comes to speak to you, and do not eat anything they may offer you. I shall take care to come to your help if you find yourself in difficulty, and in everything you will act as is expected of your understanding. From this place, the sixteenth of August, at four in the morning.

Your friend,

The Duke.

Sancho was astounded, and the bystanders showed themselves astounded too; and, turning to the steward, he said:

"What must be done now, and it must be at once, is to put Doctor Recio in a dungeon; because if anybody is going to kill me, it is he, and by the most lingering and the worst kind of death, which is hunger."

"It seems to me too," said the head steward, "that your worship should not eat any of what is on this table, because it has been presented by some nuns; and, as they say, behind the cross stands the devil."

"I do not deny it," answered Sancho, "and for now give me a piece of bread and about four pounds of grapes, for no poison can come in them; because in fact I cannot get by without eating, and if we are to be ready for these battles that threaten us, it will be necessary to be well kept up, since it is guts that carry the heart and not the heart the guts.

"And you, secretary, answer the duke my lord and tell him that what he orders shall be carried out as he orders it, without a point missing; and you shall kiss my lady the duchess's hands on my behalf, and say that I beg her not to forget to send my letter and my bundle to my wife Teresa Panza by a special messenger, since I shall take it as a great kindness and shall take care to serve her with everything my strength can reach. And on your way you may jam in a kissing of hands to my lord Don Quixote of La Mancha, so that he may see that I am grateful bread. And you, as a good secretary and a good Biscayan, may add anything you like and whatever comes best to the point. And let this cloth be taken up and give me something to eat, and I shall deal with all the spies and murderers and enchanters that may come at me and at my isle."

At this a page came in and said:

"There is a farmer here with business who wants to speak to Your Lordship on a matter, as he says, of great importance."

"This is a strange business," said Sancho, "with these people with business. Is it possible that they are so foolish as not to see that hours like these are not the ones for coming to do business in? Are we who govern, we who are judges, not by any chance men of flesh and bone, and is it not necessary that they should let us rest for as long as need requires — or do they want us to be made of marble? By God and in my conscience, if the government lasts me — which it will not, as far as I can see through it — I shall bring more than one man of business to heel. Now tell that good man to come in; but let it first be made sure that he is not one of the spies or one of my murderers."

"No, sir," answered the page, "because he looks like a soul of a pitcher; and either I know very little, or he is as good as good bread."

"There is nothing to fear," said the steward, "for we are all here."

"Would it be possible," said Sancho, "head steward, now that Doctor Pedro Recio is not here, for me to eat something with some weight and substance to it, even if it were a piece of bread and an onion?"

"Tonight at supper the shortcomings of the dinner shall be made up, and Your Lordship will be satisfied and paid," said the head steward.

"God grant it," answered Sancho.

And with this the farmer came in, who was of very good appearance, and from a thousand leagues off you could see that he was good and a good soul. The first thing he said was:

"Which is the lord governor here?"

"Who should he be," answered the secretary, "but the man sitting in the chair?"

"I bow myself, then, before him," said the farmer.

And, going down on his knees, he asked him for his hand to kiss it. Sancho refused it, and ordered him to get up and say what he wanted. The farmer did so, and then said:

"I, sir, am a farmer, a native of Miguel Turra, a place two leagues from Ciudad Real."

"We have another Get-You-Gone!" said Sancho. "Speak, brother, for what I can tell you is that I know Miguel Turra very well, and that it is not very far from my village."

"The case is, then, sir," the farmer went on, "that I, by God's mercy, am married in the peace and presence of the Holy Roman Catholic Church; I have two sons who are students, the younger of whom is studying to be a bachelor and the elder to be a licentiate. I am a widower, because my wife died — or, better said, a bad doctor killed her for me by purging her when she was pregnant. And if God had been pleased for the birth to come out into the light, and if it had been a son, I would have set him to study to be a doctor, so that he should not envy his brothers the bachelor and the licentiate."

"So that," said Sancho, "if your wife had not died, or if they had not killed her, you would not be a widower now."

"No, sir, on no account," answered the farmer.

"We are in a fine way!" replied Sancho. "Get on, brother, for it is more the hour for sleeping than for doing business."

"I say, then," said the farmer, "that this son of mine who is to be a bachelor fell in love in that same village with a maiden called Clara Perlerina, daughter of Andrés Perlerino, an extremely rich farmer; and this name of Perlerines does not come to them from their ancestry or from any other family line, but because everybody of that line is palsy-struck — palsied being perlático in our speech — and, to better the name, they call them Perlerines, as though from perla, a pearl. Although, if the truth is to be told, the girl is like an oriental pearl; and looked at from the right-hand side she seems a flower of the field — from the left not so much, because she is missing that eye, which she lost to smallpox. And although the pits on her face are many and large, those who love her well say that they are not pits but graves in which the souls of her lovers are buried.

"She is so clean that, so as not to dirty her face, she carries her nose, as they say, turned up, so that it looks for all the world as if it were running away from her mouth. And with all this she looks extremely well, because she has a large mouth; and if she were not missing ten or twelve teeth and grinders, she could pass and hold her own among the best formed. Of her lips I have nothing to say, because they are so fine and delicate that if lips could be wound on a reel they could make a skein of them; but as they are a different colour from the one commonly in use for lips, they look miraculous, because they are mottled with blue and green and aubergine. And let the lord governor forgive me if I go painting so minutely the parts of the girl who in the end is to be my daughter; for I love her well and she does not seem bad to me."

"Paint whatever you like," said Sancho, "for I am enjoying the painting; and if I had eaten, there would have been no better dessert for me than your portrait."

"That is at your service," answered the farmer, "but the time will come when we shall be, if we are not now. And I say, sir, that if I could paint her gracefulness and the height of her body it would be a thing to wonder at; but it cannot be, on account of her being bent double and drawn in, and having her knees at her mouth. And with all that, it can be seen well enough that if she could straighten up she would knock her head on the ceiling. And she would have given her hand in marriage to my bachelor before now, only she cannot stretch it out, since it is knotted up; and even so, in her long, grooved nails you can see her goodness and her good making."

"That is well," said Sancho; "and take it, brother, that you have now painted her from head to foot. What is it you want now? And come to the point without going round about or down alleys, without scraps or additions."

"I should like, sir," answered the farmer, "your worship to do me the favour of giving me a letter of recommendation to my future in-law, begging him to be pleased for this marriage to be made, since we are not unequal in the goods of fortune or in those of nature. Because, to tell the truth, my lord governor, my son is possessed, and there is not a day when the malignant spirits do not torment him three or four times; and from having fallen once into the fire, he has his face wrinkled like parchment and his eyes rather watery and running. But he has the disposition of an angel, and if it were not that he beats himself and punches himself, he would be a blessed creature."

"Do you want anything else, good man?" replied Sancho.

"I should like one other thing," said the farmer, "except that I do not dare to say it. But let it come, for after all it is not going to rot in my breast, hit or miss. I say, sir, that I should like your worship to give me three hundred or six hundred ducats to help with my bachelor's marriage portion — I mean to help with setting up his house; because in the end they must live by themselves, without being subject to the impertinences of their in-laws."

"See whether you want anything else," said Sancho, "and do not leave it unsaid out of awkwardness or shame."

"No, certainly not," answered the farmer.

And he had hardly said this when the governor got to his feet, seized the chair he had been sitting in and said:

"I swear, you rustic and ill-mannered lout, that if you do not get away and hide yourself out of my presence this instant, I shall break your head open with this chair! You whoreson rascal, painter for the devil himself — and at this hour you come and ask me for six hundred ducats? And where have I got them, you stinking creature? And why should I give them to you even if I had them, you sly idiot? And what is Miguel Turra to me, or the whole line of the Perlerines? Get away from me, I say; if not, by the life of the duke my lord, I shall do what I have said! You cannot be from Miguel Turra, but some sly rogue that hell has sent here to tempt me. Tell me, you soulless man, it is not yet a day and a half since I have had the government, and already you want me to have six hundred ducats?"

The head steward made signs to the farmer to get out of the hall, which he did with his head down and, to all appearances, afraid that the governor would carry out his rage — for the great rogue knew how to do his office very well.

But let us leave Sancho with his choler, and let peace go round the ring, and let us come back to Don Quixote, whom we left with his face bandaged and treated for the cat's wounds, which he did not get better of for a week; and on one of those days there happened to him what Cide Hamete promises to tell with the exactness and the truth with which he generally tells the things of this history, however small they may be.

Chapter 48: Of What Happened to Don Quixote with Doña Rodríguez, the Duchess's Duenna, with Other Events Worthy of Writing Down and of Everlasting Memory

The badly wounded Don Quixote was extremely vexed and melancholy, his face bandaged and marked — not by the hand of God but by the claws of a cat: misfortunes that belong to knight-errantry. Six days he spent without coming out in public; and on one of those nights, being awake and unable to sleep, thinking about his misfortunes and about Altisidora's pursuit of him, he heard somebody opening the door of his room with a key, and at once imagined that the enamoured maiden was coming to make an assault on his chastity and put him in danger of failing in the faith he owed to his lady Dulcinea of El Toboso.

"No," he said, believing his own imagination — and he said it in a voice that could be heard; "the greatest beauty on earth shall not be enough to make me leave off adoring the one I have graven and stamped in the middle of my heart and in the deepest part of my entrails, whether you are, my lady, transformed into an onion-fed peasant girl, or into a nymph of the golden Tagus weaving cloths of gold and silk, or whether Merlin or Montesinos keeps you where they please; for wherever you are you are mine, and wherever I am I have been and shall be yours."

The finishing of these words and the opening of the door were all one. He got up on his feet on the bed, wrapped from top to bottom in a coverlet of yellow satin, a nightcap on his head, and his face and his moustaches bandaged — his face because of the scratches and his moustaches so that they should not droop and fall; in which get-up he looked like the most extraordinary phantom that could be imagined.

He fixed his eyes on the door; and when he was expecting to see the conquered and wounded Altisidora come in by it, he saw come in a most reverend duenna with white headcloths, hemmed and so long that they covered her and mantled her from foot to head. Between the fingers of her left hand she carried half a lighted candle, and with her right she was shading herself so that the light should not get in her eyes, which were covered by a very large pair of spectacles. She came stepping very quietly, and moved her feet softly.

Don Quixote watched her from his lookout; and when he saw her get-up and noticed her silence, he thought that some witch or sorceress was coming in that dress to work some evil upon him, and he began to cross himself in great haste. The vision came closer; and when it got to the middle of the room it raised its eyes and saw the haste with which Don Quixote was making crosses. And if he was terrified at seeing such a figure, she was frightened at seeing his; because as soon as she saw him so tall and so yellow, with the coverlet and with the bandages that disfigured him, she gave a great shout, saying:

"Jesus! What is this that I see?"

And in her fright the candle fell out of her hands; and, finding herself in the dark, she turned her back to go, and in her fear she tripped over her own skirts and came down in a great fall. Don Quixote, terrified, began to say:

"I conjure you, phantom, or whatever you are, to tell me who you are and to tell me what it is you want of me. If you are a soul in torment, tell me so, and I shall do for you everything my strength can reach; for I am a Catholic Christian and a friend to doing good to everybody, and it was for this that I took up the order of knight-errantry that I profess, whose exercise stretches even to doing good to the souls in purgatory."

The bruised duenna, hearing herself conjured, gathered Don Quixote's fear from her own, and in a distressed and low voice answered him:

"Señor Don Quixote — if by any chance your worship is Don Quixote — I am no phantom or vision or soul out of purgatory, as your worship must have thought, but Doña Rodríguez, my lady the duchess's duenna of honour, who comes to your worship with one of those needs your worship is in the habit of relieving."

"Tell me, Señora Doña Rodríguez," said Don Quixote, "does your worship by any chance come to act as a go-between? Because I must let you know that I am of no use to anybody, thanks to the peerless beauty of my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso. I say, in short, Señora Doña Rodríguez, that so long as your worship keeps out and sets aside all messages of love, you may go and light your candle again and come back, and we shall talk over whatever you may command and whatever comes best to your pleasure — leaving out, as I say, all provoking coquetry."

"I, sir, with a message from anybody?" answered the duenna. "Your worship knows me badly. Why, I am not yet of such advanced years as to take refuge in childishness of that kind; for, God be praised, I have my soul in my flesh and all my teeth and grinders in my mouth, except a few that some catarrhs have stolen from me, which in this country of Aragon are so common. But wait a little for me, your worship: I shall go out to light my candle and come back in an instant to tell my troubles, as to the reliever of all the troubles in the world."

And, without waiting for an answer, she went out of the room, where Don Quixote was left quiet and thoughtful, waiting for her; but at once a thousand thoughts came over him about this new adventure, and it seemed to him a badly done and a worse thought-out thing to put himself in danger of breaking the faith he had promised his lady, and he said to himself:

"Who knows whether the devil, who is subtle and crafty, may want to deceive me now with a duenna, when he has not been able to do it with empresses, queens, duchesses, marchionesses or countesses? For I have heard it said many times and by many judicious people that if he can, he will sooner give her to you snub-nosed than aquiline. And who knows whether this solitude, this occasion and this silence may wake my sleeping desires and make me at the end of my years fall where I have never yet stumbled? And in cases like this it is better to flee than to wait for the battle.

"But I must not be in my right mind, since I am saying and thinking such absurdities; for it is not possible that a white-coifed, long-drawn-out, spectacled duenna could move or raise a lascivious thought in the most soulless breast in the world. Is there by any chance a duenna on earth with good flesh on her? Is there by any chance a duenna on the globe who is not impertinent and puckered and affected? Away with you, then, you duennaish herd, useless for any human pleasure! Oh, how well that lady did who they say kept two dummy duennas with their spectacles and their sewing cushions at the end of her drawing room, as though they were at work — and those statues served her as well for the dignity of the room as real duennas would!"

And, saying this, he threw himself off the bed, meaning to shut the door and not let Señora Rodríguez in; but when he got there to shut it, Señora Rodríguez was already coming back with a white wax candle lit. And when she saw Don Quixote closer to, wrapped in the coverlet, with the bandages and the nightcap, she was frightened again; and, drawing back a couple of steps, she said:

"Are we safe, sir knight? Because I do not take it for a very decent sign that your worship should have got out of his bed."

"That is the very thing I should ask, madam," answered Don Quixote; "and so I ask whether I shall be safe from being assaulted and forced."

"Of whom and from whom do you ask that safety, sir knight?" answered the duenna.

"Of you and from you I ask it," replied Don Quixote; "because I am not made of marble nor you of bronze, and it is not ten in the morning now but midnight, and even a little past, as I imagine, and in a room more shut up and secret than the cave must have been where the treacherous and daring Aeneas enjoyed the beautiful and merciful Dido. But give me your hand, madam, for I want no greater safety than that of my own continence and reserve, and the safety those most reverend headcloths offer."

And, saying this, he kissed his own right hand and took hold of hers, which she gave him with the same ceremonies.

Here Cide Hamete puts in a parenthesis and says that by Muhammad he would have given, to see the two of them going along hand in hand like that from the door to the bed, the better of the two Moorish cloaks he owned.

Don Quixote got into his bed at last, and Doña Rodríguez was left sitting in a chair somewhat away from the bed, without taking off her spectacles or putting down the candle. Don Quixote curled himself up and covered himself all over, leaving nothing but his face uncovered; and, the two of them having settled down, the first to break the silence was Don Quixote, saying:

"Your worship may now, my lady Doña Rodríguez, unstitch yourself and disgorge everything you have inside that troubled heart and those wounded entrails of yours; for it shall be heard by me with chaste ears and helped with merciful deeds."

"So I believe," answered the duenna; "for from your worship's gentle and agreeable presence nothing could be expected but so Christian an answer.

"The case is, then, Señor Don Quixote, that although your worship sees me sitting in this chair and in the middle of the kingdom of Aragon, and in the dress of a worn-out and knocked-about duenna, I am a native of the Asturias of Oviedo and of a family crossed by a great many of the best in that province. But my short luck and the carelessness of my parents, who fell into poverty before their time without knowing how or why, brought me to the court, to Madrid, where for the sake of peace and to avoid worse misfortunes my parents placed me to serve as a sewing maid to a lady of quality. And I want to make your worship knowing that in hemstitching and white work nobody has ever put a foot ahead of me in all my life.

"My parents left me in service and went back to their own country, and a few years later they must have gone to heaven, for they were exceedingly good and Catholic Christians. I was left an orphan, and dependent on the wretched wages and the pinched favours that are generally given to such servants in great houses. And at this time, without my giving any occasion for it, a squire of the household fell in love with me — a man already on in years, bearded and well set up and, above all, as much a gentleman as the king, because he came from the northern mountains.

"We did not carry on our love so secretly that it did not come to my mistress's notice; and she, to save chattering and gossip, married us in the peace and presence of the Holy Mother Roman Catholic Church. Of which marriage there was born a daughter, to finish off my good luck if I had any — not that I died in childbirth, for I had her straight and in season, but because a little later my husband died of a certain fright he had; and if there were room now to tell it, I know your worship would be amazed."

And with this she began to weep tenderly, and said:

"Forgive me, your worship, Señor Don Quixote, for it is not in my power to help it; because every time I remember my poor ill-fated man my eyes fill with tears. God bless me, and with what dignity he used to carry my lady on the crupper of a mighty mule, black as jet itself! For in those days coaches and chairs were not in use, as they say they are now, and ladies rode on the cruppers of their squires' mules. This at least I cannot leave untold, so that my good husband's breeding and punctiliousness may be noticed.

"Coming into the Calle de Santiago in Madrid, which is rather narrow, there came out along it a judge of the court with two constables in front of him; and as soon as my good squire saw him he turned the mule's reins about, making as if to go back and escort him. My mistress, who was riding on the crupper, said to him in a low voice: 'What are you doing, you wretched man? Do you not see that I am here?' The judge, out of courtesy, drew rein on his horse and said to him: 'Go your own way, sir, for it is I who ought to be escorting my lady Doña Casilda' — for that was my mistress's name.

"Still my husband kept insisting, with his cap in his hand, on wanting to go and escort the judge; seeing which, my mistress, full of choler and annoyance, took a stout pin — or I believe a bodkin — out of her case and drove it into his back, so that my husband gave a great shout and twisted his body in such a way that he brought his mistress down on the ground. Two footmen of hers ran to lift her up, and so did the judge and the constables. The Guadalajara Gate was thrown into an uproar — I mean the idle crowd that stands about there. My mistress came home on foot, and my husband went off to a barber's house saying that his entrails were pierced right through.

"My husband's courtesy got about so widely that the boys chased him through the streets; and for this reason, and because he was somewhat short-sighted, my lady the duchess dismissed him; from grief at which, without any doubt, I hold for myself that his mortal illness came on him.

"I was left a widow and unprotected, with a daughter on my hands who kept growing in beauty like the foam of the sea. Finally, as I had a name for being a great needlewoman, my lady the duchess, who was then newly married to the duke my lord, wanted to bring me with her to this kingdom of Aragon, and my daughter neither more nor less. And there, with days going and days coming, my daughter grew, and with her all the charm in the world: she sings like a lark, she steps like a thought, she dances like a mad thing, she reads and writes like a schoolmaster and she reckons like a miser. Of her cleanness I say nothing: running water is no cleaner. And she must be now, if I remember rightly, sixteen years, five months and three days old, one more or less.
