"In short: with this girl of mine there fell in love the son of an extremely rich farmer who lives in a village of the duke my lord's, not very far from here. In fact I do not know how or why, but they came together, and, under his word of being her husband, he made a mock of my daughter and will not keep it. And although the duke my lord knows about it, because I have complained to him not once but many times and asked him to order this farmer to marry my daughter, he turns a merchant's ear and will hardly listen to me. And the reason is that, since the deceiver's father is so rich and lends him money and stands surety for his debts at every turn, he does not want to displease him or give him any distress in any way.

"I should like, then, my dear sir, your worship to take in hand the undoing of this wrong, either by entreaty or by arms; since, as all the world says, your worship was born into it to undo them and to right injustices and protect the wretched. And let your worship set before you my daughter's orphaned state, her gracefulness, her youth, with all the good parts I have said she has; for in God and in my conscience, of all the maidens my lady has, there is not one who comes up to the sole of her shoe; and one they call Altisidora, who is the one they hold to be the freest and the most gallant, put in comparison with my daughter does not come within two leagues of her.

"Because I want your worship to know, my dear sir, that all is not gold that glitters; for this little Altisidora has more of presumption about her than of beauty, and more of the forward than of the modest, besides not being very healthy — for she has a certain weary breath about her that a man cannot bear to be next to for a moment. And even my lady the duchess... I had better be quiet, for they say that walls have ears."

"What of my lady the duchess, on my life, Señora Doña Rodríguez?" asked Don Quixote.

"With that adjuration," answered the duenna, "I cannot help answering what I am asked with the whole truth. Does your worship see, Señor Don Quixote, the beauty of my lady the duchess, that complexion of her face, which looks like nothing but a polished and burnished sword blade, those two cheeks of milk and carmine, which have the sun in the one and the moon in the other, and that gallantry with which she goes treading and even scorning the ground, so that she seems to be scattering health wherever she passes? Well, your worship must know that she can be grateful for it first to God and then to two issues she has in her two legs, through which all the bad humours drain away that the doctors say she is full of."

"Holy Mary!" said Don Quixote. "And is it possible that my lady the duchess has such drains? I would not have believed it if barefoot friars had told me; but since Señora Doña Rodríguez says so, it must be true. But such fountains, and in such places, must run not with humours but with liquid amber. Truly I now finally believe that this business of having issues made must be an important thing for one's health."

Don Quixote had hardly finished saying this when with a great bang the doors of the room were thrown open; and at the shock of the bang the candle fell out of Doña Rodríguez's hand, and the chamber was left like a wolf's mouth, as the saying goes. Then the poor duenna felt two hands seizing her by the throat so tightly that they did not let her squeak; and another person, very quickly and without saying a word, lifted her skirts and, with what seemed to be a slipper, began to give her so many lashes that it was a thing to pity.

And although Don Quixote did pity her, he did not stir from his bed and did not know what it could be, and stayed still and quiet, and even fearing that the round and the drubbing of lashes might come his way. And his fear was not empty; because, having left the duenna ground to a pulp, the silent executioners — and she did not dare to complain — came to Don Quixote, and, unwrapping him from the sheet and the coverlet, pinched him so thick and so hard that he could not help defending himself with his fists; and all this in an astonishing silence.

The battle lasted nearly half an hour; the phantoms went out; Doña Rodríguez gathered up her skirts, and, groaning over her misfortune, went out at the door without saying a word to Don Quixote, who, sore and pinched, confused and thoughtful, was left alone — where we shall leave him, longing to know who the perverse enchanter had been who had put him in that state. But that shall be told in its own time, for Sancho Panza is calling us, and the good order of the history requires it.

Chapter 49: Of What Happened to Sancho Panza While Going the Rounds of His Isle

We left the great governor annoyed and vexed with that painting, sly farmer — who, coached by the steward, and the steward by the duke, were making game of Sancho. But he held his own with all of them, dolt and rough thick-set fellow though he was; and he said to those who were with him, and to Doctor Pedro Recio, who, once the secret of the duke's letter was over, had come back into the hall:

"Now truly I understand that judges and governors must be, or have to be, of bronze, so as not to feel the importunities of people with business, who at all hours and at all times want to be listened to and dealt with, attending only to their own affairs, come what may. And if the poor judge does not listen to them and deal with them, either because he cannot or because that is not the time set aside for giving them audience, then they curse him and gossip about him and gnaw his bones, and even go into his family tree.

"Foolish man of business, idiot man of business, do not hurry: wait for the season and the right moment for doing business. Do not come at dinner time or at sleeping time, for judges are of flesh and bone and must give nature what nature naturally asks of them — unless it is I, who do not give mine anything to eat, thanks to the doctor Pedro Recio of Get-You-Gone here present, who wants me to die of hunger and declares that this death is life; and may God give him and all his breed the same. I mean the breed of bad doctors, for the good ones deserve palms and laurels."

Everybody who knew Sancho Panza was astonished to hear him talk so elegantly, and they did not know what to put it down to except that great offices and charges either sharpen the wits or dull them. Finally Doctor Pedro Recio Agüero of Get-You-Gone promised to give him supper that night, even if it went beyond all the aphorisms of Hippocrates.

With this the governor was content, and he waited with great anxiety for the night and the supper hour to come; and although time, to his mind, was standing still without moving from its place, still the so much longed-for hour did come round for him, when they gave him for supper a hash of beef with onion and some boiled calves' feet from a beast somewhat on in years. He fell to on it all with more pleasure than if they had given him francolins of Milan, pheasants of Rome, veal of Sorrento, partridges of Morón or geese of Lavajos; and, in the middle of supper, turning to the doctor, he said:

"Look, doctor: from now on do not bother to give me dainty things or exquisite dishes to eat, because it will be taking my stomach off its hinges. It is used to goat, to beef, to bacon, to dried meat, to turnips and to onions; and if by any chance it is given other palace dishes, it takes them squeamishly and sometimes with disgust.

"What the head steward can do is to bring me these things they call olla podridas — and the more rotten they are the better they smell — and into them he can pack and shut up anything he likes, so long as it is food, and I shall thank him for it and pay him for it one day. And let nobody make game of me, because either we are or we are not: let us all live and eat in good peace and fellowship, for when God sends the dawn, he sends it for everybody.

"I shall govern this isle without giving up a right or taking a bribe, and let everybody keep their eye open and look out for the bolt; because I let them know that the devil is in Cantillana, and that if they give me cause they shall see wonders. No — make yourself honey and the flies will eat you."

"Certainly, my lord governor," said the head steward, "your worship is quite right in everything you have said; and I offer, in the name of all the islanders of this isle, that they shall serve your worship with all punctuality, love and good will; because the gentle manner of governing your worship has shown in these beginnings gives them no room to do or think anything that could redound to your worship's disservice."

"I believe it," answered Sancho, "and they would be fools if they did or thought otherwise. And I say again that care is to be taken with my keep and with my grey's, which is what matters most and comes most to the point in this business; and, when the hour comes, let us go the rounds, for it is my intention to clear this isle of every kind of filth and of vagabond people, idlers and badly occupied folk. Because I want you to know, my friends, that idle and lazy people are in a commonwealth what the drones are in a hive, which eat the honey the working bees make. I mean to favour the farmers, keep their privileges to the gentry, reward the virtuous and, above all, have respect for religion and for the honour of religious men. What do you think of that, my friends? Am I saying something, or am I breaking my head for nothing?"

"Your worship says so much, my lord governor," said the steward, "that I am amazed to see a man as unlettered as your worship — who, as I believe, has no letters at all — say such things and so many of them, full of judgements and of warnings, so far outside everything that those who sent us and those of us who came here expected of your worship's wits. Every day new things are seen in the world: jokes turn into earnest and the jokers find themselves the ones joked with."

Night came, and the governor had supper with the doctor Recio's leave. They got themselves ready for the rounds; he went out with the steward, the secretary and the head steward, and the chronicler who had the task of putting his deeds on record, and constables and clerks, so many that they could have made up a middling squadron. Sancho went in the middle with his rod, and there was nothing else to look at; and, a few streets of the place having been walked, they heard the noise of sword-strokes. They ran there and found that it was only two men quarrelling; who, seeing the law coming, kept still. And one of them said:

"Help, in God's name and the king's! Is it to be borne that people are robbed in a settled town like this one, and that men go out to hold up travellers in the middle of the streets?"

"Calm yourself, honest man," said Sancho, "and tell me the cause of this quarrel, for I am the governor."

The other opponent said:

"My lord governor, I shall tell it as shortly as I can. Your worship must know that this gentleman has just now won more than a thousand reals in this gambling house opposite here — and God knows how; and I, being present, judged more than one doubtful throw in his favour, against everything my conscience was telling me. He walked off with his winnings; and when I was expecting him to give me at least one crown as a tip, as is the use and custom of giving it to men of quality like me, who stand by to see fair play through good and bad and to back up wrong throws and prevent quarrels, he pocketed his money and went out of the house.

"I came out after him in a rage, and with good, courteous words asked him to give me at least eight reals, since he knows I am an honourable man and have no trade or benefice, because my parents neither taught me one nor left me one; and the sly fellow — who is no more a thief than Cacus and no more a cardsharp than Andradilla — would not give me more than four reals. So your worship may see, my lord governor, how little shame and how little conscience! But upon my word, if your worship had not come along, I would have made him vomit up his winnings and he would have learnt how many notches the steelyard had."

"What do you say to this?" asked Sancho.

And the other answered that everything his opponent said was true, and that he had not been willing to give him more than four reals because he gave them him many times; and that people who expect tips must be civil and take with a cheerful face whatever they are given, without going into accounts with the winners — unless they knew for certain that they were sharpers and that what they had won was ill won. And that as a sign that he himself was an honest man and not a thief, as the other said, there was no greater one than his not having been willing to give him anything; for sharpers are always tributaries to the onlookers who know them.

"That is so," said the steward. "See, your worship, my lord governor, what is to be done with these men."

"What is to be done is this," answered Sancho. "You, winner, good or bad or indifferent, give this slasher of yours a hundred reals at once; and, what is more, you must lay out thirty for the poor prisoners in the gaol. And you, who have no trade and no benefice and go about as a spare man in this isle, take those hundred reals at once, and tomorrow in the course of the day leave this isle, banished for ten years, on pain, if you break it, of serving them out in the next life, since I shall hang you from a gibbet, or at least the hangman will by my orders. And let nobody answer me back, or I shall lay my hand on him."

The one paid out, the other took it in; this one left the isle and that one went home; and the governor was left saying:

"Now either I have little power, or I shall do away with these gambling houses; for it comes through to me that they are very harmful."

"This one at least," said a clerk, "your worship will not be able to do away with, because it belongs to a great personage; and what he loses in a year is beyond comparison more than what he takes out of the cards. Against other gaming dens of less standing your worship may show your power, for those are the ones that do most harm and cover up most insolences. In the houses of knights of quality and of great lords the famous sharpers do not dare to use their tricks; and, since the vice of gambling has turned into a common practice, it is better that people should play in great houses than in some tradesman's, where after midnight they catch some poor wretch and flay him alive."

"Now, clerk," said Sancho, "I know there is a great deal to be said about that."

And at this a bailiff came up bringing a young man gripped by the arm, and said:

"My lord governor, this young fellow was coming towards us; and as soon as he made out the law he turned his back and began to run like a fallow deer — a sign that he must be some offender. I set off after him; and if it had not been that he tripped and fell, I should never have caught him."

"Why were you running away, man?" asked Sancho.

To which the young man answered:

"Sir, to save myself from answering the many questions that officers of the law ask."

"What is your trade?"

"Weaver."

"And what do you weave?"

"Lance-heads, by your worship's good leave."

"So you are a wit, are you? You fancy yourself a joker? Very good! And where were you going just now?"

"Sir, to take the air."

"And where does one take the air in this isle?"

"Where it blows."

"Good: you answer very much to the point! You are a judicious young man; but take it that I am the air and that I am blowing you astern, and steering you to the gaol. Seize him there, and take him off, for I shall see that he sleeps there tonight without any air!"

"By God," said the young man, "your worship will make me sleep in gaol about as soon as you will make me king!"

"Why, and why shall I not make you sleep in gaol?" answered Sancho. "Have I not the power to arrest you and let you go whenever I like?"

"However much power your worship may have," said the young man, "it will not be enough to make me sleep in gaol."

"How not?" replied Sancho. "Take him off at once, where he shall see the truth with his own eyes — however much the warder may want to use his interested generosity on him; for I shall lay a penalty of two thousand ducats on him if he lets you take a single step out of the gaol."

"All that is a laughing matter," answered the young man. "The point is that all the men alive today will not make me sleep in gaol."

"Tell me, you devil," said Sancho, "have you got some angel to get you out and take off the fetters I mean to have put on you?"

"Now, my lord governor," answered the young man very charmingly, "let us be reasonable and come to the point. Suppose your worship orders me to be taken to gaol, and that there they put fetters and chains on me and shut me in a dungeon, and heavy penalties are laid on the warder if he lets me out, and he carries it out just as he is ordered: with all this, if I choose not to sleep and to stay awake all night without shutting an eyelid, will your worship, with all your power, be enough to make me sleep if I do not want to?"

"Certainly not," said the secretary, "and the man has carried his point."

"So that," said Sancho, "you would not leave off sleeping for any other reason than your own will, and not out of any wish to go against mine."

"No, sir," said the young man, "not by any means."

"Then go, and God be with you," said Sancho; "go home and sleep, and God give you a good sleep, for I do not want to take it from you. But I advise you from now on not to make game of the law, because you will come across some officer who will hit you over the head with your own joke."

The young man went off, and the governor carried on with his rounds. And a little later two bailiffs came up bringing a man gripped by the arm, and said:

"My lord governor, this person who looks like a man is not one but a woman, and not an ugly one, and she comes dressed in man's clothes."

They brought two or three lanterns up to her eyes, in whose light they made out a woman's face, apparently of sixteen years or a few more, her hair gathered up in a net of gold and green silk, and as beautiful as a thousand pearls. They looked her up and down, and saw that she was wearing crimson silk stockings with garters of white taffeta with gold and seed-pearl fringes; her breeches were green, of cloth of gold, and she wore a loose overjacket of the same, under which she had a doublet of the finest cloth of gold and white; and her shoes were white and a man's. She wore no sword at her belt but a very rich dagger, and on her fingers a great many very good rings.

Finally the girl pleased everybody, and none of those who saw her recognised her; and the natives of the place said they could not think who she might be, and those who were in on the tricks to be played on Sancho were the ones who were most astonished, because this event and discovery had not been arranged by them; and so they were in doubt, waiting to see where the business would end.

Sancho was thunderstruck at the girl's beauty, and asked her who she was, where she was going and what had moved her to dress in that way. She, with her eyes on the ground and in the deepest modest shame, answered:

"I cannot, sir, say so publicly what it mattered so much to me to keep secret. One thing I want to be understood: that I am no thief and no criminal, but an unfortunate maiden whom the force of jealousy has made break the decorum that is owing to modesty."

Hearing this, the steward said to Sancho:

"Have the people moved off, my lord governor, so that this lady may say what she wants with less embarrassment."

The governor ordered it so; everybody moved off except the steward, the head steward and the secretary. Finding themselves alone, then, the maiden went on, saying:

"I, gentlemen, am the daughter of Pedro Pérez Mazorca, the wool-farmer of this place, who often comes to my father's house."

"That does not stand up, madam," said the steward, "because I know Pedro Pérez very well and I know he has no children, neither son nor daughter. And what is more, you say he is your father and then add that he often comes to your father's house."

"I had already noticed that," said Sancho.

"Now, gentlemen, I am confused and do not know what I am saying," answered the maiden. "But the truth is that I am the daughter of Diego de la Llana, whom all your worships must know."

"That does stand up," answered the steward, "for I know Diego de la Llana and I know that he is a gentleman of quality and rich, and that he has a son and a daughter, and that since he was widowed there has been nobody in this whole place who can say he has seen his daughter's face; for he keeps her so shut up that he does not give the sun room to see her. And with all that, report says she is extremely beautiful."

"That is the truth," answered the maiden, "and I am that daughter; whether report lies or not about my beauty you will by now have found out for yourselves, gentlemen, since you have seen me."

And with this she began to weep tenderly. Seeing which, the secretary came up to the head steward's ear and said to him very softly:

"Without any doubt something of importance must have happened to this poor maiden, since in such a dress, and at such an hour, and being of such quality, she is out of her house."

"There is no doubting that," answered the head steward; "and what is more, her tears confirm that suspicion."

Sancho consoled her with the best words he knew, and asked her to tell them without any fear what had happened to her, for they would all try very earnestly and in every possible way to put it right.

"The case is, gentlemen," she answered, "that my father has kept me shut up for the last ten years, which are the same as the years the earth has been eating my mother. In our house they say Mass in a rich oratory; and in all this time I have not seen the sun of heaven by day or the moon and the stars by night, nor do I know what streets, squares or churches are, or even men, apart from my father and a brother of mine and Pedro Pérez the wool-farmer — who, because he comes into my house regularly, I took it into my head to say was my father, so as not to declare my own.

"This shutting up and this refusing to let me go out of the house, even to church, has for many days and months left me very disconsolate. I wanted to see the world, or at least the town where I was born, since it seemed to me that this desire did not go against the good decorum that maidens of quality owe to themselves. When I heard it said that they were running bulls and playing at canes and performing plays, I asked my brother, who is a year younger than I am, to tell me what those things were and a great many others I had never seen; he explained them to me in the best ways he knew, but it was all setting my desire to see them more alight.

"Finally, to shorten the story of my ruin, I say that I begged and asked my brother — and I wish I had never asked or begged such a thing..."

And she began to weep again. The steward said to her:

"Go on, madam, your worship, and finish telling us what has happened to you, for your words and your tears have us all in suspense."

"I have few left to say," answered the maiden, "though a great many tears left to weep; because badly placed desires can bring nothing with them but the like of this."

The maiden's beauty had settled in the head steward's soul, and he brought his lantern up again to look at her afresh; and it seemed to him that what she was weeping were not tears but seed pearls or the dew of the fields, and he even raised them higher and brought them up to oriental pearls; and he was hoping her misfortune might not be as great as the signs of her weeping and her sighs gave to understand. The governor was in despair at the girl's slowness in drawing out her story, and told her to leave off keeping them in suspense, for it was late and there was a great deal of the town still to be walked. She, between broken sobs and badly formed sighs, said:

"My misfortune is nothing else, and my ill luck is nothing else, but that I begged my brother to dress me in man's clothes with one of his suits and to take me out one night to see the whole town when our father was asleep. He, worn down by my entreaties, gave in to my wish; and, putting this suit on me and dressing himself in another of mine, which fits him as though he were born in it — because he has not a hair of beard and looks like nothing but a most beautiful girl — tonight, it must be an hour ago, more or less, we came out of the house.

"And, guided by our own boyish and disordered judgement, we went all round the town; and when we wanted to go back home we saw a great crowd of people coming, and my brother said to me: 'Sister, this must be the watch: make your feet light and put wings on them, and come running after me, so that they do not recognise us, for it would go badly with us.' And, saying this, he turned his back and began, I will not say to run, but to fly; and I, at less than six paces, fell down in the shock. And then the officer of the law came up who has brought me before your worships, where, for being a bad, capricious girl, I find myself shamed in front of so many people."

"So that in fact, madam," said Sancho, "no other mishap has happened to you, and jealousy, as you said at the beginning of your story, did not bring you out of your house?"

"Nothing has happened to me, and jealousy did not bring me out, but only the desire to see the world, which stretched no further than to seeing the streets of this town."

And what finished confirming that what the maiden said was true was the arrival of the bailiffs with her brother under arrest, whom one of them had caught when he ran off from his sister. He was wearing nothing but a rich petticoat and a short cloak of blue damask with fine gold braid, and his head bare of any headdress and adorned with nothing but his own hair, which was rings of gold, so fair and curly was it.

The governor, the steward and the head steward drew aside with him and, out of his sister's hearing, asked him how he came to be in that dress; and he, with no less shame and embarrassment, told the same as his sister had told — at which the enamoured head steward took great pleasure. But the governor said to them:

"Certainly, ladies and gentlemen, this has been a great piece of childishness; and to tell this piece of folly and daring there was no need for such long-drawn-out delays, or so many tears and sighs. By saying, 'We are so-and-so and so-and-so, and we came out of our parents' house on this contrivance simply out of curiosity, with no other design at all,' the story would have been over — and no little groans and little weepings and on and on."

"That is the truth," answered the maiden, "but your worships must know that the confusion I have been in has been so great that it has not let me keep the bounds I should have."

"Nothing has been lost," answered Sancho. "Let us go, and we shall leave your worships at your father's house; perhaps he will not have missed you. And from now on do not be such children, or so eager to see the world; for the honourable maiden keeps a broken leg and stays at home; and a woman and a hen are soon lost by wandering; and the girl who is eager to see is also eager to be seen. I say no more."

The young man thanked the governor for the kindness he wanted to do them in taking them back to their house; and so they made their way towards it, which was not very far from there. They arrived, then; and the brother threw a pebble at a grating, and at once a maidservant came down who was waiting for them and opened the door to them, and they went in — leaving everybody amazed both at their gracefulness and beauty and at the desire they had to see the world by night and without leaving the town. But they put it all down to their few years.

The head steward was left with his heart pierced through, and he resolved to ask her father for her hand in marriage the very next day, holding it for certain that he would not refuse him, since he was a servant of the duke's. And even Sancho was seized with a longing and a notion of marrying the young man to Sanchica his daughter, and he decided to bring it up in its own time, giving himself to understand that no husband could be refused to a governor's daughter.

With this the rounds of that night came to an end, and two days later the government came to an end too, with which all his designs were cut down and rubbed out, as will be seen further on.

Chapter 50: Where It Is Declared Who the Enchanters and Executioners Were Who Whipped the Duenna and Pinched and Scratched Don Quixote, with What Happened to the Page Who Carried the Letter to Teresa Sancha, Sancho Panza's Wife

Cide Hamete, that most exact investigator of the atoms of this true history, says that at the time when Doña Rodríguez came out of her room to go to Don Quixote's chamber, another duenna who slept with her heard her; and, since all duennas are fond of knowing, finding out and nosing about, she went after her so silently that good Rodríguez did not notice it. And as soon as the duenna saw her go into Don Quixote's chamber, so that the general habit all duennas have of being gossips should not be wanting in her, she went at that moment to blab it to her lady the duchess, telling her how Doña Rodríguez was in Don Quixote's room.

The duchess told the duke, and asked his leave for her and Altisidora to go and see what that duenna wanted with Don Quixote. The duke gave it her; and the two of them, with great care and quietness, step by step, came and set themselves next to the door of the room, and so close that they could hear everything that was being said inside. And when the duchess heard that Rodríguez had thrown the Aranjuez of her issues out into the street — Aranjuez being the royal garden famous for its fountains — she could not bear it, and no more could Altisidora; and so, full of choler and eager for revenge, they burst into the room and riddled Don Quixote and whipped the duenna in the way that has been told; because affronts that go straight at women's beauty and their vanity wake anger in them in a very great degree and set alight their desire for revenge.

The duchess told the duke what had happened to her, at which he was much amused; and the duchess, going on with her intention of playing tricks and getting entertainment out of Don Quixote, sent off the page who had played the figure of Dulcinea in the agreement about her disenchantment — which Sancho Panza had quite forgotten with the business of his government — to Teresa Panza his wife, with her husband's letter and with another from herself, and with a great string of rich coral as a present.

The history says, then, that the page was very judicious and sharp; and, wanting to serve his master and mistress, he set off very willingly for Sancho's village. And before going into it he saw a number of women washing in a stream, and asked them whether they could tell him if there lived in that place a woman called Teresa Panza, wife of a certain Sancho Panza, squire to a knight called Don Quixote of La Mancha. At which question a young girl who was washing got to her feet and said:

"That Teresa Panza is my mother, and that Sancho is my lord father, and that knight is our master."

"Then come, my girl," said the page, "and show me your mother, because I bring her a letter and a present from this father of yours."

"That I shall do very willingly, my dear sir," answered the girl, who looked to be about fourteen years old, a little more or less.

And, leaving the washing she was doing to another companion, without putting on her headdress or her shoes — for she was bare-legged and tousled — she leapt out in front of the page's mount and said:

"Come, your worship, for our house is at the entrance of the village, and my mother is in it, in great distress at having had no news of my lord father for many days now."

"Well, I am bringing her such good news," said the page, "that she has good reason to thank God for it."

Finally, leaping and running and skipping, the girl reached the village; and before going into her house she called out from the door:

"Come out, mother Teresa, come out, come out, for here comes a gentleman who brings letters and other things from my good father."

At which shouts Teresa Panza her mother came out, spinning a bundle of tow, in a brown skirt. It seemed, so short was it, that it had been cut off at her shame; and she had a little brown bodice too and a shift. She was not very old, though she looked to be past forty; but she was strong, upright, sinewy and weather-browned. And, seeing her daughter and the page on horseback, she said:

"What is this, child? What gentleman is this?"

"He is a servant of my lady Doña Teresa Panza," answered the page.

And, suiting the deed to the word, he threw himself off the horse and went with great humility to kneel down before Señora Teresa, saying:

"Give me your hands, your worship, my lady Doña Teresa, as the lawful and particular wife of Señor Don Sancho Panza, proper governor of the isle of Barataria."

"Oh, my dear sir, get up from there; do not do that," answered Teresa. "For I am nothing of a court lady but a poor farm woman, the daughter of a clod-crusher and the wife of a wandering squire and not of any governor!"

"Your worship," answered the page, "is the most worthy wife of a most archly worthy governor; and, as proof of this truth, let your worship receive this letter and this present."

And he took out of his pocket on the instant a string of coral with gold ends and threw it round her neck and said:

"This letter is from my lord the governor, and another I am carrying and this coral are from my lady the duchess, who sends me to your worship."

Teresa was thunderstruck, and her daughter neither more nor less, and the girl said:

"May they kill me if our master Don Quixote is not behind this — he must have given father the government or the earldom he had promised him so many times."

"That is the truth," answered the page: "out of respect for Señor Don Quixote, Señor Sancho is now governor of the isle of Barataria, as will be seen by this letter."

"Read it to me, your worship, sir gentleman," said Teresa; "for although I can spin, I cannot read a crumb."

"Nor I either," added Sanchica; "but wait for me here, and I shall go and call somebody to read it — either the curate himself or the bachelor Sansón Carrasco, who will come very willingly to hear news of my father."

"There is no need to call anybody: I cannot spin, but I can read, and I shall read it."

And so he read the whole of it to her; which, having been already given, is not set down here. And then he took out another from the duchess, which went in this way:

Teresa my friend:

The good qualities of the goodness and the wit of your husband Sancho moved and obliged me to ask my husband the duke to give him the government of one of the many isles he has. I have news that he governs like a gerfalcon, at which I am very well pleased, and the duke my lord likewise; for which I give many thanks to heaven for not having been mistaken in choosing him for such a government. Because I want Señora Teresa to know that a good governor is hard to find in this world, and may God make me as good as Sancho is a governor.

I am sending you here, my dear, a string of coral with gold ends; I should have been glad if it had been of oriental pearls, but the man who gives you the bone would not like to see you dead. The time will come when we shall know each other and be in each other's company, and God knows what will come of it. Commend me to Sanchica your daughter, and tell her from me to get ready, for I mean to marry her highly when she least expects it.

They tell me that in that place of yours there are fat acorns: send me a couple of dozen, which I shall value greatly for being from your own hand; and write to me at length, letting me know about your health and your well-being. And if you should need anything, you have nothing to do but open your mouth, for your mouth shall be the measure. And God keep you. From this place.

Your friend, who is very fond of you,

The Duchess.

"Oh," said Teresa when she had heard the letter, "what a good, plain, humble lady! Let them bury me with ladies like that, and not with the gentlewomen who are in fashion in this village, who think that because they are gentlewomen the wind must not touch them, and go to church with as much airs as if they were queens themselves, and look for all the world as if they held it a dishonour to look at a farm woman. And see here how this good lady, being a duchess, calls me her friend and treats me as if I were her equal — and may I see her equal to the tallest belfry there is in La Mancha!

"And as to the acorns, my dear sir, I shall send her ladyship a peck of them, and they are so fat that people can come and look at them and marvel. And for now, Sanchica, see that this gentleman is looked after: get his horse seen to, and get eggs out of the stable, and cut plenty of bacon, and let us give him a dinner fit for a prince; for the good news he has brought us and his good face deserve it all. And meanwhile I shall go out and give my neighbours the news of our good fortune, and the father curate and Master Nicolás the barber, who are and have been such friends of your father's."

"I shall, mother," answered Sanchica; "but mind you must give me half of that string, for I do not think my lady the duchess such a fool as to have sent her the whole of it."

"It is all for you, daughter," answered Teresa, "but let me wear it round my neck for a few days, for truly it seems to gladden my heart."

"They will be glad too," said the page, "when they see the bundle in this portmanteau, which is a suit of the finest cloth that the governor wore only one day out hunting, and which he is sending in its entirety for Señora Sanchica."

"May he live a thousand years," answered Sanchica, "and the man who brings it neither more nor less, and even two thousand if there is need."

At this Teresa went out of the house with the letters and with the string round her neck, and went along drumming on the letters as though they were a tambourine; and, meeting the curate and Sansón Carrasco by chance, she began to dance and to say:

"Upon my word, now there are no poor relations! We have a nice little government! No — let the smartest gentlewoman take me on, and I shall trim her up like new!"

"What is this, Teresa Panza? What madness is this, and what papers are those?"

"There is no other madness but that these are letters from duchesses and governors, and these I am wearing round my neck are fine coral; the Ave Marias and the Our Fathers are of hammered gold, and I am a governess."

"Under God, we do not understand you, Teresa, and we do not know what you are saying."

"There they can see it for themselves," answered Teresa.

And she gave them the letters. The curate read them so that Sansón Carrasco heard them, and Sansón and the curate looked at each other as if amazed at what they had read; and the bachelor asked who had brought those letters. Teresa answered that they should come with her to her house and they would see the messenger, who was a young man like a golden pine, and that he was bringing her another present worth as much again.

The curate took the coral off her neck and looked at it and looked at it again, and, making certain that it was genuine, was amazed all over again, and said:

"By the habit I wear, I do not know what to say or what to think about these letters and these presents. On the one hand I see and touch the fineness of this coral, and on the other I read that a duchess is sending to ask for two dozen acorns."

"Match me those measurements!" said Carrasco then. "Well now, let us go and see the bearer of this packet, and we shall find out from him about the difficulties that occur to us."

They did so, and Teresa went back with them. They found the page sifting a little barley for his mount, and Sanchica cutting a rasher of bacon to pave it with eggs and give the page his dinner; and his appearance and his good dress pleased the two of them very much. And, after they had greeted him courteously and he them, Sansón asked him to tell them news both of Don Quixote and of Sancho Panza; for although they had read Sancho's letter and the lady duchess's, they were still confused and could not manage to hit on what this business of Sancho's government could be, and above all of an isle — since all or most of the isles there are in the Mediterranean belong to His Majesty. To which the page answered:

"That Señor Sancho Panza is a governor there is no doubting; whether what he governs is an isle or not, I do not meddle in that, but it is enough that it is a place of more than a thousand inhabitants. And as for the business of the acorns, I say that my lady the duchess is so plain and so humble that not merely sending to ask for acorns from a farm woman — she has even been known to send and ask a neighbour of hers for the loan of a comb. Because I want your worships to know that the ladies of Aragon, although they are of such great quality, are not as punctilious and as high-flown as Castilian ladies; they treat people with more plainness."

In the middle of this talk Sanchica burst in with a lapful of eggs, and asked the page:

"Tell me, sir: does my lord father by any chance wear tied hose now that he is a governor?"

"I have not looked at that," answered the page, "but he must do."

"Oh my God!" replied Sanchica. "And what a thing it will be to see my father in trunk hose! Is it not a fine thing that ever since I was born I have wanted to see my father in tied hose?"

"Your worship will see him in such things and worse if he lives," answered the page. "By God, he is on the way to travelling in a hooded cape if the government lasts him only two months."

The curate and the bachelor saw well enough that the page was talking slyly, but the fineness of the coral and the hunting suit Sancho was sending undid it all — for Teresa had already shown them the suit. And they could not help laughing at Sanchica's wish, and still more when Teresa said:

"Master curate, look about and see whether there is anybody going to Madrid or to Toledo, to buy me a round farthingale, a proper one and well made, in the fashion and one of the best there is; for truly and truly I mean to honour my husband's government as far as I can, and even, if I get annoyed, to go off to that court and set up a coach like everybody else. For the woman who has a governor for a husband may very well keep and maintain one."

"And how, mother!" said Sanchica. "Would to God it were today rather than tomorrow, even if those who saw me riding beside my lady mother in that coach were to say: 'Look at the such-and-such, daughter of the garlic-stuffed man, and how she goes sitting and stretched out in the coach as if she were a she-pope!' But let them tread the mud, and let me ride in my coach with my feet up off the ground. A bad year and a bad month to all the gossips in the world, and let me be warm and let people laugh! Am I right, mother?"

"And how right you are, daughter!" answered Teresa. "And all these good fortunes, and even greater ones, my good Sancho has prophesied to me; and you shall see, daughter, how he does not stop until he has made me a countess. It is all a matter of beginning to be lucky; and, as I have heard your good father say many times — and he is the father of proverbs as well as yours — when they give you the heifer, run with the halter; when they give you a government, take it; when they give you an earldom, grab it; and when they chuck you under the chin with some good gift, pocket it. No — go to sleep, and do not answer the good fortunes and the good luck that are knocking at the door of your house!"

"And what do I care," added Sanchica, "if anybody who likes says, when he sees me giving myself airs and putting on style: 'The dog got himself into hemp breeches...' and the rest of it?"

Hearing which, the curate said:

"I cannot help believing that all of this line of the Panzas were born with a sackful of proverbs inside them: I have never seen one of them who does not spill them at all hours and in every conversation they have."

"That is the truth," said the page; "for the lord governor Sancho says them at every turn, and, although a great many are beside the point, they still give pleasure, and my lady the duchess and the duke make much of them."

"And does your worship still hold to it, my dear sir," said the bachelor, "that this business of Sancho's government is true, and that there is a duchess in the world who sends him presents and writes to him? Because we, though we have touched the presents and have read the letters, do not believe it, and think that this is one of those affairs of Don Quixote our fellow townsman, who thinks everything is done by enchantment; and so I am half inclined to say that I want to touch and feel your worship, to see whether you are a fanciful ambassador or a man of flesh and bone."

"Gentlemen, I know no more about myself," answered the page, "than that I am a true ambassador, and that Señor Sancho Panza is an actual governor, and that my lord and lady the duke and duchess can give, and have given, that government; and that I have heard it said that this same Sancho Panza conducts himself in it most valiantly. Whether there is enchantment in this or not, let your worships argue it out among yourselves; for I know nothing else, by the oath I make, which is by the life of my parents, whom I have alive and love and am very fond of."

"It may very well be so," replied the bachelor, "but dubitat Augustinus."

"Let doubt who will doubt," answered the page, "the truth is what I have said, and it must always float on top of a lie, as oil does on water; and if not, operibus credite, et non verbis. Let one of your worships come with me and you shall see with your eyes what you do not believe with your ears."

"That journey is mine," said Sanchica. "Take me, sir, on your nag's crupper, for I shall go very willingly to see my lord father."

"Governors' daughters must not go along the roads alone, but attended by coaches and litters and a great number of servants."

"By God," answered Sancha, "I would go as well on a she-ass as in a coach. You have found your squeamish girl, have you not!"

"Be quiet, girl," said Teresa; "you do not know what you are saying, and this gentleman is right: as the times are, so the touch; when it is Sancho, Sancha, and when it is governor, my lady — and I do not know whether I am saying something."

"Señora Teresa says more than she thinks," said the page. "And give me something to eat and send me off soon, because I mean to go back this afternoon."

To which the curate said:

"Your worship shall come and take pot luck with me, for Señora Teresa has more good will than furnishings to serve so good a guest with."

The page refused; but in the end he had to agree to it for his own good, and the curate took him along very willingly, so as to have room to ask him at leisure about Don Quixote and his exploits.

The bachelor offered to write the answering letters for Teresa; but she did not want the bachelor to meddle in her affairs, for she took him for something of a joker; and so she gave a roll and two eggs to an altar boy who could write, who wrote her two letters, one for her husband and another for the duchess, dictated out of her own headpiece — and they are not the worst that are set down in this great history, as will be seen further on.

Chapter 51: Of the Progress of Sancho Panza's Government, with Other Events as Good as They Are Entertaining

The day dawned that followed the night of the governor's rounds, which the head steward spent without sleeping, his mind taken up with the face, spirit and beauty of the disguised maiden; and the steward spent what was left of the night in writing to his master and mistress about what Sancho Panza was doing and saying, as amazed by his deeds as by his sayings — because his words and his actions went about mixed together, with glimmerings of the judicious and of the foolish.

The lord governor got up at last; and, by Doctor Pedro Recio's orders, they made him breakfast on a little preserve and four swallows of cold water — a thing Sancho would have traded for a piece of bread and a bunch of grapes; but, seeing that this was more force than free will, he put up with it, with a good deal of grief to his soul and distress to his stomach, Pedro Recio making him believe that scanty and delicate food sharpened the wits, which was what best suited persons set up in commands and in grave offices, where they have to make use not so much of their bodily strength as of the strength of their understanding.

With this sophistry Sancho suffered hunger, and to such a degree that in secret he cursed the government and even the man who had given it him. But, with his hunger and with his preserve, he set himself to give judgement that day; and the first thing that offered itself was a question a stranger put to him, with the steward and the rest of his acolytes present at the whole of it, which was:

"Sir, a great river divided two districts of one and the same lordship — and let your worship be attentive, because the case is important and rather difficult. I say, then, that over this river there was a bridge, and at the end of it a gallows and a kind of court house, in which there were ordinarily four judges who judged by the law laid down by the lord of the river, of the bridge and of the lordship, which was in this form: 'If anybody crosses this bridge from one side to the other, he must first swear where he is going and what he is going for; and if he swears the truth, let them let him pass; and if he tells a lie, let him die for it, hanged on the gallows that stands there, without any remission at all.'

"This law being known, and the severity of its condition, a great many people crossed; and then, from what they swore, it could be seen that they were telling the truth, and the judges let them pass freely. It happened, then, that, taking a man's oath, he swore and said that by the oath he was making, he was going to die on that gallows over there, and for nothing else. The judges stuck at the oath and said: 'If we let this man pass freely, he lied in his oath, and according to the law he must die; and if we hang him, he swore that he was going to die on that gallows, and, having sworn the truth, by the same law he must go free.'

"It is asked of your worship, my lord governor, what the judges are to do with this man; for even now they are still in doubt and suspense. And, having had news of your worship's sharp and lofty understanding, they sent me to beg your worship on their behalf to give your opinion in so intricate and doubtful a case."

To which Sancho answered:

"Certainly those gentlemen the judges who send you to me could have spared themselves the trouble, because I am a man who has more of the dull ox in him than of the sharp fellow. But for all that, repeat the business to me once more so that I understand it: perhaps I might hit the mark."

The questioner went over what he had said before once and again, and Sancho said:

"To my mind I can set this business out in two shakes, and it is this: the man swears he is going to die on the gallows; and if he dies on it, he swore the truth, and by the law laid down he deserves to go free and to cross the bridge; and if they do not hang him, he swore a lie, and by the same law he deserves to be hanged."

"It is just as the lord governor says," said the messenger; "and as to the completeness and understanding of the case, there is nothing more to ask or to doubt."

"I say, then, now," replied Sancho, "that of this man they should let the part that swore the truth cross, and hang the part that told a lie; and in this way the condition of the crossing will be carried out to the letter."

"Well, my lord governor," replied the questioner, "it will be necessary for this man to be divided into parts, the lying part and the truthful part; and if he is divided, he must of necessity die, and so nothing at all is achieved of what the law requires, and it is expressly necessary that the law should be carried out."

"Come here, my good man," answered Sancho. "This traveller you speak of — either I am a blockhead, or he has the same reason for dying as for living and crossing the bridge; because if the truth saves him, the lie condemns him equally. And this being so, as it is, I am of the opinion that you should tell those gentlemen who sent you to me that, since the reasons for condemning him and for absolving him are evenly balanced, they should let him cross freely; for doing good is always more praised than doing harm. And I would give you this signed with my name, if I knew how to sign.

"And in this case I have not spoken out of my own head, but there came into my memory one precept, among a great many others that my master Don Quixote gave me the night before I came to be governor of this isle: which was that when justice was in doubt I should lean and take refuge in mercy. And God has willed that I should remember it now, since it comes into this case as though it were cast in the mould."

"That is so," answered the steward, "and I hold for myself that Lycurgus himself, who gave the Spartans their laws, could not have given a better sentence than the one the great Panza has given. And let the morning's audience end with this, and I shall give orders for the lord governor to dine very much to his taste."

"That is what I ask, and fair play," said Sancho. "Give me something to eat, and let cases and doubts rain down on me, and I shall polish them off in the air."

The steward kept his word, thinking it would be a matter of conscience to starve so judicious a governor to death — and the more so as he meant to make an end of him that very night by playing him the last trick he had a commission to play.

It happened, then, that, having dined that day against the rules and aphorisms of the doctor of Get-You-Gone, as the cloth was being taken up a courier came in with a letter from Don Quixote for the governor. Sancho ordered the secretary to read it to himself, and, if there were nothing in it worth keeping secret, to read it out loud. The secretary did so; and, going over it first, he said:

"It may well be read out loud, for what Señor Don Quixote writes to your worship deserves to be stamped and written in letters of gold; and it goes like this:

Letter from Don Quixote of La Mancha to Sancho Panza, Governor of the Isle of Barataria

When I was expecting to hear news of your carelessnesses and impertinences, Sancho my friend, I heard news of your judicious sayings; for which I gave particular thanks to heaven, which knows how to raise the poor out of the dunghill and to make wise men out of fools. They tell me that you govern as if you were a man, and that you are a man as if you were a beast, so humble is the way you conduct yourself.

And I want you to note, Sancho, that many times it is fitting and necessary, for the authority of the office, to go against the humility of the heart; because the good dress of a person set in grave charges must be according to what those charges require and not according to the measure of what his humble condition inclines him to. Dress well, for a stick well got up does not look like a stick. I do not say that you should wear trinkets and finery, or that, being a judge, you should dress like a soldier, but that you should adorn yourself with the habit your office requires, so long as it is clean and well arranged.

To win the good will of the people you govern, among other things you must do two: one, be well-mannered with everybody, although I have already told you this before; and the other, take care that there is plenty of food, for there is nothing that wears at the hearts of the poor more than hunger and scarcity.

Do not make many decrees; and if you make them, try to make them good ones, and above all see that they are kept and carried out — for decrees that are not kept are the same as if they had never been made; on the contrary, they give it to be understood that the prince who had the judgement and the authority to make them had not the courage to make them kept. And laws that frighten and are not enforced come to be like the log, king of the frogs: at first it terrified them, and in time they thought nothing of it and climbed up on top of it.

Be a father to the virtues and a stepfather to the vices. Do not always be severe, nor always mild, and choose the middle way between these two extremes, for in that lies the point of good judgement.

Visit the prisons, the butchers' shops and the markets, for the presence of the governor in such places is of great importance: he comforts the prisoners, who are hoping for a quick despatch of their cases; he is a bogey to the butchers, who for that occasion make their weights even; and he is a scarecrow to the market women, for the same reason.

Do not show yourself — even if by any chance you are so, which I do not believe — greedy, a womaniser or a glutton; because when the people and those who deal with you know your settled inclination, they will lay their batteries against you there until they bring you down into the depths of ruin.

Look and look again, go over and over again the advice and the precepts I gave you in writing before you set out from here to your government, and you will see how you find in them, if you keep them, a help in hand to carry you through the labours and difficulties that come to governors at every step.

Write to your lord and lady and show yourself grateful to them; for ingratitude is the daughter of pride and one of the greatest sins there is, and the person who is grateful to those who have done him good gives an indication that he will also be grateful to God, who has done him so many good things and goes on doing them.

My lady the duchess sent a special messenger with your suit and another present to your wife Teresa Panza; we are expecting an answer at any moment.

I have been a little out of sorts from a certain cat-mauling that happened to me not very much to the good of my nose; but it was nothing, for if there are enchanters who ill-treat me, there are also enchanters who defend me.

Let me know whether the steward who is with you had anything to do with the doings of the Trifaldi, as you suspected; and you shall keep giving me notice of everything that happens to you, since the road is so short. What is more, I mean to leave soon this idle life I am in, since I was not born for it.

A business has come up for me that I believe will put me out of favour with these nobles; but although it matters a great deal to me, it does not matter to me at all, since in the end I must fulfil my profession sooner than their pleasure, according to what they say: amicus Plato, sed magis amica veritas. I say this Latin to you because I give myself to understand that, since you have been a governor, you will have learnt it. And God be with you, and may He keep you from anybody's pitying you.

Your friend,

Don Quixote of La Mancha.

Sancho listened to the letter with great attention, and it was praised and held for judicious by those who heard it. And then Sancho got up from the table and, calling the secretary, shut himself up with him in his chamber; and, without putting it off any longer, he decided to answer his master Don Quixote at once, and told the secretary to write down what he said to him without adding or taking away anything at all. And so he did; and the letter of reply was of the following tenor:

Letter from Sancho Panza to Don Quixote of La Mancha

The business of my affairs is so great that I have no time to scratch my head or even to cut my nails; and so I wear them so long that God help me. I say this, my dear lord of my soul, so that your worship should not be surprised that until now I have given no notice of how I am faring, well or badly, in this government, in which I am hungrier than when the two of us were going about through the woods and the wastelands.

The duke my lord wrote to me the other day, letting me know that certain spies had come into this isle to kill me; and up to now I have not discovered any but a certain doctor who is here on a salary to kill all the governors who come to this place. He is called Doctor Pedro Recio and he is a native of Get-You-Gone: so your worship may see what a name it is, for me not to be afraid of dying at his hands!

This doctor says of himself that he does not cure diseases when they are there but prevents them, so that they may not come; and the medicines he uses are diet and more diet, until he has the person down to bare bones — as though thinness were not a greater evil than fever. In short, he is killing me with hunger and I am dying of vexation; for when I thought I was coming to this government to eat hot and drink cold and rest my body between fine linen sheets on feather mattresses, I have come to do penance like a hermit — and, since I do not do it of my own will, I think that in the end the devil will carry me off.

Up to now I have not touched a fee or taken a bribe, and I cannot think what this means; because here they have told me that the governors who usually come to this isle, before coming into it, have been either given or lent a great deal of money by the townspeople, and that this is the ordinary custom with the rest who go to governments, not only in this one.

Last night, going the rounds, I came across a very beautiful maiden in man's clothes and a brother of hers in woman's; my head steward fell in love with the girl and picked her out in his imagination for his wife, as he has said, and I picked out the young man for my son-in-law. Today the two of us shall put our ideas to their father, who is a certain Diego de la Llana, a gentleman and as much of an old Christian as you please.

I visit the markets, as your worship advises me; and yesterday I found a stallholder selling new hazelnuts, and I established that she had mixed a bushel of new hazelnuts with another of old, empty and rotten ones. I gave the whole lot to the charity-school children, who would know how to tell them apart, and I sentenced her not to come into the market for a fortnight. They have told me that I did it valiantly; what I can tell your worship is that it is common talk in this town that there are no worse people than the market women, because they are all shameless, soulless and brazen — and so I believe, from the ones I have seen in other towns.

That my lady the duchess should have written to my wife Teresa Panza and sent her the present your worship speaks of, I am very much satisfied with; and I shall try to show myself grateful in due time. Let your worship kiss her hands on my behalf and say that I say she has not thrown it into a torn sack, as she shall see by the deed.

I should not like your worship to have any falling-out or unpleasantness with these lord and lady of mine; because if your worship gets angry with them, it is plain that it must redound to my harm — and it will not be right that, when I am given advice to be grateful, your worship should not be so with people who have done him so many kindnesses and by whom he has been treated with such indulgence in their castle.

That business of the cat-mauling I do not understand, but I imagine it must be one of the bad turns the bad enchanters generally play on your worship; I shall know when we see each other.

I should like to send your worship something, but I do not know what to send, unless it is some syringe tubes for use with bladders, which they make very neatly in this isle; although if the office lasts me I shall find something to send by hook or by crook.

If my wife Teresa Panza writes to me, let your worship pay the postage and send me the letter, for I have the greatest longing to know the state of my house, my wife and my children. And with this, God deliver your worship from ill-meaning enchanters, and bring me safely and peacefully out of this government — which I doubt, for I think I shall leave it along with my life, the way Doctor Pedro Recio treats me.

Your worship's servant,

Sancho Panza, the Governor.

The secretary closed the letter and sent the courier off at once. And the people who were playing tricks on Sancho, coming together, arranged among themselves how to get him out of the government. And Sancho spent that afternoon in making some ordinances touching the good government of what he imagined to be an isle; and he ordered that there should be no hoarders of provisions in the commonwealth, and that people might bring wine into it from wherever they liked, on condition that they declared the place it came from, so that a price could be set on it according to its value, its goodness and its reputation; and that anybody who watered it or changed its name should lose his life for it.

He brought down the price of all footwear, chiefly of shoes, since it seemed to him that it was running exorbitantly high. He set a limit to servants' wages, which were travelling at a loose rein along the road of self-interest. He laid the gravest penalties on those who sang lascivious and improper songs, either by night or by day. He ordered that no blind man should sing of a miracle in ballads unless he brought a genuine certificate that it was true, since it seemed to him that most of those the blind men sing are made up, to the damage of the true ones.

He made and created a constable of the poor, not to persecute them but to examine them as to whether they really were poor; because in the shadow of a pretended crippling and a false sore there go about thieving arms and drunken good health. In short, he ordained things so good that to this day they are kept in that place, and are named The Constitutions of the Great Governor Sancho Panza.

Chapter 52: Where the Adventure of the Second Distressed, or Anguished, Duenna Is Told, Called by Another Name Doña Rodríguez

Cide Hamete tells that, Don Quixote being now healed of his scratches, it seemed to him that the life he was leading in that castle was against the whole order of chivalry he professed; and so he decided to ask the duke and duchess for leave to set out for Saragossa, whose festival was coming near, where he expected to win the suit of armour that is competed for at such festivals.

And, being one day at table with the duke and duchess and beginning to put his intention into practice and ask for leave, see here: all at once there came in at the door of the great hall two women — as they afterwards proved to be — covered in mourning from head to foot; and one of them, coming up to Don Quixote, threw herself at his feet, stretched out at full length, her mouth stitched to Don Quixote's feet, and she gave out groans so mournful, so deep and so pained that she threw everybody who heard and saw her into confusion.

And although the duke and duchess thought it must be some trick their servants wanted to play on Don Quixote, still, seeing the earnestness with which the woman sighed and groaned and wept, it left them doubtful and in suspense — until Don Quixote, out of compassion, raised her from the ground and made her uncover herself and take the mantle off her weeping face.

She did so, and showed herself to be what nobody could ever have imagined, because she uncovered the face of Doña Rodríguez, the duenna of the house; and the other woman in mourning was her daughter, the one deceived by the rich farmer's son. All those who knew her were astonished, and the duke and duchess more than anybody; for although they took her for a fool and a good-natured creature, they did not take her for one who would come to commit follies. Finally Doña Rodríguez, turning to her master and mistress, said to them:

"May your excellencies be pleased to give me leave to have a few words with this knight, since it is needful for me to come well out of the business the boldness of an ill-meaning peasant has put me in."

The duke said that he gave it her, and that she might have as many words with Señor Don Quixote as she pleased. She, directing her voice and her face to Don Quixote, said:

"Many days ago, valorous knight, I gave you an account of the wrong and the treachery a wicked farmer has done unto my dearly loved daughter — who is this unfortunate girl here present — and you have promised me to stand up for her and to right the injustice that has been done her. And now it has come to my notice that you mean to leave this castle in search of the good adventures that God may send you. And so I should like, before you slip away along those roads, that you should challenge this untamed rustic and make him marry my daughter, in fulfilment of the word he gave her of being her husband before and ere he lay with her. Because to think that the duke my lord will do me justice is to ask pears of an elm, for the reason I have already declared to your worship in confidence. And with this, may Our Lord give your worship much health, and not leave us unprotected."

To which words Don Quixote answered with a great deal of gravity and pomp:

"Good duenna, temper your tears — or, better said, dry them and save your sighs; for I take upon my own charge the remedy of your daughter, who would have done better not to be so ready to believe lovers' promises, which for the most part are light in the promising and very heavy in the keeping. And so, with the leave of the duke my lord, I shall set out at once in search of that soulless young man; and I shall find him and challenge him and kill him whenever and however he excuses himself from keeping the word he promised. For the chief business of my profession is to pardon the humble and punish the proud — I mean, to come to the help of the wretched and destroy the harsh."

"There is no need," answered the duke, "for your worship to put yourself to the labour of looking for the rustic this good duenna complains of; nor is there any need for your worship to ask my leave to challenge him. I take him as challenged, and I take it upon myself to let him know of this challenge and to make him accept it and come and answer for himself at this castle of mine, where I shall give the two of you a safe field, keeping all the conditions that generally are and ought to be kept in such matters, and keeping his justice equally to each of you, as all those princes are bound to do who give free field to men who fight within the bounds of their lordships."

"Then with that safe conduct and with your greatness's good leave," replied Don Quixote, "from here I say that for this once I renounce my gentle birth, and level and adjust myself to the lowness of the offender, and make myself his equal, qualifying him to fight with me. And so, though he is absent, I challenge and defy him, on the grounds that he did wrong in cheating this poor girl, who was a maiden and through his fault is one no longer; and that he must keep the word he gave her of being her lawful husband, or die in the attempt."

And then, pulling off a glove, he threw it into the middle of the hall; and the duke picked it up, saying that, as he had already said, he accepted that challenge in the name of his vassal, and set the term at six days from then; and the field, in the square of that castle; and the arms, the ones customary among knights: lance and shield and articulated armour with all the other pieces, without deceit, trickery or any superstition, examined and inspected by the judges of the field.

"But before anything else, it is necessary that this good duenna and this bad maiden should put the right of their case into Señor Don Quixote's hands; for otherwise nothing will be done, and the challenge will never come to be duly carried out."

"I do put it," answered the duenna.

"And I too," added the daughter, all in tears and all shamefaced and in bad spirits.

This memorandum being taken down, then, and the duke having imagined what he would do in the case, the women in mourning went off; and the duchess ordered that from then on they should not be treated as her servants but as adventuring ladies who had come to her house to ask for justice. And so they gave them a separate suite and served them as strangers, not without alarm among the rest of the servants, who did not know where the foolishness and forwardness of Doña Rodríguez and her ill-fortuned daughter were going to end.

While they were at this, to finish making the feast merry and give the dinner a good ending, see here where there came into the hall the page who had taken the letters and presents to Teresa Panza, wife of the governor Sancho Panza; at whose arrival the duke and duchess were greatly pleased, being eager to know what had happened to him on his journey. And, on their asking him, the page answered that he could not tell it so publicly or in a few words: let their excellencies be pleased to leave it until they were alone, and meanwhile entertain themselves with these letters. And, taking out two letters, he put them into the duchess's hands.

One had on its address: Letter for my lady the duchess of such-and-such, of I do not know where; and the other: To my husband Sancho Panza, governor of the isle of Barataria, whom God prosper more years than me. The duchess's bread would not bake, as the saying goes, until she had read her letter; and, opening it and reading it to herself and seeing that she could read it aloud so that the duke and the bystanders could hear it, she read in this way:

Letter from Teresa Panza to the Duchess

Great pleasure it gave me, my lady, the letter your greatness wrote me, which truly I had wanted very much. The string of coral is very good, and my husband's hunting suit is not one step behind it. That your ladyship should have made Sancho my consort a governor has given great pleasure to this whole place, though there is nobody who believes it — chiefly the curate, and Master Nicolás the barber, and Sansón Carrasco the bachelor. But I do not care a bit; for, so long as it is so, as it is, let everybody say what they like — although, to tell the truth, if the coral and the suit had not come, I should not have believed it either, because in this village everybody takes my husband for a blockhead, and, apart from governing a flock of goats, they cannot imagine what government he can be good for. God grant it, and set it on the road as He sees His children need.

I, lady of my soul, have made up my mind, with your worship's leave, to bring this good day into my house by going to the court to stretch myself out in a coach, so as to put out the eyes of the thousand envious people I have already. And so I beg your excellency to order my husband to send me a little money, and let it be something worth having, because at court expenses are great: bread is at a real and meat thirty maravedís the pound, which is a judgement. And if he does not want me to go, let him warn me in good time, because my feet are itching to be on the road; for my friends and my neighbours tell me that if my daughter and I go about grand and puffed up at court, my husband will come to be known through me more than I through him, since a great many people will have to ask: "Who are these ladies in this coach?" And a servant of mine will answer: "The wife and daughter of Sancho Panza, governor of the isle of Barataria." And in this way Sancho will be known and I shall be respected, and off to Rome with the whole thing.

It grieves me, as much as it can grieve me, that this year there has been no crop of acorns in this village; even so, I am sending your highness about half a peck of them, which I went and gathered and picked one by one on the mountain, and I could not find any bigger; I wish they had been like ostrich eggs.

Do not let your pomposity forget to write to me, for I shall take care of the answer, letting you know of my health and of everything there is to let you know from this place, where I remain praying to Our Lord to keep your greatness, and not to forget me. Sancha my daughter and my son kiss your worship's hands.

She who wants more to see your ladyship than to write to you, your servant,

Teresa Panza.

Great was the pleasure everybody took in hearing Teresa Panza's letter, and chiefly the duke and duchess; and the duchess asked Don Quixote's opinion whether it would be right to open the letter that had come for the governor, which she imagined must be an excellent one. Don Quixote said that he would open it to give them pleasure, and so he did; and he saw that it went in this way:

Letter from Teresa Panza to Sancho Panza Her Husband

Your letter I received, my Sancho of my soul, and I promise you and swear to you as a Catholic Christian that I came within two fingers of going mad with pleasure. Look, brother: when I came to hear that you are a governor, I thought I should fall down dead there of pure joy, for you know they say that sudden gladness kills as much as great grief. As for Sanchica your daughter, her waters went from her without her noticing it, out of pure contentment.

I had the suit you sent me in front of me, and the coral my lady the duchess sent me round my neck, and the letters in my hands, and the man who brought them there present; and with all that I believed and thought that everything I saw and touched was a dream. Because who could think that a goatherd would come to be governor of isles? You know, my friend, that my mother used to say that you had to live a long time to see a great deal; I say it because I expect to see more if I live longer, for I do not mean to stop until I see you a tax-farmer or an excise-man — which are offices that, though the devil carries off whoever uses them badly, still in the end always have money and handle it.

My lady the duchess will tell you the wish I have to go to the court; think it over and let me know your pleasure, for I shall try to do you honour there by going about in a coach.

The curate, the barber, the bachelor and even the sacristan cannot believe that you are a governor, and they say it is all humbug or a matter of enchantment, as everything to do with your master Don Quixote is. And Sansón says he means to go and look for you and get the government out of your head and the madness out of Don Quixote's skull; and I do nothing but laugh and look at my string and plan out the dress I am to make for our daughter out of your suit.

Some acorns I sent my lady the duchess; I wish they had been of gold. Send me some strings of pearls, if they are in use in that isle.

The news from this place is that the Berrueca woman has married her daughter to a bad painter who came to this village to paint whatever might turn up. The council ordered him to paint His Majesty's arms over the doors of the town hall; he asked two ducats, they gave them to him in advance, he worked for a week, at the end of which he had painted nothing and said he could not manage to paint so many odds and ends; he gave the money back, and even so he got married on the strength of being a good workman. It is true that he has now dropped the brush and taken up the hoe, and goes into the fields like a gentleman.
