Pedro de Lobo's son has taken minor orders and the tonsure, meaning to become a priest; Minguilla, Mingo Silvato's granddaughter, got to know of it and has brought a suit against him, saying that he has given her a promise of marriage. Bad tongues will have it that she has been with child by him, but he denies it flat-footedly.

There are no olives this year, and there is not a drop of vinegar to be found in this whole village. A company of soldiers came through here; on their way they carried off three girls from this village; I do not want to tell you who they are: perhaps they will come back, and there will be no lack of men to take them for wives, with their good or bad blemishes.

Sanchica makes lace edging; she earns eight maravedís clear every day, which she keeps dropping into a money box to help with her dowry. But now that she is a governor's daughter, you will give her the dowry without her working for it. The fountain in the square dried up; lightning struck the pillory, and much I care.

I hope for an answer to this and for a decision about my going to the court; and with this, may God keep you more years than me, or as many, for I should not like to leave you in this world without me.

Your wife,

Teresa Panza.

The letters were made much of, laughed over, valued and marvelled at; and, to finish setting the seal on it, the courier arrived who was carrying the one Sancho was sending to Don Quixote, which was likewise read publicly, and which put the governor's foolishness in doubt.

The duchess withdrew to learn from the page what had happened to him in Sancho's village, which he told her at great length, without leaving out a single circumstance. He gave her the acorns, and a cheese as well that Teresa had given him for being a very good one, better than the cheeses of Tronchón. The duchess received it with the greatest pleasure — with which we shall leave her, so as to tell the end that the government of the great Sancho Panza came to, the flower and mirror of all island governors.

Chapter 53: Of the Wearied End and Close That Sancho Panza's Government Came To

"To think that in this life its affairs will always stay in one state is to think the impossible. Rather it seems that it all goes round in a circle — I mean, round and round: spring follows summer, summer high summer, high summer autumn, autumn winter and winter spring, and so time goes back to travelling on this continual wheel. Only human life runs to its end, lighter than time, without hope of being renewed except in the next life, which has no bounds to limit it."

So says Cide Hamete, that Mohammedan philosopher; because this business of understanding the swiftness and instability of the present life and the everlastingness of the eternal one that is looked for has been understood by many without the light of faith, and only by the light of nature. But here our author says it because of the speed with which Sancho's government ended, was used up, was undone and went off like a shadow and a smoke.

Sancho, being in his bed on the seventh night of the days of his government — not full of bread or of wine but of judging and giving opinions and making statutes and decrees — when sleep, in spite and defiance of his hunger, was beginning to close his eyelids, heard such a great noise of bells and of voices that it sounded for all the world as though the whole isle were sinking. He sat up in bed and stayed listening attentively, to see whether he could hit on what might be the cause of such a great uproar. But not only did he not find out; on the contrary, with the noise of infinite trumpets and drums adding itself to the voices and the bells, he was left more confused and full of fear and terror.

And, getting to his feet, he put on a pair of slippers because of the damp of the floor, and, without putting on a dressing gown or anything of the kind, he went out to the door of his room, just as he saw coming along some galleries more than twenty people with lighted torches in their hands and with their swords drawn, all of them shouting at the tops of their voices:

"To arms, to arms, my lord governor, to arms! For infinite enemies have come into the isle, and we are lost if your skill and valour do not come to our help."

With this noise, fury and uproar they came to where Sancho was, astounded and dumbfounded by what he was hearing and seeing; and when they came up to him one of them said:

"Arm yourself at once, your lordship, if you do not want to be lost and this whole isle to be lost!"

"What am I to arm myself with?" answered Sancho. "And what do I know about arms or about relieving people? These things had better be left to my master Don Quixote, who will polish them off and put them out of danger in two shakes; for I, sinner that I am before God, understand nothing about these emergencies."

"Ah, my lord governor!" said another. "What slackness is this? Arm yourself, your worship, for here we bring you offensive and defensive arms; and come out into that square and be our guide and our captain, since it is your right to be so, being our governor."

"Arm me then, and welcome," replied Sancho.

And at once they brought him two pavises, which they had come provided with; and they put them over his shirt without letting him put on any other clothes, one pavise in front and another behind, and through some hollows they had made in them they pulled his arms out and tied him up very tightly with cords, so that he was left walled in and boarded up, straight as a spindle, unable to bend his knees or to stir a single step. They put a lance in his hands, which he leaned on so as to be able to keep on his feet. When they had him like this, they told him to march and to guide them all and encourage them; for, he being their pole star, their lantern and their morning star, their affairs would come to a good end.

"How am I to march, wretched man that I am," answered Sancho, "when I cannot work my kneecaps, because these boards that are stitched so tight to my flesh are stopping me? What you must do is carry me in your arms and set me, laid across or upright, in some gateway, and I shall guard it, either with this lance or with my body."

"Get on, my lord governor," said another; "it is fear more than the boards that is stopping your step. Have done and stir yourself, for it is late, and the enemies are growing, and the shouting is getting louder and the danger is pressing."

At which urgings and abuse the poor governor tried to move, and came down on the ground with such a great crash that he thought he had smashed himself to pieces. He was left like a tortoise shut up and covered by its shells, or like half a side of bacon between two troughs, or exactly like a boat run aground on the sand; and, for all their seeing him fallen, those mocking people felt no compassion for him at all. On the contrary, putting out the torches, they went back to redoubling their shouts and repeating their "to arms!" in such great haste, walking right over poor Sancho and dealing him endless sword-strokes on the pavises, that if he had not gathered himself in and shrunk up, putting his head between the pavises, the poor governor would have come off very badly. Shut up in that tightness, he sweated and sweated again, and with his whole heart commended himself to God to bring him out of that danger.

Some tripped over him, others fell down, and there was one who stood on top of him for a good while and from there, as from a watchtower, directed the armies, saying at the top of his voice:

"Here, our men — the enemy is pressing harder on this side! Let that breach be guarded, let that gate be shut, let those ladders be barred! Bring fire-pots, pitch and resin in cauldrons of boiling oil! Barricade the streets with mattresses!"

In short, he named with all earnestness all the odds and ends and instruments and engines of war with which the assault on a city is generally defended; and the battered Sancho, who was listening to it all and putting up with it all, said to himself:

"Oh, if only my Lord were pleased for this isle to be finally lost, and for me to see myself either dead or out of this great anguish!"

Heaven heard his petition, and, when he least expected it, he heard voices saying:

"Victory, victory! The enemy are beaten! Come, my lord governor, get up, your worship, and come and enjoy the victory and share out the spoils that have been taken from the enemy by the valour of that invincible arm!"

"Lift me up," said the aching Sancho in a pained voice.

They helped him up; and, on his feet, he said:

"The enemy I have conquered — I want them to nail him on my forehead. I do not want to share out spoils from any enemy, but to ask and beg some friend, if I have one, to give me a swallow of wine, for I am parched, and to dry this sweat off me, for I am turning into water."

They wiped him, brought him the wine, untied the pavises; he sat down on his bed and fainted away from the fear, the shock and the labour. The people of the trick were already sorry at having made it so heavy for him; but Sancho's coming round tempered the grief his fainting had given them. He asked what time it was; they answered that day was already breaking. He said nothing; and, without saying another word, he began to dress, buried in silence, and everybody watched him and waited to see where the haste with which he was dressing was going to end.

He dressed at last; and little by little, because he was battered and could not go very fast, he went off to the stable, followed by everybody who was there. And, coming up to the grey, he embraced him and gave him a kiss of peace on the forehead, and, not without tears in his eyes, said to him:

"Come here, my companion and my friend and the sharer of my labours and my miseries: when I got along with you and had no thoughts but those that came to me from the cares of mending your harness and keeping your little body going, my hours and my days and my years were happy ones. But since I left you and climbed up on the towers of ambition and pride, a thousand miseries, a thousand labours and four thousand disquiets have got into my soul."

And while he was saying these things he was likewise putting the pack-saddle on the donkey, without anybody saying anything to him. The grey being saddled, then, with great pain and grief he got up on him; and, directing his words and arguments to the steward, the secretary, the head steward and Pedro Recio the doctor, and to a great many others who were there present, he said:

"Make way, my dear sirs, and let me go back to my old liberty; let me go and look for my past life, so that it may raise me up from this present death. I was not born to be a governor, or to defend isles or cities from enemies who may want to attack them. I understand ploughing and digging and pruning and trimming the vines better than making laws or defending provinces or kingdoms. Saint Peter is well enough off in Rome — I mean that everybody is well enough off practising the trade he was born for. A sickle fits my hand better than a governor's sceptre; I would rather have my fill of gazpacho than be subject to the misery of an impertinent doctor who kills me with hunger; and I would rather lie down in the shade of an oak in summer and wrap myself in a shaggy sheepskin in winter, in my liberty, than go to bed under the subjection of a government between fine linen sheets and dress myself in onion-sables.

"Your worships stay with God, and tell the duke my lord that naked I was born and naked I find myself: I neither lose nor gain — I mean that I came into this government without a farthing and I go out of it without one, quite the other way round from how governors of other isles generally go out. And stand aside: let me go, for I am off to be poulticed; because I believe I have all my ribs crushed, thanks to the enemies who have been walking about on top of me tonight."

"It must not be like this, my lord governor," said Doctor Recio; "for I shall give your worship a draught against falls and bruisings that will restore you at once to your first soundness and vigour. And in the matter of food, I promise your worship to mend my ways, letting you eat plentifully of everything you like."

"Too late, chick!" answered Sancho. "I shall no more leave off going than I shall turn Turk. These jokes are not for twice over. By God, I shall stay in this government, or take another, about as soon as I shall fly to heaven without wings. I am of the line of the Panzas, who are all pig-headed; and if they once say odds, odds it has to be, even if it is evens, in spite of all the world.

"Let the ant's wings stay here in this stable — the wings that raised me into the air so that swifts and other birds could eat me — and let us go back to walking on the ground on a level foot; and if it is not adorned with pinked cordovan shoes, it will not go short of rough rope sandals. Every ewe with her own mate, and let nobody stretch his leg further than the sheet is long. And let me pass, for it is getting late for me."

To which the steward said:

"My lord governor, we would very willingly let your worship go, although it will grieve us greatly to lose you, for your wit and your Christian conduct oblige us to want you. But it is well known that every governor is obliged, before leaving the place where he has governed, first to give an account of his term: let your worship give an account of the ten days you have had the government, and go in the peace of God."

"Nobody can ask it of me," answered Sancho, "except whoever the duke my lord may order; I am going to see him, and to him I shall give it to the pattern. What is more, going out naked as I do, no other sign is needed to give it to be understood that I have governed like an angel."

"By God the great Sancho is right," said Doctor Recio, "and I am of the opinion that we should let him go, because the duke will take infinite pleasure in seeing him."

They all agreed to it and let him go, first offering him company and everything he wanted for the comfort of his person and the convenience of his journey. Sancho said he wanted no more than a little barley for the grey and half a cheese and half a loaf for himself; for, the road being so short, he had no need of a bigger or a better larder. They all embraced him, and he, weeping, embraced them all, and left them astonished, both at his words and at his decision, so resolute and so judicious.

Chapter 54: Which Deals with Matters Touching This History and No Other

The duke and duchess made up their minds that the challenge Don Quixote had made to their vassal, for the reason already given, should go forward. And since the young man was in Flanders, where he had gone in flight so as not to have Doña Rodríguez for a mother-in-law, they arranged to put in his place a Gascon footman called Tosilos, first coaching him very thoroughly in everything he had to do.

Two days later the duke told Don Quixote that in four days his opponent would come and present himself in the field, armed as a knight, and would maintain that the girl lied by half her beard, and even by her whole beard, if she declared that he had given her a promise of marriage. Don Quixote took great pleasure in this news, and promised himself to work marvels in the case, and counted it a great piece of luck that an occasion had offered itself where those nobles might see how far the valour of his mighty arm reached. And so, with excitement and contentment, he waited out the four days, which, by the reckoning of his eagerness, were turning into four hundred centuries.

Let us leave them to pass, as we leave other things to pass, and let us go and keep Sancho company, who came riding along on the grey, between glad and sad, to look for his master, whose company pleased him more than being governor of all the isles in the world.

It happened, then, that, not having got very far from the isle of his government — for he never set himself to find out whether what he governed was an isle, a city, a town or a village — he saw coming along the road he was travelling six pilgrims with their staves, of those foreigners who beg for alms by singing; who, on coming up to him, drew up in a line and, all raising their voices together, began to sing in their own language what Sancho could not understand, except one word he clearly made out: alms — by which he understood that it was alms they were asking for in their song.

And as he was, according to Cide Hamete, exceedingly charitable, he took half a loaf and half a cheese out of his saddlebags, which he had come provided with, and gave it them, telling them by signs that he had nothing else to give them. They took it very willingly and said:

"Gelt! Gelt!"

"I do not understand," answered Sancho, "what it is you are asking me for, good people."

Then one of them took a purse out of his bosom and showed it to Sancho, by which he understood that they were asking him for money; and he, putting his thumb to his throat and spreading his hand upwards, gave them to understand that he had not a scrap of coin; and, spurring the grey, he pushed through them. And as he passed, one of them, having been looking at him very attentively, rushed at him, throwing his arms round his waist, and said in a loud and very Castilian voice:

"God bless me! What is this I see? Is it possible that I have in my arms my dear friend, my good neighbour Sancho Panza? I have, without a doubt, because I am not asleep and I am not drunk just now."

Sancho was astonished to hear himself named by his name and to see himself embraced by the foreign pilgrim; and, after looking at him very attentively without saying a word, he could not recognise him at all. But the pilgrim, seeing his bewilderment, said to him:

"How, and is it possible, brother Sancho Panza, that you do not know your neighbour Ricote the Morisco, the shopkeeper of your village?"

Then Sancho looked at him more attentively and began to make out his features; and finally he came to know him at every point, and, without getting off the donkey, threw his arms round his neck and said:

"Who the devil would have known you, Ricote, in that mummer's dress you are wearing? Tell me: who has turned you into a Frenchy, and how do you dare to come back to Spain, where if they catch you and recognise you it will go very badly with you?"

"If you do not give me away, Sancho," answered the pilgrim, "I am safe enough that in this dress there will be nobody to recognise me. And let us turn off the road to that poplar grove over there, where my companions mean to eat and rest; and you shall eat with them there, for they are very pleasant people. I shall have room to tell you what has happened to me since I left our village, in obedience to His Majesty's edict, which threatened the unfortunate people of my nation with such severity, as you heard."

Sancho did so; and, Ricote speaking to the other pilgrims, they turned off to the poplar grove they could see, well away from the high road. They threw down their staves, took off their pilgrims' capes and were left in their shirtsleeves; and they were all young men and very fine-looking, except Ricote, who was a man already on in years. They all carried saddlebags, and all of them, by the look of it, came well provided, at least with provoking things that call up a thirst from two leagues off.

They stretched themselves out on the ground and, making tablecloths of the grass, laid out on them bread, salt, knives, walnuts, slices of cheese and bare ham bones which, if they would not let themselves be chewed, did not forbid being sucked. They also laid out a black dish they say is called caviare, made of fish eggs, a great awakener of thirst. Nor were olives wanting, though dry and without any pickle, but tasty and entertaining. But what showed most in the field of that banquet was six wineskins, each man taking his own out of his saddlebag; even good Ricote, who had transformed himself from a Morisco into a German or a High Dutchman, took his out, which in size could compete with the other five.

They began to eat with the greatest pleasure and very slowly, savouring every mouthful, which they took on the point of the knife, and very little of each thing. And then, at that instant, all together, they raised their arms and their wineskins in the air; their mouths set to the skins' mouths, their eyes fixed on the sky, they looked for all the world as if they were taking aim at it; and in this way, moving their heads from one side to the other — signs that bore witness to the pleasure they were taking — they stayed for a good while, decanting the bowels of the vessels into their stomachs.

Sancho watched it all and grieved over none of it; on the contrary, to keep the proverb he knew very well, "when you go to Rome, do as you see done," he asked Ricote for the wineskin and took his aim like the rest, and with no less pleasure than they.

Four times the wineskins allowed themselves to be tilted up; but the fifth time it was not possible, because by then they were drier and more parched than esparto grass — a thing that withered the gladness they had shown until then. From time to time one of them would join his right hand to Sancho's and say:

"Spaniard and Dutchman, all one: good companion."

And Sancho would answer: "Good companion, by God!"

And he would let off a burst of laughter that lasted him an hour, not remembering anything just then of what had happened to him in his government; because over the hour and the time when a man is eating and drinking, cares generally have very little jurisdiction.

Finally the running out of the wine was the beginning of a sleep that came over them all, and they were left asleep on the very tables and tablecloths. Only Ricote and Sancho stayed awake, because they had eaten more and drunk less; and, Ricote drawing Sancho aside, they sat down at the foot of a beech, leaving the pilgrims buried in sweet sleep. And Ricote, without stumbling at all into his Morisco tongue, in pure Castilian said him the following words:

"You know very well, Sancho Panza, my neighbour and my friend, how the proclamation and the edict His Majesty ordered published against those of my nation put terror and fright into all of us. At least it put it into me in such a way that it seemed to me that before the time allowed us for taking ourselves out of Spain, the severity of the penalty was already carried out on my person and on my children's.

"I arranged, then — prudently, to my mind, exactly like a man who knows that at a certain time they are going to take away the house he lives in and provides himself with another to move to — I arranged, I say, to leave my village alone, without my family, and go and look for somewhere to take them conveniently and without the haste with which the rest went out. Because I saw clearly, and all our elders saw, that those proclamations were not merely threats, as some said, but real laws that would be put into execution at their appointed time. And I was forced to believe this truth by knowing the base and disordered designs our people had, and such that it seems to me it was divine inspiration that moved His Majesty to put so gallant a resolution into effect — not because we were all guilty, for there were some firm and true Christians; but they were so few that they could not stand against those who were not, and it was not right to breed the serpent in the bosom, having the enemies inside the house.

"In short, we were punished with justice by the penalty of exile — mild and gentle to the mind of some, but to ours the most terrible that could be given us. Wherever we are, we weep for Spain; for in the end we were born in it and it is our natural country. Nowhere do we find the welcome our misfortune longs for; and in Barbary and in all the parts of Africa, where we hoped to be received and taken in and treated well, that is where they most offend and ill-treat us. We did not know the good until we had lost it; and the longing almost all of us have to come back to Spain is so great that most of those — and there are many — who know the language as I do come back to it and leave their wives and children over there unprotected: so great is the love they bear it. And now I know and feel by experience what is generally said: that the love of one's country is sweet.

"I left our village, as I say, and went into France; and although they gave us a good welcome there, I wanted to see everything. I crossed into Italy and got to Germany, and there it seemed to me that one could live with more freedom, because its inhabitants do not stick at a great many niceties: everybody lives as he likes, because in most of it people live with liberty of conscience. I took a house in a town near Augsburg; I joined these pilgrims, who have a habit of coming to Spain in great numbers every year to visit the shrines of it, which they take for their Indies and for the most certain source of profit and known gain. They go over almost the whole of it, and there is no village they do not come out of fed and watered, as they say, and with at least a real in money; and at the end of their journey they come out with more than a hundred crowns over, which, changed into gold — either in the hollow of their staves or among the patches of their capes or by whatever contrivance they can manage — they get out of the kingdom and carry over to their own countries, in spite of the guards at the posts and ports where they are searched.

"Now my intention, Sancho, is to dig up the treasure I left buried — which, being outside the village, I can do without danger — and to write or go over from Valencia to my daughter and my wife, who I know is in Algiers, and lay a plan to bring them to some French port and from there take them to Germany, where we shall wait for what God may be pleased to do with us. For in short, Sancho, I know for certain that Ricota my daughter and Francisca Ricota my wife are Catholic Christians; and although I am not so much of one, still I have more of the Christian in me than of the Moor, and I always pray God to open the eyes of my understanding and let me know how I am to serve Him. And what astonishes me is not knowing why my wife and my daughter went to Barbary rather than to France, where she could have lived as a Christian."

To which Sancho answered:

"Look, Ricote, that must not have been in her hands, because Juan Tiopieyo, your wife's brother, took them; and, as he must be a thorough Moor, he went where it suited him best. And I can tell you another thing: I believe you are going in vain to look for what you left hidden, because we had news that they took a great many pearls and a great deal of money in gold off your brother-in-law and your wife, which they were carrying unregistered."

"That may well be," replied Ricote, "but I know, Sancho, that they did not touch my hiding place, because I did not tell them where it was, for fear of some mishap. And so, if you, Sancho, will come with me and help me to get it out and hide it, I shall give you two hundred crowns, with which you can put your needs right; for you know that I know you have plenty of them."

"I would do it," answered Sancho, "but I am not at all greedy. If I were, I let an office go out of my hands this morning where I could have made the walls of my house of gold and been eating off silver plates within six months. And so, both for this reason and because it seems to me I should be doing my king a treason by giving help to his enemies, I would not go with you, even if instead of the two hundred crowns you promise me you gave me four hundred here in cash."

"And what office is it you have left, Sancho?" asked Ricote.

"I have left off being governor of an isle," answered Sancho, "and such a one that upon my word they will not find another like it at three tugs."

"And where is this isle?" asked Ricote.

"Where?" answered Sancho. "Two leagues from here, and it is called the isle of Barataria."

"Be quiet, Sancho," said Ricote; "isles are out there in the sea, for there are no isles on dry land."

"How not?" replied Sancho. "I tell you, Ricote my friend, that this morning I set out from it, and yesterday I was in it governing at my pleasure like a very lord of creation; but for all that I have left it, since being a governor seems to me a dangerous office."

"And what have you gained in the government?" asked Ricote.

"I have gained," answered Sancho, "the knowing that I am not good for governing anything but a flock of sheep, and that the riches that are gained in such governments are at the cost of losing your rest and your sleep and even your food; because in isles the governors must eat little, especially if they have doctors to look after their health."

"I do not understand you, Sancho," said Ricote, "but it seems to me that everything you say is nonsense. For who would give you isles to govern? Were there no abler men in the world to be governors than you are? Be quiet, Sancho, and come to your senses, and see whether you will come with me, as I have told you, to help me get out the treasure I left hidden; for truly there is so much of it that it can be called a treasure, and I shall give you enough to live on, as I have said."

"I have told you already, Ricote," replied Sancho, "that I do not want to; be content that I shall not give you away, and go on your road and good luck to you, and let me follow mine. For I know that what is well gained is lost, and what is ill gained, itself and its owner with it."

"I will not press you, Sancho," said Ricote, "but tell me: were you in our village when my wife and my daughter and my brother-in-law left it?"

"I was," answered Sancho, "and I can tell you that your daughter went out so beautiful that everybody in the village came out to see her, and they all said she was the loveliest creature in the world. She went along weeping and embracing all her friends and acquaintances and everybody who came up to see her, and asked them all to commend her to God and to Our Lady his mother; and this with so much feeling that it made me weep, and I am not generally much of a weeper. And upon my word, a good many wanted to hide her and go out and take her away from them on the road; but the fear of going against the king's order held them back.

"The one who showed himself most passionate about it was Don Gaspar Gregorio, that rich young heir you know, who they say was very much in love with her; and after she left he has never appeared again in our village, and we all think he went after her to carry her off — but up to now nothing has been heard."

"I always had a bad suspicion," said Ricote, "that that gentleman was in love with my daughter; but, trusting in my Ricota's worth, it never grieved me to know that he loved her well. For you must have heard it said, Sancho, that Morisco women seldom or never made love matches with old Christians; and my daughter, who, as I believe, attended more to being a Christian than to being in love, would not have troubled herself about that young heir's attentions."

"God grant it," replied Sancho, "for it would go badly with them both. And let me set off from here, Ricote my friend, for I want to get tonight to where my master Don Quixote is."

"God go with you, brother Sancho, for my companions are stirring already, and it is time we went on with our journey too."

And then the two of them embraced, and Sancho got up on his grey and Ricote leaned on his staff, and they parted.

Chapter 55: Of Things That Happened to Sancho on the Road, and Others as Good as Can Be Seen

Sancho's having stopped with Ricote gave him no room to reach the duke's castle that day, although he came within half a league of it, where night caught him — rather dark and thick; but, as it was summer, it did not distress him much. And so he turned off the road, meaning to wait for the morning; and his short and unfortunate luck willed that, while he was looking for a place to settle himself better, he and the grey fell into a deep and very dark pit that lay among some very ancient buildings. And as he fell he commended himself to God with all his heart, thinking he would not stop until the bottom of the abyss. And it was not so, for at a little over three times a man's height the grey struck bottom, and Sancho found himself on top of him without having taken any hurt or harm at all.

He felt himself all over his body and held his breath, to see whether he was sound or holed anywhere; and, finding himself well and whole and catholic in his health, he could not have done thanking God Our Lord enough for the kindness He had done him, for he had certainly thought he was smashed to a thousand pieces. He also felt with his hands along the walls of the pit, to see whether it would be possible to get out of it without anybody's help; but he found them all sheer and without any handhold, at which Sancho was greatly distressed, and especially when he heard the grey groaning tenderly and painfully — and no wonder, for he was not complaining out of self-indulgence, since in truth he was in a bad way.

"Oh," said Sancho Panza then, "what unthought-of things happen at every turn to those who live in this wretched world! Who would have said that the man who yesterday saw himself enthroned as governor of an isle, commanding his servants and his vassals, would today see himself buried in a pit, with nobody at all to help him and no servant or vassal to come to his rescue? Here we shall have to perish of hunger, my donkey and I — if we do not die first, he of being battered and broken and I of grief.

"At least I shall not be as lucky as my master Don Quixote of La Mancha was when he went down into the cave of that enchanted Montesinos, where he found people to treat him better than at home, so that it looks for all the world as if he went to a laid table and a made bed. There he saw beautiful and pleasant visions, and here I shall see, as I believe, toads and snakes. Unlucky man that I am, and what have my madnesses and fancies come to! From here they will take out my bones, when heaven is pleased for them to be found — bare and white and scraped, and my good grey's along with them; from which perhaps it will be made out who we are, at least by those who know that Sancho Panza never left his ass, nor his ass Sancho Panza.

"Again I say: wretched creatures that we are, whose short luck has not willed that we should die in our own country and among our own people, where, even if our misfortune found no remedy, there would be no lack of somebody to grieve over it and to close our eyes in the last hour of our passing! O my companion and my friend, what a bad return I have made you for your good services! Forgive me, and ask fortune, in the best way you know how, to bring us out of this wretched trouble the two of us are put in; for I promise to put a crown of laurel on your head, so that you shall look like nothing but a laureate poet, and to give you your rations double."

In this way Sancho Panza lamented, and his donkey listened to him without answering him a word — such was the strait and anguish the poor creature was in. Finally, having spent that whole night in wretched complaints and lamentations, the day came, by whose brightness and light Sancho saw that it was impossible with every impossibility to get out of that well without being helped; and he began to lament and to shout, to see whether anybody could hear him; but all his shouting was done in the desert, since there was nobody in all those parts who could have heard him, and then he finally gave himself up for dead.

The grey was lying on his back, and Sancho Panza arranged him in such a way that he got him on his feet, which he could hardly keep. And, taking out of the saddlebags — which had run the same fortune of the fall — a piece of bread, he gave it to his donkey, who did not find it bad. And Sancho said to him, as though he would understand:

"All sorrows are good with bread."

At this he made out at one side of the pit a hole big enough for a person to get through if he bent over and shrank himself up. Sancho Panza went to it and, crouching down, got in through it, and saw that inside it was spacious and long; and he could see it, because through what might be called the roof there came in a ray of sunlight that showed the whole of it. He saw too that it widened out and stretched away into another spacious hollow. Seeing which, he went back out to where the donkey was, and with a stone began to crumble away the earth of the hole, so that in a little while he made room for the ass to get in easily, as he did; and, taking him by the halter, he began to travel forward along that grotto, to see whether he could find some way out at the other end. Sometimes he went in the dark, and sometimes without light, but never without fear.

"God almighty help me!" he said to himself. "This, which for me is a misadventure, would be a better adventure for my master Don Quixote. He indeed would take these depths and dungeons for flowery gardens and for Galiana's palaces, and would expect to come out of this darkness and this narrowness into some flowery meadow. But I, luckless man, short of counsel and cut down in courage, at every step think another pit deeper than the last is suddenly going to open under my feet and finish swallowing me. Welcome, trouble, if you come alone!"

In this way and with these thoughts it seemed to him that he must have travelled a little over half a league, at the end of which he made out a confused brightness that seemed to be daylight and to be coming in somewhere — a sign that this road of his to the other life had an open end.

Here Cide Hamete Benengeli leaves him and goes back to dealing with Don Quixote, who, excited and contented, was waiting for the appointed time of the battle he was to fight with the robber of the honour of Doña Rodríguez's daughter, whose wrong and injury, wickedly done unto her, he meant to set right.

It happened, then, that, going out one morning to train and rehearse himself in what he had to do in the pass he expected to be in the next day, giving Rocinante a sudden pull-up or charge, he came to set his feet so close to a cave that if he had not tugged strongly at the reins it would have been impossible not to fall into it. In short, he held him and did not fall; and, coming a little nearer without dismounting, he looked at that depth. And, while he was looking at it, he heard loud shouts inside; and, listening attentively, he could make out and understand that the man who was giving them was saying:

"Ho, up there! Is there any Christian who hears me, or any charitable knight who will pity a sinner buried alive, or an unfortunate ungoverned governor?"

It seemed to Don Quixote that he heard Sancho Panza's voice, at which he was bewildered and amazed; and, raising his voice as much as he could, he said:

"Who is down there? Who is complaining?"

"Who can be here, or who is to complain," they answered, "but the worn-out Sancho Panza, governor, for his sins and his ill fortune, of the isle of Barataria, and squire that was to the famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha?"

Hearing which, Don Quixote's astonishment doubled and his amazement grew, it coming into his mind that Sancho Panza must be dead and that his soul was doing penance there; and, carried away by this idea, he said:

"I conjure you by everything I can conjure you by as a Catholic Christian, to tell me who you are; and if you are a soul in torment, tell me what you want me to do for you. For since it is my profession to favour and help those in need in this world, I shall also be ready to help and aid the needy of the other world, who cannot help themselves."

"In that case," they answered, "your worship who is speaking to me must be my master Don Quixote of La Mancha; and indeed by the organ of the voice it is nobody else, without any doubt."

"Don Quixote I am," replied Don Quixote, "who make it my profession to help and aid the living and the dead in their needs. So tell me who you are, for you have me astounded; because if you are my squire Sancho Panza and you are dead, and if the devils have not carried you off but by the mercy of God you are in purgatory, our Holy Mother the Roman Catholic Church has intercessions enough to bring you out of the pains you are in, and I, for my part, shall solicit them for you as far as my property will reach. So finish declaring yourself and tell me who you are."

"I swear," they answered, "and by the birth of whoever your worship likes, I swear, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, that I am your squire Sancho Panza, and that I have never died in all the days of my life. Only, having left my government for things and reasons that need more room to tell, last night I fell into this pit where I lie, and the grey with me, who will not let me lie — for, as a further sign, he is here with me."

And there is more: it looked for all the world as if the donkey understood what Sancho said, because at that moment he began to bray so loudly that the whole cave rang with it.

"A famous witness!" said Don Quixote. "I know that bray as if I had given birth to it, and I hear your voice, my Sancho. Wait for me; I shall go to the duke's castle, which is close by here, and bring somebody to get you out of this pit where your sins must have put you."

"Go, your worship," said Sancho, "and come back quickly, for the one God's sake, for I cannot bear being buried alive here any longer, and I am dying of fear."

Don Quixote left him and went to the castle to tell the duke and duchess about Sancho Panza's mishap, at which they were not a little amazed, although they understood well enough that he must have fallen in by the connection with that grotto which had been there from time immemorial; but they could not think how he had left the government without their having notice of his coming.

Finally, as they say, they brought ropes and cables; and, at the cost of a great many people and a great deal of labour, they got the grey and Sancho Panza out of that darkness into the light of the sun. A student saw him and said:

"This is how all bad governors ought to come out of their governments — as this sinner comes out of the depths of the pit: dead with hunger, colourless and without a farthing, as I believe."

Sancho heard him and said:

"Eight days or ten it is, brother gossip, since I went in to govern the isle they gave me; and in all that time I never had my fill of bread for so much as an hour. In them doctors have persecuted me and enemies have crushed my bones; and I have had no chance to take bribes or to collect fees. And this being so, as it is, I did not deserve, to my mind, to come out like this; but man proposes and God disposes, and God knows what is best and what suits each man; and as the times are, so the touch; and let nobody say 'I shall not drink of this water', for where you think there are flitches of bacon there are not even hooks. And God understands me, and that is enough, and I say no more, though I could."

"Do not be angry, Sancho, or take it hard from whatever you hear, for it would be never-ending. Come with a clear conscience and let them say what they will; and to want to tie the tongues of slanderers is the same as wanting to put doors on the open field. If the governor comes out of his government rich, they say of him that he has been a thief; and if he comes out poor, that he has been a good-for-nothing and an idiot."

"For a safe bet," answered Sancho, "this time they will take me for a fool rather than for a thief."

In this talk they came, surrounded by boys and by a great many other people, to the castle, where the duke and duchess were already waiting in a gallery for Don Quixote and Sancho. But Sancho would not go up to see the duke without first having settled the grey in the stable, because he said he had spent a very bad night at his lodging; and then he went up to see his master and mistress, before whom, on his knees, he said:

"I, my lord and lady, because your greatness willed it so and through no deserving of my own, went to govern your isle of Barataria, which I entered naked and naked I find myself: I neither lose nor gain. Whether I have governed well or badly, I have had witnesses in front of me who will say whatever they like. I have cleared up doubts and given judgement in lawsuits, always dying of hunger, because Doctor Pedro Recio, native of Get-You-Gone, an isle-and-governor doctor, willed it so.

"Enemies attacked us by night; and, having put us in a great strait, the people of the isle say they came out free and victorious by the valour of my arm — and may God give them as much health as they are telling truth.

"In short, in this time I have taken the measure of the burdens that governing brings with it, and the obligations; and I have found by my reckoning that my shoulders will not be able to carry them, that they are no weight for my ribs and no arrows for my quiver. And so, before the government pitched me over the side, I chose to pitch the government over the side myself; and yesterday morning I left the isle as I found it, with the same streets, houses and roofs it had when I went into it. I have not borrowed from anybody or got into any money-making; and although I meant to make some useful ordinances, I made none, for fear they would not be kept — which is the same as making them or not making them.

"I left the isle, as I say, with no company but my grey's; I fell into a pit, I came along it until this morning, when by the light of the sun I saw the way out — but not so easy a one that if heaven had not furnished me with my master Don Quixote I should not have stayed there until the end of the world.

"So, my lord duke and lady duchess, here is your governor Sancho Panza, who in the ten days alone that he has had the government has gained the knowledge that he would not give a farthing to be governor, not merely of an isle but of the whole world. And on this understanding, kissing your worships' feet, and copying the boys' game where they say 'You jump, and now you give it me', I jump out of the government and pass over into the service of my master Don Quixote; for with him, though I eat my bread in alarm, at least I have my fill — and for me, so long as I am full, it is all one whether it is carrots or partridges."

With this Sancho made an end of his long speech, Don Quixote all the while fearing that he was going to say thousands of absurdities in it; and, when he saw him finish with so few, he gave thanks to heaven in his heart. And the duke embraced Sancho and told him it grieved him to the soul that he had left the government so soon; but that he would arrange for him to be given some other office on his estate with less burden and more profit. The duchess embraced him likewise, and ordered him to be well looked after, since he gave signs of coming badly battered and worse used.

Chapter 56: Of the Monstrous and Never-Before-Seen Battle That Took Place Between Don Quixote of La Mancha and the Footman Tosilos, in Defence of the Duenna Doña Rodríguez's Daughter

The duke and duchess were not left regretting the trick they had played on Sancho Panza with the government they gave him — and the more so as that very day their steward came and told them point by point almost all the words and actions Sancho had said and done in those days, and finally set out for them at length the assault on the isle and Sancho's fear and his departure, from which they took no small pleasure.

After this, the history tells that the day of the appointed battle came round; and the duke, having warned his footman Tosilos once and a great many times how he was to manage with Don Quixote so as to conquer him without killing or wounding him, ordered the heads to be taken off the lances, telling Don Quixote that the Christian charity he prided himself on did not allow that battle to be fought with so much risk and danger to their lives, and that he should be content that he was giving him a free field on his own land, although this went against the decree of the Holy Council, which forbids such challenges, and that he should not want to carry so hard a pass through in all its severity.

Don Quixote said that His Excellency might arrange the affairs of that business as he was best pleased, and that he would obey him in everything.

The dreaded day having come, then, and the duke having ordered a spacious scaffold to be built in front of the castle square, where the judges of the field and the duennas, mother and daughter, the plaintiffs, should sit, an infinite number of people had come from all the neighbouring towns and villages to see the novelty of that battle — for the like of it had never been seen or heard of in that country by those who were living or by those who had died.

The first to come into the field and the lists was the master of the ceremonies, who measured the ground and walked all over it, so that there should be no trick in it or anything hidden to trip over and fall on. Then the duennas came in and sat down in their seats, covered with their mantles up to their eyes and even up to their breasts, with signs of no small feeling.

Don Quixote being present in the lists, a little later, attended by a great many trumpets, there appeared at one side of the square, on a mighty horse, making the whole of it echo, the great footman Tosilos, his visor down and all stiffly encased in strong, shining armour. The horse looked to be a Frisian, broad and dapple-grey; from each fore and hind fetlock there hung a good bushel of hair.

The valorous combatant came well informed by the duke his master how he was to conduct himself with the valorous Don Quixote of La Mancha, warned that on no account was he to kill him but was to try to dodge the first charge, so as to escape the danger of Don Quixote's death, which was certain if he ran him full on. He rode round the square; and, coming to where the duennas were, he stopped a while to look at the one who was asking for him as a husband.

The marshal of the field called Don Quixote, who had already presented himself in the square; and, along with Tosilos, he spoke to the duennas, asking them whether they consented to Don Quixote of La Mancha's standing up for their right. They said they did, and that everything he did in that case they held for well done, for binding and for valid.

By this time the duke and duchess had taken their places in a gallery that looked over the lists, the whole of which was crowned with an infinite number of people waiting to see the severe and never-before-seen encounter. It was a condition of the combatants that if Don Quixote won, his opponent was to marry Doña Rodríguez's daughter; and if he were beaten, his adversary was free of the promise that was being demanded of him, without giving any other satisfaction.

The master of the ceremonies divided the sun between them and set each of the two in the place where they were to stand. The drums sounded, the sound of the trumpets filled the air, the earth trembled underfoot; the hearts of the watching crowd hung in suspense, some fearing and others hoping for the good or the bad outcome of that business.

Finally Don Quixote, commending himself with his whole heart to God Our Lord and to the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso, was waiting for the exact signal for the charge to be given him. But our footman had different thoughts: he was thinking of nothing but what I shall now tell.

It seems that when he stood looking at his enemy, she seemed to him the most beautiful woman he had seen in all his life; and the little blind boy, whom people up and down these streets generally call Love, did not want to lose the chance that offered itself of triumphing over a footman's soul and putting it on the list of his trophies. And so, coming up to him nicely without anybody seeing him, he ran a two-yard arrow into the poor footman's left side and pierced his heart right through; and he could do it in perfect safety, because Love is invisible and goes in and out wherever he likes, without anybody asking him to account for what he does.

I say, then, that when they gave the signal for the charge, our footman was carried away, thinking about the beauty of the woman he had already made the mistress of his liberty; and so he took no notice of the sound of the trumpet, as Don Quixote did, who had hardly heard it when he charged and, at the fastest gallop Rocinante allowed, set off against his enemy. And, his good squire Sancho seeing him set off, he said in a loud voice:

"God guide you, cream and flower of knights errant! God give you the victory, since you have right on your side!"

And, although Tosilos saw Don Quixote coming at him, he did not stir a step from his place; on the contrary, he called out loudly to the marshal of the field, who, coming to see what he wanted, was told:

"Sir, is this battle not being fought about whether I marry that lady or not?"

"That is so," he was answered.

"Well, I," said the footman, "am afraid for my conscience, and I should put a great load on it if I went on with this battle. And so I say that I give myself up as beaten, and that I want to marry that lady at once."

The marshal of the field was astonished at Tosilos's words; and, as he was one of those who were in on the machinery of that business, he did not know how to answer him a word. Don Quixote pulled up in the middle of his career, seeing that his enemy was not attacking him. The duke did not know why the battle was not going forward, but the marshal of the field went and explained to him what Tosilos was saying, at which he was left bewildered and extremely choleric.

While this was going on, Tosilos came up to where Doña Rodríguez was and said in a loud voice:

"I, madam, want to marry your daughter, and I do not want to get by lawsuits and quarrels what I can get in peace and without danger of death."

The valorous Don Quixote heard this and said:

"Since this is so, I am left free and released from my promise: let them be married and good luck to them; and since God Our Lord gave her him, let Saint Peter bless her to him."

The duke had come down into the castle square, and, coming up to Tosilos, said to him:

"Is it true, sir knight, that you give yourself up as beaten, and that, urged on by your timorous conscience, you want to marry this maiden?"

"Yes, my lord," answered Tosilos.

"He does very well," said Sancho Panza at this, "because what you are going to give the mouse, give the cat, and it will save you trouble."

Tosilos was unlacing his helmet, and begged them to help him quickly, because his breath was failing him and he could not bear to be shut up so long in the narrowness of that lodging. They took it off him quickly, and his footman's face was left uncovered and plain to see. Which Doña Rodríguez and her daughter seeing, they said in a great outcry:

"This is a fraud, this is a fraud! They have put Tosilos, the duke my lord's footman, in the place of my true husband! Justice of God and of the King on so much malice — not to say roguery!"

"Do not distress yourselves, ladies," said Don Quixote, "for this is neither malice nor roguery; and if it is, the cause has not been the duke but the wicked enchanters who persecute me, who, envious that I should attain the glory of this victory, have turned your husband's face into that of this man you say is the duke's footman. Take my advice, and, in spite of my enemies' malice, marry him, for he is undoubtedly the very man you want to get for a husband."

The duke, who heard this, was ready to break out into laughter and forget all his choler, and said:

"The things that happen to Señor Don Quixote are so extraordinary that I am inclined to believe that this footman of mine is not one. But let us use this trick and dodge: let us put off the wedding for a fortnight, if they like, and keep this personage who has us in doubt shut up; in which time it might be that he would go back to his first shape — for the enchanters' grudge against Señor Don Quixote cannot last so long, and the more so as they get so little out of using these humbugs and transformations."

"Oh, my lord," said Sancho, "these villains have it for a habit and a custom by now to change one thing into another where my master is concerned. A knight he conquered a few days ago, called the Knight of the Mirrors, they turned into the shape of the bachelor Sansón Carrasco, a native of our village and a great friend of ours; and my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso they have turned into a country wench. And so I imagine that this footman will live and die a footman all the days of his life."

To which Rodríguez's daughter said:

"Let this man who asks for me as his wife be whoever he may be, I am grateful to him for it; for I would rather be the lawful wife of a footman than the mistress of a gentleman who has made a mock of me — although the man who made a mock of me is no gentleman."

In short, all these tales and events came round to Tosilos's being shut up until it should be seen what came of his transformation. Everybody proclaimed the victory for Don Quixote, and most of them were left sad and melancholy at seeing that the two so long expected combatants had not smashed each other to pieces — exactly as the boys are sad when the hanged man they are waiting for does not come out, because either the injured party or the law has pardoned him. The people went off; the duke and Don Quixote went back to the castle; they shut Tosilos up; Doña Rodríguez and her daughter were left extremely pleased at seeing that, one way or the other, that business was going to end in a marriage; and Tosilos expected nothing less.

Chapter 57: Which Deals with How Don Quixote Took His Leave of the Duke, and with What Happened to Him with the Witty and Forward Altisidora, the Duchess's Maiden

It now seemed to Don Quixote that it would be as well to get out of all the idleness he was living in at that castle; for he imagined that his person was greatly missed by his staying shut up and lazy among the infinite indulgences and delights those nobles gave him as a knight errant, and it seemed to him that he would have to give a strict account to heaven for that idleness and confinement. And so one day he asked the duke and duchess for leave to depart. They gave it him, with signs that it grieved them greatly that he should leave them.

The duchess gave Sancho Panza his wife's letters, over which he wept, and said:

"Who would have thought that hopes as great as those that the news of my government bred in the breast of my wife Teresa Panza should end in my going back now to the dragged-about adventures of my master Don Quixote of La Mancha? Still, I am content to see that my Teresa answered to being who she is by sending the acorns to the duchess; for if she had not sent them, I should have been grieved and she would have shown herself ungrateful.

"What consoles me is that this gift cannot be given the name of a bribe, because I already had the government when she sent them, and it stands to reason that those who receive some kindness, even if it is only trifles, should show themselves grateful. In fact I went into the government naked and I come out of it naked; and so I can say with a clear conscience — which is no small thing — 'naked I was born and naked I find myself: I neither lose nor gain'."

This is what Sancho was saying to himself on the day of their departure; and, Don Quixote coming out, having taken his leave of the duke and duchess the night before, one morning he presented himself armed in the castle square. All the people of the castle watched him from the galleries, and the duke and duchess likewise came out to see him. Sancho was on his grey with his saddlebags, his valise and his stores, extremely pleased, because the duke's steward, the man who had been the Trifaldi, had given him a little purse with two hundred gold crowns to make up for the needs of the road — and Don Quixote did not yet know about this.

While, as has been said, everybody was watching him, all at once, among the duchess's other duennas and maidens who were looking at him, the forward and witty Altisidora raised her voice and said in a mournful tone:

	Listen, wicked knight;
	hold your reins a little;
	do not wear out the flanks
	of your badly ruled beast.
	Look, false man, that you are not fleeing
	from any fierce serpent
	but from a little lamb
	that is a long way from being a ewe.
	You have made a mock, hideous monster,
	of the loveliest maiden
	that Diana saw on her mountains,
	that Venus looked on in her woods.
	Cruel Bireno, fugitive Aeneas,
	may Barabbas go with you; settle it out there.
	You carry off — impious carrying! —
	in the claws of your hands
	the entrails of a girl who is humble
	and, being in love, tender.
	You carry off three headcloths
	and a pair of garters from legs
	that are a match for pure marble
	in smoothness, in whiteness and in blackness.
	You carry off two thousand sighs
	which, if they were of fire, could
	burn up two thousand Troys,
	if there were two thousand Troys.
	Cruel Bireno, fugitive Aeneas,
	may Barabbas go with you; settle it out there.
	Of that Sancho, your squire,
	may the bowels be so stubborn
	and so hard that Dulcinea
	never comes out of her enchantment.
	For the fault that is yours
	may the poor girl carry the penalty;
	for in my country the just
	sometimes pay for the sinners.
	May your finest adventures
	be turned into misadventures,
	your pastimes into dreams,
	your constancies into forgettings.
	Cruel Bireno, fugitive Aeneas,
	may Barabbas go with you; settle it out there.
	May you be held for false
	from Seville to Marchena,
	from Granada as far as Loja,
	from London to England.
	If you play at kings,
	or at hundreds, or at primero,
	may the kings run away from you;
	may you see neither aces nor sevens.
	If you cut your corns,
	may the cuts run blood,
	and may the stumps stay in you
	if you have your grinders pulled.
	Cruel Bireno, fugitive Aeneas,
	may Barabbas go with you; settle it out there.

While the wounded Altisidora was complaining in the way that has been described, Don Quixote stood looking at her; and, without answering her a word, he turned his face to Sancho and said to him:

"By the memory of your ancestors, my Sancho, I conjure you to tell me a truth. Tell me: do you by any chance have the three headcloths and the garters this enamoured maiden speaks of?"

To which Sancho answered:

"The three headcloths I do have; but the garters, no more than the hills of Úbeda."

The duchess was astonished at Altisidora's forwardness; for although she took her for bold, amusing and free, she did not take her for free to the point of daring such forwardnesses as these. And, since she had not been warned about this trick, her astonishment grew still greater. The duke wanted to reinforce the joke, and said:

"It does not seem well to me, sir knight, that, having received in this castle of mine the good welcome that has been given you in it, you should have dared to carry off three headcloths at the least — and at the most my maiden's garters. They are signs of a bad heart and evidences that do not answer to your fame. Give her back the garters; if not, I challenge you to mortal battle, without any fear that villainous enchanters may turn or change my face, as they have done with Tosilos my footman's, who went into battle with you."

"God forbid," answered Don Quixote, "that I should draw my sword against your most illustrious person, from whom I have received so many kindnesses. The headcloths I shall give back, because Sancho says he has them; the garters is impossible, because neither I have received them nor he either; and if this maiden of yours will look in her hiding places, it is a safe bet that she will find them. I, my lord duke, have never been a thief, nor do I mean to be one in all my life, so long as God does not take His hand off me. This maiden speaks, as she says herself, as a woman in love, for which I am not to blame; and so I have nothing to ask pardon for, either from her or from Your Excellency — whom I beg to hold me in a better opinion and to give me leave once more to follow my road."

"May God give you so good a one, Señor Don Quixote," said the duchess, "that we may always hear good news of your doings. And go with God; for the longer you stay, the more you increase the fire in the breasts of the maidens who look at you. And I shall punish my own in such a way that from now on she will not let herself go with her eyes or with her words."

"One thing more only I want you to hear from me, O valorous Don Quixote," said Altisidora then; "and it is that I ask your pardon for the theft of the garters, because, in God and in my soul, I have them on, and I have fallen into the carelessness of the man who went looking for his ass while he was riding it."

"Did I not say so?" said Sancho. "A fine one I am for hiding thefts! Why, if I had wanted to commit any, the chance came to me on a plate in my government."

Don Quixote bowed his head and made a bow to the duke and duchess and to all the bystanders; and, turning Rocinante's reins, with Sancho following him on the grey, he went out of the castle and made his way towards Saragossa.

Chapter 58: Which Deals with How Adventures Came Thick and Fast on Don Quixote, So Many That They Gave Each Other No Room

When Don Quixote saw himself in the open country, free and disencumbered of Altisidora's love-making, it seemed to him that he was at his own centre and that his spirits were being renewed for taking up the business of his chivalries afresh; and, turning to Sancho, he said:

"Liberty, Sancho, is one of the most precious gifts heaven gave to men; with it the treasures the earth encloses and the sea covers cannot be compared. For liberty, as for honour, a man can and should venture his life; and, on the contrary, captivity is the greatest evil that can come to men.

"I say this, Sancho, because you have seen well enough the indulgence and the abundance we have had in that castle we have left; well, in the middle of those seasoned banquets and those iced drinks it seemed to me that I was in the straits of hunger, because I did not enjoy them with the freedom I should have if they had been my own. For the obligations of repaying kindnesses and favours received are bonds that do not let a free spirit range. Happy is the man to whom heaven gave a piece of bread without his being obliged to thank anybody for it but heaven itself!"

"For all that your worship has told me," said Sancho, "it is not right that we should leave without a show of gratitude the two hundred gold crowns the duke's steward gave me in a little purse, which I carry over my heart like a poultice and a cordial against whatever may turn up; for we shall not always find castles where they treat us well — sometimes we shall come across inns where they thrash us."

In these and other arguments the errants, knight and squire, were going along, when they saw, having travelled a little over a league, that on the grass of a small green meadow, on top of their cloaks, about a dozen men dressed as farm labourers were eating. Next to them they had what looked like white sheets covering something that was underneath; they were propped up and spread out and set at intervals.

Don Quixote came up to the men who were eating; and, greeting them courteously first, he asked them what those cloths were covering. One of them answered him:

"Sir, under these cloths there are some images in relief and carved work that are to serve in an altarpiece we are making in our village; we carry them covered so that they may not be rubbed, and on our shoulders so that they may not be broken."

"If you would be so good," answered Don Quixote, "I should be glad to see them; for images that are carried with so much care must undoubtedly be good ones."

"And how good they are!" said another. "If not, let the price say so; for truly there is not one of them that stands at less than fifty ducats. And so that your worship may see this truth, wait, your worship, and you shall see it with your own eyes."

And, getting up, he left off eating and went and took the covering off the first image, which turned out to be Saint George on horseback, with a serpent coiled at his feet and the lance thrust through its mouth, with the fierceness with which he is generally painted. The whole image looked like a live coal of gold, as the saying goes. Don Quixote, seeing it, said:

"This knight was one of the best errants the divine soldiery ever had: he was called Don Saint George, and he was besides a defender of maidens. Let us see this other one."

The man uncovered it, and it turned out to be Saint Martin on horseback, dividing his cloak with the poor man; and Don Quixote had hardly seen it when he said:

"This knight was also one of the Christian adventurers, and I believe he was more generous than valiant, as you can see, Sancho, from his dividing his cloak with the poor man and giving him half. And it must undoubtedly have been winter at the time, for if not he would have given him the whole of it, so charitable was he."

"That must not have been it," said Sancho, "but that he must have held to the proverb that says that for giving and keeping, brains are needed."

Don Quixote laughed and asked them to take off another cloth, under which was uncovered the image of the Patron of the Spains on horseback, his sword bloody, trampling Moors and treading on heads; and, on seeing it, Don Quixote said:

"This one is a knight indeed, and of the squadrons of Christ; this one is called Don Saint James the Moor-slayer, one of the most valiant saints and knights the world ever had and heaven has now."

Then they uncovered another cloth, and it turned out to hide Saint Paul's fall from his horse, with all the circumstances that are generally painted in the altarpiece of his conversion. When he saw it so much to the life that one would have said Christ was speaking to him and Paul answering, he said:

"This man was the greatest enemy the Church of God Our Lord had in his time, and the greatest defender of it that it will ever have: a knight errant in his life and a saint standing still in his death, a tireless labourer in the Lord's vineyard, a teacher of the nations, whose schools were the heavens and whose professor and master, to teach him, was Jesus Christ himself."

There were no more images, and so Don Quixote ordered them to cover them again, and said to the men who were carrying them:

"I have taken it for a good omen, brothers, to have seen what I have seen; because these saints and knights professed what I profess, which is the exercise of arms — only that the difference between me and them is that they were saints and fought in the divine way, and I am a sinner and fight in the human way. They conquered heaven by main force, because heaven suffers violence; and I so far do not know what I am conquering by the force of my labours. But if my Dulcinea of El Toboso were to come out of the sufferings she is in, and my fortune were to improve and my judgement be mended, it might be that I should set my steps on a better road than the one I am on."

"May God hear it and sin be deaf," said Sancho on this occasion.

The men were astonished, both at Don Quixote's figure and at his words, without understanding half of what he meant to say in them. They finished eating, took up their images and, taking their leave of Don Quixote, went on their journey.

Sancho was left once more as if he had never known his master, astonished at what he knew, since it seemed to him that there could not be a history in the world or an event that he did not have at his fingertips and nailed into his memory; and he said to him:

"Truly, sir our master, if what has happened to us today can be called an adventure, it has been one of the smoothest and sweetest that has happened to us in the whole course of our wanderings. We have come out of it without cudgellings and without a fright, and we have not laid hand to our swords or beaten the earth with our bodies, and we are not left hungry. Blessed be God, who has let me see such a thing with my own eyes."

"You speak well, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "but you must note that not all times are alike, nor do they run in the same way. And these things that the common people generally call omens, which are not founded on any natural reason, ought to be held and judged for good happenings by the man who is judicious.

"One of these omen-mongers gets up in the morning, comes out of his house and meets a friar of the order of the blessed Saint Francis; and, as though he had met a griffin, he turns his back and goes home again. Another spills the salt on the table, and melancholy is spilt over his heart — as though nature were obliged to give signs of coming misfortunes by things as trifling as the ones I have mentioned. The judicious and Christian man must not go splitting hairs over what heaven means to do.

"Scipio arrives in Africa, trips as he leaps ashore, and his soldiers take it for a bad omen; but he, embracing the ground, said: 'You shall not be able to escape me, Africa, for I have you gripped and in my arms.' So, Sancho, my having met these images has been for me a most happy happening."

"I believe so too," answered Sancho, "and I should like your worship to tell me what the reason is that the Spaniards say, when they mean to give battle and are calling on that Saint James the Moor-slayer, 'Santiago, and close, Spain!' Is Spain by any chance open, and in such a way that it needs closing? Or what ceremony is this?"

"You are the simplest of the simple, Sancho," answered Don Quixote. "Look, God has given this great knight of the red cross to Spain for her patron and protection, especially in the hard passes the Spaniards have had with the Moors; and so they call on him and invoke him as their defender in all the battles they undertake, and many times they have seen him visibly in them, knocking down, trampling, destroying and killing the squadrons of Hagar. And of this truth I could bring you a great many examples that are told in the true Spanish histories."

Sancho changed the subject and said to his master:

"I am amazed, sir, at the forwardness of Altisidora, the duchess's maiden: that fellow they call Love must have wounded and run her through bravely — the one they say is a blear-eyed little blind boy who, though he has rheumy eyes, or, better said, no sight at all, if he takes a heart for his target, however small it may be, hits it and runs it through from side to side with his arrows. I have also heard it said that on the modesty and reserve of maidens the arrows of love are blunted and dulled; but on this Altisidora it looks as though they were sharpened rather than blunted."

"Note, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that love neither looks at rank nor keeps to the bounds of reason in its arguments, and that it has the same nature as death: that it attacks the high castles of kings just as it does the humble huts of shepherds; and when it takes complete possession of a soul, the first thing it does is take away its fear and its shame. And so, without any shame, Altisidora declared her desires — which bred in my breast confusion rather than pity."

"Notorious cruelty!" said Sancho. "Unheard-of ingratitude! For myself I can say that the least little loving word of hers would have conquered me and made me her vassal. Whoreson, and what a heart of marble, what entrails of bronze and what a soul of mortar! But I cannot think what it was this maiden saw in your worship to conquer and enslave her like that: what elegance, what spirit, what charm, what face — that any one of these things by itself, or all of them together, should have made her fall in love. Because truly and truly I often stop to look at your worship from the tip of your foot to the last hair on your head, and I see more things to frighten a woman than to make her fall in love; and, having also heard it said that beauty is the first and chief part that makes people fall in love, your worship having none at all, I do not know what the poor girl fell in love with."

"Note, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "that there are two kinds of beauty: one of the soul and another of the body. That of the soul shows and displays itself in the understanding, in decency, in good conduct, in generosity and in good breeding; and all these qualities can fit and be found in an ugly man. And when the aim is set on this beauty and not on that of the body, love is generally born with force and with advantages. I, Sancho, see well enough that I am not handsome; but I also know that I am not deformed. And it is enough for an honest man not to be a monster to be well loved, so long as he has the gifts of the soul I have told you of."

In these words and this talk they were going into a wood that lay off the road; and all at once, without thinking about it, Don Quixote found himself tangled in some nets of green thread that were stretched from one tree to another; and, unable to imagine what that could be, he said to Sancho:

"It seems to me, Sancho, that this business of the nets must be one of the newest adventures that can be imagined. May they kill me if the enchanters who persecute me are not trying to tangle me in them and hold up my road, as revenge for the severity I have shown Altisidora. Well, I let them know that even if these nets, instead of being made of green thread, were of the hardest diamonds, or stronger than the one with which the jealous god of the blacksmiths tangled up Venus and Mars, I should break them as though they were made of sea rushes or shreds of cotton."

And, wanting to go forward and break the whole thing, all of a sudden there appeared in front of him, coming out from among some trees, two most beautiful shepherdesses — at least dressed as shepherdesses, except that their jerkins and skirts were of fine brocade; I mean that the skirts were very rich petticoats of gold tabby. They wore their hair loose over their shoulders, which in fairness could compete with the rays of the sun itself, and it was crowned with two garlands woven of green laurel and red amaranth. Their age, to look at them, was neither under fifteen nor over eighteen.

This was a sight that astonished Sancho, bewildered Don Quixote, made the sun stop in his course to look at them, and held all four of them in a marvellous silence. Finally the one who spoke first was one of the two shepherdesses, who said to Don Quixote:

"Hold your step, sir knight, and do not break the nets; for they are stretched there not to do you any harm but for our entertainment. And, since I know you are going to ask me why they have been put there and who we are, I want to tell you in a few words.

"In a village up to two leagues from here, where there are a great many people of quality and a great many gentlemen and rich men, it was agreed among a large number of friends and relations that with their sons, wives and daughters, their neighbours, friends and relations, we should come and enjoy ourselves at this spot, which is one of the most agreeable in all these parts, forming among us all a new and pastoral Arcadia, the girls dressing as shepherdesses and the young men as shepherds. We have two eclogues by heart, one by the famous poet Garcilaso and another by the most excellent Camões in his own Portuguese tongue, which we have not yet performed.

"Yesterday was the first day we came here.
