We have some tents pitched among these branches — they say they are called field tents — on the bank of a plentiful stream that makes all these meadows fertile. Last night we stretched these nets from these trees to trap the simple little birds which, driven up by the noise we make, come and blunder into them. If it pleases you, sir, to be our guest, you shall be entertained generously and courteously; because for now neither heaviness nor melancholy is to come into this place."

She fell silent and said no more. To which Don Quixote answered:

"Certainly, most beautiful lady, Actaeon cannot have been left more bewildered or astonished when he suddenly saw Diana bathing in the waters than I have been left thunderstruck at seeing your beauty. I praise the design of your entertainments, and I thank you for your offers; and if I can serve you, you may command me with the certainty of being obeyed, because this is not my profession but to show myself grateful and a doer of good to every sort of person, and especially to the sort of quality your persons represent. And if these nets, which must take up some small space, took up the whole round of the earth, I should look for new worlds to pass through without breaking them. And so that you may give some credit to this exaggeration of mine, see that it is promised you, at the very least, by Don Quixote of La Mancha — if this name has reached your ears."

"Oh, friend of my soul," said the other shepherdess then, "what great good fortune has happened to us! Do you see this gentleman we have in front of us? Well, I let you know that he is the most valiant and the most in love and the most courteous man in the world, unless a history of his exploits that is in print and that I have read is lying to us and deceiving us. I would wager that this good man who comes with him is a certain Sancho Panza, his squire, whose drolleries have no equals."

"That is the truth," said Sancho: "I am that droll and that squire your worship speaks of, and this gentleman is my master, the very Don Quixote of La Mancha of the history and the report."

"Oh," said the other, "let us beg him to stay, my friend; for our fathers and our brothers will take infinite pleasure in it. For I too have heard the same of his valour and his charms as you have told me; and, above all, they say of him that he is the firmest and most loyal lover known, and that his lady is a certain Dulcinea of El Toboso, to whom in all Spain they give the palm of beauty."

"With reason they give it her," said Don Quixote, "unless your peerless beauty puts it in doubt. Do not wear yourselves out in detaining me, ladies, because the strict obligations of my profession do not let me rest anywhere."

At this there came to where the four of them were a brother of one of the two shepherdesses, dressed likewise as a shepherd, with richness and finery to match the girls'. They told him that the man who was with them was the valorous Don Quixote of La Mancha, and the other his squire Sancho, of whom he already had news through having read their history. The gallant shepherd offered his services and asked him to come with him to their tents; Don Quixote had to grant it, and so he did.

At this the beaters came up; the nets were filled with various little birds which, deceived by the colour of the nets, fell into the danger they were fleeing from. There gathered in that place more than thirty people, all of them splendidly dressed as shepherds and shepherdesses, and in an instant they were informed who Don Quixote and his squire were, at which they took no small pleasure, since they already had news of him from his history. They went to the tents, found the tables laid, rich, plentiful and clean; they honoured Don Quixote by giving him the first place at them; they all looked at him and marvelled at the sight of him.

Finally, the cloth being taken away, with great composure Don Quixote raised his voice and said:

"Among the greatest sins men commit, although some say it is pride, I say it is ingratitude, holding to what is generally said: that hell is full of the ungrateful. This sin, as far as it has been possible for me, I have tried to run from ever since I had the use of reason. And if I cannot repay the good works done me with other works, I put in their place the wish to do them; and when these are not enough, I publish them abroad — because the man who tells and publishes the good works he receives would also repay them with others if he could, since for the most part those who receive are inferior to those who give. And so God is above all, because He is the giver above all; and man's gifts cannot answer to God's on equal terms, by an infinite distance; and this narrowness and shortness is in a certain way made up for by gratitude.

"I, then, being grateful for the kindness that has been done me here, and unable to answer it in the same measure, keeping myself within the narrow limits of my power, offer what I can and what I have of my own growing. And so I say that for two whole days I shall maintain in the middle of that royal road that goes to Saragossa that these ladies here, counterfeit shepherdesses, are the most beautiful and the most courteous maidens in the world, excepting only the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso, the sole lady of my thoughts — be it said without offence to all the men and women who hear me."

Hearing which, Sancho, who had been listening to him with great attention, said in a great shout:

"Is it possible that there are people in the world who dare to say and swear that this master of mine is mad? Say, your worships, gentlemen shepherds: is there a village curate, however judicious and however much of a student he may be, who could say what my master has said? Or is there a knight errant, however great a reputation for valour he may have, who could offer what my master has offered here?"

Don Quixote turned to Sancho and, his face fired up and choleric, said to him:

"Is it possible, Sancho, that there is anybody in the whole globe who says you are not a fool, lined with the same and with I do not know what trimmings of the malicious and the rogue? Who brings you into my affairs, and into establishing whether I am judicious or an idiot? Be quiet and do not answer me back, but saddle Rocinante if he is unsaddled: let us go and put my offer into effect; for, with the right that is on my side, you may count as beaten all those who may want to contradict it."

And with great fury and signs of anger he got up from his chair, leaving the bystanders astonished and making them doubt whether they should take him for mad or for sane. Finally, having urged him not to put himself to such a demand, since they took his grateful good will as well enough known and there was no need of fresh demonstrations to know his valorous spirit, since those reported in the history of his deeds were enough — for all that, Don Quixote carried out his intention; and, set on Rocinante, gripping his shield and taking his lance, he placed himself in the middle of a royal road that lay not far from the green meadow. Sancho followed him on his grey, along with all the people of the pastoral flock, eager to see where his arrogant and never-before-seen offer would end.

Don Quixote, then, being placed in the middle of the road, as I have told you, struck the air with words like these:

"O you travellers and wayfarers, knights, squires, people on foot and on horseback who pass along this road, or are to pass along it in these next two days! Know that Don Quixote of La Mancha, knight errant, is placed here to maintain that all the beauties and courtesies of the world are surpassed by those shut up in the nymphs who inhabit these meadows and woods, leaving aside the lady of my soul, Dulcinea of El Toboso. Therefore let anybody who is of a contrary opinion come, for here I wait for him."

Twice he repeated these same words, and twice they were heard by no adventurer. But fortune, which was directing his affairs from better to better, arranged that a little later there should appear along the road a multitude of men on horseback, a great many of them with lances in their hands, all travelling packed together in a troop and in great haste.

Those who were with Don Quixote had hardly seen them when, turning their backs, they got well away from the road, because they knew that if they waited some danger might come to them. Only Don Quixote, with a fearless heart, stood still, and Sancho Panza sheltered himself behind Rocinante's hindquarters.

The troop of lancers arrived, and one of them, who came in front, began to say to Don Quixote at the top of his voice:

"Get out of the road, man of the devil, for these bulls will smash you to pieces!"

"Come, you rabble," answered Don Quixote, "for me there are no bulls worth anything, even if they are the fiercest that the Jarama breeds on its banks! Confess, you villains, all together and without more ado, that what I have published here is true; if not, you have me to fight with."

The herdsman had no room to answer, and Don Quixote had none to get out of the way even if he had wanted to; and so the troop of fierce bulls and of tame lead-oxen, with the multitude of herdsmen and other people who were taking them to be penned in a place where they were to be run the next day, went over Don Quixote and over Sancho, Rocinante and the grey, bringing them all to the ground and sending them rolling over the earth.

Sancho was left battered, Don Quixote terrified, the grey pounded and Rocinante not very catholic in his health; but in the end they all got up, and Don Quixote in great haste, tripping here and falling there, began to run after the herd, calling out:

"Stop and wait, you villainous rabble, for a single knight is waiting for you — one who is not of the nature or the opinion of those who say that for the enemy who flees you should build a bridge of silver!"

But the hurrying runners did not stop for that, nor did they take any more notice of his threats than of last year's clouds. Weariness stopped Don Quixote; and, more angry than avenged, he sat down in the road waiting for Sancho, Rocinante and the grey to come up. They came, master and man got up again, and, without going back to take their leave of the pretended or counterfeit Arcadia, and with more shame than pleasure, they went on their road.

Chapter 59: Where the Extraordinary Event Is Told, Which May Be Counted an Adventure, That Happened to Don Quixote

The dust and the weariness that Don Quixote and Sancho carried away from the bulls' rudeness were relieved by a clear, clean spring they found among a cool grove of trees; on whose bank, leaving the grey and Rocinante free, without halter or bridle, the two worn-out master and man sat down. Sancho went to the larder of his saddlebags and took out of them what he generally called his victuals; he rinsed out his mouth, Don Quixote washed his face, and with this refreshment their fainting spirits took heart again.

Don Quixote did not eat, out of pure grief, and Sancho did not dare to touch the food he had in front of him, out of pure politeness, and waited for his master to taste it first. But, seeing that, carried away by his imaginings, he did not remember to lift the bread to his mouth, Sancho did not open his own; and, trampling on every kind of good breeding, he began to pack into his stomach the bread and cheese that offered itself.

"Eat, Sancho my friend," said Don Quixote; "keep life going, for it matters more to you than to me, and let me die at the hands of my thoughts and by the force of my misfortunes. I, Sancho, was born to live dying, and you to die eating. And, so that you may see I am telling you the truth in this, consider me: in print in histories, famous in arms, courteous in my actions, respected by princes, courted by maidens; and in the end, when I was expecting palms and triumphs and crowns earned and deserved by my valorous exploits, this morning I have seen myself trodden on and kicked and battered by the feet of filthy and vulgar animals. This thought sets my teeth on edge, dulls my grinders, numbs my hands and takes away my appetite altogether — so that I mean to let myself die of hunger: the cruellest of all deaths."

"In that case," said Sancho without leaving off chewing hard, "your worship will not approve that proverb they say: 'let Martha die, and die full'. I at least do not mean to kill myself; on the contrary, I mean to do like the cobbler, who pulls the leather with his teeth until he makes it stretch where he wants it. I shall stretch my life by eating until it reaches the end heaven has settled for it. And let me tell you, sir, that there is no greater madness than the one that touches on wanting to give oneself up to despair, as your worship does. Believe me, and after you have eaten, lie down and sleep a little on the green mattresses of this grass, and you will see how when you wake you find yourself somewhat relieved."

Don Quixote did so, since it seemed to him that Sancho's arguments were more a philosopher's than an idiot's, and he said to him:

"If you, Sancho, would do for me what I shall tell you now, my reliefs would be more certain and my griefs not so great. And it is that, while I sleep, obeying your advice, you should go off a little way from here and, with Rocinante's reins, throwing your flesh open to the air, give yourself three or four hundred lashes on account of the three thousand and more you have to give yourself for Dulcinea's disenchantment; for it is no small pity that that poor lady should be enchanted through your carelessness and neglect."

"There is a great deal to say about that," said Sancho. "Let us both sleep for now, and afterwards God has said what will be. Let your worship know that this business of a man whipping himself in cold blood is a hard thing, and the more so if the lashes fall on a badly kept and worse fed body. Let my lady Dulcinea have patience, for when she least expects it she will see me riddled like a sieve with lashes; and until death, it is all life — I mean that I still have mine, along with the wish to carry out what I have promised."

Don Quixote thanked him for it, ate a little and Sancho a great deal, and they both lay down to sleep, leaving those two constant companions and friends Rocinante and the grey to graze at their own will and without any restraint on the plentiful grass that meadow was full of.

They woke rather late, mounted again and went on their road, hurrying to reach an inn that could be made out, apparently a league from there. I say it was an inn because Don Quixote called it so, outside his habit of calling all inns castles.

They came to it, then, and asked the host whether there was lodging. They were answered that there was, with all the comfort and indulgence they could have found in Saragossa. They dismounted, and Sancho put away his stores in a room, of which the host gave him the key; he took the beasts to the stable and gave them their feeds; he came out to see what Don Quixote, who was sitting on a stone bench, wanted of him, giving particular thanks to heaven that this inn had not seemed a castle to his master.

Supper time came round; they went to their room; Sancho asked the host what he had to give them for supper. To which the host answered that his mouth should be the measure; and so let him ask for whatever he wanted, for that inn was provided with the little birds of the air, the fowls of the earth and the fishes of the sea.

"There is no need for so much," answered Sancho; "with a couple of chickens roasted for us we shall have enough, because my master is delicate and eats little, and I am not excessively much of a glutton."

The host answered him that he had no chickens, because the kites had cleaned him out of them.

"Then let the master host," said Sancho, "have a pullet roasted, a tender one."

"A pullet? My father!" answered the host. "Truly and truly, I sent more than fifty to the city yesterday to be sold; but apart from pullets, let your worship ask for whatever you like."

"In that case," said Sancho, "there will be no lack of veal or kid."

"In the house just now," answered the host, "there is none, because it has run out; but next week there will be plenty."

"We are in a fine way with that!" answered Sancho. "I will wager that all these shortages come round to being made up by the plenty there must be of bacon and eggs."

"By God," answered the host, "my guest is a nice slow one! Why, I have told him that I have neither pullets nor hens, and he wants me to have eggs? Range over other dainties, if you like, and leave off asking for hens."

"Let us settle it, body of me," said Sancho, "and tell me finally what you have, and leave off ranging, master host."

The innkeeper said:

"What I really and truly have is a couple of cow-heels that look like calves' feet, or a couple of calves' feet that look like cow-heels; they are boiled with their chickpeas, onions and bacon, and at this hour they are saying, 'Eat me! Eat me!'"

"I mark them as mine from here," said Sancho; "and let nobody touch them, for I shall pay better than anybody else for them, because for me nothing else could be looked for that would be more to my taste; and it would not matter to me at all whether they were feet, so long as they were heels."

"Nobody will touch them," said the innkeeper, "because other guests I have, being of such quality, bring a cook and a steward and their own larder with them."

"If it is a matter of quality," said Sancho, "nobody has more than my master; but the office he follows does not allow larders or wine cellars: we stretch ourselves out in the middle of a meadow and fill ourselves with acorns or medlars."

This was the conversation Sancho had with the innkeeper, without Sancho wanting to go any further in answering him; for he had already asked him what office or what employment his master's was.

Supper time came round, then; Don Quixote went to his room; the host brought the pot just as it was, and sat down to sup very much in earnest. It seems that in another room next to Don Quixote's, divided from it by nothing but a thin partition, Don Quixote heard somebody say:

"On your life, Señor Don Jerónimo, while they are bringing the supper let us read another chapter of the second part of Don Quixote of La Mancha."

Don Quixote had hardly heard his own name when he got to his feet and listened with an alert ear to what they were saying about him; and he heard this same Don Jerónimo answer:

"Why does your worship want us to read this nonsense, Señor Don Juan? Anybody who has read the first part of the history of Don Quixote of La Mancha cannot possibly take any pleasure in reading this second one."

"For all that," said Don Juan, "it will be as well to read it, since there is no book so bad that it has not something good in it. What displeases me most in this one is that it paints Don Quixote as having fallen out of love with Dulcinea of El Toboso."

Hearing which, Don Quixote, full of anger and indignation, raised his voice and said:

"Whoever says that Don Quixote of La Mancha has forgotten, or can forget, Dulcinea of El Toboso, I shall make him understand with equal arms that he is very far from the truth; because the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso can neither be forgotten, nor can forgetfulness find room in Don Quixote. His blazon is constancy, and his profession is to keep it gently and without doing himself any violence."

"Who is it that answers us?" they answered from the other room.

"Who should it be," answered Sancho, "but the very Don Quixote of La Mancha, who will make good everything he has said, and everything he may say? For a good payer does not mind pledges."

Sancho had hardly said this when in at the door of their room came two gentlemen — for such they looked — and one of them, throwing his arms round Don Quixote's neck, said to him:

"Neither can your presence give the lie to your name, nor can your name fail to bear out your presence: undoubtedly you, sir, are the true Don Quixote of La Mancha, pole star and morning star of knight-errantry, in spite and in defiance of the man who has tried to usurp your name and annihilate your exploits, as the author of this book I hand you here has done."

And, putting into his hands a book his companion was carrying, Don Quixote took it, and without answering a word began to leaf through it; and a little later he handed it back, saying:

"In this little I have seen, I have found three things in this author deserving reproof. The first is some words I have read in the prologue; the second, that the language is Aragonese, since he sometimes writes without articles; and the third, which most confirms him for an ignorant man, is that he goes wrong and departs from the truth in the chief matter of the history — because here he says that the wife of Sancho Panza my squire is called Mari Gutiérrez, and she is not called that at all but Teresa Panza. And a man who goes wrong in so chief a matter as this may well be feared to go wrong in all the rest of the history."

To this Sancho said:

"A pretty sort of historian! Certainly he must be well up in the tale of our doings, since he calls Teresa Panza, my wife, Mari Gutiérrez! Take the book again, sir, and see whether I go about in it and whether he has changed my name too."

"From hearing you talk, my friend," said Don Jerónimo, "you must undoubtedly be Sancho Panza, Señor Don Quixote's squire."

"I am," answered Sancho, "and I pride myself on it."

"Well, upon my word," said the gentleman, "this modern author does not treat you with the cleanness your person shows: he paints you as a great eater, and simple, and not at all amusing, and quite another Sancho from the one described in the first part of your master's history."

"God forgive him," said Sancho. "He should have left me in my corner without remembering me; because let him play the tune who knows it, and Saint Peter is well enough off in Rome."

The two gentlemen asked Don Quixote to come over to their room to have supper with them, since they well knew that in that inn there was nothing suitable for his person. Don Quixote, who was always courteous, gave in to their request and had supper with them. Sancho stayed behind with the stew, with full and mixed jurisdiction over it; he sat down at the head of the table, and with him the innkeeper, who was no less fond than Sancho of his feet and his heels.

In the course of the supper Don Juan asked Don Quixote what news he had of the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso: whether she had married, whether she had been brought to bed or was with child, or whether, being still whole, she remembered — keeping her decency and good decorum — the loving thoughts of Señor Don Quixote. To which he answered:

"Dulcinea is still whole, and my thoughts are firmer than ever; our dealings are in their old dryness; her beauty is transformed into that of a coarse country wench."

And then he went on telling them point by point about the lady Dulcinea's enchantment, and what had happened to him in the cave of Montesinos, along with the orders the wise Merlin had given him for disenchanting her, which were the lashes for Sancho.

The two gentlemen took the greatest pleasure in hearing Don Quixote tell the strange events of his history, and they were as astonished by his absurdities as by the elegant manner in which he told them. Here they took him for judicious, and there he slipped away from them into an idiot, without their being able to settle what degree they should give him between judgement and madness.

Sancho finished his supper; and, leaving the innkeeper making X's with his legs, he went over to his master's room; and, on coming in, he said:

"May they kill me, gentlemen, if the author of that book your worships have does not mean that we shall not eat off the same dish; and I should like it that, since he calls me a glutton, as your worships say, he should not call me a drunkard too."

"He does call you one," said Don Jerónimo, "but I do not remember in what way — although I know the words are ill-sounding, and, what is more, lies, as I can see from the physiognomy of the good Sancho here present."

"Believe me, your worships," said Sancho, "that the Sancho and the Don Quixote of that history must be different men from the ones who go about in the one Cide Hamete Benengeli composed, which are us: my master valiant, judicious and in love; and I simple and amusing, and neither a great eater nor a drunkard."

"So I believe," said Don Juan; "and if it were possible, an order ought to be given that nobody should dare to deal with the affairs of the great Don Quixote except Cide Hamete, his first author — exactly as Alexander ordered that nobody should dare to paint his portrait except Apelles."

"Let anybody who likes paint me," said Don Quixote, "but let him not maul me; for patience often falls down when it is loaded with insults."

"None," said Don Juan, "can be offered to Señor Don Quixote that he cannot avenge, if he does not fend it off on the shield of his patience — which, to my mind, is strong and great."

In these and other talks a great part of the night went by; and, although Don Juan would have liked Don Quixote to read more of the book, to see what he carped at, they could not bring him to it, for he said that he counted it as read and confirmed it as wholly foolish, and that he did not want its author, if it should come to his notice that he had had it in his hands, to be pleased with thinking that he had read it; for from obscene and filthy things one's thoughts must be kept away, and still more one's eyes.

They asked him where he had decided to take his journey. He answered that it was to Saragossa, to be present at the jousts for the suit of armour that are generally held in that city every year. Don Juan told him that that new history related how Don Quixote — whoever he might be — had been present at a ring-tilting there, short of invention, poor in mottoes, extremely poor in liveries, though rich in silliness.

"For that very reason," answered Don Quixote, "I shall not set foot in Saragossa; and so I shall bring out into the open square of the world the lie of that modern historian, and people will see that I am not the Don Quixote he speaks of."

"You will do very well," said Don Jerónimo, "and there are other jousts at Barcelona where Señor Don Quixote can show his valour."

"That is what I mean to do," said Don Quixote; "and let your worships give me leave, for it is time for me to go to bed; and hold me and set me in the number of your greatest friends and servants."

"And me too," said Sancho: "perhaps I may be good for something."

With this they took their leave, and Don Quixote and Sancho withdrew to their room, leaving Don Juan and Don Jerónimo astonished at seeing the mixture he had made of his good sense and his madness; and they truly believed that these were the true Don Quixote and Sancho, and not the ones the Aragonese author described.

Don Quixote got up early and, knocking on the partition of the other room, took his leave of his fellow guests. Sancho paid the innkeeper magnificently, and advised him either to praise the provisions of his inn less or to keep it better provided.

Chapter 60: Of What Happened to Don Quixote on His Way to Barcelona

The morning was cool, and gave signs that the day would be so too, when Don Quixote left the inn, first finding out which was the straightest road to go to Barcelona without touching Saragossa: such was his eagerness to give the lie to that new historian who they said abused him so much.

It happened, then, that for more than six days nothing occurred to him worth putting in writing; at the end of which, going off the road, night caught him among some thick oaks or cork trees — for in this Cide Hamete does not keep the exactness he generally keeps in other things.

Master and man dismounted from their beasts; and, settling themselves against the trunks of the trees, Sancho, who had had his snack that day, let himself go headlong in at the gates of sleep. But Don Quixote, whom his imaginings kept awake much more than hunger, could not close his eyes; instead his thoughts came and went over a thousand kinds of places. Now it seemed to him that he was in the cave of Montesinos; now that he saw Dulcinea, turned into a peasant girl, jump and spring up onto her ass; now that the words of the wise Merlin were ringing in his ears, telling him the conditions and the steps that were to be taken and kept for Dulcinea's disenchantment.

He was in despair at seeing the slackness and the small charity of Sancho his squire, since, as far as he believed, he had given himself only five lashes — an uneven and small number for the infinite ones he still owed. And at this he took such distress and annoyance that he made this argument:

"If the great Alexander cut the Gordian knot, saying, 'Cutting is as good as untying,' and did not for that reason stop being universal lord of all Asia, the same might happen now in Dulcinea's disenchantment if I whipped Sancho in spite of himself. Because if the condition of this remedy lies in Sancho's receiving the three thousand and more lashes, what does it matter to me whether he gives them to himself or somebody else gives them to him, since the substance of it lies in his receiving them, from wherever they come?"

With this idea he went up to Sancho, having first taken Rocinante's reins and arranged them in such a way that he could whip him with them, and began to undo the laces — for it is held that he had only the front one, which held up his breeches. But he had hardly got there when Sancho woke up in full possession of his senses and said:

"What is this? Who is touching me and unlacing me?"

"It is I," answered Don Quixote, "who come to make up your shortcomings and to relieve my own troubles. I come to whip you, Sancho, and to discharge in part the debt you bound yourself to. Dulcinea is perishing; you live in carelessness; I am dying with longing; and so unlace yourself of your own free will, for mine is to give you, in this solitude, at least two thousand lashes."

"Not that," said Sancho. "Let your worship keep still; if not, by the true God the deaf shall hear us. The lashes I bound myself to must be voluntary and not forced, and just now I have no fancy to whip myself. It is enough that I give your worship my word to flog myself and swat myself whenever I feel like it."

"There is no leaving it to your courtesy, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "because you are hard of heart and, peasant though you are, soft of flesh."

And so he kept trying and struggling to unlace him. Which Sancho Panza seeing, he got to his feet and, rushing at his master, grappled with him at close quarters; and, tripping him up, brought him down on the ground on his back. He set his right knee on his chest and held his hands with his own hands, so that he let him neither turn over nor breathe. Don Quixote said to him:

"How, traitor? Do you rebel against your master and natural lord? Do you set on the man who gives you his bread?"

"I neither unmake a king nor make one," answered Sancho, "but only help myself, who am my own lord. Let your worship promise me that you will keep still and will not try to whip me for now, and I shall leave you free and unencumbered; if not,

	Here shall you die, traitor,
	enemy of Doña Sancha."

Don Quixote promised it him, and swore by the life of his thoughts not to touch him on a hair of his clothes, and to leave the whipping entirely to his own will and choice, whenever he liked.

Sancho got up and moved a good way off from that place; and, going to lean against another tree, he felt something touch him on the head and, putting up his hands, came upon two human feet with shoes and stockings on them. He shook with fear; he made for another tree, and the same thing happened to him. He shouted, calling on Don Quixote to help him. Don Quixote did so; and, asking him what had happened to him and what he was afraid of, Sancho answered that all those trees were full of human feet and legs. Don Quixote felt them and tumbled at once to what it could be, and said to Sancho:

"You have nothing to be afraid of, because these feet and legs you are feeling and cannot see are undoubtedly those of some outlaws and bandits who are hanged on these trees; for the law generally hangs them about here when it catches them, twenty at a time and thirty at a time. From which I give myself to understand that I must be near Barcelona."

And it was the truth, as he had imagined it.

At daybreak they raised their eyes and saw the clusters on those trees, which were the bodies of bandits. Day was breaking by now; and if the dead had frightened them, they were no less troubled by more than forty living bandits who suddenly surrounded them, telling them in the Catalan language to keep still and to stop until their captain came.

Don Quixote found himself on foot, his horse without a bridle, his lance leaning against a tree and, in short, without any defence at all; and so he thought it well to fold his arms and bow his head, keeping himself for a better season and conjunction.

The bandits set about picking the grey clean and leaving him nothing of everything he was carrying in the saddlebags and the valise; and it turned out well for Sancho that the duke's crowns, and the ones they had brought from home, were in a belt he had girt round him — and even so those good people would have weeded him out and looked even at what he had hidden between his skin and his flesh if their captain had not arrived at that moment.

He looked to be about thirty-four years old, robust, more than middling in height, with a grave look and a dark complexion. He came on a mighty horse, wearing a steel coat of mail, and with four pistols — which in that country they call flintlocks — at his sides. He saw that his squires, for so they call those who follow that trade, were about to strip Sancho Panza; he ordered them not to, and was obeyed at once; and so the money belt escaped.

He was astonished to see a lance leaning against the tree, a shield on the ground, and Don Quixote armed and thoughtful, with the saddest and most melancholy figure that sadness itself could have made. He came up to him, saying:

"Do not be so sad, good man, because you have not fallen into the hands of any cruel Busiris but into those of Roque Guinart, which have more of the compassionate about them than of the severe."

"My sadness," answered Don Quixote, "is not at having fallen into your power, O valorous Roque, whose fame there are no limits on earth to enclose; but at having been so careless that your soldiers have caught me without my bridle, when I am obliged, by the order of knight-errantry that I profess, to live constantly on the alert, being at all hours my own sentinel. Because I let you know, O great Roque, that if they had found me on my horse with my lance and with my shield, it would not have been very easy for them to overcome me; for I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, the man who has filled the whole globe with his exploits."

Roque Guinart at once knew that Don Quixote's disease touched more on madness than on valour; and, although he had heard him named a few times, he had never held his deeds for true, and could not persuade himself that such a humour could reign in a man's heart. And he was extremely glad to have met him, so as to touch close up what he had heard of him at a distance; and so he said to him:

"Valorous knight, do not despair or take this state you find yourself in for ill fortune; for it might be that in these stumblings your twisted luck may come straight. For heaven, by strange and never-before-seen roundabouts that men never imagine, generally raises up the fallen and enriches the poor."

Don Quixote was about to thank him when they heard behind them a noise like a troop of horses — and it was only one, on which there came at full fury a young man of, apparently, about twenty, dressed in green damask with gold braid, in wide breeches and an overjacket, with a hat cocked in the Walloon fashion, waxed boots fitting close, spurs, a gilded dagger and sword, a small musket in his hands and two pistols at his sides. At the noise Roque turned his head and saw this handsome figure, who, on coming up to him, said:

"I was coming to look for you, O valorous Roque, to find in you, if not a remedy, at least a relief in my misfortune. And, so as not to keep you in suspense — for I know you have not recognised me — I want to tell you who I am. I am Claudia Jerónima, daughter of Simón Forte, your particular friend and the particular enemy of Clauquel Torrellas, who is likewise yours, being one of the men of the opposite faction. And you know that this Torrellas has a son called Don Vicente Torrellas — or at least he was called that not two hours ago.

"This man, then — to shorten the tale of my misfortune, I shall tell you in a few words what has caused it. He saw me, he courted me, I listened to him, I fell in love with him, without my father's knowledge; for there is no woman, however sheltered and however careful she may be, who has not time enough to put her headlong desires into execution and effect. Finally he promised to be my husband, and I gave him my word to be his, without our going any further in deeds.

"Yesterday I learnt that, forgetting what he owed me, he was marrying another woman, and that this morning he was to be betrothed — news that disturbed my senses and made an end of my patience. And, my father not being in the place, I had to put myself into the dress you see; and, urging on this horse, I caught up with Don Vicente about a league from here. And, without stopping to make complaints or to hear excuses, I fired these muskets at him and, into the bargain, these two pistols; and, as I believe, I must have shut more than two bullets in his body, opening doors for my honour to come out of, wrapped in his blood. I left him there among his servants, who neither dared nor were able to come to his defence.

"I come to look for you so that you may take me over into France, where I have relations to live with, and likewise to beg you to defend my father, so that Don Vicente's many kinsmen may not dare to take an outrageous revenge on him."

Roque, amazed at the gallantry, the dash, the fine figure and the adventure of the beautiful Claudia, said to her:

"Come, lady, and let us go and see whether your enemy is dead; and afterwards we shall see what matters most to you."

Don Quixote, who was listening attentively to what Claudia had said and what Roque Guinart answered, said:

"Nobody need take any trouble to defend this lady, for I take it upon myself. Give me my horse and my arms and wait for me here, and I shall go and look for this knight; and, dead or alive, I shall make him keep the word he promised to so much beauty."

"Let nobody doubt it," said Sancho, "because my master has a very good hand at matchmaking; for it is not many days since he made another man marry who was also denying his word to another maiden. And if it had not been that the enchanters who persecute him changed his true shape into a footman's, by this hour that maiden would be one no longer."

Roque, who was attending more to thinking about the business of the beautiful Claudia than to the words of master and man, did not take them in; and, ordering his squires to give Sancho back everything they had taken off the grey, ordering them likewise to withdraw to the place where they had been lodged that night, he set off at once in great haste with Claudia to look for the wounded — or dead — Don Vicente.

They came to the place where Claudia had met him, and found nothing there but freshly spilt blood. But, casting their eyes in every direction, they made out some people up a slope, and gave themselves to understand — as was the truth — that it must be Don Vicente, whom his servants were carrying, dead or alive, either to treat him or to bury him. They made haste to catch them up; and, as they were going slowly, they easily did.

They found Don Vicente in his servants' arms, and he was begging them in a weary, weakened voice to let him die there, because the pain of his wounds would not let him go any further.

Claudia and Roque threw themselves off their horses and came up to him; the servants were afraid at Roque's presence, and Claudia was thrown into confusion at seeing Don Vicente's. And so, between tenderness and severity, she came up to him and, taking him by the hands, said to him:

"If you had given me these, according to our agreement, you would never have found yourself in this pass."

The wounded knight opened his almost closed eyes, and, recognising Claudia, said to her:

"I see well enough, beautiful and deceived lady, that you have been the one to kill me — a punishment neither deserved nor owing to my desires, with which, or with my deeds, I never wished or knew how to offend you."

"Then is it not true," said Claudia, "that you were going this morning to be married to Leonora, the daughter of the rich Balvastro?"

"Certainly not," answered Don Vicente. "My bad fortune must have brought you this news so that, out of jealousy, you should take my life away — which, since I leave it in your hands and in your arms, I count my lot fortunate. And, to assure you of this truth, press my hand and take me for your husband, if you will; for I have no greater satisfaction to give you for the wrong you think you have received from me."

Claudia pressed his hand, and her heart was pressed so hard that she fell in a faint on Don Vicente's blood and breast; and a mortal spasm took hold of him. Roque was confused and did not know what to do. The servants ran to look for water to throw in their faces, and brought it and bathed them. Claudia came out of her faint, but Don Vicente did not come out of his spasm, because his life ended.

Which Claudia seeing, and having made certain that her sweet husband was no longer alive, she broke the air with sighs, struck the heavens with her cries, mistreated her hair, giving it to the wind, disfigured her face with her own hands, with all the signs of grief and feeling that could be imagined from a wounded breast.

"O cruel and thoughtless woman," she said, "how easily you were moved to put so bad a thought into execution! O raging power of jealousy, to what a desperate end you lead the man who gives you room in his breast! O husband of mine, whose unfortunate lot, for being my possession, has carried you from the marriage bed to the grave!"

Such and so mournful were Claudia's cries that they drew tears out of Roque's eyes, which were not used to shedding them on any occasion. The servants wept; Claudia fainted away at every step; and that whole circuit looked like a field of sadness and a place of misfortune.

Finally Roque Guinart ordered Don Vicente's servants to carry his body to his father's village, which was close by, so that they might give it burial. Claudia told Roque that she would like to go to a convent where an aunt of hers was abbess, in which she meant to end her life, accompanied by another and a better and more everlasting husband. Roque praised her good resolution and offered to go with her wherever she liked and to defend her father from Don Vicente's relations and from all the world, if they should want to harm him. Claudia would not have his company on any account; and, thanking him for his offers in the best words she knew, she took her leave of him in tears.

Don Vicente's servants carried away his body, and Roque went back to his men; and this was the end that the loves of Claudia Jerónima came to. But what wonder, when the invincible and severe forces of jealousy wove the plot of her lamentable history?

Roque Guinart found his squires in the place where he had ordered them, and Don Quixote among them, on Rocinante, making them a speech in which he urged them to leave that way of life, so dangerous both for the soul and for the body; but, as most of them were Gascons, rough and disorderly people, Don Quixote's speech did not go into them very well.

When Roque arrived, he asked Sancho Panza whether they had given him back and restored the goods and valuables that his men had taken off the grey. Sancho answered that they had, except that he was short of three headcloths that were worth three cities.

"What are you saying, man?" said one of those present. "I have them, and they are not worth three reals."

"That is so," said Don Quixote, "but my squire values them at what he has said, on account of the person who gave them to me."

Roque Guinart ordered them given back to him at once; and, ordering his men to draw up in line, he ordered all the clothes, jewels and money to be brought there in front of him, and everything they had robbed since the last division. And, making the reckoning quickly, giving back what could not be divided and turning it into money, he divided it out among the whole company with such fairness and prudence that he did not go a point beyond distributive justice or defraud it in anything.

This done, at which they were all left contented, satisfied and paid, Roque said to Don Quixote:

"If this exactness were not kept with these men, it would be impossible to live with them."

To which Sancho said:

"By what I have seen here, justice is such a good thing that it must be used even among thieves themselves."

One of the squires heard him and raised the butt of a harquebus, with which he would undoubtedly have split Sancho's head open if Roque Guinart had not shouted to him to stop. Sancho was thunderstruck, and resolved not to unstitch his lips as long as he was among those people.

At this there came up one, or some, of those squires who were posted as sentries along the roads to see the people who came along them and give notice to their chief of what was afoot, and this one said:

"Sir, not far from here, along the road that goes to Barcelona, there comes a great troop of people."

To which Roque answered:

"Have you seen whether they are of those who are looking for us, or of those we are looking for?"

"No, but of those we are looking for," answered the squire.

"Then all of you go out," replied Roque, "and bring them here to me at once, and let none of them escape you."

They did so; and, Don Quixote, Sancho and Roque being left alone, they waited to see what the squires would bring. And in the meantime Roque said to Don Quixote:

"Our way of life must seem a new one to Señor Don Quixote — new adventures, new events, and all of them dangerous; and I do not wonder that it should seem so, because I really confess to you that there is no way of living more restless or more full of alarms than ours. What has put me into it is a certain desire for revenge, which has the power to trouble the quietest hearts; I am by nature compassionate and well-meaning, but, as I have said, the wanting to avenge myself for a wrong that was done me throws all my good inclinations so completely to the ground that I persevere in this state in spite and in defiance of what I understand. And, as one abyss calls to another and one sin to another sin, the revenges have linked themselves together in such a way that I take on not only my own but other people's. But God is pleased that, although I see myself in the middle of the labyrinth of my confusions, I do not lose the hope of coming out of it into a safe harbour."

Don Quixote was astonished at hearing Roque speak such good and orderly words, because he had thought that among men of trades like robbing, killing and holding up travellers there could be nobody with good judgement; and he answered him:

"Señor Roque, the beginning of health lies in knowing the disease and in the sick man's being willing to take the medicines the doctor orders him. Your worship is sick; you know your ailment; and heaven — or God, better said, who is our doctor — will apply medicines to you that will heal you, which generally heal little by little and not suddenly and by a miracle. And besides, judicious sinners are nearer to mending than simple ones; and, since your worship has shown your prudence in your words, there is nothing for it but to have good courage and hope for an improvement in the disease of your conscience. And if your worship wants to save the journey and set yourself easily on the road to your salvation, come with me, and I shall teach you to be a knight errant, in which one goes through so many labours and misfortunes that, taking them as penance, they will put you in heaven in two shakes."

Roque laughed at Don Quixote's advice; and, changing the subject, he told him the tragic business of Claudia Jerónima, which grieved Sancho extremely, for the girl's beauty, dash and spirit had not seemed bad to him.

At this the squires of the raid came up, bringing with them two gentlemen on horseback and two pilgrims on foot, and a coach of women with about six servants who were attending them on foot and on horseback, along with two mule-boys the gentlemen had brought. The squires took them into their midst, conquered and conquerors keeping a great silence, waiting for the great Roque Guinart to speak. And he asked the gentlemen who they were and where they were going and how much money they were carrying. One of them answered him:

"Sir, we are two captains of Spanish infantry; we have our companies in Naples and we are going to embark on four galleys which they say are at Barcelona with orders to cross to Sicily. We are carrying about two or three hundred crowns, with which, to our mind, we go rich and contented, since the ordinary tightness of soldiers does not allow greater treasures."

Roque asked the pilgrims the same as the captains; he was answered that they were going to embark to cross to Rome, and that between the two of them they might have about sixty reals. He also wanted to know who was going in the coach and where, and the money they were carrying; and one of the men on horseback said:

"My lady Doña Guiomar de Quiñones, wife of the regent of the Vicarial Court of Naples, with a small daughter, a maid and a duenna, are the ones going in the coach; six servants attend her, and the money is six hundred crowns."

"So that," said Roque Guinart, "we now have here nine hundred crowns and sixty reals; my soldiers must be about sixty; let it be worked out how much falls to each one, because I am a bad accountant."

The highwaymen, hearing this said, raised their voices, saying:

"Long live Roque Guinart for many years, in spite of the lladres — the thieves — who seek his ruin!"

The captains showed themselves distressed, the lady regent's wife was saddened, and the pilgrims were not at all pleased at seeing their goods confiscated. Roque kept them like this in suspense for a while; but he did not want their sadness to go any further, for by now it could be seen from a harquebus-shot away; and, turning to the captains, he said:

"Your worships, gentlemen captains, be so good as to lend me sixty crowns out of courtesy, and the lady regent's wife eighty, to content this squadron that goes with me — for the abbot dines on what he sings — and then you may go your way freely and unhindered with a safe conduct I shall give you, so that if you come across other squadrons of mine that I have divided about these parts, they may do you no harm; for it is not my intention to wrong soldiers or any woman, especially women of quality."

Infinite and well-spoken were the words with which the captains thanked Roque for his courtesy and generosity — for such they held it — in leaving them their own money. The lady Doña Guiomar de Quiñones wanted to throw herself out of the coach to kiss the great Roque's feet and hands, but he would not consent to it on any account; on the contrary, he asked her pardon for the wrong he was doing her, forced to it by the strict obligations of his bad trade. The lady regent's wife ordered a servant of hers to hand over at once the eighty crowns that had been assessed on her, and the captains had already paid out the sixty. The pilgrims were about to hand over all their poor pittance, but Roque told them to keep still; and, turning to his men, he said:

"Of these crowns two fall to each man, and twenty are left over: let ten be given to these pilgrims, and the other ten to this good squire, so that he may speak well of this adventure."

And, being brought writing materials, with which he always went provided, Roque gave them in writing a safe conduct for the chiefs of his squadrons; and, taking his leave of them, he let them go free, astonished at his nobility, his gallant bearing and his strange conduct, and holding him rather for an Alexander the Great than for a known thief. One of the squires said in his mixed Gascon and Catalan:

"This captain of ours is more fit to be a friar than a bandit: if from now on he wants to show himself generous, let him be so with his own property and not with ours."

The unlucky man did not say it so softly that Roque did not hear it; and he, laying hand to his sword, split his head almost in two, saying to him:

"This is how I punish loose-tongued and impudent men."

They were all thunderstruck, and none of them dared to say him a word: so great was the obedience they had for him.

Roque drew aside and wrote a letter to a friend of his in Barcelona, letting him know that the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha was with him — that knight errant of whom so many things were said; and letting him know that he was the most amusing and the most understanding man in the world, and that in four days' time, which would be the day of Saint John the Baptist, he would set him down in the middle of the city beach, armed in all his arms, on Rocinante his horse, and his squire Sancho on an ass; and that he should give notice of this to his friends the Niarros, so that they might amuse themselves with him. He wished that his enemies the Cadells could be deprived of this pleasure, but that this was impossible, because Don Quixote's madnesses and judicious speeches and his squire Sancho Panza's charms could not fail to give general pleasure to all the world.

He sent these letters off by one of his squires who, changing the bandit's dress for a farm labourer's, went into Barcelona and gave it to the man it was going to.

Chapter 61: Of What Happened to Don Quixote on Entering Barcelona, with Other Things That Have More of the True in Them Than of the Judicious

Three days and three nights Don Quixote spent with Roque; and if he had spent three hundred years, he would not have run out of things to watch and marvel at in his way of life. They woke up in one place and dined in another; sometimes they fled without knowing from whom, and other times they waited without knowing for whom. They slept standing up, breaking off their sleep and shifting from one place to another. It was all posting spies, listening to sentries, blowing on the matches of the harquebuses — though they carried few, because they all used flintlocks.

Roque spent the nights away from his men, in parts and places where they could not know where he was; because the many proclamations the viceroy of Barcelona had issued against his life kept him uneasy and afraid, and he did not dare to trust anybody, fearing that his own men would either kill him or hand him over to the law: a wretched and tiresome life, certainly.

Finally, by unused roads, by short cuts and hidden paths, Roque, Don Quixote and Sancho set off for Barcelona with six other squires. They reached its beach on the eve of Saint John at night; and, Roque embracing Don Quixote and Sancho — to whom he gave the ten promised crowns, for until then he had not given them him — he left them, with a thousand offers made on both sides.

Roque went back. Don Quixote stayed waiting for the day just as he was, on horseback; and it was not long before there began to appear over the balconies of the East the face of the white dawn, gladdening the grass and the flowers instead of gladdening the ear — although at that very moment the ear was gladdened too by the sound of a great many shawms and kettledrums, the noise of little bells, the "tramp, tramp, out of the way, out of the way!" of runners who seemed to be coming out of the city. The dawn gave place to the sun, which, with a face bigger than a buckler, was little by little rising up over the lowest horizon.

Don Quixote and Sancho cast their eyes in every direction: they saw the sea, which they had never seen until then; it seemed to them extremely spacious and long, a great deal more so than the Lagoons of Ruidera they had seen in La Mancha. They saw the galleys that were on the beach, which, dropping their awnings, showed themselves full of pennants and streamers that fluttered in the wind and kissed and swept the water; inside them sounded clarions, trumpets and shawms, which near and far filled the air with sweet and warlike notes.

They began to move and to make a kind of skirmish over the quiet waters, matched in almost the same way by an infinite number of knights who came out of the city on beautiful horses and in showy liveries. The soldiers of the galleys fired off endless artillery, which was answered by those on the walls and forts of the city; and the heavy artillery broke the winds with a terrible uproar, which was answered by the gangway cannon of the galleys. The sea glad, the earth joyful, the air clear — only now and then clouded by the smoke of the artillery — it all seemed to be pouring in and breeding a sudden pleasure in everybody.

Sancho could not imagine how those hulks that moved over the sea could have so many feet. At this, the men in liveries came running up, with shouting and cries and uproar, to where Don Quixote stood bewildered and astounded; and one of them, the man Roque had written to, said to Don Quixote in a loud voice:

"Welcome to our city, the mirror, the lantern, the star and the pole star of all knight-errantry, as far as it is contained anywhere. Welcome, I say, to the valorous Don Quixote of La Mancha: not the false one, not the fictitious one, not the apocryphal one that false histories have shown us these last days, but the true, the lawful and the faithful one that Cide Hamete Benengeli, the flower of historians, described to us."

Don Quixote answered not a word, and the knights did not wait for him to answer; instead, wheeling and rewheeling with the rest who followed them, they began to make a tangled caracole round Don Quixote. And he, turning to Sancho, said:

"These men have recognised us well enough: I would wager they have read our history, and even the Aragonese one that has just been printed."

The knight who had spoken to Don Quixote came back again and said to him:

"Let your worship, Señor Don Quixote, come with us; for we are all your servants and great friends of Roque Guinart."

To which Don Quixote answered:

"If courtesies breed courtesies, yours, sir knight, is the daughter or a very near relation of the great Roque's. Take me wherever you like, for I shall have no will but yours — and the more so if you want to employ it in your service."

With words no less civil than these the knight answered him; and, closing him in among them all, to the sound of the shawms and the kettledrums they made their way with him to the city. At the entrance of which, the Evil One — who arranges all evil — and boys, who are worse than the Evil One, two mischievous and daring ones of them pushed in through all the people; and, lifting the tail of the grey and the other the tail of Rocinante, they put and stuck a bunch of gorse under each.

The poor animals felt these new spurs and, clamping their tails down, increased their distress in such a way that, giving a thousand bucks, they brought their owners down on the ground. Don Quixote, put out and affronted, ran to take the plumage off his nag's tail, and Sancho off his grey's. Those who were guiding Don Quixote would have liked to punish the boys' impudence, and it was not possible, because they got away among more than a thousand others who were following them.

Don Quixote and Sancho got up again, and with the same applause and music they came to their guide's house, which was large and of good quality — in short, like a rich gentleman's; where we shall leave him for now, because that is what Cide Hamete wants.

Chapter 62: Which Deals with the Adventure of the Enchanted Head, Along with Other Trifles That Cannot Be Left Untold

Don Antonio Moreno was the name of Don Quixote's host, a rich and judicious gentleman who was fond of amusing himself in a decent and agreeable way; and, seeing Don Quixote in his house, he went about looking for ways to bring his madnesses out into the open without harming him — because jokes that hurt are no jokes, and there are no entertainments worth anything if they are at a third party's expense.

The first thing he did was to have Don Quixote unarmed and to bring him out to be seen in that narrow chamois suit of his — as we have described and painted him at other times — on a balcony that looked out on one of the chief streets of the city, in view of the people and of the boys, who looked at him as at an ape. Once again the men in liveries rode past in front of him, as though they had put them on for him alone and not to make that festive day merry; and Sancho was extremely pleased, since it seemed to him that he had found, without knowing how or why, another wedding of Camacho's, another house like Don Diego de Miranda's and another castle like the duke's.

Some of Don Antonio's friends dined with him that day, all of them honouring Don Quixote and treating him as a knight errant; at which he, puffed up and pompous, could not contain himself for contentment. Sancho's drolleries were so many that all the servants of the house and everybody who heard him hung on his mouth. Sitting at table, Don Antonio said to Sancho:

"We have news here, good Sancho, that you are so fond of blancmange and little meatballs that if you have any left over you keep them in your bosom for the next day."

"No, sir, it is not so," answered Sancho, "because I have more of the clean about me than of the greedy; and my master Don Quixote here present knows very well that the two of us generally get by for a week on a handful of acorns or walnuts. It is true that if it sometimes happens that they give me the heifer, I run with the halter — I mean that I eat what is given me and use the times as I find them. And whoever has said that I am an outstanding eater and not clean may take it as said that he is wrong; and I should say this in another way if I were not looking at the honourable beards at this table."

"Certainly," said Don Quixote, "the sparingness and cleanness with which Sancho eats could be written and engraved on plates of bronze, to stay in the everlasting memory of the ages to come. It is true that when he is hungry he looks something of a glutton, because he eats fast and chews on both sides of his mouth; but he always keeps his cleanness at its height; and in the time when he was a governor he learnt to eat so fastidiously that he ate grapes, and even pomegranate seeds, with a fork."

"What!" said Don Antonio. "Has Sancho been a governor?"

"Yes," answered Sancho, "and of an isle called Barataria. Ten days I governed it exactly as I pleased; in them I lost my peace of mind and learnt to despise all the governments in the world. I ran away from it, I fell into a cave where I gave myself up for dead, and I came out of it alive by a miracle."

Don Quixote told in detail the whole business of Sancho's government, at which he gave the listeners great pleasure.

The cloth being taken away, and Don Antonio taking Don Quixote by the hand, he went with him into a room set apart, in which there was no other ornament but a table apparently of jasper, held up on a foot of the same, on which there stood — in the manner of the busts of the Roman emperors, from the chest up — one that seemed to be of bronze. Don Antonio walked about the whole room with Don Quixote, going round the table many times, after which he said:

"Now, Señor Don Quixote, that I have made certain that nobody hears or listens to us and the door is shut, I want to tell your worship about one of the rarest adventures, or, better said, novelties, that can be imagined — on condition that what I tell your worship you are to lay up in the deepest chambers of secrecy."

"So I swear," answered Don Quixote, "and I shall even put a tombstone on top of it, for greater security; because I want your worship to know, Señor Don Antonio" — for he already knew his name — "that you are speaking to a man who, although he has ears to hear, has no tongue to speak with. So your worship may safely transfer what you have in your breast into mine, and reckon that you have thrown it into the depths of silence."

"On the strength of that promise," answered Don Antonio, "I want to fill your worship with astonishment at what you shall see and hear, and to give myself some relief from the pain it causes me to have nobody to share my secrets with, since they are not to be trusted to everybody."

Don Quixote was bewildered, waiting to see where so many preparations were going to end. At this, Don Antonio, taking his hand, ran it over the bronze head and over the whole table and over the jasper foot that held it up, and then said:

"This head, Señor Don Quixote, has been made and manufactured by one of the greatest enchanters and sorcerers the world has ever had — a Pole, I believe, by nation, and a disciple of the famous Escotillo, of whom so many marvels are told. He was here in my house, and for the price of a thousand crowns that I gave him he wrought this head, which has the property and virtue of answering whatever anybody asks it in its ear. He kept the bearings, drew characters, observed the stars, watched the points, and finally brought it out with the perfection we shall see tomorrow — because on Fridays it is dumb, and today, being one, it will make us wait until tomorrow. In this time your worship may prepare what you will want to ask, for I know by experience that it tells the truth in everything it answers."

Don Quixote was amazed at the head's virtue and property, and was inclined not to believe Don Antonio; but, seeing how little time there was before the test, he did not want to say anything to him except that he thanked him for having revealed so great a secret to him. They came out of the room, Don Antonio locked the door, and they went off to the hall where the other gentlemen were. In this time Sancho had told them a good many of the adventures and events that had happened to his master.

That afternoon they took Don Quixote out for a ride — not armed but in walking dress, wearing a long gown of tawny cloth which in that season could have made the ice itself sweat. They arranged with their servants to keep Sancho occupied so that they should not let him leave the house. Don Quixote went, not on Rocinante, but on a great smooth-paced mule, very well harnessed. They put the gown on him; and on his back, without his seeing it, they sewed a parchment on which they wrote in large letters: This is Don Quixote of La Mancha.

As soon as the ride began, the placard drew the eyes of everybody who came to see him; and as they read This is Don Quixote of La Mancha, Don Quixote was astonished to see that everybody who looked at him named him and knew him; and, turning to Don Antonio, who was riding at his side, he said:

"Great is the prerogative that knight-errantry contains in itself, since it makes the man who professes it known and famous through all the bounds of the earth. If not, look, your worship, Señor Don Antonio, how even the boys of this city, who have never seen me, know me."

"That is so, Señor Don Quixote," answered Don Antonio; "for just as fire cannot be hidden and shut up, virtue cannot fail to be known — and the virtue that is attained by the profession of arms shines and shows itself above all the rest."

It happened, then, that as Don Quixote was going along with the applause that has been described, a Castilian who read the placard on his back raised his voice, saying:

"The devil take you for Don Quixote of La Mancha! How is it that you have got this far without the endless beatings you have on your back having killed you? You are mad; and if you were mad by yourself and inside the doors of your madness it would be less bad; but you have the property of turning everybody who deals with you and talks to you mad and idiotic — if not, let them look at these gentlemen who are with you. Go home, you idiot, and see to your property, to your wife and your children, and leave off these emptinesses that are gnawing away your brains and skimming the cream off your understanding."

"Brother," said Don Antonio, "go your own way and do not give advice to people who do not ask you for it. Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha is very sane, and we who go with him are not fools; virtue is to be honoured wherever it is found; and be off with you, and do not meddle where you are not called."

"By God, your worship is right," answered the Castilian; "for advising this good man is kicking against the pricks. But for all that, it gives me very great sorrow that the good wits this idiot is said to have in everything should be drained away down the gutter of his knight-errantry. And the bad luck your worship has wished me be on me and on all my descendants if from this day on, even if I lived more years than Methuselah, I ever give advice to anybody again, even if they ask me for it."

The adviser moved off; the ride went on. But such was the eagerness of the boys and all the people to read the placard that Don Antonio had to take it off, as though he were taking off something else.

Night came and they went back home; there was a ladies' evening party, because Don Antonio's wife, who was a lady of quality and cheerful, beautiful and judicious, invited other friends of hers to come and do honour to her guest and enjoy his never-before-seen madnesses. Some came; they had a splendid supper, and the party began at about ten at night.

Among the ladies there were two of a mischievous and joking humour; and, though they were very decent, they were rather free, so as to give room for the jokes to make merry without annoyance. These two were so eager in pulling Don Quixote out to dance that they wore out not only his body but his soul. It was a thing to see, Don Quixote's figure — long, stretched out, lean, yellow, tight in his clothes, awkward and, above all, not at all nimble. The young ladies made love to him as though on the sly, and he, likewise as though on the sly, disdained them; but, finding himself hard pressed with compliments, he raised his voice and said:

"Fugite, partes adversae! Leave me in my quiet, ill-come thoughts. Settle your desires elsewhere, ladies; for she who is queen of mine, the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso, does not allow any but her own to enslave and conquer me."

And, saying this, he sat down in the middle of the hall on the floor, battered and broken by so much dancing exercise. Don Antonio had him carried bodily to his bed, and the first man to lay hold of him was Sancho, saying to him:

"In a bad hour, sir our master, you have danced it! Do you think all brave men are dancers and all knights errant ball-room performers? I say that if you do think so, you are mistaken; there are men who would sooner venture to kill a giant than cut a caper. If you had to do clog-dancing, I would make up for your shortcomings, for I clog-dance like a gerfalcon; but in this business of dancing I do not put a stitch in."

With these and other words Sancho gave the people of the party something to laugh at, and got his master into bed, wrapping him up so that he should sweat out the chill of his dancing.

The next day it seemed to Don Antonio a good idea to make the experiment of the enchanted head; and with Don Quixote, Sancho and two other friends, along with the two ladies who had worn Don Quixote out with dancing and who had stayed that night with Don Antonio's wife, he shut himself up in the room where the head was. He told them the property it had, charged them with the secret and told them that this was the first day on which the virtue of that enchanted head was to be tested; and apart from Don Antonio's two friends, nobody else knew the crux of the enchantment — and indeed if Don Antonio had not disclosed it first to his friends, they too would have fallen into the astonishment the rest fell into, and could not possibly have done otherwise: with such contrivance and such order was it made.

The first to come up to the head's ear was Don Antonio himself, and he said to it in a low voice, but not so low that everybody did not hear it:

"Tell me, head, by the virtue that is shut up in you: what thoughts have I now?"

And the head answered him, without moving its lips, in a clear and distinct voice, so that everybody heard it, these words:

"I do not judge of thoughts."

Hearing which, they were all astounded, and still more at seeing that in the whole room and round the table there was no human being who could have answered.

"How many of us are here?" Don Antonio asked again.

And he was answered in the same tenor, softly:

"There are you and your wife, with two friends of yours and two friends of hers, and a famous knight called Don Quixote of La Mancha, and a squire of his who has Sancho Panza for his name."

Here indeed was fresh astonishment; here indeed did everybody's hair stand on end with pure terror! And Don Antonio, moving away from the head, said:

"This is enough to give me to understand that I was not cheated by the man who sold you to me, O wise head, talking head, answering head and admirable head! Let somebody else come and ask it whatever they like."

And, as women are generally in a hurry and fond of knowing things, the first to come up was one of the two friends of Don Antonio's wife, and what she asked it was:

"Tell me, head: what shall I do to be very beautiful?"

And she was answered:

"Be very virtuous."

"I ask you no more," said the questioner.

Then her companion came and said:

"I should like to know, head, whether my husband loves me or not."

And they answered her:

"Look at what he does for you, and you will see it."

The married woman moved away, saying:

"That answer did not need a question, because in fact the deeds a man does declare the will of the man who does them."

Then one of Don Antonio's two friends came up and asked it:

"Who am I?"

And he was answered:

"You know."

"That is not what I am asking," answered the gentleman, "but that you should tell me whether you know me."

"I do know you," they answered him: "you are Don Pedro Noriz."

"I want to know no more, since this is enough to make me understand, O head, that you know everything."

And, moving away, the other friend came up and asked it:

"Tell me, head: what desires has my son the heir?"

"I have already said," they answered him, "that I do not judge of desires; but for all that, I can tell you that those your son has are of burying you."

"That is it," said the gentleman: "what I see with my eyes, I point at with my finger."

And he asked no more. Don Antonio's wife came up and said:

"I do not know what to ask you, head; I should only like to know from you whether I shall have my good husband for many years."

And they answered her:

"You shall, because his health and his temperance in his living promise many years of life, which many men shorten by their intemperance."

Then Don Quixote came up and said:

"Tell me, you who answer: was it truth or was it a dream, what I tell of what happened to me in the cave of Montesinos? Will Sancho my squire's lashes be certain? Will Dulcinea's disenchantment be carried out?"

"As to the cave," they answered, "there is a great deal to say: it has something of both. Sancho's lashes will go slowly; Dulcinea's disenchantment will come to its due execution."

"I want to know no more," said Don Quixote; "for so long as I see Dulcinea disenchanted, I shall reckon that all the good fortune I could wish for has come at one stroke."

The last questioner was Sancho, and what he asked was:

"By any chance, head, shall I have another government? Shall I get out of the tightness of being a squire? Shall I see my wife and my children again?"

To which they answered him:

"You shall govern in your own house; and if you go back to it, you shall see your wife and your children; and, leaving off service, you shall leave off being a squire."

"Good, by God!" said Sancho Panza. "I could have told myself that: the prophet Truism himself could have said no more."

"You beast," said Don Quixote, "what do you want them to answer you? Is it not enough that the answers this head has given match what it is asked?"

"Yes, it is enough," answered Sancho, "but I should have liked it to explain itself more and tell me more."

With this the questions and answers came to an end, but not the astonishment they were all left in — except Don Antonio's two friends, who knew the business.

Which Cide Hamete Benengeli decided to explain at once, so as not to keep the world in suspense, believing that some sorcerous and extraordinary mystery was shut up in that head. And so he says that Don Antonio Moreno, in imitation of another head he had seen in Madrid made by a print-seller, made this one in his house to entertain himself and to astonish the ignorant. And the making of it was in this way: the top of the table was of wood, painted and varnished like jasper, and the foot it stood on was of the same, with four eagle's claws coming out of it for greater firmness under the weight. The head, which looked like a medallion and a figure of a Roman emperor and was bronze in colour, was entirely hollow, and so was the top of the table, into which it fitted so exactly that no sign of a join showed. The foot of the table was likewise hollow and answered to the throat and chest of the head, and all of this came out into another room that lay below the room of the head. Through this whole hollow of foot, table, throat and chest of the said medallion and figure there ran a tube of tinplate, fitted very exactly, which nobody could see. In the room below, matching the one above, was placed the man who was to answer, his mouth glued to that same tube, so that, like a blowpipe, the voice went from above to below and from below to above in articulate and clear words; and in this way it was not possible to know the trick.

A nephew of Don Antonio's, a sharp and judicious student, was the answerer; and, having been told by his uncle who would be coming in with him that day into the room of the head, it was easy for him to answer the first question quickly and exactly; the rest he answered by conjecture, and, being judicious, judiciously.

And Cide Hamete says more: that this marvellous machine lasted some ten or twelve days; but that, it being noised about the city that Don Antonio had an enchanted head in his house that answered everybody who asked it, and fearing that it might come to the ears of the wakeful sentinels of our Faith, he explained the business to the lords inquisitors, who ordered him to take it apart and go no further with it, so that the ignorant crowd should not be scandalised. But in Don Quixote's and Sancho Panza's opinion the head remained enchanted and answering, more to Don Quixote's satisfaction than to Sancho's.
