The gentlemen of the city, to please Don Antonio and to entertain Don Quixote and give him room to show his silliness, arranged to hold a ring-tilting six days later; which did not come off, for the reason that will be told further on.

Don Quixote took a fancy to walk about the city plainly and on foot, fearing that if he went on horseback the boys would chase him; and so he and Sancho, with two other servants Don Antonio gave him, went out for a walk.

It happened, then, that, going along a street, Don Quixote raised his eyes and saw written over a door in very large letters: Books printed here. At which he was much pleased, because until then he had never seen a printing house and wanted to know what one was like. He went inside with his whole retinue and saw them pulling in one place, correcting in another, setting up here and revising there — in short, all that machinery that shows itself in great printing houses. Don Quixote would go up to one case and ask what it was they were doing there; the workmen would give him an account of it; he would be astonished and pass on.

He came up to one of them and asked him what he was doing. The workman answered him:

"Sir, this gentleman here" — and he showed him a man of very good figure and appearance and of some gravity — "has translated a Tuscan book into our Castilian language, and I am setting it up to give it to the press."

"What title has the book?" asked Don Quixote.

To which the author answered:

"Sir, the book in Tuscan is called Le Bagatelle."

"And what does Le Bagatelle answer to in our Castilian?" asked Don Quixote.

"Le Bagatelle," said the author, "is as though in Castilian we said The Trifles; and although this book is humble in its name, it holds and shuts up in itself very good and substantial things."

"I," said Don Quixote, "know something of Tuscan, and I pride myself on singing some stanzas of Ariosto. But tell me, your worship, my dear sir — and I do not say this because I want to examine your worship's wit, but out of curiosity and no more: have you ever found the word pignatta in your writing?"

"Yes, many times," answered the author.

"And how does your worship translate it into Castilian?" asked Don Quixote.

"How should I translate it," replied the author, "except by saying pot?"

"Body of me," said Don Quixote, "how far advanced your worship is in the Tuscan tongue! I would lay a good wager that where the Tuscan says piace, your worship says in Castilian pleases; and where it says più, you say more; and su you set out as up and giù as down."

"I do set them out so, certainly," said the author, "because those are their proper equivalents."

"I would dare to swear," said Don Quixote, "that your worship is not known in the world, which is always an enemy to rewarding flowering wits and praiseworthy labours. What abilities are lost about the place! What wits are cornered! What virtues are despised!

"But for all that, it seems to me that translating from one language into another, unless it is from the queens of languages, Greek and Latin, is like looking at Flemish tapestries from the wrong side: for although the figures can be seen, they are full of threads that darken them, and they are not seen with the smoothness and colour of the right side. And translating from easy languages argues neither wit nor eloquence, any more than it is argued by the man who transcribes or copies one paper from another paper. And I do not want to infer by this that this exercise of translating is not praiseworthy; because a man could employ himself on worse things and ones that brought him less profit.

"Outside this reckoning stand the two famous translators: the one, Doctor Cristóbal de Figueroa in his Pastor Fido, and the other, Don Juan de Jáuregui in his Aminta, where they happily put it in doubt which is the translation and which the original. But tell me, your worship: is this book being printed at your own expense, or have you already sold the licence to some bookseller?"

"At my own expense I am printing it," answered the author, "and I expect to make a thousand ducats at least with this first printing, which is to be of two thousand copies, and they will go off at six reals each in a trice."

"Your worship is well up in your reckoning!" answered Don Quixote. "It is plain enough that you do not know the ins and outs of printers and the understandings there are between one and another. I promise you that when you find yourself loaded with two thousand copies of a book, you will find your own body so battered that it will frighten you — and the more so if the book is a little crooked and not at all spicy."

"Why, then," said the author, "does your worship want me to give it to a bookseller who will give me three maravedís for the licence and even thinks he is doing me a kindness in giving them me? I do not print my books to win fame in the world, since I am already known in it by my works: it is profit I want, for without it a good name is not worth a farthing."

"God give your worship good luck," answered Don Quixote.

And he went on to another case, where he saw that they were correcting a sheet of a book entitled The Light of the Soul; and, on seeing it, he said:

"Books like these — although there are a great many of the kind — are the ones that ought to be printed; because there are a great many sinners about, and infinite lights are needed for so many people in the dark."

He went on and saw that they were likewise correcting another book; and, asking its title, he was answered that it was called The Second Part of The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha, composed by a certain man of Tordesillas.

"I already have news of this book," said Don Quixote, "and truly and in my conscience I thought it was burnt and turned to powder by now for its impertinence. But its Martinmas will come to it, as it does to every pig; for invented histories are good and delightful just so far as they come near the truth or the likeness of it, and true ones are the better the truer they are."

And, saying this, with signs of some indignation, he went out of the printing house. And that same day Don Antonio arranged to take him to see the galleys that were on the beach, at which Sancho was much delighted, since he had never seen any in his life. Don Antonio let the commander of the galleys know that he was to bring his guest, the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha, to see them that afternoon — of whom the commander and all the inhabitants of the city already had news; and what happened to him on board them will be told in the following chapter.

Chapter 63: Of the Ill That Befell Sancho Panza on the Visit to the Galleys, and the Strange Adventure of the Beautiful Moorish Girl

Great were the arguments Don Quixote made about the enchanted head's answer, without any of them hitting on the trick, and they all ended in the promise — which he took for certain — of Dulcinea's disenchantment. There he went to and fro and was glad within himself, believing that he was soon to see it carried out. And Sancho, although he loathed being a governor, as has been said, still wanted to go back to giving orders and being obeyed; for this is the bad luck that command brings with it, even if it is only in jest.

In short, that afternoon Don Antonio Moreno his host and his two friends, with Don Quixote and Sancho, went to the galleys. The commander, who had been warned of their welcome coming so that he might see the two so famous men Quixote and Sancho, had hardly seen them reach the shore when all the galleys dropped their awnings and the shawms sounded. Then they threw the skiff into the water, covered with rich carpets and with cushions of crimson velvet; and, the moment Don Quixote set foot in it, the flagship fired her gangway cannon and the other galleys did the same; and, as Don Quixote came up the starboard ladder, the whole rowing crew saluted him as is the custom when a person of quality comes aboard a galley, saying "Hu, hu, hu!" three times.

The general — for by this name we shall call him — gave him his hand; he was a gentleman of quality from Valencia, and he embraced Don Quixote, saying to him:

"I shall mark this day with a white stone, for being one of the best I expect to have in my life, having seen Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha: a time and a token that shows us that in him is shut up and summed all the worth of knight-errantry."

With no less courteous words Don Quixote answered him, extremely glad to see himself treated so much like a great lord. They all went into the stern gallery, which was very well fitted out, and sat down along the benches; the boatswain passed along the gangway and gave the signal with his whistle for the crew to strip, which was done in an instant.

Sancho, seeing so many men naked, was thunderstruck, and still more when he saw them rig the awning so fast that it seemed to him that all the devils were at work there. But all this was cakes and fancy bread compared with what I shall now tell.

Sancho was sitting on the stern post next to the aftermost rower on the right-hand side, who, having been warned what he was to do, took hold of Sancho and, lifting him in his arms — the whole crew being on their feet and on the alert — beginning from the starboard side, went passing and rolling him along on the crew's arms from bench to bench with such speed that the poor Sancho lost the sight of his eyes and undoubtedly thought the very demons were carrying him off; and they did not stop with him until they had brought him back along the port side and set him down in the stern. The poor man was left battered and panting and sweating all over, unable to imagine what had happened to him.

Don Quixote, who saw Sancho's flight without wings, asked the general whether these were ceremonies used with those who came aboard galleys for the first time; because if by any chance they were, he, having no intention of taking his vows in them, did not want to perform exercises of the kind; and he swore to God that if anybody came to lay hold of him to roll him about, he would kick the soul out of him. And, saying this, he got to his feet and gripped his sword.

At this instant they dropped the awning, and with an enormous noise let the yard fall from top to bottom. Sancho thought the sky was coming off its hinges and about to fall on his head; and, bending it down, full of fear, he put it between his legs. Don Quixote was not altogether easy either, for he too shuddered and hunched his shoulders and lost the colour in his face.

The crew hoisted the yard with the same speed and noise with which they had lowered it, and all this in silence, as though they had neither voice nor breath. The boatswain gave the signal to weigh anchor and, leaping into the middle of the gangway with his lash, began to swat the backs of the crew and to stand out little by little to sea.

When Sancho saw so many red feet moving at once — for such he thought the oars were — he said to himself:

"These really are enchanted things, and not the ones my master talks about. What have these wretched men done to be whipped like this, and how does this one man who goes about here whistling dare to whip so many people? Now I say that this is hell — or at least purgatory."

Don Quixote, who saw the attention with which Sancho was watching what was going on, said to him:

"Ah, Sancho my friend, how quickly and at how little cost you could, if you wanted, strip yourself from the waist up and place yourself among these gentlemen and make an end of Dulcinea's disenchantment! For with the misery and the pain of so many, you would not feel your own much; and what is more, it might be that the wise Merlin would count each one of these lashes, for being given by a good hand, as ten of the ones you must in the end give yourself."

The general was about to ask what lashes these were, or what disenchantment of Dulcinea, when the seaman said:

"Montjuïc is signalling that there is an oared vessel on the coast on the western side."

Hearing this, the general leapt into the gangway and said:

"Come, my sons, do not let her get away from us! This must be some brigantine of Algerine corsairs that the lookout is signalling to us."

The other three galleys came up at once to the flagship to learn what they were ordered. The general ordered two of them to stand out to sea, and he with the other would go along close in to land, so that in this way the vessel should not escape them. The crew pulled hard at the oars, driving the galleys on with such fury that they seemed to fly.

The two that stood out to sea, at about two miles, made out a vessel which by eye they marked at some fourteen or fifteen benches — and so it was. This vessel, when she made out the galleys, made off, meaning and hoping to escape by her speed; but it went badly for her, because the flagship was one of the swiftest vessels that sailed the sea, and she gained on her so fast that those on the brigantine plainly knew they could not escape. And so the captain would have had them drop their oars and give themselves up, so as not to provoke the commander of our galleys into anger.

But fortune, which was guiding it another way, arranged that, just as the flagship came so close that those on the vessel could hear the voices from her calling on them to surrender, two toraquis — which is as much as to say two drunken Turks — who were on the brigantine among these twelve, fired two muskets and killed two soldiers who were on our forecastle. Seeing which, the general swore to leave nobody alive of all he took on that vessel; and, coming on to ram her at full fury, she slipped away under his oars.

The galley went on a good way ahead; those on the vessel saw themselves lost, made sail while the galley was coming round, and once more, under sail and oar, made off; but their diligence did not help them as much as their boldness harmed them, because the flagship caught them up at a little over half a mile, laid her oars over them and took them all alive.

At this the other two galleys came up, and all four with the prize went back to the beach, where an infinite number of people were waiting for them, eager to see what they had brought. The general anchored near land and saw that the viceroy of the city was on the shore. He ordered the skiff to be let down to bring him, and ordered the yard to be lowered so as to hang at once the captain and the rest of the Turks he had taken on the vessel, who would be about thirty-six persons, all of them fine-looking men and most of them Turkish musketeers.

The general asked who the captain of the brigantine was, and he was answered by one of the prisoners in the Castilian tongue, who afterwards proved to be a Spanish renegade:

"This young man you see here, sir, is our captain."

And he showed him one of the loveliest and most gallant young men that human imagination could paint. His age, to look at him, did not reach twenty. The general asked him:

"Tell me, you ill-advised dog, what moved you to kill my soldiers, when you saw that it was impossible for you to escape? Is this the respect that is kept for flagships? Do you not know that rashness is not valour? Doubtful hopes ought to make men bold, but not foolhardy."

The captain was about to answer, but the general could not hear the answer just then, having to go and receive the viceroy, who was already coming aboard the galley, and with whom there came some of his servants and some people of the town.

"The hunting has been good, my lord general!" said the viceroy.

"And so good," answered the general, "that Your Excellency shall see it hanging from this yard in a moment."

"How so?" replied the viceroy.

"Because they have killed me," answered the general, "against all law and against all reason and usage of war, two of the best soldiers in these galleys; and I have sworn to hang all those I have taken prisoner, and chiefly this young man, who is the captain of the brigantine."

And he showed him the young man, who already had his hands tied and the cord round his throat, waiting for death.

The viceroy looked at him; and, seeing him so beautiful and so gallant and so humble — his beauty giving him at that instant a letter of recommendation — he was seized with a desire to save him from death; and so he asked him:

"Tell me, captain: are you a Turk by nation, or a Moor, or a renegade?"

To which the young man answered, likewise in the Castilian tongue:

"I am neither a Turk by nation, nor a Moor, nor a renegade."

"Well, what are you?" replied the viceroy.

"A Christian woman," answered the young man.

"A woman and a Christian, and in such a dress and in such a pass? That is a thing more to be marvelled at than believed."

"Suspend, gentlemen," said the young man, "the carrying out of my death; for not much will be lost by your revenge being put off while I tell you my life."

Who could have had a heart so hard as not to be softened by these words — or at least to wait to hear what the sad and wounded young person wanted to say? The general told him to say whatever he liked, but not to expect to obtain any pardon for his known guilt. With this leave, the young man began to speak in this way:

"Of that nation more unfortunate than prudent, on whom a sea of misfortunes has rained down these last days, I was born, engendered by Morisco parents. In the current of their misfortune I was taken to Barbary by two uncles of mine, and it did me no good to say that I was a Christian, as in fact I am — and not one of the pretended or apparent ones but one of the true and Catholic ones. It did not help me, with those who had charge of our wretched exile, to tell this truth; nor would my uncles believe it; on the contrary, they took it for a lie and an invention for staying in the land where I had been born, and so, more by force than by good will, they brought me with them.

"I had a Christian mother and a judicious and Christian father, neither more nor less; I sucked in the Catholic faith with my milk; I was brought up with good habits; and neither in my speech nor in them did I ever, as I believe, give signs of being a Morisco. Alongside and in step with these virtues — for I believe they are virtues — my beauty grew, if I have any; and, although my reserve and my seclusion were great, they must not have been so great that a young gentleman called Don Gaspar Gregorio, the eldest son of a gentleman who has an estate of his own next to our village, did not have a chance to see me.

"How he saw me, how we spoke to each other, how he was lost for me and how I was not much won by him would be long to tell, and the more so at a time when I am afraid that between my tongue and my throat the harsh cord that threatens me is going to come across. And so I shall only say how Don Gregorio chose to go with me into our exile. He mixed with the Moriscos who came out of other places, because he knew the language very well, and on the journey he made friends with two uncles of mine who were bringing me with them.

"Because my father, prudent and provident, as soon as he heard the first edict of our exile, left the village and went to look for somewhere in foreign kingdoms to take us in. He left shut up and buried, in a place that only I know of, a great many pearls and stones of great value, along with some money in gold crusadoes and doubloons. He ordered me on no account to touch the treasure he was leaving, if we were exiled before he came back.

"I did so; and with my uncles, as I have said, and other relations and connections we crossed to Barbary; and the place where we settled was Algiers, as though we had settled in hell itself. The king got to hear of my beauty, and rumour told him of my riches — which in part was my good fortune. He called me before him, asked me what part of Spain I was from and what money and what jewels I had brought. I told him the place, and that the jewels and the money had been left buried in it, but that they could easily be got if I myself went back for them. All this I told him, fearing that it would not be my beauty that blinded him but his own greed.

"While he was in this talk with me, they came and told him that there was travelling with me one of the most gallant and beautiful young men that could be imagined. At once I understood that they were speaking of Don Gaspar Gregorio, whose beauty leaves behind the greatest that can be extolled. I was thrown into confusion, considering the danger Don Gregorio was running; because among those barbarous Turks a beautiful boy or youth is held and valued more than a woman, however lovely.

"The king ordered at once that he should be brought there in front of him so that he might see him, and asked me whether what they told him about that youth was true. Then I, almost as though warned by heaven, told him that it was; but that I would let him know that it was not a man but a woman like myself; and that I begged him to let me go and dress her in her natural clothes, so that she might show her beauty entirely and appear before him with less embarrassment. He told me to go and welcome, and that the next day we would talk about the way of arranging for me to go back to Spain to get out the hidden treasure.

"I spoke to Don Gaspar; I told him the danger he ran in showing himself to be a man; I dressed him as a Moorish woman, and that same afternoon brought him into the king's presence; who, on seeing him, was astonished and formed the design of keeping her to make a present of her to the Grand Turk. And, to escape the danger he might have in his own harem and to fear from himself, he ordered her to be put in the house of some Moorish ladies of quality to guard her and serve her, where they took her at once.

"What the two of us felt — for I cannot deny that I love him — let it be left to the thoughts of those who part when they love each other well. Then the king laid the plan for me to come back to Spain in this brigantine and for two Turks by nation to go with me, who were the ones who killed your soldiers. This Spanish renegade also came with me" — and she pointed at the man who had spoken first — "of whom I know very well that he is a Christian in secret and comes with more wish to stay in Spain than to go back to Barbary. The rest of the crew of the brigantine are Moors and Turks, who serve for nothing but to pull at the oar.

"The two Turks, greedy and insolent, without keeping to the orders we had that they should put me and this renegade ashore on the first part of Spain in Christian dress, which we came provided with, chose first to sweep this coast and make some prize if they could, fearing that if they put us ashore first, through some accident that might happen to the two of us we might reveal that the brigantine was at sea; and if there happened to be galleys along this coast, they might be caught.

"Last night we made out this beach and, without knowing about these four galleys, we were made out ourselves, and there has happened to us what you have seen. In short: Don Gregorio remains in woman's dress among women, in plain danger of being lost, and I see my hands tied, waiting — or, better said, fearing — to lose my life, which by now wearies me.

"This, gentlemen, is the end of my lamentable history, as true as it is unfortunate. What I beg of you is that you let me die as a Christian; for, as I have said, in nothing have I been guilty of the guilt into which those of my nation have fallen."

And then she fell silent, her eyes swollen with tender tears, which were joined by a great many from those who were present. The viceroy, tender and compassionate, without saying her a word, came up to her and with his own hands took off the cord that bound the beautiful hands of the Moorish girl.

While the Morisco Christian woman was telling her strange history, an old pilgrim who had come aboard the galley when the viceroy came had kept his eyes fixed on her; and the Morisco girl had hardly finished her speech when he threw himself at her feet and, embracing them, with words broken by a thousand sobs and sighs, said to her:

"O Ana Félix, my unfortunate daughter! I am your father Ricote, who was coming back to look for you, unable to live without you, since you are my soul."

At which words Sancho opened his eyes and raised his head, which he had been keeping bowed, thinking about the misfortune of his ride; and, looking at the pilgrim, he knew him to be the same Ricote he had met on the day he left his government, and he confirmed that this was his daughter — who, being untied by now, embraced her father, mixing her tears with his. And Ricote said to the general and the viceroy:

"This, gentlemen, is my daughter, more unfortunate in her doings than in her name. Ana Félix she is called, with the surname of Ricote, famous as much for her beauty as for my riches. I left my country to look in foreign kingdoms for somebody to shelter and take us in; and, having found it in Germany, I came back in this pilgrim's dress in the company of some Germans to look for my daughter and to dig up a great deal of wealth I had left hidden. I did not find my daughter; I found the treasure, which I carry with me; and now, by the strange roundabout you have seen, I have found the treasure that most enriches me, which is my beloved daughter.

"If our small guilt and her tears and mine can, by the integrity of your justice, open doors to mercy, use it with us; for we never had any thought of offending you, nor did we agree in any way with the intentions of our people, who have been justly exiled."

Then Sancho said:

"I know Ricote well, and I know that what he says is true as far as Ana Félix's being his daughter goes; as to these other odds and ends of coming and going and having good or bad intentions, I do not meddle."

Everybody present being amazed at the strange business, the general said:

"Come what may, your tears will not let me keep my oath: live, beautiful Ana Félix, the years of life that heaven has settled for you, and let the insolent, reckless men who committed the offence carry the penalty of their guilt."

And he ordered at once that the two Turks who had killed his two soldiers should be hanged from the yard; but the viceroy begged him earnestly not to hang them, since what they had done had been madness rather than valour. The general did what the viceroy asked, because revenge is not well carried out in cold blood.

Then they set about laying a plan for getting Don Gaspar Gregorio out of the danger he was left in. Ricote offered for it more than two thousand ducats that he had in pearls and jewels. A great many ways were suggested, but none was as good as the one given by the Spanish renegade already mentioned, who offered to go back to Algiers in some small boat of about six benches, manned by Christian rowers; because he knew where and how and when he could and should land, and likewise he was not ignorant of the house where Don Gaspar was left.

The general and the viceroy doubted about trusting the renegade, or trusting the Christians who were to pull at the oar; Ana Félix went surety for him, and Ricote her father said he would come forward to pay the ransom of the Christians if they should happen to be lost.

Being settled, then, in this opinion, the viceroy went ashore, and Don Antonio Moreno took the Morisco girl and her father home with him, the viceroy charging him to treat them well and make much of them as far as he could; and for his own part he offered whatever there was in his house for their entertainment. So great was the good will and charity that Ana Félix's beauty poured into his breast.

Chapter 64: Which Deals with the Adventure That Gave Don Quixote More Distress Than Any That Had Happened to Him Until Then

Don Antonio Moreno's wife, the history tells, was extremely pleased to see Ana Félix in her house. She received her with a great deal of graciousness, being as taken with her beauty as with her good sense — for in both the one and the other the Morisco girl was outstanding; and all the people of the city came to see her as though a bell had been rung.

Don Quixote told Don Antonio that the plan they had settled on for Don Gregorio's freeing was not a good one, because it had more of the dangerous in it than of the convenient, and that it would be better to put him ashore in Barbary with his arms and his horse; for he would bring him out in spite of all the Moors, as Don Gaiferos had done with his wife Melisendra.

"Let your worship note," said Sancho, hearing this, "that Señor Don Gaiferos brought his wife out of dry land and took her to France over dry land; but here, if we do bring Don Gregorio out, we have no way of bringing him to Spain, since the sea lies between."

"There is a remedy for everything except death," answered Don Quixote; "for, the boat coming to the shore, we can embark on it though all the world should stop us."

"Your worship paints it and makes it easy very well," said Sancho, "but from saying to doing is a long way; and I hold by the renegade, who seems to me a very honest man with very good bowels in him."

Don Antonio said that if the renegade did not come well out of the business, the expedient would be taken of the great Don Quixote's crossing over to Barbary.

Two days later the renegade set off in a swift boat of six oars a side, manned by the most valiant of crews; and two days after that the galleys sailed for the Levant, the general having asked the viceroy to be so good as to let him know what happened in Don Gregorio's freeing and in Ana Félix's case; the viceroy undertook to do it as he asked.

And one morning, Don Quixote going out to ride along the beach armed in all his arms — because, as he often said, arms were his adornment and fighting his rest, and he never found himself without them for a moment — he saw coming towards him a knight likewise armed cap-a-pie, who carried a shining moon painted on his shield; who, coming within a distance at which he could be heard, addressed his words to Don Quixote and said in a loud voice:

"Distinguished knight and never-sufficiently-praised Don Quixote of La Mancha, I am the Knight of the White Moon, whose unheard-of exploits will perhaps have brought me back to your memory. I come to contend with you and to try the strength of your arms, so as to make you know and confess that my lady, be she who she may, is beyond comparison more beautiful than your Dulcinea of El Toboso. Which truth, if you confess it plainly and openly, you will save yourself from death and me from the labour I must take in giving it you.

"And if you fight and I conquer you, I want no other satisfaction than that, laying down your arms and holding off from looking for adventures, you should gather yourself in and withdraw to your village for the space of a year, where you are to live without laying hand to your sword, in quiet peace and profitable rest, since this is what best suits the increase of your property and the salvation of your soul. And if you conquer me, my head shall be at your discretion, and the spoils of my arms and my horse shall be yours, and the fame of my exploits shall pass to yours. Consider which is best for you, and answer me at once, because I have all today as my term for despatching this business."

Don Quixote was bewildered and astounded, as much by the Knight of the White Moon's arrogance as by the cause for which he was challenging him; and with composure and a severe air he answered him:

"Knight of the White Moon, whose exploits have not so far come to my notice, I would dare to swear that you have never seen the illustrious Dulcinea; for if you had seen her, I know you would have tried not to put yourself to this demand, because the sight of her would have undeceived you of there ever having been or ever being able to be any beauty that could be compared with hers.

"And so, not telling you that you lie but that you are wrong in what you propose, I accept your challenge with the conditions you have named, and at once, so that the day you have appointed may not go by; and I except from the conditions only that of the fame of your exploits passing to me, because I do not know what they are or of what kind: with my own I am content, such as they are. Take, then, whichever part of the field you like, for I shall do the same; and whoever God gives it to, Saint Peter bless it to him."

They had made out the Knight of the White Moon from the city and told the viceroy, who was talking with Don Quixote of La Mancha. The viceroy, believing it would be some new adventure got up by Don Antonio Moreno or by some other gentleman of the city, went out at once to the beach with Don Antonio and with a great many other gentlemen who accompanied him, just as Don Quixote was turning Rocinante's reins to take as much of the field as he needed.

The viceroy, then, seeing that the two of them were giving signs of turning to charge each other, placed himself between them, asking them what the cause was that moved them to give battle so suddenly. The Knight of the White Moon answered that it was precedence in beauty, and in a few words said him the same things he had said to Don Quixote, along with the acceptance of the conditions of the challenge made by both sides.

The viceroy came up to Don Antonio and asked him softly whether he knew who this Knight of the White Moon was, or whether it was some trick they meant to play on Don Quixote. Don Antonio answered him that he neither knew who he was nor whether the challenge was in jest or in earnest. This answer left the viceroy perplexed as to whether or not he should let them go on with the battle; but, being unable to persuade himself that it was anything but a joke, he stepped aside, saying:

"Gentlemen knights, if there is no remedy here but confessing or dying, and Señor Don Quixote sticks at his thirteen and your worship of the White Moon at your fourteen, then into the hand of God, and have at it."

The Knight of the White Moon thanked the viceroy in courteous and judicious words for the leave that was given them, and Don Quixote did the same; and he, commending himself to heaven with all his heart and to his Dulcinea — as was his custom at the beginning of the battles that offered themselves — went and took a little more of the field, because he saw that his opponent was doing the same. And, without a trumpet sounding or any other warlike instrument giving them the signal to charge, both of them at the same moment turned their horses' reins.

And, as the White Moon's horse was the swifter, he reached Don Quixote when two thirds of the course had been run, and there he met him with such mighty force, without touching him with his lance — which he raised, apparently on purpose — that he brought Rocinante and Don Quixote down in a dangerous fall. He was on top of him at once and, setting his lance on his visor, said to him:

"You are conquered, knight, and dead too, if you do not confess the conditions of our challenge."

Don Quixote, battered and stunned, without raising his visor, as though he were speaking from inside a tomb, said in a weakened and sickly voice:

"Dulcinea of El Toboso is the most beautiful woman in the world, and I the most unfortunate knight on earth; and it is not right that my weakness should defraud this truth. Press home the lance, knight, and take my life, since you have taken my honour."

"That I shall not do, certainly," said the Knight of the White Moon. "Let the fame of the lady Dulcinea of El Toboso's beauty live and live entire; I am content only that the great Don Quixote should withdraw to his village for a year, or for such time as I may order him, as we agreed before going into this battle."

All this the viceroy and Don Antonio heard, along with a great many others who were there; and they heard likewise that Don Quixote answered that, so long as he was not asked for anything that would be to Dulcinea's damage, he would carry out all the rest as an exact and truthful knight.

This confession made, the Knight of the White Moon turned his reins and, bowing his head to the viceroy, went at a half gallop into the city.

The viceroy ordered Don Antonio to go after him and by all means to find out who he was. They lifted Don Quixote up, uncovered his face and found him without colour and sweating all over. Rocinante, out of pure ill usage, could not stir for the moment.

Sancho, all sad, all grieved, did not know what to say or what to do: it seemed to him that this whole business was happening in a dream and that all that machinery was a matter of enchantment. He saw his master conquered and bound not to take up arms for a year; he imagined the light of the glory of his exploits darkened, the hopes of his fresh promises undone as smoke is undone by the wind. He was afraid that Rocinante might be left crippled, and his master's bones out of joint — though it would have been no small piece of luck if it had been his madness that came out of joint.

Finally, in a sedan chair the viceroy ordered to be brought, they carried him to the city; and the viceroy went back to it too, wanting to know who the Knight of the White Moon might be, who had left Don Quixote in such a bad way.

Chapter 65: Where It Is Made Known Who the Knight of the White Moon Was, Along with Don Gregorio's Release and Other Events

Don Antonio Moreno followed the Knight of the White Moon, and a great many boys followed him too — and even chased him — until they shut him up in an inn inside the city. Don Antonio went in, wanting to know him; a squire came out to receive him and to disarm him; he shut himself up in a room on the ground floor, and Don Antonio with him, whose bread would not bake until he knew who he was. The Knight of the White Moon, seeing, then, that this gentleman would not leave him, said to him:

"I know very well, sir, what you have come for, which is to find out who I am; and, since there is no reason to deny it you, while this servant of mine disarms me I shall tell you, without falling a point short of the truth of the case.

"Know, sir, that they call me the bachelor Sansón Carrasco. I am from the same village as Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose madness and folly move all of us who know him to pity him; and among those who have pitied him most I have been one. And, believing that his health lies in his rest and in his staying in his own country and his own house, I laid a plan to make him stay in it.

"And so, three months ago I came out onto the road as a knight errant, calling myself the Knight of the Mirrors, meaning to fight him and conquer him without doing him any harm, laying it down as a condition of our fight that the beaten man should be at the winner's discretion. And what I meant to ask of him — for I already judged him beaten — was that he should go back to his village and not leave it for a whole year, in which time he might be cured.

"But fortune arranged it otherwise, because he conquered me and knocked me off my horse, and so my plan came to nothing. He went on his way and I came back, beaten, put out and battered by the fall, which was besides a dangerous one. But this did not take away my wish to go back and look for him and conquer him, as has been seen today. And, as he is so exact in keeping the orders of knight-errantry, he will beyond any doubt keep the one I have given him, in fulfilment of his word.

"This, sir, is what is afoot, and I have nothing else at all to tell you. I beg you not to give me away or to tell Don Quixote who I am, so that my good intentions may take effect and a man may recover his judgement who has an excellent one, if only the follies of chivalry would leave him alone."

"Oh, sir," said Don Antonio, "God forgive you the wrong you have done all the world in trying to make the most amusing madman in it sane! Do you not see, sir, that the good that Don Quixote's sanity may do cannot come near the pleasure he gives with his ravings? But I imagine that all the master bachelor's contrivance will not be enough to make a man so utterly mad sane again; and if it were not against charity, I should say: let Don Quixote never get well, because with his health we lose not only his own charms but Sancho Panza his squire's, any one of which could gladden melancholy itself again. For all that, I shall be quiet and shall say nothing to him, to see whether I turn out right in suspecting that the pains taken by Señor Carrasco will have no effect."

Carrasco answered that as things stood the business was at a good point, and that he hoped for a happy outcome from it. And, Don Antonio offering to do whatever else he might order, he took his leave of him; and, having had his arms tied up on a mule, that very instant, on the horse he had gone into the battle with, he left the city that same day and went back to his own country, without anything happening to him that obliges us to tell it in this true history.

Don Antonio told the viceroy everything Carrasco had told him, at which the viceroy took no great pleasure, because in Don Quixote's retirement everybody who had news of his madnesses lost the pleasure they might have had of them.

Six days Don Quixote spent in bed, downcast, sad, thoughtful and in a bad way, his imagination coming and going over the unfortunate business of his defeat. Sancho consoled him, and among other things said to him:

"My dear sir, let your worship lift up your head and be glad if you can, and give thanks to heaven that, since it threw you down on the ground, you did not come out of it with a broken rib. And, since you know that where they give they take, and that there are not always flitches of bacon where there are hooks, snap your fingers at the doctor, for you do not need him to cure you of this illness. Let us go back home and leave off going about looking for adventures in lands and places we do not know.

"And if it is properly considered, I am the greatest loser here, although your worship is the worst used. I, who left with the government the wish to be a governor again, did not leave the wish to be a count — which will never come off if your worship leaves off being a king by leaving the exercise of your chivalry; and so my hopes come to turn into smoke."

"Be quiet, Sancho, since you see that my seclusion and retirement is not to go beyond a year; for then I shall go back to my honourable exercises, and I shall not lack a kingdom to win and an earldom to give you."

"May God hear it," said Sancho, "and sin be deaf; for I have always heard it said that a good hope is worth more than a poor possession."

They were at this when Don Antonio came in, saying with signs of the greatest contentment:

"A reward, Señor Don Quixote! Don Gregorio and the renegade who went for him are on the beach! What am I saying, on the beach? They are already at the viceroy's house, and will be here in a moment."

Don Quixote cheered up somewhat and said:

"Truly I am half inclined to say that I should have been glad if it had all turned out the other way round, because it would have obliged me to cross over into Barbary, where with the strength of my arm I should have given liberty not only to Don Gregorio but to all the Christian captives there are in Barbary. But what am I saying, wretched man? Am I not the one who has been beaten? Am I not the one who has been thrown down? Am I not the one who cannot take up arms for a year? Then what am I promising? What am I boasting of, when the distaff suits me better than the sword?"

"Leave that alone, sir," said Sancho. "Long live the hen, even with her pip; for today it is your turn and tomorrow mine; and in these matters of encounters and knocks there is no taking any measure of them, since the man who falls today can get up tomorrow — unless he wants to stay in bed; I mean unless he lets himself faint away without gathering fresh spirit for fresh quarrels. And let your worship get up now to receive Don Gregorio, for it seems to me that the people are in a stir and he must be in the house by now."

And it was the truth; because, Don Gregorio and the renegade having already given the viceroy an account of their going and coming, Don Gregorio, eager to see Ana Félix, came with the renegade to Don Antonio's house. And although Don Gregorio, when they brought him out of Algiers, was in woman's clothes, in the boat he exchanged them for those of a captive who came out with him; but in whatever he had come, he would have shown himself a person to be coveted and served and valued, because he was extremely beautiful, and his age to look at him was seventeen or eighteen.

Ricote and his daughter came out to receive him: the father in tears and the daughter with modesty. They did not embrace one another, because where there is much love there is generally not much freedom. The two beauties of Don Gregorio and Ana Félix together particularly amazed all those who were present. Silence was what spoke there for the two lovers, and their eyes were the tongues that revealed their glad and modest thoughts.

The renegade told the contrivance and the means he had used to get Don Gregorio out; Don Gregorio told the dangers and the straits he had been in with the women he had been left with — not in a long speech but in a few words, in which he showed that his judgement went ahead of his years. Finally Ricote paid and satisfied both the renegade and those who had pulled at the oar generously. The renegade was reincorporated and reconciled with the Church, and from a rotten limb came back clean and sound with penance and repentance.

Two days later the viceroy discussed with Don Antonio what way they might have of getting Ana Félix and her father allowed to stay in Spain, since it seemed to them no drawback at all that so Christian a daughter and so apparently well-meaning a father should stay in it. Don Antonio offered to come to the court to negotiate it, where he had of necessity to come on other business, giving it to be understood that there, by means of favour and gifts, a great many difficult things are brought off.

"There is no hoping," said Ricote, who was present at this talk, "in favours or in gifts, because with the great Don Bernardino de Velasco, Count of Salazar, to whom His Majesty gave charge of our expulsion, entreaties are worth nothing, nor promises, nor gifts, nor pity. Because although it is true that he mixes mercy with justice, since he sees that the whole body of our nation is contaminated and rotten, he uses on it the cautery that burns rather than the ointment that softens.

"And so, with prudence, with shrewdness, with diligence and with the fears he sets up, he has carried on his strong shoulders the weight of this great machine to its due execution, without our contrivances, stratagems, entreaties and frauds having been able to dazzle his eyes of Argus, which he keeps constantly on the alert so that none of our people may stay behind or be hidden — like a hidden root that with time may afterwards come to sprout and put out poisonous fruits in Spain, now clean and now rid of the fears our numbers held it in. A heroic resolution of the great Philip the Third, and unheard-of prudence in having entrusted it to that same Don Bernardino de Velasco!"

"Come what may, I shall take what steps I can once I am there, and let heaven do what it is best pleased to do," said Don Antonio. "Don Gregorio shall go with me to console the grief his parents must be feeling for his absence; Ana Félix shall stay with my wife in my house, or in a convent; and I know that the lord viceroy will be glad for good Ricote to stay in his, until we see how I get on."

The viceroy consented to everything proposed; but Don Gregorio, learning what was afoot, said that on no account could he or would he leave Doña Ana Félix. But, meaning to see his parents and to lay a plan for coming back for her, he agreed to the settled arrangement. Ana Félix stayed with Don Antonio's wife, and Ricote in the viceroy's house.

The day of Don Antonio's departure came, and that of Don Quixote and Sancho, which was two days later — for the fall did not let him take the road any sooner. There were tears, there were sighs, faintings and sobs when Don Gregorio took his leave of Ana Félix. Ricote offered Don Gregorio a thousand crowns if he wanted them; but he took none, only five that Don Antonio lent him, promising to repay them at court. With this the two of them set off, and Don Quixote and Sancho afterwards, as has been said: Don Quixote unarmed and in travelling dress, Sancho on foot, because the grey was loaded with the arms.

Chapter 66: Which Deals with What Will Be Seen by Whoever Reads It, or Heard by Whoever Has It Read to Him

On leaving Barcelona, Don Quixote turned to look at the place where he had fallen, and said:

"Here Troy was! Here my ill luck, and not my cowardice, carried off the glories I had won; here fortune used her turns and returns on me; here my exploits were darkened; here, in short, my good fortune fell, never to rise again!"

Hearing which, Sancho said:

"It is as much the part of valiant hearts, my dear sir, to have patience in misfortunes as gladness in prosperity; and this I judge by myself, for if I was glad when I was a governor, now that I am a squire on foot I am not sad. Because I have heard it said that this thing they call Fortune about the place is a drunken, whimsical woman and, above all, blind, and so she does not see what she is doing, and does not know whom she is throwing down or whom she is raising up."

"You are very philosophical, Sancho," answered Don Quixote; "you speak very judiciously — I do not know who teaches you. What I can tell you is that there is no fortune in the world, and that the things that happen in it, good or bad as they may be, do not come by chance but by the particular providence of heaven; and from this comes what is generally said, that every man is the maker of his own fortune.

"I have been the maker of mine, but not with the necessary prudence, and so my presumptions have cost me dear; for I ought to have thought that the mighty bulk of the White Moon's horse could not be resisted by Rocinante's weakness. I ventured, in short; I did what I could; they knocked me down; and, although I lost my honour, I did not lose, and cannot lose, the virtue of keeping my word. When I was a knight errant, bold and valiant, with my deeds and my hands I gave credit to my doings; and now, when I am a squire on foot, I shall give credit to my words by keeping the one I gave in my promise. Walk on, then, Sancho my friend, and let us go and spend the year of our novitiate in our own country; in which seclusion we shall gain fresh strength for going back to the exercise of arms, which I never forget."

"Sir," answered Sancho, "travelling on foot is not such a delightful thing that it moves and stirs me to make long stages. Let us leave these arms hanging on some tree in place of a hanged man; and, with me astride the grey and my feet up off the ground, we shall make the stages as your worship asks and measures them; for to think that I am to travel on foot and make them long ones is to think the impossible."

"You have spoken well, Sancho," answered Don Quixote. "Let my arms be hung up for a trophy, and at the foot of them, or round about them, we shall carve on the trees what was written on the trophy of Roland's arms:

	Let nobody move these
	who cannot stand the test with Roland."

"That all seems to me of pearl," answered Sancho; "and if it were not for the want Rocinante would be to us on the road, it would be as well to leave him hanging too."

"Neither he nor the arms," replied Don Quixote, "do I want hanged, so that it may not be said that for good service, bad reward!"

"Your worship speaks very well," answered Sancho, "because, in the opinion of judicious men, the ass's fault is not to be laid on the pack-saddle; and, since your worship has the blame for this business, punish yourself and do not let your anger burst out on the already broken and bloody arms, or on Rocinante's gentleness, or on the softness of my feet, by wanting them to walk more than is fair."

In these arguments and this talk that whole day went by for them, and four more, without anything happening to hold up their road. And on the fifth day, at the entrance of a village, they found a great many people at the door of an inn who, it being a holiday, were amusing themselves there. As Don Quixote came up to them, a farm labourer raised his voice, saying:

"One of these two gentlemen coming here, who do not know the parties, shall say what is to be done about our wager."

"I shall say it, certainly," answered Don Quixote, "with all uprightness, if I can manage to understand it."

"The case is this, then, my good sir," said the labourer. "A neighbour of this village, so fat that he weighs eleven arrobas — an arroba being twenty-five pounds — challenged another neighbour of his, who weighs no more than five, to a race. It was the condition that they should run a course of a hundred paces with equal weights; and, the challenger having been asked how the weight was to be made equal, he said that the challenged man, who weighs five arrobas, should put six of iron on his back, and in this way the thin man's eleven arrobas would be equal to the fat man's eleven."

"Not that," said Sancho at this point, before Don Quixote could answer. "And it falls to me, who left off being a governor and a judge a few days ago, as all the world knows, to settle these doubts and give an opinion in every suit."

"Answer and welcome, Sancho my friend," said Don Quixote, "for I am not fit to give crumbs to a cat, my judgement being so disturbed and turned upside down."

With this leave, Sancho said to the labourers, a good many of whom stood round him with their mouths open, waiting for the sentence to come out of his:

"Brothers, what the fat man asks does not stand up, and it has not the shadow of any justice in it; because if it is true what is said, that the challenged man may choose the weapons, it is not right that this man should choose such as would hinder him and stop him from coming out the winner. And so it is my opinion that the fat challenger should prune, peel, thin out, polish and trim himself, and take six arrobas of his flesh off from here or there on his body, wherever seems best and suits him. And in this way, being left at five arrobas of weight, he will be even and level with his opponent's five, and so they will be able to run equally."

"I swear," said a labourer who had heard Sancho's sentence, "that this gentleman has spoken like a blessed saint and given sentence like a canon! But it is a safe bet that the fat man will not want to take an ounce off his flesh, let alone six arrobas."

"The best thing is for them not to run at all," answered another, "so that the thin man is not ground down by the weight and the fat man is not carved up. And let half the wager go on wine, and let us take these gentlemen to the tavern for the good stuff — and on my back be the cloak when it rains."

"I, gentlemen," answered Don Quixote, "am grateful to you, but I cannot stop for a moment, because sad thoughts and events make me look discourteous and travel faster than at a walk."

And so, giving Rocinante the spurs, he passed on, leaving them astonished at having seen and noted both his strange figure and his servant's good sense — for such they judged Sancho's. And another of the labourers said:

"If the servant is so judicious, what must the master be? I would wager that if they go and study at Salamanca, in no time at all they will come to be judges of the court; for it is all a joke but studying and more studying, and having favour and luck; and when a man least expects it, he finds himself with a magistrate's rod in his hand or a mitre on his head."

That night master and man spent in the middle of the fields under the bare, uncovered sky; and the next day, following their road, they saw coming towards them a man on foot with saddlebags round his neck and a javelin or pike in his hand, exactly the figure of a foot courier. Who, on coming up to Don Quixote, quickened his step and came at a half run and, embracing him round the right thigh, since he could reach no higher, said to him with signs of great gladness:

"O my lord Don Quixote of La Mancha, what great contentment must reach my lord the duke's heart when he learns that your worship is coming back to his castle — for he is still there with my lady the duchess!"

"I do not know you, my friend," answered Don Quixote, "and I do not know who you are, unless you tell me."

"I, Señor Don Quixote," answered the courier, "am Tosilos, the duke my lord's footman, who would not fight with your worship over the marriage of Doña Rodríguez's daughter."

"God bless me!" said Don Quixote. "Is it possible that you are the man whom my enemies the enchanters transformed into that footman you speak of, to cheat me of the honour of that battle?"

"Be quiet, my good sir," replied the letter-carrier, "for there was no enchantment at all and no change of face at all: I went into the lists as much Tosilos the footman as I came out of them Tosilos the footman. I thought I would get married without fighting, because the girl had taken my fancy; but my idea turned out backwards, for as soon as your worship left our castle the duke my lord had me given a hundred strokes for having gone against the orders he had given me before going into the battle. And it has all ended in the girl's being a nun by now, and Doña Rodríguez's having gone back to Castile, and my going now to Barcelona to take a packet of letters to the viceroy that my master is sending him. If your worship would like a little drop — warm, but neat — I have a gourd full of the good stuff here, with I do not know how many little slices of Tronchón cheese, which will serve as a call and an awakener to thirst, if by any chance it is asleep."

"I take up the invitation," said Sancho, "and let the rest of the courtesies go hang, and let good Tosilos pour out, in spite and defiance of all the enchanters there are in the Indies."

"In short," said Don Quixote, "you, Sancho, are the greatest glutton in the world and the greatest ignoramus on earth, since you cannot persuade yourself that this courier is enchanted and this Tosilos a counterfeit. Stay with him and fill yourself, and I shall go on ahead slowly, waiting for you to come."

The footman laughed, unsheathed his gourd, unbagged his slices, and, taking out a small loaf, he and Sancho sat down on the green grass and in good peace and fellowship polished off and struck bottom in the whole store of the saddlebags, with such good appetite that they licked the packet of letters simply because it smelt of cheese. Tosilos said to Sancho:

"Without any doubt this master of yours, Sancho my friend, must be a madman."

"Must he?" answered Sancho. "He is in no man's debt, for he pays for everything, and the more so when the coin is madness. I see it well enough, and I tell him so well enough; but what good does it do? And the more so now that he is finished off, because he has been beaten by the Knight of the White Moon."

Tosilos begged him to tell him what had happened, but Sancho answered him that it was discourteous to leave his master waiting for him; that another day, if they met, there would be room for it. And, getting up after shaking his coat and the crumbs out of his beard, he drove the grey on ahead and, saying goodbye, left Tosilos and caught up with his master, who was waiting for him in the shade of a tree.

Chapter 67: Of the Resolution Don Quixote Took to Become a Shepherd and Follow the Life of the Fields During the Year of His Promise, with Other Events Truly Good and Entertaining

If a great many thoughts wore at Don Quixote before he was knocked down, a great many more wore at him after his fall. He was in the shade of the tree, as has been said, and there, like flies to honey, thoughts came at him and stung him: some went to Dulcinea's disenchantment and others to the life he would have to lead in his forced retirement. Sancho came up and praised the generous nature of Tosilos the footman.

"Is it possible," Don Quixote said to him, "that you still think, Sancho, that that man is a real footman? It seems to have gone out of your mind that you have seen Dulcinea turned and transformed into a country girl, and the Knight of the Mirrors into the bachelor Carrasco — all of them the works of the enchanters who persecute me. But tell me now: did you ask this Tosilos of yours what God has done with Altisidora? Whether she has wept for my absence, or whether she has already left in the hands of forgetfulness the loving thoughts that wore at her in my presence?"

"The thoughts I had," answered Sancho, "were not such as to give me room to ask foolish questions. Body of me, sir, is your worship now in a state to inquire into other people's thoughts, and especially loving ones?"

"Look, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "there is a great difference between the works that are done out of love and those that are done out of gratitude. It may very well be that a knight is unloving, but it cannot be, strictly speaking, that he is ungrateful. Altisidora loved me, apparently; she gave me the three headcloths you know about; she wept at my going; she cursed me, abused me, complained, in spite of shame, in public: all signs that she adored me, for lovers' angers generally end in curses.

"I had no hopes to give her and no treasures to offer her, because mine are made over to Dulcinea, and knights errant's treasures are, like goblins', apparent and false; and I can only give her these memories I have of her — without prejudice, though, to those I have of Dulcinea, whom you wrong by the slackness you show in whipping yourself and in punishing that flesh of yours, which I should like to see eaten by wolves, since it prefers to keep itself for the worms rather than for that poor lady's relief."

"Sir," answered Sancho, "if the truth is to be told, I cannot persuade myself that the lashes on my backside have anything to do with the disenchanting of the enchanted, which is as if we said: 'If your head aches, rub ointment on your knees.' At least I would dare to swear that in all the histories your worship has read that deal with knight-errantry you have never seen anybody disenchanted by lashes; but, one way or the other, I shall give them to myself when I feel like it and the time gives me a convenient chance to punish myself."

"God grant it," answered Don Quixote, "and may the heavens give you grace to grasp the obligation that lies on you to help my lady — who is yours too, since you are mine."

In this talk they were going along their road when they came to the very spot and place where they had been trampled by the bulls. Don Quixote recognised it and said to Sancho:

"This is the meadow where we came across those splendid shepherdesses and gallant shepherds who wanted to renew and imitate the pastoral Arcadia in it — an idea as new as it was judicious. In imitation of which, if it seems good to you, I should like us, Sancho, to turn ourselves into shepherds, at least for the time I have to be in retirement.

"I shall buy some sheep and all the other things necessary to the pastoral exercise; and, calling myself the shepherd Quixotize and you the shepherd Panzino, we shall go about the mountains, the woods and the meadows, singing here and lamenting there, drinking the liquid crystal of the springs, or of the clean little brooks, or of the great rivers. The oaks will give us with a most plentiful hand their sweetest fruit; the trunks of the hardest cork trees a seat; the willows shade; the roses scent; the wide meadows carpets tinted with a thousand colours; the clear, pure air breath; the moon and the stars light in spite of the darkness of the night; singing pleasure; weeping gladness; Apollo verses; love conceits — with which we shall be able to make ourselves everlasting and famous not only in the present but in the ages to come."

"By God," said Sancho, "that kind of life squares with me, and even corners with me. And what is more, the bachelor Sansón Carrasco and Master Nicolás the barber will hardly have got a good look at it before they will want to follow it and turn shepherds with us; and God grant the curate does not take it into his head to come into the fold too, being as cheerful as he is and as fond of a good time."

"You have spoken very well," said Don Quixote. "And the bachelor Sansón Carrasco, if he comes into the pastoral guild — as he undoubtedly will — can be called the shepherd Sansonino, or else the shepherd Carrascón; Nicolás the barber can call himself Miculoso, as the old Boscán called himself Nemoroso; for the curate I do not know what name to give, unless it is some derivative of his own, calling him the shepherd Curiambro. As for the shepherdesses whose lovers we are to be, we can pick their names as though out of a basket of pears; and, since my lady's suits a shepherdess as well as a princess, there is no call for me to wear myself out looking for another that would suit her better. You, Sancho, may give yours whatever name you like."

"I do not mean," answered Sancho, "to give her any but Teresona, which will suit her well with her fatness and with the name she has already, since she is called Teresa; and what is more, by celebrating her in my verses I come to reveal my chaste desires, since I do not go looking for better bread than wheaten in other people's houses. It will not be well for the curate to have a shepherdess, for the sake of good example; and if the bachelor wants to have one, his soul is in his own palm."

"God bless me," said Don Quixote, "what a life we shall lead, Sancho my friend! What pipes shall come to our ears, what Zamoran bagpipes, what little drums, and what jingles, and what rebecks! And then, what if among these different kinds of music the sound of the albogues rings out? There you will see almost all the pastoral instruments."

"What are albogues?" asked Sancho. "For I have never heard them named or seen them in all my life."

"Albogues," answered Don Quixote, "are certain brass plates in the shape of candlesticks which, being struck one against the other on the hollow side, make a sound that, if not very agreeable or harmonious, is not displeasing, and goes well with the rusticity of the bagpipe and the little drum. And this word albogues is Moorish, as are all those in our Castilian tongue that begin with al — that is to say, almohaza, a currycomb; almorzar, to take lunch; alhombra, a carpet; alguacil, a constable; alhucema, lavender; almacén, a storehouse; alcancía, a money-box; and others like them, which must be only a few more. And our language has only three that are Moorish and end in i, and they are borceguí, a buskin; zaquizamí, a garret; and maravedí, a coin. Alhelí, the gillyflower, and alfaquí, a Moorish doctor of the law, are known for Arabic both by the al they begin with and by the i they end in.

"This I have told you in passing, because the occasion of having named albogues brought it back to my memory. And what will help us a great deal to bring this exercise to look perfect is my being something of a poet, as you know, and the bachelor Sansón Carrasco's being one in the extreme. Of the curate I say nothing; but I would wager he must have his points and edgings of a poet; and that Master Nicolás has them too I do not doubt, because all of them, or most, are guitarists and versifiers. I shall complain of absence; you shall boast of being a constant lover; the shepherd Carrascón of being scorned; and the curate Curiambro of whatever he can best make use of — and so the thing will go along with nothing left to wish for."

To which Sancho answered:

"I am so unlucky, sir, that I am afraid the day will never come when I see myself in such an exercise. Oh, what neat spoons I shall make when I see myself a shepherd! What sops, what creams, what garlands and what pastoral odds and ends — which, if they do not earn me the name of a judicious man, will not fail to earn me the name of an ingenious one!

"Sanchica my daughter shall bring us our dinner out to the flock. But look out! For she is good-looking, and there are shepherds who are more malicious than simple, and I should not like her to go out for wool and come back shorn; and loves and unwholesome desires generally go about the fields as much as the cities, and about the shepherds' huts as much as the royal palaces; and take away the cause and you take away the sin; and eyes that do not see, a heart that does not break; and a leap over the hedge is worth more than good men's prayers."

"No more proverbs, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "since any one of those you have said is enough to give your idea to be understood. And many times I have advised you not to be so lavish with proverbs and to hold yourself back in saying them; but it seems to me it is preaching in the desert, and 'my mother beats me and I spin my top'."

"It seems to me," answered Sancho, "that your worship is like the saying: 'The frying pan said to the kettle, get away from here, black-face.' You are reproving me for saying proverbs, and your worship threads them two at a time."

"Look, Sancho," answered Don Quixote: "I bring in proverbs to the point, and when I say them they come like a ring on a finger; but you bring them in so much by the hair that you drag them rather than lead them. And if I do not remember wrongly, I have told you before that proverbs are short judgements drawn from the experience and the reflection of our wise men of old; and the proverb that does not come to the point is nonsense rather than a judgement. But let us leave this; and, since night is coming on, let us withdraw some way from the high road, where we shall spend the night — and God knows what tomorrow will be."

They withdrew, they supped late and badly, much against Sancho's will, to whom there presented themselves the hardships of knight-errantry practised in the woods and the mountains — although sometimes abundance had shown itself in castles and houses, both Don Diego de Miranda's and the wedding of the rich Camacho and Don Antonio Moreno's. But he considered that it was not possible for it to be always day or always night, and so he spent that night sleeping, and his master keeping watch.

Chapter 68: Of the Bristly Adventure That Befell Don Quixote

The night was rather dark, though the moon was in the sky — but not in a part where it could be seen; for sometimes the lady Diana goes off to take a walk among the antipodes and leaves the mountains black and the valleys dark. Don Quixote satisfied nature by sleeping his first sleep, without giving room to a second — quite the other way from Sancho, who never had a second, because his sleep lasted him from the night until the morning, which showed his good constitution and his few cares.

Don Quixote's cares kept him awake in such a way that he woke Sancho and said to him:

"I am amazed, Sancho, at the freedom of your nature: I imagine you are made of marble or of hard bronze, in which there is no room for any movement or feeling. I keep watch while you sleep; I weep while you sing; I faint with fasting while you are lazy and out of breath from pure fullness. It is the part of good servants to share their masters' pains and to feel their feelings, if only for the look of it. Look at the serenity of this night, at the solitude we are in, which invites us to put some waking in among our sleep.

"Get up, on your life, and go some way off from here, and with good courage and a grateful boldness give yourself three or four hundred lashes on account of the ones for Dulcinea's disenchantment. And I beg and entreat you to do it, for I do not want to come to grips with you as I did the other time, because I know your arms are heavy. After you have given them to yourself, we shall spend what is left of the night singing, I of my absence and you of your constancy, making a beginning from now on the pastoral exercise we are to have in our village."

"Sir," answered Sancho, "I am no monk, that I should get up in the middle of my sleep and flog myself; nor does it seem to me that a man can pass from the extreme of the pain of lashes to that of music. Let your worship let me sleep and not press me about the whipping; for you will make me take an oath never to touch a hair of my coat, let alone of my flesh."

"O hardened soul! O squire without pity! O bread badly bestowed and ill-considered favours that I have done you and mean to do you! Through me you have seen yourself a governor, and through me you see yourself with hopes close at hand of being a count, or of having some equivalent title; and the fulfilling of them will take no longer than it takes for this year to go by — for I, post tenebras spero lucem."

"I do not understand that," replied Sancho. "I only understand that while I am asleep I have neither fear nor hope, neither labour nor glory. And blessings on the man who invented sleep — the cloak that covers all human thoughts, the food that takes away hunger, the water that drives off thirst, the fire that warms the cold, the cold that tempers the heat, and, in short, the general coin with which all things are bought, the balance and the weight that makes the shepherd equal to the king and the simple man to the judicious. Sleep has only one bad thing about it, so I have heard it said, and that is that it is like death, since between a sleeping man and a dead one there is very little difference."

"I have never heard you speak, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "as elegantly as now; from which I come to see that the proverb you sometimes say is true: 'Not who you are born with, but who you graze with.'"

"Ah, confound it, sir our master," replied Sancho, "I am not the one who is threading proverbs now; for they fall out of your worship's mouth two at a time better than they do out of mine. Only there must be this difference between mine and yours: that your worship's come in season and mine out of season — but in fact they are all proverbs."

They were at this when they heard a dull uproar and a harsh noise that spread over all those valleys. Don Quixote got to his feet and laid hand to his sword, and Sancho crouched under the grey, putting the bundle of arms on one side of him and his donkey's pack-saddle on the other, shaking with fear as much as Don Quixote was startled. From moment to moment the noise kept growing and coming nearer to the two frightened men — or at least to the one, for the other's valour is well known by now.

The case is that some men were taking more than six hundred pigs to sell at a fair, and were travelling with them at that hour; and such was the noise they made and the grunting and the snorting that they deafened the ears of Don Quixote and of Sancho, who could not make out what it could be.

The spread-out, grunting herd came up in a troop and, with no respect for Don Quixote's authority or for Sancho's, went right over the two of them, undoing Sancho's trenches and knocking down not only Don Quixote but carrying off Rocinante into the bargain. The rush, the grunting, the speed with which the filthy animals arrived, threw into confusion and onto the ground the pack-saddle, the arms, the grey, Rocinante, Sancho and Don Quixote.

Sancho got up as best he could and asked his master for his sword, telling him that he wanted to kill half a dozen of those gentlemanly and ill-mannered pigs, for by now he had made out that that was what they were. Don Quixote said to him:

"Let them alone, my friend; for this affront is the punishment of my sin, and it is heaven's just chastisement that a beaten knight errant should be eaten by jackals and stung by wasps and trampled by pigs."

"It must also be heaven's punishment," answered Sancho, "that the squires of beaten knights should be pricked by flies and eaten by lice and set on by hunger. If we squires were the sons of the knights we serve, or very near relations of theirs, it would be no great matter that the penalty of their sins should reach us to the fourth generation; but what have the Panzas to do with the Quixotes? Well now: let us settle ourselves again and sleep the little that is left of the night, and God will send the morning and we shall get on."

"Sleep, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "for you were born to sleep; and I, who was born to keep watch, in the time that is left from now until daybreak shall give rein to my thoughts and vent them in a little madrigal that, without your knowing it, I composed in my memory last night."

"It seems to me," answered Sancho, "that thoughts that leave room for making verses cannot be very many. Let your worship versify as much as you like, and I shall sleep as much as I can."

And then, taking as much ground as he wanted, he curled up and slept a loose sleep, without sureties or debts or any pain hindering him. Don Quixote, leaning against the trunk of a beech or a cork tree — for Cide Hamete Benengeli does not distinguish which tree it was — to the sound of his own sighs, sang in this way:

	Love, when I think
	on the ill you give me, terrible and strong,
	I go running to death,
	thinking so to end my immense ill;
	but, on reaching that pass
	which is the harbour in this sea of my torment,
	I feel such gladness
	that life gathers strength and I do not pass through.
	So living kills me,
	since death gives me back my life again.
	O unheard-of condition,
	that death and life should deal with me like this!

Each of these lines he accompanied with a great many sighs and not a few tears, exactly like a man whose heart was pierced through with the pain of his defeat and with Dulcinea's absence.

At this daylight came, the sun struck Sancho's eyes with its rays, he woke and stretched, shaking and pulling out his lazy limbs; he looked at the havoc the pigs had made of his stores and cursed the herd and something beyond it.

Finally the two of them went back to the road they had begun; and as the afternoon was drawing in they saw coming towards them some ten men on horseback and four or five on foot. Don Quixote's heart gave a jump and Sancho's was startled, because the people who were coming up to them carried lances and shields and came very much ready for war. Don Quixote turned to Sancho and said to him:

"If I could, Sancho, use my arms, and if my promise had not tied my hands, I should count this machine that is coming at us for cakes and fancy bread; but it might be something other than what we fear."

At this the men on horseback came up and, levelling their lances, without saying a word surrounded Don Quixote and set them at his back and his chest, threatening him with death. One of the men on foot, with a finger on his lips as a sign for him to be quiet, took hold of Rocinante's bridle and drew him off the road; and the rest of those on foot, driving Sancho and the grey ahead of them, all of them keeping a marvellous silence, followed the steps of the man who was leading Don Quixote.

Two or three times Don Quixote tried to ask where they were taking him or what they wanted; but he had hardly begun to move his lips when they came to close them with the heads of the lances. And the same thing happened to Sancho, because he had hardly given signs of speaking when one of the men on foot pricked him with a goad, and the grey neither more nor less, as though he too had wanted to speak.

Night closed in, they quickened their pace, and the fear grew in the two prisoners, and the more so when they heard them saying from time to time:

"Walk on, troglodytes!"
