"Be quiet, barbarians!"

"Pay up, anthropophagi!"

"Do not complain, Scythians, and do not open your eyes, you murdering Polyphemuses, you butchering lions!"

And other names like these, with which they tormented the ears of the wretched master and man. Sancho went along saying to himself:

"Us, turtle-doves? Us, barbers, or pot-scourers? Us, little dogs that they call 'sic 'em, sic 'em' to? These names do not please me at all: this heap is being winnowed in a bad wind; all the trouble comes on us at once, as the beatings do to the dog — and I only hope what this most unfortunate adventure threatens stops at that!"

Don Quixote went along dumbfounded, unable, for all the reasonings he made, to hit on what those names full of abuse might be that they were putting on them, out of which he gathered plainly that they were to expect no good and to fear a great deal of harm. At this, almost an hour into the night, they came to a castle which Don Quixote knew very well to be the duke's, where they had been not long before.

"God bless me!" he said as soon as he recognised the place. "And what will this be? Why, in this house everything is courtesy and good civility; but for the conquered, good turns into bad and bad into worse."

They came into the chief courtyard of the castle and saw it fitted out and arranged in a way that increased their astonishment and doubled their fear, as will be seen in the following chapter.

Chapter 69: Of the Rarest and Newest Event That Befell Don Quixote in the Whole Course of This Great History

The men on horseback dismounted; and, along with those on foot, taking Sancho and Don Quixote up bodily and in a rush, they carried them into the courtyard, round which nearly a hundred torches were burning in their sconces, and along the galleries of the courtyard more than five hundred lamps; so that, in spite of the night, which showed itself rather dark, the lack of daylight was not noticed.

In the middle of the courtyard rose a catafalque some two yards from the ground, covered all over with an enormous canopy of black velvet, round which, on its steps, white wax candles were burning on more than a hundred silver candlesticks. On top of this catafalque was displayed the dead body of a maiden so beautiful that her beauty made death itself look beautiful. She had her head on a brocade cushion, crowned with a garland woven of various sweet-smelling flowers, her hands crossed on her breast and, between them, a branch of yellow, conquering palm.

At one side of the courtyard a stage was set up, and on it, seated in two chairs, two personages who, by having crowns on their heads and sceptres in their hands, gave signs of being some kings, either real or pretended. At the side of this stage, which was reached by some steps, were two other chairs, on which the men who had brought the prisoners set Don Quixote and Sancho — all this in silence and giving the two of them to understand by signs that they should be silent too. But without being signed to, they were silent themselves, because astonishment at what they were looking at had their tongues tied.

At this there came up onto the stage, with a great retinue, two chief personages, whom Don Quixote at once recognised to be the duke and duchess, his hosts, and who sat down in two very rich chairs next to the two who looked like kings. Who would not have been astonished at this, with the addition that Don Quixote recognised that the dead body on the catafalque was that of the beautiful Altisidora?

As the duke and duchess came up onto the stage, Don Quixote and Sancho got to their feet and made them a deep bow, and the duke and duchess did the same, inclining their heads a little.

At this an officer came out from the side and, coming up to Sancho, threw over him a gown of black buckram, all painted with flames of fire; and, taking off his cap, put on his head a mitre like those the Holy Office puts on penitents; and he told him in his ear not to unstitch his lips, because they would clap a gag on him or take his life.

Sancho looked himself up and down; he saw himself burning in flames; but, as they did not burn him, he did not value them at two farthings. He took off the mitre, saw it painted with devils, and put it back on, saying to himself:

"Well and good — the flames do not burn me and the devils do not carry me off."

Don Quixote was looking at him too; and, although fear had his senses in suspense, he could not help laughing to see Sancho's figure.

At this there began to come, apparently from under the catafalque, a soft and agreeable sound of flutes which, not being interrupted by any human voice — because in that place silence itself kept silence to itself — showed itself gentle and loving. Then there suddenly showed himself, next to the pillow of the apparent corpse, a beautiful young man dressed in the Roman fashion who, to the sound of a harp that he played himself, sang in a most sweet and clear voice these two stanzas:

	While Altisidora comes back to herself,
	dead through Don Quixote's cruelty,
	and while in this enchanted court
	the ladies dress themselves in haircloth,
	and while my lady clothes her duennas
	in baize and in serge,
	I shall sing her beauty and her misfortune
	with a better quill than the singer of Thrace.
	And I do not think that this office falls to me
	in life alone;
	but, with my tongue dead and cold in my mouth,
	I mean to move my voice as is your due.
	My soul, freed from its narrow rock
	and carried over the Stygian lake,
	shall go on celebrating you, and that sound
	shall make the waters of oblivion stand still.

"No more," said one of the two who looked like kings at this point; "no more, divine singer; for it would be to go on for ever to set out for us now the death and the graces of the peerless Altisidora — not dead, as the ignorant world thinks, but alive on the tongues of Fame and in the penance that Sancho Panza, who is here present, must go through to bring her back to the light she has lost.

"And so, O Rhadamanthus, who judge with me in the gloomy caverns of Dis: since you know everything that is settled in the inscrutable fates about this maiden's coming back to herself, say it and declare it at once, so that the good we hope for from her fresh return may not be put off for us."

Minos, judge and companion of Rhadamanthus, had hardly said this when Rhadamanthus, getting to his feet, said:

"Come, you officers of this house, high and low, great and small, come one after another and seal Sancho's face with twenty-four chucks under the chin, and twelve pinches and six pinprickings on his arms and his back; for in this ceremony lies Altisidora's health!"

Hearing which, Sancho Panza broke his silence and said:

"I swear I shall let my face be sealed or my cheeks be handled about as soon as I shall turn Turk! Body of me! What has handling my face got to do with this maiden's resurrection? The old woman got a taste for the greens. They enchant Dulcinea and they whip me so that she may be disenchanted; Altisidora dies of ills God chose to give her, and to bring her back to life they must give me twenty-four chucks under the chin and riddle my body with pinpricks and bruise my arms with pinches. Try those jokes on your brother-in-law, for I am an old dog and there is no 'here, boy' with me!"

"You shall die!" said Rhadamanthus in a loud voice. "Soften, you tiger; humble yourself, proud Nimrod; and suffer and be quiet, since they are not asking you for impossibilities. And do not go into establishing the difficulties of this business: chucked you must be, riddled you must find yourself, pinched you must groan. Come, I say, officers, carry out my order; if not, by the faith of an honest man, you shall see what you were born for!"

At this there appeared to be coming across the courtyard some six duennas in procession, one after another, four of them with spectacles, and all of them with their right hands raised high, with four fingers of wrist showing to make their hands look longer, as is now the fashion. Sancho had no sooner seen them than, bellowing like a bull, he said:

"I might well let myself be handled by everybody in the world; but to consent to being touched by duennas — that, no! Let them claw my face as they did my master's in this same castle; let them run my body through with the points of sharpened daggers; let them grip my arms with red-hot pincers, and I shall bear it patiently, or serve these gentlefolk; but that duennas should touch me I shall not consent to, if the devil carries me off for it."

Don Quixote broke his silence too, saying to Sancho:

"Have patience, my son, and give these lords and ladies pleasure, and give many thanks to heaven for having put such a virtue in your person that by the martyrdom of it you disenchant the enchanted and raise the dead."

The duennas were close to Sancho by now, when he, softened and more persuaded, settling himself well in his chair, gave his face and his beard to the first of them, who gave him a chuck under the chin very well sealed, and then a great curtsey.

"Less courtesy, and fewer face-washes, madam duenna," said Sancho; "for by God your hands smell of vinegar-water!"

Finally all the duennas sealed him, and a great many other people of the house pinched him; but what he could not put up with was the pricking of the pins. And so he got up out of his chair, apparently vexed, and, seizing a lighted torch that was next to him, went at the duennas and at all his executioners, saying:

"Away, you infernal ministers, for I am not made of bronze, that I should not feel such extraordinary martyrdoms!"

At this Altisidora, who must have been tired from having lain so long on her back, turned on her side; seeing which, the bystanders almost all said with one voice:

"Altisidora is alive! Altisidora lives!"

Rhadamanthus ordered Sancho to lay aside his anger, since the purpose they were after had been achieved.

As soon as Don Quixote saw Altisidora stir, he went and knelt down in front of Sancho, saying to him:

"Now is the time, son of my entrails — not merely my squire — for you to give yourself some of the lashes you are bound to give for Dulcinea's disenchantment. Now, I say, is the time when your virtue is ripened, and effectual for working the good that is hoped from you."

To which Sancho answered:

"This seems to me trick on top of trick, and not honey on pancakes. It would be a fine thing if after pinches and chucks and pinpricks the lashes came now. They have nothing else to do but take a great stone and tie it round my neck and pitch me into a well — which would not grieve me much, if to cure other people's ills I have to be the cow at the wedding. Leave me alone; if not, by God I shall throw it all up and let everything go at thirteen even if it does not sell."

By this time Altisidora had sat up on the catafalque, and at the same instant the shawms sounded, joined by the flutes and by everybody's voices, all calling out:

"Long live Altisidora! Altisidora lives!"

The duke and duchess and the kings Minos and Rhadamanthus got up, and all of them together with Don Quixote and Sancho went to receive Altisidora and to bring her down from the catafalque; and she, playing the woman recovering from a faint, bowed to the duke and duchess and to the kings, and, looking sideways at Don Quixote, said to him:

"God forgive you, unloving knight, for through your cruelty I have been in the other world, as it seemed to me, for more than a thousand years. And you, O most compassionate squire the globe contains, I thank for the life I have. From today on, Sancho my friend, dispose of six shifts of mine that I make over to you, to make yourself six shirts of them; and if they are not all sound, at least they are all clean."

Sancho kissed her hands for it, with the mitre in his hand and his knees on the ground. The duke ordered them to take it off him and give him back his cap and put on his coat and take off the gown of flames. Sancho begged the duke to let him keep the gown and the mitre, for he wanted to take them back to his own country as a sign and a memorial of that never-before-seen business. The duchess answered that they would let him keep them, since he knew what a great friend of his she was. The duke ordered the courtyard cleared, and that everybody should withdraw to their rooms, and that Don Quixote and Sancho should be taken to the ones they already knew.

Chapter 70: Which Follows the Sixty-Ninth and Deals with Matters Not to Be Left Out for the Clearness of This History

Sancho slept that night on a truckle bed in Don Quixote's own room — a thing he would have excused himself from if he could, because he knew very well that his master would not let him sleep for questions and answers, and he was in no condition to talk much, since the pains of his past martyrdoms were still with him and did not leave his tongue free; and it would have suited him better to sleep alone in a hut than in that rich chamber in company.

His fear turned out so true and his suspicion so certain that his master had hardly got into bed when he said:

"What do you think, Sancho, of tonight's business? Great and mighty is the force of unloving scorn, since with your own eyes you have seen Altisidora dead — not by any arrows, or by any sword, or by any other warlike instrument, or by deadly poisons, but by the thought of the severity and the scorn with which I have always treated her."

"She might have died in her own good time as much and how she liked," answered Sancho, "and left me at home; for I never made her fall in love or scorned her in my life. I do not know and cannot think how the health of Altisidora, a maiden more whimsical than judicious, has anything to do — as I have said before — with the martyrdoms of Sancho Panza. Now indeed I come to know clearly and distinctly that there are enchanters and enchantments in the world, from whom may God deliver me, since I cannot deliver myself. And with all this, I beg your worship to let me sleep and not to ask me any more, unless you want me to throw myself out of a window."

"Sleep, Sancho my friend," answered Don Quixote, "if the pinpricks and the pinches you have received and the chucks under the chin that have been given you leave you room for it."

"No pain," replied Sancho, "came up to the affront of the chucks — for no other reason than their having been given me by duennas, confound them. And I beg your worship again to let me sleep, because sleep is a relief from the miseries of those who suffer them awake."

"Be it so," said Don Quixote, "and God be with you."

The two of them fell asleep; and in this time Cide Hamete, the author of this great history, chose to write and give an account of what moved the duke and duchess to raise the structure of the machinery just described.

And he says that the bachelor Sansón Carrasco had not forgotten how the Knight of the Mirrors was conquered and knocked down by Don Quixote, which conquest and fall rubbed out and undid all his designs; and he wanted to try his hand again, hoping for a better outcome than the last. And so, learning from the page who took the letter and present to Teresa Panza, Sancho's wife, where Don Quixote was, he looked for fresh arms and a horse and put the white moon on his shield, carrying it all on a mule led by a farm labourer, and not by Tomé Cecial his old squire, so that he should not be recognised by Sancho or by Don Quixote.

He came, then, to the duke's castle, and the duke told him the road and the course Don Quixote was taking, meaning to be present at the jousts at Saragossa. He told him likewise the tricks he had played on him with the contrivance of Dulcinea's disenchantment, which was to be at the expense of Sancho's backside. In short, he gave him an account of the trick Sancho had played on his master, giving him to understand that Dulcinea was enchanted and transformed into a country girl, and how the duchess his wife had given Sancho to understand that he was the one who was deceived, because Dulcinea really was enchanted; at which the bachelor laughed and marvelled not a little, considering Sancho's sharpness and simplicity as much as the extreme of Don Quixote's madness.

The duke asked him that if he found him, and whether he conquered him or not, he should come back that way and give him an account of what happened. The bachelor did so; he set off in search of him; he did not find him at Saragossa; he went on and there happened to him what has already been related.

He came back by the duke's castle and told him it all, along with the conditions of the battle, and that Don Quixote was already on his way back to keep, like a good knight errant, his word to withdraw to his village for a year — in which time it might be, said the bachelor, that he would be cured of his madness; for this was the intention that had moved him to make those transformations, since it was a thing to be pitied that a gentleman of such good understanding as Don Quixote should be mad. With this he took his leave of the duke and went back to his village, waiting there for Don Quixote, who was coming after him.

From this the duke took the occasion for playing him that trick — so great was the pleasure he took in Sancho's and Don Quixote's doings. And, having the roads near and far from the castle watched on every side by which he imagined Don Quixote might come back, with a great many of his servants on foot and on horseback, so that by force or by good will they might bring him to the castle if they found him. They did find him and sent word to the duke, who, being already prepared with everything he had to do, as soon as he had news of his coming ordered the torches and the lamps of the courtyard to be lit and Altisidora laid on the catafalque, with all the apparatus that has been told, so much to the life and so well done that between the truth and it there was very little difference.

And Cide Hamete says more: that he holds for himself that the jokers are as mad as the joked-with, and that the duke and duchess were not two fingers away from looking like fools, since they took such pains to make fools of two fools.

Of whom, one sleeping a loose sleep and the other lying awake with unleashed thoughts, the day and the wish to get up caught both — for idle feather beds, whether beaten or victorious, never gave Don Quixote any pleasure.

Altisidora — in Don Quixote's opinion, brought back from death to life — following her master and mistress's humour, crowned with the same garland she had worn on the catafalque and dressed in a tunic of white taffeta sown with golden flowers, her hair loose over her shoulders, leaning on a staff of black and very fine ebony, came into Don Quixote's room. At whose presence he, troubled and confused, shrank down and covered himself almost entirely with the sheets and coverlets of the bed, his tongue dumb, unable to manage any courtesy to her.

Altisidora sat down in a chair next to his pillow, and, after giving a great sigh, said to him in a tender and weakened voice:

"When women of quality and modest maidens trample on their honour and give their tongues leave to break through every obstacle, publicly giving notice of the secrets their hearts hold, they are in a narrow strait. I, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, am one of these — pressed, conquered and in love; but for all that, patient and modest, so much so that, by being so much so, my soul burst through my silence and I lost my life. Two days ago, with the thought of the severity with which you have treated me,

	O harder than marble to my complaints,
	you stony-hearted knight! —

I have been dead, or at least judged so by those who have seen me; and if it had not been that Love, taking pity on me, laid up my remedy in the martyrdoms of this good squire, I should have stayed over there in the other world."

"Love could very well," said Sancho, "have laid it up in my donkey's, and I should have been grateful to him for it. But tell me, madam — and so may heaven fit you out with a softer lover than my master — what did you see in the other world? What is there in hell? For whoever dies in despair must of necessity have that for his lodging."

"To tell you the truth," answered Altisidora, "I cannot have died altogether, since I did not go into hell; for if I had gone in there, once I was in I could not have come out again even if I had wanted to. The truth is that I got to the gate, where about a dozen devils were playing at tennis, all of them in hose and doublet, with falling bands trimmed with Flemish lace edging and with cuffs of the same, with four fingers of arm showing so that their hands should look longer, and in them they had rackets of fire.

"And what astonished me most was that instead of balls they were using books, apparently full of wind and flock — a marvellous and new thing. But this did not astonish me as much as seeing that, whereas it is natural for gamblers that the winners are glad and the losers sad, there in that game they were all growling, all snarling and all cursing one another."

"That is no wonder," answered Sancho, "because devils, whether they play or do not play, can never be contented, whether they win or do not win."

"That must be so," answered Altisidora; "but there is another thing that also astonishes me — I mean that astonished me then — and it was that at the first volley there was not a ball left standing or fit to be used a second time. And so they went through new books and old ones one after another, which was a marvel. To one of them, new and shining and well bound, they gave such a stroke that they knocked its guts out and scattered its leaves. One devil said to another: 'Look what book that is.' And the devil answered him: 'This is the Second Part of the History of Don Quixote of La Mancha — not composed by Cide Hamete, its first author, but by an Aragonese who says he is a native of Tordesillas.' 'Take it away from there,' answered the other devil, 'and put it in the depths of hell: let my eyes never see it again.' 'Is it as bad as that?' answered the other. 'So bad,' replied the first, 'that if I set myself on purpose to make it worse, I should not manage it.'

"They went on with their game, batting other books about; and I, from having heard the name of Don Quixote, whom I love and am so fond of, took care to keep this vision in my memory."

"A vision it must undoubtedly have been," said Don Quixote, "because there is no other me in the world; and that history goes about here from hand to hand, but it stops in nobody's, because everybody gives it a kick. I have not been upset at hearing that I walk like a fanciful body through the darkness of the abyss, or through the brightness of the earth, because I am not the man that history deals with. If it is good, faithful and true, it will have centuries of life; but if it is bad, from its birth to its grave the road will not be very long."

Altisidora was going to go on complaining of Don Quixote when Don Quixote said to her:

"Many times I have told you, madam, that it grieves me that you should have placed your thoughts on me, since from mine they can sooner be thanked than remedied. I was born to be Dulcinea of El Toboso's, and the fates, if there are any, dedicated me to her; and to think that any other beauty is to take the place she has in my soul is to think the impossible. This is disillusionment enough for you to withdraw within the limits of your modesty, since nobody can be bound to the impossible."

Hearing which, Altisidora, showing herself angry and upset, said to him:

"By the Lord, Sir Codfish, soul of a mortar, date-stone, more stubborn and hard than a peasant who has been begged and has his own way — if I come at you, I shall tear your eyes out! Do you think, by any chance, Sir Beaten and Sir Cudgelled, that I died for you? Everything you have seen tonight has been pretended; for I am not the woman to let a black speck of a fingernail ache for camels of that sort, let alone to die."

"That I believe very well," said Sancho; "for this business of lovers dying is a laughing matter: they may well say it, but as for doing it — let Judas believe it."

While they were in this talk, the musician, singer and poet came in who had sung the two stanzas already given; and, making Don Quixote a great bow, he said:

"Let your worship, sir knight, count me and hold me in the number of your greatest servants, for it is many days now that I have been very fond of you, both for your fame and for your exploits."

Don Quixote answered him:

"Let your worship tell me who you are, so that my courtesy may answer to your deserts."

The young man answered that he was the musician and panegyrist of the night before.

"Certainly," replied Don Quixote, "your worship has an outstanding voice; but what you sang did not seem to me very much to the point — for what have the stanzas of Garcilaso to do with this lady's death?"

"Let your worship not marvel at that," answered the musician; "for among the unshorn poets of our age it is now the custom for everybody to write as he likes and steal from whoever he likes, whether or not it comes to the point of what he means; and by now there is no foolishness they sing or write that is not put down to poetic licence."

Don Quixote would have liked to answer, but he was prevented by the duke and duchess, who came in to see him; among whom there passed a long and pleasant talk, in which Sancho said so many droll and so many malicious things that he left the duke and duchess astonished afresh, both at his simplicity and at his sharpness.

Don Quixote begged them to give him leave to set off that same day, since for beaten knights like himself it was more fitting to live in a pigsty than in royal palaces. They gave it him very willingly, and the duchess asked him whether Altisidora was still in his good graces. He answered her:

"My lady, let Your Ladyship know that all this maiden's trouble comes from idleness, whose remedy is decent and continual occupation. She has told me here that they use lace in hell; and, since she must know how to make it, let her not let it out of her hands, for while she is busy working the bobbins, the image or images of what she loves will not be working in her imagination. And this is the truth, and this is my opinion and this is my advice."

"And mine," added Sancho; "for I have never in my life seen a lacemaker die of love; girls who are busy set their thoughts more on finishing their tasks than on thinking about their loves. I speak from my own case; for while I am digging I do not remember my missus — I mean my Teresa Panza, whom I love more than the lashes of my eyes."

"You speak very well, Sancho," said the duchess, "and I shall see that my Altisidora busies herself from now on with some white work, which she knows how to do outstandingly well."

"There is no need, my lady," answered Altisidora, "to use that remedy, since the thought of the cruelties this stray villain has used on me will rub him out of my memory without any other contrivance. And, with your greatness's leave, I want to get away from here, so as not to see before my eyes any longer his sorrowful countenance — no, his ugly and abominable face."

"That seems to me," said the duke, "like what is generally said:

	For the man who speaks abuse
	is not far off from forgiving."

Altisidora made a show of drying her tears with a handkerchief, and, curtseying to her master and mistress, went out of the room.

"I wish you," said Sancho, "poor maiden — I wish you, I say, bad luck, since you have had to do with a soul of esparto grass and a heart of oak. Upon my word, if you had had to do with me, another cock would have crowed for you!"

The talk came to an end, Don Quixote dressed, dined with the duke and duchess, and set off that afternoon.

Chapter 71: Of What Happened to Don Quixote with His Squire Sancho on the Way to Their Village

The beaten and worn-out Don Quixote went along extremely thoughtful on the one hand and very glad on the other. His sadness was caused by his defeat, and his gladness by considering the virtue that was in Sancho, as he had shown it in Altisidora's resurrection — although with some scruple he persuaded himself that the enamoured maiden had really been dead.

Sancho went along not at all glad, because it saddened him to see that Altisidora had not kept her word about giving him the shifts; and, coming and going over this, he said to his master:

"Truly, sir, I am the unluckiest doctor to be found in the world, in which there are physicians who, after killing the patient they are treating, want to be paid for their labour — which is nothing but signing a little slip for some medicines that they do not make themselves but the apothecary makes, and there is the trick done. And to me, whose other people's health costs me drops of blood, chucks under the chin, pinches, pinpricks and lashes, they do not give a farthing.

"Well, I swear that if they bring me another patient into my hands, they will have to grease mine before I cure him; for the abbot dines on what he sings, and I do not want to believe that heaven has given me the virtue I have so that I should pass it on to other people for nothing."

"You are right, Sancho my friend," answered Don Quixote, "and Altisidora has done very badly in not giving you the promised shifts. And, granting that your virtue is gratis data — since it has cost you no study — it is more than study to receive martyrdoms in your own person. For myself I can tell you that if you wanted payment for the lashes of Dulcinea's disenchantment, I should have given it you already and a good one; but I do not know whether payment will go well with the cure, and I should not like the reward to hinder the medicine. For all that, it seems to me that nothing will be lost by trying it. Look, Sancho, what you want, and whip yourself at once, and pay yourself in cash and with your own hand, since you have money of mine."

At these offers Sancho opened his eyes and his ears a hand's breadth, and in his heart consented to whip himself willingly; and he said to his master:

"Well now, sir, I am willing to get myself ready to give your worship the pleasure you want, with profit to myself; for the love of my children and my wife makes me show myself grasping. Tell me, your worship: how much will you give me for every lash I give myself?"

"If I had to pay you, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "according to what the greatness and the quality of this remedy deserves, the treasure of Venice and the mines of Potosí would be too little to pay you. Take the measure of what you have of mine, and set the price on each lash."

"They are," answered Sancho, "three thousand three hundred and so many; of them I have given myself about five: the rest are still to come. Let these five come in among the 'so many', and let us come to the three thousand three hundred — which at a quarter-real each, and I shall not take less if the whole world ordered me to, come to three thousand three hundred quarter-reals; which is, for the three thousand, one thousand five hundred half-reals, making seven hundred and fifty reals; and the three hundred make one hundred and fifty half-reals, which come to seventy-five reals; which, added to the seven hundred and fifty, make eight hundred and twenty-five reals in all. These I shall deduct from what I have of your worship's, and I shall go into my house rich and contented, though well whipped; because you do not catch trout... and I say no more."

"O blessed Sancho! O lovable Sancho!" answered Don Quixote. "How bound Dulcinea and I shall be to serve you all the days heaven gives us of life! If she comes back to the being she has lost — as it is not possible but that she will — her misfortune will have been good fortune, and my defeat a most happy triumph. And see, Sancho, when you want to begin the discipline; for I shall add a hundred reals so that you may cut it short."

"When?" replied Sancho. "Tonight, without fail. Let your worship arrange for us to have it out in the fields, under the open sky, and I shall open up my flesh."

Night came, waited for by Don Quixote with the greatest anxiety in the world, since it seemed to him that the wheels of Apollo's chariot had broken and that the day was drawing itself out longer than usual — exactly as happens to lovers, who never make the reckoning of their desires come out.

Finally they went in among some pleasant trees that stood a little way off the road, where, leaving Rocinante's saddle and the grey's pack-saddle empty, they stretched themselves out on the green grass and supped from Sancho's store. And he, making a mighty and flexible whip out of the grey's halter and headstall, withdrew some twenty paces from his master among some beeches. Don Quixote, who saw him go with boldness and spirit, said to him:

"Look, my friend, do not smash yourself to pieces; give room for one lash to wait for another; do not try to hurry so much in the race that in the middle of it your breath fails you. I mean, do not lay it on so hard that your life fails you before you reach the desired number. And, so that you may not lose by a card too many or too few, I shall stand aside counting on this rosary of mine the lashes you give yourself. May heaven favour you as your good intention deserves."

"A good payer does not mind pledges," answered Sancho. "I mean to lay it on in such a way that, without killing me, it hurts; for in this the substance of this miracle must consist."

He at once stripped himself from the waist up and, snatching up the cord, began to lay on, and Don Quixote began to count the lashes.

Sancho would have given himself six or eight when the joke began to seem to him a heavy one and the price of it very cheap; and, stopping a little, he told his master that he cried off, because each of those lashes deserved to be paid at half a real and not at a quarter.

"Go on, Sancho my friend, and do not lose heart," Don Quixote said to him, "for I double the stake on the price."

"In that case," said Sancho, "into the hand of God, and let lashes rain!"

But the sly fellow left off laying them on his back and laid them on the trees, with a sigh from time to time such that it seemed as if with every one of them his soul was being torn out. Don Quixote's soul being tender and afraid that his life would come to an end and that he would not get his wish through Sancho's imprudence, he said to him:

"On your life, my friend, let this business rest at this point; for this medicine seems to me a very harsh one, and it will be as well to give time to time; for Zamora was not won in an hour. More than a thousand lashes, if I have not counted wrong, you have given yourself: they are enough for now; for the ass, to speak coarsely, bears the load but not the overload."

"No, no, sir," answered Sancho, "it shall not be said of me: 'money paid, arms broken'. Let your worship stand aside a little more and let me give myself another thousand lashes at least; for at two goes like this we shall have finished this instalment, and there will even be cloth to spare."

"Since you find yourself in such a good disposition," said Don Quixote, "may heaven help you; lay on, and I shall stand aside."

Sancho went back to his task with such boldness that he had already taken the bark off a good many trees: such was the severity with which he whipped himself. And, raising his voice once and giving a monstrous lash to a beech, he said:

"Here shall you die, Samson, and all who are with him!"

Don Quixote ran up at once at the sound of the pained voice and of the blow of that harsh lash; and, taking hold of the twisted halter that served Sancho for a scourge, he said to him:

"Fate forbid, Sancho my friend, that for my pleasure you should lose your life, which is to serve for keeping your wife and your children. Let Dulcinea wait for a better conjunction, and I shall hold myself within the limits of a hope close at hand and wait for you to gather fresh strength, so that this business may be concluded to everybody's satisfaction."

"Since your worship wants it so, my dear sir," answered Sancho, "so be it and welcome; and throw your cloak over these shoulders of mine, for I am sweating and I should not like to catch a chill — for new penitents run that risk."

Don Quixote did so, and, staying in his shirt, he wrapped up Sancho, who slept until the sun woke him; and then they went on with their road, which they brought to an end for the time being at a place three leagues from there.

They dismounted at an inn, which Don Quixote recognised for such, and not for a castle with a deep moat, towers, portcullises and a drawbridge; for since he had been beaten he reasoned more soundly in everything, as will now be told. They lodged him in a low room, whose gilt leather hangings were some old painted serges, as they use in the villages. On one of them there was painted by a very bad hand the rape of Helen, when the bold guest carried her off from Menelaus, and on another was the history of Dido and Aeneas — she on a high tower, as though she were making signals with half a sheet to the fugitive guest, who was fleeing over the sea in a frigate or brigantine.

He noticed in the two stories that Helen did not go very unwillingly, because she was laughing on the sly and slyly; but the beautiful Dido showed herself shedding tears the size of walnuts out of her eyes. Which Don Quixote seeing, he said:

"These two ladies were extremely unfortunate in not having been born in this age, and I above all unfortunate in not having been born in theirs. If I had met these gentlemen, Troy would not have been burnt nor Carthage destroyed, since merely by my killing Paris so many misfortunes would have been avoided."

"I would wager," said Sancho, "that before long there will not be a tavern or an inn or a lodging house or a barber's shop where the history of our exploits is not painted up. But I should like it painted by the hands of a better painter than the one who painted these."

"You are right, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "because this painter is like Orbaneja, a painter who lived at Úbeda; who, when they asked him what he was painting, would answer: 'Whatever comes out.' And if by any chance he painted a cock, he would write under it, 'This is a cock,' so that people should not think it was a fox. In this way, it seems to me, Sancho, must be the painter or the writer — for it is all one — who brought out into the light the history of this new Don Quixote that has appeared: he painted or wrote whatever came out.

"Or else he must have been like a poet who went about the court in years past called Mauleón, who answered on the spot whatever he was asked; and, somebody asking him what Deum de Deo meant, he answered: 'Let it strike where it may' — for that is what the Latin sounds like in our Castilian. But, leaving this aside, tell me whether you mean, Sancho, to give yourself another round tonight, and whether you want it to be under a roof or under the open sky."

"By God, sir," answered Sancho, "for what I mean to give myself, it is all one to me indoors or in the fields; but for all that, I should like it to be among trees, for they seem to keep me company and to help me carry my labour marvellously."

"Then it must not be so, Sancho my friend," answered Don Quixote; "for so that you may gather your strength, we shall keep it for our village, where we shall arrive at the latest the day after tomorrow."

Sancho answered that he should do as he pleased, but that he himself would like to finish that business quickly in hot blood and while the mill was freshly dressed, because in delay there is often danger; and pray to God and keep hammering; and one 'here you are' is worth more than two 'I'll give you'; and the bird in the hand is worth more than the vulture on the wing.

"No more proverbs, Sancho, for the one God's sake," said Don Quixote, "for it seems that you are going back to your sicut erat. Speak plainly, smoothly, without tangles, as I have told you many times, and you will see how it is worth a hundredfold to you."

"I do not know what bad luck this is of mine," answered Sancho, "that I cannot say a sensible thing without a proverb, or a proverb that does not seem to me a sensible thing; but I shall mend my ways, if I can."

And with this their talk stopped for the time being.

Chapter 72: Of How Don Quixote and Sancho Reached Their Village

Don Quixote and Sancho spent that whole day in that village and that inn, waiting for the night: the one to finish the round of his discipline out in the open country, and the other to see the end of it, in which the end of his desire lay.

At this there came to the inn a traveller on horseback with three or four servants, one of whom said to the man who seemed to be their master:

"Here your worship, Señor Don Álvaro Tarfe, may spend today's siesta: the lodging looks clean and cool."

Hearing this, Don Quixote said to Sancho:

"Look, Sancho: when I leafed through that book of the second part of my history, it seems to me that in passing I came across this name of Don Álvaro Tarfe there."

"It may very well be," answered Sancho. "Let us let him dismount, and afterwards we shall ask him."

The gentleman dismounted, and, opposite Don Quixote's room, the hostess gave him a low room hung with other painted serges like those in Don Quixote's chamber. The newly arrived gentleman put on summer clothes; and, coming out into the porch of the inn, which was spacious and cool, along which Don Quixote was walking, he asked him:

"Where away are you travelling, sir gentleman?"

And Don Quixote answered him:

"To a village near here that I come from. And your worship, where are you travelling?"

"I, sir," answered the gentleman, "am going to Granada, which is my own country."

"And a good country!" replied Don Quixote. "But tell me, your worship, out of courtesy, your name; for it seems to me it will matter to me to know it more than I can readily say."

"My name is Don Álvaro Tarfe," answered the guest.

To which Don Quixote replied:

"Without any doubt I think your worship must be that Don Álvaro Tarfe who goes about in print in the Second Part of the History of Don Quixote of La Mancha, lately printed and given to the light of the world by a modern author."

"The very man," answered the gentleman; "and that Don Quixote, the chief subject of that history, was a very great friend of mine, and I was the man who took him out of his own country — or at least moved him to come to some jousts that were being held at Saragossa, where I was going. And truly and truly I did him a great many friendly services, and I kept the hangman from combing his shoulders for him, for being excessively bold."

"And tell me, your worship, Señor Don Álvaro: do I look at all like that Don Quixote your worship speaks of?"

"Certainly not," answered the guest: "in no way at all."

"And that Don Quixote," said ours, "did he have with him a squire called Sancho Panza?"

"He did," answered Don Álvaro; "and, although he had a name for being very amusing, I never heard him say a droll thing that had any drollery in it."

"That I believe very well," said Sancho at this, "because saying droll things is not for everybody; and that Sancho your worship speaks of, sir gentleman, must be some very great rogue, dull and a thief into the bargain. For the true Sancho Panza is me, and I have more drolleries than raindrops; and if you doubt it, let your worship make the experiment and go about after me for at least a year, and you will see that they fall out of me at every step, and such and so many that, without my knowing most of the time what I am saying, I make everybody who hears me laugh.

"And the true Don Quixote of La Mancha — the famous, the valiant and the judicious, the lover, the undoer of wrongs, the guardian of wards and orphans, the protection of widows, the slayer of maidens, the man who has for his one lady the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso — is this gentleman here present, who is my master. Any other Don Quixote and any other Sancho Panza is a joke and a thing of dreams."

"By God, I believe it!" answered Don Álvaro; "because you have said more droll things, my friend, in four sentences you have spoken than the other Sancho Panza in all I ever heard him say, and that was a great deal. He had more of the great eater about him than of the good talker, and more of the fool than of the wit; and I hold it for certain that the enchanters who persecute Don Quixote the good have chosen to persecute me with Don Quixote the bad.

"But I do not know what to say; for I would dare to swear that I left him shut up in the madhouse at Toledo to be cured — and now here another Don Quixote turns up, though a very different one from mine."

"I," said Don Quixote, "do not know whether I am the good one; but I can say that I am not the bad one. As proof of which I want your worship, my lord Don Álvaro Tarfe, to know that in all the days of my life I have never been in Saragossa; on the contrary, because I was told that this fanciful Don Quixote had been present at the jousts of that city, I chose not to go into it, so as to bring out his lie in the face of the world.

"And so I passed straight on to Barcelona: the storehouse of courtesy, the shelter of strangers, the hospital of the poor, the country of the valiant, the avenger of the injured, the pleasant correspondence of firm friendships, and, in its situation and in its beauty, unique. And, although the things that have happened to me in it are not much to my pleasure but much to my grief, I carry them without grief simply for having seen the place.

"Finally, Señor Don Álvaro Tarfe, I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, the very man fame speaks of, and not that unfortunate creature who has tried to usurp my name and honour himself with my thoughts. I beg your worship, by what you owe to being a gentleman, to be so good as to make a declaration before the magistrate of this place that your worship has never in all the days of your life seen me until now, and that I am not the Don Quixote printed in the second part, and that this Sancho Panza my squire is not the one your worship knew."

"I shall do that very willingly," answered Don Álvaro, "although it causes astonishment to see two Don Quixotes and two Sanchos at one and the same time, as alike in their names as they are different in their actions; and I say again and affirm that I have not seen what I have seen, and that what has happened to me has not happened."

"Without a doubt," said Sancho, "your worship must be enchanted, like my lady Dulcinea of El Toboso; and would to heaven that your worship's disenchantment lay in giving me another three thousand and so many lashes like the ones I am giving myself for her, for I would give them to myself without any interest at all."

"I do not understand this about lashes," said Don Álvaro.

And Sancho answered him that it was long to tell, but that he would tell him if by any chance they were going the same road.

At this the dinner hour came round; Don Quixote and Don Álvaro dined together. The magistrate of the village happened to come into the inn with a clerk, before which magistrate Don Quixote put in a petition that it was to his right's advantage that Don Álvaro Tarfe, that gentleman who was there present, should declare before his worship that he did not know Don Quixote of La Mancha, who was likewise there present, and that he was not the one who went about in print in a history entitled The Second Part of Don Quixote of La Mancha, composed by one Avellaneda, a native of Tordesillas.

Finally the magistrate gave his ruling in due form; the declaration was made with all the force that ought to be used in such cases; with which Don Quixote and Sancho were left very glad, as though such a declaration mattered a great deal to them and their deeds and their words did not plainly show the difference between the two Don Quixotes and the two Sanchos.

A great many courtesies and offers of service passed between Don Álvaro and Don Quixote, in which the great Manchegan showed his good sense, so that he undeceived Don Álvaro Tarfe of the error he was in; who gave himself to understand that he must be enchanted, since he had touched with his hand two such opposite Don Quixotes.

Evening came, they set out from that place, and about half a league on two different roads parted, one leading to Don Quixote's village and the other the one Don Álvaro was to take. In this short space Don Quixote told him the misfortune of his defeat and Dulcinea's enchantment and its remedy — all of which put Don Álvaro into fresh astonishment; and, embracing Don Quixote and Sancho, he went his road and Don Quixote his.

That night he spent among some more trees, so as to give Sancho room to carry out his penance, which he carried out in the same way as the night before, at the expense of the beeches' bark far more than of his own shoulders — which he guarded so well that the lashes could not have knocked a fly off them if there had been one on top.

The deceived Don Quixote did not lose a single stroke of the count, and found that with those of the night before they came to three thousand and twenty-nine. It seems that the sun had got up early to see the sacrifice, by whose light they went on with their road, the two of them talking about Don Álvaro's mistake and how well advised it had been to take his declaration before the law, and so authentically.

That day and that night they travelled without anything happening to them worth telling, except that in the night Sancho finished his task — at which Don Quixote was contented beyond measure; and he waited for the day, to see whether on the road he would come across his lady Dulcinea already disenchanted. And, going along his road, he did not come across a single woman without going to see whether she was Dulcinea of El Toboso, holding it for infallible that Merlin's promises could not lie.

With these thoughts and these desires they climbed up a hill from which they made out their village; which, on seeing, Sancho went down on his knees and said:

"Open your eyes, longed-for country, and see that Sancho Panza your son is coming back to you — if not very rich, then very well whipped. Open your arms and receive your son Don Quixote too, who, if he comes beaten by another man's arms, comes the conqueror of himself; which, as he has told me, is the greatest conquest that can be desired. I am bringing money, for if they gave me good lashes, I was riding well mounted."

"Leave off this foolishness," said Don Quixote, "and let us go in with the right foot to enter our village, where we shall give vent to our imaginings and to the plan we mean to carry out for the pastoral life."

With this they came down the hill and went to their village.

Chapter 73: Of the Omens Don Quixote Had on Entering His Village, with Other Events That Adorn and Give Credit to This Great History

At the entrance of it, according to Cide Hamete, Don Quixote saw that on the threshing floors of the village two boys were quarrelling, and one said to the other:

"Do not wear yourself out, Periquillo, for you shall not see her in all the days of your life."

Don Quixote heard him and said to Sancho:

"Do you not notice, my friend, what that boy said: 'You shall not see her in all the days of your life'?"

"Well then, what does it matter," answered Sancho, "that the boy said that?"

"What?" replied Don Quixote. "Do you not see that, applying those words to my own purpose, it means that I am not to see Dulcinea any more?"

Sancho was about to answer him when he was prevented by seeing a hare come running across that field in flight, followed by a good many greyhounds and hunters; and the hare, terrified, came and took shelter and crouched down under the grey's feet. Sancho caught it with his bare hand and presented it to Don Quixote, who was saying:

"Malum signum! Malum signum! A hare flees, greyhounds follow her: Dulcinea does not appear!"

"Your worship is a strange man," said Sancho. "Let us suppose that this hare is Dulcinea of El Toboso and these greyhounds that are chasing her are the villainous enchanters who turned her into a country girl: she flees, I catch her and put her into your worship's power, and you have her in your arms and make much of her. What bad sign is this, and what ill omen can be taken from it?"

The two boys who had been quarrelling came up to see the hare, and Sancho asked one of them why they were quarrelling. And he was answered by the one who had said "you shall not see her again in all your life" that he had taken a cricket cage from the other boy and did not mean to give it back to him in all his life. Sancho took four coppers out of his pocket and gave them to the boy for the cage, and put it into Don Quixote's hands, saying:

"Here, sir, these omens are broken and undone, and they have no more to do with our affairs — as I imagine, fool though I am — than with last year's clouds. And if I do not remember wrongly, I have heard our village curate say that it is not the part of Christian or judicious people to stick at these childish things; and your worship yourself told me so a few days ago, giving me to understand that all those Christians who stuck at omens were fools. And there is no need to press the point: let us go on and go into our village."

The hunters came up, asked for their hare, and Don Quixote gave it them; they went on and, at the entrance of the village, came across the curate and the bachelor Carrasco saying their prayers in a little meadow.

And it is to be known that Sancho Panza had thrown over the grey and over the bundle of arms, to serve as a saddlecloth, the buckram gown painted with flames of fire that they had put on him at the duke's castle on the night when Altisidora came round. He had also fitted the mitre on the donkey's head, which was the newest transformation and adornment that any donkey in the world was ever seen in.

The two of them were at once recognised by the curate and the bachelor, who came to them with open arms. Don Quixote dismounted and embraced them tightly; and the boys, who are lynxes there is no escaping, made out the mitre on the donkey and came running to see him, saying to one another:

"Come along, boys, and you shall see Sancho Panza's ass finer than Mingo, and Don Quixote's beast thinner today than on the first day."

Finally, surrounded by boys and accompanied by the curate and the bachelor, they went into the village and made their way to Don Quixote's house, and found the housekeeper and his niece at the door, for the news of his coming had already reached them.

News of it had likewise reached Teresa Panza, Sancho's wife, who, tousled and half undressed, leading Sanchica her daughter by the hand, came running to see her husband; and, seeing him not so well got up as she thought a governor ought to be, she said to him:

"How is it you come like this, my husband? For it seems to me that you come on foot and footsore, and you have more the look of an un-governor than of a governor."

"Be quiet, Teresa," answered Sancho, "for many times where there are hooks there is no bacon; and let us go to our house, and there you shall hear marvels. I am bringing money, which is what matters, earned by my own industry and without harm to anybody."

"Bring the money, my good husband," said Teresa, "and let it be earned here or there; for however you have earned it, you will not have brought in a new custom into the world."

Sanchica embraced her father and asked him whether he was bringing anything, for she had been waiting for him like the rain in May; and, holding on to one side of his belt, with his wife on his hand and her daughter pulling the grey, they went off to their house, leaving Don Quixote at his, in the power of his niece and his housekeeper and in the company of the curate and the bachelor.

Don Quixote, without keeping to terms or hours, at that very moment drew the bachelor and the curate aside on their own, and in a few words told them of his defeat and of the obligation he was left under not to leave his village for a year — which he meant to keep to the letter, without going a hair's breadth beyond it, exactly like a knight errant bound by the exactness and the order of knight-errantry; and that he had thought of becoming a shepherd for that year and entertaining himself in the solitude of the fields, where at a loose rein he could give vent to his loving thoughts, exercising himself in the pastoral and virtuous exercise.

And he begged them, if they had not a great deal to do and were not held up by more important business, to be so good as to be his companions; for he would buy sheep and stock enough to give them the name of shepherds. And he let them know that the chief part of that business was done, because he had given them their names, which would fit them as though cast in the mould. The curate asked him to say them. Don Quixote answered that he himself was to be called the shepherd Quixotize; and the bachelor the shepherd Carrascón; and the curate the shepherd Curiambro; and Sancho Panza the shepherd Panzino.

They were all thunderstruck at seeing Don Quixote's new madness; but, so that he should not get away from the village again to his chivalries, and hoping that in that year he might be cured, they agreed to his new intention and approved his madness as judicious, offering themselves as his companions in his exercise.

"And what is more," said Sansón Carrasco, "as everybody already knows, I am a most celebrated poet, and at every turn I shall compose pastoral verses, or courtly ones, or whatever comes best to the point, so that we may entertain ourselves along those out-of-the-way places where we are to go. And what is most needed, my dear sirs, is that each of us should choose the name of the shepherdess he means to celebrate in his verses, and that we should not leave a tree, however hard it may be, without labelling it and carving her name on it, as is the use and custom of shepherds in love."

"That is exactly right," answered Don Quixote, "although I am free of having to look for the name of a pretended shepherdess, since there stands the peerless Dulcinea of El Toboso, the glory of these banks, the adornment of these meadows, the mainstay of beauty, the cream of all charms, and, in short, a subject on whom every praise can well be settled, however hyperbolical."

"That is true," said the curate; "but we shall look about for some handy shepherdesses, who if they do not square with us will corner us."

To which Sansón Carrasco added:

"And when they run short, we shall give them the names of the stamped and printed ones that the world is full of: Phyllises, Amaryllises, Dianas, Fléridas, Galateas and Belisardas; for, since they sell them in the market squares, we can very well buy them and hold them for our own. If my lady — or, better said, my shepherdess — happens to be called Ana, I shall celebrate her under the name of Anarda; and if Francisca, I shall call her Francenia; and if Lucía, Lucinda, for it all comes out the same way. And Sancho Panza, if he is to come into this brotherhood, can celebrate his wife Teresa Panza under the name of Teresaina."

Don Quixote laughed at the fitting of the name, and the curate praised his decent and honourable resolution infinitely and offered himself again to keep him company all the time he had free from attending to his necessary obligations. With this they took their leave of him, and begged and advised him to look after his health with anything that might be good for him.

Fortune willed that his niece and the housekeeper had heard the talk of the three of them; and, as soon as they had gone, both of them went in to Don Quixote, and his niece said to him:

"What is this, my lord uncle? Now that we thought your worship was coming back to settle down in his house and to live a quiet and honourable life in it, do you want to get yourself into new labyrinths, turning yourself into

	Little shepherd, you who come,
	little shepherd, you who go?

Why, truly, the green barley is too tough now for making pipes."

To which the housekeeper added:

"And will your worship be able to bear out in the fields the summer noons, the winter night airs and the howling of wolves? Certainly not; for that is an exercise and an office for robust men, tanned and bred for such a ministry almost from their swaddling clothes. Even taking one evil with another, it is better to be a knight errant than a shepherd.

"Look, sir, take my advice — and I do not give it you on a full belly of bread and wine but fasting, and on the strength of the fifty years of age I have: stay in your house, attend to your property, confess often, favour the poor; and on my soul be it if any harm comes to you."

"Be quiet, my daughters," Don Quixote answered them, "for I know very well what suits me. Take me to bed, for I do not think I am very well; and hold it for certain that, whether I am a knight errant now or a shepherd yet to set out, I shall never leave off seeing to whatever you may need, as you shall see by the deed."

And the good daughters — for such the housekeeper and the niece undoubtedly were — took him to bed, where they gave him something to eat and looked after him as well as they could.

Chapter 74: Of How Don Quixote Fell Ill, and of the Will He Made, and of His Death

Since human things are not everlasting, always going downhill from their beginnings until they reach their last end — and especially the lives of men — and since Don Quixote's had no privilege from heaven to hold up the course of its own, his end and finish came when he least expected it. Because, whether it was from the melancholy caused him by seeing himself beaten, or by the disposition of heaven that ordered it so, a fever settled on him that kept him six days in bed, in which he was visited many times by the curate, the bachelor and the barber, his friends, and Sancho Panza his good squire never left his pillow.

These, believing that the grief of seeing himself beaten and of not seeing his desire fulfilled in Dulcinea's freedom and disenchantment kept him in that state, tried by every possible means to cheer him up, the bachelor telling him to take heart and get up so as to begin their pastoral exercise, for which he had already composed an eclogue that would put in the shade all those Sannazaro ever composed; and that he had already bought with his own money two famous dogs to guard the flock, one called Barcino and the other Butrón, which a stockman of Quintanar had sold him. But for all that Don Quixote did not leave off his sadness.

His friends called the doctor; he felt his pulse and was not much pleased with it, and said that, one way or the other, he should see to the health of his soul, because his body's was in danger. Don Quixote heard it with a quiet mind; but his housekeeper, his niece and his squire did not hear it so, and they began to weep tenderly, as though they already had him dead in front of them. The doctor's opinion was that melancholy and low spirits were making an end of him.

Don Quixote begged them to leave him alone, because he wanted to sleep a little. They did so, and he slept at a stretch, as they say, for more than six hours — so much so that the housekeeper and the niece thought he would stay in that sleep. He woke at the end of the said time, and, letting out a great cry, said:

"Blessed be almighty God, who has done me so much good! In short, his mercies have no limit, and the sins of men do not shorten them or hinder them."

The niece listened attentively to her uncle's words, and they seemed to her better ordered than he usually said them — at least in that illness — and she asked him:

"What is your worship saying, sir? Have we something new? What mercies are these, or what sins of men?"

"The mercies, niece," answered Don Quixote, "are those God has used with me at this moment; whom, as I said, my sins do not hinder. I have my judgement now, free and clear, without the murky shadows of ignorance that my bitter and constant reading of those detestable books of chivalry cast over it. Now I know their absurdities and their deceptions, and the only thing that grieves me is that this coming to my senses has arrived so late that it leaves me no time to make any amends by reading others that might be a light to my soul.

"I feel myself, niece, at the point of death; I should like to make it in such a way as to give it to be understood that my life had not been so bad as to leave me the name of a madman; for although I have been one, I should not like to confirm that truth in my death. Call me, my dear, my good friends: the curate, the bachelor Sansón Carrasco and Master Nicolás the barber, for I want to make my confession and to make my will."

But the niece was spared this labour by the coming in of the three. Don Quixote had hardly seen them when he said:

"Give me joy, good gentlemen, that I am no longer Don Quixote of La Mancha but Alonso Quixano, whom my habits gave the name of the Good. Now I am an enemy of Amadís of Gaul and of the whole infinite herd of his line; now all the profane histories of knight-errantry are hateful to me; now I know my own foolishness and the danger that reading them put me in; now, by God's mercy, having learnt at my own cost, I abominate them."

When the three heard him say this, they undoubtedly believed that some new madness had taken hold of him. And Sansón said to him:

"Now, Señor Don Quixote, when we have news that the lady Dulcinea is disenchanted, does your worship come out with this? And now that we are so near to being shepherds and passing our lives singing like so many princes, does your worship want to turn hermit? Be quiet, on your life; come to yourself and leave off these tales."

"Those I have told until now," replied Don Quixote, "which have been true to my own harm, my death shall turn, with heaven's help, to my profit. I, gentlemen, feel myself dying in great haste; let all jokes be set aside, and bring me a confessor to confess me and a notary to make my will; for at such passes as this a man must not play games with his soul. And so I beg that, while the curate confesses me, you should go for the notary."

They looked at one another, astonished at Don Quixote's words; and, although in doubt, they chose to believe him. And one of the signs by which they guessed that he was dying was his having come back so easily from mad to sane, because to the words already spoken he added a great many others so well said, so Christian and so orderly that they finally took away their doubt and made them believe that he was sane.

The curate had everybody sent out and stayed alone with him and confessed him.

The bachelor went for the notary and came back a little later with him and with Sancho Panza; which Sancho, who already knew from the bachelor's news what state his master was in, finding the housekeeper and the niece in tears, began to pull faces and to shed tears himself. The confession was finished, and the curate came out, saying:

"Truly he is dying, and truly Alonso Quixano the Good is sane; we may well go in for him to make his will."

This news gave a terrible push to the swollen eyes of the housekeeper, the niece and Sancho Panza his good squire, in such a way that it burst the tears out of their eyes and a thousand deep sighs out of their breasts. Because truly, as has been said at some point, all the time Don Quixote was Alonso Quixano the Good, plain and simple, and all the time he was Don Quixote of La Mancha, he was always of a gentle nature and agreeable in his dealings; and for this reason he was well loved not only by the people of his house but by everybody who knew him.

The notary came in with the rest; and, having drawn up the head of the will and Don Quixote having settled his soul with all those Christian circumstances that are required, coming to the bequests, he said:

"Item, it is my will that of certain moneys Sancho Panza has, whom in my madness I made my squire — since there have been between him and me certain accounts and givings and takings — he shall not be charged with them and no account shall be asked of him. But if anything should be left over after he has paid himself what I owe him, the remainder shall be his, and it will be very little, and much good may it do him. And if, when I was mad, I had a part in giving him the government of the isle, now that I am sane I would give him that of a kingdom if I could, because the plainness of his nature and the faithfulness of his dealings deserve it."

And, turning to Sancho, he said to him:

"Forgive me, my friend, for the occasion I have given you of seeming as mad as I was, by making you fall into the error I fell into, that there have been and are knights errant in the world."

"Ah," answered Sancho, weeping, "do not die, your worship, my dear sir; take my advice and live many years, because the greatest madness a man can commit in this life is to let himself die without any more ado, without anybody killing him and with no other hands making an end of him but melancholy's.

"Look, do not be lazy; get up out of that bed and let us go out into the fields dressed as shepherds, as we have arranged: perhaps behind some bush we shall find the lady Doña Dulcinea disenchanted, and there will be nothing more to see. If it is that you are dying of grief at being beaten, put the blame on me and say that they knocked you down because I had girthed Rocinante badly; and what is more, your worship will have seen in his books of chivalry that it is an ordinary thing for one knight to knock down another, and for the man who is beaten today to be the winner tomorrow."

"That is so," said Sansón, "and good Sancho Panza is very much in the right of these cases."

"Gentlemen," said Don Quixote, "let us go gently, for in last year's nests there are no birds this year. I was mad and now I am sane; I was Don Quixote of La Mancha and I am now, as I have said, Alonso Quixano the Good. May my repentance and my truthfulness bring me back with your worships to the esteem I was held in; and let the notary go on.

"Item, I bequeath my whole estate, behind closed doors, to Antonia Quixana my niece, who is here present, having first taken out of the soundest part of it what is needed to carry out the bequests I have made. And the first satisfaction I want made is the paying of the wages I owe for the time my housekeeper has served me, and twenty ducats besides for a dress. I leave as my executors the curate and the bachelor Sansón Carrasco, who are here present.

"Item, it is my will that if Antonia Quixana my niece wants to marry, she should marry a man of whom it has first been established that he does not know what books of chivalry are; and in case it should be found that he does know, and my niece should still want to marry him and should marry him, she shall lose everything I have left her, which my executors may distribute in works of charity as they please.

"Item, I beg the said gentlemen my executors that if good fortune should bring them to know the author who they say composed a history that goes about with the title of The Second Part of the Exploits of Don Quixote of La Mancha, they should on my behalf beg him, as earnestly as may be, to forgive the occasion I gave him, without thinking of it, of having written so many and such great absurdities as he writes in it; because I depart this life with a scruple at having given him a motive for writing them."

With this he closed the will; and, a fainting fit taking him, he stretched himself out at full length on the bed. Everybody was thrown into an uproar and ran to help him; and in the three days he lived after the one on which he made his will, he fainted very often. The house was in an uproar; but for all that, the niece ate, the housekeeper drank healths and Sancho Panza was merry — for this business of inheriting something rubs out or tempers in the heir the memory of the grief that it is right the dead man should leave.

In the end Don Quixote's last day came, after he had received all the sacraments and after he had abominated the books of chivalry with many and forcible arguments. The notary was present, and said that he had never read in any book of chivalry of a knight errant dying in his bed so quietly and so like a Christian as Don Quixote; who, among the compassion and the tears of those who were there, gave up his spirit — I mean that he died.

Seeing which, the curate asked the notary to give him a certificate that Alonso Quixano the Good, commonly called Don Quixote of La Mancha, had passed out of this present life and had died naturally; and he asked for such a certificate so as to take away the chance of any author other than Cide Hamete Benengeli falsely raising him from the dead and making endless histories of his exploits.

This was the end of the Ingenious Gentleman of La Mancha, whose village Cide Hamete would not name exactly, so as to leave all the towns and villages of La Mancha to contend among themselves to adopt him and claim him for their own, as the seven cities of Greece contended over Homer.

The weeping of Sancho and of Don Quixote's niece and housekeeper is left out here, and the fresh epitaphs on his tomb — although Sansón Carrasco set this one on it:

	Here lies the mighty gentleman
	who came to such an extreme
	of valour that it may be noted
	that death did not triumph
	over his life by his death.
	He held the whole world cheap;
	he was the scarecrow and the bogey
	of the world, at such a juncture
	that his good fortune was made good
	by dying sane and living mad.

And the most prudent Cide Hamete said to his pen:

"Here you shall stay, hung on this rack and this brass wire, my quill — I do not know whether well cut or badly trimmed — where you shall live for long ages, if presumptuous and villainous historians do not take you down to profane you. But before they reach you, you can warn them and say to them in the best way you can:

	Softly, softly, little poltroons!
	Let her be touched by nobody;
	for this enterprise, good king,
	was kept for me alone.

"For me alone Don Quixote was born, and I for him: he knew how to act and I to write; the two of us alone are made for one another, in spite and in defiance of that pretended writer of Tordesillas who dared, or shall dare, to write with a coarse and badly trimmed ostrich quill the exploits of my valorous knight — for it is no load for his shoulders and no subject for his frozen wit.

"And you shall warn him, if by any chance you come to know him, to let the weary and by now rotted bones of Don Quixote rest in the grave, and not to try to carry him off, against all the laws of death, to Old Castile, making him come out of the tomb where he really and truly lies stretched at full length, unable to make a third expedition and a new sally. For, to make a mock of all the many that so many knights errant made, the two he did make are enough — so much to the taste and good pleasure of the people whose notice they came to, in this kingdom as in foreign ones.

"And with this you will fulfil your Christian profession by giving good advice to the man who wishes you ill; and I shall be left satisfied and proud at having been the first to enjoy the fruit of his writings entirely, as I wished — since my desire has been no other than to make men loathe the invented and preposterous histories of the books of chivalry, which, thanks to those of my true Don Quixote, are already stumbling and will beyond any doubt fall altogether. Vale."

The End
